title: 3rd UPDATE: Singapore 2Q GDP Soars; MAS To Let  Currency  Rise
text:
(Adds comments from Citigroup, HSBC)


 
   By Gaurav Raghuvanshi, Sam Holmes and Costas Paris 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's economy continued to soar in the second quarter as manufacturing surged, prompting the government to sharply raise its growth forecasts and sending the local dollar to a three-week high.

Gross domestic product jumped 26% on a seasonally adjusted and annualized basis from the previous three months, the government said Wednesday, well above the 17.4% forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires survey.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore won't stand in the way of the local dollar's subsequent rise, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking told Dow Jones Newswires.

The city-state's rocketing growth is pacing Asia's strong recovery, which is leading the rest of the world out of the economic crisis. Asian central banks recently have become more aggressive in raising interest rates to preempt inflation, even as Europe's debt crisis and a slowing U.S. economy cast a shadow over major economies.

Given sluggish demand in those key export markets, however, Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said the island economy's sizzling growth is likely to moderate going forward, even as it revised up its first-quarter growth reading to 45.9%--the fastest on record going back to 1975--from an initial estimate of 38.6%.

"The exceptionally strong growth experienced by the Singapore economy in the first half of 2010 is therefore not likely to be sustained into the second half of the year," the ministry said in a statement. "While year-on-year growth rates in the second half will be healthy, sequential growth from current levels of economic activity will be low."

Citigroup also noted the expected shift ahead.

"Expect a slowdown (not a slump)" in the second half, two Citigroup economists wrote in a research report. "Given signs of easing momentum, and a slowdown in the U.S. and China," third-quarter GDP data should pull back 11% from the current torrid pace and be "broadly flat" in the fourth quarter--though they added that there were strong upside risks to this outlook.

On-year, GDP grew 19.3% in the second quarter, accelerating from the first quarter's 16.9% and beating the Dow Jones survey's forecast of a 16.5% rise. First-quarter growth was revised up from 15.5%.

The government raised its full-year growth forecast to 13%-15% from its May estimate of 7%-9%.

That's stronger than most economists' projections, but appears achievable, CIMB economist Song Seng Wun said.

"I suppose the only question now is how much more juice is left, but the forecasts are realistic," Song said, adding that 2010 is likely to be a tale of two halves.

The strong growth boosted the Singapore dollar, with the U.S. currency falling to S$1.3741, its lowest since June 21, from S$1.3858 before the announcement.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore likely won't intervene to curb the local currency's rise unless the U.S. dollar falls to around 1.3600, said the person familiar with the central bank's thinking.

"The U.S dollar is still well within the MAS' range. The U.S. dollar is also broadly weak against other currencies" in recent days, the person said. "You won't see any movement by the MAS unless we hit the 1.36 level or below."

The MAS uses the trade-weighted exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its main policy tool because trade flows dwarf the island's domestic economy. The central bank now targets a "gradual and modest appreciation" for the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed trading band.

The person said that at this point "there are no thoughts about further tightening by the MAS when it meets in October" for its next scheduled policy review.

But others are entertaining such thoughts. If the economy's rapid growth continues, the MAS may tighten by "re-centering" its targeted band for the Singapore dollar, HSBC economist Frederic Neumann wrote.

"There's no more slack left in the economy and the MAS may want to re-center again in October," Neumann said. "With numbers like these, it's certainly on the table."

Inflation remains relatively modest, with the government forecasting in May that consumer prices would rise 2.5%-3.5% for the full year. Wednesday's report doesn't give new inflation figures.

In the second quarter, manufacturing output rose 45.5% from a year earlier, accelerating from the first quarter's 38.2% growth.

Manufacturing expanded 58.6% on-year in May, the fastest since comparable records began in 1980, and breaking April's record of 49.7%. Services grew 11.4% on-year in the second quarter, while construction expanded 13.5%.

The main gauge of Singapore's exports rose 28.7% in June from a year earlier, topping the 26.1% rise for non-oil domestic exports forecast in the Dow Jones survey, and up from May's revised 24.3%.

All sectors expanded, with electronics shipments up 43.9% and pharmaceuticals rebounding 29.8%.

-By Gaurav Raghuvanshi; Sam Holmes and Costas Paris, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 64154 154; costas.paris@dowjones.com [ 14-07-10 0429GMT ]

text:
* Sing dollar surges briefly on record Q2 economic growth

* Won jumps as much as 1.7 pct but faces resistance

* Dollar/yuan NDFs hover near 2-week low

* Baht inches up ahead of rate decision

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, July 14 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar briefly surged to a three-week high on Wednesday after data showed the economy grew at a record pace in the second quarter, while stronger stock markets boosted the South Korean won and most other Asian currencies.

Asian stocks rose to a three-week high, led by gains in technology issues, while the euro held steady near a two-month high against the dollar, with high-yielding currencies such as the Australian dollar supported by a seemingly significant improvement in risk appetite. [ID:nSGE66D02R]

SINGAPORE DOLLAR, RINGGIT

Singapore dollar <SGD=> briefly hit a three-week high at 1.373 per U.S. dollar but later retreated to 1.3766, down slightly on the day, as investors increasingly worried that Singapore's central bank may intervene to temper the currency's strength.

The currency jumped in early trade after data showed Singapore's economy grew by a record 19.3 percent in the second quarter from a year earlier, prompting the government to raise its full-year growth forecast. [ID:nSGE66C0GX]

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose as much as 0.7 percent to 3.1800 per dollar, the highest in just over three weeks, tracking rising stock markets and the Singapore dollar.

But the ringgit later trimmed gains on short dollar covering.

"It looks like some players were still caught short (dollars) after NDF fixing. I think 3.20 should be toppish for now," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.

WON

The won <KRW=> jumped as much as 1.7 percent to 1,191.9 per dollar as foreign investors continued to buy local stocks and exporters bought the won for settlements.

But the won faces some resistance and investors appear to be reluctant to chase the won <KRW=> more aggressively on caution over possible dollar-buying intervention by the authorities.

It later pulled back to the weaker side of 1,200.

"Dollar bids are quite strong around 1,197 and it looks difficult for the won to strengthen more," said a local bank dealer.

Seoul shares <.KS11> rose 1.6 percent as foreign investors buy a net 701.0 billion won worth of stocks on the main exchange.

YUAN

Dollar/yuan NDFs hovered near a two-week low in thin activity, with gains capped by the PBOC's slightly stronger daily mid-point <CNY=SAEC> for the yuan against the dollar.

"Moves in forwards are getting smaller. They are trying to break out of the range," said a trader at a European bank in Shanghai.

One-year dollar/yuan non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) <CNY1YNDFOR=> were quoted little changed at 6.6548 bid at midday from Tuesday's close of 6.6535, with their implied 12-month yuan appreciation falling a tad to 1.81 percent from 1.90 percent.

The People's Bank of China set the yuan's mid-point <CNY=SAEC> at 6.7755 against the dollar on Wednesday, up from Tuesday's 6.7802, while spot yuan was trading at 6.7732 to the dollar at midday, down slightly from Tuesday's close of 6.7720.

The yuan has gained 0.8 percent since its depegging from the dollar late last month.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> inched up to 32.20 per dollar, tracking other Asian currencies and buoyed by expectations of a 25 basis point interest rate increase by the Bank of Thailand later in the day.

Nine out of 16 analysts polled by Reuters expect the BoT to raise its policy rate by 25 bps from a record low of 1.25 percent. Seven expect no change. [ID:nSGE66D02F]

"Investors are turning to riskier assets like stocks and commodities, pushing the dollar back. Most analysts see a 25 basis point rate rise although the expected central bank decision has mostly been factored in," a Bangkok-based trader said.

title: FX  ASIA: Asian Reserves Drop In May On  Intervention , Euro
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's official foreign exchange reserves fell 1.2% in May from April, the biggest drop in well over a year, hit by a decline in the value of euros held by central banks and the sale of U.S. dollars to stop local currencies from weakening too fast.

As global markets were hit by concerns that euro-zone economies like Spain and Portugal may need financial assistance, and a military crisis on the Korean peninsula, central banks including those in South Korea and Indonesia were suspected of heavy dollar sales late in May to curb declines in their currencies. Traders estimate Korea's central bank sold as much as $2 billion-$2.5 billion in a single day, likely its biggest intervention since the Lehman Brothers collapse in 2008.

These moves highlight the complex issues faced by central banks across the region, as they were coupled with similar, albeit generally smaller, interventions to buy dollars to contain appreciation pressures on local currencies. Analysts say many central banks may remain on both sides of the market to keep currencies in narrow ranges in coming months, balancing the need to keep their exports competitive and inflation at bay.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, excluding China's, stood at US$2.776 trillion at the end of May, down from US$2.810 trillion at the end of April. That was the largest drop since January 2009, and compared with a 1.5% increase posted in April from March.

China, which only releases its data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.447 trillion in reserves at the end of March.

Much of the decrease in Asian reserves was due to the lower valuation of euros held by central banks, since the euro lost 7.5% against the dollar in May. Euros are believed to account for around 20%-25% of total reserves.

Overall, emerging market central banks, mostly Asian, have bought around US$1 trillion worth of euros since the currency was launched in 1999, United Overseas Bank estimates. Speculation that these central banks may lose confidence in the euro has added to uncertainty in forex markets, despite recent statements by big reserve holders like China and Russia, saying they remain committed to the euro as an alternative reserve currency to the dollar.

In fact, many observers say that while a slowdown or even a freeze in future euro purchases is possible, central banks are unlikely to dump the currency even as it drops to fresh multi-year lows against the dollar, given a lack of safe, liquid alternatives -- and the fact that the U.S. fiscal situation is not much better than the European Union's.

"The biggest point here is that emerging market countries have not been accumulating reserves just in order to have more reserves; that's never been a policy goal. Rather, higher FX reserves are a side-effect, a residual of the real policy goal, which has been to keep their currencies relatively stable," analysts at UBS said in a recent report. "And this means continuing to accumulate dollars and euros."

title: *DJ MAS May  Intervene  If US Dollar Rises Well Above S$1.42 -Source
text:
23 May 2010 23:49 EDT *DJ  MAS Comfortable With Singapore Dollar Level Vs US Dlr -Source

23 May 2010 23:49 EDT *DJ  Singapore MAS Not Concerned For Now With Euro Fall - Source

23 May 2010 23:49 EDT *DJ  MAS Doesn't Expect Strong Euro Rebound In Short Term - Source

23 May 2010 23:50 EDT DJ  MAS May Intervene If US Dollar Rises Well Above S$1.42 -Source

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore central bank is comfortable with the local dollar's moves against the U.S. currency and the euro and wouldn't intervene near current levels, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said Monday.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore views the local currency's recent fall against the U.S. dollar and rise against the euro as part of global trends and won't defend the Singapore dollar unless the U.S. dollar should rise "convincingly" above S$1.4200, the person told Dow Jones Newswires.

The greenback was quoted at S$1.4069 at 0345 GMT Monday.

"The stronger U.S. dollar is not the result of any fundamental weakness in Singapore, or for that matter, Asia," the person said. "It's because of the debt issues in the euro zone, which hurt the euro. In any case, the dollar is still well within the MAS trading band."

The central bank guides the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band against a basket of other currencies. It uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates because trade dwarfs Singapore's small domestic economy.

Many Asian central banks have intervened in the past year to prevent big rises in their own currencies against the U.S. dollar from crimping their export-reliant economic recoveries. But as the U.S. currency has risen globally in recent weeks on safe-haven buying due to the European debt crisis, central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines have been selling dollars to support their own currencies, traders say.

The MAS aggressively tightened policy in April by raising its trading band for the Singapore dollar in trade-weighted terms and targeting a "modest and gradual appreciation" for the local dollar, changing its previous policy of zero appreciation.

The U.S. dollar fell as low as S$1.3646 in late April on the policy change but has steadily recovered.

The person familiar with the MAS's thinking said the city-state's central bank is "still" not concerned about the falling euro as it hasn't dented Singapore's exports to the European Union.

"There is already a slight euro recovery," the person said. "But there are no expectations of sustained euro strength at least in the short-term."

The euro fell to an eight-year low of S$1.6971 last week but had rebounded to S$1.7596.

The EU is Singapore's biggest trading partner, followed by China and the U.S. In April, Singapore's non-oil domestic exports to the EU rose 21.3% on year to S$1.9 billion, but fell 5.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis from the previous month.

title: FX  ASIA: As Asian Reserves Rise, Euro May Fall Into Disfavor
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 1.5% in April from March as continued intervention in foreign exchange markets offset a drop in the value of central banks' euro-denominated holdings.

That trend that may emerge as an additional negative for the euro if it forces some of the world's top reserve holders to review the preference they've shown for the European currency in recent years.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, not including China's, stood at US$2.810 trillion at the end of April, up from US$2.777 trillion at the end of March. That compares with a 0.3% increase posted in March from February.

China, which releases its data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.447 trillion in reserves at the end of March.

Combined, Asian central bank holdings account for around two-thirds of the world's overall amount, and analysts believe some 20%-25% of that amount is in euros. That's likely below the international average of 27.4% as of last December, according to International Monetary Fund data, but Asia's percentage has grown steadily in recent years.

Worries about a possible reduction of central bank euro holdings hit the market earlier this year and are gaining pace as the euro loses ground against the dollar, eroding its status as the top alternative to the greenback. That's important because the latest data show that while market speculators (including hedge funds) are active euro sellers, observers believe most "real-money" managers like central banks and pension funds haven't yet joined the euro-bashing party.

In a recent report, Credit Suisse analysts said the euro-zone's structural problems and handling of the Greek debt crisis have "severely damaged" the notion--particularly among managers of central bank reserve funds--that euros can be held as a "safe alternative" to the dollar.

So far this year, the euro has lost 11% against the dollar; that includes a 1.6% drop in April and a 4.9% drop so far in May. But that may be just the beginning if Asian central banks start to unload euros.

In 2002, when the euro replaced individual euro-zone currencies, it accounted for only 23.8% of global reserves. It's up 50% against the dollar since, supported by the continued decrease in the dollar as a percentage of global reserves as central banks have diversified in favor of the euro.

Meanwhile, strong purchases of dollars in forex markets continued in many Asian countries in April. That matches the recent trend as central banks remain wary of allowing their local currencies to rise on the strength of sustained flows into fast-growing Asian markets.

Seven Asian central banks reported reserves at all-time highs, including Indonesia's, where reserves grew a whopping 9.5% on-month in April on the back of continued intervention. Bank Indonesia has been trying to contain the appreciation of the rupiah, one of Asia's best performers this year with a 3.9% gain against the dollar since January on top of a 12% rise in 2009.

Strong reserve increases in Singapore and South Korea also were likely driven by continued intervention in forex markets.

"It would probably be a function of how far the officials are willing to let it go," one trader at a local bank said.

title: FX  ASIA: Singapore Dollar Will Head Higher, But Slowly
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar has soared since the central bank switched to an appreciation policy for the first time in almost two years, but precedent suggests the monetary authority won't let it run too far, too fast.

That means anyone expecting the Singapore dollar to lead the charge higher in Asian currencies will be disappointed.

The Singapore dollar has climbed over two cents against the greenback since the Monetary Authority of Singapore tightened policy Wednesday, a huge leap for a normally mild-mannered currency, which the MAS manages within an undisclosed band against a currency basket.

The rally spooked policymakers. A person familiar with the central bank's thinking told Dow Jones Newswires Thursday that MAS intervention is possible if the U.S. dollar "falls well below" S$1.3700 in coming days. It was last at S$1.3776.

The MAS dropped its neutral policy stance because the city-state's recovery has turned red hot. The economy expanded at its fastest pace on record in the first quarter and the government raised its growth and inflation forecasts for this year. Wednesday's tightening was unprecedented: never before has the MAS both revalued the currency and shifted the slope of its target band toward appreciation.

The aggressive move let Singapore dollar bulls loose: strategists tripped over themselves issuing reports predicting a sharper rally in the currency.

But the MAS doesn't appear to be looking for a much stronger currency, at least for now, since inflation--at 1% in March--remains under control.

The central bank is unlikely to allow the U.S. dollar to drop below S$1.35 in coming even months, intervening as needed to ensure the Singapore dollar gains are "modest and gradual" in line with its statement Wednesday.

"The basket peg, by definition, is a constraint for the Singapore dollar," said Tim Condon, a strategist with ING Bank.

Condon expects the U.S. dollar may drop to S$1.35, but only in about three months. That would still keep the Singapore dollar--which is up 2.3% against the greenback this year--as an underperformer compared to high-fliers like the Malaysian ringgit, which has gained 7%, and the Korean won, up 4.7%.

Standard Chartered analysts reckon the MAS may allow a 2% annual gain of the Singapore dollar against the central bank's currency basket, which would provide additional upside only if currencies like the ringgit and Chinese yuan, believed to be key basket components, gain substantial ground.

StanChart Wednesday upgraded its rating for the Singapore dollar to overweight from neutral, but anticipates the greenback will only slide to S$1.35 by the end of June, and then to S$1.33 by the end of September.

ING and StanChart assume in their forecasts that China, one of Singapore's major trading partners, will let the yuan rise against the dollar by the end of June. That means the Singapore dollar, unlike other Asian currencies, would get no additional boost if Beijing makes such a move, Condon said.

"This was a pre-emptive move, we believe, ahead of China moving on the currency," Condon said. "I think a stronger yuan is already included in (the Singapore dollar) price."

(David Roman, a regional forex reporter, has been a Dow Jones correspondent since 2002, covering economic and corporate news. He can be reached at 65 6415 4045 or by e-mail: david.roman@dowjones.com)

title: Singapore  MAS May  Intervene  If US Dollar Falls 'Well Below' S$1.37 - Source
text:
Corrected April 15, 2010 01:46 ET (0546 GMT) [ 15-04-10 0534GMT ]

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)-- The Monetary Authority of Singapore was surprised at how much the local dollar rose after the central bank tightened policy Wednesday, and the MAS may intervene if the currency keeps rising, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said Thursday.

The MAS "didn't expect such a rise in the Singapore dollar," the person told Dow Jones Newswires. The central bank "expected it to stabilize to around S$1.38 to the U.S. dollar."

The U.S. dollar fell to S$1.3722, near a two-year low, Wednesday after the MAS announced an aggressive tightening--raising the Singapore dollar's trading band and targeting a further "modest and gradual appreciation" of the currency.

At 0435 GMT the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.3735.

The local dollar is now around the midpoint of the MAS's undisclosed policy band in trade-weighted terms, the person said, adding that if the U.S. dollar "falls well below" S$1.37, "the MAS could intervene."

The central bank is concerned that if China revalues the yuan, as many expect, that will further boost the Singapore dollar, along with other Asia currencies, the person said.

Forecasting models suggest that even a "slight" yuan revaluation could prompt the U.S. dollar to fall to S$1.33 or lower within a few months, he said.

The central bank's tightening, the first in two years, marked the first time it has both raised the trading band and targeted further appreciation of the Singapore dollar. The MAS uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its main policy tool because Singapore's trade flows dwarf the island's small domestic economy.

-By Singapore Bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4150; djnews.singapore.bureau@dowjones.com [ 15-04-10 0535GMT ]

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, April 12 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose on Monday as investors bought riskier assets after European Union leaders agreed to a rescue package for Greece, with gains in the Singapore dollar sparking official intervention.

The euro <EUR=> jumped to 1.3692 from $1.3488 in New York on Friday after investors who had sold it scrambled to cover short positions, weighing broadly on the dollar. [ID:nTOE63B03E]

Euro zone finance ministers approved a 30 billion euro ($40.5 billion) aid package of loans for Greece if needed, with 10 billion euros also expected from the International Monetary Fund, a move likely to calm markets in the short term. [ID:nLDE63A0BO]

WON

The won rose in both onshore and offshore markets.

One-month offshore dollar/won non-deliverable forwards <KRWNDFOR=> dipped to 1,112 from 1,117.6 late on Friday.

"We see heavy selling this morning across dollar/Asians. Risk appetite is back," said a Singapore-based NDF trader.

The spot won <KRW=> briefly hit a 19-month high at 1,111.3 per dollar but later pulled back to 1,114 as investors were wary of a dollar-buying intervention by authorities.

Local importers also bought dollars to settle accounts.

"Investors are reluctant to chase it more as the authorities are expected to defend certain levels," said a dealer.

Seoul shares <.KS11> fell 0.8 percent with foreign investors sellers of a net 49.2 billion won worth of stocks on the main exchange.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose half of a percent to 1.3838 per U.S. dollar -- the highest in just over four months, prompting the central bank to intervene.

"The intervention makes Singapore dollar's appreciation much slower," said a Singapore-based trader.

Ten out of 18 analysts expect the central bank, which manages the currency within a secret trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies, to keep its zero appreciation policy at a review on Wednesday. [ID:nSGE62G0F6]

Emmanuel Ng, strategist at OCBC Bank, believes Singapore dollar is now around 1.6 percent above the band's central parity compared with the upper ceiling of 2 percent managed by the central bank.

"We think there is a 55 percent probability of a reversion to a gradual and modest appreciation," Ng said.

BAHT

The baht <THB=> lost as much as half of a percent to 32.38 per dollar in line with local stocks <.SETI>, bucking a bullish trend for most Asian currencies due to the political turmoil.

Thailand's government could propose early elections to defuse a month-long political crisis, a newspaper reported on Monday, although opposition "red shirts" say the time for talks is over after clashes between anti-government protesters and security forces killed 21 people. [ID:nSGE63B008].

title: EM ASIA  FX -Peso, Singapore dollar gain, yuan NDFs edge up
text:
* Peso gains, buoyed by offshore/onshore arbitrage

 * Yuan NDFs inch up as China tries to cool FX spat

 * Singapore dollar capped by suspected intervention

 By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, March 19 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso gained on Friday as investors tried to profit from a spread between offshore and onshore forwards, while suspected official intervention capped a rise in the Singapore dollar.

 Several Asian currencies, including the Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar, are on track for their sixth straight week of gains, in line with Asian stocks and supported by growing optimism about a sustained economic recovery in the region.

 Meanwhile, the euro stabilised but remained under pressure after Greece said it could not achieve promised deficit cuts if its borrowing costs remain so high. [ID:nTOE62I04M]

 PESO

 The peso <PHP=> gained a third of a percent to 45.54 per dollar, matching a 19-month high hit on Wednesday, as investors continued to profit from a gap in onshore/offshore forwards.

 "A lot of banks and some corporate accounts have been taking advantage of the arbitrage between the onshore and offshore markets, that's why dollar/peso has been trading lower despite the weakness in the euro overnight," said a dealer in Manila.

 Investors bought dollar/peso offshore and reversed the trade onshore in arbitrage trade, which translated into fund inflows.

 One-month dollar/peso NDFs <PHP1MNDFOR=> fell to 45.69 from 45.73 late on Thursday while 1-month onshore forwards <PHP1M=> eased to 45.73 from 45.741.

 The spread between one-month onshore/NDFs has narrowed to 40 points from around 110 points a week earlier.

 YUAN

 The yuan edged up NDFs in tenors up to one year after declines earlier this week, as Commerce Ministry official He Ning says on Friday that channels of communication are open for discussing trade issues, including yuan. [ID:nBJB003743].

 But traders believe yuan NDFs are unlikely to form a major uptrend before a critical semi-annual U.S. Treasury report due April 15.

 "Any bets now either way would involve lots of risk, with stakes too high for the reward. NDFs may move sideways in coming weeks," said an analyst at U.S bank in Hong Kong.

 One-year dollar/yuan NDFs eased to 6.6598 from Thursday's close of 6.6640, implying a 2.5 percent yuan rise from day's mid-point, up fractionally from Thursday.

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose a fifth of a percent to 1.3915 per U.S. dollar on growing optimism about the economy, but traders said the unit was contained by central bankintervention.

 "The only real big (dollar) buyer in the market is the central bank and they will probably continue till the next policy meeting in April," said trader in Singapore.

 Singapore dollar has gained just 0.8 percent so far this year, the second-worst performer in Asia after the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS>, which is virtually pegged to the U.S. dollar.

 Most Analysts expect Singapore's central bank to keep its neutral currency policy in the April meeting despite signs of economic recovery is gaining steam.

 RINGGIT

 The ringgit <MYR=> gained a fifth of a percent to 3.297 per dollar, extending its gains so far this year to 3.8 percent and making it the top performing Asian currency.

Morgan Stanley has raised its end-2010 forecast on the ringgit to 3.13 per dollar from 3.20, citing Malaysia's improving balance of payments and the central bank's policy tightening.

 The central bank surprised investors by raising interest rates earlier this month.

 "We also recognise that the ringgit has a potential 'bonus fundamental', given that it is perceived to benefit the most from a yuan revaluation scenario in Asia ex-Japan," analysts at the bank said in a note.

 Investors should profit from further gains in ringgit via NDFs, call spread and risk-reversals, they suggested.  Change on the day at 0654 GMT

title: FX  ASIA: Asian Reserves Up In Jan As  Intervention  Continues
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 0.8% in January from a month earlier, boosted by intervention in forex markets and large inflows into several key economies, indicating that the fast-growing region remains a strong draw for foreign capital.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, excluding China's, stood at US$2.774 trillion at the end of January, up from US$2.753 trillion at the end of December. That compares with a 1.1% decrease posted in December from November, the first decrease in 10 months.

China, which releases its data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.4 trillion in reserves at the end of December.

The U.S. dollar's surge against alternative reserve currencies such as the euro and British pound lowered the value of non-dollar reserves in January, as it did in December. However, dollar purchases in forex markets by Asian central banks - most of which want to stop their currencies from rising too much - as well as strong investment flows offset the valuation effect in January.

The dollar rose 3% in January against the euro and 0.9% against the British pound. It fell 2.8% against the Japanese yen.

The dollar also lost some ground against other key Asian currencies including the Indonesian rupiah, Thai baht and Korean won, prompting suspected interventions in these countries and elsewhere. As a result, reserves rose over 2.5% in Korea, Thailand and Indonesia, hitting an all-time high in January in all three countries.

In Taiwan, where the local central bank also is prone to intervene in forex markets, reserves increased by 0.7% to set an all-time high for the fourteenth consecutive month, the longest streak in the region.

That trend seems likely to continue. China's economic growth, which Xinhua reports the Academy of Sciences think-tank expects to be 10% this year, is driving other economies in the region to growth rates well above those in the developed world.

Many analysts expect that inflows will keep pushing Asian currencies higher, driving central banks to intervene in coming months and building up their reserves.

Central banks are likely to remain focused on protecting the competitiveness of local export industries amid concern about the strength of final demand in the developed world, leaving inflation worries as a secondary concern despite an uptick in energy and commodity prices.

UBS economist Jonathan Anderson wrote recently that policymakers in Asia and other emerging markets historically have maintained a preference for weak or stable currencies, a trend that should continue.

Anderson noted that many emerging economies face steeper inflation rates - four percentage points higher on average - than do developed markets. That increases the cost of their products and makes them lose competitiveness over time, even if their currencies remain stable against those of their trading partners in the developed world. As a result, intervention is seen as a way to protect their export industries.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker late Friday, weighed down by a selloff in most Asian currencies and equities as investors remain cautious ahead of the release of key U.S. jobs numbers.

The U.S. Department of Labor Friday releases its non-farm payrolls data for November, with economists expecting to see 125,000 jobs lost in the month and the unemployment rate steady at 10.2%.

A Singapore-based trader for a foreign bank said the Singapore dollar will take its cues from the euro's reaction to the jobs data.

However, he expects there will be some limit to the local currency's appreciation even if a strong employment number supports a burst of risk appetite, given the Monetary Authority of Singapore's recent intervention efforts.

"Even if the U.S. dollar does weaken a bit and goes down to S$1.3750, I think through fear and intervention it will come back," the trader said.

"All the central banks in Asia are trying to stop their currencies from rising too much--the MAS is not the only one."

Singapore bonds also weakened with yields rising slightly on positioning ahead of the employment data.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar ended the Asian session stronger Thursday as its U.S. counterpart continued to weaken against most currencies.

The key for the U.S. dollar's weakness was the euro rising above the psychologically significant US$1.51 level Wednesday.

The fall in the greenback against the Singapore dollar was checked in part by central bank intervention. The Monetary Authority of Singapore Thursday intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the U.S. dollar, two persons familiar with the situation told Dow Jones Newswires.

One person said that the central bank intervened around S$1.3797 and that the central bank will continue supporting the greenback if needed.

However, one trader said with the U.S. dollar having broken down through key levels on a trade-weighted basis, there is still plenty of scope for the currency to drop to the S$1.3700 level.

He said while Asian equities were slightly weaker Thursday, risk appetite is "neutral."

"There's a bit of a correction in the stock markets today but I think the trend is for more Asian currency appreciation near-term," the trader said.

Singapore government bonds were stronger at the short end, supported by the modest downturn in regional equities.

title: ANALYSIS-Asia to loosen grip on  FX  as inflation returns
text:
* Asia c.banks intervene to curb FX gains as dollar drops

* But intervention will ease as inflation revives

* Inflation muted now, but will be a concern next year

* Less pressure for intervention if China unshackles yuan

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The dollar's plunge has prompted Asian central banks to intervene to curb strength in their currencies and support exports, but they may change tack in 2010 to rely on currency appreciation to contain inflation.

Asian currencies are rallying strongly as investors pile cash into emerging markets, believing they will not only recover from the global downturn before developed economies but will start to raise interest rates first as well.

But the risk for Asian central banks is that raising interest rates as growth and inflation revives could spur yet more capital inflows, especially if it means a growing rate premium over G7 economies.

Another option would be to reduce the level of intervention and allow currency appreciation to take up the policy slack.

"At this juncture, we think central banks are seeking to prevent excessive speculative pressure while trying to accommodate endemic dollar weakness," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at OCBC Bank in Singapore.

"Probably in the first to second quarter, the global outlook would have better clarity and the central bankers would be able to sleep better when they loosen up slightly to allow their respective exchange rates to reflect better economic conditions."

For now, currency intervention is serving the purpose of helping Asian exporters in their time of need as they try to recover from the global downturn and compete with China, which has kept the yuan flat against the dollar since mid 2008.

But China is likely to unshackle the yuan early next year when export markets are expected to pick up, which will help calm fears among its smaller neighbours about losing out to Chinese exporters, analysts say.

Investors are already pricing in the prospect of stronger economic growth and higher interest rates. The South Korean won and Indian rupee have each gained 6 percent since September. The Philippine peso is up 5 percent.

The Indonesian rupiah is soaring. It's up 16 percent this year as the dollar sits at 14-month lows against major currencies.

"Obviously we see currency-strengthening despite the fact that they are intervening, and I would expect that to continue to be the case as long as there are appreciating pressures," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia currency strategist at SEB in Singapore.

A Reuters poll shows analysts expect the won and rupee to gain about 6 percent from now to the end of 2010, leading Asian currencies higher. [MKTPOLL1]

Foreign currency reserves held by Asian central banks surged by nearly $112 billion in September to a record $4.96 trillion, reflecting dollars accumulated in intervention. [ID:nSP496890]

"PRE-CONDITION"

Earlier this month, Australia became the first G20 country to raise interest rates and markets are pricing in the risk of tighter policy elsewhere in Asia, including in South Korea, India and China.

Analysts believe some Asian central banks, particularly those in Indonesia, India and the Philippines, may see inflation rising closer or beyond their comfort levels in the first half of 2010.

But raising interest rates aggressively when borrowing costs stay low in the United States would only fuel capital inflows and eventually negate the tightening effect of rate rises, analysts at HSBC said in a note.

"In other words, monetary policy decoupling in Asia virtually requires as a pre-condition that exchange rates appreciate. This is especially so the longer low interest rates are expected to persist in the West," they said.

A Reuters poll suggests Philippines inflation could hit 4.1 percent in the second quarter of 2010, inside the government's annual target of 3.5-5.5 percent. It's just 0.7 percent now.

The poll shows Indonesia's inflation will more than double to hit 5.9 percent in the second quarter of next year, against a central bank forecast of 4-6 percent.

In India, analysts expect inflation to surpass the central bank's comfort level of 5 percent before March 31 from 1.2 percent now.

Another incentive to cut back on intervention is that it can fuel inflation because of the domestic liquidity that is generated.

"That's when one of the side effects of fighting currency appreciation becomes a pressing domestic issue," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac in Sydney.

While reduced intervention may suit a policy purpose, China may hold the key to easing central bank nerves about rising currencies.

"I think in general terms, this kind of intervention is likely to step down rather than step up when China starts to let its currency strengthen again, which I expect to happen during the first quarter of next year," SEB's Prim said. (Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: EM ASIA  FX -Baht rebounds,  intervention  talk caps  Singapore  dlr
text:
* Baht rebounds from 2-week low in line with local stocks

* Singapore dollar firms, but capped by intervention talk

* Ringgit falls from 14-month high as investors book profits

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The Thai baht rebounded on Friday in step with local stocks after two days of losses sparked by concerns over the health of the country's king, while the Singapore dollar's gains were limited by talk of official intervention.

The yen <JPY=> stayed under broad pressure as investors cut some of their long positions, while sterling <GBP=D4> approached its highest level in three weeks following upbeat central bank comments. [IDnT126523]

BAHT

The baht <THB=> rebounded to 33.37 per dollar from its two-week low of 33.61 hit on Thursday, in line with a bounce back in stocks after a palace official said the king's health was improving.

The palace official said on Thursday that the 81-year-old king was on the mend but he would still need protracted physical therapy. He has been in hospital for nearly a month and is recovering from pneumonia.

Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said on Friday that Thailand has no need to adopt special measures to support the stock market after its biggest fall in a year, and added that he expected the country's economic fundamentals to remain sound. [ID:nBKT003111]

"The baht would probably hover around this level with the focus on the stock market. If stocks face a renewed broad sell-off, baht will follow," said a trader.

Other dealers said many investors may protectively close out FX positions ahead of the weekend.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> drifted towards 1.388 per U.S. dollar, but its upside was contained by talk of official intervention.

"We see good two way interest with market rumours the authority is supporting the U.S. dollar at 1.3880," said a trader.

On Thursday, traders suspected official intervention as the Singapore dollar rose to 1.3856, its highest since August 2008.

Singapore dollar has gained 4 percent since early Sept. as part of an Asia-wide rally against the beleaguered U.S. currency. Earlier this week, Singapore's central bank kept its zero appreciation stance on hold and sounded wary on the country's economic outlook.

RINGGIT

The ringgit <MYR=> eased to 3.37 per dollar, down 0.4 percent from Thursday, when it hit a 14-month high.

"Obviously the market is very short dollars, people are squaring up as we go into weekend," said a trader.

title: EM ASIA  FX - Intervention  suspected as dollar suffers
text:
* Firmer baht, peso prompt central banks to intervene

 * Traders spot U.S. dollar buying to cap Singapore dollar

 * Asian FX gains seen intact despite official intervention

 By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Renewed weakness in the U.S. dollar on Tuesday pushed the Thai baht and Philippine peso towards last week's multi-month highs, triggering fresh official intervention to curb their strength.

 The Singapore dollar rose but its gains were also limited by suspected official dollar-buying, a day after the monetary authority kept its zero appreciation policy intact and sounded wary on the economic outlook. [ID:nSP502821]

 Although central banks are tapping on the brakes, analysts expect the rally in Asian currencies against the dollar to continue as foreign investors flock to regional stock and bond markets on a view the economies will recover from the global downturn faster than the rest of the world.

 "Intervention itself cannot stop this Asia FX rally," said Suresh Ramanathan, strategist at CIMB Investment Bank.

 "If policy makers need to get out of this directional play in Asia ex-Japan FX, the need is to spell out clearly a time frame for exit strategies, this at least provides the market with a framework in gauging how far Asian currencies can strengthen."

 The dollar stayed weak against major currencies <.DXY> on Tuesday after falling overnight. Investors are shifting into higher-yielding currencies as a belief that U.S. corporate earnings will exceed expectations boosts risk appetite. [ID:nT311772]

 India's markets were shut for holiday.

 BAHT

 The Thai baht <THB=> firmed in early trade on Tuesday and was expected to move in a narrow range of 33.25-33.40, although dealers spotted the central bank providing support for the dollar.

 "The Bank of Thailand was in the market to support dollar/baht at 33.30," said a Bangkok-based trader.

 It reached an intraday peak of 33.25, moving close to a 14-month high struck last week of 33.22

 PHILIPPINE PESO

 The peso <PHP=> rose briefly to 46.49 per dollar, up 0.3 percent from Monday's close, edging back towards last week's 2009 high of 46.45.

 But it soon pulled back to 46.50 as traders spotted official intervention around the day's high.

 "The central bank is at 46.50," said a Manila-based trader, adding the such intervention was not aggressive.

 The peso has gained only 2 percent against the dollar so far this year, trailing the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, which has rallied nearly 17 percent, and the South Korean won's 8 percent gain <KRW=>.

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR

 Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained a quarter of percent to 1.3962 per U.S. dollar but it was capped by suspected U.S. dollar-buying by local banks on the behalf of the central bank, some traders said.

 "Agent names have been on the bid (for USD) since yesterday and they are still bidding, while the market prefers to sell U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar," said a trader.

 Singapore's central bank kept its zero appreciation policy on Monday was cautious about the economic outlook. [ID:nSP502821]

 "We continue to expect the Singapore dollar to trade close to the top of the authority's target band and believe the central bank will manage the balance of payments surplus via intervention in the spot and forward FX markets, with a view towards keeping short-term interest rates low and stable," analysts at Barclays Capital said in a note.

The analysts forecast the Singapore dollar would rise to 1.38 to the U.S. dollar by the end of this year and rise further to 1.34 by the end of 2010.

 YUAN

 The Chinese yuan was little changed to 6.8260 per dollar, even though many analysts expect Chinese policy makers to allow the currency to resume its steady appreciation once the country's exports rise again.

 A banking regulator was quoted on Tuesday by Chinese media as calling for Beijing to let the yuan rise smartly against the dollar if the U.S. currency weakens, even though Chinese exports are already under pressure. [ID:nPEK313727]

title: UPDATE 2-Singapore dlr eases on profit-taking after MAS policy
text:
* Singapore dollar falls in line with regional peers

 * MAS caution on economy, intervention talk hurt sentiment

 * Further gains in store on U.S. dollar's expected weakness  (Adds fresh comments)

 By Kevin Yao

 SINGAPORE, Oct 12 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar eased on Monday as investors took profits from its recent gains after the central bank stuck to a neutral bias in its policy review but appeared wary about prospects for exports and global growth.

 The Singapore dollar fell in tandem with other Asian currencies against a broadly firmer U.S. dollar, with sentiment overshadowed by talk of official intervention.

 In an expected move, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which steers monetary policy by managing the currency's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) within a undisclosed band, kept its zero appreciation policy unchanged.

 The move came as the economy expanded 0.8 percent in the third quarter of 2009 from a year earlier, returning to growth after three quarters of annual contraction.

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell as far as 1.4010 per U.S. dollar, down nearly 0.4 percent from Friday's close and compared to levels of 1.3950 just before the policy announcement.

 "U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar is higher on profit taking and also on comments from MAS that the economy is not seen sustaining strong third-quarter expansion and that export demand has yet to recover fully for a place that lives and dies on exports," said a trader.

 The central bank intervened in offshore trading late on Friday by buying U.S. dollars at 1.3910-1.3920 to curb the rise in the local unit, which has gained 10 percent against the U.S. dollar since early March, traders said.

 Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at OCBC Bank, said he expected the pro-growth central bank to limit further gains in the Singapore dollar, which is seen near its the upper end of its trade-weighted band.

title: ANALYSIS-Singapore seeks balancing act on  currency , rates
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank is seen playing a delicate balancing act in the months ahead by keeping the currency stable and borrowing costs low to cement an economic recovery while heading off possible asset bubbles.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is tipped to keep its zero appreciation policy next Monday, while concerns about asset bubbles, particularly in the housing market, may have persuaded it to prevent further declines in already ultra-low money rates, analysts say.

"The MAS's money market operations may have helped put a floor under money market rates recently," said Mirza Baig, strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.

Singapore's short-term interest rates, which track U.S. funding costs as the country imposes few capital controls, have fallen sharply since the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, but they have stabilised in recent months.

The central bank had acted to keep market liquidity flush at the height of the credit crunch, analysts said, and they suspected it may have achieved that by sterilising less local money from the banking system after currency interventions.

"The MAS can engage in money market activities to push down rates and logically they could continue to be doing so in one form or another, though the degree of activity could vary," said Vishnu Varathan, economist at Forecast in Singapore.

He predicted Singapore's rates would be kept low for the next 6-12 months, but may drift higher later as the U.S. Federal Reserve and other central banks begin to tighten policy.

The Singapore 6-month swap offered rate (SOR), a benchmark for mortgage and commercial lending in the economy <SGDDFIX=ABSG>, has fallen steadily to 0.8 percent on Friday from 2.2 percent in September 2008.

The three-month interbank market rate (SIBOR) <SISGDD=ABSG> has been hovering near 0.7 percent since January, but its spread over three-month dollar LIBOR rates <LIBOR> has widened to 40 basis points since turning positive in May.

Singapore's central bank calibrates policy by guiding the exchange rate within a undisclosed trade-weighted band rather than interest rates. It eased policy in April through a mild devaluation to stimulate the flagging economy.

The economy leapt out of its worst-ever recession in the second quarter, but the government has maintained its 2009 forecast for the economy to contract 4-6 percent.

CONCERNS

Low borrowing costs would help boost Singapore's domestic demand but exports, the key growth engine for the economy, remain weak despite improvements in the global economy, analysts say.

"The preference is probably for more accommodative interest rate stance given the credit contraction concerns for corporates, especially small- and medium-size enterprises," said Selena Ling, head of treasury research and strategy at OCBC Bank in Singapore.

Official data this week showed total bank lending in Singapore rose 1.03 percent in August to S$274.6 billion ($193.8 billion) from S$271.8 billion in July.

A wave of fund inflows into the country's stock and property markets, meanwhile, have raised concerns about asset bubbles.

Singapore's private home prices surged nearly 16 percent in the third quarter from the previous quarter, the biggest jump this decade despite the government's recent move to release more land and make it harder for home buyers to defer payments.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> has rallied 11 percent against the dollar since March, but Singapore's monetary authority has not been seen intervening very aggressively even though analysts believe the unit has risen close to the upper end of the band.

Singapore's foreign currency reserves climbed by $2 billion in the first eight months of 2009 to $176.3 billion, far trailing increases in South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand.

Analysts say the central bank's forward book -- a tally of its holdings of U.S. dollar swaps -- rose to $49 billion in August from $37 billion in May, indicating that the MAS has drained more liquidity from the market in recent months.

TIGHTENING RISKS

The central bank is expected to tighten policy by allowing trade-weighted currency appreciation early next year, when the economy shows sustained recovery and inflation rises.

"The policy will be kept neutral for now," said Tim Condon, head of Asia research at ING, predicting a change in April 2010, when the bank next reviews policy.

Wei Zheng Kit, economist at Citigroup, also expects the central bank would tighten policy only in April 2010.

"Nevertheless, incipient inflation risks, and MAS's somewhat hawkish bias recently, suggests that risk of early tightening should not be ignored completely," he said in a note.

Three-month SIBOR rates may rise in line with expected U.S. interest rate rises early next year, but the spread between the SIBOR and LIBOR may turn negative again due to market expectations of a firmer Singapore dollar, Kit said.

"Continued demand for loans amidst a gradual easing of liquidity/deposit growth may also impute slight upward pressure on SIBOR rates into 2010," he added. (Reporting by Kevin Yao; Editing by Kim Coghill)

SINGAPORE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose on Tuesday against a broadly weaker U.S. currency but its gains were capped by fears of possible official intervention, while the South Korean won's strength prompted authorities to buy dollars.

The U.S. dollar eased broadly after rallying on Monday when traders took profits on short dollar positions ahead of key events such as a Federal Reserve policy meeting and a Group of 20 summit. [ID:nT239170] Markets in Japan, Malaysia and Indonesia were shut for a holiday.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose 0.3 percent to 1.4145 per U.S. dollar, but it failed to advance further as investors weighed the prospect of a possible official intervention because the currency could be reaching the upper end of its secret band.

"The Singapore dollar is so far stuck in a tight range," said a Singapore-based trader. "It seems that the Singapore dollar is close to the stronger end of the band, so I reckon support for U.S. dollar will be at 1.4140-50."

The Singagpore dollar has jumped 10 percent since early March, buoyed by optimism about the global economy.

Some investors were keen to sell the Singapore dollar against the euro and the Australian dollar, traders said.

(Adds detail from source, analysis.) 


 
   By Costas Paris and Se Young Lee 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank may intervene in the foreign exchange market to support the U.S. dollar if it falls convincingly below S$1.4200, a person familiar with the situation said Wednesday.

The Singapore dollar has seen a "steep rise" as it has climbed to its highest since December, the person told Dow Jones Newswires. "It will hurt the country's exports at a time when they are expected to turn around after being very weak this year."

This person said the Monetary Authority of Singapore won't intervene if the U.S. dollar stays around current levels, and if it does step in, it "will initially try to smooth the greenback's fall and then see what happens." The MAS doesn't want to fire its "big ammunition right from the start."

But in a recognition of the limits of intervention to curb rises in a single currency when the U.S. dollar is falling broadly, the person said, "All the calls are for the U.S. dollar to keep falling, so there is only so much a central bank can do."

The MAS uses the exchange rate as its chief policy tool because trade dwarfs Singapore's tiny domestic economy. The central bank targets an undisclosed trading band for the local dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.

The person familiar with the situation said the strong end of the band for the Singapore dollar would now equate to the U.S. dollar trading around S$1.4150. The greenback was quoted at S$1.4238 at 0340 GMT, off the day's 2009 low of S$1.4232.

A stronger Singapore dollar could hurt the island state's competitiveness at a time when the economy remains weak due to the global downturn that has severely undercut demand for its exports.

The concern comes as the greenback falls broadly on expectations other countries will emerge from recession faster than the U.S., as gold has risen and as firmer equities markets have given a bid to riskier assets, such as those denominated in Asian currencies.

Foreign reserves held by 11 key Asian countries, excluding China rose 2.2% in August from July, partly as central banks bought dollars to curb rises in their own currencies, according to Dow Jones Newswires calculations.

The dollar's broad decline over the past 24 hours has given the MAS "some breathing room" as other currencies in the basket have strengthened along with the Singapore dollar, said Sean Callow, a currency strategist at Westpac in Sydney.

Callow estimates the trade-weighed Singapore dollar is as high as 1.7% above the midpoint of the MAS band, but said this is "not an unusual level over the past few months and not implying an immediate intervention threat."

"It shouldn't hit the band just yet, but not too far away obviously," he said. "We're getting close, for sure."

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share Sensitive Index could rally to 16,230, indicate charts.

Tuesday's price action suggests weariness and profit-taking at higher levels. The occurrence of a "shooting star" candlestick pattern indicates a waning upside momentum.

The index must progress beyond the resistance at 16,430 to negate the chances of a short-term downward correction. A close below 15,850 will mark the start of the corrective phase and the index could then test support at 15,360.


 
 
US STOCKS 

U.S. stocks began the unofficial start to autumn just as they did this summer, with Alcoa, Chevron and General Electric at the forefront of a rally in energy, commodities and industrial companies.

Overall, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 56.07 points, or 0.59%, at 9497.34, marking a gain for the third straight session. The Dow is up 45% from its 2009 low on March 9.

Helping push the index higher was another round of buying in several types of commodities including gold, silver and oil. From an economic standpoint, investors touted an expectation of growth globally that will, in turn, drive demand for each of these products into the end of the year.

The move in these commodities lifted several Dow components, such as aluminum giant Alcoa, up 3.5% at $12.60, and Chevron, which rose 2.2% to $70.48.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Peso rises on money inflows, rupiah NDFs fall
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso firmed on Tuesday due to remittance inflows and firmer stocks, while the Singapore dollar inched up towards nine-month high hit the previous day amid fears of official intervention.

Asian shares touched a one-year high while gold prices hit $1,000 an ounce for the first time in six months in a sign of investor concerns about the sustainability of the global economic recovery. [ID:nSP506640]

PESO

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose as far as 48.37 per dollar, up half of a percent from Friday's close, buoyed by remittance inflows during the long weekend. The market was shut on Monday for holiday.

"Accumulated inflows over the long weekend have pushed down dollar/peso today, aided also by the overall weak state of the dollar" said a dealer in Manila.

He added the peso was supported on the rise in Asian shares which attracted more fund inflows into the region.

"The global markets have embraced another round of risk appetite and have assumed further bullishness lead by the advance in gold prices," the dealer said.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained a fifth of a percent to 1.4310 per U.S. dollar but was held off its nine-month high at 1.4308 hit on Monday as investors fretted about possible central bank intervention to curb its strength.

"U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar is drifting lower as the euro getting paid up on the surge in gold," said a trader.

The Singapore dollar has gained almost 9 percent against the dollar since early March, fanning fears among investors that the central bank might step in the market to curb the currency.

The central bank manages Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) within a secret band.

RUPIAH

The rupiah <IDR=> gained 0.6 percent to 10,000 per dollar, while dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards fell further although the past week's decline in one-month NDFs has brought them so close to the spot rate that scope for further tightening in forward points seems limited.

One-month dollar/rupiah NDFs <IDRNDFOR=> eased to 10,025, implying in a 0.2 percent rupiah depreciation from the spot.

"It's a better risk environment overall and it's one of the few countries where yields are still high. So there has been good client interest in bonds and short-term bills," said a trader in Singapore.

"But at current levels it does seem a little overdone. Spot has gone from 12,000 to current 10,000, so people are looking to square their positions now," the trader added.

Spot rupiah traded close to 12,000 per dollar in March, and one-year NDFs were then pricing in a 16 percent rupiah depreciation. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah rises on risk-taking, Sing dlr at 1-mth high
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 7 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah firmed on Monday as investors bought risky assets on optimism about the global economy, while Singapore dollar was boosted by news that Abu Dhabi's state fund ATIC would invest in a local chipmaker.

Asian stocks rose on Monday after better-than-expected U.S. jobs data on Friday reinforced optimism about economic recovery and a pledge by G20 leaders over the weekend to keep stimulus measures in place for longer. [IDnL7493885]

The Philippine markets were shut for holiday.

RUPIAH

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR=> gained 0.6 percent to 10,050 per dollar, as investors bought local stocks <.JKSE>.

The rupiah, Asia's best performer this year with a gain of just over 9 percent against the dollar, is often the currency of choice when investors increase risk.

"I think it's the story of the return of risk appetite," said Enrico Tanuwidjaja, strategist at OCBC Bank.

The bank has raised its year-end rupiah forecast to 9,700 per dollar from 10,200 due to economic recovery and capital inflows.

Meanwhile, one-month dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards <IDR1MNDFOR=> fell to 10,070, implying a 0.1 percent rupiah fall from the spot compared to 0.4 percent at Friday's close.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

"Singapore dollar gained on the belief that ATIC will have to sell U.S. dollar and buy Singapore dollar to pay for the deal," said a trader.

Some traders suspected central bank intervention to cap the Singapore dollar, which has risen almost 9 percent against the U.S. dollar since early March due to optimism about the global economy.

text:
* Singapore dollar edges up, buoyed by capital inflows

* Thai baht attempts go higher but c.bank keeps it on leash

* Most Asian currencies move in tight ranges in slow trade

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar edged up on Friday amid signs of capital inflows, while the Thai baht's rise was contained by suspected central bank intervention.

The Australian dollar hit an 11-month high against the dollar after Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens hinted at higher interest rates [ID:nSYD342603], but most emerging Asian currencies moved in narrow ranges in tandem with stocks.

BAHT

The baht <THB=TH> gained a third a percent to 33.95 per dollar but was repeatedly pushed back to the weaker side of the 34 level by suspected intervention by the central bank, which has almost become a daily routine.

The Bank of Thailand has been closely guarding the psychologically important 34 level in recent sessions.

"Dollar/baht is under selling pressure, but the central bank keeps buying dollars," said a Bangkok-based trader.

The baht has gained almost 7 percent since early March, in line with its regional peers buoyed by optimism about a recovery in the global economy.

The baht's rise came to a halt in June as the central bank frequentely intervened to shackle the unit within a tight 33.9-34.3 range for fear that a stronger currency would hurt the already ailing export sector.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained a fifth of a percent to 1.44 per U.S. dollar, but its strength was capped by worries about possible central bank intervention.

Investors have been fearful of intervention to curb the rise in the Singapore dollar, which has risen almost 8 percent against the U.S. currency since early March, even though the island's economy has only showed modest recovery from a deep recession.

The central bank steers monetary policy by managing the currency within a trade-weighted band and intervention may be warranted if the unit breaches the upper end of the secret band.

Wei Zheng Kit, economist at Citigroup, said the Singapore dollar has been underpinned by a return of net capital inflows into the country since May, which pushed up asset prices.

"Capital inflows have pushed the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) towards its strong side of the policy band since mid-April," he said in a note.

Kit reckoned that Singapore dollar's NEER has been hovering more than 100 basis points above the mid-point of the band.

The central bank eased policy by lowering the mid-point of the band in April help the economy. The bank is widely expected to keep its neutral stance when it reviews policy in October.

"We see the electronics momentum deteriorating rapidly. There

 "The sharper-than-expected contraction in NODX is in part
due to high base, but the continued and deeper weakness in

and EU.

 "Both electronics and biomedical were much weaker. We
already expected a sharp fall in Q4 GDP, led by the biomedical
sector, but the rest of the areas are likely to remain sluggish.
So this is consistent with the view that we are likely to see a
big sequential contraction in Q4 GDP."	

 "Biomedical was very strong in Q3 and that was due to
cyclical reasons. Business surveys indicate that it is going to
fall sharply in Q4. Electronics hinge more on the global
environment, especially in the U.S. and Europe, and confidence

 "Singapore's monetary policy is likely to remain in the

 "It has actually raised the odds of negative

 "I think for now the existing monetary policy is still

 "U.S. retail sales are holding up well so there could be

title: DJ UPDATE: Asia Central Banks Tap  FX  Reserves To Support Their  Currencies
text:
-- Official reserves in Indonesia, Philippines, South Korea, Singapore fall in September

-- Central bank action to slow currencies' slide aimed at reassuring markets

-- Reserve levels remain ample to guard against future shocks

By Martin Vaughan

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Several Asian central banks dipped into their vast foreign exchange reserves in September to stem sharp declines in their currencies hit by global market turbulence driven by the euro-zone's debt crisis.

While Asian currencies have stabilized this week, the authorities still have ample firepower to support them if global appetite for risky assets takes another turn for the worse, analysts say.

The scale of the declines in reserves suggests most central banks were trying to smooth volatile movements in their currencies, rather than taking a no-holds-barred approach to defend specific levels.

"What they are doing is just trying to reassure markets: 'Just because we have a slip doesn't mean everyone has to pile out and put their money in dollars,'" said Robert Ryan, FX strategist at BNP Paribas. "They're saying, 'You don't need to run for the exits, we will be there.'"

Reserves held by Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest economy, fell by $10.1 billion to $114.5 billion as of Sept. 30 from a month earlier, Bank Indonesia said Friday, reflecting interventions to slow the rupiah's tumble as foreign investors pulled capital out of the country.

Foreigners cut their holdings of rupiah-denominated government bonds by 12% in September, a pace on par with a selloff in October 2008 at height of the global financial crisis, DBS says.

The Philippines' reserves declined by a more modest $301 million to $75.639 billion. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas attributed the drop to debt payments made by the government and losses from a revaluation of the central bank's gold holdings. But the central bank has also been suspected by traders of intervening as recently as Tuesday to support the peso.

Singapore's reserves fell by $15.56 billion to $233.62 billion at the end of September. The reason for the decline was unclear, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore doesn't comment on reasons for changes in official reserves.

South Korea reported Wednesday its reserves fell by $8.8 billion to $303.3 billion at the end of September, the sharpest monthly fall since November 2008. Analysts attributed the drop to both won-supportive interventions and a fall in the euro, which hit the value of its euro-denominated assets in dollar terms.

Even after the declines in September, reserves remain more than ample to guard against shocks, economists said. Indonesian reserves are sufficient to cover 6.5 months of imports and government debt payments, said Bank Indonesia deputy governor Hartadi Sarwono.

Asian currencies swooned in September as foreign investors pared holdings in emerging markets and snapped up dollars on worries European banks were vulnerable and the global economy was tipping toward recession. Many have regained some ground this week as European officials have shown renewed resolve to support banks in the region and help Greece get its debt problem under control.

But analysts see room for the dollar to rise more in the short-term, as appetite for riskier currencies is vulnerable to negative signals from Europe and bad news out of the U.S., which some say could be headed for a recession.

Indonesia has been among the most aggressive in defending its currency.

"We think Indonesia's September foreign reserves data reveals an investor-friendly policy shift," ING chief Asia economist Tim Condon said. "Bank Indonesia will intervene heavily to prevent maxi-devaluations."

title: EM ASIA  FX -Funds keep slashing bets on Korean won, Singapore dollar
text:
* Range of funds keep cutting FX positions in Asia ex-Japan

* Leveraged, macro funds sell Singapore dollar

* Real money funds, bond outflows hit won

* Asian c.banks buy own currencies, may intervene less

(Updates text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The South Korean won on Monday fell to its lowest against the yen since March 2009 and the Singapore dollar saw the biggest single-day loss since early August, with a broad range of funds pulling money out of emerging Asia on fears of a Greek default.

Asian authorities stepped into currency markets and sold some of their big piles of U.S. dollar reserves to keep their own currencies from falling too rapidly, having spent billions of dollars since last Wednesday, traders estimated.

Leveraged investors, macro-driven funds and interbank speculators sold the Singapore dollar, and offshore institutional investors were the main players dumping the won.

After months of resilience, emerging Asian currencies have quickly given way over the past week, led by moves in offshore forwards.

The position reduction and in some cases liquidation was by no means focused only on Asia, with the 1-month non-deliverable forward for dollar/Brazilian real on Friday hitting the highest since November 2010.

Still, the degree of the selloff in Asia has surprised traders and analysts as the relatively strong underlying fundamentals in the region have not changed much. Strategists were busy recommending trades that anticipated further weakness in Asian currencies.

"We are positioning for further softness in Asia ex-Japan currencies. What stands out in the current environment is the Hong Kong dollar... it makes sense to use the HKD to remain long against shorting the rest of AXJ FX - including the AUD and NZD," said Suresh Kumar Ramanathan, regional rates and foreign exchange strategist for CIMB Investment Bank in Kuala Lumpur.

Asian foreign exchange authorities are expected to keep buying their own currencies to ease volatility, though would only slow the move lower in their currencies rather than draw a clear line in the sand, especially since weaker currencies ultimately help their exports.

"Asian central banks are allowing FX weakness as a buffer, to some degree, to economic headwinds as a way of easing monetary conditions," said Sacha Tihanyi, senior currency strategist for Scotia Capital in Hong Kong.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar weakened past a 200-day moving average, shedding 1.4 percent against the U.S. dollar.

The Singapore dollar may weaken more, probably to 1.2626 per dollar, the 50 percent Fibonacci retracement of its strength between November last year and late July, if it ends the day softer than the 200-day moving average of 1.2491.

WON

The South Korean won hit a six-month low against the dollar on real money funds' selling and touched its weakest in two and a half years against the yen.

The won also came under pressure from bond outflows, dealers said.

The foreign exchange authorities were spotted buying the won, especially when it weakened past 1,120 per dollar, but investors took the intervention as chances to sell the won on rallies, dealers said.

Some dealers say authorities may not actively cap the won's falls.

"They may be concerned more about exports amid worries over Europe. They may not waste bullets around this level," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

RUPIAH

The Indonesian central bank was spotted buying the rupiah

from 8,800 per dollar to 8,850.

"It totally depends on how many dollars the central bank is willing to give. If it is a small amount, USD/IDR could break 8,900 even today. If BI cannot guard the volatility, it will be exaggerated by short term investors and will drag the IDR even weaker. It will hit the long-term investors eventually," said a Jakarta-based dealer.

Another dealer, saying the central bank had not been too aggressive, estimated that it sold $250 million to support the rupiah.

title: WSJ BLOG/MarketBeat: Singapore's Second Quarter Disappoints
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Market Beat blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/marketbeat.)

By Matthew Allen and Philip Vahn

Credit Suisse said its Singapore second-quarter report card had 18 disappointments versus 11 positive surprises, with the remaining 27 results in line with expectations.

"Overall, [second-quarter] net earnings for these companies fell 3% on-year," it said. This was "despite a 15% on-year jump in revenue as net margins decreased from 10.8% in [the second quarter of 2010] to 9.3% in [the second quarter of 2011]."

After this "poor" results season, the house has lowered its 2011 fiscal year market earnings estimate by 4.5%.

Among the second quarter's positives, Credit Suisse said six came from the offshore marine sector, which has underperformed defensives by 16% in share-price terms on recession concerns, while dividends rose 13% from last year.

"While the overall reporting season is disappointing, the key question for investors is whether this is already priced in. Even post-downgrades, we are looking for 3% [earnings per share] growth in [fiscal year 2011] while the [Straits Times Index] is down 11% in local currency terms and down 5% in U.S. dollar terms so far this year."

Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar's rise is posing a challenge for exporters but it will be premature for the Monetary Authority of Singapore to ease its current exchange-rate policy in the upcoming policy review, DBS Group Research said in a note.

Apart from diluting export competitiveness, the stronger Singapore dollar has created a negative currency effect on the export numbers, the house says, adding that local exporters are now getting less in Singapore dollar terms unless they have hedged their U.S. dollar exposure.

The Singapore dollar rose by about 12% against the greenback over the past year. Still, the house warns that inflation remains a concern in Singapore and any drastic intervention to soften the Singapore dollar on the back of the strong capital inflows will prove to be a costly affair for the authority.

"Stability is probably the best option in times of volatility," it cautions.

The U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar was trading at 1.2064 Thursday.

title: Moody's Analyst: BOJ Easing, Japan  FX Intervention  Are 'Positive Actions'
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--New easing measures by the Bank of Japan and intervention to weaken the yen are "positive actions," but their impact is likely to be limited over time and they don't remove the "big credit challenges" the country faces, a senior analyst at Moody's Investors Service said Thursday.

Japan stepped into the currency market Thursday, launching a yen-selling campaign that was backed up by Y10 trillion in easing measures from the central bank, as officials said they needed to tame market speculation threatening a fragile economic recovery.

Moody's lead sovereign analyst for Japan Tom Byrne told Dow Jones Newswires that the BOJ's easing would help to offset deflationary pressures and to some extent aid the recovery of economic activity from various constraints caused by March's devastating earthquake.

He noted that the yen's climb was becoming the No. 1 concern for exporters, now that the quake-damaged supply chain is normalizing.

"BOJ easing and MOF intervention are positive actions, although they will probably have limited effects over time," Byrne said.

"However, Japan's big credit challenges remain--fiscal consolidation and economic growth revitalization."

Moody's is nearing the end of a three-month assessment period on Japan's Aa2 sovereign rating, having put it on review for possible downgrade May 31.
