title: Asian Shares Mostly Up; Yen Tumbles, Tokyo Shares Climb On  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Most Asian shares rose Thursday, with the yen tumbling against its rivals and buoying Tokyo stocks after Japanese authorities intervened to weaken the currency.

Japanese Finance Minister Yuhioko Noda said the Ministry Of Finance conducted yen-selling intervention after weeks of warning about "one-sided" moves, as authorities step up efforts to cap the high flying yen as it threatened to damage the export economy as it recovers from the March 11 earthquake and tsunami.

Bank of Japan Governor Masaaki Shirakawa said he strongly expects the MOF action will stabilize the yen's recent moves.

"The Ministry of Finance faces a tough battle in the months ahead against yen strength while the situation with the U.S. economy and possible sovereign downgrade remains uncertain, keeping pressure on the dollar," said Koji Fukaya, director of fixed income and global foreign exchange research at Credit Suisse.

The U.S. dollar rose to Y78.31 from Y77.10 earlier in the day, and compared with Y77.06 in late New York trade Wednesday. The euro was also up at Y112.24, from Y110.35 in New York, while against the dollar it was at $1.4325 compared with $1.4320.

"The market is breathing a sigh of relief for now, but the yen remains firm and investors are expecting more rounds of intervention later in the day," said Takuya Yamada, senior portfolio manager of ITC Investment Partners.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average rose 1.0%. Most export sector stocks surged on the intervention, overshadowing news Hitachi and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries plan to merge some operations. Toyota Motor rose 1.9% and Sony added 1.0%.

Hitachi and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries rose 2.4% and 3.7%, respectively, on news of a possible merger of several of their infrastructure operations, which could lead to the creation of one of the world's largest global players in a number of key sectors.

"While it's not certain whether the deal will go through, this could signal further consolidation among the more traditional companies," said Yutaka Miura, senior technical analyst at Mizuho Securities.

Lead September Japanese government bond futures were up 0.20 at 142.43 points.

Most other regional equity markets were only modestly higher in cautious trade after the recent heavy selloffs amid persistent concerns about the global economic outlook. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.1%, recovering from an 11-month low touched earlier, supported by resources and bank plays.

South Korea's Kospi Composite fell 0.2% and New Zealand's NZX-50 tacked on 0.2%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 66 points in screen trade.

September Nymex crude oil futures are up 27 cents at $92.20. Spot gold was at $1,663.20 per troy ounce, up $2.10 from New York trade.

title: Asian Rubber Settles Lower; Eyes On Yen As Japan  Intervenes
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian rubber settled lower Thursday, with the weakening yen not giving much upside support to the bellwether Tokyo Commodity Exchange, as macro-economic concerns put downward pressure on prices.

Benchmark January Tocom natural rubber settled Y0.6 lower at Y390.5 a kilogram, even as the Japanese Ministry of Finance sold the yen for the first time since March, while the Bank of Japan announced additional monetary easing, coordinating efforts to stem export-damaging rises in the currency.

Tocom rubber is usually boosted when the yen weakens as this makes it more competitive than the dollar-denominated physical commodity.

"It's about time the Japanese government did something about the yen, but it may already be priced in," said a Hat Yai-based trader at a major exporter.

"Tocom players are nervous about setting up new positions with the volatility in yen today [Thursday]," Kaname Gokon, Tokyo-based deputy general manager at commodity brokerage Okato Shoji Co, said, adding that traders are watching the Japanese currency for further cues.

Tocom will make a break upward with resistance at Y396.5/kg, if USD/JPY breaks above Y80 decisively. Otherwise, Tocom will likely continue to trade in a Y380-Y395/kg range, Gokon said.

Japan's finance minister hinted Thursday that the government will intervene further in the currency market if necessary, saying its efforts to weaken the yen are not complete and he will "do what is deemed necessary."

Asked about the impact of the intervention so far, Yoshihiko Noda said: "We are still halfway through, so I'll sum up the results after this is over."

January Tocom rubber closed Y2.6 higher at Y393.1/kg in the night session as the yen weakened further. The night session is considered part of the next trading day.

Natural rubber on the Shanghai Futures Exchange settled 0.3% lower, taking cues from SHFE metals amid persistent concerns over the health of the global economy.

   By Martin Vaughan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies have snapped a two-month funk, testing recent highs and prompting some intervention from central banks Friday as investors put Europe's debt crisis behind them for the moment and as encouraging U.S. data spurred regional share gains.

Central banks in South Korea, the Philippines and Taiwan apparently sold their currencies to slow the resumed gains, local traders said. Most of the region's authorities had been sidelined since early May, when Greece's fiscal crisis flared up, sapping demand for risky assets.

With the next bailout payment apparently headed toward Athens, risk appetite has perked up in recent days, boosting Asian currencies. Strong U.S. job data Thursday helped propel them back toward their highs, with the Singapore dollar resuming its record run against the U.S. currency.

Craig Chan, Asian currency strategist at Nomura Bank in Singapore, predicted the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah will be among the biggest gainers in coming months, as global growth picks up again and the region's authorities allow more appreciation to counter rising inflation.

Asia's central banks have tolerated significant gains in their currencies as the region has led the global economic recovery, but they still step in when they feel the rises are too abrupt or out of line with the trends of their trading partners.

"It's too early to say that we're at the end of the solvency issue for Greece," said Nomura's Chan. "But now there seems to be a little bit more clarity, and people are getting more hopeful that we're moving through the soft patch."

The U.S. private sector added 157,000 jobs in May, well above the forecast 95,000 increase, said payroll giant Automatic Data Processing Inc., boosting expectations that Friday's closely watched nonfarm payrolls will also be strong.

With investors bidding up the Singapore dollar along with other Asian currencies Friday, the U.S. dollar slid below its May 2 record low to S$1.2177. It had traded above $1.2500 several times in May as global risk aversion sent investors into the safe-haven greenback.

As the won climbed to its highest since the U.S. subprime crisis went global in August 2008, the Bank of Korea bought an estimated $200-$300 million, apparently in a bid to defend the KRW1,057.00 line after the dollar fell to the day's low of KRW1,056.20, traders said.

The head of the BOK's foreign-exchange market team declined to comment.

Seoul traders predicted the authorities will be less aggressive than in recent forays into the market, probably because a strong won helps to keep imported inflation from feeding the rapid rise in domestic consumer prices.

Traders in Manila said the Philippine central bank appeared to buy $50-$100 million, but the dollar still ended at a two-month low of PHP42.75. Taiwan's central bank appeared to buy the U.S. currency around NT$28.760, Taipei traders said.

The Philippine and Taiwan central banks couldn't immediately be reached for comment.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Weaker, Yen At Post- Intervention  High Before ECB
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The dollar was broadly weaker in holiday-thinned Asia trade Thursday, with the yen ticking to its highest levels since Japan's March intervention as investors awaited a rate decision from the European Central Bank.

The euro, caught between a hawkish ECB outlook and worries about the sovereign-debt crisis on the euro-zone periphery, firmed slightly against the dollar and yen as market participants adjusted positions, with markets closed in Japan, South Korea and Thailand.

The ECB is expected to keep its key interest rate on hold in its 1145 GMT decision, with markets closely watching President Jean-Claude Trichet's subsequent news conference for nuances that could point to the timing of future interest-rate rises.

With inflation climbing further above the ECB's target of 2%, some economists expect Trichet to signal a further rate hike as early as June, by using the key phrase that the bank is showing "strong vigilance" on price pressures.

Michael Wolfolk, a strategist at Bank of New York Mellon, said that if Trichet fails to convey a heightened vigilance on inflation, it could spark a substantial relief rally for the dollar. Alternatively, hawkishness from Trichet could boost the euro toward $1.5000, he said.

The euro was at $1.4868 at 0537 GMT, up from $1.4827 late Wednesday in New York, and Y119.43 against Y119.47.

The yen, benefiting from safe-haven flows along with the Swiss franc as risk aversion swept through markets. The dollar fell below Y80.44 in Asia, the lowest since the Group of Seven joined Tokyo in selling the Japanese currency March 18. At 0537 GMT, the dollar was at Y80.45, off its session low Y80.36, according to EBS via CQG, but down from Y80.62 late Wednesday in New York.

Analysts are looking to Y80.00 as a major support level, which would trigger expectations that Japan would intervene again to support the greenback.

The Swiss franc also gained, with the dollar at CHF0.8595, down from CHF0.8616 in New York.

The commodity-linked Australian dollar -- savaged against the U.S. dollar overnight with silver, copper, oil and gold all lower - tumbled to a seven-session low of US$1.0689 from US$1.0766 after the Australia's March retail sales unexpectedly fell 0.5% from February, vs a forecast rise of 0.5%.

The Aussie was at US$1.0739 vs US$1.0748 in New York.

The pound was also mildly supported before the Bank of England's 1100 GMT rate decision. The U.K. central bank is expected to leave its key interest rate at its all-time low of 0.5% for the 26th consecutive month.

Sterling was at $1.6520 vs $1.6489 in New York.

The dollar got a brief boost from Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Dennis Lockhart, who struck a hawkish tone, saying in a speech there's little chance of a double-dip recession or of the Fed embarking on a third round of "quantitative easing." The ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the U.S. dollar against a basket of currencies, shot up to 73.196 from 73.11 on the comments, though the move quickly reversed. title: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  Again As  Currencies  Extend Rally
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The dollar continued to sell off sharply in Asia Thursday, prompting central banks in South Korea and Malaysia to try to curb the surge in their currencies to long-term highs by intervening for the second day running.

South Korean authorities also said they will inspect foreign-exchange transactions at banks, focusing on activity in the overseas non-deliverable forward market. The move comes as heavy dollar selling by offshore players, largely via the NDF market, has pushed the Korean won to multi-month highs in recent weeks.

China fixed the yuan at another record high against the dollar, setting the tone for Asian trading where sentiment was also given a boost by upbeat U.S. economic data and a strong earnings-driven rally on Wall Street. Strategists said authorities are trying to smooth sudden market moves, but likely won't stand in the way of the broad appreciation trend in Asian currencies.

"Asian central banks and government officials have made it very clear that they're going to use currencies to fight inflation," said Stuart Oakley, head of emerging market trading at the Royal Bank of Scotland. "They're allowing their currencies to move faster than they have before, and China is leading the way on that."

Traders said the Bank of Korea bought dollars at KRW1,080.00, after the greenback hit KRW1,079.70 in early trading hours. The central bank used multiple foreign banks to execute trades, traders said. The BOK intervened again later, pushing the U.S. currency up to KRW1,080.50, according to traders in Seoul.

The head of BOK's foreign exchange market team declined to comment.

Bank Negara Malaysia bought dollars at MYR3.0120, and then later at MYR3.0080 as the dollar fell to 13-year lows against the ringgit, local traders said.

The actions came as the U.S. dollar took a beating across the board, falling against the euro and other currencies. Commodity-linked currencies soared into rarely-seen territory. The Australian dollar hit a 29-year high of $1.0760, while the U.S. dollar touched C$0.9482 against the Canadian Loonie, a level not seen since 2007.

The U.S. dollar fell to a fresh record low against the Singapore dollar, which has paced the gains in Asian currencies, reaching a low early Thursday of S$1.2358.

Traders in Thailand were on vigil against further intervention by the Thai authorities to weaken the baht, following suspected market activity Wednesday by the Bank of Thailand.

Better-than-expected U.S. housing data overnight helped to spur risk appetite Thursday as Asian equity markets opened higher.

But the main thing pushing Asian currencies higher against the U.S. dollar remains the sense that the U.S. Federal Reserve is lagging the European Central Bank and others in its willingness to tighten policy.

"We've had pretty clear signals from the majority on the [Fed's Federal Open market Committee] that they don't see any problem with keeping monetary conditions in the U.S. as loose as possible for as long as possible," said Cliff Tan, a foreign exchange strategist at Societe Generale in Hong Kong.

In contrast, Asian central banks have been tightening since last year to try to blunt higher food and fuel prices, and the ECB lifted its key policy rate earlier this month.

A stronger currency makes exports more expensive abroad, and central banks in Asia's export-oriented economies have historically intervened to soften the blow of a sharp currency rise.

Korea is brandishing various tools to curb gains in the won. It announced Thursday it would conduct "inspections" into non-deliverable forward trades at four banks. Offshore investors have taken short positions on the dollar in the forward market, pushing the won higher.

Analysts said the inspections might perturb the banks, but authorities can do little concretely to limit NDF trades, which are done beyond the jurisdiction of Korean authorities.

title: DJ Asia Central Banks  Intervene  Again As Asian  Currencies  Climb
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks in South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia intervened Wednesday to slow a surge in their currencies in a broad Asian rally that carried the Singapore and Australian dollars to fresh highs against the U.S. currency.

The People's Bank of China's decision to fix the yuan at a fresh high record against the U.S. dollar added to bullish views on Asian currencies, which have been trending upward as central banks around the region tighten monetary policies to fight rising inflation.

The Asian currency rally Wednesday appeared to be driven by a rebound in risk-taking sentiment. Recovering from temporary misgivings about U.S. fiscal health following Standard & Poor's rating warning, investors warmed to risk again, pumping more money into Asia's fast-growing economies.

Wai Ho Leong, senior regional economist at Barclay's Capital, said improved risk appetite and also continued high oil prices are some of the factors influencing Asian currencies' move higher. High commodity prices "give policymakers the willingness to tolerate a stronger currency" as a check on inflation, he said.

Many Asian countries have intervened in recent months to stem a decline in the U.S. dollar, which could hurt their export industries. The foreign exchange interventions by the Korean, Thai and Malaysian authorities Wednesday appeared to be aimed at tempering gains in the won, baht and ringgit rather than an effort to stop the upward trend in those currencies.

The Australian dollar reached a new post-float high against the U.S. dollar, fetching US$1.0611 before easing back to $1.0602. Its climb was in part driven by a Dow Jones Newswires report that Australia is weighing a tax break on passive investments by sovereign funds.

The Singapore dollar also notched record highs, as the greenback fell to S$1.2400. The Singapore currency's nearly year-long rally gained momentum last week when the island's central bank revalued the currency and pledged to continue to guide it higher to curb rising inflation.

The PBOC, which tightly controls the yuan, fixed the dollar's exchange rate at CNY6.5294, down from Tuesday's fixing of CNY6.5346 and close of CNY6.5305 in the over-the-counter market. Traders said they expect the PBOC to let the yuan rise further ahead of a May 24-25 U.S.-China strategic economic dialogue in Beijing, since China has a record of yuan strengthening ahead of such international events.

The Bank of Korea likely bought about $500 million Wednesday in an effort to curb the won's ascent, traders said. The dollar dipped to KRW1,082.00 before ticking up to KRW1,082.20 late in Asian trade.

Against the Malaysian ringgit, the U.S. dollar fell to MYR3.0160, its lowest level since September 1997. That was down from MYR3.0230 at Tuesday's close. The ringgit rebounded somewhat on buying by Bank Negara Malaysia, traders in Kuala Lumpur said. The dollar was last at MYR3.0155, with the central bank suspected of more buying at that level.

Further gains could be in store for the ringgit, as it has lagged recently against regional peers like the Singapore dollar, which it tends to track closely. Continued high oil prices will support the ringgit, as will expectations of a rate hike at Bank Negara's next policy meeting, set for May 5.

The Bank of Thailand was suspected of buying dollars as the baht gained ahead of a monetary policy meeting at which the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points--as expected--and said interest rates remain on an upward trend. The action helped keep the dollar supported at THB30.02, traders said.

title: DJ US Dollar To Remain Pressured Despite Singapore  Currency  Move
text:
-- Asian central banks unlikely to end dollar recycling

-- Singapore's currency move not likely to herald regional shift in policy

-- U.S. dollar set to remain under pressure By Siva Sithraputhran Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar is set to remain under pressure over the long term because most Asian central banks are seen as being unlikely to slow the pace of greenback sales, even after Singapore signaled that it might do just that.

Asian central banks typically buy the dollar against local currencies to slow any export-denting bouts of strength, but then churn the dollars into euros, Australian dollars, and other currencies to spread the risks, so the greenback falls. This 'recycling' of reserves has been at the heart of the dollar's weakness against a range of currencies--including the euro--over recent years.

That relationship came under scrutiny Thursday after the Monetary Authority of Singapore opened up to more currency strength by raising the trading band of the Singapore dollar, initially boosting the currency to a record high against the greenback and dragging other Asian currencies higher with it. Tellingly though, the immediate reaction from Singapore's closest neighbor, Malaysia, was to intervene in the market to stem the rise of its currency--the ringgit--indicating that there is still lot of resistance to allow local currency gains.

Recycling quickly kicked in, and the U.S. dollar plunged, sinking fast against the euro, the Australian dollar, and other major currencies.

Valentin Marinov, a strategist at Citigroup in London, remains of the opinion that emerging-market currencies will be allowed to rise only gradually, maintaining that pressure on the dollar.

'This set-up could be particularly damaging for the dollar against its liquid alternatives in the G-10 world,' he said. 'We think this should continue to generate sufficient upside momentum for the euro and Australian dollar against the greenback,' he added.

Over the past few months, there have been waves of interventions by the central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia to arrest the rises of their respective currencies. By keeping their currencies from rising too fast, the central banks want to make sure their exports don't lose competitiveness.

'There is no monetary coordination in Asia, with most policymakers running mercantilist-type policies that favor their own exports via undervalued exchange rates,' Win Thin, New York-based strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman said.

Singapore has been 'more open to currency appreciation in [a] controlled way' than some regional competitors, said Ken Dickson, investment director at Standard Life Investments in Edinburgh, which manages GBP143 billion in assets worldwide.

To some extent, China too has been allowing its currency to rise very gradually as it tries to rein in inflation.

The amount of currency reserves held by Asian central banks has continued to mount, suggesting that the wider market impact of any region-wide change in policy could be huge, even if only a fraction of these reserves are moved in or out of dollars.

At the end of March, China's foreign exchange reserves surged to a record, topping $3 trillion. In Singapore, reserves have been climbing steadily since November, to reach just over $233 billion in March. That indicates that the central banks have been carrying out smoothing operations to keep their currencies within the required trading bands. Data for April will be eagerly awaited for signs that the pace of gains has moderated.

Singapore's move last week means it will be able to trim these smoothing operations, said Dickson at Standard Life.

But as other regional central banks are still loathe to let their currencies rise, the impact of Singapore's action on the U.S. dollar looks set to be drowned out. -By Siva Sithraputhran, Dow Jones Newswires; 44-20-7842-9462; siva.sithraputhran@dowjones.com.

title: UPDATE: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  As US, France Press China On Yuan
text:
-- South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand intervene to curb gains in their currencies

-- China sets yuan at a record-high against the dollar

-- U.S and France press China to let yuan rise

(Adds Thailand's intervention in the lead and paragraph 11, Korea intervention size in paragraph 4, comments by Korea finance ministry official in paragraphs 5-6, updates forex quotes.)


 
   By Arran Scott and Jieun Shin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand were seen intervening to slow the rise of their currencies Thursday, as China set the yuan at a record-high while the U.S. and France called for more exchange-rate flexibility--code for wanting Beijing to let its currency rise faster.

The developments highlighted both the reservations in Asian nations about the speed of their currencies' rise and the urgency felt in the U.S. and Europe, where governments argue a stronger yuan is essential to reducing trade imbalances that threaten global economic stability.

Asia's large trade surpluses, a major source of economic growth for the region, has put strong pressure on the local currencies to rise, which authorities have resisted by selling their currencies in foreign-exchange markets. The trade surplus of China, now the world's second-biggest economy, has soared while the U.S. has run a persistent deficit, an imbalance Washington blames in part on an artificially weak Chinese currency.

The Bank of Korea apparently bought $1 billion for won, Seoul-based traders said, citing dollar purchases near KRW1,100 in early trading and additional buy orders at KRW1,095 in the afternoon. It was the first time since March 25 that the BOK was seen intervening.

Korea's Finance Ministry, which sets the country's foreign exchange policy, is closely watching the won and will counter any one-sided moves but isn't targeting a particular level, said Kim Ik-joo, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

"Capital is flowing into the local financial system with foreigners buying a lot of local shares as they focus more on positive factors. We are closely monitoring the currency market to make sure there aren't any rapid one-sided moves," Kim said.

The dollar ended trading at KRW1,096.7, down from KRW1,104.20 late Wednesday.

Bank Negara Malaysia, similarly, sold ringgit to slow its rise, two Kuala Lumpur dealers said, spotting dollar purchases by the central bank at MYR3.0250. The U.S. currency was at MYR3.0250 in late Asian trade, down from MYR3.0255 late Wednesday.

In Singapore, some traders said there was speculation that the central bank had been in the market, but intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore couldn't immediately be confirmed.

Dealers said banks known to be MAS agents bought U.S. dollars around S$1.2617 in the morning. But the Singapore dollar faced strong upward pressure throughout the trading session, with the U.S. currency falling to a record low of S$1.2592 late in the afternoon, down from S$1.2622 late Wednesday.

Thailand's central bank was suspected of buying $100 million to $200 million around THB30.24-THB30.27, traders said. The U.S. currency was last at THB30.25.

A record-high fixing for the yuan in the morning set a bullish tone for Asian currencies. The People's Bank of China set its dollar parity at CNY6.5564, the lowest ever and down from Wednesday's fixing of CNY6.5586.

The yuan, which ended trading at CNY6.5485 to the dollar in the onshore spot market, has risen 4.2% against since June, when China effectively ended its two-year currency peg and vowed to make the yuan more flexible. Other Asian central banks watch Beijing closely, and to varying degrees have also allowed their currencies to rise against the dollar.

China appeared to be under renewed pressure Thursday to move faster on the currency front at an informal meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of 20 industrial and developing nations held in the former Chinese capital of Nanjing.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, in prepared remarks at the meeting, argued forcefully for flexible exchange rates, calling the mismatch between fixed and floating exchange rates "the most important problem to solve in the international monetary system today."

"This asymmetry in exchange rate policies creates a lot of tension," Geithner said. "It magnifies upward pressure on those emerging market exchange rates that are allowed to move and where capital accounts are much more open. It intensifies inflation risk in those emerging economies with undervalued exchange rates. And, finally, it generates protectionist pressures."

Geithner didn't mention the yuan in his prepared remarks, but there is little doubt his message was aimed at least in part at China.

French President Nicolas Sarkozy said the global currency system in its current form has fueled growing global imbalances. The world needs to move toward a more flexible exchange rate regime, he said.

China Vice Premier Wang Qishan said Beijing will work with others toward "a more equitable global monetary system" but avoided any reference to the yuan's exchange rate.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Surges Against Yen As Japan MOF  Intervenes
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)-- The U.S. dollar and euro surged against the yen Friday after the Group of Seven finance ministers agreed to joint intervention to weaken the yen, as Japan struggles with multiple natural disasters and an ongoing nuclear emergency.

The dollar spiked as high as Y81.84 from around Y79.50 earlier, as G-7 finance ministers issued a communique following a conference call. The dollar was recently at Y81.64.

Traders said the united stand added "clout" to the announcement. It marked the first joint G-7 intervention since 2000.

"We express our solidarity with the Japanese people in these difficult times, our readiness to provide any needed cooperation and our confidence in the resilience of the Japanese economy and financial sector," the communique said. "We will monitor exchange markets closely and will cooperate as appropriate."

Japan's finance minister told reporters that market intervention that occurred from 0000 GMT was from authorities in Japan, and each G-7 country would intervene in their own market.

"At a time when Japan is in a difficult situation, it is extremely significant that G-7 authorities agreed to act in concert and cooperate for the stability of the markets," Yoshihiko Noda said.

Dealers said the U.S. dollar was likely to continue rising against the yen over the next 24 hours as central banks take their turn at providing support.

"It looks like central banks will intervene as their markets open, which means round the clock intervention and support. We'll probably see dollar/yen two or three big figures higher over the next 24 hours," said Richard Grace, head of currency strategy at the Commonwealth Bank.

Westpac Global Markets strategists Sean Callow and Robert Rennie said that with the Bank of Japan flooding markets with liquidity in recent days, "this yen intervention is likely to be successful."

The G-7 action was more about preventing a one-sided speculative market than the actual level of the yen, they added. "The G-7 does not like one-sided speculative markets."

The euro also surged against both the yen and the greenback on the G-7 announcement on expectations the European Central Bank will do its part to keep the Japanese currency low. There has been no indication from the central bank yet that it has intervened.

"If the ECB is ever to step into the market, that will be during European trading hours, not Asian," one dealer said.

After the G-7 announcement the euro climbed to as high as $1.4087 from $1.4020 in late New York trade and to Y115.27 from Y110.62.

The euro's and dollar's rallies came against a backdrop of escalating tensions in the Middle East with the United Nations earlier sanctioning a no-fly zone over Libya, setting the stage for a potential vote on a military move within a few hours.

The Pentagon was already fine-tuning military options for "serious" strikes against ground and air targets should the White House order them, U.S. defense officials said.

OCBC strategists say the current environment may remain inhospitable for excessively strong risk appetite because oil prices remain elevated.

"However, some improvement in investor sentiment may be expected near term if investors perceive the latest G-7 solidarity to extending beyond just the FX front, especially in terms of stabilizing markets and providing liquidity as needed," OCBC said.

Nymex crude oil futures were recently $1.83 higher at $103.25 a barrel on Globex.

title: DJ Asian Shares Rise, Yen Falls As G-7 Agrees To  Intervene
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Japan led Asian stock markets higher Friday, as the Group of Seven industrialized nations agreed to a coordinated intervention to staunch the yen's recent surge, providing some relief to Tokyo as the nation grapples with last week's crippling earthquake and an ongoing nuclear crisis.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average rose 2.5%, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 advanced 0.8%, South Korea's Kospi Composite was up 0.6% and New Zealand's NZX-50 tacked on 0.7%.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 63 points in screen trade.

Tokyo stocks rallied on the G-7 news, on relief that Japan's key exporting companies won't be hobbled by a rising yen as the nation struggles to cope with last week's devastating earthquake and tsunami.

The yen pulled back sharply against the U.S. dollar after the G-7 statement and as Japan's Ministry of Finance intervened in foreign exchange markets. Japanese finance minister Yoshihiko Noda said each central bank would intervene in its own timezones.

'In response to recent movements in the exchange rate of the yen associated with the tragic events in Japan, and at the request of the Japanese authorities, the authorities of the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and the European Central Bank will join with Japan, on March 18, in concerted intervention in exchange markets,' the G-7 statement said.

This was the first agreement on joint intervention since September 2000.

Ahead of the outcome, traders have been anticipating some form of joint action after the dollar slumped to a new all-time low of Y76.25 early on Thursday.

'What G-7 is telling us is that they will simply not tolerate a rapid strengthening in the yen,' said Sean Callow, strategist at Westpac bank. 'Now in our view, the actual cost of the yen surge will not be significant. We estimate an economic loss of 3% of gross domestic product to Japan's economy from the earthquake and tsunami, but the impact of the subsequent yen rise should be much smaller,' he said.

'This is more about preventing a one-sided speculative market than it is about the actual level of the yen in our view. And G-7 does not like one-sided speculative markets,' Callow added.

The dollar surged to Y81.11, from Y78.93 late Thursday in New York, and the euro was buying Y113.61, from Y110.58, and $1.3992 against the dollar, from $1.4020.

The yen could lose more ground on the coordinated intervention effort, said Richard Grace, chief currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. 'It looks like central banks will intervene as their market opens, which means round the clock intervention and support,' he said. 'We'll probably see dollar/yen two or three big figures higher over the next 24 hours.'

Japanese exporters such as Honda Motor, Toyota Motor, Sony and Canon were up 2.2%-4.2%.

Buying was spread across the market, with economically-sensitive stocks such as Asahi Glass and Fast Retailing also advancing 2.4% and 6.0% respectively.

Some traders were circumspect about the Tokyo market's rise, noting that the coordinated G-7 action had been anticipated and Japanese officials still have a massive recovery and rebuilding task on hand.

'The problems at the nuclear plant are far from over, and we have a three-day weekend ahead, so it's hard to keep buying on the weaker yen alone,' said Yumi Nishimura, deputy general manager at Daiwa Securities Capital Markets.

Japanese authorities claimed modest gains Thursday in their efforts to tame a heavily damaged nuclear-power plant that has caused worries around the world.

Markets in Australia, Korea and New Zealand were also buoyed by G-7 news.

In Sydney, energy stocks were stronger, aided by the rise in crude oil futures after the U.N. endorsed a no-fly zone in Libya and set the stage for a potential vote on a military move within a few hours.

April Nymex crude oil futures were up $1.39 at $102.81 per barrel on Globex.

Woodside Petroleum, Santos and Oil Search were up 1.8%-3.0%. In Seoul, shipbuilders led gains on hopes for more orders with Hyundai Heavy Industries up 0.7% and Samsung Heavy Industries up 1.3%.

Lead June Japanese government bond futures were down 0.13 at 139.57 points, weighed by the Nikkei's rise and the yen's sharp fall. The yield on the 10-year cash JGB was down two basis points at 1.22%

Spot gold was at $1,407.20 per troy ounce, up $3.20 from its New York settlement Thursday.

title: CORRECT: Asian  Currencies  Hit Multi-Year Highs As Risk Appetite Revives
text:
("Asian Currencies Hit Multi-Year Highs As Risk Appetite Revives," at 0507 GMT, misstated the time in the 11th paragraph. The correct version follows:)


 
   By Arran Scott 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Several Asian currencies hit multi-year highs against the dollar Tuesday as revived risk appetite encouraged investors to plough money back into the region.

A rally in regional share prices, triggered in part by strength on Wall Street overnight and a decline in crude oil prices, set a bullish tone in Asia. Investors appear to be buying into the notion Asian central banks will use a combination of stronger currencies and higher interest rates this year to temper inflation.

The Malaysian ringgit and Taiwan dollar rose to their highest levels since October 1997, when the Asian financial crisis sent those and other regional currencies into a tailspin. The South Korean won, which has lagged in the broad Asian currency appreciation last year, struck levels not seen since the Lehman Brothers collapse in September 2008 clobbered Asian currencies.

The Indonesia rupiah added to gains it has made since Friday, when the country's central bank raised interest rates and signaled it would use a stronger local currency to rein in inflation that has surged above its target band. The rupiah had been hurt by concerns that Jakarta was falling behind the curve in containing inflation, but has now nearly recovered the losses it had logged since mid-November when such worries began to escalate.

Inflation has been picking up in Asia, fueled by fast economic growth, loose monetary policies and soaring prices of food and commodities on global markets. Central banks across the region have increased interest rates and taken steps to soak up liquidity that has gushed into the region as investors hunted for higher returns that were available in low interest-rate environments in the U.S. and Europe.

"The final tool in the armory of the region's authorities is FX appreciation," Fiona Lake, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a research note. "Korea, Indonesia and Taiwan have shown greater desire for currency appreciation to help tackle inflation."

The won has some catching up to do with Asia's strongest currencies of the past year: the Singapore dollar, the Malaysian ringgit and the Thai baht. The Bank of Korea has also turned more hawkish in its comments on tackling rising inflation. Economists at Nomura expect the BOK to deliver its first back-to-back 25 basis-point hike at its next meeting Friday, followed by 25 basis points of moves in April and June, lifting the official rate to 3.50% by the end of the year.

What's more, the U.S. has put the won on its list of currencies for which "there is room for a greater degree of exchange-rate stability and less intervention."

The Treasury Department, in its annual foreign exchange report Friday, cited International Monetary Fund calculations that the won is 5%-20% undervalued. The U.S. likely has more leverage with Korea than with China on currency matters. Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac, points out that Congress hasn't ratified the U.S.-South Korea free trade agreement signed by Presidents Barack Obama and Lee Myung-bak in December.

The dollar fell to KRW1,102.50 from KRW1,107.50 late Monday. It was last at KRW1,104.20.

Against the Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was at NT$28.9180 at 0500 GMT, after earlier touching NT$28.900, its lowest intraday level since October 1997, on foreign capital flows into Taipei stocks on the first trading day after the Lunar New Year holidays. A trader said the market is on the lookout for the Taiwan central bank, which is thought to intervene regularly near the close of trading to smooth out moves in the currency.

Against the rupiah, the dollar was around IDR8,910, back near the IDR8,890 level at which it traded in mid-November, before concerns over inflation started to permeate the market.

The dollar carved out a fresh 13-year low against the ringgit, last trading at MYR3.0330. That was down from MYR3.0360 late Monday, when traders said the Malaysian central bank intervened in the market to temper the local currency's rise. Dealers were on the alert for the possibility of further intervention Tuesday to curb the ringgit.

Against the Singapore dollar, which has recently logged record highs, the U.S. currency was at SGD1.2734, down from SGD1.2746 late Monday as risk appetite gathers momentum, especially for regional currencies, said a trader with a foreign bank. "Flows are coming back into Asia mainly because investors are betting on the strong (economic) fundamentals in the region," he said.

The baht and Philippine peso were also higher Tuesday, helped by the broader rally in Asian currencies.

-By Arran Scott, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4042; arran.scott@dowjones.com

-Mark Cranfield in Singapore, I Made Sentana in Jakarta, Ankur Relia in Kuala Lumpur, P.R. Venkat in Singapore, and Fanny Liu in Taipei contributed to this article. [ 08-02-11 0616GMT ]

title: =DJ Asian Central Banks  Intervene  As  Currencies  Rise; Yuan At Record High
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand intervened in foreign-exchange markets Thursday as Asian currencies surged against the dollar on optimism about the region's economic outlook, underscored by data showing the Chinese industrial sector expanded strongly in December.

Taiwan, meanwhile, unveiled measures to buttress its banking system against rapid movements in foreign capital, the latest Asian country to introduce stricter regulations to control the risks posed by so-called "hot money" flows.

The currency moves were exagerated by thin trading conditions with many investors away for year-end holidays. But traders said an upward trend for most Asian currencies appears set to continue, with China's decision to guide the yuan to a modern record high against the dollar cementing the bullish sentiment.

"People are making a bet that growth in emerging markets will still be on an uptrend and that currencies will continue with their appreciation," said Lum Choong Kuan, head of fixed income research at CIMB Group in Kuala Lumpur. "With the debt crisis in Europe and with the U.S. still showing protracted slow growth, investors will have no other place to put their money but here."

Capital has been flooding into Asia this year, helping to finance investments in one of the world's fastest-growing regions. But the influx of foreign money has raised concerns in Asian capitals about the perils of fast-moving capital flows, given the damage the region's economies suffered during the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s, when a previous boom ended suddenly and foreigners rushed for the exits.

Fresh data Thursday from China, the powerhouse of the Asian economy, showed manufacturing growth eased slightly in December but was still at relatively high levels. The HSBC China Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index, a gauge of nationwide manufacturing activity, fell to 54.4 in December from 55.3 in November; any reading above 50 indicates expansion.

Hongbin Qu, HSBC's chief economist for China, said that despite the moderation in the PMI inflation remains Beijing's top policy concern, rather than economic growth.

He expects China to take further tightening measures to curb inflation--which hit 5.1% in November--including additional modest interest rate hikes. China's central bank raised interest rates Dec. 25, its second hike in less than three months.

CIMB's Lum said central banks in emerging markets are looking at tightening monetary policy next year, which means interest-rate differentials between emerging markets and the developed economies of the U.S., Europe and Japan should grow wider. That leaves Asian central banks looking for ways to control inflows of capital chasing higher returns.

In Kuala Lumpur, traders said Malaysia's central bank was suspected of buying dollars to curb a rise in the ringgit, which hit a three-month high Thursday. Bank Negara Malaysia may have bought dollars around MYR3.0810-MYR3.0820, dealers said. The dollar was last at MYR3.0846.

Traders in Seoul said they suspected the Bank of Korea entered the market, buying more than $500 million at intervals around KRW1,135, KRW1,136, and KRW1,140. The dollar closed at KRW1,134.80, bringing the won's gains to 2.6% for the year.

In Bangkok, the dollar was last at THB30.15--down from THB30.16 late Wednesday--with suspected buying by the central bank around that level to limit the downside, two dealers said.

"I don't think the dollar/baht will move much on the final trading day of this year, especially with the central bank supporting the pair," one Bangkok-based dealer said.

In Taipei, which has been trying to temper gains in the New Taiwan dollar--a favorite among investors seeking exposure to China, given Taiwan's increasingly close economic ties to the mainland--the Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) announced new measures to control capital flows.

Starting Saturday, local banks will have to set aside 90.00% of foreign investors' new deposits as reserves, a quantum leap from the current level of 9.775%.

The central bank also raised its benchmark interest rate by 12.5 basis points, the third hike this year as it seeks to normalize lending costs and cool a sizzling property market. Central bank Governor Perng Fai-nan said inflation will likely accelerate next year.

Also Thursday, Taiwan's financial regulator also said it will inspect banks' use of foreign funds to determine whether there has been speculative trading in the local currency. Earlier Thursday, the Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) said it had found "unusual" trading strategies at a small number of banks.

"Over the past few days, a small number of authorized foreign-exchange banks have targeted specific times of the day to sell off large quantities of foreign exchange," the central bank said in a statement.

"Our inquiry has revealed that the funding for these transactions originates exclusively from the inward remittance made by certain foreign investors," the bank said, adding that it "asked the authorities concerned to probe into the final beneficiaries behind these foreign investors."

The central bank didn't name the banks in question or give details on the timing of the trades.

It's not unusual for Asian central banks to intervene in foreign exchange markets when volatility in their currencies rises. Many have taken regulatory steps in recent months to try to slow capital inflows and make their banking systems more resilient to movements in foreign funds.

On Wednesday, Indonesia's central bank said it would increase the amount of reserves commercial banks must hold at the central bank against foreign currency deposits, among others steps. Also Wednesday, South Korea said it would announce lower ceilings on banks' foreign-exchange forward positions in January.

For many countries, the main consideration has been to make sure their currencies don't rise so much that they hurt export industries. Still, stronger currencies would reduce the cost of imports, tempering inflationary pressures that are on the rise regionally on surging commodities prices. For that reason, many economists expect authorities to permit their currencies to rise further.

An official at the People's Bank of China Thursday echoed that sentiment, saying that a small, gradual appreciation in the yuan presents more benefits to the Chinese economy than costs.

In an article in the Financial News, Sheng Songcheng, director of the PBOC's Statistics and Analysis Department, said the yuan's rise against the dollar since the exchange rate was made more flexible has had only a small impact on employment and growth. At the same time, Sheng wrote, the yuan's gradual rise has cut import costs, reduced inflationary pressures and prompted Chinese companies to become more competitive.

The yuan has appreciated 3.4% since June 19, when China pledged to increase the currency's trading flexibility, effectively ending a two-year-long peg to the dollar.

The State Council, or China's Cabinet, has the final say on major policies such as yuan reform. But Sheng's article, which featured prominently in the central bank-run newspaper, may reflect growing confidence that Beijing can allow the yuan to rise further without severe consequences.

The dollar fell to a record low against the yuan Thursday after the PBOC, which tightly controls the currency, set the dollar/yuan parity rate at an all-time low of 6.6229, down from Wednesday's rate of 6.6247. It marked the eighth straight session that the central bank has set the parity rate lower.

In the over-the-counter market, the dollar was at CNY6.6008 around 0830 GMT, down from Wednesday's close of CNY6.6212. The dollar traded Thursday between CNY6.6000--the lowest intraday level since the yuan began regularly trading in 1994--and CNY6.6232.

The impact of yuan demand from bank customers was exaggerated by the thin year-end trading, one Shanghai-based trader at a local bank said.

"The market is rather one-sided right now," he said. "The yuan's gain today is definitely bigger than what people had anticipated."

Elsewhere, the U.S. currency also fell against its major rivals, as U.S. Treasury bond yields fell overnight following strong demand at a seven-year auction, again exaggerated by a thin market. The dollar slipped to a seven-week low of Y81.28 and a fresh all-time low of CHF0.9418.

The dollar also was weaker against its Australian and New Zealand counterparts: The Australian dollar surged to a fresh post-float high of $1.0197, and the Kiwi dollar rose to a high of $0.7691.

Many participants "dumped quite a few (U.S.) dollars," said Satoshi Tate, senior vice president of the forex division at Mizuho Corporate Bank.

text:

27 Oct 2010 00:00 EDT *DJ  MAS: Singapore 2010 GDP On Track To Grow 13%-15%

27 Oct 2010 00:00 EDT *DJ  Singapore MAS: Risk of Developed Econs Slipping Into Recession Receded

27 Oct 2010 00:00 EDT DJ  MAS: May Intervene To Curb Singapore Dollar; Asia Faces Capital-Inflow Risk

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank said Wednesday it may intervene to curb rises in the local dollar as Asia faces risks from a surge of capital flowing into the region.

But the Monetary Authority of Singapore, in its annual macroeconomic review, said that it sterilizes its currency interventions to keep the city-state's monetary base stable and that its interventions have little impact on local banks' current accounts.

"Singapore has seen strong capital inflows since the second half of 2009 amidst broad-based weakness of the U.S. dollar and the relatively positive outlook for the Singapore economy," the MAS said. "In such instances, MAS may intervene in the foreign exchange markets to dampen upward pressures on the Singapore dollar."

It is rare for the MAS to discuss its currency interventions. People familiar with the matter told Dow Jones Newswires twice last month that the central bank had sold Singapore dollars to slow the currency's rise.

The MAS said in its review that its decision this month to tighten monetary policy was based on the assessment that economic activity would remain high and Singapore's economy would keep expanding, though at a slower and more sustainable pace. At the same time, domestic cost pressures have been rising and strong income growth has placed pressure on the prices of some consumption items, it said.

The MAS surprised financial markets Oct. 14 by announcing it would guide the trade-weighted Singapore dollar upward at a slightly faster pace and let it rise a bit further from its targeted midpoint.

The central bank uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates as its key policy tool because trade flows dwarf the island's tiny domestic economy.

The MAS said it tightened because of rising cost pressures. Data released Monday showed that consumer prices rose 3.7% on year in September, the fastest pace in 20 months.

In its review the central bank forecast CPI inflation will rise close to 4% by the year end and stay high in the first half of 2011 before moderating. Full-year inflation will average between 2.5%-3% in 2010 and 2%-3% next year, the report said.

The MAS said the economy is "on track" to grow by 13%-15% in 2010. The estimate matches that of the government.

The government said Oct. 14 the economy contracted 19.8% in annualized, seasonally adjusted terms in the third quarter after rocketing 27.3% in the second and a record 45.9% in the first. A stronger-than-expected 26.2% growth in manufacturing output reported Tuesday, however, may lead to an upward revision of third-quarter growth numbers, economists said.

Singapore could slip into a technical recession, or two quarters of on-quarter contraction, in the second half of 2010, Senior Minister of State in the Ministry of Trade and Industry and Ministry of Education S. Iswaran said in Parliament Oct. 18.

"These short-term adjustments are not indicative of an imminent relapse into broad-based weakness in the economy and the level of economic activity is expected to remain high in the quarters ahead," the MAS report said.

On the global economy, the MAS said recovery has lost momentum in recent months and the outlook for Singapore's key trading partners will remain uneven.

"After a strong start in the first half of 2010, the global recovery has lost momentum in recent months, partly due to the scaling back of government stimulus packages and the fading of inventory restocking effects," it said. "Thus, while the risk of the developed economies slipping back into recession has generally receded, final demand is likely to remain sluggish.

Growth in Asia, which exited the recession earlier, appears to have peaked in the first quarter and has slowed to a more sustainable rate, the MAS said. The pace of growth in trade-dependant economies such as Korea and Taiwan was unsustainable as it came from inventory replenishment arising from a robust demand for information technology products.

In comparison, growth has been more stable in the domestic-oriented economies of China, India and Indonesia, underpinned by continued strength in consumption and investment spending, the report said.

title: SE Asia Stocks-Up on commodity-led buying; KL sets 33-month high
text:
* S'pore posts biggest gain in 4 mths; Thai index near 1,000

* Philippines, Indonesia claw back to near records

* Palm oil, energy shares lead regional gains

By Viparat Jantraprap

BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian stock markets gained on Wednesday amid expectations of fresh U.S. economic stimulus, with rising crude oil prices swelling demand for heavily weighted commodity shares across the region.

Share markets recouped recent losses as growing risk appetite lured more inflows into equities, although that pushed up their currencies, which made investors wary about possible intervention moves by the authorities.

Singapore's Straits Times Index <.FTSTI> rose 1.7 percent, its biggest one-day rise in almost four months, Malaysia <.KLSE> gained 0.7 percent, setting a 33-month high, and Indonesia <.JKSE> jumped 1.8 percent, moving near a record hit last week.

Thailand <.SETI> climbed 1.6 percent, approaching the 1,000 mark last seen before the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, while the Philippines <.PSI> ended up 0.7 percent. Vietnam <.VNI> rose 0.7 percent.

Asian and European shares in general rose on increasing expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will ease policy to support the economy and following a positive fourth-quarter forecast from computer chipmaker Intel.

The dollar remained weak after details of the last meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve suggested the central bank was closer to injecting fresh stimulus into the ailing economy. [ID:nN12191658]

By 0938 GMT, the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index <.MIAPJ0000PUS> was up 1.2 percent, led by a 2.3 percent gain in MSCI's India index <.MIIN00000PIN> and a 2.04 percent rise in Singapore <.MISG00000PSG>.

In Singapore, the local index hovered around 28-month highs, led by palm oil companies, with Golden Agri-Resources jumping 9.2 percent and Indofood Agri Resources climbing 7.9 percent amid firm palm oil prices.

Malaysia's IOI Corp rose 2.5 percent while Indonesia's Astra Agro Lestari gained 3.2 percent and Thailand's top energy firm, PTT , rose over 1 percent.

In Thailand, the imposition of a 15 percent withholding tax on interest payments and capital gains earned by foreign investors on Thai bonds did little to affect stock market sentiment, dealers said. [ID:nSGE69B0A6]

Bangkok-based Sukit Udomsirikul, a strategist at broker SCB Securities, said the measures had no significant impact on stocks or bond markets. But he said investors were still cautious over further possible measures to deal with the rising baht.

"The policy interest rate may be maintained at an upcoming meeting on Oct. 20 to help ease inflow pressure as the baht tends to appreciate further," he added. (Editing by Alan Raybould)

title: =DJ  FX  ASIA: Region's  Currencies  To Pull Back 4Q On  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Most Asian currencies will pull back this quarter as central banks step up their foreign-exchange intervention, helping the dollar pause in its steep slide, analysts predict.

After sharp rallies across the Asia region last month, only the Chinese yuan and the South Korean won will keep rising through December--although at a slower pace--according to a Dow Jones Newswires poll of 10 foreign-exchange strategists.

The dollar fell against the 10 main regional currencies in September to long-term or, in the case of Singapore, record lows. This prompted the region's central banks to be more aggressive in selling their currencies against the greenback, especially after Japan returned to the currency markets for the first time in more than six years.

With Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega proclaiming that an "international currency war" has begun and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn warning that large-scale intervention is a growing concern, the aggressive central bank moves are expected to give the swooning dollar a temporary respite.

The Dow Jones poll forecasts on average that the dollar will fall just 0.6% against the yuan this quarter, slowing from the 1.7% decline of last month when Beijing accelerated its currency's rise. Against the won, the dollar is tipped to fall 1.6%, adding to September's 4.9% swoon.

But against the rest of the region's currencies, the greenback is expected to get a lift this quarter.

In the most dramatic turnaround, the dollar is forecast to make its biggest bounce, 2.0%, against the Indonesian rupiah, against which it logged the biggest September drop, at 5.3%. Asia's other best performers this year, the Malaysian ringgit and the Thai baht, are also expected to correct in the fourth quarter as their economies slow after surprisingly strong rebounds in the first half.

Aside from the yuan, which was essentially pegged to the dollar for two years until June, most Asian currencies weakened significantly during the 2008-2009 financial crisis as investors fled risky assets. They have risen sharply as the global economy recovered, but the region's policymakers now want to curb the rises in their currencies to protect export-reliant growth as the global economy slows.

"In recent weeks, some Southeast Asia authorities appear to have become more concerned about local-currency appreciation, given the sharp rally in regional real effective exchange rates," analysts at Standard Chartered said, noting that stronger intervention in the area is a rising possibility.

All the strategists polled expect the yuan to keep strengthening through year end, with several cutting their dollar/yuan forecasts after last month's faster move.

China is under increasing political pressure from the U.S., with President Barack Obama joining the call for a stronger yuan and the House of Representatives this week passing a bill to penalize China for allegedly keeping its currency undervalued. This should compel Beijing to keep the yuan on a rising trend into next year, the strategists say.

By contrast, the won--one of the worst Asian performers this year and among the few regional currencies that haven't recovered to pre-2008 levels--has recently been playing catch-up. The Bank of Korea intervenes regularly, local traders say, but it still has more leeway to allow appreciation than some of its fellow central banks around Asia.

title: MARKET TALK:USD/KRW Sustains Marginal Fall; 1,139-1,143 Tipped
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; 
MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0541 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/KRW sustains marginal losses in afternoon trade at 1,141.0 vs 1,142.0 late yesterday on persistent exporter USD selling. But pair little moved from morning levels amid lack of momentum to push pair further down, while euro weakens in Asian trade, failing to give local unit extra boost, traders say. "There's quite a lot of dollar selling from exporters, but given the likelihood of authorities' intervening (to buy dollars) at levels below KRW1,140, the pair will likely hover around current levels for rest of the session," says local bank trader. Tips pair in 1,139-1,143 range. (min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com)

0535 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesia shares by midday +0.3% at 3055.011 in light volume, off earlier low of 3489.812, led by buying in select resources, automotive stocks on hopes for strong 3Q earnings, traders say; tip resistance at 3520. "I think the main index is set to close at another fresh record high in a generally cautious trend," says fund manager at state-owned pension fund. Among gainers: tin miner Timah (TINS.JK) +5.3% at IDR3,000, gold, nickel miner Antam (ANTM.JK) +3.3% at IDR2,350. Profit-taking hits toll road builder, operator Jasa Marga (JSMR.JK), down 3.0% at IDR3,200. (edhi.pranasidhi@dowjones.com)

0510 GMT [Dow Jones] Kospi turns lower, down 0.2% at 1862.91 as investors taking breather before 3Q earnings season; "foreigners are buying KRW220 billion worth of domestic stocks and it's keeping the main index from falling further," says Lee Kyoung-min at Woori Investment & Securities. Says if major companies come up with strong 3Q results next month, Kospi may get hefty boost to test 1900 level; 1855-1870 band tipped for today. Stocks helping to limit Kospi's fall include technology, shipbuilding, transport shares. Samsung Electronics (005930.SE) +0.7% at KRW777,000, Hynix Semiconductor (000660.SE) +1.1% at KRW22,100, Hyundai Mipo Dockyard (010620.SE) +1.9% at KRW188,500, Korean Air Lines (003490.SE) +1.8% at KRW77,400. Some shares falling after recent gains: Hyundai Engineering & Construction (000720.SE) down 2.5% at KRW71,800, SK Energy (096770.SE) off 2.3% at KRW148,500, LG Chem (051910.SE) down 1.7% at KRW327,000. (kyong-ae.choi@dowjones.com)

0502 GMT [Dow Jones] China likely to continue using targeted measures such as Wednesday's property curbs to rein in excesses in certain parts of the economy, rather than turning to broad-based tightening such as interest rate hikes; Wednesday's measures only the latest example of this strong policy preference. Consumer prices rose 3.5% in August, but mostly on one-off factors such as higher food prices, and economists almost universally expect inflation to ease in coming months. Inflation rates were also much higher during last round of interest rate hikes, over 6% in 2H 2007 and as high as 8.7% in February of 2008. See: =MONEY TALKS: China To Focus On Property, Not Broad Tightening. (aaron.back@dowjones.com)

0501 GMT [Dow Jones] Nikkei 225 December futures down 1.3% at 9440, extending morning losses on concerns about firmer yen (USD/JPY at 83.52 and EUR/JPY at 113.59). "In addition to the stronger yen, the decline in banking shares to fresh year-to-date lows is souring overall sentiment," says Hideki Horikawa, chief analyst at Himawari Securities. MUFG (8306.TO) down 4.0% at Y388 and SMFG (8316.TO) off 3.9% at Y2,432; both hit fresh 2010 lows on concerns over consumer lender affiliates and renewed European debt worries. Puts successive futures index near-term support levels at 9400, then 9200. (kana.inagaki@dowjones.com)

0447 GMT [Dow Jones] KLCI +0.2% at 1,464.08 midday in range-bound morning session as investors grope for leads from global markets amid dearth of local cues; index caught in tight 6 point range through morning session; Dealer says markets likely to continue to consolidate through rest of session; tips 1,460-1,467 range for rest of session. Immediate resistance at recent high of 1,479.59, with support at Friday low of 1,445.33. Market breadth negative with 348 decliners vs 253 advancers. Advancers led by property, construction stocks with Kimlun Corp. (5171.KU) +1.9% at MYR1.09 on MYR70 million contract win from Malaysian Resources (1651.KU), which +1.4% at MYR2.19; MMC Corp. (2194.KU) +2.0% at MYR3.00. Decliners led by Unisem (5005.KU) down 2.0% at MYR1.98, IOI Corp. (1961.KU) down 1.1% at MYR5.49. (ankur.relia@dowjones.com)

0442 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/JPY briefly falls below 83.50, lowest level since Sept. 15, when Japan's government intervened in foreign-exchange market, amid persistent speculation Fed likely to ease monetary policy further soon, says Yuzo Sakai, senior dealer at Tokyo Forex & Ueda Harlow; adds, selling by Japan's exporters also pushing pair lower. But notes "if the dollar extends falls against the yen, expectations could grow that the government will step into the currency market again to sell the yen, which could discourage investors from actively buying" JPY. Tips support at 83.20 for now; last 83.51 vs session high of 83.81. (tomoyuki.tachikawa@dowjones.com)

0441 GMT [Dow Jones] Action in Singapore stock market notably subdued as investors generally staying on sidelines after digesting solid gains from past weeks. STI +0.3% at 3095.66 midday, but +5.3% since start of September, with support at last week's 3069 low. "The index won't come off too much because everyone knows this year is a good year for the Singapore economy," says dealer at foreign brokerage; "we have had a good month in September. It's time to take a break, have a Kit Kat, as it's the end of the month." Overall market volume light at 894.4 million shares worth S$1.24 billion, with good mix of large, small, mid caps among most active, including Genting Singapore (G13.SG), off 1.1% at S$1.88, Innovalues (591.SG), flat at S$0.17, Genting Hong Kong (S21.SG), off 2.3% at US$0.43, Transcu Group (E15.SG), flat at S$0.125, SingTel (Z74.SG), off 1.0% at S$3.14. (frankie.ho@dowjones.com)

0441 GMT [Dow Jones] Nikkei down 1.1% at 9450.77 after hitting new intraday low of 9436.59 in afternoon session. "It's futures-led selling; it's not like new selling factors are hitting the cash market," says Japanese brokerage manager, adding Europeans appear to be selling on slightly weaker USD/JPY (now 83.53 vs 83.80 earlier); December Nikkei futures off 1.2% at 9450, in line with cash market. Adds, Nikkei may be supported at 9400. All 33 Topix subindexes in negative territory, with heavily-weighted banks down 3.1% as a group; MUFG (8306.TO) down 2.5% at Y390 on concerns about rising credit default swap levels for consumer lender affiliate Acom (8572.TO). Nintendo (7974.OK) continues fall, now off 9.5% at Y20,820 after slashing FY forecast. Tokyo Electric Power (9501.TO) stabilizing somewhat, off 2.4% at Y2,055 (vs midday close of Y2,031) after announcing details of massive equity capital increase plan. (ayai.tomisawa@dowjones.com)

0440 GMT [Dow Jones] HK market's resilience, with HSI ending midday only down 0.3% at 22,316.98, despite ICBC (1398.HK) stake cut by Goldman Sachs, China's further property tightening, should be taken as sign of market's underlying strength. Market volume strong at HK$46.97 billion at interval, doesn't appear index would slide more; week's lowest of 22,109 likely won't troubled. ICBC down 3.2% at HK$5.78, China Overseas Land (0688.HK) tumbles 3.7% to HK$16.20, China Resources Land (1109.HK) off 4.5% at HK$15.76, but weakness in part offset by rally in Hutchison (0013.HK), big HK developers Cheung Kong (0001.HK), SHK Properties (0016.HK). Overall, given HSI's about 9% gain in September, "we believe the market will enter a period of consolidation over the next few trading sessions," says Celestial Securities. (robert.li@dowjones.com)

0429 GMT [Dow Jones] PREVIEW: Hong Kong August retail sales growth likely remained in double digits, but likely slowed vs July on fading base factor. By value, tipped +16.0% on-year in August vs July's +18.9%; by volume +13.2% in August vs July's +16.0%, according to Dow Jones poll of 5 economists. "Domestic demand remains buoyant with the fall in the jobless rate and tourist arrivals continue to be resilient, but the higher base of comparison last year also weighs on the headline figure," Core Pacific-Yamaichi analyst Keith Lo says. Bank of East Asia economist Paul Tang says retail sales growth likely fell to "high single digits" in 4Q due to higher base of comparison, as city's retail sales returned to growth since September last year. Data due 0830 GMT Monday. (chester.yung@dowjones.com)

0424 GMT [Dow Jones] While central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia were suspected of intervening in FX markets overnight, following confirmed moves by Japan earlier this month, don't expect Reserve Bank of Australia to do any such thing, say traders and strategists. With surging mining sector, robust banking system, inflation a very real concern, RBA is looking to cool the economy any way it can, with gains in AUD helping central bank. "If the Aussie dollar wasn't as high as it is, we could see more than one rate hike by the end of the year as it's doing some heavy lifting for the RBA. A high Aussie dollar curbs importers and inflation, creating a dampening affect that is exactly what the RBA wants," says JPMorgan Economist Helen Kevans. AUD/USD last at 0.9670 after hitting 26-month high around 0.9730 overnight. (geoffrey.rogow@dowjones.com) [ 09-30-10 0141ET ]

0651 GMT [Dow Jones] The euro zone is still bearing the weight of event risks Wednesday, with the cost of the Anglo Irish bailout and a Moody's downgrade of Spanish debt both expected this week. title: FX  ASIA: Malaysian Ringgit May Sail Past  Intervention  Threat
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The ringgit, Asia's best-performing currency so far this year, may rise further ahead of key milestones for Malaysia's economic reform plans -- as long as the country's central bank sticks to its policy of not curtailing currency strength.

The ringgit is up 11% against the U.S. dollar since January, the result of strong foreign inflows to an economy growing at an 8.9% annual pace in the second quarter.

Analysts say the ringgit may receive additional good news next month. The government is expected to present its 2011 annual budget on Oct. 15, including measures that top officials say will lower the deficit significantly from an estimated 5.6% of gross domestic product this year -- one of Asia's highest levels and a significant concern for investors.

Also in October, Petronas Petrochemicals Group Bhd., a unit of Malaysia's government-controlled oil and gas company Petronas, is slated to complete the country's largest initial public offering, surpassing last year's $3.6 billion IPO from Maxis Bhd (6012.KU).

That may be followed by more IPOs later this year, as Malaysia's government implements the New Economic Model it announced in April to boost economic growth.

This is a favorable environment for the ringgit, which on Wednesday hit MYR3.0800 to the dollar, its highest level since the 1997-98 Asian crisis. That followed news that index provider FTSE had re-classified Malaysia as an advanced emerging economy, opening the door for inflows of up to $2.4 billion from managers of indexed funds over the next year, Barclays Capital estimates.

BarCap last week raised its ringgit forecasts and now expects the dollar to trade at MYR2.92 in a year's time, versus a previous forecast of MYR3.05. Some analysts anticipate even faster gains, with the dollar possibly falling to MYR3.0 as early as December.

Standard Bank economist Patrick Bennett recently noted that Malaysia, whose main commodity exports are denominated in dollars, may refrain from intervening in forex markets to cap ringgit rallies. That would be a stark contrast to the concerted forex intervention in East Asian economies that export mainly manufactured products.

Bennett said this suggests the dollar could fall next year toward MYR2.80 -- a level unseen since the height of the Asian crisis.

"The government and central bank have been accommodating of ringgit gains and have no reason to turn back now," Bennett said.

Kuala Lumpur traders say Malaysia's central bank has likely intervened in recent weeks around MYR3.10. But recent data show any intervention has likely been in tiny amounts aimed at smoothing out currency trading, rather than putting a floor beneath the currency as Japan did earlier this month.

Recent data show that as of Sept. 15, Malaysian central bank reserves had risen just 0.7% since the end of August, to $95.9 billion. The small increase is likely explained by the higher valuation of Malaysia's euro-denominated reserves, given the euro's 2.6% rise against the dollar in the period, and implies that few if any dollars were purchased.

title: Asian Central Banks Keep Up  Intervention  As Dollar Weakens
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia were suspected of intervening in forex exchange markets Wednesday to contain gains in their currencies, but analysts say the continued weakness of the U.S. dollar means Asian units should extend their rallies.

The wave of intervention, which has continued across the region for most of this year, hasn't been strong enough to reverse the strengthening trend in Asian currencies, as many policymakers are allowing their currencies to rise slowly to limit imported inflation.

That stance was reinforced after China, the top trading partner for key Asian countries, said in June it would let the yuan strengthen against the dollar -- meaning that other Asian countries can maintain their export competitiveness against China even if their currencies rise a bit.

On Wednesday the Thai baht and the Malaysian ringgit hit their highest levels since the 1997 Asian currency crisis, while the Singapore dollar rose to an all-time high.

In a note to investors, Standard Chartered analysts said global dollar weakness, closely tied to market expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve may launch another round of quantitative easing by boosting purchases of U.S. securities, is likely to keep Asian and other emerging market currencies in strong demand. In recent days, the central banks of countries ranging from Russia to Colombia have been suspected of intervening in forex markets because of dollar weakness.

"The prospect of another round of quantitative easing by the Fed in the fourth quarter of 2010 should be seen as broadly negative for the dollar," StanChart said.

Intervention Wednesday was particularly significant in Indonesia, which has attracted a surge of inflows thanks to its solid economic performance and high interest rates.

Jakarta-based traders said the central bank was suspected of buying around $50 million at IDR8,950 in early trade, and then an unspecified amount at IDR8,945. Neither move managed to send the rupiah lower, however, and the dollar last traded at IDR8,935.

"The dollar is still under pressure against the rupiah, as investors' appetite for riskier assets is improving," one dealer in Singapore said.

Intervention by Bank Indonesia has continued for the past two years, but is now likely at its highest volume ever. Bank Indonesia's forex reserves rose 9% in the first three weeks of September, a huge amount even by East Asian standards, mostly due to dollar-buying in forex markets.

The Bank of Thailand and Monetary Authority of Singapore also were suspected of early intervention moves Wednesday. In Bangkok, traders said the BOT was spotted intervening at THB30.50 against the dollar, but the baht rose further and last traded at THB30.46.

In Singapore, the MAS managed to weaken the local dollar slightly after it soared to an all-time high at S$1.3152 against the greenback. The Singapore dollar last traded at S$1.3170.

Seoul traders said intervention by the Bank of Korea was relatively mild, as the Korean won is still some distance away from two-year highs hit earlier this year. The dollar last traded at KRW1,141, having fallen as low as KRW1,139 earlier in the day.

title: Singapore Dollar Flat Late As MAS Steps In To Defend Greenback
text:
Latest   Change 
   USD/SGD               1.3228   +0.0007 
   Overnight rate        0.13%    Unchanged 
   Two-year bond yield:  0.41%    +3 bps 
   10-year bond yield:   2.00%    Unchanged 
   Two-year swap offer:  0.85%    -1 bp 
   10-year swap offer:   2.43%    Unchanged 
   2-10-yr swap curve:  158 bps   +1 bps 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was flat against the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade Tuesday, coming off its early morning highs after the island's central bank intervened to stem the greenback's slide.

A person familiar with the central bank's thinking told Dow Jones Newswires earlier in the day that the Monetary Authority of Singapore "briefly intervened around S$1.3204" to smooth the U.S. dollar's decline.

The U.S. dollar had hit a record low of S$1.3192 overnight.

"They (MAS) can't change the trend of the weak dollar against Asia currencies but they will try to make the fall orderly. At this point they will continue intervening at around S$1.3200," the person said.

Traders and analysts said broad market sentiment toward Asian currencies remains strong.

"Global sentiment continues to remain strong and demand for the U.S. dollar as a safehaven is likely to remain subdued," a trader with a foreign bank said.

In the government bond market, prices were mostly flat with some selling seen at the short-end of the curve.
