title: News Highlights: Top Economic Stories Of The Day
text:
GERMAN GFK CONSUMER SENTIMENT UP, EXPECTATIONS AT 3-YEAR HIGH 

German consumer sentiment is set to rise in October as economic expectations rose to a three-year high in September thanks to falling unemployment levels and moderate consumer prices, market research group GfK said Tuesday. (published 0628 GMT)


 
YUAN APPRECIATION IN CHINA'S, WORLD'S INTERESTS - ADB 

It's in the interests of both China and the world for China to allow its currency to appreciate and increase exchange-rate flexibility, as a stronger yuan will strengthen household consumption power, the Asian Development Bank's chief economist said Tuesday. (published 0532 GMT)


 
JAPAN'S FINANCE MINISTER WARNS AGAINST NEW DEBT ISSUANCE 

Japan's finance minister sounded a warning Tuesday against issuing more government debt to pay for a planned stimulus package amid growing calls from both ruling and opposition lawmakers for the government to go down this well-trodden road. (published 0509 GMT)


 
S KOREA PLANS TOTAL SPENDING OF KRW309.6 TLN IN 2011, UP 5.7% 

The South Korean government unveiled Tuesday a budget plan for next year that aims at fiscal prudence as the local economy recovers fully from the worst global economic downturn in decades. (published 0200 GMT)


 
JAPAN METI MINISTER: INVESTIGATING IMPACT OF SLOWING IMPORTS FROM CHINA 

Japan is investigating the impact on its domestic companies of slowing imports from China, aiming to gather sufficient facts to encourage China to resolve any problems in the trade flow, Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Akihiro Ohata said Tuesday. (published 0355 GMT)

SINGAPORE MAS BRIEFLY INTERVENES TO CUSHION US DOLLAR FALL -SOURCE 

The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market Tuesday after the Singapore dollar hit an all-time high against the greenback, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said. (published 0143 GMT)


 
S KOREA SEPTEMBER CONSUMER SENTIMENT INDEX AT 14-MONTH LOW 

A key index measuring consumer confidence in South Korea fell for a second straight month to a 14-month low in September, reflecting rising concerns about a possible slowdown in the pace of recovery in the domestic economy. (published 0309 GMT)


 
CHINA OFFICIAL: 2010 INDUSTRIAL OUTPUT GROWTH COULD HIT 13%-14%

title: Singapore  MAS Briefly  Intervenes  To Cushion US Dollar Fall -Source
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market Tuesday after the Singapore dollar hit an all-time high against the greenback, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said.

The person said the MAS "briefly intervened around S$1.3204" to smooth the U.S. dollar's decline.

The Singapore dollar overnight hit a record high, with the U.S. dollar falling to S$1.3192. At 0140 GMT the greenback was trading at S$1.3222.

"They (MAS) can't change the trend of the weak dollar against Asia currencies but they will try to make the fall orderly. At this point they will continue intervening at around S$1.3200," the person said.

It was the second time this month that the MAS has intervened in the foreign exchange market.

The central bank uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates as its main policy tool because Singapore's trade flows dwarf the island's small domestic economy.

The MAS aggressively tightened policy in April by raising the trading band for the Singapore dollar and targeting a "modest and gradual appreciation" for the local dollar, changing its previous policy of zero appreciation.

-By Singapore Bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4150; djn.singapore.bureau@dowjones.com [ 28-09-10 0143GMT ]

title: MONEY TALKS: Fed's Mending Ways May Put Asia In A Bind
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--As Ben Bernanke maneuvers the Federal Reserve closer to further quantitative easing, Asian policy makers may find themselves bearing some of the pain of keeping the U.S. economy afloat.

The Fed made it amply clear this week it is concerned about low inflation--and indeed the risk of deflation--in the U.S. and stands ready to act to fulfil its mandate of promoting maximum employment and price stability.

It's likely that Bernanke & Co. will be compelled--unless they are blessed with a sudden and apparently-sustainable improvement in data prints--to embark on another round of monetary loosening. An announcement on QE looks a distinct possibility at the next policy meeting in November.

Flooding the market with more U.S. dollars to lower the cost of credit and inflate the economy may be the way to go; in Asia, however, we may see some fallout from the Fed's actions.

Further easing from the Fed could send the U.S. dollar down and already-strong Asian currencies up, endangering the region's export-dependent economies.

Asian central banks could be forced to continue intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the dollar and temper the impact on exporters. Japan last week was forced to intervene massively for the first time in six years, as a surging yen threatened an already-sluggish economic recovery. Other countries in the region, such as South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, have intervened to prop up the greenback.

Asia will also have to contend with the potential surge in hot money flows to sectors such as housing, heightening the risk of asset price bubbles. With Treasury yields likely to ease on any fresh QE, more investors will turn to Asia for yield.

Central banks in the region may lay low for some months on rates, but if they start hiking to curb inflation that will only accentuate rate differentials.

Such a scenario will pose a policy dilemma for Asia's central banks. Thailand is already moving to introduce rules to boost capital outflows, while the Philippine central bank said Thursday it's mulling changes to foreign exchange regulations to address a surge in portfolio investments that has buoyed the peso.

With Asia already battling rising currencies, the last thing it needs is for the Fed to further frustrate the situation.

Still, the way the cards are stacked up, policy makers in the region will probably be the first to acknowledge that the Fed cannot sit on its hands and risk deflation in the U.S.

text:
Latest   Change

   Overnight rate        0.13%    unchanged 
   Two-year bond yield:  0.49%    unchanged 
   10-year bond yield:   2.16%    +3 bps

   10-year swap offer:   2.48%    +4 bps 
   2-10-yr swap curve:   153 bps  +2 bps 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was marginally weaker in late Asian trade Wednesday, retreating from the record high it struck in offshore trade after the Japanese government intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend a sliding U.S. dollar.

The greenback fell sharply against the euro and Asian currencies in offshore trade as speculation the Federal Reserve may need to do more to support the U.S. economy weighed on the dollar.

Japan's Finance Ministry, operating through the Bank of Japan, sold yen aggressively from Wednesday morning for the first time since March 2004, driving the U.S. currency sharply higher against the yen from 15-year lows and against other Asian currencies such as the Singapore dollar.

A person familiar with the Monetary Authority of Singapore's thinking Wednesday said the local central bank is gauging the impact of Japan's currency-market intervention, which is expected to help other Asian authorities cope with their strong currencies.

The MAS may intervene if the U.S. dollar falls back to around S$1.3300 from current levels but is watching the market for now, the person told Dow Jones Newswires.

However, a trader at a local bank said the U.S. dollar is unlikely fall back toward S$1.3300 in the next few days with the risk of central bank intervention in Asia still high.

"There's always the risk of intervention by the MAS and other central banks as well because of Japan's move," the trader said.

Resistance for the greenback is likely around S$1.3400.

Singapore government bond yields were higher at the longer end as firmer equities markets pushed up yields.

title: Singapore  MAS Waiting To See Impact Of Japan  Intervention  On US Dollar - Source
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Monetary Authority of Singapore is gauging the impact of Japan's currency-market intervention, which should help other Asian authorities cope with their strong currencies, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said Wednesday.

The MAS may intervene again if the U.S. dollar should fall back to around S$1.3300 from current levels around S$1.3370, but for now it is watching the market, the person told Dow Jones Newswires.

Japan's Finance Ministry, operating through the Bank of Japan, sold yen aggressively from Wednesday morning for the first time since March 2004, driving the U.S. currency sharply higher against the yen from 15-year lows.

The U.S. currency also rose against the Singapore dollar and other regional currencies, taking some heat off the authorities, who fear their currencies' strength could hurt their export-reliant recoveries.

"The BOJ move makes it easier for other Asia central banks to manage the (U.S.) dollar's fall," the person said, reflecting the broadly held view that Asia can't change the weak-dollar trend but wants to keep moves under control.

title: MONEY TALKS: Japan Takes On The $4 Trillion Monster
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Those working on the foreign exchange intervention desk at the Bank of Japan may find themselves selling lots and lots of yen in the next 24 hours.

For Japan to succeed in breaking the yen-buying psychology of the four trillion dollar FX market, the Ministry of Finance, via the BOJ, may have to be willing to buy U.S. dollars on a scale it has never previously done and be prepared to fight the world's largest market, all day and all night.

For inspiration Japan can look back at its successful attack on the yen in April 1995. With dollar/yen just below 80, Japan started buying billions of dollars; traders at the time estimated it bought over twenty billion dollars in one day, starting in Tokyo and continuing into the North American trading session. It worked; within one month the yen had weakened 8% and by the end of 1995 it had weakened 23%.

However in the mid-1990s the U.S. economy was enjoying a much better time than it is today; unemployment was much lower and economic growth was on an uptrend at the start of the technology-led boom.

Contrast that with 2010 and the U.S. may not stand idly by and let Japan weaken its currency too far before it puts Japan in the dock alongside China to accuse it of manipulating its currency.

Partly for that reason, Japan is likely to be on its own in this contest with the market; notably there are no bank economists forecasting the U.S. Treasury will join Japan as a partner to weaken the yen and strengthen the dollar this time around.

Thus-far intervention appears to have been in the range of three to five billion dollars; significantly the Bank of Japan has apparently agreed to leave the intervention unsterilized for now, which could help convince traders that Japan is serious about its job.

In 2010 Japan may also be satisfied with a more modest degree of success.

If the market can be persuaded to stop buying yen for long enough to question the notion that dollar/yen is a one-way bet, it may be enough to bring foreign investors back into the Japanese stock market. The slide in the Nikkei Stock Average index below the 9000 mark in late August could have been the tipping point which led to selling of yen Wednesday.

Wherever the market is heading from here, the next 24 hours may be crucial for the MOF and the Bank of Japan as it carries out the MOF's instructions. Pizza delivery anyone?

(Mark Cranfield is an analyst for Dow Jones CommentaryPlus. He was previously a currency and bond trader for major banks in London, Hong Kong & Singapore. He can be reached on 65-6415-4034 or via email: mark.cranfield@dowjones.com)

title: FX  ASIA: Japan  Intervention  Could Prompt Copycats Around Asia
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--A Japanese intervention in forex currency markets might well fail to weaken the yen, but should have a near-term impact on other Asian currencies.

Japanese authorities have ratcheted up their rhetoric against a strong yen as the currency rises steadily, hitting a 15-year high against the dollar Tuesday.

Some analysts say Japanese intervention would embolden other Asian central banks, many of which have intervened heavily so far this year, to increase their own dollar purchases to protect their exporters. Likely candidates for a quick correction under that scenario would be the Taiwan dollar, Korean won and Singapore dollar, all currencies closely watched by their central banks.

Asian central banks "would be more likely to intervene" after a potential Japanese move, as it "would make them more comfortable with intervention," said Sean Callow, a forex strategist with Westpac. "All Asian central banks keep an eye on what the others are doing; they haven't been shy about intervening."

Japanese intervention might become likelier if Ichiro Ozawa, a kingmaker in the ruling Democratic Party of Japan, wins an internal party election Tuesday to replace Naoto Kan as party leader and prime minister. Ozawa has espoused a more activist line to curb the yen and protect Japanese exporters.

That could become a matter of concern for Japan's competitors, including South Korea and Taiwan, which have taken market share from Japanese exporters in fields such as automobiles and electronics.

Over the past two years, as the yen rose 19% against the U.S. dollar, the Korean won has lost 5% against the greenback and the Taiwan dollar has been flat. That has helped those economies -- which grew more than 7% on-year in the second quarter, compared with 1.5% growth in Japan -- to recover faster from the global slowdown.

Westpac's Callow said China's response to any Japanese intervention also would be key, as the Chinese yuan has become an increasingly relevant benchmark for Asian currencies. With Japan hectoring China to intervene less to weaken the yuan, China could react to Japanese intervention by slowing or even reversing the pace of yuan appreciation.

Singapore, where the local dollar rose to an all-time high against the greenback earlier this week, is another candidate to mirror any Japanese intervention. A person familiar with the Monetary Authority of Singapore's thinking said the central bank would be more likely to step in if Tokyo does.

On the other hand, Indonesia could find it hard to increase its intervention. As of last month Bank Indonesia's forex reserves stood at $81.3 billion, up 36% on the year -- among the world's largest gains -- as a result of sustained dollar purchasing in forex markets.

Bank Indonesia has expressed reservations about the quick buildup and announced several measures to increase monitoring of investment inflows in recent months, looking to find other ways to lessen pressure on the rupiah.

That's because Indonesia's high policy rates, now at 6.5%, make it more expensive to keep dollar reserves there than in other countries, as commercial banks must be paid interest in local currency in exchange for keeping dollars with the central bank.

(David Roman, a regional forex reporter, has been a Dow Jones correspondent since 2002, covering economic and corporate news. He can be reached at 65 6415 4045 or by e-mail: david.roman@dowjones.com)

(Costas Paris in Singapore contributed to this story.)

title: UPDATE: MAS To  Intervene  If US Dollar Stays Below S$1.34010-Source
text:
(Adds quotes, Bank Negara intervention, background) 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank is poised to intervene in the currency market, selling the local currency for the second time, this month if the U.S. dollar trades "consistently" below S$1.3410, a person familiar with the situation said Thursday.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is watching the local currency's rise "very closely," the person told Dow Jones Newswires. "If (the U.S. dollar) trades consistently below S$1.3410," the MAS "will likely intervene."

The Singapore dollar hit a record high Thursday, with the greenback falling to S$1.3407 as Asian currencies climbed on renewed global risk appetite. At 0405 GMT it was quoted at S$1.3428.

The MAS, which had largely stayed out of the market since April, intervened Sept. 3 after the U.S. dollar fell to S$1.3425.

The person said the MAS would have intervened again Thursday if it wasn't for the U.S. currency's weakness against other Asian currencies like the yen, the Thai baht, the Malaysian ringgit and the Korean won that make up part of the basket of currencies the central bank uses to guide the Singapore dollar.

The U.S. dollar has been sliding against Asian currencies this year, first as Asia's strong economic recovery has attracted heavy investment and, more recently, on expectations that the Federal Reserve will need to loosen U.S. monetary policy further as the world's biggest economy slows.

Authorities in export-reliant countries are growing concerned about the rises in their currencies, and a growing number of Asian central banks has been intervening in an attempt to keep their exporters competitive.

The Bank of Thailand and the Bank of Korea have been steadily buying dollars and the Bank of Japan has repeatedly threatened to intervene for the first time in more than six years as the yen hits 15-year highs.

Bank Negara Malaysia, which had also been standing aside since April, has begun to intervene to curb the ringgit around 13-year highs, traders in Kuala Lumpur say. The central bank bought dollars last week and as recently as Wednesday at MYR3.1110-MYR3.1120, the traders said.

As with its peers in Asia, Bank Negara appears to be trying to smooth its currency's rise and keep moves orderly, rather than reversing the ringgit's strength. Traders expect the dollar to fall to around MYR3.1000 in the near term from MYR3.1100 early Thursday.

"This is what every Asian central bank is doing," said the person familiar with MAS thinking.

"They all expect a weaker dollar, but they are trying to make the fall orderly and discourage speculation," the person said. "There are of course red lines and in Singapore, at this point, anything below S$1.34 will prompt action which will be beyond what they call 'smoothing.'"

The MAS also views the Singapore dollar's rise as part of a trend among Asian currencies after China decoupled the yuan from the U.S. dollar in mid-June, the person said. Although the yuan has barely risen, the de-pegging by the People's Bank of China paved the way for other export-reliant Asian economies to let their own currencies gain further, the person said.

The MAS aggressively tightened policy in April by raising the trading band for the Singapore dollar and targeting a "modest and gradual appreciation" for the local dollar, changing its previous policy of zero appreciation.

Singapore's economy grew a blistering 18.8% in the second quarter from a year earlier, accelerating from 16.9% in the first quarter and after contracting last year due to the global economic crisis. The government expects the economy to grow 13%-15% for the full year.

Analytical models show the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is well within the confines of the central bank's secret policy band, suggesting the MAS may act to smooth but not stop further losses in the near term.

The modest injection suggests that Singapore isn't yet facing a severe liquidity squeeze.

"They're willing to add liquidity but right now it's not needed," the trader said.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar plummeted Friday as escalating credit concerns prompted speculators to liquidate positions in emerging market assets.   

Traders said that liquidity in global markets will remain the focal point in the near term, and the currency will suffer if the credit woes evolve into a crisis.   

"We're watching credit markets very closely," a trader said. "The Singapore dollar may hold steady until there's news on the subprime front, but if this thing comes further undone there will be more damage."   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the currency within a secret trade-weighted band, and currently has a policy of modest and gradual appreciation.   

Analytical models indicate that the currency is near the center of the band, suggesting the central bank won't intervene unless the Singapore dollar makes a sharp dive.   

United Overseas Bank estimated that if the Singapore dollar held steady against other currencies, the greenback would have to climb to S1.5446 before hitting the edge of the policy band - the point where the MAS is likely to act.   

Singapore government bonds took a cue from U.S. Treasurys, which surged Thursday after French bank  BNP Paribas said it was unable to value three of its funds invested in collateralized debt obligations.   

BNP's struggle led to a surge in demand for cash across Europe, prompting the European Central Bank to inject almost EUR100 billion into the money market.   

The MAS was the first central bank in Asia to follow the ECB's lead, with a central bank official stating early Friday that the MAS was ready to offer liquidity if needed.   

"We will stand ready to inject liquidity," Ong Chong Tee, deputy managing director at the MAS told reporters at a press conference. "If there are liquidity bottlenecks certainly we could be willing."   

Later Friday, the MAS injected S$1.5 billion of cash into the money market, two traders told Dow Jones Newswires.   

The central bank regularly acts in the money market to ensure sufficient liquidity, but analysts said the cash infusion marked a symbolic gesture to reinforce Ong's statement.   

Despite the injection, the overnight deposit rate paid by banks rose 50 basis points to a high of 2.75% Friday morning as cash demand surged.

title: UPDATE:Asia Central Bks Inject Cash; Play Dn Liquidity Worry
text:
(Adds central bank comments, FX intervention, money market rates.)   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks in Japan, Australia and Singapore leapt into the fray to calm jittery financial markets Friday, injecting cash into their local money markets in an echo of overnight action by the European Central Bank and the U.S. Federal Reserve.   

The authorities in Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia meanwhile intervened to support their currencies against the U.S. dollar.   

However, central bankers and government officials across the region were circumspect about the prospects for a credit crunch here, likely for fear of feeding the panic that has arisen out of the snowballing U.S. subprime crisis. Concerns about subprime have prompted a flight to highly rated assets and made it more difficult for investors to access ever more cautious markets.   

"Any impact on the Philippines will be largely indirect, mainly in the form of risk aversion," said Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Amando Tetangco said.   

"There is sufficient domestic liquidity," he added.   

In Korea, where the finance ministry has just wrapped up a meeting with officials from the central bank, the Financial Supervisory Commission and commercial banks to discuss the global market volatility, Vice Finance Minister Lim Young-Rok warned the impact from the subprime may continue for some time but that sufficient liquidity meant the bank wasn't planning to inject any fresh money into the market.   

Asia broadly has been raising interest rates of late to slow hefty liquidity growth, with South Korea and Australia tightening policy earlier this week and regional economic giants China and Japan expected to follow suit in coming weeks or months.   

Speculation will now turn to whether and how much the snowballing credit market fallout will change the Asian rate cycle or damage local economies and whether governments and central banks are ready to act.   

"Suddenly, central banks have changed their tune from a wait-and-see stance on the subprime issue to a move to stabilize the financial system,"  Barclays Capital analyst Masuhisa Kobayashi wrote in a research note Friday.   

He said that the start of action could either mean that the credit market and financial system have destabilized so much that central banks had to act or that the action was meant to prevent such a situation, and things should calm down going forward.   

"The market seems to have taken the former, more pessimistic view," he added.   

For their part, Japanese government officials played down worries, with economy minister Hiroko Ota saying the U.S. subprime issue would wreak little damage on the Japanese economy and that Japanese monetary policy would be based on the state of the local economy and prices.   

Still,  Credit Suisse said the chances of a rate hike at the BOJ meeting later this month had fallen to 37% Friday from 64% Thursday.   

The Bank of Japan injected Y1 trillion into the local money market Friday after the overnight call rate rose above the bank's target rate of 0.5% for overnight loans. Sharp gyrations followed but by mid afternoon the overnight rate was quoted at 0.5049%.   

Banks weren't facing fund-raising problems but wanted to preemptively ensure as much funding as possible amid growing credit anxiety, said one senior money trader in Tokyo. He added that banks that borrowed money through the BOJ's injection were holding the funds, encouraging other banks to raise their bid rates.   

The Reserve Bank of Australia injected A$4.95 billion of liquidity into Australia's financial system, double the A$2.44 billion needed.   

Spokesmen for both played down the actions as part of normal dealing operations.   

Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore also injected S$1.5 billion into the market in what they said was a symbolic gesture, coming as it did shortly after Deputy Managing Director Ong Chong Tee said the MAS was ready to step in to offer liquidity if necessary.   

Following the injection, the overnight deposit rate jumped to 2.75% before falling to 2.56% in mid afternoon. That was still higher than 2.25% at the start of the day.   

On the foreign exchange markets, where high-yield currencies were slammed by the rush to safe-haven units, dealers said the Malaysian central bank sold US$3 million at MYR3.48 to smooth the pair's gains and that the Indonesian central bank was also in the market supporting the rupiah.   

Traders in Manila said the Philippine central bank was selling U.S. dollars at PHP45.75 to infuse liquidity into a market due to heavy U.S. dollar buying from oil firms and banks.   

The action across Asia followed decisions by the ECB and the Federal Reserve to inject EUR94.84 billion and $24 billion respectively into their markets.   

That was sparked by spiking overnight rates after  BNP Paribas SA, France's biggest bank, said Thursday it had stopped withdrawals from three investment funds due to volatility in the U.S. asset-backed securities market.   

Subsequent market jitters overnight sent a shockwave through move Asian markets Friday.   


 
   -By Karen Lane, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415-4043; karen.lane@dowjones.com

  SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose Friday as momentum from Thursday's rally kept it on an upward course, and traders say the strong bias may extend into the new week.    

One trader said he sold a fair amount of U.S. dollars for institutional clients during the day, and that he expects the greenback to drop sharply if it breaks through S$1.5100.   

"It's definitely the next important level," he said. "I can see us dropping 30 pips right away if we make a clean break through S$1.5100."   

Singapore's central bank manages the appreciation of the local currency, but most analytical models suggest it can rise substantially further without prompting intervention.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore's current policy of modest, gradual appreciation allows the currency to fluctuate within a secret trading band.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose to a seven-week high against the greenback Tuesday after data showed second-quarter economic output rose much faster than expected, underlining the currency's fundamental value.   

A foreign exchange trader said the U.S. dollar "is still heavy" against the Singapore dollar, and may continue to grind lower in coming sessions.   

Singapore's economy expanded 12.8% from the first quarter on a seasonally adjusted and annualized basis after growing a revised 8.5% in the previous three months, the Ministry of Trade & Industry said. Economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had on average forecast a 7.8% expansion.   

The Singapore dollar jumped in response to the data release at 0000 GMT, with the greenback slipping to S$1.5170 from S$1.5200. It was the lowest level the U.S. dollar had touched since May 16.   

Another trader said that the U.S. dollar has ample room to fall against the local currency in the medium term without risk of intervention by the Singapore central bank.   

"This data will make it easier to justify a long Singapore dollar position," he said. "We could see more interest and I don't think there's any way the authorities will come in."   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses exchange rate targeting as its chief policy tool, and manages the currency within a secret trading band.   

Analytical models indicate the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is near the middle of the undisclosed range, suggesting it could appreciate at least 1% before breaching the band's top.   

In the government bond market, prices rose as the strong economic data encouraged investors to seek Singapore dollar-denominated assets.   

"In the morning, we saw strength in the Singapore dollar show up in bonds and the market was well-bid into the afternoon," a fixed-income trader said.   

The trader added that interest rate swap levels stayed relatively supported as investors taking new long positions in bonds wanted to hedge against fixed-rate coupons.   

"Investors have been in the market bidding up (interest rate swaps), so there was some bond-swap widening," the trader said.   

Market-watchers will tune into a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke later Tuesday that may offer clues on the Fed's outlook on inflation.

title: ANALYSIS- Intervention  costs impel Asia to loosen  FX  grip
text:
SINGAPORE, July 4 (Reuters) - Rising asset prices and the mounting cost of foreign exchange intervention are prompting Asian policy makers to step back from markets, setting the stage for a faster rise in regional currencies.   

 In a region that routinely curbs currency strength to help underpin exports, official concerns about higher exchange rates have been further soothed by the resilience of overseas sales this year despite a slowdown in the U.S. economy.   

 Most Asian countries tightly manage their currencies while trying to run an independent monetary policy.   

 This can create a conflict. Tighter monetary conditions can attract capital, putting pressure on the currency to rise, which becomes costly to control. This is known as the impossible trinity.   

 "They have seen the limits of the system, though they are not going to end intervention completely by any means," said Marshall Gittler, chief Asia strategist at  Deutsche Bank Private Wealth Management.   

 Underlining the tolerance for higher exchange rates, Malaysia's Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz said last week that a firm ringgit had not hurt the country's exports, and local firms are taking the currency's strength in their stride.   

 Indonesian officials have said they were comfortable with a stronger rupiah.   

  India's central bank admitted in its April policy review that "dealing with the impossible trinity of fixed exchange rates, open capital accounts and discretion in monetary policy had become more complex than before".   

 For that reason, it allowed the rupee <INR=IN> to jump 10 percent versus the dollar in about three months from early March to achieve monetary policy control to fight against inflation.   

 The rupee is the best-performer in Asia so far this year, although with inflation easing, India's central bank may well tighten its currency reins once again, analysts say.   

 MORE DIFFICULT   

 Tim Condon, head of Asia research at ING, said in theory it's impossible to manage the so-called impossible trinity, although Asian countries have tried.   

 "But it's becoming more and more difficult in a globalised world," he said.   

Morgan Stanley says India, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Thailand are all struggling to check their currencies while controlling monetary policy with relatively open capital accounts.   

 In theory, fixing an exchange rate alongside an independent monetary policy can only work with capital controls.   

Foreign exchange reserves in Asia ex-Japan have doubled from 2003 to $2.4 trillion as central banks limited currency gains, but the costs of piling up such reserves are mounting.   

 These include the cost of mopping up the local currency that is injected into the economy when a central bank buys foreign exchange and the fall in the value of the dollar, which makes up the majority of most reserves.   

 "The costs of reserve accumulation for a number of countries have reached levels which would appear difficult to sustain,"  HSBCcurrency strategist Richard Yetsenga said.   

 He estimated the cost of accumulating foreign exchange reserves had reached around 4 percent gross domestic product in India, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand and Singapore.   

 ASSET-PRICE BUBBLE   

 Capital is flowing into the region's high-flying stock markets while property prices are also booming.   

 This raises concerns about future inflation, prompting Asia's more tolerant policy makers to tighten monetary conditions by letting currencies rally.   

 Analysts believe the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> would benefit from the new policy tolerance.   

 Standard Chartered has raised its end-2007 forecast on the rupiah to 8,900 per dollar from 9,000, and its June 2008 forecast to 8,700 from 8,800. It was trading around 9,000 per dollar on Wednesday.   

 "The economy looks relatively sound and also there are signs of tolerance for currency appreciation. We are definitely bullish on the rupiah," said Thomas Harr, the bank's currency strategist.   

 Asian emerging currencies have regained most of the ground lost in the 1997/98 financial crisis but analysts see room for further gains.   

 "I think Asia will survive very well with exchange rates 20 or 30 percent above where they are now, so long that everybody in Asia moves at the same time," said Huw McKay, senior economist at Westpac.   

 China, with reserves of more than $1.2 trillion, has also shown signs of tolerance for a faster rise in its yuan as it tried to tackle its soaring trade surplus -- a major point of contention with the United States.   

 Most analysts expect the yuan to rise 5-6 percent versus the dollar this year, compared with last year's 3.4 percent.   

 The yuan's rise has quickened since the central bank widened its daily trading band to 0.5 percent from 0.3 percent in May.   

 "While I would not expect them to make any announcement of formal change in policy, it's quite reasonable that they will let the yuan to appreciate more within the band," Gittler said.   

 A noticeable exception to the more tolerant currency attitude is South Korea, where officials have voiced repeated concerns about the won's <KRW=> strength against the dollar and particularly the yen <JPYKRW=R>, the currency of key export rival Japan.   

 In recent months, the won has hit its highest levels against both currencies since the Asian financial crisis.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady in Asia Wednesday, but traders say the local currency is exposed to a spillover effect if the Malaysian ringgit continues to fall.   

"The Malaysian ringgit has trended weaker, and the Singapore dollar would follow if (the ringgit) has a major breakout," a trader said.   

"If the U.S. dollar moves much beyond MYR3.4200 the Singapore dollar could break out of its range as well."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was flat in Asia Monday, and although estimates suggest central bank intervention is unlikely, the currency has been slow to rise as traders remain guarded.   

"For now, there is still room for the (Singapore dollar) to strengthen further without challenging the policy threshold,"  United Overseas Bank said in a report.   

UOB estimates that if the Singapore dollar holds steady against other currencies, the greenback would need to reach S$1.5050 to prompt the central bank to act.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses the exchange rate as its primary policy tool and manages the currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.   

"The U.S. dollar dipped below S$1.5100 Friday but the market's a bit jittery and there's been some short covering," a trader at a foreign bank said.   

Another trader said that when the central bank last apparently intervened on April 12, the trade-weighted Singapore dollar was below the currency band's upper limit.   

"Since they came in unpredictably before, we think they want to keep the market guessing, so the U.S. dollar may have a hard time breaking S$1.5100," he said.   

The trader added that the greenback may encounter a short-term ceiling between S$1.5130 and S$1.5140, a level it remained beneath late last week.   

In the government debt market, the yield curve steepened as strong demand in a T-bill auction resulted in the lowest yield in over 18 months.   

A S$1.9 billion auction of three-month government T-bills priced at a cutoff yield of 1.94%, the lowest level since September 2005.   

Foreign purchases of Singapore dollars have lifted the currency to the top of the secret trading band in recent months, and analysts say the inflows have given government paper a major boost.   

"It's still a capital inflows story," said Selena Ling, a fixed-income strategist at OCBC.   

Central bank watchers say the MAS historically conducted money market operations to keep short-term rates stable, but it's been notably absent in 2007.   

Singapore benefits from external price competition, and a very low inflation rate has also been a prop for fixed-income assets.   

Singapore's consumer prices rose just 0.7% from a year earlier in March, similar to the 0.6% rise in February.

"The U.S. dollar is heavy, and if we can drop below S$1.5100 it's possible we'll go to S$1.5050 early next week," a trader at a Japanese bank said.   

The U.S. dollar has edged below the psychologically important S$1.5100 level in recent sessions - touching new 10-year lows - but hasn't made a decisive breakthrough.   

The trader said that the Singapore dollar has correlated closely with the Japanese yen recently, and both currencies failed to carry momentum Friday.

Traders say that if the Singapore dollar does stage a rally, the Monetary Authority of Singapore won't intervene at current levels.   

"We don't think there's much chance of the central bank coming in here, but we could always get a surprise," another trader said.   

The central bank uses the exchange rate as its primary monetary policy tool and manages the currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.   

According to  United Overseas Bank, the U.S. dollar would have to decline to S$1.4982 to lift the trade-weighted basket to the top of the secret currency band.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia up,  intervention  fears cap rupee's gains
text:
SINGAPORE, April 18 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose against a weaker dollar on Wednesday, but the Indian rupee retreated amid growing concerns about fresh central bank dollar-buying intervention.   

 The Thai baht <THB=TH> gained nearly 0.3 percent to 34.75 to the dollar. It had hit 34.70 in early onshore trading, its highest level in almost a month.   

 The dollar sank to a 26-year low against sterling <GBP=> and weakened against other major currencies after data showing weaker U.S. core consumer inflation in March, bolstered the view that the Federal Reserve may lean towards a rate cut this year.   

 "The dollar is under pressure. The low consumer prices could be positive for U.S. equities as it helped take some pressure off the Fed, and that was a helpful lead to Asian equity markets," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Bank.   

 The rupee <INR=IN> eased back to around 41.95 per dollar surrendering most of its daily gains after briefly hitting 41.80, which was still off its 9-year high of 41.63 hit on Tuesday.   

 Analysts are concerned that the rupee's rapid gains in recent days might push the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to intervene. So far they say the central bank appears to have accepted the strength in the currency, which helps hold down inflation.   

 "Following aggressive intervention in February and March, the central bank appears to have scaled back their dollar buying significantly this week," currency strategists at UBS said in a research note.   

 The RBI bought $1.14 billion of reserves in the first week of April, central bank data shows, implying a slowdown from a record $11.9 billion it bought in February to prevent the rupee's gains.   

INTERVENTION LIKELY   

 But UBS cautioned that the RBI was standing aside to wait for a clearer economic picture, and its dollar-buying intervention will resume if money supply and inflation eased.   

 "We would therefore not be surprised if the RBI returns to the rupee market before the week is up," UBS said, adding they were cautiously shifting their 1-month dollar/rupee forecast to 42.50.   

 The won <KRW=> rose as high as 927.3 per dollar, its highest since early January, despite concerns about intervention by the Bank of Korea, which traders said had stepped into the market this week to cap the currency's gains.   

 The baht has gained about 3.8 percent this year, trailing the rupee's 5.5 percent rise as the best-performing currency in Asia, despite Bangkok's attempts to cap the baht's rise to protect its exporters.

title: ANALYSIS-More than meets the eye in Singapore rates policy
text:
SINGAPORE, April 17 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank announced last week it was sticking to a three-year policy of modest monetary tightening -- just as it intervened to weaken the Singapore dollar and drive money market rates to their lowest in more than a year.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) words and actions further confused a market that has always struggled to fathom Singapore's complicated, currency-based monetary settings.   

Like every other central bank in Asia, the MAS seemed to want policy to be tight and loose at the same time, to check rising asset prices on the one hand but cushion the economy from flagging electronics exports on the other.   

It suggested that, while nominally sticking to its moderately tight policy, Singapore's central bank would keep intervening to weaken its currency and encourage the drop in short-term money market rates that intervention would engender.   

"Buy property. I am sure mortgage rates will soon fall," said one Singapore-based economist.   

Three-month interbank rates fell to 2.78 percent on Tuesday, their lowest level since November 2005.   

Monetary policy is conducted by guiding the Singapore dollar <SGD=> within a secret band determined by its trade-weighted levels. Since April 2004, the MAS has had a policy of allowing a gradual appreciation of the mid-point of that band.   

Notwithstanding the confirmation of that policy last week, currency analysts said they would position for some weakness in the Singapore dollar, particularly against the currencies of countries Singapore trades with.   

"It is surprising how dovish they were in the statement, which is backed up by the intervention they have done and the short-term interest rates remaining very low," said HSBC economist Robert Prior-Wandesforde.   

Policy was designed to ensure the currency remained competitive to shore up exports, he said, although HSBC expects the electronics sector to recover shortly anyway.   

Analysts estimate the Singapore dollar has stuck near the top of its secret band for the past six months, underpinned by a robust economy and capital inflows into soaring property and stock markets.   

It hit a 9-1/2-year peak of 1.5110 against the U.S. dollar on April 10 -- the day of MAS's twice-yearly policy review -- but has since retreated a little. It was around 1.5130 on Tuesday. "The risk is that the Singapore dollar will underperform regional currencies as growth risks may mean a more interventionist and dovish MAS," JPMorgan analyst Claudio Piron said in a note to clients.   

IMPOSSIBLE TRINITY   

The MAS's policy statement showed it was in a tight corner. It highlighted the 7.2 percent annualised first-quarter economic growth and buoyancy in the construction and service sectors.   

A potential slump in U.S. housing -- and therefore the U.S. economy -- and weak demand in the global electronics industry were risks, it said.   

For the moment, the U.S. problems remain little more than threats, so it would have been premature to ease policy. Singapore's economy is still expected to grow at its normal potential rate of 4.5 to 6.5 percent this year, while prices are likely to rise after the sales tax climbs 2 percentage points in July to 7 percent.   

However, electronics exports, the mainstay of growth, are weak, and the MAS has been struggling to keep the Singapore dollar in check. Singapore's currency reserves have swollen to $137.5 billion, roughly equalling GDP, and the MAS has gathered another $66 billion through swaps.   

Nowadays, analysts say, the MAS has stopped sterilising its intervention. That means it buys up foreign currency from the market in exchange for Singapore dollars but lets the local currency remain with banks rather than issue bonds to absorb it.   

Piron reckons the ensuing decline in yields is deliberate, aimed at alleviating the upward pressure on the Singapore dollar without explicitly altering the monetary stance.   

"The other dilemma is that allowing lower interest rates could fuel an asset boom and risks of instability," he said.   

That may be the lesser evil for a country that aspires to be Asia's financial conduit and is courting multinationals that might otherwise head for Hong Kong or Shanghai.   

Singapore also has a heavy dependence on trade. Annual exports are estimated to be more than twice its economic output.   

A popular hypothesis in international economics states that if a country allows free capital movement, it can only control either its currency or interest rates, not both.   

Singapore needs free movement of capital but at the same time it must ensure its currency does not become too uncompetitive.   

That means interest rate policy has to give. Under present circumstances, that means rates are falling, and at least some economists reckon the central bank -- worried about the currency and economic risks -- is glad they are.

"The (nominal effective exchange rate) is nowhere near the top of the trading band right now."   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses exchange-rate targeting as its chief policy tool, and since April 2004 has advocated a modest and gradual appreciation of the local unit.   

The Singapore dollar fell against currencies such as the Malaysian ringgit at the start of the week, which reduced the local unit's trade-weighted value.

"We're beginning to think that the liquidity is here to stay and interest rates are going to be soft for a while," a trader said.   

Although interest rate swap levels moved sharply lower, bond yields made a smaller adjustment.   

"The swap market led the way, and even though bond yields came down, there's a big lag," a trader said.   

"Bonds won't necessarily follow the entire move because we were due for a bit of a correction in the bond-swap spread."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against the greenback in Asia Monday as the local unit eased versus other currencies, reducing pressure on the central bank to intervene, traders say.   

"The trade-weighted Singapore dollar has come down from last week," a trader said.   

"There's room for the U.S. dollar to test the S$1.5100 level before (the central bank) comes in."   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses exchange-rate targeting as its chief policy tool, and since April 2004 has advocated a modest and gradual appreciation of the local unit according to a trade-weighted calculation.   

The currencies of trading partners other than the U.S. gained against the local unit since Friday, lowering the Singapore dollar's weighted value.   

The euro reached highs near S$2.0600 early Monday from lows around S$2.0450 late Friday.   

The trader said that further strength in the Chinese yuan - linked to political pressure in the U.S. - may boost the Singapore dollar in coming sessions.   

"With the U.S. getting impatient on China and urging it to move faster on the yuan, we expect that this could yield more speculation of another revaluation this week," he said.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore apparently intervened last week, and another trader said it sold about S$6 billion to restrain the currency's strength.   

In the local debt market, short-dated government bonds gained following a T-bill auction that was priced at the lowest yield since September 2005.   

A S$1.9 billion auction of three-month T-bills sold at a cutoff yield of 2.20%, far below yields above 3.00% as recently as February.   

One trader said that the results were "on the low side" of expectations, but that short-term rates may remain suppressed for some time.   

"There's been aggressive bidding from the local banks that can't afford to miss a buying opportunity because T-bills are rarely traded in the secondary market," he said.   

Surging capital inflows have led new deposits to grow much faster than new loans in recent months, and banks have been compelled to match assets to the swelling liabilities.   

Singapore's M2 money supply, a broad measure that spans from cash to certificates of deposit, surged 22% in the year to February, according to the latest government data.

"A lot of our customers seem willing to sell U.S. dollars whether the central bank comes in or not," a trader at a foreign bank said. "If the central bank doesn't come in, I think the U.S. dollar can keep drifting lower."

text:
SINGAPORE, April 12 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit a three-week low on Thursday on suspected central bank buying of U.S. dollars to cap local currency strength, while wariness about intervention helped keep other Asian currencies in a tight range.   

Markets in the Philippines, Malaysia, South Korea, India as well as Singapore have all been watchful this week of official intervention to limit currency gains against a backdrop of firm equities and optimism about economic growth.   

Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was probably buying U.S. dollars in the market again on Thursday, helping push the Singapore dollar <SGD=> to a three-week trough at 1.5220 per U.S. dollar.   

The Singapore dollar is down about 0.6 percent from Tuesday's 9-1/2-year peak at 1.5110.   

"They are getting increasingly frustrated with Sing dollar strength and will increasingly come into the market," said one trader. He thought the MAS had intervened earlier from the 1.5170 per dollar level to 1.5220.   

The MAS is determined to squeeze out short U.S. dollar    


positions against the Singapore dollar -- bets that the U.S.
currency will weaken -- said Tim Condon, head of research at
   

ING.   

But such trades are likely to remain in favour given that the central bank has just maintained a moderately tight monetary policy, he said.   

The MAS, which uses the exchange rate instead of interest rates to conduct monetary policy, on Tuesday reiterated its stance of allowing "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the trade-weighted currency.   

"The night before the MAS meeting the Sing dollar was 2.5 percent above the mid-point of its band and very much in intervention territory," said Westpac currency strategist Sean Callow, referring to his estimate of the band.   

"Now it's about 1.9 percent above the mid-point, so intervention has helped pull it back."   

CENTRAL BANK WATCHING   

The Philippine peso <PHP=> dipped to the weaker side of 48 per dollar but held near Wednesday's six-year high of 47.90.   

Dealers said the central bank may have intervened, but any dollar buying was probably smaller than earlier in the week.   

"Maybe they were there today and yesterday, but not as actively as they were on Tuesday," said one Manila trader, referring to the central bank.   

In South Korea, the won <KRW=> touched a one-week high at about 931 per dollar amid foreign buying of Korean shares, which hit a fresh record peak. A move to 930 is expected to be met by central bank intervention, helping to limit won gains.   

The won also rose to 7.7895 against the yen <JPYKRW=R>, its highest since Feb. 27.   

Markets showed little immediate reaction to a widely expected decision by the Bank of Korea to hold its benchmark interest rate steady at 4.50 percent.   

A meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations, starting on Friday in Washington, helped keep most Asian currencies range-bound, dealers said.   

Analysts say the G7 may renew calls for currency flexibility in Asia, with a focus on China, to help correct global imbalances.   

China's foreign exchange reserves, the world's largest, rose by $135.7 billion in the first quarter to $1.202 trillon, the country's central bank said on Thursday.   

This could add fresh ammunition to any calls at the G7 meeting for faster appreciation in the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS>, analysts said. China has said top officials will not be attending the G7 meeting.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was down in Asia Thursday as the central bank returned to the market for the third time in a week to stem the currency's rise.   

"The central bank wants to keep the market guessing," a trader said. But he added that the U.S. unit's new-found upward movement may have some momentum behind it, and its near-term floor "may keep getting higher and higher."   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened late Thursday morning to push the U.S. dollar up from S$1.5170 to S$1.5220, several traders said.   

Tuesday, the MAS intervened in two waves, first lifting the greenback from S$1.5115 to S$1.5185, and later from S$1.5160 to S$1.5215.   

But a greenback upside bias may now be taking hold, as minutes from the recent meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve released overnight suggest monetary tightening remains possible.   

"If the Federal Reserve is skewed towards a hike, people may start buying into the U.S. dollar, and the base will move higher and higher, probably testing S$1.5250," another trader said.   

In its policy statement Tuesday, the MAS said the trade-weighted Singapore dollar has recently traded near the upper end of its undisclosed policy band.   

The MAS uses exchange-rate targeting as its chief policy tool, and since April 2004 has advocated a modest and gradual appreciation of the local unit.   

In the local debt market, government bonds fell, mirroring a move in U.S. Treasurys.   

"Yields were pretty low at these levels, and the move in U.S. Treasurys gave some people an excuse to sell bonds," a trader said.   

U.S Treasury yields rose one to two basis points across maturities in overnight trade.   

But another trader said Singapore's overnight deposit rate remains low enough to anchor short-dated yields in coming sessions.   

"Even if yields creep up in the U.S., the market here is still flushed with cash so bonds aren't likely to sell off," the trader said.

text:
SINGAPORE, April 11 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso touched a six-year high due to strong remittance inflows on Wednesday, while the South Korean won pushed higher as heavy foreign buying helped lift the local stock market index to a record high.   

In contrast, the Singapore dollar retreated from Tuesday's 9-1/2-year peak amid jitters about central bank intervention to curb its strength.

The Thai baht <THB=TH> was steady at about 34.95 per dollar onshore after the Bank of Thailand delivered a 50-basis-point cut in the one-day repurchase rate to 4.00 percent, in line with expectations.   

The cut, aimed at boosting the economy, is also seen as a measure to weaken the baht, which has remained strong despite capital controls aimed at pushing it down. The baht has risen just over 3 percent this year after a 14 percent increase versus the dollar in 2006.   

"They should have done this before the capital controls were introduced and it would have been a better way to curb speculative flows and slow currency strength," said UBS currency strategist Nizam Idris.   

The peso hit 47.90 per dollar <PHP=>, a six-year high, as remittances that had bunched up over the Easter holiday continued to push the currency higher.   

But suspected central bank intervention stalled the gains, dealers said.   

"Basically it's still strong remittances," said one trader in Manila, explaining the peso's rise. "We believe they (the central bank) were there -- that's why the market has had a hard time piercing 47.90."

"They bought about 2.5 to 2.7 billion U.S. dollars in the global day yesterday and I think they are in again this morning," said one trader.

text:
SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar was knocked back from 9-1/2-year highs on Tuesday by suspected central bank intervention, but the Philippine peso climbed to a six-year peak thanks to inflows that had piled up over Easter.   

 Wariness about official intervention to curb currency gains kept other Asian units in a tight range, although sentiment remained positive due to the firm tone in equity markets.   

 Stronger-than-expected economic growth and the central bank's decision to stick to a policy of modest currency appreciation lifted the Singapore dollar to 1.5110 per U.S. dollar <SGD=>.   

 But the gains proved fleeting and it fell as low as 1.5188 on suspected U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).   

 Still, dealers said the central bank's monetary policy stance and optimism about the economy meant that bullish sentiment towards the local dollar would hold sway.   

 "We definitely had first-quarter GDP on the strong side of expectations, so that would seem to indicate that Singapore is handling the downturn in the electronics cycle quite well," said Magnus Prim, chief strategist for Asia at SEB.   

 "The MAS still has a modest tightening bias and that basically translates into a stronger currency, even though at this point in time we are at the stronger end of the band and that is why we probably saw them intervening."   

Singapore's economy grew an annualised 7.2 percent in the first quarter, well above forecasts, although a little slower than in the previous quarter.   

 The central bank maintained its policy of a "gradual and modest appreciation" in the Singapore dollar. It uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates to conduct monetary policy and guides the currency in a secret trade-weighted band.

title: 2nd UPDATE: Singapore Keeps SGD Policy; 1Q GDP Tops Views
text:
(Adds comments from economists, breakdown of first quarter GDP, background.)   

By John Jannarone   

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank maintained its slightly restrictive monetary policy, and economists say the stance may remain through the year despite an outlook for slower economic growth.   

At its first semiannual review of 2007, the Monetary Authority of Singapore reaffirmed its preference for a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar - a policy in place since April 2004.   

First quarter economic growth figures, also released Tuesday, confirmed economists' views that the economy decelerated, but the growth was faster-than-expected.   

On a seasonally adjusted and annualized basis, the economy expanded 7.2% from the fourth quarter, after growing 7.9% in the previous three months. A Dow Jones Newswires poll had forecast a 3.7% expansion.   

Citigroup economist Chua Hak Bin said the modest deceleration in growth from the fourth quarter is an encouraging sign as it shows the economy "has held up well despite a slowdown in the electronics cycle."   

He expects the economy to grow 6.2% in 2007, slower than 7.9% in 2006, but near the top end of the government's 4.5% to 6.5% target.   

Compared with a year earlier, the economy grew 6.0%, slower than the 6.6% growth in the fourth quarter. The Dow Jones poll forecast on-year growth of 5.4%.   

Singapore's exports and manufacturing were weak in the first quarter due to softer demand from the U.S. for the country's mainstay electronic products.   

Manufacturing output grew 6.1% in the first quarter from a year earlier, slowing from 7.7% in the fourth quarter, with strength in ship and oil rig construction helping offset weak electronics.   

But investment in transport and marine equipment, which contributed nearly three percentage points to economic growth in the fourth quarter, may not be sustainable in 2007, said HSBC economist Robert Prior-Wandesforde.   

"The growth in the first quarter is still very much driven by transport equipment," he said.   

"I do think the area is vulnerable and if transport equipment investment does fall back at some point, it would leave the economy exposed."   

The services sector grew 6.1%, down modestly from 6.6% in the fourth quarter, while construction output surged 7.0% after posting only 2.7% growth in the fourth quarter.   

Improved construction output partly reflected the recovery in Singapore's residential and commercial property markets.   

Current Policy Offers Cushion   

Most analysts predicted the MAS would leave its policy unchanged, and many contend the stance will hold again at the next review in October.   

They say the currency, which the MAS manages within a secret band, has sufficient room to depreciate without an outright change in overall policy.   

"The MAS will have flexibility to allow a weaker currency without a change," Prior-Wandesforde said.   

In its statement, the central bank confirmed a widely-held view that the trade weighted Singapore dollar has fluctuated near the top of its policy band since October.   

Prior-Wandesforde said that economy is "not quite weak enough" to warrant a shift to a more accommodative policy.   

HSBC forecasts 4.9% growth in 2007, but Prior-Wandesforde said the target "is beginning to look a bit pessimistic."   

But if demand for Singapore's key electronics exports doesn't rebound in the second half, some say there's a chance the MAS will opt for monetary stimulus.   

Standard Chartered economist Joseph Tan said that Singapore's trade-dependent economy remains closely tied to the U.S., where downside risks are substantial.   

"The U.S. economy is not looking that hot," Tan said.   

"Whether or not the second half is going to look weak depends on the U.S. economy."   

Standard Chartered expects the U.S. economy to expand by 1.7% in 2007, but says the chance of a recession could prompt the MAS to switch to a neutral stance for the Singapore dollar.   

Ultra-low Inflation   

Tan said the MAS isn't expecting major inflationary pressure to result from an increase in the goods and services tax to 7% from 5%, due to take effect in July.   

The MAS said a two percentage point increase in the GST will add 0.5 percentage points to the CPI in 2007 and 2008.   

Tan said the last hike to 5% from 3% resulted in a 0.8 percentage point increase in the inflation rate.   

"The passthrough effect is not going to be as strong as the previous round - at least the MAS is not expecting it to be," he said.   

Tan said if prices for imports like fuel decline before October, the MAS may have even greater scope for looser policy.   

Following the GDP data and policy statement, the U.S. dollar fell to around S$1.5115 from S$1.5130 just before the announcement, but the momentum quickly faded.   

One trader said the stronger-than-expected growth figures pressured the Singapore dollar to appreciate, but the chance of central bank intervention prevented a sustained rise.   

The U.S. dollar has dropped to its lowest level against the Singapore dollar since 1997 in recent weeks, and analysts expect further declines in the months ahead.   

UBS expects the U.S. dollar to reach S$1.4800 by the end of the year, as encouraging growth prospects continue to draw capital inflows.   

The MAS primarily targets the exchange rate rather than domestic interest rates because import prices are the main driver of inflation in the city-state.

title: UPDATE: Singapore MAS Keeps Modest, Gradual SGD Rise Policy
text:
(Adds comments from the MAS, influences on the Singapore dollar, growth and inflation outlook.)   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank maintained its policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the currency, as the economy is expected to remain healthy this year and inflation remains low.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said Tuesday it won't re-center the undisclosed trade-weighted policy band for the currency, nor change the band's slope or width.   

All 10 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had expected the MAS to maintain the modestly tight policy stance.   

The central bank said the trade-weighted Singapore dollar has fluctuated near the top of its policy band during the last six months.   

The MAS operates monetary policy using the currency rather than interest rates, and intervenes to keep the Singapore dollar within a secret band that market participants estimate.   

Strength in the Singapore dollar reflected the broad-based weakness of the U.S. dollar, capital inflows into Asia and the relatively buoyant Singapore economy, the MAS said in a statement.   

The MAS reiterated its target for economic growth of between 4.5% and 6.5% in 2007, slowing from 7.9% in 2006, and maintained its forecast for full-year inflation to be in a range of 0.5% to 1.5%.   

"Looking ahead, the external environment is expected to remain broadly supportive of sustained growth," the central bank said.   

Growth from Singapore's export sector has moderated but economic activity will be buttressed by the services sector, it said.   

Ministry of Trade & Industry figures - also released Tuesday - showed that the Singapore economy slowed in the first quarter but still beat expectations.   

On a seasonally adjusted and annualized basis, the economy expanded 7.2% from the fourth quarter, after growing 7.9% in the previous three months. A Dow Jones Newswires poll of economists had forecast a 3.7% expansion.   

The MAS said a two-percentage-point increase in the goods and services tax that takes effect in July this year will add 0.5 percentage point to the CPI in 2007 and 2008.   

The increase in inflation will be tempered by offsetting fiscal measures and import costs being contained by the stronger Singapore dollar, it said.   

-By Singapore Bureau; Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4150; djnews.singapore.bureau@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Sing dlr retreats from highs,  intervention  suspected
text:
(Updates with latest price move, quote)   

SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit a 9-1/2-year high on Tuesday but then retreated, with dealers suspecting the central bank of buying U.S. dollars to curb the local currency's gains.   

By 0345 GMT the currency was trading at 1.5188 per U.S. dollar, down about 0.5 percent from the peak of 1.5110 hit earlier.   

Stronger-than-expected economic growth and a central bank decision to stick to a policy of modest currency appreciation had boosted the currency.   

"It does feel like they are in but it's hard to be sure," said one trader in Singapore, referring to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the central bank.   

Another trader said he suspected the central bank was intervening in the market, but not on a large scale.   

Singapore's economy grew an annualised 7.2 percent in the first quarter, well above forecasts although a little slower than in the previous quarter.   

The central bank maintained its policy of a "gradual and modest appreciation" in the Singapore dollar. It uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates to conduct monetary policy.   

"We were in the minority expecting the central bank to tighten by means of an increase in the slope of the band," Tim Condon, head of research at ING, said in a note.   

"We think it's only a matter of time before the MAS tightens, which makes us bearish U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar reached its highest level since 1997 in Asian trade Thursday on weakness in the U.S. dollar and strength in the Malaysian ringgit and the Chinese yuan.  

Traders need not worry about volatility in the market for the next week as the central banks in Malaysia and Singapore would intervene if their currencies appreciate too fast, said Alvin Liew, an economist from United Overseas Bank.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore has a policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar.  

The greenback weakened against major currencies after Wednesday's Federal Open Market Committee statement, and the Singapore dollar "went along with the regional currencies and strengthened against the U.S. dollar," said Liew.  

After announcing its widely expected decision to keep interest rates at 5.25% for a sixth straight meeting, the Fed softened its tightening bias and referred to "future policy adjustments" rather than specifying the possibility of future rate hikes as it has in past post-decision statements.  

The Singapore dollar also tracked the strength of the yuan and the ringgit. The U.S. dollar hit a post-reevaluation low of CNY7.7297 and touched a new nine-year low of MYR3.4570.  

Liew said the U.S. dollar would likely stay in the S$1.5100-$1.5200 range for the next week, with very strong support at S$1.5122, as the MAS is expected to intervene at this level.  

Another local bank dealer said the MAS would likely only slow the pair's fall and wouldn't intervene too aggressively to avoid volatility in the market.  

Singapore government bonds rallied, tracking the U.S. Treasurys, which rose after the Fed softened its tightening bias.  

"There's not much key data in the coming sessions, so I would expect to see some position readjustments in the Singapore bonds if the U.S. Treasurys move sideways in the near term," said a local bond dealer.  

He said the market would have to readjust the positions to accommodate S$2.9 billion worth of new bonds in April.  

The MAS announced the size of the next five-year Singapore bond auction after the market closed Wednesday. The amount was near the top end of market expectations.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia powers ahead as Fed modifies tone
text:
SINGAPORE, March 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies extended this week's gains on Thursday as the Federal Reserve removed a reference to possible interest rate rises in a policy statement, dealing a blow to the U.S. dollar.  

 However, as the regional currencies rallied, investors grew wary of central bank intervention to cap the gains.  

 Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=> hit a nine-year high at 3.4560 per dollar after the country's central bank governor expressed support for a stronger currency late on Wednesday.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose 0.5 percent to a 9-½   year peak at 1.5165 per U.S. dollar, the South Korean won <KRW=> hit a one-month high at about 936 per dollar and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> jumped 0.8 percent to a three-week high at 9,070 to the dollar.  

 On Wednesday, the Fed left rates steady at 5.25 percent, as expected. But the shift in tone in its policy statement knocked the dollar to a two-year low versus the euro <EUR=>.  

 The statement also triggered a rally in stocks, helping markets to recover further from the beating they took earlier this month on worries that weakness in the U.S. housing sector could spread to the broader economy.  

 Asia's stock markets notched up strong gains <.MSCIAPJ>. Tokyo's Nikkei share average <.N225> rose to a three-week high. The high-yielding Australian dollar <AUD=> briefly touched a 10-year peak against the dollar in another sign of a pick up in risk appetite.  

 "The Fed statement seems to be taken favourably by emerging markets and this is reflected by the weaker yen and stronger Aussie, which is an indication of the return of carry trades," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

 "This puts Asian currencies that have been suffering on the rebound."  

 Asia's high-yielding currencies have seen some of the strongest gains in the region this week. The rupiah, for instance, has risen almost 1.7 percent against the dollar.  

 SPOTLIGHT ON MALAYSIA  

 In Kuala Lumpur, an apparent change in the authorities' long-held view of favouring a cheap currency hogged the spotlight.  

 In the past two days, both the prime minister and central bank governor have expressed support for a stronger ringgit.  

 On Wednesday Malaysia further relaxed foreign exchange rules.  

 But some analysts say that rather than signalling a change in policy, Malaysia is reiterating its tolerance of gradual appreciation in the currency, with the central bank still expected to intervene in the market to limit sharp moves.  

 "They are now warming up to ringgit strength if the currency moves gradually," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur, referring to the government and central bank. "What they don't want is a shock to the market."  

 Still, the latest measures were seen boosting investor sentiment towards the ringgit and paving the way for fresh gains.  

 "Malaysia's currency measures encourage inflows and outflows. But in the current environment they encourage more inflows and this has been endorsed by the central bank, so the ringgit is staged for further appreciation," said Tan at Bank of America.  

CENTRAL BANK SPOTTING  

 Malaysia's central bank was suspected of intervening, while dealers said the Philippine central bank was seen buying dollars for pesos around 48.25 <PHP=>.  

 In Singapore, traders said that although there was some caution, the central bank was not expected to intervene just yet given the momentum behind the Singapore dollar's rally.  

 The currency has firmed about 0.6 percent in the past two days.  

 "Dollar/Sing after breaking 1.5240 support should have momentum to 1.5150 and lower," said a trader.  

 "Intervention is just to smooth the fall.. and I don't think the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) will be too keen to buy U.S. dollars at this level as the Sing dollar is strong on the crosses."  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0754 GMT

title: Singapore dollar rises to 9-1/2-year high
text:
SINGAPORE, March 21 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to its highest level in 9-½   years on Wednesday, benefiting from weakness in the U.S. dollar after a report that China would stop amassing currency reserves.  

 It rose as far as 1.5240 to the U.S. dollar, its highest level since October 1997. In late trade on Tuesday it was quoted at 1.5255.  

 China will stop stockpiling foreign reserves, China's central bank governor, Zhou Xiaochuan, said in an interview published on Tuesday.  

 The comments undermined the U.S. dollar in overnight trade although analysts questioned whether China would in practice be able to stop accumulating reserves.  

  Dealers said wariness about central bank intervention in the currency market could limit gains in the Singapore dollar.  

 "The China story overnight and selling of the U.S. dollar is driving the Sing dollar," said one trader in Singapore.  

 "I don't see them (the central bank) in the market, but there were rumours that they were there earlier. If they were there, dollar/Sing would not have come down so fast."  

 The Singapore dollar has also been boosted in the last few days by talk of a possible tightening in Singapore's monetary policy.  

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which is expected to meet in April, sets monetary policy through the currency instead of interest rates. It guides the Singapore dollar within a secret, trade-weighted band. title: Emerging  FX -Asia nudges up with yuan after China rate rise
text:
SINGAPORE, March 19 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies edged up against the dollar on Monday, with sentiment slightly bullish after a weekend decision by China to raise interest rates boosted hopes of faster yuan appreciation.  

 The yuan <CNY=CFXS> touched a post-revaluation high of 7.7330 to the dollar, while China's main stock index <.SSEC> bounced back from early losses to jump nearly 3 percent.  

 The reaction in Chinese stocks to the rate move was in focus given recent volatility in global markets and its rally, together with gains in other Asian equity markets <.MSCIAPJ>, supported local currencies.  

 "The Shanghai stock index, and other equity markets in Asia, shrugged off the rate hike. One possible reason for the reaction could be that some in the market inaccurately perceive this as the end of rate hikes in China," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

 "I doubt the rate move has a significant impact on where the yuan is trading right now, but it is a possible endorsement of further yuan appreciation."  

 China lifted its benchmark one-year yuan lending and deposit rates by 0.27 percentage point each, taking the one-year deposit rate to 2.79 percent and the lending rate to 6.39 percent.

 Malaysia's ringgit strengthened to about 3.4960 per dollar <MYR=>, its highest in just over two weeks, while in onshore trade in Thailand, the baht <THB=TH> hit 34.79 to the dollar -- its strongest since about September 1997.

 "So people are just taking this into consideration and maybe also that the MAS might change their policy next month. I doubt this will happen though."
