SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened in line with broad U.S. dollar weakness in Asian trade Friday.  

"The dollar story is slowing beginning to come back. It is coming back into play with the risk aversion story, so next week should be interesting," said Emmanuel Ng, a forex strategist from the Overseas Chinese Banking Corp.  

He said U.S. dollar weakness has been "the flavor for the day" following weak manufacturing data from New York and Philadelphia Thursday night. The stronger February U.S. producer price index didn't help the greenback, he said.  

"The dollar-Sing will continue to be heavy (next week), with support first at S$1.5250, then at S$1.5200," Ng said. He doesn't expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene until it is near S$1.5200.  

The MAS manages the currency within an undisclosed trading band as its key monetary policy tool.  

Another local bank dealer said the yen carry trade would likely continue to affect the U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar, but he thinks the pair should remain heavy in the long term, due to a strong Singapore economy.  

He said the decline in Singapore's February non-oil exports had little effect on the overall health of Singapore's economy.  

In the Singapore bonds market, prices fell, tracking the U.S. Treasurys.  

"The market is stabilizing now, though the rates are still quite soft," said a local bond dealer. "People are trying to figure out what the right levels are."  

She said liquidity in the shorter-dated bonds is drying up, as "the value for holding the current yield is way too low," which caused a bigger fall in the price in the shorter-dated bonds Friday.  

Overnight rates also spiked on "an outflow of funds, resulting in a lack of liquidity," she said.  

"People may buy the belly part of the curve if they need bonds," the dealer said. "However, there's an auction in (the first week of) April for five-year bonds, so response may be mixed."  

The five-year bonds traded at 2.73% at 0654 GMT Friday.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar traded sideways in Asia on Monday, with capital outflows from the weak stock market offset by some investors who bought the currency because of the local economy's strong prospects.  

"Domestic equities are still selling down, so there's capital outflow," said Selena Ling, head of treasury research at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.  

"At the same time, there are people who are buying the Singapore dollar, so the two-way interest offsets each other."  

A local bank dealer said investors who are bullish about the Singapore economy are taking this opportunity to buy the Singapore dollar despite an equities sell-down, resulting in a tight range in Monday's trade.  

The Straits Times Index fell below 2940 for the first time this year, with all 50 component stocks in the negative territory.  

Ling said people are waiting for more U.S. data later in the global session.  

"If there's good data, the selling of Wall Street may reverse slightly, and the Asian outlook will be more positive as well," she said.  

The U.S. ISM non-manufacturing index is due at 1500 GMT.  

The local bank dealer said the Monetary Authority of Singapore isn't likely to intervene unless the pair falls to S$1.5200.  

Dealers expect the pair to trade between S$1.5210 and S$1.5350 for the rest of the week.  

The MAS operates monetary by managing the currency in an undisclosed trading band.  

Singapore government bond prices were higher across the board.  

"The bond market is traditionally a safe haven," said a local bond dealer.  

"The key's still the equity market. If equities continue to fall tomorrow, bond prices will continue to rise."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly in Asian trade Thursday on weak sentiment toward the U.S. dollar and as regional currency markets that were roiled Wednesday were more stable.  

Emmanuel Ng, a forex strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp., said reduced aversion to risk, a rebound in regional stock markets and reduced liquidation of carry trades between the yen and the long Singapore dollar stabilized the local market.  

Foreign exchange markets were shaken Wednesday by a global selloff in stock markets that began in Shanghai on Tuesday.  

"If the risk aversion goes away, the pair will head lower," Ng said. "There's still weak dollar sentiment now, keeping the USD/SGD top heavy."  

A local bank dealer said bearish sentiment toward the major currencies should see the U.S. unit continue to weaken against the Singapore dollar.  

He said the pair isn't in danger of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore with the market "too calm" to warrant any action.  

Ng said the Singapore dollar's trade weighted index isn't near the extreme strong end of its trading band and so intervention isn't likely.  

The MAS conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed policy band. The central bank currently has a policy stance of allowing a gradual and modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar.  

Traders expect the pair to trade in the familiar range between S$1.5260 and S$1.5300 for the rest of the week.  

Singapore government bonds fell slightly, tracking U.S Treasurys.  

"There was too much action the past two days, the market is trying to catch its breath now," said a bond dealer.  

"The equities market is recovering, so prices for the bonds will fall a little. Overall, it should consolidate after the strong rally."

title: Indonesian rupiah, peso off lows,  intervention  cited
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso were pushed off their lows on Wednesday by suspected central bank dollar selling, but both currencies remained weak amid heightened risk aversion in global markets.   

Traders said the Indonesian and Philippine central banks sold the dollar for their local currencies which had come under pressure as investors unwound yen-funded carry trades following a steep sell-off in global stock markets.   

By 0315 GMT, the rupiah was quoted at 9,175 per dollar <IDR=>, down 1 percent from levels seen late in Asia on Tuesday, but off a three-month low hit earlier at 9,195.   

The peso <PHP=> stood at about 48.60 to the dollar, down about 0.4 percent and just off a three-week low of 48.65. "They just want to smooth the movement, nothing more than that," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the suspected intervention in Indonesia and the Philippines.   

Dealers said they suspected that Bank Indonesia had bought the rupiah around the 9,200 level against the dollar, while a trader in Manila said the central bank there stepped into the market when the peso weakened to 48.65 per dollar.   

"They were just there to dampen the volatility and prevent things from getting out of hand," the trader said.   

"The market does seem to have settled down a bit and I don't think there is any panic."

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah leads weak Asia on equity falls
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah led the decline in Asian currencies on Wednesday as regional stock markets fell and investors unwound yen-funded carry trades following a steep sell-off in global stock markets.   

Traders said the Indonesian and Philippine central banks sold the dollar for their local currencies as the rupiah and peso led a broad decline in most Asian currencies.   

The rupiah <IDR=> recovered from a three-month low of 9,195 per dollar, but was still down about 0.8 percent at 9,150 per dollar. The peso <PHP=> was near 48.50 per dollar, down a quarter of a percent and just off three-week lows.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell a third of a percent to 941.6 per dollar, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> also dipped nearly 0.3 percent to around 1.53 per U.S. dollar.   

Analysts remained bullish about the underlying strength of Asian currencies in general, citing the region's solid economic growth and hefty balance-of-payment surpluses.   

"I think what we see right now in the market is just a reaction to what happened yesterday, so you see people starting to get a bit risk averse again," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia currency strategist at SEB.   

"But I see the fundamentals are still pretty good and the falls should prove to be a short-term correction," he said.   

The yen <JPY=> fell against the dollar, taking a breather after surging to 10-week highs in the previous session as investors unwound risky trades on fears of rising volatility.   

A tumble in global stock prices including the biggest daily fall in Chinese stocks in a decade, soft U.S. economic data and growing tensions with Iran jolted investors from complacency and prompted them to cut exposure to risk.   

The Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index, or VIX <.VIX>, rose 70 percent on Tuesday in another sign of investor jitters. The VIX typically rises as investors become anxious about the stock market and tends to fall when fear subsides.   

Asian equity markets <.MSCIAPJ> were weaker on Wednesday, but Chinese stocks <.SSEC> rose about 4 percent on Wednesday after falling nearly 9 percent on Tuesday.   

China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit a new intraday post-revaluation high of 7.7378 per dollar, extending the previous day's gains.   

RUPIAH, PESO FACE BIGGER PRESSURE   

Aslim Tadjuddin, a deputy Indonesian central bank governor, said that the bank views a sharp fall in the rupiah as temporary and will do "everything necessary" to defend the currency.   

But traders said the central banks would not over-react.   

"They just want to smooth the movement, nothing more than that," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the suspected intervention in Indonesia and the Philippines.   

JPMorgan analysts Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho said in a research note that the rupiah, the peso and the Indian rupee would face greater pressure as investors had borrowed the cheaper yen to build long positions in the units.   

"While we struggle to identify fundamental changes in the external backdrop that warrants a fundamental reversal of the carry backdrop, we acknowledge that the technical environment of market caution, heavy long risky asset positions and tight valuations mean pressures could remain for some time."   

The Thai baht, which has been caught in a two-tier market since the government imposed currency controls in December, gained about 0.3 percent to 35.43 per dollar onshore <THB=>.   

But it was volatile in offshore trading <THB=W>, moving between 33.05 and 34.10 per dollar.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened slightly in Asian trade Tuesday on continued U.S. dollar weakness against regional currencies, but traders expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene soon.  

"The Singapore dollar is edging quite close to the level where the MAS could intervene. The threshold is about 0.1% to 0.2% from its current level," said Nizam Idris, an analyst at UBS.  

"I don't think the MAS wants to intervene significantly to push it (the local currency) down. It's too much volatility in the market, and it's not what they usually want to do."  

Idris, therefore, predicts that the pair could stay in its current range for a "long, long time".  

Singapore's central bank manages the local currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

Another foreign bank trader said that some dealers are buying the U.S. unit "in anticipation of an intervention" and that they would take profit if the pair reaches S$1.5310.  

Singapore longer-dated bonds rose, tracking a rally in the U.S. Treasurys.  

"The bonds will follow the U.S. market this week," said a local bond dealer.  

Bonds had also rallied Monday after the first auction of 20-year Singapore government bonds was at a lower-than-expected yield.  

"There's enough supply in the 20-year bond. Traders were just adjusting their positions (yesterday)," the local dealer said.  

The market is also waiting fourth-quarter U.S. gross domestic product, which will be released Wednesday, and the February ISM Manufacturing Index data, which will be released Thursday.

"The (U.S.) dollar sentiment will remain soft (for this week)," said a foreign bank dealer.

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  talk as Philippine peso at 6-year high
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 20 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso stalled at a six-year high against the dollar in holiday-thinned Asian trade on Tuesday, reined in by suspected central bank intervention.  

Other Asian currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Thai baht <THB=> maintained extremely tight ranges, with much of the region still closed for the Lunar New Year holiday.  

Markets in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam were closed. China and Taiwan are shut for the whole week.  

The peso <PHP=> went back up to 48.03 per dollar, a six-year peak it struck on Monday, at which point it had gained one percent in a week.  

Traders said dollar bids from the central bank, seen several times in the past week, persisted.  

"Dollar/peso should be consolidating at these levels. There are some strong bids coming in at levels below 48.05 which may be from the central bank," said one Manila-based trader.  

Yet the trader said he would position for further gains in the peso and other Asian currencies.  

"Look at the euro's strength. Everyone's coming to the conclusion that we are in a weaker dollar scenario for a few more days," he said.  

The euro hit a six-week peak against the dollar on Tuesday, extending its rally on mounting expectations the Federal Reserve's next move would be to cut interest rates later this year.  

A two-day Bank of Japan policy meeting ends on Wednesday and operators remain divided over the chances of a rate rise. That lent little support to the yen <JPY=>, which weakened to near 120 to a dollar.  

PHILIPPINE GROWTH SURGE?  

Fundamental support for the peso seemed to be growing.  

An aide to President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo said on Tuesday economic growth might accelerate to seven percent this year from 5.4 percent in 2006, and eventually to a higher rate of 9 percent by 2009.  

Strong inflows of remittances from overseas workers and a rally in local stocks have bolstered the peso. The currency has gained 2 percent versus the dollar this year, making it Asia's best-performing unit.  

"Fundamentally it is a strong currency, and the risks are mostly cyclical," said UBS currency strategist Nizam Idris.  

Structural flows from exports and remittances remained strong and there was low risk of the government compromising on an improving fiscal position by spending more ahead of the May congressional elections, Idris said.  

"We could, however, see a slower pace of growth in remittances going forward."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened in Asian trade Wednesday after the government raised the city-state's 2007 growth forecast, but its upside was limited by suspected intervention by the central bank, traders said.  

"I think the only thing hindering the market from selling (the U.S. dollar) is the authorities. They had been rather aggressive (in intervening) two days ago, so the market will stay pat and wait for the level to stabilize," said an analyst at a research firm who declined to be named.  

Singapore's economy expanded an annualized 7.9% in the fourth quarter of 2006 from the third, faster than the government's advance estimate of 7.6%, and the 2007 growth target was raised to a range of 4.5%-6.5% from 4%-6%.  

Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened when the pair reached S$1.5380-S$1.5385.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore operates monetary policy by managing the local currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

A trader at a foreign bank said the Singapore government's budget, due Thursday, may influence trade because the size of a corporate tax cut and the timing for an increase in the goods and services tax are likely to be announced.  

The pair is likely to trade between S$1.5350 and S$1.5450 next week, the analyst from the research firm said.  

"It's a short week next week, so I doubt the pair will move much, unless the dollar-yen creeps lower or Bernanke says something dovish in his speech these two days."  

Markets in Singapore are closed Monday and Tuesday for the Lunar New Year Holiday.  

In the Singapore bond market, prices were mostly flat though shorter-dated bonds rose marginally on inflows, a local bond dealer said.  

"Right now, everyone is just focused on the 20-year auction," the dealer said. "Players are on the sideline, no one wants to make any bets before the 20-year."  

The size of the 20-year auction is likely to be announced Thursday or Friday.

title: Emerging  FX -Singapore dollar gets GDP boost, rest of Asia firm
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 14 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose on Wednesday following the release of stronger-than-expected economic growth numbers, but gains were tempered as the market remained wary of central bank intervention.  

Other Asian currencies also edged up against the U.S. dollar, supported by rallying stock markets, but trade was subdued ahead of U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's congressional testimony, which starts later in the day, and Japanese gross domestic product data on Thursday.  

The Singapore dollar rose as far as 1.5365 per U.S. dollar <SGD=>, up about 0.5 percent from Tuesday's one-month low, as data showed the Singapore economy grew at a faster-than-expected annualised rate of 7.9 percent in the fourth quarter.  

Economists had forecast 7.6 percent.  

"The GDP figure is good news for the Singapore dollar," said Alvin Cheng, a trader at Fortis Bank Hong Kong Branch.  

There was some caution as the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was suspected of intervening aggressively in the market on Monday to cap local currency strength. Traders said the central bank was probably in the market again on Tuesday.  

"Many traders love to sell dollar/Sing but the MAS intervention two days ago was very aggressive," Cheng said.  

"The Sing dollar is definitely a buy. People are waiting for dollar/Sing to move higher before selling for fear of running into MAS intervention."  

The 2007/08 Singapore budget on Thursday was the next focus for local markets.  

"Downside risks in the budget for the Singapore dollar include a one percent corporate tax cut instead of the expected 2 percent and increases to stamp duties or other negative changes to property-related items," United Overseas Bank said in a note.  

A FRESH STEER  

Asian currencies were expected to take their direction from the Bernanke testimony and Japan's fourth quarter GDP data.  

The Japanese figures could shed light on the interest rate outlook. At the moment, analysts are split on whether the Bank of Japan will raise rates at a meeting next week.  

"Everything is focused on the Q4 GDP number. The market is trying to hang its hat on that and it is a nice target but I'm not sure if it will be conclusive," said Ben Simpfendorfer, a currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

"The Taiwan dollar is interesting -- it is increasingly the region's funding currency and so what happens tonight and tomorrow could be important for it."  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> briefly touched a 3-1/2-month low at 33.098 per U.S. dollar before turning round, helped by stock market gains and a firmer yen.  

In India the rupee <INR=IN> was pushed higher after the Reserve Bank of India raised the cash reserve ratio -- the percentage of banks' total deposits they have to keep with it -- to 6.0 percent from 5.5 percent on Tuesday.  

The increase will take place in two stages, the first on Feb. 17 and the second on March 3, and follows a quarter-point increase in the main lending rate in January.  

"With the pace of monetary tightening having now ratcheted up, the chances of a meaningful correction in asset markets must be increasing," HSBC economist Robert Prior-Wandesforde said in a note.  

"The key issue is that demand growth has been exceeding supply for a long time now, largely as a result of a monetary policy that has been far too loose," he said in the note.

title: Emerging  FX -Sing dlr at 1-month low, c.bank's hand suspected
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 13 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit a one-month low against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday, extending falls on suspected central bank intervention, while a soft tone in equities kept other Asian currencies on the back foot.  

 A sharp sell-off in the Singapore dollar began overnight when the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was suspected of buying U.S. dollars and dealers said the central bank was probably in the market again on Tuesday.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> weakened as far as 1.5440 per U.S. dollar, its lowest level since Jan. 12, taking its drop so far this week to about 0.7 percent.  

 While MAS intervention to cap strength in the currency is not unusual, dealers said the scale of the latest bout of dollar buying had taken them by surprise.  

 "The intervention last night was pretty strong, we think it was in the region of $600-700 million," said a trader in Singapore. "We are at a bit of a loss as to why they intervened. Maybe they were trying to pre-empt any fall in dollar/yen."  

 Another market estimate put the overnight intervention as high as $1 billion.  

 The MAS conducts monetary policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates, holding the Singapore dollar in an undisclosed band. Its current policy is to pursue "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the trade-weighted currency.  

 To some analysts, the MAS intervention reflected a bid to stop speculators from pushing the Singapore dollar too high.  

 "Recent MAS intervention has been weak and not sufficient to dislodge offshore speculative positions. This time around, their intention has been clearly not just to cap Singapore dollar strength but squeeze out the spec positions," said one analyst.  

 "They're basically saying enough is enough -- let's be a bit more aggressive now."  

 Position-covering ahead of Thursday's Singapore budget and next week's Chinese New Year holiday also weighed on the Singapore dollar, another trader said.  

 EQUITY WEAKNESS  

 Other Asian currencies were undermined by a sell-off in regional equity markets <.MSCIAPJ> and failed to draw comfort from a rally in the Japanese yen <JPY=>.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> dipped to about 33.09 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest level since Nov. 2, as foreign investors dumped Taiwan shares for a second day.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=> slipped as much as 0.2 percent to a two-week low at about 939.40 per dollar, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell a third of a percent to about 9,075 per dollar, its lowest in about a week.  

 "There has been some dollar buying interest from local banks," said a trader in Jakarta. "Market sentiment is moderately bullish, and we could move to 9,080."  

 Market attention was turning to this week's main events -- congressional testimony on the U.S. economic outlook from Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on Wednesday and Thursday and Japanese economic growth data on Thursday.  

 "We have the Japanese GDP numbers and the Bernanke testimony coming up, so we won't see strong direction in the market for the next 48 hours," said OCBC Bank currency strategist Emmanuel Ng.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0757 GMT

However, the U.S. dollar is likely to slide in the next few sessions as the Chinese New Year holidays approach, a local bank economist said.  

"The Chinese market will be closed, and the offshore (non-deliverable forwards) will push the yuan up and that may put appreciative pressure on the Singapore dollar," he said.  

The outlook "will be clearer after the Chinese New Year."  

He doesn't expect the MAS to intervene again and questioned whether MAS did intervene.  

"I don't see why MAS would want to intervene though the Singapore dollar is at its toppish side," he said. "The other currencies are all range-bound."  

He expects the pair to trade between S$1.5300 and S$1.5450 for the rest of the week.  

One trader said the MAS employed DBS Bank to sell more than S$1 billion to drive the pair from around S$1.5340 to over S$1.5415 in the European session Monday. A DBS spokeswoman declined to comment.  

The MAS' main monetary policy tool is managing the currency in an undisclosed trading band.  

Another local bank dealer dismissed the market interest in the rumors and said, "It doesn't matter. MAS or no MAS, the damage is already done."  

Contrary to the economist's view, the local bank dealer predicts that the pair could rise in the near future.  

"There will be unwinding of yen crosses and one of them involves the Singapore dollar, so the Sing will fall," he said.  

The pair will be well-supported at S$1.5390, the dealer said.  

The dealer said the Singapore budget Thursday would likely be a nonevent for the market.  

The government has "already said what they wanted to do" and the market has priced in the effects of a cut in the corporate tax rate and an increase in consumption tax, the dealer said.  

In the Singapore bond market, there was little movement ahead of the auction of the Singapore government's first 20-year bond, which is expected Friday.  

"I don't expect much movement before the auction - what happens after that, it really depends on the issue size. This bond is out of the curve, so no one knows what it is like," said a local bond dealer.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was a tad higher in Asian trading Wednesday on expectations of a stronger Japanese yen in coming sessions.  

A local bank dealer said the U.S. dollar rose slightly against the Singapore dollar in the morning on buying by an American bank, but the effect was offset by the overall weak sentiment for the greenback ahead of the G7 meeting this weekend.  

Although U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and various Japanese officials had indicated that the yen issue won't be a major topic at the G7 meeting, German Finance Minister Peer Steinbruck said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal published Wednesday that he would push for a meeting of the G7 to discuss the low value of the yen.  

The G7 buzz has boosted the yen and other Asian currencies.  

Suan Teck Kin, an economist at United Overseas Bank, said the Monetary Authority of Singapore may decide not to intervene even if the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar fell to the bottom end of the trading band, he said.  

"If the dollar-Sing does not cross the S$1.5300 level, we are quite safe," Suan said. "If it strengthens beyond that level, official action may be expected. But this is difficult to say as authorities may let it run in view of the (G7) event coming up."  

The MAS' key monetary policy tool is managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

Dealers expect the U.S. dollar to trade between S$1.5300 and S$1.5350 for the rest of the week.  

The government bond market remained quiet.  

"The past three days' (trade has) been practically nonexistent," said a local bond trader. "In view that Chinese New Year is coming up, the whole of February is burned."  

"Everyone is playing a waiting game. Maybe it's calm before a storm," the trader said.  

She said everyone was anxiously waiting for the auction of the 20-year bond, which will likely fall on Feb. 26.  

The dealer predicts that the size of the 20-year bond would be large and would carry attractive yields.  

-By Wei Yi Lim, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4036; weiyi.lim@dowjones.com [ 07-02-07 0730GMT ]

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady in Asian trade Monday, as traders await the G7 meeting in Cologne this weekend.  

"Dollar-sing is currently traveling in no man's land," said one foreign strategist. "But the overall dollar-Asia tone is still heavy," with dollar declines expected over time.  

He said the Singapore dollar is trading "dangerously" near the top of the undisclosed trading band within which the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the currency, which could attract intervention.  

"Obviously the MAS will intervene again; it's part of the policy ... but it won't be massive intervention like what we saw last November," when the MAS was rumored to have aggressively sold dollars amid the week dollar tone.  

He said mid-term currency movements would largely depend on signals from the U.S.  

"If there's a higher expectation of a (U.S.) rate hike, dollar-sing will strengthen in the coming weeks," he said. "Otherwise, dollar-Asian will remain in range-trade."  

Another local bank dealer agreed the pair would trade in a tight range for the rest of the week.  

"Traders have no new leads at all. Everyone is focusing on the euro and the yen now, so we can only watch for the G7 this weekend," he said.  

Traders expect the pair to trade between S$1.5300 to S$1.5400 for the rest of the week.  

The Singapore bond market was equally quiet, mirroring U.S Treasurys.  

However, a local bond trader said more buying can be expected in the shorter-dated bonds for the rest of the month.  

"The old seven-year bond will expire on March 1," she said. "Traders are not rushing to replace it with the new 20-year bonds, as this is the first issuance, and they do not know what the size of the bonds will be, nor what to expect. So they will replace the expiring bonds with short-end bonds."  

-By Wei Yi Lim, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4036; weiyi.lim@dowjones.com

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged up in Asian trade Wednesday, but looks unlikely to gain further ahead of a host of key events in the U.S. tonight, market participants said.  

U.S. Treasury secretary Henry Paulson testifies before the U.S. Congress later in the day, while the Federal Open Market Committee will decide on interest rates and issue an accompanying statement. Also watched will be the U.S. preliminary fourth-quarter gross domestic product data.  

"The market's focus is more on the Paulson testimony," said DBS currency strategist Philip Wee.  

There is speculation that Paulson will not only be questioned about the Chinese yuan's value, but also about the recent weakness of the yen versus both the U.S. dollar and euro.  

"You will notice that ever since the U.S. dollar crossed Y120, the Asian currencies' appreciation has stalled," said Wee.  

If Paulson signals any sympathy with Europe's discomfort over the yen's weakness ahead of the G7 meeting of finance ministers starting Feb. 9, the yen, the Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies could rise.  

Currently the Singapore dollar is still near the top end of its trade-weighted band, according to United Overseas Bank.  

"SGD (Singapore dollar) should be capped at 1.5324 level in the extreme case, as it corresponds to the NEER (net effective exchange rate) at 2.5% above the midpoint," said a UOB report, implying this level would be an automatic trigger for central bank intervention.  

The Singapore central bank operates monetary policy by keeping the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

The Singapore bond market saw yields edge down in muted trade ahead of the FOMC decision.  

"Yields have gone up quite significantly in recent sessions so perhaps players are thinking the pendulum has swung too far and decided to reposition before the Fed statement," OCBC fixed income strategist Selena Ling said.  

A more hawkish Fed stance in response to recent strong U.S. economic data would likely provoke Singapore bond weakness tomorrow.  

Ling said that fears of this were probably overdone and that the Fed is unlikely to adjust its stance significantly.  

-By Singapore Bureau; Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4150; djnews.singapore.bureau@dowjones.com [ 31-01-07 0839GMT ]

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly higher in Asian trade Tuesday, but market participants say the unit still lacks a catalyst to break out of its recent tight trading range.  

"Sideways will still be the catch phrase for the next 24 to 36 hours," said a currency strategist at a local bank.  

The sideways trading pattern reflects investor caution ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve interest rate meeting that begins Tuesday, the strategist said.  

He added that Asian currencies as a group were starting to consolidate against the U.S. dollar ahead of the G7 meeting of finance ministers in Germany that starts Feb. 9.  

The meeting is likely to discuss the recent weakness of the Japanese yen and could act as a pivot for the value of the yen vs the euro and U.S. dollar, subsequently providing direction for regional currencies like the Singapore dollar.  

He expects solid near-term U.S. dollar support at S$1.5340 - where intervention could be triggered - and resistance at S$1.5430.  

Singapore's central bank manages the local unit within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band, and is suspected of recently intervening to stem Singapore dollar appreciation.  

Singapore unemployment and money supply data due Wednesday are likely to be overshadowed by external factors, according to United Overseas Bank.  

"We expect trading to be led by U.S. data releases and developments on the RMB (Chinese Yuan)," UOB said in a report.  

Singapore government bonds inched lower in quiet trade.  

"We are just tracking Treasurys," said a local bond trader. "There's some apprehension that the Fed statement may be more hawkish than previously expected, and that's keeping some players out of the market," he said.  

The Federal Reserve statement is due around 1800 GMT Wednesday.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was almost flat in Asian trade Thursday, but capital inflows continue to exert upward pressure on the local currency, traders say.  

"The Asian currencies (ex-Japan) are still being driven higher by strong equity-related inflows, and it is difficult to identify possible negative catalysts," a strategist at a local bank said.  

The prospect of an intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore is preventing a breakout of the Singapore dollar from its current range, analysts said.  

The central bank controls money supply by exchange-rate targeting and manages the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

At current levels, the Singapore dollar is close to the upper edge of the policy band, according to analyst estimates.  

United Overseas Bank estimated in a note that if the greenback fell to S$1.5330, the trade-weighted Singapore dollar would be 2.5% above the midpoint, or at the stronger edge of the policy band.  

Market participants said the MAS sold the city-state's currency overnight, driving the U.S. dollar up from S$1.5335 to S$1.5380.  

Thursday's appreciation of the yen against the Singapore dollar could have lessened the likelihood of further intervention, they said.  

The Singapore dollar weakened to Y78.37 from around Y78.85 earlier Thursday, easing the local unit away from the top of the band.  

A local trader said a decline in the greenback to S$1.5325 could trigger intervention, but said "much depends" on the yen.  

He added that the U.S. dollar would need a sustained break below Y120 before the Singapore dollar could continue its trend to the upside.  

In the government bond market, limited buying interest supported short-dated maturities, but activity was otherwise "very quiet," a local trader said.  

"The only real theme is the expected steepening of the yield curve in advance of the issue of the new 20-year bond," the trader said.  

Singapore is scheduled to issue its first 20-year government bond on Mar. 1.  

The next market catalyst may be U.S. existing home sales data expected later Thursday, and players will watch for a possible reaction by U.S. Treasurys.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia gets a supportive hand from the yen
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were largely steady on Thursday, underpinned by a strong recovery in the yen on reports that European officials may complain about yen weakness at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in February.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> was in focus before an interest rate decision, with comments earlier this week from the central bank governor dampening expectations for a rate reduction.  

 Gains in some regional currencies, such as the Singapore dollar <SGD=>, South Korean won <KRW=> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> were limited by wariness that authorities would or had stepped into the market to cap currency gains.  

 Westpac Bank analysts said the market was wary of central bank intervention on the Singapore dollar around the 1.5350 per U.S. dollar area.  

 In Seoul, the won ended the day around 936 per dollar after what dealers called "smoothing operations" by the authorities.

 A trader in Bangkok said dollar selling by exporters had pushed the baht up in thin volumes.  

 "There's also a rumour that maybe the Bank of Thailand will take action soon on the exchange rate -- there is a lot of pressure on it to ease the capital control regulations."  

 Since the central bank unveiled capital controls in December, there has essentially been a two-tier market in the baht, with an offshore and an onshore aspect.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly in Asia Wednesday, but growing concerns of central bank intervention may restrain further gains, traders said.  

Analysts said the currency is trading near the top of its undisclosed trade-weighted band, within which the central bank manages the currency as its chief policy tool.  

One trader said there were "good bids" for the U.S. dollar around S$1.5350, but "no sign of intervention" by the central bank Wednesday.  

Analysts said the Singapore dollar could gain further against the greenback if the local unit loses substantial ground against other currencies in the trade-weighted basket, especially the Japanese yen.  

The yen rose against most currencies late Wednesday, as short-sellers exited a carry-trade linked to the Australian dollar.  

The Singapore dollar weakened to Y78.80 from around Y79.20 late in the day, easing the local unit away from the top the band.  

One trader identified S$1.5340 as the nearest crucial support for the greenback, and a break below that could prompt a further short-term drop.  

Singapore government bonds rose slightly, despite U.S. Treasurys falling overnight.  

"The SGS market outperformed today, despite the negative cues from Treasurys and swap rates this morning," said a local market maker. "Buyers emerged early which led to stalemate in the market," she said.  

She added that long-dated issues also held up well, as the market is comfortable with the estimated $2.5 billion size of the new 20-year bond auction scheduled for Mar. 1.

title: Singapore Dollar Down Slightly, Remains Near Top Of Band
text:

 10-year bond yield:    3.14%    +3 bps

 10-year swap offer:    3.53%    +2 bps 
 2-10-year swap curve:  +7 bps   +1 bp 
   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar sounded a weak note in Asian trade Monday after a string of gains last week, with analysts saying the currency is unlikely to resume an upward momentum as the chance of central bank intervention remains high.  

"On Friday it was quite clear that the Singapore dollar was at the edge of the strong side of the band," a strategist said. "It corrected a little bit, but we're still bordering on the edge."  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses exchange rate targeting as its chief policy tool, managing the local currency within an undisclosed trade-weighted band.  

The local unit hit its recent peak Friday, with the U.S. dollar touching a low near S$1.5340. But by Monday, the trade-weighted Singapore dollar fell some 0.5%, temporarily reducing the chance that the MAS would intervene, another strategist said.  

But analysts say even a modest decline in the greenback against the Singapore dollar could prompt the central bank to act.  

"I think if (the U.S. dollar) reached S$1.5370, we could see the MAS turn up," the first strategist said, adding that without intervention the first support is at S$1.5340.  

The second strategist said the central bank wouldn't intervene unless the greenback dipped to S$1.5325.  

Meanwhile, Singapore government bonds fell slightly, with the yield curve steepening as a bid for shorter-dated maturities appeared mid-session, traders said.  

"Yields were up at first, but there was some buying later...and the short end held up the best," a trader said.  

The Singapore dollar overnight deposit rate, currently at 3.125%-3.000% remains relatively low, and may be supportive of short-dated issues in coming sessions, another trader said.  

"The cost of funding is fairly low, and it's helping the short-end," the second trader said.  

The MAS announced Monday that it would issue S$1.7 billion in two-year government notes in a reopening of an existing issue.  

However, the auction size met expectations, and didn't prompt a reaction in the market, the trader said.  

-By John Jannarone, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4152; john.jannarone@dowjones.com

title: Thai fin min: job of halting baht rise done-report
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Thailand had no choice but to intervene to stop the rise of the baht, a job that has now been done, the country's finance minister said in an interview published in the Singapore Straits Times newspaper on Saturday.  

Pridiyathorn Devakula, also Thailand's deputy prime minister, reiterated the threat to exports posed by the currency's rise, the original reason given for capital controls imposed on Dec. 18.  

"Exports comprise 60 percent of gross domestic product. Thailand owes its growth to exports," he told the newspaper.  

Thailand's central bank announced rules on Dec. 18 targeting short-term speculators with limits to the amount of money they could pull out of the country within a year of investing it.  

The rules were diluted the next day after a near 15 percent one-day fall in the Thai stock market forced the bank into a U-turn.  

Despite the market reaction, and strong criticism of the central bank from investors, Pridiyathorn said he had to give bank governor Tarisa Watanagase full credit for taking the strong measures necessary to curb the baht's rise, the Strait Times reported.  

The Thai minister said China's currency controls were part of the reason for having to arrest the rise of the baht.  

"If China allows its currency to appreciate, Thailand would not have to do this," he told the newspaper. Pridiyathorn also defended changes to the Foreign Business Act aimed at limiting the ability of foreign companies to control Thai firms through the use of nominees.  

He said that if a police investigation found that Singapore's state investment firm Temasek Holdings had used nominees to exert control over Shin Corp., other companies in the same boat would be forced to hurriedly sell off shares.  

"I had to prevent that nightmare," he said.  

The rules ban foreign firms from owning 50 percent or more of Thai companies, but nominees are often used to gain de facto control. Thai police are investigating whether Temasek followed this route after buying its stake in Shin Corp. from ousted former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker in Asian trade Friday because of suspected intervention by the central bank and on generally bullish U.S. dollar sentiment due to a soft Japanese yen and euro.  

"The Singapore NEER (net effective exchange rate) was at the top of the band, so something definitely had to be done," said a foreign bank dealer.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore operates monetary policy by keeping the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

The dealer said the performance of the pair in the short term will be dependent on the Bank of Japan's interest rate decision next week.  

"If there's no rate hike, the dollar-yen will go higher, and the dollar-Sing will have to follow suit," he said.  

Another local bank dealer was optimistic about the greenback in the short term.  

"We will see some upward bias (for USD/SGD) next week and it may test S$1.5500," he said. "The (U.S.) dollar is bullish now, but I think it is only for the time being."  

CMC Markets analyst Ashraf Laidi said the most immediate downside risk to the U.S. dollar remains a rebound in the oil price.  

Crude oil futures fell below US$52 per barrel for the first time since May 2005 on Thursday in the U.S. If the price rose to US$57-US$59, the euro would likely see a resurgence of buyers and the U.S. dollar would likely be capped at Y121.00, he said.  

In the Singapore bond market, prices fell, tracking the global bond market.  

A local bond dealer said the Bank of England's surprise interest rate hike and "reasonably good data" in the U.S. overnight caused bond prices to fall globally.  

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported initial unemployment claims fell 26,000 to 299,000 in the week to Jan. 6 - the first reading below 300,000 since July 2006 and another sign of economic strength for the U.S.  

The dealer said bond investors will be watching the U.S. December retail sales due at 1330 GMT. A Dow Jones Newswires survey of 21 economists produced a median estimate of a 0.7% gain in sales.  

Next week, the Singapore market has export data to look forward to.  

Emmanuel Ng, a strategist from Overseas Chinese Banking Corp., said the December non-oil exports are unlikely to disappoint on the downside, considering reasonably good data from the region, such as the Taiwan exports.  

"If the data doesn't disappoint on the downside, the bond yields would be fairly supported," he said.  

The December non-oil exports data are due Wednesday.  

-By Wei Yi Lim, Dow Jones Newswires, 65-6415-4036, weiyi.lim@dowjones.com [ 12-01-07 0703GMT ]

text:

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar gained Wednesday in Asia on the first trading day of 2007, reflecting investors' strong appetite for Asian currencies, traders said.  

"Asian currencies are in demand now," said one foreign bank dealer. "It is looking very bright for all the Asian currencies and a lot of hot money is coming in."  

"The U.S economy is slowing down...so, naturally, investors would choose the strong Asian economies, which in turn benefit the Singapore dollar," he said.  

The Singapore dollar's appeal was underscored by a government report Wednesday that said gross domestic product grew a seasonally adjusted 7.6% in the fourth quarter from July-September, faster than the third quarter's 5.6% expansion.  

Thio Chin Loo, a foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas, said Asian currencies look very bright and they will "start the year very well."  

She predicts the U.S. dollar to be supported at S$1.5250 in the near term.  

But the currency's strength means there is a risk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

"I don't dismiss MAS intervening. MAS is always there to smoothen any market swings," she said.  

"The level of the decline is not so important. Instead, if the pair falls too quickly or it's not in level with the rest of its major trading partners, then MAS would step in."  

The MAS operates monetary policy by managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

The Singapore dollar's gains sparked a rally in the bond market, especially in the shorter-dated bonds.  

"We are trading on our own today because of the strong Singapore dollar. After this, we will continue to track the U.S. Treasurys as per normal," a local bond dealer said.  

Traders are watching the U.S. December ISM Manufacturing Index and the Federal Open Market Committee Meeting later in the global session.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Slightly, Chance Of MAS Action Higher
text:

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar gained modestly on light volume in Asian trade Thursday but lost momentum as the possibility of central bank intervention increased, traders said.  

"I'm not sure the Singapore dollar will hold here," a trader said. "The (trade-weighted) exchange rate is pretty high, and I think the central bank could come into the market."  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore uses the exchange rate as its chief policy tool, managing the local unit within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

Early in the Asian day, the trade-weighted Singapore dollar gained from Wednesday, but retraced some of its rise to about 1.0% above the center of the band, DBS currency strategist Philip Wee said.  

Wee estimates that if the U.S. dollar fell to S$1.5290 - with the Singapore dollar steady against other basket currencies - the trade-weighted unit would reach the top of the band, about 1.5% over the midpoint.  

But traders say the MAS recently acted when the unit was inside the band's upper limit and that there is significant chance of intervention at current levels.  

Singapore government bond yields opened three to four basis points higher after yields on U.S. Treasurys rose five to six basis points overnight on stronger-than-expected housing data in the world's largest economy.  

But buyers in the local market later reversed much of the losses, reflecting year-end volatility that may extend through Friday.  

"There was late bottom-picking that brought the long end back toward yesterday's levels," a trader said. "The market is thin, and it doesn't take much to move it."  

Speculators' modest appetite for government paper was forceful enough to drive yields below the day's opening levels, the trader said.  

U.S. November existing home sales data, due later Thursday, could have an impact on fixed-income markets, but only on a major surprise.  

"It would have to deviate far from what the market has already positioned for," the trader said.

Singapore government bond yields opened three to four basis points higher after yields on U.S. Treasurys rose five to six basis points overnight on stronger-than-expected housing data in the world's largest economy. But buyers in the local market later reversed much of the losses, reflecting year-end volatility that may extend through Friday. 'There was late bottom-picking that brought the long end back toward yesterday's levels,' a trader said. 'The market is thin, and it doesn't take much to move it.' Speculators' modest appetite for government paper was forceful enough to drive yields below the day's opening levels, the trader said. U.S. November existing home sales data, due later Thursday, could have an impact on fixed-income markets, but only on a major surprise. 'It would have to deviate far from what the market has already positioned for,' the trader said. -By John Jannarone, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4152; john.jannarone@dowjones.com -Edited by Ven Ram -0-

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady in Asian trade Wednesday after the Federal Open Market Committee again left interest rates unchanged. That will likely leave the local currency rangebound, as market activity wanes prior to the year-end holiday.  

The Fed announced Tuesday that the U.S. policy rate would stay steady at 5.25%, the fourth consecutive pause after 17 straight increases.  

One foreign bank analyst said market players now have lower expectations for the Singapore dollar since the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened heavily two weeks ago to hold the currency down.  

"That was probably the last wave of intervention for the year," the analyst said. "There may be some players who are interested to have the Singapore dollar leap back to the higher levels seen last week, but liquidity of the Singapore dollar will have to surge by the end of the year to see that kind of level again."  

But that is unlikely, as "the year is closing and hence, the market is thinning," said one local bank dealer.  

Last Thursday, the Singapore dollar reached its highest intraday level in nine years at S$1.5364.  

The analyst said the Singapore dollar's trading band is now "moving away from the persistent strength and has found a new, comfortable, lower level."  

But the local bank dealer said that while the Singapore dollar may not be as strong as it was last week, the greenback is still relatively heavy, and there are still heavy Singapore dollar inflows.  

"Besides the casino-resort-linked inflows, there are Asian currency inflows across the board," he said.  

Traders expect inflows for financing the multi-billion-dollar casino-resort that was awarded Friday to Genting International (G13.SG) and its consortium partner Star Cruises Ltd. (S21.SG), both units of Malaysian gaming company Genting Bhd. (3182.KU).  

The local bank dealer expects resistance for the U.S. dollar at S$1.5420, and support at a "risky" S$1.5300 for the rest of the week.  

In the Singapore bond market, prices were up slightly, tracking U.S. Treasurys, with traders echoing the view that there is no story in the local bond market for this year.  

"There's really nothing" said one local bank dealer.  

However, he said the 20-year bond auction, likely to be held in February next year, would be noteworthy.  

"It's the first issue of the extended yield curve, so it's anyone's guess on how it would perform," the dealer said. "For such a long-term bond, it will usually attract investors and foreign funds, so it will be interesting to judge the foreign demand."  

"For the rest of this year, just keep watching the U.S. Treasurys," he said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia up, Thai baht rally sparks  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand bought dollars on Tuesday to rein in the baht as Asia's best performing currency hit its highest since the Asian financial crisis, while other regional currencies followed its firm tone.  

 The baht <THB=> retreated to 35.32 per dollar after reaching 35.23, its strongest since October 1997, strengthening beyond its previous high of 35.46 per dollar set in December 1998.  

 Assistant governor at Bank of Thailand, Suchada Kirakul, told reporters that the central bank had intervened, buying dollars to try to slow the rise of the baht.  

 But she said the bank would take time to consider whether fresh measures were needed to deter foreign speculation in the baht after it imposed curbs last week to block access by foreign speculators through domestic bond and debt paper transactions.  

 A dealer at Bangkok Bank said he expected the central bank to impose new curbs to target currency speculation in the baht to prevent the currency from breaching the key 35-per-dollar level.  

 "A break below 35.00 could herald more selling, although we expect the BOT to guard this level religiously," said Thio Chin Loo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas.  

 Christy Tan, currency analyst at Bank of America in Singapore, said markets were betting on a decision from the Bank of Thailand to keep interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, which would underpin the Thai currency.  

 The Thai central bank meets on Wednesday to review its monetary policy, but 8 of 9 analysts surveyed by Reuters predicted the central bank would leave its 14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.  

 The baht has gained around 16.6 percent so far this year, prompting worries among local exporters that the currency's rise could crimp their revenues and make their goods less competitive.  

 OPTIMISTIC  

 Most analysts and dealers remain optimistic about the near-term outlook on Asian currencies as capital flows into the region and trade surpluses persist, despite a wave of verbal and actual intervention by central banks to cap currency strength.  

 But some analysts believe currencies such as the baht and the South Korean won, so far leading the rally, would probably lose pace while the Malaysian ringgit and Indian rupee were likely to outperform in the weeks ahead, since they have lagged the rally.  

 The won <KRW=>, which led declines in Asian currencies in the past two sessions, gained about a third of a percent on Tuesday to 922.4, with dollar purchases from exporters outweighing suspected intervention by local authorities.  

 The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> strengthened to as far as 3.538 per dollar, its highest level in nearly nine years, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> gained a fifth of a percent to 49.45.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained about a quarter of a percent to 1.54 per U.S. dollar, still off a nine-year high of 1.5362 struck last week.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> hovered between 32.41 and 32.55

title: Emerging  FX -S.Korean won down on  intervention , rest follow
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 8 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention forced the South Korean won to retreat on Friday from the previous session's nine-year high and other Asian currencies fell, too, with analysts suspecting a three-week rally was losing steam.  

The dollar's listlessness against the majors played a part as traders held back ahead of U.S. non-farm payrolls data that could provide fresh pointers to the way Federal Reserve policy is headed.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> straddled 1.54 per U.S. dollar, barely changed from Thursday and less than half a cent away from a nine-year high of 1.5362 struck earlier this week.  

The won <KRW=> fell to levels on the weaker side of 920 per dollar, slipping fast from Thursday's high of 912.6.  

At those highs, the won had gained 11 percent this year.  

Traders said the Bank of Korea could have bought up to $1.8 billion.  

"Today, it's profit-taking and intervention," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist with Deutsche Bank, referring to the won's decline.  

The won's rally on Thursday to nine-year highs surprised analysts because it followed a Bank of Korea announcement that the reserve ratio on foreign currency deposits was being raised from later this month.  

That measure was seen aimed at curbing foreign funds flowing into Korea, which were partly responsible for pushing up asset prices and the won.  

Baig said he was still positive on the Asian currencies.  

"I expect one to two percent more upside from here regionally but I would be keeping an eye out for positioning getting stretched," he said.  

PICKING THE WINNERS  

The Thai baht <THB=> was quoted as high as 35.49 per dollar, continuing to hit eight-year highs. The baht has risen in spite of Bank of Thailand measures announced this week to rein the currency in.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose, reaching a 3-1/2-month high near 9,040 per dollar in early deals before finding resistance.  

But some analysts said currencies such as the won and Thai baht, so far leading the rally, would probably lose pace while the laggards caught up.  

"I still think dollar/Asia is biased lower, but the market will be a lot more discriminating in which currencies it favours," said Sue Trinh, a currency strategist with RBC Capital Markets.  

"The Korean won should underperform the region, given it is expensive and given increased flexibility of the Asians," she said.  

Analysts reckon the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> and Indian rupee <INR=IN> are likely to outperform the region in the weeks ahead, since they have lagged the rally so far.  

"It seems those two currencies are standing out as leading contenders in 2007. In contrast, I expect Sing dollar and the won have had their time in the sun, which is not to say they won't appreciate, but gains will slow on a relative basis," Trinh said.  

The ringgit has appreciated 6 percent this year and the rupee less than 1 percent. That compares with a 15 percent gain for the baht and 8.5 percent for the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady in Asian trade late Thursday, as traders took a breather after the Singapore dollar reached its highest intraday level in nine years.  

Global U.S. dollar weakness pushed the unit to S$1.5368, its lowest level since October 1997, and is likely to continue to weigh on the greenback.  

"The U.S. dollar will continue to fall," said a foreign bank dealer.  

He said the major currencies would prolong their gains against the greenback, and the Singapore dollar "will dutifully track the yen and the euro, at least till the end of the year."  

Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at United Overseas Bank, said market watchers can take leads from the U.S.  

"(Treasury Secretary Henry) Paulson and (Federal Reserve Chairman Ben) Bernanke will be in China next week - they seem to be trying to shape the market's view to be less bullish on the Asian currencies," in case they don't achieve any change in forex policy in the meeting, he said.  

Locally, Koh doesn't expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene until the greenback trades at S$1.5240, but it will take "some time" to get to that level.  

The MAS' key monetary policy tool is managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

Koh predicts the greenback will continue trading between S$1.5320 and S$1.5400 for this week.  

In the debt market, bond prices were mixed in a relatively quiet market.  

"Bonds are generally muted because bonds had already reacted (to robust November U.S. non-manufactuturing data) yesterday," said Selena Ling, head of Treasury Research at Overseas Chinese Banking Corp.  

While market players may watch for the U.S. November nonfarm payroll data due 1330 GMT Friday, it may not have a great impact on the market, she said.  

"Treasurys have already adjusted prices after the ADP report, so it may be a non-event unless there's any big surprises," she said.  

An employment indicator published by Automatic Data Processing and Macroeconomic Advisers forecasts a 158,000 increase in the nonfarm payrolls, above economists' expectations for a 110,000 increase in jobs in a Dow Jones Newswires survey earlier this week.  

She also warned that bonds may be more volatile than usual in December, as liquidity is thin.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher, won shrugs off  intervention  fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies extended gains against a weak dollar on Wednesday as optimism about the region's economic picture offset worries about official intervention to curb currency strength.  

The South Korean won <KRW=>, backed by the yen's <JPY=> gains, jumped 0.9 percent and went as high as 915.9 per dollar, its strongest since October 1997.  

It has gained about 10 percent this year.  

The U.S. dollar slipped towards a four-month low against the yen and inched nearer a 20-month trough versus the euro due to expectations that its interest rate advantage would be eroded further.  

"I think it's still a weak dollar story -- Asian currencies that are backed by strong fundamentals are able to catch up," said UBS currency strategist Nizam Idiris. "The won is following the dollar story, but it's not that alarming for the Bank of Korea for now."  

The won's strength in recent days has been underpinned by dollar sales by exporters, despite caution over possible intervention by the Bank of Korea.  

Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=>, which jumped 0.8 percent on Tuesday, rose another 0.4 percent on Wednesday to 3.544 per dollar, its highest level in nearly nine years.  

On Tuesday a leading Malaysian think tank predicted it could rise to 3.5 in the first quarter of 2007 and called for the central bank to loosen its grip on the currency, which was depegged from the dollar in July 2005.  

It has gained about 6.7 percent so far this year but has underperformed other regional currencies, such as the Singapore dollar, South Korean won, Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht.  

FUNDAMENTALS MATTER  

A renewed rally in Asian currencies in recent weeks has sparked a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to curb their strength to protect exporters.  

"The symptoms of excessive liquidity remain, with regional bonds and equities rallying and showing an increasing mistrust of the dollar, despite all the policy makers' attempts to cajole the market into buying the dollar," Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at JPMorgan said in a research note.  

Sustained foreign capital flows into the region's equity markets and solid economic fundamentals, including large trade surpluses, are providing support for Asian currencies despite worries over a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy.  

The Thai baht <THB=>, which took a hit on Monday when the Bank of Thailand announced measures to tighten foreign exchange rules, rose a quarter of a percent on Wednesday, while the Indonesian rupiah traded between 9,094 and 9,115 per dollar.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger in Asian trade Wednesday, tracking a stronger Japanese yen.  

"The yen has finally moved higher, and this will likely continue," said one local bank dealer. "When the yen becomes stronger against the U.S. dollar, the Singapore dollar will follow suit."  

This could potentially lead to intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said Suan Teck Kin, an economist from United Overseas Bank.  

"The Singapore dollar will of course be dictated by the broad movement in the yen. The risk of intervention could be quite high if the U.S. dollar reaches S$1.532," Suan said.  

The MAS' key monetary policy tool is managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

The greenback could still fall further against the Singapore dollar, said another foreign bank dealer.  

"The Singapore dollar hardly moved relative to the regional currencies," so it may try to track the ringgit, he said.  

On Wednesday, the U.S. dollar fell to an intraday low against the ringgit of MYR3.5380, the lowest since March 1998.  

In the bond market, bond prices fell, especially in shorter-dated bonds, flattening the curve.  

"It's the year-end, people are going on leave so they are just clearing their positions," said a local dealer. "The liquidity in the short-end is very soft, so it actually doesn't make much sense to sell it."  

"Traders, however, are holding back on selling the long-end," she said. "They are unsure what is going to happen. If the U.S. declares a spike in interest rates, they will start selling the longer-dated bonds."

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar ended slightly lower Friday after the central bank apparently intervened to erase the local currency's early gains, and analysts said the local authority may remain active in days ahead.  

"The central bank wants to keep the market guessing," said a local trader.  

Traders say the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the local currency, intervened Thursday and Friday to dampen volatility and to keep the unit within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

One bank estimated that the trade-weighted Singapore dollar has weakened in the last two days, largely due to strength in basket currencies other than the greenback.  

As a result, there is some scope for the U.S. dollar to continue its decline without lifting the trade-weighted Singapore dollar beyond the policy band limit, a strategist said.  

However, the net effective exchange rate is still in the upper half of the MAS' target range, and intervention remains possible, the strategist said.  

He said the central bank may also intervene to minimize drastic fluctuations in the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar exchange rate, even if its market operations have only short-term effects.  

"There are actually two considerations," the strategist said. "The second is the volatility of the spot rate itself."  

Last week and on Thursday, the MAS bought U.S. dollars to weaken the Singapore dollar, but the rise in the spot rate retraced within hours.  

On Friday, traders said the MAS bid the U.S. dollar up to around to S$1.5470 from about S$1.5370, but the greenback eased back to S$1.5430 by 0600 GMT.  

In the debt market, government bond prices rose following a weaker-than-expected November manufacturing report in the U.S. that sent Treasury prices higher.  

The Singapore government bond yield curve steepened slightly, and some investment banks are predicting the two- to 10-year spread to rise by more than 30 basis points by the end of 2007.  

"If you look to the U.S., we may be entering a period of monetary easing, and the yield curve should get steeper," said Lee Wee-Kok, a strategist at Standard Chartered. "In Singapore it will be comparable."

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher, shrug off  intervention  jitters
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Sustained capital inflows sent Asian currencies higher on Friday as the U.S. dollar weakened globally, with the Thai baht <THB=> leading the rally amid signs of easing market concern about central bank intervention.  

Underscoring solid fundamentals buoying most regional currencies, South Korea said on Friday the country's exports in November grew a faster-than-expected 19.8 percent to a monthly record from a year earlier, maintaining surprising strength.  

"The risk appetite is still very good and there is no sign that any growth slowdown is impacting inflows into the region at the moment, and the dollar is softer," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

"So strong inflows plus a soft dollar, even with central banks intervening, means the trend remains in place," he said.  

Renewed strength in most Asian currencies in recent weeks has triggered a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to cap further currency appreciation.  

"Looking ahead, renewed interests for short dollar positions should place dollar/Asia on track to end this week with another decline," currency strategists Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at JPMorgan wrote in a research note.  

Thio Chin Loo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas, said she remained bullish about the near-term strength of Asian currencies, with the latest gains helped by dollar weakness.  

The dollar hit a 14-year low against sterling <GBP=> on Friday and a new 20-month trough versus the euro <EUR=> as the U.S. currency suffered from expectations a weakening economy will prompt the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates next year.  

BEST PERFORMERS  

The Thai baht and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> were Friday's best performers, with the baht gaining more than two thirds of a percent to 35.71 per dollar, its strongest level in eight years.  

The Bank of Thailand has been intervening both verbally and through actual dollar buying this week, traders said.  

Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said the baht, which has gained about 15 percent so far this year, was also supported as political uncertainty after a military coup in September eased.  

"People took another look at Thailand and said okay, inflation has peaked, growth is set to accelerate so quite a few investors who were underweight Thailand have come back in the past few months," he said.  

The latest Reuters poll on positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors stepped up long positions in the Thai baht and remained bullish on the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

The ringgit strengthened to about 3.5915 per dollar, up about 0.75 percent from levels traded late on Thursday. A trader said the ringgit's unusually sharp gains were largely due to technical selling of the dollar.  

The South Korean won <KRW=>, underpinned by third-quarter gross domestic product data that was revised upward, rose to as high as 927.1 per dollar, gaining moderately but still off a nine-year high this week of 925.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> firmed as high as 32.25 per U.S. dollar, hitting its highest level in about 4-½ months, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> briefly hit 1.5372 against the U.S. dollar, matching a nine-year high set on Thursday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR; Change on the day at 0728 GMT

* Rupiah falls on dollar-covering, steady after rate cut

 * Singapore dollar is seen near top end of its secret band

 * Vols drop as intervention fears shackle Asian currencies

 By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah fell on Wednesday as investors took a drop in local stocks as a cue to book profits, while most Asian currencies moved in tight ranges amid worries about possible official intervention.

 Suspected intervention by some Asian central banks to curb currency appreciation to help local exporters have driven down volatilities, with those of the Chinese yuan <CNYVOL>, Thai baht <THBVOL> and Korean won <KRWVOL> hitting multi-month lows.

 RUPIAH

 The rupiah <IDR=> lost 0.4 percent to 9,900 per dollar, a day after hiting its highest level since October 2008.

 It was little moved after Bank Indonesia cut its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.5 percent, in line with market expectations. [ID:nJAK372576].

 Traders expect the rupiah to strength further.

 "At this juncture, we continue to favour the rupiah on fundamental grounds," Emmanuel Ng, strategist at OCBC Bank, said in a note

 The rupiah, the best performing currency in Asia, has gained just over 11 percent against the dollar so far this year, supported by a revival in risk appetite amid optimism that the the global economy is on a path of recovery.

 One-month dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards <IDRNDFOR=> eased a tad to 9,880, implying little change from the spot. The NDFs traded 63 points below the one-month onshore forwards <IDR1M=> compared to 24 points on Tuesday.

 The South Korean won <KRW=> fell slightly in step with local stocks after a 4-day rally. [ID:nSEO354145]

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was stuck in a 1.4321-1.4345 range against the U.S. dollar, amid speculation that the central bank may intervene to stem the local currency's strength.

 The Singapore dollar has rallied 8 percent since early March, riding on fund inflows fanned by optimism about the global economy.

 "I reckon investors all see that the Singapore dollar is on the stronger end of the band and are worried that the authority might be around," said a Singapore-based trader, predicing the unit would move in a range of 1.4310-1.4350 for a while.

 Singapore's central bank steers monetary policy by managing the currency within a trade-weighted band against a basket of foreign currencies, rather than using interest rates.

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit fell against a broadly firmer dollar on Wednesday, while the Singapore dollar eased as investors fretted about possible intervention by the central bank to curb the currency's strength.

The dollar stayed firm against major currencies after gaining on safe-haven bids the previous session after an unexpected fall in U.S. consumer confidence cooled optimism about an economic recovery. [ID:nT146254]

Trading was lacklustre with Thailand's markets closed for holiday.

RINGGIT

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell 0.4 percent to 3.5260 per dollar, pressured by the U.S. currency's broad strength.

"Overnight euro softness on dollar short covering made dollar/ringgit biddish," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.

On Tuesday the ringgit hit its highest since mid-June after Prime Minister Najib Razak unveiled steps to attract foreign investment.

Some analysts suspect Malaysia's central bank, or BNM, may have been trying to weaken the ringgit to help exporters as its rate-cutting cycle draws to an end.

"We think BNM used dollar weakness to accommodate ringgit depreciation pressure and this explains the move in the Singapore dollar/ringgit cross rate earlier this month above its long-term 2.38-2.42 trading range," analysts at ING said in a note.


 "In view of the policy constraints -- BNM's easing cycle is
over and there will be no more fiscal packages -- we expect


Singapore dollar/ringgit to remain above 2.42 for the rest of the year," they added.

The Singapore dollar has gained 7 percent since early March, fanned by tentative signs of a recovery in the global economy.

In April, the central bank eased policy by lowering the mid-point of the undisclosed currency band to help the economy.

title: UPDATE: Singapore April Exports Fall At Faster Pace
text:
(Adds more details, background, analysts' comments)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's key exports fell for a 12th straight month in April - and at an accelerated pace - underscoring how fragile the economic crisis has left the island's main trading partners.

Non-oil domestic exports declined 19.2% in April from the same month a year earlier and compared with a revised 17.3% drop in March, the trade promotion agency International Enterprise Singapore said Monday.

Eight economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had forecast an 18.6% decline from April a year ago.

Tiny Singapore, which is highly dependent on external demand, is suffering its worst-ever recession.

Significantly, exports to China, which rose 14% in March and 8% in February, turned back down in April, falling 15% from the same month in 2008.

All eyes are on China and the pace at which it imports components from Asian neighbors, only to assemble them into products which it exports abroad, largely to the West.

"There is lot of uncertainty still hanging over (global demand)," said David Cohen of Action Economics. He expects the second half of 2009 to usher in a slight recovery in Singapore's exports.

According to the data, exports to all of Singapore's top 10 markets fell in April; the E.U., U.S. and Indonesia led the decline.

Exports to the U.S. - Singapore's largest export market - fell 35% from a year earlier after declining 31% in March. Shipments to the European Union fell 31% on year compared with a 24% decline the previous month.

Electronics exports to China fell 21% on year in April, mainly due to weaker demand for disk drives and personal computer components.

Overall electronics exports declined 25.6% in April from a year earlier on reduced shipments of personal computer parts, disc drives and semiconductors. Non-electronics exports slid 14.8% on year as exports of petrochemicals and disk media products declined.

Shipments to Japan fell 34% on year in April after dropping 33% the previous month; exports to Indonesia fell 33% in April compared with the same month in 2008.

"Perhaps the worst of the contraction may be behind us, but in terms of the headline numbers it's not really looking like we're on track for any meaningful V-shaped recovery," CIMB-GK economist Song Seng Wun said.

"There may be occasional sprouts of green shoots, but...I think the numbers we're seeing is a reminder that it's dangerous to extrapolate," Song said.

For the full year, Singapore's government now expects non-oil domestic exports to fall between 10% and 13%; the government earlier forecast exports would contract between 9% and 11%.

Seasonally adjusted and on a month-by-month basis, exports fell 1.3% in April, compared with a 10.4% rise in March; the surveyed economists had forecast a 0.5% drop in April.

The Singapore dollar barely budged on the export data, largely because the decline was close to expectations. The local currency last traded at 1.4690 at 0719 GMT.

In a related development, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has intervened in currency markets at least three times this month, buying U.S. dollars to smooth the Singapore dollar's rise, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Singapore's export competitiveness is highly dependent on the strength of its currency relative to major partner's currencies, especially the U.S. dollar.

Singapore is "happy" with the local dollar's current level but the MAS will buy the U.S. dollar again if it falls convincingly below S$1.4600, the person said.
