   By Costas Paris and P.R. Venkat 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore is ready to intervene in the currency market to brake the local dollar's rise, a person familiar with the situation said Thursday, while the central bank reaffirmed there is no change in its policy for the currency.

The Monetary Authority will buy the U.S. dollar "if it falls below S$1.4700, around S$1.4690," the person familiar with the situation told Dow Jones Newswires. He said S$1.4700 to the U.S. dollar roughly equates with the strong end of the Singapore dollar in terms of the undisclosed trade-weighted band that the MAS uses to guide the currency.

These remarks were "a very strong signal" to the market that the MAS doesn't want the Singapore dollar pushing too high, said a trader with a foreign bank. But he predicted the local currency will continue to rise in coming days if there are no negative economic surprises.

And indeed, a top central bank official separately reiterated the MAS doesn't plan to deliberately drive the Singapore dollar lower over time.

"We keep our monetary policy on the medium-term inflation outlook and taking into account growth prospects," Managing Director Heng Swee Keat told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. "We don't use the currency for competitiveness because it is not sustainable to align currencies just for competitiveness."

Heng declined to comment on specific levels for the Singapore dollar.

The MAS uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its chief policy tool, because trade flows dwarf the island's small domestic economy.

The central bank last month eased policy by lowering the midpoint of the Singapore dollar band. But it kept the slope of the trading band flat, surprising some market players who had expected the MAS to drive the local currency lower, via a downward slope for the policy band, in order to help exporters.

The MAS has been rumored to be intervening quietly in the market in recent days, traders say. The Singapore dollar has joined other Asian currencies and stock markets in climbing on improved risk appetite as the global recession shows signs of slowing and markets take heart at reported results of U.S. "stress tests" of the nation's major banks.

The U.S. dollar, which had traded as high as about S$1.58 in early March, has slid steadily in the past two months as global sentiment has rebounded. It dipped Thursday to four-month low of S$1.4691 - just at the levels signaled as the MAS intervention zone - before rising modestly. The greenback was quoted at S$1.4718 around 0840 GMT.

In addition to its importance for the MAS trading band, the S$1.4700 level is represents a key technical level for the U.S. dollar.

Daily charts show strong support in the S$1.4620-S$1.4700 area, but a weekly close below that zone could target a rapid decline to the U.S. dollar's December trough of $1.4150, said Dow Jones CommentaryPlus analyst Mark Cranfield. The greenback closed Wednesday below its 200-day moving average at S$1.4804, adding to bearish signals as it is already trading below its 30-, 55-, and 100-day averages.

"The U.S. dollar is weakening in response to the risk rally," said Citigroup economist Kit Wei Zheng. Singapore "is also attracting capital inflows on the equity side, so that's pushing the Singapore dollar stronger."

But while the mood among investors has brightened, export-dependent Singapore remains mired in its worst recession since independence in 1965.

"Fundamentally as far as the Singapore economy, nothing has changed," said OCBC strategist Selena Ling, who forecasts the city-state's economy to contract 7.6% this year - within the government forecast range of between 6% nd 9% contraction. "It's just all sentiment. It's just that people had expected the worst, so going from here they're looking for the upside - or they want to believe in the upside."

The MAS's Heng said the central bank will stick to its policy.

"Our assessment is that the current monetary policy stance remains appropriate," he said. "There are no new developments that cause us to change our stance."

* Singapore dollar falls but supported by intervention talk

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, March 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies retreated on Wednesday as investors took profits from their recent rallies, with the high-yielding Indonesian rupiah suffering sharp losses in both spot and offshore forwards.

The rupiah <IDR=> slid just over 1 percent to 11,590 per dollar, down from its two-month high hit on Tuesday fanned by the U.S. government's plan to purge toxic bank assets from banks.

"There has been some profit-taking and the majors are also retreating a bit against the dollar," said a Jakarta-based trader.

Meanwhile, one-year offshore dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards <IDR1YNDFOR=> jumped about 2.5 percent to 13,000, implying an 11 percent depreciation from the spot.

The Thai baht <THB=TH> lost 0.7 percent to 35.60 per dollar at one point, but later pulled back to 35.50.

"The baht moves lower in line with regional currencies. The dollar/baht should meet resistance at 35.50 and 35.83 respectively," said a trader in Bangkok.

The baht is still up nearly 2 percent this month as part of an Asia-wide rally fuelled by optimism that the global financial system may be stabilising and the dollar's broad retreat against major currencies.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> shed a third of a percent to 1.5177 to the U.S. dollar as investors moved to cover their short U.S. dollar positions, but it later pared losses amid talk of possible official intervention.

Traders reckon the Singapore dollar is near the bottom of its secret trade-weighted band which is widely expected to be shifted lower when the central bank reviews policy in early April.

"We see no convincing argument against a loosening of monetary policy at the April review," Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac, said in a note.

"Unlike most economies, its currency is Singapore's policy instrument so there is no question of 'beggar thy neighbour' policy," he said.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> was little changed at 6.832 per dollar, while one-year offshore dollar/yuan NDFs <CNYNDFOR=> rose slightly to 6.80, implying a 0.5 percent rise from the spot.

"We remain convinced that 'basic stability' will be maintained in the exchange rate," Patrick Bennett, currency strategist at Societe Generale, said in a note.

Using the NDF to hedge China investment or exposure at current levels in still uncertain times is an appropriate move," he added.

The South Korean won <KRW=> hit a two-month high of 1,357.9 per dollar, bucking regional weakness as investors who were long on U.S. dollars rushed to dump the currency on stop-losses.

Traders said stop-losses in closing trader were triggered by heavy dollar sales by exporters and talk of POSCO converting its dollar bond proceeds.

title: =DJ FOCUS: Singapore  Central Bank  Likely To Ease Policy In April
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank will likely ease monetary policy in April, weakening the local currency in an effort to stem the damage to the small trade-dependent nation from the global downturn.

But given doubts that driving down the currency sharply would rescue the recessionary economy from the collapse in external demand, the Monetary Authority of Singapore is unlikely to shift to a policy of sustained currency depreciation, analysts say.

The city-state's outlook has grown increasingly bleak.

Gross domestic product shrank at an annual rate of 16.4% in the last three months of 2008 - the biggest contraction since the government began releasing seasonally adjusted data in 1976. Exports and manufacturing output plunged at record rates in January. Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew said GDP could contract by much as 10% this year, which would be by far be the worst fall on record.

The dire signals are putting heavy pressure on the authorities to take additional steps to limit downside risks. The government has ramped up fiscal policy and now the heat is on the central bank.

The MAS uses the Singapore dollar exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its chief policy tool because trade dwarfs the island's small domestic economy. The central bank, which manages the Singapore dollar in an undisclosed trade-weighted band, is to hold its next half-yearly policy review in April, although a date hasn't been set.

Citigroup economist Kit Wei Zheng said the MAS has been "consistently intervening to weaken the Singapore dollar" to keep it within the bottom quartile of the policy band.

"If our model is correct, this suggests that MAS has already engineered a de facto easing of policy within the parameters of the current 'neutral' policy stance," he said. "But this de facto easing has already reached its natural limits, and, therefore, the next step would be to be to engineer an explicit easing of policy."

Assuming an April easing, Westpac forecasts the U.S. dollar will rise to S$1.61 by the end of June. Standard Chartered expects the greenback to hit S$1.57 by midyear but end the year lower at S$1.48.

The U.S. currency, quoted at S$1.5268 around 0630 GMT Wednesday, has risen 6.3% so far this year against the Singapore currency and is far above the all-time low of S$1.3438 it hit July 15.

The central bank last eased policy at October's policy review by shifting to a neutral stance, ending a policy of guiding the Singapore dollar gradually higher to fight previously rising inflation.

Kit is among many analysts who say the MAS will ease policy in April, likely through a downward re-centering of the Singapore dollar's trading band - a move that would immediately weaken the Singapore currency - rather than a more aggressive shift to a downward sloping band, which would aim to steadily weaken the local currency.

MAS Deputy Managing Director Ong Chong Tee in January suggested the authorities were reluctant to commit to guiding the Singapore dollar lower over a sustained period. "The current slowdown reflects a sharp slowdown in global demand and not on (Singapore's) competitiveness," he said, adding there was "no reason, in our view, for a persistent weakening of the Singapore dollar."

Singapore's non-oil domestic exports contracted for a 10th straight month in February, falling 23.7% from a year earlier. While that wasn't as bad as January's record 34.9% drop, shipments to almost all major trading partners, such as the U.S. and the European Union, remained weak.

Driving down Singapore's currency could also lead to other headaches, such as further downward pressure on asset prices that could trigger fund outflows.

"Weakening the Singapore dollar to gain a competitive edge in trade could also backfire and lead to retaliatory actions by regional economies and major trading partners," said Standard Chartered economist Alvin Liew in a report. "In such a competition no one wins, but everyone pays dearly."

Nevertheless, a move by MAS to aid the economy is likely.

"There do not seem to be solid grounds to believe that fiscal policies will carry the torch for the rest of the way," market research firm 4CAST said in a report. "Complementary monetary policy easing will be imperative in creating economic conditions more conducive for a recovery when conditions begin to pick up once again. "

Citigroup's Kit said the October easing stopped but didn't reverse a tightening of monetary conditions that occurred when the MAS re-centered the Singapore dollar's trading band upward in April to curb inflation. He said the currency's real effective exchange rate (REER) in fact appreciated in January and has strengthened by 10%-20% against most Asian counterparts since end of 2007.

"The Singapore dollar REER appreciation, alongside the rise in real interest rates (due to moderating inflation) has resulted in a tightening of overall monetary conditions since January at a time when it is least needed," he said.

Kit said a sufficiently aggressive move from the MAS will "do the trick," in which case it will simply need to maintain the status quo for "another two policy meetings or so."

"Maybe in the second half of 2010 when you have firmer sign of a more decisive pickup, then maybe they will shift towards a more appreciation stance again," he said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rises on stock gains, China stimulus hopes
text:
SINGAPORE, March 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Wednesday as investors snapped up stocks in the hope that China will step up efforts to spur its economy, with suspected intervention boosting South Korea's won and the Singapore dollar.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose a third of a percent to 48.65 per dollar as a senior central bank official said falling inflation had created room for the central bank to cut interest rates, a day before the interest rate review.

Deputy central bank governor Diwa Guinigundo also said the central bank would avoid intervention given the peso's relative stability. [ID:nSP405920]

The peso is down 2.4 percent against the dollar so far this year -- the second best performing currency after the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> in those that are tracked daily by Reuters.

Meanwhile, the Thai baht <THB=TH> gained almost 0.4 percent to 36 per dollar.

The volatile South Korean won <KRW=> rose as much as 1 percent to 1,535.2 per dollar as dealers suspected the authorities were selling dollars to support the ailing unit.

The won, the worst performing Asian currency, is still down 19 percent against the dollar this year.

A senior Chinese planning official said on Wednesday the government will increase spending in areas such as infrastructure and manufacturing on top of the 4 trillion yuan ($585 billion) stimulus package unveiled in November. [ID:nL4384]

The comment, along with signs of a recovery in China's economy highlighted by a big improvement in the purchasing managers' index, helped boost Asian stocks.

The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> rising 1.5 percent as of 0747 GMT.

"The bounce in equities probably is the most obvious cue while the broad dollar index has stabilised somewhat, with the additional boost coming from in China of course," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at OCBC Bank.

But he cautioned that the near-term outlook for most Asian currencies remained grim due to the worsening global downturn.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> hovered near 6.84 per dollar, but one-year dollar/yuan non-deliverable forwards <CNYNDFOR=> eased to 6.9553, which implied a fall of 1.6 percent from the spot.

Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> edged up to 1.5510 to the U.S. dollar as traders cited official intervention to limit the currency's losses.

"There was a lot of U.S. dollar buying this morning by U.S. houses and funds," said a Singapore-based trader, adding the unit is supported by U.S. dollar sales by the central bank.

A second trader said the intervention may reflect official concerns about excessive currency weakness as Singapore dollar is believed to be near the lower end of its undisclosed trading band. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

Even with the gains in Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong, sentiment was cautious; trading ranges remained very wide and markets swung often from negative to positive and back again.

"Given the 'trading mentality' within Asia, the key question remains how long this change in sentiment will last," said IG Markets dealing head Oliver Stevens.

Brown Brothers Harriman analysts said the GDP data would be poor, and could be a catalyst for further declines: "Bad news for the U.S. to be sure, but worse news for many other countries whose growth was largely a function of exports to the U.S.," they said.

title: Singapore's money rates fall on c.bank fund injection
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Singapore's money market rates fell on Tuesday after the central bank injected funds to ease credit strains caused by global financial turmoil, traders said.

 One-month interbank market rates (SIBOR) <SISGDD=ABSG> fell to 1.85 percent on Tuesday from 2.06 percent on Monday and retreated from a nine-month high at 2.275 percent hit on Friday.

 Singapore's overnight rates <SGDF=> fell to 0.875 percent on Tuesday from 2.125 percent on Monday, traders said.

 Traders said the falling money market rates indicated the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had injected money.

 "No doubt the MAS will be there to stabilise the money market conditions, but they are dealing in a global environment that has turned irrational," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist at JPMorgan Chase in Singapore.

 "There are signs around the region that counter-party risk and risk aversion is starting to push rates high as banks limit their credit," he said.

 The MAS may have sold U.S. dollars in recent weeks to support the weakening Singapore dollar, which required it to add  liquidity into the local market to help offset the effect of such intervention, analysts said.

Singapore's interbank rates had long been held down by steady inflows of foreign money, which put pressure on the Singapore dollar to rise and in turn force the MAS to buy U.S. dollars to curb its strength.

 It then released money into the local money market, keeping rates low as it failed to sterilise the intervention, analysts say.

 But the picture has changed in recent weeks as the global credit turbulence has prodded foreigners to dump Singapore's stocks <.FTSTI>, which have fallen by a quarter since early June.

 "Outflows and concerns over counterparty risks naturally put some upside pressure on the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar," said Han Sia Yeo, currency strategist at Bank of America.

 Reflecting the trend of capital outflows and weakening exports, Singapore's foreign exchange reserves fell by $4.86 billion in August to $170.1 billion.

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.4345 per U.S. dollar on Tuesday, down some six percent from its record high of 1.3453 hit on July 15 amid a region-wide squeeze on the U.S. dollar funding.

 Most analysts expect the MAS, which steers monetary policy by managing its currency within an undisclosed trading band rather than adjusting interest rates, is likely to slow the pace of currency gains when it reviews policy on October 10.

 The central bank shifted the centre of that band upwards in April to try to quell inflation, which has started easing.

 Mark Tan and Michael Buchanan, analysts at Goldman Sachs, said in a note that they expected the Singapore dollar to fall to 1.45 and 1.47 per U.S. dollar over the next six and 12 months.

 Singapore's data issued last week showed the country's August factory output fell a seasonally adjusted 1.9 percent from July and dropped 12.2 percent from the same month in 2007.  (Reporting by Kevin Yao; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

title: Singapore dollar's volatilities jump as spot rate rises
text:
SINGAPORE, July 17 (Reuters) - Implied volatilities on the Singapore dollar jumped higher as the currency hit a record high this week, but analysts caution that the authorities would prevent sharp currency gains even as they try to quell inflation.

One-month implied volatilities <SGDVOL> reached as high as 5.0 percent on Wednesday, the strongest level since June 27. They eased a tad to 4.8 percent on Thursday.

On Tuesday, the volatilities registered their sharpest daily percentage gain in three years, when the Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a record high at 1.3453 against the U.S. dollar.

Rising implied volatilities, a measure of how much the market expects the currency to move, indicate the options market expects the currency will become increasingly volatile.

Traders said investors rushed to buy protection through options to hedge against further falls in the U.S. dollar.

"The Singapore dollar's volatilities were begging for a retrace given that they had come off significantly since June," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at OCBC Bank.

"Implied option skews had moved to uncharacteristically favour U.S. dollar calls, but in the past few sessions the downward move in the U.S. dollar versus Singapore dollar has 'corrected' the skews," Ng said.

The volatilities had been falling since it hit as high as 6.8 percent in early June.

Investors have significantly increased their long positions in the Singapore dollar in the first half of July as they expect the authorities to tolerate further currency rises to help fight inflation, a Reuters poll showed. [ID:nSP231499]

But analysts sounded a cautious note, predicting Singapore's authorities would try to prevent any sharp move in the currency, which would hit exports and in turn weigh on the economy.

"I think the market needs to be a little bit cautious in taking this currency too far. If it rises beyond 1.3450, I think it will face strong resistance from the central bank," said Joseph Tan, currency strategist at Fortis.

"As long as the currency's move is on a very gradual basis, the central bank is OK with that, but any volatile move will be met with intervention," he added.

title: Singapore cbank dollar buying to depress money rates
text:
SINGAPORE, July 15 (Reuters) - Singapore's depressed money market rates will stay that way for a while as the central bank continues to buy dollars to limit currency appreciation, flooding the market with money, analysts said on Tuesday.

Three-month interbank market rates (SIBOR) <SISGDD=ABSG> fell to 1.157 percent on Monday from 1.163 percent on Friday, staying close to a three-year low of 1.156 percent hit last week.

Six-month interbank rates fell to 1.50 percent on Monday from from 1.813 percent in early June.

Singapore's interbank rates have been falling steadily from the middle of 2006, when the three-month rate peaked at about 3.6 percent, coinciding with steep gains in the local dollar since then.

Analysts expect the short-term rates to stay weak in the coming months as foreign money flows in, putting pressure on the Singapore dollar to rise and forcing the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to buy U.S. dollars to curb its strength.

"The easier money rates have been an 'anomaly' that are probably partly attributable to continued inflows that are keeping interbank liquidity flush," said Emmanuel Ng, a currency strategist at OCBC Bank in Singapore.

"There is little impetus (for the rates) to rise significantly in the near term unless we see a generalised withdrawal of investor flows out of Asia en masse," he added.

But Chia Woon Khien, an analyst at Royal Bank of Scotland, said she believed that Singapore's money rates would bottom out later this year as weakening exports reduce the amount of U.S. dollar inflows and ease upward pressures on the currency.

"Considering that liquidity conditions are still flush, money market rates have fallen quite a lot lately, but I'm not so sure if rates have more room to fall," she said.

The MAS, which is torn between the dilemma of containing inflation running at 26-year highs while trying to avoid a sharp economic slowdown, is expected to stick to its tight policy at its review in October but refrain from tightening further.

The central bank, which conducts monetary policy by managing the currency within a secret trading band against a basket of currencies instead of setting interest rates, shifted the centre of that band upwards in April to try to quell inflation.

CURRENCY RISES

Analysts say this unique policy constrains the central bank because it has to intervene to control the currency, and in the process it has no sway over rates in the money market.

Han Sia Yeo, a currency strategist at Bank of America, said he expected the Singapore dollar to stay close to the estimated upper end of the band in the near term, but gradually drift lower towards its mid-point later this year as inflation risks begin to recede.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, viewed by investors as a safe bet in Asia, gained 0.3 percent on Tuesday to 1.3504 per U.S. dollar, its highest level since April 23.

The Singapore dollar has gained 6.6 percent this year despite frequent dollar-buying intervention by the authorities, trailing behind the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP>.

By contrast, fears of inflation and credit woes have hit most Asian currencies this year, particularly the South Korean won <KRW=>, the Indian rupee <INR=IN> and Philippine peso <PHP=>, prompting dollar-selling intervention to prop up the units.

Meanwhile, Singapore's bond yield curve <0#SGBMK=> is flattening with yields on two-year bonds rising 25 basis points in the past week and the spread between 2- and 20-year bonds narrowing to 270 basis points from 305 basis points a week ago.

Analysts said the flattening yield curve was partially influenced by recent data which showed that the economy shrank by an annualised and seasonally adjusted 6.6 percent in the second quarter -- the sharpest contraction in five years.

Citigroup has cut its forecast for Singapore's 2008 economic growth to 4.1 percent from 4.7 percent, citing slowing exports amid the U.S. slowdown, analyst Kit Wei Zheng said in a note.

"Given the growth slowdown, moderating inflation and lagged effects of past policy tightening, we expect the MAS to maintain its current policy stance in October," he said. (Editing by Jacqueline Wong)

title: UPDATE: SGD Hits Record High After MAS Tightens Policy
text:
(Adds market response, comments from economists.) 
 
   By John Jannarone 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rocketed to an all-time high Thursday after the central bank aggressively tightened policy to fight mounting inflationary pressures.

The U.S. currency went into temporary free-fall against the local dollar, dropping to a record low of S$1.3616 from S$1.3790 just before the policy statement release at 0000 GMT.

At 0130 GMT the greenback was at S$1.3627.

Analysts said the Singapore dollar may continue to rise under the new policy stance, and any intervention by Monetary Authority of Singapore would reflect an effort to slow, but not block further gains.

"The central bank made an implicit 1%-1.5% tightening," said Joseph Tan, senior strategist at Fortis Bank in Singapore.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it would re-center its undisclosed trade-weighted policy band for the currency, which analysts believe to have a width of 2%-3%.

The MAS said in the statement that the currency has fluctuated near the top of the policy band since the last meeting in October.

"The U.S. dollar could fall to S$1.3560 after the tightening," said Selena Ling, an economist at Singapore's OCBC Bank.

Similarly, UBS estimates that the U.S. dollar could fall to S$1.3500 without exceeding the limits of the new policy.

The policy tightening shows that the central bank is making price stability a priority as the economy feels the impact of weaker global demand just as food and commodity prices surge.

But Ling said first quarter economic growth data, also issued Thursday, may have given the central bank some comfort in its decision.

On a seasonally-adjusted annualized basis, gross domestic product grew 16.9% in the first quarter, reversing the 4.8% contraction in the previous quarter, according to the Ministry of Trade and Industry's advance estimate.

A Dow Jones Newswires Poll of economists had forecast a 6.8% rise.

The central bank maintained its 4%-6% economic growth target for 2008, but warned that price pressures have intensified, likely leading 2008 inflation to come in at the top of its 4.5%-5.5% target range.

"CPI inflation has increased and is expected to remain elevated in the first half of this year," the MAS said.

"Against this backdrop of continuing external and domestic cost pressures, an upward shift of the policy band at this point will help to moderate inflation going forward, while providing support for sustainable growth in the economy."

The MAS uses exchange-rate targeting rather than interest rates as its chief policy tool because external trade dwarfs the domestic economy.

Thursday's policy shift follows a move at the last policy review in October to increase the slope of the trade-weighted band.

In recent months, consumer prices have risen at their fastest rate in 25 years as surging global food and energy costs have added to higher rents across the island.

The island's economy expanded 7.2% from a year earlier, faster than the 5.4% rise in the fourth quarter and higher than a poll forecast for a 5.7% growth.

-By John Jannarone, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4153; john.jannarone@dowjones.com [ 10-04-08 0133GMT ]

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  currencies  rise, some hit decade highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies firmed strongly on Wednesday, propelled by the prospects of falling U.S. interest rates, with some hitting their strongest levels since 1997.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as far as 1.3979 as the U.S. dollar slumped to a record low against the euro <EUR=> and a basket of major currencies <.DXY>.   

It marked the first time that the Singapore dollar had pierced S$1.4 since January 1997, just before the Asia financial crisis.   

The Singapore dollar was also supported by expectations the central bank needs a stronger currency to curb price pressures. Data on Monday showed the island's annual inflation accelerated to a 25-year high of 6.6 percent in January.   

The Singapore dollar gained almost half of a percent on Wednesday, bringing its appreciation versus the U.S. currency so far this year to 2.9 percent.   

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose as far as 3.201 per dollar, up about 0.3 percent and its highest since late 1997. The Thai baht <THB=TH> briefly hit 32.09 per dollar, up half of a percent to its highest since August 1997.   

"The dollar/baht is still heavy from exporters' dollar sales plus expectations about lifting capital controls," said a trader in Bangkok.   

Investors believe Thai authorities will soon scrap capital controls imposed in late 2006, which were designed to curb the baht's strength to protect local exporters.   

The Bank of Thailand kept its policy interest rate steady at 3.25 percent on Wednesday, as expected.   

The Thai rate -- the lowest in emerging Asia, is still higher than the U.S. fed funds rate, which has fallen rapidly to 3 percent.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> hit 9,037 per dollar, up almost 0.6 percent from late Asian trade on Tuesday.   

"Unless there is another wave of inflows today, the rupiah should retrace a bit," said a trader in Jakarta.   

WEAK DOLLAR AND INFLATION   

The dollar slumped after weak economic data and comments from a Fed official signalled that U.S. interest rates will continue to head lower. [ID:nN26322234]   

Fed Vice Chairman Donald Kohn said on Tuesday that a weak U.S. economy was a bigger worry than higher inflation risks. [ID:nN26364877]   

Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke is expected to provide a similar message when he presents the central bank's twice-yearly monetary policy report to Congress on Wednesday and Thursday. [ID:nN24651396]   

In Asia, inflation risks are likely to prod policy makers to tolerate stronger currencies to curb import costs, fuelled by lofty oil prices, analysts said.   

"The driver for Asian currencies is a combination of a Fed being backed into further cuts amid a climate of rising global inflation," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist at  JPMorgan.

"Singapore is uniquely positioned in that its FX rate is the tool of choice in combating inflation and is widely seen as credibly applied," he added.   

But he cautioned that Singapore's central bank would keep intervening in the market to ensure currency rises are gradual.   

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> hit a three-year high at 30.903 per U.S. dollar amid fund inflows, bringing its gains this year to 5 percent, overtaking the baht as Asia's top performer.   

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> rose to 7.1450 per dollar but was still off its post-revaluation high at 7.1413 hit last week.

title: Emerging  FX -Taiwan dlr jumps, Singapore dlr capped by c.bank
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar hit a new high on Monday after the island's politicians pledged to boost direct flights with China, while suspected intervention stalled gains in the Singapore dollar, despite strong inflation.   

Meanwhile, most Asian currencies were shackled in narrow ranges, mirroring regional stocks <0#.INDEXA>.   

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> hit a fresh 2-1/2-year high at 31.25 per U.S. dollar, up 0.8 percent from Friday's close, buoyed by a promise from the island's presidential candidates during a weekend debate to step up direct flights with China.   

The Taiwan dollar has gained around 3.3 percent since the opposition KMT party's landslide win in legislative elections last month, which raised expectations that its candidate, Ma Ying-jeou, will win the presidential elections in March.   

That would help reduce cross-straits tensions and spur the island's economy, but some analysts believe prospects of rising inflation would support the currency in the longer term.   

"The Taiwan dollar's strength, led by the recent strong portfolio inflows, could serve as an extra channel for the central bank to tackle inflationary pressure more effectively," Goldman Sach analyst Enoch Fung said in a note.   

The bank raised its forecast on the Taiwan dollar, expecting the unit to hit 30.75, 30.5 and 30.25 in 3, 6 and 12 months, respectively, up from 32, 32 and 31.5 previously.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> briefly rose to 946.2 per dollar as local shares rose, but analysts said foreign investors were selling local stocks and that would support the dollar.   

C.BANK CAPS SINGAPORE DOLLAR   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> pulled back to 1.4060 per U.S. dollar after briefly hitting an 11-year high of 1.4050 as the central bank was suspected of buying U.S. dollars, but analysts expect the Singapore unit to rise to help curb inflation.   

"They have been there since last week, but all they can do is slow the pace of the U.S. dollar's decline," said a trader.   

A second dealer agreed: "I reckon they will try to prevent spot falling below 1.4050."   

Dealers expect the currency to rise past the psychologically important 1.40 level in the near future.   

Consumer prices in January rose 6.6 percent from a year earlier, the fastest pace since 1982, government data showed on Monday. [ID:nSGC001786] [SGCPIY=ECI]   

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> eased slightly to 7.15 per dollar, but the currency jumped in offshore non-deliverable forwards <CNYNDFOR=>, pricing in more than 10 percent gains in 12 months.   

Analysts expect the pace of appreciation to gain steam again after the central bank said on Friday it would step up use of the currency to help rebalance the economy.   

"We are likely to see the continued appreciation of the currency at a pace of around 8-10 percent this year and the next," analysts at  UBS said in a note.   

Goldman Sachs has forecast a 12 percent rise in a year.   

The yuan has gained a further 13.5 percent since it was revalued in July 2005, including by 2.2 percent so far this year.

title: Singapore  dollar capped by c.bank  intervention -traders
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank was suspected of intervening in the currency market on Monday as the Singapore dollar rose to an 11-year-high of S$1.4050 and as data showed inflation at its highest since 1982, traders said.   

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> eased back to S$1.4060 per U.S. dollar from the high as dealers suspected the central bank was buying U.S. dollars.   

 "The granny (central bank) is around," said a Singapore-based trader. "They have been there since last week, but all they can do is slow the pace of the U.S. dollar's decline."   

 A second dealer agreed: "I reckon they will try to prevent spot falling below S$1.4050."   

 Still, dealers and analysts said they expected the Singapore dollar to rise beyond the S$1.4 level in the near term as the central bank is under pressure to quell inflation even as economic growth slows.   

 Analysts also estimate the currency is at the top end of its undisclosed policy band, based on the value of a trade-weighted basket of currencies, within which the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the currency.   

 Consumer prices in January rose 6.6 percent from a year earlier, the fastest pace since 1982, government data showed on Monday. [ID:nSGC001786] [SGCPIY=ECI]  (Reporting by Kevin Yao; Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: MONEY TALKS:  Central Bank Currency  Angst On The Rise In Asia
text:
By Rosalind Mathieson   

A Dow Jones Newswires Column   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian central banks have been getting a bit twitchy as their currencies continue to rise, but that doesn't mean they will try and put an end to it.   

There may be a pickup in spot market intervention, rhetoric or even administrative measures (as evidenced by Taiwan's actions of late).   

This, though, will be aimed at slowing the appreciation in regional currencies, rather than stopping it altogether.   

Governments tend to prefer weaker currencies, given the competitive advantage this provides to exporters.   

Central banks aren't as one-sided, however. Especially in times like these, when they are faced with a slower economic growth outlook but also rising price pressures.   

Letting their currencies gain - in a managed fashion - can help take some of the steam out of inflation (though only to some extent, it can't really do much about domestically-originating inflation pressures).   

So the question becomes one of relativity: Asian central banks are likely to accept some appreciation in their currency, but don't want people trying to capitalize on that by pushing currencies up in wanton fashion.   

The central banks have therefore been making their presence felt of late in several countries, in particular Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia, where currencies have been especially strong.   

There has been suspected spot market intervention in Singapore, Malaysia and Taiwan, to buy the U.S. dollar.   

There have also been moves by the central bank in Taiwan to curtail speculation in the onshore non-deliverable forwards market, including by exporters who reportedly have been straying from using plain currency forward contracts.   

But there hasn't been the sort of barrage of rhetoric and large-scale intervention that would accompany a bid to halt a trend.   

In some cases, authorities have even cited the higher currencies as a sign of economic strength, i.e. of resilience in the face of the offshore headwinds coming from the U.S.   

And none of the central banks are likely to be silly enough to do something like slap on capital controls. They tend to not work well, for one thing.   

In the medium term, anyway, Malaysia, Taiwan and Singapore may find their currencies do some deflating on their own.   

Some of the momentum in the first two countries right now is tied up with coming elections.   

In Malaysia, that has led to some fairly large spending promises for infrastructure and other developments aimed at luring in foreign investors. Some of those pledges though may turn out to be little more that hot air, once the elections are out of the way.   

In Taiwan, the hype is all about the potential for a change in government, and for that new government to warm up the relationship with Beijing.   

That has led to a level of excitement about the potential for rapid progress in allowing investment between China and Taiwan and greater tourism. But those expectations are also at risk of disappointment - any thawing is likely to come pretty slowly, and the doors aren't going to be swung wide open to a flood of tourists from the mainland, all armed with cash and credit cards to burn.   

For Singapore, the currency is the main policy management tool, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been well-concerned about inflation, so authorities would think some local dollar strength is warranted. But the relatively small and export-dependent economy there is heading for a slowdown, and that may yet help bring rents and other costs down.   

Look for continued action from central banks to try and keep a lid on their currencies. But unless it turns into a large speculative attack, the action should remain relatively modest.

"Yesterday there was talk that there was official presence near the 1.4100 level," a local trader said.   

The MAS manages the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band, and traders said the currency is near the top of that range.   

The suspected intervention and weak performances by regional bourses kept the local currency range-bound despite the U.S. dollar's overnight weakness and inflation pressures from rising oil futures, traders said.

The local trader said the MAS may have to tighten its monetary policy and allow for faster appreciation of the Singapore dollar should oil futures remain above US$100 a barrel.   

But the strategist disagreed, saying high oil prices may only lead to more MAS intervention because the government appears unwilling to shift its monetary policy. Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam said last week an excessive appreciation of the Singapore dollar could hurt economic growth.   

Trade in the local bond market was lackluster on lack of major news, a local bond trader said.   

The size of the 20-year bonds scheduled to be reopened Feb. 27 is to be announced after the market's close Wednesday, the trader said.

title: Emerging  FX -Yuan leads ringgit, Singapore dollar to highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies extended gains for a third day on Friday, riding on improving risk appetite after an aggressive U.S. rate cut and a jump in the Chinese yuan, with the Singapore dollar hitting its highest level in a decade.   

 The Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit hit 10-year highs, and the Philippine peso saw the biggest gains in the region on while the yuan <CNY=CFXS> climbed to 7.2070 per dollar, its highest levels since its July 2005 revaluation.   

 Analysts said the yuan was boosted by a report indicating Chinese growth will remain strong in 2008, notwithstanding the risks of a U.S. recession, and another report suggesting China will allow a faster pace of appreciation of its currency. [nPEK85240] [nPEK96371]   

 "Comments from China do seem to be confirming that they are using the currency as an inflation-fighting tool," said Sean Callow, a strategist with Westpac Bank.   

 "This encourages expectations dollar/China will be substantially lower in the coming months, and it's a vote of confidence that most dollar/Asian pairs will be heading lower."   

 Even if there was a resurgence in market volatility in the coming days, for instance if the Federal Reserve refrained from cutting rates as expected next week, this medium term trend in the Asians would persist, Callow said.   

 STOCKS RECOVER   

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose by 0.7 percent to hit a 10-1/2-year high at 1.4205 per dollar, helped by a 3.6 percent rally in its stock market <.FTSTI> as well as the country's close ties to China.   

 Traders said the currency was close to the top of its policy band, and suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to curtail further gains.   

 The ringgit <MYR=> rose 0.9 percent to hit a decade high at 3.2350 per dollar as local stocks <.KLSE> rose by 1.8 percent.   

 "Money is coming into the market to buy local stocks and bonds," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.   

 The broad appreciation in Asia was furthered by firm global equity markets, which in turn were buoyed by a return of some confidence in the U.S economy after solid employment data and a congressional fiscal package, coming just days after the Fed's hefty 75 basis points rate cut.   

 The Bush administration's fiscal package includes $150 billion of tax rebates and business incentives meant to prevent a slowdown in the country's economy. [ID:nN24242910]   

 MSCI's measure of Asian equities excluding Japan [.MIAPJ0000PUS] gained more than 5 percent, after overnight gains in the Dow Jones index <.DJI>.   

 The Japanese yen <JPY=>, borrowed widely as a cheap funding currency for higher-yielding investments, fell in a sign market participants were gradually renewing their interest in risky trades.

"The stock markets of the world aren't doing very well as a general trend," a local trader said.

title: UPDATE: Asian Stocks, Dlr Hit By  Merrill Lynch Report
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks turned lower in afternoon trade Friday, after a report that  Merrill Lynch is set to disclose further losses due to the U.S. subprime mortgage crisis soured fragile sentiment.   

Shares in Hong Kong were among those hardest hit, with the Hang Seng Index recently down 1.3% after spending much of the day in positive territory.   

Elsewhere, the Nikkei 225 ended down 1.9%, and near 19-month lows, while South Korea's Kospi Composite lost 2.3%. The S&P/ASX 200 in Australia fell 1.6%.   

Markets had started the day on the back foot, after a profit warning from American Express Co. cast a shadow over earlier comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke indicating that the U.S. central bank is prepared to deliver bigger rate cuts to ward off an increasing chance of recession.   

The renewed focus on the Fed's next interest rate move, and expectations of even weaker yields on the U.S. dollar, was the main driver for currency trading. The dollar has given up early gains against the yen, and is at multi-year lows against several other Asian currencies, although it has fared better against Asia-Pacific's barometers of risk aversion, the higher-yielding Australian and New Zealand dollars.   

The drops in Asian stocks come despite gains on Wall Street overnight, which saw the Dow Jones Industrial Average rise 117.78 points, or 0.9%, to 12,853.09. While Asian markets earlier seemed to be weighing the advantages of rate cuts against the threat of a U.S. recession, the  Merrill Lynch news seemed to tip them over the edge.   

The New York Times reported that  Merrill Lynch is expected to suffer $15 billion in losses stemming from soured mortgage investments, almost double its original estimate.   

The company is expected to disclose the huge write-down when it reports earnings next week, the paper said, citing people who have been briefed on Merrill's plans.   

Not all markets have been hit, though. Extending their recent immunity from financial troubles in the U.S., shares in India remain strong, with the Sensex up 1.1% and buyers targeting banks in particular. In Malaysia, stocks again hit record highs.   

Still, a cautious tone is likely to dominate Asia's stock markets for some time, said Khiem Do, head of Asian multi asset at  Barings Asset Management.

Not only are concerns about technology stocks weighing on tech-heavy markets like Korea and Taiwan, but "the more cynical commentators and investors believe that the Fed and the U.S. government are too late in easing policies in order to avoid a recession," he said. That's keeping investors hesitant.   

Currency markets, meanwhile are also turbulent. The dollar was recently trading as low as Y108.64, after earlier having risen to a high of Y109.71. But, following declines in Korean shares, the dollar has strengthened against the Korean won, to recently trade at KRW937.50.   

Elsewhere, though, dollar weakness prompted the monetary authority in Singapore to intervene and buy the U.S. currency, according to traders, after it fell to levels not seen since 1997 against the Singapore dollar. The dollar was also at its weakest since 1997 against the Malaysian ringgit.   

Gold prices reacted to the falling dollar by returning to a record high in early Asian trading Friday. Gold was recently off that record, but up $2.45 a troy ounce from the close of trading in New York to $893.35 and within reach of the $900 mark.   

-By Mohammed Hadi; Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4147; mohammed.hadi@dowjones.com [ 11-01-08 0742GMT ]

title: Asia Stks Volatile; Mkt Weighs Rate Cuts Vs Weaker US Econ
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stock markets are volatile Friday, as investors weigh the greater prospect of interest rate cuts in the U.S. against fears over the impact of a weakening U.S. economy.   

The focus on interest rate policy, and expectations of even weaker yields on the U.S. dollar, is also driving trading in the currency markets. The dollar was recently stronger against the yen after a drop in overnight trading, but remains lower against several other Asian currencies.   

Among stocks, shares in Australia are faring particularly poorly, as cautious statements from U.S. credit card issuer American Express Co. (AMEX) prompt concerns about the country's banks. The S&P/ASX 200 is down 1% to 6015.2, with financial stocks among the worst hit.   

"I think that investors gave the Australian banking system the benefit of the doubt, but this benefit of the doubt is being questioned," said Khiem Do, head of Asian Multi-Asset at  Baring Asset Management Ltd.

Resources stocks, which dominate the Australian stock market, are also hurting on worries about the impact of the slowing U.S. economy on commodity prices. Overnight, crude oil prices slipped on fears that a U.S. recession would crimp demand.   

Meanwhile, shares in Japan and South Korea have erased early gains, though expectations for further interest rate cuts in the U.S. are driving shares higher in Hong Kong, where the monetary authority maintains a peg to the dollar and automatically follow U.S. rate moves.   

The Kospi Composite in Korea was recently down 0.2% to 1821.67, and the Nikkei 225 in Japan was off 0.8% to 14,272.38. The Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong was up 0.3% to 27,319.41.   

But Baring's Do notes that a cautious tone is likely to dominate Asia's stock markets for some time. Not only are concerns about technology stocks weighing on tech-heavy markets like Korea and Taiwan, but "the more cynical commentators and investors believe that the Fed and the U.S. government are too late in easing policies in order to avoid a recession," he said. That's keeping investors hesitant.   

Indeed, traders expect markets to remain volatile as investors seek more clarity on the outlook for the U.S. economy and interest rates.   

The Straits Times Index in Singapore was recently up 0.8%. "I think we could bounce around a bit like the Nikkei, but basically I think we'll be heading sideways for the next couple of days," a trader in Singapore said.   

The volatility follows a mixed bag of news from the U.S.   

Shares rose on Wall Street overnight after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said that the central bank is prepared to cut interest rates in response to weakening economic conditions. Also bolstering U.S. markets was word that  Bank of America is in talks to buy troubled U.S. mortgage lender  Countrywide Financial.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 117.78 points, or 0.9%, to 12,853.09.   

But Asian traders have more to consider. After U.S. trading ended, U.S. credit card issuer  American Express said it is seeing signs of a weaker U.S. economy and noted slowing spending by cardholders and an upturn in delinquencies and loan write-offs, sending its stock sharply lower.   

Trading in currency markets, meanwhile, reflects the disparity in interest rate policy among central bankers in the U.S. and Asia.   

Fed-funds futures traded in the U.S. are now pricing in an 88% chance that the Fed will cut interest rates by 50 basis points at its next meeting.   

The dovish comments offered by Bernanke, as well as market expectations on rate cuts, make an "overall environment that should bode positively" for immediate Asian foreign exchange trading, said  JP Morgan in a note.   

Indeed, with the Bank of Korea leaving its interest rate targets unchanged, the Korean Won strengthened against the dollar. The dollar was recently trading at 934.20 won, down 3.30. The dollar was also weaker against the Singapore dollar, prompting the monetary authority there to intervene, according to traders, and has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 against the Malaysian ringgit.   

One exception is the yen, which is giving back some overnight gains against the dollar as bargain hunters step in. The dollar was recently up slightly at Y109.50, from an overnight low of 109.13 following Bernanke's comments.   

Gold prices reacted to the falling dollar by returning to a record high in early Asian trading Friday. Gold was recently off that record, but up $3.65 a troy ounce from the close of trading in New York to $894.55.   

Darren Heathcote, head of trading at Investec in Sydney, said: "The reason for (gold's strength) is the weaker dollar...primarily on the back of Bernanke's comments."   

Heathcote said he expects gold to push above $900 Friday, although the market will likely wait until London or New York trading to break that historic mark.   

-By Mohammed Hadi; Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4147; mohammed.hadi@dowjones.com [ 11-01-08 0257GMT ]

title: Emerging  FX -Asia listless amid uncertainty,  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steady on Thursday as investors held back because of uncertainty over the outlook for the U.S. economy and rate decisions due in Europe later in the day.   

 Traders said the market was also cautious because central banks in the Philippines, Malaysia, India and Singapore were suspected of having intervened this week to curb strength in their currencies.   

 The U.S. dollar recovered against the yen and other major currencies overnight and held near a nine-month high against sterling <GBP=> in Asia.   

 But Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA>, where foreigners have been heavy net sellers this year, barely moved, giving little direction to currencies.   

 The South Korean won <KRW=> initially rose 0.3 percent to hit 934.0 per dollar as local equities <.KS11> rallied, but it soon pared the gains to trade around 937.   

 A trader in Seoul said the won was stuck between 933 and 945 per dollar.   

 "There's a solid bottom for the dollar at 930 because oil companies are buying more dollars and equity outflows are continuing," the trader said.   

 "But there's also interest from shipping companies to hedge their earnings above 940 and exporters are selling options," she said.   

 Another trader felt the won would weaken to around 970 per dollar over the next few weeks, owing to outflows for dividend payments and  SK Telecom's purchase of a stake in Korean broadband provider  hanarotelecom , valued at nearly $1.2 billion.   

 SK is buying the stake from a consortium led by  American International Group and private equity fund Newbridge Capital.   

 Options traders said there was demand to sell won around 940 for one month and up to 1,000 per dollar through one-year options.   

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> was steady around 1.4310 per U.S. dollar while the Philippine peso <PHP=> fell half a percent from its previous close, backing off the highest level in nearly eight years hit on Wednesday.   

 In a volatile session, the peso rose from a low of 40.78 per dollar to hover around 40.60 before slipping again in late trading as the dollar gained against sterling and the yen.   

 "I think the peso will still appreciate. Any dollar upticks will be sold," a trader in Manila said.   

 But some analysts said the peso's long rally may have run its course for now.   

 They said a report earlier on Thursday showing Philippine exports in November fell 2 percent from a year earlier raised worries the currency's 20 percent appreciation in the past 12 months may be hurting the economy.   

 Many investors kept to the sidelines ahead of meetings by the European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England (BoE), and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke later on Thursday.   

 Analysts expect the ECB to hold interest rates steady at 4.0 percent but see the BoE cutting rates due to weak consumption, which has sparked fears of a slowdown in the economy.   

 The next Fed rates decision is due on Jan. 30 and market expectations are shifting increasingly towards a cut in the Fed funds rate of as much as 50 basis points, although the majority in a Reuters poll still expected a more modest 25 basis points.

title: Asia  Forex : Dollar Nudges Higher As Market Reverses ISM Sales
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar pulled gently higher against the yen Thursday as players started to reverse early sales and take off some positions that have sent the U.S. unit some Y5 lower since Dec. 27.   

The euro also came off its highs against its U.S. counterpart.   

But traders remain nervous about the dollar in the wake of a discouraging manufacturing survey overnight and in the run-up to key jobs data due to be released Friday.   

The Institute of Supply Management's December manufacturing index, which contracted after 10 consecutive months of expansion, prompted a drop in U.S. stocks and a spike in risk aversion. In turn, the trading day started on a sour note for the dollar before some light buying kicked in.   

U.S. jobs data out Friday should provide more clues to the direction of the economy, traders said.   

But "very weak" jobs data will be needed for the yen, euro, sterling and Australian dollar to break above key resistance levels against the dollar, said Easy Forex senior dealer Francisco Solar, noting the U.S. labor market has been resilient and largely supportive of the economy so far.   

He pegged resistance for the euro at $1.48, at $0.8850 for the Australian dollar and at $2.00 for sterling.   

Another Singapore-based trader said strong buy orders for the dollar are placed at Y109.20-Y109.25 and Y108.70 and Y108.75.   

Economists forecast that U.S. non farm payrolls will rise an average 50,000 in December after a 94,000 rise in November.   

The dollar hit a high of around Y114.65 on Dec. 27 but was at Y109.68 at 0518 GMT, off its intraday low of around Y109.24. The euro was at $1.4710, off its high hit earlier in the morning of around $1.4725.   

Elsewhere, the U.S. dollar sank to S$1.4350, its lowest against the Singapore currency since July 1997. By early afternoon, though, it had nudged off that low as players turned wary about central bank intervention with the Singapore currency now very close of the central bank's policy band.   

The U.S. unit was at S$1.4361, down from the S$1.4386 close Wednesday.

title: UPDATE: Asian Stocks Fall; Oil Prices Raise Inflation Worry
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks are lower Thursday as investors worry about the impact of high energy prices and a weakening U.S. economy after crude prices touched a key threshold overnight.   

Meanwhile the Japanese yen remains firm amid the risk-averse market mood with the Singapore dollar hitting a 10-year high against the U.S. dollar. Other Asian currencies, like the Taiwan dollar, are weaker against the U.S. dollar.   

Markets are taking their cue from crude oil after it touched $100 a barrel for the first time ever on Wednesday. February Nymex crude ended $3.64, or 3.8%, higher at $99.62 a barrel in New York, and was recently down 31 cents in electronic trade on Globex at $99.31.   

The move to $100 is largely symbolic, particularly given it was the result of a single trade, but it has prompted analysts to revisit the question of just how high oil prices might climb and what that could do to economic growth around the globe.   

For now, the consensus seems to be that the factors supporting crude prices will be intact for the foreseeable future. Some are very bullish with CLSA analyst Gordon Kwan saying oil may rise to $150 a barrel in 2008, possibly as soon as the next three months.   

For traders in other markets, the concern is high oil will create inflationary pressure at a time the U.S. economy is showing signs of weakness, raising talk the U.S. may yet face a period of stagflation. Inflation also creates a problem for Asia's central bankers, who are pinned between concerns about economic growth and suppressing prices.   

Beyond that is the risk $100-a-barrel oil will weigh on consumer confidence - in part via higher gasoline prices.   

Crude's next move may rest on the release later Thursday of weekly U.S. inventory data, with a Dow Jones poll of six analysts expecting an average drawdown in crude stocks of 1.8 million barrels.   

Meanwhile, spot gold hit a record high of $861.15 a troy ounce, taking out the previous peak of $852 in 1980, helped by a weaker U.S. dollar. Recently gold was $1.50 lower from the overnight close.   

Soft commodity prices have also gained, led by palm oil, a biofuel feedstock that can substitute for crude.   

Palm oil opened at an all-time high on the Bursa Malaysia Derivatives exchange of MYR3,159 a metric ton for March delivery, before slipping back a touch. The March contract is now MYR50 higher on the day at MYR3,132/ton.   


 
   More Cues Sought On US Economy 
    

Traders are now looking to Friday's release of a monthly non-farm payrolls report in the U.S. for further leads on the economy, after data Thursday showed the Institute of Supply Management's December manufacturing index fell to 47.7 from 50.8 in November, the weakest reading in nearly five years and an indication of contraction in the manufacturing sector of the economy.   

"The reaction to the much weaker than expected ISM indicator shows how sensitive the market is to negative news out of the U.S.," said Standard Chartered in a research note. "We do believe there are significant downside risks to U.S. domestic demand and the global credit markets in the coming quarters, which will be felt globally."   

Asian stocks are tracking Wall Street's decline, though liquidity remains thin with Japanese markets closed until Friday.   

The S&P/ASX 200 in Australia has fallen 1.4% to 6,263.7, while the Kospi Composite in South Korea is off 0.8% to 1,839.24. Losses in Korea are limited as the market already fell 2.3% Wednesday.   

Shares in Hong Kong are also faring poorly with the Hang Seng down 1.7% to 27,089.41, and the Straits Times Index in Singapore off 1.5% to 3,409.84.   

Among market sectors, gold, oil and alternative energy shares are faring well, while companies that rely heavily on energy faring poorly.   

Korean petrochemical companies are lower as analysts say these companies will find it difficult to pass on higher input costs as quickly as oil prices are rising. LG Chem (051910.SE) was recently down 4.5%.   

Among alternative energy companies, Taiwan's Gintech Energy (3514.TW) was up 1.3%, and E-Ton Solar Tech (3452.OT) up 1.7%, while Korean solar energy companies are also on the rise with DC Chemical (010060.SE) up 2.6%.   

Oil-sensitive airline shares are generally weaker, though some airlines may benefit from a weaker U.S. dollar, as it cuts the cost of funding their dollar-denominated debt.   

The rise in gold prices has aided shares of gold miners across the region. China's Shandong Gold-Mining (600547.SH) has gained 8.5%, while in Australia, Newcrest (NCM.AU) has added 5%.   

Among currencies, the dollar is still weak against Japanese yen after an overnight tumble, recently around Y109.55.   

Meanwhile the Singapore dollar reached a ten year high against the U.S. dollar, with traders watching for signs of intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore.   

Analysts generally look for further dollar declines in the near term. "The trend will be for a weak dollar over the first few months of the year," said  Citigroup economist Stephen Halmarick.   

Still, CMC Markets' chief currency analyst Ashraf Laidi looks for a dollar recovery going into 2008, and adds this can come in tandem with prolonged gold gains.   

Global interest rates are likely to head lower with investors hit by a double whammy of rising inflation and falling nominal yields, "two reasons prompting the shift to higher-yielding gold," he said.   

At the same time, U.S. interest rate cuts won't occur in a vacuum, while prolonged selling in equities should trigger falls in higher-yielding currencies against the dollar, he said.   

Bond markets are rising after a gain in U.S. Treasurys overnight, with bonds taking their cue from the poor ISM reading.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar ended slightly higher on thin volume Wednesday in Asian trade, with few traders around and the market having priced in domestic inflationary pressures.   

"The Singapore dollar has been quite flat in the past few trading sessions on thin trading," a strategist with a local bank said. "Not a lot of traders are around, and there's not a lot of trading interest."   

Although Singapore's November consumer price index data - released Monday - showed the highest rate of inflation in 25 years at 4.2% on year, the strategist said the upward movement was already priced in by the market.   

Another trader said the market is wary of another intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which seeks a gradual appreciation of the domestic currency against the U.S. greenback.   

The strategist said the U.S. dollar should close the year around S$1.45, but said the currency will continue to slide next year on an anticipated slowdown in the world's largest economy and expectations of further rate cuts by the U.S. Federal Reserve.   

The strategist also said that continued international pressure on the Chinese government to let the yuan appreciate faster will serve to strengthen most other Asian currencies.   

In the local bond market, trading was thin, with short-term yields moving up on selling pressure following the domestic inflation data.   

A local trader said that most market players were closing their positions ahead of the year-end.   

-By Se Young Lee, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4154; vincent.lee@dowjones.com [ 26-12-07 0734GMT ]

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)-- The Singapore dollar ended slightly higher in Asian trade Thursday, but its gains were capped by the possibility of another intervention by the Singapore central bank.   

Traders said a broad decline in Asian equity markets also halted the local currency from rising further.   

A trader with a local bank said the Monetary Authority of Singapore's suspected market intervention Tuesday, after the U.S. dollar dropped to S$1.4372, continues to keep players on their toes.   

"I don't think it (the U.S. dollar) can go significantly lower (than at current levels), because the MAS will do something if it does," the trader said.   

The market also largely ignored the joint actions of the U.S. Federal Reserve and four other central banks to ease the global bank funding crisis, the trader said.   

The market's indifference to the Fed's 25-basis-point rate cut and that the year is almost over will keep the greenback's trading levels at around S$1.44 right into early 2008, the trader added.   

Local government bond prices rose again, another trader with a local bank said, on foreign investors' strong appetite for short-to-medium range papers, as they bet that the Singapore dollar is expected to appreciate further for some time to come.   

By Se Young Lee, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4154; vincent.lee@dowjones.com [ 13-12-07 0823GMT ]

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar finished marginally lower in Asian trade Tuesday as traders saw some large buying interest in the U.S. dollar.   

Some traders suspect that Singapore's central bank could have been in the market, buying the greenback after it hit an intra-day low of S$1.4372, close to a 10-year low of S$1.4363 tested in November.   

"There was a sudden spike in the U.S. dollar from S$1.4382, and there was (follow-through) buying interest," said a trader.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which has said that it prefers a modest and gradual appreciation of the local currency against its major trading currencies, doesn't comment on its market operations.   

Traders now await the outcome of December's Federal Open Market Committee in the U.S. later tonight.   

Though most expect the Fed to cut interest rate by 25 basis points, a 50-basis point cut could send the US dollar sliding against higher-yielding currencies as risk appetite will increase further.   

"The reaction of Wall Street to the Fed meeting will be a key driver for Asian currencies," said another trader.   

Local government bond yields were flat on thin volumes as players were sitting on the sidelines ahead of the Fed meeting.   

"Given concerns of domestic inflation and with the market the already having discounted a 25 basis points interest rate cut by Fed, there isn't much movement that could be seen in the bond market," said a trader.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar ended higher in Asian trade Tuesday as investors were selling U.S. dollars, given the greenback's weak outlook, while the absence of an intervention by the central bank in the past few sessions boosted the local currency, traders said.   

They, however, said that investors were still cautious about placing any big bets, as they await the U.S. non-farm payrolls data due Friday that might give hint to the Federal Reserve's decision on policy rates at its Federal Open Market Committee meeting next week.   

The fact that the Monetary Authority of Singapore hasn't been in the market since its last intervention Thursday gave comfort to some investors selling U.S. dollars, said a trader with a foreign bank.

title: Emerging  FX -Central banks step in as Asians reach for highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar, Korean won and Malaysian ringgit hit fresh 10-year highs on Friday after weak U.S. data led to renewed selling of the dollar and spurred some Asian central banks to step into the market.   

The dollar fell broadly after Thursday's soft durable goods orders, coming on top of the previous day's data showing existing home sales at a record low in September, which intensified expectations of another rate cut by the Federal Reserve next week.   

U.S. crude oil prices at $92 a barrel and the jump in gold prices to 28-year highs also hurt the dollar.   

The dollar hit a record low of $1.4377 against the euro <EUR=>.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was capped at a 10-year high of 1.4523 per U.S. dollar, after a rally of a quarter percent. It retreated in later deals to 1.4595, but analysts remained bullish.   

"I would sell rallies on the U.S. dollar whenever the MAS intervenes. Inflation is creeping higher, so the Sing dollar will eventually appreciate," said a trader.   

That seemed to be the predominant view.   

BNP Paribas analyst Thio Chin Loo said she sees the Singapore dollar at 1.40 by the year-end.   

JPMorgan's strategists said Asian central banks were likely to intervene to rein in their currencies but would progressively have to buy dollars at lower levels since bad news from credit markets and views on U.S. rates would weigh on the dollar.   

Analysts said the Singapore dollar had outperformed some of its neighbours and was near the top end of the secret trade-weighted band in which the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the currency.   

"Intervention seems very plausible to me," said Westpac Bank's Sean Callow, who felt that long positions in the Indian rupee <INR=IN> and Philippine peso had better potential for returns.   

RINGGIT, PESO   

The ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.345 per dollar, rising past the 3.35 level for the first time since late 1997 and taking its gains in just 3 sessions to more than 1 percent.   

Traders said the central bank had bought dollars through some banks, but the momentum of ringgit-buying was too strong.   

Suresh Kumar Ramanathan of CIMB Bank said the ringgit would see a sudden jump if the 3.345 level was breached, with the next resistance coming in only at 3.33 - a level seen in Nov. 1997.   

Earlier in the day, Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz was quoted by media as telling businesses they should learn to cope with ringgit fluctuations even if it worked against them.   

The Philippine central bank (BSP) was suspected of buying dollars to keep the peso <PHP=> from hitting the 44-per-dollar level. The currency stalled at a seven-year high of 44.02 per dollar, just a fraction higher than Thursday's 44.03 peak.   

"BSP is buying dollars heavily but the market flows are all on one side -- selling," a trader in Manila said.   

South Korea's central bank warned market participants it would take steps if the won <KRW=> rose excessively. The won stopped short of 909 per dollar, but hit 10-year highs.   

The Japanese yen <JPY=> was fickle on Friday, rising initially on the dollar's weakness to near 114 per dollar and then falling as the Nikkei average <.N225> and other Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA> rose and investors seemed to be selectively returning to risky assets.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> hit a record high of 572.20, surpassing the previous peak of 569.13 set on Oct. 11.
