title: Emerging  FX -Asia dithers on listless stocks, U.S. dollar
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar recovered a quarter of a percent on Wednesday but other Asian currencies were listless, trapped in tight ranges by the dollar's vacillations and uncertainty about risk appetite.   

Asian stock markets also wavered, hurt in later trades by reports that  Merrill Lynch & Co. was expected to add more losses related to declining market values for its debt holdings.   

The dollar slipped overnight but clawed back in Asian trading against the euro <EUR=> and a broad basket of currencies as markets waited for Wednesday's U.S. existing home sales data.   

But it has been volatile this week, falling after the Group of Seven officials failed to explicitly mention its weakness, rising subsequently from what some considered oversold levels on Monday and weakening again on Tuesday.   

The yen <JPY=> rallied, indicating another bout of risk aversion as investors exited carry trades.   

In emerging Asia, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.4614 per U.S. dollar, and the Malaysian ringgit rose 0.2 percent to 3.3670 per dollar.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell to 918 per dollar after an initial 0.1 percent rise to 916.6 per dollar, in spite of verbal and suspected dollar-buying intervention by the Korean authorities in the previous session.   

"Investors are still cautious on Asia FX as the trend has not been as strong or defined as the equity markets," said Claudio Piron, a strategist at JPMorgan Chase Bank.   

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> rose to 39.455 per dollar, then pared gains as the stock market <.BSESN> fell.   

The rupee has, however, rebounded sharply from lows of 39.96 struck last Wednesday after regulators proposed restrictions on derivatives used by foreigners investing in the Indian market. The measures could be implemented on Thursday.   

CHINA SPECULATION   

Meanwhile, the non-deliverable forwards <CNYNDFOR=> market showed the yuan at fresh highs after media quoted an in-house report by the National Development and Reform Commission as suggesting China should consider a one-off 15-20 percent yuan revaluation.   

A news department official at NDRC said he was unaware of this report, but it gave markets the ammunition to speculate further on the possibility China will allow the tightly-managed yuan to rise faster.   

Spot yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit 7.4928 per dollar, its highest since the yuan was revalued in July 2005. One-year NDFs took the yuan to the firmer side of 7-per-dollar for the first time, to 6.996 or a 7.1 percent effective appreciation in 12 months.   

"With the implied yuan 12-month gain now sitting just short of 7 percent, either the recent speculative selling is an inspired bet on an imminent yuan surge or it is time to buy NDFs on a range-play heading back to a more typical 5 percent handle," Westpac Bank's Sean Callow said in a note.   

Callow said he would bet on the latter, but added that sentiment on the dollar would have to improve considerably for NDFs to move back to being less bullish yuan.   

Elsewhere, the fear of intervention kept Singapore dollar bulls from chasing the currency higher.   

The currency is still some way off 10-year highs of 1.4577 struck last week, when the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was suspected of intervening to hold it down. It has moved between 1.46 and 1.4678 this week.   

"Eventually, Sing dollar has to rise but, in the short term, there's MAS to deal with," a trader in Hong Kong said.   

Westpac Bank's Callow said that while the MAS's policy of encouraging currency appreciation to rein in inflation reinforced the firm tone for the Singapore dollar, it had still outperformed trading partners such as the yuan and rupiah in recent weeks.   

"Hence while the Singapore dollar does have the appeal of less vulnerability to passing global jitters, there is limited prospect for returns on short U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar to beat the U.S. dollar/Asia average since MAS bids won't be far away," he said in a note.

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  currencies  weaker despite stocks rally
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies weakened on Tuesday, yielding ground to a recovering U.S. dollar and failing to find any support from a rally in stock markets as traders groped for direction.   

 The Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit led the decline in the Asian currencies.   

 The dollar rebounded sharply from its record lows struck against the euro <EUR=> on Monday after what traders interpreted as G7 indifference towards the currency's weakness. It also climbed back against the yen <JPY=> and other currencies.   

 But trading was marked by confusion, with some looking for bargains in the oversold dollar against the Asians and others returning to risky assets. Some traders also felt the dollar's decline had been overdone -- its trade-weighted basket <.DXY> has fallen nearly 2 percent in two weeks.   

 In Asia, stocks rebounded. MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> climbed to 554 from Monday's lows near 540. The index had its steepest fall since Aug. 16 on Monday.   

 At its weakest, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> shed 0.4 percent to hit 1.4678 per U.S. dollar, the ringgit <MYR=> lost 0.3 percent to hit 3.38 per dollar and the high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> dropped a quarter of a percent to 9,135 per dollar.   

 The Singapore dollar subsequently rallied to 1.4650, with traders preparing for the currency to appreciate in anticipation of tighter monetary policy as inflation accelerates.   

 "There's marginal downward pressure on U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar due to inflationary pressures," said Standard Chartered Bank's strategist Thomas Harr.   

 "We are in strong end of band already. I see the pair at 1.46 by year-end."   

 Singapore's annual inflation in September was 2.7 percent, softening from a 12-year high hit in August of 2.9 percent. Still, high oil and house prices are expected to keep inflation levels elevated.   

 The currency has come off a 10-year high of 1.4577 hit last week.   

 But it has still risen 2.6 percent in the past month, a rally sparked by the Fed's 50-basis-point rate cut on Sept. 18 and positioning for Singapore's policy review on Oct. 10, when the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) increased the pace of appreciation of the currency.   

 COPYCAT RINGGIT   

 The ringgit has so far dropped half a percent in two sessions. Traders said the ringgit and Singapore dollar were moving in tandem, both undermined by suspected intervention by their respective central banks after hitting decade highs last week.   

 Traders said they would not buy the ringgit against dollars unless there was a big rise in the Singapore dollar as well.   

 "After all dollar/ringgit is negative carry if you sell dollars, so Bank Negara can always afford to buy dollars," a trader in Hong Kong said, referring to the intervention.   

 Malaysia's 3.5 percent overnight policy rate is below the fed funds rate at 4.75 percent, making it more profitable to hold dollars.   

 Analysts at  JPMorgan Chase said that in contrast with the Singapore dollar, which was on the strong side of its trade-weighted band, the ringgit was trading about 180 basis points on the weaker side of an estimated informal trade-weighted policy band.   

 They also expect Malaysian inflation data due on Wednesday to show some upward pressure on consumer prices.   

 "Still, the challenge remains that the ringgit is sensitive to risk appetite and the vagaries of equity market sentiment. In this respect, we expect long ringgit positions to experience some downside and volatility this week,"  JPMorgan said.   

 Elsewhere, the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> tested the upper end of its 7.75-7.85 linked exchange rate system to the U.S. dollar, driven by cash flows into the stock market and speculation that the peg might either be abandoned or recalibrated. [nSHA15826].

title: MAS Tightening Puts Singapore Dollar On Track For New Record
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--A surprise monetary tightening by Singapore's central bank Wednesday vaulted the Singapore dollar up sharply and put it on track to rise to its all-time high set during the 1990s boom.   

The stronger Singapore dollar will help cap mounting price pressures in the city state but won't cause exporters to lose their competitive footing against regional rivals because other Asian currencies are also on an upward course against a swooning U.S. dollar, analysts say.   

"The stronger Singapore dollar is not going to put a massive downward pressure on exports," said Prakriti Sofat, an economist at  HSBC in Singapore.   

"The appreciation is still going to be very gradual and we think the government is going to be very cautious about maintaining economic growth."   

The Singapore dollar sprung to a 10-year high against the U.S. currency early Wednesday after the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it would "increase slightly" the slope of its undisclosed trade-weighted currency band. The U.S. dollar fell to S$1.4631 - a point last reached in July 1997 - from S$1.4720 just before the central bank issued the statement.   

Citigroup economist Chua Hak Bin said the new policy may allow the trade-weighted currency to rise an extra 0.2-0.5 percentage point each year beyond the estimated 1.9% rate allowed previously. He now expects U.S. dollar to finish 2008 at S$1.3900 compared to a previous forecast of S$1.4100.   

That target is just above the Singapore dollar's record high set in May 1995, when the U.S. currency fetched only S$1.3835. And the local currency may approach the record more quickly if Singapore's red-hot economy maintains momentum, Chua said.   

"Further MAS tightening may be necessary next year, via more 'slight' fine-tuning," Chua said. "Lower Singapore dollar interest rates, following the Fed rate cuts, have moreover exacerbated demand pressures."   

The more hawkish stance by Singapore's central bank stems from concerns that rising inflation could pose a growing risk to the economy, which has been booming on growth in financial services and surging output of pharmaceuticals and offshore oil rigs.   

The central bank's statement noted the local three-month interbank interest rate has fallen to about 2.5% from 3.5% in February. It forecast inflation will stay within a 1.5%-2% range this year and 2%-3% in 2008, but warned about the impending impact of rising residential rents and property prices.   

That means Singapore, which uses the foreign exchange rate to influence prices because external trade dwarfs the domestic economy, is likely willing to let its currency rise at a moderately faster pace.   

"Against a robust growth backdrop, the MAS is clearly taking no chances when it comes to the inflation outlook, hence the tightening step,"  Rabobank said in a note to clients.   

Rabobank now forecasts the U.S. dollar will drop to S$1.4300 by the end of 2008, lower than its forecast of S$1.4400 before the MAS policy statement.   

To be sure, the central bank will be vigilant against sharp swings in foreign exchange rates. It has demonstrated a willingness to keep a tight grip on the currency.   

JPMorgan Chase Bank and Societe Generale noted unconfirmed talk in the market Wednesday that the Singapore authorities had intervened to cushion the U.S. dollar's early plunge, though other traders played down such speculation.   

Still, traders have said the MAS was active in the market during periods of heightened volatility last month to prevent drastic appreciation. And late last year the central bank added tens of billions of U.S. dollars in currency forward exposure in an apparent effort stem the local currency's rise.   

HSBC's Sofat said the strength in the Singapore dollar is in line with gains in other Asian currencies. The Singapore dollar has gained about 5% against the U.S. dollar in 2007 while the Chinese yuan has risen 4% and the Malaysian Ringgit is up nearly 10%.   

"The Singapore dollar has been appreciating, but the rest of the currencies across Asia are also moving higher," Sofat said. "The MAS is keeping a conservative view and it's unlikely we'll see exports threatened," she added.   

She said Singapore's economy may decelerate only slightly next year from the MAS's 7%-8% target for 2007.   

The central bank said it expects the economy to expand by 4%-6% in 2008, but both  HSBC and  Citigroup expect a higher rate of expansion.

title: 2nd UPDATE: Singapore MAS Tightens Policy As Inflation Picks Up
text:
(Adds market response, economists' comments, additional background.) 
 
   By John Jannarone 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
    

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore shifted monetary policy a notch tighter Wednesday in response to rising inflationary pressure and an upbeat economic growth outlook, a surprise move marking the first change in the central bank's stance in over three years.   

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it would increase slightly the slope of its undisclosed trade-weighted currency band but that it hadn't changed the width or centering of the policy target.   

The news caused the Singapore dollar to jump to a 10-year high as investors speculated the authorities are now willing to let the currency rise at a faster pace to temper increases in consumer prices.   

The U.S. dollar fell to S$1.4631 from S$1.4720 just before the announcement, putting traders on guard for possible intervention by Singapore authorities seeking to smooth sharp movements. The U.S. currency later rebounded to just above S$1.4650, amid unconfirmed rumors that the MAS had entered the market.   

The monetary tightening suggests that Singapore policy makers are serious about getting inflation under control, even at the expense of slower growth. The MAS's more hawkish stance led some analysts to predict the central bank might tighten policy again as soon as its next meeting in April.   

The decision also highlights the need for Asian central banks to tailor policy to suit local economic conditions, even as the Federal Reserve recently moved to an easier money policy. For Singapore, which uses the foreign exchange rate to influence prices because external trade dwarfs the domestic economy, that means that a tighter monetary policy - or stronger Singapore dollar - is warranted.   

"In Singapore the business cycle is not exactly in synch with the U.S., so there's a need for fine-tuning," said Chua Hak Bin, an economist at  Citigroup in Singapore.   

Wednesday's move marked the first time since April 2004 that the Monetary Authority of Singapore has altered its monetary policy. Since then, the central bank had kept a preference for a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, paving the way for the currency to rise 16% against the U.S. dollar over that period.   

Behind the change in stance is concern that inflation is starting to become a problem for the city state, analysts said.   

Inflation in Singapore may "have breached the central bank's comfort zone," said Chua, noting the MAS expects the consumer price index to rise by 3.5% in the first half of 2008.   

"Inflation is going to ease back, but it will be near a historical high," he said.   

The central bank said inflation will average between 2%-3% in 2008 after coming in at 1.5%-2% in 2007.   

A recent increase in Singapore's sales tax is partly to blame for the higher rate of inflation. The MAS estimates that 0.7 percentage point of each year's rise reflects a one-time impact of the tax hike to 7% from 5% on July 1.   

But there is reason to believe that price pressures have deeper roots. The MAS warned that prices for food, oil and other commodities are expected to continue to pick up, while higher property prices will also begin to feed into consumer inflation.   

Private property prices in Singapore are still below the peak from 1996, but the local real estate market continues to boom with few signs of a slowdown.   

Third-quarter private property prices rose 8% from the second quarter after rising 8.3% in the previous three months. The second quarter increase was the fastest in eight years.   


 
   Broad-Based Expansion 
    

Robust economic growth is underpinning the real estate boom and a tight labor market.   

The economy grew 6.4% in the third quarter from the second on an adjusted, annualized basis, led by strength across the economy and a faster expansion in manufacturing, Singapore's trade ministry said in a separate release.   

That was a slower pace than in the second quarter, when gross domestic product expanded 14.4%, but it beat analysts' projections. A Dow Jones Newswires poll of economists forecast the economy had expanded 5.6%.   

The ministry said the economy is "well on track" to meet the government's 7%-8% growth forecast in 2007.   

Singapore's mainstay manufacturing expanded 12.3% in the third quarter from a year earlier after growing 8.3% in the second quarter.   

The services sector grew 8.1% from a year earlier after rising 8.4% in the second quarter.   

The sizzling property market continued to support construction, which jumped 15.5% following a 18.8% expansion in the previous three months.   

Compared with a year earlier, the economy grew 9.4%, compared with 8.6% growth in the second quarter.   

The Dow Jones poll pointed to on-year growth of 9.1% in the third quarter.   

The advance GDP figures are mainly based on data from the first two months of the quarter.   


 
   Hawkish Tone 
    

Economists say Wednesday's monetary policy tweak sets a precedent for further adjustments if price pressures persist.   

"We see room for further MAS tightening at the next monetary policy meeting in April 2008," said Matthew Hildebrandt, an economist at  J.P. Morgan in Singapore.   

He said Wednesday's statement had "a much more hawkish tone than the last, with concerns about inflation clearly outweighing those about growth."   

The central bank's statement said the U.S. economy has weakened and other economies are also likely to soften, but Singapore may post economic growth of 4%-6% in 2008.   

"The global economy is expected to remain resilient, particularly in Asia," the MAS statement said.   

As the economy expands apace, wage growth has picked up, adding to inflationary pressures.   

Wages rose 8.5% from a year earlier in the second quarter, the fastest pace in seven years.   

Also, major gauges of money supply show expansion exceeding 20%, the fastest expansion since the early 1990s.   

"Given the strong growth numbers clearly inflationary pressures are building in the economy," said Prakriti Sofat, an economist at  HSBC in Singapore.   

"We think there are signs of overheating."

text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 2 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit fell half a percent on Tuesday, leading a retreat in Asian currencies as investors exited stretched positions ahead of a string of U.S. economic data that could determine direction for the U.S. dollar.   

The ringgit <MYR=> gave up all of this week's gains to hit 3.4110 per dollar, down 0.8 percent from Monday's 4-month high of 3.3850.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> shed 0.5 percent, swinging from a high of 1.4753 per U.S. dollar to a low of 1.4835.   

And the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was forced off a 2-month high of 9,055 per dollar and pushed to levels around 9,100, slightly down on the day.   

"I think there was some intervention in the Singapore dollar," said a trader.   

"But, in general, people are also worried about the sharp sell-off in dollar/Asia, and some fast money accounts are covering their shorts now," he said.   

Worries about excessive positioning against the dollar also saw high-yielders such as the Australian dollar <AUD=> decline.   

The dollar stayed just off record lows against the euro <EUR=>, helped in part by a record high close in the Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> on Monday.   

It also got a breather as markets waited for a series of data and central bank policy meetings, including the Bank of England and European Central Bank on Thursday.   

The U.S. Institute for Supply Management's non-manufacturing index and non-farm payrolls reports are due later this week, and could offer clues on whether U.S. rates will be cut again to offset the impact of a housing market slump.   

The Philippine peso gained 0.2 percent to 44.74 per dollar in early deals before ending local trade slightly weaker at 44.915.   

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> retreated to 32.57 from the previous session's 9-month high of 32.465.   

Markets in India and China were closed for holidays.   

BULLISH RUPIAH   

Foreign demand for Indonesian stocks and bonds has helped drive the rupiah up nearly 4 percent in 3 weeks. Some analysts expect it will continue to be strong near term.   

The rupiah has been underpinned by investment inflows into a rising Jakarta stock market <.JKSE>, whose index hit an all-time high on Tuesday.   

Analysts said expectations that the authorities will cut policy rates again and also encourage rupiah appreciation to rein in imported inflation from higher oil prices were behind the growing foreign appetite for Indonesian assets.   

Indonesia's one-month policy rate, now at 8.25 percent, has already been cut 13 times in line with falling inflation, but there are signs now that price pressures are returning.   

"The broad U.S. dollar backdrop continues to be weak... and the balance of payments surplus will continue to support rupiah appreciation,"  JPMorgan Chase said in a note.   

"This, in our view, will drive dollar/rupiah to 8,700 by year-end and may also dampen inflationary pressures through softer import prices,"  JPMorgan said.

title: Emerging  FX -Singapore dollar at 10-yr high, rupiah rises
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 1 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a 10-year high on Monday, leading a rally in Asian currencies after weakness in U.S. inflation data renewed selling pressure in the U.S. dollar.   

The Singapore dollar rose nearly 1 percent to hit 1.4765 per dollar, its strongest since July 1997.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> also gained strongly, each rising by at least half a percent.   

The rupiah hit a 2-month high of 9,079 per dollar. The Philippine peso <PHP=> hit a 2-month high of 44.85 per dollar, then stalled on fears of central bank intervention.   

The dollar hit another record low against both the euro <EUR=> and a basket of currencies after a tame reading in the Federal Reserve's favoured price index stoked expectations of another cut in U.S. rates.   

The dollar's decline was spurred by the Fed's large half point rate cut on Sept. 18, one that was designed to buffer the economy from the problems in the subprime mortgage sector.   

Traders expect trading volumes in Asia to thin this week as Chinese markets are closed for National Day holidays.   

Some also were getting nervous about selling the dollar too aggressively ahead of the Group of Seven nations' meeting in Washington in mid-October.   

"There is a sizeable short-dollar position," said  Bank of Americacurrency strategist Han Sia Yeo.   

"The dollar could see a bounce this week on prospects of stronger-than-expected U.S. data," he said.   

OCBC Bank strategist Emmanuel Ng said in a note he expected the momentum of dollar-selling to persist although there were signs of positions getting excessively extended.   

He also warned that Asian central banks could intervene to slow gains in the regionals.   

Analysts at DBS told investors to anticipate more volatility ahead of the G7 meeting.   

European policy makers have been calling for a stronger dollar and expressing worry about the euro's rapid rise.   

Meanwhile, Federal Reserve Governor Frederic Mishkin said last week Europe's economy will have to adapt with the changing value of the dollar.   

"The market will be looking out for rhetoric out of G7 officials that will suggest whether or not the U.S. dollar and the Chinese yuan will be mentioned in the G7 communique, something that the Europeans appear to favour, and the Americans opposed," DBS said in a note.   

SINGAPORE DOLLAR   

Traders, meanwhile, were pricing in more appreciation for the Singapore dollar, partly on belief the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will retain a gradual tightening bias when it reviews policy on Oct. 10.   

The currency is the MAS's main policy tool. It has gained more than 3 percent in the past three weeks, but traders estimated it was still on the weaker side of the secret trade-weighted or nominal-effective-exchange-rate (NEER) band within which the MAS guides the currency.   

"Most of the people have missed out on this move as they kept thinking MAS would intervene at some point of time," a Singapore-based trader said.   

"Technically, there aren't any supports for U.S. dollar before the 1.45-handle, so I think we have enough room to move to the downside, particularly in the run up to the monetary policy."   

Analysts at  UBS said the Singapore dollar had stayed within 0.65 percent of the mid-point of the MAS's policy band in the past four months. But the central bank's recent upward revision to its inflation forecasts for the year suggested it was happy to have the currency appreciate, they said.   

"This in our view signals the MAS is not about to let down its guard on inflation despite the recent market volatility. We think the MAS is pretty happy seeing the NEER rising,"  UBS said in a note. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0757 GMT

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  caps peso, but Taiwan dollar jumps
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The Philippine central bank's suspected dollar buying stalled rises in the high-yielding peso on Friday, while the Taiwan dollar and South Korean won jumped as investors raised their bet on further U.S. interest rate cuts.   

The low-yielding Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose as far as 32.50 per U.S. dollar, up 0.6 percent from Thursday's close to a nine-month high, amid signs that the central bank was selling the U.S. currency along with local exporters.   

"They (the central bank) think the Taiwan dollar should strengthen slightly to help reduce the inflationary risk," said a trader in Singapore. "And the U.S. dollar/Asia go lower."   

The won <KRW=> gained 0.6 percent to 914.80 per dollar, a two-month high.   

The peso <PHP=> pulled back to the weaker side of 45 per dollar after its attempt to break the two-month peak of 44.90 was foiled by suspected central bank intervention.   

"The central bank was spotted at the 44.90 level. There was also some mild profit-taking," said a trader in Manila.   

"Probably it wants to prevent a sharp drop for the dollar/peso to limit volatility," said a second trader.   

The peso has gained nearly 9 percent against the dollar so far this year, trailing behind the 11 percent gains in the Indian rupee <INR=IN>, another high-yielding currency in Asia.   

Asian currencies, led by the high-yielders, have rallied alongside rising regional stocks after the Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate by 50 basis points last Tuesday.   

"In general, we expect the trend to continue, maybe not at the (current) pace," said Magnus Prim, SEB's chief Asia currency strategist.   

"We are positive on the rupiah and peso -- these two probably have more to go. The Singapore dollar is also one," he said.   

EYE ON U.S. ECONOMY   

The dollar stuck near record lows against the euro <EUR=> and a basket of major currencies after U.S. data showed sales of new homes plunged in August, cementing expectations that the Fed would cut interest rates again next month.   

Investors awaited reports on U.S. business activity and inflation data to gauge the health of the world's largest economy and how far the Fed is likely to loosen its monetary policy further.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, another high-yielder, moved in a tight range between 9,125 and 9,158 per dollar.   

"The rupiah might move between the 9,120 and 9,170 range for the next week," said a trader in Jakarta.   

Analysts are increasingly bullish about the rupiah, which remains the worst performer in Asia this year, but some caution that foreigners might pull out from the country's bond markets as higher inflation could stifle the chance of another rate cut.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a fresh 10-year high at 1.4887 to the U.S. dollar, bringing its gains in the past week to 1 percent amid expectations that the central bank will stick to its modest tightening policy in a meeting early next month. title: Sing dollar at one-month high, spurred by yen, yuan
text:
SINGAPORE, March 1 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit its highest level in a month on Wednesday, lifted by a rising Japanese yen and Chinese yuan, but operators were wary of central bank intervention to rein the currency in.  

The Sing dollar <SGD=> hit 1.6198 per U.S. dollar in early deals, its strongest level since the end of January, taking its gain to more than one percent in less than two weeks. It later steadied around 1.6205/15.  

Traders suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened on Tuesday to slow down the Sing dollar's rise.  

"MAS has been tempering the pace of appreciation. But I expect both the yuan and yen to appreciate strongly over the next 10 to 15 days and these will pull the Sing dollar with them," one Singapore-based trader said.  

The yen <JPY=> was quoted around 115.95 a dollar. It has risen more than 2.5 percent in a week on expectations of a near-term end to Japan's ultra-easy monetary policy.  

The Chinese yuan has risen this week to its highest level since its revaluation last July.  

Analysts estimated that the Sing dollar's rise this year had taken it to the top end of the MAS's policy band.  

The MAS conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band based on a trade-weighted basket of currencies.  

JPMorgan strategist Claudio Piron said in a note the Sing dollar was particularly susceptible to any decline in the yen.  

But traders were bullish. "I don't think it's too expensive. We do have a reasonable chance to go towards 1.6120," one said.

title: Singapore Dollar Falls, Bonds Stabilize After Losses
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell Tuesday due to pent-up corporate buying of the U.S. dollar to meet month-end payments and on talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

Government bonds stabilized after two days of losses as corporate buyers returned to seek bargains, dealers said.  

At 0615 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6241, up from S$1.6230 in late New York trade Monday. It traded at S$1.6244 in late Asian trade Friday.  

The U.S. dollar moved between S$1.6215 and S$1.6259 intraday.  

The U.S. unit pulled up from a morning low of S$1.6232 to S$1.6255 on talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have checked the Singapore's unit rise, a trader at a local bank said.  

Later, importers came back into the market to buy the greenback to meet corporate payments, dealers said.  

Against the yen, the U.S. unit rose to a session high of Y116.49 on the EBS before slipping to Y116.32, compared to Y116.20 at the New York close.  

Traders said the Singapore dollar's recent gains were due to strength in the yen, but room for more gains was limited.  

Sean Callow, a currency strategist at Westpac Bank, said he favors long U.S. dollar positions against the Singapore dollar because the trade-weighted Singapore dollar has, he believes, reached the top of Monetary Authority of Singapore's undisclosed target band.  

"Hence we would not be in the least surprised if Tuesday's market anecdotes of MAS intervention on USD/SGD are correct. Short-term, we continue to see risk/reward in favor of long USD/SGD with a S$1.62 handle," Callow said in a note to clients.  

He said his outlook should stay intact until the MAS reviews its policy in April. Many in the market expect the central bank to push for a steeper appreciation of the local unit to contain inflation.  

Bonds consolidated after two days of heavy selling, sparked by last week's 10-year government bond auction, where yields rose sharply.  

Both the two- and 10-year bonds closed flat at 2.86% and 3.52% respectively after some weakness in the early session, when the 10-year opened at 3.53%, dealers said.  

The 10-year bond has risen 20 basis points from 3.32% late Thursday.

title: Singapore Dollar Lifted By Yen, Bonds Extend Losses
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar extended gains Friday, reacting to a strong Asian rally in the Japanese yen on expectations the Bank of Japan may soon end its ultra-easy monetary policy.  

Government bonds declined, reacting to overnight losses in U.S. Treasurys and concerns over Singapore's inflation, dealers said.  

At 0647 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6250, slightly down from S$1.6253 in late New York trade Thursday. It traded at S$1.6288 in late Asian trade Thursday.  

The U.S. dollar moved between S$1.6226 and S$1.6272 intraday.  

Traders said the Singapore forex market was tied to the movements in the dollar-yen,  

The Japanese yen rallied after BOJ Governor Toshihiko Fukui told a government financial committee Thursday conditions for ending the quantitative easing policy are "gradually ripening."  

On Friday, the U.S. unit briefly dropped to Y116.42 - the lowest level since Y116.12 on Jan. 27 - after selling by U.S. banks and macrofunds triggered stop-loss orders around Y116.50, traders said. It had closed Thursday's New York session at Y117.11.  

However a dealer at Singapore bank said the U.S. dollar erased some of its early losses after having slipped to S$1.6226 on fears Singapore's central bank would intervene.  

January's inflation data for Singapore that showed consumer price index rising 1.7% from a year earlier in January - the largest gain since November 2004 - has also made players bullish about the currency despite belief that the local unit is on the stronger side of trade-weighted band, traders said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore had forecast inflation to remain between 0.5% and 1.5% in 2006, up from 0.5% last year.  

Higher prices and a strong economy has increased the likelihood of the central bank shifting to a tighter monetary policy and allowing a steeper appreciation of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate, bankers said.  

DBS Bank said any upside surprise on inflation in the run-up to the April policy announcement could increase the risk of a tighter monetary policy.  

"This could be carried out via a steeper appreciation bias or a level shift of the (Singapore dollar) exchange rate. Since the start of the year, the SGD nominal effective exchange rate has been trading on the strong side of the band," DBS said.  

Yields on the two-year bond rose eight basis points to 2.82% - its fourth consecutive rise - while the 10-year bond yield rose four basis points to 3.36% after losses in U.S. Treasurys overnight and concerns over inflation.  

Friday's auction for sale of S$1.1 billion 10-year government bonds also increased anxiety as the cutoff yield of 3.45% showed market participants weren't keen to buy bonds at lower yields.

title: Singapore Dolllar Flat Late; Rumored MAS Action Early
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar ended a choppy Asian trading session nearly flat against the U.S. dollar Thursday, ahead of the second day of new U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's congressional testimony.  

Government bonds weakened slightly in the wake of robust Singapore data, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6294, almost unchanged from Wednesday's New York close of S$1.6291. It was quoted at S$1.6298 in Asia Wednesday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. dollar rose to an intraday high of S$1.6320 on interbank-led short-covering spurred by rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

The central bank apparently bought the U.S. currency in the S$1.6292-S$1.6295 area via local banks in the morning, prompting interbank players to buy back U.S. dollars, they added.  

Foreign exchange market participants shrugged off the early morning release of stronger-than-expected Singapore data, focusing more on this suspected intervention.  

Fourth-quarter gross domestic product grew 8.7% from a year earlier. This beat the 8.2% average growth forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of economists.  

Citing stronger domestic and external demand, export-dependent Singapore raised its forecast for gross domestic product growth in 2006 to 4%-6% from 3%-5%.  

Some players who had bought back U.S. dollars in the morning took profit in the afternoon, causing the greenback to fall back to the S$1.6290 area.  

Late in the session, the U.S. dollar consolidated with a firm tone against the local dollar ahead of the second leg of Bernanke's two-day congressional testimony later in the session.  

Bernanke is expected to reiterate the Fed's message that further rate hikes will depend on how U.S. economic data unfold in the coming months. This continuity of former Chairman Alan Greenspan's policy stance could extend the recent U.S. dollar gains versus its rivals.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds were higher across the curve, mostly owing to the robust data, dealers said.  

Volume was low ahead of an announcement later in the session of the auction size for the reopening of the 10-year government bond.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late On Positive Data Expectations
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against its U.S. counterpart in Asia Tuesday, bolstered by expectations of strong major domestic data later this week.  

The government bond yield curve flattened, in line with Monday's inversion of the U.S. Treasury curve.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6269, down from Monday's New York close of S$1.6294. It was quoted at S$1.6303 in Asia Monday.  

From early in the session, the U.S. dollar gradually fell against the Singapore dollar, eventually hitting an intraday low of S$1.6265 late afternoon.  

The market expects Wednesday's retail sales and Thursday's final reading for fourth-quarter gross domestic product to indicate robust economic growth, said dealers.  

United Overseas Bank expects December retail sales growth to pick up to 9.0% on year, from 2.4% in November. "This will be boosted in part by the rebound in vehicle sales, given the increase in new car registrations in December," it said in a research note.  

Friday's non-oil domestic exports for January, though, is likely to indicate some moderation from December's torrid 31.6% on-year growth, dealers said.  

A further fall of the U.S. currency versus the Singapore dollar may be limited by possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

Although there were no apparent signs of central bank intervention by late local trade Tuesday, one trader cited rumors that the central bank had bought U.S. dollars via local banks in Asia late Monday to curb a sharp rise in the Singapore currency.  

Yields on short-dated Singapore government bonds rose while those on very long-term issues fell, leading to mild curve flattening, dealers said.  

Proprietary traders were rumored to have bought 15-year government bonds, dragging their yield down to 3.38% Tuesday from 3.40% Monday.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Expectation Of Hawkish Bernanke
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell in Asia Monday on expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve's new chairman might sound a hawkish note at his first congressional testimony later this week.  

The government bond yield curve flattened slightly in thin trading ahead of this week's batch of U.S. and Singapore events, dealers said.  

At 0640 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6303, up from Friday's New York close of S$1.6258. It was quoted at S$1.6282 in Asia Friday.  

From early in the session, interbank players bought U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars to cover short positions, lifting the U.S. unit to a morning high of S$1.6299, dealers said.  

The short-covering was spurred by prospects that Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke, at his two-day testimony starting Wednesday, could reaffirm his predecessor Alan Greenspan's upbeat view of the U.S. economy and signal more interest-rate hikes in the coming months.  

For the rest of the session, the U.S. dollar consolidated around the psychologically important S$1.6300 resistance level, largely owing to the U.S. unit's resilience against other Asian currencies such as the Japanese yen.  

At 0640 GMT, the U.S. unit was at Y117.92, up slightly from Y117.90 in New York Friday.  

One trader said another factor driving the U.S. currency's rise against the Singapore dollar was expectations that the Monetary Authority of Singapore could again intervene after it apparently bought U.S. dollars late Friday, when the U.S. unit fell to a one-week low of S$1.6222.  

But there were no signs of central bank intervention by late local trade Monday.  

Government bonds hugged tight ranges as players were reluctant to take any large positions ahead of Bernanke's testimony Wednesday and Singapore Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's budget presentation Friday, dealers said.

title: Weak dollar forces Asia's hand on  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Just when a large stockpile of foreign currency reserves and strong domestic demand was finally weaning Asia off its currency-weakening intervention habit, weakness in the U.S. dollar has thrown a spanner in the works.  

Central bank data showed Asia's reserves, excluding China's, jumped in January by $29 billion, more than in any month in the past year, as a weaker U.S. dollar and portfolio inflows forced central banks to intervene to hold their currencies down.  

 South Korea's $6.5 billion growth in reserves in January was the highest since December 2004, Singapore's $3.55 billion increase was the biggest since April last year and the Philippines reported its largest monthly gain in reserves on record, taking total Asian reserves to just over $2.7 trillion.  

 The figures were evidence of the overwhelming flows the region has received, giving central banks little choice but to absorb some of them and temper the rise in their currencies.  

 Even with the intervention, the Korean won <KRW=> rose nearly 5 percent in January, the Thai baht <THB=> rose 5 percent and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> 2 percent.  

 "January was clearly a month of enormous pressure on Asian currencies to appreciate. I would have been surprised if Asian central banks hadn't intervened," said Merrill Lynch's head of Asian currency strategy, Simon Flint.  

 It could be a sign of how 2006 will shape up on the currency policy front.  

 Asia's reserves grew by just $251 billion in 2005, compared with $538 billion in 2004 and $473 billion in 2003, as Japan stopped buying dollars and other regional central banks grew less obsessed with export-driven growth and more tolerant of currency gains.  

 Besides, the dollar was rising through most of 2005.  

 But, with U.S. rates probably close to a peak, the dollar started 2006 on a weak footing. If that trend persists and strong growth in the United States and elsewhere leads to higher Asian trade surpluses and portfolio investment in Asian markets, the region's reserves could very well surge, as they did in 2003 and 2004, analysts say.  

 "A number of countries, Korea in particular, are trying to move away from intervention policy," Flint said.  

 "They intend to intervene less. It's just that the market conditions dictate that they continue to intervene significantly."  

 STRONGER CURRENCIES

 Asia has a number of reasons to intervene less and let its currencies rise faster, the main one being the still high cost of the oil the region imports.  

 Also, analysts believe China and Malaysia are allowing a faster pace of appreciation in the yuan and ringgit than immediately after they unlinked the two from the dollar in July 2005.  

 Growth is more broad-based, with consumption and investment demand picking up and reducing Asia's reliance on exports. Japan's deflationary pressures have abated.  

 Moreover, rates in the United States may peak just as Asia steps up monetary tightening. That means the cost of issuing paper to absorb the local currency released in dollar-buying intervention, known as sterilisation, could mount just as returns on dollar assets stop rising.  

 "The current environment of increased inflation risk should prompt Asian countries to be more willing to accept domestic currency strength. So should ongoing, albeit modest, yuan appreciation," said Jan Lambregts, head of Asia-Pacific research at Rabobank.  

Intervention therefore should not be as big a factor in the currency market as in 2003 and 2004, Lambregts said in a note.  

 "At the same time, there's some early evidence of Asian countries falling back on bad intervention habits in the face of the U.S. dollar's weak start to the year that warrants monitoring," he wrote.  (For a table detailing Asian countries' reserves, click on [nSP89186])

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weakness on US rate view seen brief
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly weaker on Thursday, retreating from the previous day's multi-year peaks as markets pushed the dollar higher to price in more U.S. rate rises.  

But most analysts said weakness in Asian currencies would be short-lived because flows into regional equity markets were strong and positioning in favour of the regionals was still light.  

The dollar rose to a seven-week high above 118 yen <JPY=> and also rallied against the euro <EUR=> and other European currencies as interest rate markets priced in further monetary tightening in the United States this year.  

The Federal Reserve raised the fed funds rate on Tuesday for the 14th time in 19 months and hinted further rises could follow.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> dropped a percent on the day to around 974 a dollar, pulling further back from Wednesday's eight-year peak around 957.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> were also big losers. The Singapore dollar slipped to the weaker side of 1.63 per U.S. dollar, ceding more than a cent from the previous day's high.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose early to 52.03 per dollar, its strongest level since May 2003, and then slipped. It has risen about 1.8 percent since Jan. 23, buoyed by expectations of foreign portfolio inflows and a possible upgrade in the country's credit ratings.  

Markets in China and Taiwan were closed for Lunar New Year holidays.  

Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the dollar's rebound was no surprise.  

"The market did get a little bit carried away with the notion that the dollar should decline as soon as the Fed even hints at finishing tightening.  

"There is no guarantee that they have finished hiking yet and that the yield story will be broadly supportive of the dollar overall," he said.  

Still, the strength of economic fundamentals would support currencies such as the won, ensuring their losses were limited, Callow said.  

"Dollar/won could track higher in the short-term but it is hard to argue for a major pullback on any of the won crosses. The fundamental story for the won is very strong," he said.  

INTERVENTION

Analysts suspected central banks in Korea, India, the Philippines and Singapore had intervened this week to rein in the strength of their currencies.  

"They are never going to sit passively while markets take their currencies stronger against the dollar," Tim Condon, ING's currency strategist said.  

"They are always going to be dollar defenders but I suspect that means they slow but not reverse the pressure," he said, while citing the strength of flows underpinning Asian currencies.  

South Korean foreign exchange reserves jumped $6.5 billion in January, the biggest monthly gain in 14 months, which dealers said indicated heavy dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Korea.  

Yet, the commerce ministry said on Wednesday the central bank had been complacent and had allowed the won to strengthen rapidly.  

This week, the won hit an 8-year high near 8.14 per yen <JPYKRW=R>, as Asian currencies outperformed the yen.  

ABN AMRO Bank's Shahab Jalinoos said the outperformance against the Japanese currency would persist.  

"This reflects the fact that low-yielding yen is currently a global funding currency in a risk-loving environment, while Asian currencies are beneficiaries of risk-seeking global capital seeking returns in their asset markets," he said in a note. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Higher,  intervention  fears surface
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bucked the dollar's strength against the yen on Wednesday and hit multi-year highs against the U.S. currency, raising concerns that regional central banks will step up intervention.  

In late Asian trading, the Korean won <KRW=>, Singapore dollar <SGD=>, Thai baht <THB=> and Philippine peso <PHP=> were off their intra-day peaks against the dollar. Traders suspected central banks in India and Korea had intervened to buy dollars.  

The moves took place even as the U.S. dollar remained near a four-week high against the yen <JPY=> after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates as expected on Tuesday for the 14th time in a 19-month tightening cycle. The Fed also indicated further tightening could follow.  

The peso ended at 52.09 per dollar, just off a high of 52.05, its strongest level since May 2003 as markets positioned for foreign investment in Philippine equities.  

The won briefly hit 957 per dollar, last seen when Asia was in the midst of a financial crisis in November 1997, before retreating modestly.  

The Thai baht crept to the firmer side of 39 per dollar and then fell back, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> stayed close to 9,300 per dollar and at its highest since March.  

The Singapore dollar met resistance near 1.6207 per U.S. dollar, some distance away from last week's highs around 1.6170.  

Markets in China, Malaysia and Taiwan remained closed for the Lunar New Year holidays.  

Mirza Baig, a Deutsche Bank currency strategist, said operators who had been bearish were now buying Asian currencies.  

However, he said he would hesitate to buy Asian currencies at these levels.  

"The speculative position overhang has become extended and there is a higher probability of a squeeze like the one we saw in dollar/yen overnight.  

"People have realised that Asia is appreciating and have jumped on the bandwagon and we are likely to see a correction in the next few days."  

Manila-based traders said the peso was approaching resistance between 52 and 51.80, the latter level being the May 2003 peak.  

Expectations of foreign portfolio inflows underpinned sentiment. Foreigners have bought a net $2.35 billion of South Korean shares in the past 10 sessions.  

In the Philippines, news that 80 percent of power producer First Generation Corp.'s 8.5 billion peso IPO had been sold to overseas investors buoyed the peso.  

SING DOLLAR SEEN CAPPED  

Analysts said the Sing dollar's 2.5 percent rise last month had pushed it to the top of what they estimated was the central bank's policy band for the currency, and that markets should be on guard for possible intervention.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.  

Rising asset prices, robust export growth and the strength in economic growth numbers have prompted thinking among economists that the MAS is on the verge of announcing a policy suggesting a faster pace of appreciation for the currency.  

UBS's currency strategist Ashley Davies said the currency was about 1.8 percent stronger than his estimate of the mid-point of the band. UBS assumes the band is 4 percent wide and the central bank allows a modest pace of appreciation for this mid-point, he said.  

Davies said the Singapore dollar would now be stable, but could gain further in the medium term.  

"We still think that SGD will perform well on a medium-term view given the potential for the MAS to adopt a more aggressive tightening bias, should the strong data continue," he said in a note.

title: Singapore dollar near top of band, seen capped
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar's 2.5 percent rise last month has pushed it to the top of the central bank's policy band for the currency, and markets should be on guard for possible intervention, analysts said on Wednesday.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to around 1.6207 per U.S. dollar on Wednesday, half a cent away from last week's highs near 1.6170 and defying the U.S. dollar's strength against the yen.  

"The market is unwilling to push the Sing dollar higher because it is already close to the top of the band and the strong data will not let it go lower," said UBS's currency strategist Ashley Davies.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.  

The central bank has maintained a tightening bias by permitting a gradual appreciation of the trade-weighted band since April 2004.  

Davies said the currency was about 1.8 percent stronger than his estimate of the mid-point of the band. UBS assumes the band is 4 percent wide and the central bank allows a modest pace of appreciation for this mid-point, he said.  

Some analysts who track the currency based on a 2 percent wide band had said last week the currency has breached the top extremity of that band.  

Rising asset prices, robust export growth and the strength in economic growth numbers have prompted thinking among economists that the MAS is on the verge of announcing a policy suggesting a faster pace of appreciation for the currency.  

The government reported on Wednesday that the island's unemployment rate fell in the fourth quarter to 2.5 percent, the lowest since the second quarter of 2001.  

Davies said the Singapore dollar would now be stable, but could gain further in the medium term.  

"We still think that SGD will perform well on a medium-term view given the potential for the MAS to adopt a more aggressive tightening bias, should the strong data continue," he said in a note.  

Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's strategist, estimated the Singapore dollar was around 2.1 percent above the mid-point of a band he assumes is 4 percent wide.  

He said in a note to clients it was possible the MAS would drop the word "modest" from the appreciation bias it has held for nearly 2 years when it reviews policy this April.  

"But until then, there can be little doubt that the speed and extent of the SGD rise since mid-Nov will be causing some unease at the MAS."  

The gains seemed stretched, Callow said, adding he would not buy the Singapore dollar at these levels.

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late After FOMC Signals More Tightening
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell slightly in Asia Wednesday after the Federal Reserve raised U.S. interest rates as expected but signaled the possibility of more monetary tightening.  

Prices on government bonds rose in the short end but slipped in the long end, resulting in yield curve steepening, dealers said.  

At 0710 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6232, up from Tuesday's New York close of S$1.6219. Singapore's markets were closed for Lunar New Year holidays Monday and Tuesday, with the U.S. unit having ended local trade Friday at S$1.6245.  

The U.S. dollar edged up to an intraday high of S$1.6245 very early in Wednesday's Asian session following the Federal Open Market Committee's statement hinting at more tightening at its next policy-setting meeting on Mar. 28, dealers said.  

In its statement, the Fed dropped the word "measured," which it had use to describe the previous pace of its rate hikes since it began its tightening in June 2004, and also noted that "some further policy firming may be needed."  

Although the U.S. dollar consolidated within a S$1.6210-S$1.6240 range for the rest of Wednesday's Asian session, the U.S. currency could extend its rebound against the local dollar in the coming sessions, analysts said.  

"We would prefer not to chase SGD much higher at current prices and see scope for some (downward) retracement (of the Singapore dollar) in the near term," said Westpac Institutional Bank in a research note.  

Westpac said the Singapore dollar's current level "is very much in (the Monetary Authority of Singapore's) intervention territory."  

Market speculation believes central bank intervention may have contributed to the brevity of the recent U.S. dollar decline below the psychologically important S$1.6200 level, Westpac said.  

Yields on short-dated Singapore government bonds fell on domestic investor demand while those on longer-term bonds rose due to higher U.S. Treasury yields Tuesday, leading to a modest steepening of the local bond yield curve, dealers said.

title: Singapore  Dlr Up Late; Rumored  Intervention  Curbs Rise
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose in Asia Wednesday on foreign fund flows into Singapore equities and domestic corporate demand for the local currency, but rumored central bank intervention curbed the local currency's rise, dealers said.  

Government bonds were mostly weaker, tracking Tuesday's fall in U.S. Treasury prices, dealers said.  

At 0706 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6221, down from Tuesday's New York close of S$1.6227. In Asian trade Tuesday, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.6216.  

From early in Wednesday's Asian session, the U.S. dollar fell steadily against the Singapore dollar, eventually hitting a new 10-month low of S$1.6187 in the afternoon. The S$1.6187 level was the lowest since March 14, 2005.  

Traders and analysts said foreign investors' flows into the Singapore stock market and local companies' demand for Singapore dollars ahead of the coming Lunar New Year holiday were behind the U.S. dollar's fall.  

Foreigners typically invest in Asian stock markets such as Singapore's Straits Times Index to build long Asian equity positions to hold over the holidays, one local analyst said. At 0706 GMT, the Straits Times Index was up 16.75 points at 2385.07.  

In the run-up to the Lunar New Year holiday which starts Jan. 28 and ends Jan. 31 in Singapore, local corporations have also been buying Singapore dollars, as many of them traditionally give money out as gifts in red envelopes at this time of year.  

The U.S. dollar then recovered to around the S$1.6220 level late in the session on suspected U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in the S$1.6190-S$1.6195 zone to temper the Singapore unit's sharp rise, dealers said.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds were mostly pulled up by Tuesday's mild rise in U.S. Treasury yields, but local trading was thin due to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's auction of S$2.4 billion worth of five-year government bonds, traders said.  

Around mid-day, the MAS sold the five-year bonds at a cutoff yield of 3.15%, in line with market expectations.  

Bids totaled S$4.78 billion and the average yield was 3.09%, according to data posted on the central bank's Web site.

title: Sing dlr hovers near 10-mth high, barrier at 1.62/dlr
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 24 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar traded on Tuesday near a 10-month high reached in late Asian trading the previous day, as investors moved out of U.S. dollar assets on signs that U.S. interest rates were close to peaking.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> traded as strong as 1.6205 per dollar, close to Monday's 10-month high of 1.6195, as the U.S. dollar dropped to a four-month low against the euro <EUR=>.  

Dealers said local banks were buying U.S. dollars in late trading on Monday, apparently on direction from the local central bank, to support the U.S. currency at S$1.62.  

"The local banks were intervening quite aggressively yesterday evening to support the 1.62 level," said a Singapore dealer.  

"This morning those who were short dollars were buying back on seeing their inability to break the 1.62 level."  

Dealers said there was little evidence of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in early trading on Tuesday.  

They said the Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies were unlikely to gain on their own merit because foreign inflows into their stock markets have ebbed after a spurt at the start of the year.  

But the Singapore dollar could break the 1.62 level if the U.S. dollar falls below 114 yen, a dealer said. The dollar traded as low as 114.3 yen on Tuesday, compared with 114.62 yen in late Asian trading on Monday.  

The dollar dropped to a four-month low against the euro and Swiss franc <CHF=> after Federal Reserve officials, including St. Louis Fed President William Poole and New York Fed President Timothy Geithner, suggested the central bank's 18-month tightening cycle is nearly over and pointed to the dangers of U.S. deficits.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Fall from highs,  intervention  in focus
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on Friday, retreating from this week's multi-month peaks, as a narrowing in the U.S. trade deficit and the absence of a strong hawkish tone from the European Central Bank bolstered the dollar.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> led the decline in regionals, shedding more than 1 percent, with dealers citing hefty dollar-buying intervention after Finance Minister Han Duck-soo pledged a concerted effort to curb won strength.  

 The won closed local trade at about 988 per dollar, after it had weakened from Thursday's highs near 974 -- its strongest since the Asian crisis in 1997.  

 Indonesia added its voice to warnings in the region against sharp currency gains. Indonesian Vice President Jusuf Kalla said on Friday steps needed to be taken to prevent the rupiah <IDR=> from getting too strong.  

 Still, after a week marked by ups and downs in currencies, analysts remained bullish on Asian regionals and viewed the U.S. dollar's recovery as short-lived.  

 "We had the U.S. trade numbers yesterday and that caught everyone by surprise, so dollar/Asia moved higher. We've also had intervention as well," said a trader in Hong Kong.  

 "But people are still looking to sell dollar/Asia as there are those who weren't fast enough to get on to the trend. So the bias is still down for the dollar."

 Concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) may intervene contained the Singapore dollar <SGD=>, pushing it back from Thursday's 10-month highs near 1.6200.

 "Some overshooting has taken place," said Jimmy Koh, head of economics and treasury at United Overseas Bank in Singapore. "The market is getting excited and this could be part of a new year phenomenon when hedge funds have a lot of money to invest."

title: Singapore Dollar Weakens Late On US Dlr Short-Covering
text:
By Michael Kitchen  

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was moderately weaker in Asia Friday, as interbank players bought back the U.S. dollar in the wake of Thursday's better-than-expected U.S. data.  

Government bonds weakened across the board, bucking Thursday's gains in U.S. Treasury prices, dealers said.  

At 0620 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6312, up from S$1.6223 in Asia Thursday.  

After opening near its intraday low of S$1.6271, the U.S. currency rose as high as S$1.6328 in the morning as interbank players covered short U.S. dollar positions against the local dollar, dealers said.  

Sparking this U.S. dollar short-covering was U.S. Commerce Department data released Thursday that showed the November trade deficit contracted to US$64.21 billion from a revised record high of US$68.13 billion in October. Economists had forecast a US$66.5 billion deficit for November.  

Traders also said some market participants sold Singapore dollars on the view that the local currency had climbed to the upper limit of the band within which the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the currency.  

The MAS operates a managed float regime for Singapore, which allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band and intervenes to prevent it from breaching the band.  

Singapore government bonds, which closely track U.S. Treasurys, defied expectations for price gains Friday, as their prices slipped across the curve on selling by local banks, dealers said.  

One trader said a large-sized domestic bank was behind the local bond sell-off, possibly aimed at taking profit on recent gains in local bond prices.  

"We are not following the U.S. today, and most of the trades are betting on a steepening of the curve," the dealer added.  

Curve steepening trades have picked up following recent robust economic data such as the city-state's gross domestic product, which expanded at a faster-than-expected pace of 7.7% in the fourth quarter of 2005 from the same period of 2004.  

The 7.7% growth figure was better than the average forecast of 6.7% by six economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Hitting new highs after a pause
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies hit fresh multi-month highs against the dollar on Thursday as traders bet that the U.S. currency had further to fall after a brief consolidation early this week.  

 Hawkish comments from the Swiss central bank, expectations that the European Central Bank would sound a hawkish note at a meeting later in the day and anxiety ahead of U.S. trade data all weighed on the dollar. It has already shed about 2.5 percent in trade-weighted terms <=USD> this month.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to its highest level in nearly 10 months at about 1.6220 per U.S. dollar, and the Thai baht <THB=> rose to about 39.38 per dollar, its highest since May 2005.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> strengthened more than one percent from Wednesday's domestic close to 973.8 per dollar, its strongest level since November 1997.  

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> also added more than one percent to its strongest level in almost 10 months, while the Taiwan dollar <TW1D=TP> firmed to 31.831 per U.S. dollar -- its highest level since early August.  

 "There's been a lot of appreciation against the dollar but, the way these currencies are managed, I doubt there's been much trade-weighted appreciation," said Tim Condon, head of research at ING in Singapore.  

 Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said that while there had been a huge move in currency markets at the start of 2006, similar rapid moves in the early weeks of the past three years had not been sustained.  

 "We will see some degree of consolidation. However, we are very much in the camp that believes in medium-term dollar weakness so any consolidation will be a further opportunity to offload more dollars," he said.  

 WATCHFUL CENTRAL BANKS  

 The Thai baht's rise versus the dollar has made it a "bit too strong" and its appreciation should require central bank action, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakul said on Thursday. "No one has confirmed central bank intervention but everybody is talking about it," said a trader in Bangkok. "The central bank is worried that a strong baht is not good for exports so intervention would not be a surprise."  

 So far this month, South Korea has warned against won strength, while Taiwan has intervened in the market to curb Taiwan dollar strength.  

 Analysts said that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had been less aggressive than expected in its intervention to cap Sing dollar gains and this had encouraged some investors to push the currency higher.  

 The Sing dollar has risen nearly 3 percent in the past three weeks.  

 "The entire street seems to be short Sing dollar against the basket," said a local trader.  

 He said the U.S. dollar's weakness, driven by the view that U.S. monetary tightening was close to an end, had left those betting against the Sing dollar in the red and led to short-covering.  

 "And with MAS intervening only in bits and pieces, it is making life for those Sing dollar shorts pretty miserable."  

 The MAS's chief monetary policy tool is the currency, which it manages within an undisclosed trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0825 GMT

title: Singapore Dollar Again Tests 10-Mo High Vs US Dollar Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose again to a near 10-month high Thursday, as market participants sold the U.S. dollar on concerns over major U.S. economic data due out later in the day.  

Government bond yields were higher in the long end than in the short end, resulting in curve steepening, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6223, down sharply from S$1.6375 in Asia Wednesday.  

After opening near its intraday high of S$1.6298, the U.S. dollar fell to S$1.6214, its lowest since Mar. 17, 2005, as speculators and other players dumped the U.S. currency for the local dollar amid worries over the 1330 GMT release Thursday of U.S. trade deficit data for November.  

Traders said a wider-than-expected U.S. trade deficit could fuel the prevailing bearish sentiment toward the greenback and pave the way for the U.S. currency to fall further toward the six-year low of S$1.6161 set in March 2005 in coming sessions.  

In an apparent effort to temper the Singapore dollar's surge versus its U.S. counterpart Thursday, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have bought a small amount of U.S. dollars around the S$1.6250 level in the morning, dealers said.  

Given the Singapore dollar's recent strength, analysts such as DBS Bank's senior market strategist Philip Wee estimate that the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is very near to the upper limit of the band within which the central bank manages the currency.  

The MAS operates a managed float regime for Singapore, which allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band, and intervenes to prevent it from breaching the band.  

In the Singapore government bond market, the yield on the 10-year bond rose more than that on the two-year bond, as Wednesday's rise in U.S. Treasury yields lifted the long end of the local yield curve more, dealers said.

title: Singapore dollar rises to 10-month high vs weak USD
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar extended its January gains to hit its highest levels in nearly 10 months on Thursday, buoyed by the U.S. dollar's broad weakness and the belief that Singapore authorities wanted a stronger currency.  

 The Sing dollar <SGD=> rose overnight to levels around 1.6270/80 per U.S. dollar, its highest since March 2005, taking its gains in the past 3 weeks to nearly 3 percent.  

 "The entire street seems to be short Sing dollar against the basket," said one local trader.  

 He said the U.S. dollar's weakness, driven by the view that U.S. monetary tightening was close to an end, had pushed those bets against the Singapore dollar into the red and led to a short-covering.  

 Besides, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the central bank, had not intervened to rein in the rallying Sing dollar as aggressively as other regional central banks, he said.  

 "And with MAS intervening only in bits and pieces, it is making life for those Sing dollar shorts pretty miserable."  

 The MAS's chief monetary policy tool is the currency, which it manages against an undisclosed trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies.  

 Analysts estimated the Sing dollar was now close to the top extremity of that band.  

 Bhanu Baweja, UBS's currency strategist, said in a note it was not advisable to be buying the Sing dollar against the U.S. dollar at these levels. But investors should try and be long the Sing dollar through options, he said.  

 "This is based on our view that Singapore has stepped up the tightening of monetary policy as the economy has remained strong, and pressure on headline inflation is rising," Baweja said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Undermined by  intervention  worry
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slipped in holiday-thinned trading on Tuesday, weighed down by profit-taking after their sharp rises in the past week and the anxiety about possible central bank intervention.  

 Markets in Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia were closed for a Muslim festival holiday. That kept trading volumes thin.  

 The won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> closed local trade around 982 per dollar, just off Monday's high of 975 which was the currency's strongest level since the Asian financial crisis in 1997.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell to 52.645 per dollar, off Monday's peak of 52.25 which was its highest level since May 2003.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> gave up some ground, easing to 39.93 from Monday's 8-month high of 39.69 a dollar.  

 "Seems like some players took profit, but when we were back up above 39.90 some exporters came to sell dollars," said a baht trader based in Bangkok.  

 Regional currencies slipped as the dollar staged a slight rebound from three-month lows struck the past couple of sessions against the euro <EUR=> and yen <JPY=>.  

 Also, markets paused to see the extent to which central banks around the region would intervene to cap their currencies, which have risen sharply since the start of the year.  

 South Korean authorities kept up their normal run of comments.  

 The Vice Finance Minister said the won had risen too fast and steps would be taken as necessary, soon after a Bank of Korea official said the currency had risen above an equilibrium range against the dollar but authorities would not force it lower.  

 "Korean authorities clearly are not comfortable with either the pace of the move or the rate of the won," Richard Yetsenga, HSBC's currency strategist, said.  

 "But it unlikely that they will be successful in preventing the won moving at all."  

 Shahab Jalinoos, currency strategist with ABN AMRO Bank, said in a note the comments suggested there would be no concerted attempt to cap the won.  

 "This backs our view that strong growth means Korea will not want to risk the liquidity headaches implied by concerted intervention. Korean intervention in 2006 will be tactical rather than  strategic," he said.  

 That view would be confirmed if the Bank of Korea raised interest rates at its policy meeting on Thursday, he said.

Also, markets were taking a breather while watching how far central banks around the region would intervene to cap their currencies, which have risen sharply since the start of the year.

title: Singapore Dlr Hits Strongest Since Mar; Bonds Up Slightly
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar surged to an almost 10-month high Monday, tracking sharp gains in the Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar on signs U.S. interest rate increases may end soon.  

Government bonds edged up slightly in thin trade as a further easing of the overnight rate and a local holiday Tuesday kept investors on the sidelines, dealers said.  

Around 0609 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6324, down from S$1.6464 in Asia Friday.  

This was the lowest level for the U.S. dollar since March 22, when it dipped as low as S$1.6291.  

Intraday the U.S. dollar traded between S$1.6322 and S$1.6389.  

A dealer at a European bank said the local pair rallied as it tracked gains in the yen against the U.S. dollar triggered by Friday's weaker-than-expected December U.S. non-farm payrolls number.  

In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at Y113.84, down from Y114.39 in New York Friday.  

Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank, said the rally in Asian currencies was triggered by an unwinding of carry trades, especially in the Japanese yen.  

Last year, the forex market undertook massive carry trades - where market players borrow in a cheaper currency such as the Japanese yen and buy high-interest yielding currencies such as the U.S. dollar.  

The trades began after China disappointed the market by appreciating its currency by a lower-than-expected 2% and on expectations the Federal Reserve would aggressively tighten monetary policy which would support the U.S. dollar.  

Recent signals from the Fed suggest the rate hikes may be coming to an end, leading to the unwinding of these carry trades, Wee said.  

But traders are also worried the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate from breaching the band's upper limit.  

The Singapore dollar was 1.3% above the midpoint of the band - the highest level since April 2004 when the MAS first tightened policy - according to a report from United Overseas Bank.  

UOB treasury economist Jimmy Koh expects the U.S. dollar to find strong support at S$1.6300 while it should stabilize against the yen around Y113.50.  

In the bond market, the 10-year yield fell one basis point to 3.24%. The two-year yield also slid one basis point to 2.74%.  

While the yield curve was unchanged, JPMorgan said the recent easing of short-term rates should encourage curve steepening trades. The overnight rate dropped to 2.250% from 2.625% Friday.
