title: DJ Singapore Dlr Hits Strongest Since Mar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar surged to an almost 10-month high Monday, tracking sharp gains in the Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar on signs U.S. interest rate increases may end soon.  

Government bonds edged up slightly in thin trade as a further easing of the overnight rate and a local holiday Tuesday kept investors on the sidelines, dealers said.  

Around 0609 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6324, down from S$1.6464 in Asia Friday.  

This was the lowest level for the U.S. dollar since March 22, when it dipped as low as S$1.6291.  

Intraday the U.S. dollar traded between S$1.6322 and S$1.6389.  

A dealer at a European bank said the local pair rallied as it tracked gains in the yen against the U.S. dollar triggered by Friday's weaker-than-expected December U.S. non-farm payrolls number.  

In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at Y113.84, down from Y114.39 in New York Friday.  

Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank, said the rally in Asian currencies was triggered by an unwinding of carry trades, especially in the Japanese yen.  

Last year, the forex market undertook massive carry trades - where market players borrow in a cheaper currency such as the Japanese yen and buy high-interest yielding currencies such as the U.S. dollar.  

The trades began after China disappointed the market by appreciating its currency by a lower-than-expected 2% and on expectations the Federal Reserve would aggressively tighten monetary policy which would support the U.S. dollar.  

Recent signals from the Fed suggest the rate hikes may be coming to an end, leading to the unwinding of these carry trades, Wee said.  

But traders are also worried the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate from breaching the band's upper limit.  

The Singapore dollar was 1.3% above the midpoint of the band - the highest level since April 2004 when the MAS first tightened policy - according to a report from United Overseas Bank.  

UOB treasury economist Jimmy Koh expects the U.S. dollar to find strong support at S$1.6300 while it should stabilize against the yen around Y113.50.  

In the bond market, the 10-year yield fell one basis point to 3.24%. The two-year yield also slid one basis point to 2.74%.  

While the yield curve was unchanged, JPMorgan said the recent easing of short-term rates should encourage curve steepening trades. The overnight rate dropped to 2.250% from 2.625% Friday.

title: ANALYSIS-Asian  FX intervention  may have less bite this time
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Asian central banks have made it clear they are not happy with a surge in their currencies as 2006 gets under way, but analysts doubt they will intervene on a large scale, saying economic strength warrants firmer exchange rates.  

South Korea vowed on Friday to do its utmost to stall a jump of nearly 3 percent in the won against the dollar in the new year while the central banks of Taiwan and Singapore sold dollars to halt a month-old rally in their currencies.  

Asian currency intervention peaked in 2004 -- Japan leading the region with massive dollar purchases in an attempt to hold the yen down -- as Japan and South Korea struggled to pull out of a prolonged economic downturn.  

Asian authorities were worried that strong currencies would make their exports less competitive, which would hamper the recovery of their export-dependent economies.  

Asia's top 10 holders of foreign reserves together bought $44 billion a month on average that year.  

This time it's different, analysts said. The rise in Asian currencies is part of a broad dollar decline, triggered by expectations that U.S. interest rates may be close to peaking, and Asian economies are on a stronger footing.  

"The market is not afraid of intervention," said Roh Sang Chil, a currency trader at Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

"The fundamentals of the Korean economy are getting better. There's not much reason for the Korean won to depreciate. The intervention is going to be just a smoothing operation."  

The same holds true for the rest of Asia, analysts said, where economies from Taiwan to India are set to accelerate thanks to an upturn in domestic demand while China remains the engine of growth in the region. The improving outlook, which contrasts with an expected slowdown in the United States, has led to a rush of foreign equity investors into India, Taiwan, Thailand and other Asian countries in the past month.  

Stock indices in South Korea <.KS11>, India <.BSESN> and Indonesia <.JKSE> hit record highs this week while those in Singapore <.STI>, Thailand <.SETI> and the Philippines <.PSI> reached or approached multi-year peaks.  

"Hence the underlying flows remain solidly in favour of regional Asian currencies," Shahab Jalinoos, Asian currency strategist at ABN AMRO Bank, said in a note.  

In fact, Asian currencies have been rising against the U.S. dollar since December. The foreign equity inflows in the new year merely accelerated the process, with the won <KRW=> hitting an eight-year high of 985.1 per dollar on Thursday.  

BROAD-BASED MOVE  

Claudio Piron, Asian currency strategist at JPMorganChase Bank, noted that this year's Asian rally differed from rallies in 2004 and the early part of 2005, which were driven by speculation about a sharp appreciation in the Chinese yuan.  

This time the Asian currencies are moving more in line with the yen, an indication that their gains are more broad-based and can be sustained, Piron said.  

"We seem to be having a broader move, which the yen is joining in, and it is always hard to turn that tide," he said.  

"It seems to be driven by equity flows and that's premised on an upward assessment of currencies."  

Some believe the rise in the won and the Taiwan dollar may have run its course for the time being. Roh at Kookmin Bank said the Bank of Korea was likely to defend the 990 won per dollar level for now.  

But, analysts said, other currencies have more room to appreciate.  

"For those wishing to be short dollar/Asia, it seems safer at this stage to look at the Indian rupee and especially the baht and rupiah rather than the won and Taiwan dollar, which are already overstretched," said Jalinoos at ABN AMRO.  

Others think the central bank bark may be stronger than its bite this time round.  

Central bank intervention over the past few years has already bloated foreign currency reserves in many countries and adding to them would be both expensive and counterproductive.  

"There is increased concern about the rising cost to the Bank of Korea from holding large amounts of FX reserves," Merrill Lynch said, adding that the won's appreciation had not had a significantly detrimental impact on the South Korean economy. Asian central banks, including the Bank of Korea, have been raising interest rates to quell inflation pressures and Japan is set to end its ultra-loose monetary policy.  

Efforts to reverse currency appreciation -- which typically loosens monetary conditions -- would run counter to those policies.  

"The amount of intervention so far has not been that significant and the danger is that if Korea and Taiwan intervene heavily, they could create an opportunity for the market," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won, Taiwan dlr down,  intervention  in focus
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mixed on Friday, with the South Korean won and Taiwan dollar down as regional authorities moved to cap currency strength but the Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht extending recent gains.  

The won <KRW=><KRW=KTFC> eased as far as 996.9 per dollar after finance ministry and central bank officials held an emergency meeting after Thursday's sharp rise to about 985 per dollar, its highest level in more than eight years.  

South Korea would do its utmost to stabilise the foreign exchange market, Vice Finance Minister Kwon Tae-shin said after the meeting on Friday morning.  

Dealers in Seoul said they spotted no dollar-buying intervention and the won, which has risen about 5 percent in the past month, had recovered some ground by late Asian trade.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> eased as much as 0.9 percent to 32.31 per U.S. dollar, with the central bank seen intervening after the currency hit a 4-1/2-month peak on Thursday.  

Dealers said that despite intervention, Asian currencies would remain in demand, given expectations that U.S. monetary tightening may end and brighter economic data in Asia.  

"Intervention is unlikely to turn the tide in Asian currencies," said JPMorgan currency strategist Claudio Piron.  

"This is part of a broad dollar move that is also reflected in the equity markets. If data from Asia is strong, currency appreciation is justified and the best central banks can do is slow the level of that appreciation."  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> recovered from lows hit in early trade despite suspicion that the central bank was still checking levels.  

Traders suspected that intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had caused the Sing dollar to retreat from an overnight high of 1.6450 per U.S. dollar.  

They had been expecting the MAS to intervene after the currency hit a seven-month high this week and moved near to the top end of its presumed trade-weighted band.  

RINGGIT, BAHT FIRM  

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> extended this week's rise to about 3.7505 per dollar -- its strongest level in 4-½ months.  

Investors have been encouraged by this week's relatively big move in the ringgit, which has traded in narrow ranges since its peg against the dollar was abandoned last July, dealers said.  

They said the ringgit was bolstered by gains in Malaysia's stock market index <.KLSE>, which hit a two-month high on Friday, and expectations of foreign fund inflows this quarter.  

"People have got used to the fact that the ringgit doesn't move much. They have been shocked by the move this week and so there have been short-term players coming into the market," said Callum Henderson, Standard Chartered's head of currency strategy.  

The Thai baht <THB=> hit its strongest level in seven months at about 40.04 per dollar as the market tried to test a key chart barrier in the 40 baht per dollar area, dealers said.  

The focus turned to the U.S. non-farm payrolls report, due later on Friday. Analysts said the data would be the litmus test for whether the dollar could stage a rebound.  

"I am in the dollar-bear camp, but remember what happened at the start of last year when the dollar sold off then reversed?" said Henderson. "That's why there is a focus on the payrolls numbers. All we need is one strong number and everything could reverse the other way."

text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 6 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar recovered from lows hit in early trades on Friday despite suspicion in the market that the central bank was still checking levels.  

 Traders suspected that intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had caused the Sing dollar <SGD=> to retreat from an overnight high of 1.6450 per U.S. dollar.  

 At 0350 GMT, the Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.6475/80, off a low of 1.6495.

 "They (MAS) possibly bought U.S. dollars overnight. But their agents have been sellers all morning. Even now they are selling at 1.6482," said the trader.  

 Talk of MAS intervention gained credence after traders reported that other central banks, such as South Korea's and Taiwan's, had intervened to rein in their rallying currencies on Friday.  

 The won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> was forced off Thursday's eight-year high.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Regional  currencies  rise to multi-month highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Asia's currency markets enjoyed another day of stellar gains on Wednesday as the minutes from the last Federal Reserve meeting fuelled talk that the U.S. central bank is almost done with lifting interest rates.  

Most regional currencies, in a rally led by the Japanese yen <JPY=>, hit multi-month highs against the dollar.  

The South Korean <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> strengthened past the psychologically important 1,000 mark to hit an 8-month high at 997.9 per dollar.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a 4-½ month peak at 1.6461 per dollar, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> set its highest level in almost a month at about 9,635 per dollar and the Taiwan dollar rose as much as one percent in local markets to hit a 4-month high of 32.33 per U.S. dollar.  

The minutes of the Fed's Dec. 13 meeting, released on Tuesday, showed the central bank's top officials believed the number of additional rate increases would not be large although its future action would depend on economic data.  

Asian currencies had already started the new year on a strong footing, helped by a view that the U.S. monetary tightening that bolstered the dollar last year was unlikely to last much longer.  

Analysts said the minutes and data on Tuesday showing a drop in the U.S. Institute for Supply Management's factory index gave the rally in Asian currencies fresh momentum.  

"People are looking at what the big trade of this year will be and there are enough houses saying the dollar will have a poor year," said Westpac senior currency strategist Sean Callow.  

"So people are either putting on new positions or receptive to news confirming their suspicions -- such as the ISM data."  

The sharp rise in regional currencies raised the spectre of central bank intervention.  

A dealer in Singapore said the market was wary of intervention to curb the Singapore dollar's sharp gains but had so far seen no signs of such action.  

South Korea's central bank was suspected of intervening in the market on Tuesday to cap the won's strength. A central bank official said on Wednesday that the won's latest rise was the result of an excessive reaction to the Fed minutes.  

"The market is unlikely to be afraid of the threat of intervention from Korea," said Callow. "Korean authorities are aware that they are unlikely to stem the tide of a broad trend in the currency market."  

MORE THAN JUST A DOLLAR STORY  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> gained more than half a percent from Tuesday's close in local markets to a fresh 2-½ year peak of 52.37 per dollar, while the Thai baht <THB=> strengthened to 40.50 -- its strongest level against the dollar in 7 months.  

Dealers said besides a soft tone in the U.S. dollar, investors were also responding to strong local equity markets, brighter economic data and favourable technical patterns.  

"There was strong (dollar) support in the 40.70/85 area and this has been broken," said a trader in Bangkok, referring to the baht. "We have also seen heavy offshore selling of dollar/baht this morning."  

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose and the yuan, traded in offshore derivative markets <CNYNDFOR=>, was pulled higher in line with the regional currency strength.  

Six-month non-deliverable forwards moved to price the yuan at 7.8675 per dollar, compared with 7.8730 late on Tuesday. The one-year contract priced the yuan at 7.7200 against the dollar from 7.7350 late the previous session.  

"The move in the NDFs is consistent with the move in the spot market and with the forecasts for a decline in the dollar in the months ahead," Callow said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0818 GMT

title: Singapore dollar highest in over 4 mths, data helps
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 3 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar climbed on Tuesday to its highest level against the U.S. dollar in more than four months, boosted by data showing stronger-than-expected economic growth.  

 Singapore's economy grew at an annualised rate of 9.7 percent in the fourth quarter of 2005, thanks to a big boost in manufacturing and stronger domestic demand, government data showed earlier. The figure was higher than a 7.2 percent growth rate forecast by economists in a Reuters poll last week.  

 Together with a generally firm tone in Asian currencies, the data pushed the Singapore dollar <SGD=> to 1.6578 per U.S. dollar, its strongest level since mid-August.  

 "The data continues to hint that there is a big chance that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will tighten policy at the April meeting and I think the market is reacting to that," said John Cairns, head of research at IDEAglobal in Singapore.  

 "We've seen strong data throughout the fourth quarter and that raises the risk of tightening in April. It's not a sure thing but there may be some speculation on this."  

 The MAS conducts monetary policy by guiding the trade-weighted Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band.  

 Estimates on the width of the currency band vary, but analysts and traders said the Singapore dollar was now trading in the strong side of the band.  

 A trader said the central bank could intervene in the currency market to prevent the Singapore dollar moving too fast, too soon.  

 "I think people are trying to test what levels the MAS will start to come in. According to our internal calculator, we are already testing the stronger side of the band -- a 1-½   percent band on either side of the mid-point," he said.  

 "If they do not come into the market, I think we should see further gains in the Sing dollar."

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was flat against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Wednesday amid extremely thin trading ahead of year-end holidays.  

Government bond prices rose across the curve, in line with U.S. Treasurys' price gains Tuesday, dealers said.  

At 0615 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6665, unchanged from Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6662 and S$1.6688 intraday.  

Throughout the Asian session, the U.S. dollar's movements versus the Singapore dollar were somewhat choppy within a narrow range of roughly 26 pips, tracking the U.S. currency's fluctuations against the yen, dealers said.  

Traders added that the absence of many Singaporean and foreign players due to year-end holidays was the main factor behind the very low volume of trading.  

"Nobody is trading" the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar, a dealer with a Singapore-based foreign bank said.  

But, recent robust Singapore data such as the better-than-expected 22.4% on-year growth in industrial output for November reported Tuesday have spurred expectations among some analysts for a stronger Singapore dollar in the short term.  

The trade-weighted Singapore dollar "still has an upward bias toward the strong side" of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's policy band, DBS Bank's senior market strategist, Philip Wee, said. He estimated the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is about 0.7% above the perceived midpoint of the band.  

The MAS allows the trade-weighted Singapore dollar to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band, and intervenes to prevent the currency from breaching the band.  

Singapore conducts monetary policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates because trade amounts to three times the country's S$184 billion domestic economy.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Singapore dlr at 4-mth high, Indian rupee up
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 19 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose to a four-month high on Monday thanks to a year-end sell-off in the U.S. dollar, while the Indian rupee hit a 1-1/2-month high as foreign investors spurred local stocks to record highs.  

Similar stock buying pushed the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> to a three-month peak of 33.104 per dollar. But concerns the central bank may step in to check the currency's rise checked the gains by midday.  

Analysts said dollar-buying intervention by central banks or indications that authorities might intervene prevented stronger appreciation in the Indian rupee <INR=IN>, South Korean won <KRW=>, Singapore dollar <SGD=> and Thai baht <THB=>.  

"The intervention figures show the smoothening out of the exaggerated moves in Asian currencies in the past few weeks rather than any efforts to cap those moves," said Jimmy Koh, currency strategist at United Overseas Bank in Singapore.  

"I don't think the Asian central banks want to be that aggressive."  

Asian currencies have rallied this month on the back of the yen's <JPY=> recovery against the dollar.  

As the year drew to a close, investors who had borrowed low-yielding currencies such as the yen and Singapore dollar earlier in the year to buy higher-yielding assets such as the U.S. dollar, reversed the carry trades before closing their books.  

The reversals have helped the yen climb 4.5 percent since it hit a 2-1/2-month low against the U.S. dollar earlier this month.  

The Singapore dollar rose to 1.6635 per dollar on Monday. The currency has strengthened 2.2 percent in the past month, helped by the reversal of the carry trades and strong economic data.  

Koh said the trade-weighted Singapore dollar was almost 0.3 percent stronger than the mid-point of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's band for the currency.  

CARRY TRADE  

"The gains are mainly due to year-end unwinding of carry trades," said a Singapore currency dealer.  

The dealer said investors could start borrowing low-yielding currencies again in the new year to exchange them for the U.S. dollar if markets price in benchmark U.S. interest rates higher than 4.5 percent by the middle of 2006.  

Another dealer said the carry trades seemed to have run their course and volumes could thin out as year-end holidays approach.  

"We have seen most of the adjustment for this year," said Koh at United Overseas Bank, adding the yen is likely to trade in the range of 115-120 per dollar going into the new year.  

The yen weakened to 116.58 on Monday, but was still close to a seven-week hit earlier in the day.  

In the new year, Koh said, conducting the carry trade by borrowing Asian currencies to exchange them with U.S. dollars could become riskier as regional interest rates are catching up with those in the United States.  

"That'll make shorting of Asian currencies that much more expensive," he said.  

Moreover, recent economic data from across Asia indicated the region is heading for another strong quarter following buoyant exports and retail sales in the third quarter. The improved outlook triggered buying of local stocks by foreign investors.  

Singapore's non-oil exports in November rose a higher-than-expected 14 percent to S$12.9 billion from a year earlier, the biggest annual rise in a year, data showed Friday.  

Optimism about a strong earnings outlook for Taiwan exporters in the first quarter of 2006 drove the local stock index <.TWII> to a four-month high on Monday. Data showed foreigners have been net buyers of local stocks on all but one day this month.

title: Singapore Dlr Rises To 4-Mo High; Bonds Little Changed
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose to a four-month high against the U.S. dollar Monday as a recent rebound in the Japanese yen and strong economic data for the city-state encouraged players to take fresh positions in the local unit.  

Government bond yields were little changed amid thin volume ahead of holidays, dealers said.  

At 0618 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6658 - its lowest level since Aug. 18 when the greenback slipped to S$1.6631 a few weeks after China switched to a managed float against a basket of currencies, causing the yuan to appreciate 2% against the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar traded between S$1.6633 and S$1.6663, down from S$1.6685 late Friday.  

Early in the Singapore trading session, the U.S. dollar slipped to an intraday low of S$1.6640 after it breached key support of S$1.6645, which triggered stop-losses, said a trader at a foreign bank.  

However, a rebound in the U.S. dollar against the yen allowed it to claw back above the Singapore dollar support, said a second dealer at a local bank.  

The U.S. dollar had recovered to Y116.35 in afternoon trade after falling as low as Y115.52 in early trade, the weakest since late October.  

The trader said fears the central bank would intervene also prevented the Singapore dollar from appreciating more, especially after the Monetary Authority of Singapore was suspected to have bought back small amounts of U.S. dollars to provide a floor for the U.S. unit Friday.  

The Singapore dollar has gained 2.3% against the U.S. currency since Nov. 14, when it slipped to S$1.7065, its lowest since early July. It started rallying after a spate of data showed the local economy was strengthening while global markets speculated the Federal Reserve may be nearing the end of its monetary tightening cycle.  

"The change in expectations was because of the FOMC statement which encouraged market players to pare back some extended positions in the U.S. dollar going into the new year," said Thomas Lam, a treasury economist at United Overseas Bank.  

Lam said the major position-squaring came in the dollar/yen, which also lifted other Asian currencies.  

Singapore data released Friday showed non-oil domestic exports in November grew 14.0% from a year earlier to S$12.92 billion, beating a Dow Jones Newswires poll forecast of 11.4% growth.  

The data also boosted hopes that the trade-dependent economy will be able to sustain strong growth for a second quarter in a row after gross domestic product grew 7% in the third quarter.  

Deutsche Bank said in a report that the stronger economy means the MAS will likely continue its current policy of currency appreciation, which would trigger more gains for the Singapore dollar in the first half of 2006.  

On the Singapore government bond market, the 10-year bond yield was flat at 3.34%, while the two-year yield edged up one basis point to 2.77%, flattening the yield curve slightly in thin trade.

title: Singapore dlr at 4-mth high, investors reverse sales
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 19 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose to a four-month high on Monday as investors bought back the low yielding currency to close their books before the year-end.  

 The trades helped reverse earlier bets when investors had borrowed the currency to exchange it for higher yielding assets such as the U.S. dollar.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.6635 per dollar. The currency has strengthened 2.2 percent in the past month, helped by the reversal of the earlier carry trades and strong economic data from the island nation.  

 Similar reversals in carry trades have also helped the Japanese yen <JPY=> climb 4.5 percent since it hit a 2-1/2-month low against the U.S. dollar earlier this month.  

 "The unwinding of carry trades continues," said a Singapore currency dealer who expects the Singapore dollar to strengthen further to 1.6620/1.6630 during the day.  

 She said some overseas banks were seen squaring off their previous sales of the Singapore currency in early Asian trading.  

 Another trader said gains could be restricted given that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been intervening in the market occasionally last week to stem the rise in the Singapore dollar.  

 Recent economic data from Singapore indicated that the city-state held on to its strong economic performance in the fourth quarter.  

 Non-oil exports rose a higher-than-expected 14 percent to S$12.9 billion in November, the biggest annual rise in a year, government data showed on Friday.  

 On a seasonally adjusted basis, non-oil exports fell a much smaller-than-expected 0.6 percent from October.  

 "Singapore data are coming out pretty strong," said a dealer. "Everything is pointing to a stronger currency in the near term."

title: Singapore  Dlr Dn Late After Suspected  Forex Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar in Asia late Friday after suspected central bank intervention on the foreign exchange market.  

Government bond yields were mostly higher, mainly due to a rise in short-dated domestic interest rates, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6685, up from S$1.6676 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6667 and S$1.6716 intraday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. dollar slipped to an intraday low of S$1.6667 due to its weakness versus the yen.  

But, the U.S. currency soon rose as high as S$1.6716 on rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to prevent the Singapore dollar from appreciating too much, dealers said.  

"They apparently came in this morning," a trader at a European bank said.  

MAS probably bought U.S. dollars around S$1.6685-S$1.6690, a Singapore dealer said.  

The MAS's suspected intervention in the currency market during Singapore trading hours is unusual as it typically acts during European hours. The central bank said it doesn't comment on its market operations.  

After the apparent intervention by the MAS, the U.S. gradually drifted back down to around S$1.6680 in extremely thin trade by late afternoon, dealers said.  

On the Singapore government bond market, a rise in short-dated local interest rates pushed up yields across most of the curve, dealers said.  

The bid side for the domestic overnight interbank rate rose as high as 4.25%, its highest since October 1998, while the benchmark three-month Singapore interbank offered rate, or SIBOR, rose to 3.25%, its highest since Nov. 25, on strong borrowing interest from Singapore-based banks amid very thin liquidity, dealers said.

text:

title: Singapore Dlr Rises To New 3-Mo High For 3rd Straight Day
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar climbed to a new three-month high for the third straight session in Asia late Thursday, mainly owing to speculator-led profit-taking on long U.S. dollar positions.  

Government bond yields rose more in the short end than in the long end, leading to a flattening of the curve, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6676, down from S$1.6718 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6664 and S$1.6705 intraday.  

From early in the session, U.S. funds unwound long U.S. dollar positions against the Singapore dollar to take profit ahead of the year-end, thereby dragging the U.S. currency down as low as S$1.6676 in the morning, dealers said.  

Another negative factor for the U.S. dollar against its Singaporean counterpart was Wednesday's U.S. data showing that the trade deficit widened by 4.4% to a fresh record high of US$68.89 billion in October from September's revised US$66 billion gap. The October figure was worse than economists' expectations for a US$63 billion deficit.  

Traders said the U.S. currency's weakness versus the Singapore dollar appears to reflect a change in market sentiment away from the U.S. dollar after the U.S. Federal Reserve removed its reference to monetary policy being accommodative, which many players perceived as a signal that the central bank is approaching the end of its interest-rate hike cycle.  

But, the U.S. dollar soon rebounded to near the psychologically important S$1.6700 level in the morning on rumors that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in the foreign exchange market to cap a further rise in the Singapore dollar versus the U.S. currency, dealers said.  

Late in the session, the U.S. currency resumed its decline versus the Singapore dollar, dropping to as low as S$1.6664, its lowest level since Aug. 23, due to more selling of U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars by U.S. funds, dealers said.  

In the Singapore government bond market, the yield curve flattened slightly in extremely thin markets, as local players were reluctant to build any positions ahead of the year-end.

title: Singapore Dlr Rises To Fresh 3-Mo High Vs US Dlr Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose to a fresh three-month high in Asia late Wednesday, as players bought the local unit and other Asian currencies in the wake of Tuesday's meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-making board.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds flattened slightly after the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting, dealers said.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late On Limited Upside; Bonds Weaker
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly lower in thin trade Thursday as local players saw little incentive to push the local unit near a key resistance level.  

Dealers said the Singapore dollar has limited upside as the greenback is already close to its support level.  

Government bonds were weaker with the long end leading losses, causing a steepening of the yield curve, they said.  

At 0725 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6861, up from S$1.6854 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6846 and S$1.6866.  

The U.S. dollar slipped to a seven-week low against the Singapore dollar earlier this week, but has consolidated after market players saw less room for the Singapore dollar to rally.  

"The market is pretty much rangebound ahead of the holidays," a dealer at a foreign bank said. Despite the yen's gains against the U.S. dollar and euro, players weren't interested to buy the Singapore dollar.  

Sabrina Jacobs, currency strategist at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein, said the Singapore dollar has limited room to strengthen because the U.S. dollar is "very close to its support level of S$1.6300."  

She said fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene if the market pushed the Singapore dollar too high also kept players cautious.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Broadly firm, rupiah in focus after rate move
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly firm against the dollar on Tuesday, boosted by gains in regional equities and optimism about economic growth in the region.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> hit a one-month peak at about 9,910 per dollar as investors cheered changes to the cabinet's top economic positions, but it dropped back slightly after Bank Indonesia delivered a smaller-than-expected interest rate rise.  

The central bank raised the BI rate <BIPG>, its target rate for one-month certificates <BISBI01>, by 50 basis points to 12.75 percent to contain inflation, which is at a six-year high.  

This disappointed some in the currency market who had been looking for a rise of between 75 and 100 basis points.  

Still, analysts said sentiment was likely to stay upbeat after President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono named respected former Finance Minister Boediono as his chief economics minister, replacing Aburizal Bakrie.  

Planning Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati moves across to take on the finance portfolio from Jusuf Anwar.  

"Indonesia has been raising interest rates and hiring and firing the right people, so it is on the right track," said JPMorgan currency strategist Claudio Piron. "The rupiah is likely to close up on the day but it will give up some of its gains."  

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KTFC> gained more than a third of a percent to 1,033.0, boosted by foreign buying in the local equity market, whose index <.KS11> hit an all-time high.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> added a quarter of a percent to a three-week high of 33.405 per dollar, helped by expectations that the victory of Taiwan's opposition party in local government elections at the weekend would spur more foreign fund inflows.  

Its success has been welcomed by financial markets because the opposition is viewed as having a more conciliatory approach to China, the island's top trading partner.  

GROWTH OPTIMISM  

Analysts said favourable economic data meant Asia's currencies were holding up well against the dollar.  

"We are getting stronger-than-expected numbers for the third quarter and the export numbers are also showing that growth will be a bit better going into the first quarter despite high oil prices," said Jimmy Koh, head of economics and treasury at United Overseas Bank.  

Thailand's economy expanded 2.2 percent in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating market forecasts, data on Tuesday showed.  

Optimism about the economic outlook and rising short-term interest rates in Singapore helped push the Sing dollar <SGD=> to a two-month peak of about 1.6830 per dollar.  

Three-month rates <SGDF=> have risen to their highest level since early 2000. Traders said the upward pressure on rates was aimed at raising the appeal of local assets as interest rates around the region rise.  

"There is very strong macro data, a very strong push higher in domestic yields and a general recognition of the fact that the Sing dollar is cheaper against the basket," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.  

Dealers in the Philippines said central bank intervention to cap the peso's strength had undermined the currency in early trade.  

The peso <PHP=> underperformed other Asian currencies for much of the day before strengthening slightly to about 53.87 per dollar in late trade.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Singapore dollar, Philippine peso up
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose and the Korean won weakened on Thursday as the U.S. dollar steadied after recent falls, helped by markets having second thoughts about speculation that U.S. monetary tightening may soon end.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> hit a 6-½   month peak of 54.17 per dollar, helped by foreign investment and remittances from Filipinos working overseas, although it pared some of those gains towards the close of trading.  

 Traders had sold the U.S. dollar after minutes of the Federal Reserve's November policy meeting released on Tuesday suggested some board members were wary of raising rates too much.  

 But by Thursday many in the market were veering to the view that they may have over-reacted and the Fed was merely signalling U.S. policy was no longer that accommodative.  

 Some felt that even if the Fed paused early next year in a tightening cycle that began in June 2004, it could raise rates once again later in 2006.  

 The yen <JPY=> came off Wednesday's highs around 118.20 per dollar, to trade around 118.65/70. That weighed on the South Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> and the Thai baht <THB=>.  

 Analysts said Asian currencies could rally in the short term as markets unwind heavy speculative holdings of dollars.  

 "For the time being, the won can strengthen because the dollar is going through a bit of an adjustment," Jan Lambregts, head of Asia-Pacific research at Rabobank, said.  

 But the U.S. dollar will be underpinned by it's yield advantage in the longer term, he said.  

 "On a six-month horizon, the yen will struggle to make gains. The dollar can still perform reasonably well here."  

 SINGAPORE PUZZLE  

 Traders continued to be puzzled by developments in Singapore's money markets, as the Singapore dollar <SGD=> rallied to a 4-week high of 1.6902 per U.S. dollar and money market rates eased from their highest levels in nearly 6 years.  

 At Thursday's peak, the Singapore dollar was more than a cent up from the week's lows. Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in the money markets could not be confirmed.  

 James Malcolm, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist, said the Singapore dollar's rally was on account of the yen's recovery.  

 "It is just a product of the U.S. dollar losing steam and some lumpy flows," he said.  

 Overnight money market rates <SGDF=> eased to about 2.5 percent from the day's high of 3 percent, as did other rates which had been rising for 3 weeks owing to several factors including the weakness in the currency, rising bank lending and speculation that the MAS wanted to keep rates tight.  

 On Thursday, traders suspected the Singapore dollar's rally had led to rates being received in the money and fixed income markets, although no one was really sure.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR   Change on the day at 0918 GMT

title: Weak Sing dlr,  intervention  push up  Singapore  rates
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Extended weakness in the Singapore dollar and suspected central bank intervention to support it have pushed up short-term interest rates in Singapore to their highest in over four years, traders said on Thursday.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a 4-month low of 1.7065 against the U.S. dollar on Monday.  

It has recovered since, and was quoted around 1.7020/25 on Thursday, helped partly by central bank intervention which some analysts suspect was to the tune of over U.S.$1 billion.  

But inter-bank rates have continued to climb higher. Three-month inter-bank rates <SGDF=> were quoted at 2.75/3.00 percent on Thursday, their highest levels since early 2001.  

The rate, which has been rising in the past 3 months, has jumped quite sharply from about 2.25 percent in early November.  

Analysts said one reason for the spike in yields has been a market belief that the Sing dollar will stay weak, despite the central bank's efforts to shore up the unit.  

"When people think that the exchange rate is not going to appreciate, they demand higher returns on money market deposits," said Deutsche Bank currency strategist Mirza Baig.  

"The central bank is preventing a further currency depreciation, but if they want the Sing dollar to outperform the basket, they need to be much more aggressive."  

Unlike most central banks, the Monetary Authority of Singapore's main policy tool is the trade-weighted currency, which it manages in an undisclosed band.  

Analysts say the Sing dollar is in the weaker half of its policy band, although estimates on the width of the band vary.  

Bhanu Baweja, UBS's currency strategist, said interest rates and exchange rates in Singapore were closely linked.  

Singapore's markets adhered to uncovered-interest-parity theory, he said, which states that the expected movement in a currency pair equals the interest rate differential.  

"The Sing dollar remains weak and you need to be compensated for holding it through a higher interest rate," Baweja said.  

The MAS has had a tightening stance of allowing a "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the currency since April 2004.  

When it adopted that bias, the 3-month rate was about 0.44 percent, and the U.S. fed funds rate was 1.00 percent. The fed funds rate now stands at 4.00 percent and is expected to rise to 4.50 percent by the end of January next year.  

Other analysts said interest rates had also been driven up by banks covering a rising demand for consumer loans, especially mortgages.  

Moreover, by intervening the central bank was tightening the short-term supply of funds by selling U.S. dollars and soaking up Singapore dollars from the financial system, they said.  

Dealers added that the main focus for the Singapore dollar would remain the yen <JPY=>, which has weakened this week to 27-month lows against the dollar.  

"The key to dollar/Sing in the past few months has been dollar/yen," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered in Singapore.  

"There is still a very high correlation between the two because the yen is a key component of the trade-weighted basket and so if dollar/yen goes up, dollar/Sing goes up."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dollar, won higher but peso slips
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mixed on Monday as the Taiwan dollar and South Korean won hit multi-week highs as foreigners bought stocks, while the Philippine peso succumbed to profit taking after sharp gains in the past month.  

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KTFC> firmed about 0.4 percent to a 5-week peak against the dollar at 1,037.7, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> strengthened about a third of a percent to a 4-week high at 33.372 per U.S. dollar.  

Sentiment towards the north Asian currencies was boosted by foreign buyers of the country's stocks. This is a contrast to last month, when heavy foreign selling of South Korean and Taiwan shares sent the won and Taiwan dollar to multi-month lows.  

Seoul's benchmark share index <.KS11> on Monday hit a record high and Taiwan's TAIEX stock index <.TWII> closed at a 5-week peak.  

"Korea and Taiwan are tracking tech stocks," said Philip Wee, currency strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore. "In the NDF market, the won and the Taiwan dollar are the most sensitive currencies to equities."  

Foreign institutions bought a net 10.6 billion Taiwan dollars worth of local stocks on Monday.

title: Singapore  dollar above low on  intervention  fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 14 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar on Monday pulled away from 4-month lows hit on Friday, supported by wariness that the central bank might intervene to bolster the currency, dealers said.  

 At 0200 GMT, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> was trading at about 1.7010 per U.S. dollar, steady from late Asian levels on Friday but above a 4-month low at about 1.7045 hit that session.  

 Broad-based U.S. dollar strength and a break of key chart support levels have undermined Singapore's currency.  

 Dealers said talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's central bank, could intervene in the market to bolster the currency was providing support, although no actual intervention had so far been seen.  

 "There is talk that the MAS could check currency rates at about 1.7025, so the market is wary about intervention," said a trader in Singapore.  

 The Singapore dollar is managed within a secret trade-weighted currency band.  

 An analyst estimated the currency was trading about 0.5 percent weaker than the mid-point of a 1.5 percent-wide trading band.  

 Despite support for the currency, dealers said further near-term weakness was likely.  

 "The Singapore dollar is taking its direction from the U.S. dollar," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore.  

 "Unless there is a reversal in the dollar's trend against the euro and the yen, the bias will be towards more dollar strength against the Singapore dollar."  

 The Singapore dollar has been weakening against the U.S. currency since about mid-August, shedding almost 3.5 percent.

title: Singapore Dlr Flat In Asia, Bonds Fall Led By Short End
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was little changed against the U.S. dollar in Asian trade Monday, shrugging off early losses after the U.S. unit weakened against major currencies.  

Government bonds eased, led by selling at the front end of the yield curve, which further led to a flattening of the 2-10 year curve, dealers said.  

At 0714 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.7010, nearly unchanged from S$1.7011 late Friday. It traded between S$1.7005 and S$1.7028 intraday.  

A dealer at a foreign bank said the Singapore dollar erased early losses after the U.S. dollar slipped against the euro and the yen.  

Despite fears that the central bank may step in to stem the slide in the Singapore dollar, the central bank hasn't intervened in the market for the past few days, said a second dealer.  

The U.S. dollar hit a four-month high of S$1.7045 during intraday trading Friday, but started easing in the late session that day.  

"As long as the Singapore dollar is trading within the band they don't seem to be worried," the trader said.  

The Singapore dollar is currently estimated at 0.8% below the midpoint of the band, traders said.  

Looking ahead, United Overseas Bank said it expects the local unit to focus on a raft of economic data due this week with October's non-oil domestic exports - or NODX - being key.  

The NODX data due Thursday are expected to show exports resuming a growth trend after faltering to a 0.4% on-year decline in September.  

Analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires expect NODX to rise 4.2% on year in October because of improving electronics shipments and a recovery in pharmaceutical exports.  

In the Singapore government bond market, yields on the short end continued to lead the selloff in the market.  

Yields on the government bonds have been rising because of selling in U.S. Treasurys while short positions in the Singapore dollar lately further squeezed liquidity from the front end, said a strategist at a foreign bank.  

The two-year bond yield rose to 2.68%, up by two basis points, and the 10-year bond yield edged up by one basis points to 3.18%.

title: Singapore Dlr Falls To Fresh 3-Month Low Vs US Dlr Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell to a fresh three-month low against the U.S. dollar in Asia late Friday, due to factors such as Thursday's release of robust U.S. data.  

Government bond prices tumbled for the seventh straight trading session after U.S. Treasury prices slipped in New York Thursday, dealers said.  

At 0710 GMT, the U.S. unit was S$1.6983, up from S$1.6942 late Wednesday. The range was between S$1.6974 and S$1.6998 intraday. Singapore's financial markets were closed Thursday due to a public holiday.  

The U.S. dollar kicked off Friday's Asian session on a firm footing against its Singaporean counterpart after Thursday's batch of strong U.S. data, dealers said.  

Late Thursday, the U.S. Labor Department said productivity growth nearly doubled during the third quarter of 2005, with non-farm business productivity lifting a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.1%, the biggest quarterly increase in more than year. That was stronger than the 2.1% second-quarter increase and expectations of a 2.7% rise.  

The Institute for Supply Management in the U.S. also reported that its non-manufacturing index, which comprises mostly services and details performance in the single largest sector of the economy, rose 60.0 last month from 53.3 in September. Economists had been looking for a reading of 57.0 in October.  

Thursday's slew of better-than-expected U.S. data spurred speculation that the U.S. October nonfarm payrolls due out at 1330 GMT Friday could surprise on the upside, which fueled U.S. dollar-buying that lifted the U.S. unit as high as S$1.6998, its highest since July 11, in Friday's Asian session, dealers said.  

The median estimate of 22 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for an increase of 124,000 in October payrolls, reversing the 35,000 decline in the preliminary report for September.  

But, the U.S. dollar's rise above the psychologically important S$1.7000 resistance level was capped by rumored intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

"There's quite a lot of (U.S. dollar) selling interest above S$1.7000, so the market is suspicious" that the MAS has placed those offers, said a Singapore dealer.  

Given prospects that the U.S. dollar could retest the S$1.7000 resistance level if tonight's U.S. nonfarm payrolls report beats expectations, the MAS could intervene again to curb a further fall of the Singapore dollar versus the U.S. currency, dealers said.  

In the bond market, yields rose sharply across the board due to both the strong U.S. data and the continued weakness of the U.S. Treasury market, traders said.  

"Local players are selling bonds, as the market is very bearish," said a bond dealer at a local bank.

title: ASIA DEBT: Singapore Curve Flattening May Not Last
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's market intervention to support its currency is draining liquidity from the money market, pushing up short-term interest rates and flattening the yield curve to a level last seen in the middle of the year.   

The shape of the curve is odd at a time when the economy is strengthening from a period of slowdown. A strengthening economy generally acts to steepen the yield curve.   

Analysts expect that the Monetary Authority of Singapore will in coming weeks need to continue to support the currency to meet its goal of gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar so the yield curve could flatten even further.   

But in the longer-term the stronger economy and a possible rise in yields on U.S. Treasurys, which Singapore's bond market closely tracks, will lead to a curve steepening.   

Some analysts say that volatility in the curve's shape makes it difficult for investors to take short-term positions on Singapore's curve movements alone.   

They say it makes more sense to execute trades that link the Singapore and U.S. yield curves. They say Singapore's strong economic performance means that the Singapore curve will lag any U.S. curve flattening and will outsteepen any U.S. curve steepening.   

Chia Woon Khien, a fixed-income strategist at UBS bank, has recommended investors do a box trade. That is, they should buy Singapore 2-10-year interest-rate swap steepener against a U.S. 2-10-year swap flattener.   

The Singapore 2-10-year spread is 68 basis points while the U.S. 2-10-year spread is 24 basis points, making the difference between the two 44 basis points. Chia said the target for this relative value trade is for a widening to 66 basis points over the next three months.   

She believes Singapore's term structure is unlikely to stay flat for long because its economy is strengthening.   

Singapore's industrial output rose more than expected in August due to robust growth in the pharmaceutical and transport-engineering sectors. This has prompted some economists to revise upward their economic growth forecasts for the third quarter.   

The data also likely mean that the economy is on track to meet the government's projected growth of 3.5%-4.5% for the whole year, moderating from last year's 8.4%, when the economy rebounded from a SARS outbreak in 2003.   


 
    MAS Action Accelerated Flattening 
    

The recent flattening trend was partly driven by suspected central bank intervention in the foreign-exchange swap market, which led market participants to cover short positions in the local currency, pushing up sharply the overnight rate.   

The overnight rate hit a high of 2.35% on Sept. 23, its highest level since late 2001, and up from a year-low of 1.25% in January. It has averaged 1.75% so far this year. At the same time, yields on Singapore government bonds have remained relatively low, in line with long-term U.S. Treasury yields.   

The spread between the two- and 10-year yields, a measure of the curve's shape, narrowed to 53 basis points Thursday from 82 basis points on August 30.   

That is near to the 46-point level set in June which was the narrowest spread since the Asian financial crisis in 1997-98.   

"We see a flattening bias because there's a risk the overnight rate may rise to 2.5%," said Selena Ling, a fixed-income analyst at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.   

Ling said that with strong resistance for the yield on 10-year bonds at 3.0%, the two-10-year spread could test the June low in coming weeks. The 10-year bond currently yields 2.86%.   

Others say that the MAS will likely reduce its intervention in the foreign-exchange market and allow liquidity in the short-term money market to rise after its semiannual policy review in the middle of October.   

The MAS at that time will likely maintain its policy of targeting a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, which could give the currency a psychological boost and allow MAS to pull back from the market.   

Singapore targets the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its monetary policy tool since its exports and imports amount to three times the city-state's S$184 billion economy.   

The Singapore dollar is currently 0.6% below the midpoint of its estimated trade-weighted band, United Overseas Bank said in a note Thursday. The U.S. dollar was last quoted at S$1.6893 at 0507 GMT.

title: Singapore Dlr Little Changed Late On Suspected MAS Moves

Singapore government bonds were weak at the short end, catching up with recent weakness in U.S. Treasurys amid a firm overnight rate, and flat at the long end, which helped flatten the yield curve.

title: Singapore curve inversion signalling tight policy
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Singapore's short-term interest rates have risen and the yield curve has inverted this month, signalling to markets that the central bank will retain its tightening bias at October's semi-annual policy review.  

Over the past two weeks, overnight rates in the low-yielding economy have climbed 55 basis points.  

Overnight rates <SGDDFIX=ABSG> were quoted on Monday at 2.57 percent, higher than a one-month rate of 2.38 and a six-month rate of 2.34 percent -- a negatively sloping money market curve.  

Analysts said this inversion of the curve suggested the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was intervening to push up short-term rates, to signal that its tightening bias was intact.  

Monetary policy in Singapore is run through the currency. The MAS conducts policy by guiding the Singapore dollar <SGD=> within a secret trade-weighed band and, since April last year, has tightened policy through a gradual appreciation of the band.  

"Heading into the beginning of October, the MAS will start guiding the Sing dollar towards where it wants it to be," said Chia Woon Khien, an interest rates strategist with UBS in Hong Kong.  

The central bank's effort to push the currency higher ahead of its mid-October policy review was forcing speculators and traders with short Sing dollar positions to borrow the currency, pushing up rates out to a month, Chia said.  

The currency had been trading in the strong half of what economists estimated to be its policy band earlier this year when expectations were high that China would revalue the yuan, bringing speculative cash into Asia.  

The Sing dollar weakened to the bottom of the band after the size of China's July 21 yuan revaluation disappointed markets.  

Economists said it was unlikely the MAS will accelerate the pace of tightening, but the currency might be allowed to move up to the top end of the band. The MAS has not disclosed the rate at which it has allowed the Sing dollar's policy band to appreciate.  

The Sing dollar was quoted around 1.6890 per dollar on Monday. Some analysts estimated it was still trading about 0.75 percent weaker than the mid-point of the trade-weighted band, so it had room to rise going into the review.  

"With the Singapore dollar trading at the weaker end of its trading band, we expect front-end Singapore rates to keep pace with the gradual increase in the U.S., unless in the unlikely event MAS drops its appreciation stance," Adrian Khoo, BNP Paribas's interest rates strategist said in a note.  

Some analysts said markets were forcing short-term rates up as investors sought a better return to justify buying the Singapore dollar in exchange for the higher-yielding U.S. dollar.  

One interest rate trader said the MAS had been spotted intervening through currency swaps to push up Singapore rates.  

"Previously, we saw them leave more liquidity in the market because the economic numbers were printing quite poorly," he said. "But, over the last few weeks they want to keep rates a bit firmer. They don't really need to have this liquidity bias any more and a loose policy can push inflation up."  

The economy reported a quarterly contraction in output between January and March but has since rebounded, with the manufacturing sector expanding at a healthy rate and inflation showing signs of picking up in August.

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: Singapore To Keep Policy Tight
text:
By Saeed Azhar 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires column 
   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank is widely expected to reaffirm a tight monetary policy at October's semiannual review as persistently high oil prices mean it will be wary of inflation pressures, analysts say.  

Maintaining a tight policy, which has been in place since April 2004 and targets modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, will also reflect central bank confidence that the economy has regained a stable footing after an annualized contraction in the first quarter.  

"If they view the risk to growth as very limited, and price pressures are translating into higher inflation, then the intended stance of monetary policy would remain that of modest and gradual appreciation," said Sanjay Mathur, an economist at UBS Bank.  

MAS has only said the monetary policy review will be in October, and analysts expect it to be in the second week of the month.  

For much of this year, prices in Singapore have been very subdued, picking up only in the last couple of months as record high oil prices start being passed through to consumers. For instance, Singapore's transport operators recently increased bus and taxi fares to protect their profit margins.  

The consumer price index fell in June before picking up to a 0.1% year-on-year rise in the seven months ended July. And in August, inflation rose faster than expected at a 0.7% year-on-year pace although the CPI registered a still meek 0.2% for the January-August period. In the first half, the inflationary impact from higher oil prices was partly offset by lower car prices and competition among gasoline retailers.  

MAS has forecast inflation of between 0% and 1.0% for 2005.  


 
   Policy Stance Likely Unch In Next 12-18 Mos - UOB 
   

Jimmy Koh, an economist at United Overseas Bank, thinks the MAS will maintain a tight policy as inflation is "creeping up."  

In Singapore's case, this means allowing the local dollar to strengthen. The republic won't be alone in adopting such a stance, he added, noting that other Asian economies are also allowing currencies to strengthen to overcome the impact of expensive oil imports.  

Koh doesn't expect the current policy stance to change over the next 12 to 18 months as Singapore isn't likely to be hit by recession although economic growth may slow.  

Structural changes in the economy, such as a move away from electronics to biomedical manufacturing, and toward a greater reliance on financial sector growth will help cushion Singapore from a major slowdown, he said.  

Singapore uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its monetary policy tool because trade amounts to three times the city-state's S$184 billion economy - one of the highest such ratios in the world.  

The MAS operates a managed float regime for Singapore, which allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band, and intervenes to prevent it from breaching the band.  

The last monetary policy review was in April, a few months before China and Malaysia revalued their currencies and loosened their link to the U.S. dollar. Since then, however, both currencies have strengthened very marginally to the disappointment of many currency watchers expecting a sharp rise in regional units.  

Daniel Hui, an economist at JPMorgan, said that historically, the MAS has only turned accommodative in the wake of major external shocks that posed a significant risk to Singapore's growth.  


 
   Last Shift To Neutral In 2003 
   

The last shift to a neutral policy came in 2003 when the city state and its regional trading partners were reeling from the outbreak of SARS virus.  

"While Singapore began the year on the weak side and growth indicators firmed only at the end of the second quarter, the recent external demand recovery should ensure a solid second half" for the Singapore economy, said Hui.  

Gross domestic product grew 5.2% in the second quarter, recovering from a lower-than-expected 2.7% growth in the first, when output from the volatile biomedical sector slumped.  

Thus, although the economy won't grow as fast as 2004's 8.4% when it rebounded from the previous year's SARS outbreak, GDP could still expand as much as 4.5% this year, according to the government.  

As the policy review draws near, the central bank will likely intervene to push the Singapore dollar back near the midpoint of the band which may tighten liquidity as players short of Singapore dollars cover their positions.  

At 0821 GMT Friday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6837, significantly higher from S$1.6449 around the April policy review.  

Against its trade-weighted exchange rate, the Singapore dollar is likely about 0.6% below the estimated midpoint of the band, said United Overseas Bank, which reckons the lower end of the band is at S$1.6988 and upper end at S$1.6322. The midpoint is likely at S$1.6655, assuming 2% on each side, UOB said.  

Strength recently seen in economic indicators hasn't been translated into a higher currency because of a resurgent U.S. dollar and weakness in the Indonesian rupiah, which has generally been a drag on most other regional currencies.  

Still, forecasters are generally positive about the Singapore dollar's medium term prospects.  

Citigroup forecasts the U.S. dollar at S$1.6500 by the end of the year, JPMorgan is looking S$1.6200 and the United Overseas Bank projects the U.S. dollar to weaken to S$1.6400.

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: Singapore To Keep Policy Tight
text:
By Saeed Azhar 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires column 
   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's central bank is widely expected to reaffirm a tight monetary policy at October's semiannual review as persistently high oil prices mean it will be wary of inflation pressures, analysts say.  

Maintaining a tight policy, which has been in place since April 2004 and targets modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, will also reflect central bank confidence that the economy has regained a stable footing after an annualized contraction in the first quarter.  

"If they view the risk to growth as very limited, and price pressures are translating into higher inflation, then the intended stance of monetary policy would remain that of modest and gradual appreciation," said Sanjay Mathur, an economist at UBS Bank.  

MAS has only said the monetary policy review will be in October, and analysts expect it to be in the second week of the month.  

For much of this year, prices in Singapore have been very subdued, picking up only in the last couple of months as record high oil prices start being passed through to consumers. For instance, Singapore's transport operators recently increased bus and taxi fares to protect their profit margins.  

The consumer price index fell in June before picking up to a 0.1% year-on-year rise in the seven months ended July. And in August, inflation rose faster than expected at a 0.7% year-on-year pace although the CPI registered a still meek 0.2% for the January-August period. In the first half, the inflationary impact from higher oil prices was partly offset by lower car prices and competition among gasoline retailers.  

MAS has forecast inflation of between 0% and 1.0% for 2005.  


 
   Policy Stance Likely Unch In Next 12-18 Mos - UOB 
   

Jimmy Koh, an economist at United Overseas Bank, thinks the MAS will maintain a tight policy as inflation is "creeping up."  

In Singapore's case, this means allowing the local dollar to strengthen. The republic won't be alone in adopting such a stance, he added, noting that other Asian economies are also allowing currencies to strengthen to overcome the impact of expensive oil imports.  

Koh doesn't expect the current policy stance to change over the next 12 to 18 months as Singapore isn't likely to be hit by recession although economic growth may slow.  

Structural changes in the economy, such as a move away from electronics to biomedical manufacturing, and toward a greater reliance on financial sector growth will help cushion Singapore from a major slowdown, he said.  

Singapore uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its monetary policy tool because trade amounts to three times the city-state's S$184 billion economy - one of the highest such ratios in the world.  

The MAS operates a managed float regime for Singapore, which allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band, and intervenes to prevent it from breaching the band.  

The last monetary policy review was in April, a few months before China and Malaysia revalued their currencies and loosened their link to the U.S. dollar. Since then, however, both currencies have strengthened very marginally to the disappointment of many currency watchers expecting a sharp rise in regional units.  

Daniel Hui, an economist at JPMorgan, said that historically, the MAS has only turned accommodative in the wake of major external shocks that posed a significant risk to Singapore's growth.  


 
   Last Shift To Neutral In 2003 
   

The last shift to a neutral policy came in 2003 when the city state and its regional trading partners were reeling from the outbreak of SARS virus.  

"While Singapore began the year on the weak side and growth indicators firmed only at the end of the second quarter, the recent external demand recovery should ensure a solid second half" for the Singapore economy, said Hui.  

Gross domestic product grew 5.2% in the second quarter, recovering from a lower-than-expected 2.7% growth in the first, when output from the volatile biomedical sector slumped.  

Thus, although the economy won't grow as fast as 2004's 8.4% when it rebounded from the previous year's SARS outbreak, GDP could still expand as much as 4.5% this year, according to the government.  

As the policy review draws near, the central bank will likely intervene to push the Singapore dollar back near the midpoint of the band which may tighten liquidity as players short of Singapore dollars cover their positions.  

At 0821 GMT Friday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6837, significantly higher from S$1.6449 around the April policy review.  

Against its trade-weighted exchange rate, the Singapore dollar is likely about 0.6% below the estimated midpoint of the band, said United Overseas Bank, which reckons the lower end of the band is at S$1.6988 and upper end at S$1.6322. The midpoint is likely at S$1.6655, assuming 2% on each side, UOB said.  

Strength recently seen in economic indicators hasn't been translated into a higher currency because of a resurgent U.S. dollar and weakness in the Indonesian rupiah, which has generally been a drag on most other regional currencies.  

Still, forecasters are generally positive about the Singapore dollar's medium term prospects.  

Citigroup forecasts the U.S. dollar at S$1.6500 by the end of the year, JPMorgan is looking S$1.6200 and the United Overseas Bank projects the U.S. dollar to weaken to S$1.6400.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late After Fed Signals More Tightening
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker against its U.S. counterpart in late Asian trade Wednesday, after the U.S. Federal Reserve signaled it would maintain its measured pace of monetary tightening.  

Short-dated government bonds slipped in response to the Fed's decision to raise rates, while the rest of the curve was relatively steady, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6809, up from S$1.6775 Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6805 and S$1.6841.  

Late Tuesday, the Federal Open Market Committee voted to hike the key federal fund's rate by 25 basis points to 3.75% and indicated in its accompanying statement that it would continue to tighten policy at a measured pace.  

The hawkish statement from the FOMC spurred some U.S. dollar short-covering against the Singapore dollar, lifting the U.S. unit to S$1.6841, its highest since Aug. 31, very early in the session.  

But Singapore companies sold the U.S. currency around S$1.6841, apparently to hedge their foreign exchange exposure, dragging the U.S. unit back down as low as S$1.6806 in the afternoon, dealers said. Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might have intervened to curb the U.S. dollar's rise beyond S$1.6841 was another factor that pulled the U.S. currency down, said traders.  

But technical analysis show the overall tone of the U.S. dollar is still positive, said United Overseas Bank in a research note.  

"Key resistance remains at S$1.6860 and a move above this level will lead likely to higher acceleration," UOB said, adding "it is unlikely that we will move below S$1.6765 from here."  

As a short-term trading strategy, UOB recommended buying the U.S. dollar at S$1.6800, and placing stop-loss orders below S$1.6765  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose moderately in the short end but edged down in the long end, resulting in a flatter yield curve, dealers said.  

"It looks like the flattening trend is back," in the wake of the FOMC meeting, said a Singapore dealer.  

Traders said the Fed rate hike put upward pressure on short-term yields, but lingering uncertainty over future rate direction prevented longer-dated yields from rising too much.

title: Singapore Dollar Down Late On Weak Euro; Bonds Fall
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell in late Asian trade Monday, hurt by the euro's weakness after unconvincing election results in Germany, Europe's biggest economy.  

Singapore government bond prices fell, tracking overnight losses in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said.  

At 0654 GMT, the U.S. unit was S$1.6833, up from S$1.6782 Friday. It traded between S$1.6810 and S$1.6840.  

Dealers said the Singapore dollar opened weaker after the euro tumbled to a one-month low against the U.S. dollar in early trade.  

The common currency was hurt after conservative challenger Angela Merkel's party won most votes in German elections Sunday but fell short of a clear mandate to govern against incumbent Gerhard Schroeder.  

The euro fell to as low as $1.2132 as of 0518 GMT, its lowest since Aug. 19. Any weakness in the euro hurts the Singapore dollar as the common currency is about 15% of Singapore's trade-weighted currency basket, analysts said.  

A dealer at a Singapore bank said despite early weakness, the local unit remained stuck in a narrow range because of strong support at S$1.6850.  

Dealers said the market was wary of central bank intervention because the Singapore dollar was trading on the weaker side of its trade-weighted band.  

JPMorgan in a report said the Singapore dollar's current weakness is at odds with strong economic data last week, including faster-than-expected growth in non-oil exports and retail sales.

title: Singapore Dollar Lower Late; Pares Losses On MAS Fears
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was lower in late Asian trade Thursday as broad gains in the U.S. dollar hurt most Asian currencies.  

The local unit recovered from early lows on fears the central bank may intervene.  

Singapore government bond prices fell, tracking overnight selling in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said.  

At 0701 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6801, up from S$1.6790 Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6781 and S$1.6812 intraday.  

In the morning session, the U.S. dollar rose to S$1.6812, following the greenback's rise against the yen and the euro, said a dealer at a Singapore bank.  

However fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may prevent larger weakness in the local currency prevented players from taking the dollar further higher, he said.  

Speculation that Singapore's state-owned investment company, Temasek Holdings, may be in the market to buy foreign currency to fund recent acquisition of stakes in Chinese banks has also kept the Singapore dollar under downward pressure, traders said.  

However most analysts have recently made calls for the Singapore dollar to strengthen because MAS is likely to continue with its current policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the exchange rate adopted in April 2004.  

DBS Bank in its currency strategy said the Singapore dollar should rebound from the weak limit of its trade-weighted band toward the stronger half as the MAS is unlikely to change policy in its next review in October.  

It recommends buying the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies comprising the U.S. dollar, euro and Japanese yen.  

Sabrina Jacobs, forex strategist at Dresdner Kleinwork Wasserstein, said the upside for the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar is likely to be capped at S$1.6830 because of tight MAS policy.  

She said the U.S. dollar may have strongly rebounded recently, but a firm outlook on the greenback would likely depend on a spate of economic data due this week.  

Key would be the consumer price index, which may determine the outlook for the Federal Reserve's current tightening stance.

title: Singapore Dollar Edges Up Late On US Dlr Profit-Taking
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged higher in late Asian trade Wednesday on U.S. dollar profit-taking sparked by rumored central bank intervention late Tuesday.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds flattened slightly, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6790, down from S$1.6800 Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6767 and S$1.6818 intraday.  

In the wake of suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore late Tuesday to curb the U.S. dollar's rise against its Singaporean counterpart, the U.S. currency opened Wednesday's session with a negative tone versus the local dollar, dealers said.  

Singapore-based players used the apparent central bank intervention as an excuse to take profits on their long U.S. dollar positions against the Singapore dollar, thereby pushing the U.S. unit down as low as S$1.6767 in the morning, dealers added.  

Analysts said the MAS' rumored intervention is a typical pattern that occurs when the Singapore dollar comes close to the weaker boundary of the currency's nominal effective exchange rate, or NEER, band.  

The MAS doesn't disclose its policy band, but Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi economist Wong Keng Siong in a research report Wednesday said he estimates that the Singapore dollar weakened late Tuesday to around 0.85% below the policy midpoint.  

"By logical extension, the likelihood is that the Singapore dollar would firm toward the S$1.6700 per (U.S.) dollar mark later today," Wong said.  

Despite the U.S. dollar profit-taking early in the session, the U.S. currency soon rebounded to near the psychologically important S$1.6800 level in the afternoon, supported by improved sentiment spurred by Tuesday's release of a narrower-than-expected U.S. trade deficit for July.  

The U.S. deficit in international trade of goods and services contracted to US$57.94 billion in July from June's revised US$59.49 billion. The July figure was smaller than the US$60 billion trade gap which Wall Street had expected.  

In Singapore's government bond market, the yield curve flattened by around five basis points, as the two-year yield rose on tight liquidity while the 10-year yield tracked the 10-year U.S. Treasurys yield lower, dealers said.  

Reflecting this tight liquidity, the overnight interbank rate remained high at 2.0625% in Asia late Wednesday.  

OCBC Bank, in a weekly report, said the tight liquidity conditions are suspected to be linked to the MAS' policy need to curb speculative interest to sell the Singapore dollar against the U.S. dollar.  

"We suspect that current firmness in Sibor (Singapore interbank offered rate) levels may persist until the October monetary policy review when the future path of the SGD monetary policy becomes clearer," OCBC said.
