title: DJ Singapore Dollar Edges Up Late On US Dlr Profit-Taking
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged higher in late Asian trade Wednesday on U.S. dollar profit-taking sparked by rumored central bank intervention late Tuesday.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds flattened slightly, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6790, down from S$1.6800 Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6767 and S$1.6818 intraday.  

In the wake of suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore late Tuesday to curb the U.S. dollar's rise against its Singaporean counterpart, the U.S. currency opened Wednesday's session with a negative tone versus the local dollar, dealers said.  

Singapore-based players used the apparent central bank intervention as an excuse to take profits on their long U.S. dollar positions against the Singapore dollar, thereby pushing the U.S. unit down as low as S$1.6767 in the morning, dealers added.  

Analysts said the MAS' rumored intervention is a typical pattern that occurs when the Singapore dollar comes close to the weaker boundary of the currency's nominal effective exchange rate, or NEER, band.  

The MAS doesn't disclose its policy band, but Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi economist Wong Keng Siong in a research report Wednesday said he estimates that the Singapore dollar weakened late Tuesday to around 0.85% below the policy midpoint.  

'By logical extension, the likelihood is that the Singapore dollar would firm toward the S$1.6700 per (U.S.) dollar mark later today,' Wong said.  

Despite the U.S. dollar profit-taking early in the session, the U.S. currency soon rebounded to near the psychologically important S$1.6800 level in the afternoon, supported by improved sentiment spurred by Tuesday's release of a narrower-than-expected U.S. trade deficit for July.  

The U.S. deficit in international trade of goods and services contracted to US$57.94 billion in July from June's revised US$59.49 billion. The July figure was smaller than the US$60 billion trade gap which Wall Street had expected.  

In Singapore's government bond market, the yield curve flattened by around five basis points, as the two-year yield rose on tight liquidity while the 10-year yield tracked the 10-year U.S. Treasurys yield lower, dealers said.  

Reflecting this tight liquidity, the overnight interbank rate remained high at 2.0625% in Asia late Wednesday.  

OCBC Bank, in a weekly report, said the tight liquidity conditions are suspected to be linked to the MAS' policy need to curb speculative interest to sell the Singapore dollar against the U.S. dollar.  

'We suspect that current firmness in Sibor (Singapore interbank offered rate) levels may persist until the October monetary policy review when the future path of the SGD monetary policy becomes clearer,' OCBC said.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late As Worries Over Katrina Diminish
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar slipped in late Asian trade Tuesday on U.S. dollar purchases spurred by diminishing worries over the negative impact from Hurricane Katrina on the U.S. economy.  

Government bonds also fell along the curve, mainly on Monday's weakness in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said.  

At 0635 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at its intraday high of S$1.6800, up from S$1.6747 Monday. Its intraday low was S$1.6766.  

Bearish sentiment toward U.S. economic growth prospects that had accumulated in the wake of Hurricane Katrina continued to decline, prompting Singapore players to buy U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars early in Tuesday's Asian session.  

Some Singaporean companies also bought the U.S. currency, helping to lift the U.S. dollar as high as S$1.6800 in the afternoon, dealers said.  

While the hurricane caused extensive damage to the U.S. Gulf Coast, the storm is unlikely to prevent the Federal Reserve from hiking interest rates, even at the Federal Open Market Committee's next meeting on Sept. 20.  

But lingering speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may not tolerate excessive weakness of the Singapore dollar capped the U.S. dollar's upside in the Asian session, dealers said.  

Singapore's central bank is rumored to have intervened late Friday and Monday to curb the U.S. currency's rise beyond the psychologically important S$1.6800 resistance, dealers said.  

From a technical analysis perspective, however, the U.S. dollar is likely to extend its gains versus the Singapore dollar in Tuesday's global session, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"Having said that, previous attempts to move higher have failed at S$1.6800 and even a (U.S. dollar) move above this level will likely be limited to S$1.6820-S$1.6825," UOB said.  

In the Singapore government bond market, yields rose between four and eight basis points along the curve, in line with higher yields on U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. The 10-year Treasury yield hit a post-Katrina high overnight as many investors' worst fears about the overall economic impact of the hurricane subsided.  

Moreover, new corporate bond issuance in the form of S$500 million worth of bonds from Hongkong Land Holdings, which plans to sell the bonds this week, put downward pressure on local bond prices.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late On Yen's Early Poll-Linked Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose in late Asian trade Monday, reacting to the yen's early gains after a landslide election victory for Japan's ruling coalition.  

Government bonds fell at the short end as the overnight rate rose, and was little changed at the long end, which helped steepen the yield curve, dealers said.  

At 0624 GMT, the U.S. dollar was S$1.6747, down from S$1.6779 late Friday. It traded between S$1.6725 and S$1.6751 intraday.  

The election victory of Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi's Liberal Democratic Party and its coalition partner, New Komeito Party, pushed the U.S. dollar to Y108.96 in early trade, the yen's strongest level since Sept. 5.  

Later, the U.S. dollar recovered ground and was little changed from its New York close of Y109.61 as selling by Japanese importers offset the wave of election-related yen-buying.  

The brief yen rally provided support for the Singapore dollar, which had already stabilized from suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore late Friday, traders said.  

Amy Yeo, treasury economist at United Overseas Bank, said the Singapore dollar was poised for more gains if the yen rallies further.  

Another important factor would be if Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average climbs above 13,000 points, which would be a psychological boost for the yen and Asian currencies, she said. Monday, the Nikkei 225 closed up 204.39 points at 12896.43.  

"This would trigger yen longs and would further weaken the dollar-Sing (U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar), she said.  

Other traders were cautious over the outlook for the local currency.  

Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. said in a note that it saw strong support for the U.S. dollar at S$1.6700, while saying it would rather wait for U.S. trade data Tuesday before forming a short-term outlook for the Singapore dollar.  

On the money market, the overnight rate rose to 2% from 1.9250% Friday, pushing the two-year yield up two basis points to 2.07%.  

Dealers said they suspected the MAS may be behind the higher overnight rate since last week as it was trying to squeeze liquidity to curb speculative selling of the Singapore dollar.

title: Singapore Dollar Relatively Steady Vs US Dollar Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was relatively steady late in Asia Wednesday, caught between sales of the local currency for non-U.S. dollar currencies and prospects of central bank intervention to limit the Singapore dollar's fall.  

Short-dated government bonds slipped on tighter liquidity, causing the curve to flatten, dealers said.  

At 0655 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6765, almost unchanged from S$1.6766 late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6744 and S$1.6780 intraday.  

From early in the session, the U.S. dollar steadily advanced against the local dollar, reaching an intraday high of S$1.6780 in the afternoon, as some speculators sold the Singapore dollar for non-U.S. dollar currencies such as the euro, dealers said.  

"It's all cross (buying) plays against the Singapore dollar," said a Singapore dealer.  

But lingering speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may continue intervening to cap the U.S. dollar's rise against the Singapore dollar weighed down the U.S. unit later in the session.  

Singapore's central bank was rumored to have intervened Tuesday evening to curb the U.S. dollar's rise versus the local currency, dealers said.  

"Signs of MAS action appear to be capping near-term upside. We expect the immediate USD/SGD upside to be limited from here," JP Morgan Chase Bank said in a research report.  

In its weekly report, OCBC Bank said it expects the U.S. dollar to hold on to support at S$1.6700, which is roughly 50% retracement of the rise from the May low of S$1.6339.  

But OCBC added that any U.S. dollar fall below the S$1.6700 support level would target next support in the S$1.6650-S$1.6660 region in the coming days.  

Singapore government bonds weakened at the short end of the curve, mainly due to a rise in the overnight interbank rate to 2.1250% Wednesday from 2.0625% Tuesday, dealers said.  

With yields on long-term securities rising less than those on short-dated bonds, however, the yield curve flattened slightly. The spread between two- and 10-year local bond yields narrowed to 77 basis points Wednesday from 79 basis points Tuesday.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Continued Strength In Oil Prices
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar slipped against its U.S. counterpart in late Asian trading Wednesday, undermined by the unrelenting march ofoil prices during the session.  

Government bond prices were flat to higher across the curve, more or less in line with Tuesday's rise in U.S. Treasurys.  

At 0637 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6865, up from S$1.6833 late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6829 and S$1.6871 intraday.

"MAS monetary policy as articulated in its Monetary Policy Statement of April 12, (2005), remains. The next policy review will be in October," the central bank said in an e-mail to Dow Jones Newswires.  

Its response came after economists raised concerns that Singapore's economy and its currency may be feeling the pressure of the Indonesian crisis as well as record-high oil prices.  

Still, the U.S. dollar steadily rebounded against the local currency during the rest of the session, reaching as high as S$1.6871 late in the afternoon, as oil prices continued their rally amid fears over possible damages to oil refineries along the U.S. Gulf Coast from Hurricane Katrina.  

Growing worries that high oil prices could adversely affect economic growth in Asian countries have contributed to a recent weakness in regional currencies, including the Singapore dollar.

title: Singapore Dlr Falls To 5-Week Low Vs US Dlr Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell to a five-week low against its U.S. counterpart in late Asian trade Tuesday, dragged down by receding worries over the impact of high oil prices on the U.S. economy and by weakness in regional currencies.  

Singapore government bonds were weaker across the board following a disappointing auction of 15-year bonds Monday, dealers said.  

At 0642 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6833, up from S$1.6753 late Monday. It traded between S$1.6782 and S$1.6849 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar kicked off Tuesday's Asian session on a positive note against the local dollar, bolstered by diminishing concerns over the adverse effects of higher oil prices on the U.S. economy and by the pronounced weakness of the yen and the Indonesian rupiah.  

Singapore-based interbank players eventually boosted the U.S. currency to S$1.6849, its highest level since July 21.  

Tuesday, the U.S. unit soared as high as Y111.09. At 0642 GMT, it was quoted at Y111.00, up from Y110.61 in New York late Monday.  

The rupiah, meanwhile, continued tumbling Tuesday, with the U.S. dollar rising above IDR11,000, marking the lowest level for the rupiah since July 2001.  

Given lingering concerns over high oil prices, sentiment toward Asian currencies such as the Singapore dollar remained negative, analysts said.  

But traders said wariness over possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to curb excessive depreciation of the Singapore dollar could slow the current rally of the U.S. dollar versus its Singaporean counterpart in coming sessions.  

"Caution about intervention may emerge should (the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar) rally too quickly," OCBC Bank said in a research report.  

From a technical analysis perspective, the S$1.6870-S$1.6880 area is a strong resistance region and a clear U.S. dollar rise above there seems unlikely for the global session, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

Having said that, however, UOB also said only a U.S. dollar pullback below the S$1.6770 support level would suggest that the U.S. currency is entering a consolidation phase against the Singapore dollar.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose along the curve, mainly due to Monday's weaker-than-expected auction of S$2.7 billion worth of 15-year bonds, dealers said.

Singapore government bonds were weaker across the board following a disappointing auction of 15-year bonds Monday, dealers said.  

At 0642 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6833, up from S$1.6753 late Monday. It traded between S$1.6782 and S$1.6849 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar kicked off Tuesday's Asian session on a positive note against the local dollar, bolstered by diminishing concerns over the adverse effects of higher oil prices on the U.S. economy and by the pronounced weakness of the yen and the Indonesian rupiah.  

Singapore-based interbank players eventually boosted the U.S. currency to S$1.6849, its highest level since July 21.  

Tuesday, the U.S. unit soared as high as Y111.09. At 0642 GMT, it was quoted at Y111.00, up from Y110.61 in New York late Monday.  

The rupiah, meanwhile, continued tumbling Tuesday, with the U.S. dollar rising above IDR11,000, marking the lowest level for the rupiah since July 2001.  

Given lingering concerns over high oil prices, sentiment toward Asian currencies such as the Singapore dollar remained negative, analysts said.  

But traders said wariness over possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to curb excessive depreciation of the Singapore dollar could slow the current rally of the U.S. dollar versus its Singaporean counterpart in coming sessions.  

'Caution about intervention may emerge should (the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar) rally too quickly,' OCBC Bank said in a research report.  

From a technical analysis perspective, the S$1.6870-S$1.6880 area is a strong resistance region and a clear U.S. dollar rise above there seems unlikely for the global session, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

Having said that, however, UOB also said only a U.S. dollar pullback below the S$1.6770 support level would suggest that the U.S. currency is entering a consolidation phase against the Singapore dollar.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose along the curve, mainly due to Monday's weaker-than-expected auction of S$2.7 billion worth of 15-year bonds, dealers said.  

With a cutoff yield of 3.30% and an average yield of 3.18%, the so-called 'tail' of the auction was 12 basis points, which was considered overly long and was indicative of weak investor demand, dealers added.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Mostly steady, rupiah hits 3-½ year low
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah hit a fresh 3-½ year low on Thursday but recovered slightly after central bank intervention, while most Asian currencies were little moved against the dollar.   

A retreat in oil prices, which hit a record high of $67.10 last Friday, supported regional currencies, hurt this week by worries that firm oil prices would dent economic growth.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> <SGD=D4> and South Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KTFC> pulled away from two-week lows hit against the dollar on Wednesday. The Thai baht <THB=> was up about a fifth of a percent at 41.19 per dollar -- above Wednesday's almost two-week trough at 41.33.   

The rupiah <IDR=> hogged the spotlight as it stepped closer to the key psychological level of 10,000 rupiah per dollar.   

Domestic demand for dollars pushed the rupiah to a 3-½ year low of about 9,980, before the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the battered currency.   

A Bank Indonesia spokesman confirmed the intervention.   

Seeking to support the rupiah, the central bank also said it would offer four-day instruments carrying an interest rate of 5.75 percent on Thursday to absorb excess rupiah liquidity.   

"Everyone is focusing on the 10,000 level, whether or not it goes and when," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore.   

"Intervention will be an obstacle to this in the short term. But more weakness is likely -- you have a balance of payments deterioration because Indonesia is a net oil importer, capital inflows are not picking up the slack, while interest rates are too low," Henderson said.   

The rupiah has lost more than 6 percent of its value since the start of the year, due mainly to rising inflation and soaring oil prices, which have increased dollar buying to finance oil imports. It has shed about 1.5 percent this week.   

RINGGIT WEAKER   

Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=> dipped to its weakest level since the currency was unpegged from the dollar a month ago, pressured by foreign investors selling local assets, traders said.   

They said the ringgit eased to a low of 3.7695 per dollar, taking it to its weakest level since July 22 -- the day after Malaysia abandoned the ringgit's peg to the U.S. currency.   

"Initially, when investors bought the ringgit at 3.8 they parked the money in ringgit assets, in bonds and equities," said one dealer in Kuala Lumpur.   

"When the currency tested the 3.7450 area it looked quite strong but didn't move further, so most investors sold their bonds and converted their ringgit back into dollars."   

Asian currencies were also likely to be held back by equity flows into Japan from the rest of Asia, dealers said.   

Foreign investors bought a net 721.9 billion yen ($6.58 billion) of Japanese stocks last week, up from 495 billion yen the previous week, official data from Japan showed on Thursday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaker but yen rally helps curb losses
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were weaker on Tuesday, weighed down by worries about the impact of high oil prices on economic growth, but trimmed some of their losses as the yen hit a seven-week high against the U.S. currency.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> extended Monday's falls to hit its lowest level since March 2002 at about 9,920 per dollar.   

Dealers said they suspected the central bank had intervened in the market to support the rupiah, helping the currency pull away from its lows.   

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> underperformed most other Asian currencies.   

The ringgit eased more than a third of a percent to 3.767 per dollar. Analysts said offshore speculators were selling the currency on expectations that the ringgit was unlikely to strengthen as much as anticipated against the dollar near term.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, which hit a two-week low against the U.S. currency overnight, and the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP>, which slipped to a one-month low earlier, pared their falls.   

"The sell-off has been fairly contained, although the rupiah is the one that looks dicey given the break out of its recent range," said BNP Paribas senior currency analyst Thio Chin Loo.   

"The yen is a factor that is helping mitigate losses, so by and large Asian currencies haven't been suffering too much despite the rebound in the dollar against European currencies."   

The yen <JPY=> hit a seven-week peak against the dollar on growing optimism about Japan's economy.   

One Singapore-based dealer said equity flows out of Asia, excluding Japan, into the world's second-largest economy were helping the yen outperform other regional currencies.   

Analysts at UBS said in a note that a decrease in the market's appetite for risk had meant that a strong run of portfolio inflows into Asia, excluding Japan, was now moderating.   

"However, this is a bigger worry for economies in Southeast Asia, where declining terms of trade and higher import volumes have also meant a sharp contraction in current account surpluses," the note said.   

RUPIAH WOES   

Analysts said the technical outlook for the rupiah was bleak after the currency broke through key chart support in the 9,900 per dollar area.   

"The next test will be the 10,000 psychological level and if that breaks, I would see little resistance for dollar/rupiah until 10,220," said Wayne Wong, a technical analyst at IDEAglobal in Singapore.   

Dealers said suspicions of central bank intervention limited selling in the rupiah. A trader in Singapore said comments from Bank Indonesia also supported the currency.   

Indonesia's central bank governor said on Tuesday a government target of 9,400 rupiah per dollar in 2006 was realistic.   

The rupiah has lost more than six percent of its value since the start of the year, due mainly to rising inflation and soaring oil prices, which have increased the dollar buying of state oil company Pertamina to finance oil imports.   

Pertamina has bought a total of about 18.23 million barrels of oil products for September, its highest monthly volume of imports this year and 15 percent more than in August, industry sources said on Tuesday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Yen;Off Early Highs On MAS Fears
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly against its U.S counterpart late Friday following gains in the Japanese yen, but lost some of its early shine on fears of central bank intervention.  

Government bonds rose at the long end on overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys and were slightly weaker at the front end, which flattened the yield curve.  

At 0637 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6474, down from S$1.6480 late Thursday. The U.S. unit slipped to S$1.6440 Thursday, its lowest level since May 11, but suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore lifted the greenback in late trade.  

Friday, the U.S. currency slid to S$1.6462 early in the session, when the Japanese yen was rallying ahead of the data release for gross domestic product in the second quarter. The U.S. dollar had dipped to Y109.59 against the dollar in the early session, before bouncing back to Y109.94.  

A trader said the Singapore dollar could have gained more, but fears of central bank intervention capped the rise.  

The local unit has been bolstered by stronger-than-expected 5.2% growth in the economy in the second quarter from a year ago.  

United Overseas Bank said in its technical analysis that the U.S. dollar's medium-term trend is bearish, and it may hit a low of S$1.6400. A move back above S$1.6530 will suggest that a recovery for the U.S. dollar is underway, the bank said.  

The next major economic data release for Singapore is on Wednesday, when the Ministry of Trade and Industry announces non-oil domestic exports for July. If the data are stronger than market expectations, they may trigger more gains for the local currency.  

Daniel Hui, economist at JPMorgan, said Singapore's exports should show a modest bounce in July, but a strong recovery is likely to come only in August on a possible rebound in global electronics demand.  

JPMorgan expects month-on-month seasonally adjusted non-oil exports growth of 2.5%. It expects on-year growth of 1.2% - a conservative projection compared with broader market estimates of 3.9%.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Equity Inflows; Long Bonds Flat
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended firmer against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Thursday on equities-linked inflows and strength in the Japanese yen, a regional trendsetter, dealers said.  

The baht finished off its high, however, on late intraday weakness in the Singapore dollar and on dollar buying by local importers, they said.  

Long-term government bonds ended mostly unchanged, as sharp recent declines in prices finally attracted some demand from big funds and insurance companies.  

The dollar finished at THB40.905, versus THB40.965 at the Asian close Wednesday.  

The U.S. currency opened at THB40.855 and fell to an intraday low of THB40.800 as offshore players chased the baht for portfolio investment, dealers said.  

Foreign investors have been persistent net buyers of Thai shares since July 25.  

However, some players bought the dollar back after it rebounded from a three-month low against the Singapore dollar on suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and on fears of equities-related outflows after a selloff in the Singapore stock market.  

"Some (Thai) importers also entered the market to buy the dollar in late trade, fearing the U.S. currency would shoot up significantly during the long weekend," a dealer at a major local bank said.  

Thai financial markets will be closed Friday to mark the queen's birthday.  

Traders expected the dollar to trade over the long weekend in a range between THB40.80 and THB41.10, barring any excessive volatility in other major regional units. [ 11-08-05 1112GMT ]  

Thai long-term government bond bid yields ended mostly unchanged, as big funds and insurance companies returned to buy long bonds after sharp increases in the last two weeks brought yields to attractive levels, dealers said.  

Yields are likely to continue rising gradually in the coming weeks due to the rising interest-rate trend, but the market will likely be calmer next week as renewed demand restrains the curve, they said.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid on the government bond due August 2008 finished up one basis point at 4.31%. Dealers said the March 2012 bid was flat at 4.83%, and the August 2019 bid was unchanged at 5.25%.  

The most-active overnight interbank rate was expected to have remained unchanged from Wednesday's most-active level of 2.70%, dealers said.  

Quotes for most term interest rates rose slightly, under pressure from the rising trend in offshore and onshore interest rates.

title: Bk Indonesia: Has Stabilised Rupiah Exchange Rate
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Foreign-exchange intervention by Bank Indonesia has likely stabilized the local currency's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar, a central bank official said Friday.  

"We are quite confident that our actions have stabilized" the rupiah, said Perry Warjiyo, head of the economic research and monetary policy directorate at Bank Indonesia.  

He said the government's moves to impose capital controls are also likely supporting the rupiah.  

"Of course, we see blips" in the exchange rate, Warjiyo said at an economics forum in Singapore.  

The rupiah is down around 4% versus the U.S. dollar from the start of the year, but has gained gradually in recent weeks after reaching its weakest point this year on July 5.  

UBS estimates that intervention by Bank Indonesia since April cost the central bank almost $5 billion, or 14% of its total reserves.

title: Indian rupee virtually pegged to US dollar -study
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee, contrary to market perceptions, is virtually pegged to the U.S. dollar, according to a study presented by two economists on Friday.  

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) says it follows a "managed float" for the rupee <INR=IN>, implying that it guides the currency against a basket of currencies of India's major trade partners.  

But an analysis from Tony Cavoli of the University of Adelaide and Ramkishen S. Rajan from Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy suggests that the central bank guides the rupee's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar.  

In contrast, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the Singapore dollar <SGD=> against a basket of currencies of its top trade partners, the study found, confirming Singapore's official stance.  

"The Indian rupee appears to be a de facto U.S. dollar peg while the Singapore dollar is a genuine basket pegger," Cavoli said, presenting the paper at the Singapore Economic Review Conference.  

"The degree of influence of the U.S. dollar on the rupee is quite high."  

Central bank officials often cite the rupee's real effective exchange rate (REER) to indicate that the rupee is overvalued or undervalued against a basket of currencies of its main trade partners.  

"The perception that RBI is targetting the REER is not right," said Rajan. "Since 1996, that's not true. That's not what we find."  

Other currencies have a negligible influence on the rupee, he said, although the the euro <EUR=> is gradually gaining in importance.  

"The euro is becoming more important at the expense of the pound sterling <GBP=> and the yen," Cavoli said.  

For the Singapore dollar, the Japanese yen <JPY=> has been growing in influence since 1998, he said.  

The study also found that the degree of flexibility in currency movements allowed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore was lower than that allowed by the Reserve Bank of India.  

That means the degree of intervention by the Singapore authority to keep the currency within its preferred trading band is higher than that of the Indian central bank, Cavoli said. title: Singapore Dlr Surges To One-Week High Vs US Dlr Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar surged to a fresh one-week high against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Tuesday, bolstered by speculation that Malaysian authorities may be letting the ringgit rise against the U.S. dollar.  

Government bonds weakened along the curve, in line with Monday's drop in U.S. Treasurys prices.  

At 0637 GMT, the U.S. dollar was S$1.6568, down significantly from S$1.6611 late Monday. It traded between S$1.6566 and S$1.6618 intraday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. currency slid to S$1.6566, its lowest level since July 22, dragged by speculator-led selling of U.S. dollars for other Asian currencies, dealers said.

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly weaker against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Monday, weighed down by expectations of possible central bank intervention.  

Prices on government bonds were lower, in the wake of a fall in U.S. Treasury prices Friday, dealers said.  

At 0635 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6611, up from S$1.6600 late Friday. It traded between S$1.6605 and S$1.6657 intraday.  

Despite the U.S. dollar's fall to as low as S$1.6605 on its weakness against the yen early in the session, the U.S. currency soon found support above the psychologically important S$1.6600 level amid prospects of the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervening around that level to curb further appreciation of the local dollar, dealers said.  

Traders said the MAS is perceived to be keen to temper any excessive rise of the Singapore dollar that may hurt growth in the city-state's export-reliant economy. The government is targeting growth of 2.5%-4.5% in 2005, down from 8.4% last year when the economy rebounded from a SARS outbreak in 2003.  

The U.S. dollar then consolidated steadily in the low-S$1.6600s for the rest of the session, as market players waited for the 1400 GMT release Monday of the U.S.'s Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index in July.  

The median estimate of 15 economists surveyed Friday by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for a reading of 54.0 for the ISM manufacturing index in July, compared with 53.8 in June.  

For this week, the U.S. dollar is likely to remain relatively supported versus the Singapore dollar as the yen could come under pressure ahead of Friday's vote by Japan's upper house on the privatization of the nation's postal system, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

"If unsuccessful, (Prime Minister Junichiro) Koizumi could decide to dissolve the parliament's lower house, which could put upward pressure on the USD/JPY," UOB said.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Profit-Taking On Yen Weakness
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Monday, as weakness in the Japanese yen led to unwinding of short positions in the U.S. unit that were built after China revalued its currency last week.  

Government bonds ended flat at the short end and slightly higher at the long end, helped by a recovery in U.S. Treasurys Friday.  

At 0755 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6649, up from S$1.6609 late Friday.  

The U.S. dollar was lower at S$1.6597 at the start of trading in Singapore and slipped further to S$1.6585 in midday trade as players looked at gains in the Malaysian ringgit.  

But as the day progressed, banks sold the Singapore dollar due to weakness in the Japanese yen, said a trader.  

"When the market realized the Chinese yuan and the Malaysian ringgit weren't going anywhere for now they decided to offload short positions in the U.S. dollar," said a banker at a foreign bank.  

Fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene also kept players from pushing the Singapore dollar upward in early trade.  

The MAS last week said it will only intervene if the Singapore dollar breaches its trade-weighted exchange rate band or if market conditions are too volatile.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research report that it expects the U.S. dollar to find strong resistance at S$1.6700. Therefore the bank maintains a bearish outlook for the U.S. currency in the medium term.

title: = UPDATE: Asian  Currencies  Pare Gains, Stks Mixed On Yuan
text:
SINGAPORE, Jul 22, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --   

A number of Asian currencies Friday gave back a portion of their sharp gains that followed China's revaluation of the yuan against the U.S. dollar late Thursday, while regional stock markets were mixed and local-currency bonds recovered from an initial slump.   

Reaction in oil and commodities markets was mostly muted.   

Local currencies responded quickly to China's decision to scrap the yuan's decade-old peg to the dollar and shift to an undisclosed basket of currencies to manage the currency's exchange rate.   

The yen surged against the dollar, with the U.S. unit tumbling more than two yen to a low of Y109.87 after the announcement. But the dollar bounced back Friday in Tokyo as traders decided to wait and see how China would actually control the yuan under the new system before pushing up the yen further.   

At 0920 GMT, the dollar was at Y110.89, more than half a yen back up from Y110.28 late Thursday in New York.   

The Australian dollar shot up above US$0.7650 from US$0.7600 before China's move on perceptions that Australia's commodity-heavy economy will benefit from the yuan move. It, unlike the yen, continued to climb and was last at US$0.7676.   

In the Singapore market, the U.S. dollar fell to S$1.6511 from S$1.6804 in late Asian trading Thursday, but recovered Friday on suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The intervention encouraged companies to step up U.S. dollar buying, traders said.   

Speculative buying of the Singapore dollar was also helped by Malaysia's decision to abandon its peg to the dollar and move to a currency basket regime.   

Despite Malaysia's policy change, the U.S. dollar didn't weaken much against the ringgit and was last quoted at MYR3.7775.   

Chua Hak Bin, an economist at Singapore's DBS Bank, said Asian currencies may rally more, led by the Japanese yen and the Taiwan dollar, because of their huge trade with China.   

But he said the Chinese appreciation is smaller than expected, which will prompt market players to speculate on more currency revaluation in the months ahead.   

Nikkei Slumps On Fears For Exporters
   

Asia-Pacific stock markets were mixed.   

Chinese shares led the region's gainers. Airline, property and paper-related companies in the mainland did especially well.   

The Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares in China, ended up 2.5% at 1046.32. The Shenzhen Composite Index ended up 2.2% to 245.57.   

Japan, which was hurt by concerns that a stronger yen would cut into exporter's profits, led the region's decliners.   

Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average ended down 0.8% at 11695.05. Japanese exporters were susceptible to profit-taking following their recent run-up, which were driven by hopes that their earnings would get a boost from a weaker Japanese currency.   

China's currency reform offered "a perfect incentive" for selling, as Tokyo stocks were due for a correction after their near-continuous gains since May, said Takashi Miyazaki, senior strategist at UFJ Partners Asset Management.   

Taiwan's Weighted Price Index ended down 0.2% at 6380.73. Technology shares accounted for 72% of turnover, down from their more usual level recently of around 80%.   

The Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, ended down 0.04% at 1074.22.   

Bonds Claw Back Losses
   

Asian local currency bonds fell early Friday in a knee-jerk response to the yuan revaluation, but recovered quickly in anticipation that currency appreciation in the region staves off rate hikes.   

Stronger Asian currencies are also ultimately likely to ease the debt burden for those countries and companies - like the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand and China - that have local currency revenues and large U.S. dollar-denominated liabilities.   

The oil futures market reacted largely coolly to China's move.   

Toward the end of the Asian trading day, with European markets opening for business, Nymex benchmark light sweet crude for September delivery was trading at $57.40 a barrel, up 27 cents from the New York floor trade close.   

The yuan revaluation had triggered a brief oil price rally as a stronger currency makes imports of dollar-priced oil cheaper for China.   

Reaction in commodities markets was muted, apart from trading in palm oil, as the size of the yuan revaluation was smaller than expected. Palm oil prices fell on fears that a de-pegged Malaysian ringgit will make it less competitive in the international market.   

In the long term, prices of rubber, iron ore, grains, copper and gold could rise as the yuan's revaluation has made it cheaper for China to import such commodities, analysts said.   

China is the world's largest buyer of soybeans as also natural rubber, iron ore and several other commodities. It also buys several other commodities such as gold in large quantities.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Jump on yuan, central banks restrict gains
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies jumped on Friday after China, bowing to years of international pressure, let its currency appreciate, but dollar purchases by central banks and lack of a further rise in the yuan pared gains.  

On Thursday China let the yuan <CNY=CFXS> appreciate by 2.1 percent to 8.11 per dollar, dropping the peg of 8.28 per dollar to adopt a system of valuing the currency against a basket made up of the currencies of major trading partners.  

"We think the biggest gainers will be the Japanese yen and Taiwan dollar, second will be Korean won, Singapore dollar and Indian rupee," DBS Bank economists Chua Hak Bin and Chris Leung, said in a report.  

The South Korean won <KRW=KFTC> gained as much as 1.5 percent to a three-week high of 1,020.0 per dollar before closing local trading at 1,021.3.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as much as 1.7 percent from late Asian trading on Thursday to 1.6516 per dollar before losing some ground to 1.6635 on suspected central bank dollar buying. It hit a two-month high of 1.6490 in overnight trading.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose to a three-week high of 31.55 per dollar but central bank dollar buying helped cut gains. The Indian rupee <INR=IN> was the only Asian currency that weakened on Friday. It lost more than half a percent from the previous day after suspected central bank dollar buying pushed it from a six-year high of 43.115 per dollar.  

YUAN OUTLOOK  

Traders said Asian authorities were likely to check gains in their currencies until China lets the yuan appreciate further.  

"The (Korean) government has clearly said they're going to intervene any time if there is a rapid change and if they find out the action is driven by speculators," said Lee Yoon Ho, a currency options trading manager at Shinhan Bank in Seoul.  

"The market participants see the yuan strengthening further because a 2 percent rise is not enough. But the problem is that the China government is not satisfied with that kind of expectation. We'll have to wait and watch the yuan rate in the next couple of days."  

Although the yuan will be allowed to rise or fall by 0.3 percent per day, the currency barely moved on Friday. The yuan opened local trading on Friday at 8.11 per dollar and weakened by 0.01 percent to close local trading at 8.1111.  

"Expectation for a bigger appreciation of the yuan's value was, and will be, unrealistic," the state-run China Daily said in an editorial.  

But investors betting on the yuan's future value using non-deliverable forward contracts <CNYNDF=> priced in as much as a 6.3 percent rise in the Chinese currency in the next 12 months.  

"My intuition is that the market is in for a fight if they expect today's one-year forward contracts to mature in the money," Huw McKay, senior economist at Westpac Bank in Sydney said in a report.  

SINGAPORE DOLLAR BOOST  

Claudio Piron, currency strategist at JPMorgan Chase Bank, expects the Chinese currency to rise by another 5 percent against the dollar by the end of 2005 and lift other regional units. Citigroup said it expected a further 3 percent gain by year-end.  

The Singapore dollar stood to gain the most initially "as it benefits from the potential double revaluation of the yuan and the ringgit", Piron said in a note.  

Malaysia dropped the ringgit's peg against the dollar on Thursday and moved to a system of managing the currency against a basket of currencies.  

The ringgit <MYR=> appreciated as much as 0.7 percent from its earlier peg of 3.8 per dollar to 3.7750 per dollar but dealers said dollar buying by the Malaysian central bank pushed it lower to 3.7790 in late Asian trading.  

JPMorgan said the ringgit was still undervalued by about 7 percent.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Friday it would intervene in the currency markets when the currency nears the top end of its undisclosed policy band but reiterated its aim for a gradual and modest appreciation in the currency. Despite MAS intervention, Piron expects the Singapore currency to advance further, along with the South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar.  

"Appreciation pressure on the Singapore dollar could also be exacerbated for lack of other alternatives in Southeast Asia as the Philippine peso, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah are beset with either political woes, trade deficits or dollar-oil demand," Piron said. title: UPDATE 1-MAS will  intervene  if Sing dollar nears policy band
text:
(Adds details, background)  

SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank said on Friday it would intervene when the Singapore dollar nears its policy band and reiterated its commitment to a policy of gradual and modest appreciation of its currency.  

Ong Chong Tee, deputy managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Singapore dollar <SGD=> was currently trading at the top half of its band.  

"We will come into the market when the Singapore dollar looks to reach the policy band," Ong told a news conference where the bank presented its 2004/05 annual report.  

The central bank also said China's revaluation of its yuan on Thursday would not have a major impact on the Singapore dollar.  

"Our policy has allowed us to accommodate the changes that have taken place. We see no need to change the regime," said Heng Swee Keat, MAS managing director.  

The MAS conducts monetary policy by steering the Singapore dollar in a band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, rather than setting an interest rate as many central banks do.  

The band and the basket of currencies are kept secret.  

The city-state's central bank added that persistently high oil prices were posing an upside risk to external inflation.  

GROWTH TO SLOW  

On the economic front, the bank said in its annual report that Singapore's growth will ease in 2005, as a slowdown in the electronics sector weighs on the global economy.  

"The Singapore economy is poised to descend from its cyclical high in 2004, and is expected to grow between 2.5 percent and 4.5 percent in 2005," the MAS said, reaffirming the government's forecast in May.  

The MAS said it expected inflation in 2006 to rise to 1 to 2 percent from zero to 1.0 percent in 2005.  

On Thursday, the Singapore dollar strengthened by about two percent to 1.6498 against the U.S. dollar compared to Wednesday's close after China and Malaysia revalued their currencies.  

But after rallying to a near two-month high, the Singapore dollar eased back to 1.6574 within half an hour, which traders said was due to central bank intervention.  

The bank said on Friday that Thursday's two percent move in the Singapore dollar was "not considered too volatile".  

The monetary policy will be reviewed again in October, the bank said. ($1=1.686 Singapore Dollar)

title: Asian  Currencies  Pare Gains, Stks Mixed After Yuan Shift
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies gave back some of their sharp gains Friday after China revalued the yuan against the U.S. dollar late Thursday, while regional stock markets were mixed and local currency bonds recovered from an initial slump.  

Reaction in oil and commodities markets was muted.  

Local currencies responded quickly to China's decision to scrap the yuan's decade-old peg to the dollar and shift to an undisclosed basket of currencies to manage the currency's exchange rate.  

The yen surged against the dollar, with the U.S. unit tumbling more than two yen to a low of Y109.87 after the announcement. But the dollar bounced back Friday in Tokyo as traders decided to wait and see how China would actually control the yuan under the new system before pushing up the yen further.  

At 0532 GMT, the dollar was at Y111.05, almost a full yen back up from Y110.28 late Thursday in New York.  

The Australian dollar shot up above US$0.7650 from US$0.7600 before China's move on perceptions that Australia's commodity-heavy economy will benefit from the yuan move. It was last at US$0.7647.  

In the Singapore market, the U.S. dollar fell to S$1.6511 from S$1.6804 in late Asian trading Thursday, but has since partly recovered on suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The intervention encouraged companies to step up U.S. dollar buying, traders said.  

Speculative buying of the Singapore dollar was also helped by Malaysia's decision to abandon its peg to the dollar and move to a currency basket regime.  

Despite Malaysia's policy change, the U.S. dollar didn't weaken much against the ringgit and was last quoted at MYR3.7825.  

Chua Hak Bin, an economist at Singapore's DBS Bank, said Asian currencies may rally more, led by the Japanese yen and the Taiwan dollar, because of their huge trade with China.  

But he said the Chinese appreciation is smaller than expected, which will prompt market players to speculate on more currency revaluation in the months ahead.  


 
   Nikkei Slumps On Fears For Exporters 
   

Asia-Pacific stock markets are mixed.  

The Nikkei 225 Stock Average is down around 0.8% at 11689.91. Analysts believe the yuan revaluation is generally positive for Japanese shares because it reduces trade tensions between Tokyo and Beijing. But some said a stronger yen may squeeze some Japanese exporters. Nikkei's weakness so far Friday is likely due to "sell-on-news" mentality, as the yuan revaluation had long been anticipated, analysts said.  

China's stock markets are rising, with airline stocks surging as they are expected to benefit from a strong yuan regime because many of those companies have outstanding U.S. dollar debt, which will be easier to service.  

The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, rose 0.6% by mid-morning.  

The Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, is down 0.1%, Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 is up 0.3%, and Singapore's Straits Times Index is up around 0.3%. Taiwan's Weighted Price Index is down around 0.3%.  


 
   Bonds Claw Back Losses 
   

Asian local currency bonds fell early Friday in a kneejerk response to the yuan revaluation, but recovered quickly in anticipation that currency appreciation in the region staves off rate hikes.  

Stronger Asian currencies are also ultimately likely to help those countries and companies - like the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand and China - which have local currency revenues and large U.S. dollar-denominated liabilities.  

The oil futures market reacted largely coolly to China's move.  

By the middle of the Asia trading day, and shortly before European markets got going, Nymex benchmark light sweet crude for September delivery was trading at $57.42 a barrel, up 29 cents from the New York floor trade close.  

The yuan revaluation had triggered a brief oil price rally as a stronger currency makes imports of dollar-priced oil cheaper for China.  

Reaction in commodities markets was muted as China's decision to revalue its currency by 2% to CNY8.11 to the U.S. dollar was a smaller shift than expected. However, prices of commodities could rise in the long run as the revaluation has made it cheaper for China to import the goods.  

China is the world's largest buyer of soybeans as also natural rubber, iron ore and several other commodities. It also buys several other commodities such as gold in large quantities.

title: USD/SGD At 1.6578 Vs 1.6565 As MAS  Intervenes -Dealers
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar came back from early Friday morning highs after suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6578 after the suspected intervention, recovering from its early lows around S$1.6565.  

"They seem to have come in," said a trader at a local bank.  

The suspected intervention came after the MAS said late Thursday the move by China to revalue its currency won't have a major impact on the Singapore dollar or the MAS exchange rate system.  

"Our current exchange rate policy stance remains appropriate. The fundamentals of the economy have not changed, nor have the factors influencing the growth prospects for the Singapore economy," MAS said in a statement.  

MAS will continue to maintain the current policy of a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar against a trade weighted basket of currencies, the central bank said.  

-By Saeed Azhar, Dow Jones Newswires;  

65-6415-4157; saeed.azhar@dowjones.com [ 22-07-05 0024GMT ]  

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--In the wake of China's revaluation of the yuan, the Monetary Authority of Singapore reiterated Friday that its Singapore dollar policy stance of modest and gradual appreciation remains appropriate.  

Speaking at the central bank's annual review, Deputy Managing Director Ong Chong Tee said the central bank will only intervene if the Singapore dollar breaches its trade weighted exchange rate band.  

"We will only come in when the trade weighted index has breached its policy band and if market conditions are volatile," he said. [ 22-07-05 0406GMT ]  


   Ong said the local dollar is currently in the "upper half of the band."   

He wouldn't confirm if MAS had intervened in the foreign exchange market since last night to tackle excessive gains in the Singapore dollar.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6630 at 0445 GMT, recovering from an early low of S$1.6511 on suspected MAS intervention, traders said.  

The Singapore dollar had rallied by more than 1.7% before shedding some of its gains against the U.S. dollar.  

MAS doesn't disclose its policy band, but United Overseas Bank in a research report Friday said assuming 2% on each side of the midpoint, the band is currently S$1.6878 to S$1.6548 with the midpoint at S$1.6217.  

Ong said the MAS is comfortable with its current policy band.  

Heng Kwee Keat, managing director of MAS, said moves by China and Malaysia to reform their exchange rate system are a positive development for Asia.  

"It just gives us (Asia) better buffer to absorb shocks in the future," he said.  

When asked if the monetary authorities were looking at movements in the Malaysian currency after the change in its regime, he said the MAS is monitoring the situation.  

But he noted the statement by Malaysian officials that the ringgit won't deviate too much from the value it had when it was pegged to the U.S. dollar.  

The Malaysian ringgit gained only 0.4% by midday.  

On the economy, Heng said the outlook for Singapore remains positive because electronics sector demand will improve in the second half of the year.  

"Our assessment is that we will see a pickup in IT in the second half which will help the Singapore economy," he said.  

The latest data from the U.S. and the Chinese economy have also reinforced the central bank's view that the second half will be better for the local economy, he said.  

Heng said MAS expects Singapore's economy will grow between 2.5% to 4.5% in 2005, reiterating a government forecast for economic growth.  

He said the current monetary policy stance remains appropriate and the next policy statement will be released in October.  

Heng said MAS remains vigilant against inflation despite headline inflation being low in the first half.  

"The economy is close to its potential output level and there are upside risks to the external inflation environment including, from the persistently high oil prices," he said.  

-By Saeed Azhar and Kevin Lim, Dow Jones Newswires;

title: ANALYSIS-End to dollar peg in Asia to fuel  FX  reserve shift
text:
LONDON, July 21 (Reuters) - Increasingly flexible Asian currencies following China and Malaysia's moves to abandon dollar pegs on Thursday could prompt the region's central banks to diversify further away from the dollar, analysts say.  

China revalued the yuan by 2.1 percent and adopted a basket of currencies to manage the currency, allowing it to appreciate to 8.11 per dollar from the previous 8.28. Malaysia also dropped its 7-year-old dollar peg in favour of a managed float.  

There were no details on the new basket of currencies the yuan is pegged against, but analysts say China could buy fewer dollars and re-adjust its foreign exchange reserves -- the world's largest after Japan at above $700 billion.  

"This China move, especially given the anticipation that this might be replicated in other countries in the region, I imagine that investors will now assume the stock of dollar reserves Asian central banks hold will be reduced," said Michael Metcalfe, senior strategist at State Street.  

Diversification by central banks worldwide, who have nearly $4 trillion of reserves, is a sensitive topic for the foreign exchange market.  

In the three years to 2004, the dollar lost 30 percent against the euro, due partly to expectations central banks in emerging countries are shifting away from the dollar.  

On Thursday, the dollar lost more than two yen to a three-week low of 110.16 yen <JPY=> after China's move. Against the euro however, the fall was limited and it traded near $1.2130 <EUR=>.  

The Bank of New York said the dollar and yen might have equal effective weightings in the basket of around 40 percent each with the euro at 20 percent.  

Citigroup said in a note to clients: "Today's move is a conclusive signal that the yuan likely will become progressively less linked to the dollar over time."  

"Given our expectations for China to lead a broader move by Asia economies away from their dollar-linked currencies, this implies that foreign official purchases of U.S. assets eventually will decline."  

DIVERSIFICATION EVIDENCE  

There has already been some evidence that foreign central banks are buying less U.S. Treasuries this year.  

HBOS Treasury Services estimates in the first 5 months of this year, U.S. Treasury asset holdings by the 25 largest emerging countries including China rose by $79 billion, compared with a gain of $113 billion in the same period last year.  

At the same time, these countries' combined FX reserves rose by $175 billion in 2005, compared with the increase of $145 billion last year.  

HBOS estimates these central banks sold more than $1 billion a day against other developed market currencies in the fourth quarter of last year. It also said China already has 40 percent of reserves in non-dollar currencies after a recent shift.  

"In the first 4 months of this year reserve diversification is ongoing. As the exchange rate becomes more flexible, China will start managing euro/yuan or yen/yuan more actively as part of the basket and accumulate these currencies in the course of its FX intervention other than the dollar," Pearson said.  

HBOS estimates the euro's share in the FX reserves of the 25 emerging countries has risen to 30 percent from 25 percent in the past two years.  

The Bank for International Settlements gives the dollar's share in global reserves at 69 percent in 2004 while the euro's share was 21 percent.  

Pearson said the net effect from Asia's FX flexibility can actually be dollar positive as Asian central banks accumulate less reserves.  

"Reserve accumulation in Asia is bad for the dollar against G10 currencies and good for the dollar against developing countries. This is totally the opposite of what is required to rebalance the global trade," he said.  

"But the move to greater flexibility in China is going to start to correct that imbalance. Eventually it means regional central banks accumulate less reserves in dollars and they will have less dollars for sell for other currencies."  

Even with the evidence of diversification, the dollar gained around 10 percent against the euro since January.  

INTERVENTION THREATS  

During the dollar's three-year fall, Asian central banks have intervened heavily in the FX market to prevent export-damaging strength in their local currencies.  

Japan, which spent more than $300 billion in yen-selling intervention in the five quarters through the end of March 2004, has already fired a warning shot after China's move, saying it would take action if needed.  

Dealers reported Singapore's central bank was seen intervening in the market on Thursday to smooth the appreciation of the local currency, after it surged 2 percent against the U.S. dollar.  

"Short-term, if there is the evidence of disorderly moves, central banks would like to come in and smooth the move," Metcalfe said.  

"Looking further ahead, China has revalued now, in theory it should increase all the Asian authorities' tolerance for domestic currency strength against the U.S. dollar."

title: UPDATE 3-Yen surges after China abandons dollar  FX  peg
text:
(Updates price moves, adds official reaction)  

LONDON, July 21 (Reuters) - The yen rose 2 percent versus the dollar and rallied against the euro on Thursday after China abandoned its dollar peg in favour of a basket of currencies to manage the yuan, allowing it to appreciate to 8.11 per dollar.  

The yen's gains, which also came after Malaysia changed the ringgit currency peg to a managed float, triggered a chain reaction in other Asian currencies.  

The Singapore dollar surged 2 percent before dealers reported the country's central bank was seen intervening in the currency to smooth its appreciation.  

China's long-awaited revaluation from the previous 8.28 per dollar was smaller than many economists had expected. But it nevertheless sent a shockwave through the currency market as investors were losing patience with their unprofitable bets on the yen -- used as a proxy for yuan revaluation speculation.  

"It was going to happen at some point. They have introduced a very modest appreciation to kick the whole thing off," said Ian Gunner, head of foreign exchange research at Mellon Financial Corporation.  

"The market is now going to be interested in how much further there is to go. There could be another adjustment in a few months but I do not think they will want to get into a timetable here."  

The Japanese currency has risen to a three-week high of 110.18 per dollar, a whole 2 yen gain from pre-announcement levels around 112.40.  

The Japanese currency was on track for its biggest daily gains since March 2002 on percentage terms. However, by 1445 GMT it had trimmed gains to 110.78.  

The yen also rose to 134.26 per euro from around 136.60 before the announcement, around 1 percent higher from late New York levels. Within 30 minutes of the yuan news the yen rose 1.2 percent.  

The dollar's reaction was muted against the euro. It fell initially to the day's low of $1.2255 per euro from around $1.2140 but reversed losses to stand at $1.2115, up a quarter percent on the day.  

State-run Xinhua news agency said China would continue to manage the yuan in a range of plus/minus 0.3 percent against the dollar and would aim to keep the yuan basically stable at a balanced and rational level.  

MORE TO COME?  

The Singapore dollar, widely used with the yen to bet on a yuan move, shot higher to a two-month high of 1.6503 per U.S. dollar, up 2 percent on the day compared with 1.6843 on Wednesday, before dealers reported the intervention.  

Singapore said it will maintain its policy of gradual and modest strengthening of the Singapre dollar and said fundamentals of the city-state's economy had not changed.  

Hong Kong said it would not consider changing its currency peg to the dollar even if the yuan keep appreciating and said the Hong Kong dollar will remain very stable.  

The Indian rupee rose to a six-year peak against the dollar around 43.20, up more than half a percent.  

"The move is clearly positive for Asian currencies first, and to some extent the euro. It is pretty clear that the basket will involve a reasonable chunk of Asian currencies," said Emanuele Ravano, European strategist at PIMCO in London.  

The Korean won's non-deliverable forward prices, used by offshore investors to trade the won, showed investors are factoring in a 2.2 percent rise in the won/dollar rate in one-month's time.  

The won closed at 1,035.5 per dollar in the local market.  

"It's still difficult to interpret. We don't know vital elements like the weights of the different currencies in the basket -- indeed if we ever get to know that," said Adam Cole, senior currency strategist at Royal Bank of Canada.  

Politicians worldwide welcomed China's move although the 2.1 percent revaluation to 8.11 per dollar stopped short of what many of China's trading partners had hoped for.  

U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow welcomed China's move to let its currency trade more freely and noted that the United States expects more currency moves from Beijing.  

Following the yen's rise of more than two percent, Japan's top financial diplomat Hiroshi Watanabe said he is watching the market carefully and would take action if needed.  

Japan has been urging China to reform the rigid FX regime but it had repeatedly said the yuan revaluation doesn't mean a higher yen and it has hinted it would intervene if necessary.

title: Asian  currencies  to rise on China move, for a while
text:
SINGAPORE, July 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose sharply on Thursday after China and Malaysia announced they were abandoning currency pegs with the dollar and analysts said they would rise further, at least, in the next few weeks.  

But speculative money that had flowed into Asia betting on a yuan and ringgit revaluation could start to leave Asia, undermining Asian currencies against the dollar in the longer term, they said.  

"People are going to get out of this trade at this point," said Tim Condon, head of Asian research at ING. "The incentive to hang around for another big move is diminished considerably."  

Asia's traditionally interventionist central banks were quick to warn markets against pushing regional currencies up too sharply.  

Japan and South Korea issued such warnings, while authorities in Singapore were suspected of intervening to curb strength in the Singapore dollar.  

China said it was scrapping the yuan's dollar peg, revaluing its currency by 2.1 percent to 8.11 per dollar, and tying it to a basket of currencies of China's major trading partners.  

Shortly after that, Malaysia's central bank said it was dropping its ringgit-dollar peg and adopting a managed float.  

The announcements came after Asian markets had closed trading for the day.  

Still, traders in Singapore and London pushed the Singapore dollar <SGD=> up 2.2 percent from the day's low to a two-month high of 1.6498 per U.S. dollar. The Thai baht <THB=> moved to a 3-week high after China's move.  

"It will have a significant impact. We expect dollar/won to hit our forecast of 990 by the end of September, and expect dollar/Taiwan to hit 29," said Claudio Piron, a currency strategist with JPMorgan in Singapore.  

"Hong Kong will fly as well but because it has a peg it will be reflected in the property and stock markets," he said.  

The Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> was traded around 1,025 per dollar in thin offshore dealings late on Thursday, up 1.5 percent from the day's low, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> was quoted around 31.65, up a percent from the day's trough.  

China's yuan was also quoted in offshore non-deliverable forwards <CNY=CFXS> <CNYNDF=> at 7.9 per dollar at the end of one year, reflecting the market view that the managed float will result in a steady appreciation of the currency.  

Piron said JPMorgan expected a 7 percent appreciation in the yuan by the end of the year, and that would keep other Asian currencies under pressure to rise, even if speculative money flowed out of the region.  

HOT MONEY  

Investors had poured billions of dollars into Asia in the past three years betting that China would revalue the yuan, taking the competitive heat off its neighbours in export markets.  

Analysts said the Singapore dollar, won and Taiwan dollar, the most popular proxies used until now to bet on a yuan revaluation will be the fastest to rise over the next few days.  

While most Asian currencies compete with China in global export markets, China is also a big buyer of Asian exports. Hong Kong and Taiwan sell about 40 percent of their exports to China.  

"Once the dust settles from this knee-jerk move, the dollar will resume its strengthening trend and these gains in Asian currencies will prove short-lived, I suspect," Condon said.  

According to Morgan Stanley's economist Andy Xie, about $700 billion in speculative money is parked in Asia -- three times the amount that left the region in the Asian financial crisis and far higher than Asia's $200 billion annual trade surplus.  

Xie estimates half that money is invested in China, with another 25 percent in Japan and the rest in other Asian currencies.  

In a report issued earlier this month, Xie said China should not revalue the yuan and should tighten policy to prevent a flight of capital.  

Simon Flint, head of Asian currency strategy at Merrill Lynch, said there was no such danger.  

China's central bank might limit the yuan's moves initially, but the country's mounting trade surplus and foreign fund inflows will force the yuan higher, he said.

title: UPDATE 2-Singapore sticks to  currency  policy after yuan move
text:
(Adds details, background)  

SINGAPORE, July 21 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the city-state's central bank, said on Thursday it will maintain its policy of a gradual and modest strengthening of the Singapore dollar following the revaluation of the Chinese yuan.  

"Our current exchange rate policy stance remains appropriate. The fundamentals of the economy have not changed, nor have the factors influencing the growth prospects for the Singapore economy," the MAS said in a statement.  

The MAS said it will continue to maintain its policy of a "modest and gradual appreciation" of the Singapore dollar policy band as announced in April.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> strengthened by about two percent to 1.6498 per U.S. dollar, a two-month high. That compared with 1.6804 in late trade on Thursday, before news of the revaluation, and a close on Wednesday of 1.6908.  

After hitting the intraday high, the currency pulled back to 1.6574 within half an hour after the Singapore central bank was seen intervening in the currency market, dealers said.  

After the MAS statement, the Singapore dollar eased further to 1.6580.  

The MAS conducts monetary policy by steering the Singapore dollar in a band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, rather than setting an interest rate as many central banks do.  

The band and the basket of currencies are kept secret.  

EYES ON RINGGIT  

"We're hearing that the MAS wants to cool the market a bit... maybe they are not happy with the pace of the move and may want to cool the market down," said a currency dealer who declined to be identified.  

A dealer with a Singapore bank said the Singapore dollar's direction in the coming days would depend to a large extent on the movement of the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=>.  

Soon after China said it had let its yuan <CNY=CFXS> appreciate, Malaysia announced it had also dropped a policy of fixing its currency to the U.S. dollar in favour of a managed float of the ringgit.  

The ringgit had been pegged at 3.8 to the dollar since September 1998 when it was imposed to help Malaysia cope with the Asian financial crisis.  

"At this point we are at the stronger side of the band, but where it heads to after this depends on the dollar-ringgit level," said a dealer with a Singapore bank.  

Malaysia is Singapore's top trading partner, followed by the European Union, the United States and China.  

The last time the MAS intervened was in the fourth quarter of 2004 and in early 2005, when speculation of China and Malaysia changing their currency regime drove the Singapore dollar higher.  

The MAS is due to present its annual report on Friday morning. (Additional reporting by Fayen Wong, Mia Shanley and Vidya Ranganathan) (Writing by Geert De Clercq; mia.shanley@reuters.com; Reuters Messaging: mia.shanley.reuters.com@reuters.net; +65-6870-3305))

title: Singapore Dollar Down Late; Near 9-Month Low On Yen Fall
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell to nearly a nine-month low against the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade Friday, dragged down by a surge of the U.S. unit against the Japanese yen following a rate hike by the Federal Reserve.  

Singapore government bond prices rose slightly after overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys.  

The U.S. unit traded between S$1.6823 and S$1.6908, its highest level since S$1.6906 on Oct. 8. At 0722 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6894, up from S$1.6820 late Thursday.  

"Although there's a long weekend in the U.S., the market went a bit wild after the Japanese yen fell," said a dealer at a local bank.  

Dealers said they were expecting some consolidation Friday ahead of the weekend and the July 4 holiday in the U.S. However, selling in Asian currencies accelerated after the U.S. dollar rose to a near-nine-month high of Y111.13.  

Most Asian currencies are at multi-month lows against the U.S. dollar due to high oil prices, weakening speculation of a yuan revaluation, and rising U.S. interest rates. The Federal Reserve, as expected, on Thursday raised its key target rate to 3.25% from 3%.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research report the U.S. dollar should face resistance above S$1.6900 because market players will be cautious of any intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's central bank. The Singapore dollar has support because the MAS doesn't appear to be in the mood of abandoning its policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the local dollar against a basket of currencies in the next few months, UOB said.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late On Yen Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against the U.S. dollar late Thursday, gaining back some of the ground it lost Wednesday as it tracked the recovering Japanese yen.  

Singapore government bond prices fell across the curve, but a bigger upward move at the short-end yield on firmer overnight rates, slightly flattened the yield curve.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6820, up from S$1.6847 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6819 and S$1.6870.  

The U.S. dollar failed to stay above the S$1.6850 resistance level, which prompted banks to cut positions, said a trader.  

There was also talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene above S$1.6850, making players cautious, he said.  

Despite Thursday's recovery most technical analysts are still suggesting a bearish trend for the Singapore dollar. The local unit suffered a blow recently after weaker-than-expected manufacturing and export data for May.  

The U.S. dollar's outlook has turned bullish in the medium-term after its global rally in past few days, said the United Overseas Bank in a report Thursday. It recommends buying the U.S. unit at S$1.6820, with the next target at S$1.6980. It recommends selling the U.S. dollar if it weakens below S$1.6720.  

BNP Paribas said a move above S$1.6800 opens further upside potential for the U.S. currency, allowing it to test S$1.700.  

"A break of a major downtrend line at S$1.6825 hints of a new trend in motion which is a bullish U.S. dollar," it said in a report.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steadier after falling on euro
text:
SINGAPORE, June 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies steadied on Wednesday after falling for two days, in line with the euro's moves, but markets braced for further weakness on account of reduced expectations for a Chinese yuan revaluation.   

The euro <EUR=> steadied briefly in Asian trade but soon extended a slide that began on Monday to hit a 7-1/2-month low below $1.2294 in European trading.   

The steep euro drop was triggered by political and economic concerns after France's rejection in a referendum of a proposed European Union constitution, and the euro was seen staying weak on Wednesday as the Dutch began voting in a similar referendum.   

In Asia, the Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> and the Thai baht <THB=> were the biggest losers.   

The won came within striking distance of a 100-day moving average around 1,013 a dollar, taking its decline this week to 1.2 percent, before paring losses.   

The Thai baht breached key support at 40.70 per dollar. The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.6710, its lowest level against the dollar since October.   

Currency analysts said the dollar's euro-driven rally and the paring of bets on a change in policy for China's virtually pegged yuan had undermined regionals. Banks had to hurriedly cover their bullish Asian positions, they said.   

China decided on Monday to scrap export tariffs on 81 textile products in a tit-for-tat move after the United States and Europe curbed Chinese textile exports.   

"One theme that continued to permeate through Asia was shorts in dollar-Asia," Westpac Bank said in a note.   

"The very aggressive push back from China on trade sanctions suggests that they have little interest in responding to foreign pressure," Westpac said   

The market still has a lot of positions betting on a yuan revaluation, so there was potential for Asian currencies to be sold further, it said.   

Traders suspected several regional central banks had intervened.   

"It seems the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) has been trying to contain the Sing dollar's fall but the BOK (Bank of Korea) is leaning into the move today," a trader said, referring to talk that the South Korean authorities had bought dollars to weaken their currency.   

BUCKING THE BEARS   

The Philippine peso <PHP=> and the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> stood firm, the latter still underpinned by strong equity flows as players adjust positions after Taiwan's reweighting in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index on Tuesday.   

"Of the top 3 performing currencies of the year -- peso, won and Taiwan dollar -- the weakest link of them all is won," said said Claudio Piron, currency strategist with JP Morgan in Singapore.   

"And the most robust one is Taiwan because you still have some combination of domestic and external performance complementing one another."   

Morgan Stanley Capital International Inc., a global stock index compiler, said last year it would raise the weighting of Taiwan stocks in its emerging markets index.   

Taiwan weightings in the index were raised in 2 stages. The second phase took effect on Tuesday.   

Foreign funds have been pumping money into Taiwan in anticipation of the reweighting, although they turned net sellers on Wednesday.   

Data from Nomura International shows overseas investors bought a net $13.9 billion of Taiwan equities in the 250 days to May 29.   

The Taiwan dollar was quoted around 31.38/39 per dollar on Wednesday and has shed about a quarter of a percent this week.   

"Due to the Taiwan MSCI reweighting, we actually saw only 2 days of net foreign equity selling last month," Piron said.   

"One should think that most of the participants have moved now but there should still be some support coming from there." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0825 GMT

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late, Rebounds From Key Support
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose modestly against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Friday, rebounding from a key support level while tracking range-bound trade in other Asian currencies.   

Government bonds were flat at the short end, but the 10-year yield rose fractionally in lackluster trading, snapping alonger-end rally in the past two weeks, dealers said.   

At 0605 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6587, down from S$1.6617 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6574 and S$1.6608 intraday.   

A trader said the U.S. dollar met resistance around S$1.6000 amid fears since Thursday that Singapore's central bank may intervene to stem a bigger weakness in the local currency.   

The U.S. dollar, meanwhile, rallied against the euro in anticipation of a likely rejection of a referendum vote on the European Union in France over the weekend.   

"Most Asian currencies were generally range-bound, which also kept the Singapore dollar in a tight range," the trader said. Trading volume was also thin ahead of a three-day weekend in the U.S. and the U.K.   

Technical analysis suggests U.S.-dollar bullishness in the medium term. The tone will be neutralized only if the U.S. unit weakens below S$1.6510, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.
