title: Singapore  Dlr Steady Late On Threat Of  FX Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was relatively steady against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Wednesday, as the threat of possible central bank intervention kept a lid on the local currency's upside.  

Prices on government bonds edged up, tracking slightly higher U.S. Treasurys prices late Tuesday.  

At 0650 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6547, nearly unchanged from S$1.6550 late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6527 and S$1.6564 intraday.  

Early in the session, speculators used a media report that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had reaffirmed its current stance of gradual and modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar as an excuse to push the U.S. dollar down as low as S$1.6527, dealers said.  

The central bank's reported remarks came on the heels of the International Monetary Fund's economic survey released Monday, in which the IMF recommended that Singapore may need to change its current tight monetary policy to a supportive one if its economic slowdown worsens. Since April 2004, the MAS has maintained a tight policy that allows a "modest and gradual appreciation" of the Singapore dollar to counter inflationary pressures.  

The U.S. currency soon rebounded to the mid-S$1.6500s on speculation that the MAS had checked the prevailing U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar exchange rates with Singapore-based banks, a move that was widely interpreted as a prelude to potential currency intervention, dealers said.  

The U.S. unit then consolidated in the mid-S$1.6500s for the rest of the session, ahead of the 1230 GMT release of the U.S. durable goods orders data for April. The median estimate of 21 economists surveyed Monday by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for a 1.5% increase in new orders for durable goods.  

In the short term, the U.S. currency is likely to dip, then rise again to test immediate resistance at S$1.6610, based on technical analysis, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"As long as the critical support at S$1.6510 is not taken out, the probability of a resumption of the recent (U.S. dollar) up-move is still good," UOB said.  

As a short-term trading strategy, UOB recommended buying the U.S. unit at S$1.6540 and placing stop-loss sales orders below S$1.6510 in anticipation of a potential rise to S$1.6620.

title: UPDATE:HK, Asia Markets Stay Strong After HKD Peg Change
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Currencies and stock prices across East Asia stayed strong Thursday despite Hong Kong's move to deter the inflows of speculative "hot money" which have been buoying markets across the region.  

Hong Kong traders said that after an initial outflow of funds from the territory on Wednesday night, there was no sign of major outflows on Thursday, and there were even some fresh inflows of foreign money into the stock market. The Hang Seng index ended 0.5% higher at 13698.93 points, confounding fears that it would slide.  

"We saw some of these speculators closing positions yesterday and going away, and now they are back again," said Francis Lun at Fulbright Securities.  

Elsewhere in Asia, Hong Kong's action only served to increase speculation that China would soon change its currency peg, allowing the yuan to appreciate against the U.S. dollar. Taiwan was one market buoyed by such hopes; its benchmark stock index closed up 1.4% at 5970.71, also helped by Wall Street's strong performance Wednesday, while the Taiwan dollar firmed to 31.300 against the U.S. dollar from its previous close of 31.383.  

On Wednesday evening, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said it was introducing a ceiling for the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar to discourage its use as a trading proxy for speculation about a revaluation of the Chinese yuan.  

The surprise announcement raised the possibility that other economies experiencing big inflows of funds speculating on the yuan - China itself, as well as Malaysia and to a lesser extent Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea - could take similar action. Any reversal of the flood of hot money into Asia could deal a major short-term blow to the region's markets.  

But on Thursday morning, most investors were clearly betting that because China has sovereignty over Hong Kong, the HKMA may have been informed of an imminent yuan revaluation and was making preparations to keep the Hong Kong dollar stable at that time.  

RBC Capital Markets said the HKMA's move was part of a series of events that "will eventually lead to a yuan revalue in the coming weeks". It predicts China will move from a de facto yuan peg against the U.S. dollar to a trade-weighted basket of currencies, producing a rise of the yuan against the dollar of between 3% and 5%.  

Many analysts, however, think that theory is wrong, noting that Chinese leaders have in recent days strongly indicated they won't be bullied by foreign pressure into rushing a yuan revaluation.  

Bank of America's Robert Sinche said he didn't believe  


Hong Kong's move was linked to knowledge of any imminent yuan policy change. Instead, he argued, it "merely reflects the HKMA's interest in maintaining stable conditions in local markets. With large on-again, off-again speculative capital inflows since 2003... the HKMA began to consider the need for a two-sided commitment."   

Merrill Lynch, while noting that a yuan revaluation was only a matter of time, said it doubted the HKMA would have had advance knowledge of a yuan revaluation. title: Singapore Dollar Surges To 5-Week High Vs US Dollar Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar surged to a five-week high against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Friday, boosted by increased speculation that the Chinese authorities might revalue the yuan during week-long holidays in China next week.  

Prices on Singapore government bonds edged up in the wake of higher U.S. Treasury prices late on Thursday, dealers said.  

At 0715 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6423, down from S$1.6467 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6326 and S$1.6477 intraday.  

After consolidating around the S$1.6470 level in the morning, the U.S. dollar soon plunged to as low as S$1.6326, its lowest since March 22, on rising expectations that China could move to a more flexible currency regime.  

Fueling these expectations was a surprisingly sharp fall in the U.S. dollar to as low as CNY8.2700 from Thursday's close of CNY8.2765, dealers said.  

Although the spot dollar-yuan stayed within the official daily trading band of 0.3% on either side of CNY8.277, analysts said the unexpected plunge in the dollar spooked market participants into selling the U.S. currency against the Singapore dollar and other regional currencies and heightened speculation that China may be preparing to adopt a freer exchange rate sooner rather than later.  

This speculation arose despite China's central bank spokesman saying Friday that there is no plan to adjust yuan policy during the Labor Day holiday.  

"As far as we know, there's no adjustment expected in the yuan exchange rate," Bai Li, spokesman for the People's Bank of China, told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Bai made the comment in response to a question on whether the central bank would revalue the yuan during the week-long holiday starting May 1.  

Given the U.S. currency's tumble against the Singapore dollar, the Monetary Authority of Singapore apparently intervened around the intraday low of S$1.6326, lifting the U.S. unit back up to near the mid-S$1.6400s, dealers said.  

Yet the foreign exchange market remained jittery, with some players saying the U.S. dollar could retest S$1.6326 if U.S. economic data to be released later in the global session surprise on the downside.  

The U.S. first-quarter employment cost index, March personal income and March personal spending data will be released at 1230 GMT. These data will be followed by the final University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index for April at 1345 GMT and the April Chicago purchasing manager index at 1400 GMT.

Singapore government bond prices were slightly higher across the board, in line with strength in U.S. Treasurys on Friday, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6474, down from S$1.6506 late Friday. It traded between S$1.6436 and S$1.6478 intraday.  

Early in the session, market participants sold the U.S. currency down to as low as S$1.6436, its lowest since April 14. The selling was mainly because of bullish sentiment toward the Singapore dollar on expectations that China would move to a more flexible foreign exchange regime sooner rather than later, dealers said.  

Although concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore could intervene to curb a sharp rise in the Singapore dollar spurred light U.S.-dollar buybacks that lifted the U.S. unit to around the S$1.6480 level in the morning, the U.S. currency continued to be weighed down against the local dollar by sell-on-rally interest for the rest of the session.  

Fueling the yuan revaluation speculation were fresh remarks from Chinese officials over the weekend. A Chinese regulator said Sunday that China may speed up preparations for changes to its exchange rate regime, though emphasized that any such reforms will continue to be driven by domestic priorities and not criticism from its trading partners.  

"I agree that the economy is growing well, and probably it's time for China to consider to take the change. In general terms, a more flexible exchange rate is beneficial to the economy," said Wei Benhua, deputy director of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. "We can positively and prudently accelerate reform of the renminbi exchange rate regime," he said.  

At the same time, however, Wei said "there is no timetable" for any change to the renminbi regime. The currency, also known as the yuan, is effectively pegged around 8.28 to the U.S. dollar.  

Wei's remarks came on the heels of comments made Saturday by the governor of the People's Bank of China, the central bank.  

"We are making some preparations," Zhou Xiaochuan said, pointing specifically to ongoing reforms in the domestic banking system.  

However, he also said it was a gradual process and that "we have our own sequencing of reforms according to the Chinese situation."

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6474, down from S$1.6506 late Friday. It traded between S$1.6436 and S$1.6478 intraday.  

Early in the session, market participants sold the U.S. currency down to as low as S$1.6436, its lowest since April 14. The selling was mainly because of bullish sentiment toward the Singapore dollar on expectations that China would move to a more flexible foreign exchange regime sooner rather than later, dealers said.  

Although concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore could intervene to curb a sharp rise in the Singapore dollar spurred light U.S.-dollar buybacks that lifted the U.S. unit to around the S$1.6480 level in the morning, the U.S. currency continued to be weighed down against the local dollar by sell-on-rally interest for the rest of the session.  

Fueling the yuan revaluation speculation were fresh remarks from Chinese officials over the weekend. A Chinese regulator said Sunday that China may speed up preparations for changes to its exchange rate regime, though emphasized that any such reforms will continue to be driven by domestic priorities and not criticism from its trading partners.

'We can positively and prudently accelerate reform of the renminbi exchange rate regime,' he said.  

At the same time, however, Wei said 'there is no timetable' for any change to the renminbi regime. The currency, also known as the yuan, is effectively pegged around 8.28 to the U.S. dollar.  

Wei's remarks came on the heels of comments made Saturday by the governor of the People's Bank of China, the central bank.  

'We are making some preparations,' Zhou Xiaochuan said, pointing specifically to ongoing reforms in the domestic banking system.  

However, he also said it was a gradual process and that 'we have our own sequencing of reforms according to the Chinese situation.'

'Expect the strong support at S$1.6400 to be tested, but currently it is unclear whether a sustained down-move is possible,' UOB said.  

UOB also said a rebound of the U.S. dollar above resistance at S$1.6515 would indicate that the downside risk has diminished.

title: Singapore  Dlr Steady Late After Suspected  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was relatively steady against its U.S. counterpart late Thursday in Asia after suspected central bank intervention to curb the local currency's appreciation.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose in the short end but fell in the long end, leading to the curve flattening, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. currency was at S$1.6481, nearly unchanged from S$1.6485 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6455 and S$1.6495 intraday.  

After opening near its intraday low of S$1.6455, the U.S. dollar surged to as high as S$1.6495 early in the session, as the Monetary Authority of Singapore apparently intervened to limit a further rise in the Singapore dollar, dealers said.  

But the U.S. currency's weakness against its major rivals throughout the session and ongoing worries over U.S. economic growth weighed down the U.S. dollar against its Singaporean counterpart in the afternoon.  

Looming event risks later in the global session, such as the 1230 GMT release of U.S. initial jobless claims and the 1400 GMT speech by Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Sandra Pianalto on the "Power of Price Stability," kept market participants mostly sidelined.  

From a technical analysis perspective, there is no sign of stabilization for the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair yet and a further decline in the U.S. unit is likely, despite oversold conditions, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"As the downward momentum is not very strong, (we) expect any down-move to be slow and grinding," UOB said. "On the upside, only a move above S$1.6530 will suggest that a recovery is on the way."  

As a short-term trading strategy, UOB recommended selling the U.S. unit at S$1.6500 and placing stop-loss orders above S$1.6530, in anticipation of a possible fall to S$1.6430.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Speculation Over China  FX  Move
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose late Wednesday in Asia, as growing speculation that China may shift to a more flexible foreign exchange regime outweighed rumored intervention by Singapore's central bank.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds fell more in the long end than in other sectors, resulting in curve flattening, in line with Tuesday's flattening in the Treasurys yield curve, dealers said.

Late Tuesday, both Bush and Snow reiterated recent remarks calling on the Chinese authorities to move now toward a more flexible currency regime.  

In a research note, Morgan Stanley said these comments are likely aimed at diffusing efforts by the U.S. Senate to debate protectionist steps. The Senate is considering legislation to impose steep tariffs if China doesn't allow its currency to rise.

title: Singapore  Dlr Down Late;Rumored MAS  Intervention ,Yen Fall
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell significantly against its U.S. counterpart late Friday in Asia, dragged down by suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the weakness of the yen.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose in the front end, but were flat to lower in the medium- to long-term sectors, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6600, up sharply from S$1.6510 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6548 and S$1.6618 intraday.  

Early in the session, Singapore's central bank apparently stepped into the currency market to buy the U.S. dollar around the S$1.6570 level, sparking short-covering that eventually lifted the U.S. currency as high as S$1.6618 in the afternoon, dealers said.  

The rumored intervention may have been aimed at scaring away speculators from betting on a sharp rise in the Singapore dollar against the U.S. currency in the coming sessions after the central bank decided earlier this week to retain its current policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, dealers added.  

The yen's weakness against the U.S. and most other currencies in the session also helped weigh down the Singapore dollar. At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at Y108.28, up from Y108.11 late Thursday in New York.  

But, with both the two-day meeting of the finance ministers and central bankers of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations and the Treasury International Capital flows data looming later in the global session, market participants refrained from pushing the U.S. currency sharply higher against the local dollar.  

According to technical analysis, the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar's medium-term outlook is still neutral, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"Critical resistance is at S$1.6700 and unless this level is taken out, we are probably caught in a wide sideways consolidation," UOB said.  

Yields on short-dated Singapore government bonds rose slightly on tightening liquidity conditions in the money market, as reflected by the rise in the overnight interbank rate to 1.9375% Friday from 1.8750% Thursday.  

Longer-dated local government bond yields, however, were flat to lower, given Thursday's strength in U.S. Treasurys.

title: INSTANT VIEW 2-Singapore MAS maintains monetary policy stance.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 12 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the city-state's central bank, retained on Tuesday its year-old tightening stance of allowing a stronger currency to curb inflation risks, even as economic growth slows.  

The MAS said it would maintain its policy of allowing "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the trade-weighted Singapore dollar, which was adopted last April when Singapore's economy was undergoing rapid economic expansion.  

KEY POINTS:  

- Most economists had expected the MAS to leave its year-long policy of "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the Singapore dollar unchanged because of inflation risks.  

- A Reuters poll of 11 analysts take after Monday's unexpectedly weak economic growth data found that more than two-thirds expected the MAS to keep its tighter policy stance.  

- The MAS cut its forecast for headline CPI inflation to 0-1 percent for 2005 against previous forecast of 1-2 percent. For 2006, the MAS expects headline CPI inflation of 1-2 percent.  

- The MAS expects Singapore's gross domestic product growth to come in at the lower half of the government's forecast range of 3-5 percent.  

- MAS said it intervened significantly in the fourth quarter of 2004 and into early 2005 to moderate excessive upward pressure on the Singapore dollar.  

COMMENTARY:  

SIMON FLINT, HEAD OF EMERGING ASIA CURRENCY STRATEGIST, MERRILL LYNCH  

"This was very much in line with my expectation and to some extent, you can see this in the market place - there has been some fairly modest appreciation by the Sing dollar. But because of the recently, relatively poor GDP numbers and the very low inflation numbers, some people may have thought they would change. The impact of growth will be very minor.  

"The things that have interested me so far are two-fold. First of all, their slightly muted outlook for inflation this year and saying between 0 to 1 percent.  

"Also this mention of intervention was used to curb Singapore dollar strength which I would interpret as them intervening in order to prevent the speculative pricing of either Chinese or Malaysian regime change on the Sing dollar.  

IRENE CHEUNG, HEAD OF ASIA CURRENCY STRATEGY, ABN AMRO BANK  

"Probably they are still looking at better numbers for GDP for the rest of the year and despite the worse-than-expected GDP growth for the first quarter of this year. They have lowered their inflation forecast to 0 to 1 percent from 1 to 2 percent and I think that is in line with what we see from the lastest CPI numbers.  

"They are having a very, very slight appreciation of the Sing dollar so it won't have a major impact on growth."  

PHILIP WEE, TREASURY MARKET STRATEGIST, DBS BANK  

"It signals that the economy is seeing a soft patch and not a recession. We are also being consistent with what's happening around us, which is that interest rates are being tightened."  

MARKET REACTION:  

- The Singapore dollar was trading at 1.6461 to the U.S. dollar after the announcement, compared with 1.6502 just before 0000 GMT.  

- The stock market was not open when the review was announced. The Straits Times Index ended flat at 2,181.58 points on Monday.  

LINK  

- To view the full report, please go to the Web site of the Monetary Authority of Singapore at  http://www.mas.gov.sg ("http://www.mas.gov.sg").  

BACKGROUND:  

- The MAS conducts monetary policy by steering the Singapore dollar in a band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, rather than setting an interest rate as many central bank do.  

- The band and the basket of currencies are kept secret, though most major financial institutions have developed models to broadly mirror the central bank's system.  

- Singapore's economy grew 8.4 percent in 2004, its fastest in four years, but analysts polled by Reuters have forecast the growth rate would halve to 4.2 percent this year.  

- The economy contracted at an annualised 5.8 percent rate in the first quarter, far worse than market expectations.  

- The MAS has estimated that consumer prices in 2005 will rise between 1 percent and 2 percent.  

- The inflation rate in 2004 hit a 7-year high of 1.7 percent after a rise in a goods-and-services tax and power tariffs.  

($1=1.65 Singapore Dollar).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing, Taiwan dlr weaken on  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, March 11 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar led
Asian currencies lower on Friday on worries central banks may
again step in after some intervened a day earlier to pull their
currencies from multi-year highs to keep exports competitive.
 
    The Singapore dollar, which touched a 6-1/2-year high on
Thursday, fell 0.2 percent to 1.6212 per dollar.
    The Taiwan dollar, Asia's second-best performing currency
against the dollar this year, slipped a tenth of a percent to
30.820 per dollar, easing from a 4-1/2-year high on Thursday.
    Analysts said the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which
  

guides the trade-weighted Singapore dollar within an  

undisclosed band, may no longer want a stronger currency

because of the dim outlook for electronics and bio-medical  

exports. MAS has maintained a bias towards appreciation since  

last year.  

"There may be a chance that the MAS may shift to a neutral  

policy come April," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at  

ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore, referring to the next MAS policy  

meeting.   


 
    "The Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate has
been kept on a tight leash in the year to date."
    Ng said inflation may not be a major cause for concern for
MAS because the effects of high oil prices are likely to be
limited. That weakens the argument for a stronger currency.
    South Korea made it clear it was uncomfortable with the
  

won's rise, which has made South Korean exporters less  

competitive against regional rivals. The won has surged 10  

percent against the yen since the start of November and touched  

a 5-1/2-year high of 9.52 per yen on Thursday.  

The won weakened to 9.6 per yen on Friday after South  

Korea's deputy finance minister, Bahk Byong-won, said the  

government would not stay idle in the face of rapid currency

movements, which he said were driven by speculation.  

Given that backdrop, ABN AMRO expected the won to  

strengthen only 1 percent in the next three months to about 990  

against the dollar, despite a revival in domestic consumer  

demand.  

JPMorgan Chase Bank said in a report that although South  

Korea does not want a sharp weakening of the dollar, it may not  

stand in the way of any longer-term weakness.  

"The monetary authorities will unlikely attempt to turn  

broader market trends (dollar weakness) and should gradually  

cede local currency appreciation," JPMorgan said in a note to  

clients.  

Concern about the dollar's long-term decline was fuelled on  

Friday when India's central bank governor, Yaga Venugopal  

Reddy, said diversification of foreign exchange reserves was  

being discussed within the bank and that it was a subject of  

ongoing debate among all central banks.  

The rupee was steady at 43.58 per dollar.  

The peso, Asia's best performer this year, was the only  

Asian unit to gain on Friday, rising a quarter of a percent.  

Ng said the peso was benefitting from foreign investment in  

stocks, remittances from overseas Filipinos and expectations of  

foreign direct investment in its mining and power industries.

text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, March 11 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar led
Asian currencies lower on Friday on worries central banks may
again intervene to keep their currencies competitive after they
had pulled Asian units down from multi-year highs a day
earlier.
    The Singapore dollar, which touched a 6-1/2-year high on
Thursday, fell 0.3 percent to 1.6230 per dollar. The South
Korean won edged down to 1,002 per dollar, extending its
retreat a seven-year high of 989 on Thursday.
    Analysts said South Korea, which was estimated to have
spent $2 billion on Thursday to block the won's strength, may
spend more in buying dollars to keep the country's exporters
competitive, particularly against Japan.
    The South Korean unit has surged almost 10 percent against
the yen since the start of November, to reach its strongest
level since and mid-1999.
  


    "Until we get concrete evidence that the domestic
consumption recovery is firmly entrenched, we believe the 9.50
level for the yen-won will provide good support," said Emmanuel
Ng, currency strategist at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore.
    South Korean deputy finance minister Bahk Byong-won said
the government would not stay idle in the face of rapid
currency movements, which he said were driven by speculation.
    Given that backdrop, ABN AMRO expected the won to
strengthen only 1 percent in the next three months to about 990
per dollar, despite a revival in domestic consumer demand.
    The Taiwan dollar, Asia's best performing currency against
the dollar this year after the Philippine peso , also
slipped a tenth of a percent on worries the central bank may
intervene for a second day.
 
    Foreign investors, who have buoyed the currency this year,
turned net sellers on Thursday for the second time this month.
    The currency has also been weighed by a bill being debated
  

in China's parliament that would authorise China to use force  

to prevent Taiwan from seceding from the mainland. Traders were  

waiting on Taiwan's response to the bill.  

The rupiah, Asia's worst performer after the Japanese yen  

this year, remained pressured by dollar demand from importers  

and near-record oil prices, which analysts say could worsen the  

country's balance of payments position.  

The peso was the only Asian currency to strengthen on  

Friday morning, on expectations authorities would allow gains  

to help counter inflation pressures from high oil prices.  

Ng said the peso continued to benefit from foreign  

investments in stocks, strong remittances from Filipinos living  

abroad and expectations of foreign direct investments into its  

mining and power industries.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Knocked from multi-year highs by c.banks.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, March 10 (Reuters) - The South Korean won,
Taiwan dollar and the Singapore dollar were knocked off
multi-year highs on Thursday when some Asian central banks
intervened to stop their currencies strengthening and keep
exports competitive.
    The South Korean won ended local trading at 1,000.3 per
dollar, barely changed from the previous day's close of 1,001
but off a seven-year high of 989 hit in the morning.
 
    Traders said the government bought almost $2 billion in the
currency markets to pull the won off its highs.
    "That's definitely a step up (in intervention) from what
  

we've seen in recent times but they haven't got a lot of bang  

for it," said David Simmonds, emerging markets strategist at  

Royal Bank of Scotland's Singapore office.   


 
    "The intervention efforts may be quite persistent from here
on for a while. Some of the fast money has already been made."
    The Taiwan dollar ended local trading 0.1 percent stronger
  

at 30.79 per dollar. The currency yielded ground after hitting  

a 4-1/2-year high of 30.67 following dollar buying  

interventions by the central bank.  

The Singapore dollar hit a 6-1/2-year high of about 1.6162 per  

dollar before softening, while the yen gained 0.7 percent from  

late Asian trading on Wednesday to trade at about 103.87 per  

dollar.   


 
    The Asian currency gains were triggered by South Korean
data which showed consumer sentiment hit a two-year high.
    Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi fueled the rally
further by telling a parliament committee that it was necessary
for Japan to diversify its record foreign currency reserves.
    Japan had until now refrained from echoing other Asian
  

policy makers who have publicly announced plans to diversify  

their holdings away from dollar-denominated assets. Asian  

central banks hold about $2.5 trillion of foreign currency

reserves.  

DAMAGE CONTROL  

As Asian currencies soared, Japanese finance ministry  

officials said Japan had no plans to change the composition of  

the country's $840.56 billion reserves, the world's largest.   


 
    South Korean finance ministry and central bank officials
joined in the damage control.
    Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung called for "international
  

action" to counter the dollar's weakness and promised  

aggressive steps to check the gains in the won, which he said  

was excessively strong.  

The won has gained 3.5 percent this year, making it Asia's  

best performing currency after the Taiwan dollar which has  

strengthened 3.7 percent. The won gained 15.2 percent in 2004.  

"The won and the Taiwan dollar have been our top picks (in  

Asia) for the last six months and there's no reason to change  

that now," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at Deutsche  

Bank in Singapore.  

"Investor interest is shifting back to Asia because other  

economies are not looking that attractive. This is the region  

where the growth will be the strongest, this is the region  

where the currencies are undervalued."  

Malcolm said speculators who had been on the sidelines  

since the start of the year after bidding up Asian currencies

in the last quarter of 2004 were once again buying them.  

Although the U.S. economy is on a rebound, investors are  

revisiting the longer-term problems facing the dollar such as  

the bloated U.S. current account deficit, he said.  

With investors in north Asian currencies facing  

intervention, traders bid up the Philippine peso and Indonesian  

rupiah on expectations their central banks would not mind  

stronger currencies as they battle inflationary pressures from  

near-record high oil prices.  

The Philippine peso gained as much as half a percent to set a  

fresh 19-month high of 54.15 per dollar. The country has  

benefitted from strong inflows into its stock market, which  

drove the benchmark stock index to a 5-1/2-year high this week.  

Simmonds said further moves in Asian currencies would  

depend on oil prices, terms of trade of each country and equity  

inflows. But he ruled out any joint interventions by Asian  

authorities.   


 
    "I'd be very surprised if there's any sort of coordinated
efforts," he said. "At best these are smoothening-off efforts."

title: Singapore Bonds Tumble On Treasurys, Tight MAS Policy
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--A sharp fall in U.S. Treasurys sparked fresh selling at the longer end of Singapore's bond market Thursday, driving the benchmark 10-year bond yield to a five-month high.  

The 10-year bond opened at a yield of 3.22% and rose to 3.24% by 0400 GMT, up from 3.18% Wednesday. The market reacted to selling in the U.S., where Treasurys sank to new session lows overnight, sending the 10-year U.S. yield above 4.50% for the first time since July.  

The selling shows the city-state is facing a double-edged sword - the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been on a tightening trend since October to contain inflation, while yields on the U.S. Treasurys are moving higher at a faster pace.  

In order to keep the Singapore dollar competitive, the MAS has been intervening in the foreign exchange market to prevent a sharp fall in the U.S. dollar.  

Even on Thursday, suspected MAS intervention allowed the U.S. dollar to rebound from a new six-year low of 1.6160 in early trade. The central bank declined to comment.  

However, at the same time, MAS is also sterilizing surplus liquidity through the sale of domestic securities which, in fact, is leading to funds outflow and higher rates, said Thomas Lam Tai Loong, treasury economist at United Overseas Bank.  

He said the shorter end of the yield curve is reacting to the MAS action and rising U.S. rates - which have been firming up since the start of the year.  

The longer-dated bonds may still have support at 3.25%, said one dealer at a local bank, but other analysts said the bearish sentiment for the bond market is far from over.  

"For the 10-year Treasurys, our year-end forecast is 5.6%, so we should expect the Singapore bond yield to hit 3.6% by the end of the year," said Simon Klassen, fixed-income research analyst at JP Morgan.  

However, an expected rise in yields won't force companies to "to rush to the doors" for more corporate bond issuances because they have already covered themselves last year, he said.

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against its U.S. counterpart late Thursday in Asia after a Japanese yen rally, but retreated from a new six-year high due to suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

Singapore bonds rose, with the longer-dated 10-year yield hitting a five-month high, reacting to the second day of a selloff in U.S. Treasurys overnight.

'Koizumi's comments had a big impact on the market, but after the clarification, the pressure on the U.S. dollar eased a bit,' said a Singapore dealer.  

The U.S. currency's downside against its Singaporean counterpart was also supported by rumored intervention by the MAS, with some dealers saying the U.S. unit could find strong support at S$1.6150.

title: DJ Singapore Bonds Tumble On Treasurys, Tight MAS Policy
text:
SINGAPORE, Mar 09, 2005 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

A sharp fall in U.S. Treasurys sparked fresh selling at the longer end of Singapore's bond market Thursday, driving the benchmark 10-year bond yield to a five-month high. The 10-year bond opened at a yield of 3.22% and rose to 3.24% by 0400 GMT, up from 3.18% Wednesday. The market reacted to selling in the U.S., where Treasurys sank to new session lows overnight, sending the 10-year U.S. yield above 4.50% for the first time since July. The selling shows the city-state is facing a double-edged sword - the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been on a tightening trend since October to contain inflation, while yields on the U.S. Treasurys are moving higher at a faster pace. In order to keep the Singapore dollar competitive, the MAS has been intervening in the foreign exchange market to prevent a sharp fall in the U.S. dollar. Even on Thursday, suspected MAS intervention allowed the U.S. dollar to rebound from a new six-year low of 1.6160 in early trade. The central bank declined to comment. However, at the same time, MAS is also sterilizing surplus liquidity through the sale of domestic securities which, in fact, is leading to funds outflow and higher rates, said Thomas Lam Tai Loong, treasury economist at United Overseas Bank. He said the shorter end of the yield curve is reacting to the MAS action and rising U.S. rates - which have been firming up since the start of the year. The longer-dated bonds may still have support at 3.25%, said one dealer at a local bank, but other analysts said the bearish sentiment for the bond market is far from over. "For the 10-year Treasurys, our year-end forecast is 5.6%, so we should expect the Singapore bond yield to hit 3.6% by the end of the year," said Simon Klassen, fixed-income research analyst at JP Morgan. However, an expected rise in yields won't force companies to "to rush to the doors" for more corporate bond issuances because they have already covered themselves last year, he said. Foreign companies issued S$3.42 billion in local currency bonds in 2004, almost double the amount from 2003.

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger late Tuesday in Asia on mild, broad-based strength in the yen, although the local currency's upside was curbed by fears of potential intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

Prices on government bonds slipped after a fall in U.S. Treasurys late Monday, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6247, down from S$1.6258 late Monday. It traded between S$1.6216 and S$1.6261 intraday.  

After falling to a six-year low of S$1.6214 late Monday in New York, the U.S. currency opened Tuesday's Asian session on a negative note against the local dollar, dealers said.  

Despite light short-covering led by a U.S. bank that lifted the U.S. dollar as high as S$1.6261 early in the session, the U.S. unit was weighed down against the local dollar on the yen's slight rise against other currencies in the afternoon.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at Y104.48, down from Y104.52 Monday in New York. The euro was at Y137.93, down from Y138.42 Monday in New York.  

Traders said yen-bullish sentiment continued to bolster the Singaporean and other regional currencies in Tuesday's Asian session after strong Japanese economic data were released Monday.  

Monday, the Japanese government said the nation's industrial production rose 2.1% in January from December, reversing the revised 0.8% fall of the previous month and beating market expectations for a 1.6% rise. Japan's overall retail sales rose 2.2% in January, against expectations of 0.3%.  

However, the U.S. dollar managed to hold above the six-year low of S$1.6214, given concerns that Singapore's central bank could intervene to stem any sharp fall below the psychologically important S$1.6200, a level which hasn't been broken since early November 1998.  

According to technical analysis, the U.S. dollar's downward momentum against its Singaporean counterpart is strong and there are no signs of stabilization just yet, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

"It looks like a further down-move is likely from here. Only a move above S$1.6275 will indicate that we have seen a temporary short-term low," UOB said.  

As a short-term trading strategy, UOB recommends selling the U.S. dollar at S$1.6250 and placing stop-loss orders above S$1.6275 in anticipation of a possible fall to S$1.6180.  

Yields on Singapore government securities rose across the curve, in the wake of a sharp rise in U.S. Treasury yields late Monday in New York, dealers said.  

But trading flows in the local bond market were relatively thin ahead of this week's slew of U.S. economic data, including the 1500 GMT release of the Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index for February.

By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The South Korean won pared

surging on economic data.

    The Indian rupee gained a fifth of a percent after the
  

finance minister presented the country's budget for 2005/2006,  

cutting corporate taxes and taking steps to boost growth in  

infrastructure and rural areas.  

The won was lifted earlier on Monday by data which showed  

South Korea's factory output rose a faster-than-expected 3.1  

percent in January from December.  

Signs of a revival in the domestic economy attracted  

overseas investors to its stock markets this month, pushing its  

benchmark stock index to a five-year high on Monday. Foreign  

investors have bought a net 2.32 trillion won in shares so far  

this year.

990," said Christy Tan, an analyst at 4CAST Ltd. in Singapore.
    Yet, analysts said intervention concerns may keep the won
  

from breaching the 1,000 won per dollar barrier in the near  

term. South Korea could sell more bonds to fund intervention

in the currency markets to stem the won's rise, Irene Cheung,  

head of Asian currency strategy at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore,  

said in a report.  

The South Korean data was followed by statistics from  

Japan which showed industrial production rose a  

faster-than-expected 2.1 percent in January from a month

slowdown.

    SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on
Friday in line with a weakening Japanese yen and on fear of

 of Korea had not resumed its intervention on Friday, although   

 the finance ministry said it could issue more bonds to mop up

 Meanwhile, a local Taiwan newspaper reported the central   

 bank had warned foreign investors against speculating in the   

currency.   

Currency analysts said short-term factors such as the focus   

 on yields, which was undermining the yen, and the worry of   

intervention, would weigh on the regionals, despite the longer   


 
    "With the focus on yield, Asia is obviously not the
favourite," said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist with UBS.
    Baweja said the decline in the regional currencies provided
an opportunity for investors to establish fresh long positions.
    He said he would pick the Taiwan dollar, Sing dollar,
Indian rupee  and Thai baht, although he would wait for
the currently high volatility levels to drop.
    Even the rise in crude oil prices to more than $50 a barrel
was overshadowed by other factors for currencies in the
oil-importing Asian markets.
    These included a boost for Asian currencies early this week
  


when a Korean document outlining plans to diversify foreign
  


reserves sparked a dollar sell off. Asian authorities have
  


since assured markets they are not selling the dollar.

But markets continued to speculate on what could have been
  


discussed at a closed-door meeting of Asian policy makers in
  


Bangkok on Tuesday.

held to discuss how to cope with a weak U.S. dollar and the

Policy makers from South Korea, Japan, China and the

Bangkok. Japanese officials said there was no discussion on

rise earlier this week had markets assuming that the policy
  


makers might have decided to accommodate some currency


strength.

title: Singapore  Dollar Falls Late On Suspected MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell against its U.S. counterpart late Friday in Asia, after apparent intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to absorb heavy selling by U.S. investment banks.  

Government bonds were weaker across the board, especially for short-dated securities, resulting in curve flattening, dealers said.  

At 0649 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6329, up from S$1.6277 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6284 and S$1.6332 intraday.  

The U.S. currency kicked off Friday's Asian session on a positive note against the local dollar after broad-based U.S. dollar strength on the back of a climb in U.S. Treasury yields and U.S. equities late Thursday.  

But U.S. investment banks soon sold the U.S. dollar down to as low as S$1.6284 early in the session, supposedly to bet on a renewed decline of the U.S. currency against its Singaporean counterpart in the near term, dealers said.  

In an apparent effort to stem the U.S. unit's slide against the local dollar, the MAS was rumored to have bought the U.S. dollar around the intraday low of S$1.6284, thereby lifting the U.S. unit to the S$1.6330 level in the afternoon, dealers added.  

Speculation that Singapore's central bank could continue to curb an excessive appreciation of the Singapore currency put a floor under the U.S. dollar in the S$1.6330 area for the rest of the Asian session.  

Traders also cited the 1330 GMT release of the U.S.'s preliminary gross domestic product data for the fourth quarter as another factor providing support for the U.S. dollar.  

U.S. GDP growth in the fourth quarter is expected to be revised upward, reflecting a narrowing in the trade deficit, among other things. The median estimate of 20 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for growth to be revised up to a 3.8% annual rate from the 3.1% rate in the advance report.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds rose, particularly at the front end, leading to flattening of the yield curve, dealers said.  

A flattening of the U.S. Treasurys yield curve late Thursday and a rise in Singapore's short-term interbank rates Friday boosted yields on short-dated securities.  

Since the start of this year, the three-month Singapore interbank offered rate, or Sibor, has risen to 1.87% from 1.50%, Standard Chartered Bank said in a research report.  

While seasonally tight liquidity conditions around the Lunar New Year holidays earlier this month resulted in higher interbank rates, Standard Chartered said the fact that this rise in Singapore interest rates isn't abating is a potential concern and could quicken economic growth deceleration.

By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Feb 24 (Reuters) - The Korean won and the Taiwan
dollar were pulled off intra-day highs on Thursday by talk of
dollar-buying by the authorities, but markets remained bullish
on the two currencies after their run-up earlier in the week.
    The won hit a seven-year peak of 998 a dollar on Wednesday
after a Bank of Korea document referring to diversification of
foreign exchange reserves sparked a dollar sell-off against
major currencies.
    A Korean media report suggesting Asian policy makers met in
Bangkok on Tuesday to discuss their approach to the dollar's
weakness also boosted the regionals.
    Traders said speculation the policy makers might have
agreed to accommodate some strength in their currencies had
underpinned the regionals.
  


    And, although the Korean authorities were suspected of
intervening earlier this week, their failure to stop a 2
percent rally from 1,024 to levels above 1,000 won a dollar had
intensified the dollar selling, traders added.
 
    But at 0740 GMT on Thursday, the won had slipped to 1,006 a
dollar, down a quarter percent from the morning's levels.
    The Taiwan dollar fell to 31.17 a dollar from a 4-=   year
peak of 31.09 it struck in morning deals.
    Traders suspected the Korean authorities might have mopped
  

up around $200 million in the morning to cap the won, alongside  

heavy verbal intervention. The Korean finance minister said the  

won's gains were temporary and central bank chief Park Seung  

said the won might decline around April.  

"I think we will not see any bouts of outperformance in  

these currencies for a few days. They will move sideways for a  

while," said John Cairns, head of research at IDEAglobal.com.  

A Japanese finance ministry official said on Thursday there  

had been no discussion of trying to halt the dollar's decline  

at the Bangkok meeting.   


 
    At their highs, the won had risen 2 percent since Monday
and the Taiwan dollar had risen 1.4 percent.
    The Singapore dollar also slipped slightly on Thursday
after its one percent rise since Monday.
    The Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah held steady.
    Referring to remarks by authorities in Taiwan, Korea and
  

Japan playing down the idea of reserves diversification, JP  

Morgan strategist Claudio Piron said the regional central banks  

were clearly sensitive to sentiment on the dollar.  

"Policy makers will not, through their own actions,  

exacerbate U.S. dollar losses. Currency stability or gradual  

appreciation remains the dominant policy mandate and it serves  

no interest for policymakers to accelerate dollar losses,"  

Piron said in a note.   


 
    "In this context, any effort to diversify reserves will not
be designed as a destabilising influence on the dollar."
    YEN-WON CROSS
    Meanwhile, the yen rallied during Asian trading, shrugging

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late On Lingering US Dlr Bearishness
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened late Thursday in Asia on lingering bearish sentiment toward the U.S. dollar, despite suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

Government bonds were stronger after the MAS auctioned S$1.2 billion worth of 10-year government bonds, dealers said.  

At 0705 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6277, down from S$1.6295 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6263 and S$1.6298 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar came under downward pressure against the local currency early in the session as speculators sought to test the U.S. unit's one-month low of S$1.6250 set on Tuesday, following disappointing U.S. data and a lack of any positive surprises in the minutes from the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee's Feb. 1-2 meeting.  

Underpinning bearish sentiment toward the U.S. currency was Wednesday's U.S. data showing slower-than-expected growth in consumer prices in January. The U.S. government reported that the consumer price index rose 0.1% in January, and that core consumer prices increased 0.2%.  

Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires had forecast a 0.2% rise in both the overall index and the core component, which strips out food and energy prices.  

Traders said the minutes from the FOMC's meeting, released Wednesday, also contributed to the U.S. dollar's weakness against the local dollar, as Fed policymakers said they see little evidence that the large U.S. trade deficit will narrow.  

Although the U.S. dollar slid as low as S$1.6263 in the morning, it soon found support around that level on suspected MAS intervention aimed at slowing the U.S. unit's fall against its Singaporean counterpart, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar consolidated with a steady bias in the high-S$1.6200s for the rest of the session, bolstered by expectations that the MAS wouldn't hesitate to step back into the market to support the U.S. unit against the local dollar, dealers added.  

Despite its oversold condition, however, the U.S. currency has yet to form a short-term base against the Singapore dollar, based on technical analysis, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

"Any recovery is expected to be short-lived and another exhaustive down-move toward the next support at S$1.6230 is expected," said UOB.  

"Only a move above S$1.6340 will indicate that a stronger recovery is on the way," it said.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds flattened after the MAS's auction of S$1.2 billion in 10-year government bonds appeared to have been well-received by the local market, dealers said.  

The MAS sold S$1.2 billion in 10-year bonds at a cutoff yield of 3.00%. Bids totaled S$2.7 billion and the average yield was 2.97%, according to data posted on the central bank's Web site.  

A total S$94.1 million of the 10-year issue was allotted to noncompetitive applications, none of it to the MAS.  

The bonds, which will be issued March 1, are a reopening of an existing paper that matures July 1, 2014.

title: DJ Singapore Dollar Up Late On Lingering US Dlr Bearishness
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened late Thursday in Asia on lingering bearish sentiment toward the U.S. dollar, despite suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

Government bonds were stronger after the MAS auctioned S$1.2 billion worth of 10-year government bonds, dealers said.  

At 0705 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6277, down from S$1.6295 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6263 and S$1.6298 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar came under downward pressure against the local currency early in the session as speculators sought to test the U.S. unit's one-month low of S$1.6250 set on Tuesday, following disappointing U.S. data and a lack of any positive surprises in the minutes from the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee's Feb. 1-2 meeting.  

Underpinning bearish sentiment toward the U.S. currency was Wednesday's U.S. data showing slower-than-expected growth in consumer prices in January. The U.S. government reported that the consumer price index rose 0.1% in January, and that core consumer prices increased 0.2%.  

Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires had forecast a 0.2% rise in both the overall index and the core component, which strips out food and energy prices.  

Traders said the minutes from the FOMC's meeting, released Wednesday, also contributed to the U.S. dollar's weakness against the local dollar, as Fed policymakers said they see little evidence that the large U.S. trade deficit will narrow.  

Although the U.S. dollar slid as low as S$1.6263 in the morning, it soon found support around that level on suspected MAS intervention aimed at slowing the U.S. unit's fall against its Singaporean counterpart, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar consolidated with a steady bias in the high-S$1.6200s for the rest of the session, bolstered by expectations that the MAS wouldn't hesitate to step back into the market to support the U.S. unit against the local dollar, dealers added.  

Despite its oversold condition, however, the U.S. currency has yet to form a short-term base against the Singapore dollar, based on technical analysis, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

'Any recovery is expected to be short-lived and another exhaustive down-move toward the next support at S$1.6230 is expected,' said UOB.  

'Only a move above S$1.6340 will indicate that a stronger recovery is on the way,' it said.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds flattened after the MAS's auction of S$1.2 billion in 10-year government bonds appeared to have been well-received by the local market, dealers said.  

The MAS sold S$1.2 billion in 10-year bonds at a cutoff yield of 3.00%. Bids totaled S$2.7 billion and the average yield was 2.97%, according to data posted on the central bank's Web site.  

A total S$94.1 million of the 10-year issue was allotted to noncompetitive applications, none of it to the MAS.

title: =DJ ASIA DEBT: Singapore IRS Debate: To Steepen Or Flatten?
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column  

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Not long ago, the dominant theme in Singapore's fixed-income market was that interest-rate curves here would follow those in the U.S. by flattening.  

Some strategists and traders insist the island city-state's bond yields and interest rate swaps are bound to mimic the months-long flattening trend seen in U.S. Treasurys and IRS. But now, even before the steep Singapore curves have had a chance to flatten, others are arguing that there's room for the gap of long-term over short-term yields and IRS rates to widen further.  

Proponents of flattening, such as DBS Bank, say persistently strong appetite for local fixed-income assets and tamedinflation don't warrant sharply higher long-term interest rates here, while the central bank is expected to support short-term rates with a tight bias in monetary policy.  

But those in the steepening camp are this week citing fast-rising long U.S. Treasury yields and talk of a bulging local bond pipeline to argue that the long end of the Singapore interest rate curves should gather upward momentum, pushing short and long rates even farther apart.  

Since talk began at the start of the year of an impending flattening here, the spread of the 10-year Singapore dollar IRS swap over the two-year rate has instead widened 15 basis points to 114 basis points. The similar spread on Singapore government bond yields has also widened 15 basis points, to 118 basis points.  

During the same period, the U.S. interest rate curves have flattened rapidly, with the IRS 2-10-year spread shrinking by 32 basis points to around 83.7 basis points. Playing for a similar flattening in the U.S. Treasurys curve has been a major trade in that market since last year, despite the Federal Reserve's steady diet of interest rate rises at the short end.  

The phenomenon has become pronounced enough for Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan last week to brand it a 'conundrum,' sparking a sharp rebound of U.S. long yields as traders and investors wondered whether the one-way flattening ride was over.  

Singapore, despite predictions of a flattening, has been decoupled from U.S. curve moves this year largely because of the Fed's inexorable tightening, which contrasts with an outlook for slower growth in the island republic. The 2-10-year spread in Singapore has widened a further 4 basis points in the past week, fueled by talk that a company was preparing to issue a long-dated Singapore-dollar bond as soon as this week.  

'We heard the new issue size could be pretty big,' said a trader at a Singapore bank. 'If the market doesn't have the appetite for it, the curve could steepen further.'  

In addition, the post-Greenspan steepening in the U.S. Treasury curve has begun spilling over into the Singapore market.  

While the market has so far responded calmly to an unexpectedly large S$1.2 billion reopening Thursday of a 10-year government bond, uncertainty will likely linger until the bond's auction Thursday. The market had mostly expected the reopened issue to be worth S$800 million to S$1 billion. If demand for the bond is weak, paying interest may increase at the long end of the IRS curve, pushing swap rates up.  

But despite such upward risks for long-dated rates, some strategists are standing by their curve flatteners.  

DBS recommends investors sell the two-year bond and buy the 10-year, targeting a flattening 100 basis points in one to three months.  

Historically, the yield-curve spread can narrow only to 100 basis points 'in a rising-rate environment,' says DBS strategist Chia Woon Khien. 'Unless the current hiking cycle is coming to a halt, there's no reason to disrupt the flattening strategy, especially in U.S. Treasurys, which have more scope for further flattening.'  

Chia said the IRS curve will behave in a broadly similar fashion but that she sees more room for the bond-yield curve to flatten. Indeed, DBS recommends a widener on the 10-year bond-swap spread.  

She is also adamant that long rates in Singapore will remain in check thanks to yield-hungry investors, as inflation stays benign and the local economy transforms itself to a productivity-oriented nature from an investment-driven one in past decades. 'On an asset-allocation basis, you look at nominal growth, which is no longer like the go-go days,' Chia said. 'People would still want to seek relatively more comfort in bonds than equities.'  

The debate over the Singapore rate curves also hinges on the outlook for monetary policy here, with the flattener camp expecting the Monetary Authority of Singapore to maintain its tightening bias at its next policy meeting in April but steepener fans looking for the central bank to ease.  

'We deem the chance next to nil,' Chia said, adding that the government's new pro-growth budget would offset some of the current weakness in exports. 'Besides, the MAS's tenet is that the Singapore dollar policy is to defend inflation, not exports.'  

The MAS uses the Singapore dollar exchange rate rather than interest rates as monetary policy tool for this small, trade-dominated economy. But when the authority intervenes to buy the local currency, the resulting drain of Singapore dollar liquidity from the interbank market puts upward pressure on short-term rates.  

In the midst of this heated debate, some traders say both arguments may in fact prove right and that it's best to stay flexible - anticipating a steepening for the next week or two due to the bond-supply pressures, then reverting to a longer-term flattener trade after long rates stabilize.  

The 2-10 IRS spread has an immediate upside of 125 basis points, where investors could consider taking profits and entering a flattener with a target of 100 basis points, traders say.  

-By Shen Hong, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4032; hong.shen@dowjones.com

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Weak Yen, Rumored MAS Rate Check
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged lower against its U.S. counterpart in Asia Wednesday on broad-based yen weakness and on speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore was checking on foreign exchange rates.  

Singapore government bonds were nearly flat ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's two-day semiannual congressional testimony that begins later in the global day.  

At 0640, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6414, above S$1.6412 late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6374 and S$1.6419 intraday.  

The U.S. currency kicked off the Asian session on a positive note against the local dollar as interbank players bought U.S. dollars on rumors that the MAS had called several banks about the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair when the U.S. unit was trading around S$1.6380, dealers said.  

Concerns that Singapore's central bank would intervene to support the U.S. dollar against the local dollar spurred the interbank-led short-covering that helped to boost the U.S. unit as high as S$1.6419 in the afternoon.  

The yen's slide against major rivals throughout most of the session also contributed to the U.S. dollar's climb against its Singapore counterpart, dealers said.  

Early in the session, the Japanese government said Japan's real gross domestic product shrank 0.1% in the October-December period from the previous quarter, undershooting economists' expectations for GDP growth of 0.1%. The government also lowered previous GDP figures to a 0.3% decline in the July-September period and a 0.2% fall in the April-June period.  

"Technically, Japan is in a recession," said a local dealer.  

The technical definition of a recession is at least two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.  

The U.S. dollar continued to trade firmly in the low-S$1.6400s later in the session, though its upside was capped by rumored offers from a U.K. bank in the S$1.6410-S$1.6415 area, dealers said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won slips, Sing dollar softer.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Feb 11 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell and
most Asian currencies were soft on Friday after the Japanese
yen's decline overnight and North Korea's declaration that it
had nuclear weapons.
    The Japanese yen's recovery in later trades helped some of
the regional currencies recoup, leaving only the won and the
Sing dollar down over a quarter percent since they were last
traded earlier in the week.
   The Philippine peso was steadier around 54.80 per dollar,
having come off its highest levels in over a year earlier this
week.
    Japanese markets were closed on Friday. Other regional
markets in Taiwan and Hong Kong also remained shut for extended
Lunar New Year holidays, exaggerating currency moves.
    The won fell in early deals as trading resumed after the
festival holidays. It hit 1,038 per dollar, down from Monday's
levels near 1,029.
  


    North Korea declared on Thursday for the first time that it
possessed nuclear weapons, and it pulled out indefinitely from
six-nation talks on its atomic ambitions, saying it needed a
defense against a hostile United States.
 
    Korean stocks fell, paring some of the rapid gains the
index has made in the past month.
    Traders played down the impact of the North Korean
statement on markets and attributed the won's decline more to
the Japanese yen.
    "While all three rating agencies have listed the North
  

Korean issue as an impediment to a ratings upgrade, only  

Moody's has adjusted the ratings in response to developments in  

the nuclear issue," Dominique Dwor-Frecaut of Barclays Capital  

wrote in a note to clients.  

"Some FX and equity market weakness has been attributed to  

North Korea's latest announcement, but we expect this to  

subside since, as explained above, we do not see any lasting  

significant consequences from this statement," she said.  

James Malcolm, a currency strategist with Deutsche Bank,  

said the yen's cross rate against the won showed the won was  

not badly hit.  

"Yen/Korea is still below 9.8. The market is not taking it  

(the North Korea declaration) terribly seriously," said  

Malcolm.  

The yen was off its three-month low of 106.86 against the  

dollar after U.S. data showed the country's trade deficit hit a  

record $617.7 billion last year. But it had shed nearly 3  

percent during the week after upbeat comments by Federal  

Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on the U.S. current account  

deficit.  

The won was quoted at 9.78 per yen, near its overnight  

levels of 9.70, which were the highest in over 2 years. It has  

remained stronger than 10 per yen this month, a level markets  

believe Korean authorities and businesses are sensitive to when  

evaluating the won's competitiveness in export markets.  

Deutsche's Malcolm said markets had become less responsive  

over time to North Korea's threats and declarations of nuclear  

ambitions.   


 
    He cited an instance in late 2003, when the won fell beyond
11 per yen.
    "It is so difficult to gauge that kind of tail risk. Over
time the reaction becomes smaller and smaller.
    "I don't see it being a major factor at the moment,"
Malcolm said, referring to the North Korea news.
    Markets were becoming increasingly bullish on South Korea,
he noted, citing reports of improving retail sales and the
surge in stocks to five-year highs on Monday.
    SING DOLLAR - INTERVENTION?
    Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar recovered from two-month
lows near 1.66 reached late on Thursday in offshore trading.
But it stayed on the weaker side of 1.65 a dollar.
    Economists at UBS said the Monetary Authority of Singapore

might intervene to contain volatility in the currency. The MAS  

manages the Sing dollar within a trade-weighted basket of  

currencies of its trading partners.  

As per UBS estimates, the Sing dollar trade-weighted index  

or nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) was now 0.5 percent  

below the mid-point of that secret band, compared with 0.5  

percent above the mid-point around January 19.   


 
    "The MAS not only manages the level of the NEER but also
the volatility within the band," UBS said.
    "As such the risk of MAS intervention to buy Sing dollar
  

has increased even though the Sing dollar NEER is still well  

within the plus/minus 2 percent trading range around the  

mid-point," UBS said.

year after being the second-worst performer in 2004 -- rose 0.4
percent to a 15-month high of 54.67 per dollar.
    The Philippines and Thailand both expect their economies to
grow about 6 percent this year. The booming stock markets in
both countries got a further boost this week when Calpers, the
U.S. pension fund, decided to include Thailand and retain the
Philippines in the list of countries where it plans to invest.

willing to take Asian currency risks and look at the other
catch-up candidates such as the peso," said David Simmonds,
currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore.
    The peso has been helped in the past month by sustained
foreign investment in the country's stock and bond markets and
by signs the government is taking steps to boost its tax
revenue to reduce the fiscal deficit.

five-year high this week and traded near that level on Friday.
    ABN AMRO said in a report that the baht, Asia's second-best

weekend that Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's ruling Thai

interest rates would help stabilise the won against the dollar.

authorities would still sell the won if it strengthened beyond  

9.80 per yen, Simmonds said.

weakening from a five-year high on Thursday, on concern the  

central bank would act against further appreciation.

attractive trading opportunities in Asia was to sell the rupee
for other regional currencies such as the Taiwan dollar     A
  

government decision on Thursday to raise interest rate paid by  

the Employees Provident Fund by one percentage point could add  

to the government subsidies and fiscal deficit, Michael  

Spencer, Deutche's chief economist for Asia, said in a report.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down as China, G7 expectations pared.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were pushed
lower on Monday as markets scaled back their expectations for
an imminent Chinese yuan revaluation and for the upcoming Group
of Seven nations' meeting to put more pressure on the region.
    That happened after fresh comments from Chinese top
officials suggested they were in no hurry to reform the yuan
regime, and the U.S. dollar found support ahead of key data and
a Federal Reserve  policy meeting.
    Traders braced for a volatile week that will end with the
Group of Seven nations' meeting in London on Friday and
Saturday and could see U.S. rates raised by another 25 basis
points.
    U.S. Treasury Undersecretary John Taylor added to the
pressure on regionals with his remarks that there was no need
for the dollar to crash and that the G7 statement would not be
different from the one issued last year in Florida.
  


 Officials
from China, India and other emerging economies have been
invited to talks with the seven industrialised nations.
 
    The Korean won fell from near Friday's 7-year high of 1,023
a dollar to around 1,026.
    The Singapore dollar fell about a quarter percent to 1.64 a
dollar and then trimmed losses. The Thai baht and Indonesian
rupiah were down.
    There was talk of intervention in Singapore and in the
  

Philippines, where the peso barely moved after its rapid 2.3  

percent gains in 3 weeks, helped by a 12 percent rally in  

stocks  

Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said even if  

the G7 called on Asia to share in the adjustment of the massive  

U.S. trade deficit by letting currencies rise, the region would  

not oblige readily.  

"Even if the rhetoric is stepped up on level to  

burden-sharing, I believe it will not be very significant for  

currency moves."  

"What is central for Asian authorities is that economic  

growth in most areas is clearly off the peak. They will  

continue to intervene to protect against sharp appreciation in  

their currencies, thereby trying to keep exports competitive,"  

he said.  

The Philippines released data on Monday showing annual  

gross domestic product grew 6.1 percent in 2004, the quickest  

pace in 15 years. But growth in the last quarter of 2004 was  

disappointing, and analysts warned the currency market was  

probably overestimating potential investment inflows and  

remittances.  

DOLLAR SUPPORTED  

Meanwhile, the see-sawing on the prospects of China  

revaluing its virtually pegged yuan continued, with China's  

deputy central bank governor Li Ruogu dashing expectations by  

saying China did not have the capacity to address global  

economic imbalances and was not willing or able to do it.  

The premium on one-year yuan in non-deliverable forwards  

was down to 3,850 points, pricing in 4.9 percent gains,  

compared with 5.6 percent on Friday.  

Global oil prices fell, with U.S. oil below $47 a barrel,  

after OPEC producers left output unchanged and Iraq's election  

passed without disruption to oil exports.   


 
    "The dollar will bounce this week," said Claudio Piron,
currency strategist with JP Morgan.
    "Oil prices are lower and that should help the dollar. The
Fed FOMC will be delivering 25 basis points and positioning in
Asia is very aggressive," he said.
    YEN-WON CROSS
    Piron said the north Asian currencies would suffer, but
that markets would be divided on whether to buy the won against
the yen. The yen-won cross rate showed the yen at 9.89 won.
    Markets have been torn between the urge to buy the yen-won
  

cross below the 10 mark - which they believe is the highest  

level for the won Korean authorities can tolerate - and the  

belief that South Korea will not intervene heavily, since the  

government is running out of bonds to offset the intervention.  

Traders waited for data on foreign exchange reserves from  

Korea for evidence of intervention in January and confirmation  

of their view that Korea intervened less in order to stabilise  

its bond markets.  

The finance ministry's announcement on Friday that it would  

issue 5 trillion won in fiscal bonds in February, however,  

frustrated some won bulls. That came after Korea said it would  

cut down on the amount of treasuries issued in February.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Yuan talk,  intervention  worry limit moves.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were trapped
in tight ranges on Friday, with the Korean won pushed to a
7-year high, caught between fresh speculation of an imminent
Chinese yuan revaluation and the fear of central bankintervention.
    The Philippine peso bounced off a one-year high of 55.03 a
dollar, the Taiwan dollar was capped at 31.77 a dollar, and the
Singapore dollar was almost a cent off an overnight peak of
1.6280.
    The initial rally was spurred by comments from Yu Yongding,
a Chinese economist and member of the central bank's monetary
policy committee, who told a seminar at the World Economic
Forum in Davos it was time China made the yuan more flexible.
    But the yen and other regionals fell after a Dow Jones
report quoted a Chinese central bank official as saying Yu's
comments were not an official view. Separately, the central
bank reiterated its policy of keeping the yuan stable.
  


    Worries about intervention ahead of next week's Group of
Seven meeting also weighed on the regionals. As well, the
dollar was supported ahead of U.S. jobs and GDP data and a
Federal Reserve policy meeting next week.
    Analysts said they expected more comments from Chinese
officials in coming days, aimed at toning down market
speculation ahead of the G7 meeting on Feb. 4 and 5. China,
India and other emerging economies have been invited to talks
with G7 officials.
    "We believe that the Chinese authorities are keen to
maintain some semblance of two-way risk in the market in
preparation of when they do gradually introduce greater
flexibility," UBS said in a note.
    "As such, it would not be surprising to see official
comments over the coming days that emphasise that a stronger
yuan does not automatically follow a move to greater
flexibility."
    Chinese yuan offshore non-deliverable forwards were
unaffected by the swings in the yen, and priced in a higher
premium on the yuan. Yuan NDFs were dealt at 4,150 points
premium for one-year yuan, pricing in 5.3 percent gains.
    Yu's comments came near the end of a volatile week for yuan
forwards and regional currencies, driven by comments from U.S.,
European and Chinese officials for and against a yuan shift.
    Speculation China would free up the pegged yuan fed through
to the Malaysian ringgit. One-year ringgit NDFs were quoted at
3.695 per dollar, stronger than the peg level at 3.8.
    WON RISES
    The Korean won rose to a fresh seven-year peak near 1,023 a
dollar, continuing to receive support from the view that it
would be boosted by turbulence in the bond markets caused by
worries over issuance.
    That stems from the view the Bank of Korea would intervene
less to buy dollars if their capacity to issue bonds to offset
that intervention was reduced.
    But David Simmonds, markets strategist with Royal Bank of
Scotland, said recent measures by Korean authorities did not
mean the risks of intervention were lower.
    The won, Asia's best performer in 2004, was at its highest
since late 2000 in trade-weighted terms, Simmonds said. He said
the won would not outperform its trading partners but would
gradually move up to 1,000 per dollar in coming months.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late As Yuan Talk Continues To Shift
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was relatively steady against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Friday as speculation over a possible move by China to a flexible foreign exchange regime continued to swing back and forth.  

The yield curve of Singapore government bonds steepened, in line with Thursday's steepening of the U.S. Treasury yield curve, dealers said.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6341, almost unchanged from S$1.6344 late in Asia Thursday. It traded between S$1.6278 and S$1.6347 intraday.  

In the run-up to the Feb. 4-5 meeting of finance officials from the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations, expectations that China might adopt a more flexible currency have seesawed almost every day as an increasing number of Chinese officials join the chorus of commenting on the nation's foreign exchange policy.  

People's Bank of China's monetary policy committee member Yu Yongding said Thursday that now is the time for the central bank to revalue the Chinese yuan.  

"Now is the time to revalue," Yu told journalists at the World Economic Forum after a dinner discussion on the dollar's weakness. "We need more flexibility. That means revaluation."  

Yu's remarks prompted speculators to dump U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars, pushing the U.S. unit as low as S$1.6278 early in Friday's Asian session, dealers said.  

But China's central bank soon doused speculation of an imminent revaluation of the yuan, saying Friday that Yu's comments don't represent Beijing's view on the matter.  

"(Yu Yongding's) remarks are only his personal view, and the opinions of an academic. They do not represent the central bank's policy," an official in the PBOC's information office told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Yu is an academic adviser to the PBOC's monetary policy committee. Though he isn't a government official, Yu advises the central bank on its policies.  

The PBOC's clarification of Yu's comments, along with suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, boosted the U.S. currency as high as S$1.6347 in the morning, traders said, adding that the MAS was rumored to have bought a small amount of U.S. dollars around the S$1.6310 level.  

The rest of Friday's global session could see more volatile trading in the U.S. dollar against other currencies, including the Singapore dollar, especially given the 1330 GMT release of U.S. advance fourth-quarter gross domestic product data.  

The median estimate of 20 economists surveyed Monday by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for a 3.6% annual rate of GDP growth with a 2.0% rate of increase for the chain-weighted price index.
