title: Singapore  Dlr Dn Late Amid Concerns MAS Might  Intervene
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged lower against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Tuesday, pressured by speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to prevent a sharp slide of the U.S. unit.  

The yield curve for Singapore government bonds flattened slightly, in tandem with Monday's flattening of the U.S. Treasurys yield curve, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6341, slightly up from S$1.6326 late in Asia Monday. It traded between S$1.6318 and S$1.6349 intraday.  

After rising as high as S$1.6345 on broad-based U.S. dollar strength early in the session, the U.S. currency soon came under downward pressure from various players looking to rebuild short positions against the local dollar ahead of major upcoming events such as the weekend elections in Iraq.  

The U.S. dollar was also dragged lower against the Singapore unit by speculator-led selling of euros for Singapore dollars after European policy-makers continued to make veiled calls on Asian countries to adopt a more flexible foreign exchange rate stance.  

Late Monday, French Finance Minister Herve Gaymard said the Feb. 4-5 meeting of G-7 finance ministers will provide a necessary forum for commitments to correct fluctuations in currency rates.  

"In Europe we're aware of the need to boost the growth potential, while the U.S. is well aware of the need to act on its deficit and Asia is conscious of a need for more flexibility," Gaymard said at a Franco-German summit of ministers and central bankers.  

Although the U.S. dollar fell as low as S$1.6318 at midday, it later rebounded to as high as S$1.6349 on mild short-covering spurred by speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to prevent a sharp slide of the U.S. unit below the psychologically important S$1.6300 level, dealers said.  

While the overall outlook for the U.S. dollar against the Singapore currency still appears weak, based on technical analysis, the downward momentum isn't strong and the solid support at S$1.6275 will likely hold for the global day, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"In other words, expect another down-move but this should be followed by a rebound later on," UOB said.  

As a short-term trading plan, UOB recommends buying the U.S. currency at S$1.6300 and placing stop-loss orders below S$1.6275, in anticipation of a rise to S$1.6360.

title: Singapore  Dlr Down Late On Suspected MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell moderately in Asia late Thursday as suspected U.S. dollar buying by the Monetary Authority of Singapore overwhelmed heavy selling of the U.S. currency by U.S. hedge funds.  

Yields on Singapore government bonds were lower in the front end than in the rest of the curve, leading to curve steepening, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6380, up from S$1.6335 late in Asia Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6299 and S$1.6392 intraday.  

Increased speculation that China may revalue the yuan next month and renewed expectations that Malaysia could change the ringgit peg this year prompted U.S. funds to sell the U.S. dollar down to as low as S$1.6299 early in the session, dealers said.  

Speculation on the revaluation of the yuan was fueled by a news article citing a report by consultancy firm Medley Global Advisors that China might revalue the yuan by up to 5% after the weeklong Lunar New Year holiday, which starts Feb. 9, dealers added.  

Recently, U.S. and European policy-makers have increasingly called on Asian nations, and China in particular, to share more of the burden of the U.S. dollar's long-term weakness, sparking expectations that the Group of Seven major industrialized nations will pressure China to shift to a more flexible foreign exchange regime at the G7 meeting of finance officials Feb. 4-5.  

Moreover, Malaysia's former Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad was quoted by national news agency Bernama as saying late Wednesday that Malaysia's ringgit peg, which has been in place for more than six years, should be reviewed as the weak U.S. dollar has made imports more expensive than they should be.  

The peg of 3.80 ringgit to the U.S. currency has served the economy well since its introduction in September 1998, although some analysts say the U.S. dollar's sharp fall in recent months and expectations of a revaluation of the yuan imply the ringgit is undervalued.  

Thursday, Malaysian Prime Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi and central bank Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz reassured markets that no change to the ringgit peg was imminent.  

Although U.S. funds used the two news reports as reasons to sell U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars throughout the session, traders said the MAS apparently stepped into the market at least twice to prop up the ailing U.S. currency against the local dollar, eventually lifting the U.S. unit as high as S$1.6392 in the afternoon.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell moderately in Asia late Thursday as suspected U.S. dollar buying by the Monetary Authority of Singapore overwhelmed heavy selling of the U.S. currency by U.S. hedge funds.

Increased speculation that China may revalue the yuan next month and renewed expectations that Malaysia could change the ringgit peg this year prompted U.S. funds to sell the U.S. dollar down to as low as S$1.6299 early in the session, dealers said.  

Speculation on the revaluation of the yuan was fueled by a news article citing a report by consultancy firm Medley Global Advisors that China might revalue the yuan by up to 5% after the weeklong Lunar New Year holiday, which starts Feb. 9, dealers added.  

Recently, U.S. and European policy-makers have increasingly called on Asian nations, and China in particular, to share more of the burden of the U.S. dollar's long-term weakness, sparking expectations that the Group of Seven major industrialized nations will pressure China to shift to a more flexible foreign exchange regime at the G7 meeting of finance officials Feb. 4-5.

currencies lower on Tuesday on worries that U.S. capital

officials could ease market concerns about the U.S. dollar's
prospects.
    The Taiwan dollar lost a quarter of a percent and the
Singapore dollar, Indian rupee and the rupiah each lost around
a fifth of a percent, following the lead of the yen, which
weakened almost a percent from Monday's five-year high against
the dollar.
    U.S. capital inflow figures for November are due at 1400
GMT on Tuesday. A reading close to the record U.S. trade
deficit of $60.3 billion for November would alleviate some
worries that the United States is unable to plug its record
current account deficit.
    "Stronger-than-expected net inflows may lend the dollar a
bit of support against the Asian currencies," said David
Simmonds, a currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in
Singapore.
  


    Traders will monitor comments from four U.S. Federal
Reserve officials, due to speak on Tuesday, for signals that
U.S. interest rates might rise faster than expected.
    Royal Bank of Scotland expects the U.S. central bank to

    "The Fed is sounding hawkish," said Simmonds. "Asia would

behind the inflation curve and starts tightening much harder.
We're not there yet."
    INTERVENTION FEAR

after several had reached multi-year highs on Monday. South
Korea's won traded at a seven-year high on Monday.
    Analysts say central banks in South Korea, Taiwan,

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down on yen,  intervention .
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Despite the renewed pressure
from western policy makers for Asian currencies to rise, the
regionals fell on Friday owing to a weaker Japanese yen and the
fear of central bank intervention.
    The Singapore dollar        suffered the heaviest losses,
retreating nearly 2 cents from a fresh six-year peak of 1.6235
struck overnight on talk that the Monetary Authority of
Singapore was intervening through local banks.
    The Korean won                   fell over half a percent,
coming off an offshore 7-year high of 1,032.7, as the yen too
ceded some ground to the dollar despite gaining against the
euro.
    The Indonesian rupiah        was also a loser, pushed below
Thursday's one-month high by scepticism over the benefits of
debt relief granted by the Paris Club of creditors.
    The U.S.
  


 dollar rallied against the euro overnight after
European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet said the
consensus within the Group of Seven nations was for an orderly
appreciation in Asian emerging-market currencies.
    Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Paul Jenkins and New
York Fed President Timothy Geithner also urged exchange rate
flexibility in Asia.
    Ahead of a G7 meeting in the first week of February, many
analysts were expecting further rhetoric for Asia to take up
its share of a broad dollar downtrend, aimed at helping correct
a record U.S. trade deficit.
    Ray Farris, markets strategist with CSFB, said there was
little to suggest that the United States would make any major
statements on foreign exchange at the G7 and that U.S.
authorities appeared to prefer markets to determine currency
levels.
 
    Still, he said, "There may very well be some G7-related
pressure on Asia."
    "It is unlikely that China will alter its exchange rate
regime simply because of criticism or pressure from G7," Farris
said.
    Economists at UBS also said that the Asian authorities
would now begin to fret about further currency gains.
    "The end game for the U.S. dollar does indeed require the
  

dollar to fall more against Asian currencies in order to help  

the greenback fall on a broad trade-weighted basis," UBS said  

in a note.  

"But we are not convinced that Asian policy makers are  

willing at this stage to tolerate much stronger currencies from  

here, any more than they were following last February's G7."  

RUPIAH RETREATS  

The rupiah's decline did not surprise many analysts. It  

comes after a 2.4 percent rise in a week, driven by  

expectations of aid inflows after the tsunami and the debt  

moratorium.  

The club agreed to an initial three-month debt moratorium  

for th countries hit by the disaster and said it could be  

extended.   


 
    Indonesian chief economics minister Aburizal Bakrie said it
would be good if the country got a year's moratorium.
    JP Morgan's strategist Caludio Piron said in a note the
risk was that only the immediate three-month relief would
materialize.
    "While near-term sentiment could drive further rupiah
gains, the eventual agreement is not expected to turn
underlying balance of payments trends," he said.
    "The potential debt relief compares unfavorably to the $21
billion of private and public external debt servicing due for
the country this year," he said.
    Citigroup's strategist Cliff Tan said the rupiah might have
  

over-reacted to the debt relief plans, given that Indonesia was  

getting only some time to pay its debt, not money. Also,  

rebuilding the tsunami-struck areas would require future  

imports, Tan said.

title: ANALYSIS-Capital curbs,  intervention  stifle Asia  FX  market
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Corporate demand for deep, liquid currency markets is rising in Asia, but such thirst will hardly be slaked unless governments relax capital controls and resist the urge to control exchange rates through intervention.  

The corporate pressure is adding to the political pressure from western nations for Asian governments to relax capital controls and foreign exchange policies to help resolve global economic imbalances.  

However, few analysts expect change to occur quickly even as the International Monetary Fund adopts a new role of international currency policeman.  

Huw McKay, senior economist at Westpac Bank, believes more Asian countries will liberalise capital accounts as they benefit from strong growth and improving banking systems, but change will be gradual.  

Ultimately, the foreign exchange market would be a clear winner, he said.  

"Turnover in foreign exchange market will be a high beta respondent to liberalisation of Asia's international financial arrangements," he wrote in a recent research report.  

His figures show trade in the emerging currencies of Asia is just a fraction of the region's contribution to global output, underlining the depth of capital controls.  

But equally, Asia runs large trade and current account surpluses, which regional exporters want to hedge.  

Daily foreign exchange turnover in seven countries -- China, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, South Korea -- currently amounts to just $36 billion, McKay says, based on data from the Bank for International Settlements.  

That is less than 2 percent of turnover in the $2-trillion-per-day global currency market, yet the region generates 26 percent of world economic output.  

"Pent-up demand for freer access to deeper foreign exchange markets in Asia is in evidence. That predicts a rapid rate of catch-up for turnover once the 'supply side' policy adjustment process begins in earnest," McKay said, referring to capital account liberalisation.  

Illustrating the demand for access to more open markets, Chinese banks were active participants in the offshore yuan non-deliverable forwards market until the government imposed a ban in October because it wants to develop its domestic markets.  

GRADUAL REFORMS  

China revalued the yuan by 2.1 percent in July 2005 and has since introduced a string of steps to help firms hedge risk, but the markets are small, limiting the volume of trade.  

South Korea and Taiwan have relaxed capital controls. The latest major policy initiative has come from India with a five-year plan for fuller capital account convertibility.  

China has pledged to make the yuan <CNY=CFXS> fully convertible, though it has yet to commit to a firm timetable.  

In addition, most Asian countries have yet to dismantle capital curbs imposed in the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis to deter currency speculators, although policy makers have shifted the focus to restricting capital inflows, rather than capital flight.  

Asian countries are reluctant to relax capital flows partly because of their lopsided economies that rely on exports for growth in the absence of strong domestic consumption.  

That has left currencies under pressure to appreciate as consistent trade surpluses have produced around $3 trillion in foreign currency reserves across Asia, including Japan's holdings.  

It has also drawn criticism from the West, led by the United States, who want Asian currencies to rise at a faster pace to help reduce trade imbalances.  

INTERVENTION

But Asian governments fear that allowing their currencies to rise too fast could hurt exports and weaken their economies, so they intervene in the foreign exchange market to limit currency gains.  

In Thailand, where the baht <THB=> has risen 14 percent so far this year against the dollar, central bank chief Tarisa Watanagase said on Wednesday that the bank had acted to slow the baht's rise and would keep monitoring the currency.  

Dealers estimate South Korean authorities spent $1 billion on Wednesday to curb the won's <KRW=> strength. It wasn't the first time the government had intervened this year.  

"Traditionally, Asian countries always want to maintain stable exchange rates. Whenever there is a surge in volatility in currencies, authorities step in and intervene," said Wang Qing, senior currency strategist at Bank of America.  

"Little volatility can be expected if governments don't want to nurture foreign exchange markets and there is little demand for currency derivatives if there is no volatility," he said.  

Tim Condon, economist at ING, said it would take time for Asian countries to remove their capital restrictions due partly to their less developed capital markets, despite the changing economic landscape since the Asian financial crisis.  

"I think it's just a matter of capital market development and they will get around with it eventually, but they have to get over the strong desire to limit fluctuations in the currency."  

Analysts say any shift in policies would hinge on Asian countries' willingness to change their export-led growth model.  

"Ultimately, any shift in policies hinge on whether the countries are willing to change their export-led growth model. But but right now, they haven't fully embraced such changes," said Wang at Bank of America.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher despite  intervention  worries
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose against the dollar on Thursday, buoyed by economic fundamentals justifying their underlying strength, despite lingering market concerns about possible central bank intervention.  

But a spike in crude oil prices capped gains in Asian currencies, while traders continued to be wary of regional central banks intervening to rein in their currencies.  

Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas, said she remained bullish about the near-term strength of most Asian currencies because of funds flowing into Asian equity markets.  

"It looks likely a quite good picture for Asian currencies. The only ones seeing less inflows are the Philippines and Indonesia because they have been front-runners, so there is a bit of consolidation as markets move from the high-yielder to the laggard," she said.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a fresh nine-year high of 1.5421 against the U.S. dollar before retreating to 1.5440, while the South Korean won <KRW=> reversed earlier losses to hit around 929 per dollar, slightly off a nine-year high this week of 925.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> hit 32.42 per U.S. dollar, the highest level in 4-½ months as exporters tried to offload their dollar holdings.  

"Sentiment is quite firm and when you see price action on the Korean won, where everyday you get comments on currency strength, it is testiment to strength in local currencies," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Bank.  

RUNNING AHEAD  

The Thai baht <THB=> gained about a third of a percent versus the dollar to 36 per dollar, hitting its strongest level in almost eight years.  

"The Bank of Thailand will not resist a lower dollar/baht if the broad global trend is for a lower dollar," said Philip Wee, DBS Bank currency strategist.  

But based on current euro/dollar and dollar/yen levels, the baht should be closer to 36.40 per dollar, he said. The euro <EUR=> was trading around $1.3145, having come off Wednesday's 20-month highs, while the yen weakened to 116.50 per dollar.  

"This sort of tells you why Bank of Thailand is uncomfortable that the baht strength may have run ahead of itself," he said.  

The Bank of Thailand (BOT) has been intervening both verbally and by buying dollars this week, traders said.  

The BOT said on Wednesday the baht had risen too fast and its rise was not justified by fundamentals. On Monday it had said it would ask the finance ministry to allow exporters to hold their overseas receipts for up to 15 days instead of the seven-day limit now in place.  

Shahab Jalinoos of ABN AMRO Bank said baht had risen this year on higher baht interest rates and the relative cheapness of Thai stocks. The currency has gained about 14 percent so far this year despite months of political uncertainty that culminated in a bloodless coup in September.  

The strength of the trade account, which has propelled Thailand's current account to swing into surplus in the later half of this year, was also behind the baht's rally, he said.  

"Until now, strong global demand has overwhelmed the effect of baht strength, allowing exports growth to remain solid.  

"If the data show more evidence that this is still the case, we see room for further baht gains through 36.00 towards 35.50, given that the central bank has already thrown in the towel on its ability to stop this trend," Jalinoos said in a note to clients. title: Emerging  FX -Asia edges down as stocks, oil weigh
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies edged down against the dollar on Tuesday, undermined by a sell-off in equities, a rise in oil prices and wariness about central bank intervention to rein in local currency strength.  

U.S. equities fell sharply on Monday, hurt by doubts over holiday spending after a disappointing sales estimate from Wal-Mart Stores Inc. . A 1.36 percent fall in the broad S&P 500 index <.SPX> was the biggest since early June.  

Latin American markets, tracking Wall Street, also suffered heavy losses with the Brazilian real <BRBY> falling 1 percent.  

This in turn hurt Asia's high-yielding currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Philippine peso <PHP=>, and led to their underperformance within the region.  

"Obviously the overnight equity market losses have restrained Asian currencies and introduced two-way risk into the market," said Claudio Piron, a currency strategist at JPMorgan.  

The rupiah shed almost 0.6 percent to 9,188 per dollar, its weakest in nearly two weeks, and the peso fell to 49.92 per dollar -- down 0.6 percent from Monday's 4-1/2-year highs.  

"The tension in Latin American markets yesterday and the sharp fall in the Dow Jones is spilling over," said a Manila trader.  

Asian shares were broadly lower, with the MSCI's broadest index of shares <.MSCIAPJ> in the region excluding Japan, down about 1.6 percent by 0801 GMT.  

Oil prices, meanwhile, extended gains above $60 a barrel <CLc1>, weighing on local currencies.  

Some analysts pointed to a fall in the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index <.VIX>, or VIX, as a bearish signal for regional markets.  

The VIX, often called Wall Street's fear gauge, on Monday jumped more than 13 percent to 12.23 in its biggest one-day percentage surge since mid-July when record oil prices were pushing stock prices around.  

"The VIX index has broken to new levels, so the external environment suggests Asian currency appreciation may encounter some bumps," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

JPMorgan's Piron said U.S. economic data and a speech by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on the economic outlook later on Tuesday could provide markets with fresh direction.  

Elsewhere, the South Korean won <KRW=> hovered around 930.70 per dollar, off the previous day's nine-year highs, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> was up a touch at about 32.65 to the U.S. dollar -- but down about 0.4 percent from three-month peaks, touched in early trade.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was quoted at about 1.5518 to the U.S. dollar, little changed from levels traded late in Asia on Monday, and off a nine-year peak struck last week at 1.5467.  

"The market is calm but I think it is wary about intervention," said a Singapore dollar trader. "But the trend is bearish U.S. dollar."

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  worries cap Asian  currencies
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Monday as the dollar took a beating against the euro and yen, but wariness about central bank intervention to limit local currency strength dampened the bullish sentiment slightly.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=> was quoted at its highest level in more than nine years at 925 per dollar, before paring gains on suspected dollar-buying intervention by Korea's central bank.  

 The Bank of Thailand said the baht's rise had been too fast and it might allow exporters to hold dollars for up to 15 days, longer than the current 7-day limit. The baht <THB=> was capped at about 36.38 per dollar, a hair's breadth away from 7-1/2-year highs of 36.36 struck earlier this month.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> gained almost 0.7 percent to 32.62 to the U.S. dollar, its highest since mid-August, before paring some gains. The Philippine peso <PHP=> ended local trade off a fresh 4-1/2-year high at 49.60 per dollar.  

 "Dollar weakness pressure was felt first in Asia," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist with Deutsche Bank.  

 But intervention by the regional central banks had reined the Asian currencies in, he said.  

 "Now, the G10 currencies have taken up the torch, and emerging Asia is lagging."  

 The euro hit a 20-month peak at about $1.3180 <EUR=> on electronic trading platform EBS and the dollar fell to a three-month low at 115.40 yen <JPY=> on Monday.  

 Although the dollar subsequently clawed back some ground against the majors, analysts suggested the Asian rally would continue even if they had underperformed so far.  

 "The fundamental picture continues to shift in favour of Asian currencies gaining in strength and it would be reasonable to expect local central banks to intervene," said Richard Yetsenga, a currency strategist at HSBC in Hong Kong.  

 "But Asian currencies have underperformed the move in the majors versus the dollar."  

 Expectations for further euro zone interest rate increases have bolstered the euro. The dollar, in general, has also been hurt by position adjusting and ongoing talk of central banks diversifying their foreign exchange reserves away from the U.S. currency.  

 Some traders said central bank intervention may be limited in the face of a strong dollar downtrend.  

 "They (the central banks) will come in on and off, but I don't think they will be too aggressive because dollar sentiment is very bearish," said a Singapore dollar trader.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, meanwhile, retreated to 1.5515/25 per U.S. dollar, up about 0.15 percent from levels traded late on Friday but off a nine-year high hit last week at 1.5467.  

 Elsewhere, the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> firmed to 7.8410 to the dollar, its strongest level since the July 2005 revaluation and analysts continued to expect a further pick-up in gains.  

 "Dollar/yuan is now under major pressure to move lower quickly given the influence of euro/dollar and dollar/yen," ABN AMRO currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell considerably against the U.S. dollar in afternoon trades in Asia Friday on rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

"The market is quite cautious of the downside of USD/SGD next week with the presence of the official bid," a local forex strategist said. "The buying is more frequent than historically."  

The U.S. dollar, which was trading below S$1.5500 before the rumored intervention, pulled up to S$1.5582 around 0452 GMT.  

The MAS' key monetary policy tool is managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band. It doesn't traditionally comment on any market intervention.  

"If the pace of decline of the U.S. dollar is fast again next week to uncomfortable levels, the MAS may intervene again," BNP Paribas forex strategist Thio Chin Loo said.  

She predicts that the greenback will continue to be soft next week.  

"With more U.S. data such as October home salesand a lot of speeches by Fed officials upcoming, the market is going to price in interest rate cuts by the Fed," she said. This is because the data are supposed to signal a weak housing market.  

The first strategist didn't rule out the possibility of the U.S. dollar revisiting this week's low of S$1.5481 if it continues to be bearish against the yen.  

Thio said there isn't much support for the U.S. unit until S$1.5400, and the next level of support would be at S$1.5250.  

The Singapore bond curve was flat.  

"A local bank has been selling its two-year bonds since yesterday, while the long end is still in demand," a local bank dealer said. "The yield curve will likely remain flat next week as there are still consistent offers and bids at the respective ends of the curve."  

The two-year bond rose on persistent demand despite selling by the local bank.  

U.S. October home sales data next week will influence local bonds since participants have no other news to track, another local bank dealer said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  currencies  retreat on  intervention  fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies fell on Friday, giving up some of Thursday's stellar gains amid worries about central bank intervention to rein in currency strength.  

Dealers suspected that intervention played a hand in falls in the Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Indian rupee <INR=IN>, while South Korea reiterated its warnings against a rising won <KRW=>.  

Rhee Gwang-ju, head of the Bank of Korea's international department, said the central bank was closely watching currency market movements.  

"It is more to do with intervention concerns and maybe a bit of position squaring," said Royal Bank of Scotland currency strategist Ben Simpfendorfer, referring to the general weakness.  

The Singapore dollar eased to 1.5581 per U.S. dollar, down about half a percent from Thursday's nine-year high at 1.5467, while the Indian rupee fell a similar amount to 44.95 per dollar.  

"They have been in pretty heavily today," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the country's central bank.  

The won shed about a 0.25 percent to almost 933 per dollar, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> eased to 49.80 to the dollar -- down about a third of a percent from Thursday's 4-½ year high.  

Strong gains in the yen versus the dollar <JPY=> late in the Asian day helped some regional currencies trim losses, but most of them remained in negative territory.  

Some traders in Europe were focusing on reports of comments made by Wu Xiaoling, vice governor of the People's Bank of China, that the value of east Asian currency reserves were at risk from their exposure to the U.S. dollar.  

Dealers said the comments had had little impact on Asian markets.  

Most regional currencies had racked up firm gains on Thursday as position adjusting ahead of holidays in the United States and Japan triggered a broad sell-off in the U.S. dollar.  

"We don't think the move in Asian currencies is sustainable said Jimmy Koh, a currency strategist at United Overseas Bank.  

"They will be driven by the majors and unless we see signs of Japanese interest rates rising, dollar/yen is unlikely to fall sharply."  

DIFFERING VIEWS Others, however, took a different view, saying there was scope for further currency gains.  

"Although the Fed is talking a bit more hawkishly, we've already got an eye on next year and potential BOJ tightening and yen strength," said Simpfendorfer at Royal Bank of Scotland.  

"With that in mind, you might expect markets to be looking for reasons to extend the Asian rally but there is not a huge amount of conviction there at the moment."  

The Thai baht <THB=> was little moved at about 36.55 per dollar, drawing some support from news that martial law in Thailand could be lifted in most areas by the end of the year.  

General Sonthi Boonyaratglin, who led a military coup that overthrew Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra on Sept. 19, said in an interview with CNN television aired on Friday that he wanted a return to normal as soon as possible.  

"I think it is positive for the baht, as it is good to think that everything here is returning to a normal situation," said a Bangkok trader. "But the baht will still be driven by the capital flows and also the U.S. dollar trend."  

Dealers in Malaysia turned their attention to an interest rate decision from the country's central bank later on Friday.  

The central bank is expected to keep its overnight policy rate at 3.50 percent, especially after data this week showed Malaysia's consumer prices in October rose 3.1 percent from a year earlier -- the slowest increase since July 2005.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rallies, central banks watch closely
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rallied on Thursday, with the Singapore dollar hitting a nine-year high and the Philippine peso touching a 4-1/2-year peak, in reaction to a broad sell-off in the U.S. currency overnight.  

Renewed strength in local currencies triggered a wave of comments from officials. South Korea warned against won strength and the Thai central bank said it may relax its capital controls further to help ease upward pressure on the baht.  

Central bank intervention to curb currency strength was suspected in South Korea and India.  

Trade was generally subdued with U.S. and Japanese markets closed for a holiday. But with the dollar taking a beating overnight as investors adjusted positions ahead of the break, Asia's currency markets held their firm tone.  

"Over the last few weeks we have seen bouts of intervention on some currencies, while some central banks have said they are not concerned about currency strength," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank.  

"But the bias is for further Asian currency strength and we have had a major move in the dollar in the last 24 hours, albeit on thin liquidity."  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose to 44.66 to the dollar, its highest level in about 4-½ years, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> extended Wednesday's gains to a new nine-year high of about 1.5520 per U.S. dollar.  

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> rose to 7.8575 per dollar, the strongest since its July 2005 revaluation, while the Japanese yen <JPY=> was at 116.58 per dollar, up about 0.75 percent from late Wednesday's levels in Asia.  

SPOTLIGHT ON WON  

The South Korean won <KRW=> added as much as 0.5 percent to about 929.20 per dollar -- its highest in just over 1-½ weeks.  

It was supported by a South Korean central bank decision on Thursday to raise reserve requirements on short-term deposits.  

The chief foreign exchange official at South Korea's central bank warned the bank would take steps whenever necessary to stabilise the currency market, adding the won had overshot fair value.  

"It is more a case of the authorities wanting not only just to stem won strength because of concerns about exporters but also because it is starting to detect that speculative flows are behind won gains," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

The won by some measures was still at record highs, raising concerns about export competitiveness, Tan said.  

The won gapped higher at Thursday's opening -- a sign of market strength, according to technical analysts.  

In Singapore, dealers said they did not suspect the central bank of intervening to cap gains in the Singapore dollar despite market wariness in early trade about such action.  

A trader in Manila said it also appeared that the Philippine central bank had stayed away from the market as weakness in local stocks helped limit the peso's rally.

title: DATA VIEW: Singapore Oct CPI Contained; MAS Could Loosen
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's consumer price inflation stayed beneath the government's target range last month, which, analysts said, gives the central bank room to adopt a looser policy in the event of an unwelcome economic slowdown.  

The consumer price index rose 0.4% from a year earlier, holding steady with the rate of increase in September, the government said Thursday. The rise was slightly higher than the average forecast of 0.3% in a Dow Jones Newswires poll.  

The very low level of inflation could signal a softer economy in the months ahead, but analysts say the central bank is well positioned to respond if the risk of deflation increases or output growth drops sharply.  

"If it looked like we were going down toward zero inflation, more accommodative policy could be an option," David Cohen, an economist at Action Economics, said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, and is believed to intervene in the foreign exchange market to keep the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

It has a target range for inflation of 1% to 2% this year, and 0.5% to 1.5% next year.  

Though Cohen doesn't expect a policy shift to be "imminent", he said that a more accommodative policy would imply a Singapore dollar that holds steady versus a basket of currencies.  

"They might say that (the Singapore dollar) should stay at a flat level," he said.  

DBS strategist Philip Wee said he expects the current policy to remain in place, but even a switch to looser policy wouldn't preclude further weakening of the U.S. dollar.  

"If the U.S. dollar stays heavy, it could still decline (against the Singapore dollar), but the decline would be slower," Wee said.  

He estimates that the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is 0.9% above the central bank's undisclosed policy band midpoint.  

Since the beginning of this year, the Singapore dollar has appreciated about 7% against the U.S. dollar, which began the year around S$1.6620 and is now at S$1.5525.  

The stronger local currency has helped shield Singapore against external price pressures, the main source of inflation in the city-state.  

Among all sources of inflation, Cohen expects oil to be the central bank's main focus in the months ahead.  

"A lot will depend on oil prices," he said.  

After rising to a high of around $78 in July, Nymex crude is now trading below $60 a barrel.  

In October, the consumer price index also rose 0.4% from September when adjusted for seasonal variations, just above a poll forecast of 0.3%.  

Lower fuel costs eased price pressures in the transport and communications sector. The inflation sub-index for the sector fell 1.9% from a year earlier.  

A possible sales tax increase next year could add to domestic price pressures, but Cohen still expects inflation to be tame.  

"The tax incrase could add maybe 0.5%...and the full-year rate would be 1.5% in 2007," he said.  

Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong recently announced plans to increase the tax on goods and services to 7% from 5% now.  

Among other key components, housing costs, which make up 21% of the index, gained 1.5% from a year earlier, and rose 0.7% from September due to higher electricity tariffs.  

The cost of food, which is the biggest component in the index with a 23% weighting, climbed 1.5% from a year earlier and 0.1% from September.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar traded steady in Asian trade Tuesday, ahead of holidays in the U.S. and Japan on Thursday.  

"The pair's going to be trading in tight range this week," said a foreign bank dealer. "Once it breaks the S$1.5550 support level, the pair may go down all the way. But traders must be wary of intervention by MAS."  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore's key monetary policy tool is managing of the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

With a lack of news until the end of the year, "traders would be most concerned with the yen-carry trades," said a local bank market strategist.  

Under yen-carry trade transactions, hedge funds and other investors borrow funds cheaply, exploiting low Japanese interest rates, and sell yen to invest in higher-yield financial instruments overseas for a profit.  

The Bank of Japan in mid-July ended its zero-interest-rate policy and raised its key call rate to 0.25%. BOJ Governor Toshihiko Fukui Friday downplayed the chance of an imminent rate hike, saying that the possibility of an interest rate hike in December isn't high.  

"If there's another interest rate hike in Japan, it would also encourage more traders to stay short dollar against the Asian currencies till the end of the year," the strategist said.  

In the Singapore bonds market, there was aggressive selling in the two-year bonds to take advantage of higher yields offered by the three-month treasury bills.  

But, bond trading is "likely to remain range-bound for the rest of the month," said one local bank dealer. "The U.S. data are very mixed; there's strong employment, weak housing data, and so on. The market is still trying to get the whole picture."

title: Emerging  FX -Philippine peso bucks Asian weakness
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on Friday on further unwinding of positions by traders fearing more central bank intervention and on the dollar's strength despite the softness in U.S. inflation data.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> was the biggest loser, shedding nearly 0.4 percent as it hit a one-week trough of 36.60 per dollar.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> was the lone exception to the weakness, as a heavy bunch of export earnings forced it to rally 0.2 percent to around 49.96 per dollar.  

 "When spot failed to go above 50.20 yesterday, a lot of exporters placed orders to sell," said one Manila-based trader, referring to the peso's rally.  

 Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the peso has traditionally been driven more by flows from trade transactions.  

 "So it is less likely to participate in any knee-jerk moves that, for example, the Sing dollar and Korean won have when broad dollar sentiment changes," he said.  

 But this week's decline in the Asian currencies has raised worries about whether this is merely a result of intervention or the start of a bigger sell-off of emerging markets.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> lost a quarter of a percent to hit a low of 1.5633 per U.S. dollar, taking losses from 9-year highs struck this week to half a percent and prompting speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have intervened, as several other central banks did this week.  

 The Bank of Thailand was suspected of intervening to rein in the baht after it hit its strongest level in nearly seven years on Tuesday. The Reserve Bank of India and the Bank of Korea were also spotted buying dollars to halt the appreciation in their respective currencies, the rupee <INR=IN> and the won <KRW=>.  

 The won was slightly weaker at 938 per dollar on the day, but strong dollar earnings for Korean shipmakers and electronics exporters had helped lift it from lows near 944 on Thursday.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> fell a quarter of a percent on Friday.  Analysts at UBS said selling of Asian currencies was spurred not just by intervention fears but by warnings from central banks in New Zealand and Japan on the heavy accumulation of carry trades.  

 The yen and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> have been the favoured funding vehicles in Asia for carry trades, which involve borrowing low-yielding currencies to invest in high-yielding assets.  

 "The combination of these has contributed to position squaring particularly in high-yielding Asian currencies," UBS said.  


 "The high-yielding currencies -- Indonesian rupiah,
Philippine peso, Korean won, Indian rupee -- weakened
  

significantly while the lower-yielding currencies such as the
Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar have largely remained
resilient."  

 The yen <JPY=> was trading near its weakest level this
week, changing hands around 118.33/35 per dollar, as markets
discounted tame U.S. inflation data to focus on a likely soft
landing for the U.S. economy and steady U.S. rates for a
while.

title: Emerging  FX -S.Korean won recovers, other Asians steady
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The South Korean won recovered some ground it had lost to the dollar over the past couple of days, helped by a large bout of dollar inflows on Thursday for local businesses and by the absence of central bank intervention.  

 Other Asian currencies also stabilised as markets waited for U.S. consumer prices data to give them a sense of direction for Federal Reserve policy.  

 The Japanese yen <JPY=> rallied briefly to 117.75 per dollar on a report that China's central bank had been buying yen for its reserves but soon gave up those gains, pushing the dollar to levels near 118 yen traded overnight after the Fed said in minutes of its October meeting that reducing inflation was its biggest concern.  

 Asian currencies, many of which had hit multi-month and multi-year highs at the start of this week, slipped in early deals but stabilised subsequently.  

 After hitting a six-month high of 927.8 per dollar on Monday, the won <KRW=> had gradually lost ground this week, falling earlier on Thursday to around 944 per dollar, its weakest level since late October.  

 However, by 0730 GMT, it had rebounded slightly to be quoted around 937 per dollar.  

 "The upside in dollar/won changed to downside as the yen rose and offshore markets sold dollars," said Yun Jin Ko, a dealer with Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

 "Exporters of ships and electronics joined in," she said.  

 Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist said a surge in export orders for Korean manufacturers of ships, oil platforms and power plants had created a steady stream of strong foreign exchange earnings, putting pressure on the won to appreciate.  

 "The absence of the Bank of Korea makes it easier for spot to fall," he said.  

 Fearing rapid and volatile appreciation in their currencies, central banks in South Korea, Thailand and India are suspected of having sold their currencies this week. Traders estimated Bank of Korea had bought about $1.5 billion on Monday and Tuesday.  

 Baig said only a few exporters seemed to be testing the Bank of Korea's tolerance.  

  "Not all segments of the market play this cat and mouse game with BOK. Exporters generally just want a good level to sell," he said.  

 WON, RUPEE CAPPED?  

 Gerrard Katz, head of currency trading for North Asia at Standard Chartered Bank, said this stream of export earnings will put a floor under the won, despite the Bank of Korea's attempts to rein it in.  

 "Dollar/won will find 945-950 tough resistance. I heard a lot of exporters forecast a 900-940 range for next year so they will be (dollar) sellers," he said.  

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.5611 per U.S. dollar in early trades, having gradually come off the 9-year highs around 1.5545 hit this week. It then pared back to be traded at 1.5575/80.  

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> rallied nearly half a percent from Wednesday's close near 45.34 per dollar.  

 JPMorgan Chase said in a note to clients the risk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) remained high with the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted level now estimated to be at the top end of the MAS's secret policy band.  

 It also said the Reserve Bank of India's aggressive intervention had moved the rupee's inflation-adjusted trade-weighted levels away from overvalued territory, and that it was technically now more favourable to be buying the rupee <INR=IN>.  

 "Foreigners remain net buyers of local equities and oil prices below $60 a barrel should sustain market impetus for dollar/rupee downside," JPMorgan said.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR   Change on the day at 0733 GMT

title: Emerging  FX -Asia  currencies  slip on yen,  intervention  fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slipped on Wednesday due to persisting worries about central bank intervention, even as the dollar edged up against the yen ahead of more U.S. data that could shape interest rate expectations.  

Still, many analysts expected Asian currencies to resume their advances against the dollar in the near future once the outlook for the U.S. economy and for rates is clearer.  

"It looks like the Asian central banks are getting their way right now, and now we're seeing the Thai baht looking vulnerable too after the Bank of Thailand said it's too volatile," ABN AMRO analyst Shahab Jalinoos said in a research note.  

"We still think dollar/Asia is a longer-term sell, but for now it's better not to fight the contagion risk."  

Thai central bank Governor Tarisa Watanagase said on Wednesday that the baht <THB=> is too volatile and the Bank of Thailand will smooth its volatility. The baht fell to 36.5 per dollar from Tuesday's highs around 36.36, its strongest in nearly seven years.  

In recent weeks, Asian currencies have been driven up by inflows of foreign portfolio investments and more recently by a Chinese central bank comment that Beijing planned to diversify its $1 trillion in foreign exchange reserves.  

Fearful that stronger currencies could hurt exporters, central banks in South Korea, Thailand and India are suspected of having sold their currencies.  

"Asian currencies took their cue from the latest dollar/yen development, but I think they should strengthen over time," said Wang Qing, currency strategist at Bank of America in Hong Kong.  

"Once the outlook of a U.S. soft-landing becomes more confirmed, I think Asian central banks should feel easier in handling their currency appreciation," Wang said.  

STOCK RALLY  

Solid gains in Asian stocks, buoyed by capital inflows, would provide some support for Asian currencies, analysts say.  

Asian stocks outside of Japan hit a record high on Wednesday following a rally on Wall Street. The MSCI index of Asian stocks outside Japan <.MSCIAPJ> hit a record high of 370.97 in early trade, before pulling back to around 370.54.  

The dollar edged up against the yen <JPY=> on Wednesday after sliding on Tuesday on soft U.S. produce prices and retail sales figures that suggested a slowing economy.  

The United States releases consumer prices data on Thursday and housing starts figures on Friday.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> slipped for the third straight session on Wednesday, shedding nearly half a percent as investors covered dollar short positions. It briefly touched a session low of 942.1, the weakest since 943.4 on Nov. 7.  

But the Bank of Korea was not spotted intervening during the day, dealers said, having bought an estimated $1.5 billion over Monday and Tuesday.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> shed nearly half a percent to 9,168 per dollar while the Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell a quarter of a percent against the dollar.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> slipped around 0.20 percent to 1.5590 per U.S. dollar, moving further back from a nine-year high of 1.5545 that it struck late on Friday and matched overnight.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Higher on China reserves plan, yen
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose against the dollar on Friday supported by news of China's plans to diversify its $1 trillion foreign exchange reserves and a firmer Japanese yen.  

The dollar lost ground against the yen <JPY=> and the euro <EUR=> after China's central bank said it had a clear plan to diversify its foreign exchange reserves, although it was not clear whether China would sell dollar assets.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> rose as high as 932.40 against the dollar on Friday, brushing a six-month high after Japan's central bank chief expressed concern about a sharp unwinding of carry trades in the low-yielding currency.  

"Asian currencies are taking their cue from the yen and the yuan," said Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank.  

"There is a quite a bit of interest in the yen and this is supportive."  

China's central bank chief, Zhou Xiaochuan told Reuters on Thursday that China had a clear plan to diversify its reserves. On Friday, he said such diversification would be across different currencies and investment instruments in emerging markets.  

Many currency strategists expect Beijing to face greater foreign pressure to let the yuan rise faster after the country posted a record trade surplus of $23.83 billion for October.  

China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> rose as far as to 7.8633 per dollar on Friday, its strongest level since the July 2005 revaluation.  

RALLY VS INTERVENTION

A further rally in Asian currencies towards the end of the year is widely expected, but some analysts also fear that recent strength in regional currencies might trigger central bank intervention amid concerns about a possible export slowdown.  

"Lower global rates encourage risk-taking among developed country investors, implying increased flow into emerging markets asset classes", Richard Yetsenga at HSBC said in a research note.  

Yun Jin Ko, a dealer at Kookmim Bank, said she saw no sign of intervention from the Bank of Korea on Friday, but cautioned that the central bank may step in if the won rises above the 930 mark.  

"I still believe 930 is our supporting line with probable intervention expected," she said.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained nearly a quarter of a percent and traded as high as 1.5565 per U.S. dollar, close to nine-year highs around 1.5560 reached earlier in November.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> firmed to T$32.78, just off a seven-week high reached on Wednesday, while the Thai baht <THB=> traded in a narrow range between 36.59 and 36.67 per dollar, near Wednesday's seven-year high of 36.56.  

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> rose to about 44.35 per dollar on Friday, its strongest level in nearly eight months, before retreating to around 44.60.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and dollar short-covering dragged the Singapore dollar lower Tuesday.  

"There was talk of the MAS in the market at different levels," said one local bank dealer.  

The MAS' key monetary policy tool is to manage the currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

"There shouldn't be any significant downside in the pair (in the near term)," said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at United Overseas Bank. "According to my estimation of the band, the pair is already 2.26% stronger than the midpoint. The MAS normally intervenes when it is 2.1% above the midpoint."  

Koh also predicted that the greenback would be supported at S$1.5580, unless the USD/JPY falls below Y116.50.  

Another local bank dealer said that the U.S. dollar is "still heavy" and that will only change if October U.S. nonfarm payrolls data due Friday is stronger than expected.  

In the Singapore bond market, prices were almost unchanged.  

"There was some rally in the three- to four-year bonds on customers' purchases," said a local bank dealer.  

"With no new issuances locally, we can only track U.S. data," he said. "Expect volatility as there are a lot of U.S. data, starting tonight."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rally but traders wary of  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies, led by the Japanese yen, were broadly firm against the dollar on Monday after soft U.S. economic growth numbers reinforced a view that U.S. interest rates would stay steady for a while.  

But wariness about central bank intervention to curb strength in local currencies tempered some of the gains.  

Dealers said they suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had stepped into the market to buy U.S. dollars and sell Singapore dollars.  

The Bank of Thailand said its had again intervened on the baht -- which rose to a 7-year high -- although the currency had started to stabilise after inflows slowed.  

"The move in some Asian currencies has been aggressive in the past week, and generally there is no resistance to the direction of the move but the magnitude," said DBS Bank currency strategist Philip Wee. "Generally the big picture is still not changed -- everyone is still looking for a weaker dollar."  

The Thai baht <THB=> climbed to 36.66 to the U.S. dollar, its strongest level since July 1999, before pulling back slightly by late trade.  

A Bangkok trader said there was strong support for the dollar around 36.35, but the outlook still suggested further baht gains.  

"Sellers of dollars are still strong," he said. "They (the central bank) may just come in to calm the market down."  

The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.5610/20 <SGD=> per dollar, up about a quarter of a percent, but pulling away from a nine-year peak hit in offshore trade on Friday at about 1.5580.  

A dealer said he suspected the MAS had intervened on Monday in the 1.5605 to 1.5620 per dollar area.  

FED OUTLOOK  

The U.S. economy grew at an annualised rate of 1.6 percent in the third quarter, its weakest pace in more than three years, due to a slump in the housing market, data showed on Friday.  

This set a backdrop for fresh gains in Asian currencies, which hit multi-week highs last week on foreign investment inflows, gains in the Chinese yuan and weakness in the U.S. dollar.  

The yen strengthened more than 1 percent from levels traded late on Friday to about 117.20 yen per dollar <JPY=>, while the South Korean won firmed to a one-month high at about 942.60 to the dollar <KRW=>.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose about a quarter of a percent to 33.19 per U.S. dollar, its highest in just over a week.  

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> strengthened to about 3.6380 per dollar, its highest in more than three months, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> gained about a fifth of a percent to 49.73 to the U.S. dollar, its highest level in more than four years.  

"Dollar/yen weighed on dollar/peso at the open, but we are also seeing demand for pesos and some corporates are coming into the market," said a trader in Manila.  

"The central bank could come in at the 49.70 area." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0745 GMT

title: Sing dollar off fresh 5-mnth high, ringgit surges
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Heavy foreign investment inflows into Asian asset markets and the Chinese yuan's rise to fresh highs buoyed Asian currencies on Friday, pushing the Malaysian ringgit to its highest level in seven weeks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -At multi-week highs, Thai c.bank steps in
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rallied to multi-week highs against the dollar on Friday, propped up by foreign investment inflows, the Chinese yuan's steady rise and the weakness in the U.S. currency.  

The Chinese yuan's <CNY=CXFS> rise to 7.8870 per dollar, its highest level since its revaluation in July 2005, helped boost Asian currencies across the board.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.5650 per U.S. dollar, a 5-month peak, with the market wary of any intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Traders said the MAS had been suspected of intervening on Thursday.  

"But the market is still looking to buy the Singapore dollar, presumably still taking the unit as a proxy to yuan views. The Sing dollar has remained as the currency with the highest correlation and beta to the yuan," analysts at UBS said in a note to clients.  

The Thai baht <THB=> climbed to 36.84 to the U.S. dollar, its strongest level since January 2000, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as far as 9,075 per U.S. dollar, its strongest since Sept. 6.  

Thailand has received a net $446 million worth of net foreign portfolio investments so far this month, stock exchange data showed, taking total net investments this year to more than $3 billion.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said on Friday the central bank may raise the limits on offshore investment to ease pressure on the baht. She had warned markets earlier this week that the baht's rise had been too rapid.  

The dollar's broad weakness underpinned regional currencies. It was under pressure as the market priced in expectations the Fed would continue to keep rates on hold after it kept them steady this week for a third straight meeting.  

The ringgit <MYR=> was quoted at a seven-week high of 3.6480 per dollar, propped up by foreign inflows into Malaysian assets. The South Korean won <KRW=> hit a one-month high.  

Analysts said portfolio investments into Asia could increase after Chinese lender Industrial & Commercial Bank of China's solid trading debut on Friday following its record US$19 billion IPO.  

"It's blue sky ahead for risky assets. What's driving the Asian currencies is confidence-sensitive portfolio flows into regional equity markets," said Tim Condon, ING Bank's regional economist and strategist.  

"The trend is your friend in this case," he said, adding Asian currencies would continue to appreciate until the end of the year.  

Still, the yen <JPY=> lagged the rise in most other Asian currencies after softer-than-expected Japanese inflation data. It rallied to levels around 118.50 per dollar from 118.74 late in Asian trade the previous session but hit a record low against the euro <EURJPY=>. Japan's core consumer price index in September climbed 0.2 percent from a year earlier, lower than forecasts, sparking expectations that the Bank of Japan could wait until 2007 to raise interest rates.  

The weakness in the yen was a hurdle for the rallying Asian currencies, analysts said.  

"The story in Japan is capital outflows, given the outlook for the economy as well as financial policies are very supportive of dollar/yen," Condon said.  

"So it will be difficult for this appreciation of regional currencies to become a real strong trend, given the headwind of well supported dollar/yen," he said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0806 GMT

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar added to recent gains in Asian trade Friday on broad strength in Asian currencies, and traders say the unit could remain near the strong end of the central bank's target range.  

"The (U.S. dollar) is looking heavy against the rest of Asia...the central bank may come in to slow the Singapore dollar's strength, but it can remain strong," said a dealer at a foreign bank.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, and intervenes in the foreign exchange market to keep the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

The dealer said the next support level for the U.S. dollar is near S$1.5630, but the dollar has potential to move lower.  

The dealer also said that the Singapore dollar is a "very close proxy" for the Chinese yuan, which Friday reached a new high against the U.S. dollar.  

At 0730 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at CNY7.8891. Earlier in the session, it dipped to CNY7.8870, the lowest since Beijing moved to a more flexible foreign exchange regime in July 2005.  

Market players may buy the relatively liquid Singapore dollar in lieu of a long Chinese yuan position, as the two units tend to move in tandem.  

In the Singapore bond market, prices followed U.S. Treasurys higher in early action, but retraced their gains as the overnight rate moved higher.  

The overnight rate reached 3.63% in late trade Friday, bringing the cost of short-term funding above bond yields across maturities.  

A trader at a local bank said that despite a five-basis-point drop in U.S. Treasury yields overnight, Singapore government paper will remain under pressure due to relatively high short-term funding costs.  

"There is negative funding throughout the curve...it will be a major challenge for bonds," said a trader at a local bank.  

"We had buying interest in the morning, when yields were originally down three to four basis points in the long end...now they're down maybe one basis point," the trader added.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Thai baht off highs, Sing dlr supported
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Verbal intervention by the Bank of Thailand reined in the Thai baht on Wednesday after foreign investment flows boosted it to its strongest level in nearly seven years, close to 37 per dollar.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was underpinned by flows from funds betting on Asian currency gains, pushing it to what analysts said was the top of the secret trade-weighted band within which the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages it.  

Markets in Indonesia and Malaysia were closed but other Asian currencies firmed, shrugging off the yen's weakness as foreign investment flowed into the region. The South Korean won <KRW=> rose 0.4 percent to around 955 per dollar.  

Southeast Asian stock markets have been the bigger beneficiaries of foreign investment flows, with the Hong Kong and Indonesian markets near recent highs and Singapore's Straits Times Index <.STI> hitting a record high on Wednesday.  

The yen <JPY=> remained in a 119.10-119.20 per dollar range as nervousness ahead of a Federal Reserve policy decision trapped the U.S. dollar.  

The Fed's two-day policy meeting ends on Wednesday.  

Economists expect U.S. rates to be left unchanged this week. The Fed raised rates 17 times in two years up to June, but kept them steady in August and September.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose a quarter of a percent to 1.5721 per U.S. dollar.  

"Much of the flow pressure seems to be coming from models, which presumably are rebuilding positions they had closed in the run-up to this month's policy review," said Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist.

"And foreign equity purchases have been very strong relative to the rest of the region."  

Data from the stock exchange showed net foreign portfolio inflows into Thailand have been about $389 million so far in October.

title: Singapore Growth To Moderate But Stay Healthy In 07 -MAS
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's growth will likely slow to a moderate pace in 2007, as high oil prices and weaker external demand weigh on the domestic economy, the central bank said Wednesday.  

"For 2006 as a whole, Singapore's GDP growth is expected to come in at the upper half of the official forecast range of 6.5% to 7.5%. The economy is likely to register more moderate growth in 2007 in line with its medium-term potential rate," the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in its semiannual macroeconomic review.  

Singapore's medium-term potential growth rate is estimated at 3% to 5%.  

The MAS said that high energy price will contribute to a lower rate of economic expansion.  

"Demand-supply conditions suggest that global oil prices could stay high, at above $60 per barrel," it said.  

After reaching a high of around $78 dollars in July, Nymex crude has pulled back recently to levels just under $60 a barrel.  

The MAS said that while a sharp global downturn is unlikely, it does anticipate slower expansion worldwide.  

"Both developed countries and emerging Asian economies are predicted to record slower growth in 2007 compared to this year," it said.  

"Nevertheless, the outlook remains generally sanguine and should support continued healthy expansion."  

The MAS said Singapore's mainstay electronics sector will experience "knock-on" effects from lower demand, but the cycle is not in a typical downturn.  

"On balance, barring a sharp adjustment in the U.S. economy, the global IT industry will grow at a slightly slower pace in 2007 compared to this year."  

The report cites industry analyst projections of 6% to 8% growth in chip sales in 2007 compared with 8% to 10% growth in 2006.  

Biomedical manufacturing, which is another important sector of the economy, may continue growing at a steady clip, as pharmaceutical plants add capacity in 2007, the bank said.  

The MAS also highlighted the construction sector, which it expects to benefit from developments in the Marina Bay area and a recent increase in residential housing prices.  

Inflation In Check, Policy On Track  

Despite some passthrough effects of higher energy costs in 2006, consumer prices have been contained by relatively low import price inflation and subdued pressure on wages.  

Nominal wage growth is expected to be just 3.5% to 4.0% in both 2006 and 2007, comparable to 3.5% in 2005.  

The recent strengthening of the Singapore dollar has helped shield Singapore against external price pressure, the main source of inflation in the city-state.  

The MAS advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, and intervenes in the foreign exchange market to keep the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

The MAS reaffirmed its slightly contractionary monetary policy on October 10, and it expects the current policy will serve to contain inflation through next year.  

"CPI inflation will be contained in 2006 and 2007 under the current policy stance," the report said.  

The MAS said that the Singapore dollar has stayed in the upper half of the central bank's policy band since April.  

Since the beginning of 2006, the Singapore dollar has appreciated by about 5% against the U.S. dollar, which began the year around S$1.6620 and is now near S$1.5770.  

However, the MAS said the real exchange rate has remained low due to low costs and prices in Singapore relative to its trading partners.  

"The level of Singapore's real exchange rate at this point of the business cycle suggests that our competitiveness has not been undermined by the appreciation of the trade-weighted (Singapore dollar)," the report said.  

Monetary conditions tightened earlier this year, as the Singapore dollar three-month interbank rate rose to 3.56% in August from 3.44% in May.  

The three-month interbank rate retraced to 3.44% at the end of the third quarter, and the MAS expects it to hold near the current level through the fourth quarter.  

The Singapore dollar three-month interbank rate is "expected to stabilize at around current levels for the rest of 2006, against the backdrop of a pause in US Fed funds rate hikes in August and September," the report said.

title: DATA VIEW: Singapore Inflation At 14-Month Low In Sept
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's inflation rate remained below the government's official forecast range in September, and economists say that stable price levels give the central bank room to ease policy in the event of a sharp economic slowdown.  

The consumer price index rose 0.4% from a year earlier in September, the slowest pace since July 2005, according to official figures released Monday.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore has a target range for inflation of 1% to 2% for 2006, and it expects similarly low inflation of 0.5% to 1.5% in 2007.  

Seasonally adjusted, the consumer price index contracted 0.1% from August after remaining unchanged the previous month.  

September's data were below the average of a Dow Jones Newswires poll of seven economists, which forecast the CPI would rise by 0.7% from a year earlier.  

United Overseas Bank economist Alvin Liew said he expects the current monetary policy to keep prices well-contained through 2006.  

"The strong Singapore dollar will be quite effective in limiting import price inflation in the last months of the year," he said.  

He added that ahead of Monday's CPI release, UOB had forecast full-year inflation between 1.3% and 1.4%, but that it now forecasts inflation between 1.1% and 1.2% for 2006.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, and intervenes in the foreign exchange market to keep the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

Since the beginning of 2006, the Singapore dollar has appreciated by about 6% against the U.S. dollar, which began the year around S$1.6620 and is now at S$1.5742.  

The stronger Singapore dollar has helped shield Singapore against external price pressure, the main source of inflation in the city-state.  

Action Economics economist Mayank Mehta said lower oil costs also benefited consumers in September, when prices in the transport and communication sector eased.  

Prices in the sector, which accounts for 22% of the inflation index, fell 2.7% from a year earlier in September.  

"We haven't seen the full impact from lower oil prices as yet so we can expect it later this year," Mehta said. "We may revise our inflation forecast down."  

Action Economics forecasts 1.2% full-year inflation for 2006, but may lower its prediction to 1.1%, Mehta said.  

The MAS recently noted in a report that "domestic petrol companies...cut pump prices twice by a total of 11 cents in September following the plunge in global oil prices."  

After reaching a high of around $78 dollars in July, Nymex crude is now trading below $60 per barrel.  

Liew said the risk of inflation won't prevent the central bank from loosening monetary conditions if global economic prospects deteriorate.  

"Given the benign situation for inflation, the central bank may switch to a neutral policy...but it would only need to change its stance in the unexpected event of a drastic change in the external environment," Liew said.  

CIMB-GK economist Song Seng Wun said monetary policy is "on track" for now, but that the central bank could switch its stance in April, when it will hold its next policy review, if the economy falters or overheats.  

"Until we see signs of much stronger growth or much slower growth, this inflation level would be supportive of a reiteration of a monetary policy that is keeping inflationary pressure at bay," Song said.  

Among other key components, housing costs, which make up 21% of the index, gained 2.0% from a year earlier, and fell 0.5% from August due to lower maintenance charges and garbage collection fees.  

The cost of food, which is the biggest component in the index with a 23% weighting, climbed 1.8% from a year earlier and held steady from August.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing dlr, Thai baht at multi-week highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies edged up on Friday, with the Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar hitting multi-week highs as weak U.S. data hurt the U.S. dollar.  

A survey by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia on Thursday showed a surprise fall in business activity in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region, renewing worries about U.S. economic growth.  

The Singapore dollar rose to a six-week high at 1.5710 per U.S. dollar <SGD=>, making traders wary about central bank intervention to curb its strength.  

The Thai baht gained a quarter of a percent to a one-month peak at about 37.20 per dollar <THB=>, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose as much as half a percent to 33.02 to the U.S. dollar -- its strongest level in about 2-½ weeks.  

The Japanese yen was up about a third of a percent at 118.30 per dollar <JPY=>, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was steady near Thursday's one-month peaks. The Philippine peso held around 50 per dollar <PHP=>.  

China's central bank, meanwhile, set the mid-point of the yuan's exchange rate against the dollar <CNY=CFXS> at 7.8995, its highest mid-point since the July 2005 revaluation.  

"After a rough night for the dollar, Asian currencies are keeping in step with the move in dollar/yen," said Sean Callow, a senior currency strategist at Westpac Bank in Singapore.  

A rally in local share markets also provided support.  

South Korea's key stock index <.KS11> closed up 0.75 percent, Taiwan's share index <.TWII> rose 0.6 percent and Singapore's benchmark Straits Times Index <.STI> pushed up to a record high as overnight gains on Wall Street boosted regional markets.  

Dealers said firm equity markets suggested investor risk appetite remained high despite tensions over North Korea.  

They added that despite weakness in overnight U.S. data, there was still uncertainty about the U.S. economic outlook and this kept most currencies in familiar ranges versus the dollar.  

"When it comes to the dollar, there still doesn't seem to be a strong conviction on where it is headed," said Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank. "I'm looking ahead to the Fed next week and that could provide some direction."  

SING DOLLAR SHINES  

In Singapore, this week's 1 percent gain in the local currency versus the U.S. dollar made some traders nervous about central bank intervention -- although the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has not been spotted in the market this week.  

There have been differing views on whether Singapore dollar gains are related to expectations of Singapore state investment firm Temasek [TEM.UL] selling shares in Thai telecommunications group Shin Corp. to resolve a foreign-ownership dispute.  

The Shin Corp. sale by the family of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra sparked street protests in Thailand aimed at forcing him to quit before he was ousted in September's military coup. Critics have said the Shin deal broke foreign ownership rules.  

"There are no flows related to Temasek as far as I can see," said a Singapore trader. "I'm not aware of the MAS being in the market today," he added.  

Wee at DBS said the Singapore dollar probably remained at the strong end of its undisclosed trade-weighted currency band. He estimated the mid-point of the band at about 1.5870 per dollar.  

A trader in Bangkok said strong offshore demand for the baht was helping to push the currency higher.  

"Dollar/baht is lower because of some capital inflows from offshore," he said. "I think it's related to direct investment."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Touch lower on yen weakness
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 19 (Reuters) - A softer tone in the yen pushed most Asian currencies down on Thursday, but trade was generally subdued as the market waited for fresh direction.  

A degree of caution also lingered amid concerns about North Korea following last week's nuclear test.  

The yen shed about 0.4 percent to around 119 per dollar <JPY=>, but had trimmed some of its falls by late trade.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> eased to about 958 per dollar, down 0.6 percent from this week's one-week highs, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> dipped to about 33.23 to the U.S. dollar -- heading back towards last week's 10-month low at 33.34.  

The Thai baht <THB=> slipped to about 37.40 per dollar, down a quarter of a percent from Wednesday's one-month high at about 37.30, although the Singapore dollar <SGD=> touched a fresh 5-1/2-week high at about 1.5735.  

U.S. data on Wednesday was mixed, while reports this week that Russia has started to buy the yen for its foreign exchange reserves and the Bank of Japan plans to increase its monitoring of carry trades appear to have given the yen only a modest boost.  

"In the last few weeks, Asian currencies have done reasonably well and risk appetite has rebounded," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank.  

"But we are still stuck in a range and we still need to see a clear trend in the dollar."  

Henderson said that in the current environment the appeal of trading Asian currencies against each other instead of versus the dollar had risen.  

"The Philippine peso, for instance, has outperformed the Sing dollar and the won," he said. "The crosses are where the opportunities are."  

WATCHING THE FLOWS  

Analysts said the Singapore dollar probably remained at the strong end of its undisclosed trade-weighted currency band.  

But traders said the central bank was unlikely to intervene to curb strength in the local currency given slight yen weakness.  

Markets had been wary of such intervention on Wednesday as the Singapore dollar rallied.  

There was some talk that the gains were related to Singapore state investment firm Temasek [TEM.UL] selling share holdings in Thai telecommunications group Shin Corp to resolve a foreign ownership dispute.  

IDEAglobal analysts said the deal could potentially see flows of as much as $1.5 billion, with the Singapore currency likely to benefit if the proceeds are converted back to Singapore dollars.  

"The market is not particularly worried about intervention at the moment as the yen is staying here," said the trader.  

"The Temasek news has been digested and yesterday the sell-off in dollar/Sing was by model funds, and more speculative or long liquidation."  

Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose a fifth of a percent to about 3.6680 per dollar.  

It continues to draw support from cash flows into Malaysia related to the acquisition of about $2 billion of Malaysian OYL Industries Bhd by Japanese air-conditioner maker Daikin Industries Ltd. , dealers said.  

Asian currencies showed little reaction to Chinese data.  

China's annual economic growth slowed a little in the third quarter to 10.4 percent, from 11.3 percent in the second quarter.
