title: DATA VIEW: Singapore Inflation At 11-Month Low In Aug
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's inflation rate slipped below the government's targeted range in August, but economists expect the central bank will maintain its modestly tight monetary stance when policy is reviewed in October.  

The consumer price index rose just 0.7% from a year earlier in August, the slowest pace since September 2005, according to official figures released Monday.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore has a target range for inflation of 1% to 2% for 2006, and has said it expects inflation in the bottom of the same range in 2007.  

Seasonally-adjusted, the consumer price index remained unchanged from July.  

August's data was below the average of a Dow Jones Newswires poll, which forecasted the CPI would rise by 1.0% from a year earlier.  

David Cohen, an economist at Action Economics, said prices are not at a great risk of rising or falling too quickly, and that current inflation levels are unlikely to motivate a change in the central bank's policy stance.  

"I don't think there's any hurry to shift from the slightly appreciating band," Cohen said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore advocates a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar, and intervenes in the foreign exchange market to keep the local dollar within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band.  

Some market players have speculated that benign inflation would allow the monetary authority to weaken the Singapore dollar, but economists say the current policy allows sufficient room for fluctuation.  

"The band is already quite flexible," said Sim Moh Siong, economist at Citigroup.  

Sim said that an overly-strong Singapore dollar could be a liability in the event of a recession, but such a scenario is unlikely.  

"We are in the soft-landing camp," Sim said. "We are not looking at a 2001 scenario. U.S. growth should still be 3% next year."  

Since the beginning of 2006, the Singapore dollar has appreciated by about 5% against the U.S. dollar, which began the year around S$1.6620 and is currently at S$1.5840.  

The stronger Singapore dollar has helped shield Singapore against external price pressure.  

DBS strategist Philip Wee said that lower oil prices have eased external pressures further.  

After reaching a high of around $78 dollars this summer, Nymex crude is currently trading around $60 per barrel.  

Wee said that domestic inflation is also "quite benign" because of subdued wage pressure and a decline in the cost for Certificates of Entitlement, which allow Singaporeans to own cars.  

He said COE prices declined ahead of the August CPI sampling, which accounts for much of the decline in transportation costs.  

The cost of transport and communication, which represents 22% of the inflation index, fell 1.8% from a year earlier in August and fell 0.1% from July.  

Among other key components, housing costs, which make up 21% of the index, rose 2.1% in August from a year earlier, but fell 0.1% from July.  

The cost of food, which makes up 23% of the index, rose 1.7% from a year earlier and remained unchanged from July.

title: Singapore Dlr Down As MAS Action Expected; Bonds Stable
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker in Asian trade Tuesday on expectations that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene, as the Singapore dollar has been trading at the strong end of its policy band.  

A local bank dealer said his bank estimated that the Singapore dollar was just shy of 2% above the center of the central bank's trading band.  

The MAS operates monetary policy by managing the currency within an undisclosed trading band rather than using interest rates.  

A foreign bank dealer said the IMF and World Bank meeting this week in Singapore is "still the focus. But it has yet to release any major news."  

Emmanuel Ng, a foreign exchange strategist from the Overseas Chinese Banking Corp., said market players would also be looking overseas for cues.  

"If there is a removal of reference on deflation in the Japanese Cabinet Office economic report this Friday, the Japanese yen will get support," Ng said. "There is also the U.S. trade deficit numbers tonight."  

The Singapore dollar tracks the yen closely.  

The U.S. July trade deficit data will be released later in the global session. A survey by Dow Jones Newswires predicts the deficit at US$64.5 billion, compared with US$64.8 billion in June.  

At 0655 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.5787, up from S$1.5767 at New York close and S$1.5744 in late Asian trade Monday.  

In the government debt market, the two-year bond yield remained flat at 3.03%, while the 10-year bond yield rose one basis point to 3.33%.  

"The bonds are holding steady," a local dealer said. "There is a little shedding of the prices."  

"It's a quiet market today, but the market is a little nervous, as the U.S. Treasurys are trading lower," the trader said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Yen lends support, spotlight on G7
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies held steady on Friday, supported by a rally in the yen after a German finance official said the currency's weakness would be a topic at this month's Group of Seven meeting.  

The yen hit one-month highs against the euro <EURJPY=R> and rose to about 116.10 per U.S. dollar <JPY=>, up about 0.7 percent from late on Thursday.  

A firmer yen helped push the South Korean won <KRW=> briefly to about 954 per dollar, the strongest level since the end of July, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.5657 per U.S. dollar overnight -- its highest since mid-May.  

But dealers suspected that the Monetary Authority of Singapore stepped into the market to curb currency gains in overnight trade and wariness of further central bank action kept the market in a tight range on Friday.  

"It looks like there was intervention overnight, but not so far today," said a Singapore trader. "People seem to be paying full attention to any comments on forex and it looks like this will be a big issue during the G7 and IMF meetings."  

Finance ministers and central bank governors from the G7 industrial nations will meet on Sept. 16 in Singapore, Japan's Finance Minister Sadakazu Tanigaki said on Friday. Singapore, China and Thailand have been invited to join part of the discussions.  

Tanigaki said currencies would be discussed but declined to say if the yen would be at the centre of such talks.  

As most traders had been expecting the Chinese yuan and not the yen to be a key focus, Thursday's comments by German Deputy Finance Minister Thomas Mirow came as a surprise and prompted short covering of the yen.  

"Yesterday's comments from the German Deputy Finance Minister woke the market up to the risks that there could be major fireworks at this G7 meeting," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered. "Today's comments confirm that the focus is very much on the need for Asian currencies to appreciate. Asia has to play its part."  

Henderson added that the move in the euro to almost 150 yen has encouraged European officials to suggest that Asia should take up more of the burden of reducing global imbalances.  

Bank of Japan Governor Toshihiko Fukui said on Friday, however, that he did not expect the yen to be the centre of the G7 finance ministers' discussions.  

YUAN IN SPOTLIGHT TOO  

The yuan <CNY=CFXS> was also in the spotlight ahead of this month's meetings of the G7 and International Monetary Fund, with markets digesting a raft of comments from officials on Friday.  

China rejected blame for global economic imbalances, while U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said that the United States and China agree currency flexibility is "very important."  

The official Financial News, meanwhile, said China may widen the yuan's trading band against the dollar to allow greater fluctuation in the currency.  

Recent volatility in the currency suggested Beijing may make such a move, the paper said, without giving a timeframe.  

The yuan has risen about 0.8 percent in the past three weeks to hit 7.9367 per dollar on Tuesday, its highest level since it was revalued by 2.1 percent in July 2005. Some analysts say a widening of the yuan's trading band is likely to happen soon.  

"The political mileage that the Chinese can gain from widening the band ahead of the (G7) summit is a powerful incentive to act early," said Deutsche Bank currency strategist Mirza Baig. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change of the day at 0740 GMT

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Yen, yuan behind rally, c.banks seen
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 5 (Reuters) - A rising Japanese yen and Chinese yuan pushed Asian currencies to multi-week highs on Tuesday, prompting the Philippine central bank to intervene verbally.  

The yen <JPY=> rallied to 2-week highs near 115.60 per dollar after Monday's capital spending reinforced expectations for rate rises in Japan. Those expectations had been subdued by soft July inflation data.  

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit its highest level since being freed from a virtual dollar peg last July. The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=>, buoyed by official comments made last week that a stronger currency would help contain inflation, rose to 3.6445 per dollar, its highest in two months.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rallied less than a quarter of a percent, although it hit 50.33 per dollar, its strongest in four years. Central bank Governor Amando Tetangco said the strong peso posed a risk to inflation because of the additional supply of funds.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.5658 per U.S. dollar, its highest since mid-May. Analysts said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened to cap the currency on Monday, ensuring it remained within its secret, trade-weighted policy band.  

"The MAS seems quite determined not to let the NEER (nominal effective exchange rate) move beyond the band. It is still sitting close to the upper limit," said Sabrina Jacobs, a currency strategist at Dresdner Kleinwort.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> barely budged after Bank Indonesia cut its one-month policy rate by 50 basis points, as many in the market had expected.  

YEN POSITIONS  

The yen's rally was spurred by heavy squaring of short yen positions. Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission showed bets against the yen hit a record high in the week to Aug. 29.  

Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the yen's rally was driven more by "fear and greed" and short covering rather than fundamentals, such as the strong capital spending and rising Nikkei average <.N225>.  

Some of the Japanese data preceding this week's capital spending numbers had been weaker than expected, particularly the rise in the July consumer price index (CPI) that tempered market expectations of monetary tightening.  

"Dollar/yen historically goes up by the stairs, down in the elevator. But unless the G7/IMF is huge, then this is not the big move," Callow said.  

Callow was referring to the World Bank and IMF annual meetings taking place in Singapore later this month.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Firmer thanks to yen, yuan, stocks
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly firm on Monday as the Japanese yen rebounded from last week's lows, the Chinese yuan hit a fresh post-revaluation high and regional equity markets posted strong gains.  

Friday's data showing the U.S. economy created 128,000 jobs in August, just above expectations, did little to alter the view that U.S. interest rates would be on hold for the rest of the year, adding momentum to the Asia currency rally.  

"The U.S. numbers were not particularly good and there continues to be a scaling back of rate-hike expectations," said BNP Paribas currency strategist Thio Chin Loo.  

The yen <JPY=> rose about three quarters of a percent from levels traded late on Friday, lifted by news on Monday that Japanese firms increased capital spending by 16.6 percent in the second quarter compared with a year earlier.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> broke through a key chart level to hit its highest in about 3-½ months at 1.5665 per U.S. dollar, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> extended last week's gains to rise to a four-year high at 50.48 to the dollar.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> added roughly a third of a percent each. The Thai baht <THB=> rose about 0.5 percent to a 2-1/2-week high at about 37.33 per dollar, while the Malaysian ringgit broke out of recent ranges to firm to 3.6550 per dollar, its highest in almost a month.  

The yuan <CNY=CFXS> strengthened as far as 7.9400 per dollar, its highest since it was revalued in July 2005.  

It was expected to remain in focus ahead of this month's meeting of finance ministers of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations, with China facing pressure to step up the pace of currency appreciation.  

"Currencies like the Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit are doing well because there is a risk of concerted pressure on the Chinese currency," said Richard Yetsenga, a currency strategist at HSBC in Hong Kong. "They are the ones to benefit."  

INTERVENTION SUSPECTED  

Some traders said they suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in the market to cap gains in the Singapore dollar, which they felt was probably trading at the strong end of its secret trade-weighted band.  

Others said it was less clear.  

"I'm not too sure about intervention -- but one of the local banks has been selling Sing dollars and that is surprising," said a trader. "With 2-3 weeks left to the next MAS policy review, everyone is trying to second guess what they will do."  

The latest Reuters poll on market positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors have stepped up long Singapore dollar positions versus the U.S. dollar.  

Taking a long position on a currency is essentially a bet that it will strengthen.  

Elsewhere, the ringgit continued to benefit from positive sentiment following Friday's 2007 Malaysian budget.  

The budget unveiled the first cut in corporate tax since 1998 and dealers said this, together with a comment in the economic report also released on Friday that a stronger ringgit would help contain inflation, boosted the currency.  

"About 80 percent of the move in the ringgit is related to the budget reaction," said a Kuala Lumpur-based trader.  

"There were comments from finance ministry officials about the ringgit being used to fight inflation and this saw an immediate 100-point reaction which is continuing today."  

Malaysia's benchmark stock index <.KLSE> rose to its highest level in almost four months, bolstering the ringgit.  

Other Asian equity markets were also firmer and in Taiwan foreign funds bought a net 10.71 billion Taiwan dollars of shares compared with about 6.8 billion on Friday.

title: Singapore dlr at 3-½   month high, mkt wary of MAS
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose to its highest level in about 3-½   months versus a generally soft U.S. dollar on Monday, after breaking through key chart levels.  

 Dealers said that with the Singapore dollar <SGD=> most probably trading at the strong end of its secret trade-weighted band, they were wary of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) in the market to curb currency gains.  

 The Singapore dollar strengthened as far as 1.5665 per U.S. dollar, its strongest since about mid-May and up about a third of a percent from levels traded late on Friday.  

 "Local banks have been selling dollar/Sing and the move through 1.57 triggered a wave of stop-loss selling," said a trader in Singapore.  

 "So far we have not seen any signs of official intervention, but if dollar/Sing continues to drift lower, they (the MAS) are likely to come in."  

 Traders said the absence of the central bank in the market in recent weeks has encouraged investors to push the Singapore dollar higher.

title: Singapore Dlr Tracks Yen Strength; MAS Seen Paring Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose through key support levels Monday, tracking strength in the Japanese yen, but the central bank likely intervened to contain the local currency's appreciation.  

"The Japanese yen started the day stronger, and the capital expenditures numbers from Japan gave a lift to both the yen and the Singapore dollar," said a dealer at a local bank.  

The Singapore dollar followed the yen higher in early trade, gaining against the U.S. dollar, but players say the central bank entered the market to cut its appreciation short.  

"(The U.S. dollar) fell to S$1.5660 with the rising yen, and there is talk the MAS is around to support it at S$1.5670," a trader at a foreign bank said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the value of the local currency against a basket of other currencies within an unspecified band, and traders say the MAS intervened to weaken the Singapore dollar in recent weeks.  

Last week, the central bank likely intervened when the U.S. dollar was slightly stronger, above the S$1.57 level.  

But a strategist at a foreign bank said the value of the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies has not changed from last week, even though the U.S. dollar declined to S$1.5670 in intraday trade Monday.  

Other currencies in the basket, including the Japanese yen and the Malaysian ringgit, have gained in recent days, reducing the value of the Singapore dollar against the overall basket.  

At 0811 GMT, the U.S. dollar traded at Y116.20, down Y0.90 from Friday's New York close.  

Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.5698, from S$1.5721 at the close of New York trade Friday and S$1.5722 in late Asian trade Friday.  

Traders expect the U.S. dollar to be supported at S$1.5670 and face resistance at S$1.5720 in the next few days.  

In the Singapore government debt market, prices fell slightly across maturities, and the yield curve flattened modestly.  

Despite a modest bid for short-dated U.S. Treasurys in Friday's global session, Singapore players shunned short-dated Singapore government paper after poor results at an auction for Singapore three-month bills.  

The cutoff yield was 3.23% for the S$1.6 billion auction of bills.  

"The auction results that were weaker than expected had a negative effect on the two-year note, and its yield was up two or three basis points," said Selena Ling, strategist at OCBC Bank.  

"Activity was light in the long end beyond the seven-year note," Ling said.  

The two-year Singapore government bond bid-side yield was two basis points higher at 3.14%, while the 10-year bid-side yield rose one basis point to 3.38%.  

There will be little economic data from the U.S. this week, but the market will watch for an indication of the Bank of Japan's future policy when the Bank holds a meeting Thursday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Touch firmer, fresh 4-year highs for peso
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a touch firmer ahead of key U.S. jobs numbers due later on Friday, with the Philippine peso extending this week's rally to hit a four-year peak against the dollar.  

The peso <PHP=> rose as far as 50.70 per U.S. dollar, taking its gains this week to about 1.2 percent.  

Strong foreign demand for local bonds and stocks, remittances from overseas workers, an easing of political worries and upbeat economic data have all been pushing the peso higher.  

But after a week of gains, the peso rally was starting to run out of steam, dealers said. "Dollar/peso has been oversold in the last few days so it is time for a pause and there was bit of profit taking around 50.70," said a trader in Manila.  

He said it was not clear if the central bank had intervened in the market to curb peso strength.

The U.S. August non-farm payrolls report is due at 1230 GMT and economists polled by Reuters forecast a median 120,000 new jobs were created compared with 113,000 in July.

title: Singapore Dlr Hits  Central Bank  Policy Ceiling; Bonds Up
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged higher in Asian trade Friday but encountered resistance as it reached the strong end of the central bank's undisclosed trading band.  

"Everyone wants to be short the (U.S.) dollar against Asia, but the Singapore dollar basket is trading at the high end of central bank's target range," a dealer at a foreign bank said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the value of the local currency against a basket of other currencies within an unspecified band, and market players say the MAS intervened this week to stem gains in the Singapore dollar.  

"MAS came in to bring (the U.S. dollar) back up to the S$1.5715-S$1.5720 level," the dealer said.  

At 0636 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.5722, from S$1.5732 at the close of New York trade and S$1.5717 in late Asian trade Thursday.  

Some players use the relatively liquid Singapore dollar to take on exposure to Asian currencies, which many believe have the potential to gain against the U.S. dollar in the coming months.  

"Only Asia has been lacking against the U.S. dollar. Currencies from other regions - like the euro, British pound and Australian dollar - have already gained quite a bit," said Emmanuel Ng, a strategist at OCBC bank.  

"The big picture is that the market expects some Asian currency appreciation, and the Singapore dollar also reflects strength in (the Chinese yuan)," Ng said.  

But some analysts think the Singapore dollar has already traded outside of the central bank's target band for the last few sessions, and some players may take short positions as they perceive upside risk to be minimal.  

"Gains are seen as limited for the Singapore dollar, so it is a good funding currency for a carry trade with the Indonesian rupiah or Philippine peso, which have higher interest rates," a local dealer said.  

Investors can benefit from interest rate differentials by taking loans in Singapore dollars and buying currencies that offer higher rates of interest on deposits.  

Traders expect the U.S. dollar to be supported at S$1.5680 and face resistance at S$1.5750 next week.  

In the Singapore government debt market, longer-dated issues posted significant gains after an overnight rally brought yields on U.S. 10-year Treasury notes to a five-month low.  

"The three or four basis-point fall in yields was a catch-up from earlier this week," a local trader said.  

On Wednesday and Thursday, Singapore government bonds held steady, despite gains in U.S. Treasurys.  

The two-year Singapore government bond bid-side yield was one basis point lower at 3.13%, while the 10- and 15-year bid-side yields each fell four basis points to 3.36% and 3.43%, respectively.  

"The overnight rate is still high, so the market was buying the long end of the curve to avoid negative carry," another trader said.  

Recently, short-dated bond yields have fallen beneath the overnight rate.  

Traders say the timing of a possible interest rate cut in the U.S. is the bond market's key focus in coming weeks.  

The release of the U.S. August nonfarm payroll figure, slated for tonight, may give an indication of whether the U.S. economy is cooling, and how soon the Fed may cut rates.  

"Payrolls will be the main focus into next week," a local trader said.

title: Singapore Dlr Edges Up;Resistance Seen At Top Of MAS Band
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar gained slightly in Asian trade Thursday but was restrained by market perceptions that it was strengthening beyond the central bank's target range.  

"The one key factor keeping the Singapore dollar from moving higher is that current levels put it at the top end of the trading band," said UBS currency strategist Nizam Idris.  

At 0755 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.5717, down from S$1.5736 at the close of New York trade and S$1.5727 in late Asian trade Wednesday.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the value of the local currency against a basket of other currencies within an unspecified band. The MAS may intervene to limit gains in the Singapore dollar, and financial analysts make calculations on the trading levels that might prompt central bank action.  

"The trade-weighted index is at its strongest point since the last policy meeting in April," said Irene Cheung, a currency strategist at ABN Amro.  

Weakness in the Japanese yen also likely contained the rise of the Singapore dollar, and some analysts say there is downside risk for both currencies if the yen weakens further.  

"If (the U.S. dollar) breaks out to the upside through Y117.50, there could be a big move further, even though the market is already very short yen," said ABN's Cheung. "And if there is a breakout, we could see some retracement in the Singapore dollar."  

The yen declined Thursday morning in Asia on weaker-than-expected Japanese industrial output data that suggested the Bank of Japan might not raise rates again this year.  

At 0755 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at Y117.25, compared with Y117.08 at the beginning of Asian trade.  

The yen has weakened recently as prospects for higher rates in other economies weigh against Japan's rates, which are likely to stay low.  

ABN's Cheung notes there is a 417-basis-point spread between the two-year U.S. Treasury yield and the two-year Japanese Government Bond yield, the largest since July.  

Traders expect the U.S. dollar to be supported at S$1.5700 and face resistance at S$1.5770 in the next few days.  

In the Singapore government debt market, a modest bid for mid-dated maturities reflected demand for U.S. Treasurys overnight, when the market showed healthy appetite in an auction for new five-year Treasury notes.  

The two-year Singapore government bond yield was flat at 3.14%, while the five- and seven-year yields each fell one basis point to 3.27% and 3.31%, respectively. The 10-year yield was flat at 3.40%, as was the 15-year yield at 3.47%.  

"The five-year was catching up after the 15-year rallied earlier in the week," a local trader said. "There was a lot of flattening on the five- to 15-year curve and it is correcting."  

At a reopening of the 15-year Singapore government bond Tuesday, the auction closed at a cutoff yield of 3.48%, below the 3.50%-3.60% some had expected.  

Players in the Singapore bond market will watch for signs of inflation in economic data releases from the U.S. this week, especially the personal spending data due later Thursday, and nonfarm payrolls due Friday.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late On PM's Speech; Bonds Weaker
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose in Asian trade Monday in response to the prime minister's optimistic speech about the economy Sunday and a stronger euro. "The Singapore dollar is quite strong...so there's concern of (Monetary of Singapore intervention) in the market," said Jimmy Koh, a treasurys economist from United Overseas Bank. "Traders may not want to push the Singapore dollar significantly higher."  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the value of the local currency against a basket of other currencies within an unspecified policy band.  

At 0746 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.5706, down from S$1.5737 at the New York close and from S$1.5740 late Friday in Asia.  

A foreign bank trader said that investors would be looking out for Japan's July consumer price index released this Friday.  

"A strong Japanese CPI will result in a stronger yen, which may lead to a more bearish U.S. dollar," he said.  

He also said investors would be paying attention to any change in China's policy on the yuan after last Friday's Chinese interest rate increase sparked more speculation that the government may let the yuan appreciate at a faster pace.  

China's benchmark one-year bank lending rates and one-year deposit rates rose by 0.27 percentage point to 6.12% and 2.52% from last Saturday.  

The Singapore dollar also got a boost from a speech by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, the foreign bank trader said. "Foreign investors feel positive about his speech."  

Lee said Singapore's economy is expected to grow about 7.0% this year. Over the long term, he expects gross domestic product growth to average 3%-5% a year. He also welcomed more foreigners to work in Singapore.  

The Singapore dollar also benefited from the undermining of sentiment in the U.S. dollar resulting from a strengthening euro, the trader said. At 0742 GMT, the euro was trading at US$1.2894, up from US$1.2839 at the New York close.  

Traders predict the greenback to be supported slightly below S$1.5700, with resistance at S$1.5740-50.  

In the Singapore bond market, the two-year bond yield rose four basis points to 3.07%, while the 10-year bond yield rose two basis points to 3.40%.  

"There's more selling in the short end because the three-month (Singapore treasury bill) was not so well-received," a local dealer said.  

The three-month Singapore treasury bill was sold in an auction at 3.15% today, compared with 3.1% last week.  

The government will auction 15-year bonds Tuesday.

title: Singapore  Dlr Down On Rumored MAS  Intervention ;Bonds Down
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell in Asian trade Friday, which traders suspect was due to intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to keep the currency within its trading band.  

Traders say the U.S. dollar is likely to continue to gain in the near term, as the MAS is still monitoring the local currency and other factors, such as key data and world events, could add to the greenback's strength.  

"The important technical level would be S$1.5770-S$1.5780," said a dealer from a foreign bank. "If it breaks above this level, we can see some short-covering of the U.S. dollar."  

At 0644 GMT, the U.S. unit was trading at $1.5756, up from S$1.5714 at the New York close and $1.5687 late Thursday in Asia.  

United Overseas Bank treasury economist Jimmy Koh said investors should be alert to the possibility of China announcing more flexibility for its foreign exchange regime in the next few weeks.  

China is likely to face more pressure from the international community at the International Monetary Fund meeting in September and may adopt a more flexible currency policy ahead of the meeting so it's not "seen as bowing to international pressure," he said.  

If this happens, the U.S. dollar will have a downside bias, he said.  

The foreign bank dealer said the Singapore dollar was trading 2% above the suspected band early Friday on selling of the greenback by speculative sellers. However, the Singapore dollar soon turned around, which prompted rumors of MAS intervention.  

Singapore manages its currency in a band but doesn't disclose its parameters, leaving market participants to estimate the lower and upper limits of the trading band.  

"The weak yen did not help the Singapore dollar either. Japanese oil companies were buying a lot of the U.S. dollar against the yen," the foreign bank dealer said.  

At GMT 0646, the U.S. dollar was trading at Y115.69, up from Y115.27 at New York's close.  

In the Singapore bond market, the two-year yield rose three basis points to 2.95%, while the 10-year yield rose three basis points to 3.40%.  

"A local bank started selling the 15-year bonds and it started a downturn in the bond market," a dealer from a local bank said.  

He said traders will be eyeing the tender of the 15-year Singapore Government Securities late next week.

title: Singapore Dlr Gains Slightly On US Data; Bonds Up
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose for the third consecutive session in Asian trade Monday after weaker-than-forecast U.S. nonfarm payrolls raised expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will take a break from raising interest rates.  

"The U.S. dollar dropped too fast this morning," said Suan Teck Kim, an economist with United Overseas Bank. "Thus, there could be a possible rebound of the U.S. dollar tomorrow, even if the Fed paused the rate hike" cycle at its meeting Tuesday.  

At 0638 GMT, the U.S. unit was trading at $1.5713, down from S$1.5731 at the New York close and $1.5770 late Friday in Asia.  

The U.S. dollar fell against the Singapore dollar due to the payrolls data released Friday in the U.S.  

Nonfarm payrolls grew 113,000 in July, less than the predicted 150,000 increase, adding weight to the view that the Fed will leave rates unchanged.  

Further gains in the Singapore dollar could be capped by fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore will intervene to slow the currency's rise.  

"There is the fear of the MAS to keep the Singapore dollar in check," Suan said.  

Some 22 of 23 primary dealers polled by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC believe the Fed will keep its overnight target rate fixed at 5.25%.  

"The effect of a pause in the rate hike is already priced in," a trader from a foreign bank said.  

"So the pause in the rate hike is unlikely to change the U.S. dollar drastically tomorrow. Rather, we are more concerned about the statement to check for clues for future rate hikes."  

Suan said that the U.S. dollar is likely to remain in the S$1.5700-S$1.5800 range.  

In the Singapore government debt market, the two-year bond yield fell one basis point to 2.97%, while the 10-year yield fell five basis points to 3.43%.  

"The Singapore bonds rallied because of the weak nonfarm payrolls in the morning and rose by five basis points across the board," a local bank dealer said."  

"During lunch, the cutoff yield of the three-month (treasury bill) tender was much higher than expected, so there was a lot of selling in the short end. In the end, the shorter-dated bonds remained unchanged."  

The dealer said the market had expected the treasury bills to be sold at a yield of 2.93% or below compared with the 3.00% they were actually sold for in the auction.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Higher as Fed rate pause anticipated
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose across the board on Monday, as weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data on Friday lifted expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve would this week pause a two-year campaign of raising interest rates.  

 Upbeat news on the Philippine economy at the weekend helped boost the peso <PHP=> to a three-month high at 51.33 per dollar.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.5704 to the U.S. dollar, its highest in about 2-½   months.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> set its strongest level in almost three months at 37.68 a dollar and the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> added 0.5 percent to 3.6550 per per dollar.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=>, which took a beating last week on worries about the country's deteriorating trade balance, rose to levels near 961 per dollar, up 0.7 percent from Thursday's four-month lows around 967.  

 The dollar held near two-month lows hit against the euro <EUR=> and yen <JPY=> on Friday after data showed the U.S. economy created 113,000 new jobs in July.  

 This tilted market expectations towards the U.S. Fed leaving its key interest rate at 5.25 percent when it meets on Tuesday.  

 "The sell off in the dollar is coming on the back of slower growth in the U.S. and that environment is not particularly positive for Asian growth and equity markets," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

 "But in a soft-dollar backdrop, the dollar is probably the predominant theme. If you look at correlations, the correlation between Asian currencies and dollar/yen is much stronger than with equity markets."  

 Some analysts said high oil prices, which surged more than 2 percent on Monday, and a U.S. economic slowdown that could hurt equity markets were reasons to be cautious about chasing Asian currencies too high for now.  

 "The best bets in the region for a short-term rally are the rupee, the ringgit, and Taiwan dollar as these currencies have already priced in negative local news to the greatest extent," ABN AMRO senior currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note.  

 "The won still looks the most vulnerable regional currency, as it is only just starting the process of pricing in negative local developments."  

 PESO EXTENDS GAINS  

 A rally in the Philippine peso gathered pace after news at the weekend that government revenues from a broadened sales tax in the first six months were 23 percent above target and the central bank had raised its 2006 growth projection on remittances from overseas Filipino workers.  

 "There is a bunch of good news moving the peso," said a Manila trader. "This is the reason why we have already breached the 51.40 level, an important technical level since last Friday."  

 Traders in Singapore said they were wary of intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to curb gains in the local currency, although there have been few signs of central bank intervention in recent weeks.  

 "Probably they are seeing some pass through of imported inflation on the economy and so are essentially happier with a stronger Sing in the extreme short term," said a trader.  

 Lim Hng Kiang, Singapore's minister for trade and industry and deputy chairman for the MAS, said on Monday the country's exports are growing despite the strengthening of the Singapore dollar.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0751 GMT

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Up after Fed survey suggests US slowdown
text:
SINGAPORE, July 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies firmed on Thursday after a survey by the Federal Reserve that suggested the U.S. economy may be slowing, which renewed talk that U.S. interest rates could soon peak after two years of rising.  

 The Fed's Beige Book survey, released on Wednesday, said U.S. economic activity grew overall between June and mid-July, but that there were many local reports of slowing growth.  

 That set the dollar up for sharp losses against the yen and euro, setting the tone for Asian currency trade, with many regionals hiting two-week highs.  

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose to 9,045 per dollar, its strongest since July 12, but it had given up most of its gains by late trade.  

 A dealer in Jakarta said central bank orders to buy dollars around 9,060-9,070 had capped rupiah gains, while some investors stepped in around that area to take profits.  

 "The central bank doesn't want to see the rupiah strengthen too quickly," he said.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose for the third straight day to 51.51 per dollar, its strongest level in about 2-½   months. It has gained about 1.25 percent so far this week.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> gained about a third of a percent each.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> hit a two-week peak at about 37.78 per dollar, while the Malaysian ringgit firmed to 3.6685, also the highest in about two weeks.  

 TIME FOR RISK?  

 Dealers said the rally in Asian currencies suggested investors were slowly moving back into riskier assets after a rout in emerging markets in May and early June.  

 "While the Beige Book has reinforced the move in emerging currencies, it had already started well ahead of that," said Sabrina Jacobs, emerging market currency strategist for Asia at Dresdner Kleinwort.  

 "The correlation between nominal yields and FX performance has been very high and positive since around mid-June, a time when risk aversion started to moderate."  

 Jacobs said the move became obvious across markets on Wednesday, with fresh demand for emerging currencies such as the South African rand.  

 In Asia, high-yielding currencies such as the rupiah and peso are expected to benefit the most from a pick-up in risk appetite.  

 Rupiah sentiment was boosted on Wednesday by Standard & Poor's upgrading of Indonesia's credit rating.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> firmed to its highest in more than two weeks at 1.5775 to the U.S. dollar and analysts said it remained at the strong end of its secret, trade-weighted band.  

 Data on Wednesday showing Singapore's factory output grew at the fastest pace in more than two years in June bolstered the currency, dealers said.  

 One trader said there had been some talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to cap its strength but it was not clear the central bank had intervened in the market.  

 "I have been expecting intervention for 6-7 days now and we continue to trade at the top end of the band," another trader said. "The MAS is probably looking at a flow we in the market don't know about. Once that flow is through, they may come in and buy U.S. dollars."  

 The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS>, meanwhile, rose to 7.9760 per U.S. dollar, the highest level since its July 2005 revaluation, supporting other Asian currencies. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Singapore Dlr Up On Casino Inflow Talk;Bond Curve Steeper
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose late Wednesday in Asian trade on continued expectation of remittances linked to Singapore's first casino project.  

"The Singapore dollar is strengthening, as the market is still speculating that the Las Vegas Sands Corp. (LVS) is going to remit foreign exchange to Singapore within these few days," a trader said.  

In late May, Singapore named Sands the winning bidder for the casino project. Sands will have to pay the Singapore government about US$750 million before the end of August to cover the cost of the waterfront site at Marina Bay as well as various taxes.  

At 0616 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.5905, down from S$1.5929 in New York and S$1.5925 late Monday in Asia.  

The greenback is well supported at the S$1.5900 level, another trader said. The U.S. dollar reached an intraday low at S$1.5888 around 0200 GMT.  

"There is a possibility that the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) is intervening to prevent the greenback from falling further, but I doubt they will intervene that greatly as the Singapore dollar is within range" of the central bank's policy trading band, the second trader said.  

In the debt market, government bond prices were mixed, with prices falling in the longer end, further steepening the yield curve.  

The two-year bond yield remained unchanged at 2.94%, while the 10-year bond yield gained four basis points to 3.55%, steepening the curve.  

"The bond market will remain rangebound until the government seven-year bond auction announcement later today," a dealer said.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is expected to announce the auction size of the seven-year paper later in the Asian day, with market participants expecting the amount to be between S$1 billion and S$1.3 billion.

title: Singapore Dlr Gains On Hopes Of  FX  Inflows; Bonds Weak
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar gained Monday on expectations of more foreign exchange inflows linked to a new casino project, as well as mergers and acquisition activity in the city-state.  

Government bonds were weaker and the curve flatter, but trading volumes remained thin even after an auction for five-year bonds, dealers said.  

At 0646 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.5788, below S$1.5802 at the close of the New York session. In Asian trade late Friday, the greenback was at S$1.5800.  

The U.S. dollar opened on a weak note against the local unit on last Friday's announcement that Las Vegas Sands' S$5 billion proposal made them the successful bidder for Singapore's first casino and integrated resort project.  

The US-based casino giant has to pay S$1.2 billion within the coming weeks, which the market saw as an opportunity to sell the greenback, a local bank dealer said.  

The selling in the U.S. dollar came despite early gains against the yen which failed to spillover into the Singapore market, as investors had positioned themselves for more gains in the local currency.  

The local unit was also helped by news that Indonesia's Lippo is buying a 55.04% stake in Overseas Union Enterprise from Singapore's second biggest bank, United Overseas Bank (U11.SG), and three associated companies for S$989.9 million in cash, triggering a takeover offer for OUE.  

However thin volumes due in part to a U.S. holiday Monday prevented larger gains, they said.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research note that the short-term downside for the U.S. dollar was capped at S$1.5750, considering an absence of direction from regional currencies and recent sharp gains in the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate.  

A huge rise in the rate, which the Monetary Authority of Singapore doesn't disclose, risks central bank intervention in favor of the U.S. dollar, since it counters its current policy of allowing only modest and gradual gains in the currency.  

In the bond market, the two-year yield rose by four basis point to 2.90% in thin, cautious trade ahead of the U.S. holiday. The 10-year yield rose one basis point to 3.49%.  

However after the central bank's auction for five-year bond met market expectations, trading remained lackluster, traders said.  

The central bank sold S$1.1 billion in five-year bonds at 3.27%, in line with market expectations of 3.25%-3.30%, dealers said.  

The market is looking for excuse to buy at the shorter end of the curve and waiting for clues on when the Federal Reserve may end its tightening policy, dealers said.  

The near-term trend for the curve is to steepen, led by a fall in short-term yields, a local bank dealer said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  as won, Sing dlr hit 8-year highs
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - The currencies of South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia hit their highest levels in more than eight years on Wednesday, prompting central bank intervention, as the U.S. dollar fell on speculation U.S. interest rates would stop rising soon.  

The won <KRW=> hit a high of 933.2 per dollar, its strongest level since October 1997.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as high as 1.5730 per dollar, its highest since November 1997, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.6049 per dollar, a level last seen in April 1998.  

Traders said central banks across the region stepped in with dollar purchases to stifle further gains in their currencies. Some central banks intervened through state lenders.  

"The state-run banks have been buying dollars aggressively," said a Singapore currency dealer at a foreign bank.  

The dealer said investors held off from bidding the Singapore dollar higher after seeing the authorities intervene at 1.5730/35 levels. The currency could retreat to levels around 1.58 before traders pushed it higher again, dealers said.  

Similar intervention was noted in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.  

Asian authorities are worried that stronger currencies, could hurt Asian exports to the United States, Europe and Japan, particularly when China is keeping the yuan on a tight leash.  

Data on Wednesday indicated that the South Korean authorities had been intervening in the foreign exchange market since April. The country's foreign exchange reserves jumped $5.55 billion last month to $222.89 billion, the fourth largest in the world.  

"The authorities are afraid of the pace and further appreciation of the won. That's why they came into the market to support the dollar. But the intervention is a smoothing operation -- they want to moderate the pace and not stop the trend," said Roh Sang Chil, a currency trader at Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

Swiss bank UBS said concerns about the record U.S. current account deficit, attempts by central banks to diversify their reserves away from the dollar and expectations that the Fed may end its rate-rise cycle after another increase this month were likely to dominate currency markets.  

It expects the yen <JPY=> to strengthen to 108 per dollar in three months from about 113.25 now. The euro <EUR=> could climb to $1.3 from about $1.26 over the same period, it said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Stall near highs, Korean  intervention  seen
text:
SINGAPORE, April 25 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention by central banks in South Korea and Singapore on Tuesday and a pause in the Japanese yen's rally led to a slight retreat in the won, Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies.  

The won, Sing dollar, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah had hit fresh multi-year highs in early trade after European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet called for an adjustment in Asian exchange rates, echoing statements from the Group of Seven nations and the International Monetary Fund.  

The won <KRW=> climbed to a fresh 8-1/2-year high near 936 per dollar overnight and was underpinned by data showing faster-than-expected first-quarter economic growth.  

It slipped later and shed more than half a percent after the Bank of Korea's suspected dollar-buying intervention.  

"With the big move in dollar/yen over, the fears of intervention has bubbled to the surface again and we may see a short squeeze in Asia," said Ben Simpfendorfer, a regional economist with The Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

Although loss of momentum in the Asian currencies had stalled the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP>, the support from continuing equity inflows would eventually push the currency to 31.50 per U.S. dollar, Simpfendorfer said.  

The Taiwan dollar rose to 31.86 per U.S. dollar, its highest in more than 3 months, but then pulled back to 31.97/99.  

Traders said the Asian rally was also undermined by the yuan's failure to strengthen despite renewed pressure from Western policy-makers for China to play a greater role in the adjustment of global trade imbalances.  

China's central bank fixed the central point of the yuan's trading band for Tuesday at 8.0160 per dollar, weaker than Monday's close at 8.0150. It later rose marginally to 8.0120.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> retained some gains but retreated to levels around 1.5880/85 per U.S. dollar from the overnight high of 1.5850, its strongest level in nearly 8 years.  

The Thai baht <THB=> was briefly quoted at a 6-year high of 37.48 per dollar, before it followed the regional trend.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> pulled back to levels around 8,800 from around 8,780 per dollar, its strongest level since May 2004.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> remained an exception to the wider trend in Asia, undermined by concerns over the country's fiscal position. It continued falling and hit a 2-month low of 51.90 per dollar. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0800 GMT

title: Singapore Dollar Slightly Up; Bonds Gain On Local Buying
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly in Asia Friday, tracking early weakness in the U.S. dollar, but more gains were capped by fears of central bank intervention.  

Government bond prices rallied, led by local buying in the 10-year paper, which unexpectedly flattened the yield curve, dealers said.  

At 0659 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.5980, compared with S$1.5985 at the close of New York trade. In late Asian trade Thursday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.5981.  

The U.S. dollar traded in a range of S$1.5974 and S$1.6002.  

Dealers said trading was lackluster as the local currency tracked the U.S. dollar's movement against major currencies.  

After slipping to Y117.38 early, the U.S. dollar stabilized to Y117.61 in afternoon trade, little changed from the New York close.  

Comments by Singapore's trade minister about the currency also failed to move the market.  

"The adjustment in the Singapore dollar is due to market forces, and it also reflects the strength of the Singapore economy," Trade and Industry Minister Lim Hng Kiang told reporters Friday.  

The Singapore dollar is near an eight-year high and has risen 6.6% since late November when the rally began.  

Recent suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been preventing a decline in the U.S. dollar after it recovered from Thursday's intraday low of S$1.5959 - the lowest in eight years.  

BNP Paribas said in a note the U.S. dollar should find support at S$1.5973 and resistance at S$1.6007.  

The 10-year bond yield slipped four basis points to 3.49%, while the 10-year interest-rate swap rate briefly dropped below 3.90% from a peak of 3.97% Thursday, after a local bank stepped up buying to adjust positions, said a dealer.  

The gains were unexpected after U.S. Treasurys fell overnight and traded flat in Tokyo trade Friday.  

The two-year yield slipped one basis point to 3.08%, flattening the curve by three basis points to 41 basis points.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Hu's visit disappoints, rupiah supported
text:
SINGAPORE, April 21 (Reuters) - China's yuan slipped in offshore forwards on Friday and some Asian regionals fell after being sold by speculators disappointed with Chinese President Hu Jintao's comments on the currency during his U.S. visit.  

The Thai baht <THB=> fell a quarter of a percent and the Philippine peso <PHP=> hit a 1-½ month trough of 51.71 per dollar.  

But the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, South Korean won <KRW=> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> were supported by foreign investment inflows. The won <KRW=> rose to about 946 per dollar, just shy of the 8-1/2-year peak of 944 struck on Wednesday.  

"It is a disappointment, undoubtedly. The easiest thing would have been for dollar/China to have made it below 8 and it could not even do that," said Claudio Piron, JPMorgan Chase's currency strategist, referring to Hu's statements while in Washington.  

Traders had speculated that the bigger gains allowed in the yuan <CNY=CFXS> by the Chinese authorities earlier this month were aimed at pushing it through the 8-per-dollar mark before Hu's visit. But the yuan peaked at around 8.0022 per dollar on April 10. It was traded on Friday between 8.0140 and 8.0180.  

Traders had been expecting that Hu's meeting with U.S. President George W. Bush on Thursday would result in a commitment to a faster appreciation of the yuan. Hu said China would continue to liberalise the yuan regime but gave no specifics.  

That led to the yuan being sold in offshore forwards markets.  

But speculative positions in the Asian currencies were small, Piron said, and hence any disappointment with Hu's comments was unlikely to result in a big sell-off.  

"If anything, the risk gets skewed to the other direction and we could see trade tensions and protectionist measures coming through. That is more of a slow-burning fuse and a Q3/Q4 risk to Asia and, potentially, currency tensions," Piron said.  

Other analysts said the selling of the Asian currencies would be limited ahead of the Group of Seven nations' meeting that starts on Friday and IMF meetings on the weekend.  

RUPIAH SUPPORTED  

Craig Chan, a currency strategist with the Royal Bank of Scotland, said equity flows into South Korean and Taiwan equity markets had been strong, underpinning those currencies, but suspicion that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was intervening had capped the Singapore dollar.  

Taiwan's stock market data showed foreigners have invested nearly a net $4.3 billion in the country's equity market so far in April.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> stopped short of hitting 1.6000 per U.S. dollar and stayed close to Wednesday's peak around 1.5960, which was its strongest in nearly 8 years.  

The rupiah owed its strength to comments by Indonesia's chief economic minister Boediono on Thursday, that the authorities would let market forces guide the currency and that tight monetary policy would soon be relaxed, Chan said.  

The rupiah <IDR=> matched Thursday's high of 8,860 per dollar, its strongest since July 2004, before settling around 8,890/8,895. It is Asia's top performer this year, with gains of more than 10 percent.  

"Boediono opened the gates for more appreciation. That is stimulating more bond related inflows and pushing the equity market to record highs," Chan said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0800 GMT

title: Singapore Dlr Hits 8-Year High Before Suspected MAS Move
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar hit a fresh eight-yearhigh in Asia Wednesday on hopes U.S. rate increases will soon end, before suspected central bank intervention pared some of the gains.  

Government bond prices rallied, tracking gains in U.S. Treasurys overnight following the release of the minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting that signaled an early end to U.S. monetary tightening, dealers said.  

At 0633 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.5983, off its near eight-year low of S$1.5975 in early trade, and compared with S$1.5989 at the close of New York trade. In late Asian trade Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6021  

A Singapore dealer said stop-losses were triggered very early in the session after the U.S. dollar breached the S$1.5990 level.  

This pushed the greenback to a low of S$1.5975 - the lowest since May 6, 1998, when the pair had dipped to S$1.5827.  

At that juncture suspected interventions by the Monetary Authority of Singapore prevented further gains in the local dollar, dealers said.  

An MAS spokesperson told Dow Jones Newswires the central bank doesn't comment on its money-market operations.  

The main reason for the rise Wednesday in Asian currencies such as the Singapore dollar was the belief that the end of the Fed's rate tightening phase will trigger another spell of weakness for the U.S. dollar.  

"Most members thought that the end of the tightening process was likely to be near, and some expressed concerns about the dangers of tightening too much, given the lags in the effects of policy," according to the FOMC minutes, released after a normal three-week period Tuesday.  

Reacting to such expectations, the greenback briefly hit a seven-month low of $1.2369 to the euro on the EBS dealing system, while it dropped to a two-week low of Y116.76 versus the Japanese yen in Asia.  

However, Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank, said more gains in the Singapore dollar were likely capped since it had moved toward the stronger end of the MAS trading band.  

The central bank has in the past defended the currency if it breaches the stronger or weaker end of the undisclosed trading band.  

The rally in government bond prices was led by the 10-year paper, which led to a flattening of the yield curve.  

The 10-year bond yield fell five basis points to 3.58%, while the two-year yield dropped three basis points to 3.08%.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late Ahead Of U.S. Data, Holidays
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar gained slightly in Asian trade Thursday due to moderate profit-taking on the U.S. dollar and caution ahead of the release of key U.S. retail sales data.  

The government bond yield curve steepened as weaker U.S. Treasuries pushed long-term yields higher while the two-year bond yield rose only modestly, dealers said.  

At 0600 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6088, below S$1.6120 at the New York close Wednesday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6120 in late Asian trade Wednesday.  

Early in the day, investors sold the U.S. dollar, tracking the stronger Japanese yen, on the view it had gone as high as it can go in Asia, dealers said.  

They said some investors also bought the Singapore dollar as part of cross-currency deals but were unclear on the specifics of such deals.  

However, overall caution ahead of the release of U.S. March retail and food sales data later Thursday and the long holiday weekend ahead is expected to temper any sharp fluctuations overnight and keep the U.S. dollar rangebound between its Asian close and upward resistance of S$1.6138, a dealer with a local bank said.  

Analysts said the Singapore dollar should remain in a narrow range in the short term with upside potential capped by fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent the currency from going outside its policy band.  

MAS Deputy Chairman Tharman Shanmugaratnam reportedly said Wednesday there is no need for a faster appreciation of the Singapore dollar over the medium term.  

He said the decision by MAS to maintain its current policy was appropriate.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Pre-MAS Review, Bond Curve Steepens
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened in Asia Monday as the issue of another set of strong economic data reinforced expectations of monetary tightening, market participants said.  

Government bond prices fell at the long end, but were flat at the short end, causing the yield curve to steepen, dealers said.  

At 0600 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6048, below S$1.6073 at the New York close Friday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6065 in late Asian trade Friday.  

The U.S. dollar opened little changed from the New York close in the Singapore session, but soon drifted downward as expectations grew that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may tighten its policy Tuesday.  

According to advance estimates issued earlier Monday, Singapore's economy grew 9.1% in the first quarter from a year earlier, its strongest growth rate in two years.  

Soon after the data were issued, the U.S. dollar slipped to S$1.6036 before stabilizing as bigger losses were capped by fears that the MAS might intervene to stem gains in the Singapore dollar, said a dealer at a local bank.  

The local unit has been rising of late due to expectations that Singapore's central bank would either allow a one-time upward shift of the currency's trading band or choose a steeper appreciation path. Last week, the U.S. dollar slid to near an eight-month low of S$1.6016 before recovering on suspected MAS intervention.  

The central bank's current stance is to allow a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate - a policy unchanged since April 2004.  

Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. said in a note that it expects the MAS to shift the midpoint of the exchange rate upward, which would still leave sufficient room for policy flexibility if global growth slows toward the end of the year.  

BNP Paribas said the next key support level for the U.S. dollar is at S$1.6000, which, if broken, might push the greenback to S$1.5775.  

In the bond market, the yield on the two-year paper was flat, but the 10-year yield climbed two basis points to 3.60%.  

A dealer at a local bank said the market wasn't volatile despite selling in U.S. Treasurys Friday because short-end bonds were supported by inflows from foreign funds, which are targeting greater gains for the Singapore dollar after the MAS policy review.

title: Sing dlr seen hitting 1.6/dollar on tighter policy
text:
SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar could hit the psychologically important 1.6 per U.S. dollar mark after a likely tightening of monetary policy on Tuesday but further gains may be limited by the central bank, traders said on Monday.  

The Singapore currency <SGD=> has strengthened 3.6 percent this year and on Monday rose as high as 1.6035 per dollar, just short of last Wednesday's 1.6020, its highest since June 1998.  

Analysts have speculated that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which controls monetary policy by guiding the trade-weighted currency, would let the Singapore dollar appreciate at a faster pace to fight off imported inflationary pressures.  

"The market is pricing a 70-80 percent chance that they will tighten policy. If that happens, we could see a break of 1.6 for a brief while," said a Singapore dollar trader.  

A Reuters poll of 13 analysts last week showed that eight expected the MAS would allow the currency to rise further, while sticking to its two-year policy of a gradual and modest appreciation bias.  

The other five economists said MAS would leave its policy unchanged at its meeting on Tuesday.  

A tighter policy could mean either strengthening the mid-point of the MAS's secret trading band for the trade-weighted currency or widening the band to allow for sharper currency moves.  

Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Banking Corp., said he expected the MAS to strengthen the mid-point of the band by 3 percent to adjust for the currency's rise since the last policy meeting in October.  

"This does not mean, however, that the MAS will be inviting further sharp appreciation -- it has already seen such a move," Callow said in a note.  

"After all, the global growth environment will not look so benign by the October review if the U.S. economy has slowed down."  

He expects the MAS to maintain its policy of a gradual and modest rise in the trade-weighted currency which he expects would allow for a 0.5 percent appreciation in the next 12 months.  

"So, while as of Tuesday theoretically MAS might not feel obliged to intervene to support U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar until the low 1.57 area, more realistically they will be unhappy about a sudden rapid rise," he said.  

IDEAGlobal said in a report that the Singapore currency could be capped at the 1.6 per dollar level for the time being, even if the MAS strengthened the mid-point of its preferred trading range.  

That was because a one-off tightening of policy had already been factored into the exchange rate with the trade-weighted currency 2.5 percent above the estimated mid-point.  

"Thus, the risks are for a 'sell-on-the-fact' after the meeting," the report said.  

To profit from a Singapore dollar sell-off, investors could buy the South Korean won against the Singapore currency for a target of 0.1700 Singapore cents per won <KRWSGD=R> and then 0.1720, it said. The pair traded at about 0.1682 on Monday.

title: Singapore Dollar Gains Capped By MAS Talk; Bonds Weaken
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose in Asia Friday, benefiting from a broad rally in key Asian currencies, but shed some early gains on suspected central bank intervention.  

Government bond prices dropped in thin trade as players focused on the release late Friday of U.S. non-farm jobs data that might signal future U.S. interest rate moves, dealers said.  

At 0650 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6065, below S$1.6074 at the New York close Thursday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6059 in late Asian trade Thursday.  

Earlier in the session the U.S. dollar dipped to S$1.6030 as foreign hedge funds were seen buying the Singapore dollar, the Korean won and the Thai baht, said a dealer at a local bank.  

However, talk emerged in the afternoon session that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened, helping the U.S. dollar to recover from its morning low, traders said.  

Nevertheless, analysts said interest in Asian currencies will remain strong ahead of Chinese President Hu Jintao's summit meeting with U.S. President George W. Bush on April 20.  

The market is speculating about a possible Chinese goodwill gesture during the visit, such as allowing its currency to strengthen - which U.S. Congress has been demanding, analysts said.  

The local unit is also benefiting from talk that the MAS may further tighten policy when it announces its semiannual review next Tuesday.  

United Overseas Bank said in a report there is a 70% chance the MAS will move the midpoint of the trading band upward as a one-off tightening move to fight rising inflationary pressures.  

Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank, said the market doesn't have a consensus on whether the central bank will change policy. However, he said, the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis has been trading on the stronger side of the band.  

The Singapore dollar will continue to benefit from broad dollar weakness.  

"If broad dollar is going down, especially against the Asian currencies, dollar-Sing will also move down," he said  

If the MAS tightens monetary policy, it would be either allowing a one-time upward shift of the currency's trading band or choosing a steeper appreciation.  

The central bank's current stance is to allow a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate - a policy adopted in April 2004.  

In the bond market, yield on the two-year paper rose two basis points to 3.14%, while the 10-year yield climbed one basis point to 3.58%, slightly flattening the curve.  

The market was cautious ahead of U.S. non-farm payrolls data later on Friday, dealers said.

title: Singapore Dlr Stronger Late; Bonds Up On SGD-Linked Flows
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar extended gains in Asia Thursday, as players stayed long on the local unit ahead of the central bank's monetary policy review next week.  

But larger gains were capped after suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore overnight when the U.S. dollar fell to near an eight-year low.  

Government bond prices were stronger for a third straight day as foreign players targeted the shorter-end of the yield curve to take advantage of the strengthening currency, a trader said.  

At 0704 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6059, below S$1.6070 at the New York close Wednesday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6072 in late Asian trade Wednesday.  

A dealer at a foreign bank said the local unit consolidated in a narrow range after Wednesday's volatile trade, when most Asian currencies rallied.  

He said the next key support for the U.S. dollar was at S$1.600, while it should find resistance at S$1.6120.  

The U.S. dollar dropped to S$1.6016 overnight - the lowest since June 1998, when the greenback hit S$1.5890.  

JPMorgan said in a note that the Singapore dollar's testing of the stronger side of the MAS trading band is a signal for an impending move at next week's policy meeting.  

If the MAS tightens monetary policy in its half-yearly statement on April 11, it would be either allowing a one-time upward shift of the currency's trading band or choosing a steeper appreciation, traders said.  

The central bank's current stance is to allow a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate - a policy adopted in April 2004.  

The Asian Development Bank said in a report that it expects the MAS to maintain its 'moderately' tight monetary policy in view of strengthening domestic demand and increasing inflationary pressures.  

In the bond market, a stronger currency triggered inflows into the shorter-end of the yield curve, lifting prices of two-year bonds and easing the overnight rate.  

The two-year yield dropped two basis points to 3.14%, while the 10-year yield slipped one basis point to 3.56%, steepening the yield curve.  

"A stronger currency has sparked (foreign) fund flows into the Singapore bond market," said a dealer at a local bank.

title: Singapore Dollar Weak Before FOMC; Bonds Lower On US Tsys
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fell in Asian trade Tuesday, hurt by weakness in the Japanese yen with sentiment cautious ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee's interest rate decision later in the day.  

Government bond prices fell at the long end of the yield curve on weaker U.S. Treasurys, but declined at a modest pace at the short end ahead of a two-year bond auction Wednesday, they said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6195, up from S$1.6183 at the close of New York trade Monday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6184 in Asian trade late Monday.  

Traders said the U.S. dollar found support in anticipation of another 25-basis-point U.S. rate hike, sending the yen and other Asian currencies lower.  

However, currency traders are looking for clues on future interest-rate moves in the FOMC statement and weren't keen to go long on the U.S. dollar amid uncertainty about U.S. monetary policy.  

In the short term, the U.S. dollar should trade in a narrow range since it was finding strong support at S$1.6150 and its gains were capped at S$1.6200, said Selene Ling, a treasury economist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.  

The U.S. dollar's downside support was driven by fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent the local unit from rising to sharply, dealers said.  

Market participants continued to debate what to expect from an MAS policy review in April.  

Deutsche Bank, in a note to its clients, said it expects the central bank to maintain a tight monetary stance because of a strong economy and inflationary pressures.  

But the German bank cautioned the central bank won't change the current path of modest and gradual appreciation.  

Sanjeev Sanyal, an economist at Deutsche Bank, said he expects the MAS to maintain what he thinks is a 3% appreciation target that it has pursued in the past year against the trade-weighted basket. The MAS has never disclosed its target.  

Deutsche Bank expects the U.S. dollar to slide to S$1.55 over 12 months, he said.  

JPMorgan said the Singapore dollar stands out as the most likely Asian currency to continue its steady appreciation against U.S. dollar despite the Federal Reserve's rate hike.  

The U.S. bank expects the MAS to allow a one-off tightening in April, when it recenters the midpoint of the trading band 1.0%-1.5% above the current level to help ward off inflationary pressures.  

In the bond market, yields on 10-year government bonds rose three basis points to 3.53%, while the two-year yield rose by one basis point to 3.09%.  

Players were waiting for the FOMC outcome and were cautious ahead of a two-year bond auction Wednesday.  

OCBC expects the market to bid a 3.1%-3.2% yield in the auction for the S$1 billion of bonds. The current benchmark bond was trading at 3.09%, while the bond that will be reopened Wednesday was trading at 3.15% late Tuesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steady ahead of Fed, firm undertone
text:
SINGAPORE, March 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies barely moved on Tuesday as traders waited for the outcome of a Federal Reserve policy meeting at which U.S. rates were expected to be raised for the 15th time since mid-2004.  

 Yet, despite the caution, the tone on the Asian regionals remained firm as markets anticipated more gains in the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, possible policy tightening in Singapore and the likelihood of faster appreciation in the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS>.  

 On Tuesday the yuan hit its highest level since its July revaluation, rising to 8.0205 per dollar after the central bank set a record-high daily mid-point, around which the currency is allowed to fluctuate in a tight band.  

 U.S. Senators Charles Schumer and Lindsey Graham, proponents of a bill that threatens China with tariffs on its exports if it does not allow the yuan to rise faster, visited the country last week.  

 That, and Chinese President Hu Jintao's planned visit to the United States in mid-April, have stoked speculation Beijing will allow faster appreciation.  

 Analysts said a rising yuan and Japanese yen <JPY=> would push up currencies such as the Singapore dollar <SGD=> that are used as proxies to trade the yuan. Others such as the Korean won <KRW=> that had already raced ahead might not gain so much.  

 The won fell marginally to near 977 per dollar, weighed down by expectations of seasonal dollar demand as Korean corporations pay dividends to foreigners.  

 Philip Wee, DBS Bank's currency strategist, said he expected the won to weaken to about 8.5 per yen from levels around 8.36 on Tuesday.  

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, in contrast, firmed modestly to a 15-month high of 9,000 a dollar, with traders bracing for technical factors and flows into high-yielding Indonesian bonds to push it to levels around 8,800.  

 "I am bullish rupiah on the 12-month view. The rupiah has become a policy tool for policy makers," said Lim Su Sian, regional economist with the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.  

 Lim said currency appreciation was a better approach to tackling Indonesia's inflationary pressures, given there was limited room to raise double-digit interest rates further.  

 SING DOLLAR  

 Elsewhere, although the Singapore dollar weakened on demand for U.S. dollars from importers, there was little impact from news that state-owned investment firm Temasek [TEM.UL] was buying a stake in bank Standard Chartered Plc .  

 The Sing dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.6202 per dollar, inching close to Monday's low of 1.6210 and half a cent away from the previous session's highs. Traders rejected the possibility of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to rein in the Sing dollar.  

 Temasek's announcement on Tuesday that it had agreed to buy an 11.55 percent stake in Standard Chartered, worth approximately $4 billion, was old news, traders said. "That talk was on the streets about 10-12 days ago, when a large sterling-Sing dollar deal had gone through," said one Singapore-based trader.  

 Analysts maintained their bullishness on the currency, saying it would gain against the U.S. dollar irrespective of whether the Fed announces another rate rise on Tuesday.  

 JPMorgan strategist Claudio Piron said the Sing dollar was supported by expectations that the MAS would probably move up the centre of the trade-weighted band within which it manages the currency when it reviews policy in April.  

 The MAS conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar against an undisclosed band based on a trade-weighted basket of currencies. It has maintained a stance of gradual and modest appreciation since April 2004.  

 Lim differed. She said she did not expect the MAS to further tighten policy given inflation was benign and likely to remain so, except for some upward pressure in May when recently announced budgetary hand-outs to low-income groups were made.
