title: Emerging Asia  FX -Firmer but wary of c.bank  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, March 17 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose against a generally soft dollar on Friday, but gains in the Malaysian ringgit and Indian rupee were curbed by suspected central bank intervention.  

 Wariness that Singapore's central bank may step into the market to cap gains in the Singapore dollar <SGD=>, pushed the currency off a two-week high hit in early trade although traders said there had been no signs of actual intervention.  

 Regional currencies were underpinned as investors trimmed expectations for further U.S. dollar-friendly interest rate increases following tame U.S. inflation data on Thursday.  

 A rise in the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> to its highest level since last July's revaluation and speculation over further gains also supported Asian currencies.  

 In Kuala Lumpur, traders said that banks acting on behalf of the central bank had bought dollars for ringgit <MYR=>. This capped the ringgit's gains at the psychologically important 3.70 per dollar level -- the strongest level since a peg against the dollar was abandoned last July.  

 Dealers said the central bank did not want to see the ringgit strengthen too far, too fast, although the trend for a stronger ringgit remained.  

 Malaysia's Second Finance Minister Nor Mohamed Yakcop said on Friday that a higher ringgit would result in lower imported inflation.  

 "This is the first ringgit comment from a senior official in a while, but given that it comes at a time when dollar/ringgit is trying to push to new year lows below 3.7000 it will be seen as a green light for further currency strength," said Shahab Jalinoos, a currency strategist at ABN AMRO in Singapore.  

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> was pushed off a one-week high at 44.34 per dollar on suspected central bank intervention, dealers said.  

 SING DOLLAR OFF HIGHS  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a two-week high at 1.6165 per U.S. dollar before trimming gains as investors suspected that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) may intervene to prevent a sharp rise in the currency.  

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar was probably trading at the strong end of its currency band. The MAS conducts monetary policy by guiding the trade-weighted currency within an undisclosed trading band.  

 It has a tightening stance of allowing "a modest and gradual appreciation" of the trade-weighted currency and traders expect the central bank to tighten monetary policy further next month.  

 "I am surprised that there hasn't been intervention because the currency is at the top half of the band," said Mirza Baig, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

 "This may be because the policy review is coming up and they don't want to do anything ahead of that."  

 The South Korean won <KRW=> hit a two-week high at 970.4 per dollar. The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, which hit its highest level since January 2005 on Wednesday, inched lower. A Jakarta trader said the slight weakness was due to a covering of short positions on the dollar ahead of the weekend.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> hovered around 39.06 per dollar, trading firmer with other Asian currencies, but dealers said the currency remained vulnerable to political uncertainty in Thailand.

title: Singapore Dollar Up On Yen; Bonds Down On Treasurys
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened Tuesday, reacting to a stronger Japanese yen, but further gains were capped due to fears of forex outflows if DBS Bank succeeds in its effort to buy South Korea's fifth-biggest lender.  

Government bond prices declined after prices of U.S. Treasurys dropped overnight on continued fears of higher U.S. interest rates, dealers said.  

At 0611 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6250, compared with S$1.6254 at the close of New York trade Monday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6278 in Asian trade late Monday.  

The greenback traded between S$1.6236 and S$1.6262.  

A dealer at a foreign bank said interbank players stepped in after the U.S. dollar dipped to S$1.6240 in early trade.  

News that DBS will bid for a 50.5% stake in Korea Exchange Bank, which is controlled by U.S. Lone Star Funds, also lent support to the currency pair after some estimated that the bid could be around US$6 billion, dealers said.  

Most analysts don't expect DBS to emerge the winner, as it faces tough competition from two South Korean lenders.  

Analysts were also wary of central bank intervention since the Singapore dollar is trading 1.3% above its midpoint on a trade-weighted basis.  

One reason for its surge is the recent decoupling from movements in the Japanese yen, which has been volatile since the Bank of Japan's recent tightening of monetary policy, JPMorgan said in a note.

title: Singapore Dollar Flat Late Despite Weaker Yen, Bonds Down
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was little changed Monday despite a weaker yen as there was little corporate demand for the U.S. dollar after recent flows from mergers and acquisitions, dealers said.  

Government bonds fell across the board. The slide was led by the front end, which helped to flatten the yield curve, dealers said.  

At 0618 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6278, compared with S$1.6279 at the close of New York trade Friday. The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6297 in Asian trade late Friday.  

The greenback traded between S$1.6258 and S$1.6294.  

A dealer at a foreign bank said that corporates stepped back after they realized there was little demand out there for the U.S. dollar on speculation that foreign exchange transactions needed for Temasek's proposed purchase of Thailand's Shin Corp had already been put through.  

He said that some corporates also sold the greenback early in the session before it stabilized to current flat levels.  

Dealers said they expect some more corporate inflows over the next few days from mergers and acquisitions taking place in Singapore.  

One such inflow could come from theproposed sale of SembCorp Industries' 60% stake in SembCorp Logistics to Australia's Toll Holdings for S$749 million. If SembCorp accepts Toll's full takeover offer, the transaction could be worth S$1.4 billion.  

However, JPMorgan cautioned in a note Monday that recent gains in the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate are unlikely to continue because of fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore despite broad expectations that it might move to a tighter policy in April.  

It said the Singapore dollar is 1.20% above the midpoint of the band, but it faces strong support if it slips to 0.7% above midpoint.  

In the bond market, the two-year yield rose six basis points to 3.11%, reacting to stronger-than-expected U.S. non-farm payrolls data, which raised expectations the Federal Reserve may push benchmark rates above 5% from 4.5% now.  

The 10-year yield rose two basis points to 3.52%, which helped flatten the yield curve by another four basis points to 41 points.

title: Sing dollar hits highest more than 7 yrs vs USD
text:
SINGAPORE, March 3 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit its highest levels in more than 7 years in overnight deals as foreign investors poured money into Asian assets, leading to sharp gains in one of the region's more liquid currencies.  

Analysts said a breach of resistance around 1.6160-1.6170 per U.S. dollar on Thursday triggered some stop-loss buying of Sing dollars.  

It was traded as high as 1.6127 per U.S. dollar, a level last seen in October 1998 towards the end of the Asian financial crisis, and has risen 1.5 percent in two weeks. On Friday morning it was trading around 1.6140.  

"We saw stops go out yesterday after the highs of the previous two runs were taken out," Callum Henderson, Standard Chartered Bank's head of currency strategy, said.  

Henderson said rises in the Thai baht <THB=>, Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, South Korean won <KRW=> showed foreigners were keen on Asian assets. Yet they were being selective, and the Singapore dollar was perceived to be a low-risk currency, he said.  

Some traders have been wary of buying the Sing dollar for fear the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will intervene, given market estimates that it is trading near the top of its secret trade-weighted policy band.  

Henderson said the top end of the central bank's band as per his estimates was now around 1.61 per U.S. dollar. That estimates assumes the band is 3 percent wide and its mid-point appreciates at an annual pace of 2 percent.

title: Singapore  Dollar Slips Late Vs USD On  Intervention  Fears
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar, which surged to a seven-year high against the U.S. dollar in overnight trades, fell in Asia Friday due to a pullback in the yen and on fears of intervention by the local central bank.  

Government bonds extended recent losses, with the two-year yield surging to its highest level since December 2000 after an overnight selloff in U.S. Treasurys and continued issuance of corporate bonds, dealers said.  

At 0602 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6210, up from S$1.6178 in New York trade Thursday. In overnight dealings, the U.S. dollar slid to S$1.6128, the lowest level since trading at S$1.6050 on Oct. 16, 1998, but recovered ground in Asian early morning trades.  

The U.S. dollar was at S$1.6187 in Asian trade late Thursday.  

A dealer at a local bank said the U.S. dollar regained strength against the local unit after erasing losses against the yen in early trade.  

The U.S. dollar had dipped to Y115.91 in New York close, but rebounded to Y116.39 by Friday afternoon, while pushing ahead against other Asian currencies.  

Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore won't tolerate swift gains in the Singapore dollar also prevented the local currency from extending overnight gains, said a second dealer.  

Despite the weakness, some banks improved their forecast for the local currency this year because of a strong economy and expectations that the central bank may allow a steeper rise in the exchange rate to counter inflation.  

Goldman Sachs said in a report said that it is revising upward its forecast for the Singapore dollar because of an expansionary budget that will promote economic growth and an expected tightening of monetary policy to attack inflation.  

It expects the dollar to slide to S$1.58 in three months, S$1.54 in six months and S$1.50 in 12 months. Its previous forecast for the three periods were S$1.62, S$1.60 and S$1.58.  

It also expects the MAS to allow a steeper appreciation of the trade-weighted exchange rate without signaling an actual change in its policy stance.  

Calyon Bank said it expects the U.S. dollar to slide to S$1.55 by the end of the year because of an expected tightening in policy and a strong economy.  

In the bond market, weaker U.S. Treasurys and continued issuance of corporate bonds dragged prices lower.  

The Housing Development Board has priced a S$100-million, 10-year bond at 3.73%, a week after it sold a S$400 million five-year bond, bankers said Friday.  

The two-year bond yield climbed seven basis points to 2.97% - its since Dec. 2000. The 10-year bond yield rose five basis points to 3.57%, the highest level for the yield since July 2004.  

Selena Ling, a fixed-income analyst at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp., said that bond market sentiment is bearish because players are willing to pay in the interest rate swap market amid concerns that rates might climb further.

title: Singapore  Dlr Down Late On  Intervention  Fears;Bonds Lower
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly weaker in Asia Thursday on fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent more gains and on a slight recovery in the U.S. dollar against major currencies.  

Singapore government bonds fell across the board after overnight weakness in U.S. Treasurys and on local corporate issuance in the primary market, dealers said.  

At 0647 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6187, up from S$1.6178 in New York trade Wednesday. It was at S$1.6203 in Asian trade Wednesday.  

A dealer at a Singapore bank said foreign funds sold the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar early in the session, but the selling halted after talk emerged the central bank was ready to intervene.  

A second dealer said talk that the MAS was willing to intervene around S$1.6170-S$1.6180 forced speculators to step back.  

The early push for a stronger Singapore dollar was due to renewed speculation that China and Malaysia may allow their currencies to rise, traders said.  

The speculation rose as U.S. Undersecretary of Treasury for International Affairs Timothy Adams reiterated Wednesday the U.S. view that China needs to introduce more flexible forex policies.  

Jimmy Koh, treasury economist at United Overseas Bank, said that in the medium term the Singapore dollar will continue to face upward pressure because of hopes China may allow its currency to rise.  

He said unwinding of carry trades was also helping the Japanese yen and as a result pushing up Asian currencies.  

Speculation about further monetary tightening by the MAS in its next policy review due in April is another factor pushing the Singapore dollar higher, Koh said.  

"We think they will not jump the gun. Inflation is not running away therefore there's no need to further tighten policy," he said.  

The next key level for the U.S. dollar is S$1.6162 - the lowest level for the greenback last year, he said.  

"This is a critical level that the market will be watching closely," said Koh.  

In the bond market, weaker U.S. Treasurys and the issue of new corporate debt weighed on the market.  

Southeast Asia's biggest property company, CapitaLand Ltd., sold S$200 million in fixed- and floating-rate five-year bonds Thursday.  

Earlier in the day, Frasers Centrepoint sold S$200 million five-year bonds at 4.045%, a source familiar with the deal said.  

The bond sales had the biggest impact on the five-year government bond, whose yield rose five basis points to 2.33%, while the two-year yield climbed six basis points to 2.91%.

title: Singapore Dollar Up Late Amid Broadly Weak U.S. Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger late Tuesday in Asia amid broad U.S. dollar weakness sparked by renewed fears of further global terrorism after an Israeli missile attack Monday killed Palestinian Hamas founder Ahmed Yassin.  

Singapore government bonds were also slightly higher at the end of the session, in line with U.S. Treasurys, reflecting the heightened fears of terrorism.  

At 0750 GMT, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.6878, down from S$1.6927 late Monday in Asia. It traded in the S$1.6874-S$1.6996 range intraday.  

The missile attack, which was condemned by governments in the Arab world, Europe and Japan, reignited geopolitical worries, prompting some players to push the U.S. dollar down as low as S$1.6877 in the morning.  

But the U.S. currency later rebounded slightly on light buybacks spurred by jitters that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to support the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair.  

Traders said market participants were wary of driving the U.S. currency down toward S$1.6860, the three-week low set last week where the MAS was rumored to have called banks to ask about the currency pair.  

Despite the possibility of MAS intervention, however, the U.S. dollar edged back down against the local currency late in the session, hitting a fresh intraday low of S$1.6874 on continuing fears of more terrorism globally.  

Although the U.S. currency managed to hold ground in the high S$1.6800s, technical analysis suggests the U.S. currency's short-term corrective rebound may have ended at S$1.6960 Monday, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

But UOB added the U.S. dollar's downward momentum against the local currency isn't strong and the S$1.6840 support will likely be difficult to break. It also recommended selling the U.S. currency at S$1.6910 and placing a stop-loss order above S$1.6940 as a short-term trading strategy. [ 23-03-04 0834GMT ]  

Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly marginally higher as they tracked U.S. Treasurys on heightened concerns about global terrorism after Monday's assassination of the Hamas founder.  

Bonds, however, showed little reaction to the release of Singapore's February consumer price index, which rose 1.5% on year, at the high end of expectations of a 1.0%-1.5% increase.  

Analysts said although theoretically bonds should have reacted to the bigger-than-expected increase, in practice Singapore bonds tend to take their cue from U.S. Treasurys instead.  

The yield on the two-year Singapore government securities was 0.92%, down four basis points from Monday's close. At the longer end of the curve, the yield on 10-year bonds was flat at 3.02%, while the 15-year yield slipped two basis points to 3.44%.  

Interest rate swaps also were mostly slightly lower. The two-year swap offer was at 1.31%, against 1.35% late Monday, while the five-year offer was at 2.31%, versus 2.34%. The 10-year swap offer fell one basis point to 3.33%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps widened to 202 basis points from 199 points late Monday.  

The overnight rate fell to 0.1875% from 0.3125%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dollar weak, peso at low.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 22 (Reuters) - Political risks undermined
the Taiwan dollar and the Philippine peso on Monday, after the
controversy surrounding Taiwan's weekend presidential elections
and worries ahead of the Philippine elections in May.
    The Philippine peso        hit a fresh all-time low of
56.45 per dollar, while the Taiwan dollar  fell 0.3
percent from Friday. Central banks in both countries were
suspected of intervening to defend their respective currencies.
    Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar       , Korean won
 , Indonesian rupiah  and Thai baht       , were
also marginally weaker as the Japanese yen  slid further
from last week's one-month highs.
    Traders said markets were wary of testing the Japanese
authorities' tolerance of a stronger yen, despite the belief
that their aggressive yen-weakening intervention ahead of the
fiscal year end on March 31 had eased.
  


    Markets also waited for news out of Pakistan, where troops
have rounded up a group of Islamic militants and their tribal
allies, possibly including a senior al Qaeda figure whose
capture could boost the dollar.
    Analysts dismissed the swings in the regionals, led by the
yen, as temporary noise and said Asian currencies would
appreciate in the longer term.
    "The best way to trade Asian currencies is to stick to the
fundamental script. Here, the story for the yen and other Asian
currencies continues to be bullish," Lehman Brothers said in a
commentary.
 
    "Japanese capital markets are increasingly outperforming
their G3 peers," it said.
    Asian trade balances were rising and equity inflows also
remained strong, the note said.
    "Avoid getting caught in the noise and be prepared to deal
with the occasional intervention hiccup. But as long as the
fundamentals remain positive, stay long Asian currencies."
    POLITICAL UNCERTAINTY
    The Taiwan government said on Sunday the central bank would
intervene in markets if necessary to maintain exchange rate
stability.
    But President Chen Shui-bian's narrow election victory, a
puzzling assassination attempt and the large number of invalid
votes have sparked protests and a call for a recount.
    Even though the authorities have pledged to limit
volatility in the currency and stocks, analysts said the
election outcome was a negative for the Taiwan dollar.
    A win by the opposition candidate Lien Chan, whose KMT
  

(Nationalist Party) holds a slim majority in parliament, would  

have helped Taiwan make progress with tough banking reforms and  

attracted foreign investment, said UBS strategist Bhanu Baweja.  

The Taiwan dollar had been among the strongest in  

Asia earlier this year, rising 3.5 percent from December to  

mid-February. It has since been volatile.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dollar hurt, peso at new low.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 19 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar fell on
Friday after President Chen Shui-bian and Vice-President
Annette Lu were shot while campaigning on the eve of the
presidential election.
    Offshore traders bought the dollar not just against the
Taiwan dollar but also against the Philippine peso, driving the
latter to a fresh record low of 56.38 per dollar.
    The Singapore dollar and Korean won found some support
during the day, as they followed the yen's moves and waited for
its rally to resume.
    Taiwan's currency was hurt by the possibility a sympathy
vote may help the President retain the presidency in the face
of a strong challenge from the opposition Nationalist Party.
    The Taiwan dollar hit a low of 33.29 per dollar, a 0.2
percent drop, after the news broke. The currency stabilised
after dealers said they saw the central bank intervening in the
market to contain the fall.
  


 
    "If this increases the chances of the DPP coming to power,
then I think it is negative for the Taiwan dollar,"
    "The markets had already expected largely that the KMT is
  

going to win, and if the stock market goes lower then you will  

see a lot of the good work undone for the Taiwan dollar bulls,"  

said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist with UBS.  

The KMT holds a slim majority in the legislature and if the  

president belonged to the same party, it would help Taiwan make  

progress with tough banking reforms and attract foreign  

investment, Baweja said.   


 
    However he added the currency's weakness would be limited
even if the Chen retained the presidency.
    INTERVENTION
    The rest of the Asian currencies spent the day in narrow
ranges, reassessing the yen's trend and speculation that Japan
would moderate its currency intervention.
    The yen was off Thursday's one-month high of 106.35 per
dollar, straddling 107.
    Analysts said the Asian forex sluggishness was a sign
markets had got ahead of themselves in buying the yen, driving
it up nearly six percent in 10 days, and were now wary.
    David Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of
  

Scotland, Singapore, said the scale of Japanese intervention

may have moderated but markets were being too aggressive in  

buying the yen.  

Other Asian central banks were also likely to intervene

less, although they would remain watchful ahead of elections in  

many countries, Simmonds said.  

"I do feel we are in the early stages of a shift in balance  

here, away from such huge levels of intervention and reserves  

accumulation and towards a slightly faster pace of currency

gains," Simmonds said.  

"But I am quite sure that CBC (Taiwan's central bank), BOK  

(Bank of Korea), MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) are  

still vigilant around the fringes of these markets and they are  

not going to disappear either."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Off highs, rethinking  intervention .
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies retreated
from early highs on Friday, following the yen's moves as
markets reassessed speculation that Japan would moderate its
currency intervention.
    The dollar was almost a yen        up from Thursday's
one-month low of 106.35 per dollar. Late on Thursday it was
hurt by security concerns after a bomb scare affected train
services between Britain and France.
    News that a senior al Qaeda member may have been cornered
in Pakistan boosted the dollar, as did a view that the yen's
nearly six percent rally in 10 days may have been too rapid.
    The Singapore dollar        fell back to 1.6920/30, levels
seen in Thursday's Asian trading and down from the 1.6861 highs
struck in offshore deals.
    The Korean won                   gave up four won from an
offshore one-month peak near 1,155 per dollar.
  


 The Taiwan
dollar  was also off a one-month high, of 33.16 per
dollar, and treaded warily ahead of Saturday's presidential
elections.
    Analysts said the sluggishness in currencies was a sign
markets had got ahead of themselves in buying the yen, and were
now wary.
    "I am convinced that a $50 billion a month run rate of
(Japanese) intervention is utterly unsustainable and unwise and
that we have seen the peak," said David Simmonds, markets
strategist with the Royal Bank of Scotland, Singapore.
    "The problem is the temptation to look for extremes, that
either they continue at the same extraordinary rate of
intervention that they have shown over the last few months,
which is ridiculous, or that they suddenly disappear
altogether," he said.
    ASIA TO INTERVENE LESS
    The other Asian central banks were also likely to intervene
less, although they would remain watchful ahead of elections in
many countries, Simmonds said.
    "I do feel we are in the early stages of a shift in balance
here, away from such huge levels of intervention and reserves
accumulation and towards a slightly faster pace of currency
gains," Simmonds said.
    "But I am quite sure that CBC (Taiwan's central bank), BOK
(Bank of Korea), MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) are
still vigilant around the fringes of these markets and they are
not going to disappear either."
    The Thai baht        rose in a belated catch-up with the
region's uptrend but the Indonesian rupiah  was weighed
down by uncertainty ahead of that country's long election
period, which begins next month.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said while the
Korean authorities were managing the won less closely than
before, they would not let it trade freely until investment and
employment improved.
 
    Moreover, there was a threat from the recent drop in
leading indicators for Asian exports, he said.
    "If this situation does not change soon, and growth in
  

Korean export incomes begins to slow even when domestic economy  

recovery has not yet shifted into top gear, it will induce the  

authorities to once again be more interventionist in the  

market," Baweja said.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late As US Dlr Weakens Versus Regionals
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was markedly stronger against its U.S. counterpart late in Asia Thursday, hitting a three-week high in the early afternoon amid broad-based U.S. dollar weakness against regional currencies.  

Meanwhile, Singapore government bond prices were slightly weaker in line with softer U.S. Treasurys prices overnight.  

At 0800 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6922, down from S$1.6966 late in Asia Wednesday. It traded a S$1.6895-S$1.6993 range intraday.  

The U.S. currency's plunge to as low as S$1.6895, its lowest level since Feb. 25, was fueled by heavy selling from various banks, including foreign houses, to cut losses on long U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar positions or to bet on a further fall in the U.S. unit against the local unit, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar has been falling against the yen in Asian trade Thursday and is now trading at Y107.07, down from Y108.25 late in New York Wednesday. The U.S. unit fell as low as Y106.75 during Asian trading.  

But local banks immediately bought the U.S. dollar around the psychologically important S$1.6900 level, lifting it back into the low-S$1.6900s. One trader said the domestic banks might have acted on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, although another dealer said the banks were likely trading for their own account.  

Nonetheless, the MAS is widely known to be averse to excessive volatility in the Singapore dollar, and is suspected to have intervened last month to curb the local currency's rise when the U.S. dollar slid to a four-year low of S$1.6675.  

However, with the U.S. unit's close below S$1.7005 late in New York Wednesday, the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair has triggered a bearish double-top pattern that suggests a fall to at least S$1.6823 in coming days, based on technical analysis.  

The S$1.7005 level is the March 9 low between the two tops - the March 4 high of S$1.7193 and the March 12 high of S$1.7180.  

Another negative factor for the currency pair in the near term is the U.S. dollar's fall below both its 50-day moving average at S$1.6958 and its 30-day moving average at S$1.6952 in Thursday's Asian session. [ 18-03-04 0812GMT ]  

Singapore government bond prices fell following the results of a five-year bond auction earlier in the session.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore had sold S$1.3 billion in five-year paper at a relatively high cutoff yield of 2.10%.  

Late Thursday, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds rose to 0.95% from 0.92% late Wednesday. At the longer end of the curve, the yield on 10-year bonds was higher at 2.92% from 2.87%, and the 15-year yield was 3.35% versus 3.34% previously.  

The five-year benchmark was bid at 2.00%.  

Interest rate swaps were also higher in line with local bond yields. The two-year swap offer was at 1.32% from 1.29% late Wednesday, while the five-year offer was 2.25% versus 2.20%. The 10-year swap offer was 3.23%, up from 3.20%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps was unchanged at 191 basis points.  

The overnight rate rose to 0.4375% from 0.3750%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Nervous about  intervention .
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were just
a shade weaker on Wednesday morning with trading still driven
by wariness over Japanese intervention and expectations of
longer-term appreciation in the regionals.
 
    As with Japan, markets in Korea and Taiwan worried about
possible dollar-buying intervention by their central banks.
    Weak Asian equity markets following losses on Wall Street,
provided further impetus to bearishness on the regionals.
    Mimicking the yen's decline of over a yen from levels close
to 110 per dollar in overnight trade, the Sing dollar
bounced off 1.70 offshore and lost more than half a cent.
    The Taiwan dollar          was flat around 33.32 per U.S.
dollar and the Thai baht  was slightly weak.
    An exception was the Korean won                  , which
  

was about a quarter percent stronger than levels around 1,174  

late on Tuesday. It fell from a three-week high near 1,167 on  

Tuesday after the Bank of Korea was believed to have  

intervened.  

Analysts said the suspected intervention in Korea and  

Taiwan seemed to be aimed at slowing the appreciation in their  

currencies, unlike in Japan, where markets believe the dollar  

is being defended at 110 yen.  

"Overall, I don't think that the markets' view that the  

Korean authorities have adjusted their stance is incorrect,"  

said John Cairns, head of research at IDEAglobal Ltd.,  

Singapore.   


 
    "It is just that the Korean authorities are not going to
allow sudden and large appreciation."
    Cairns estimated the Bank of Korea had bought about $200
million on Monday and over $1 billion on Tuesday and Wednesday,
to slow the won's gains both against the dollar and the yen.
    Traders were however betting on longer-term gains in some
regionals and indicated a preference for buying the Sing dollar
and the north Asians -- the won and Taiwan dollar.
    Some traders in Singapore were already positioning for
heavy inflows that Singapore Telecom  would receive
when it sells its stake in Belgian telephone operator Belgacom
         which is preparing for an initial public offering.
    LESS BULLISH ON BAHT, RUPIAH
    Elsewhere, the Philippine peso        stayed in a narrow
56.15-56.25 range, just above its lifetime low of 56.35 which
the central bank is believed to be defending.
    The Indonesian rupiah        was near 8,550 per dollar,
sidelined ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections
starting from next month.
    Analysts said they would avoid taking any bets, especially
bullish ones, on the peso and rupiah because of the political
risk even though they offered high yields.
    IDEAglobal's Cairns said he would also be wary of buying
the baht as the bird flu outbreak had hurt exports and
authorities seemed reluctant to let the currency rise.
    "The bird flu is not a major worry but it has altered the
balance of payments significantly enough to suggest that the
downside on dollar/baht has slowed considerably," Cairns said.
    The baht was quoted at 39.35/40 a dollar.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pinned down by doubts over yen.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 8 (Reuters) - Asian currency markets were
restless on Monday as doubts swirled about the U.S. dollar's
global trend and over Japanese intervention to weaken the yen.
    The Singapore dollar        rose almost a cent, from
Friday's three-month low of 1.7186, and the Korean won
  moved in a narrow range around 1,172 per dollar.
 
    The baht        was almost unchanged from Thursday's close
around 39.45 as Thai markets opened after a long weekend.
    The Thai economy grew a better than expected 2.7 percent in
the fourth quarter of 2003, helping it to its biggest annual
expansion in eight years, official data showed on Monday.
    But, with the yen hitting a five-month low of 112.30 per
dollar on Friday in New York, markets were taking no chances.
    While the regionals had indeed parted ways with the yen's
  

three-week fall versus the U.S. dollar, analysts said there was  

a lingering risk that Japanese intervention to weaken the yen  

would continue, and eventually pull down regional currencies.   


 
    "Dollar/yen has to come down and so does dollar/Asia," said
Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS.
    "The only risk is that of BOJ intervention," he said,
adding that buying the yen at this time could be likened to
going against "a moving train."
    The yen has shed over 3.6 percent of its value against the
  

dollar in two weeks. In comparison, the won is up about a  

percent, the Taiwan dollar has lost over half a  

percent and the Singapore dollar is about 1.2 percent down in  

two weeks.  

Traders said cross-currency trades, involving short  

positions in the yen against the regionals, were becoming too  

crowded and the ambiguity about the yen made things worse.  

Markets were also confused about the U.S. dollar's  

direction in major markets after Friday's surprisingly weak  

U.S. jobs data and some comments from European policymakers  

appreciating the dollar's rebound versus European currencies.  

While the U.S. dollar climbed against the yen in the face  

of the jobs data, it fell against other major currencies like   


the euro , Swiss franc  and sterling       .
  

BUY THE RUPIAH  

Elsewhere, the Philippine peso moved in a tight  

56.32-56.35 per dollar band. It was supported at the 56.35  

record low by suspicion the central bank was defending the  

currency as political uncertainty continued to hurt sentiment.  

The Indonesian rupiah recovered gradually in opening  

deals, crossing over from the weaker side of 8,600 to the  

dollar.   


 
    Baweja said he would place bets on a rally in the rupiah
against the dollar, by buying rupiah in the offshore forwards.
    Bank Indonesia had defended the rupiah from falling past
8,600, and hence they might not confuse markets by buying
dollars too at those levels, he said.
    "Given BI's greater FX reserves ammunition compared to
  

recent years, and the high probability of a near-term turn in  

dollar/yen, we see value in selling near-dated dollar/rupiah  

non-deliverable forwards," he said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaker but outperform yen.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened
slightly on Friday ahead of key U.S. jobs data but outperformed
the yen, which was undermined by wariness of Japanese
intervention.
    The Singapore dollar        hit a three-month low of 1.7190
per dollar on Thursday but found some support during Asian
trading.
    The Korean won        and Taiwan dollar          were
slightly weaker but supported by foreign equity investment
inflows. Markets in Thailand were closed.
 
    Analysts said the yen       , pinned near four-month lows
around 111.30/40 per dollar and down nearly six percent from
3-=   year highs struck last month, had room to fall further
and that could keep Asian currencies under some pressure.
    "Technically the yen is looking at 112.75 as the next
  

hurdle and that means there could be a further fallout on Asian  

currencies," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist with  

Standard Chartered Bank.   


 
    Markets were hoping the U.S. non-farm jobs data would help
determine if the dollar was set for further gains.
    Piron said he believed the dollar's rally was temporary and
not a reversal in its longer term downtrend.
    CROSSES
    Yen/Asia cross rates showed regional currencies were
treating their Japanese counterpart's decline lightly and
traders recommended buying the regionals against the yen.
    "When dollar/yen goes up, yen/Asia goes down and Asian
  

currencies will outperform the yen when the yen is falling,"  

said David Simmonds, a markets strategist with the Royal Bank  

of Scotland.  

The Sing dollar/yen cross was at 64.85 yen, the  

strongest the Sing dollar has been against the yen since  

September. The Taiwan dollar/yen cross showed the  

Taiwan dollar yielding about 3.34 yen, the highest since  

September.  

Simmonds said the trend was reminiscent of the yen's big  

fall after a prolonged rally against the dollar towards the end  

of 1999, when foreign equity flows and a strong growth outlook  

propped up Asian currencies and helped them outperform the yen.  

RUPIAH WEAK  

The Indonesian rupiah hit a four-month low near  

8,590 per dollar but the decline was checked by expectations of  

inflows from a $1.0 billion sovereign bond issue and a  

suspicion that the central bank was selling dollars.  

Still, the currency has fallen 2.5 percent since early  

February and is being undermined by worries over upcoming  

parliamentary and presidential elections that start in April  

and could last till September, if a presidential run-off is  

required.  

"The one major overhang is the election process in  

Indonesia," said M.R.Madhavan, regional strategist with Bank of  

America. "The elections in Indonesia are much more closely  

fought and volatile. It is also a long process and that gives  

rise to a lot of uncertainty."

title: WRAPUP 1-Singapore's economic outlook brightens in 2004.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Singapore got a surprising boost from its rapidly growing pharmaceuticals sector in January, and the government raised its growth forecast for 2004, suggesting the economy is set for its best performance in four years.  

With drug and electronics production gathering pace due to growing demand from global markets, the government said on Thursday growth this year was likely to be around 3.5 to 5.5 percent, up from its previous forecast of 3.0 to 5.0 percent.  

Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) grew at an 11 percent annualised rate in the three months through December after adjustment for seasonal patterns, the government said, topping market expectations for growth of about nine percent.  

This brought 2003 growth to 1.1 percent, revised up from an estimate issued last month of 0.8 percent but only half of the 2.2 percent growth seen in 2002.  

"The external sector has helped lift the figures in the final sprint. But it's still an uneven pace, led primarily by the external sector," said Song Seng Wun, an economist at G.K. Goh.  

Unemployment has come off 17-year highs, but the city state is grappling with structural pressures and factories face intense competition from China and India.  

Economists polled by Reuters say Singapore should hit the top of the government's new range with growth of about 5.2 percent this year as busy factories drive the recovery.  

From U.S hard disk drive maker Seagate Technology to the world's largest drug manufacturer, Pfizer Inc, factories are ramping up production.  

"The first quarter will be much more important in signalling the underlying trend. On the whole, we are still quite bullish," said Lian Chia-liang, an economist at JP Morgan Chase. He expects first-quarter annualised growth of six percent.  

BIRD FLU RISK  

But the Ministry of Trade and Industry tempered the optimism, pointing to risks posed by outbreaks of bird flu sweeping parts of Asia, political uncertainty in the region and a weak U.S. dollar.  

Friedrich Wu, director, economics division of the ministry, told a news conference that a sharp correction in the U.S. dollar could trigger a sell-off of U.S. dollar assets and a rise in U.S. interest rates, which would drag down the economy.  

"We believe that Asian central banks are likely to intervene heavily to prevent this from occurring as their economies remain highly dependent on U.S. demand," he said.  

Asked if the central bank would intervene if the U.S. dollar continued to slide against the Singapore dollar, a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) official declined comment.  

"We do not comment on intervention policy and reiterate we maintain the exchange rate against a basket of currencies and there is no change in that regime," Khor Hoe Ee, an assistant managing director at the MAS said.  

The growth data helped the Singapore dollar withstand a broad-based rally in the U.S. dollar on Thursday, but dealers said it would not entirely shield the local currency.  

The Sing dollar traded around 1.6955 per U.S. dollar in late afternoon, off late Wednesday's 1.6900 level but above three-week lows around 1.7020 per dollar hit on Monday.  

BOUNCING FROM SARS  

The December quarter marked a slowdown from brisk third quarter annualised growth of 16.1 percent, the fastest since 1997, as Singapore rebounded from a SARS slump that sent its $90 billion economy into its worst ever quarterly contraction.  

Manufacturing output rose a surprising 18.1 percent in January from December, after adjustment for seasonal patterns, as drug makers offset slower factory activity elsewhere due to the Lunar New Year.  

Analysts said leading indicators such as the U.S. semiconductor book-to-bill ratio signal a positive trend.  

The stronger outlook could pave the way for Goh Chok Tong, prime minister since 1990, to hand power to Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.  

Goh has said he would be comfortable making way for Lee - son of founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew - if the economy were growing at a full-year rate of three to four percent.  

"You might as well have early elections while the economy is still running hot," said Lian of JP Morgan, who saw a snap poll in the third quarter as a possibility. (Additional reporting by Jennifer Tan).

title: Asia likely to act if dlr falls sharply - Singapore.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Asian central banks were likely to intervene heavily in currency markets to prevent a sharp fall in the U.S. dollar that could threaten demand for the region's exports, a Singapore government economist said on Thursday.   

Friedrich Wu, director, economics division of the Ministry of Trade and Industry, told a news conference that a sharp correction in the U.S. dollar could trigger a sell-off of U.S. dollar assets as well as a rise in U.S. interest rates, which would drag the economy down.   

"We believe that Asian central banks are likely to intervene heavily to prevent this from occurring as their economies remain highly dependent on U.S. demand," he told reporters after the release of Singapore's economic growth figures.   

Asked if the central bank would intervene if the U.S. dollar continued to slide against the Singapore dollar , a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) official declined comment.   

"We do not comment on intervention policy and reiterate we maintain the exchange rate against a basket of currencies and there is no change in that regime," Khor Hoe Ee, an assistant Managing Director at the MAS told the news conference.   

Asian central banks hold over $2 trillion worth of foreign exchange reserves, mostly in dollars. Reserves have risen sharply over the last two years or so as central banks have fought the weakening trend in the U.S. dollar in an attempt to keep their exports competitively priced in the key U.S. market.   

The practice has been strongly criticised by European and U.S. policymakers as distorting currency markets and handing Asia an unfair trade advantage.

title: Singapore  Warns Of Asian  Intervention  To Halt USD Fall
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian central banks are expected to "intervene heavily" to slow the U.S. dollar's decline as the region's economies begin to grow again, a top Singapore official said Thursday.  

The falling U.S. dollar is also a threat to Singapore's export-driven economy, which expanded by 1.1% in 2003 and is expected to grow 3.5%-5.5% this year, said Friedrich Wu, the chief economist at Singapore's Ministry of Trade & Industry.  

"A sharp fall of the U.S. dollar under the downward pressure of the twin deficit" could pose a risk to Singapore's economic growth. "But Asian central banks are likely to intervene heavily to prevent this."  

These are the first public comments from officials in Singapore on the U.S. dollar's decline and indications of a concerted Asian effort to stem the fall.  

(MORE)  

Asian central banks, including the Bank of Japan, have been intervening in foreign exchange markets to curb the U.S. dollar's sharp decline in recent months. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is also said to have intervened but the central bank has declined to comment on it.  

Asian governments are worried a weak U.S. dollar would hurt their exports and therefore hurt economic growth.  

Japan's real gross domestic product grew 7.0% in annualized terms in the October-December period, a pace of expansion that marked a 13-year high. The growth was driven by overseas shipments, capital investment to produce those goods and improved consumer outlays.  

Malaysia and Thailand have also reported strong economic growth, and expect exports to continue to underpin GDP growth in 2004.  

(MORE)  

Since the Group of Seven statement in September, the U.S. dollar has fallen by 20% against the euro and by 5.4% against the Singapore dollar.  

A senior central bank official also said Thursday that Singapore's inflation rate will likely rise slightly to 0.5%-1.5% this year compared with 0.5% in 2003 as economic growth picks up.  

The statement by Khor Hoe Ee, an assistant managing director at the MAS, reiterates the central bank's outlook for the consumer price index issued late last year.  

"As economic activity picks up, it's not unreasonable to expect inflation to rise from last year," he told reporters.  

On the exchange rate, which the MAS controls, Khor remained tightlipped about any possible change to the central bank's current neutral monetary policy stance.  

The MAS continued to keep the Singapore dollar within the trade-weighted policy band it has set for the currency. The extent of this band isn't made known to the public.  

"There has been no change to that," he said.  

Khor didn't discuss implications for monetary policy from the expanding economy, saying the policy stance will be announced in April.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late As Players Jump Back Into US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker late in Asia Thursday as various participants jumped back into long U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar positions after the U.S. currency's strong rally in New York Wednesday.  

Around 0730 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6826, up sharply from S$1.6727 Wednesday. It traded a range of S$1.6780-S$1.6833 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar's rally against major currencies from new lows overnight spooked Singapore banks and U.S. investment houses into buying back the U.S. unit against its Singaporean counterpart just one day after the U.S. currency had fallen as low as the psychologically key S$1.6700 level in Asia Wednesday.  

The turnaround in the U.S. unit's fortunes overnight stemmed from heavy buying by investors, especially hedge funds, to unwind huge short U.S. dollar positions against the euro, the sterling pound and other currencies for profit.  

The U.S. unit climbed against the local currency early in the session on the buying by domestic and U.S. investment banks, but it soon ran into thick offers from Singapore companies just above the psychologically important S$1.6800 level.  

Later in the session, however, the U.S. dollar finally overcame the persistent selling from those firms to hedge their foreign exchange exposure, extending its gains to the low S$1.6800s.  

With the U.S. unit having found solid support at S$1.6770-S$1.6780, it could rise further toward its key psychological resistance of S$1.6900 in the coming sessions, dealers said.  

But technical analysis still suggests the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar is in a short-term downtrend. The U.S. unit hasn't yet hit S$1.6638, the minimum target of a bearish right triangle triggered earlier this month. Also, the three-point downtrend line from the end of January that comes in today at S$1.6891 (and falling S$0.0012/day) is intact.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds fell on supply-related concerns, following news that U.S. mortgage finance agency Fannie Mae was selling a further S$150 million of its Singapore-dollar bond due 2009 and that the Monetary Authority of Singapore will sell S$1.2 billion of an existing government bond due 2011 next week.  

There was also lingering interest to hedge a recent Housing Development Board issue, which pushed interest rate swaps higher, traders said.  

Overnight, prices of U.S. Treasurys ended little changed as evidence of weakness in housing was offset by a rebounding dollar, suggesting that foreign central banks may not need to buy as many U.S. bonds as part of currency intervention.  

Late Thursday, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was 1.07%, up from 1.04% Wednesday. The yield on 10-year bonds also rose to 3.29% versus 3.24%, while the yield on 15-year bonds was at 3.72% against 3.66% previously.  

The two-year swap offer climbed to 1.46% against 1.43% late Wednesday, while the five-year offer was at 2.54%, compared with 2.48%. The 10-year swap rose to 3.63% from 3.58%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps was 217 basis points from 215 basis points previously.  

The overnight interbank offer rate rose to 0.3125% from 0.1875%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dlr hits high,  intervention  eyed.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 17 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar
touched it highest level in about 19 months on Tuesday, but
most other Asian currencies stepped back from recent highs on
fears that central banks would intervene to curb exchange rate
gains.
    The Taiwan dollar          hit 33.075 per U.S. dollar, its
strongest since July 2002, before the central bank stepped in
to cap the rise, dealers said.
    Dealers in Singapore said settlement of stock purchases by
foreign investors pushed the currency up. Foreign investors had
bought over $700 million of Taiwan stocks last week, they said.
    Central bank intervention was also suspected in South
Korea, where the won             touched a high of
1,157.0 per dollar in local trade, just shy of Friday's
four-month high of 1,156.0 hit in offshore trade.
    The Singapore dollar        weakened as far as 1.6783 per
U.S. dollar before recovering, but it stayed well clear of last
Friday's four-year peak of 1.6675.
  


 Dealers said the fall came
after a sharp fall in the Thai baht  on Tuesday morning.
    The baht fell to a one-week low of 39.05 per dollar amid
talk that a foreign bank was buying U.S. dollars on behalf of
the central bank to curb currency gains, dealers said.
    However, rising exports and capital inflows into Asian
equities meant the appreciation pressure on regional currencies
was expected to continue despite the efforts of central banks.
    APPRECIATION PRESSURE
    Peter Redward, strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore,
said the upward pressure on the Taiwan dollar and South Korean
won, on a day when the Japanese yen  eased against the
dollar, showed the amount of capital rushing into these
economies.
    "Central banks have been in the market all along but the
pressure is so much that I think on average they are now
letting some of that pressure pass through," he said.
    The Singapore dollar has gained almost 1.5 percent so far
this year, against a nearly two percent rise for the whole of
2003. The Taiwan dollar has gained about 2.6 percent, against
2.2 percent in 2003, and the Korean won has risen nearly three
percent versus a depreciation of about one percent last year.
    Speculation of revaluation of the Chinese yuan           ,
which is managed in a narrow range near 8.28 per dollar, and
its potential strengthening impact on regional currencies has
been another major factor attracting inflows into the region.
    The yuan non-deliverable forward           premium on the
three-month tenor  traded around Monday's one-month
high of 1,400 points to the U.S. dollar.
    The premium on the one-year tenor was around 4,600 points,
against Monday's 4,900 points. The one-year premium hit an
all-time high of 5,200 points in October last year.
    At 4,600 points, the premium implies an expected
appreciation of close to six percent against the U.S. dollar in
a year's time.
    A senior Chinese state official said speculation on the
yuan has hindered plans to reform the exchange rate regime, but
analysts said delaying an adjustment of the Chinese currency
was not the solution.
 
    "If anything, the pace of capital inflows have accelerated
dramatically in recent weeks," Redward said.
    The Philippine peso        edged down to hit 56.17 per
  

dollar, even as the market in Manila speculated on the  

possibility of new central bank regulations aimed at tougher  

monitoring of foreign exchange transactions by local companies.  

However, dealers said demand for dollars was genuine as  

companies were trying to hedge their requirements ahead of the  

import season that usually begins in the second quarter.  

Earlier this month the peso hit an all-time low of 56.22  

per dollar.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Edge up but off recent highs.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Most Asian regional
currencies edged up on Monday but were still shy of recent
highs as the U.S. dollar steadied against major currencies.
    A one-day holiday in the United States was also seen
sapping trading interest, lowering volume and restricting
ranges in currency markets, dealers said.
    The Singapore dollar        traded as high as 1.6730 per
U.S. dollar, from late Friday's 1.6745 but was far from its
four-year peak of 1.6675 hit on Thursday.
    The Taiwan dollar          tested 33.10 per U.S. dollar,
its strongest in 18-months which was also hit on Thursday. The
South Korean won             rose to a new four-month
high of 1,157.6 in local trade, but was off Friday's offshore
high of 1,156.0.
    Dealers in Singapore said the won was helped after the Bank
of Korea said authorities planned to ease restrictions,
introduced last month, on domestic institutions' trading of
non-deliverable forwards.
  


 The move was aimed at curbing
speculation.
    The Thai baht        was steady at around 38.90 per dollar,
against last week's one-month high of 38.80. The Indonesian
rupiah  hugged a tight range around 8,400 per dollar.
 
    The Philippine peso        lingered at around 56.10 per
dollar, not far from its all-time low of 56.22 hit in January.
    "After last week's run (to new highs), the market needs
fresh factors," said a dealer of regional currencies in
Singapore.
    Dealers said fear of central bank intervention, to curb
currency strength, and volatility due to low volume was
expected to keep players cautious across the region.
    PRESSURE TO APPRECIATE
    However Philip Wee, strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore
  

said despite the caution markets were more confident that most  

Asian currencies, backed by strong economic performance and  

diplomatic pressure, would appreciate in the medium term.  

"We believe that Asia will be coming under pressure to  

rebalance the asymmetric weakness in the dollar's adjustment to  

address global imbalances," said Wee, referring to the fact  

that over the last two years the U.S. unit has depreciated  

mainly against currencies of Europe, Australia, New Zealand and  

Canada.  

Asian currencies gained last week following the Group of  

Seven industrial powers' implicit call on Asia to allow  

appreciation against the dollar.  

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments on  

Wednesday added to the dollar's woes. Greenspan said there was  

no rush to tighten monetary policy and that a weak dollar would  

help narrow the country's large current account deficit.   


 
    Dealers said for players in Asian regionals, a test of 105
yen  could provide a fresh cue to sell U.S. dollars.
    European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet's
  

testimony before the European Parliament, due later on Monday,  

was also seen as an opportunity for Europe, worried over the  

euro's strength, to take a jab at China's policy to keep the  

yuan virtually pegged at 8.28 per dollar.  

Speculation over this drove the yuan non-deliverable  

forwards premium back to its recent high of 1,200  

points on the three-month tenor . The premium on the  

one-year tenor was around 4,450 points, implying an expected  

appreciation of close to 5.7 percent in a year's time.  

"We believe that as the pressure on yen and yuan intensify,  

the mileage may be in selling dollars against Asia, except for  

the Philippine peso," Wee said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Off highs after week of gains.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies pulled back
from recent highs on Friday as players reduced short U.S.
dollar positions after repeated central bank intervention
during the week and ahead of a long U.S. weekend.
    Dealers said profit-taking emerged after a week of
reasonable gains that began with the Group of Seven industrial
powers' implicit call on Asia to allow appreciation against the
dollar.
    Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments on
Wednesday added to the dollar's woes. Greenspan said there was
no rush to tighten monetary policy and that a weak dollar would
help narrow the country's large current account deficit.
    The Singapore dollar        pulled back almost a full cent
from Thursday's four-year high of 1.6675 per U.S. dollar, the
South Korean won             was off its four-month high
of 1,159.9 and the Taiwan dollar  at one point was down
a quarter percent from Thursday's 18-month high of 33.10.
   


    The Thai baht        went as low as 38.94 per dollar, off a
one-month high of 38.80, the Indonesian rupiah  was on
the weaker side of the 8,400 per dollar level and the
Philippine peso  hit 56.105 per dollar, its lowest in
about a week.
    TESTING CENTRAL BANK RESOLVE
    Dealers in Singapore said suspected dollar-buying
intervention against the Singapore dollar throughout the week,
mainly through local banks, turned aggressive on Thursday.
    They said local banks were spotted early Friday at around
the 1.6730 level, prompting more covering of short dollar
positions but interest to buy the Sing dollar was also seen
below 1.6760.
    "The Sing dollar was testing the upper boundary of the
estimated central bank tolerance band," said Thio Chin Loo,
currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore.
    The Monetary Authority of Singapore targets the Sing dollar
within an undisclosed trade-weighted policy band to ensure it
remains competitive against those of major trade partners.
    "The rebound from there and the congestive tone in the U.S.
dollar against other majors suggest that spot dollar/Sing is
likely to range between 1.6680 to 1.6800 in the near term,"
Thio said.
    Dealers said the South Korean won repeatedly ran into what
they believe were central bank-driven dollar purchases at the
1,160 per dollar level.
    The Taiwan dollar was capped at levels just shy of 33.10.
    Dealers said even after losses on early Friday, most Asian
currencies were hanging on to a large part of their recent
gains.
    The Singapore dollar has gained about 1.4 percent so far
this year, against near two percent gains for the whole of
2003. The Taiwan dollar has gained about 2.5 percent, against
2.24 percent in 2003 and the Korean won has risen by 2.8
percent versus a depreciation of close to one percent last
year.
    YUAN MOVE
    Taking a cue from the regional bias, the Chinese yuan
non-deliverable forwards  premium traded at around
1,100 points on the three-month tenor , versus 1,200
points on Thursday.
    The premium on the one-year tenor was around 4,200 points,
against a high of 4,450 points on Thursday. At 4,200 points the
premium implies an expected appreciation of slightly above five
percent in the yuan  in a year's time.
    A Reuters poll of 25 analysts from banks, investment houses
and consultancies in Asia, Europe and the United States showed
China was expected to change its currency regime this year
which would allow the yuan to strengthen at least a little.
    "More appreciation pressure on the yen and Asian regionals
will be exerted as a result of the China move towards
flexibility," said Bhanu Baweja, strategist at UBS.
    "We have not factored this in our FX forecasts but
recognise that this poses an upside risk to Asian currencies."

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, Sets Another 4-Year High Vs US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar climbed to another new four-year high against the U.S. currency late in Asia Wednesday as offshore speculators and other players heavily sold the U.S. unit.  

At 0830 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6744, down from S$1.6758 late in Asia Tuesday. It traded a range of S$1.6686-S$1.6760 intraday. On Tuesday, the U.S. unit dropped to around S$1.6748, its lowest since late January 2000.  

The U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar selling was triggered by remarks from New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen early in the session that the government has "options" to halt the rise in the New Zealand dollar.  

"Cullen's comments prompted speculators to unwind long Australian and New Zealand dollar positions against the Singapore dollar," said a Singapore dealer.  

Other speculators, many of whom were taking the Group of Seven's call for "more flexibility" from major nations or economic areas that "lack such flexibility" to heart, also joined in the U.S. dollar-selling spree against the local currency.  

Analysts said these speculators could be selling the U.S. dollar against the Singaporean and other Asian currencies on a bet that the G7 wants Asian nations to allow their currencies to rise in order to share more of the burden for the U.S. dollar's weakness.  

The U.S. currency fell as low as S$1.6686 but later recovered to the mid-S$1.6700s on buying by Singapore banks, probably at the behest of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

After apparently staying out of the markets since the G7 meeting, the MAS is suspected to have intervened Wednesday to prevent the sharp rise in the Singapore dollar from hurting the city-state's exports.  

The MAS is likely to keep intervening to curb a rapid appreciation in the local currency, but the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair's short-term outlook remains bearish, dealers said.  

"I'm looking at S$1.6620 then S$1.6500," said a local dealer.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds ended lower as they trailed the overnight retreat in U.S. Treasurys.  

The overall tone in the domestic bond market was generally subdued ahead of testimony later Wednesday by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan before the House Financial Service Committee on the state of the U.S. economy and the outlook for monetary policy.  

But the retreat in local bonds was somewhat tamed by the sharp rise of the Singapore dollar.  

At the end of Wednesday's session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds closed one basis point higher at 1.12%. At the longer end of the curve, the yield on the 10-year bonds rose six basis points to 3.31%, while the yield on 15-year bonds rose three basis points to 3.68%.  

Interest-rate swaps were also higher in line with local bond yields. The two-year swap offer was at 1.54% versus 1.51% late Tuesday, the five-year offer rose to 2.58% from 2.52%, while the 10-year swap gained to 3.64% from 3.58%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 200 basis points from 207 basis points Tuesday.  

The overnight interbank offer rate slipped to 0.6250% to 0.6875%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing, Taiwan dlr at new highs, cbanks eyed.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies pushed
higher against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday on growing
speculation that central banks may have less resistance to
exchange rate strength.
    Dealers said that while the presence of central banks was
being felt across the region, there was a growing feeling that
the gradual gains this week showed they were smoothing the rise
rather than defending levels.
    The Singapore dollar rose past the 1.6700 per dollar level
to briefly touch a new four-year high of 1.6690. It pulled back
to 1.6720 at the first sight of strong U.S. dollar bids from
local banks, which sparked talk the central bank was in the
market.
    "The fear (of intervention) is there and maybe they (the
Monetary Authority of Singapore) were in the market," said a
dealer at a foreign bank in Singapore.
    "But at the same time no one is sure if they have actually
intervened.
   


 If anything, gains this week suggest they have
eased a bit on dollar bids."
 
    The Taiwan dollar hit a fresh 18-month high of 33.121 per
dollar, despite concerns about possible intervention.
    The South Korean won extended its four-month highs to
   

1,610.6 per dollar, even as a finance ministry official said   

authorities were concerned about "excessive" volatility in   

exchange rates and planned to take action if necessary.   

"We are worried that intensifying speculation on currency

rates has caused excessive moves in the exchange rates," the   

official told Reuters.   

He also said there had been no change in the government's   

stance that exchange rates should reflect the country's   

economic fundamentals.   

Still, dealers said there was growing talk in the market   

that the new finance minister, Lee Hun-jai, named late on   

Tuesday, would be more tolerant to currency strength.   

G7 FALL-OUT   

David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in   

Singapore, said the Bank of Korea was unlikely to step   

completely out of the way of the won's rise against the dollar,   

but central banks appeared to be less eager to intervene.   

"This is kind of a post-G7 fall-out the market was looking   

for," he said, referring to the weekend meeting of the Group of   

Seven industrial powers that made an implicit call on the   

region to allow more exchange rate flexibility.   

"Our anticipated change in intervention policy appears to   

be materialising," wrote James Malcolm, strategist at JP Morgan   

Chase, in a morning note.    


 
    "Policy signals are tilting increasingly towards smoothing
the pace of decline, rather than defending specific levels."
    Simmonds said the same was true for the Singapore dollar,
unless the central bank stepped in to conduct an aggressive
intervention.
    On the South Korean won, Simmonds said the crucial factor
was its cross against the Japanese yen which had been testing
the 11-per-won level, up from lows around 11.20 won last month.
    The speculation of a shift in currency bias in the region
   

pushed the Chinese yuan non-deliverable forwards premium to   

1,200 points on the three-month tenor versus 850 points last   

week. The premium on one-year tenor reached 4,450 points. That   

suggested the market expected the yuan to appreciate by about   

5.5 percent in a year's time.   

Encouraged by its peers, the Thai baht rose to 38.91 per   

dollar, its strongest in nearly a month. It had touched 38.85   

in offshore trade.   

The Philippine peso held steady at around 55.85 per dollar,   

although dealers in Manila said the market was cautious after   

official campaigning for the May presidential election kicked   

off on Tuesday.   

The Indonesian rupiah held on to three-week highs on the   

stronger side of the 8,400 per dollar level.

title: Singapore Dlr Surges Late To Fresh 4-Year High Vs US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar surged to a fresh four-year high against the U.S. currency late in Asia Tuesday as broad-based U.S. dollar weakness returned to the foreign exchange markets with a vengeance.  

Offshore players, banks and companies sold the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair to either accumulate short positions or hedge their currency exposure, driving the U.S. unit down to around S$1.6748, its lowest level since late January 2000.  

Traders said a U.S. bank was rumored to have sold U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars in a "large" quantity out of Hong Kong, triggering stop-loss sales orders in the high-S$1.6700s and exacerbating the U.S. unit's slide against the Singaporean currency.  

At 0800 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6758, sharply lower from S$1.6851 late in Asia Monday. It traded a range of S$1.6748 to S$1.6844 intraday.  

Rising sentiment that the Group of Seven's warning against "excess volatility" lack teeth and that the U.S. authorities will continue tolerating gradual U.S. dollar weakness prompted players to dump the U.S. unit against the Singaporean and other currencies.  

The near-term outlook for the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair continued to look bleak as there were no apparent signs of intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore to prop up the ailing U.S. currency, dealers said.  

While the MAS is suspected to have intervened in recent weeks to prevent a strengthening local dollar from hurting Singapore exports, this week's rise in Asian currencies may have prompted the central bank to stay out of the markets in order to allow the local currency to appreciate in tandem, dealers added.  

"The U.S. dollar could fall to S$1.6600-S$1.6700" soon, said a local dealer.  

According to technical charts, the U.S. dollar has also been in a downtrend against its Singaporean counterpart since Jan. 20.  

Technical analysis shows that the U.S. dollar triggered a bearish right triangle last Friday with its daily close below the horizontal lower edge of the pattern at S$1.6893 and that the downside target for the U.S. dollar is S$1.6638.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds were barely changed in very thin dealings Tuesday in line with the subdued activity in the overnight U.S. Treasurys market, which is awaiting Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to Congress later this week.  

There could be some buying interest in local bonds if the Singapore dollar continues to strengthen, a trader said, noting the currency's rise to a new four-year high against the U.S. dollar late in the session.  

Earlier Tuesday, JP Morgan said the bullish trend in Singapore government bonds that started at the beginning of the year has ended. It expects a mild steepening in the bond curve and said Singapore's yield discount to Treasurys "still has potential to widen but will require higher U.S. rates first."  

At the end of Tuesday's trading, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was down at 1.10% from 1.13% Monday. The 10-year bond yield was slightly higher at 3.25% versus 3.23% previously, while the 15-year bond yield was at 3.65% against 3.64%.

their currencies appreciate against the dollar.
    The Singapore dollar        rose to 1.6827 per dollar, up

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Test Of G7 Resolve Over Warning
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against the U.S. currency in late Asia Monday, as speculators tested the resolve of the Group of Seven major industrialized nations to back its warning against "excess volatility" with action.  

At 0750 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6851, sharply down from S$1.6938 late in Asia Friday. It traded a range of S$1.6830 to S$1.6877 intraday.  

While the U.S. currency initially rebounded on short-covering following a new four-year low of S$1.6820 set late New York Friday, various players soon sold the U.S. unit amid sentiment the G7 might not jointly act against further U.S. dollar weakness.  

"Market participants think (the G7 statement) will be only words and no action," said a local dealer.  

In a joint communique issued after their meeting in Boca Raton, Fla., over the weekend, the G7 finance officials added a new phrase warning that "excess volatility" and "disorderly movements" in exchange rates were "undesirable for economic growth."  

Later in the session, however, the U.S. dollar's slide against the Singapore dollar was slowed by rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore via domestic banks, dealers said.  

While the G7's castigation of "excess volatility" may slow the U.S. dollar's slide somewhat in the short term, "(the statement) in and of itself is not strong enough to halt, let alone reverse it in the coming few months," said Bank of America in a research report.  

The G7's call for "more flexibility" from "major countries and economic areas that lack such flexibility" targets China and other non-Japan Asian nations and puts more diplomatic pressure on them to let their currencies rise, though rapid currency appreciation will continue to be resisted by central banks, Bank of America added.  

Given this international pressure on Asian countries to allow their currencies to strengthen and the underlying U.S. dollar bearish sentiment, the U.S. currency could probe the psychologically key S$1.6800 level this week although the unit's downside is likely to be supported by MAS intervention, dealers said.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds closed higher Monday following a gain in U.S. Treasurys Friday on weak U.S. jobs numbers.  

The U.S. created 112,000 jobs in January, the fastest monthly rate for three years, but the figure was well below expectations of a 160,000 rise.  

Treasurys continued their ascent Monday in Tokyo, where traders viewed the G7 statement as positive for Treasurys because it didn't criticize Japan's intervention in the foreign exchange market.  

"There is a high expectation in the market that Japan's intervention funds will be invested at the week's refunding tender for short-term (U.S. Treasury) notes," a trader said.  

At the end of the session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was down at 1.13% from 1.15% Friday. At the longer end of the curve, the yield on the 10-year bond was lower at 3.24% from 3.30%, while the 15-year bond yield was 3.64% from 3.70%.  

"Fears of bird flu was another factor helping Singapore bonds today; but with strong equity markets, the 10-year (government bond) should soon rise toward the 3.4%-3.5% region," a market strategist said.  

Interest-rate swaps were lower in line with local bond yields. The two-year swap offer was at 1.54% versus 1.57% late Friday, the five-year offer fell to 2.55% from 2.61%, while the 10-year swap fell to 3.58% from 3.66%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 204 basis points from 209 basis points Friday.  

The overnight interbank offer rate fell to 0.6250% from 0.7500% Friday.

delivered a bullish surprise.

data for December.

gaining 3.9 percent from November to beat analysts' forecasts

absorbed by Singapore banks, which had been buying U.S. dollars
since Friday morning, sparking fears of central bankintervention.
    "When local banks in Singapore are buying dollars
aggressively, others don't usually want to test and see who is
behind the order," said a dealer at a European bank.
  


    Overall sentiment on Asian currencies stayed depressed
because of recent moves in South Korea and Thailand to curb the
strength of the won and baht.
    South Korea imposed limits on Thursday on domestic
financial institutions' trade with the offshore non-deliverable
forward market -- a move seen aimed at curbing the won's
  rise.

intervened recently to stem the baht's  gains.

currencies weak.

appreciation by authorities and looked to book profits on its

    SINGAPORE, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Concerns over central bankintervention rose to the fore once again in Asian currency
markets on Friday, keeping the Japanese yen and the rest of the

said.  

The continuing underperformance expected across Asia called
