title: Emerging Asia  FX -Strong but wary on euro's retreat.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies were
mostly higher on Wednesday, but suspected central bankintervention and the U.S. dollar's recovery from record lows
against the euro were expected to cap gains.
    The Singapore dollar        was firm but off the fresh
44-month peak of 1.6951 per dollar it had hit in offshore trade
overnight. The South Korean won             was off a
three-week high of 1,186.4 it had touched on Tuesday.
    The Taiwan dollar          and Thai baht        rose to
their strongest since the middle of October at 33.78 and 39.06
respectively, before coming off.
    The Indonesian rupiah        was steady at around 8,335, a
level not traded since July. The Philippine peso  tested
55 per dollar, its highest in two months. The peso has not
traded on the stronger side of the 55 level since October.
  


    Dealers said investors and speculators were watching the
euro's retreat from Tuesday's record high of $1.2812, to judge
if there was scope for a larger correction of the European
currency's recent sharp rise against the U.S. dollar.
 
    A correction in the euro would put a halt to gains in Asian
regional currencies, they said.
    CORRECTION RISK
    Peter Redward, strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore,
  

said that was a risk, but it was not clear if the euro was  

taking a temporary breather or was at the start of a big  

retracement.  

"It is a tough question to answer. The market is too  

bullish and is relatively long (on the euro), so there is a  

possibility of a sharp correction," he said.  

Redward said after an almost linear rise, the euro could  

ease to around $1.2550 and the yen could fall to around  

107 to the dollar, moves that could push the Singapore dollar  

back to the weaker side of 1.7000, the Korean won to 1,195 and  

the Taiwan dollar to 33.90.   


 
    "But so far it seems like a very shallow correction and is
likely to be only temporary," he said.
    Redward said he was not expecting a big retracement of
Asian currency gains, even if the euro undergoes a large
correction, because the regionals had lagged gains in the euro.
    Dealers said suspected intervention by Asian central banks,
  

directly or through other banks, had not been very aggressive  

so far. But a U.S. dollar rebound could turn this situation  

around very quickly, they said.   


 
    "We have felt the presence of dollar bids from central
banks all along," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Singapore.
    The Bank of Japan has been suspected of intervening
repeatedly since Monday to stop the yen  from
appreciating through the 106 per dollar level.
    Early on Wednesday, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold
HK$4.27 billion in three interventions to buy U.S. dollars and
curb the Hong Kong dollar's  rise.
    The Hong Kong dollar traded at 7.7628/38, against the
  

pegged level of HK$7.80 per dollar. Wednesday's interventions

followed sales of HK$505 million on Monday and HK$4.06 billion  

on Tuesday.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late;Foreigners Buy, Local Bks Cap Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged higher against the U.S. currency in Asia Wednesday on some buying by foreign investment banks but its upside was curbed by light selling from domestic banks.  

Mounting U.S. dollar bearishness fueled buying of the Singaporean currency by overseas speculators, although the Monetary Authority of Singapore was suspected to have intervened in small lots to prop up the U.S. unit.  

While the specter of possible Singapore dollar selling intervention by Singapore's central bank was expected to continue to haunt players, and keep the local dollar from rising too sharply, the market forces behind the U.S. unit's slide could prove tough to fight, dealers said.  

Indeed, the U.S. dollar set a fresh 47-month low of S$1.6955 late Tuesday in New York, as the U.S. unit weakened against most other currencies on concerns over the huge U.S. current account deficit and apparent indifference of U.S. monetary authorities toward the U.S. dollar's weakness.  

The U.S. dollar is set to lose even more ground over the next few months, with analysts projecting it around S$1.6840 by the end of June.  

At 0910 GMT Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6979, down from S$1.6997 Tuesday in Singapore. Intraday, it traded between S$1.6962 and S$1.6986.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds rose early in the session on buying by market players to accumulate long positions, but mostly declined on profit-taking by some participants toward the session's close.  

The weakness of U.S. Treasurys in thin trading in Asia and worries about supply of new bonds from U.S. Treasury auctions this week also weighed on the prices of Singapore government bonds, dealers said.  

Singapore government bonds may weaken in the coming sessions as market participants could take more profit on the bonds they bought earlier this week.  

At the end of the session, the yield on the two-year bonds had fallen one basis point to 1.05%. The yield on the 10-year bond had risen one basis point to 3.69%, while the 15-year bond yield moved up four basis points to 4.10%.  

The two-year interest rate swap was unchanged at 1.76%, while the five-year swap was offered three basis points higher at 3.06%. The 10-year offer ended four basis points higher at 4.16%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 230 basis points from 236 basis points late Tuesday.  

In the local money market, rates were mostly steady, with the overnight interbank rate falling to 0.3125% from 0.3750% Tuesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Strong despite suspected  intervention .
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies rose
against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday, even as suspicion grew that
central banks were in the market to restrict further gains.
    The Singapore dollar        traded in a narrow range just
shy of a 44-month peak of 1.6970 per dollar hit on Monday. The
Thai baht , Taiwan dollar  and Indonesian rupiah
  traded near highs last seen in mid-October and the South
Korean won  touched three-week highs.
 
    The region-wide bullishness also helped the troubled
Philippine peso  to a two-month high of 55.06 per dollar.
    "It seemed like the peso was lifted with the regional
tide," said Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at Union Bank of
the Philippines.
    Dealers in Manila said as the peso rose above the 55.15
  

level, where most corporate dollar buying orders were placed,  

players scrambled to get out of short dollar positions and in  

the process pushed the peso higher.  

The peso was Asia's worst performer in 2003, giving up  

about four percent of its value against the dollar on worries  

about the economic and political outlook of the Philippines.  

Dealers said with the dollar now hitting fresh lows against   


the euro  almost daily, and with the yen        around
  

September 2000 highs, Asian currencies were set to rise  

further.  

TRADE-WEIGHTED WEAKNESS  

Another suspected intervention by the Bank of Japan, after  

one on Monday, only helped to pull the yen slightly away from  

the 106 level and had a modest impact on regional currencies.  

Analysts said on a trade-weighted basis most Asian  

currencies should have weakened because most of them have  

lagged gains in other currencies versus the dollar.  

Jimmy Koh, head of research at Singapore's UOB Bank said  

that despite the Sing dollar's recent gains, the currency was  

still more than one percent weaker from the mid-point of the  

central bank's trade-weighted policy band.  

Thio Chin Loo, an analyst at BNP Paribas said that meant  

currency players would continue to build long Sing dollar  

positions against the U.S. dollar.  

"This only means that the Sing dollar has room to  

appreciate on a nominal basis against a universally weak  

dollar," she said.  

Dealers said the most aggressive players in the market were  

offshore investment banks and funds bidding almost all Asian  

currencies higher against the dollar.  

"People believe that the U.S. is very happy with the weak  

dollar situation and the Europeans and Japanese are not  

opposing it sufficiently so until they see things prove  

otherwise they are going to continue selling the dollar," said  

Simon Flint, strategist at Bank of America in Singapore.  

Dealers said U.S. dollar purchases by some local or  

state-run banks in Singapore, Thailand, Taiwan and Korea early  

on Tuesday had raised suspicion that central banks were trying  

to manage the currency gains.  

YUAN SPECULATION  

China's announcement that it had pumped $45 billion into  

two of its debt-ridden state banks had no impact on the yuan  

or other currency markets in the region.  

The transaction was made late last year and analysts said  

it probably involved a direct transfer of assets from the  

central bank's reserves without any currency exchanges.  

Speculation that China would this year allow some  

appreciation of the currency, which is virtually pegged to the  

dollar at around 8.3 yuan, pushed the U.S. dollar discount on  

one-year non-deliverable forwards to near record  

levels at above 5,000 points - implying a yuan rate of 7.7780  

per dollar.  

Flint said the weakening U.S. dollar would continue to fuel  

speculation of a yuan revaluation. However, he said any  

appreciation of the yuan would be modest and sometime in the  

third quarter of this year.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late But Rumored MAS Action Curbs Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose against the U.S. currency Tuesday on buying by foreign players, though it later curbed those gains on suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.  

European investment banks and others bought the Singapore dollar amid heightened U.S. dollar bearishness, following the greenback's persistent losses against regional currencies late Monday.  

But their efforts consistently ran into a wall of U.S.-dollar bids placed around S$1.6970-S$1.6990 by domestic banks, which some dealers speculated may have been on behalf of the central bank.  

While these bids should place a floor under the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair in that range for the rest of the global session, dealers said the pair could fall further to S$1.6900 by the end of this month.  

Given the weekend comments by Federal Reserve Governor Ben Bernanke that the chances of a U.S. dollar crisis are "quite low" and that interest rates are likely to stay low for some time, the U.S. unit faces a further downside risk against most currencies, dealers said.  

At 0828 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6997, down from S$1.7002 Monday in Singapore. Intraday, it traded between S$1.6970 and S$1.6999.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds rose Tuesday as some institutions bought bonds in a buy-and-hold strategy, while other participants bought them to cover short positions, dealers said.  

The medium-to-long-end of the bond curve was especially popular among market players, with yields falling roughly eight basis points for five- to seven-year maturities and dropping 10-15 basis points for 10- to 15-year maturities.  

Singapore government bonds should remain firm in the near future amid what dealers consider to be relatively low supply of new issues coming out this year.  

At the end of the session, the yield on the two-year Singapore government bonds had fallen four basis points to 1.06%. The yield on the 10-year bond had declined 16 basis points to 3.69%, while the 15-year bond yield moved down 11 basis points to 4.06%.  

The two-year interest rate swap dropped eight basis points to 1.76%, while the five-year swap was offered 10 basis points lower at 3.03%. The 10-year offer ended 10 basis points lower at 4.12%.

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Jan 5 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit a new
44-month high on Monday, as most Asian regional currencies
strengthened against the U.S. dollar after it fell to fresh
record lows against the euro.
    The Singapore dollar        touched 1.6975 per dollar, a
level not seen since April 2000, before giving up some of the
gains, but was still on the stronger side of the 1.70 level.
    The Taiwan dollar          rose to 33.80 per dollar -- its
highest in about two months -- and the Thai baht  and
Indonesian rupiah  posted highs not seen since the middle
of October at 39.30 and 8,388 per dollar respectively.
 
    Dealers said offshore players who had kept a low profile
during the holiday season had returned in an aggressive mood.
    "What this largely reflects is that investors have come in
  

essentially to the first trading day of the new year and have  

established short dollar/Asia positions," said Peter Redward,  

currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.  

"The central banks have realised that this is a short-term  

flow and are allowing currencies to temporarily strengthen  

before they come back and intervene," he added.  

Dealers said most regional currencies were at record lows  

against the euro. This meant they had weakened on a  

trade-weighted basis, and could be pushed higher without fear  

of immediate intervention by regional central banks.   


 
    The central banks have been sensitive that currency
strength would eat into export competitiveness.
    The trade-weighted weakness was a key trading factor in
  

currencies like the Singapore dollar where authorities manage  

exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of currencies,  

with the U.S. dollar, yen and euro as its main components.  

POLICY REMINDERS  

But suspected intervention by the Bank of Japan to curb  

recent gains by the yen and similar action by the  

central bank in Taiwan served as reminders that Asian central  

banks policies have not changed.  

"Central banks may allow some moderate appreciation in the  

next two, three days but I don't see a trend appreciation  

here," Redward said.   


 
    He said policy makers would be cautious ahead of elections
in several Asian countries this year.
    Substantial gains in Asian currencies would only follow a
  

policy move by China on its yuan , he added. China has so  

far refused to bow to international criticism that its  

currency, pegged to the U.S. dollar, is undervalued.   


The South Korean won             rose to touch a
  

two-week high at 1,192.0 per dollar, but fear of central bank

intervention restricted further gains, dealers in Singapore

said.  

Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $155.35  

billion at the end of December from $150.34 billion a month  

before, helped by a surge in the dollar value of euro  

denominated assets, the central bank said.  

A Reuters poll of 10 dealers found they expected the won to  

move between 1,188.1/1,199.0 this week, with pressure to firm  

coming from inflows of stock funds by foreign investors and  

hopes for a peaceful resolution to the North Korean nuclear  

row.  

The Philippine peso rose to 55.26 per dollar, from  

last week's lows around 55.50, before giving up some of those  

gains as news broke that authorities in Manila were checking a  

suspected case of SARS.  

Dealers in Manila said the peso was helped by some residual  

year-end remittances from overseas Filipinos.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Edges Near Key S$1.7000 Intraday
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly against the U.S. unit in Asia Tuesday on light corporate demand for the local currency ahead of the New Year holidays.  

While the Singapore dollar edged up toward the psychologically key level of S$1.7000 against the U.S. currency, expectations that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may buy the greenback capped the Singapore dollar's rise.  

At 0825 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7015, down from S$1.7042 late Monday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7010 and S$1.7025 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7022 in Singapore and drifted lower as some banks sold U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars to fulfill the year-end demand from commercial customers.  

But concerns that the MAS would step in to prevent an excessive U.S. dollar fall - which would hurt the republic's exports, the main engine of its nascent economic recovery - curbed its decline, dealers said.  

In recent sessions, the MAS is suspected to have been quietly stepping into the local currency market to smooth the U.S. dollar's slide against the Singapore dollar, making most players wary of testing the central bank's resolve, the dealers added.  

For the rest of the week, potential intervention by Singapore's central bank is expected to keep the U.S. dollar above S$1.7000, although underlying U.S. dollar bearishness and improving domestic economic fundamentals could push the U.S. unit below that level early next year.  

"I'm targeting S$1.6600 by the middle of next year," said a Singapore dealer.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds drifted lower in Asia in the wake of U.S. Treasurys' fall overnight, but most market participants refrained from trading actively ahead of the New Year holidays.  

After Wednesday's half-day session, Singapore's government bond market will be closed until Jan. 2.  

Singapore government bond yields were slightly higher across the curve, but further swings in yields may be limited as overall trading could be subdued until next week, dealers said.  

At the end of the session, the yield on two-year government bonds was unchanged at 1.01%. The yield on the 10-year bond rose three basis points to 3.75%, while the 15-year yield gained two basis points to close at 4.05%.  

The two-year interest rate swap was two basis points higher at 1.73%, while the five-year swap rose four basis points to 2.98%. The 10-year offer ended four basis points higher at 4.06%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps widened to 233 basis points from 231 basis points late Monday.  

In the local money market, rates were mostly steady, though the overnight interbank rate slipped to 0.3750% versus 0.4375% late Monday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Preparing for strength in 2004.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed
bunch on Monday as the Japanese yen's fickle-mindedness and
economic data kept them from settling down in holiday-thinned
trading.
    The Singapore dollar        first fell as fears of Japanese
dollar-buying intervention lifted the U.S. dollar off lows, but
recovered as geopolitical worries and concerns over the U.S.
current account deficit resurfaced to undermine the U.S. dollar
once again.
    The Sing dollar was close to last Friday's highs of 1.7023
in afternoon trade and the Korean won             too
rallied off one-month lows as markets took the yen back up to
107 per dollar.
    "Asian currencies remain bid as strong data coupled with
good stock market performance prepare the market for another
strong year," BNP Paribas' currency analyst Thio Chin Loo said.
  


    "The Sing dollar is seeking new highs as the year closes,
and we expect the Sing dollar to move below 1.7000 when the new
year begins."
    Thailand on Monday forecast a robust 8.3 percent GDP growth
next year, after an expected 6.4 percent in 2003, and also
forecast an over 14 percent export growth in 2004.
 
    But Korean data disappointed markets as the industrial
output fell in November from October.
    As the yen rallied past 107 and South Korean stocks
  

recovered, markets shed their worries about the central bank

wanting to keep the won weak for end-of-year accounting and  

pushed the currency from 1,201 up to 1,198 per dollar.  

The won is among the few Asian currencies to have fallen  

against the U.S. dollar in 2003, beleaguered by Korea's  

consumer debt problems, including accounting irregularities at  

SK Global Co (01740.KS) and the recent cash crunch at LG Card  

Co , and the anxiety over North Korea's nuclear  

ambitions.  

The Thai baht was stable around 39.60 per dollar.  

After rising nearly nine percent against the dollar this year,  

the baht is one of Asia's best performers after the yen.  

Little reaction was seen to news of a suspected SARS case  

in China as traders braced for more U.S. dollar weakness at the  

start of 2004.  

The exception was the Philippine peso . Among Asia's  

weakest currencies in 2003, the peso was set for more weakness  

from seasonal factors and political worries heading into  

presidential elections early next year.  

"There is no aggressive position-taking from here on, but  

the medium term bias may tilt towards more gradual weakening of  

the peso," said Rovic De Guzman, the head of trading at the  

Union Bank of the Philippines.  

The peso opened steady after a week of holidays  

around 55.53 to 55.60 per dollar. It bounced off an all-time  

low of 55.85 per dollar on November 27, but markets have  

remained jumpy.  

"I won't be surprised to see the market retest historical  

peso lows in the near term," De Guzman said, adding the  

seasonal inflows from expatriate Filippinos at the end of the  

year was starting to wane.

title: Singapore dollar hits three-year high.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 8 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar firmed past the key 1.71 level on Monday afternoon to its highest since August 2000, benefiting from the rallies in the yen and euro after Friday's U.S. jobs data.  

The Singapore dollar was traded at 1.7092 per dollar in some deals as it rallied over a cent from Friday's lows. It has strengthened more than one percent since the end of November.  

It had traded around 1.7095 in mid-November briefly before worries the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene capped its gains.  

The U.S. dollar fell to three-year lows against the yen and plumbed record lows against the euro on Monday. Weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data accelerated the downward momentum on the dollar.  

Traders said the Singapore dollar was only around 0.3 percent on the stronger side of the mid-point of the undisclosed trade-weighted band the monetary authority is believed to manage it in and the uptrend merely reflected moves by major currencies.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Unexcited by U.S. dollar descent.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were
marginally firmer on Thursday morning, seemingly unimpressed by
the sliding U.S. dollar and unwilling to test the intervention
habits of regional central banks.
    The U.S. dollar was near record lows against the euro
  and just off a five-year trough against sterling       ,
undermined by weak sentiment and persisting anxiety over the
U.S. current account deficit and the Iraq violence.
    But the yen        bounced off two-week lows near 108 per
dollar as markets got worried the Bank of Japan would cap its
gains.
    The Singapore dollar        was near the past week's peaks
around 1.7150/60 per dollar, the Korean won
was headed for Wednesday's two-week highs of 1,190 per dollar,
and the rest of the regionals were slightly higher on the day.
    Yet, notwithstanding recent improvements in regional
economic data, market players seemed to be wary of buying the
regional currencies aggressively.
  


    This week's data showed Korean exports soaring and
Singapore's manufacturing activity expanding for the sixth
straight month in November.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said the end of
the year was probably not the right time to be taking up fresh
bullish positions on Asia.
    "Based on the recent raft of data globally and within Asia,
we become more convinced of an eventual move up in Asian
currencies versus the U.S. dollar, though it may be early to
call for that just yet," he said.
    With portfolio flows no longer as strong as they had been
and volumes thinning into the year-end, it was also likely that
dollar-buying central bank intervention would become the bigger
force in markets, he said.
 
    "I would be more wary of intervention in December than at
any other point in time."
    "Hence my view that in the short term, you want to be long
or neutral dollar/Asia and in the long term, you want to be
short dollar/Asia," Baweja said.
    Baweja recommended positioning for this eventual Asian
  

appreciation through spreads, such as buying one-month  

dollar/won non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) and  

selling the six-month forwards.  

SING DOLLAR STILL NEUTRAL  

The Philippine peso was steadier around 55.27/35,  

off last week's life lows.  

Yet, markets were nervous about policy instability after  

the decision by film star Fernando Poe Junior to contest next  

year's presidential elections, finance secretary Jose Camacho's  

resignation and the likelihood of a deterioration in the budget  

deficit next year.  

The Taiwan dollar made light gains, in line with  

the won, and the Indonesian rupiah was virtually  

unchanged.  

Despite the Sing dollar's rise, traders said it was merely  

mirroring the euro's and yen's moves and was still unchanged in  

trade-weighted nominal exchange rate terms. The currency is  

managed in an undisclosed trade-weighted band.  

Traders said markets were slightly disappointed with the  

dip in the Singapore Purchasing Managers' Index reading for  

November, despite it being the sixth month of expansion.  

But, more than that, the fear of intervention by the  

Monetary Authority of Singapore would keep markets from pushing  

the Sing dollar towards 1.71, to three-year highs it struck  

last month.  

"The data has been good. But the market is not in a hurry  

to move the Sing dollar to the top end of the band," Baweja  

said.  

"I don't expect the dollar/Sing to do more than 1.71 this  

year."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Philippine peso falls on Camacho resignation.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso fell
sharply to near a record closing low on Friday after Finance
Secretary Jose Camacho said he would resign at the end of the
month.
    The peso        ended local trading down half a percent
from Thursday's close at 55.585 per U.S. dollar. This was near
its early November lows and within striking distance of its
all-time low of 55.75 per dollar.
    It has been Asia's weakest currency this year, dogged by
worries over the budget deficit and politics, and this
development raised the policy uncertainty, analysts said.
    "I would imagine there will be a little bit of pressure on
the spot rate, a bit of pressure on the ROP (sovereign bond)
spreads and little bit of pressure on the domestic bond market
until things settle down," said John McGowan, treasurer of
HSBC, Philippines.
  


 
    "If there's uncertainty it is bound to create some sort of
pressure locally."
    Other Asian currencies also fell on Friday, undermined by
the violence in Turkey and Iraq, weak equity markets and the
worry over intervention by local authorities.
    The yen's moves were erratic. It benefited from the
  

dollar's decline after the suicide bombings in Turkey and  

blasts in Iraq but fear of Japanese dollar-buying intervention

weighed.   


The Korean won             fell as far as 1,198 per
  

dollar in early deals, its weakness exacerbated by recent  

comments from Korean authorities that they favoured a currency

policy that supported exports.  

REFLATION DOUBTS  

Equity markets in the region were mostly weak on Friday  

too, and analysts said the bombings had merely given traders an  

excuse to trim their long positions on Asia ahead of the year  

end.  

"Equity markets are being challenged, reflation is being  

challenged and therefore Asian currency longs are being  

challenged," said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist with UBS.  

The Sing dollar was over a cent off Wednesday's  

three-year highs near 1.71 per dollar, with some traders  

suspecting the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened

to rein in the rallying currency.  

"As you can see from the dollar, from the lack of upside in  

the Aussie and from stock markets, the market has begun  

to challenge the reflation theme," Baweja said.  

"And that's combined with continued intervention. The  

authorities continue to believe that exports are the only  

bastion of support for their economy."

title: Singapore  Dlr Down Late;  Intervention  Talk Lifts US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar tumbled to its lowest level in three sessions Friday, pressured by talk the government was intervening in the market to support the U.S. unit.  

Market participants said the Monetary Authority of Singapore was thought to have been buying U.S. dollars in small amounts since it hit a three-year low of S$1.7105 against the Singapore dollar early Wednesday.  

"They appear to have been in the market over the past few days to keep the (U.S.) dollar above the S$1.7100 level," a trader at a U.S. bank said.  

It is MAS policy not to comment on its foreign exchange market activities.  

After opening trading Friday around S$1.7175, the U.S. dollar climbed steadily to an intraday high of S$1.7240 late afternoon.  

At 0820 GMT, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.7230, up from S$1.7185 late Thursday in Asia.  

An improving economic outlook has helped make the Singapore dollar one of the region's best performing currencies since the end of October (up 1.5%).  

But further gains will be more difficult to come by in the near term, United Overseas Bank said in a research note.  

Next week's scheduled report on October industrial production should confirm the economic recovery is continuing, but "unless the data outperforms spectacularly, it is unlikely to provide a further boost to the Singapore dollar, given that the recent appreciation has probably factored in all the good news for now already," the bank said.  

Singapore government bond prices rose modestly across the curve, continuing the three-week rally that has been inspired by recent gains in U.S. Treasurys.  

At the end of the session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was down three basis points at 1.12%.  

The yield on the five-year bond was down four basis points at 2.83%.  

The yields on the seven- and 10-year bonds were each down three basis points at 3.22% and 3.79%, respectively.  

The yield on the 15-year bond was down two basis points at 4.40%  

Interest rate swaps were also lower, with the two-year offer down four basis points at 1.80%. The five-year offer was at 3.03%, while the 10-year offer was at 4.18%, both down six basis points.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 232 basis points from 234 basis points late Thursday.

of falling Asian currencies on Thursday as the yen's retreat in

on sentiment.

violence in Iraq and the U.S. decision to impose quotas on
Chinese textile imports, Asian currencies found little support.

drivers," National Australia Bank said in a commentary.
    "The first is the degree of capital inflow into the Asian
  

economic region. While this has been very strong in the past  

quarter, there are signs that foreign investors are becoming  

less enamored with Asian equity assets with the rate of inflow  

into Taiwan dropping away sharply," it said.   


 
    The second factor was the value of the yen and market
perceptions of changes to China's currency regime, it said.
    "The trend towards a stronger yen has exerted a strong
gravitational force, but the opposing force has been the yuan
peg."

Hong Kong were all weak on Thursday.

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late; US Dlr Rebounds From 39-Month Low
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar rebounded smartly against its Singapore counterpart Thursday after hitting a 39-month low a day earlier.  

Buying by U.S. banks, broad-based U.S. dollar short-covering, and concern over possible Singapore government currency market intervention supported the U.S. unit, dealers said.  

At 0820 GMT, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.7185, up from S$1.7127 late Wednesday in Asia.  

The U.S. dollar's level late Thursday represented nearly a half-percent gain from its 39-month low of $1.7105 reached early Wednesday.  

The rebound in the U.S. dollar that started Wednesday was thought to be at least partly due to intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, United Overseas Bank said in a research note.  

"Now that MAS has been suspected to be in the market, it will probably make the market more wary of pushing dollar/Sing down too aggressively," according to UOB, which added that the U.S. dollar should find near-term support around the S$1.7100 level.  

The MAS doesn't comment on its currency market operations, but is believed to have sold Singapore dollars from time to time to prevent currency gains from hurting demand for the country's exports.  

The Singapore dollar, helped by strong economic data, has been strengthening steadily since the start of November when the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7475.  

Prices of most Singapore government bonds fell after U.S. Treasurys slumped overnight amid concerns of new corporate issuance.  

Yields were up from 4-5 basis points across the curve early in the Singapore session before buying interest perked up later in the day and helped cut some losses.  

The yields on the 15- and 10-year Singapore government bonds, which were up as much as 5 basis points each in the morning, were just 1 basis point higher in late trading at 4.42% and 3.83% respectively.  

The yield on the seven-year bond was 1 basis point lower at 3.26%, after trading as high as 3.31% in the morning.  

The yield on the five-year bond was up 3 basis points at 2.87%, while the yield on the two-year bond was unchanged at 1.13%.  

In the interest rate swaps market, the two-year offer was up up 3 basis points at 1.84%. The five-year offer and seven-year offer were unchanged at 3.09% and 4.18% respectively.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies barely moved
on Thursday morning as growing evidence of higher growth in the
United States and data pointing to heavy currency intervention
by local authorities put markets in a quandary.
    The yen        was weaker, having fallen below 110 per
dollar after another batch of U.S. data pointing to improving
growth.
    In Asia, the Indonesian rupiah        and Philippine peso
 , the two least correlated with the yen, were slightly
weaker. The rest were unchanged.
    The Sing dollar        held a 1.7415/25 range and the
Korean won             was stable around 1,182 per
dollar.
    "I think it is a choppy period now with the struggle
between data coming out of the United States as well as
elsewhere, and Asian central bank intervention," said Cliff
Tan, currency and interest rates strategist at Citigroup.
 
    "We are maintaining our focus to buy Asian currencies on
dips," he said.
   


    Still, it was a period in which traders ought to be
   


cautious, Tan said, with market positions still heavily short
   


on dollars and recent surprises on the upside in data coming
   


out of Europe, Japan and other parts.
   


It could be the beginning of a policy tightening cycle too,
   


after Australia led with a rate hike on Wednesday and the Bank
   


of England expected to do so soon.
   

INTERVENTION


Recent months have been tumultuous for currency markets,
   


beginning with the September Group of Seven meeting, calling
   


for flexible currency policies in Asia, to last week's
   


surprisingly reticent report on global foreign exchange policy
   


by U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow.
   


But central bank data showed Asian central banks had
   


continued intervening aggressively through October. Japan spent
   


about $25 billion on yen-weakening intervention and China's
   


reserves rose to over $400 billion.
   


James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan, said
   


reserve accumulation in a narrow block comprising China, Japan,
   


Korea and Taiwan amounted to $58 billion in September and an
   


estimated $54 billion in October, against a 2003 monthly
   


average of $31 billion.
   


"In terms of Asian currencies, growth and recovery continue
   


to unfold in Asia so if the dollar rebounds and it is because
   


of growth, that has been generally supportive for Asian
   

currencies, almost counter-intuitively sometimes," Tan said.
   


"But currency politics may remain quite important for the
   


Greater China block and may return again in spite of the fact
   


that the market has got calmer since Snow's testimony."
   


Tan said Asian central banks may reduce the intervention to
   


keep their currencies weak as they head into better growth in
   


2004.
   


But the lack of confidence with the political leadership in
   


some places, such as Korea and Taiwan, could mean those central
   


banks would be cautious about currency appreciation for some
   


more time, he said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; Dlr Up On US Data,  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The dollar rose across the board against its Asian competitors Thursday, helped by an improving economic outlook in the U.S. and continued efforts by governments in the region to curb the strength of their currencies.  

A better-than-expected index reading in the New York Federal Reserve Bank's October survey of manufacturers and positive retail sales data for September set a firm tone for the dollar in Asian trading.  

Central banks and government officials in the region have been taking advantage of the dollar's recent upward momentum to push their currencies lower through regulation and market intervention.  

"Given that G7 pressures to allow market forces to prevail (in currency markets) is really directed toward China and Japan, the remaining central banks have hidden behind the big boys and continue to intervene to protect their currencies' competitiveness and hurt speculators," UBS said in a research note.  

The South Korean won, in a volatile session, fell by more than 1% in the opening hour of trading as fears of central bank intervention continued to flush out short-dollar positions.  

"A central bank-driven short squeeze in dollar/won continued for the third day in Asia today, pushing the pair back toward the KRW1,180 mark," UBS said.  

The dollar hit a 10-week high of KRW1,184.4 in morning trade before reversing course as interest in the local stock market perked up.  

The Korean Composite Stock Price Index rose 1.7% to finish at its highest level in a year. Foreign investors bought a net KRW89 billion worth of shares in the cash market and a net 8,548 futures contracts.  

The dollar slipped to an intraday low of KRW1,117.2 late in the session. State banks acting on behalf of the government then stepped in to support the U.S. unit. That helped lift the dollar to its closing level of KRW1,174.9, up from KRW1,170.5 late Wednesday and its best finish since Sept. 2.  

The Thai baht was little changed as the initial shock from capital controls imposed by the central bank earlier this week began to wear off.  

The dollar was quoted at THB39.850 late in Asia, about the same level as a day earlier.  

The U.S. unit rose to an intraday high of THB39.96 before profit-taking wiped out its gains.  

Dealers said some players are starting to build short dollar positions again, hoping that the steep correction in the baht since the central bank announced its new regulations Tuesday will allow the Thai unit to resume its appreciation on trade and investment capital flows.  

Taiwan's central bank helped keep a lid on the local dollar by reiterating that the bank would not allow the currency to become a manipulation target in the foreign exchange market.  

The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.950, up from NT$33.900 late Wednesday.  

The New Taiwan dollar's rise to a 14-month high Monday fueled concerns that the surging currency could deal a setback to the country's export-reliant economy.  

The Singapore dollar tracked its regional peers lower in relatively calm trading after a string of recent volatile sessions.  

Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7410, up from S$1.7375 late Wednesday.  

The U.S. unit hit a session high of S$1.7450 in early trading before succumbing to profit-taking.  

With little in the way of domestic news to drive trading the Singapore dollar's moves were mainly dictated by the yen and the baht, dealers said.  

The Philippine peso also followed the yen lower after surrendering early gains.  

The dollar closed at 54.66 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.62 late Wednesday.  

The local currency's rally over the past few sessions was cut short after the dollar's rise against the yen triggered a round of dollar/peso short-covering, dealers said.  

Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar was quoted at IDR8,440 in late Asian trade, up from IDR8,425 late Wednesday.  

Traders said players sold the rupiah in sympathy with the yen due to a lack of other news on which to trade.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Volatility Dominates Session
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies were mixed against the dollar Wednesday in a choppy trading session.  

The U.S. currency weakened against the New Taiwan dollar, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah, while extending its gains versus the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

The short-covering rally that sent the dollar soaring against Asian currencies a day earlier appeared to have largely run its course in some markets, leaving the U.S. unit vulnerable to renewed selling pressure, analysts said.  

"The market has once again been caught out looking for a clearout of dollar shorts only to encounter good demand to sell the dollar into rallies," UBS said in a research note.  

U.S. President George W. Bush also contributed to some of the dollar's weakness, vowing Tuesday to press China and Japan to allow their currencies to move freely against the dollar.  

Bush told reporters he will raise the issue with Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi during a visit Friday to Tokyo and with Chinese officials during an economic summit in Bangkok next week.  

The Thai baht recovered from a three-week low in morning trade to finish the Asian session modestly stronger against the dollar.  

Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at 39.775 baht, down from THB39.970 late Tuesday.  

The baht opened on a weak note following the Bank of Thailand's move Tuesday to introduce further measures to discourage speculators from taking long positions in the Thai currency.  

Central Bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the initial weakening of the baht after the new rules were unveiled showed that the policy was working.  

However, after peaking at THB40.240 in the first hour of trading, the dollar reversed course and proceeded to weaken for the balance of the session.  

A trader at a local bank said exporters viewed the dollar's rise above the THB40 level as a good selling opportunity.  

The won fell for the second straight session after hitting a 35-month high against the dollar earlier in the week.  

An official at South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy attributed the won's slide to market players covering "excessive short-positions" in the dollar.  

The dollar closed at 1,170.5 won, up from KRW1,166.4 late Tuesday.  

Suspected government intervention pushed the dollar to a six-week high of KRW1,175.0 in afternoon trading before the rally began showing signs of fatigue.  

The U.S. dollar's rise against its Singapore counterpart in volatile trading fueled speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened to support the U.S. currency.  

Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7375, up from S$1.7360 late Tuesday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7330 and S$1.7470 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7350 and quickly reached its session high of S$1.7470 on buying led mainly by large local banks, sparking speculation they were acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

The U.S. currency spent the rest of the session gyrating between S$1.7380 and S$1.7450, with market attention dominated by its moves against the Thai baht, dealers said.  

A hands-off approach taken by Taiwan's normally interventionist central bank allowed the local currency to rise modestly against its U.S. counterpart.  

The U.S. dollar ended at NT$33.900, down from NT$34.051 Tuesday.  

Trading volume totaled US$809 million, down from US$1.16 billion in the previous session.  

"The central bank wasn't as active (Wednesday), after its big move yesterday," a dealer at a foreign bank said.  

The peso was buoyed by dollar remittance inflows from Filipinos working overseas.  

The dollar closed at 54.620 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP54.720 Tuesday.  

Many Filipinos working abroad traditionally increase their repatriation of funds in the fourth quarter to give family members more spending money for Christmas.  

The peso will remain vulnerable, however, due to political concerns ahead of the presidential elections in May next year, analysts say.  

The rupiah benefited from expectations of capital inflows into the local stock market.  

The dollar closed at 8,425 rupiah, down from its close Tuesday at IDR8,450.  

The ongoing initial public offering of a 36% stake in Bank Rakyat Indonesia, which is scheduled to close early next month, is expected to attract foreign investors' interest, helping the local currency.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Central bank  moves bring big falls.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Several Asian currencies
posted their biggest losses in months on Tuesday, reversing
most of the gains since the Group of Seven meeting last month
that was seen as a call on Asian countries to let their
currencies rise.
    Dealers said players scrambled to cover their short U.S.
dollar positions as central banks, almost across the region,
conducted aggressive dollar-buying intervention.
    The baht        fell about two percent to near 40 per
dollar, a two-week low, after the Bank of Thailand placed fresh
restrictions, including a limit on the amount of baht
foreigners can keep in Thai bank accounts. The moves were aimed
at curbing speculation in the currency market, BOT said.
    The Korean won            posted its biggest fall since
March, to a near one-month low of 1,169.5, amid what dealers in
Singapore suspected was sporadic dollar-buying intervention by
the Bank of Korea.
  


    The Taiwan central bank was spotted buying U.S. dollars to
push its dollar  to a near one-month low on the weaker
side of the 34 per U.S. dollar.
    The Hong Kong Monetary Authority was also in the market to
buy U.S. dollars and sell Hong Kong dollars , pushing the
spot market to around 7.75 per dollar -- its closest to the
official peg rate of 7.8 to the U.S. dollar since late
September.
 
    The region-wide swing in sentiment pulled the Singapore
dollar  to its lowest in more than three weeks.
    "The move was aided by rumours of intervention and
  

increasing concerns in the market about the post-G7 pace of  

Asian currency appreciation, and overstretched short dollar  

positions," said Bank of America's strategist Sameer Goel.  

He said the move was also partly in response to the U.S.  

dollar's rise against major currencies after European Central  

Bank President Wim Duisenberg said the G7 call last month for  

exchange rate flexibility was not directed at the euro .  

"There is still this issue of fear of floating where they  

had been scared in the aftermath of the Asian crisis," said  

Claudio Piron, strategist at Standard Chartered commenting on  

Thailand's steps to restrict capital flows.   


 
    "There is also an issue here of kind of protecting the
constituency, the exporters."
    Dealers said the move in the market has defied general
bullish expectations ahead of President George W. Bush's visit
to Asia next week and the APEC summit in Thailand.
    Traders had expected Asian central banks to intervene less,
  

given United States' persistent criticism of the foreign  

exchange policy of many Asian nations to keep their currencies

weak.   


 
    However, David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of
Scotland said the weak U.S. dollar trend was still intact.
    "I think we are in a parameter shift here in terms of Asian
currencies going stronger against the U.S. dollar. That is the
trend and I don't think that's altered," he said.
    "Periodically we're going to get some pretty sharp and
unpleasant corrections and this is one of them," he said.
    Elsewhere, losses in the Philippine peso were limited by
fresh dollar remittances from overseas workers.
    Dealers said with the import season having peaked, and
  

overseas workers remitting dollars for the school admission  

season, the peso was likely to see stronger levels in coming

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Fall on US dollar rise, policy caution.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies gave up some
of their recent gains early on Tuesday, prompted by the U.S.
dollar's rebound against major currencies and as caution grew
over authorities' response to further appreciation.
    Dealers in Singapore said they suspected there was
aggressive intervention by the Bank of Korea and the Taiwan
central bank on Tuesday to pull their currencies down to weaker
levels.
    Dealers were wary of the Thai baht as well after it fell to
a one-week low, down from Monday's three-year highs above 39 to
the dollar, despite Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra saying
the government had not yet made any decision on whether to use
tax measures to discourage currency speculation.
    Thai Finance Minister Suchart Jaovisidha was quoted on
Monday as saying Thailand was considering taxing currency
transactions to help stem growing speculation on the strong
baht.
  


    The South Korean won was down to its lowest in three weeks
compared with Monday's three-year high, and the Taiwan dollar
fell to its one-week low from a 14-month high.
 
    The region-wide swing in sentiment pulled the Singapore
dollar to its lowest in over two weeks.
    Dealers said the move in the market has defied general
bullish expectations ahead of the President George Bush's visit
to Asia, next week, and the APEC summit in Thailand.
    Traders had expected Asian central banks to intervene less,
  

given United States' persistent criticism of the foreign  

exchange policy of many Asian nations to keep their currencies

weak.  

"Even if you're bearish dollar/Asia, which I am, you have  

to except the reality that these central banks are not going to  

look the other way," said David Simmonds, strategist at Royal  

Bank of Scotland in Singapore.  

"Pending a convincing pick up in domestic demand they  

(central banks) are going to remain pretty sensitive to  

exchange rate moves. That certainly does seem clear," he added.  

However, Simmonds said Asian currency losses could be a  

corrective move within the well established weak U.S. dollar  

trend, which is unlikely to reverse anytime soon.   


 
    "Periodically we're going to get some pretty sharp and
unpleasant corrections and this is one of them," he said.
    Elsewhere, the Philippine peso edged off a one-month high
hit on Monday but dealers in Manila said fresh remittances from
overseas workers were supporting the peso.
    Dealers said with the import season having peaked, and
  

overseas workers remitting dollars for the school admission  

season, the peso was likely to see stronger levels in coming  

days.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -New highs on U.S. dollar fall.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose to
new highs early on Wednesday, following the U.S. dollar's fall
to fresh lows against major currencies.
    The South Korean won            hit a 35-month high, the
Thai baht  set a new three-year high, the Singapore
dollar  probed fresh four-month peaks and the Taiwan
dollar  closed in on one-year highs.
    The baht also received a boost after Standard and Poor's
upgraded its credit ratings by one notch. The agency also
upgraded Indonesia and Malaysia. For a detailed story click on
           .
    Dealers said the Japanese yen's        rise through the
psychological barrier of 110 per dollar, to new three-year
highs, would raise expectations that central banks in the
region might allow their currencies to set fresh highs against
the U.S. dollar as well.
  


    "The 110-level was the next line in the sand where people
had feared that (Japan's) ministry of finance would order
intervention," said Bank of America's strategist in Singapore,
Simon Flint.
    "With that level broken it means people are adding to their
short dollar/Asia positions at the moment, so you are beginning
to see new (U.S. dollar) lows across the region."
    However, Flint added that Asian central banks would not
completely stand out of the way of currency appreciation and
would continue to limit the move.
    Earlier a senior official at South Korea's finance ministry
told Reuters there had been no change in the government's
foreign exchange policy -- a reference to recent dollar-buying
intervention by Korean authorities.
    Asia's policy to keep currencies weak to help boost exports
has come under increasing criticism from the United States and
Europe and the focus has been China's yuan currency, which is
virtually pegged at around 8.278 per dollar.
    Chairman of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, Charles
Grassley, on Tuesday sent a letter to the Chinese government,
threatening action unless the country moves to a flexible
exchange rate and upholds trade commitments.
    The yuan's one-year non-deliverable forward contract had
risen to record premium above 5,000 points per U.S. dollar,
pricing an appreciation of about six and a half percent.
    The U.S. Treasury Department is scheduled to report on
Asia's currency policies to Congress on October 16, ahead of
President George Bush's appearance at an APEC summit.
    Dealers said speculation on a move in the yuan has
intensified ahead of the APEC gathering in Thailand later this
month, in which the region's currency management policies are
expected to be raised.
    Given China is a major trading partner of most Asian
economies, any move in the yuan, whenever it comes, will be
matched by other regional currencies.
    Such speculation has also spilled over into the Hong Kong
dollar  market, pushing the two-decade old peg of 7.8 per
U.S. dollar to strengthen to levels not seen since October
1997.
    Dealers said currency players would still be cautious in
Korea and Singapore where monetary policy announcements are due
on Thursday and Friday, respectively.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht rallies, but gains worry others.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies held a
stronger bias on Thursday, helped by stock market gains, with
the Thai baht rallying to a three-year high as a ratings agency
placed the country on review for possible upgrade.
    Led by the yen       , Asian currencies have strengthened
in the two weeks since the Group of Seven called for more
flexibility in exchange rates, although most regional
currencies have been wary of bettering the highs they set early
last week.
    Dealers said markets were still cautious for any
dollar-buying intervention by their respective central banks,
amid talk that the Bank of Japan might have intervened to curb
the yen's rise in early trade.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS in Singapore, said
Japan's yen policy was an important determinant of how the rest
of the region would respond to their currency strength.
  


    "Whether or not reduced intervention from Japan will result
in reduced intervention from the rest of the region; that is
theme number one," he said.
    He said Asian authorities were suspicious of the
sustainability of export growth, and were thus wary of currency
appreciation.
    "But they might change their reaction as a result of good
numbers. So we do believe currencies will appreciate backed by
better economic data," he said.
    Baweja said such a change in attitude was apparent in
Thailand, where policymakers have shown tolerance to currency
strength as the economy outperformed most in the region.
    Moody's Investor Services placed the country's foreign
currency ratings on review for possible upgrade on Thursday,
citing the strength of the economy.
    On Thursday the baht        rallied over half a percent to
39.58 per dollar, its strongest since July 2000, taking its
year-to-date gains to close to nine percent.
    Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said early
in the afternoon the bank had not intervened to weaken the
baht.
    "Today the baht is strengthening slightly too fast but we
haven't intervened yet," Pridiyathorn told reporters in
Bangkok.
    Dealers in Bangkok suspect authorities do step in
frequently to buy dollars, and said the Bank of Thailand
probably did on Thursday to smooth out volatility as the baht
surged.
    CENTRAL BANK TALK
    But elsewhere, worries about dollar-buying intervention
capped the South Korea won  and the Taiwan dollar
 .
    Equity- and export-related dollar sales kept the won to
near 1,150 per dollar, a level it has failed to convincingly
breach in the last week due to intervention by authorities.
    Dealers in Singapore said state banks had pulled the won
down to a near one-week low on Wednesday, a move they suspected
was on behalf of the central bank. Data on Thursday showed
Korean reserves rose by over $5 billion in September to $141.5
billion.
    Currency players in Singapore, however, braved rumours of
central bank intervention and pushed the local dollar  to
a four-month high of 1.7227 per U.S. dollar, dealers said.
 
    Dealers said the move was exacerbated after stop-loss U.S.
dollar sell orders kicked in around 1.7250.
    Dealers said they suspected Wednesday's U.S. dollar

Monetary Authority of Singapore. Some local banks were seen  

buying dollars on Thursday as the Sing dollar approached  

four-month highs.  

Meanwhile, Indonesia's central bank said it was happy for  

the rupiah to remain in the 8,200-8,700 per dollar  

range.  

Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah also said Fitch Ratings would

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht at 3-yr highs, others watchful.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies stayed
in sight of their recent highs on Thursday, helped by buoyant
stock markets, with the Thai baht  leading the way as it
explored three-year highs.
    Dealers said markets were still on the watch for
dollar-buying intervention by their respective central banks,
amid talk that the Bank of Japan might have intervened early on
to curb the yen's  rise.
    "The overriding question at this point in time is on the
dollar/yen," said Sameer Goel, analyst at Bank of America in
Singapore.
    "If you do believe that dollar/yen is actually floored at
110 yen and its going to be defended vigorously by the MOF
(Japan's Ministry of Finance), then obviously there is not much
downside to dollar/Asia in general," he said.
    The baht was pressing against 39.70 per dollar, its
strongest since July 2000, after first hitting the level in New
York trade. It has risen by about 8.5 percent so far this year.
  


    Late on Thursday morning, Moody's Investor Services placed
Thailand's foreign currency ratings on review for possible
upgrade, citing the strength of the economy.
    The baht has rallied since the Bank of Thailand said on
Wednesday that it was at an appropriate level, was not
threatening exports, and that the bank had not intervened to
stop its rise.
    Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik also said that even if
the baht strengthened to 38-39 per dollar by next year, exports
would still be competitive.
    Goel said the baht, like most Asian currencies, would
remain supported by optimism over Asia's economic recovery and
by foreign investment flows into the region's stock markets.
    CENTRAL BANK FEARS
    But elsewhere, worries about central bank intervention to
keep currencies weak persisted.
    Helped by equity-related dollar sales, the South Korean won
  rose to near 1,150 per dollar, a level it has failed
to convincingly breach in the last week due to dollar-buying
intervention by Korean authorities.
    Dealers in Singapore said state banks had pulled the won
down to a near one-week low on Wednesday, a move they suspected
was on behalf of the central bank. Data on Thursday showed
Korean reserves rose by over $5 billion in September to $141.5
billion.
    Finance Minister Kim Jin-pyo said it was not necessary for
the won to match the strength of other Asian currencies if
those economies were growing faster than that of Korea.
    The Singapore dollar        closed in on four-month highs
past 1.7230 per dollar, but players were cautious on rumours
that Wednesday's U.S. dollar purchases by some local and
foreign banks were on behalf of the Monetary Authority of
Singapore.
    Still, dealers said the U.S. dollar sales by corporates,
spotted in the past couple of sessions, were likely to continue
and that would limit the Sing dollar's downside.
    Dealers said the U.S. dollar sales, led by a local bank and
a state enterprise, were likely related to either the purchase
of stakes in two Indonesian state banks or to hedging of new
quarter requirements.
    Indonesian is expected to complete the sales of majority
stakes in Bank Internasional Indonesia Tbk (BNII.JK) and PT
Bank Lippo Tbk (LPBN.JK) by next month. The sales are expected
to raise around $500 million.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late; Stuck In Tight Range Vs US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady late Thursday, after moving in a very tight range amid a lack of strong interest to trade in the local market, dealers said.  

Around 0810 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7338, barely changed from S$1.7342 late in Asia Wednesday. The U.S. dollar traded between S$1.7320 and S$1.7340 intraday.  

The U.S. dollar slipped to its session low of S$1.7320 early in the session after comments by Federal Reserve officials overnight provided market participants with further incentive to sell the already weak U.S. dollar.  

The fall, however, turned out to be brief, as the U.S. dollar recovered to S$1.7330-S$1.7340 by midday, mirroring its rise back up above Y112 against the yen, dealers said. By late Thursday, the U.S. dollar had slipped to just below that mark, trading at Y111.95.  

Market participants in Singapore remained especially cautious over the possibility that the local dollar's strength may prompt the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene to limit the rise, dealers said.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research report that there had been "pockets of talk" that the central bank had intervened to buy U.S. dollars earlier in the week, though dealers said this seemed highly unlikely.  

Even so, trade in the Singapore market has been very thin over the past two sessions, especially with the MAS' monetary policy statement due early next month.  

Market participants said they generally think the MAS is comfortable with the current Singapore dollar levels and thus don't expect any change to the central bank's currently neutral policy stance.  

Over the next few sessions, dealers expect the U.S. dollar to stay between S$1.7300 and S$1.7400 against the local currency.  

Prices of Singapore government bonds ended slightly lower Thursday after giving up their early gains on profit-taking, traders said.  

Local bonds had opened higher after an overnight rise in U.S. Treasurys, but the gains were eroded as selling interest emerged by late afternoon.  

At the end of the session, the yield on two-year bonds was one basis point higher at 1.14%, while at the longer end of the curve, the yield on 10-year bonds rose three basis points to 3.56%. The yield on the longest tenor, the 15-year bonds, rose four basis points to close at 4.01%.  

Interest rate swaps moved generally in tandem with the bond yields, with the two-year offer rising four basis points to 1.40%, while the five-year rose two basis points to 2.58%. The 10-year offer was three basis points higher at 3.71%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 231 basis points from 232 basis points late Wednesday.  

In the local money market, rates were mostly steady with the overnight offer unchanged at 0.5000%.

title: IMF/INTERVIEW:Singapore Econ Rebound Likely Underway-Min
text:
DUBAI (Dow Jones)--Singapore's economy is showing signs of recovery after a sharp contraction in the second quarter, but a top official declined to comment on whether the improvement will prompt a monetary policy shift.  

Second Finance Minister Lim Hng Kiang told Dow Jones Newswires in a recent interview that he is optimistic the recovery has begun as the world economy picks up and Singapore tackles its structural problems such as cutting business cost and diversifying the manufacturing base.  

"The economic recovery is taking place on a cyclical and structural level," Lim said on the sidelines of annual International Monetary Fund and the World Bank meetings here.  

In a separate interview, Lim was quoted as saying the economy will expand by 0.5%-0.7% this year, well within the government's twice downgraded zero to 1% growth forecast, the Singapore Business Times newspaper reported Wednesday.  

Lim's comments come as evidence emerge of an economic recovery in the U.S. and Asia - crucial export markets for Singapore whose trade volume is three times the S$160 billion gross domestic product.  

Sure signs of a turnaround from the second quarter's 11.4% on-quarter contraction when Singapore was hit by the SARS outbreak and the war in Iraq also suggests the government would be under less pressure to ease monetary policy.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore, where Lim is a deputy chairman, will early next month decide whether to shift the current neutral policy stance.  

In July, while the government retained the neutral stance, it re-centered the trade-weighted Singapore dollar at lower levels within the undisclosed band, effectively easing policy.  

Lim declined to be drawn into discussing the policy when directly asked whether further easing was a possibility, as several economists are predicting.  

"Our approach has always been to track the movement of a basket of currencies that reflects our major trading partners," he said, referring to the long-standing government policy. "That has served us well in the past, as it allows flexibility and lets the market decide the value of the Singapore dollar," said Lim.  

In Singapore, where the impact of trade dominates a small domestic economy, the MAS conducts monetary policy via the exchange rate, rather than interest rates. It intervenes to push up the Singapore dollar when it wants to control inflation or an overheating economy and sells the local unit when the economy needs a boost.  

The authority guides the Singapore dollar in a narrow but undisclosed range - analysts estimate it is plus or minus 1% to 2% - against an unspecified trade-weighted basket of currencies.  

Lim said economic weakness in the first half of the year was due both to weaker growth in the world economy, and new competitive challenges particular to Singapore.  

"The weakness at the beginning of this year was partly cyclical and partly structural," he said. "Singapore faces a new competitive environment, and some sectors that had previously been doing well will have to be replaced by new value-added sectors," the minister added.

title: Asian  Currencies  Soar On G7; Ctrl Bks Fail To Curb Gains
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Despite central bank intervention, Asian currencies surged Monday after Group of Seven finance ministers made an unprecedented call for increased flexibility in currency regimes to address global economic imbalances.  

Several Asian currencies soared to multi-month highs against the U.S. dollar, while the forward discount on the dollar-China yuan pair steepened to record levels during the day.  

The G7 communique at the weekend didn't target any country, addressing its message to "major countries or economic areas."  

Nevertheless, currency traders immediately turned to the yen and other more freely-traded Asian currencies, interpreting that remark as confirming the end of Washington's "strong dollar" policy of the late 1990s and conversely, the start of stronger Asian currencies.  

"The (G7) statement is a bit of a watershed. It explicitly said they want more flexibility in exchange rates," said BNP Paribas Senior Currency Analyst Thio Chin Loo.  

"The market thinks it (G7) is pointing towards Asia where there is the greatest trade imbalances with the U.S.," Thio added.  

As a result, the dollar plunged to a 33-month low versus the yen in Asia Monday, and a 34-month low against the Korean won. The dollar was also sharply weaker against the Singapore dollar - at a near three-month low - and reached a 13-month low against the Taiwan dollar. Stock markets across the region, meanwhile, fell as investors fretted over what stronger currencies mean for corporate profits.  


 
   Korea Bought Dlrs; China Says Policy Stance Unchanged 
   

Even jawboning from the Bank of Korea did nothing to stop dollar sales versus the won.  

"The recent trend in the market is not appropriate given Korea's economic fundamentals and we hope to see balance restored in the market on its own," said a high-ranking official at the Korean central bank.  

The Bank of Korea comments follow similar dollar-supportive remarks from the Ministry of Finance and Economy earlier Monday. The ministry followed through on its verbal intervention by buying dollars via state-run banks, according to dealers.  

The dollar fell to as low as KRW1,150 intraday Monday, tracking the dollar-yen's sharp fall, and ended at a 34-month low of KRW1,151.2, versus Friday's close of KRW1,168. The yen-won cross was at 10.2620 late Monday, from Friday's 10.2501.  

The dollar sank in the market for forward delivery against the yuan, which can be used in place of the spot market to make bets on the yuan's long-term direction. The dollar's one-year discount steepened to a record 2400 points at one stage, implying expectations of the dollar falling to 8.0374 yuan over the next 12 months, a nearly 3% drop from the tight spot range that Beijing now allows around CNY8.277.  

These expectations linger even though Chinese authorities insist nothing has changed post-G7.  

China's position on its current forex regime remains unchanged from the firm support for that policy expressed by People's Bank of China Governor Zhou Xiaochuan earlier this month, a central bank spokeswoman said Monday.  

Separately, a State Administration of Foreign Exchange spokesman said, "We will continue to keep the renminbi (or yuan) exchange rate basically stable."  

"The NDFs imply the yuan is under intense pressure," BNP Paribas' Thio said.  

"But China's (forex) stance should stay for another one or two years," she added.  


 
   Taiwan Central Bank Supplied NT$ 
   

Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.805, its lowest level since Aug. 14, 2002, versus Friday's close of NT$34.058. Dealings were valued at US$1.412 billion, the highest volume since May 30, 2002, compared with Friday's US$779 million.  

Players in the non-deliverable forward market dumped the U.S. dollar, while the Taiwan central bank was "supplying Taiwan dollar unlimitedly" to absorb dollar offers, said a local bank trader.  

The dollar slid to as low as 1.7295 Singapore dollars, its lowest level in almost three months. But by the end of the local session, the dollar was well off its early lows due to concerns Singapore's central bank may intervene and a possible easing of local monetary policy next month.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research report, "Over the next few days, U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar direction will be totally dependent on U.S. dollar-yen's outlook and whether the Bank of Japan will show up (to buy dollars)."  

Late Monday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7322, down sharply from S$1.7490 late in Asia Friday.  

Against the Thai baht, the dollar reached a 38-month low of THB39.93 and was at THB40.05 late Monday, versus late Friday's THB40.51. No Bank of Thailand intervention was spotted though dealers said any baht sales by the authorities would likely have been easily absorbed.  

The dollar ended at 55.07 pesos Monday, down from Friday's close of PHP55.165, largely in tandem with regional markets and the dollar-yen pair. The market shrugged off the Philippine central bank's as-expected decision to keep rates unchanged.  

The Indonesian rupiah was barely traded as markets were shut for a religious holiday. Traders expect the rupiah to strengthen against the dollar Tuesday as the Indonesian unit catches up with the rises in its regional counterparts.

title: Asian  fx  rally may not herald end to  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rallied sharply on Monday after the world's richest countries called for an end to intervention, but regional policymakers were still uneasy about the surge and threatened to curb the gains.  

The Group of Seven over the weekend called for more flexibility in exchange rates, which markets saw as criticism of the U.S. dollar-buying policies of Asian economies.  

"The communique is a clear swipe at Japan, China and the rest of Asia's tampering in currency markets," Sydney-based Macquarie Bank analysts said in a report.  

The immediate reaction would have pleased European and United States policymakers. The yen surged to a high of 111.37 per dollar, its highest level in over two and a half years, and pulled Asian currencies along in its slipstream.  

However, Asian monetary authorities had a different take, and dealers in Seoul said the central bank bought U.S. dollars on Monday after the won firmed to its strongest in nearly three years.  

Zembei Mizoguchi, Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs, said the G7 statement was not intended to curb Japan's intervention to cap yen gains and, in response to a reporter's question, said the yen's surge had been too rapid.  

"We reaffirmed our view on currencies and it is unchanged. Therefore, our stance of closely monitoring markets and taking action as needed is unchanged," Mizoguchi told reporters.  

ONE SIDED  

In South Korea, an official at the central Bank of Korea said authorities were concerned about one-sided sentiment in the won.  

In Taiwan, dealers waited for the central bank to appear after the Taiwan dollar traded at a 13-month high.  

Analysts said the goal posts had changed, but not the game.  

"I don't think that they would necessarily intervene less, but they will intervene at lower dollar/Asia levels. The intervention band levels have just been lowered," said Peter Redward, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist in Singapore.  

Asian revaluation now tops the agenda for politicians from Berlin to Washington because of Asia's massive export flows, China's emergence as the world's factory floor, and a stubbornly weak U.S. labour market ahead of the 2004 presidential election.  

Asian currencies make up around 40 percent of the Federal Reserve's trade-weighted dollar index, so any rise in their value makes U.S. exports more competitive. This, U.S. lawmakers say, should ease stubbornly high unemployment and boost growth.  

YUAN SPECULATION  

Regional currencies lagged the strength of gains in the yen on Monday - the closely watched yen/won cross jumped to a five-month high as the won underperformed - and stock markets weakened as exporter shares came under pressure.  

The Thai baht rallied to its strongest level since July 2000 and markets also grew more confident that China would allow the yuan to strengthen within 12 months.  

Chinese authorities manage the yuan in a tight 8.2760-8.2800 band per dollar, so the market reaction to the G7 showed up in the offshore non-deliverable forwards market, where the yuan premium against the dollar rose to a record high.  

The one-year contract traded at 2,520 points, which equates to a yuan rate in a year's time of about 8.026 per dollar - three percent stronger than now.  

The rationale for Asia's intervention has been to protect export markets, a key economic engine for the region.  

That has led to a massive surge in the region's foreign exchange reserves - over $1.66 trillion and largely made up of U.S. dollar assets.  

But the policy has attracted European criticism that the euro - which has rallied over 25 percent since the start of 2002 - has had to bear the brunt of adjustment for the massive U.S. current account deficit. Signs of upturn in Japan as parts of Europe slipped into recession added to the complaints. (Additional reporting by Ovais Subhani).
