title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late;USD/CNY NDF Discount Widens
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar weakened against most Asian currencies Tuesday, including a widening in the discount versus the Chinese yuan to a record level in the nondeliverable forwards market. 

 The dollar-yuan NDF discount has been steadily widening in recent months, reflecting a perception by market participants that China will eventually loosen the narrow trading band for the local currency and allow it to appreciate against the dollar. 

 The NDF market allows investors to make plays on potential moves in the dollar-yuan, despite the fact the yuan isn't freely traded. 

 The one-year dollar-yuan discount widened to an unprecedented 2,100 points Tuesday, just days ahead of The Group of Seven finance ministers meeting in which China's tight control over the yuan is expected to be an issue. 

 "There's just too much pressure from all over the world," a Hong Kong-based trader at a major U.S. bank said. 

 The yen's rise to a one-week high against the dollar in late Asian trading contributed to the widening of the dollar's discount versus the yuan. 

 Yen moves are catalysts for shifts in the yuan and Hong Kong dollar NDF markets because significant strength in the Japanese unit is viewed as placing pressure on those two fixed-currency regimes. 

 Signs that the U.S. economic recovery may not be as robust as originally thought weighed on the dollar-yen. Late in Asian trading the dollar was quoted at Y116.40, down from Y117.50 late Monday in New York. 

 Elsewhere in Asia, the South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht strengthened. The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso weakened. 

 The won was buoyed by the yen's strength, as well as foreign inflows into the local stock market. 

 The dollar closed at 1,170.0 won, down from KRW1,172.7 a day earlier. 

 Foreigners bought a net KRW37.3 billion worth of shares, helping push up the Korea Composite Stock Price Index by 1.3% on the day. 

 The won's gains were muted, however, by government intervention to support the dollar around the KRW1,170 level, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar overcame heavy central bank intervention to strengthen against the dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.103, down from NT$34.147 Monday. 

 Dealers said that central bank intervention aimed at cushioning the local currency's strength accounted for between a third and half of Tuesday's total trading volume of US$605.5 million. 

 The peso weakened as demand for the U.S. currency started to build in preparation for the quarter-end corporate dollar requirements. 

 The dollar closed at its intraday high of 55.05 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.965 a day earlier. 

 Traders said they expect the dollar to gather more momentum during the week as importers and other companies build up their dollar holdings to pay for overseas purchases and settle debts. 

 Citigroup forecasts the dollar to reach PHP55.75 within a month due to a range of factors, including the lingering political concerns in the Philippines, the drain in dollar liquidity due to foreign debt payments, lower remittance inflows from migrant Filipino workers during the third quarter, and higher demand for dollars from importers. 

 With little in the way of news to drive trading, the Thai baht tracked other regional currencies higher. 

 Toward the end of the Asian session the dollar was quoted at 40.510 baht, down from THB40.650 late Monday.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies crept
higher on Tuesday, helped by a modestly higher yen and an
irresolute U.S. dollar, but remained wary of central bankintervention.
    Uncertainty over policy dominated trade. The Singapore
dollar  was pressured by worries over next month's
monetary policy review, and Philippine markets debated whether
the central bank would remove a six-month limit on forward peso
contracts.
    In Korea, markets wondered if the won
would be allowed to rise beyond 1,170 per dollar as they
awaited an inflow of $1.2 billion from U.S-based Lone Star
Fund's investment in Korea Exchange Bank (04940.KS).
    After Taiwan media reports suggested foreign institutional
investors would be allowed to sell their holdings of Taiwan
stocks overseas, markets there speculated whether that opening
of equity markets would be accompanied by currency
appreciation.
  


    And as the Thai baht        shied away from 40.50 in
offshore deals and stayed a bit weaker, analysts said Asian
dollar-buying intervention would remain the hot topic heading
into IMF and Group of Seven meetings on the weekend.
    "Although intervention appears to be an ongoing short-run
reality, the event calendar in the coming months would argue
against expecting the status quo," Lehman Brothers said in a
note, citing the weekend meetings and preparations for U.S.
presidential elections next year.
    Lehman said solid growth in China, the Japanese economic
rebound, and the strong flow of foreign money into Asian
equities justified bullishness on Asian currencies.
    "Better global growth expectations and rising equity
markets have been part of the reasoning behind our pro-Asia
view, it is hardly the only reason. Asian currencies are cheap
and the Asian business cycle has been growing on its own for
some time," the note said.
    PRICING HIGHER TAIWAN DOLLAR
    While the Taiwan dollar stayed near 34.10/12, a level it
has struggled to rise past since early September, the
non-deliverable forwards were pricing in a higher currency.
    The one-year premium on the Taiwan dollar           was
quoted at 57 points, the highest in 14 months and pricing the
currency up 1.7 percent in a year.
    "The Taiwan dollar will appreciate over coming months, and
potentially much more strongly than we have been used to seeing
it for a long period," said David Simmonds, markets strategist
at the Royal Bank of Scotland.
    "The central bank will remain cautious about currency gains
and competitiveness pending direct, tangible evidence that
stronger economic recovery is here," he said.
    Other factors, such as whether Japan would ease its policy
of yen-selling intervention and China's currency policy, would
also play a big role in influencing Taiwan's policymakers, he

By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were caught
between a number of conflicting factors on Monday, including
weak U.S. data, falling north Asian stock markets and Europe's
fresh criticism of the region's currency policies.
    The yen        remained steady with Japanese markets closed
for a holiday. The euro  was under slight pressure after
Swedish voters decided not to join the single currency, but the
U.S. dollar continued to be undermined by Friday's weak retail
and consumer confidence data.
    The Thai baht        was among the few currencies to rise,
recovering from a sharp fall after the central bank last week
imposed short-term capital controls to curb speculation.
    Chinese non-deliverable forwards (NDF) showed a rising
premium on the yuan after Europe's top financial officials
again urged China and Japan to share the burden of the U.S.
current account adjustment.
  


 There were specific calls for China
to shift from a virtually fixed dollar peg to managing the yuan
against a basket of currencies.
    The one-year yuan NDF premium           hit 1,900,
equalling a record high struck in June, and pricing the yuan
  at around 8.09 in a year, compared to the narrow
8.2760/8.2800 band it is managed in.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan, said the
debate over Asia's weak currencies and policies would surely
heat up heading into the Group of Seven meeting on the weekend,
and it was likely regional currency intervention would
moderate.
 
    "I don't think there's anything new from G7 for Asia as a
whole, but it is a continued build-up of pressure," he said.
    "The direction is very clear, a downside dollar bias. But
it is really a question of how it is managed in terms of
central bank intervention," he said.
    ASIA WON'T BUCKLE YET
    U.S. Fed data showed Asian central banks remained heavy
buyers of U.S. treasuries and agency debt in early September.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS, said that judging
  

by the indifference of the yen to recent euro and dollar moves  

and the recent measures by the Bank of Thailand, Asia had not  

succumbed to the growing pressure to intervene less.  

"We feel that for Asia to be seen giving in to global  

demands of currency flexibility that are once again likely to  

be made at the G7 and IMF meetings in Dubai later this month,  

it is important that the hopes on global reflation continue  

push foreign money into Asian equities," Baweja said in a note.   


The Korean won             weakened on Monday as

intervention. Korean markets had been shut for three days of  

holidays.

By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar slipped
late on Tuesday after the government confirmed the world's
first case of the deadly SARS virus since the World Health
Organisation declared a global outbreak over in July.
    The Singapore dollar        slipped past $1.7570 per U.S.
dollar in late trade after the Ministry of Health said a
27-year old man had tested positive for the Severe Acute
Respiratory Syndrome virus, but it remained clear of Monday's
lows.
    Before the confirmation, the Singapore dollar had rebounded
about three-quarters of a cent after falling to a one-month low
of 1.7618 in New York trade on initial reports of the SARS
case.
    "The impact on price action was very much muted. I don't
see much speculative flows as such," said a dealer at a foreign
bank in Singapore.
    Analysts said if it was an isolated case, which the
government said it was, any impact on the Singapore dollar
would be brief.
  


 SARS killed over 800 people in a global
outbreak, including 33 in Singapore, and savaged Asian
economies earlier this year.

    Elsewhere, the Thai baht        hit a 14-month high, and
dealers in Bangkok suspected the Bank of Thailand had
intervened through local banks to cap the rise when it hit
40.43 per U.S. dollar, its strongest since July 2002.
    Dealers said the intervention was not as aggressive as
previous bouts, and that had left the market looking for more
gains.
    David Simmonds, currency strategist at Royal Bank of
Scotland in Singapore, said Thailand's economic outperformance
should allow authorities to be comfortable with some currency
strength.
    "It would be unrealistic to expect Thailand to stand
completely out of the way of appreciation, one has to be a
little bit wary. But by and large, I do think we are seeing a
catch up to fundamentals here," he added.
    A senior dealer at a local bank in Thailand said players
were targetting 40.25 as the next level to test. However, he
said he had heard some state enterprises were looking to buy
dollars around those levels.
   The South Korean won                   rose to a two-week
high of 1,168.0 per dollar, helped by equity inflows. The Bank
of Korea policy meeting left interest rates steady, and the
central bank governor voiced concern that an anticipated
recovery was yet to appear.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Yen  Intervention  Helps Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar was mixed against Asian currencies Monday, drawing some support from the Japanese government's efforts to prop up the U.S. unit against the strengthening yen. 

 The Bank of Japan, acting on behalf of Japan's Ministry of Finance, bought dollars for the third straight session, boosting the U.S. currency by nearly one full yen in early morning trading. 

 The dollar, which was changing hands around Y116.80, soared to Y117.72 after the BOJ bought as much as $5 billion, according to some analysts' estimates. 

 The sharp rise against the yen triggered a round of dollar buying that boosted the U.S. currency across the region. 

 But the yen battled back, supported by a strong stock market, improving economic numbers and expectations that Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi will be re-elected as leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party later this month. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar had slipped back below the Y117 threshold and was trading around Y116.97, up from Y116.83 from late Friday in New York. 

 The dollar backtracked against other Asian currencies as the day progressed. The dollar finished slightly stronger against the South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar, and Philippine peso. It weakened against the Singapore dollar and Thai baht, and was unchanged against the Indonesian rupiah. 

 The won was pulled off its intraday lows with the help of foreign inflows into the local stock market and dollar sales by exporters. 

 The dollar ended at 1,171.5 won, up from KRW1,170.6 at Friday's close. 

 Foreign investors were net buyers of KRW142.7 billion worth of local shares Monday, although the size of their net purchases has shrunk from previous days. 

 The dollar was also pressured by corporate sales ahead of a local holiday. 

 South Korean financial markets will be closed Wednesday through Friday for Chuseok, a thanksgiving holiday. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit closed at NT$34.129, up from NT$34.117 Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar strengthened to NT$34.167 in the morning on the back of its gains against the yen, but lost ground in afternoon trading. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was helped by the recovering yen, as well as net inflows of NT$9.65 billion into the local stock market. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from its early losses, helped by the selling of the U.S. dollar by foreign banks in afternoon trading. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7572, down from S$1.7580 late in Asia Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7580 in Singapore and after a quiet start drifted higher to touch its session high of S$1.7610 in tandem with its rise against the yen. 

 But the U.S. dollar failed to retain its gains as foreign banks unwound long U.S. dollar positions and took profit from midday. 

 The peso was pressured by lingering political and security concerns. 

 The dollar ended at its intraday high of 55.130 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP55.020 Friday. 

 The stability of the Philippine government has been called into question following corruption charges against President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's husband, as well as a recent failed mutiny by some members of the military. 

 Traders said further peso weakening could be expected in the run-up to the May 2004 general election. 

 The Thai baht finished stronger on the heels of the yen's late recovery. 

 The dollar ended at 40.73 baht, down slightly but little changed from THB40.775 at the Asian close Friday. 

 Sentiment toward the baht remains positive due to the strength of the local economy and local stocks. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar was unchanged at 8,490 rupiah. 

 Traders said expectations for further gains in the local stock market could boost the rupiah in the coming days. 

 Jakarta stocks ended at a three-and-a-half year high Monday, ending up 0.8% at 587.057 points.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Yen down on  intervention  talk, Tokyo stocks gain.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Japan appeared to be intervening to weaken the yen on Monday after poor U.S. jobs data undermined the dollar, traders said, but hopes for better news on the Japanese economy lifted Tokyo shares.   

 An index of stocks elsewhere in the Asian-Pacific region continued to touch levels unseen since early 2001, led by gains in technology shares and despite losses in Hong Kong and Seoul.   

 The yen slipped nearly one percent against the dollar and euro in early trade amid persistent talk of intervention by the Japanese authorities.   

 But it soon began to creep back up in the absence of official confirmation or further evidence of central bank action.   

 "It seems the Bank of Japan has bought (dollars) this morning in thin market conditions," said a senior manager at a Japanese trust bank. "It's a bit unnatural to see such a big spike around this time of the day."   

 The yen fell towards 117.75 to the dollar compared with 116.80 in late New York trade on Friday and 3-1/2-month highs around 115.75 set last week. But by 0225 GMT, the yen had clawed back up to around 117.35 to the dollar.   

 The Japanese currency also fell beyond 130 to the euro for the first time in more than two weeks. The euro was steady against the dollar at around $1.11 holding onto gains made on Friday on the weak U.S. jobs data.   

 The jobs report showed non-farm payrolls fell 93,000 versus forecasts for a 12,000 rise, while the jobless rate declined to 6.1 percent from 6.2 percent, when no change was expected.   

 ASIAN STOCKS MIXED   

 That weakened U.S. stocks, with a knock-on effect on shares in Hong Kong, South Korea and Singapore Benchmark indices for all three markets were around 0.3 percent weaker.   

 But Tokyo's Nikkei average ended morning trade up half a percent at 10,707.83 and an MSCI index of shares elsewhere in Asia Pacific climbed a quarter of a percent, led by its technology component.   

 Japanese shares moved back towards 14-month peaks on hopes that a string of data this week will reinforce signs of a brighter outlook for the economy.   

 That optimism was reflected in gains in bank shares such as Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, which rose 4.5 percent.   

 Traders are looking forward to a batch of economic data this week, with July machinery orders, a gauge of capital spending, on Tuesday, followed by revised gross domestic product (GDP) data for April-June on Wednesday.   

 "There's a very good chance that GDP data will be revised up this week, which could prove the trigger for a charge towards 11,000 by the Nikkei," said Koji Muneoka, head of domestic sales trading at HSBC Securities.   

 Sony Corp, the world's biggest consumer electronics firm, rose three percent, while office equipment and camera giant Canon Inc was up almost two percent.   

 Taiwan rose 0.5 percent, helped by gains of more than two percent in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co and United Microelectronics Corp Australia advanced a third of a percent.   

 Despite the weak jobs report, Wall Street strategists expect U.S. stocks to gain in coming days following positive economic data in recent weeks and a bullish revenue forecast from technology bellwether Intel Corp   

 The jobs data provided indirect support for Japanese government bond (JGB) prices, which jumped across the board after U.S. Treasuries surged on the weak data.   

 The key September 10-year JGB futures contract hit its highest level since August 27, traders said.   

 Oil gained and gold weakened.

strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.  

However, Redward said China was unlikely to heed the call  

any time soon, and at best a modest widening of the band in  

which China allows the currency to move could be expected in  

the next six to 12 months.  

Analysts say authorities across Asia would continue to  

resist significant currency appreciation unless they gained  

more confidence over economic recovery at home and abroad.  

Reflecting those views, the U.S. dollar discount priced in  

the one-year yuan non-deliverable forwards pulled  

back to 1,750 points, from Thursday's close of 1,875, just shy  

of its record level of 1,900 points on June 17.  

The U.S. dollar premium on one-year Hong Kong Dollar  

forwards moved to 46 points, from an early high of 70  

but was still far from Thursday's one-year low of 35 points.

Elsewhere, the only currencies to edge slightly up were the   


South Korean won             and Taiwan dollar         .
  

Both were helped by equity-related inflows but were  

constrained by fear of dollar-buying intervention by their  

respective central banks a day after they intervened

aggressively to cap currency gains.  

The Singapore dollar retreated through 1.7600 per  

U.S. dollar, from late Thursday's 1.7558 with some major funds  

spotted covering short U.S. dollar positions.  

The Thai baht edged back from 13-month highs, after  

some local banks were spotted buying dollars late on Thursday  

following Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's comments that the  

central bank would try to keep currency strength from hurting  

exports.   


 
    The baht declined to 40.89 per dollar, from Thursday's
40.73, its strongest since July 2002.
    Dealers in Singapore said local corporates were hedging
  

their future dollar requirements, while three days of net  

selling of local stocks by foreign investors has also hit  

sentiment.  

Foreign investors' net selling of local stocks has reached  

more than a billion baht so far this week, and dealers say that  

money could chase the dollar higher.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;Japan  Intervention  Lifts Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar strengthened against selected Asian currencies Thursday after Japan's Ministry of Finance intervened in the currency market to support the U.S. unit against the yen. 

 The dollar had been weakening against its Asian counterparts early in the session, including the yen, when the MOF stepped into the market. 

 The ministry is believed to have bought as much as $3 billion in the widely-rumored intervention to curb the yen's strength, analysts said. 

 The MOF, through the Bank of Japan, began buying dollars after speculative selling pushed the U.S. currency to a 15-week low of Y115.75 in the early hours of Asian trading. Within 20 minutes, the dollar jumped to Y116.90 as the intervention triggered a wave of dollar short-covering. 

 "Dollar-Asia was supported pretty much across the board this morning after the aggressive, unconfirmed, intervention by the Bank of Japan ...," Bank of America said in a note to clients. 

 Japanese authorities have worked to cap the yen's appreciation for fear excessive currency strength could jeopardize the country's fragile economic recovery. 

 The dollar rose sharply against all regional currencies after the intervention. It held onto its gains against the New Taiwan dollar, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah, but retreated later in the session against the South Korean won and Thai baht. The U.S. dollar was little changed against the Singapore dollar. 

 The New Taiwan dollar posted a fresh one-year intraday high in early trading before reversing course after the Japanese intervention. 

 The U.S. dollar traded as low as NT$34.030 in the morning session. It climbed steadily after the intervention, finishing the day at NT$34.120, up from NT$34.095 at Wednesday's close. 

 Taiwan's central bank apparently took advantage of the U.S. dollar's momentum against the yen and jumped into the market to buy the U.S. currency against the New Taiwan dollar. 

 Many players who were short U.S. dollars were then forced to cover their positions, providing an even bigger boost to the U.S. unit. 

 The U.S. currency succumbed to selling pressure against the won in afternoon trading as foreign investors continued to pour money into the South Korean stock market. Foreign investors bought a net KRW215.3 billion worth of shares Thursday. 

 Domestic corporations also unloaded the dollar in favor of the local currency. 

 The dollar closed at KRW1,173.1, down from KRW1,174.3 at Wednesday's close. The dollar had changed hands as high as KRW1,176.5 after the Japanese intervention. 

 The baht initially weakened in line with the yen, but later rallied to finish at a fresh 14-month high against the dollar. 

 Traders said Fitch Ratings' upgrade of Thailand's sovereign ratings Wednesday continued to support a bullish view of the local currency and they expected the baht to continue its climb Friday. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 40.770 baht down from THB40.885 late Wednesday. 

 Comments by the Thai prime minister published in the local press Thursday that the dollar isn't likely to fall beyond THB39 gave investors the impression that the central bank may not heavily intervene in the foreign exchange market until the pair gets closer to that level, a Bangkok-based trader said. 

 The peso snapped a three-day winning streak as it tracked the yen lower and gave way to corporate demand for dollars. 

 The dollar rebounded from an intraday low of PHP54.620 to finish Asian trading at PHP54.950, up from PHP54.755 late Wednesday. 

 Corporations bought dollars as the U.S. currency's losses earlier this week have brought it down to levels that are perceived to be attractive for debt servicing purposes. 

 The Singapore dollar was supported by persistent buying interest from some market participants despite a sharp fall in the yen. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7558, compared with S$1.7562 late in Asia Wednesday. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar was quoted at IDR8,480 rupiah in late Asian trading compared with IDR8,475 late Thursday. 

 Dealers said demand from local importers drove the U.S. currency up to an intraday high of IDR8,495 before inflows into the local stock market pulled the unit lower.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pulls back after yen  intervention .
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were
stronger on Thursday but pulled back from early highs after
Japan heavily intervened to cap the yen's  rise against
the U.S. dollar.
    The intervention came even as the chatter among
policymakers about Asian currencies' undervaluation grew louder
as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting got
underway.
 
    U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow said he would keep
pushing Asia to adopt more flexible currency policies.
    South Korean Deputy Finance Minister Kwon Tae-Shin played
  

down the impact of a rising won on his country's economy,  

saying 40 percent of its exports competed on quality and brand  

name, rather than price.  

But earlier in the day, dealers in Seoul said they had  

spotted dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Korea that   


pulled the won             to weaker levels.
  

Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, whose recent  

remarks had encouraged the baht hit its strongest since July  

2002, said the baht was on an uptrend, but the central bank

would try to prevent it from hurting exports.  

Analysts said it was unrealistic to expect Asian  

authorities to let their currencies appreciate unless they  

became more confident over the durability of economic recovery  

at home and abroad.  

"To the extent that the discussion is now on that is  

something of a change, but whether that leads to a change in  

attitude of FX policies I sort of doubt it," said David  

Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore.  

The U.S. complained that the yuan, also called the  

renminbi, was too cheap at its current pegged level of around  

8.3 per dollar, and it was becoming a key issue ahead of the  

2004 U.S. Presidential election.   


 
    China maintains that the yuan would eventually float
freely, but has resisted calls to speed up the process.
    The Thai baht        pared its early gains from a 13-month

behalf of the central bank.

    The Singapore dollar        rose to S$1.7520 per U.S.

    Sentiment remained weak as a key manufacturing activity
report showed the Singapore economy was struggling to recover.
    The purchasing managers' index in August eased to 51.3,
from July's 51.4, showing the manufacturing sector was barely
growing.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Thai baht buoyed, others track yen.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The Thai baht gained nearly
half a percent early on Thursday to its strongest in over a
year, as Asian currencies benefited from the Japanese yen's
rise to three-month highs against the U.S. dollar.
    Later, heavy intervention by the Bank of Japan pushed up
the U.S. dollar, and the move also pulled most Asian currencies
back from their early peaks.
    In Thailand dealers said importers and local corporates
were spotted buying U.S. dollars early on and there were fears
of intervention by authorities but foreign funds and banks were
still lapping up the baht.
    The baht was bought up to 40.73 per U.S. dollar, its
strongest since July 2002, by mostly Hong Kong and Singapore
names, a dealer at a foreign bank in Singapore said.
    The dealer said breach of the 40.80 level, beyond which
most players thought the central bank would cap gains
aggressively, supported the currency's rise.
  


    Baht stands as the lead gainer among Asian regionals,
rising close to six percent so far this year on the back of
strong economic growth and portfolio investments.
    Comments by government officials over the baht's potential
strength and Wednesday's credit ratings upgrade by Fitch
Ratings have further buoyed market sentiment.
    "The dollar/baht can be around 39.75 in the next three
months," said Simon Flint, Bank of America's strategist in
Singapore.
    He said the baht would appreciate even more on a
trade-weighted basis, even if gains against the U.S. dollar
were cut short.
    C.BANK PULLS BACK WON
    The Taiwan dollar rose to T$34.03 per U.S. dollar, its
strongest in more than a year, aided by U.S. dollar sales by
exporters.
    Equity-related inflows and exporters' dollar sales also
pushed the South Korean won higher, before dealers spotted
intervention by the central bank pushing the currency weaker
against Wednesday's close of local trade.
 
    The won touched a high of 1,170.8 per dollar, before the
dollar-buying intervention pulled it down to 1,176.5.
    The Singapore dollar rose to S$1.7520 per U.S. dollar,
before it retreated to S$1.7537.
    Sentiment remained weak as a key manufacturing activity
report showed the economy was struggling to recover.
    The purchasing managers' index in August eased to 51.3
percent, from July's 51.4 percent, showing the manufacturing
sector was barely growing.
    "The Singapore dollar never deserved to appreciate when
people were buying into the Asian reflation trades," Flint
said.
    "The economy still faces quite significant cyclical and
structural challenges," he added.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Tokyo stocks fall, Japan  intervenes  to weaken yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Tokyo shares fell for the first time in five sessions on Thursday on worries stocks had risen too fast and the yen tumbled as Japan apparently intervened to weaken the currency and protect an economic recovery.   

 The jitters in Japan were mirrored in South Korea and Taiwan. But shares in Hong Kong and Australia scored 14-month highs on signs of an improving global economy, helping to lift an MSCI index of Asia Pacific stocks ex-Japan 0.5 percent to levels unseen since February 2001.   

 "You're starting to see signs of recovery in most major economies - China, Japan, the U.S. is starting to turn around, in Europe there's a flicker of light at the end of the tunnel," said Mick Coombes, director at Australia's Macquarie Equities.   

 Oil and gold prices were little changed, but Japanese government bonds rallied for a second day after the Bank of Japan vowed to stick to its ultra-loose monetary policy.   

 The yield on the 10-year bond tumbled 14 basis points to 1.475 percent.   

 In another move intended to keep a budding economic recovery on track, the Bank of Japan was spotted intervening in the currency market to stem export-damaging strength in the yen, traders said.   

 They said yen sales by the central bank pulled the currency more than one percent off multi-month highs versus the dollar and the euro.   

 The dollar shot up more than one yen to 116.84 yen from a 3-1/2-month low of 115.75 hit in early trade. The euro rose about 1.5 yen from the day's low to 126.60 yen after hitting an eight-month low of 125.05 yen on Wednesday.   

 ECONOMY OFF SICK BED   

 "The Japanese economy is like a bedridden man who has finally recovered but has only just started to walk a little bit," said Seiya Nakajima, chief economist at Itochu Corp. "It's clear the government doesn't want to kill the nascent recovery."   

 The yen has been rising on foreign demand for Japanese stocks, encouraged by indicators such as a capital spending report on Thursday that suggest the economy is improving.   

 Although laggards in the recent rally such as drug makers continued to gain, concern that stocks were overheating pulled the Nikkei average lower. The market had gained more than 15 percent in less than a month to hit 14-month highs.   

 "We seem to be losing some of our momentum after the market rocketed higher earlier this week," said Norihiro Fujito, senior strategist at Mitsubishi Securities.   

 The Nikkei closed down 0.6 percent at 10,646.95 as top technology stocks fell. Tokyo Electron dropped 4.4 percent and Toshiba Corp fell 3.3 percent.   

 Top drug maker Takeda Chemical Industries Ltd rose 3.7 percent and rival Sankyo Co Ltd surged 8.4 percent.   

 South Korea and Taiwan also fell prey to worries stocks had risen too far on hopes a U.S. economic recovery would boost exports from Asia - their benchmark indices fell 0.3 percent and 0.8 percent respectively.   

 But Hong Kong stocks reached 14-month peaks, with the Hang Seng Index ending morning trade up 0.6 percent at 11,171.68. Australian shares hit the same milestone, climbing half a percent.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Snow,  intervention  talk dominate.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Asian currency trading was
dominated for a second day by the higher yen and expectations
that dollar-buying intervention by regional central banks will
be subdued while U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow is in the
region.
    Snow was in Tokyo on Monday and due in Beijing on Tuesday.
    The yen        kept to steady ranges after Japanese
authorities said a further rise in the currency was not
warranted, but Asian traders braced for more aggressive
intervention next week, after Snow leaves Asia.
    The Singapore dollar        stayed within a narrow band,
the Taiwan dollar  struggled to rise past Monday's
one-year highs and the Korean won             was a shade
lower.
    Even the Thai baht        was forced off 13-month highs.
    "Dollar yen remains the driving influence in Asia," said
Michael Jansen, markets strategist with National Australia
Bank.
  


    There was pressure on the yen to rise, and it remained to
be seen if the Bank of Japan would tolerate yen strength, he
said.
    "BOJ intervention is only a matter of time and may take
place only once Treasury Secretary Snow has left the region
over the weekend," Jansen said.
    "We could be looking towards yen strength to persist for
most of this week and then a stronger dollar-yen exchange rate
next week."
    It was no surprise that the Singapore dollar had found
heavy resistance at 1.75, traders said. The Sing dollar failed
to capitalise on the yen's weekend rally but would be pushed
lower if the yen pared gains, they said.
    BAHT GIVES UP GAINS
    The baht came under sudden downward pressure on Tuesday
morning, after it struggled to get past a 13-month high of
40.91.
 
    One Bangkok-based trader said its drop below 41 triggered
dollar demand both locally and from overseas players.
    The baht has been rallying for months and with increased
momentum in the past three weeks.
    "A lot of the strength in the baht is coming to a close.
  

There have been very strong capital inflows and a lot of that  

is skewed or possibly positioned towards how Thailand is going  

to trade as an economy in the next 12 months," Jansen said.  

"But that is running its course and we need to see overall  

a much stronger period of global economic indicators for the  

baht to maintain its upside."  

Markets have been confused after the central bank last week  

said the currency was strong and that it had intervened, while  

government officials forecast even higher levels for the baht.   


 
    Jansen said even if the baht continued to rise, its gains
would be capped at 40 per dollar.
    Elsewhere, the won continued to underperform the yen
  on expectations the Bank of Korea would intervene.
    The Philippine peso tested 55 again and then kept to the
higher side of that figure.
    The Indonesian rupiah        weakened slightly while
  

markets in Jakarta awaited the verdict in the treason trial of  

Muslim cleric Abu Bakar Bashir, who authorities say is the  

spiritual leader of the Jemaah Islamiah network blamed for  

violence in Southeast Asia.  

But there was positive news from Indonesia's Bank  

Restructuring Agency, which announced foreign investors were  

keen on stakes in two more banks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pressured by Korea talks,  intervention  fears.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Barring the Taiwan dollar,
most Asian currencies disregarded a rising Japanese yen on
Friday and were either steady to lower.
    As the yen reached a six-week high against the dollar,
after Japanese data showed improving industrial output and the
Nikkei rose, the Taiwan dollar neared its highest in a year.
    The Korean won suffered from worries as six-nation talks in
China over North Korea's nuclear crisis ended inconclusively,
with the delegates agreeing to meet again in October and
Pyongyang highly critical of the U.S. stance.
 
    Worries the Bank of Korea was still intervening to contain
won appreciation also pushed the currency down against the yen.
    The Thai baht too was haunted by the fears of intervention,
forcing it to halt a three-week uptrend. The Bank of Thailand
hinted on Thursday it had been intervening.
    On Friday, Thai central bank governor,  Pridiyathorn


 Devakula, said the bank was monitoring speculative flows 

 betting on the baht's rise and would find ways to deal with 

 them. 

 "The uncertainties inherent in the (Korea) talks represent 

 one set of reasons why, though we like baht and Taiwan dollar 

 in reflecting the global reflation trade, we are more wary of 

 won," Bank of America said in their commentary. 

 "Bank of Thailand launched another salvo against 

 speculation in the currency. This makes sense in the context of 

 them wishing to limit baht appreciation as a result of 

 speculation," it said. 

 The Singapore dollar fell as it moved towards the centre of 

 the trade-weighted band authorities manage the currency in, a 

 day after the authorities announced cuts to employer 

 contributions to the country's pension system. 

 RUPIAH WEAK AFTER RATE CUTS 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered from two-week lows towards 

 afternoon after falling under the pressure of month-end imports 

 and market expectations that falling interest rates will erode 

 its attractiveness to investors. 

 The central bank cut overnight rates on Friday, the seventh 

 time since May and said it saw no need to intervene to defend 

 the rupiah. 


 
    Vincent Low, markets strategist at Merrill Lynch, said the
rate cut ought to impact the rupiah adversely.
    But Low disagreed with some economists who suggest



Indonesia ought to be less aggressive in cutting rates and



should focus on attracting investment and building foreign



exchange reserves as it prepares to exit an IMF funding



programme.



 
    "I'm not sure about using the exchange rate as a stimulus
in a closed economy like Indonesia," Low said.
    "Interest rates are a more direct way for macro economic
objectives, and the way to build reserves is not through
intervention but by looking for alternative sources to the
IMF."     The Indonesian central bank was comfortable with some



weakness in the rupiah, which has been one of Asia's best



performers this year, and other than politics, Indonesia's



economic fundamentals were sound, he said.



Elsewhere, the Philippine peso was back on the weaker side



of 55, after having closed above that level for the first time



in 10 days on Thursday and despite the central bank's remark it



expected the peso around 54 per dollar at the end of 2003.



The country's Defence Secretary Angelo Reyes said on Friday



he was resigning in the wake of the July 27 failed mutiny, and



warned of a well-funded plot to bring down the government.



The peso had rallied over the past two days from near



record lows after a government warning and a slight monetary



tightening.



The central bank announced on Thursday after the market



closed that it was scrapping a tiered system on overnight



borrowing that discouraged banks from making larger deposits



with the central bank.

the central bank's target zone," the note said

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht succumbs to  intervention  fears.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Thai baht       , among
the only Asian currencies to have escaped intervention anxiety
in a sharp three-week rally, pared gains on Thursday after the
central bank hinted it had moved to contain the currency's
appreciation.
    The threat of intervention by central banks hung around
other regional currencies, preventing them from gaining on
continuing foreign investment inflows and relative growth
prospects.
    The baht        rose to a 13-month high of 41.07, boosted
by Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's remarks that the central
bank could do little to curb the rallying baht in the past
week.
    It pared gains after Bank of Thailand director Chakramon
Phasukvanich said the bank was monitoring the baht and had
intervened. Some traders suspected the BOT bought dollars.



    "The Thai baht was the only currency that continued to move
down over the last couple of days, so I am not surprised," said
James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan.
    But, despite worries that the market was getting too long
the baht, traders had hesitated positioning against the
currency.
    Besides strong exports and domestic consumption, Thailand
has seen foreign portfolio investment of a net 19.04 billion
baht of Thai stocks so far, 33 percent more than in all of
2002.
 
    UBS said the Bank of Thailand (BoT) had allowed the baht to
effectively appreciate four percent since May.
    Central bank measures to allow more capital outflows have
not reined in the bullishness on the baht.
    On Thursday, traders were sure the currency would hit 41 in
the next few sessions.
    BULLISH ON ASIA
    The rupiah        was the region's weakest currency,



falling over half a percent to 8,530 to the dollar on talk of



demand for dollars from an oil firm and covering of stop-losses



triggered by the drop past 8,480.



But, amid expectations of positive U.S. data later this



week and fears of Japanese intervention, local traders were



betting Asian currencies would rise soon.



 
    "On a medium-term outlook, we would still be comfortable
recommending long Asia, short dollar trades," Malcolm said.
    The Singapore dollar        was off Wednesday's two-week



lows but stayed on the weaker side of 1.75 as Prime Minister



Goh Chok Tong announced a cut in employer contributions to the



city state's pension scheme and said a consumption tax hike due



on January 1 would be implemented as scheduled.



The Philippine peso  closed on the firmer side of 55



for the first time in two weeks, extending a rebound from



31-month lows after Wednesday's warning by authorities against



speculation.



Meanwhile, intervention pressures on the won



  subsided, although traders suspected the Bank of



Korea was still vigilant and would step in if the won tried to



firm past 1,170 again.



The Taiwan dollar  was virtually unchanged, torn



between the weakening won and a rising domestic share market.

By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 27 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar fell to
a two-week low early on Wednesday while the South Korean won
and Taiwan dollar stepped further back from their recent highs.
    The Thai baht        stayed buoyed on hopes of improving
economic growth prospects, while consolidation of positions
helped the Philippine peso  and Indonesian rupiah
bounce off their recent lows.
    The Singapore dollar        was at 1.7555 per U.S. dollar,

    Dealers said the Singapore dollar's retreat had gathered
pace on worries ahead of a relief package and a planned cut in
employers' contributions to the state-run pension scheme,
likely to be announced on Thursday.
    Chia Woon Khien, strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank, said
the Singapore dollar's decline was triggered after it briefly
breached the stronger end of the central bank's policy band
last week.



    The Monetary Authority of Singapore targets the Singapore
dollar against an undeclared basket of trade-weighted
currencies, of which the U.S. dollar, Japanese yen  and
euro  are supposed to be major components.
    "While the rest of Asia regionals can target the U.S.
dollar on a bilateral basis, positions in Sing dollar have to
be managed against the basket currencies," she said.
    The Singapore dollar was still on the stronger side of the
band which suggested more downside was possible in line with
the recent decline of the euro  and the yen's retreat
from a one-month high against the dollar, she said.
    Woon Khien said a test of 1.7600 per dollar was possible
this week, depending on how the market reacts to the pension
cuts aimed at lowering the cost of doing business in Singapore.

protecting export competitiveness, was seen pulling the Korean
won             and the Taiwan dollar          off their
recent 13-month and 11-month highs respectively.
    Dealers in Singapore said while foreign investors had been
buying stocks in Korea and Taiwan, the amount of net purchases

built in anticipation of capital inflows.
    However, net selling of local stocks by foreign investors
had little impact on the baht , which stayed in sight of
its 13-month high hit on Monday.

strength.

prospects.

fell to a fresh 31-month trough on Tuesday, just shy of its
record low, while other regionals retreated in anticipation of
possible Japanese intervention to stem the yen's recent rise.

lowest since January 17, 2001, when it hit a record low of

presidency.
    Speculation the central bank was intervening to prop up the
peso helped it bounce off the lows. But some dealers said the
sharp dip in the peso had sparked a brief dollar sell-off by
exporters prompting other players to cover their short peso
positions.
    "Some exporters had already placed orders within
55.50-55.60 range," said Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at
the Union Bank of the Philippines.



    The peso, already down by about seven percent since May,
would suffer from a seasonal rise in imports and low
remittances from workers abroad, he said.
    Sentiment for Philippine assets has soured after a failed
mutiny by renegade soldiers last month and on worries over
potential instability ahead of presidential polls next year.
    The fall came a day after the central bank's Deputy
Governor Amando Tetangco said the bank was ready to inject
liquidity into the foreign exchange market if needed.

"We see scope for a dollar/yen move to 115 over a

rise in imports and falling remittances from expatriate
workers.
    Sentiment for Philippine assets has soured after a failed

potential instability ahead of presidential polls next year.
 
    "From here onwards the next target will naturally be the
all-time low of 55.75," said a dealer at a local bank.
    Dealers said the peso backed up a bit, after some foreign

 The fall came a day after the central bank's Deputy

INTERVENTION WARINESS

Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS, said the BOJ had

"The fear is there. It's not just a question of speculative

Asian forex markets, especially in Korean and Taiwan,

    SINGAPORE, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Wariness over central bankintervention dominated trade in Asian currencies on Monday,
limiting the Philippine peso's fall and capping the rise of the
South Korean won and Thai baht.
    The Philippine peso slipped to a fresh 31-month low of
55.47 against the U.S. dollar, before ending local trade a
touch higher, helped by the central bank's verbal intervention.
    The peso is perilously close to its record low of 55.75,
hit in January 2001 amid the turmoil of Joseph Estrada's forced
exit from the presidency.
 
    The central bank said it was ready to inject liquidity into
the foreign exchange market if needed.
    "We will provide liquidity as necessary. That policy has
never changed," Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco said.
    Dealers in Manila said the peso, which has lost about 6.5
percent since May, had been under pressure from a seasonal rise
in imports and falling remittances from overseas workers.



    Sentiment on Philippine assets has worsened after a failed
mutiny last month and on worries over potential instability
ahead of the presidential election next year.
    The central bank wrote to the finance department that it



was worried its foreign exchange reserves, at around $16



billion, might drop in 2004 due to the huge gap between the



government's planned foreign borrowings and its debt



maturities.



"Such news will add to concern about the central bank's



ability to support the currency given the reserves level," said



a dealer at a local bank in Manila.



WON CAPPED



The won fell back after dealers in Seoul cited possible


intervention through state-run banks.



A senior official at the Finance and Economy Ministry told



Reuters that South Korea would continue to take steps to curb



the currency's strength not justified by fundamentals.



 
    "The won's recent gain has been driven by speculative
forces, rather than economic fundamentals," he said.
    The comment came after the won hit a new 13-month high of
1,166.0 per dollar, shy of a 20-month high of 1,164.0 reached
in July 2002.
    Fear of central bank intervention also capped the Taiwan
dollar at a fresh 11-month high.
    Simon Flint, strategist at Bank of America in Singapore,



said central banks in Asia would continue to manage currency


strength until they become comfortable with the global growth



outlook.



"Currencies will appreciate but you'll have to be patient



and realise that the central banks are going to be quite



cautious."



The baht edged back slightly from its 13-month high of



41.32 hit on Friday in New York trade, after local players and



some foreign funds booked profits on the move, fearing



authorities might step in if the bath rose too far, too fast.



The Singapore dollar lost its early gains, although its



downside was limited by the yen's strength and investors



building long positions in anticipation of a global growth



pick-up later this year.



Dealers said fears the central bank might be preparing to


intervene had pulled the Singapore dollar off its two-month

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Some Ctrl Bks Help Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The yen's strength and portfolio flows into regional stock markets lifted most Asian currencies Friday, with the South Korean won ending at its strongest level in more than a year and the New Taiwan dollar chalking up its best finish in more than 11 months. 

 Monetary authorities in several countries were suspected of buying U.S. dollars to temper their currencies' gains, but the broad trend remained intact. 

 Policymakers in the region are unwilling to allow their currencies to strengthen too much for fear of losing out on export competitiveness. 

 The Singapore dollar was a notable exception to the general trend as investors bought the U.S. unit after it slid to a two-month low in the overnight global session. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7454, up from $1.7398 in Asia late Thursday and S$1.7330 overnight. 

 A foreign bank dealer said local banks were supporting the U.S. dollar. He wasn't sure if they were acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore but "I wouldn't be surprised," he said. 

 But an Asian bank dealer said offshore banks were the main buyers of U.S. dollars when it staged a rebound around mid-afternoon. 

 A research report by JP Morgan Chase calling for investors to sell the Singapore dollar in favor of the basket of currencies against which the MAS guides the currency may have contributed to the move, he said. 

 The MAS guides the local dollar within an undisclosed trading band against the basket of currencies of major trading partners. It occasionally intervenes to iron out excess volatility and keep the Singapore dollar within the band. 

 As "the SGD (Singapore dollar) is hitting the upper limit against its trade-weighted index, concerns over central bank intervention to slow the SGD's rise will help support the USD," BNP Paribas said in a research report. 

 "Nonetheless, it should not alter the bullish trend for the SGD, which has leeway to appreciate further as the JPY and other Asian currencies continue their rise," the French bank said. 

 Meantime, the dollar ended at the intraday low of 1,169.5 won - its lowest close since July 2002 - and down from Thursday's KRW1,173.0. 

 The U.S. unit extended losses toward the close despite steady dollar purchases likely on behalf of the government. The state-run Korea Development Bank was buying the dollar, dealers said. 

 "The market was deluged with dollars by foreign stock investors, but investors (in the foreign exchange market) were getting cannier about more interventions from the government, which had already intervened at every level today," said Seo Jiwang, a dealer at State Street. 

 Foreign investors, who were net buyers of more than KRW1 trillion in shares on the Korea Stock Exchange this week, are selling dollar for won to settle purchases. 

 Dealers expect dollar sales to continue into Monday, possibly leading the dollar as low as KRW1,165. 

 "The authorities won't let the dollar/won free fall, but I think it's heading downward anyway," said a dealer at Kookmin Bank. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit ended at NT$34.217, its lowest since ending at NT$34.122 last Sept. 5, and down from NT$34.238 Thursday. 

 Dealers said strong inflows from overseas investors to invest in Taiwan's equity markets lifted the local dollar. Foreign investors bought a net NT$7.20 billion in shares Friday, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange. 

 Trading volume totaled US$1.02 billion, up from US$731 million in the previous session and the heaviest in over a month. 

Central bank intervention to keep the local dollar from rising further accounted for a big portion of the volume, a Taipei dealer said. Another dealer estimated the monetary authority bought around US$600 million in the session. 

 Taiwan's central bank often intervenes to stem sharp movements in the New Taiwan dollar, and to keep it from strengthening too much for fear it might hurt exports. 

 The Thai baht was lower as investors, mainly offshore, unloaded the dollar, though agents of the central bank were spotted buying the U.S. unit, traders said. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted at 41.50 baht, down from THB41.55 late Thursday. 

 A bank trader in Singapore reported heavy dollar sales at the THB41.48-THB41.50 level earlier in the session, but "those levels will be supported by Bank of Thailand." 

 He said, however, that the central bank seems to be trying to slow the baht's rise, rather than reverse the trend. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was lower in subdued trading as traders covered short-dollar positions ahead of the weekend. 

 The dollar closed at 8,425 rupiah, up from IDR8,390 Thursday. 

 Philippine markets were closed for a holiday Friday.

title: Singapore Dlr Weaker Late; Selling Led By Foreign Banks
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar weakened Friday on selling led by foreign banks in a very thin illiquid market. 

 At 0820 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7454, up from S$1.7398 late in Asia Thursday. It traded between S$1.7390 and S$1.7467 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7392, near its session low, and at first couldn't establish a clear course after rising strongly against the euro but falling against the yen in New York overnight. 

 The U.S. dollar held steady for much of the morning session as market participants were concerned the sharp overnight fall would prompt central banks in the region, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore, to intervene to support the U.S. currency. 

 But the U.S. dollar rebounded sharply around midafternoon as foreign banks aggressively bought the U.S. dollar from around S$1.7400, pushing it up to S$1.7467. The move may have been somewhat exaggerated by thin liquidity, dealers said. 

 "The offshore banks were the main buyers. But it's pretty much the Sing (Singapore dollar) all on its own. All the other currencies are generally steady," an Asian bank dealer said. 

 A research report by JPMorgan Chase Bank calling for investors to sell the Singapore dollar in favor of the basket of currencies against which the MAS guides it may have also contributed to the moves, he added. 

 The MAS guides the Singapore dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. It occasionally intervenes to iron out excess volatility and to keep the local currency within the undisclosed band. 

 Although there were some concerns that the MAS may have played a role in the U.S. dollar's afternoon rebound Friday, there seemed to be little evidence to support that, dealers said. 

 Although the U.S. dollar was off its intraday high by the end of the Asian session, dealers said further gains were possible in the global trading day, though "I think it should be capped at S$1.7500," another trader said. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were higher Friday, after recovering from their early falls, thanks to bargain hunters, dealers said. 

 Local bonds opened lower after sharp losses in U.S. Treasurys overnight. But bonds rebounded around midday, said market participants, on continued relief after the MAS announced a smaller-than-expected issue size of new 15-year bonds due Sept. 1. 

 The MAS said Wednesday that it would auction S$1.5 billion in new 15-year bonds Aug. 27, smaller than market expectations of between S$2 billion and S$2.5 billion, easing concerns that the market would be flooded with new issues. 

 At the end of Friday's session, the yield on two-year bonds was down two basis points at 1.38%, while the yield on five-year bonds shed three basis points to 2.51%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was also three basis points lower at 3.18%, while the yield on 10-year bonds fell four basis points to 3.56%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was one basis point lower at 3.77%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site: 

http://www.sgs.gov.sg("http://www.sgs.gov.sg")

 In the interest rate swaps market, offers were also mostly lower, tracking local bond yields. The two-year offer, bucked the trend though, holding steady at 1.55%, while the five-year swap offer slipped one basis point to 2.76%. The 10-year offer was five basis points lower at 3.77%. 

 The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 222 basis points from late Thursday's 227 basis points.

By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 21 (Reuters) - An early spike in some Asian
currencies was capped by actual and suspected central bankintervention on Thursday, but dealers said forecasts of a
global recovery and portfolio inflows pointed to further
strength.
 
    The expection remained the Philippine peso, which ended
local trade at another record closing low of 55.265 per dollar.
    The South Korean won                   pulled back from a


 seven-month high of 1,171.9 per dollar, after selling from 

 local banks sparked speculation the authorities were behind the 

 move. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar was blocked at an 11-month 

 peak of 34.225 per dollar on intermittent but aggressive 

central bank intervention. 

 The Singapore dollar hit a two-month high of 1.7366 per 

 dollar. Traders decided to book profits rather than risk 

 testing the resolve of authorities by pushing deeper into the 

 strong side of an undisclosed policy band. 

 "The strength of the Singapore dollar has pushed it to the 

 upper half of its trade-weighted index, suggesting that 

intervention risks have risen," said Thio Chin Loo, senior 

currency analyst at BNP Paribas. 

 She said the Singapore dollar could rise up to 1.7250, 

 which she calculated as the stronger end of the targeted policy 

 band. 


 
    "Gains beyond would depend on how much further the yen and
other regional currencies can go," she said.
    Dealers and analysts said most Asian central banks have



acted this year to limit their currencies strength to protect



export competitiveness. Currency gains also counter the easier



monetary policy stances many central banks have adopted this



year.



The Thai baht  rose to a month high as the stronger



regional bias helped it overcome Wednesday's selling pressure,



triggered after the central bank said it was allowing foreign



debt investment applications of $2.45 billion.



 
    That was about five times the limit it had announced when
it relaxed foreign exchange controls last month.
    The Indonesian rupiah rose to the stronger side of 8,400



per dollar for the first time since July 22, to be about four



percent higher than the lows hit after a Jakarta hotel was



bombed on August 5.



Aslim Tadjuddin, the deputy governor of the central bank,



told Reuters the strengthening of rupiah was a vote of



confidence by foreign and domestic investors.



PESO EYES RECORD LOWS



In Philippines, however, the euphoria of the expected



economic recovery in the region was lost amid political worries



ahead of the May presidential elections.



The peso  fell to 55.28 per dollar, its weakest since



January 2001 when it hit a record low of 55.75 amid the turmoil



of Joseph Estrada's forced exit from the presidency.



"The irony is that it (peso) should benefit from the U.S.



recovery given its export profile, but obviously the odd thing



out here is the politics," said Claudio Piron, strategist at



Standard Chartered in Singapore.



The peso has fallen more than six percent from this year's



high in May, pressured by political and security concerns,



including a failed mutiny on July 27.



Dealers in Manila said a combination of lean remittances



from overseas workers and a seasonal peak in dollar demand from



importers would keep the peso under pressure.



But they said the market was cautious amid speculation that



the central bank had sold U.S. dollars around 55.20 on



Wednesday.



A dealer at a local bank said some long U.S. dollar



unwinding was also spotted by players trying to shed their



exposures ahead of a long weekend. Financial markets in



Philippines would be closed on Friday for a local holiday.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Yen, Local Stks; Off 2-Mo High
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was stronger late Thursday, but off a fresh two-month high, supported by a stronger yen and fund flows into the local stock market, dealers said. 

 At 0805 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7398, down from S$1.7488 late in Asia Wednesday. It traded between S$1.7365 and S$1.7420 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7390 after its broad overnight retreat against the yen in New York. 

 It initially hovered around S$1.7380-S$1.7390 but dropped further to S$1.7360, its lowest in two months, mirroring its move against the yen. 

 Fund flows into a buoyant local stock market also aided the Singapore dollar to its two-month high, with the benchmark Straits Times Index up 0.9% at 1626.69 points late Thursday. 

 But the U.S. dollar managed to recoup some losses against the Singapore currency midafternoon, also in line with the yen, amid concerns the sharp intraday U.S. dollar fall might cause the local central bank to intervene to slow the descent. 

 At the end of the session, the U.S. currency was trading at Y118.00 off its session low of Y117.83, but still weaker compared with Y118.56 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 Standard Chartered Bank said in a research report that with the local dollar having appreciated about 1% since July, "This means that we are fast approaching the limit of (Singapore dollar) strength and the risk of intervention is increasing." 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore guides the Singapore dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. It occasionally intervenes to iron out excess volatility and to keep the local currency within the undisclosed band. 

 Later Thursday, the U.S. dollar is expected to stay between S$1.7360 and S$1.7450, though trade is likely to be thinner as the weekend nears. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended higher Thursday, but generally off their early peaks, as an overnight fall in U.S. Treasurys damped a relief rally in the local bond market. 

 Local bonds opened sharply higher as market participants welcomed the announcement that the MAS would auction S$1.5 billion in new 15-year bonds on Aug. 27, smaller than market expectations of between S$2 billion and S$2.5 billion. 

 The smaller size eased concerns that the market would be flooded with new issues and was expected to fuel a sharp rally through Thursday's session. 

 But some tenors trimmed their early gains as attention switched back toward the sharp overnight retreat in U.S. Treasurys and the implications for trends in the local bonds market. 

 At the end of the session, the yield on two-year bonds was down three basis points at 1.40%, while the yield on five-year bonds shed four basis points to 2.54%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was six basis points lower at 3.21%, while the yield on 10-year bonds fell seven basis points to 3.61%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was two basis points lower at 3.78%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site: 

http://www.sgs.gov.sg("http://www.sgs.gov.sg")

 In the interest rate swaps market, offers were also lower, tracking local bond yields. The two-year offer slipped one basis point to 1.55%, while the five-year swap offer also slipped one basis point to 2.77%. The 10-year offer was four basis points lower at 3.82%. 

 The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 227 basis points from late Wednesday's 230 basis points. 

 In the local money market, rates were steady as liquidity remained sufficient in the banking system.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Peso at 31-mth low, Taiwan dlr up.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 20 (Reuters) - The persistent weakness of
the Philippine peso  stuck out like a sore thumb on
Wednesday as other Asian currencies rose on the back of a
stronger Japanese yen.
    The beleaguered peso fell to 55.18 per dollar, its lowest
since January 2001 when it hit a record low of 55.75 amid the
turmoil of Joseph Estrada's forced exit from the presidency
during an army-backed popular revolt.
    John McGowan, treasurer of HSBC, Philippines, said the
uncertainty after recent events in the Philippines -- a failed
mutiny and a court-ordered one-year suspension of central bank
Governor Rafael Buenaventura, which has been appealed -- were
keeping the peso under pressure.
    It was likely demand for dollars to hedge liabilities had
increased from corporates who had been complacent during the
peso's stability in the months before the July mutiny, he said.



    The peso held a tight 55.10-55.13 range in early trade, but
a large order for dollars pushed it through its March low of
55.16.
     "I heard of a sizeable demand for dollars. It seems to be
a temporary thing, although the move is in line with our long
term view," said Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at the Union
Bank of the Philippines.
    YEN BOOSTS REGION
    The yen's strength, derived from the Nikkei average's
  rise to 13 month highs, boosted other regional
currencies.
    The Taiwan dollar          hit its highest since July 11,
backed by continuing foreign equity inflows into a rising share
market and the suspicion that the central bank was not
intervening to cap its gains.
    The Singapore dollar        was stuck in familiar ranges
around 1.7480-1.7500 per U.S. dollar, although against the euro
  it has risen for two weeks, to 1.9422 per euro from
2.01.
    "The trade-weighted Sing dollar has been reasonably firm,"
said David Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of
Scotland.
    Singapore's stock markets have been enthused by the
government's decision, announced on the weekend, to cut
employer contributions to employees' pension funds.
    But some currency traders worried that the move could be
accompanied by a monetary loosening, which the central bank
operates through the trade-weighted band for the currency.
    The Thai baht        was languid, following the yen with
markets apathetic after the authorities said they saw the baht
gradually appreciating this year and said the current strength
was not hurting exports.
    The Korean won                   recovered to be slightly
stronger in local trade after a drop to 1,180 per dollar in
offshore deals.
    "It looks like a bear trap on the won. The false breakout
stalled at 1181," a trader said of the drop, which was possibly
because dollar bears had been forced to cut positions.
 
    The won however was shy of the sensitive 1,175 level amid
suspicion the Bank of Korea had bought dollars this week.
    Data on Tuesday showing a $1.87 billion rise in foreign
exchange reserves in the first half of August, following a $1.2
billion rise in July, strengthened those fears.
    But the Taiwan dollar's rise suggested the intervention
there to contain the gains may have lessened, Simmonds said.
    "There are these big equity inflows into Taiwan. And the



CBC (central bank) periodically steps out of the way and lets



the Taiwan dollar strengthen when there are overwhelming



inflows."



"But, I don't think this is the beginning of the end of the



Asian intervention story," he said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Succumb to U.S. dollar strength.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies finally
yielded ground to a rising U.S. dollar on Tuesday, as the
optimism about a U.S. recovery overshadowed the region's
surging stock markets and foreign investment inflows.
    Taiwan's central bank contributed to the dollar strength
when the head of its foreign exchange department told Reuters
that now was a good time to buy U.S. Treasuries, and said the
euro was too expensive.
    Traders said with the euro at four-month lows, the yen
  giving up resistance and the interventionist policies of
regional central banks, Asian currencies were bound to feel
some pressure.
 
    The Singapore dollar        slipped to the weaker side of
1.75, making it among the weakest regional on the day.
    The Thai baht        shrugged off repeated comments from
the central bank and other policymakers that its strength was
not hurting exports and therefore not worrying, and fell.



    Japan's Nikkei average         rose to its highest level in



13 months, the Korean stock market  hit an 11-month



high, and Thai stocks  reached their highest in over



four years.



The Taiwan dollar  ended onshore trade almost



unchanged, paring gains as stocks ended lower and amid talk of



dollar-buying intervention to pull the Korean won



  down.


Singapore's stock market  was also in negative



territory on Tuesday afternoon, having hit 13-month highs the



previous day, as the impact of a government plan to cut pension



costs borne by employers seemed to be wearing off.



"That the government has employed such drastic measures on



the fiscal front, the risk is that some sort of Sing dollar



weakness will also be employed as added cushions," United



Overseas Bank said in their commentary.



RUPIAH FIRM, PESO WEAK



The Indonesian rupiah  was the only currency in the



region to gain substantially, rallying in relief after the



National Day holiday weekend passed without any militant



attacks.



 
    The peso fell in early trade to 55.15, a five-month low,
and stayed weak as politics remained the overriding concern.
    Traders said they suspected the central bank had sold some
dollars to stop it falling to 55.16, the low struck in March.
    Allegations about the business dealings of President Gloria
Macapagal's Arroyo husband, made by an opposition senator in a
privileged speech on Monday, kept Philippine markets unsettled.
    "The market seems to be reacting to today's headlines plus
weaker regional currencies. We're watching the market," central
bank deputy governor Amando Tetangco told Reuters.
    On Tuesday, the Philippines reported its first monthly



trade surplus for this year in June, owing to increased demand



for its electronics exports, but it offered little comfort to



the peso.



Political and policy continuity concerns have been



heightened after a failed mutiny on July 27 and a recent court



order suspending central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura for



a year over the closure of a commercial bank. The suspension



cannot be enforced until the appeals are exhausted.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Support From Stock Markets
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Monday as stronger stock markets generally supported gains, but rises were tempered by suspected government intervention in South Korea and Taiwan. 

 The South Korean won ended weaker and the New Taiwan dollar finished steady. The Philippine peso drifted lower, but the Singapore dollar and Thai baht were modestly stronger. Indonesian financial markets were closed for a public holiday. 

 Overall bids and offers were fairly well matched, which kept trading ranges tight, a trader at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 "It's pretty mixed. There was a sell-off earlier (in the dollar versus regional currencies), but now they (market players) are buying back. It's the same guys (who were buying and selling)," he said. 

 Analysts said regional currencies are underpinned by expectations of better global growth in the current half-year, led by the U.S., which is a major export market for Asia. 

 Hence "people are still looking to expand positions in Asian currencies," said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist at UBS AG. 

 Security issues, which were in the spotlight recently, appeared to have largely subsided, except in the Philippines, he said. 

 "I don't think the market is going to trade off that (security concerns) until it (something untoward) happens." 

 After the deadly bombing at a major hotel in Jakarta on Aug. 5, there were fears that Sunday's Independence Day celebrations in Indonesia could be a target for similar terrorist attacks, but the day passed without incident. 

 Meantime, some traders suspected the South Korean government had a hand in reversing the won's gains. Others said an exchange of warning shots between North and South Koreas in the afternoon also helped pushed the dollar higher. 

 South Korea's navy fired warning shots Monday after a North Korean fishing boat entered waters controlled by the South, the military said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,178.2 won, up from KRW1,176.6 at Thursday's close. The market was closed for a holiday Friday. 

 Some dealers said the authorities likely bought the dollar around the intraday trough of KRW1,174. 

 "The dollar suddenly soared when it was just about to go below KRW1,174," said a dealer at Chohung Bank. 

 Taiwan's central bank was also suspected of intervening in the currency market, resulting in the local dollar erasing early gains to close unchanged at 34.358 to the U.S. unit. 

 The New Taiwan dollar's initial rise was related to inflows for equity investments. 

 Trading volume amounted to US$450 million, up from US$433.50 million in the previous session. One dealer said the central bank's trades may have accounted for as much as US$150 million of total volume. 

 "It looked like the central bank was in the market a lot during the afternoon," said a foreign bank dealer in Taipei. 

 Taiwan's central bank prefers to have the local dollar move in tandem with the currencies of export competitors such as South Korea and Japan in order to preserve competitiveness. 

 Both the South Korean and Taiwanese governments don't usually comment on specific interventions. 

 The Singapore dollar rose on the back of fresh investments in the local stock market, and hopes of a brighter economic outlook, dealers said. 

 The U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7472 late in the local session, down from S$1.7480 late Friday. 

 Interbank players unwound long U.S. dollar positions amid hopes the government's plans to lower business costs through cuts in mandatory pension fund contributions would help buoy the economy. 

 Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong late Sunday outlined wage and pension reforms as two key ways of lifting the city state out of its worst ever economic slump. 

 The release of non-oil export data in the afternoon session didn't have much impact on the market, traders said. 

 Non-oil domestic exports, a key gauge of Singapore's economic health, rose 10.8% on year in July, slower than the previous month's 18.7% expansion. 

 The Thai baht moved in a similar pattern to the Singapore dollar. Late in Asia, the U.S. unit was quoted around 41.61 baht, down from THB41.66 late Friday. 

 Elsewhere, lingering security concerns and anticipation of sustained dollar demand from importers pushed the beleaguered Philippine peso to yet another new five-month closing low, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at the intraday high of 55.090 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP55.060 Friday. This was the dollar's strongest finish since its record closing high of PHP55.099 on March 12. 

 Traders said many banks didn't want to unload their dollar holdings on hopes the U.S. unit would rise to breach PHP55.160, its highest intraday level so far this year. 

 "Many are holding their dollars close to their chest," said a local bank trader. 

 Among the factors fueling bullish sentiment on the dollar are a seasonal rise in imports, and continued worries over the country's security situation after the July 27 mutiny by over 300 soldiers in Manila's financial district.
