title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pare early gains, peso struggles.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso struggled
to make a convincing move from five-month lows on Wednesday,
and other Asian currencies pared early gains after the Japanese
yen eased to the weaker side of 119 per U.S. dollar.
    The peso ended local trade with some gains, but the fear
of
 central bank intervention was a factor after it had slipped
towards Tuesday's low of 54.97 per dollar in morning trade.
    Dealers said the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to leave
key rates unchanged, as had been expected, had little impact on
regionals outside its influence on the yen .
    The South Korean won                   hit a one-month high
of 1,177.2 in early trade but then retreated to near the lows
it saw on Monday. The Taiwan dollar  touched a two-week
high of 34.357 per dollar, before also pulling back. Traders in
both currencies remain wary of intervention to cap gains.



    The Singapore dollar       , Thai baht        and the
Indonesian rupiah  were all a touch lower, but within
familiar ranges.
    "The Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged hardly made
markets excited. As such, activity on the FX front remains
dull," said Thio Chin Lo, senior currency analyst at BNP
Paribas.
    She said the summer holiday season in the United States was
keeping markets lacklustre, although key U.S. data this week --
including retail sales, business inventories and import prices
-- could inspire some action.
    The peso hit a low of 54.945 in morning trade, just shy of
Tuesday's five-month low, before wariness of intervention
prompted traders to unwind long dollar positions.
    Dealers in Manila said the seasonal rise in dollar demand
for imports in August and September, and political worries as
the trial of one of the leaders of last month's failed mutiny
began, were weighing down the peso.
    Traders suspected the central bank had sold dollars just
ahead of the local close on Tuesday, and expect that it would
continue to defend 55 per dollar.
    "There was no activity by the central bank but corporates
are still in the market for dollars, although demand seems to
taper off as we approach 54.95," said chief dealer of a local
bank.
    The Indonesian rupiah        fell from Tuesday' highs
around 8,500 per dollar, and dealers in Jakarta said security
worries ahead of the Indonesia's national day on Sunday could
pull it down further.
    Good two-way interest kept the Sing dollar in a
1.7540-1.7580 range. Dealers said some long-term players were
spotted unloading U.S. dollars, but that was easily absorbed by
the market.
    The baht sat at 41.80 per dollar, with support from

central bank dollar sales aimed at keeping exports competitive.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Bombing impact eases, risks linger.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah managed
to post some gains on Wednesday as Asian currencies trimmed the
losses they sustained after bombing of a Jakarta hotel, but
worries about regional security kept markets cautious.
    Currencies were still weaker from the start of the week as
worries over the U.S. economy and volatile asset markets, the
sustainability of foreign equity inflows into the region, and
the threat of more attacks remained.
    The rupiah        fell as far as 8,720 per dollar in
morning deals, near the three-month low of 8,725 low struck two
weeks ago, in a sell-off triggered by Tuesday's bombing of
Jakarta's JW Marriott Hotel, which claimed up to 16 lives.
    It rallied over 100 rupiah, and stayed there, after the
central bank's senior deputy governor told Reuters that the
bank would try to limit the impact of the bombing on the
rupiah, a sign it was ready to intervene to check the fall.



    Forwards on the rupiah betrayed some of the nervousness in
the market. The three-month dollar premium rose to 182 points,
last seen in late May and sharply up from 165 on Tuesday.
    Analysts said the bearishness following the bombing would
linger for some days. More importantly, the incident gave
markets an excuse to offload Asian currency holdings built up
on hopes of stronger growth and foreign investment inflows,
they said.
    "The tone is a little bit on the soft side, firstly as we
may have seen a peak in the equity capital inflows for a little
while at least," said David Simmonds, markets strategist at the
Royal Bank of Scotland.
    "If the currencies have not been allowed to go any stronger
over the last couple of weeks, on the back of the relative
growth optimism and the equity capital inflows, at some point
there will be periods of reappraisal and position-squaring."
    "The dip in the equity inflows combined with events in
southeast Asia and Jakarta may provide some impetus to the
position squaring," Simmonds said.
    The Thai baht       , perceived to be a currency backed by
strong fundamentals and rising foreign interest, was steady at
42.04/08.
    Analysts said this bout of weakness gave central banks some
respite from having to intervene to contain currency
appreciation, particularly in Korea, Taiwan and Singapore.
    "Definitely Singapore is one candidate that would not be
averse to further Sing dollar weakening, so long as it remains
within their policy band," said Claudio Piron, currency
strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
    The Singapore dollar        was sold heavily in early

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Recover a bit, wary after bombing.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah's
weakness after the bombing of a Jakarta hotel undermined Asian
currencies on Wednesday, preventing them from benefitting from
the U.S. dollar's decline.
    The currencies pared part of their falls after the bombing
at Jakarta's JW Marriott Hotel which claimed 16 lives on
Tuesday.
    But the risk of further attacks, the fear that foreign
investment into the region will ebb and the inconsistency in
economic indicators stopped markets from buying back Asian
currencies.
    "This increases the risk premium in the near term, so in
the next week or two the bias is certainly for weakening (of
Asian currencies)," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist
with Standard Chartered Bank.
 
    "In a way, they (central banks) were intervening already to
weaken the currencies and this makes it all the more potent."
    The rupiah        inched closer to a two-week low of 8,725


 in morning deals and then recovered. The central bank said it 

 would try to limit the impact of the bombing on the currency, a 

 sign it was ready to intervene to limit any sharp fall. 


 
    The Singapore dollar        was sold heavily, but stopped
short of Tuesday's three-month lows around 1.7668.
    Analysts said this bout of selling would persist for a
short while, with the uncertainty in U.S. markets about
economic recovery providing additional reason for nervousness.
    "While we continue to look for a medium term appreciation



in Asian currencies, a near term stalling of equity inflows



could see the market building small long U.S. dollar/Asia



positions as short term tactical trades," UBS said in a note to



clients.



This weakness would suit some of the Asian central banks,



such as those in Korea and Taiwan, that have been intervening


heavily to contain gains in their currencies, analysts said.



The bombing also highlighted the vulnerability of the



Philippine peso , which has been under attack after a



failed mutiny on July 27 and the subsequent risks of political



instability.



 
    The peso, which the central bank is believed to have
defended from the key 55 level, was range-bound on Wednesday.
    TOLERATING WEAKNESS
    Deutsche Bank economist Sanjeev Sanyal said in a note the
bombing had occurred at a time when Indonesia had stabilised
its economy and was planning to exit a IMF loan programme.
    The country would need to accumulate reserves aggressively
and hence would have to keep interest rates high and stop the
rupiah from appreciating, he said.
    Even elsewhere, central banks in the region would tolerate
some decline in their currencies after being glutted by foreign
investment inflows in recent months, analysts said.
    "Definitely Singapore is one candidate that would not be
averse to further Sing dollar weakening, so long as it remains
within their policy band," Piron said.
    Even Korea managed to push up the sensitive yen-won cross



rate , a measure of its competitiveness against



Japan, to 9.9 won per yen from 9.78 a week ago, he said.



Meanwhile, the risk that U.S. asset markets could price in



similar attacks to the Indonesian bombing remained, and that



could upset the U.S. dollar.



"We would have to watch whether the U.S. follows by raising



their national threat level to orange. Then that may again put



pressure on the equity market in the U.S. and the dollar,"



Piron said.



"But, the benefactors there may likely be the Swiss franc



and euro rather than Asian currencies."

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Rupiah Taking Respite
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Led by the rupiah, Asian currencies were mostly higher against the U.S. dollar late Wednesday, recovering from the previous day's jitters brought on by a bomb blast in the Indonesian capital. 

 The dollar's slide against the Japanese yen and the threat of central bank intervention also helped regional currencies, notably the Singapore dollar, move higher, observers said. 

 "The ability of Asian currencies to withstand such an event in Jakarta is a good thing," said Thio Chin Loo, a currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. 

 However, Thio was quick to warn that the steadiness in regional units Wednesday "could be a bit artificial because central banks are stepping up vigilance." 

 The blast at a leading Jakarta hotel Tuesday killed at least 10 people and renewed security concerns across Southeast Asia. The Al-Qaida-linked Islamic militant group Jemaah Islamiyah has claimed responsibility for the bombing in Jakarta and has warned of further attacks. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted at 8,608 rupiah, down from IDR8,625 Tuesday. 

 Although Bank Indonesia has vowed to defend the currency following Tuesday's plunge on the terrorist bombing attack in Jakarta, some observers expect the rupiah to resume heading south in the near future, particularly as political instability could rise ahead of Indonesia's mid-2004 presidential election. 

 "We are moving back to an environment where political risks are underpriced...and these sorts of event risks will be more of an issue in the run-up to the election," said James Malcolm, a strategist at JPMorgan Chase in Singapore. 

 Despite Bank Indonesia's efforts to limit the rupiah's downside, "people will be looking to reduce exposure to Indonesia," Malcolm added. "The trend of dollar-rupiah should be up, rather than down." 

 Malcolm said JPMorgan Chase expects the U.S. dollar to rise gradually to IDR9,500 by the end of this year. 

 The Singapore dollar also rebounded from a three-month low it hit Tuesday, taking advantage of the spillover impact of a stronger yen. The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7622 late in the session, down from S$1.7640 Tuesday. 

 The Thai baht, which tends to take its cue from its Singapore counterpart, was unchanged late in Asia, following a brief rebound earlier Wednesday. The U.S. dollar was quoted flat at THB42.07, after dipping to an intraday low of THB41.96. 

 The Philippine peso also reversed direction Tuesday, capitalizing on better corporate demand and fears of central bank intervention. 

 The dollar closed at PHP54.790 on the Philippine Dealing System, compared with PHP54.815 Tuesday. 

 In Northeast Asia, the South Korean won ended the day higher, as foreign investors sold dollars to pay for local stock purchases, but narrowed gains toward the close on suspected government intervention. 

 The dollar closed at 1,184.6 won, down from KRW1,187.9 Tuesday. 

 Foreign investors were net buyers of KRW84.3 billion worth of Korean shares Monday and Tuesday, before turning net sellers Wednesday. 

 Market participants also suspected the authorities stepped into the market right before the close to support the dollar. The Korean authorities never specifically comment on their activities in the market. 

 Traders expect the dollar to trade between KRW1,183 and KRW1,190 Thursday, with any downside limited by the government's clear aversion to a rising won as it tries to keep local exports competitive. 

 "The market's consensus is that it will be difficult for the dollar-won to fall below 1,180," said a trader at Korea Exchange Bank. 

 In China, Premier Wen Jiabao's reaffirmation that the country would maintain the basic stability of the yuan exchange rate led to a narrowing in the one-year yuan nondeliverable forward discount in the offshore market. 

 The one-year dollar NDF was quoted at a discount of 1500 to the yuan late Wednesday, compared with 1585 Tuesday. This implies that market players expect the U.S. dollar to weaken to CNY8.1273 in 12 months' time. 

 The yen's strength against the U.S. currency also lifted the New Taiwan dollar, sparking a slew of dollar selling from Taiwanese domestic banks. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.446, down from NT$34.466 Tuesday. 

 The Taiwanese currency often tracks the yen, because the island imports large amounts of goods from Japan and as the two compete in some export categories. 


The U.S. dollar is expected to remain steady Thursday between NT$34.42
and NT$34.47, said a dealer at a foreign bank in Taipei.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Ctrl Bk Presence Detected
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, with traders reporting the presence of at least two central banks in the markets during the session. 

 The Philippine peso's woes continued unabated and the currency closed at yet another four-month low, marking its fourth straight day of declines since Sunday's mutiny by junior army officers. 

 The dollar ended at 54.720 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.700 Wednesday. 

 Despite pressure on the peso, the central bank left its closely watched overnight rates unchanged at its policy-setting meeting Thursday, saying the currency's recent weakening hasn't affected the country's inflation outlook and isn't interest rate-related. 

 The Singapore dollar and the New Taiwan dollar were also weaker, while the Indonesian rupiah was flat, and the South Korean won and Thai baht were modestly stronger. 

 The currencies all kicked off the session on a weak note following the yen's overnight fall, but either narrowed or reversed losses as the yen made a mild recovery in Asia. 

 At 0945 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y120.17, down from Y120.27 overnight in New York but up from Y119.82 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 Traders detected the presence of the central banks of Taiwan and Thailand in the markets. Some also suspected intervention in the South Korean won market. 

 A Singapore trader said agents of Bank of Thailand were looking to sell dollars at the 42.05-42.10 baht level. 

 He didn't think it was because the central bank is more amenable to the idea of a stronger baht. Rather, he said it was an exercise to smoothen volatility in currency movements, noting the central bank also buys dollars when the baht firms sharply. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 41.94 baht, down from THB41.97 late Wednesday. 

 The South Korean won reversed direction, tracking the yen's mild recovery, and aided also by dollar sales from local exporters, traders said. 

 The dollar, which opened at the intraday high of KRW1,182.0, finished at KRW1,179.7, slightly down from KRW1,180.0 Wednesday. 

 "Exporter dollar sales were heavier than expected," a dealer at the Industrial Bank of Korea said. "They must have been waiting for the dollar to pick up (to sell dollars)." 

 But investors were too cautious to test further downside for fear of attracting government intervention. Some traders in Seoul suspected the government provided limited support for the dollar indirectly during the session. 

 "It seemed that the government was in smoothing operations...absorbing some of (the) dollar sales," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit ended at NT$34.417, up from Wednesday's NT$34.400. 

 Taipei dealers said the central bank intervened to keep the currency low in line with the yen to maintain the local dollar's competitiveness. 

 The New Taiwan dollar generally follows the yen as Taiwan and Japan compete in several export categories. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7593 late in Asia, up from S$1.7558 late Wednesday. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said there was a lot of activity in cross trades on the local dollar, notably against the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah. 

 Investors were selling the U.S. dollar/baht pair to buy the U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar pair because they see limited upside in the former, he said. 

 "This (cross trades) is probably the trades to put on in the next few sessions," he said. 

 The release of preliminary unemployment numbers for the second quarter didn't create any major market reaction, though some dealers said the data generally reflected the still-uncertain outlook for the local economy. 

 Singapore's unemployment rate was surprisingly steady in the second quarter, but a closer look at the data revealed a continued worsening of the job market, economists said. 

 The seasonally adjusted jobless rate stayed at 4.5% as of end-June, unchanged from the end of the first quarter, although more people lost their jobs as the economy shrank 4.3% because of SARS and weak global conditions. The jobless rate held steady only because of people exiting the work force and various seasonal factors. 

 The rupiah finished steady in a choppy session as dollar selling by foreign investors offset month-end dollar demand from local companies, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed unchanged at IDR8,510. 

 Earlier, dollar sales by foreign investors who had to settle their purchases of Bank Danamon shares Monday drove the U.S. unit to an intraday low of IDR8,475, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency sold a 20% stake in Bank Danamon to raise cash for the state budget. Almost half shares - worth around IDR1.3 trillion - were sold to foreign investors. 

 Dealers said most speculators chose to stay on the sidelines ahead of the 10-day annual convention of the nation's highest legislature, which begins Friday. 

 Some market players expect the session to be dominated by rising political tensions, although these aren't likely to threaten Megawati Sukarnoputri's presidency. 

 The market is also concerned the session could be tarnished by terrorism, recalling the bomb blast at the parliament building earlier this month.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late, Peso Trims Early Losses
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine peso clawed out of intraday troughs Monday but remained at a four-month low following a failed mutiny over the weekend. But regional counterparts barely reacted to the incident. 

 Analysts and traders viewed the mutiny by junior soldiers in the Philippines Sunday as an event that was specific to that country, with little danger of contagion. 

 "The coup in the Philippine is very much a domestic issue, opposed to, say, a terrorist act, which has wider implications for the region. Hence, we expect any spillover impact to be limited," BNP Paribas wrote in a late note Monday. 

 The dollar ended at 54.380 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.010 Friday. 

 The dollar kicked off the session at PHP54.500 and rose as high as PHP54.600 before retreating. It failed to hit the PHP55 level some had predicted earlier. 

 Traders and analysts said the peso wasn't badly mauled because the mutiny was resolved quickly and peacefully. 

 The currency was also saved from a free-fall by the fact that foreign investment in the Philippines has already been limited by economic and security concerns. As a result, there was no rush by foreign investors to sell their peso holdings. 

 "That's why the peso didn't weaken big time," said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist at UBS AG in Singapore. 

 The Philippine central bank said it didn't intervene to prop up the peso during the session. 

 Generally, analysts expect Asian currencies to keep to a strengthening bias against the U.S. dollar over the course of the year as they remain bearish on the U.S. unit. But the peso's gains will likely be more modest as topside is capped by economic and security issues, they said. 

 The PHP (peso) will remain on the defensive in the near-term, but a dramatic collapse is unlikely," BNP Paribas said. The central bank will likely defend the PHP55.00 level vigorously, the French investment bank added. 

 This week, investors will be closely watching a slew of U.S. data for confirmation of whether the economy has indeed begun to improve. 

 It will also be an important week for data in Asia. Exports data from South Korea due Friday, for instance, "will provide the first hints of how the region's exports are holding up after the impressive performance in June," Bank of America said in a note. 

 Against the South Korean won, the dollar closed at 1,178.8, a tad below Friday's KRW1,180.1, due to selling by local exporters and foreign investors in local shares, traders said. 

 The selling wasn't aggressive and overall trading was slow. 

 "The market was in for another quiet session. The global currency market as a whole remains slow," said Koo Sang-Jun, a dealer at KorAm Bank. 

 Meantime, weaker-than-expected manufacturing output data for June pulled the Singapore dollar off earlier highs, dealers said. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7480, down from S$1.7488 late Friday. 

 The Economic Development Board Monday said industrial production fell 7.3% on year in June, marking a third straight month of contraction. The drop was worse than the average 4.3% decline forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires poll. 

 Higher share prices and U.S. dollar selling by exporters helped lift the New Taiwan dollar, but gains were partly offset by suspected central bank intervention, dealers said. 

 The U.S. unit closed at NT$34.388, down from NT$34.405 Friday. 

 Trading was relatively quiet and the currency pair was confined to a narrow range during the session after the central bank called some bank traders last week to express concern over their short U.S. dollar positions, said a Taipei-based dealer. 

 Trading volume totaled US$236 million, down from US$260 million in the previous session. 

 The rupiah gave up early gains to close slightly lower on month-end dollar demand from importers, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,530 rupiah, edging up from IDR8,520 Friday. 

 The dollar earlier slid to a low of IDR8,480 as investors sold back the currency after its recent rise to three-month highs. 

 But local importers, led by state-owned oil and gas company Pertamina, snapped up the dollar to finance their imports, dealers said. 

 Profit-taking on rupiah-denominated assets, which was responsible for the dollar's recent rally, appeared to have died out. 

 "It seemed to be only temporary and most foreign investors are still comfortable in parking their funds in Indonesia," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "There is no negative news on Indonesia as macroeconomic pictures continue improving although slowly." 

 The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency said Monday it has sold another 20% stake in Bank Danamon since Friday, raising IDR1.3 trillion. Although most of the shares were sold to local investors, the offer drew strong interest from foreign investors. 

 The Thai baht also gave up early gains and moved to a slightly softer footing. Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted around THB41.98, slightly up from THB41.95 Friday.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 24 (Reuters) - The nose-diving Indonesian
rupiah overwhelmed Asian trading once again on Thursday morning
as traders said the central bank persisted with U.S. dollar
sales to try to stem its losses as it slumped to three-month

    The rupiah        hit 8,725 per dollar, taking its losses

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Foreign Banks Unwind Long USDs
text:

 The U.S. dollar opened lower around S$1.7550 following its retreat against the euro and yen overnight. It initially held steady during a lackluster morning session, but gradually drifted lower as foreign banks unwound their long positions as other Asian currencies extended their early gains. 

 "It was persistent but gradual (selling). Some offshore names sold from around S$1.7520 and pushed it (the U.S. dollar) further down," said an Asian bank dealer. 

 Around midafternoon, the U.S. dollar's retreat was partly accelerated by its slide against the baht after the Thai central bank said a recent easing of restrictions on foreign investment by some local institutions wasn't aimed at weakening the Thai currency. 

 The changes, which included allowing exporters to hold onto their foreign exchange earnings for longer periods, were to allow capital flows and to let foreign exchange rate stabilize, Bank of Thailand said. 

 "The dollar-baht fall seems to have prompted more dollar-Sing selling," a dealer said. 

 But the U.S. dollar's fall was stemmed just before the Asian session ended as selling momentum eased. 

 Overnight, dealers expect the U.S. dollar to stay between S$1.7480 and S$1.7530. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended lower Thursday, reversing early gains that followed an overnight rise in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah falls sharply to 11-week low.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah lost
almost two percent on Wednesday as it fell to 11-week lows,
with suspected central bank intervention unable to counter the
pressure from foreign investors withdrawing their funds.
    The mood was apprehensive even in the rest of Asia as
traders watched funds move out of high-yielding currencies into
growth plays, as a result of which the currencies of leveraged
economies such as Singapore and Taiwan found support.
    Additionally, local factors held sway after authorities in
Singapore intervened to calm a runaway rise in bond yields and
Korean policymakers tried to talk down the won.
    "Confidence in global reflation is beginning to jeopardise
capital flows into the high-yielding markets, as previously
popular global carry trades are coming unstuck," said James
Malcolm of JP Morgan in a note to clients.



    The rupiah        fell to 8,640 in morning deals, its
lowest low since May 5, on Wednesday -- the second anniversary
of Megawati Sukarnoputri's taking over as Indonesia's
President.
    The rupiah's slide had probably been triggered by the news
that BP Plc (BP.L) and global mining giant Rio Tinto
 (RIO.L) (RIO.AX) were selling their stake in Indonesia's PT
Kaltim Prima Coal to a local firm, traders said
 
    "Some of the hot money that entered Indonesia is getting
out," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS.
    "And the BP deal highlights the problems in Aceh, and the
difficulty Indonesia is likely to have in attracting foreign
investment," he said.
    With interest rates falling rapidly and investors flocking
to the more technology-dominated stock markets in the region,
foreign investment was bound to leave Indonesia, he said.
    JP Morgan's Malcolm said Jakarta's markets had been
complacent about the local risks of political stability and
success in sales of bad loans during the past 18 months.
    Slowing growth, the possibility reforms will be put on the



backburner heading into parliamentary elections in 2004, and



the uncertainty over financing as the country opts out of a IMF



loan programme could all weigh on the rupiah, he said.



Meanwhile, a Indonesian central bank official said the



market could determine the rupiah's level and there was no need



to intervene continuously - although traders said they thought



Bank Indonesia had been active on both Tuesday and Wednesday.



PESO WEAKENS



Elsewhere, a top finance ministry official in Korea said



the won's             strength was not justified, given



the weak economy.



 
    The Philippine peso        was initially steady, but
slipped in later trades to 53.95, a four-month low.
    The rest of the regionals were stuck in ranges, like the



Japanese yen which barely reacted to reports of the deaths of



former Iraqi leader Sadddam Hussein's sons and the resultant



bullishness on the U.S. dollar.



The Sing dollar  moved in a 1.7560-1.7590 band, and



some traders said market nerves had calmed after suspected bond



purchases by the Monetary Authority of Singapore on Tuesday, to



contain the volatility that pushed 10-year yields to a



nine-month high of 3.45 percent.



The Taiwan dollar  was steady, but poised to rally



when the central bank was prepared to let it appreciate,



Malcolm said.



"The US dollar/Taiwan dollar has one of the highest



correlations to global growth of all the U.S. dollar crosses we



track globally, so we expect the Taiwan dollar to benefit



disproportionately in a recovery scenario," Malcolm said in a



note.

title: REPEAT: Asian  Currencies  Mixed; Rupiah Looking Vulnerable
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian central bank intervened in the currency market Wednesday to halt the slide in the rupiah, which is showing signs of fatigue after a 20-month bull run. 

 Elsewhere in the region, the Philippine peso and Thai baht weakened, while the Singapore dollar, New Taiwan dollar and South Korea won ended stronger. 

 In Jakarta, Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said the central bank stepped in to support the local currency, which has fallen nearly 4% from levels just two days ago. 

 The dollar hit a three-month high of IDR8,650 in morning trading before the intervention helped the local unit recover slightly. Late in Asian trading the dollar was quoted at IDR8,610, up from IDR8,425 late Tuesday in Asia and IDR8,320 Monday. 

 At its peak in May, the rupiah had rallied more than 35% from a low of 11,000 to the dollar in November 2001. 

 Analysts have attributed the rupiah's recent decline to a number of factors, including Indonesia's plan to exit the International Monetary Fund program at the end of the year, the potential for increased political risk linked to next year's presidential elections, and the narrowing in Indonesia's interest-rate differential. 

 "While we once had the rupiah overshooting to 7,500 (per dollar) in the third quarter, we will be changing the numbers this week to around 9,000 by end-September," JP Morgan strategist James Malcolm said in a research report. 

 Over the past five years, IMF funding has widely been seen as a disciplinary mechanism for the Indonesian government to push through much-needed economic reforms, said Fauzi Ichsan, an economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Last year, however, the parliament issued a decree requesting the government not to extend the program into 2004. 

 In Manila, the peso hit a four-month low against the dollar as businesses continued to accumulate dollars to be used for imports of goods for the Christmas shopping season. 

 The dollar ended at PHP54.025 on the Philippine dealing system, up from PHP53.850 late Tuesday. That was the dollar's strongest close against the peso since March 25, when it ended at PHP54.300. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar gained ground after the central bank announced it would ease restrictions on investment in foreign-currency debt, and raise the time limit on exporter dollar holdings to six months from three months. 

 The dollar climbed as high as THB42.080 after the announcement, but relinquished some of those gains to trade around THB41.980 late in the session versus THB41.810 late Tuesday. 

 The new rules should increase institutional demand for dollars and could decrease supply from exporters. The dollar demand will also help to prevent any excessive appreciation in the baht. 

 The New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and won benefited from spillover strength in the yen. Against the Japanese currency, the dollar was quoted at Y118.72 in late Asian trading, compared with Y119.04 late Tuesday in New York. 

 The New Taiwan dollar got an additional boost from continued foreign inflows to the local stock market. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.417, down from  NT$34.441 late Tuesday. 

 Foreign investors bought a net NT$1.23 billion in Taiwan shares Wednesday, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange. 

 In Seoul, dollar sales by local corporations added to the pressure on the U.S. currency. 

 The dollar's fall was firmly supported around KRW1,180, however, as importers continued to buy dollars, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,180.9, down from KRW1,182.8 late Tuesday, after trading within a narrow range of KRW1,179.9-KRW1,182.8. 

 Improving prospects for Singapore's economic recovery helped fuel the local currency's gains. 

 Near the end of Asian trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7562, down from S$1.7581 late Tuesday. 

 Although the Singapore economy contracted by an estimated 4.3% in the second quarter from a year ago due largely to the SARS outbreak, economists widely expect a sharp rebound in the second half of the year. 

 United Overseas Bank said the improved outlook should keep the trade-weighted Singapore dollar trading in the stronger half of the policy band in which the central bank guides the local dollar. 

 -By Alan Yonan Jr., Dow Jones Newswires; 65 9862-0905; alan.yonan@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Asia Bonds-Sing yields soar in growth-inspired rout.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Singapore bond yields lurched to nine-month highs on Tuesday as government bond prices across Asia fell in a sell-off driven by tumbling U.S. Treasuries as investors embrace signs of improving U.S. growth. 

 Yields could rise further if economic numbers continue to improve, raising hopes of a global turnaround and fuelling expectations of higher inflation, but fixed income analysts said it was premature to call an end to the Asian bond rally. 

 Treasuries have fallen markedly since late June, after a smaller than expected rate cut from U.S. Federal Reserve, and the losses gathered pace last week after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan spoke of improving growth in Asia's biggest export market. 

 "The notion of a U.S. and global economic recovery has spooked bond markets in the trade-oriented Asian economies," said Vasan Shridharan, regional economist with HSBC. 

 The carnage in Singapore led 10-year yields to nine-month highs of 3.45 percent on Tuesday, in a steep ascent from historic lows of 1.78 in mid-May, before easing slightly. 

 In Taiwan, ten-year yields have risen 70 basis points to 2.1 percent this week. 

 "Singapore is highly geared to the external world, hence its bonds are underperforming. Leverage tends to cut you both ways," Shridharan said. 

 Tuesday's volatility raised speculation that Singapore's central bank had intervened to limit the fall in bond prices. 

 "They appear to have bought a small amount of long term bonds with the aim of promoting liquidity in a fairly illiquid market. They did that two years ago when there was a similar sell-off," said Bert Gochet, interest rates strategist with UBS. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore did not comment on the intervention rumours. In an e-mailed response to Reuters, it said it would use various instruments as part of its daily operations, including the outright purchase and sale of government bonds, to ensure there was sufficient liquidity in the banking system. 

 Analysts said Singapore's sell-off had been more severe than in the United States, where 10-year yields have leapt 110 basis points since mid-June. 

 Shridharan said the return on 10-year U.S. bonds had been a negative eight percent since mid-June. 

 But Asian central banks, sitting on a pile of investments in U.S. Treasuries whose value is being eroded, would not be griping too much, analysts said. 

 Some of the Treasury holdings have been built up as central banks around the region try to limit their currencies' gains against the U.S. dollar to protect export competitiveness. 

 "They would be happy to withstand the losses if they have a global upturn and weaker currencies," said Simon Klassen, fixed income strategist with JP Morgan. 

 SUSPICIONS ABOUT GROWTH 

 Implicit in the steepening of most of bond curves, including the United States where the spread between 10 and two-year bonds is at decade highs, was a tenuous view that long term rates will rise as stronger growth brought inflation, analysts said. But that may be overly upbeat on Asia. Singapore has just posted its biggest ever contraction in quarterly growth, Korea's economy is in recession - and data is expected to show Hong Kong is also. Much of the region is also struggling against deflation. 

 Barclays Capital said in a note to clients the fall in bond prices provided a buying opportunity and the high correlation between Asian bonds and U.S. Treasuries would soon snap. 

 Asia's tight fiscal policies, still rampant disinflation, abundant liquidity and the possibility of further rate cuts in places such as Thailand, Korea and Indonesia, would mean an interest rates rally in the region still has legs, it said. 

 Meanwhile, analysts said investors were selling bonds and holding cash but not quite ready to invest in risky equities. 

 And they advised those still holding their bond investments to switch to the short end, which would limit damages from a sell-off and guarantee some benefit if official rates were cut to try to spur economic activity.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Greenspan Remarks Lift Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies weakened along with the yen Wednesday after the U.S. dollar received a leg-up from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy. 

 "Basically, what happened overnight after Greenspan (addressed the House Financial Services Committee) gave the dollar a bit of a boost. All the dollar/Asians reacted the same," said a trader at a European bank in Singapore. He was referring to the U.S. dollar's rally against major rivals. 

 "Everything (the dollar versus Asian units) just gapped up," the trader said. 

 Traders suspected Japan's Ministry of Finance followed through on overnight yen-selling activities in Asia, which helped pushed the dollar above the Y118 mark. 

 At 1001 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y118.30, up from Y117.79 overnight in New York and Y117.69 in Tokyo late Tuesday. 

 There was no sign of intervention by central banks in the region, traders in Singapore said. 

 The European bank trader said, however, that some market players began to sell the dollar at its peak against Asian currencies. 

 "There is some topside selling coming in. People are looking to sell," he said, noting that investors were becoming cautions over how the dollar will move later in the global session. 

 Given the U.S. Treasury sell-off overnight, "It will be interesting to see if Greenspan changes his tone or language in the session (later Wednesday) to the Senate banking committee in an attempt to dampen the rise in yields," Goldman Sachs said in a research note. 

 The South Korean won snapped a six-session winning streak and fell in tandem with the yen, though it pared most of the initial losses due to heavy dollar sales by foreign stock investors and exporters, dealers said. 

 The dollar rose as high as 1,183.0 won but closed at the intraday low of KRW1,176.7 won, only slightly up from KRW1,176.0 Tuesday. 

 Local markets will be closed for a holiday Thursday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended the session at its weakest in almost two weeks as interbank players covered short positions on the U.S. unit following Greenspan's remarks. 

 Importers were also buyers of the U.S. dollar, which ended at NT$34.410, up from NT$34.364 Tuesday, marking its highest close since July 3. 

 However, dealers said demand for the local dollar remained solid as the key stock index rose 1.5% to a one-year high Wednesday. Foreign investors were net buyers of NT$4.6 billion worth of local shares during the session. 

 Some dealers said anticipation of continued foreign inflows into the stock market gives an upward bias to the local dollar. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7612 late in Asia, up from S$1.7554 Tuesday. 

 Most market participants said they viewed the current U.S. dollar level against the local unit to be near the midpoint of the monetary authorities policy band for the local currency. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore guides the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 The U.S. unit's overnight gains against major rivals sparked off dollar buying in the Jakarta interbank foreign exchange market, dealers said. 

 The dollar rose to an intraday high of IDR8,250 before ending the local session at IDR8,235, up from IDR8,225 Tuesday. 

 But dealers said the underlying bullish sentiment for the rupiah remains intact due to Indonesia's improving macroeconomic outlook. 

 Also, the interest-rate differential between the rupiah and dollar remains high despite Bank Indonesia cutting its benchmark rate Wednesday. 

 The central bank cut the benchmark weighted average rate on the one-month Sertifikat bank Indonesia notes to 9.21% at its weekly auction, from 9.23% last week. 

 The one-month rupiah interest rate at banks in Jakarta is now around 9.2%, while the dollar interest rate for the same maturity is 0.95%, which makes it attractive for traders to hold rupiah. 

 The weaker yen and rising demand for dollars from importers pulled the Philippine peso down, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;Some Central Banks  Intervene
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Tuesday at the tail end of a generally lackluster session in which some central banks intervened to cap strength in their units, traders said. 

 The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso were weaker, the Indonesian rupiah and South Korean won were little changed and the New Taiwan dollar was stronger. 

 The Thai baht was firmer compared with pre-weekend levels but was lower from offshore levels Monday, when local markets were shut for a holiday. 

 Monetary authorities in Thailand, Taiwan and South Korea were those suspected of buying dollars in Tuesday's session. 

 Traders said these central banks were in the market to smooth the movements of their currencies rather than attempt to reverse the strengthening trend. 

 Strong portfolio inflows into regional stock markets are a key factor supporting Asian currencies. 

 But policy-makers in Asia are reluctant to allow their currencies to strengthen too much for fear of losing export competitiveness amid a still uncertain outlook for the global economy, especially the U.S. 

 They are also unlikely to allow their currencies to rise significantly as long as China resists pressure to revalue the yuan, analysts said. 

 Overall, Tuesday's session mirrored that of the previous day as many investors kept to the sidelines to hear what Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has to say about the U.S. economy later in the global session. 

 Greenspan will address the House Financial Services Committee Tuesday and the Senate Banking Committee Wednesday. 

 The yen didn't provide much of a lead for its counterparts in the region as market players shrugged off early sharp gains in Tokyo share prices and the Bank of Japan's decision to keep monetary policy unchanged. 

 "There's nothing happening on the forex front," in the run-up to Greenspan's address, a European bank trader in Singapore said. 

 "There's some portfolio inflows" into regional stock markets, which are weighing on the dollar, and "the central banks are buying it (the dollar) up," he said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,176.0 against the South Korean won, a touch below Monday's KRW1,176.3, but off the intraday trough of KRW1,174.6. This was the won's sixth straight session of gains. 

 There was suspicion the government intervened to prop up the dollar when it fell to the intraday low on continued foreign buying of local shares, but traders had mixed views about this. 

 "Suspicious - but I don't think so. It was not that aggressive," a Seoul-based trader said, although a Singapore-based trader was sure the Bank of Korea was in the market. 

 Another Seoul-based trader said the dollar was also supported by news that a National Assembly committee approved a KRW4-trillion-won increase in this year's foreign exchange stabilization bond issue limit. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit ended at NT$34.364, slightly down from NT$34.376 Monday. 

 Dealers said demand from exporters and inflows of funds from foreign investors buying local stocks buoyed the local dollar. 

 But dollar purchases by the central bank and demand for the U.S. currency from importers tempered the local unit's rise, they said. 

 Falling volumes suggested the central bank wasn't very aggressive, a Taipei-based dealer said. Trading volume dropped for the third straight session Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened after a listless session as investors were reluctant to take strong positions ahead of Greenspan's address. 

 The U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7553 late in the local session, up from S$1.7540 late Monday. 

 Earlier Tuesday, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said its current neutral monetary policy stance will be appropriate to keep inflation in check and support the economy for the rest of the year. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was steady as dollar demand from local importers offset selling by foreign investors buying into local stocks and bonds, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 8,223 rupiah, virtually unchanged from IDR8,225 Tuesday. 

 Continued capital inflows showed that foreign investors are undeterred by a small bomb blast at the Indonesian Parliament building Monday. There were no casualties in the incident. 

 "The market seemed to have fully forgotten Monday's blast," a Jakarta-based dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The Philippine peso was weighed down by seasonal demand for the dollar from importers, and also security concerns following the escape Monday of three suspected terrorists from a Manila prison, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.585 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.545 Monday, but off the intraday high of PHP53.635. 

 The peso trimmed some losses on news of the Supreme Court ruling in favor of the government on the disputed Swiss deposits of late president Ferdinand Marcos, traders said. 

 The Supreme Court Tuesday forfeited in favor of the government the frozen Swiss deposits, which had increased to $658.2 million early last year. 

Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the court's ruling "would be good not only for the peso, but for the government budget as well." 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around THB41.54 late in Asia, up from THB41.50 in offshore trading Monday, but down from THB41.64 at Friday's local close. 

 Traders in Singapore said Bank of Thailand intervened during the session to cap the baht's strength, which came amid a rise in Thai share prices. 

 "Bank of Thailand (was) squeezing some shorts (on the dollar), but essentially, the range and volume was small and thin," a European bank trader said. 

 A trader at another bank said the monetary authority bought dollars at the THB41.52 to THB41.53 levels.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Talk of  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly lower Friday in a typically subdued pre-weekend session. 

 The Singapore dollar experienced the greatest swing as it lost more ground after a choppy ride in the previous session following the de facto loosening of monetary policy. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7568, up from S$1.7510 previously. 

 The New Taiwan dollar and the Philippine peso were clustered on the weak side of late Thursday's levels. The South Korean won, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah were little changed. 

 Concerns about intervention continued to support the dollar as central banks in the region stand ready to act against any sharp appreciation of their currencies for fear of losing export competitiveness. 

 Left to themselves, economic fundamentals would justify broadly stronger Asian currencies, analysts say. 

 Indeed, such intervention may even prompt protectionist measures from the U.S. and Europe, warned Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 "That's the real risk," he said. 

 However, "I do think that combined with a little bit of political pressure and also better equity environment, they will dilute the impact of intervention," he added. 

 Meantime, interbank players were forced to cover short U.S. dollar positions as Taiwan's central bank continued to aggressively buy the currency, traders said. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.400, up from Thursday's NT$34.341. Volume shrank to US$552.5 million from US$1.051 billion previously. 

 A local bank trader in Taipei estimated that the central bank bought about US$200 million during the session, mostly during morning trade. 

 An outflow of funds to cover oil purchases by local oil importers also added to the U.S. dollar's strength, traders said. 

 In South Korea, the dollar ended at 1,178.2 won, just a tad below Thursday's KRW1,178.4. 

 "There is a great deal of dollars in the market on foreign stock purchases and exporters' dollar sales," said a Seoul-based trader. 

 The government didn't actively step into the market to defend the U.S. dollar, according to traders. 

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso ended slightly lower as banks bought dollars ahead of an expected rise in demand next week, though trading was largely range-bound amid a lack of fresh news, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.44 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.41 Thursday. 

 Volume thinned to $90 million from $161 million previously as banks chose to hold on to their dollars on expectation of better rates next week when importers buy the U.S. currency to service their requirements. 

 As against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar closed at 8,218, barely moved from Thursday's IDR8,220. 

 Dealers said most market players stayed on the sidelines ahead of the weekend, amid a lack of fresh leads. 

 "I didn't get any calls at all today (Friday)," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The dollar was also little changed against the Thai baht and was quoted at 41.64 late in Asia, compared with THB41.645 Thursday.

title: WRAP: Singapore Eases Policy, Weakening SGD As GDP Sinks
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Singapore effectively eased monetary policy Thursday as it acknowledged SARS and the Iraq war had hammered the city-state's economy more severely than expected in the second quarter. 

 The government said gross domestic product shrank 4.3% in the three months through June from a year earlier, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore slightly altered policy to allow a one-time weakening of the Singapore dollar. 

 The MAS "took the opportunity to be a bit accommodating," said economist David Cohen at MMS International. The policy tweak is a "recognition of the fact" that the economy took "quite a blow" in the second quarter. 

 The GDP fall, the first in five quarters, was worse than the 2.3% contraction forecast by 11 economists in a Dow Jones Newswires survey, showing the harsh impact on tourism and trade of the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome and the war. The island nation's economy grew 1.6% on year in the first quarter. 

 Singapore's advance GDP data mark Asia's first official report on economic performance covering the quarter that SARS ravaged what had been the world's liveliest economic region. 

 Taiwan and Hong Kong, two trade- and services-driven economies also severely affected by the deadly virus, will report second-quarter data in August. 

 But on the policy front, Singapore is clearly playing catch-up. Central banks in Taiwan, Thailand and Indonesia have all recently cut interest rates, as did the Bank of Korea on Thursday. In Hong Kong, the local dollar's peg to the falling U.S. currency has eased monetary conditions in the city and made its companies more price-competitive abroad. 

 The Singapore central bank, in a semiannual policy review lowered its target for the local currency by "re-centering" its trading band for the unit around the current exchange rate - which it is acknowledged was near the bottom of its unpublished trading band. 

 "By re-centering the band and keeping the same width of the band, they are lowering the potential low point for the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis, and that is easier policy," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS Warburg. 


                Cheaper SGD OK



In a country where the economic impact of trade flows dwarfs the
amount of activity in the tiny domestic economy, the MAS regulates
policy via the exchange rate, rather than interest rates.



It targets the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed range -
generally thought to be plus or minus 1% to 2% - of an undisclosed,
trade-weighted basket of currencies. The central bank intervenes to push
up the Singapore dollar when it wants to control inflation or an
overheating economy and sells the local unit when the economy needs a
boost.



The MAS said the Singapore dollar's "nominal effective exchange rate,"
after starting 2003 nearer the top of its trading range, had slipped in
the past two months or so to the "the lower half of the policy band."
This weaker exchange rate "is conducive to supporting the incipient
recovery in the Singapore economy and to maintaining domestic price
stability in a low-inflation environment," the MAS said



The Singapore dollar tumbled on the news that the central bank will
tolerate a weaker currency, but later crawled back from its lows.



The U.S. dollar spiked 0.7% to S$1.7608 from around S$1.7480 before
the GDP and MAS announcements. Around 0740 GMT, the U.S. unit was at
S$1.7505, down from S$1.7552 late in Asia Wednesday, amid speculation
the MAS intervened to curb market volatility.



Indicating its policy is now back on hold till at least October, the
MAS said it will continue its "neutral" policy stance and keep the width
of the re-centered trading band the same.



But data released Thursday called into question the government's
0.5%-2.5% full-year growth forecast. And the MAS gave itself more
flexibility on policy by announcing its next review will be in three
months, rather than six.



"I assume, though they have not said it yet, the government will have
to lower the full-year forecast," said MMS International's Cohen.



With inflation in the first five months of the year at a
lower-than-expected 0.6% on year, the central bank also cut its
full-year consumer price index forecast to 0.5%-1% from 0.5%-1.5%
previously.



                Lingering SARS Pain



On an annualized basis, Singapore's GDP shrank 11.8% in the second
quarter from the January-March period, when it expanded at a 1.2% annual
rate on a quarter-to-quarter basis.



Suan Teck Kin, an economist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp., said
that while the second-quarter contraction "is probably the worst we'll
see," a sharp rebound this quarter isn't in the cards. Suan plans to cut
his full-year growth forecast by about half a percentage point to "1% or
less."



Suan expects the services sector, especially hard-hit by SARS, to
recover only gradually in the third quarter, probably by about 1% on
year, as sentiment remains weak and the job market soft.



The Ministry of Trade and Industry acknowledged that SARS, which
killed 32 people here, also took an unexpectedly heavy economic toll,
although the ministry expects the economy to improve in the current six
months.



Indeed, the Purchasing Managers' Index, considered a key leading
indicator of Singapore's manufacturing trends, put in a
better-than-expected showing in June by marking its first expansion
after three months of contraction. The PMI is the first set of June
manufacturing data to be published.



The key manufacturing industry contracted by 7.5% on year in the
second quarter, while the services industry shrank by 3%, the ministry
said. The construction sector continued to contract, shrinking by 10.9%.



The flash estimates are intended as an early indicator of GDP
performance in the quarter, and are based largely on data in April and
May. A more detailed report will be issued in August.



Singapore's weak data cast doubt over Taiwan's official 1.2% on-year
GDP growth forecast. "I suspect that for Hong Kong and Taiwan, the
numbers will be worse off," said Joseph Tan, an economist at Standard
Chartered Bank in Singapore.



For one thing, SARS was more widespread in those places than Singapore
and lasted longer. Singapore was taken off the World Health
Organization's list of SARS-affected regions May 30. Hong Kong, which
suffered 298 deaths from the illness, got the WHO green light June 23;
Taiwan, with 84 deaths, was cleared only last week.



   -By Shen Hong and Izham Ahmad, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4150;
hong.shen@dowjones.com; izham.ahmad@dowjones.com



-Edited by Billy Mallard

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, July 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar fell
sharply on Thursday when the island's central bank unexpectedly
eased monetary policy and data showed a large contraction in
the economy, but pared its losses in afternoon trade.
    Equity-related inflows boosted the South Korean won
  to a five-month closing high even after the central

recovered towards 1.7500 as foreign funds that had held long
U.S. dollars positions booked some profits.

 It seems

    The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which targets the
trade-weighted exchange rate rather than interest rates, said
it would re-centre its policy band around the current level of
the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate.
    Analysts said as the Singapore dollar was about 1.4 to 2.0
percent on the weaker side of the previous mid-point, the
adjustment meant MAS would target a weaker currency.
    "The MAS is conducting a policy of gradual devaluation of
the trade-weighted Sing dollar," said Adam Le Mesurier, an
analyst at Goldman Sachs in Singapore. He said the MAS has now
weakened its NEER target by five percent in the last 18 months.
    Separate data showed the economy shrank an annualised 11.8

markets had forecast. The government has said it expects an

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late; FX  Reserves Rise Sparks Easing Talk
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was weaker late Tuesday, after a reported surge in foreign exchange reserves fueled speculation of a possible central bank easing this week, dealers said. 

 At 0810 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7555, up from S$1.7498 late in Asia Monday. It traded between S$1.7540 and S$1.7570 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7570, keeping pace with its advances against counterparts such as the yen and the euro in overnight trade. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency held on to its gains on speculation the central bank might have bought U.S. dollars ahead of a monetary policy easing this week, after data issued late Monday showed a sharp rise in foreign exchange reserves for the second straight month. 

 In Singapore, where the impact of trade swamps a small domestic economy, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy via the exchange rate, rather than interest rates. It intervenes to sell the Singapore dollar when the economy needs a boost or push up the local unit when it wants to control inflation or an economic overheating. 

 Singapore's foreign exchange reserves rose 1% on month to US$86.62 billion in June, according to MAS data. 

 "That this comes two days before the widely-watched MAS policy statement has only led to further speculation of possible change by the central bank," United Overseas Bank said in a research report. 

 The MAS will issue its semiannual monetary policy review Thursday, but most market participants expect the central bank to maintain its currently neutral policy stance. 

 The Singapore government will also issue key second-quarter economic data on Thursday, which are widely expected to show a contraction in gross domestic product. Most analysts, however, expect growth to resume in subsequent quarters. 

 The U.S. currency is expected to stay between S$1.7500 and S$1.7580 in overnight trading. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended lower Tuesday as they tracked continued weakness in Japanese government bonds, and following the overnight fall in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. 

 Local bonds have also been under pressure after recent signs emerged that the trade-reliant Singapore economy, although expected to contract in the second quarter, could rebound in subsequent quarters. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was up 5 basis points at 0.86%, while the yield on five-year bonds was up 7 basis points at 1.61%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was 6 basis points higher at 2.07%, while the yield on 10-year bonds rose 10 basis points to 2.51%.

text:

    SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly

  and Thai baht        saw their strongest in over a week.
The Philippine peso  ended local trade slightly higher.



    "Today's moves in Asia regionals and even dollar/yen
suggest that the comments at Bali were not totally ignored,"
said David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland.
    In closed-door meetings, European ministers pressured Asian
governments to let their currencies rise against the dollar,
and stop Europe from bearing the economic brunt of a weaker
dollar.
    The International Monetary Fund also urged China adopt
greater foreign exchange flexibility. While China manages the
yuan in a 8.2760/8.2800 per dollar band, many Asian countries,
including Japan, intervene to keep their currencies weak.
    The discount on one-year yuan non-deliverable forwards to
buy U.S. dollars  rose to 1,525 points on Monday, from
Friday's 1,350 pips. It later pulled back to around 1,450 pips.
    Last month it hit a record of 1,900 points.
    Analysts said while traders would want to keep the
revaluation trade alive, authorities in Beijing are more likely
to live up to their repeated denial of any imminent move.
    "We have to keep expectations at a realistic level,"
Simmonds said, adding neither Japan not China, countries that
make up the largest chunk of Asia's trade surplus, were likely
to make any dramatic changes to their currency policy stance
soon.
    Late on Monday, Bank of Japan Governor Toshihiko Fukui said
foreign authorities would likely tolerate "smoothing"
operations in the yen by Japan, and added he did not expect
China to change its yuan policy soon as it would lead to
unsteady growth.
    POLICY REVIEW
    Trade in the Singapore dollar was the most volatile of the
regionals as the market speculated over the contents of
Thursday's semi-annual monetary policy review.
    A poll by Reuters last week had most analysts looking for
no change in the neutral policy stance of the Monetary
Authority of Singapore, which uses the exchange rate as its
main policy tool.
    The Singapore dollar touched 1.7476 per U.S. dollar, its
strongest since June 26, before falling back to the 1.7500
level.
    In Taiwan, a government decision to abolish a ceiling on
foreign investment in the the local stock market added to the
regional momentum and pushed the TAIEX index  to a near
one-year high, supporting the local currency.

    SINGAPORE, July 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed

    The won                   hit 1,180.0, its strongest level
since February 7, aided by foreign portifolio investments that
have crossed a two year record.
    However, a dealer in Singapore said fears of central bankintervention, with some local banks spotted buying U.S.
dollars, had limited the won's gains.
 
    The Taiwan dollar          touched a 10-month high of

    Elsewhere, dealers said a weaker bias in the Japanese yen
  and position squaring ahead of the weekend pressured
regionals downward.
    But a general lack of trading interest in currency markets
due to a holiday in the United States made players reluctant to
build aggressive positions.



    Data showing early signs of recovery in Singapore's



manufacturing sector failed to spark significant activity in



the Singapore dollar , leaving it in a range of 1.7512 to



1.7530 per U.S. dollar, against late Thursday's 1.7511.



Singapore's Purchasing Managers' Index rose 1.4 points to



50.8 percent in June, after posting three consecutive months of



readings below 50, which suggested contraction.



"The improvement is not surprising given that a rebound has



been expected with key event risks such as the Iraq war and



SARS outbreak out of the way by last month," said Jimmy Koh,



head of treasury research at UOB Bank in Singapore.



Still Koh said the rise in some components of the PMI, such



as new orders and export orders, suggested higher production



ahead and confirmed the view that second quarter was Singapore



economy's lowest point this year and that a recovery was due in



the second half.



Data reflecting a less promising exports outlook weighed



down the Philippine peso  to 53.455 per dollar, against



53.39 at close of local trade on Thursday.



Philippine exports were down nearly four percent from a



year earlier, testing hopes of stronger economic growth in the



second half of the year.



Price pressures also brought bad news, with the inflation



rate for the 12 months to June coming in at 3.4 percent, higher



than most estimates and the 2.7 percent rise in the year to



May.



The Philippine central bank said inflationary growth was



unlikely to be sustained in coming months and would not affect



its easier monetary policy.



On Wednesday, the central bank had delivered an unexpected



25 basis point cut in its overnight rates, taking them to their



lowest level in more than 11 years. It was the first adjustment



since March 2002.



 
    The Thai baht        held firm at around 41.65 per dollar,
just shy of one-week high of 41.63 hit on Thursday.
    Dealers said equity-related foreign investment inflows and
dollar sales by exporters had pushed the baht higher.
    But fears of central bank intervention to protect export

positions were likely to limit gains.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late, Focus On FOMC Meeting
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were on a modestly stronger footing late Friday, but off their intraday highs as the dollar clawed back some lost ground. 

 For the most part, market players focused on squaring positions ahead of the weekend, and ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting next week. 

 The market is "oscillating between a 25-basis-point and a 50-basis-point," rate cut expectation, said a foreign bank trader in Singapore. The dollar bounced off an intraday low of around Y118.01 as speculation once again swung toward a 25-basis-point cut. 

 At 0830 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y118.32, little changed from Y118.30 overnight in New York, but still down from Y118.60 in Tokyo Thursday. 

 With few local leads, Asian currencies were largely content to follow the dollar/yen movements. 

 "By and large, dollar/Asians are in a position squaring mode and are looking better-bid on-the-day (as the dollar regained some ground)," said a U.S. bank trader in Singapore. 

 Like in the previous session, traders suspected Bank of Korea intervened in the final minutes of trading to push the dollar up after it breached the 1,190-won support, although they said the dollar buying wasn't as heavy as Thursday. 

 A foreign bank trader in Singapore said the central bank seemed to be taking advantage of thin liquidity near the close of trade to maximize the impact of intervention. 

 "Liquidity is in the final minutes, so light intervention can have a major impact," he said. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,190.6, down from KRW1,198.5, but off the intraday low of KRW1,187.0. 

 The won continued to be supported by foreign buying of local shares. 

 Foreign investors, who bought Korean shares for the 17th straight day, were selling dollars to settle those purchases, while exporters also unloaded dollar holdings. 

 Earlier Friday, Edaily, an Internet news service, quoted an unidentified official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy as saying that the government will take steps to curb the dollar's sharp fall versus the won, if necessary. 

 "It's not desirable for investors to have excessive expectation of further won strength," the official said, noting such expectation comes from "a speculative mind rather than analysis over economic fundamentals." 

 He said the government is closely watching the foreign exchange market. 

 "If required, the government may consider using proceeds of regular treasury issues, not only those of foreign exchange stabilization bonds, to stabilize dollar/won," he said. 

 The South Korean government can use funds raised from forex stabilization bond issues to intervene in the market. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened after local banks sold the currency late in the session, probably to cover short U.S. dollar positions ahead of the weekend, dealers said. 

 Talk in the afternoon of a French bank shutting its equity operations in Singapore may also have given the U.S. dollar a mild leg up, though many dealers said there was no link between the two. 

 Late Friday, Societe General SA confirmed that it will close its Singapore equity operations amid further cost-cutting and efficiency measures. 

 "It's hard to connect the two events," said a dealer, "Personally I think the market was just a bit short (U.S. dollars) and they wanted to cover before the weekend," he added. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7360, up from S$1.7320 late Thursday. 

 The Philippine peso was up for the third straight day as some banks trimmed long-dollar positions on expectations of a U.S. rate cut next week, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.300 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.350 Thursday. 

 The peso also continued to benefit from improved market sentiment on signs the government is finally regaining control of its finances. The government Thursday reported a budget deficit of PHP9.9 billion in May, just half of the PHP20 billion ceiling for the month. 

 But news of a much lower current account surplus for the first quarter pared the peso's gains. 

 The country's current account surplus in the three months to March fell to $338 million from $1.68 billion in the year-ago period due to an unusual rise in imports. 

 "Toward the close, some banks bought back the dollars they sold earlier in the day," said a trader with a foreign bank. 

Central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura earlier Friday said he expects the dollar to average PHP53 in 2003. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was up on continued capital inflows, but dollar short covering and corporate demand for the U.S. unit tempered gains, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,240 rupiah, down from IDR8,245 Thursday. 

 A local newspaper quoted Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah as saying $4 billion of funds has flowed into the country since early April. About half of that was for foreign direct investments, $1 billion was parked in government bonds and mutual funds, and the rest was for speculative dollar-rupiah trades. 

 The New Taiwan dollar rose as foreign investors continued to buy the currency to invest in the local share market, dealers said. 

 But they said the U.S. dollar was supported by importer purchases, including state-run Chinese Petroleum Corp., which was buying to pay for oil imports. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.593, down from NT$34.614 Thursday. 

 The Taiwan Stock Exchange said overseas investors bought a net NT$4.26 billion worth of local shares Friday. 

 The Thai baht was little changed as offshore dollar buying in the afternoon trimmed most of its earlier gains. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 41.60 baht, just a tad below Thursday's THB41.615.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing slips, others hold small gains.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, June 20 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar slipped
to a one-week low on Friday afternoon, wiping out its early
gains even as other Asian currencies found some support from
the U.S. dollar's soft tone against the yen .
 
    The Singapore dollar weakened as far as 1.7361 per U.S.
dollar, after opening local trade just shy of 1.7300.
    Dealers said persistent Sing dollar offers from some


 foreign banks around 1.7300-1.7320 prompted a trimming of long 

 Sing dollar positions they were reluctant to hold over the 

 weekend. 

 That reluctance stemed from uncertainty over the U.S. 

 dollar, which could become more volatile as markets debate the 

 size of an expected rate cut by the U.S. Federal Reserve next 

 week. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore releases its policy 

 review in early July, which should provide some medium term 

 direction for the Singapore dollar, its main policy tool. 

 "The Fed meeting has become a focal point here as most 

 people think their decision would have a strong influence on 

 Singapore's policy," said a senior dealer at a local bank in 

 Singapore. 

 Elsewhere, players were cautious of currency gains after 

 profit-taking in the region's stock markets trimmed some of 

 their recent gains, although foreign portfolio investors 

 continued to be net buyers in most Asian markets. 

 "Asian economies will do well even if the recovery in the 

 U.S. is a sluggish one and that is what most fund managers are 

 positioning for," said Philip Wee, strategist at DBS Bank. 

 Those portfolio inflows have put pressure on Asian 

currencies to appreciate, a proposition unacceptable to central 

 banks in the region given their sensitivity to export 

 competitiveness. 

 BAHT CONTAINED 

 Authorities in Thailand are among those dealers said had 

intervened heavily this week, to counter the impact of foreign 

 portfolio inflows which have topped 18 billion baht this year. 

 The baht held a 41.56-41.60 per dollar range, holding above 

 Thursday's one-week low of 41.64, its upside capped by worries 

 of intervention and the stock market edging off three-year 

 highs. 

 "The baht at the moment is quite stable which is good for 

 the real sector," Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn 

 Devakula told reporters on Friday. "And we are monitoring the 

 baht to ensure competitiveness." 

 Worries about central bank intervention capped the South 


Korean won's             rise on Friday even though



foreign investors purchased a net 114 billion won worth of



local shares.

about $400 million on behalf of the central bank on Thursday,



surpassing the $325 million worth of stock purchases made by



foreign investors on the day.



Foreign equity investors have been net buyers of Korean



shares for 17 consecutive sessions, and have bought a net 1.11



trillion won in shares so far this year.



The Philippine peso  rose to a near two-week high of

gains, pulling it down to 53.30 by close of local trade,

to a four-month high on Thursday, but other Asian currencies

weeks.

believed some Korean banks in recent sessions had been buying



U.S. dollars on behalf of the central bank to protect export
