text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, June 17 (Reuters) - The Korean won rose to a 3-=
  month high alongside a surging Korean stock market and China
curtailed some of the intense speculation in yuan forwards by
reiterating its currency policy had not changed.
    Other Asian currencies were rangebound on Tuesday, watching
a listless U.S. dollar which was waiting on U.S. consumer price
data for clues as to whether the Fed would cut rates next week.
    And, as in Japan where fears of intervention capped the
yen, traders suspected regional central banks were the reason
for the limited moves in the Asian currencies.
    The Singapore dollar        made light gains during the day
but was shy of 1.7250, from where it bounced lower last month,
and traders remained apprehensive about possible intervention
by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.



    "They (the MAS) are keeping it fairly close-ranged, within
a one to two percent band," James Malcolm, currency strategist
at JP Morgan said, referring to the undisclosed trade-weighted
band authorities manage the Sing dollar in.
 
    Malcolm advised positioning for an appreciation in the
Singapore dollar, but over three to six months.
    He said even the Thai authorities seemed to have been
intervening to rein in the baht, although less aggressively
than in the past.
    The Thai baht        clung to 41.50, after it had equalled
a near 11-month high of 41.40 in offshore deals. The Philippine
peso's  spike higher past 53.40 was fleeting.
    Malcolm said it was too far-fetched for markets to position
for firmer Asian currencies on the basis of the ongoing
speculation in the yuan , or renminbi, forwards.
    Forward premiums on the one-year yuan           hit a
record 1,900 points but then fell back after China said there
was no change to its policy of keeping the yuan stable.
    Premiums have been rising since last week and the



speculative trade gathered steam early on Tuesday after U.S.



Treasury Secretary John Snow said the United States would back



any plan by China to move toward a more flexible exchange rate.



Malcolm said some banks had suggested a yuan revaluation



would boost other Asian currencies because it would reduce the



worries about export competitiveness against China.



 
    "That's a very long-term thing, not one to position for
immediately," he said.
    RUPIAH STALLS, WON GAINS
    The Taiwan dollar          rose in line with the Korean won
             as Korean stocks         hit six-month highs.
    The won's gains were also reflected in the yen-won cross
rate . The cross rate moved to 10.05 from Monday's
10.16, showing the won was gaining ground against the yen.
    The rupiah, Asia's strongest currency against the dollar



this year, could not progress much beyond 8,185. The rupiah has



encountered resistance and bounced several times in recent



weeks off a rising trendline drawn through the its 33-month



high of 8,085 on May 26 and its June 10 high of 8,150.



Traders said heavy foreign investment inflows, the latest



being the approximate $365 million received by Indonesia's Bank



Restructuring Agency for a 51 percent stake sale in Bank



Danamon (BDMN.JK), had also waned.



And analysts said despite the central Bank Indonesia's (BI)



apparent approval of a firmer currency, the competitiveness of



the currency against others in the region still mattered.



"Thus, the rupiah should stay firm, but resistance is



likely to be found at 8,000, as long as the Bank of Japan



resists yen appreciation beyond 115, keeping other Asian



central banks on the defensive," DBS Bank said in a



commentary.

title: Singapore  Dlr Up Late; Off High On Yen  Intervention  Talk
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was stronger late in Asia Monday after some banks unwound their long U.S. dollar positions, but the local currency was pulled off a session high on talk of intervention in the yen market, dealers said. 

 At 0815 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7294, down from S$1.7338 late Friday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7255 and S$1.7300 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened lower around S$1.7280 in Singapore after losing ground during Friday's trading session in New York, as market players unwound positions and took profit in the wake of weak U.S. consumer sentiment data. 

 The U.S. currency slipped to a session low of S$1.7255 before recovering to around S$1.7280, and subsequently S$1.7300, late in the session, supported by its rebound against the yen. 

 At the end of the Asian trading day, the U.S. dollar was quoted at Y117.58 compared with its earlier low of Y117.16 on speculation Japan's finance ministry may have bought U.S. dollars to weaken the Japanese currency, dealers said. 

 But trade in the local market was generally thin, as market participants were cautious of the Monetary Authority of Singapore taking similar action to keep the Singapore dollar competitive. 

 Traders are also focused on the MAS' semiannual monetary policy review in early July. 

 While many analysts believe the MAS isn't likely to change its neutral policy bias, they're on the lookout for any hint that the central bank might do otherwise. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk economic growth and low inflation. It guides the Singapore dollar in an undisclosed trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 Until then, most market participants expect thin trade to persist, with major currencies like the yen setting the tone for the Singapore dollar. 

 In the near term, the U.S. dollar is expected to stay between S$1.7250 and S$1.7320 overnight. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended mostly higher Monday, buoyed by late Friday gains in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. 

 But the rise in local bond prices was limited as market participants maintained a generally cautious stance ahead of a fresh supply of 10-year government bonds due July 1. 

 The Singapore government is expected to auction between S$2 billion and S$2.5 billion of the bonds later this month, according to dealers. 

 The yield on two-year bonds slipped four basis points to 0.65%, while the yield on five-year bonds fell one basis point to 1.30%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds fell two basis points to 1.72% and the yield on 10-year bonds slipped two basis points to 1.95%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds ended three basis points lower at 2.37%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site: 

http://www.sgs.gov.sg("http://www.sgs.gov.sg")


In the interest rate swaps market, swap offers were also mostly softer
as they tracked local bonds yields.



The two-year offer was, however, unchanged at 0.85% but the five-year
offer slipped one basis point to 1.46%. The 10-year offer shed one basis
point to 2.25%.



The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 140 basis points
from 141 basis points late Friday.



In the local money market, rates were mixed though liquidity remained

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Resist gains, watching China, Japan.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, June 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stalled
after early gains on Monday as traders fretted about possible
central bank intervention, the erosion in export
competitiveness against the Chinese yuan and the yen's
reluctance to rally.
    The opening gains came after the U.S. dollar was weakened
by soft U.S. data that heightened expectations of a U.S.
interest rate cut later this month.
    The Singapore dollar        rose over a cent from Friday's
lows, the Indonesian rupiah  was back on an uptrend that
stalled in late May, the Korean won             tested
three-month onshore highs and the Thai baht  rose to a
10-day peak.
    But as markets speculated over Japanese intervention to cap
the yen and placed bets on China yielding to pressure to widen
the yuan's tight trading band, regional currencies dithered.
    "Asia wants to join the trend of a weak U.S.



 dollar and, at
the same time, Asian central banks want to make their currency
competitive mainly due to the fact that despite the weaker
dollar, China still keeps its currency pegged," said Frank
Gong, head of Asian markets strategy at Bank of America.
 
    China has become an increasingly important trading partner
for many Asian economies, Gong said.
    "And, of course, the Bank of Japan has been intervening to
hold the dollar-yen up. Both of those factors are limiting how
much Asian currencies can strengthen," Gong said.
    Yuan revaluation trades, which bet on the Chinese yuan



being allowed to appreciate from the 8.276-8.28 range it now



keeps to against the dollar, have picked up in the past week,



with one-year forward yuan premiums in the non-deliverable



market rising to a historic high of 1,500 points .



The Singapore dollar was restricted after its early gains



by expectations of investment outflows and the risk of


intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore ahead of



next month's semi-annual policy review.



The Philippine peso  opened firmer after a holiday



weekend, boosted by bunched dollar inflows and the regional



trend, but then stalled.



Traders said authorities were suspected to have intervened


in Taiwan, where the Taiwan dollar's  gains halted



around 34.60 - still its strongest local close in three



months.



 
    The rupiah could not progress much beyond 8,185 and the
Thai baht met resistance even before touching 41.50.
    Still, Gong said, South East Asia was less susceptible to
the pressures of keeping pace with the yen.
    Currencies such as the baht were backed by strong
fundamentals, while the rupiah had the appeal of its high
yield.
    "South East Asia, in general, would have a better chance to



strengthen against the U.S. dollar because they are influenced



less compared to North East Asian currencies by dollar-yen and



the Chinese renminbi," he said.



The yen-won cross rate was steady at 10.12 ,



showing the won's gains were limited while the yen was capped.

Last week's widely-held view that the Monetary Authority of


Singapore had been intervening by buying dollars, after a $2.4



billion monthly rise in reserves in May, was also giving way to



scepticism, traders said.



Speculation next month's policy review would see the MAS



widen the undisclosed trade-weighted band the Sing dollar is



allowed to move in, effectively easing policy, had also

"Singapore has passed the worst of the SARS outbreak," Thio



said, referring to the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)

"If the MAS did not widen policy then, at the peak of the

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Flat, musing on policy.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, June 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly
flat on Friday against a backdrop of rising regional stock
markets, a steady yen and U.S. dollar, and wariness over policy
moves to curtail gains and protect export competitiveness.
    The worries over intervention and possible investment
outflows hemmed in the Singapore dollar  and dampened
moves in others such as the Thai baht  and Indonesian
rupiah .
    Traders in Singapore said the market was still worried
about dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of
Singapore after a $2.4 billion monthly rise in reserves in May.
Next month's semi-annual monetary policy review also added to
the market anxiety.
     More immediate was the concern that there will be demand
for U.S. dollars as a consortium led by Singapore's Temasek
Holdings and Germany's Deutsche Bank (DBKGn.DE) makes the final
payment for a majority stake in Indonesia's Bank Danamon
 (BDMN.JK).



    The consortium has already paid $15 million and Indonesia's
Bank Restructuring Agency said the rest of the total estimated
$363 million payment would be made by Friday. The cash payment
would be split evenly between rupiah and dollars.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan, said he
did not expect an impact on the Singapore dollar from the
payment. It was anticipated and the MAS would likely ensure the
market did not feel the pressure, he said.
    Yet, the worries over intervention seemed justified.
    "We know that the MAS are very concerned about the local
and global economic picture and outlook. Anecdotally, they
continue to be very active in the market in terms of keeping
Sing dollar at a weak level,"Malcolm said.
    "Even when you strip out the euro valuation effects and so
on, they must have bought well over a billion (U.S.) dollars in
the market in May to keep the Sing dollar weak," he said.
    The Sing dollar was being kept about one to two percent on
the weaker side of the mid-point of the undisclosed
trade-weighted band that authorities manage it in, he said.
    Yet, the chances that the MAS would widen this band to ease
monetary policy at its July review were significantly less than
50 percent, he said.
    WON INDIFFERENT
    The Korean won                   was steady, shrugging off
central bank comments on Thursday that exports were expected to
strengthen in the second half of the year and spur the economy.
    It was also indifferent to possible intervention after a
finance ministry official said on Thursday authorities would
counter the won's strength if necessary, saying currency gains
were undesirable given slowing exports and economic activity.
    "It's partly a reflection of the weak U.S. dollar
continuing," said Greg Gibbs, senior currency strategist at the
Royal Bank of Canada Capital Markets.
    That weak dollar trend could keep the won firm over the
next month or so, although the policy intentions implied the
authorities would fight the appreciation of the won, Gibbs
said.
    "The authorities there will resist that for sure," he said.
    Markets in Philippines were closed on Friday. The peso
  hit a 10-week low of 53.65 on Thursday after rating
agency Fitch downgraded its sovereign foreign currency rating.
    The Indonesian rupiah        was listless, as it has been
for over a week, after a steep rally from mid-March to late
May. The central bank cut overnight rates by half a percentage
point on Thursday, the fifth cut since May.
 
    But analysts said the currency remained attractive for its
high yield.
    "It is attractive for yield play. It has just had such a



strong run," Gibbs said.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, June 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies held tight
ranges on Thursday as traders mulled mixed signals from rising
equities, more grim economic data from Korea, and the threat of
central bank intervention in the regional markets.
    The U.S. dollar's fall to its low for the week against the
euro  amid expectations of rate cuts in both the United
States and euro zone had little influence on the local markets.
    The Thai baht        was the strongest in the region,
supported by its rising stock market and the foreign investment
inflows. In contrast, the Singapore dollar  was weighed
down by fears of intervention.
    Traders said the huge $2.4 billion monthly rise in reserves
in May, reported last weekend, has been interpreted as a sure
sign of dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of
Singapore and has weighed on the Singapore dollar this week.
    Some analysts were sceptical of the intervention talk.



    "While we would never rule out the possibility of
intervention, the likelihood is that the generally soft
economic outlook is becoming more manifest in the Singapore
dollar, if not in other Asian currencies," National Australia
Bank said in a commentary.
    "The other factor suggesting intervention has not taken
place being the fact that the Sing dollar NEER (nominal
effective exchange rate) remains mid-range," it said, referring
to the undisclosed trade-weighted band the MAS manages the
currency in.
    The Korean won                   strengthened after the
central Bank of Korea kept rates steady, as expected, despite a
rise in unemployment to a 17-month high.
 
    The Bank of Korea said it expected stronger growth in the
second half of the year, supported by strong exports.
    Traders said that could mean they would also try to keep



the won competitive in trade-weighted terms. That view was



supported when a finance ministry official said authorities



would counter the won's strength if necessary, saying currency


gains were undesirable given slowing exports and economic



activity.



 
    Korea was not alone in its woes, and National Australia
Bank said the regional economic outlook was not bullish.
    "One reason we have been bearish Asian currencies is due to
the struggling local economies," the National Australia Bank
report said.
    The Philippine peso        softened after rating agency



Fitch downgraded its sovereign foreign currency rating to BB



from BB+, citing the weak fiscal position. Late on Thursday,



the government said the May budget deficit was 13.4 billion



pesos against a target of 20.5 billion.



Manila-based traders said the peso's decline stalled around



53.65, a technical resistance for the dollar and an end-March



low, and it then retraced some losses ahead of a holiday



weekend. Markets there are closed on Friday.



The Indonesian rupiah  extended its decline as



offshore players booked profits after a long rally. The



Indonesian central bank cut interest rates for the fifth time



since the start of May, bringing the overnight intervention


rate to 9.75 percent - still the highest in Asia.



Indonesia also said it had signed a deal on economic



reforms with the International Monetary Fund, which would pave



the way for the release of the next tranche of an IMF loan of



about $450 million by early next month.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed On Equity Flows, Intervention  Fear
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies put up a mixed showing Thursday supported by strong equity inflows, but with the central bankintervention theme a strong deterrent to attempts to take the units too high. 

 The Singapore dollar, the Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah slipped, while the South Korean won, the Thai baht and the New Taiwan dollar were modestly higher. 

 Analysts said central banks in the region are loathe to allow their currencies to appreciate too fast for fear of losing export competitiveness at a time of uncertainty for the global economy. 

 "Across the board, central banks are still not sufficiently confident of a turnaround (in the economies), at least until the end of the year," said Chong Hui Chin, a currency strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a one-month low during the session, but managed to trim losses. Late in the local session, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7380, up from S$1.7365 late Wednesday. 

 A trader at a European bank in Singapore said there were a lot of U.S. names buying the currency pair, continuing a trend seen in the last few days. 

 There's been talk in the market in recent days that the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been supporting the U.S. dollar, which has damped any enthusiasm to push up the local unit. 

 Talk of such intervention seems to be supported by the recent foreign reserves data, which showed a sharp rise in reserves last month, analysts said. 

 The trader said he believes the government wants to weaken the Singapore dollar to make it more competitive against countries like neighboring Malaysia, whose currency, the ringgit, is pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Philippine peso was weighed down by a ratings downgrade from Fitch Ratings, and also as banks bought dollars ahead of a long weekend. However, strong equity inflows into the local stock market put a floor under the peso. 

 The dollar closed at 53.610 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.535 Wednesday. 

 Fitch lowered the long-term foreign currency rating on the Philippines by a notch to "BB". The move had to a large extent been anticipated as it was reported in a local newspaper in the previous session.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Market Wary Of  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies followed the yen lower Wednesday, with market players remaining wary of provoking intervention by regional central banks. 

 The South Korean won initially proved the exception as equity related dollar selling by foreign investors pushed the U.S. unit to an intraday trough of KRW1,190.7. Foreign investors snapped up local shares for a 10th session, ending as net buyers of KRW155.9 billion of stocks. 

 But the Bank of Korea intervened to support the dollar, buying the currency at the KRW1,191 level, pushing it all the way to an intraday high of KRW1,196.4, a foreign bank trader in Singapore said. 

 The dollar closed at KRW1,195.4, modestly higher from KRW1,194.5 Tuesday. 

 State-run banks bought as much as $700 million-$800 million, likely on behalf of the authorities, a Seoul-based trader said. 

 Foreign equity inflows have been a key factor underpinning the strength of Asian currencies in recent days. Bank of America said Asian stock markets, led by Taiwan and Korea, have seen equity investments of over $1.3 billion to date in June. 

 However, "we remain convinced that export competitiveness is seen as a critical goal by most central banks in the region, especially in an environment of slowing global income," the bank said in a research note. 

 "We expect most central banks to maintain a policy toward trade-weighted weakness, and this would also entail absorbing any large capital inflow to prevent a sharp appreciation," Bank of America added. 

 Continued U.S. dollar buying related to military equipment purchases, and also the yen's weakness, weighed on the New Taiwan dollar, although this was partly offset by foreign inflows to the stock market, traders said. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.682, up from NT$34.677 Tuesday. 

 Foreign investors bought more than NT$4 billion worth of shares Wednesday, although the main index fell 0.6% to snap a four-session winning streak. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a one-week low as market players exercised caution on talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been intervening in recent days to keep the local unit weak to aid the city-state's flagging economy. 

 Singapore's foreign exchange reserves data, issued over the weekend, appear to lend support to the speculation. 

 "Singapore's foreign exchange reserves grew by $2.4 billion to $85.8 billion in May, suggesting that intervention was fairly aggressive as trade flows were unlikely to have improved in that month, although this is pure conjecture at this stage with trade data not released yet," BNP Paribas said in a research note. 

 "Intervention to slow the ascent of the SGD (Singapore dollar) falls into the current monetary policy stance of the Authority, where a guarded growth outlook justifies an accommodative monetary policy stance," the French bank added. 

Intervention fears also kept the Thai baht on a weaker footing, although this was offset by equity related dollar selling by offshore institutional players, a trader in Singapore said. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 41.81 baht, marginally up from THB41.79 Tuesday. The trader said the dollar selling took hold when it reached the "high 80s." 

 The Philippine peso closed lower as banks bought dollars in anticipation of a possible downgrade of the country's credit rating, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.535 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.365 Tuesday. 

 A Manila newspaper reported Wednesday that Fitch Ratings will downgrade its long-term credit rating on the Philippines to "BB" from "BB+" due to the government's growing debt burden, fiscal deficit, and election-related concerns that raise doubts on the continuity of economic policies. 

 But traders said the market can't actively push the dollar higher as the central bank is believed to be selling dollars at PHP53.55. 

Central Bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco called the peso's weakness a "knee-jerk reaction" to reports of the possible downgrade and not an adverse view of the macroeconomic fundamentals which remain "sound." 

 "There has been an improvement on the revenue collection, (economic) growth is consistent, and inflation is low," Tetangco said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was marginally lower as market players took profit amid fears of central bank intervention. 

 The rupiah is trading at more than two-year highs after a 10% rally since the start of the year, as overseas investors put money into high-yielding stocks and bonds. 

 But the central bank last week said any further slide in the dollar would hurt exporters, and this has resulted in traders turning more cautious and taking profit on the rupiah. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,230 rupiah, up from IDR8,210 Tuesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late;Mkt Wary Of  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies gave up early gains to move to a weaker footing late Tuesday as market players covered short-dollar positions after selling it down earlier in the session. 

 The Singapore dollar, Thai baht, Indonesian rupiah and New Taiwan dollar drifted lower. However, the Philippine peso and South Korean won eked out modest gains. 

 The dollar's recovery against regional units during the session surprised analysts and traders, who had expected the currency to come under pressure in the wake of the management shake-up at Freddie Mac and weaker U.S. share prices. 

 Concerns about central bank intervention appeared to be a major factor that helped crimp regional currencies' gains. The central banks are keen to rein in the strength of their currencies to keep exports competitive. 

 "The dollar opened lower (versus regional units) and then people took the opportunity to cover short positions. It's a whippy, two-way market," a Singapore-based European bank trader said. 

 Singapore's latest foreign exchange reserves data seemed to give credence to speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been supporting the U.S. dollar, analysts said. 

 The data, issued over the weekend, showed reserves rose $2.44 billion in May - the largest monthly gain in a couple of years, according to J.P. Morgan Chase Bank. 

 "While some of this reflects EUR (euro) valuation effects and interest accrual, the underlying message is of strong USD (U.S. dollar) buying by the MAS," the bank said in a research note Tuesday. 

 "It's definitely making people nervous. That's part of the reason why the dollar/Sing (Singapore unit) is well-bid today," noted Sameer Goel, a currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7318, up from S$1.7285 late Monday. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around THB41.80 late in Asia, up from THB41.69 Monday, taking a cue from its rise versus the Singapore currency. 

 Market players were also wary of provoking Thailand's central bank, especially with memories of last week's intervention still fresh in their minds. Bank of Thailand bought dollars Friday when the baht spiked to a fresh 10-month high, traders said. 

Intervention fears also caused the Indonesian rupiah to reverse early gains. The dollar recovered from an intraday trough of 8,155 rupiah to end the local session at IDR8,210, up from IDR8,195 Monday. 

 Dealers said market talk of dollar buying by central banks elsewhere in the region helped push the U.S. unit up versus the rupiah. 

 In Taiwan, U.S. dollar demand from government-controlled banks helped weaken the local unit. Several dealers said the dollar buying was likely related to purchases of military equipment. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.677, up from NT$34.662 Monday. 

 Dealers said government-controlled Farmers Bank of China bought an estimated $100 million, while International Commercial Bank of China was also busy buying U.S. dollars. 

 Over the weekend, the local language China Times newspaper quoted unidentified Defense Ministry officials as saying Taiwan will sign a deal this month to buy four decommissioned Kidd-class destroyers from the U.S. Navy for US$28.4 billion. 

 Dollar selling by foreign buyers of South Korean shares, and also exporters, pushed the won marginally higher, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at a two-and-a-half week closing low of 1,194.5 won, down from KRW1,196.7 Monday. 

 Foreign investors bought stocks for a ninth session Tuesday, ending as net buyers of KRW20.2 billion worth of shares. 

 There was also market talk that Daewoo Shipbuilding may soon be unloading some of the $255.6 million it raised last week in a Global Depositary Receipts offering. 

 "We expect they (Daewoo Shipbuilding) will sell at least $230 million," a Seoul-based dealer said. 

 However, the dollar isn't expected to slip under KRW1,190 as the government is likely to step in to support the U.S. currency at that level, dealers said. 

 The Philippine peso ended higher as exporters unloaded some of their dollar holdings when the U.S. unit began to gain ground during the session, traders said. 

 The dollar ended at PHP53.365 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.380 Monday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late, Support From Share Buying
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies turned in a mixed performance Monday as they recovered or trimmed early losses on the back of dollar selling. 

 Broadly stronger regional equities' markets provided support to the currencies, although upside was capped by concerns about central bankintervention. 

 The Singapore dollar, Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht were weaker late Monday. The South Korean won, the New Taiwan dollar and the Philippine peso were stronger. 

 A Singapore-based trader at a European bank said the dollar started on a stronger footing against regional currencies but lost momentum later in the session. 

 "I thought it (the dollar) was going higher, so I was kind of surprised (when gains weren't sustained). The market started turning around" as participants started selling back dollars, he said. "The market is very short term. Nobody wants to be caught long (dollars)," the trader added. 

 The overall market was quiet, with trading thinned by holidays in Australia and some parts of Europe, traders said. 

 Some analysts said regional currencies may be losing steam after a strong run-up in recent weeks on the back of broad dollar weakness. 

 Firming oil prices, weak economic data and a general reluctance by regional central banks to see their currencies appreciate too fast - and hence erode export competitiveness - may well keep regional units on the defensive. 

 China's pegged currency regime, which gives it price advantage in the export market, is a "very strong motivating factor" for regional central banks to want to curb the strength of their own units, said David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at Royal Bank of Scotland. 

 China pegs the value of the yuan to the dollar, allowing it to trade in a very narrow band. 

 With such factors at play, a weak dollar wouldn't necessarily translate into stronger regional units, Simmonds said. However, resilient equity markets combined with a weak dollar would be bullish for Asian currencies, he noted. 

 The South Korean won closed at a two-week high on a wave of dollar selling by exporters and foreign investors in the local stock market. Foreigners were net buyers of Korean stocks for an eighth straight session, net buying KRW223.7 billion in shares. 

 The dollar finished at 1,196.7 won, down from KRW1,200.3 Thursday, marking its strongest close since May 23. South Korean markets were closed for a holiday Friday. 

 Market players who had been expecting the authorities to support the dollar at KRW1,200 were encouraged to test the downside by the central bank's absence from the foreign exchange market Monday. 

 "Everyone expected the BOK (Bank of Korea) to intervene, but they didn't come," a dealer in Seoul said, adding that the won is expected to continue to trend higher. He projected the dollar's new support at KRW1,190. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended modestly higher, helped also by foreign buying of local stocks. Foreign investors bought nearly NT$3.6 billion net in stocks Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.662, slightly down NT$34.665 Friday. 

 The market was very quiet as most players remained on the sidelines after last week's intervention by the central bank. 

 "Many players who shorted the U.S. dollar Friday were bitten, that is why a lot of them were kind of sluggish today," said a foreign bank trader in Taipei. 

 The central bank, which intervenes in the foreign exchange market regularly, bought an estimated US$100 million in the final minutes of Friday's session. 

 The Philippine peso snapped a four-day losing streak and finished higher on the back of remittance inflows and thin demand for dollars, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.38 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.45 Friday. 

 A Manila-based trader said there was also some profit-taking on the dollar in the afternoon as the market apparently overbought the currency earlier in the session in anticipation of central bank buying to boost international reserves. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7285 late in the local session, up from S$1.7235 Friday, but off the intraday peak of S$1.7310. 

 Lingering uncertainties about the local economy weighed on the Singapore dollar. 

 Local newspapers cited Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong as predicting flat on-year economic growth in the third quarter. 

 Whether the city-state slips back into recession this year will depend on the fourth quarter, the report cited Goh as saying. 

 Goh said a contraction in the current quarter is a foregone conclusion as the economy was hurt by SARS. 

 The Indonesian rupiah weakened slightly as the market took a breather amid fears of central bank intervention. 

 The dollar closed local trading at 8,195 rupiah, marginally up from IDR8,180 Friday. 

 Speculative investors have been moving money into Indonesian stocks and bonds in recent months in search of high returns. 

 But the central bank has signaled it may intervene to protect exporters if the dollar falls much further. Traders said fears of such intervention are deterring investors from building up large short-dollar positions. 

Intervention fears also kept the Thai baht on a weaker tone after the central bank bought dollars to rein in the currency Friday, when it rose to a fresh 10-month high. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 41.68 baht, up from THB41.63 Friday. 

 Over the weekend, Finance Minister Suchart Jaovisidha said he believed the recent rise in the baht may end within one to two weeks as the global decline in the dollar likely comes to a halt. 

 Suchart said the central bank is closely monitoring the situation. 

 "Let's be frank. If the baht gets very strong (the central bank governor) has to do something to make it weaker. He has the mechanisms in his hands," Suchart said.

    By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, June 6 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention pulled
the Thai baht off 10-month highs on Friday after the central
bank governor said he expected the currency to ease.
    Singapore dollar and Indonesian rupiah also eased from

currencies was of caution ahead of crucial U.S. jobs data due 

 later in the day. 

 Regionals had strengthened after the dollar faltered on 

 some weak U.S. data, but their gains were restrained in morning 

 trade by caution about possible Bank of Japan intervention

 which was fuelled by a series of government comments on the 

 yen. 

 Korean markets were closed for a holiday on Friday. 

 The Thai baht  eased to 41.66 per dollar, off a 

 10-month high of 41.41 hit in overnight New York trade, after 

 dealers in Bangkok said they spotted dollar bids from banks 

 that were usually active on behalf of the central bank. 

 "There were dollar bids, small but enough to let the market 

 know authorities don't want the currency to appreciate any 

 further," said a dealer at a local bank in Bangkok. 

 The baht has gained about 3.5 percent against the dollar so 

 far this year, boosted by a rallying stock market and prospects 

 of strong growth driven by healthy domestic demand. 

 Thailand's central bank governor, Pridiyathorn Devakula, 

 said he expected the Thai baht to soften after its gains this 

 week. 


 
    "It will soften later," he told reporters, without giving
any timeframe.
    When asked why he expected the baht to ease, Pridiyathorn
said: "Because I say so."
    Analysts said while the Bank of Thailand (BOT) has allowed



the baht to appreciate against the dollar on a nominal basis,



it has managed to keep the rise limited in trade-weighted



terms.



Sameer Goel, analyst at Bank of America in Singapore, said



the baht has gained only 1.9 percent against the yen since May



1, and has declined 0.2 percent and 3.1 percent against the



Singapore dollar and euro respectively.



"BOT has also recently noted the possibility of core



inflation undershooting its targets, and will be reluctant to



tighten monetary conditions through undue appreciation in the



exchange rate," he added.



At the start of the week, the BOT held its benchmark 14-day



repurchase rate steady at 1.75 percent, saying economic



recovery has not generated any perceptible upward pressure on



prices.



PESO HITS TWO-MONTH LOW



Elsewhere, the Philippine peso  weakened in afternoon



trading to hit a two-month low of 53.46 per dollar.



The easier tone in peso, which had lost about three percent



since May 8 when it hit an eight-month high of 51.80, was



helped by an effective easing of monetary policy on Thursday.



While the central bank did not cut official interest rates,



it did restore a tiered system of interest rates that pays



banks a decreasing rate on larger deposits held at the central



bank.



The step was a de facto easing as it would boost liquidity.



The tiered system was scrapped for a flat rate in March, when



the peso was threatening record lows and money supply was



rising.



The Singapore dollar  edged back to around 1.7235 per



U.S. dollar after rallying in New York trade to 1.7162, its



strongest since May 15 when it hit a 33-month high.



The Indonesian rupiah , Asia's strongest currency


against the dollar this year, also stepped back to around 8,280



per dollar from Thursday's one-week high of 8,130.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Regional Ctrl Bks Buy Dlrs
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Intervention by regional central banks and short covering on the dollar ahead of the weekend reined in Asian currencies late Friday despite the weak tone of the U.S. unit. 

 The Thai baht and the Philippine peso were lower; the Indonesian rupiah was firmer; and the Singapore dollar and New Taiwan dollar were steady. South Korean markets were closed for a public holiday. 

 Most of the currencies kicked off the session on a broadly stronger note on the back of a firmer yen; the Thai baht rose to a fresh 10-month high of 41.47 to the dollar. 

 Traders in Singapore said Thailand's central bank, via agent banks, aggressively bought dollars from the THB41.50 level through the session. 

 Around early afternoon, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters he expects the dollar to regain ground against the baht. He said the baht will soon weaken because it's likely to move in line with regional counterparts. 

 "We are monitoring its movement," he said. At the time of his comments, the dollar was trading around THB41.53. 

 At 0911 GMT, the dollar was quoted around THB41.65, up from THB41.58 at the Asian close late Thursday. 

 Last week, Pridiyathorn confirmed the central bank had been buying dollars to stem the baht's sharp rise. The baht has consistently chalked up fresh 10-month highs in recent weeks 

 Analysts and traders said the baht is getting a boost from the inflow of foreign capital into the local stock market. Foreign investors have been net buyers of stocks on most days since the beginning of May. 

 Meantime, there was also talk that the Monetary Authority of Singaporeintervened to support the U.S. currency Friday, although several traders said there was little evidence to support the speculation. 

 A European bank trader said several U.S. and local banks were buyers of the U.S. currency, but that they were likely covering short positions ahead of the weekend. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. unit was quoted at $1.7235, little changed from S$1.7233 late Thursday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar snapped a four-session winning streak to end flat on heavy intervention by Taiwan's central bank late in the session, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at its intraday high of NT$34.665, unchanged from Thursday. 

 The U.S. currency had traded below NT$34.635 for most of the session amid the inflow of foreign funds into local stocks, and also the strong yen, traders said. 

 But a flurry of dollar buying by the central bank in late trading pulled up the U.S. unit. 

 "The central bank was the most important pillar for the U.S. dollar today," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Taipei. 

 She estimated the central bank accounted for about half of Friday's turnover, including nearly US$100 million in the final 15 minutes of trading. Friday's total dealings were valued at US$347 million, compared with US$415 million Thursday. 

 The Philippine peso was driven to its lowest closing in more than two months by higher corporate demand for dollars, and also as banks built up dollar positions amid lower domestic interest rates, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at PHP53.450 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.330 Thursday, marking its strongest finish since March 31. 

 Banks bought dollars to capitalize on the narrowing of differential between U.S. and domestic rates after the central bank's de facto easing of monetary policy Thursday. 

 The central bank reinstated the tiered interest rate system on its overnight borrowing, which effectively lowered the overnight borrowing rate to a three-tiered rate of 1%, 4% and 7%, from a flat 7%. 

 "The restoration of the tiering system makes banks more liquid in pesos, and the dollar is the only attractive instrument to place these funds at this time," said a Manila-based trader with a local bank. 

 Other factors that pressured the peso were the central bank's revised balance of payments projection, and the planned lifting of the maturity limit on non-deliverable forwards, or NDFs, of banks. 

 The central bank earlier Friday said it expects the balance of payments to swing to a deficit of $1.1 billion this year from last year's $660 million surplus. It was originally expecting surplus of at least $100 million for 2003. 

 Traders said the central bank's plan to lift the six-month limit on the maturity of banks' NDFs later this month, announced Thursday, could push up the dollar. 

 "Banks' clients will be able to spread their exposure between maturities, which could lower the swap rates a bit, but this will have an inverse impact on the exchange rate," said another local bank trader in Manila. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was boosted by continued inflows of funds into the local capital market by investors seeking higher returns, traders said. 

 After a choppy session, the dollar closed local trading at 8,180 rupiah, down from IDR8,225 Thursday. 

 Although profit taking pulled the dollar out of its intraday trough of IDR8,170, traders said it remains on track to head lower. 

 "People still believe the dollar will fall to IDR8,100," said a dealer with a local bank. "It's only a matter of time."

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late, Pares Early Gains; Tracks Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was little changed late Friday as the U.S. currency steadily recovered from opening lows, keeping in tune with its movements against the yen, dealers said. 

 At 0830 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7235, compared with S$1.7233 late Thursday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7180 and S$1.7235 intraday. 

 The U.S. currency opened near its session low of S$1.7180, reflecting a broad retreat after weaker-than-expected U.S. jobless claims data and as players shifted funds into the euro after the European Central Bank's 50 basis-point interest rate cut. 

 The U.S. dollar staged a modest rebound midway through the morning session, but hovered around S$1.7210-S$1.7220 for rest of the day, before short covering ahead of the weekend pushed it higher late in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar's late rise in Singapore also tracked its movements against the yen, which weakened to Y117.99 compared with Y117.30 earlier. 

 The late weakening of the local dollar sparked speculation the Singapore central bank had intervened to support the U.S. unit, though many dealers said there was little evidence to support that theory. 

 Concern about the domestic economy's pace of recovery continued to weigh on the local dollar. Some players also noted that the thin market liquidity somewhat exaggerated moves. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to trade sideways later Friday as the weekend nears, keeping to a range of between S$1.7180 and S$1.7250. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mixed Friday, with long bonds mostly lower on pre-weekend profit taking, tracking the overnight retreat in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. 

 Trade in the local bonds market was, however, thin ahead of a key U.S. employment report due later Friday which could show further signs of weakness in the labor market, dealers said. 

 The yield on two-year bonds slipped two basis points to 0.70% as the curve continued to steepen while the yield on five-year bonds inched up one basis point to 1.35%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was steady at 1.72% and the yield on 10-year bonds rose two basis points to 1.94%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds rose one basis point to 2.35%.

SINGAPORE, June 3 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on
Tuesday, led by the Thai baht  which hit a 10-month high,
as the U.S. dollar eased against the closely watched yen
 .
    Sentiment on the dollar was hurt after the Group of Eight
summit in France failed to discuss currency rates, bucking
market expectations after some leaders had shown concern about
the dollar's decline.
 
    The market was also unimpressed by President George W.
Bush's support for a strong dollar.
    "Nobody in the market really took him seriously," said Thio
Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore.
    Currency investors can now go back to chasing high yields
without worrying about a coordinated G8 effort to help the weak
dollar, analysts said.
    However, fears of intervention by Japanese authorities to


 curb the yen's rise and reluctance to trade aggressively ahead 

 of Thursday's European Central Bank interest rate meeting would 

 cap the upside for most Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 Recent data from across the region indicating slowing 

 exports was also likely to keep central banks on guard and keep 

currency gains modest.

to remain the main driver of currency strength in the region.
    The Thai baht        was propelled to a high of 41.51 per

inflows swelled.
    Foreign investors were net buyers for the eleventh straight

taking purchases to 8.38 billion baht so far this year.
    Dealers in Bangkok said given the baht's high correlation

    Portfolio inflows and hopes of more direct investment also

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late But  Intervention  Fears Linger
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were stronger Friday in the wake of the dollar's overnight weakness against major rivals, especially the yen, which provides broad direction to regional units. 

 Buoyant equity markets also helped support Asian currencies. 

 But gains were tempered by Japanese government warnings against the yen's rise. Market players also kept a wary eye on intervention by central banks in the region. 

 "Basically, central banks in Asia will increasingly deter any trade weighted gain to defend export competitiveness," Bank of America said in a research note Friday. 

 "Asian economies are heavily export-dependent, and need to protect this in an environment of global and U.S. growth concerns," the bank added. 

Currency players are waiting to see what emerges from the weekend's meeting of the Group of Eight leading nations, particularly for further hints on the U.S.' dollar policy. 

 President George W. Bush, in an interview with a group of foreign news organizations Thursday, said he will assure the G-8 meeting that he backs a strong dollar. 

 Bush's comments came amid growing market perception that the U.S. has retreated from its so-called strong dollar policy, fueled largely by remarks made by Treasury Secretary John Snow earlier this month. 

 The South Korean won closed up at 1,205.2 to the dollar, from KRW1,207.0 Thursday, after trading in a tight band of between KRW1,203.8 and KRW1,206.5. 

 Besides riding on the yen's gains, the won was also bolstered by dollar sales by exporters, and also by foreign investors who have been snapping up local shares for the past three days. 

 But fears that the government might step in to support the dollar below 1,200-won kept the local unit from appreciating further. 

 "People are worried about intervention," a Seoul-based trader said. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7318 near the end of the local session, down from S$1.7362 late Thursday. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$34.712, down from Thursday's NT$34.772. 

 The Taiwan dollar typically moves in line with the yen owing to export competition between the two economies. 

 Dealers said heavy U.S. dollar sales by Taiwanese exporters to settle accounts ahead of the month end and foreign buying of local shares boosted the local unit. 

 One Taipei-based dealer said the local central bank stepped in to support the U.S. dollar at around NT$34.70. 

 "Throughout Asia, central banks are supporting the U.S. dollar," he said. 

 Meantime, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula Friday said the baht has now stabilized following its recent sharp rise to 10-month highs, which prompted central bank intervention earlier this week. 

 "The baht has gained stability," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 At 0928 GMT, the dollar was quoted around 41.71 baht, down from THB41.855 Thursday, mirroring the regional trend. 

 The Philippine peso rebounded from the previous session's two-month lows, propelled by the stronger yen amid thin corporate demand for dollars, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at PHP53.240 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.350 Thursday. 

 Traders said demand for dollars tapered off as most companies had covered in advance their month-end import and debt payment requirements. 

 Indonesia's financial markets were closed for a public holiday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late On Dlr's Overnight Gains
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly weaker Wednesday on the U.S. dollar's overnight gains, although they were off their intraday troughs as dollar selling re-emerged, traders said. 

 Trading was, for the most part, range-bound, with no clear direction apparent. However the underlying sentiment for the dollar remains bearish, they noted. 

 "There's no trend. It's been rangy. It started with the dollar getting bid on short-covering because of the bounce overnight against the euro and yen," said a trader at a U.S. bank. But going into the latter part of the day, the dollar began to be sold off again, he said. 

 Given the weak dollar sentiment, the market expects more upside for Asian currencies, but players will remain vigilant of central bankintervention. 

 "The central banks would be there to smoothen the rise (of Asian currencies)," the trader said. He doesn't think the monetary authorities will try to reverse the upward trend in the currencies. 

 "The big trend is (for the) dollar (to go) down, so they probably can't fight that," he said. 

 The Thai baht was barely changed from late Wednesday levels after hitting fresh 10-month highs in overnight trading. At 0900 GMT, the dollar was quoted around THB41.69 compared with THB41.68 Tuesday. 

 Earlier, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the central bank has tried to manage the Thai baht at an appropriate level amid the broad dollar weakness. 

 "We did our best," he told reporters, but declined to say how much of dollars the central bank had bought to cap the baht's strength. 

 Pridiyathorn said huge capital inflows from foreign investors parking money in local stocks have also pushed up the baht recently. 

 "The high foreign reserves and seven straight days' of gains in Thai stocks show you how much (foreign) money is flowing into Thailand," he said. 

 Foreign net buying of Thai stocks so far this year totals THB4.77 billion. Thai foreign reserves stood at $38.8 billion as of May 16, up from $38.4 billion a week ago. 

 Also Wednesday, the Ministry of Finance said Thailand's gross domestic product likely grew 6.3% in the first quarter of 2003 due to strong export growth and consumer demand but is expected to slow in coming quarters as a result of the SARS outbreak. 

 The Ministry is maintaining a 5.1% GDP growth forecast for 2003. If not for the SARS outbreak, 2003 growth would have exceeded last year's 5.2%, the ministry's fiscal policy office director Wisudhi Srisuphan said. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.7274 late in the local session, up from S$1.7240 late Tuesday. 

 Speculation that the local central bank intervened to weaken the local dollar Tuesday also kept the U.S. currency on a stronger note, although analysts said there was little evidence to support the rumors. 

 Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, in a research note, said intervention couldn't be justified as the trade-weighted Singapore dollar wasn't anywhere near the limits of the policy band within which the local dollar is guided. 

 The South Korean won closed above the 1,200 to the dollar mark for the first time in two weeks as the yen slipped against the U.S. unit. 

 Gains were partly offset by some dollar sales by exporters ahead of month-end settlements, market players said. Anticipated won buying by foreign stock funds that bought Korean shares recently also capped the dollar's rise. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,200.4, up from KRW1,198.6 Tuesday. 

 Investors have been wary about selling dollars in view of the South Korean government's commitment to support the U.S. unit. 

 Earlier Wednesday, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said it will auction KRW1 trillion of five-year foreign exchange stabilization bonds June 3, which will equip authorities with more funds to boost the dollar if necessary. 

 The announcement came two days after the ministry's strong warning that the government will take action to curb the won's sharp rise. 

 "It's not that people are strongly interested in buying (the dollar) but they just can't sell (given the expectation of intervention)," said a dealer at Chohung Bank. 

 The Philippine peso closed at its weakest level in a month as banks covered short dollar positions in a shortened trading session, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.10 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP52.88 Tuesday 

 Trading closed an hour early as heavy rains drenched the capital. The central bank was closed after the government shut its offices as a result of flooding caused by typhoon Linfa. 

 A foreign bank trader said banks are now going long on the dollar as local interest rates start to decline due to huge liquidity in the financing system. 

 Treasury bill rates fell sharply at Monday's auction, with the yield on the benchmark 91-day treasury bill falling to 6.302% from 6.842% in the previous auction. 

 "The peso is correcting," the trader said. "Interest rates are becoming unattractive." 

 First-quarter economic growth data, which the government will issue early Thursday, however, may help support the peso, a local bank trader said. 

 The government is projecting growth in the first quarter to be around 4.6% on year, slightly better than market expectations of a 4.48% rise. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended at its lowest level in more than two weeks as the yen's fall encouraged short-covering in the U.S. unit, traders said. 

 Buying of U.S. dollars by importers and insurers also helped lift the currency, which closed at NT$34.730, its strongest close since May 9, and up from NT$34.712 Tuesday. 

 Foreign banks bought U.S. dollars early in the session, pushing it to the intraday high of NT$34.740, after the government reported a 1% on-month decline in the April leading indicator. 

 However, U.S. dollar selling by exporters "gushed out in large amounts" in the afternoon, driving the unit to an intraday low of NT$34.708, said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Dollar buying emerged again near the end of the session as banks covered short positions on the back of the yen's weakness, traders said. 

 The local dollar often tracks the yen as Taiwan imports large amounts of goods from Japan and the two compete in some export categories. 

 The Indonesian rupiah weakened slightly in choppy trading due to demand for dollars from importers and companies with foreign debt to repay by the end of the month. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,220 rupiah, up from IDR8,195 Tuesday.

title: Singapore  Dlr Dn Late;  Intervention  Talk Supports USD
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was weaker late Tuesday on U.S. dollar buying by a large local bank, sparking speculation the central bank had intervened on behalf of the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 At 0820 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7240, up from S$1.7212 late Monday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7175 and S$1.7265 intraday. 

 The U.S. currency opened around S$1.7175 and drifted higher initially in line with its moves against the yen, dealers said. 

 Around midafternoon, the U.S. dollar spiked to S$1.7265 on buying by the large local bank, which some players believed was at the behest of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The rise turned out to be brief, and the U.S. dollar slipped to S$1.7250 soon after as market participants took profit, suggesting the talk of MAS intervention may not be true, dealers said. 

 An MAS spokeswoman wouldn't comment on the speculation when contacted by Dow Jones Newswires. "We do not comment on market operations," she said. 

 "The rumors were going round, but they are generally not strong, just here and there," said an Asian bank dealer about the MAS' purported involvement. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise to its intraday high against the Singapore currency coincided with its rise above Y117 against the yen, dealers added. The greenback has since come off that level and was changing hands at Y116.82 at the end of the Asian session. 

 Still, the fact that the stiff U.S. dollar buying emerged around S$1.7220 has been taken to mean the central bank may not tolerate the U.S. dollar falling beyond that mark, dealers said. 

 Dealers expect the U.S. currency to keep between S$1.7220 and S$1.7270 in overnight trade later Tuesday. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were higher Tuesday, as market participants, facing a lack of leads due to the closure of U.S. Treasurys market overnight, focused on the weak domestic economic outlook, dealers said. 

 Bonds have resumed moving higher after a mild sell-off late last week drove prices down to very attractive levels, dealers added. 

 "Expectations of further weakness in the domestic economic numbers in the coming months would allow Singapore Government Securities to remain well-bid in coming weeks," DBS Bank said in a research note. 

 At the end of the session, the yield on two-year bonds was two basis points lower at 0.69%, while the yield on five-year bonds also slipped two basis points to 1.31%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds also fell two basis points to 1.66% and the yield on 10-year bonds fell three basis points to 1.86%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds ended three basis points lower at 2.25%.

By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, May 26 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah
jumped to its strongest level in almost three years early on
Monday, helped by speculation of investment inflows, and most
other Asian currencies also rose against a weakening U.S.
dollar.
    The rupiah rose to around 8,100 per U.S. dollar, a high
since August 2000, powered by last week's central bank comments
that the currency was not overvalued despite recent gains and
could reach the 8,000 per dollar.
    From a four-month low of 9,145 per dollar in March, the
rupiah has surged about 12 percent, backed by global investors
chasing high yields, the government's asset sales programme,
and Jakarta's acceptance of a stronger currency.
 
    The military offensive against Aceh separatists has had
little impact on the rupiah.
    Last week, the Indonesian central bank signalled it would


 give the green light for the sale of a 51 percent stake in Bank 

 Danamon (BDMN.JK) to Singapore's government investment agency, 

 Temasek Holdings, and Deutsche Bank (DBKGn.DE). The sale is 

 expected to raise around $350 million dollars. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said most of the dollar sales on Monday 

 were from Singapore-based banks, while their was talk of some 

 flows related to the asset sales. 

 But a dealer at a European bank in Jakarta said trading 

 volume was just around $40 million in early hours, lending 

 support to views that the move was more sentiment driven. 


 
    He said the rupiah rise was exacerbated by stop-loss dollar
sell orders triggered at 8,250 and then at around 8,200.
    Analysts said that given the market was illiquid, only a
small order was needed to push the rupiah higher.
    "The asset sales picture is driving the rupiah, not so much
the flow but the sentiment itself," said Craig Chan, analyst at
Forecast Ltd.
    Chan said depending on where Bank Indonesia steps in to



curb the rise, the rupiah could touch 8,000 in the near-term



before players reasses the risk of holding the rupiah. The



rupiah has not strengthened past 8,000 per dollar since May



2000.



SUBDUED



Elsewhere, dealers expected trade would be subdued because



markets in both London and New York are closed for a holiday.

    Given the sensitivity to moves in the dollar/yen       ,



dealers said the Singapore dollar was likely to be capped

yen's rise against the dollar.

    Dealers said players were keeping an eye on any central
bank moves to cap baht's rise, even after the bank last week
said the baht was competitive despite recent gains.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Rupiah At 33-Mo High
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies strengthened Monday, prompting verbal intervention by some central banks. 

 The Indonesian rupiah retreated from its intraday peak but remained at a 33-mohth closing high after the central bank governor warned a strong currency would hurt exporters. 

 The dollar ended the local session at 8,175 rupiah, down from IDR8,275 Friday, although off the session low of IDR8,095. Traders said capital inflows into Indonesia and the dollar's broad weakness against regional currencies were factors behind the rupiah's rise. 

 The dollar recouped some of its losses after Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said that "a too rapid rupiah appreciation is not good for business." 

 But he also said the market should set the rupiah's level, indicating that the central bank isn't yet considering significant intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 The chairman of the Indonesian Textile Producers' Association Benny Sutrisno added that the rupiah's rise is likely to cause problems for local manufacturers who export most of their products. 

 "The rupiah's strength is not competitive and bad for exporters," said Benny. "The costs in terms of dollars will go up, while our export revenues in rupiah terms will fall." 

 Meantime, an appreciating won prompted South Korea's central bank to warn it would actively take measures to support the dollar, resulting in the local currency giving up all its early gains. 

 The dollar, which earlier fell to a low of KRW1,190.0, finished at KRW1,199.0, up from 1,194.4 Friday. 

 "The government is concerned over the negative impact of an excessive fall in the dollar-won rate and the consequent market jitters on the local economy," Choi Joong Kyung, director general at the Ministry ofFinance and Economy's international finance bureau, said in a statement. 

 The government will take "various" steps to stabilize the foreign exchange market, including issuing won-denominated foreign exchange stabilization bonds, Choi said. 

 There was speculation the authorities began to buy dollars in the market via state-run banks even before the finance ministry statement was released in the afternoon, traders said. 

 For the most part, regional currencies continued to take their cue from the dollar/yen pair, which stayed below Y117.0 in Asia ahead of holidays in U.S. and U.K Monday. 

 At 0921 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y116.88 compared with Y116.85 in New York and Y117.36 in Tokyo late Friday. 

 "Mostly it's still (a) dollar/yen (story). Support for regional currencies is coming from the yen," said Philip Wee, markets strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. 

 But he noted that domestic demand in the region has been damped by the outbreak of SARS. 

 "That leaves most countries relying on external factors for growth. Increasingly, if there's no improvement in the external outlook, it's quite hard to see currencies (in Asia) continuing their appreciating path," Wee added. 

 "We need to see the dollar/yen's weekly closing (at) below Y116 to see much more downside in dollar/Asia," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar was buoyed by the broadly weaker U.S. currency, with the market shrugging off weaker-than-expected April industrial output data, traders said. 

 Trading volumes dropped sharply ahead of holidays in the U.S. and U.K. Monday. 

 Near the end of local trading hours, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7212, down from S$1.7228 late Friday. 

 Singapore's industrial output fell 5% on year in April due to weak output of electronic goods. A Dow Jones Newswires poll had predicted an average 3.2% rise. 

 Dollar selling and equities-related inflows pushed the Thai baht up to a fresh nine-month high. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 41.745 baht, down from THB41.91 Friday. 

 Traders said Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's remarks on the baht's level, carried in the Thai language Kaohoon tabloid, helped spur dollar sales. 

 The newspaper cited Thaksin as saying the baht's level at around THB41 to the dollar is appropriate and not too strong. Thai exports are still competitive despite the stronger baht, he said. 

 Foreign investment inflows are also supporting the Thai currency but the baht's strength is mainly due to the broad dollar weakness, he said. 

 The Philippine peso firmed on the back of weekend dollar remittance inflows by Filipino working abroad, even as demand for the U.S. unit thinned, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 52.760 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP52.790 Friday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was a tad weaker after the currency of its export competitor South Korea slipped late in the session, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.709, up from NT$34.707 Friday. Trading volume totaled US$327 million, its lowest in two weeks. 

 A Taipei dealer said the central bank may have intervened to ensure the local dollar remained in line with the won, since Taiwanese firms compete with South Korean companies for export markets. 

 Demand for the local dollar by overseas investors trading Taiwan shares remained brisk, dealers said. 

 Foreign investors bought a net NT$3.63 billion worth of shares Monday, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Robust rupiah extends rally.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 21 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah's persistent rally took it to fresh 21-month highs on Wednesday, while the rest of the region kept to dull ranges after an offshore rally driven by the U.S. dollar's fall. 

 Most regionals were rangebound but strong, with the Singapore dollar stuck up a cent from late Tuesday, benefitting from the U.S. dollar's weakness after billionaire investor George Soros said he was selling the greenback. 

 Fears the Japanese authorities will intervene to curb yen gains capped Asian regionals also. Additionally, worries over the rising cases of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) hit the Taiwan dollar. 

 The Thai baht firmed past 42 per dollar to a nine-month high, and the Thailand central bank said the currency was still competitive and it was not intervening. 

 The rupiah, which is up 9.9 percent in two months, has shrugged off the military offensive against Aceh rebels and drew comfort from the new central bank governor Burhanuddin Abdullah's remark on Tuesday that the rupiah was still competitive. 

 "It's a combination of factors - a very weak dollar, very low U.S. interest rates and a decent yield on the rupiah," said David Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of Scotland. 

 But at Wednesday's high of 8,320, which is close to a technical resistance level at 8,300, traders were speculating the rally had to halt soon. 

 Exporters were aggressively selling their receivables in foreign currency, spot and future, and would soon be worried about losing competitiveness, traders said. 

 Meanwhile, the Korean authorities effectively stalled the rallying won by hinting in an unusual manner at intervention. 

 The won paused near 1,193 per dollar after the finance ministry announced plans to issue won-denominated exchange stabilisation bonds soon. 

 "It seems to be a pre-emptive sterilisation of intervention," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS Warburg, Singapore. 

 "The signal out here is that we are going to be issuing these bonds to sterilise intervention, which means we are going to intervene. And, irrespective of whether they issue these bonds, I think they will intervene to protect the won's competitiveness." 

 The Philippine peso ended stronger in light onshore trading, boosted by the yen's rally in offshore deals. 

 Elsewhere, Malaysia unveiled a stimulus package to boost a slowing economy, cutting intervention rates by half a percentage point to 4.5 percent, boosting incomes and announcing plans for an increase in direct spending. 

 The ringgit is pegged at 3.8 per U.S. dollar. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had said there were no plans to move the ringgit peg down despite the dollar's weakness. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0850 GMT Change on the day

text:

 "...the Malaysian economy on Tuesday." (corrects day)


 A corrected story follows. 

 By Vidya Ranganathan 

 SINGAPORE, May 20 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah bucked a regional bearish trend on Tuesday, resuming a rally it had halted last week as bullishness on improving fundamentals prevailed over the risks of the conflict with separatists in Aceh province. 

 On the second day of the Indonesian military offensive in Aceh, the rupiah  hit 8,360 per dollar, its strongest since August 2001 when it had rallied as far as 8,200 per dollar after Megawati Sukarnoputri became president. 

 In late trade, it pared some gains as traders booked profits but still ended up three-quarters of a percent on the day. 

 "It has been counter-intuitive and counter-trend. Either the market is overly complacent over the Aceh issue or the market is treating it as an internal security issue rather than a geopolitical flashpoint," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist with Standard Chartered Bank. 

 "And, it is fair to say that Aceh has been a long-standing situation and to a certain degree is an internal security issue," he said. 

 The rupiah has rallied 9.4 percent in two months, helped by the high yields Indonesian assets offer and the government's willingness to allow the currency to appreciate. 

 At his swearing in ceremony on Tuesday, central bank governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said the rupiah was still competitive. 

 Better than expected first-quarter GDP data on Monday helped prop up the rupiah as the U.S. dollar hit multi-year lows against the yen and euro on Monday, before talk of Japanese intervention lifted the greenback off its lows. 

 The rupiah's low correlation to other high-yielding currencies has also guarded it from the sell-off seen in currencies such as the South African rand over the past week, analysts said. 

 "The attraction of the rupiah is that it has a low correlation with some of the high-yielders and with Asian markets in general, so it has just been left to its own devices," Piron said. 

 "But that is also symptomatic of the fact that it is an illiquid market and contains some restrictions in terms of foreign investment." 

 REST SHADOW YEN 

 The rest of the Asian currencies fell on Tuesday, shadowing the Japanese currency's two yen fall against the dollar from a two-year high on Monday of 115.10 per dollar on talk of sizeable Japanese intervention.

number of probable cases of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) on
Tuesday, as well as the weak yen.

 make their exports expensive.

title: FX  Options-Bets on Sing dlr, won gains as vols rise.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 13 (Reuters) - Asian options traders are betting on another swift and sharp gain in the Singapore dollar, with implied volatilities rising even as it hit multi-month highs against a globally weak U.S. dollar on Tuesday. 


The Singapore dollar  has risen 3.4 percent against the dollar in two
weeks, on the back of a soaring euro       , U.S. economic
uncertainties and signs that the U.S. authorities do not mind a weaker
currency.


 But as the Sing traded around 1.73 on Monday and Tuesday, a level seen in late January where some traders suspect the central Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) intervened to cap its strength, options traders were still betting on further gains. 

 Implied volatility on the one-month Sing dollar option  climbed to 5.15 percent, from 4.5 on Monday and levels below four percent last week. 

 Several risk-reversal deals were reported, involving dual option contracts. One-month risk reversals were quoted at 0.25 on Tuesday, favouring Sing dollar call options 

 "People are buying downside (on dollar/Sing) and selling topside," an options trader said. 

 "They are buying U.S. dollar puts and Sing dollar calls, and financing them by selling U.S. dollar calls and Sing dollar puts," he added. 

 Under those deals, holders stood to make huge profits if the Sing dollar rose further and big losses if it fell fast, but see little impact if the currency steadied at current levels. 

 Risk reversals measure the premium investors are prepared to pay to buy call options over put options. 

 In the Korean market, players were clearly bullish on the won, which was trading around 1,200 per dollar on Tuesday. 

 The bullishness saw traders buying won call, dollar put options, even after the Bank of Korea cut its overnight call rate to 4.00 percent - matching its record low - on Thursday. 

 The won has stabilised after rising to a one-month high near 1,189 last week. Implied one-month won volatility was also steady at 8.75 percent.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Knocked by euro,  intervention  risk.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies could not
rise against a troubled U.S. dollar on Friday because traders
feared intervention to protect exports, and they weakened
sharply against the euro as it surged to a record high against
the yen.
    Dealers blamed the snap in the regional currency rally on
the yen. Worries, and threats, about Japanese intervention saw
it pull back from Wednesday's 10-month highs near 116 per
dollar, and it also hit a life low against the euro.
    That move weakened the Singapore dollar past 2.0 per euro
to its lowest against the single European currency since its
launch in January 1999.
    Dealers and analysts believe most Asian central banks had
been buying dollars in recent sessions to protect export
competitiveness in the key U.S. market, and this had triggered
profit-taking that kept regional currencies off their highs.
    Against the U.S.



 dollar, the Singapore dollar, Thai baht,
Korean won and the Taiwan dollar all held below two-month highs
hit after the Federal Reserve had warned about the risk of
deflation on Tuesday.
 
    "Asia is quasi-pegged against the yen," said Ray Farris,
Credit Suisse First Boston's strategist in Singapore.
    "They (Asian central banks) are quasi-pegging against the



yen, so if euro/yen goes higher, euro/Asia goes higher, and



they are doing that essentially to ensure that their



trade-weighted indices are stable or depreciating," he added.



The Singapore dollar and South Korean won have lost about



0.4 percent and 1.2 percent respectively against the U.S.



dollar so far this year, but against the euro their losses are



about 11 percent each in the same period.



Even the high yielding Philippine peso and Indonesian



rupiah, which have gained about two percent and 4.7 percent



respectively against the dollar, have lost some 7.5 and 4.6



percent of value against the euro this year.



Analysts said those losses against the euro showed that



while some Asian currencies may have gained against the dollar,



the overall trade-weighted performances was not as strong.



 
    NEW LOW
    The euro/Sing cross traded as high as 2.0088 on Friday.
    Dealers said the trade has gained popularity in recent days



as the euro, along with the yen and U.S dollar, was a major



component of the undisclosed trade-weighted index the Singapore


Monetary Authority manages the currency against.



"I suspect part of this story is the euro/yen game or the



Sing dollar trade against its (trade weighted) basket," said



Simon Flint, strategist at Bank of America in Singapore.



He said players who had been recently taking a bullish view



on the Sing dollar against the basket currencies, on the back



of U.S. dollar weakness, had been hit by the euro's persistent



rise.



Some dealers said the pullback from two-month highs against



the U.S. dollar may also have contributed to some players



taking what seems to be a safer bet - short Sing dollar and



long euro.



The Singapore dollar weakened past 1.74 per dollar late on



Friday, having avoided Wednesday's high of 1.7365 in the



morning.



The Thai baht fell to around 42.60 per dollar before paring



some of the losses, but it remained clear of this week's



two-month high around 42.40.



 
    The peso eased to around 52.41 per dollar, a day after it
hit 51.88, its strongest since September 13 last year.
    The Indonesian rupiah rose back to Thursday's 11-month high
