title: Most Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; Yen Casts Shadow On Region
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies tumbled Friday, caught in the downdraft of a falling yen. 

 The yen fell against both the dollar and the euro, prompting speculation that the Japanese government was covertly intervening in foreign exchange markets to weaken the local currency. 

 The euro climbed as high as Y135.26 in late afternoon trade, its strongest performance against the yen since the European currency debuted in January 1999. The euro also drew support from the European Central Bank's decision Thursday to stand pat on interest rates. 

 The dollar remained comfortably above the Y117 level for the entire session, adding to talk that the Ministry of Finance was keeping a floor under the dollar. Japanese authorities believe a weaker yen will stimulate export growth and help the country escape its long-running economic malaise. 

 The yen's tumble pressured other Asian currencies lower, except for the rupiah, which continued to lure investors attracted by relatively higher returns in Indonesia. 

 Analysts say the dollar's sharp recovery to a high of Y117.50 Friday from a low of near Y116 Thursday bore the fingerprints of official intervention. 

 "We have been expecting for some time that Japanese intervention would resume ...," UBS Warburg said in a research note. 

 The intervention rumors were fueled by comments from Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa that he believes the yen is too strong against the dollar. Shiokawa declined to comment on possible intervention. 

 The Singapore dollar lost ground after climbing to a two-month high against the U.S. dollar Thursday. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7420, up from S$1.7372 late Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar briefly dropped below S$1.7400 in the morning session, before bouncing back in line with its gains against the yen. 

 Despite the decline in the Singapore dollar, dealers said sentiment toward the currency remained positive in light of the city-state's progress in the fight against severe acute respiratory syndrome. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also tracked the yen lower in thin trading. The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.775, up from NT$34.719 Thursday. Trading volume fell to US$257 million from US$402 million Thursday. 

 Importers and exporters were mostly on the sidelines Friday, looking for clear signs as to the near-term direction for the local currency. 

 Taiwanese exporters hold large amounts of U.S. dollar's which could limit the currency's upside in coming sessions. However, continuing reports of new SARS cases in Taiwan have damped sentiment toward the local currency. 

 Some dealers in Seoul said the dollar's rise against the won may have been partly the result of intervention by South Korean monetary authorities aiming to cap the local unit's recent strength. 

 The won's appreciation of nearly 5% against the dollar over the past month has caused South Korean authorities to worry that the country's export competitiveness could suffer. 

 "The government made it clear that it doesn't want the dollar to fall further," a dealer at KorAm Bank said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,200.4 won, up from Wednesday's close of KRW1,199.0. The Seoul foreign exchange market was closed Thursday due to holiday. 

 The rupiah continued to hover near a 21-month high against the dollar as investors remained bullish about economic prospects in Indonesia. 

 The dollar was quoted at IDR8,545 in late Asian trading, down from IDR8,555 late Thursday. 

 The sale of the 51% Bank Danamon stake to a consortium comprising Singapore's Temasek Holdings and Deustche Bank has helped boost market confidence that the government is serious in implementing economic reform programs. 

 The central bank also cut short-term interest rates Friday for the fourth time this year in a move that is expected to spur economic growth, and help relieve the bad-debt problem in the country. 

 The Thai baht weakened in line with its regional counterparts. Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 42.545 baht, up from THB42.450 late Thursday. 

 However, the Thai baht is expected to draw support from the country's strong export performance going forward. 

 Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik said Friday he expects April exports to grow 15% to 20% from a year earlier, based on strong preliminary data from the customs department. Customs-based exports were up 16% on year in March. 

 Against the peso, the dollar closed at PHP52.340, up from PHP52.150 Thursday. 

 Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura Friday said he was satisfied with the peso's current level against the U.S. dollar. 

 Over the past two weeks, remittance inflows from overseas Filipino workers, sending their pay home for tuition fees ahead of the start of a new school term, have fueled a rally in the peso recently.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Gains checked by  intervention  fears.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
SINGAPORE, May 8 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso pulled
back from an eight-month high and the Indonesian rupiah pared
its rally to an 11-month peak on Thursday as suspected
intervention stalled the regional slide in the U.S. dollar.
The Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar edged
back from two-month highs as the Japanese talked the yen down
from 10-month highs near 116 yen.
Dealers said suspected intervention by several Asian
central banks, to cap currencies and protect export
competitiveness, had prompted some closing of short dollar
positions.
Korean financial markets were closed for a holiday.
"Asian being an export-oriented region, the central banks
here have an incentive to try and stem any rapid appreciation
in their currencies, as the recovery in the U.S. and global
economy is still very uncertain," Bank of America analyst
Sameer Goel said.
The peso ended local trade at 52.15 per dollar after
opening at 51.88, its strongest since September 13 last year.



It has risen about six percent since mid-March, when it was
above 55 per dollar and targetting record lows.
Dealers in Manila said remittances from overseas workers
for the school admission season in May had helped the peso.
An added boost came from the weak dollar and the search for
higher yield by investors, overshadowing worries about ratings
downgrades and large budget deficits.
But talk of central bank activity pushed the peso to the
weaker side of 52 per dollar in afternoon trade.
Central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the peso
should hold steady around current levels.
"This is the rate we always thought it should be if we did
not have the extraneous factors," he said after the bank left
its official rates unchanged at its meeting on Thursday.
Another Asian high yielder, the Indonesian rupiah, rallied



to 8,495 per dollar, its strongest since June 2002, even as



benchmark interest rates eased. But talk the central bank was



buying dollars pulled it back to around 8,550.



The rate on one-month Bank Indonesia paper fell to 10.91



percent at Wednesday's auction from 11.06 percent last week,



while three-month paper fell to 10.89 percent from 11.29 last



month.



However, dealers said the rupiah, which has risen about



seven percent since March, was still attractive as interest



rates would be double-digit for some time.



A Reuters poll this week found an average forecast of 10.28
percent for the benchmark one-month paper by the end of 2003.
SARS RISK UNWOUND
The Singapore dollar stayed close to a two-month high of
1.7365 per U.S. dollar, but was wary of further gains.
Dealers said the weak U.S. dollar and a market view the



deadly SARS virus, which killed 27 people on the island, was



under control had prompted an unwinding of the SARS risk



premium priced into the currency during March and April.



But the Sing was checked by the steadier dollar and


intervention fears after dealers said the Monetary Authority of


Singapore might have checked rates with local banks on



Wednesday - seen as a warning against sharp currency moves.



The Thai baht held a 42.40-42.44 per dollar range amid



suspicion the Bank of Thailand was buying dollars for a second



day.



Dealers said a desire to avoid triggering stop-loss



dollar-sell orders lined beyond 42.40 also helped cap the baht.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Up after Fed, fear  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies gathered upward momentum on Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve's warning of economic weakness drove the U.S. dollar to deeper lows, but fears of intervention by local central banks restricted their gains. 

 The Singapore dollar, Korean won, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar all climbed to nearly two-month highs in morning deals, but then pared some gains. 

 The Philippine peso rose to an eight-month high of 52.0, extending its recent bull run after the country's tax agency reported tax collections in April exceeded the target, but then it also stalled. 

 "The U.S. dollar downtrend is still pretty much entrenched," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist with BNP Paribas. 

 "I think the central banks are watching the markets, otherwise we'd see the Asian currencies higher." 

 Traders said they suspected the Bank of Thailand had intervened. They also suspected the Philippine central bank had checked the peso around 52, and Korean authorities might have intervened to buy dollars after warning against excessive strength in the won early on Wednesday. 

 Japanese authorities also repeated their resolve to act against excessive currency moves. 

 The U.S. dollar fell to four-year lows against the euro and nearly two-month lows against the yen after the Fed left rates steady at Tuesday's meeting and warned of the risks to growth. It got some respite after U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow reiterated support for the strong dollar policy. 

 SARS UNWOUND 

 The rise in regional currencies also reflected the unwinding of trades centred around the risk from the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) outbreak, traders said. 

 At its morning high of 1.7385/90, the Sing dollar was up three cents or two percent from Friday and had reversed the losses it incurred since mid-March, when the Iraq war began and the first local cases of SARS were detected. 

 Barclays Capital said the move might reflect a policy desire to have a neutral trade-weighted index. 

 "We believe that the Sing dollar's strength mainly reflects the MAS' desire to steer the Sing dollar back to a neutral monetary policy setting now that the SARS epidemic has been brought under control in Singapore," it said in a note. 

 BANK INDONESIA SURPRISES 

 The rupiah fluctuated between a 10-week high of 8,525 per dollar struck offshore and a low of 8,595, before ending near the highs which took its gains in two weeks to three percent. 

 But the central Bank Indonesia surprised markets with a statement hinting the gains were substantially due to short-term capital inflows seeking some of Asia's highest yielding papers. 

 "In regards to indications about the inflows of short-term funds...Bank Indonesia sees it as necessary to create a conducive climate to lure long-term funds," the bank said. It did not elaborate. 

 Traders had suspected foreign money for the privatisation of a majority stake in Bank Danamon had primarily boosted the rupiah, besides funds seeking the high yield in the country. 

 The baht's rise beyond 42.50 was fleeting. It stayed just a shade weaker than 42.50 with markets turning cautious after its 1.5 percent rise in under two weeks and amid talk the central bank was buying dollars. 

 The Korean won ended onshore trade at a two-month high of 1,199 per dollar, after coming off a 1,188 peak. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0827 GMT Change on the day

title: Sing dlr, baht rise on yen gains, worries linger.
text:
0040 GMT - The Singapore dollar        edges slightly
higher, following the U.S. dollar's decline against the yen
  and euro       .
    - Singapore dollar rises to around 1.7775 per U.S. dollar,
from a one-week low of 1.7801 hit late Thursday.
    - Dealers say given the consensus that the Sing dollar was

 band of the central bank, the U.S. dollar weakness prompted 

 players to square out of their long U.S. dollar positions. 

 - "The central bank has in the past said that it does allow 

 the currency to trade beyond its policy band for sometime 

 before it decides to intervene," said a dealer at a U.S. bank 

 in Singapore. 

 - Most analysts believe the weaker end of the policy band, 

 used by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to manage its 

 monetary policy, was around 1.7780. 

 - However, a lack of confidence on the yen's strength and 

 worries about the economic impact of the Severe Acute 

 Respiratory Syndrome is likely to keep U.S. dollar demand 

 intact at dips.

the 42.80 per dollar level in early offshore trade.
    - Dealers in Singapore say baht likely to take cue from



moves in yen and Sing dollar and could edge slightly higher to



around the 42.70 level before fresh dollar demand from



importers kicks in.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed, Singapore Dlr Still Pressured
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Wednesday at the tail end of a lack luster trading session during which the Singapore dollar's malaise continued as worries over the economic effects of the deadly SARS outbreak lingered, traders said. 

 Concerns over SARS also loomed large in Hong Kong and China, the two countries where SARS has claimed the most victims. The premium on one year Hong Kong dollar forwards remained at five-month highs despite a HK$11.8 billion government relief package to cushion the economic impact of the SARS outbreak. 

 The one-year forward was quoted at a premium of 305-315 to spot late Wednesday, up from 290-300 Tuesday. 

 Meantime, the discount on the benchmark one-year non-deliverable forward rate on the Chinese yuan continued to narrow, and was quoted around 105/65 points to the spot rate late Wednesday, from 145/85 late Tuesday, and 350/330 Monday. 

 In Singapore, the other main SARS-hit country in Asia, concerns about the health of the economy continued to damp market sentiment, dealers said. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7770, up from S$1.7758 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Tuesday, the government said visitor arrivals slumped 68% on year to 48,600 for the week of April 8-14 as tourists continued to stay away to avoid contracting SARS. So far, the outbreak has killed 16 people and infected around 178 in the city state. 

 Still, any further weakness in the Singapore dollar may be limited in the near term by the widely-held view that it is currently trading near the limits of the central bank's policy band. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore last week reaffirmed its neutral monetary policy, in effect putting a cap to further Singapore dollar selling as players worried about triggering central bank intervention, dealers said. 

 Among other currencies, the Philippine peso was also modestly weaker, while the Indonesian rupiah, South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar were marginally stronger. The Thai baht was little changed. 

 The dollar closed at PHP53.510 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP52.495 Tuesday. 

 Apart from follow-through dollar buying by companies for month-end requirements, worries over the government's continuing budget deficit overshoot and the economic impact of SARS, also dominated the market. 

 "The peso's fall, however, was capped on speculation that the central bank stepped in to provide dollar liquidity in defense of the local unit," a trader said. Central bank officials couldn't be immediately reached. 

 As against the South Korean won, the dollar closed at KRW1,218.9, down from KRW1,219.4 Tuesday. 

 Market players took profits following the dollar's sharp gain in the previous session, while exporters sold above KRW1,220, traders said. 

 "There seems to be a consensus in the market that the dollar's 10-won surge yesterday (Tuesday) was overdone," said a trader at a major South Korean bank. 

 Trading wasn't very active as players monitored developments in Beijing where the U.S., North Korea and China are holding talks on Pyongyang's suspected nuclear arms program. The talks are scheduled to conclude Friday. 

 "People aren't expecting big results from the talks and prospects for the Beijing meeting aren't at all rosy," said another trader at a foreign financial institution. 

 Selling by Taiwan exporters and offshore players pulled the U.S. unit down a tad to end at 34.812 versus the local dollar, from NT$34.816 at the previous close. 

 Bids for U.S. dollars from local insurers and importers at the NT$34.80 level capped the local unit's gains, traders said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah resumed its upward march after a brief breather in the previous session following six days of gains. 

 The dollar ended Wednesday at IDR8,730, down from IDR8,740 Tuesday. Analysts attribute the rupiah's upward momentum to investors' search for higher yields. 

 As against the Thai baht, the dollar ended the local session at THB42.755, quite steady compared with THB42.760 Tuesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; Coalition War Advance Lifts Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Broad dollar strength fueled by the progress of coalition military forces in Iraq kept most Asian currencies on the defensive Friday. 

 The Singapore dollar, under additional pressure due to concerns over the spread of a lethal strain of pneumonia, fell to a five-month low against the dollar. 

 Reports that soldiers from the U.S. 3rd Infantry Division were in the process of securing control of Baghdad's main airport boosted the dollar against its major rivals, as well as regional currencies. 

 However, a further weak U.S. economic data and uncertainty about how the "battle of Baghdad" may play out tempered the enthusiasm for the U.S. unit. 

 The Institute for Supply Management reported Thursday that U.S. service-sector activity contracted in March due to war concerns, ending 13 straight months of expansion. The Labor Department, meanwhile, said claims for unemployment insurance rose to their highest level in 11 months. 

 "We see a sluggish (U.S.) postwar recovery as the main risk to any forecast - although likely a limited one, since interest rate cuts would follow," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 For Asian economies, however, a more immediate concern is the impact of severe acute respiratory syndrome, a deadly virus that has claimed 73 lives in the region and infected hundreds more. 

 The Singapore dollar has been particularly hard hit by the negative sentiment fueled by SARS. 

 In late Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7790, up from S$1.7715 late Thursday. The U.S. dollar had hit a five-month high of S$1.7800 in overnight trading. 

 Market participants were emboldened to sell the Singapore dollar after it weakened beyond a level at which some analysts thought the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to support the currency. 

 This was interpreted by some traders as an implicit indication of the MAS's willingness to allow a weaker Singapore dollar to act as a cushion against a slowing economy. 

 Against the South Korean won, the dollar edged up to KRW1,258.0 at Friday's close from KRW1,255.0 a day earlier in light trading. 

 The U.S. currency's gains were limited by anticipated exporter dollar sales above the KRW1,260/dollar level and rumors of possible government intervention. 

 Importers, meanwhile, were believed to be looking at the U.S. unit falling to KRW1,255 before stepping in to buy the greenback, players said. 

Intervention by Taiwan's central bank helped the U.S. dollar gain against the New Taiwan dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.825, up from Thursday's NT$34.812. 

 The official intervention pulled the U.S. dollar off its intraday low of NT$34.801 late in the session. 

 Taiwanese authorities routinely intervene to weaken the local currency when they believe it is trading out of line with its regional peers. Weakening the currency is seen as a way of preserving the country's export competitiveness. 

 The Philippine peso was pressured by dollar demand from oil importers. 

 The dollar closed at its intraday high of 53.250 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.110 Thursday. 

 Traders said oil companies stepped up their dollar purchases to cover their import requirements ahead of a long weekend. 

 The Philippine financial markets are closed Monday for a public holiday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah strengthened slightly as fears of violent anti-war protests in the country continued to subside. 

 The dollar was quoted at 8,885 rupiah in late trading, down from IDR8,990 late Thursday. The dollar had traded as high as IDR8,910 during the session. 

 Market participants have been concerned that the U.S.-led military attacks on Iraq would spark a fierce anti-west backlash in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim country. But, so far anti-war protests remain largely peaceful. 

 Against the baht, the dollar was quoted at THB43.090 near the end of Asian trading, up from THB42.980 a day earlier. 

 The pair traded in a fairly narrow range of THB43.050 to THB43.140 during Friday's session.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Down Late; SARS, War News Boost Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies weakened against the dollar Thursday, pressured by a combination of dollar-positive Iraq war news and concerns that a deadly pneumonia virus could derail regional economic growth. 

 The advance of U.S. troops to within miles of Baghdad, with relatively few casualties, provided a lift for the dollar as hopes were renewed that the war could be relatively short-lived. 

 However, some market participants expressed concern that once inside the Iraqi capital, coalition forces might get bogged down in bloody street fighting that could include the use of chemical or biological weapons by Iraqi troops. 

 "It is still not clear how the war will turn out," DBS Bank said in a research note. "The significant push by U.S.-led forces toward Baghdad over the past 24 hours does provide some hope that the war may end soon." 

 The parade of investment banks cutting their economic growth forecasts for Asia due to the spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome continued Thursday. 

 ING Financial Markets was the latest to weigh in, trimming its 2003 growth forecast for Hong to 2.5% from 3%. Over the past few days more than half-a-dozen banks and brokerages have cut their forecasts for various Asian economies, citing the negative impact SARS is having on the tourism, retail and consumer services industries. 

 Asia has been the epicenter of the SARS outbreak, accounting for more than 90% of the 2,223 cases reported worldwide. In addition, 72 of the 78 SARS deaths globally have occurred in Asia. 

 The Singapore dollar has been hit particularly hard by the SARS outbreak. Singapore ranks third behind China and Hong Kong in reported SARS cases, although officials said there are signs the situation is stabilizing in the city-state. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7715, up from S$1.7690 late Wednesday. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise was kept in check by concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene to keep the local currency within a trade-weighted band that the MAS uses as a guideline for managing the Singapore dollar's movements. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar closed at its intraday high of NT$34.812, up from Wednesday's close of NT$34.798. 

 Exporters helped slow the local currency's fall by selling U.S. dollars above the NT$34.80 level, traders said. 

 The South Korean won gave up its early gains to finish marginally weaker. Foreigners' sales of local stocks weighed on the won late in the session. 

 Foreigners sold a net 58.6 billion won in shares Thursday. 

 The dollar finished at KRW1,255.0, slightly up from Wednesday's close of KRW1,254.0. 

 A stronger yen and a report from local online news provider MoneyToday underpinned the won early in the session, dealers said.

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, April 1 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar
tripped off one-week highs early on Tuesday amid further signs
that the outbreak of a killer virus in Asia was affecting
sentiment.
 
    Most other regional currencies were pushed higher by the
U.S. dollar's weakness against major currencies.
    However, gains were slim. War in Iraq, tensions in North
Korea and recent economic data both in the region and outside
have weighed on sentiment.
    The Singapore dollar eased to around 1.7670 per dollar from


 Monday's one-week high of 1.7623 following news that the killer 

 virus - Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) - claimed 

 its fourth victim in the island-state on Monday. Schools in the 

 city have been shut and 945 people quarantined. 

 However, analysts said the impact of the outbreak, that has 

 also killed people in Hong Kong, Vietnam and China, had been 

 muted so far in other currency markets. 

 "Equity markets in Asia suffered huge losses overnight as 

 players worried about the impact of SARS virus on economic 

 growth, but this has thus far not found sympathy from the forex

 markets," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS 

 Warburg. 

 Singapore-based Baweja said several economies in the region 

 risked growth downgrades if the outbreak hit the region's 

 multibillion dollar tourism industry. 

 Dealers in Singapore said some caution in pushing the Sing

 The Thai baht  held steady at around 42.85 per dollar

title: FX  Asia: SARS, Weak Econ To Drive Singapore Dollar South
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column



SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A cold wind has been blowing from the north,
giving much of Asia - and its currencies - the chills.


 The mysterious flu-like disease - known as the severe respiratory syndrome or SARS because the virus that causes it has yet to be identified - has killed at least 62 and infected over 1,600 across three continents. Most of the victims were in mainland China, where the disease is believed to have originated, and Hong Kong. 

 In Singapore, one of the worst affected places in the region, tourism has borne the brunt of the health scare, and with it the Singapore dollar. Four people in Singapore have died and over 90 have the disease. 

 Since the first cases were reported in early March, the U.S. dollar has risen to S$1.7740 in intraday trading - the highest level this year. At 0655 GMT Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was changing hands at S$1.7665. 

 The scare couldn't have come at a worse time. The Singapore economy was already poised to turn in a weaker performance, taking the impact of the Iraq war into consideration. 

 Now, with the SARS virus on the loose, the economy could weaken even further. Over the weekend, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Lee Hsien Loong said gross domestic product could expand at the lower end of the government's forecast 2%-to-5% this year. Some private-sector economists have slashed their gross domestic product forecasts to a range of between 2.0% and 3.5%. 


   NODX Up, Production Index Falls In Feb



G.K. Goh Research, for instance, now expects GDP to expand 2% from
3.8% previously, and for GDP in the second quarter to grow 1.7% from 3%
previously. The firm's forecasts assume the health problem will stretch
another six to seven months.



"It's the combined effect of everything, the impact of SARS, and the
risk of the war going into the third quarter, and the
weaker-than-expected manufacturing numbers," Song Seng Wun, G.K. Goh's
regional economist, said.



Recent economic data have begun showing the impact of the global
uncertainties. The important manufacturing sector, for instance, has
shown a conflicting performance.



Non-oil domestic exports for February rose a nominal 23% over the year
to S$7.75 billion, stronger than January's 18.3% increase, as sales of
both electronic and non-electronic products remained strong. However,
the more forward-looking industrial output index slipped 1.4% over the
year for the same month. The index's fall spooked the currency market
which had expected a rise of 12.5%. The news sent the Singapore dollar
down about 15 points to S$1.7682 against the U.S. dollar.



Meanwhile, analysts are also starting to assess the potential damage
on the economy from the SARS-related concerns. One industry they are
looking at closely is tourism, and the knock-on effects on the commerce
and retail sectors.



The stock market has already started to reflect some of these
concerns. Share prices of several hotel operators, airlines and retail
firms with both local and regional operations have already fallen as
investors expect these firms to be hard hit.



Tourism, which accounts for about 10% of GDP, depends heavily on
visitors from regional countries, the number one market being Indonesia.
Last week, the Indonesian government issued a statement warning its
citizens not to travel to countries affected by SARS, including
Singapore.



G.K. Goh's Song said the impact on tourism could last right through to
the end of the year, especially taking into account the prospects of a
more prolonged war.



The Singapore Tourism Board told Dow Jones Newswires exclusively last
week that preliminary indicators showed that 440,682 visitors arrived in
Singapore in the March 1-23 period, 8.8% lower than a year ago.



   Tourism Board's 2003 Forecasts To Stay



Official data for February have yet to be released, but for January,
tourism arrivals were up 7.4% over the year, with the increase coming
mostly from the China market.



For the full year, the tourism board had forecast growth of 1%-to-3%
for both visitor arrivals and revenues from tourism-related services.
The board said that it remained confident of that forecast as long as
the war doesn't drag and the global economy isn't "severely affected."



"Domestically, the economic impact of the SARS outbreak on top of the
hesitant economic numbers, will limit any undue SGD strength," Bank of
Tokyo-Mitsubishi said in a research report Monday.



The local currency's response to the SARS scare has so far been
orderly, which means that the Monetary Authority of Singapore is
unlikely to intervene in any way. It is also unlikely to change its
policy stance, which currently is in neutral. This means that the MAS
lets the Singapore dollar trade within an undisclosed band against a
basket of its trade partners' currencies.



If the economy weakens further, there is a likelihood that the
authority could loosen policy further to help exports, economists said.
In that situation, the Singapore dollar can be expected to soften even
more.



In the meantime, the currency pair is expected to test the upper limit
of the MAS's preferred range. Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at
United Overseas Bank Ltd., who believes the upper limit is between
S$1.7800 and S$1.7815, said that, on a trade-weighted basis, the
Singapore dollar is currently at its weakest point since January 2002.



Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi economist Emmanuel Ng, also said the
trade-weighted Singapore dollar currently stands in the weaker half of
the policy band, and believes the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair
could test his estimated limit of S$1.7780-S$1.7800.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won's woes multiply, peso plunges.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 12 (Reuters) - The Korean won led the pack of weakening Asian currencies on Wednesday after an accounting scandal spurred an onslaught on the currency which was already pressured by persistent geopolitical risks. The Philippines was the other weak spot in the region. The peso dropped as low as 55.10 per dollar, a fresh 26-month low. 

 The weakness in these two overshadowed the Singapore dollar's slide to a three-week low as the yen and regional currencies ceded ground to a U.S. dollar benefitting from Washington's delay of a U.N. vote on military action against Iraq. 

 SK GROUP SCANDAL HURTS WON 

 Traders said the unearthing of a $1.2 billion accounting scandal at Korea's fourth biggest conglomerate SK Group hurt all Korean markets. Stocks fell to a 17-month low, the won ended onshore trade at a five-month low of 1,245, credit swap spreads widened, and bonds fell sharply. 

 The won market even disregarded warnings by authorities and some suspected intervention through state banks. 

 Even an assurance by the central bank that it was considering providing funds to financial companies to stabilise the markets did not calm the won. 

 "Markets are beginning to realise that what looked a couple of months ago like a story that was rosy on all fronts for Korea now looks exactly the opposite," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan. 

 "You have got global and local geopolitical risks, a new government that seems to be messing up everything they touch, such as bilateral relations with the U.S., the corporate sector." 

 And, because the authorities had been slow in voicing concern over the moves, bearishness had been amplified, he said. 

 Additionally, a tolerable cost of carrying a short won position and a still not-so-steep forward curve implied there would be no hurry to unwind short won positions, Malcolm said. 

 The SK Group scandal took some attention away from tensions over North Korea's nuclear plans and missile tests, which had been bothering the won, amid reports of further deployment of U.S. warplanes in the South. 

 Bank of America said in its commentary on Wednesday the Korean authorities may be quite content with a weakening won. 

 "The policy preference during a weakening economy would likely be a weaker currency. The discomfort is probably due to the sharp move. We stay won negative," it said. 

 PESO'S SLOW ROUT 

 The peso closed at its third 26-month low in as many days this week as demand for dollars from oil companies building up their reserves before a likely Gulf war continued. But other fundamental and technical reasons were also working against it. 

 For one, the steep drop has brought the peso close to its historic low of 55.75, hit in volatile trade in January 2001 as President Joseph Estrada was being forced from office, which puts it into uncharted territory where there are were no technical barriers. 

 Fundamentally, last week's bombings in the southern Philippines only added to the peso's woes, which include rising oil prices, a growing budget deficit, and uncertainty over whether its new anti-money laundering laws would be approved by the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force. 

 On Wednesday, central bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco told reporters the peso was affected by war jitters. 

 "As soon as this source of uncertainty is over, peso should recover," he said. 

 RUPIAH, BAHT FOLLOW 

 The Thai baht followed the Sing dollar, with traders reporting some short positions in both these currencies being squeezed out as they fell. 

 But analysts also pointed to the consistent sales of Thai stocks by foreign investors in the past week. 

 Analysts dismissed market speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to push the Sing dollar down, saying even at its highest it had been within the undisclosed trade-weighted band authorities manage it in. 

 The Taiwan dollar finally succumbed to the weakness in neighbouring Korea and fell to a one-week low. 

 The Indonesian rupiah fell only slightly. Markets were paying close attention to the varying news of asset sales by the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA). 

 A Singapore-led consortium is leading a bid for a stake in Bank Danamon, but IBRA also said it would halt the restructuring of Asia Pulp & Paper's Indonesian debts until creditors clarified a letter sent to the country's president. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0901 GMT Change on the day

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late; Off Early High Vs US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was steady late Monday after selling by local banks pulled it off its morning high against the U.S. currency and amid broader U.S. dollar weakness, dealers said. 

 At 0830 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7360, flat with S$1.7357 late Friday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7340 and S$1.7365 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7345 in the local market and briefly touched a session low of S$1.7340, before bouncing back up to around S$1.7340-S$1.7350 midmorning as it strengthened versus the yen. 

 The U.S. dollar inched up to its session high after the midday break, allegedly lifted by modest bids by local banks, despite the U.S. currency having gained little ground against other regional currencies, including the yen. 

 "I expected (U.S. dollar) support to be around the late Friday low of S$1.7325, but we didn't even reach there, before the (U.S.) dollar bounced," an Asian bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 According to traders, the buying may have been on behalf of the local central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, even as concerns of similar intervention by other regional central banks were circulating in the market. 

 The MAS currently retains a neutral exchange rate-driven monetary policy stance, though it's believed to prefer only a limited strengthening in the local currency against the U.S. dollar in the interest of maintaining the republic's export competitiveness. 

 Most dealers said continued fears over the prospects of a U.S.-led war with Iraq, and its implications for the global economy, will continue to be the focus of regional financial markets. The U.S. dollar will be under pressure as a result. 

 "All the talk that war may be imminent is expectedly keeping the (U.S.) dollar heavy on the topside here in Asia," the Asian bank dealer said. 

 Looking ahead, dealers expect the U.S. dollar to continue to face selling pressure and support at S$1.7325 isn't likely to hold in the near-term. Next support lies at the psychologically important S$1.7300 mark. 

 The U.S. currency is expected to meet resistance at S$1.7380. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were higher late Monday, as they tracked the late Friday rally in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. 

 Local bond yields tumbled yet again to fresh historic lows in brisk buying activity, as investors, concerned about the prospects of a war, continued to seek refuge in safe-haven instruments, especially longer-term bonds.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up;Singapore $ Ignores Econ Data
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- A firmer yen guided most Asian currencies higher late Thursday amid generally muted reaction to local economic data and other news. 

 But trading ranges were narrow as suspicion of stealth intervention by Japanese authorities put a floor under the dollar-yen rate. 

 "The dollar/yen has been the main factor in the market. The rest of the dollar/Asians are being weighed down," by the U.S. unit's weakness against the yen, said a regional currency trader at a European bank. 

 "Generally, the dollar looks a bit heavy," against regional units, said a trader at another foreign bank in Singapore. 

 The U.S. unit briefly breached the Y117.00 psychological support for the first time since Sept. 3. 

 Japan's Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Zembei Mizoguchi reiterated the ministry is watching the foreign exchange market closely and is "always ready" to intervene if needed. 

 He declined to comment on whether the MOF has been carrying out covert interventions this week. 

 There was little sign of other Asian monetary authorities intervening to check the dollar's slide against their own currencies, though some traders think the Bank of Thailand may have bought the U.S. unit when it neared the 42.65 baht level earlier in Asia. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around THB42.58, down from THB42.75 at the close of the local session Wednesday. 

 United Overseas Bank in a report also noted some talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have been in the market, though it was skeptical of those rumors. 

 The bank said the local dollar was not anywhere near the stronger end of the MAS's current policy band - which it estimates to be between $1.7300-$1.7450 to the U.S. unit - so there was no need for intervention. 

 Late in the local session, the Singapore dollar was quoted around S$1.7349 per U.S. unit, from S$1.7344 late Wednesday. 

 Market players largely ignored the Ministry of Trade and Industry's detailed assessment of the city state's economic performance for last year. 

 The ministry confirmed the earlier 2.2% GDP growth estimate for 2002, despite a revision of fourth-quarter growth to 3% from the previously estimated 2.6%. It also issued a mixed outlook for the domestic economy amid continuing uncertainty over a possible U.S.-led war with Iraq. 

 The data came a day before Singapore's budget statement for the next fiscal year starting April 1. 

 The Taiwan dollar rose as exporters sold the U.S. currency to pay salaries and other monthly expenses on the last trading day for the month, traders said. 

 The yen's gains were also a boost for the local dollar, which closed at its intraday high of NT$34.746 to the U.S. unit, strengthening from Wednesday's NT$34.784. 

 Traders suspected the central bank of intervening in the afternoon session, but this was offset by U.S. dollar selling by exporters. 

 Taiwan's financial markets will be closed Friday for a public holiday. 

 Against the South Korean won, the dollar ended at KRW1,187.0, slightly down from KRW1,188.5 in the previous session. The intraday range was a narrow KRW1,185.1 to KRW1,189.0. 

 Regular end-of-month dollar selling by exporters was "less than expected this month" and mostly offset by importers' buying, a dealer in South Korea said. 

 There was little reaction to the naming of Kim Jin-Pyo as South Korea's new finance minister. A trader said the appointment wasn't a surprise. 

 Generally, market sentiment is toward buying dollars on dips "considering lingering geopolitical concerns about North Korea and worries about the current account deficit (in Korea) and rising oil prices," another dealer said. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar closed at the intraday high of 54.375 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.350 Wednesday. 

 A foreign bank trader said there was dollar inflow from Filipinos working overseas, but this failed to aid the peso as they were snapped up by corporates and banks building up their holdings of the U.S. currency. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar ended at 8,895 rupiah, from IDR8,890 Wednesday. 

 Fear of central bank intervention capped any further rises in the dollar, traders said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down as  intervention  fears resurface.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Asian currencies erased part of their offshore gains on Wednesday, following the yen down as worries over Japanese intervention and the sensitivity of regional central banks to currency strength resurfaced. 

 North Korea's missile test on Tuesday, after a series of claims about its nuclear intentions, remained a factor for the Korean won but seemed unimportant to other regional markets. 

 Apart from the yen, local growth concerns amid the risk of a Gulf war still influenced trade, currency analysts said 

 The Singapore dollar, Thai Baht and the Korean won struck multi-week highs offshore as the yen reached its strongest in nearly six-months. 

 But those gains were pared after market sources said Japan had intervened to sell the yen on Tuesday, and Japanese officials warned they were monitoring the currency. 

 That put a brake on the yen's bull run, spurred by the nomination of Toshihiko Fukui as Bank of Japan governor and encouraged by Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa's comment that he had agreed with his Group of Seven counterparts to leave foreign exchange rates to market forces. 

 "North Korea seems to be a risk, predominantly for Korea. But, even there, the main risk is the unknown of how a war in Iraq will affect global trade and how long it will keep oil prices high, which depresses global growth," said Ray Farris, currency strategist with Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 "You have dollar-yen going lower but most of the governments in the region reluctant to see their currencies appreciate in line with the yen, so a lot of these governments are effectively engineering weaker exchange rates on a trade-weighted basis," he added. 

 The Singapore dollar settled around 1.7340 after failing to hold on to a three-week high of 1.7320 per U.S. dollar. Analysts said the Sing dollar, up 1.7 percent in two weeks, was nearing levels beyond which its appreciation was difficult. 

 Singapore had another encouraging data release on Wednesday, with industrial production expanding 13.6 percent on the year in January. Gross domestic product figures for 2002 are due on Thursday and the annual budget will be released on Friday. 

 "Significant Sing dollar upside is unlikely to stretch for now. For one, market is watching the critical 1.73 level, at which MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) presence was previously cited," said a commentary from United Overseas Bank. 

 Also, there would be U.S. dollar short-covering if an invasion of Iraq was launched, UOB said. 

 The Taiwan dollar came off a two-week high as the yen slid, while the Indonesian rupiah maintained a listless range just above 8,900. 

 The Thai baht weakened to 42.74/78 towards close of Asian trading, moving slowly away from an offshore three-week high quote of 42.60. 

 The Korean won ended onshore trade weaker at 1,188.5. The yen-won cross rate was 10.115, showing the worries over North Korea were still weighing on the won, putting it in a relatively weaker position versus the yen. 

 PESO WEAK AGAIN 

 The Philippine peso slipped once again to 54.40 but markets, wary of more verbal or physical intervention, were assured by the central bank that it had not defended the peso on Wednesday. 

 Philippine markets were closed on Tuesday for a holiday. The peso had hit a two-year low of 54.48 on Monday. 

 The announcement of the January budget deficit in the afternoon also surprised markets, both because it came a day early and at 13.95 billion pesos was below the target of an average monthly deficit of 16.8 billion pesos in 2003. 

 The peso closed at 54.35, but markets were braced for persistent pressure on the currency on account of high global oil prices and worries about sanctions if the Philippines does not pass an anti-money-laundering law.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Constrained by N.Korea, c.banks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies saw little benefit from a weakening U.S. dollar on Friday as tensions over North Korea's nuclear programme and concerns regional central banks will not let their currencies appreciate weighed them down. 

 Traders said foreign investment and fund houses were seen picking up dollars against the regionals. 

 "The North Korean issue is standing in the way of regionals (firming)," a Singapore-based chief dealer said. 

 "We can see all these funds picking up the dollar against Asians, and they are probably quite right in betting that even if the dollar falls a lot, the regional central banks will be intervening against their currencies," he added. 

 The Singapore dollar  visited lows near 1.76 again in offshore deals, but was higher at 1.7530/40 by the time Asian trading started. 


The Korean won             also managed to withstand another bear
attack that took it past 1,206, and was back hugging the 1,200 level in
morning trade.



Markets remained jittery over the North Korean standoff, despite the
United States saying it is not seeking sanctions against the country,
which Pyongyang has said it would view as a declaration of war. On
Wednesday, North Korea was declared in breach of the United Nation's
atomic safeguards and the matter was referred to the U.N. Security
Council.



The U.S. dollar held its ground against the yen  around 120.40, after a
half percent fall on Thursday amid worries over terror attacks and the
approaching deadline for the U.N. arms inspectors' report on Iraq.



Asian markets also worried about oil prices at 28-month highs and about
how far the Japanese authorities would let the yen rise before
intervening, while they waited for the Bank of Japan to end a two-day
policy meeting.



The National Australia Bank said in its weekly report it expected the
dollar to be supported in Asia.



"Throughout the next few weeks we should expect Asian currencies
generally to trade at the lower end of recent ranges as the current
macro environment is not conducive to growth assets, the North Korean
crisis has further in which to run, and secondly the Japanese Ministryof Finance has engaged in a concerted effort to weaken the yen," it
said.



BEARISHNESS WIDESPREAD



All the major Asian currencies were flat or marginally up from
Thursday's levels, while the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah were
the only ones stronger from the end of 2002.



But traders said the baht  has limited room to appreciate, given
expectations the central bank will use any regional downtrend to buy
dollars as the early repayment of IMF loans begins.



On Friday, Thailand repays $950 million of an IMF-arranged loan,
leaving $3.85 billion outstanding. The government intends to clear the
loans by July.



The Sing dollar will stay under pressure until strong evidence of
economic recovery emerges, given its open economy and susceptibility to
global trends, traders said. Analysts said it had however moved into
the lower half of the undisclosed trade-weighted band that authorities
manage it in.



"The Sing dollar is now at the weaker half of the NEER band. Besides
euro's strength, this is largely due to dollar/Sing downside limited by
intervention fears, increasing geopolitical tensions and the domestic
economy in a bad shape," United Overseas Bank said in a market note.



WON'S RESPITE



The dollar's woes gave the Korean won some respite, despite its
proximity to North Korea. It held around 1,200 even as the country's
main stock index  hitting a 15-month low, with foreigners among thoses
selling stocks.



Earlier this week, Moody's Investors Service downgraded its outlook on
South Korea's A3 rating to negative.



But on Thursday, ratings agency Fitch said it expected a diplomatic
resolution to the crisis, said South Korea's economic fundamentals
leave it well placed to withstand even a prolonged period of heightened
tension. Fitch has an A rating on South Korea.



The Philippine peso  recovered from Thursday's close at 53.95, marking
time as traders braced for further weakness.



It struck a 18-month low of 54.10 per dollar last week, from where it

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Find a footing, but vulnerable.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies settled in narrow bands against the U.S. dollar after early some choppiness on Thursday, but analysts said there was high risk of them falling sharply if the tensions over Iraq or North Korea rose. 

 The Singapore dollar and the Korean won were hemmed in after having rallied from two-month lows this week, while the Thai baht and the Taiwan dollar have been rising after revisiting their end-2002 lows this week. 

 The U.S. dollar see-sawed against the yen in Asia, pressured by worries over the Iraq stand-off and rumours the United States might again raise its security alert level, while the yen benefitted from Japanese exporter sales and fund repatriation. 

 Traders said Asian currencies were expected to hold their ground until Friday, when U.N. weapons inspectors report on Iraq's compliance with a directive to disarm. 

 "From now until Friday, Asian regionals will be hovering in a range. But the bias will be weak on account of geopolitical risks, the yen, and intervention by the regional central banks," said Jimmy Koh, currency strategist at United Overseas Bank. 

 Koh said the Korean won would be most susceptible. The won weakened at the open after North Korea was declared in breach of the United Nation's atomic safeguards and the matter was referred to the U.N. Security Council, but it then headed back towards Wednesday's close. 

 "Clearly, this is the next flash point to watch for - North Korea had said that if further sanctions are imposed, that would be tantamount to a declaration of war - but we take the view that the actual military confrontation is extremely unlikely," JP Morgan currency strategist James Malcolm said in a note. 

 SING DOLLAR, BAHT RECOVER 

 The Singapore dollar weakened as far as 1.7592 as the yen softened towards 121.50 per dollar, and then rallied. 

 But analysts said the currency is still quite expensive in trade-weighted terms, implying it had substantial room to move lower. They also said trade in regional crosses, involving short Sing dollar positions against the won or Thai baht, was keeping it on the defensive. 

 The baht found support around 43 per dollar, and on Thursday was the only regional currency to be stronger than its 2002 close against the U.S. dollar. 

 It touched a six-week low of 43.20 on Tuesday, but analysts say the central bank will use any regional downtrend to buy dollars as the early reprepayments of IMF loans begin. 

 On Friday, Thailand will repay $950 million of an IMF-arranged loan, leaving $3.85 billion outstanding. The government intends to clear the loans by July. 

 Meanwhile, analysts were mixed about the impact of a decision by the influential California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) to review investments in the region. 

 Earlier this week, a CalPERS consultant recommended the fund put Thailand and Malaysia back on its list of approved investments and drop the Philippines. 

 Analysts said the amounts the fund had previously invested in these countries was quite low, and the impact, if any, would be on sentiment rather than flows into these currencies. 

 PESO STILL VULNERABLE 

 The Philippine peso slipped slightly to end at 53.95, raising concern it may head back to last week's 18-month low of 54.10 per dollar, from where it was pulled away by central bank warnings on dollar hoarding and some suspsected intervention. 

 It got some brief respite from selling after reports that the January budget deficit was around 15 billion pesos, under the government target of 16.8 billion for the month. 

 But the country's budget problems and worries about a sovereign ratings downgrade, combined with its exposure to global oil prices, placed the peso under considerable stress, analysts said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was volatile, moving close to Tuesday's six-week lows of 8,980 per dollar and then rallying to 8,938. Traders said there was no central bank intervention. 

 Indonesian markets, along with those in Malaysia and Singapore were closed on Wednesday for a public holiday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0840 GMT Change on the day

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Peso Continues Recovery
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The threat of government intervention helped the embattled Philippine peso to continue its recovery Monday, while other Asian currencies weakened against the dollar. 

 Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo over the weekend reiterated the government's pledge to defend the peso after the currency hit an 18-month low versus the dollar last week. 

 "We will do all within our power to keep the rate stable, and I ask the cooperation of the financial sector in this effort," Arroyo said in her weekly radio broadcast. 

 The peso breached the key psychological level of 54 to the dollar Friday as concerns about the impact of a possible war in Iraq cast a shadow on the economy in the Philippines and elsewhere in Asia. 

 The threat of war in Iraq, which has provided enormous downward pressure on the dollar so far this year, is now being viewed by market players as negative for Asia as well, analysts say. 

 In addition, the aggressive dollar selling in recent weeks appears to have subsided in advance of this Friday's U.N. weapons inspectors' report to the U.N. Security Council. 

 "Ironically, given that a war is almost fully priced in, a negative report by (Chief U.N. weapons inspector Hans) Blix could have a more positive impact on the dollar than a negative one," UBS Warburg said in a research note. 

 That's because a negative report could compel the anti-war element in the Security Council to conclude that all options for a peaceful resolution to the crisis have been exhausted, forcing support for the U.S. hawkish stance, UBS Warburg said. 

 The dollar closed at PHP53.880 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.940 Friday. 

 Traders said they were hesitant to sell the peso for fear the government would intervene in the market to keep a bid under the local currency. 

 A trader with a local bank speculated that the central bank may have sold around $40 million, mainly at the PHP53.950 level. Central bank officials weren't immediately available to comment. 

 The South Korean won ended at its lowest level in five weeks. The dollar closed at 1,192.3 won, up from KRW1,183.8 Friday. 

 Offshore players were especially active Monday, with most traders saying the dollar buying was for hedging purposes. 

 Opinion was split over whether rising tensions between the U.S. and North Korea were having an impact on the won. 

 "Offshore players I've talked to have said that North Korea isn't going to have an impact because nothing has actually materialized, just threats," one dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened to its lowest level in four weeks, driven in part by local banks buying U.S. dollars in what was thought to be options-related trade, dealers said. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7528, up from S$1.7433 late in Asia Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise also coincided with its climb against the yen. 

 The Japanese currency's slippage also weighed on the New Taiwan dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.779, up from Friday's NT$34.757. 

 Weaker-than-expected trade data issued late Monday is expected to pressure the New Taiwan dollar when trading reopens Tuesday. 

 The government announced that exports rose 4% in January, much lower than market expectations of an average 18% increase. 

 Corporate demand for U.S. dollars and Iraqi war fears added mild downward pressure to the rupiah. 

 The dollar closed at 8,880 rupiah, up from IDR8,870 at Friday's close. 

 Investors fear that a war in Iraq could destabilize Indonesia - the world's most populous Muslim nation. Over the weekend, tens of thousands took to the streets in an anti-U.S. protest, but the event passed peacefully. 

 Dollar strength in the region prompted players to cover their short positions in the currency against the baht. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at THB43.07, up from THB42.88 late Friday. 

 After opening in Asia around THB42.93, the dollar's early rise on offshore demand triggered short-covering at THB43.00, a foreign bank dealer said. 

 Local oil importers joined the dollar buying in the afternoon, prompting more short-covering at THB43.05.

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar strengthened against its U.S. counterpart Wednesday, but stayed in a tight trading range, as uncertainty over the prospects of a U.S.-led war with Iraq continued to plague market sentiment, dealers said. 

 At 0830 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7380, down from S$1.7412 late Tuesday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7375 and S$1.7390 intraday. 

 The U.S. currency opened around S$1.7380 in Asia after retreating overnight against its regional rivals, particularly the yen, dealers said. 

 It briefly rose early in the session, but slipped back to S$1.7375 midmorning and then spent the rest of the session trading around that level, dealers said. 

 Market participants continued to look for levels to sell the U.S. dollar and take profit following gains chalked up since Friday. 

 Overall market sentiment was still generally uncertain, especially ahead of U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell's address to the U.N. later Wednesday. 

 His address is expected to give the markets a clearer view of geopolitical developments, particularly with regard to possible strikes against Iraq. 

 Until market participants obtain a better picture of what the U.S. plans to do, most expect the U.S. dollar to continue to be pressured, though concerns over possible intervention by the Singapore monetary authorities may keep the falls limited, dealers said. 

 The U.S. currency will find immediate support at S$1.7370, its intraday low for the past two global sessions, with resistance at S$1.7430. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds rose sharply Wednesday sparked by an overnight rise in U.S. Treasurys, as concerns over the possibility of war and global economic uncertainties continued to favor sentiment toward lesser-risk bonds, dealers said. 

 At the end of the session, most bond yields were hovering near their historic lows, as the local market remained flush with liquidity and funding costs remain cheap, dealers said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Worried about war, oil,  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose off their lows on Wednesday as U.S. President George W. Bush said "crucial hours may lie ahead" for U.S. forces in the Gulf, but their gains were limited by concerns over intervention and rising oil prices. 

 The Singapore dollar saw the largest swings, weakening in New York after U.S. Treasury Secretary designate John Snow affirmed the strong U.S. dollar policy and then started rising ahead of Bush's State of the Union address. The Sing dollar hit a high of 1.7285 per U.S. dollar and then settled around 1.73. 

 The U.S. dollar weakened on rumours that Bush would declare war during his speech. He did not, but vowed to use the full force of the U.S. military to disarm Iraq if necessary, which kept the U.S. dollar on the defensive. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also benefitted, rising past a key resistance at 8,850 and leaving behind a week-long range around 8,890. 

 Another bout of verbal intervention kept the Korean won reined in around 1,170, helped by the yen's resistance to rallying too far past 118 per dollar. 

 The Philippine peso fell to a two-month low of 53.82 per dollar after the government, in preparation for any Gulf war, activated an oil contingency plan requiring refiners to maintain a minimum 30-day inventory of crude and products by February 3. 

 "The peso's fall is demand-driven. Oil companies have been asked to beef up their reserves and have been buying dollars," said Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at Union Bank of the Philippines. 

 The Thai baht was wedged in a 42.60-42.68 range by the rising war risks, as well as suspicion that the central bank was continuously mopping up the heavy influx of foreign investments. 

 Foreign investors have been net buyers of 7.8 billion baht of Thai stocks so far this year, over half the 14.34 billion baht they bought in all of 2002. 

 Traders believe the central bank is accumulating dollar reserves to facilitate the proposed early prepayment of some $4.8 billion on IMF loans by mid-2003. 

 WAITING FOR EVENTS 

 Traders said Bush's speech suggested the United States could take unilateral action to force Iraq to disarm, yet markets would wait for signals from Bush's meeting on Friday with British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell's presentation on Iraq to the United Nations on February 5. 

 In a commentary, Bank of America said Bush's speech was sufficiently hawkish to suggest the United States would not waver in its resolve to disarm Iraq, and, by flagging Powell's U.N. appearance, appeared to accelerate the timetable for war. 

 Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS Warburg, said the bearishness on the dollar would persist until Powell's presentation next week. 

 "He (Bush) hasn't set any deadlines, but the dollar's not coming off. Fundamentally, even at current high levels of short dollar positioning, the market does not want to take profits," said Baweja. 

 "The probability of war is unchanged. The market is basically just switching its focus from January 29 to February 5," he said.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, Broad USD Falls; Mkt Ignores Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was stronger late Monday as market participants continued to hold their weak outlook for the U.S. dollar, but ignored better-than-expected Singapore industrial output data, dealers said. 

 At 0820 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7278, down from S$1.7310 late Friday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7265 and S$1.7298 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.7270, after recovering from its sharp plunge to S$1.7235, its lowest since late 2000, during the New York trading session Friday, dealers said. 

 That was also well below the 2002 low of S$1.7260 against the local dollar, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar extended its rise from early in the session, mainly because some market participants were concerned that the sharp U.S. dollar fall would draw intervention from the central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The rise was halted around midday but resumed late in the session, though sporadic sell on rally trades caused it to slip several times through the local session. 

 Overall market sentiment for the U.S. unit was largely negative, but market participants are hoping for a better picture of how the U.S. might act against Iraq after U.N. weapons inspectors issue a key report on their work later Monday. 

 With market attention intently focused on external developments, Singapore dealers generally ignored the issue of December industrial output data, which showed production rising by a better-than-expected 19% year-on-year. 

 This beat the average forecast of a 8.9% rise by seven economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires. 

 The data also suggests that a double-dip recession in the fourth quarter of last year can be effectively ruled out, economists said. 

 All this failed to inspire the market, though, with the U.S. dollar hovering around S$1.7280 before and after the data was issued. 

 Later Monday, dealers expect the U.S. dollar to keep to a similar range against the local currency ahead of a slew of events scheduled this week, including the weapons inspectors' report, President George W. Bush's State of the Union address, and the Federal Open Market Committee meeting. 

 The U.S. dollar will find support at S$1.7230 with resistance at S$1.7300. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were modestly higher late Monday as fears of a war in the Middle east fueled buying in instruments deemed safer than equities, dealers said. 

 But overall trade in the local bond market was generally quiet, as participants waited for direction from the U.S. Treasury's market once the weapons inspectors' report on Iraq is issued.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Won Ends At New Six-Month High
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won soared to a new six-month closing high Friday as a firmer yen set the tone for Asian currencies and the dollar skidded under the weight of war concerns 

 The dollar managed to just claw out of an intraday trough of 1,170.4 won to end at KRW1,170.8 won, down from KRW1,175.8 Thursday. 

 Dealers said offshore players and a few exporters unloaded the U.S. currency, but overall trading was mostly quiet as market participants were wary that a stronger won would prompt intervention by the authorities. 

 "Some people believe that if the dollar/won goes below 1,170, the government will intervene," said a dealer. 

 Frank Gong, Bank of America currency strategist in Hong Kong, said the won's rise reflected global dollar weakness. 

 "The yen/won rate has been relatively stable, so that tells you it's basically a dollar story and not a won story," he said. 

 Analysts warned of more downside to the dollar if market players become convinced that a war in Iraq is inevitable. 

 "Continued hawkish commentary from U.S. officials on Iraq remains the greenback's biggest bugbear, with the market not only concerned by the prospect of war itself, but much more worried by clear signs that the U.S. is prepared to go to war without the support of the rest of the U.N. Security Council," UBS Warburg said in a note. 

 With that in mind, market players will be keeping close tabs on several events next week, starting with Chief U.N. weapons inspector Hans Blix's report to the U.N. Security Council Monday on progress made in carrying out the resolution calling for Iraq to give up its weapons of mass destruction. 

 President George W. Bush's State of the Union address Tuesday will be closely followed, as will Treasury Secretary nominee John Snow's confirmation hearing the same day. Market players will be waiting to see if he says anything about the U.S.' strong dollar policy, though analysts say they don't expect him to stray from the official line. 

 The Federal Open Market Committee Meeting on Jan. 28-29 will also be closely watched, though most expect the Fed to stand pat on interest rates. 

 Analysts generally are convinced that the dollar will remain in the doldrums in the near term at the very least, which could keep the yen strengthening, and bolster Asian currencies. 

 Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank in a report Friday ratcheted up near term forecasts for the Indonesian rupiah, the South Korean won, the Singapore dollar, after revising upward targets for the yen. 

 But "in the second half of the year, we expect a number of Asian currencies to decouple from the yen, moving stronger," due to divergent fundamentals. 

 "We expect Asia to accelerate along with the U.S. while Japan continues to stagnate," Salomon said, adding that the biggest move will likely be in the won. 

 At 0923 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y117.84, down from Y118.06 overnight in New York, and Y118.73 late Thursday in Tokyo. 

 Meantime, the yen's gains versus the dollar and foreign buying of local stocks helped support the New Taiwan dollar. 

 The U.S. currency ended at NT$34.575, down from NT$34.658 Thursday. 

 The intraday range was between NT$34.555 and NT$34.722, but it remained below NT$34.65 for much of the session. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen higher in thin trade ahead of the weekend. 

 Near the end of the local session, the dollar was quoted at S$1.7310, down from S$1.7326 late Thursday. Its intraday range was between S$1.7295 and S$1.7320. 

 U.S. dollar sentiment remained weak as market participants refrained from taking large positions amid continued concerns of a war in the Middle East, dealers said. 

 But Singapore-based dealers weren't keen on pushing the local dollar up too high for fear of sparking intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht was just marginally higher as investors were wary of trying to build on recent gains, given the central bank's recent dollar buying, traders said. 

 Market players were also reluctant to make more big bets on dollar weakness ahead of the weekend. 

 The dollar finished at 42.68 baht, down a tad from THB42.69 Thursday, after trading between THB42.65 and THB42.70.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Follow Yen Moves Vs Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies fluctuated within generally tight ranges Thursday, mostly following in the footsteps of the yen. 

 The session kicked off with most regional currencies weakening along with the Japanese currency amid short-covering in the dollar. 

 But the yen later bounced back from session lows after Japan's Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa suggested in parliamentary questioning that Japan is no longer on red alert for intervention to stem the yen's strength. 

 Regional units mirrored the yen's rebound, and by late Thursday, they were mixed against the dollar. 

 The South Korean won, the Philippine peso and the Thai baht were modestly higher, while the Singapore dollar, the New Taiwan dollar and the Indonesian rupiah softened slightly. 

 Overall, underlying sentiment on the dollar remains bearish. A regional currency trader at a Singapore-based foreign bank said there was a lot of interest to sell dollars into rallies, but the number of buyers was limited. 

 The dollar/yen's fluctuations in recent days have confused many market players and "a lot of people are sidelined," the trader added. 

 At 0954 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y118.16, from Y118.31 overnight in New York and Y118.19 in Tokyo late Wednesday. 

 "With the backdrop of poor U.S. data, Wall Street's struggles and war risks, it remains difficult picking a bottom for the U.S dollar," BNP Paribas wrote in a research note. 

 Meanwhile, heavy dollar selling by exporters and offshore players helped support the South Korean won, market participants said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,175.8 won, down from KRW1,176.7 Wednesday, after trading between KRW1,175.2 and KRW1,180.7. 

 Sales from exporters were linked to traditional month-end book balancing, but dealers couldn't explain the offshore selling. 

 "I think the market was pretty active today," a dealer said. "There was lots of selling from offshore and exporters, and I think it followed the yen closely." 

 Lower corporate demand for the U.S. currency helped the Philippine peso extend gains from the previous session. 

 The dollar ended at 53.665 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.675 Wednesday, after moving between PHP53.650 and PHP53.750. Transaction volume dropped to $75.7 million from $90.5 million previously. 

 Traders said a dearth of fresh leads kept most market participants on the sidelines. A Manila-based dealer said trades were mostly from a handful of banks which took short-term positions for quick profits. 

 The Thai baht firmed slightly as the dollar's early rebound lost steam toward the end of the session, traders said. 

 "Exporter dollar-selling during the day also helped push the dollar lower amid a thin market," a trader at a local bank in Bangkok said. 

 The dollar erased early gains that took it to a high of 42.77 baht to end the local trading session at THB42.69 baht, down from THB42.74 Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened, but came off its intraday trough, as the U.S. currency failed to hang on to its early gains as market participants trimmed positions and took quick profits. 

 Toward the close of the local trading session, the U.S. dollar was quoted around S$1.7326, from S$1.7322 late Wednesday. Intraday, it traded between S$1.7320 and S$1.7352. 

 Dealers said worries that a U.S.-led war against Iraq was inevitable kept sentiment very bearish on the dollar in Asia. 

 "We expect the U.S. dollar to continue to drift lower toward end-week, with the U.S. dollar remaining at risk from another round of selling upon new adverse developments on the Iraqi war front," United Overseas Bank said in a research report. 

 But the local dollar's gains were limited by concerns over the domestic economic outlook and potential intervention by the local central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar weakened, but ended off-lows as exporter demand helped offset earlier short covering on the U.S. currency. 

 Sentiment on the local dollar was also aided by a 1.7% rise in the key stock index, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.658, mildly higher than Wednesday's NT$34.644, after trading between NT$34.651 and NT$35.765. 

 The rupiah drifted lower as local companies bought dollars, possibly to finance imports and to hedge future dollar obligations, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 8,895 rupiah, up from IDR8,885 Wednesday. 

 State-owned oil company Pertamina was suspected of being the main dollar buyer for financing fuel imports, dealers said. 

 Indonesia is the only South East Asian member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC. But, the country imports most of its fuel products for domestic use from Singapore. 

 Underlying sentiment remains positive on the local unit as offshore participants are still attracted by the healthy differentials between the rupiah and the dollar rates while political stability seems to improve, dealers said.
