title: Emerging Asia  FX -Trapped by growth and war risks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies spent a relatively quiet Thursday in the midst of volatile major currencies, pinned by worries over central bank intervention, higher oil prices and tensions of war on Iraq. 

 The Singapore dollar, Korean won and other regionals softened in the morning as the yen remained wary of intervention, and then settled into tight ranges ahead of the January 27 deadline for U.N. inspectors to submit their report on Iraq's weapons. Markets were also uneasy ahead of next week's State of the Union address by U.S. President George. W. Bush, after he stepped up the war rhetoric recently, and U.S. Treasury Secretary nominee John Snow's Senate hearing. 

 The dollar extended its recovery against the yen to over 118.70/80 and then fell back. But the euro struck fresh 3-= year highs against the yen, boosted by safe-haven flows. 

 Frank Gong, head of Asian markets strategy at Bank of America, said the euro was the biggest beneficiary of the dollar's weakness and the fear of coordinated central bank action to weaken the yen was weighing on the latter. 

 "The yen seems to be the weakest currency, the dog of all the G10 currencies, and the euro is the star, and traders continue to stay long euro/yen," Gong said. 

 "Regionals are torn between the weaker dollar and the weaker yen and, at the same time, the geopolitical uncertainties and the clouds over the global economy is making Asian currencies underperform relative to trade-weighted baskets and the major currencies." 

 GROWTH PIVOTAL 

 The Singapore dollar kept to a 1.7330-1.7350 range, after failing to hold on to late-Wednesday's highs around 1.73. 

 The Korean won fell to 1,180, but recovered to finish local trade slightly stronger. 

 Analysts said the upside for Asian currencies was limited, given how keen their central banks are to preserve export competitiveness during these periods of uncertain global growth. 

 "The growth outlook is pivotal for Asian currencies going forward as a lack of upturn will see Asian central banks act to keep their currencies competitive," National Australia Bank said in a report. 

 "With market sentiment souring the threat of intervention is more real, and this is keeping both the Singapore dollar and Korean won from gaining against either the yen or the dollar. 

 "We see no immediate improvement in the macro framework so by implication we continue to see Asian regional currencies capped," the report said. 

 OIL IMPORTERS HEDGE 

 Oil prices eased from two-year highs, but traders said importers around the region were playing safe and hedging foreign currency liabilities. 

 Foreign equity investments cushioned the moves in Thailand and Korea. Foreign investors have bought a net 6.8 billion baht of Thai stocks so far in 2003, after net purchases of 14.34 billion baht in all of the previous year. 

 The Thai baht moved in a 42.70-42.80 range. 

 Traders in Jakarta said the central bank may have intervened to defend the rupiah around 8,890 after heavy dollar buying by local importers and profit-booking by offshore speculators. 

 Traders said Wednesday's news that international donors have pledged $2.7 billion of fresh funding for 2003 had been discounted and so was having little impact. 

 The Philippine peso was supported by exporter sales at one-month lows around 53.75, which emerged as the yen jumped off intra-day lows around 118.83. Traders said there was no intervention.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late On Yen; Peso Ignores Budget Gap
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies bounced back Wednesday as the dollar succumbed to war fears, though its decline against the yen was tempered by intervention warnings from the Japanese Prime Minister. 

 The broadly firmer tone helped lift the Philippine peso out of the one-month troughs of the past two days as market players largely ignored record high budget deficit data for 2002, which traders said was already priced in. 

 In the familiar refrain heard in recent days, traders said regional currency markets remain focused on the dollar's gyrations against the yen. 

 But the roller coaster has left market players scratching their heads and wondering about the dollar's direction. 

 "The market has been very confused," declared a regional currency trader at a European bank. 

 "At the moment, it's (dollar versus regionals) all on a soft tone, basically on the back of the dollar/yen," he said. 

 Hawkish remarks from the Bush administration reignited fears of an impending war in Iraq and sent the dollar plunging to Y117.00 overnight after the currency rallied to Y119.15 Tuesday. 

 But in Asia Wednesday, the yen's decline was cushioned by unexpected intervention remarks from Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi. 

 Asked at the Upper House of Parliament about the yen's recent strength, Koizumi warned that "if necessary, our stance is unchanged that we will take the appropriate steps." 

 Though Koizumi was repeating the standard Japanese currency policy, it caused the dollar to briefly rally to a high of Y118.41 in Tokyo. 

 At 0934 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y118.36, up from Y118.04 overnight in New York. Late Tuesday in Tokyo, the dollar was at Y118.76. 

 For the near term, sentiment on the dollar remains bearish, especially as most of the recent economic data haven't been very encouraging, analysts said. That could lead to foreign exchange market players building up positions against the dollar, they said. 

 The Philippine peso was buoyed by the firmer tone of regional currencies as recent dollar demand from oil companies tapered off. 

 The dollar closed at 53.675 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.740 Tuesday, after ranging between PHP53.650 and PHP53.750. 

 Earlier Wednesday, the government announced a record 2002 budget deficit of PHP212.7 billion, or 5.3% of gross domestic product, sharply wider from PHP147 billion in 2001, but lower than the revised ceiling of PHP223 billion for 2002. 

 "The market had been expecting quite a bad number," said a dealer with a foreign bank, adding that it had already been priced in by the market. 

 In South Korea, the dollar closed at 1,176.7 won, down from KRW1,180.0 Tuesday, after trading between KRW1,173.9 and KRW1,179.8. 

 The U.S. currency was confined to a tight range by importers buying at the lows and exporters selling at the highs, traders said. 

 Interbank players also bought dollars on dips, providing some support for the currency. 

 "Actually, we're in a very boring market these days - just stuck within tight ranges," said Seung-hyun Kim, a member of the foreign exchange corporate sales team at BNP Paribas. "There's no fresh momentum to break through the upper or lower levels." 

 The Singapore dollar and the Thai baht tracked the yen higher amid weak market sentiment on the U.S. currency. 

 Near the close of the local trading session, the dollar was quoted around S$1.7322, down from S$1.7362 late Tuesday. Intraday, it traded between S$1.7300 and S$1.7345. 

 An uncertain outlook for the domestic economy and fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore kept the dollar from falling past the psychological S$1.7300 per U.S. dollar mark, traders said. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around THB42.73 late in Asia, down from THB42.825 Tuesday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar rose in tandem with the yen, but closed off-highs as the central bank intervened at the peak to limit its gains, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.644, down from NT$34.680 Tuesday, after trading between NT$34.590 and NT$34.702. 

 The Indonesian rupiah closed unchanged at 8,885 per dollar amid talk the central bank again intervened to support the local currency. 

 Earlier, the dollar rose as high as IDR8,890 on bids from local companies looking to hedge future dollar obligations. 

 The market ignored reports that international donors agreed to pledge $2.7 billion in aid to Indonesia this year, though dealers said the news was positive for the rupiah.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Easier on dlr bounce, data worries.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 21 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar
and Taiwan dollar  fell to one-week lows and the
Philippines peso  closed in on one-month lows on Tuesday
as the U.S. dollar extended its rebound against the yen.
    The U.S. dollar bounced off an early 3-=   year low against
the euro, ahead of a knockout option at $1.0700, and was lifted
to around 118.80 yen  on stop-loss buying.
    Dealers said the move in the majors prompted players in
regional currencies to resume triming of short U.S. dollar
positions, after a pause in late Asian and offshore trade.
    They said while the dollar's upside remains checked by
fears of a possible war in Iraq, players net short of dollars
were looking for opportunities to cover those positions amid
wariness of potential Japanese intervention against the yen.
The yen has weakened since hitting a four-month high around
117.40 on Friday.



    Analysts said a weakening bias in regional currencies could
also be creeping in after recent data showed some pressure on
Asian exports.
 
    "We remain cautious of forming Asia longs," said Naomi
Fink, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore.
    "Not only due to the possibility of upcoming yen weakness



on intervention and expectations of further monetary easing,



but because of signs that exports are contracting, a clear



negative for the current account surplus economies of Asia,"



she added.



She said currency sentiment was likely to suffer after



Friday's surprisingly weak export numbers from Singapore and



Monday's sharp contraction of Philippines trade surplus.



POOR DATA UPS C.BANK FEARS



Dealers said Singapore's exports data had reinforced fears



of intervention by the island's central bank to protect



competitiveness against export rivals.



The Singapore dollar touched 1.7348 per U.S. dollar, its



weakest since January 15, as heavy offers scuttled its early



rise to levels near 1.7300, beyond which dealers believe the


central bank might come into action.



 
    The Singapore dollar had hit a six-month high of 1.7284 on
Friday, before the trade data was released.
    Already reprimanded by the central bank on Friday, currency


players in Taiwan took the cue from the yen's fall and sold off



the Taiwan dollar to 34.538 per U.S. dollar, its lowest level



since January 14. For a detailed report,



Dealers in Singapore said the Taiwan central bank had


intervened aggressively on Friday to pull the currency off a



two-month high of 34.401 per U.S. dollar.



 
    The Philippine peso touched a low of 53.75 per dollar, just
shy of one-month low of 53.76 hit on Monday.
    Dealers in Manila said peso was weighed down by Monday's
data showing a falling trade surplus and on wariness ahead of
final budget deficit numbers for 2002 expected this week.
    After three revisions of the deficit target, Manila hopes



to keep last year's deficit to within 5.6 percent of gross



domestic product, or 223 billion pesos. For this year, it aims



to trim the deficit to 4.7 percent of GDP, or 202 billion



pesos.



The Thai baht  held around 42.80 per dollar, slightly



down from late Monday and not far from Friday's one-week low of



42.85. Dealers in Singapore said dollar sales by exporters were



limiting the baht's downside, while most of the dollar demand



was from offshore players.



As widely expected, the Bank of Thailand left its benchmark



interest rate unchanged at 1.75 percent on Monday, saying



robust economic growth and low inflation meant neither monetary



easing nor tightening was necessary.



The Indonesian rupiah  touched a one-week low at



8,897 per dollar, as some offshore players covered their short



dollar positions.



Dealers in Jakarta said comments by officials of the



International Monetary Fund and World Bank may have added to



the overall bullish sentiment on the rupiah, but they were not



trading factors for the day.



The officials said donors had an understanding attitude



toward Indonesia's moves to reduce earlier announced rises in



fuel prices.



That was interpreted as suggesting Indonesia would get all



or most of the $2.8 billion in aid it is seeking at a two-day



meeting of the Consultative Group on Indonesia donors, which



began on Tuesday.



 
    Dealers said successful aid talks were already factored in,
and the rupiah was only suffering technical pressure.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Late; But Dlr Vulnerability Looms
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar staged a mild comeback against Asian currencies Friday after a struggling in the region for most of the week. 

 Friday's gains illustrate how the U.S. currency can benefit from occasional bouts of short covering. But analysts say the dollar will remain mired in a downward trend globally at least until the outcome of the confrontation with Iraq becomes clear. 

 Even then, the widening U.S. current account deficit will pose a major impediment to any chance for a sustained dollar recovery, they add. 

 Less than three weeks into the new year, the dollar is down 1.1% against the South Korean won, 0.8% against the New Taiwan dollar, 0.6% against the yen, and 0.3% against the Singapore dollar. 

 "The U.S. dollar is under downward pressure and the Asian currencies are facing upward pressure. This isn't a trend that will change anytime soon," said Geoffrey Barker, HSBC's chief economist for Asia. 

 The U.S. will find it increasingly difficult to attract the huge flows of foreign capital it needs to fund its current account gap, thereby leaving the dollar vulnerable to further weakness, he said. 

 The dollar's decent performance against the yen set the tone for its gains against other Asian currencies Friday. Regional currencies often track the direction of the yen as a reflex mechanism to preserve price competitiveness on trade. 

 The dollar traded as high as Y118.17 during the Asian session. Late in the day it was quoted at Y117.99, up from Y117.83 late Thursday in New York. 

 The Singapore dollar came off a six-month high to trade slightly weaker late Friday. Fears of central bank intervention and a disappointing trade report weighed on the local currency. 

 Near the end of trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7334, up from S$1.7327 late Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar's drop below the psychological S$1.7300 support level, hitting S$1.7290 in early trade, fueled fears of possible intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore to cap the local currency's gains, traders said. 

 The government reported that non-oil domestic exports, a key measurement of the trade-driven economy's health, rose a weaker-than-expected 4.4% in December from a year earlier. Analysts had been looking for a 13% rise. 

 The New Taiwan dollar weakened for the first time in five trading sessions after the central bank intervened in the market to cap the currency's appreciation. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.467, up from Thursday's NT$34.450. 

 Traders said the New Taiwan dollar is likely to continue to test the central bank's resolve next week, especially given poor outlook for U.S. dollar. 

 The dollar closed at a four-week high of PHP53.610 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.470 at Thursday's finish. 

 Traders said the peso lost ground from late morning as it tracked the losses in some regional currencies and due to modest corporate demand for dollars. 

 The local unit extended its weaker performance through to the closing, with its losses exacerbated by some banks covering their short dollar positions ahead of the weekend, traders said. 

 Against the South Korean won, it edged lower after trading in a narrow range for most of the session. 

 The dollar closed at 1,173.5 won, compared with KRW1,173.2 at Thursday's close. 

 With few domestic developments to drive trading, the won largely tracked the yen's moves, dealers said. 

 Dollar short covering by local corporations helped keep a bid under the U.S. currency against the Thai baht. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at THB42.750, up from THB42.670 late Thursday. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah the dollar was unchanged at IDR8,785 after trading in a narrow range of IDR8,870 to IDR8,885.

title: Singapore Dlr Slightly Dn Late On MAS Fears, Dec Exports
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar came off a new six-month high against the U.S. dollar to trade a touch weaker late Friday due to central bank intervention fears and a worse-than-expected trade report. 

 At 0819 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7334, slightly up from S$1.7327 late in Asia Thursday. It traded between S$1.7292 and S$1.7339 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar kicked off the Asian session around S$1.7310 and later ticked down to S$1.7292, its lowest level since July 19, 2002. 

 Local banks were said to be big sellers in early trading, taking advantage of spillover bearish sentiment toward the U.S. dollar amid mounting worries over an imminent war in Iraq. 

 But the U.S. dollar's retreat proved to be short-lived, as the drop below the previous psychological S$1.7300 support triggered fears of possible intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the island's central bank, traders said. 

 Short-covering and bargain hunting soon pushed the U.S. currency back to levels it closed late in Asia Thursday, thanks in part to Singapore's worse-than-expected trade performance in December. 

 Non-oil domestic exports, a key measurement of the trade-driven economy's health, rose 4.4% on year to S$8.0 billion in December, sharply below the average growth forecast of 13% by 10 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires. 

 While the focus is on the U.S. dollar's bearish tone at the moment, there is also caution over any excessive strength in currencies of emerging markets, said a chief trader at an Asian bank. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to trade between S$1.7290 and S$1.7350 Monday, traders said, but added that the session could be subdued due to a public holiday in the U.S. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were higher late Friday, despite mixed U.S. Treasurys overnight, traders said. 

 The turning point in the session was the disappointing trade data, which prompted a slew of buying after some mild selling at the open, traders said. 

 Lingering geopolitical concerns such as a war in Iraq also revived appetite for safe-haven products, they added. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was one basis point lower at 1.10%, while the yield on five-year bonds was down four basis points at 1.73%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was one basis point lower at 2.13%, while the yield on 10-year bonds fell one basis point to 2.59%.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late Vs US Dlr After ECB Issing Remarks
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened late Wednesday in Asia after a senior European Central Bank official said Asian countries needed to do more to accommodate the weakening U.S. dollar.  

Singapore government bonds were flat to weaker, in line with weakness in U.S. Treasurys late Tuesday, dealers said.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6390, down from S$1.6421 late in Asia Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6376 and S$1.6420 intraday.  

ECB chief economist Otmar Issing said at a conference Tuesday that Asian nations, and China in particular, aren't contributing enough to reduce global imbalances stemming from the large U.S. current account deficit.  

"China is still putting off its contribution, but it will no doubt at some stage act," he said, reiterating comments by other European policy-makers that Europe has unfairly borne the brunt of weakness in the U.S. dollar.  

Traders said Issing's remarks reaffirmed the view that U.S. and eurozone policy-makers are still keen on pressuring China to move to a more flexible foreign exchange rate regime from its current system that effectively pegs the yuan to the dollar.  

Chinese authorities are widely expected to announce a change to the country's foreign exchange rate regime this year. Any such change could put upward pressure on Asian currencies, including the Singapore dollar, against the U.S. dollar and the euro.  

As a result, the U.S. currency fell to a one-week low of S$1.6363 in New York late Tuesday before rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore curbed the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar's slide, dealers said.  

Speculation that the MAS might intervene again in Wednesday's Asian session sparked short-covering among interbank players, boosting the U.S. currency as high as S$1.6420 in the morning.  

But other players capitalized on the U.S. dollar's rally, selling the U.S. unit back down to just below the psychologically important S$1.6400 level in the afternoon.  

"For now, we can expect the dollar-sing to trade around S$1.6350-S$1.6450. Only a decisive move above S$1.6420 would take out the downside bias," said United Overseas Bank in a research report.

declines in Asian currencies on Wednesday, following an

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah gains on debt-relief hopes.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Jan 4 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah, Asia's
worst-performing currency in 2004, gained on Tuesday on hope
overseas lenders may cut the country's foreign debt to help it
recover from the tsunami disaster.
 
    The rupiah        gained as much as half a percent, to
9,255 per dollar, compared with late Asian trades on Monday.
    Other Asian currencies were little changed, as concerns
about central bank dollar-buying intervention weighed on a
largely bullish outlook for the regional units this year.
    Indonesia might gain the most if, as expected, the Paris
  

Club of creditor governments offered debt relief to countries  

hit by the Dec. 26 disaster, analysts said. The forum is to  

meet on Jan. 12.  

"The Italians have suggested cutting Indonesia's foreign  

debt," said Song Seng Wun, an economist at Singapore-based G.K.  

Goh Securities. "It's a nice gesture. Every little bit will  

help."   


 
    G.K. Goh expects the rupiah to strengthen to 8,500 per
dollar by the end of this year.
    INTERVENTION RISK
    The South Korean won       , the Taiwan dollar          and
  

the Singapore dollar were held back by worries central  

banks might step up dollar-buying intervention to cap gains in  

the local currencies and bolster exports that are seen slowing  

this year.  

The won rose to a seven-year high and the Taiwan dollar  

ended local trading on Monday at 31.845 per dollar, a four-year  

closing high. The Taiwan currency closed Tuesday at 31.846 per  

dollar.  

Analysts said the Taiwan dollar and the won may outperform  

Asian rivals in 2005 as the U.S. current account deficit  

extends the dollar's decline against Asian currencies for the  

fourth straight year.  

Still, risks of central bank intervention remained,  

threatening their outlook for the next few weeks, dealers  

said.  

Central bank data showed South Korea's foreign exchange

reserves rose 3.4 percent in December, indicating authorities  

had stepped up attempts to slow the surge in the won, which  

gained 15 percent in 2004 to be Asia's best performing  

currency.  

A finance ministry official said the government would  

increase, if necessary, the ceiling on bond sales to fund  

dollar-buying intervention in the local currency market.  

"The finance ministry appears poised to step up foreign  

exchange intervention," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist  

at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore.  

Still, the central bank's dollar-buying intervention has so  

far slowed the won's gain rather than reversed it, he said,  

adding the currency intervention was not at any unprecedented  

level.   


The baht  and the Indian rupee        gained
  

modestly  

as currency analysts downplayed the impact of the tsunami.  

"The shock to regional tourism is unlikely to reach  

SARS-like proportions," said Piron. "Indonesia was not hit in  

major tourist spots, India has small reliance on tourist  

receipts and Malaysia was relatively less hit."  

JP Morgan Chase cut its first-quarter growth outlook for  

Thailand but said it would be wrong to view the calamity as an  

economic trend-turning event, despite its human costs.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Vs US Dlr Late Amid Choppy Trading
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was steady against its U.S. counterpart late Wednesday in Asia after a choppy holiday-thinned trading session.  

Singapore government bonds were flat to weaker, after U.S. Treasurys closed nearly unchanged in New York late Tuesday.  

At 0700 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6344, nearly flat from S$1.6348 late in Asia Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6341 and S$1.6382 intraday.  

With most local players away on year-end holidays, the Singapore dollar closely tracked the movements of the currencies that comprise its trade-weighted basket, such as the U.S. dollar, the yen and the euro, dealers said.  

Choppy trading in these currencies - especially the U.S. currency against the yen - generated sharp fluctuations of the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair throughout the session.  

At 0700 GMT, the U.S. unit was at Y103.22, up from Y103.13 in New York late Tuesday. The euro was at US$1.3635, up from US$1.3606 in New York late Tuesday.  

Looking ahead, the U.S. unit is expected to maintain its long-term downtrend against regional currencies, although the Monetary Authority of Singapore is likely to continue intervening to curb any excessive volatility in the Singapore dollar, dealers said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Gains capped by  intervention  worry.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 24 (Reuters) - The Korean won, Taiwan dollar
and Singapore dollar set 2-week highs in holiday-thinned
trading, but fears of central bank intervention capped further
gains on Friday as the U.S. dollar hit fresh lows against the
euro and ceded ground to the Japanese yen.
    The won                   was up about a quarter percent,
coming off a high near 1,045 per dollar amid worries the Bank
of Korea would buy dollars. Its gains outpaced even the yen's
since Thursday and have put it on track to become Asia's top
performer in 2004.
    It has risen about 14 percent so far this year. The Taiwan
dollar, the next best performer, has managed less than half
that gain.
    A mixed batch of U.S. data, including weak new home sales,
and technical factors drove the euro up to above $1.35. The yen
moved more cautiously, and was quoted around 103.72/75 at 0800
GMT.
    Trading volumes have shrunk in the final weeks of the year.
  


Traders said the euro had a good chance of appreciating because
markets had unwound their heavy euro long positions in the
first half of December, as data from the U.S. Commodity Futures
Commission showed.
    "We expect the U.S. dollar to weaken further in the first
half of 2005 against developed and emerging market currencies,
given the U.S. twin deficits and the perception the U.S.
authorities are happy to see the U.S. dollar weaken, so long as
the process is orderly," Standard Chartered Bank said in a
commentary.
    The Singapore dollar        moved between 1.6360 and 1.64,
with the fear of intervention by the Monetary Authority of
Singapore surfacing intermittently as local banks bought U.S.
dollars.
    Even offshore premiums on the Chinese yuan were higher as
markets disregarded a statement from authorities earlier this
week that they had no plans to shift their stance on the
tightly managed currency.
    Speculation has intensified in the market that China might
shift its stance before the end of the year. But a central bank
spokesman said on Wednesday, "At present there is no change in
the exchange rate policy."
    One-year non-deliverable forwards           were quoted at
4,900 points, pricing in a 6.3 percent appreciation in the yuan
in a year. The yuan is effectively pegged around 8.28 per U.S.
dollar.
    "There is no extra special news that has triggered the
speculation. I think it is the broad dollar trend," said Tai
Hui, Standard Chartered Bank's economist for Greater China,
referring to the move in NDFs.
 
    Standard Chartered expects China to widen the yuan's narrow
trading band in the first half of 2005.
    Meanwhile, the Taiwan dollar retreated from 32.05 as
markets trod warily, fearing intervention near the 32 mark.
    Hui said 32 was a level to watch. Yet recent economic data
had been strong and the central bank might not be averse to
currency gains, he said.
    Taiwan's export orders showed a robust 30 percent annual
growth in November.
    "Export orders data released yesterday was still quite
  

strong," said Hui. "From that perspective, I don't think the  

central bank is concerned about the level. Smoothing out the  

ups and downs in the currency might be their objective."  

Markets in the Philippines were closed.  

The Indonesian rupiah traded conclusively on the  

firmer side of 9,300 for the first time in a week, seemingly  

overcoming recent downward pressures from commercial outflows,  

political and security worries.

Thursday, aided by higher local stock markets and the yen,

currencies, such as the won and Thai baht

title: Singapore  Dlr Down Late After Rumored MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was slightly weaker in Asia late Thursday as rumored intervention in the currency market by the central bank overcame heavy U.S. dollar-selling by various banks.  

Singapore government bonds were slightly lower in thin trading ahead of the Christmas holiday.  

At 0745 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6416, up slightly from S$1.6410 late in Asia Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6369 and S$1.6417 intraday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. dollar plunged as low as S$1.6369, its lowest since Dec. 8, as some Singapore-based banks sold the U.S. unit on behalf of corporate customers seeking to make last-minute position adjustments ahead of the year-end holidays.  

But the U.S. currency's slide against the local dollar immediately ran into buying interest from domestic banks, which were apparently acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar buying by local banks continued through the morning, and by early afternoon, the U.S. currency had been pushed as high as S$1.6418.  

Traders said the MAS may continue intervening in the foreign exchange market later in the global day if the U.S. dollar resumes its fall against the local currency. This could happen if tonight's slew of U.S. economic data - including November durable goods orders - disappoints market participants.  

U.S. durable goods orders are expected to have staged a modest rebound in November. The median finding of analysts surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for a 0.6% increase in durable orders after a 1.1% decrease in October.  

The Singapore government bond market, meanwhile, was very subdued ahead of the Christmas holiday in the U.S. on Friday, dealers said.  

For 2005, DBS Bank said in a research report that it recommends going long on government bonds in those Asian economies with fundamental currency strength, such as Singapore.  

"In particular, since SGS (Singapore Government Securities) will receive an extra boost from the inclusion of SGS in Citigroup's World Government Bond Index (WGBI), launching in Jan. 2005, SGS will remain bullish," DBS said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Offshore yuan softer, Sing dollar capped.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies surrendered
their meagre gains on Wednesday after China quashed rumours of
an imminent yuan policy change and Thailand said it will keep
the baht competitive for exports.
    The regionals moved less than a quarter of a percent during
the day as a lacklustre yen and thinning holiday trade pinned
the market down. The yen  has marked time in a one yen
range around 104.25 per dollar since Monday, robbing Asian
currencies of direction.
    The Singapore dollar's        moves to the firmer side of
1.64 a dollar were short-lived. Fear of intervention by the
Monetary Authority of Singapore, coupled with China's statement
that it had no plans to revalue the tightly managed yuan before
the year-end, dragged the currency down.
 
    The denial also took the steam out of Chinese yuan
non-deliverable forwards.
  


    One-year NDFs were quoted at 4,700 points, down 100 points
from the day's peak, which had priced in a 6.2 percent
appreciation in the yuan in a year.
    "This is a market rumour," a central bank spokesman said
when asked about the speculation in offshore currency markets.
"At present there is no change in the exchange rate policy."
    The yuan premium had risen this week as traders positioned
themselves for a possible change in the yuan's virtually fixed
rate around 8.28 per dollar.
    "The market was trying to second-guess the Chinese
  

authorities," said Bhanu Baweja of UBS in Singapore. He saw no  

reason to expect a one-off yuan revaluation or, indeed, any  

move at all before the end of the year or in early 2005.  

"A big revaluation, in terms of market thinking, is driven  

by political pressure, severe yuan undervaluation and the need  

to slow down the economy by massive revaluation.  

"I don't think they are going to move for any of these  

reasons. They will move for a structural reason and that will  

be a modest move," Baweja said.  

Elsewhere, the baht stayed in a tight range just a  

shade weaker than 39 per dollar. Bank of Thailand Governor  

Pridiyathorn Devakula said the central bank will try to keep  

the baht at a level that is competitive for exporters.   


The South Korean won             was also hemmed in a
  

narrow range of 1,053-1,058 per dollar, with little incentive  

to break out after a steep 9 percent rally since October that  

has made it Asia's top performer so far in 2004.  

Wariness over intervention capped the Taiwan dollar  

, forcing it to retreat from a 2-week high of 32.22 a  

dollar even as the stock market extended its rally  

since the start of the month.  

Expectations of heavier inflow of dollars from Filipinos  

working overseas propped up the Philippine peso , despite  

the threat of a sovereign ratings downgrade as lawmakers  

struggle to rein in a bulging budget deficit.  

INDONESIA INDIFFERENT  

The Indonesian rupiah showed almost no reaction to a  

ratings upgrade by Standard & Poor's.  

S&P lifted the country's foreign currency rating by a notch  

to B-plus, citing progress in macroeconomic stability and  

fiscal management as well as declining debt and favourable  

external liquidity.  

The rupiah was steady around 9,325 a dollar, maintaining  

its weak bias as markets priced in security and political  

fears.  

Indonesian Vice-President Jusuf Kalla's weekend victory in  

the contest to lead Golkar, the biggest opposition party, is  

widely seen as a bonus for President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.  

Yet some analysts are concerned Kalla's larger backing  

could be a threat in the event of disagreements over policy in  

Indonesia's fragmented cabinet.  

The rupiah has also been hurt by security alerts. This  

week, an old grenade was found in the compound of the Hilton  

hotel in Jakarta, just days after warnings that militants might  

attack one of the country's three Hilton hotels.

title: Singapore Dollar Edges Up Late; Government Bonds Weaker
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged higher against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Wednesday in thin trading, while Singapore government bonds were weaker across the board on profit-taking, dealers said.  

At 0730 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6410, down slightly from S$1.6420 late in Asia Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6400 and S$1.6425.  

With the approach of the Christmas holiday in the U.S. and many other countries at the end of this week, trading was confined to a narrow range and was largely driven by movements in major currencies such as the yen throughout Wednesday's Asian session.  

Most market participants have already closed their books on foreign exchange transactions for the year, with just a few of them tinkering with U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar positions.  

"Not much is happening. It's very quiet," said a Singapore dealer.  

Traders said the U.S. currency appears to have found strong support around the S$1.6390 level, where the Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have intervened during the past two sessions to stem the U.S. unit's slide against the local dollar.  

At the same time, however, the U.S. dollar faces somewhat strong resistance at S$1.6435, the downtrend line from the Dec. 10 high of S$1.6605, based on technical analysis.  

The U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair has formed a symmetrical triangle bounded by the downtrend line from the Dec. 10 peak and by a minor uptrend line (now at S$1.6391) from the Dec. 15 low. The downtrend in 10-day momentum suggests the most likely direction of any breakout would be down, which would target the S$1.6200 area.  

The Singapore government bond market, meanwhile, bucked the overnight trend of strength in the U.S. Treasurys market, as local bond yields rose along the curve, especially at the long end, dealers said.  

The brief break of the 2-year vs 10-year yield spread below the psychologically important 100 basis-point level early in the session prompted some players to unwind curve flatteners for profits.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late After US Dlr Falls Vs Most Majors
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger in Asia late Tuesday in the wake of the U.S. dollar's weakness against most major currencies in New York late Monday.  

Singapore government bond prices were flat to lower in subdued trade ahead of the Christmas holiday later this week, dealers said.  

At 0805 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6420, down from S$1.6457 late in Asia Monday. It traded between S$1.6390 and S$1.6428 intraday.  

After the U.S. currency fell against most of its major rivals late Monday, U.S. funds sold U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars at the start of Tuesday's Asian session, pushing the U.S. unit as low as S$1.6390 in the morning.  

Traders said the U.S. funds appeared to be placing fresh bearish-U.S.-dollar bets versus the local currency on the prevailing market view for further weakness of the U.S. currency in coming months.  

But domestic banks soon stepped into the foreign exchange market to buy the U.S. unit around the S$1.6390 level, lifting it as high as S$1.6428 later in the morning.  

Speculation was rife that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened via local banks to prop up the U.S. dollar against its Singaporean counterpart. Since the middle of last week, the MAS has been rumored to have intervened occasionally, either to stem the U.S. dollar's slide against the local currency or to curb excessive volatility of the Singapore dollar.  

The U.S. unit then consolidated steadily above the psychologically important S$1.6400 level in the afternoon, and is likely to stay above S$1.6388, which is the support on the minor uptrend line from the Dec. 15 trough, for the rest of the session.  

Based on technical analysis, the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair is forming a symmetrical triangle bounded by the minor uptrend line (now at S$1.6388) from the Dec. 15 low and by the downtrend line (now at S$1.6477) from the Dec. 10 peak. The downtrend in 10-day momentum suggests the most likely direction of any breakout would be down, which would immediately target the Dec. 15 low of S$1.6370.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late In Thin Pre-Holiday Trading
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar edged up against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Monday in thin, range-bound trading ahead of holidays later this week.  

Singapore government bond prices were flat to higher in subdued trading, dealers say.  

At 0630 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6457, down from S$1.6478 late in Asia Friday. It traded between S$1.6442 and S$1.6463 intraday.  

Throughout the Asian session, the U.S. dollar hugged a very narrow range against the Singaporean currency as many banks and other financial institutions that make the local market move have closed their books for this year.  

"It's hard to quote prices to clients," said a Singapore dealer, who pointed to a sharp reduction in market liquidity that typically occurs at year-end bookclosing.  

Trading volume in the currency market is expected be low and largely directionless, with a public holiday in Japan on Thursday and in the U.S. on Friday, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's economist Wong Keng Siong said in a research note.  

"In an absence of fresh positive news, the Singapore dollar is likely to be range bound at S$1.6400-S$1.6600 per U.S. dollar this week," he said.  

Wong added that a "line of defense" may have been established at the S$1.6400 level and at the S$1.6300 level against the U.S. currency.  

Last week, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have intervened in the foreign exchange market, either to stem the U.S. dollar's slide against the local currency or to curb excessive volatility of the Singapore dollar, dealers said.  

Wednesday, the U.S. unit fell to as low as S$1.6370, its lowest level since Dec. 8.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won, Sing dlr fall on  intervention  worry.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and the
Singapore dollar led Asian currencies down on Friday on worries
central banks may step up dollar-buying to stem a two-month
rally in their currencies that may threaten exports.
    The two currencies weakened almost a third of a percent
each, taking the won to 1,060 per dollar and the Singapore
dollar to 1.6482/1.6492 per dollar.
    Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore checked
rates with some banks -- a signal that it might be thinking of
buying dollars.
    The central banks of South Korea, Singapore and India have
stepped up dollar buying since November to stem a rally sparked
by concerns the United States seemed unable to attract enough
capital from abroad to plug its record current account deficit.
  


    The Bank of Korea said Friday it had carried out further
"smoothing operations" in the local currency market in the
first half of December, boosting the country's foreign exchange
reserves by $3.4 billion in the fortnight to Dec. 15.
 
    "These levels of intervention are not sustainable," said
Sani Hamid, a currency analyst at 4CAST in Singapore.
    Bank of Korea had to step up dollar-buying since November
to absorb the dollars sold by local firms as exports soared, he
said. But he added this may ease off.
    "With technology exports slowing down next year, the
current account surplus is likely to taper off a bit," he said.
    The won has gained 13 percent this year, making it Asia's
  

best performing currency. The currency surged to a seven-year  

high this month against the dollar as exporters dumped their  

dollar earnings on worries about the weakening dollar.  

SINGAPORE EXPORTS SLUMP  

The Singapore dollar, which has underperformed the won, the  

Taiwan dollar and the yen this year, weakened after the  

government reported a higher-than-expected 9.1 percent decline  

the country's non-oil exports in November. A Reuters poll of  

economists had forecast a 1.9 percent decline.  

The Singapore dollar is now on the weaker side of the  

trade-weighted range within which the Monetary Authority of  

Singapore maintains the currency, ABN AMRO Bank said in a  

report, adding that gains are likely to be modest without a  

boost from overseas portfolio investments, like those seen in  

South Korea and Taiwan.  

The Indonesian rupiah weakened as much as half a percent to  

9,325 per dollar, closer to a 3-= month low reached on  

Wednesday, on concerns about end-of-year purchase of dollars by  

local companies to repay overseas debt.  

The currency has been hurt by a widening budget deficit and  

increased security concerns as several countries warned their  

citizens not to travel to Indonesia during the holiday season.  

The rupiah was unlikely to weaken further, Hamid said,  

because the government had received a $400 million loan  

committment from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank  

to help plug a widening budget shortfall.   


 
    ADB will disburse $100 million this week, a senior
Indonesian finance ministry official said on Thursday.
    The Indian rupee lost almost half a percent to 44.03 per
dollar as stocks paused, after a run up this year.
    Record foreign investments in Indian stocks this year and
slowing inflation were likely to limit further losses, JP
Morgan Chase and ABN AMRO said in separate reports.
    The Indian government reported a decline in the rate of
  

increase in wholesale prices to 7.02 percent in the 12 months  

to Dec. 4, from 7.3 percent in the year through the previous  

week.

text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and the
Singapore dollar led Asian currencies down on Friday on worries
central banks may step up dollar-buying to stem a two-month
rally in their currencies that may threaten exports.
    The two currencies weakened almost a third of a percent
each, taking the won             to 1,060 per dollar and
the Singapore dollar  to 1.6482/1.6492 per dollar.
    Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore checked
rates with some banks -- a signal that it might be thinking of
buying dollars.
    The central banks of South Korea, Singapore and India have
stepped up dollar buying since November to stem a rally sparked
by concerns the United States seemed unable to attract enough
capital from abroad to plug its record current account deficit.
  


    The Bank of Korea said Friday it had carried out further
"smoothing operations" in the local currency market in the
first half of December, boosting the country's foreign exchange
reserves by $3.4 billion in the fortnight to Dec. 15.
 
    "These levels of intervention are not sustainable," said
Sani Hamid, a currency analyst at 4CAST in Singapore.
    Bank of Korea had to step up dollar-buying since November
to absorb the dollars sold by local firms as exports soared, he
said. But he added this may ease off.
    "With technology exports slowing down next year, the
current account surplus is likely to taper off a bit," he said.
    The won has gained 13 percent this year, making it Asia's
  


best performing currency. The currency surged to a seven-year
  


high this month against the dollar as exporters dumped their
  


dollar earnings on worries about the weakening dollar.
  


SINGAPORE EXPORTS SLUMP
  


Taiwan dollar  and the yen        this year, weakened
  


after the government reported a higher-than-expected 9.1
  


percent decline the country's non-oil exports in November. A
  


Reuters poll of economists had forecast a 1.9 percent decline.
  


The Singapore dollar is now on the weaker side of the
  


trade-weighted range within which the Monetary Authority of
  


Singapore maintains the currency, ABN AMRO Bank said in a
  


report, adding that gains are likely to be modest without a
  


boost from overseas portfolio investments, like those seen in
  


South Korea and Taiwan.
  


The Indonesian rupiah  weakened as much as half a
  


percent to 9,325 per dollar, closer to a 3-= month low

The currency has been hurt by a widening budget deficit and

The rupiah was unlikely to weaken further, Hamid said,

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won weakens on  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won weakened
on Friday as indications of increased dollar-buying
intervention by the South Korean central bank and
better-than-expected U.S. current account data helped the
dollar.
    The won        lost a quarter of a percent to 1,059 per
dollar after the Bank of Korea said it had carried out
"smoothing operations" in the won market in the first half of
December, boosting the country's foreign exchange reserves by
$3.4 billion.
    Analysts said the central banks of South Korea, Singapore
and India had stepped up dollar-buying intervention since
November to slow an Asian currency rally triggered by concerns
that a record U.S. current account deficit would hurt the
dollar.
 
    Stronger currencies make Asian exports, a key source of
growth in the region, less competitive in the United States.
  


    "With domestic demand still fragile (in South Korea),
expect such smoothing' behaviour to persist if the won renews
its strong appreciation trend," ABN AMRO Bank said in a report.
    The won has led the rally in Asian currencies since the
  

start of October and is Asia's best performing currency this  

year, having gained almost 13 percent. It hit a seven-year high  

near 1,037 per dollar on December 6, but has since lost ground.  

It has fallen one percent since the end of November.  

The Taiwan dollar has gained 5 percent and the  

Singapore dollar strengthened 3.2 percent as the yen has  

appreciated 2.6 percent this year.  

Data showing the U.S. current account deficit was narrower  

than expected in the third quarter, even though at a record  

high, helped ease some concerns about the dollar.  

"Taken collectively, the data suggests that the financing  

of the current account deficit was not a major problem in the  

third quarter, in the context of solid but not spectacular  

official inflows," said Alan Ruskin, an analyst at 4CAST, in a  

report.  

"The bad quarters, in contrast, see the dollar under marked  

pressure, and the current account and financial account data  

for the fourth quarter is likely to provide a far less  

encouraging picture longer-term," he said.  

The third-quarter data came a day after U.S. Treasury  

figures showed net inflows into the United States in October  

were not enough to cover that month's record $55.5 billion  

trade deficit.  

TAIWAN DOLLAR, BAHT  

The Taiwan dollar and the Thai baht are expected to lead  

another Asian rally against a weakening dollar because of the  

strength of their economies and greater central bank tolerance  

for currency strength, JP Morgan said in a report.  

Improving labour markets in South Korea, Hong Kong and  

Singapore and increased foreign equity investment in South  

Korea, Taiwan and Thailand would support currencies, JP Morgan  

said.  

The baht weakened a quarter of a percent to 39.25 per  

dollar, paring gains made on Thursday after a surprise 25 basis  

point interest rate rise by the Bank of Thailand.  

The Indonesian rupiah lost half a percent on renewed  

concerns about a drop in foreign direct investment and higher  

fuel subsidies which have widened the budget deficit.  

On Thursday, Japan's trade minister, Shoichi Nakagawa, said  

Indonesia needed to tackle corruption and improve law  

enforcement if it wanted Japanese investment to return.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah, won down on yen, c.bank fears.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 8 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit a
two-month trough and the Korean won tripped more than half a
percent on Wednesday as the fear of central bank intervention
and the decline in the Japanese yen undermined Asian
currencies.
 
    The U.S. dollar was above record euro lows and 12-year lows
against sterling hit on Tuesday.
    After falling steeply for two months, the U.S. currency has
  

been supported this week by increasing rhetoric from European  

and Japanese officials worried about the rise in their  

currencies.  

The dollar was up around 103 yen on Wednesday after  

Japanese GDP data showed the economy barely expanded in the  

third quarter.  

The Singapore dollar weakened to around S$1.64, down 0.7  

percent from last week's six-year high. South Korea's won was  

down some 11 won from seven-year highs struck on Monday.  

"It is pretty clear that not just Korea but most Asian  

central banks are intervening quite strongly at the moment,"  

said Simon Flint, strategist with Bank of America in Singapore.   


 
    "They would have been alarmed at the speed and extent of
the move we have seen of late," he said.
    The won has risen nearly seven percent since November. The
Taiwan dollar is up four percent in that period and the Thai
baht nearly 5 percent.
    Reserves data showed more than $10 billion of the $14
  

billion increase in Korea's November reserves could have  

resulted from dollar-buying intervention to curb the won's  

strength.  

Analysts said around $3 billion of a $4.3 billion increase  

in Singapore's November reserves could not be explained by  

simply valuation effects. The reserves totalled $110.1 billion.   


 
    "This is one of the largest implied intervention numbers we
have seen in Singapore," Flint said.
    Analysts also said this week's retreat in the yen had
  

provided the region's central banks an opportunity to intervene

effectively, buying dollars at a time when their currencies

were not being bought aggressively by the market.  

RUPIAH BLUES  

Traders said the rupiah's fall to a two month low of 9,140  

per dollar followed dollar-buying by oil companies and other  

importers.  

Still, the rupiah has been among the region's worst  

performers this year, bucking the rally of the past few months  

and shedding about 8 percent so far in 2004.  

A prolonged national and presidential election process  

robbed it of some of last year's popularity as a high-yielder  

and President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's fragmented cabinet has  

raised worries about economic reforms.  

"The rupiah is really not seen as part of the whole Asian  

revaluation story. The rupiah is not particularly undervalued  

in real effective exchange rate terms," Flint said, referring  

to the currency's inflation and trade-weighted value.  

"The market thinks of the Asian revaluation story as a  

correction of the U.S. current account deficit, so those  

countries with large current account surpluses should benefit  

the most.   


 
    "Indonesia barely has a current account surplus anymore,"
Flint said.
    Indonesia said on Tuesday it sold 20 percent of its seventh
  

largest bank, PT Bank Permata Tbk., for about $128 million. The  

news of the inflow did not help the rupiah.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Juggling  intervention  risks, weak dollar.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies ended local
market trading on Tuesday slightly weaker but off lows,
balancing the risks of regional central bank intervention and
the renewed U.S. dollar downtrend.
    The U.S. currency hit fresh lows against the euro as
markets overcame early fears of European intervention. The head
of the European Central Bank and euro zone finance ministers
said in a joint statement on Monday they were unhappy with the
euro's surge and they were closely monitoring exchange rate
swings.
    But in Asia, the dollar was about a yen off five-year lows
against the Japanese currency. It rallied from seven-year lows
against the South Korean won on suspicion the Korean
authorities had intervened.
    The dollar rallied over 6 won from Monday's seven-year low
near 1,037 against the South Korean unit. But the won closed
local trade slightly higher and was a shade stronger against
the yen.
  


    The Taiwan dollar retreated further from last week's
four-year high of 31.96, ending local trade on the weaker side
of 32. Thailand's markets opened after a holiday and pushed the
baht down after thin offshore trading had taken it past 39 per
dollar to a February high on Monday.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS in Singapore,
said the stepped-up rhetoric from the Japanese and the
Europeans had given markets an excuse to book profits on their
extended dollar-bearish positions. Yet, he did not expect the
European authorities to intervene to rein in the euro.
 
    "We seem to be entering a consolidation phase," Baweja
said.
    That would also give Asian central banks some breathing
  

space although they would intervene if the pace of currency

gains continued to be as rapid as it has been in the past two  

months, he said.  

Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah weakened to around 9,090  

from Monday's 9,060 a dollar. It has lagged the rally in the  

region, weighed down by worries over how new President Susilo  

Bambang Yudhoyono's fragmented cabinet will approve key  

reforms.  

It has not reacted to news that the country would sell  

another 20 percent of its seventh largest bank, PT Bank Permata  

Tbk., this week. That stake is estimated to be worth $120  

million.  

The Philippine peso stayed on the weaker side of 56 per  

dollar even after Fitch Ratings merely lowered its outlook on  

Philippines debt to negative, after fears there would be a  

downgrade.  

"The rupiah and peso prove that it is not just a dollar  

call, and the balance of payments does matter," Baweja said,  

explaining that the currencies in Asia with the strongest  

external accounts were rallying the most.  

SING DOLLAR STRENGTH  

The Singapore dollar initially weakened to near 1.64, over  

a cent lower than last week's six-year peak, before settling  

around 1.6350.  

Jimmy Koh, head of research at United Overseas Bank said  

the Sing was about half a percent stronger than the mid-point  

of the undisclosed trade-weighed band within which the Monetary  

Authority of Singapore guides the currency.  

"This means we could see the Sing stretching towards  

1.6320. However, with the key Chinese meeting out of the way,  

it does not look like dollar/Sing will move out of its current  

range anytime soon," Koh said in a note.  

Koh was referring to China's annual closed door economic  

summit on the weekend, where top officials pledged to keep  

monetary and fiscal policies stable in 2005 but made no  

explicit reference to the possibility of a yuan revaluation.  

On Tuesday, China's central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan  

was quoted as saying upside risks to inflation remained and  

monetary policy would be fine-tuned next year using  

market-oriented measures.  

Some analysts interpret that as a signal rates will rise  

and the yuan policy will be reformed.

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Dollar up on  intervention  hints, Asian shares dip.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - The dollar rallied on Tuesday on central bank intervention hints, underpinning shares in Asian exporters, but stocks in the region were mostly lower on nerves over Japan economic data and Hong Kong IPOs due this week.  

Shares in Amcor, the world's largest maker of plastic bottles, fell 8 percent on news it had ousted its chief executive after finding some staff may have acted illegally to drive up box prices.  

Crude oil continued a rally from three-month lows to stand above $43 a barrel, as traders eyed signals from OPEC that it might take action to stem a slide that knocked 14 percent off prices last week. The producer cartel meets in Cairo on Friday.  

Gold weakened as the dollar climbed, and Japanese government bonds were flat ahead of economic data out Wednesday and Thursday.  

On Monday, European Central Bank and euro-zone finance ministers built on recent rhetoric against their currency's surge, saying in a joint statement that sharp moves in exchange rates were unwelcome and that they were closely monitoring swings.  

"It hints at intervention because they (the ECB and European finance ministries) together control currency policy for Europe," said Jake Moore, a currency strategist at Barclays Bank.  

"The market's getting a bit nervous and that's prompted a bit of profit-taking," he said, adding that intervention would probably not occur unless the euro rose to around $1.38.  

The dollar was around $1.3408 against the euro up slightly from late levels in New York, where it rose about 0.4 percent. It marked a record low of $1.3461 on Friday.  

The U.S. currency bought around 103.02 yen little changed from late New York, where it rose 1 yen, due in part to concerns about Japanese intervention. It was well off a five-year low of 101.83 yen hit last week.  

GDP, IPOS AWAITED  

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei stock average fell 0.25 percent to 10,954.01 by its mid-session close, Hong Kong's Hang Seng was up 0.14 percent at 14,283.58 in early trade, while an MSCI index of Asian non-Japan shares was 0.46 percent lower at 255.79.  

Mitsui Trust Holdings Inc, Japan's seventh-largest bank by assets, supported the Nikkei, climbing 4.1 percent after Goldman Sachs raised its rating on the stock to "outperform" from "in line". The broker said continued operating profit growth would give it enough retained earnings to pay back the funds it owes from a state bail-out in the late 1990s. Daiei Inc. jumped 7 percent, extending gains into a fifth straight session as foreign and domestic investors, including Wal-Mart Stores Inc., queued up to submit proposals to the state-backed Industrial Revitalisation Corp. of Japan (IRCJ) for reviving the debt-laden retailer.  

Tokyo traders said investors were on the sidelines ahead of revised gross domestic product (GDP) figures for the July-September quarter, due on Wednesday, and October machinery orders data due on Thursday to get a better idea of how Japan's economy is faring.  

"The Nikkei is basically stuck around 11,000 and we're all waiting for a signal for which way to go next," said Koji Muneoka, head of domestic sales trading at HSBC in Tokyo.  

BIG HK IPOS  

In Hong Kong all eyes were on two large IPOs - Air China and the Hong Kong Housing Authority's Link's property trust - due to raise a combined US$4.1 billion this week. Singapore's Straits Times rose half a percent, led by Sembcorp, which announced a special dividend. Taiwan's benchmark index dropped a third of a percent ahead of legislative elections on Saturday. Australia's S&P ASX 200 fell 0.31, dragged down by Amcor. South Korea's KOSPI fell 0.61 percent. Global stocks as measured by the MSCI World Index were down 0.36 percent.  

U.S. stocks offering no clear direction to Asian markets, closing mixed. The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 0.43 percent at 10,547.06 as oil prices nudged higher. The Nasdaq Composite Index finished up 0.15 percent at 2,151.25 as Apple Computer Inc. rose 5 percent.  

Gold fell to $452.75 an ounce from $454 overnight. January NYMEX crude climbed 8 cents to $43.06. Ten-year JGB futures were flat, yielding 1.4 percent.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  fear forces retreat.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were
forced off their recent multi-year peaks on Tuesday after a
joint statement from European officials helped the U.S. dollar
rally.
    The U.S. currency was well off recent record lows against
the euro and five-year trough against the Japanese yen after
the head of the European Central Bank and euro zone finance
ministers said in the joint statement they were unhappy with
the euro's surge and they were closely monitoring exchange rate
swings.
    In Asia, the dollar rallied over 6 won from Monday's
seven-year low near 1,037 against the South Korean unit. Still,
the won was a shade stronger against the yen.
    The Sing dollar was on the firmer side of 1.64 but well off
last week's six-year peak and the Taiwan dollar retreated
further from last week's four-year high of 31.96.
  


    Thailand's markets opened after a holiday and pushed the
baht down after thin offshore trading had taken it past 39 per
dollar to a February high on Monday.
    Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS in Singapore,
said the stepped-up rhetoric from the Japanese and the
Europeans had given markets an excuse to book profits on their
extended dollar-bearish positions. Yet, he did not expect the
European authorities to intervene to rein in the euro.
 
    "We seem to be entering a consolidation phase," Baweja
said.
    That would also give Asian central banks some breathing
  


space although they would intervene if the pace of currency


gains continued to be as rapid as it has been in the past two
  


months, he said.
  


RUPIAH, PESO LAGGARDS
  


The Indonesian rupiah displayed characteristic lethargy,
  


holding steady levels around 9,060/9,070 a dollar.
  


The Philippine peso stayed on the weaker side of 56 per
  


dollar, with markets in Manila on alert after newspaper reports
  


that Fitch Ratings was likely to downgrade Philippines debt.
  


"The rupiah and peso prove that it is not just a dollar
  


call, and the balance of payments does matter," Baweja said,
  


explaining that the currencies in Asia with the strongest
  


external accounts were rallying the most.
  


The rupiah has been weighed down by worries over how new
  


President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's fragmented cabinet will
  


approve key reforms.
  


It has not reacted to news that the country would sell
  


another 20 percent of its seventh largest bank, PT Bank Permata
  


Tbk., this week. That stake is estimated to be worth $120
  


million.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Currencies  weaken on  intervention  fear.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 3 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar and the
Thai baht weakened more than half a percent on Friday, leading
declines in Asia as authorities increased warnings they might
sell their currencies to stem a two-month rally.
    The Singapore dollar       , which hit a six-year high
against the dollar on Wednesday, traded at about 1.6422 per
dollar. The baht  weakened to 39.37 per dollar, paring
gains that took it to a seven-month high on Thursday.
    South Korea must be ready to prevent excessive gains in its
currency and work with other countries to stem sharp currency
moves that hurt exporters, President Roh Moo-hyun said at a
press briefing in London on Thursday.
    The won        surged 14 percent this year to a seven-year
high on Thursday, leading gains in Asian currencies against a
broadly weakening dollar.
    Roh's comments resonated among other Asian officials,
particularly in Japan, who may be preparing to intervene,
analysts said.
  


    "The authorities may be signalling that enough is enough,"
said Song Seng Wun, economist at G.K. Goh Securities in
Singapore.
    "With the holiday season coming up, and liquidity low, they
may think that this is the best time to intervene because they
don't want to waste too much ammunition."
 
    South Korea has already intervened by buying dollars with
won last month, data showed this week.
    UBS expects more intervention from the Bank of Korea as
authorities seek to protect the country's biggest companies
which are also the country's largest exporters.
    The won        weakened 0.3 percent on Friday to about
1,044.30 per dollar. The Taiwan dollar  lost half a
percent to about 32.15 per dollar.
    "Considering that the Korean domestic economy is not
exactly humming along it's not surprising that the authorities
should be whining about the won's gains," said Song.
    JAPAN INTERVENTION
    UBS also expects the Bank of Japan to start dollar-buying
intervention, for the first time since March, this month, to
stall the yen.
    The yen        plunged 1.3 percent to about 103.33 per
dollar on Friday, coming off a five-year high reached on
Thursday.
    The Christmas and year-end holiday season reduces trading,
  

making it easier for Asian central banks to reverse the rally  

in their currencies by selling relatively light amounts of  

currency, analysts said  

Worries that Asian central banks might slow down the  

purchase of U.S. treasuries to fund the U.S. deficit were eased  

by data on Thursday showing foreign central banks turned net  

buyers of U.S. Treasuries in the week ending Dec. 1.  

Asian central banks, packing the world's largest foreign  

currency reserves, have some of the biggest holdings of U.S.  

treasuries.  

Speculation that some might cut purchases of U.S.  

government debt to shift to euro assets was partly responsible  

for the dollar's decline against Asian currencies, analysts  

said.  

Dealers expect the dollar to weaken longer term, but say  

the currency could find some support short term on the strength  

of the U.S. economy as reflected by rate increases by the U.S.  

Federal Reserve this year.   


 
    Analysts expect the U.S. central bank to increase its
benchmark rate again at a meeting this month.
    "People may have underestimated the resilience in the U.S.
economy," said Song. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dlr at 4-yr high, won at 7-yr high.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar surged to a
four-year high on Thursday, outperforming most other Asian
currencies, after a plunge in oil prices bolstered the outlook
for oil-importing Asian economies.
    The 7.5 percent drop in oil prices in New York on Wednesday
led overseas investors to buy shares across Asia, pushing up
the region's benchmark stock indexes and triggering further
dollar sales by Asian exporters already spooked by a two-month
plunge in the U.S. currency.
    The Taiwan dollar appreciated over 0.7 percent to 31.96 per
dollar, strengthening beyond 32 per dollar for the first time
since November 2000. The South Korean won strengthened almost
half a percent to a new seven-year high of 1,041 per dollar.
    "Those countries should benefit after the oil prices came
off sharply," said Ashley Davies, a currency strategist at UBS
in Singapore.
  


    UBS expects the Taiwan dollar to appreciate further, along
with the Indian rupee and the Singapore dollar, because of
their strong domestic economies which complement strong trade
surpluses.
    The Indian rupee surged for a fourth day to a new
seven-month high against the dollar. The dollar dropped to a
low of 44.08 rupees in later trades, from 44.41 on Wednesday.
    The rupee's gains were pared in later deals after the
central bank stepped up dollar buying and the securities
regulator decided to put a cap on investment in local corporate
debt by overseas institutional investors.
 
    The Singapore dollar was trading at about 1.6320 per
dollar, near a six-year high of about 1.6292 set overnight.
    The rupee and the Singapore dollar have underperformed the
  

Asian rally since the start of October on concerns that the  

central banks would not allow excessive strength in their  

currencies which could jeopardise prospects for their  

exporters.  

The Thai baht surged half a percent to trade at a  

seven-month high of 39.12 per dollar, gaining for a third day,  

as optimism about the economy's growth prospects after the drop  

in oil prices added to Tuesday's better-than-expected exports  

data.  

INTERVENTION LOOMS  

Christy Tan, a currency analyst at 4CAST in Singapore, said  

that as Asian exporters dumped their dollars, the region's  

currencies were likely to extend their rally through the end of  

the year.  

That was unless central banks in Japan and South Korea  

jointly started buying dollars to stem the rally in their  

currencies.  

South Korean data released on Thursday showed the  

authorities had intervened heavily in the currency markets in  

November.  

That contrasted with data from Japan that showed the  

central bank continued to stay out of the market despite  

repeated warnings that it might intervene for the first time  

since March.  

"We're not expecting further gains in the won," said UBS'  

Davies. "We expect the won to hold above 1,000 (per dollar)  

because the government will get into trouble with the large  

conglomerates if they allow the won to appreciate further."  

The won has appreciated 14.5 percent against the dollar  

this year, making it the best performing Asian currency. The  

Taiwan dollar and the yen are the next best performers, gaining  

over 6 percent and 5 percent respectively.  

UBS expects the Bank of Japan to intervene by the end of  

this year to halt the yen's gains. The yen gained on Thursday  

to its strongest level against the dollar since March 2000.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, Though Rumored MAS Action Caps
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was higher against its U.S. counterpart late Thursday on speculative buying, but gains were capped by rumored central bank intervention.  

Singapore government bonds were relatively stable in thin trading, dealers said.  

At 0638 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6321, down from S$1.6348 in Asia late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6300 and S$1.6333 intraday.  

Despite a batch of positive U.S. economic data Wednesday, the U.S. dollar maintained its downtrend against the Singapore currency, falling to a fresh six-year low of S$1.6293 in New York.  

U.S. October personal income and consumer spending data were slightly better than expected, while the Institute for Supply Management said U.S. manufacturing activity expanded at a quicker pace in November.  

Players are still fretting about the U.S. current account and fiscal deficits, traders said.  

Early in Asia Thursday, non-Singapore speculators sold the U.S. dollar down to around the psychologically important S$1.6300 level from the open of S$1.6310.  

Then, rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore around there spooked the speculators into buying back the U.S. currency, giving the U.S. dollar a boost to as high as S$1.6333, dealers said.  

"(MAS) came in a bit and scared the market," said a local dealer.  

For the rest of the session, the U.S. dollar consolidated in the low-S$1.6300s, underpinned by talk that the MAS still had bids placed around the S$1.6300 level, dealers said.  

From a technical analysis perspective, the U.S. dollar's fall against the Singapore dollar appears to be stronger than expected, as support at S$1.6350 was breached, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

"Downward momentum is picking up again and a clear move below S$1.6300 will likely lead to acceleration lower towards the next support at S$1.6220," said UOB.  

UOB added that it lowered its trailing stop to S$1.6430, and that only a rebound above this level would imply the market had seen a temporary low. [ 02-12-04 0716GMT ]  

Singapore government bonds were relatively steady Thursday after a mixed performance by U.S. Treasurys in New York.  

The yield on the two-year bond fell one basis point to 1.54%, while that on the 10-year paper was unchanged at 2.89%.  

Interest rate swaps were also mixed from Wednesday. Late in the session, the two-year swap offer was unchanged at 1.71%, while the 10-year offer was down three basis points to 3.06%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 135 basis points from 138 basis points the day before.  

Some prices quoted are pre-settlement bids obtained from dealers and are subject to change.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaken on data,  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on
Tuesday after disappointing economic data from Japan and
comments from Asian leaders calling for concerted action to
stall a two-month rally in their currencies.
    The Taiwan dollar lost about 0.4 percent in early deals to
32.28 per dollar. The South Korean won shed 0.1 percent to
about 1,048 per dollar.
    Last week, the Taiwan dollar had climbed to its strongest
level in four years while the won had appreciated to a
seven-year high.
    The rally stalled on Monday due to worries about likely
central bank interventions across Asia. South Korea's
presidential office said on Monday that the leaders of Japan,
China and South Korea agreed on the sidelines of the
Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Laos
on the need for stable exchange rates.
    Meanwhile, industrial production data from South Korea and
Japan disappointed markets.
  


 Japanese data showed industrial
output unexpectedly fell 1.6 percent in October from a month
earlier. On Monday, South Korea said industrial output fell 0.9
percent in October.
    "The weak Japanese and Korean data are making people
conclude that the U.S. economy is cyclically the strongest
now," said Simon Flint, a currency strategist at Bank of
America in Singapore.
    Some traders and investors, who had bid up the won and
other Asian currencies this month on concerns about prolonged
weakness in the dollar, probably rewound their bets after the
agreement among Asian leaders that the rally in their
currencies was overdone, Flint said.
    "The talk about that meeting may have had an impact on the
market," he said. "The decline in the dollar has been arrested
for the time being."
    Further data from Japan, including gross domestic product
figures and the Tankan survey due early next month, is likely
to reconfirm that the Japanese economy may be slowing.
    Bank of America still expects the dollar to weaken to 100
yen by the end of the year, from around 103.15 on Tuesday, and
to $1.35 per euro, from $1.325 on Tuesday, because of the
widening U.S. current account deficits.
    Traders are looking for further clues on whether Asian
central banks are curtailing purchases of U.S. treasury bills
and other dollar assets in their foreign currency reserve
holdings.
    A Chinese economic adviser said last week U.S. government
data showed that China, which holds the world's second-largest
foreign currency reserves, reduced its dollar holdings.
    Many other Asian central banks could reduce their dollar
holdings if the dollar weakness persists and that could lead to
further dollar weakness in the longer term, Flint said.
    "I don't think this question is going to go away soon,"
Flint said. "There's enough structural themes pointing to a
dollar weakness in the longer term." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR
