title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaker on  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on
Monday, led by the Taiwan dollar, on concerns the region's
central banks may come together and buy dollars to stall a
two-month rally which has driven some currencies to multi-year
highs.
    The Taiwan dollar weakened 0.2 percent to 32.16 per dollar
and the Singapore dollar fell as low as 1.6410, before
recovering some lost ground.
 
    The South Korean won pared its losses after weakening as
much as 0.6 percent in early trading.
    Some investors took profits, winding down bets for a
weakening dollar, on the run-up in the won and other Asian
currencies this month.
    The won has surged nearly 7 percent and the Taiwan dollar
  

has appreciated about 4 percent since the end of October,  

beating the less than 3 percent gain in the yen against the  

dollar.  

Others refrained from further purchases of Asian currencies

on worries the central banks in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and  

Singapore may not tolerate further gains in their units,  

traders said.  

"The market and the central banks are staring at each  

other, trying to call each other's bluff right now," said  

Philip Wee, treasury markets strategist at DBS Bank in  

Singapore.  

"We're monitoring for any signs of a possible coordinated  

move among Asian central banks to intervene."  

South Korean Deputy Finance Minister Chin Dong-soo said the  

won was rising faster than other currencies and that the  

government would coordinate with the central bank to check the  

volatility in the local currency market.  

The verbal warnings followed dollar purchases by state-run  

banks, which traders said were acting on behalf of the  

government.  

The Singapore dollar has gained the least among the major  

Asian currencies this month on concern the Monetary Authority

of Singapore may not tolerate sharp gains in the currency. The  

currency appreciated 1.3 percent since the end of October.  

Singapore traders said there were no indications of  

intervention by the MAS on Monday although the market remained  

cautious of pushing the currency too high.  

WON CROSSES  

Traders are particularly worried about Korean intervention

after the won strengthened against the Singapore dollar and the  

yen this month.  

The won has gained to 10.16 per yen on Monday from about  

10.57 per yen at the end of October. The South Korean currency

has surged to almost 637.5 per Singapore dollar from 673 over  

the same period.  

"The Korean central bank needed to calm down the markets  

for the shorter term," said Mark Cranfield, head of treasury  

and capital markets at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg.  

"Trading was frantic and truly became reckless last week,"  

he said, referring to a 1 percent surge in the won on Friday as  

local exporters dumped their dollar receipts on worries that  

the U.S. currency may continue its decline against the won and  

other currencies in the absence of central bank intervention.  

Traders and investors are also watching for further signs  

about the global demand for U.S. treasury bills and other  

dollar-assets, said Wee at DBS Bank.  

Central banks of Japan, China, South Korea and other Asian  

currencies are among the biggest holders of U.S. treasury bills  

outside the United States.  

Russia indicated earlier this month it plans to boost the  

proportion of its foreign currency reserves made up by euros  

while a Chinese newspaper report on Friday cited a local  

central bank advisor saying China may have trimmed its holdings  

of U.S. treasuries.  

The advisor later said he was only citing U.S. government  

data, but the issue continues to worry traders and put pressure  

on the dollar over the longer term.  

"It's a subject that nobody wants to talk about but is  

there at the back of everyone's mind," Cranfield said. "Is Asia  

still buying U.S. treasuries?" CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won, Taiwan dollar weaken on  intervention .
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on
Monday, led by the South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar,
after state-run banks stepped in to buy dollars to curb a rally
that drove regionals to multi-year highs last week.
    The South Korean won lost as much as 0.6 percent against
the dollar to 1,053 per dollar in local trades on suspected
central bank intervention, before recovering most of its lost
ground. The Taiwan dollar weakened 0.3 percent to 32.205 per
dollar.
    Government officials in Japan and South Korea have
threatened to intervene over the past month to stem the
dollar's broad-based slide that drove the won to a 7-year high
and the Taiwan dollar to a 4-year high last week.
    South Korea is particularly hurt by the weaker dollar
because the won has appreciated 10 percent in the past three
months to outperform other Asian currencies.
  


 
    The currency gained 1 percent on Friday as the rally
triggered sales of dollar receipts by the country's exporters.
    "The Korean central bank needed to calm down the markets
for the shorter term," said Mark Cranfield, head of treasury
and capital markets at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg.
    "Trading was frantic and truly became reckless last week. I
wouldn't be surprised if the Bank of Japan was in the market
too."
    The won also came under pressure after data showed South
  

Korea's industrial production fell a seasonally adjusted 0.9  

percent in October from the month earlier. Analysts in a  

Reuters poll had expected a median rise of 0.7 percent.  

While South Korea's current account surplus has tripled in  

the first 10 months of this year, export growth has slowed  

since the second quarter, dragging on the outlook for the  

economy already weakened by a slump in domestic consumer  

demand.  

CHINA FACTOR  

The Singapore dollar traded at about 1.6385/90, close to a  

6-year high.  

Other Asian currencies were weighed down by Chinese Premier  

Wen Jiabao's statements on Sunday signalling the country was in  

no rush to revalue the yuan.  

Jiabao said China needed a stable economy and a healthy  

financial system before making changes to the yuan's peg to the  

dollar.  

Speculation that China might soon relax controls over its  

currency and allow the yuan to trade in a broader band had  

fuelled the rally in Asian currencies.  

"I think you can believe (Premier Wen)," said Cranfield.  

"The bottomline is that China would do only what's important  

for them. It'll never do what the rest of the world wants them  

to do."  

Cranfield said the dollar was likely to continue on its  

weakening trend against most major currencies in the longer  

term.  

Since the start of this year, the dollar has weakened  

almost 14 percent against the won, nearly 6 percent against the  

Taiwan dollar and over 4 percent against the yen as U.S.  

officials voiced concerns about the country's widening current  

account deficit.  

Several U.S. Federal Reserve officials have argued that the  

shortfall could be met by a drop in the value of the dollar  

against the currencies of major trading partners of the U.S..

title: Singapore Dlr Up At Another 6-Yr High Vs US Dlr Late
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose to another six-year high against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Friday, boosted by speculator-led buying spurred by a newspaper report that China had cut its U.S. bond holdings.  

Singapore government bond prices were higher late Friday, the result of continued bull-flattening trades in the local market, dealers said.  

At 0800 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6390, down from S$1.6404 in Asia late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6376 and S$1.6409 intraday.  

After falling to S$1.6382 on selling by U.S. investment banks in the morning, the U.S. currency edged down further to S$1.6376 in the afternoon following a Chinese newspaper report quoting the People's Bank of China's policy board member Yu Yongding as saying China has reduced its U.S. bond holdings to about US$180 billion.  

The newspaper report didn't provide details of China's previous holdings of U.S. bonds, though the report said around 80% of China's estimated US$515 billion worth of foreign reserves are usually held in U.S. dollar assets.  

Traders said the newspaper report also generated worries that China could further decrease its holdings of U.S. Treasurys, which would likely lead to more U.S. dollar weakness against Asian currencies, including the local dollar.  

But the U.S. currency managed to garner support from rumored buying by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in the high-S$1.6300s throughout the session. Recently, the MAS has apparently stepped up its intervention to buy U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars, due to enhanced bearishness toward the U.S. unit, dealers said.  

As a result, speculators who had sold the U.S. dollar down to S$1.6376 in the afternoon bought back the U.S. currency later in the session to take profit on their short positions, lifting the U.S. unit up to near the psychologically important S$1.6400 level. [ 26-11-04 0840GMT ]  

Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly higher late Friday on continued buying mainly at the long-end, resulting in a further flattening of the yield curve, dealers said.  

At the end of the local session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was flat at 1.51%. At the longer end of the curve, the 10-year yield fell 3 basis points to 2.78%, while the 15-year yield fell 5 basis points to 3.17%.  

In the interest rate swaps market, the two-year swap offer was unchanged at 1.67% from late Thursday, the five-year swap offer was at 2.32% versus 2.33%, while the 10-year offer fell to 2.99% from 3.01%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 132 basis points from 134 basis points late Thursday.  

In the interbank market, the overnight rate inched up to 1.1250% from 0.6250% late Thursday.  

Prices quoted are pre-settlement bids obtained from dealers and are subject to change.

title: CORRECTED - CORRECTED-GLOBAL MARKETS-New dollar low caps Tokyo stocks, buoys.
text:
In SINGAPORE story headlined "New dollar low caps Tokyo
 stocks, buoys gold" please read in first paragraph ... on
 Friday ... instead of ... on Thursday ... (corrects day).
  

A corrected story follows.  

SINGAPORE, Nov 26 (Reuters) - The dollar hit a record low against the euro on Friday as traders tested the will of central banks to stop its slide, leaving Tokyo stocks flat on worries about a strong yen and keeping gold near a 16-year high.  

Gains in steel makers and other basic industries shares underpinned Asian stock markets, driving a regional index of shares outside Japan to its highest level in nearly 5 years.  

"The market remains emboldened that the USD can fall further," said Greg Gibbs, senior currency strategist at Asia Royal Bank of Canada Capital Markets. "As it probes the resistance of authorities to accept appreciation of their currency, it finds very little."   


With trading thinned by the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday,
Tokyo traders beat the dollar down to a record low of $1.3283 per euro
. The yen  traded near a 5-year high of 102.37 yen        reached in
London.
  

Steel producer shares firmed for the second day in a row amid growing evidence of a shortage of the metal among Japanese carmakers and the prospect of higher product prices.  

Nippon Steel Corp. (5401.T) climbed 2.4 percent and JFE Steel Corp. (5411.T) rose 2.9 percent after Nissan Motor Co. (7201.T) said the shortage would force it to stop some production.  

Nissan, which procures steel from Nippon Steel and JFE, has also asked South Korea's POSCO for emergency supplies. POSCO shares touched a record high and stood 2.9 percent ahead on the day. Nissan fell half a percent.   


Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei average  was flat at 10,897.87. An MSCI index
of non-Japan shares            climbed 0.42 percent to its highest
level since March 2000, pushing MSCI's World Index           up 0.3
percent to a 3-year high.
  

DRUG MERGER  

Japan's Dainippon Pharmaceutical Co. (4506.T) gained 5 percent after agreeing to a merger with the drug unit of Sumitomo Chemical Co. Ltd. (4005.T), up 2.4 percent.  

Their gains offset slippage elsewhere on concerns about the effect of yen strength on exports.  

In Hong Kong, shares in state controlled CNOOC (0883.HK) slipped 4.5 percent after it issued a US$850 million convertible bond, a record size for a mainland Chinese firm.  

Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 0.22 percent.  

LCD makers gained in Taiwan on news of production delays at rivals using faulty equipment made by Canon Inc. (7751.T).  

AU Optronics (2409.TW), the world's third largest display screen maker, was up 3.64 percent.  

"The problems with Canon's equipment could slow down the increase in supply, and that is good news. This sector has not had real good news for a long time," said Alvin Teng, assistant research manager at SinoPac Securities.   


Taiwan's benchmark index  rose 0.67 percent, Australia's S&P ASX 200
     climbed more than 0.2 percent to another record high, while South
Korea's KOSPI         added 0.91 percent. Singapore's Straits Times
   rose 0.14 percent.
  

VERBAL INTERVENTION NOT ENOUGH  

Gold hovered $1 below a 16-1/4-year high of $452.75 struck in Europe on Thursday.  

The dollar was trading at $1.3258 per euro, compared with $1.3270 in very thin, late New York trade, and at 102.55 yen, little changed from New York.  

A repeat of a warning against dollar weakness from Japanese Finance Minister Sadakazu Tanigaki, who threatened to take action against sudden moves, had little impact.  

"It's just a matter of when monetary authorities are going to crank up the tone of verbal intervention, but at this point verbal intervention isn't going to stop the dollar's fall," said Hideaki Furumaya, currency manager at Trust and Custody Services Bank.  

Even so, the market was looking forward to comments later in the day from European Central Bank chief Jean-Claude Trichet, who is due to speak in Rio de Janeiro, along with ECB council member and Spanish central bank governor Jaime Caruana.  

Trichet, who referred to recent currency movements as "brutal" earlier in the month, has become the most vocal European policymaker on dollar weakness.  

Traders were expecting market liquidity to remain thin because of the extended U.S. holiday.  

In such thin trading, many said a fall in the dollar past 102 yen and $1.33 per euro was a real possibility.  

Brent crude oil for January delivery was indicated slightly higher in early Asian trade, bid at $44.71 a barrel, up from up from $44.66 in London. The U.S. NYMEX crude market was closed.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Boosted by China talk, won surges.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Increased speculation of a
Chinese yuan revaluation boosted Asian currencies on Thursday,
taking the South Korean won to a seven-year high, the Taiwan
dollar to a four-year high and the Sing dollar to fresh
six-year highs.
    The Sing dollar        firmed to 1.6395 per dollar, Reuters
data showed, a level last seen in December 1998, as the
rallying yen and rising premium on the yuan buoyed Asian
regionals.
    Talk of intervention by Singapore's central bank and the
Bank of Korea did not deter markets, although a Singapore-based
trader said dollar/Sing was "quite well supported" around 1.64.
 
    Asian regionals were already on a firm footing as the U.S.
dollar extended a two-month slide to another record low against
the euro        and 4-=   year lows versus the yen       ,
undermined by concerns over the U.S. trade deficit.
    The apparent lack of U.S.
  


 concern over the dollar's descent
and the possibility Russia's central bank might increase euro
holdings has hurt the dollar this week.
    The yuan premiums on near-term non-deliverable forwards
  rose to their highest since October 2003 on talk that
Beijing would decide on a yuan regime change soon.
    The speculation was fuelled by research reports that
suggested a desision on the yuan could be taken at an annual
Central Economic Work Conference at the weekend.
    Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard
  

Chartered Bank in Singapore, said he'd be surprised if China  

announced a shift in the yuan policy at the meeting. He expects  

China will move only in the first quarter of 2005.  

"The risk is not zero, but if people are trading on  

expectations that China will announce a band widening or a  

revaluation on Monday, they are likely to be disappointed,"  

Henderson said.  

For over two years markets have speculated China would  

alter its trading band for the yuan, ceding to pressure from  

the United States and other industrialised nations that say an  

undervalued yuan gives Chinese exporters an unfair advantage.   


 
    The yuan has been kept in a narrow band around 8.28 a
dollar since late 1997.
    The one-month yuan NDF premium quoted as high as 720 points
  

on Thursday, although it eased in later deals. That level  

prices in an appreciation of nearly 1 percent in the yuan  

within a month.  

GO SLOW   


The South Korean won             strengthened nearly
  

a percent to 1,057 per dollar, a level last seen during the  

Asian financial crisis in November 1997, as it shrugged off the  

threat of Bank of Korea intervention.  

The central bank was suspected of buying dollars to cap the  

won around 1,060 per dollar on Monday and Tuesday, and the  

government has voiced concerns about the won's rise.   


 
    The Taiwan dollar          rose to 32.18 per dollar, its
strongest since November 2000.
    Even the Indonesian rupiah managed small gains, rising to
levels around 8,960 a dollar.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist with Deustche Bank, said
markets need not fear Asian central bank intervention.
    "We are in a new regime, a new environment for
intervention," he said.
    "Increasingly, intervention will be seen as something which
does not work and which simply subsidises fresh market
positions."
    Standard Chartered's Henderson said he would however advise
  

trimming some of the long Asian currency positions heading into  

the end of the year, especially in outperformers such as the  

won and Taiwan dollar.  

"Stay long (Asia) in the medium term but start taking some  

money off the table as we head into the year-end," he said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  hurts won, baht rises.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention pulled
the Korean won away from seven-year highs on Wednesday while
the Thai baht, one of Asia's laggards in the two-month long
rally against the dollar, rose to a new seven-month high.
    The threat of intervention loomed large in north Asia. Even
as Russia's proposal to review the share of euros in its
foreign exchange reserves pushed the euro  to record
highs, the yen  stalled about half a yen before last
week's peaks near 102.75 per dollar.
    The Korean won                   fell as far as 1,068.8 a
dollar, off a 7-year high of 1,060 hit on Monday and Tuesday,
after state-run banks were seen buying dollars aggressively.
    Other Asian currencies retained their upward bias.
    Reuters data showed the Singapore dollar
strengthened to 1.6420, a new 6-year high, and the Thai baht
  was quoted at 39.67, its highest since April.
  


 The Taiwan
 
dollar          equalled Friday's 3-=   year peak of 32.352 per
dollar.
    "Foreign exchange appreciation in Asia will not occur in a
  

straight line. There are already some signs of profit-taking  

and position-squaring, these will likely continue as the year  

comes to an end," Vincent Low, head of Asian currency strategy  

at Merrill Lynch, said in a note.  

Low said some signs of weakness in equities - foreigners  

turned net sellers of Korean and Taiwan shares this week after  

being net buyers for most of this month - were among the  

factors that could test authorities' tolerance of stronger  

currencies.  

"Authorities in Japan, and by default the rest of Asia, may  

be less willing to tolerate currency strength if there are  

signs that their economies are not able to withstand tighter  

policies.   


 
    "Continued signs of equity weakness could be a precursor to
central bank intervention," Low said.
    WON STALLS
    Traders were not surprised to hear Korean authorities may
have intervened to rein in the won.
    "The won has outdone even the yen and is too strong
relative to the region. The Koreans have a case for smoothening
the won's move," said Philip Wee, a strategist with DBS Bank.
    The won has risen nearly 5 percent this month, compared
with the yen's 2 percent, the Taiwan dollar's 3 percent and the
Singapore dollar's 1 percent gains.
    The yen-won cross            moved to 10.3 won per yen this
week from 10.7 in late October, reflecting the won's strength.
    On Monday, the finance ministry was reported to have asked
  

the Bank of Korea to take a more aggressive stance on the  

currency. On Wednesday, a Korean business leader said the  

finance ministry had asked firms to moderate their dollar  

selling.   


 
    Merrill's Low said he would exclude the won from any
long-Asia basket trades.
    "Given that a short dollar/won trade has done well in 2004
  

and that the macro dynamics in Korea - central bank cutting  

rates, still-fragile household balance sheets - are somewhat  

different from the region's norm, we will likely exclude the  

won in future Asia baskets," Low said.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Purchase By US Funds; Bonds Up
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger in Asia late Wednesday as U.S. funds used bullish remarks on the baht by Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra as a reason to buy the island's currency.  

Singapore government bond prices were also higher, mainly due to lower interbank rates and dip-buying interest, dealers said.  

At 0640 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6431, down from S$1.6465 in Asia late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6420 and S$1.6448 intraday.  

Given rife speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened late Tuesday to stem the U.S. currency's slide to a fresh six-year low of S$1.6414, the U.S. unit kicked off Wednesday's Asian session on a positive note near the mid-S$1.6400 level.  

But the U.S. dollar dropped as low as S$1.6420 in the morning after Thaksin said that the strong baht shouldn't have much adverse effect on Thailand's exports. Thai exporters must adapt to a stronger baht as the currency is likely to rise further against the U.S. dollar, he said.  

"U.S. funds sold dollar-Sing and dollar-baht" on Thaksin's comments, said a Singapore dealer.  

Analysts said Thaksin's comments on the baht may have sparked similar notions among U.S. funds that Singapore authorities may be resigned to a stronger local dollar and won't do much to support the beleaguered U.S. currency.  

Early in the afternoon, the U.S. dollar recovered slightly to around S$1.6435 levels on its mild rebound against major currencies such as the yen.  

For the rest of the week, the U.S. unit is likely to trade in a relatively narrow S$1.6400-S$1.6480 range, United Overseas Bank said in a research report.  

"With the euro struggling above US$1.3100, the U.S. dollar still above Y103.00 and talk of MAS in the market, the dollar-Sing's downside should be limited to S$1.6400 for now," it said. [ 24-11-04 0651GMT ]  

Government bonds were mostly higher late Wednesday, aided by an overnight rise in U.S. Treasurys and softer local interbank rates, which keep borrowing costs down, dealers said.  

Late in the local session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was down six basis points at 1.53%. At the longer end of the curve, the 10-year yield fell six basis points to 2.88%, while the 15-year yield shed seven basis points to 3.30%.  

Interest rate swaps were mostly lower too, in line with local bond yields.

Korea had intervened to sell won caused the currency to trim

curtailed the Taiwan dollar and the Japanese yen.
    Asian currencies hit fresh multi-year highs on Friday and
in Monday morning deals after the Group of 20 nations' meeting
over the weekend failed to address the U.S. dollar's descent.
    The U.S. unit's drop came on the back of Federal Reserve
Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments that a weaker currency might
be needed to trim the U.S. current account deficit.
    The markets had expected the G20 meeting to discuss
curtailing the dollar's steep fall since October. However, the
issue was not raised in the group's final communique despite
calls from European leaders for calm in currency markets.
    The euro        was near record highs on Monday but the
Japanese yen  strayed half a yen off Friday's multi-year
peak.

per dollar, a fresh seven-year high and a level last seen in
the midst of the 1990s Asian financial crisis. But it soon
dropped as far as 1,068 per dollar in some local deals on talk
the Bank of Korea (BOK) bought dollars.

bank's dollar-buying intervention was around 1,063 and it
spurred the market to push the won down to 1,068 per dollar.
    There were reports the finance ministry had asked central
bank to take a more aggressive role in the local currency
market. The head of the Bank of Korea's foreign exchange market

Singapore.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late After Snow's Remarks On  Forex
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger in Asia late Thursday, bolstered by U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow's remarks that suggest the U.S. won't take steps to support the ailing U.S. dollar.  

Singapore government bond prices were mostly higher, especially at the long end, in line with overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys, traders said.  

At 0715 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6453, down from S$1.6502 in Asia late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6450 and S$1.6470 intraday.  

Late Wednesday, Snow said "the history of efforts to impose non-market valuations on currencies has at best been unrewarding and checkered."  

He added that "no one has ever devalued their way to prosperity" and the "only way to get prosperity is to follow the marketplace," although he did reiterate his support for a "strong dollar policy."  

Overall, Snow's comments reinforced a market perception that the U.S. government is tolerant of the U.S. dollar's weakness, prompting some non-Singapore investment banks to drive the U.S. unit down to S$1.6450 early in the session.  

This was followed by rumored intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to curb a further fall of the U.S. currency, which sparked light profit-taking on short U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar positions and lifted the U.S. unit back up to around S$1.6465.  

But despite talk of MAS supporting the U.S. dollar over the past few days, the risk is that it will trade lower in the coming sessions, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

UOB cited the U.S. dollar's broad-based weakness and expectations that the Group of 20 industrial and developing nations could at this weekend's meeting in Berlin put more pressure on China to allow the yuan to appreciate.  

"For now, we expect the currency pair to hold at S$1.6400, with the upside likely to be capped at around S$1.6520-S$1.6530," UOB said.  

Technical analysis points to a further U.S. dollar fall against the local currency in the short term after negative 10-day momentum divergence Wednesday, which implies the U.S. unit may retest initial support at S$1.6448 as soon as later in the global day.  

Any clear break of the U.S. currency below S$1.6448 would immediately target secondary support in the S$1.6420-S$1.6430 area, which consists of the lows set in early December 1998. [ 18-11-04 0730GMT ]  

Singapore government bonds were mostly higher late Thursday following an overnight rally in U.S. Treasurys, with gains mainly seen in longer-term maturities, dealers said.  

At the end of the session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was unchanged at 1.57%.  

But at the longer end of the curve, the 10-year yield fell four basis points to 2.99% and the 15-year yield eased five basis points to 3.43%.  

Interest rate swaps were also mostly lower, in line with local bond yields.  

The two-year swap offer was at 1.74%, down from 1.75% late Wednesday. The five-year swap offer was at 2.44% versus 2.49%, while the 10-year offer fell to 3.19% from 3.26%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 145 basis points from 151 basis points late Wednesday.  

In the interbank market, the overnight rate held steady at 1.2500% from late Wednesday.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Bullishness; Outlook Strong
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger against its U.S. counterpart in Asia late Wednesday, underpinned by bullish sentiment toward the local currency after it hit a fresh near six-year high in overseas markets late Tuesday.  

Singapore government bond prices were steady in extremely thin trade, as players ignored the overnight slide in U.S. Treasurys and weaker-than-expected Singapore gross domestic product and export data.  

At 0645 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6502, down from S$1.6526 in Asia late Tuesday. It traded between S$1.6490 and S$1.6518 intraday.  

Throughout the session, the U.S. dollar was caught in a tug-of-war between Singapore dollar bulls seeking to sell the U.S. currency on any upticks and participants wary of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore after the central bank was rumored to have stepped into the market late Tuesday.  

Traders said the MAS apparently intervened to buy U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars when the U.S. unit slid as low as S$1.6475 late Tuesday, its lowest since December 1998.  

Looking ahead, analysts said the U.S. dollar is likely to fall further against the local currency, despite signs that Singapore's economy is slowing.  

"For now, the risk remains on the downside for the currency pair, with the market targeting S$1.6450," said United Overseas Bank in a research report, citing ongoing concerns about the huge U.S. fiscal and current account deficits.  

Separately, ING Financial Markets said it expects the U.S. dollar to decline to S$1.6370 in the next three months.  

Early Wednesday, the Ministry of Trade & Industry said Singapore's GDP grew by 7.5% in the third quarter from a year ago, narrower than the government's earlier estimate of 7.7% expansion. The government also narrowed its full-year growth forecast to 8.0%-8.5% from an earlier 8%-9%.  

International Enterprise Singapore also said Wednesday that the city-state's non-oil domestic exports rose 11.9% on year to S$11.96 billion in October, which was below the average forecast of a 14.2% gain by eight economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires. [ 17-11-04 0702GMT ]  

Late Wednesday, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was 1.55%, up from 1.54% Tuesday. The 10-year yield was flat at 3.03%, while the 15-year yield was also steady at 3.48%.  

A trader said bond yields traded in a very narrow range of two basis points during the session.  

Interest rate swaps were mixed. The two-year swap offer was at 1.75%, up from 1.72% around the same time Tuesday. The five-year swap offer was 2.49% versus 2.48%, while the 10-year offer fell to 3.26% from 3.29%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 151 basis points from 157 basis points.  

In the interbank market, the overnight rate inched up to 1.2500% from 1.1875%.

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was nearly flat in Asia late Friday after selling by local banks, rumored to have been on behalf of the central bank, pulled it off the early high against the U.S. dollar, dealers said.  

Singapore government bond prices were almost unchanged in very thin trade ahead of U.S. economic data due out later in the global day and a long weekend in Singapore.  

At 0715 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6552, almost unchanged from S$1.6550 in Asia late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.6513 and S$1.6569 intraday.  

Singapore's financial markets were closed for a holiday Thursday and will be shut again Monday.  

Despite strong selling by foreign investment banks, the U.S. dollar continued to gain on persistent buying on dips by local banks. It hit the mid-S$1.6500s by the early afternoon.  

Traders said the buying may have been on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore aimed at tempering the renewed U.S. dollar weakness against the local currency.  

At its lowest point of S$1.6513 Friday, the U.S. unit was about 0.6% below its Wednesday high of S$1.6610, and could continue lower in the coming weeks.  

In a monthly research report, HSBC said it doesn't expect the Singapore dollar, whether measured against its trade-weighted basket or the U.S. dollar, to wane anytime soon even though the island's gross domestic product growth is expected to moderate to around 4.0% next year from an estimated 8.5% to 9.0% in 2004.  

That is because the economy will remain close to full capacity, which means MAS will likely keep its stance of seeking a steady and gradual appreciation in the trade-weighted Singapore dollar.

Thursday after a sharp fall in the yen and some gains in the
dollar on a narrowing of the U.S. trade deficit and the Federal
Reserve's fourth rate rise this year.
    The Korean won                  pulled back from a
seven-year high hit this week, helped by some suspected
intervention, and the Singapore dollar was about one cent off a
near-five-year high seen on Monday.
    The Taiwan dollar          extended its retreat from
Tuesday's seven-month high of 32.85 per dollar, while the
Philippine peso  and Thai baht        were hampered by
domestic worries.
    The yen        retreated 1 percent against the dollar in
offshore trade, to back over 107 per dollar, and that helped
pull most regional currencies lower.
    "There was lots of suspicion that Japan's monetary
authorities were involved in the move, but no evidence to
support that speculation," BNP Paribas analysts said in a

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late As US Dlr Bearishness Persists
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar rose slightly against its U.S. counterpart late Tuesday in Asia, bolstered by lingering bearish sentiment toward the U.S. currency.  

Local government bond prices were slightly higher, as bond yields fell in line with falls in local interest-rate swaps amid strong receiving interest across the swap curve, dealers said.  

At 0805 GMT, the U.S. unit was at S$1.6525, down from S$1.6535 late Monday in Asia. It traded between S$1.6497 and S$1.6539 intraday.  

After falling to a five-year low of S$1.6493 late Monday in New York, the U.S. currency rebounded to S$1.6539 early in the Asian session on the unwinding of short U.S. dollar positions by some domestic and foreign banks to take profits.  

But by late morning, the U.S. unit had slumped back to the low-S$1.6500s, as other players sold into its rebound amid overall U.S. dollar bearishness, before consolidating around S$1.6520 for the rest of the session.  

Traders said worries over the massive U.S. "twin" deficits -budget and trade - and speculation that China may move to a more flexible foreign exchange regime in the near term, continued to weigh on the U.S. dollar while buoying Asian currencies.  

The Singapore dollar has risen roughly 1.4% against the U.S. unit since rumors of an imminent revaluation of the Chinese yuan intensified last week, said United Overseas Bank in a research report.  

Further U.S. dollar declines are expected, with the currency market expecting the yuan to appreciate 3%-5% in the next three to six months, UOB said.  

Technical charts also appear to support this, with the general bearish outlook likely to result in further lows for the U.S. dollar with respect to the Singapore dollar, UOB said.  

But dealers warned that a further downside could be limited should the Monetary Authority of Singapore step in to restrict the slide, dealers said.  

Analysts pointed to an increase in the level of foreign exchange reserves in September as evidence that the central bank may already have intervened to buy U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars in recent weeks.  

Singapore's official foreign reserves were up about 3%, to US$105.83 billion at the end of October, from US$102.75 billion in September, according to preliminary data issued by the MAS Monday. [ 09-11-04 0828GMT ]  

Singapore government bonds ended marginally higher late Tuesday, in tandem with a broad rise in U.S. Treasurys overnight and aided by strong receiving interest in local interest rate swaps, dealers said.  

But trade was generally modest, especially ahead of Wednesday's U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting.  

With the Federal Reserve expected to raise key interest rates by 25 basis points - and possibly another 25 basis points at the next meeting in December - government bond yields could head higher, UOB said.  

"As most of the economic data is out of the way, SGS is likely to track external developments for now," with the two-year yield moving toward 1.60%, while the longer-dated 10-year yield could rise to 3.3%, UOB added.  

Late in the session, the yield on two-year Singapore government bonds was down 1 basis point at 1.55%, while the 10-year bond yield was also 1 basis point lower at 3.15%. The 15-year bond yield fell 3 basis points to 3.58% by the end of the session.  

Interest rate swaps were also mostly lower, after seeing some heavy receiving interest right across the swap curve ahead of the FOMC meeting, dealers said.  

The two-year swap offer was at 1.70%, versus 1.74% late Monday. The five-year swap offer fell 5 basis points to 2.51% from 2.56%, while the 10-year offer fell to 3.35% from 3.39%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps was unchanged at 165 basis points from late Monday.  

In the interbank market, the overnight rate was up at 1.2500% from late Monday's 1.1250%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -South Korean won near 4-year high.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won tested a
four-year high on Tuesday after data showed strong export and
record foreign exchange reserves while other Asian currencies
steadied ahead of U.S. presidential elections.
    The won ended domestic trading at 1,114.8 per dollar, its
strongest close since September 2000, and traded at 1,114.1 in
offshore deals on speculation the central bank may hold off
cutting interest rates next week after the strong trade data
and figures showing a rise in core inflation.
    "The latest figures have given the currency a bit of a
boost," said David Simmonds, a currency strategist at the Royal
Bank of Scotland.
    "Export growth stays pretty strong and the trade surplus
remains extremely large. So there's strong supply of dollars in
the market.
  


 That reduces the risk that the ministry of finance
may intervene aggressively in the market."
    The won has strengthened about 4.5 percent in the past
three months against the dollar, mirroring similar gains in the
yen against the U.S. currency.
    South Korean exporters compete with Japanese and Chinese
companies in the U.S. and European markets. Analysts say the
government tries to keep the won's gains in line with gains in
the yen to keep exports competitive.
    U.S. ELECTION UNCERTAINTY
    Other Asian currencies, which had posted gains during
October, were little changed ahead of the U.S. elections that,
polls suggest, may not throw up a clear winner between
incumbent President George W. Bush and Democratic contender
Senator John Kerry.
 
    That could lead to a protracted legal wrangle, just as the
previous election in 2000.
    "The election uncertainty is weighing on the market," said
Thio Chin Loo, a currency strategist at BNP Paribas.
    "The fundamentals still point to a weaker dollar."
    Record U.S. trade deficits and concerns about an economic
  

slowdown in the world's largest economy owing to record high  

oil prices drove the U.S. dollar last week to its weakest level  

against the Singapore dollar in six months and to its weakest  

in five months against the Taiwan dollar.   


 
    The Taiwan dollar set a new five-month high of 33.38 per
U.S. dollar on Tuesday.
    The Singapore dollar gave up some gains, weakening at one
  

point to 1.6679 per dollar. The currency has traded within a  

range of 1.66 to 1.6679 per dollar for the last seven days -  

unable to rise further on concerns that the Monetary Authority

of Singapore may intervene to prevent further gains.  

The authority, which conducts monetary policy by guiding  

the currency within an undisclosed trade-weighted band, has  

said it would allow a gradual and modest appreciation of the  

currency to curb inflationary pressures.  

If the Singapore dollar breaches its April highs of around  

1.66 per dollar, it would trade at its strongest level against  

the U.S. currency since January 2000.  

It has gained 3.3 percent in the past quarter against the  

dollar and it may have some more room for gains before it  

reaches the top end of its trade-weighted band, BNP Paribas'  

Thio said. She said the Singapore currency could strengthen  

to 1.65 if the U.S. dollar weakens further against major world  

currencies following the U.S. elections.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Clinging to gains ahead of US election.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won steadied
near its strongest level in four years on Tuesday and other
Asian currencies held on to October's gains as traders braced
for an indecisive U.S. presidential election that could hurt
the dollar.
    As many as 24 out of 25 currency strategists polled by
Reuters out of London on Monday expected the dollar to weaken
against the world's major currencies if Tuesday's U.S. election
produced no clear winner and the outcome was prolonged by legal
wrangles.
    "If the dollar falls further against the major currencies,
Asian currencies will get a boost," said Thio Chin Loo,  a
Singapore-based currency strategist at BNP Paribas.
    "The fundamentals still point to a weaker dollar."
    The dollar's weakness in the last week of October, caused
by concerns of widening U.S.
  


 trade and budget deficits and a
economic slowdown due to record high oil prices, drove the
Singapore dollar to a six-month high and the Taiwan dollar to a
five-month high.
 
    The Taiwan currency set a new five-month high of 33.38
against the dollar on Tuesday.
    Concerns about central bank intervention were partly
  

responsible for thwarting gains in the South Korean won. The  

won hit a four-year high around 1,114 per dollar on Friday but  

has shed some of those gains in the past two sessions.  

Still, analysts said intervention by currency regulators in  

Asia had been few and far between in the past six months,  

indicating they are inclined to let their currencies strengthen  

in line with the dollar's broad-based weakness.  

"There's been no heavy-handed intervention by Asian central  

banks so far," said Thio. "The kind of intervention we saw in  

the first quarter is absent."  

There was a strong case for a further strengthening of the  

won against the dollar, Claudio Piron, a strategist at J.P.  

Morgan, said in a report.  

"This was underscored yesterday by the sturdy October trade  

performance and still high headline inflation and rising core  

consumer-price-index growth," Piron said.  

Piron said the risks of a dollar rebound remained,  

particularly if the U.S. election threw up a clear winner and  

that outcome was followed by strong U.S. non-farm jobs data,  

due later this week, and a rise in the U.S. Federal Reserve's  

benchmark interest rate next week.  

"Nevertheless, on the big-picture, longer-term view, we  

would prefer to take the opportunity and establish long Asia  

versus U.S. dollar positions," he said.  

SING DOLLAR  

The Singapore dollar, quoted around 1.6645 per dollar, was

against the dollar in the last seven trading sessions on  

concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) may  

intervene, by buying U.S. dollars, to prevent further gains in  

the Singapore currency.  

If the Singapore dollar breaches its April highs around  

1.66 per dollar, it would trade at its strongest level against  

the U.S. currency since January 2000.  

The MAS, which conducts monetary policy by guiding the  

currency within its undisclosed trade-weighted band, has said  

it will allow a gradual and modest appreciation of the currency

to curb inflationary pressures.  

Thio expected the Singapore authorities to let the currency

strengthen to 1.65 per dollar if the U.S. dollar weakened

elections.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Clinging to gains ahead of US election.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won steadied
near its strongest level in four years on Tuesday and other
Asian currencies held on to October's gains as traders braced
for an indecisive U.S. presidential election that could hurt
the dollar.
    As many as 24 out of 25 currency strategists polled by
Reuters out of London on Monday expected the dollar to weaken
against the world's major currencies if Tuesday's U.S. election
produced no clear winner and the outcome was prolonged by legal
wrangles.
    "If the dollar falls further against the major currencies,
Asian currencies will get a boost," said Thio Chin Loo,  a
Singapore-based currency strategist at BNP Paribas.
    "The fundamentals still point to a weaker dollar."
    The dollar's weakness in the last week of October, caused
by concerns of widening U.S.
  


 trade and budget deficits and a
economic slowdown due to record high oil prices, drove the
Singapore dollar  to a six-month high and the Taiwan
dollar  to a five-month high.
 
    The Taiwan currency set a new five-month high of 33.38
against the dollar on Tuesday.
    Concerns about central bank intervention were partly
  

responsible for thwarting gains in the South Korean won  

. The won hit a four-year high around 1,114 per  

dollar on Friday but has shed some of those gains in the past  

two sessions.  

Still, analysts said intervention by currency regulators in  

Asia had been few and far between in the past six months,  

indicating they are inclined to let their currencies strengthen  

in line with the dollar's broad-based weakness.  

"There's been no heavy-handed intervention by Asian central  

banks so far," said Thio. "The kind of intervention we saw in  

the first quarter is absent."  

There was a strong case for a further strengthening of the  

won against the dollar, Claudio Piron, a strategist at J.P.  

Morgan, said in a report.  

"This was underscored yesterday by the sturdy October trade  

performance and still high headline inflation and rising core  

consumer-price-index growth," Piron said.  

Piron said the risks of a dollar rebound remained,  

particularly if the U.S. election threw up a clear winner and  

that outcome was followed by strong U.S. non-farm jobs data,  

due later this week, and a rise in the U.S. Federal Reserve's  

benchmark interest rate next week.  

"Nevertheless, on the big-picture, longer-term view, we  

would prefer to take the opportunity and establish long Asia  

versus U.S. dollar positions," he said.  

SING DOLLAR  

The Singapore dollar, quoted around 1.6645 per dollar, was  

little changed. It has traded in a range of 1.66 to 1.6679  

against the dollar in the last seven trading sessions on  

concerns that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) may  

intervene, by buying U.S. dollars, to prevent further gains in  

the Singapore currency.  

If the Singapore dollar breaches its April highs around  

1.66 per dollar, it would trade at its strongest level against  

the U.S. currency since January 2000.  

The MAS, which conducts monetary policy by guiding the  

currency within its undisclosed trade-weighted band, has said  

it will allow a gradual and modest appreciation of the currency

to curb inflationary pressures.  

Thio expected the Singapore authorities to let the currency

strengthen to 1.65 per dollar if the U.S. dollar weakened  

against the yen and other major currencies after the U.S.  

elections.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steady after Oct surge, wait on US.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies steadied at
strong levels on Monday, after surging against the dollar
through October, as investors refrained from placing new bets
ahead of a closely contested U.S. presidential election.
    The South Korean won            strengthened to a new
four-year high against the dollar in local trade before losing
some ground, after a 3 percent gain in October. The Singapore
dollar  traded near a six-month high while the Taiwan
dollar approached it's highest level in almost five months.
    "Everybody's looking at the U.S. presidential elections,"
said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at Singapore's United
Overseas Bank.
    "While the consensus is to buy the dollar if a clear winner
emerges, the outcome of the elections remains uncertain.
Eventually, the widening U.S. fiscal and trade deficits will
weigh on the dollar."
    President George W.
  


 Bush and Democratic contender John
Kerry are tied nationwide ahead of Tuesday's elections,
according to a Reuters/Zogby poll released on Sunday.
    Asian currencies have surged over the past month, led by a
5 percent surge in the yen  against the dollar, and a 3.4
percent gain of the Singapore dollar , as concerns about
record high oil prices and the yawning U.S. current account
deficits weighed on the dollar.
    U.S. data on Friday showed gross domestic product grew at
an annualised rate of 3.7 percent in the third quarter, falling
short of analysts' expectations, while an index of U.S.
consumer sentiment was stronger than expected.
    If U.S. non-farm payrolls, due on Friday, were weak, it
could prompt the Federal Reserve to hold back on raising
interest rates, hurting the dollar against Asian currencies,
said BNP Paribas in a report.
    The bank expects the Singapore dollar to test its six-month
high of about 1.66 per dollar before the Monetary Authority of
Singapore intervenes. It traded on Monday at 1.6642/52 per U.S.
dollar.
 
    "We reckon it's a matter of time before this level gives
way, towards the next support at 1.65," BNP said.
    The Singapore central bank, which conducts monetary policy
  

by guiding the currency within its undisclosed trade-weighted  

band, has said it will allow a gradual and modest appreciation  

of the currency.  

Worries about intervention kept the South Korean won from  

extending its early morning gains. Adding to market caution, a  

senior South Korean commerce ministry official said a stronger  

won could hurt the economy's competitiveness.  

The comments came after the won hit a four-year high on  

data showing core inflation jumped to a 19-month high in  

October and exports grew a faster-than-expected 20.9 percent in  

the year through October. This boosted expectations the central  

bank may hold back further rate cuts at its meeting next week.  

"While the trend is still of monetary easing, there's a  

50-50 chance of no change in the central bank's monetary  

policy," said Christy Tan, a currency analyst at 4CAST Ltd.

text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 1 (Reuters) - The South Korean won
approached a four-year high against the dollar on Monday while
other Asian currencies steadied after October's gains, as
uncertainty ahead of the U.S. presidential elections weighed on
the dollar.
    The won was boosted by government data that showed South
Korea's core inflation rose to a 19-month high in October,
bolstering expectations the central bank may hold off further
interest rate cuts.
    "The core consumer index is still quite high," said Christy
Tan, a currency analyst at 4CAST Ltd in Singapore. "While the
trend is still of monetary easing, there's a fifty-fifty chance
of a change in central bank's monetary policy."
    Korean data showed exports grew a faster-than-expected 20.9
percent in the year through October, but the increase was the
slowest in 11 months.
  


    Asian currencies have jumped over the past month, with the
Singapore dollar surging to a six-month high and the Taiwan
dollar trading near a five-month high last week, as concerns
about the outlook for the U.S. economy under a new
administration and record high oil prices weighed on the
dollar.
    Tuesday's election is a dead heat with President George W.
Bush and Democratic contender John Kerry tied nationwide in the
race for the White House, according to a Reuters/Zogby poll
released on Sunday.
 
    An indecisive election or a legal battle to determine the
winner will further hurt the dollar, analysts say.
    But gains in Asian currencies were curtailed on Monday by
  

worries that central banks may buy dollars to keep their  

country's exports competitive against those of their Asian  

rivals.   


 
    A senior South Korean commerce ministry official said on
Monday a stronger won could hurt the economy's competitiveness.
    "Although the authorities have allowed the won to
appreciate, there's caution in the market about intervention,"
said Tan.
    The Singapore dollar was little changed around 1.6630/40
  

per dollar. Many analysts said it may be close to the top end  

of the Monetary Authority of Singapore undisclosed  

trade-weighted band.  

The central bank, which conducts monetary policy by guiding  

the currency within the band, has said it will allow a gradual  

and modest appreciation of the currency.  

The Singapore dollar has strengthened about 3.4 percent  

against the U.S. dollar in the past three months. The yen has  

gained 5 percent against the dollar in the same period.  

China's surprise rate rise last week, its first in nine  

years, also held back Asian currency gains as exporters fretted  

that demand from Asia's fastest-growing economy may cool.  

Japan's Nikkei average lost half a percent in morning  

trade, pulling the yen lower against the dollar.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were
steady to lower on Wednesday, paring some of their recent heavy
gains as economic data and a stock market recovery boosted the
U.S. dollar.
    Traders said fear of regional central bank intervention
helped push the Sing dollar  away from a five-year high
it neared this week and brought the Philippine peso
closer to an all-time low of 56.45.
    The Thai baht        fell slightly to 41.05/08 a dollar,
amid market concern about Thailand's south where almost 80
Muslims, arrested after Monday's riot, suffocated to death
while being transported by trucks to army barracks.
    The Korean won                   and Taiwan dollar
bucked a general weak trend, with the latter trading flat
around 33.66-33.70 a dollar.
    "The major movement last night was in the U.S. stock
market.
  


 All the top performers of last week, both high-yielders
and majors, have seen heavy profit-taking," said Philip Wee,
markets strategist with DBS Bank in Singapore.
    The Dow Jones industrial average        broke a 5-day
losing streak with its strongest one-day advance since early
June.
    Asian stocks and currencies were expected to be weighed
down by a rise in the benchmark US light crude  price
back above $55 a barrel.
    INTERVENTION WORRY
    The won hit a fresh four-year high of 1,131 in offshore
deals, but was seen succumbing to the yen's decline in morning
trade as traders debated the authorities' tolerance for gains
in the unit.
    South Korean officials said on Tuesday monetary policy
would be kept accommodative, to boost domestic demand, and that
a weaker dollar would help ease inflationary pressures.
    Separately, a Bank of Korea official said the won was
following the yen and the currency's rise should not be linked
to the chances of further rate cuts.
    "On balance, it would appear that Korean authorities are
preparing for gradual won appreciation so long as yen/won
maintains an upward bias and corporate export performance is
not visibly impaired," Claudio Piron, strategist at JP Morgan,
said in a note.
    Markets believe Korean authorities are sensitive about the
won's competitiveness in export markets, especially against the
yen.
    The won had lagged the yen's gains this month, falling to
10.68 won per yen on Monday from about 10.28 in late September.
The cross  was down to 10.58 on Wednesday.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Worries about central bankintervention capped gains in the Japanese yen and some Asian
currencies on Tuesday despite continuing U.S. dollar weakness.
    The dollar hit fresh lows against the euro        and other
European currencies and the Australian dollar . But it
bounced off Monday's six-month low against the yen .
    In Asia, the Korean won                   met with
resistance near Monday's four-year high of 1,133 a dollar. The
Sing dollar  went within striking distance of 1.66 a
dollar to levels last seen in April and near five-year highs.
 
    The Thai baht        was flat near 41 a dollar. Spikes
above that level proved short-lived.
    Concerns over the U.S. trade deficit and the upcoming U.S.
  

presidential election have weighed on the dollar since last  

week, boosting the regionals even as record oil prices weighed  

on their share markets.  

But, analysts said the Asian currencies had lagged their  

major counterparts and some of the high-yielding currencies,  

such as the Aussie and kiwi , in the latest dollar  

decline.  

"Obviously with the U.S. dollar index doing what it is  

doing it is not a surprise to see dollar/Asia lower," said  

David Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of  

Scotland.  

"But Asian markets are not where the action is. You have  

Asian currencies lagging the yen and the yen lagging other  

major currencies such as the Swiss franc and kiwi on the  

crosses.   


 
    "Therefore, the Asian regionals are not really prominent in
this weak dollar move," Simmonds said.
    The Taiwan dollar          was among Asia's top performers
  

on Tuesday, catching up with the region after a typhoon forced  

markets to close on Monday. It hit 33.60 per dollar, the  

highest since June, shrugging off a weak stock market .  

"The Taiwan stock exchange has been in decline for the  

better part of the last three weeks and risk aversion seems to  

be going higher - these factors will limit the upside in the  

Taiwan dollar," Bhanu Baweja of UBS said in a note to clients.  

In South Korea, a Bank of Korea (BOK) official said a  

stronger won would help ease inflationary pressures in the  

economy, but the won was following the yen and its recent rise  

did not indicate a change in policy.  

"The BoK has suggested a stronger currency as a possible  

route to control inflationary expectations before, but it is  

the MoFE (Ministry of Finance and Economics) that eventually  

owns FX policy in Korea, and they don't seem to be in a hurry  

to let the currency move higher," Baweja said.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on
Monday, with the Korean won hitting a four-year high, as the
region ignored high oil prices and falling stock markets to
claim ground from a declining U.S. dollar.
    Worries about the widening U.S. trade deficit and the
approaching U.S. presidential election drove the dollar to an
eight-month low against the euro  and a six-month trough
against the yen .
    The Japanese currency was up one yen since Friday at
106.70/75, undeterred by the nearly 2 percent fall in the
Nikkei average  and Saturday's massive earthquake.
    The won                  met with some resistance near
1,135 a dollar, a November 2000 peak and a rise of half a
percent since Friday, prompting speculation that the Bank of
Korea was intervening to rein in the currency.
    A Singapore-based trader said spikes in the won on the
higher side of 1,135 were short-lived, suggesting won-selling
intervention.
  


    The Sing dollar        hit 1.6620, stopping short of an
April high near 1.66. A break above that would take it to its
strongest levels since January 2000.
 
    Markets in Thailand were closed for a holiday and a typhoon
forced businesses in Taiwan to close.
    "The threat of the Korean authorities has been enough to
keep dollar/won constrained, and the market is starting to fear
the Bank of Japan," IDEAglobal.com said in a commentary.
    "As such, further (dollar/won) downside is still possible,
driven obviously by the majors but also good export orders,"
IDEAglobal.com said.
    Economists at UBS said the won's appreciation had been
slower than that of most other Asian currencies and the majors.
    "The BoK was rumoured to be present around the 1,135 level
but the bid was not heard to be strong," UBS said in a note.
    The underperformance has driven the won to a three-month
trough of about 10.67 per yen, down from 10.28 at the end of
September.
    The spike in oil prices weighed on the region's stock
markets , dragging Korean shares to an eight-week
low and Philippine stocks to a one-month low.
    The Philippine peso        lagged the region, rising very
marginally to 56.26 a dollar. The Indonesian rupiah  also
managed meagre gains.
    SINGAPORE INFLATION
    Singapore released data showing consumer prices rose a
faster-than-expected 0.5 percent in September over August, as
oil prices boosted transport and food costs.
    "It remains a challenge for authorities in Asia to control
the second-round effects of oil price inflation," UBS said.
    "Therefore authorities in economies where the output gap
  

continues to close despite a modest slowdown in growth - China,  

India, Singapore, Thailand and Taiwan - have all been biased  

towards tightening monetary conditions in one way or the  

other."  

UBS said the volatility of output in Singapore had,  

however, fallen and that meant the Monetary Authority of  

Singapore was likely to maintain the tightening bias it  

announced in April for a long time.   


 
    The MAS runs monetary policy by guiding the Sing dollar
within an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies.
    "According to UBS's calculations, the Sing dollar nominal
  

effective rate is still one percent below the top end of the  

basket in which the MAS tracks this currency, but the pace of  

appreciation may invite the MAS' hand," UBS said.  

UBS recommended booking profits on long Sing dollar  

positions and waiting for better levels to reestablish that  

bullish Sing view.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, Hits 6-Mo High As USD Falls
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was sharply higher late Friday amid a U.S. dollar-bearish market in Asia, breaking a key resistance level and hitting a fresh six-month high.  

Government bond prices were either flat or slightly lower, with some tenors tracking an overnight fall in U.S. Treasurys. Overall trade, however, was subdued ahead of the weekend.  

At 0815 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6688, down from S$1.6720 late Thursday in Asia. It traded between S$1.6680 and S$1.6743 intraday.  

At the start of the local session, the U.S. dollar was around S$1.6740, supported by talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened overnight to keep the U.S. unit from falling too sharply against the local dollar.  

But the speculation soon faded as the market's focus returned to the U.S. current account deficit and how higher oil prices could affect U.S. economic and monetary policies.  

With the U.S. dollar resuming its downtrend against the yen and euro, the U.S. currency later broke below the psychologically and technically important S$1.6700 level.  

At 0815 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at Y107.58 versus Y107.56 in New York overnight, while the euro was at US$1.2630, up from US$1.2603.  

In Singapore, the U.S. dollar extended its fall to the session low of S$1.6680, its weakest level since April 13, the day after the MAS moved to a tightening policy bias by favoring a stronger Singapore dollar.  

Looking ahead, dealers expect the U.S. dollar to fall further in the coming sessions on concerns over rising oil prices and their impact on the U.S. economy.  

UOB Treasury said in a research report that some players were already "talking about S$1.6650, then S$1.6610," and suggested that a break below Y107 could be a possible trigger. [ 22-10-04 0829GMT ]  

Singapore government bond prices were mostly steady, though some maturities fell from early in the session after an overnight drop in U.S. Treasurys.  

Late Friday, the yield on two-year bonds was unchanged at 1.52%. The 10-year bond yield rose one basis point to 3.17%, while the 15-year yield also closed flat at 3.68%.  

Interest rate swaps were also either flat or slightly lower as they tracked local bond yields.  

The two-year swap offer was up at 1.75% versus 1.74% late Thursday, the five-year swap offer was at 2.54% against 2.53% previously, while the 10-year offer was steady at 3.38%.  

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 163 basis points from 164 basis points late Thursday.  

In the interbank market, the overnight rate slipped to 1.2500% from 1.3125% previously.  

Prices quoted are pre-settlement bids obtained from dealers and are subject to change.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  caps some, rest rise.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a
mixed bag on Thursday as a suspicion central banks were
intervening halted rallies in the Sing dollar and the north
Asians while the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah rose on
recovering stock markets.
 
    Asians started the day slightly weaker as their stock
markets succumbed to the drop in U.S. stocks on Wednesday.
    But as Chinese offshore forwards renewed their move to
  

price in a greater appreciation of the tightly managed yuan and  

foreigners flocked back to Asian stock markets ,  

some of the currencies resumed gains.  

The Indonesian rupiah rose as far as 9,010 per  

dollar, its highest in two months, as markets positioned for  

currency gains after the presidential elections on Sept. 20.   


 
    The Thai baht's        rise was capped around 41.20, near
Wednesday's seven-week high of 41.18.
    "Everyone's buying Asian equities. Seems to be a mix of
  

bargain-hunting in stocks and the view that one must hold as  

little of fixed income as possible when yields are rising,"  

said one Singapore-based trader.  

Also, Chinese yuan non-deliverable forwards moved  

to price in a higher premium on the yuan, and that provided  

another boost to the Asians.  

Market attention is focused on China ahead of an Oct. 1  

Group of Seven meeting in Washington, to which China has been  

invited. On Wednesday, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow called  

for accelerated currency reform in China.  

One-year NDFs were quoted at 2,800 points, pricing in an  

appreciation of 3.5 percent in the yuan in a year. The yuan is  

effectively pegged around 8.28 per U.S. dollar.  

INTERVENTION

But the fear of intervention and in some cases suspicion of  

actual central bank dollar-buying capped some of the regionals.  

The Sing dollar stayed between 1.6890 and 1.69 a  

dollar, unable to re-visit this week's four-month high near  

1.6880.  

"Asian central banks were out yesterday, putting a steady  

hand on things," said David Simmonds, markets strategist with  

the Royal Bank of Scotland.   


 
    "Secondly, the dollar rallied a bit on some second-tier
data," he said.
    "It's no surprise to see dollar/Asia better bid," he said,
although he added that the rise had been limited.
    Analysts said there was also selling of the Sing against
  

currencies of its trading partners by funds speculating the  

currency had appreciated to the highest end of the undisclosed  

trade-weighted band authorities manage it in.  

The Taiwan dollar held between 33.80 and 33.90 a   


dollar and the Korean won             fell to 1,147 but
  

returned soon to straddle 1,145 for a fourth day.  

These two currencies failed to follow the rest of the  

region higher this week amid suspicion their central banks were  

active in the market to prevent large moves.  

The Indian rupee was forced off two-month highs  

near 45.70 on Wednesday after the central bank was reported to  

be making enquiries. On Thursday, it was pushed closer to 46 by  

dollar-buying by state-owned banks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Southeast Asians at multi-month peaks.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies
extended their rallies to multi-month peaks on Wednesday,
buoyed by surging stock markets, foreign portfolio inflows and
the seeming absence of central bank intervention to curb gains.
    The Singapore dollar firmed through another key level at
1.69 per dollar in offshore deals to hit fresh four-month highs
near 1.6880, despite concern the monetary authority might
intervene if the Sing rose too rapidly against currencies of
trading partners.
    The Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah were both at
seven-week highs, hitting 41.18 and 9,050 per dollar
respectively in morning deals.
    Major currencies had little influence on the firming trend
in these regionals, with the dollar and yen caught in tight
ranges after data showed the U.S. current account deficit
surged to a record in the second quarter and retail sales fell
in August.
  


 
    Markets are waiting for a Federal Reserve policy meeting
next week, expecting U.S. rates will be raised again.
    Analysts said the interest to buy the Asians was gathering
pace, evidenced in the return of foreign capital to the region
and stock markets hitting new highs.
    Moreover, there was speculation that the authorities had
  


been encouraging the currency appreciation in India, Thailand
  


and Singapore, through either suspected dollar sales or by
  


refraining from intervening to sell their currencies.
  


The rupee hit a two-month high on Tuesday and has risen one
  


percent in a week, driven mainly by speculation that the
  


authorities wanted a stronger currency to fight rapidly rising
  


prices. Annual wholesale price inflation is over eight percent.
  


Bhanu Baweja of UBS said it was extremely interesting that
  


the Reserve Bank of India had not intervened in the rupee
  


markets in the past two days "not only because the move was
  


sharp, but also because most of these inflows have been driven
  


by onshore-offshore arbitrage, which the RBI has historically
  


frowned upon".
  


He said the RBI also had difficulty soaking up the domestic
  


funds released through dollar-buying intervention, because of
  


the high inflation and because the central bank did not want
  


yields to rise.
  


BAHT CATCHING UP
  


Baweja said the baht, which has been an underperformer in
  


the region this year, was likely to benefit from government
  


spending on the economy and markets ahead of elections early in
  


2005.
  


"While the BoT (Bank of Thailand) have not come in to
  


impact the value of the baht either way, we believe the BoT
  


does regard baht as unfairly weak due to temporary factors such
  


as the bird flu and the problems in the Southern Thailand that
  


have undermined confidence in the Thai economy," Baweja wrote
  


in a note.
  


"If a stronger stock market was to push the baht somewhat
  


stronger, we don't think the BoT would stand in the way,
  


especially as they don't see equity inflows as interest rate
  


driven speculation on a stronger baht," he said.
  


Elsewhere, the Korean won was virtually unchanged and the
  


Taiwan dollar slightly higher, with markets suspecting the
  


authorities in these two countries were controlling the
  


movements in their currencies.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late Following Overnight USD Strength
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was lower late Thursday in Asia, hurt by the U.S. dollar's surge against the yen in New York trading overnight.  

Singapore government bonds were barely changed, as players kept to the sidelines ahead of U.S. jobless data later in the global day.  

Around 0700 GMT, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7242, up from S$1.7231 around the same time Wednesday. The U.S. dollar started the Asian day around S$1.7264 and kept to a range of S$1.7240 to S$1.7286, as its rally against the yen lost momentum during Asian hours.  

The U.S. dollar climbed to its highest level in nearly two months against the yen as traders viewed a surge in oil prices Wednesday as positive for the U.S. unit, offsetting disappointment over a U.S. durable goods report that showed orders rose 0.7% in June, well short of the consensus for a 1.5% gain.  

Around 0700 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at Y111.63, slightly down from its late New York level of Y111.71.  

Movements in the U.S. dollar against the Singapore unit "very much depended on external factors such as dollar-yen (trading) and how the dollar is faring against European currencies," a dealer said of Thursday's trading.  

Looking ahead, United Overseas Bank said in its daily technical commentary there's no change to its bullish outlook on the U.S. dollar against its local counterpart.  

"While S$1.7300 is a formidable resistance, a move above this level is anticipated for an acceleration toward the target at S$1.7400," the bank said.  

Putting a cap on the U.S. dollar were fears of further steps by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in support of the local unit.  

Suspected MAS intervention to boost the Singapore dollar Wednesday was a "reminder" that the mild appreciation exchange rate policy is still very much in effect, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said.  

In April, Singapore's central bank tightened monetary policy to allow a "modest and gradual appreciation" of the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. [ 29-07-04 0713GMT ]  

There was light selling of Singapore government bonds midafternoon Thursday due to caution ahead of U.S. jobless claims data due later in the global day.

space against the U.S. dollar on the suspicion that Asian
