title: Asian central banks step in as  currencies  trip up.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian central banks appear
to be intervening in foreign exchange markets this week after a
three-month lull, but this time they have been buying their
currencies against a resurgent U.S. dollar, traders say.
    Central banks in India, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and
Indonesia are all suspected to have intervened as some of their
currencies hit lows for the year against the dollar this week.
    That represents a change in tack after the heavy
dollar-buying intervention they conducted through all of 2003
and the first few months of 2004, boosting their combined
foreign reserves to over $2 trillion.
 
    Traders cited dollar-selling intervention in India, where
the rupee hit a fresh one-year low of 46.35/40 on Wednesday.
    The Taiwan dollar has shed about 1.5 percent in less than
   

three weeks and on Wednesday hit 33.23, its lowest in eight   

months. Traders in Singapore said they had heard that the   

central bank offered U.S. dollars in onshore markets above   

34.20.   

Expectations of higher yields in a rebounding U.S. economy,   

weakness in technology stocks and diminishing interest in the   

once-popular Chinese yuan revaluation trade seemed to be   

driving foreign funds out of Asia, analysts said.   

But they felt that policy makers might be reacting too   

quickly, given they had been battling strength in their   

currencies for a couple of years, until April.    


 
    "Some of them are hypersensitive at this moment in time,"
said Claudio Piron, a strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
    "And it seems to be a combination of where the currencies

are in historical terms, where they are in their trade-weighted   

baskets and also in terms of managing inflationary   

expectations."   

POLICY DILEMMA   

Piron said the Thai baht's two percent slide in two weeks   

had taken it to its lowest levels historically in   

trade-weighted terms. The baht hit 41.45, its weakest since   

August 2003, on Wednesday.   

Although Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula   

said the weak baht would not hurt the economy, traders   

suspected the authorities would sell dollars if there were   

further losses.   

Similarly, analysts said it was reasonable for the Monetary   

Authority of Singapore (MAS) to worry if the Sing dollar moved   

too far to the weaker side of the trade-weighted band it is   

managed in, particularly after the central bank announced in   

April it wanted to tighten policy by guiding the currency

higher.   

Local banks in Singapore were seen buying their currency

this week, spurring suspicion they were acting on behalf of the   

MAS.    


 
    South Korean markets have been baffled by conflicting
statements from policy makers.
    More than any country in the region, South Korea is faced
   

with the dilemma of whether to continue with a policy of   

boosting exports through a cheap currency, despite the risk of   

higher imported inflation from rising oil and commodity prices.   

"In Korea, they are getting a bit more sensitive in terms   

of price expectations and some of the inflationary pressure,"   

Piron said. "Some of the growth picture has started to fade,   

but they don't want price inflation to also deteriorate."   

Nonetheless, analysts said inflation was still benign in   

Asia and central banks might be acting to curb market   

volatility rather than signalling a shift in policy.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  fears limit losses.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on
Tuesday, some to new lows for the year, as foreign investors
kept up their liquidation of Asian assets though the fear of
intervention by local central banks lent some support.
    The Singapore dollar        fell as far as 1.7235 before
returning to the firmer side of 1.72 on heavy sales of U.S.
dollars by local banks that markets suspected were acting on
behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
    The Indonesian rupiah        hit a three-week low of 9,150
per dollar before rebounding as Bank Indonesia said it had not
intervened but would do so if the currency became too volatile.
 
    The Philippine peso        rose slightly from an early
level of 56.135, its lowest in a week.
    The U.S. dollar gave up some of the gains it made against
  

the yen and European majors as markets waited for U.S. GDP and  

consumer confidence data to confirm Federal Reserve Chairman  

Alan Greenspan's bullish testimony on the U.S. economy last  

week. That too provided the region some relief.  

"Inasmuch as Asian central banks are concerned about export  

competitiveness implied by softness in equities worldwide, they  

are unlikely to tolerate excessive currency weakness either,  

due to supply-side inflation pressures," Philip Wee, a  

strategist with DBS Bank, said in a note to clients.  

"We don't expect runaway depreciation in Asian currencies."  

Still, traders said the early losses showed foreigners were  

still pulling their money out of Asian stocks and  

currencies, partly because of rising yields in the United  

States and because of waning expectations of a revaluation of  

the tightly controlled Chinese yuan .  

The Taiwan dollar slipped to 34.16, a fresh low  

for 2004, and the Thai baht fell to 41.25 a dollar, its  

lowest since August 2003.  

Wee said the baht was the most vulnerable because Thailand  

ranked second in the region in its exposure to the risks of  

oil, the yen and stocks. The Taiwan dollar was sensitive to  

movements in its stock market, he said.  

Asian markets have also been pressured by the fall in the  

prices of U.S. technology stocks. The technology-packed Nasdaq  

Composite Index posted its lowest close since last  

October and the Philadelphia Stock Exchange's semiconductor  

index fell to an 11-month low on Monday.

title: Singapore rates leap and sink, baffling markets.
text:
(Fixes headline)    

 SINGAPORE, July 15 (Reuters) - Singapore's money market rates more than quadrupled in the first 12 days of July before softening swiftly this week, leaving dealers clueless about where the cash went and whether the central bank was behind the move.    

 Overnight rates  rose from 0.39 percent at the end of June to 1.65 percent on Monday, and then dropped to 0.97 percent on Thursday.    

 Other rates on the short-term curve were slightly less volatile but also rose and fell in quick succession.    

 When rates started rising, many traders speculated the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was intervening, to push rates higher and thereby force the Singapore dollar  up.    

 Nizam Idris, an analyst with IDEAglobal.com, said recent evidence of strength in the economy had fed speculation of intervention by the MAS.    

 "You can't discount that possibility altogether," he said.    

 "Although I don't suppose it is MAS style to induce volatility," he said.    

 MAS officials said the central bank does not comment on its money market operations.    

 The MAS runs its monetary policy by guiding the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed trade-weighted band of currencies of the city-state's trading partners.    

 On April 12, the MAS said it was tightening policy through the exchange rate to pre-empt any inflationary pressures.    

 But the Singapore dollar weakened in nominal and trade-weighted terms until early July. It was quoted around 1.7040/50 per dollar on Thursday, below its four-year high of 1.6605 hit on April 13.    

 Analysts reckoned it was about time the currency rose so that policy can tighten. Recent data, showing GDP expanding strongly, inflation at a three-year high and industry growing robustly, vindicated the MAS's decision in April to tighten, they said.    

 FED RESPONSIBLE?    

 Several traders said speculation surrounding the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to raise rates for the first time in four years was the reason behind the spike in Singapore rates.    

 In the weeks before the June 30 decision by the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points from a 46-year low of 1.0 percent, traders cited heavy purchases of U.S. dollars versus Sing dollars through the spot market and forwards, betting that a rate rise would boost the greenback.    

 "Those positions were being funded on a daily basis, and that put pressure on overnight rates," said a trader.    

 And there were many in the market who showed no surprise at what they termed a "July phenomenon". Rates shot up inexplicably in July 2003 too, and have done sporadically in the past.    

 Bhanu Baweja, a UBS currency strategist, said Singapore dollar forwards and money market rates were likely to remain tight for some more time.    

 "It is a small, open economy where monetary policy targets the exchange rate. Money supply in Singapore is going to be endogenous and interest rates are going to be decided abroad," he said.

title: FX  Asia:Singapore Dlr Hasn't Caught Up With Fundamentals
text:
By Ron Harui and Kevin Lim 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
 
   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is stubbornly refusing to rise despite strong economic growth and creeping inflation in the city-state. But analysts are confident the local currency will gain in the coming months.  

Major banks expect the Singapore dollar to rise 2% to 3% against the U.S. currency by the end of the year as the market catches up with Singapore's fundamentals.  

"Our longstanding view has been that the Singapore dollar's secular trend is biased towards appreciation, because of its fundamental support - economic recovery, a strong external balance and fiscal prudence," Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said in a recent report.  

The island's economy grew 7.5% on year in the first quarter and is expected to accelerate further, while prices are edging higher. And yet the Singapore dollar has weakened in the three months since the central bank changed policy and targeted a rise in the local unit.  

Factors weighing down the currency include the U.S. dollar's resilience in the face of America's widening trade and budget deficits, and weak sentiment toward Asian currencies due to concerns over a hard landing for China's white-hot economy.  

Uncertainty arising from Monday's Indonesian presidential election, which is expected to drag on to a September runoff, has also been cited as a reason for weakness in Asia currencies. But United Overseas Bank treasury economist Jimmy Koh noted this didn't stop the rupiah from hitting a six-month high this week.  

Given the Singapore dollar's weakness during the past few months, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have intervened in the foreign-exchange market on several occasions to boost the local currency. MAS may also have tightened liquidity in the local money markets to bolster the Singapore dollar, J.P. Morgan said in a research note Wednesday.  


 
       U.S. Dlr May Fall To S$1.6600 End-Dec 
   

The central bank, citing growing inflationary pressures, shifted April 12 from a policy of "zero appreciation" of the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies to seeking "modest and gradual appreciation."  

The MAS targets the local dollar's exchange rate, rather than interest rates, to spur or damp the economy because trade flows dwarf the island's small domestic economy. The U.S. dollar and currencies pegged to it - such as the Malaysian ringgit, Hong Kong dollar and Chinese yuan - are believed to account for more than half of MAS's undisclosed currency basket.  

Despite the central bank's desire for a stronger local unit and the fundamental case for such a rise, the U.S. dollar has risen 2.8% Since April 12 to S$1.7128 around 0450 GMT Wednesday. Against the MAS currency basket, UOB reckons the local dollar is 0.3% weaker than the midpoint of allowed trading band, compared with just above the pivot before MAS tightened monetary policy, and 1.5% above the center in the "immediate aftermath" of the monetary policy statement.  

But eventually, analysts say, the local currency should appreciate again - as the MAS wants.  

"There is really little reason why the Singapore dollar (trade-weighted rate) should trade around current levels," UOB said in a report Tuesday.  

UOB thinks the Singapore dollar should be worth around S$1.7034 to the U.S. dollar based on a level of 0.5% above the midpoint of its currency band. The bank expects the U.S. dollar to fall to S$1.6900 by the end of September and S$1.6700 by year's end.  

DBS Bank projects the U.S. dollar will be at S$1.6700 at the end of September and S$1.6600 at the end of the December. The U.S. dollar's trading range should be closer to S$1.6800-S$1.7000 than its current S$1.7000-S$1.7200, given the strong local stock market, strong economic numbers coming out of Singapore and the rise of inflation to the 2% level, said DBS currency strategist Philip Wee.  

A bit less Singapore dollar-bullish is Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, which sees the U.S. currency falling to S$1.7050 by the end of September and S$1.6800 at the end of December.  

Other players predicting a stronger Singapore dollar include Morgan Stanley, which forecasts the U.S. dollar falling to S$1.6700 at year's end, and J.P. Morgan, which tips the U.S. unit at S$1.6600 by then.  

After a long period of sluggish growth following the 1997 Asian economic crisis, with two recessions thrown in for good measure, Singapore has roared back to life with double-digit growth in exports and retail spending since the start of this year.  

After the strong first quarter, gross domestic product for the second quarter, due out next week, is expected to accelerate beyond 10% on year. Inflation is also making a comeback, hitting 2% on year in May after several years of stable prices.

But United Overseas Bank treasury economist Jimmy Koh noted this didn't stop the rupiah from hitting a six-month high this week.    

Given the Singapore dollar's weakness during the past few months, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have intervened in the foreign-exchange market on several occasions to boost the local currency. MAS may also have tightened liquidity in the local money markets to bolster the Singapore dollar, J.P. Morgan said in a research note Wednesday.    

U.S. Dlr May Fall To S$1.6600 End-Dec    

The central bank, citing growing inflationary pressures, shifted April 12 from a policy of 'zero appreciation' of the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies to seeking 'modest and gradual appreciation.'    

The MAS targets the local dollar's exchange rate, rather than interest rates, to spur or damp the economy because trade flows dwarf the island's small domestic economy. The U.S. dollar and currencies pegged to it - such as the Malaysian ringgit, Hong Kong dollar and Chinese yuan - are believed to account for more than half of MAS's undisclosed currency basket.    

Despite the central bank's desire for a stronger local unit and the fundamental case for such a rise, the U.S. dollar has risen 2.8% Since April 12 to S$1.7128 around 0450 GMT Wednesday. Against the MAS currency basket, UOB reckons the local dollar is 0.3% weaker than the midpoint of allowed trading band, compared with just above the pivot before MAS tightened monetary policy, and 1.5% above the center in the 'immediate aftermath' of the monetary policy statement.    

But eventually, analysts say, the local currency should appreciate again - as the MAS wants.

title: ANALYSIS-Dollar at risk as inflation deters Asian  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, June 24 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar may be heading for a big fall, with analysts saying that rising inflation will force Asian central banks to cut the currency intervention that has been financing the massive U.S. current account deficit.   

"The price to pay for the type of intervention we saw last year...is typically that you get inflationary pressure," said Jan Lambregts, Rabobank's head of Asia-Pacific research.   

"Last year that price did not have to be paid, but this time around, in an environment where inflationary pressure is on the rise, such intervention could really throw fuel on the fire."   

Last week's record U.S. current account deficit of $144.9 billion for the first quarter was a reminder to markets fixated on next week's U.S. Federal Reserve meeting that the United States still has a funding problem.   

In 2003 the United States ran a current account deficit of $530.6 billion - broadly, the imbalance between its exports and imports and the income it received from or paid to foreigners.   

Asian central banks were happy to finance that deficit by buying U.S. dollar assets, such as Treasury bonds, to hold down their currencies and keep their exports competitive. In 2003, they increased their foreign exchange reserves by almost $520 billion.   

That intervention occured when deflation was a worry for much of Asia, which was also struggling with the impact of the war in Iraq and the SARS outbreak.   

Now deflation has gone in most Asian countries, where prices are not only rising but accelerating. On Wednesday, China said inflation was moving to near five percent, a rate seen as a possible trigger for a rate rise, while Singapore reported its highest inflation rate since December 2000.   

Allowing a currency to strengthen is one way to slow an economy and hold down inflation. Intervening to hold a currency down, on the other hand, tends to pump up the amount of money in the economy, stoking inflation.   

LESS AGGRESSIVE   

"With inflationary pressures starting to pick up, it's a bit more of a two-way street as to what you should let your currency do," Standard Chartered Bank currency strategist Claudio Piron said.   

"I think that is perhaps a rationale why we may see Asian central banks being less aggressive in terms of supporting the dollar in coming quarters, especially if oil prices remain high."   

Prospective U.S. rate rises have pushed the current account deficit into the background, but it should reappear as the market becomes more comfortable with rising rates.   

"We would argue that the latest trade, current account and balance of payments data dramatically emphasise the negative case for the dollar," Jim O'Neill, head of global research at Goldman Sachs, said in a report.   

Goldman Sachs estimates that to cut the current account deficit to three percent of GDP from about five percent now, the dollar would need to fall by about 20 percent.   

Looking at the dollar from another angle, Goldman Sachs reckoned that a 31 percent fall would be needed to make U.S. assets attractive enough for foreigners to support it.   

In recent years Asia has blocked such a correction for fear of losing export competitiveness. So in the first quarter, for example, the United States could turn to Asia to fund its current account needs of $1.6 billion a day.   

U.S. ASSETS   

In these three months Japan spent a record 14.83 trillion yen - about $138 billion based on the average dollar/yen rate for the quarter - trying to prop up the dollar.   

All up, foreign exchange reserves at Asia's central banks rose by $247 billion in the first quarter. Most of that is thought to have been invested in U.S. assets.   

Asian central banks have already scaled down their dollar buying, but not because of inflation.   

Instead, the reason appears to have been that the dollar rose in April and May because investors bet on an early rise in U.S. interest rates. So intervention was not needed to hold Asian currencies down.   

Since March, Japan has not intervened. Excluding China, which has not released figures yet, Asian central bank reserves rose by only $2 billion in the two months to May 31.   

Economists expect the intervention to strengthen again - and it certainly will not disappear entirely - but inflation should prevent Asia's central banks from being such willing financiers of the U.S. current account.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Increased Terrorism Concerns
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was stronger late Monday in Asia on increased concerns about terrorism in the wake of a suspected al-Qaida attack on foreigners working in Saudi Arabia's oil industry over the weekend.  

Singapore government bond prices were lower, following the U.S. Treasurys' weaker close late Friday, in quiet trade as U.S. markets were shut for a holiday Monday.  

Around 0800 GMT, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.6975, down from S$1.6990 late Friday in Asia. It traded a S$1.6940-S$1.7000 range intraday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. dollar swiftly slipped from its opening level of S$1.7000 to its morning low of S$1.6975 following news of the weekend rampage by gunmen that killed 22 people, including several foreigners, in the Saudi city of Khobar.  

Market participants were concerned that the weekend rampage could fuel tensions in the Middle East and might be a prelude to a possible terrorist-related attack in the U.S. on its Memorial Day holiday today.  

Only fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene in the currency market to curb excessive volatility of the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair prevented the U.S. currency from extending its slide against its Singaporean counterpart in the morning, dealers said.  

"Players were cautious about pushing (the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar) down further due to (ongoing) rumors that the authorities had intervened last Friday" to prop up the currency pair, said a local dealer.  

These rumors were sparked Friday when the U.S. dollar recovered somewhat after falling to a three-week low of S$1.6960 early in that day's session.  

But ongoing worries over terrorism, rising instability in the Middle East and growing notions that the Federal Reserve's expected interest-rate hikes are already factored into the markets kept the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar under downward pressure, dealers said.  

Later in the Asian session, the U.S. dollar slipped further from around S$1.6975 to an intraday low of S$1.6940, its lowest since May 7, as stop-loss sales orders in the mid-S$1.6900s were triggered by the U.S. unit's persistent weakness against the yen.  

According to technical analysis, the U.S. dollar remains short-term bearish against the local currency this week after it broke below several important support levels last week, including its uptrend line from mid-April and Fibonacci support at S$1.7041 (the 38.2% retracement of the rise from mid-April).  

Although the U.S. unit held quite strong support at S$1.6958-S$1.6959 (the 50- and 100-day moving averages and the 50% retracement) last Friday and for most of today, its break below this area late in today's session means it could target the 61.8% retracement level of S$1.6875 in coming days. [ 31-05-04 0829GMT ]  

Singapore government bonds drifted lower at the start of the local session, following a weaker close in U.S. Treasurys late Friday.  

But trade in the local market wound down soon after the early slide, with market participants holding positions ahead of a holiday in the U.S. Monday.  

At the end of the session, the yield on the two-year government bond was 1.11%, up from late Friday's close of 1.09%. The yield on the 10-year paper rose to 3.30% versus 3.27%, while the 15-year bond yield rose one basis point to end at 3.84%.  

Interest rate swaps were also slightly higher, in line with local bond yields. The two-year swap offer was at 1.65% from 1.61% late Friday. The five-year swap was at 2.70% from 2.65% previously, while the 10-year swap was at 3.70% from 3.66% late Friday.  

The spread between the two- and 10-year swaps was unchanged at 205 basis points from late Friday.  

The interbank overnight rate slipped to 0.4375% from 0.5000%.  

Prices quoted are pre-settlement bids obtained from dealers and are subject to change.  

Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site:

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steady but risks remain.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, May 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies steadied on
Thursday after recent volatile trade but investors remain
nervous about a choppy U.S. dollar, high oil prices and the
threat of terror attacks.
    Oil prices        fell from near 21-year highs on Wednesday
but there are concerns high prices would persist until the end
of June, when the United States is expected to hand over power
in Iraq to a local administration.
    The dollar was also hit by weaker-than-expected U.S. data
and news reports on Wednesday suggesting U.S. officials had
information about terror attacks planned in the summer.
    With the yen        stuck between 111.40 and 112 a dollar,
the Singapore dollar  initially fell to the weaker side
of 1.71 and then rallied to 1.7060, a three-week high.
  


    The Korean won                   caught up with the
regional appreciation after a market holiday on Wednesday,
opening domestic trade sharply up at a three-week high close to
1,170 per dollar and creating a big gap on the dollar/won
chart.
    "It is very difficult. When you have security issues in the
U.S., the possibility of higher volatility in oil prices until
the end of next month, those factors are going to mean that
upside potential for Asian FX is not that significant," said
Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at Westpac Bank,
Sydney.
    Investors would be unwilling to commit fresh capital to
Asian assets, and those flows had been the prime drivers of
regional currency gains this year, he said.
 
    "If for any reason we see the situation in Iraq resolved,
the value in Asia will become much more compelling," he said.
    In Thursday's trading, the Indonesian rupiah        was
  

still under some pressure from liquidation of positions by  

foreigners and stop-loss trades. It hit 9,300 per dollar,  

edging closer to Tuesday's 19-month trough of 9,350.  

The Philippine peso barely moved, staying near the  

56 per dollar level as an official counting of presidential  

election votes got underway. Leaked unofficial results showed a  

narrow victory for incumbent Gloria Macapagal Arroyo.  

PICK SING DOLLAR  

Rennie said the Sing dollar and the Korean won offered the  

best value in the region, based on a ranking system that  

included macroeconomic factors, sensitivity to oil prices,  

foreign exchange regime and intervention.  

Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said the  

Singapore dollar was on the verge of an uptrend. The worry  

China might slow sharply had moderated and Singapore shares  

had outperformed other markets in the recent wave of  

equity selling, he said. Besides, risk aversion was easing, he  

said.  

"In fundamental terms the Singapore story remains a good  

one," he said, referring to a deepening economic recovery,  

especially in manufacturing.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it was tightening  

policy in early April. The MAS conducts its policy through a  

trade-weighted Sing dollar basket, guiding the currency higher  

to tighten policy.  

Baweja said the Singapore dollar had lost 1.4 percent  

against that trade-weighted basket since the policy was  

tightened.  

"MAS' policy bias, which is executed through the exchange  

rate, together with our fundamental negative view on the U.S.  

dollar means we see U.S. dollar/Sing dollar as a sell."  

"In addition, short-term factors that had kept the Sing  

dollar under the cosh seem to be abating now."

title: Singapore Dollar Down Late On Signs Of U.S. Inflation
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was weaker late Friday, having hit a fresh six-month low overnight and again during Asian trading as signs of inflation in the U.S. sparked heavy buying of the U.S. currency.  

Singapore government bond prices were also lower on U.S. inflation fears as the market awaited the U.S. April consumer price index due later in the global day.  

Around 0715 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7273, up from S$1.7240 late Thursday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7245 and S$1.7305 intraday.  

The U.S. unit touched a six-month high of S$1.7294 late Thursday in New York, its highest level since Nov. 13. It rose further to S$1.7305 Friday afternoon in Asia.  

Although it fell slightly from its opening level of around S$1.7269 on profit-taking early in the session, the U.S. currency soon began to climb toward the psychologically key S$1.7300 level on buying by domestic and non-Singaporean players, who were betting on a further U.S. dollar rise in the near term.  

They based their bets partly on a stronger-than-expected U.S. producer price index for April, which increased expectations that the Federal Reserve could hike interest rates soon.  

The U.S. Labor Department reported Thursday that the PPI rose 0.7% in April, well above the consensus forecast for a 0.3% increase. The PPI excluding food and energy rose 0.2%, in line with expectations.  

Although energy prices fueled the PPI rise, some economists fear these energy price increases could spill over into the consumer sector. Those fears are likely to take centerstage when the U.S. April CPI is released at 1230 GMT. Economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC project a 0.3% rise in April CPI and a 0.2% increase when food and energy prices are taken out.  

Although the U.S. dollar ran into strong psychological and technical resistance in the S$1.7293-SS1.7300 zone, the U.S. unit later climbed to S$1.7305 on persistent buying by U.S. investment houses.  

Growing concerns over inflationary pressures in the U.S., the negative impact on Asia from high oil prices and diverging interest-rate paths between the U.S. and Asian nations in favor of the U.S. spurred the U.S. banks' purchases of the U.S. currency, dealers said.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late Vs US Dlr After Choppy Trade
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was relatively steady against its U.S. counterpart late Friday after choppy trading ahead of this weekend's meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations in Washington.  

Singapore government bonds were higher, following U.S. Treasurys' gains in New York and Tokyo as investors tempered their expectations for any move by the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.  

At 0740 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6950, nearly flat from S$1.6955 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.6953 and S$1.7010 intraday.  

Early in the session, the U.S. dollar hit a five-week high of S$1.7010 as domestic and non-Singaporean players bought the U.S. currency to bet on an increase in U.S. interest rates in the near future.  

Despite a smaller-than-anticipated fall in U.S. weekly jobless claims released late Thursday, expectations remained high that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates this summer. The latest weekly jobless claims fell by 9,000 but economists were expecting a fall of 20,000.  

But some local banks immediately sold into the U.S. dollar's surge above the psychologically important S$1.7000 level in order to take profits prior to this weekend's G7 meeting, dragging the U.S. currency back down to the mid-S$1.6900s.  

Analysts expect the G7 meeting's wording on foreign exchange to stay basically unchanged from the previous statement in Boca Raton, given that the U.S. currency has been trading at levels broadly acceptable to the U.S., Japan and Europe in recent weeks.  

The G7 finance officials at the Boca Raton meeting in February said they generally supported flexible currency exchange rates but expressed concern over "disorderly" fluctuations.  

The early afternoon release of Singapore's consumer price index for March, which rose 1.3% from a year ago, had little impact on the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair as the data were largely in line with market expectations for an on-year rise of 1.4%, dealers said.  

With the city-state's inflation staying relatively steady for the first three months of the year, there are few signs so far that price pressures are building here, which could give the Monetary Authority of Singapore less reason to intervene to moderate Singapore dollar weakness, analysts said.  

In the short term, the U.S. currency's outlook is still bullish, as technical analysis shows that its rise above S$1.6894 Wednesday has triggered a reverse head and shoulders pattern on the daily chart, targeting S$1.7160. [ 23-04-04 0808GMT ]  

Singapore government bonds ended higher Friday, tracking the movements of U.S. Treasurys in New York and Asia.  

Singapore dealers said local bond prices managed to recover from sharp falls earlier this week when U.S. Treasurys tumbled following comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan which raised the possibility of a U.S. interest rate hike sometime this year.  

Local bonds, however, responded little to the Singapore March CPI data, mainly because the 1.3% on-year rise was within expectations, dealers added.  

At the end of local session, the yield on the two-year government bond was at 1.03%, down from the previous close of 1.05%. The 10-year yield was at 3.27% against 3.33% previously, while the 15-year yield was nine basis points lower at 3.71%.  

Interest rate swaps were, however, mixed with the two-year swap offer unchanged at 1.57%, the five-year swap offer at 2.69% from 2.71% late Thursday, while the 10-year swap offer was at 3.69% from 3.76%.  

The spread between the two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 212 basis points from late Thursday's 219 basis points.  

The interbank overnight rate rose to 0.5000% versus 0.3750% late Thursday.

title: MAS Econ Review: Singapore Dlr Up 3% Vs US Dlr In Oct-Mar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was higher by around 3% against the U.S. dollar at the end of March from where it was at the start of the fourth quarter in 2003, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in its semiannual macroeconomic review Tuesday.  

The central bank said the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, or NEER, has been under general upward pressure since late last year, reflecting the firmer economic recovery in Singapore and the region and the U.S. dollar's weakness.  

The call of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations for more flexible foreign exchange rates also led to an influx of short-term capital, the MAS said.  

At 0220 GMT Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6800 compared with S$1.6988 at the start of the year. It hit a four-year low of S$1.6608 on April 13.  

The MAS reiterated that it intervened to moderate the strength of the Singapore dollar and to curb excessive volatility, thereby keeping the trade-weighed index fairly stable within the policy band.  

The more recent appreciation of the Singapore dollar NEER toward the upper half of the policy band was supported by positive economic data, the central bank added.  

While the MAS didn't disclose any forecasts for the local currency in its macroeconomic review, analysts expect further Singapore dollar appreciation in the coming months after the MAS unexpectedly tightened monetary policy April 12.  

JPMorgan Chase Bank cut its year-end forecast for the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair to S$1.6200 from S$1.6500 projected previously, while IDEAglobal economist Nizam Idris forecast the U.S. dollar to drift down to S$1.6400 by then.  

In its biannual monetary policy statement issued last week, the MAS said it would shift from a zero percent appreciation path to a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar NEER, starting from the midpoint of the current policy band, without changing the width of the band.  

Since October last year, the general strengthening in global economic activity, coupled with the uncertainty over the outlook for the major currencies, has given foreign exchange trading activity in Singapore a significant boost, the MAS said.  

Compared with the year-ago period, foreign exchange trading turnover rose 22% in the October 2003-February 2004 period, with the bulk of the increase attributed to transactions of the U.S. currency against the euro, the Australian dollar and East Asian currencies, the central bank said.  

Of the instruments traded, currency swaps accounted for around 49% while spot transactions represented about 39% of total turnover, with the rest attributed to forward contracts.

title: Singapore To Tighten Monetary Policy
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--In a surprise move, the Monetary Authority of Singapore Monday said it will tighten monetary policy by shifting from neutral to allow a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar.  

"Against a more favourable growth outlook for the Singapore economy, and the risk of rising inflationary pressures, MAS is shifting from a 0% appreciation path to a policy of modest and gradual appreciation of the S$NEER, starting from the mid-point of the current policy band," MAS said.  

The width of the band will remain unchanged, the central bank added. [ 12-04-04 0007GMT ]  

Most economists had expected Singapore to continue with a neutral monetary policy until the next policy statement in October, although they said there was a chance MAS may signal tolerance of a relatively firm Singapore dollar against its nominal effective exchange rate, or NEER.  

Because of the open nature of the island's trade-driven economy, MAS uses the Singapore dollar's exchange rate against an undisclosed basket of currencies, rather than interest rates, to support economic growth while maintaining domestic price stability.  

In its statement Monday, MAS also revised its forecast for consumer-price inflation in 2004 to 1.5%-2.0%, from 0.5%-1.5% previously.  

"Consumer price inflation has trended up in recent months, averaging 1.4% year-on-year in January-February 2004, compared to 0.5% and 0.7% in the last two quarters of 2003, respectively, " MAS said.  

It said the increase largely reflected supply-side factors, including the passthrough effects of global commodity-related price increases and the goods-and-services tax hike in January 2004.  

It added: "Domestic price pressures remain subdued but could intensify if the growth momentum remains strong over the next few quarters, causing the labor market to tighten."  

MAS also said the Singapore dollar "NEER has generally been under upward pressure since late last year, reflecting the firmer economic recovery in Singapore and the region, and the weakness of the U.S. dollar. The G7's call for more flexible exchange rates also led to an influx of short-term capital."  

MAS had intervened "to moderate the strength of the Singapore dollar and to damp excessive volatility," it said.  

"The Singapore dollar NEER remained fairly stable until January, but more recently has appreciated towards the upper end of the policy band, supported by the release of encouraging economic data including on exports and industrial production," it added.  

On the economy, MAS said the Ministry of Trade and Industry has assessed that the gross domestic product growth range for 2004 is likely to exceed the current forecast of 3.5-5.5%.  

"While downside risks to the outlook remain, on balance, the upturn in the global economy and IT markets is likely to be sustained," the central bank added.  

-By Kevin Lim, Dow Jones Newswires; (65) 6415 4156; kevin.lim@dowjones.com [ 12-04-04 0044GMT ]

title: Singapore Dlr Sharply Higher Vs US Dlr Late As Yen Surges
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar continued to gain sharply Wednesday, touching a two-month high of S$1.6750 against its U.S. counterpart as the greenback went into a free fall against the Japanese yen.  

Singapore government bonds were barely changed in thin trading as the market awaited a U.S. employment report due at the end of this week. Traders said the outlook for bonds remains bearish.  

At 0810 GMT, the U.S. currency was trading at S$1.6756, down from S$1.6838 late Tuesday in Asia. It changed hands between S$1.6750 and S$1.6830 during the day.  

Traders said that the main sellers of U.S. dollars against the local currency were Japanese banks, and that there was no sign of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore during Asian trading.  

The U.S. currency was initially supported at S$1.6780 in the morning, but dropped below this level in the afternoon after the greenback failed to stay above its Y104.50 support against the yen.  

According to Tokyo traders, the dollar selling Wednesday was triggered by U.S.-based hedge funds on growing market speculation that Tokyo has abandoned its policy of aggressive intervention to prevent the yen from appreciating sharply.  

Despite verbal intervention by Japanese officials, including Finance Minister Sadakazu Tanigaki, who said the government would take steps against excessive movements if necessary, the dollar's fall was exacerbated by stop-loss sell orders and new sell orders coming out of Europe.  

Late Wednesday, the dollar was trading at Y103.82, down sharply from Y105.64 late Tuesday in New York.  

Traders said the Singapore dollar's performance going forward will depend on movements in the U.S. dollar-yen pair.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late On Yen; SGD Uninspired
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar continued to be left out in the cold, uninspired by the gains of other Asian currencies late Wednesday. 

 The relatively stable yen - which buoyed most of the region's currencies - and the rupiah's rise to new six-month highs failed to check the Singapore dollar's descent past the psychologically important S$1.8500 threshold to the U.S. currency earlier in the day. 

 The Singapore dollar skidded to an 11-week low of S$1.8507, as participants continued to cover their short U.S. dollar positions - as the near-term rebound in the Singapore currency they had been waiting for didn't materialize. 

 However, the U.S. dollar retreated swiftly after a large Singapore bank unloaded the currency all the way from around S$1.8500 to S$1.8470, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar late in the day extended its correction, as local banks led the selling in the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 At 0910 GMT (4:10 a.m. EST), the Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.8439 to the U.S. unit, little changed from S$1.8438 late Tuesday. 

 U.S. dollar sales by Singapore banks sparked concerns of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, but some observers said such fears were unjustified as the local currency remained well within the MAS' undisclosed policy band. 

 They noted that the MAS has largely given participants a free rein in the foreign exchange market - provided the Singapore dollar was within the policy band - since the middle of last year as the authority moves to gradually liberalize the city-state financial markets. 

 The Singapore dollar has weakened about 1.2% against the currencies of its major trading partners over the last two days, pushing the currency to the middle part of its estimated trade-weighted band from the stronger end earlier this week, said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at UOB Group. 

 Given Singapore's improving economic outlook, analysts doubt if the MAS will leave the Singapore dollar to trade in the weaker half of the band. 

 Some observers attributed the U.S. dollar's retreat to the increasingly expensive cost of shorting the Singapore dollar - Singapore dollar offshore swaps have moved to the right. This should restrain the U.S. dollar's rise, at least for now. 

Foreign exchange participants were also keen to square positions ahead of the long weekend. Singapore's markets are closed for Good Friday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah relinquished its gains after having earlier extended its climb to a six-month high of IDR9,525 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Short-covering in U.S. dollars and demand for the U.S. currency from local corporations needing to meet foreign debt repayment pushed the rupiah back to IDR9,630 late in the day, little changed compared with IDR9,620 late Monday. 

 The rupiah had recently staged a strong recovery after U.S. investment fund Farallon Capital's acquisition of the Indonesian government's 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia - the country's largest retail bank - earlier this month. 

 Returning capital inflows, political stability and optimism surrounding Indonesia's meeting with the Paris Club of official creditors next month helped reverse the rupiah's fortunes. 

 Mild gains in the yen, traditional month-end U.S. dollar sales by domestic exporters and foreign equity fund inflows bolstered the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar finished at 1,327.0 won, lower than KRW1,329.3 Tuesday. 

 Seoul's benchmark stock index jumped 2.4% to a two-year closing high Wednesday. After a selling spree over the last four days, foreign investors turned into net buyers of South Korean shares, picking up KRW16.1 billion worth of stocks. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$35.024, lower than Tuesday's NT$35.037. 

 Foreign institutional investors bought a net NT$2.81 billion worth of shares on the Taiwan Stock Exchange Wednesday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the U.S. dollar closed at 51.005 pesos, from PHP51.145 Tuesday. 

 Month-end U.S. dollar sales by exporters and the trimming of long positions in the U.S. currency ahead of the Easter holidays buoyed the peso, dealers said. Markets in Manila are closed Thursday and Friday. 

 Supported by its regional peers, the Thai currency was slightly stronger at 43.335 baht to the U.S. dollar, compared with THB43.360 late Tuesday.

title: FX  ASIA: Singapore Dlr's Dive Won't Scuttle Uptrend
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column



SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar plummeted to an 11-week
low Wednesday - but analysts believe the currency fell by the wayside
largely because of transient factors and little to do with fundamentals.


 They said market participants were caught short in U.S. dollars when their hopes for a near-term rebound in the Singapore currency didn't materialize. 

 Indeed, Singapore will likely be one of the first to recuperate from the region-wide economic malaise, with the local currency poised to recover to S$1.7800 against its U.S. counterpart by the end of the year. 

 Recent economic data have reinforced the growing optimism surrounding the Singapore economy. Although industrial output fell 11.3% year-on-year in February, it was still better than the average decline of about 16% that analysts were expecting. 

 A rebound in the Singapore dollar - which as one of the most actively traded currencies in the region often sets the direction for other Asian units - will likely support other Asian currencies, particularly the Thai baht and the Philippine peso which tend to mimic its movements. 

 But in the near term, dealers don't rule out the possibility that the Singapore dollar could retest its 11-year low of S$1.8552, reached on Dec. 27 last year, given the yen's fragility. 

 However, dealers said that level would likely pose as a strong support for the Singapore currency. 

 Extending its recent precipitous decline, the Singapore dollar briefly skidded past the psychologically important S$1.8500 threshold against its U.S. counterpart to hit an 11-week low of S$1.8507 earlier Wednesday. 


   Trade-Weighted SGD Within Policy Band - Observers



The U.S. dollar pulled back after a large Singapore bank unloaded the
currency all the way from around S$1.8500 to S$1.8470, sparking fears
that it could have been intervening on behalf of the central bank, also
known as the Monetary Authority of Singapore, or the MAS.



"It gave the market the impression that the MAS was in," said the head
of foreign exchange trading at an Asian bank. Most dealers believe the
bank is an MAS agent bank, through which it regularly deals.



After that brief dive, the Singapore dollar stabilized around S$1.8470
most part of the morning, before resuming its correction to S$1.8435 at
0845 GMT as local banks led the selling in the U.S. currency. Late
Tuesday, the Singapore dollar was trading around S$1.8438.



The MAS uses the currency, not interest rates, as its primary
monetary-policy tool to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The
Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of
currencies of the country's major trading partners.



Some observers doubted, however, that the central bank intervened as
the trade-weighted Singapore dollar remained well within the MAS'
undisclosed policy band.



They noted too that the MAS has largely given participants a free rein
in the foreign exchange market - provided the Singapore dollar was
within the policy band - since the middle of last year as the authority
moves to gradually liberalize the city-state's financial markets.



Instead, they attributed the U.S. dollar's retreat to the increasingly
expensive cost of shorting the Singapore dollar - Singapore dollar
offshore swaps have moved to the right, observers said. This should
restrain the U.S. dollar's rise, at least for now.


Foreign exchange participants are also keen to square out of their
positions ahead of the long weekend. Singapore's markets are closed for
Good Friday.



The Singapore dollar - which has depreciated by almost 2% against its
U.S. counterpart since early March - has ostensibly taken over the
rupiah's unenviable position as the black sheep of Asia's foreign
exchange markets since the end of last week.



The rupiah's fortunes have changed for the better after U.S.
investment fund Farallon Capital's acquisition of the Indonesian
government's 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia - the country's largest
retail bank - earlier this month.



Returning capital inflows, political stability and optimism
surrounding Indonesia's meeting with the Paris Club of official
creditors next month helped propel the rupiah to a six-month peak of
around IDR9,525 against the U.S. dollar earlier Wednesday, observers
said.



But even a combination of the rupiah's 3.7% rally, the stable yen and
firmer Asian currencies has failed to salvage the Singapore dollar.



As a result, the Singapore dollar has weakened about 1.2% against the
currencies of its major trading partners over the last two days, pushing
the currency to the middle part of its estimated trade-weighted band
from the stronger end earlier this week, said Jimmy Koh, head of
treasury research at UOB Group.



Given Singapore's improving economic outlook, analysts doubt if the
MAS will allow the Singapore dollar to trade in the weaker half of the
band.



   Options Market Reaction Subdued



The reaction in the currency options market to the Singapore dollar's
sharp drop was fairly subdued, as market participants wonder whether the
currency's downward momentum could be sustained - especially after it
appeared to be finding support around S$1.8500 against the U.S.
currency.



"The options market wasn't too flustered with the spot move," said a
dealer at a U.S. bank. "There are no substantial positions."



Volatilities implied by one-month U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar
currency options edged up about 0.3 point to trade at 4% earlier
Wednesday, following the U.S. currency's brief spike above S$1.8500.



One-month quarter delta risk-reversals remained well bid, favoring
U.S. dollar call/Singapore dollar put options by 0%/0.8%, dealers said.



Risk-reversals measure the market preference for either put or call
options by the premium or discount applied. Delta measures the change in
the option value for a change in the underlying foreign exchange rate.



Market watchers blamed the unwinding of short U.S. dollar positions
against the Singapore currency by international investors - particularly
U.S. investment houses - for the Singapore dollar's relentless slide in
recent sessions.



These investors were taken aback by the apparent weakness in recently
issued data, which were distorted by the fewer working days in February
this year. The Lunar New Year holidays fell in February this year; last
year, the holidays were in January.



"Superficial weakness in some headline economic indicators for
February, a product of fewer working days due to the Lunar New Year,
appears to be the main culprit," J.P. Morgan Chase Bank said in a report
Wednesday.



Singapore's key non-oil domestic exports - a barometer of the
trade-dependent city state's economic health - fell a
steeper-than-expected 23.4% in February year-on-year.



To a lesser extent, the Monetary Authority of Singapore's move last
week to further liberalize its policy of non-internationalization of the
Singapore dollar - in its bid to lure international investors to the
country's capital markets - also undermined the local currency as
participants, betting on further yen weakness, braced for more volatile
trading, observers said.

netty.ismail@dowjones.com

title: Singapore Dlr Briefly Hits 11-Week Low Of S$1.8507 Vs Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar briefly fell to an 11-week low of S$1.8507 against its U.S. counterpart Wednesday, before regaining its footing after local banks stepped in to sell U.S. dollars, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar had touched a high of S$1.8500 in overnight trading in New York. It started the Asian trading day lower around S$1.8490 against the local currency but up from S$1.8428 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Aggressive U.S. dollar buying by U.S. investment banks to cover their short positions pushed the U.S. currency above the key psychological level of S$1.8500 in early Asian trades. 

 The U.S. dollar last traded above S$1.8500 Jan. 10, when it touched a high of S$1.8510. Before that, the U.S. currency had risen to an 11-year high of S$1.8550 Dec. 28, 2001. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise above S$1.8500 prompted a large local bank to sell the U.S. currency, pushing it down by around 30 cents to S$1.8475. This sparked fears that the bank may have been acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 "It's hard to say (if it was intervention)," a European bank dealer said. "That local bank may have just been selling to take profit, but it's natural for the market to think this could be intervention. It can't be confirmed," he added. 

 The U.S. dollar has since pulled back further and was quoted at S$1.8467 around 0508 GMT (00:08 a.m. EST). Dealers said the U.S. dollar was unlikely to retest S$1.8500 locally again Wednesday, as market participants are wary of intervention. 

 According to a JPMorgan Chase research report, a combination of superficially weak industrial production numbers, and the recent liberalization of Singapore dollar lending rules by the central bank "encouraged a bout of unwinding of short U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar positions, primarily by international investors." 

 Data issued Tuesday showed that industrial production fell 11.3% year-on-year, compared with a 4.3% increase in January, although this was due mainly to a seasonal effect of having fewer working days in the month because of holidays. 

 JPMorgan currency strategist James Malcolm said suspected selling of U.S. dollars on behalf of the central bank suggests the MAS is reluctant to allow the local dollar to slide into the weak range of its undisclosed currency policy band. 

 "This makes sense as officials are likely to want some flexibility in its policy management regime should dollar/sing spike higher on any dollar/yen near-term rally," he said. 

 Looking ahead, JPMorgan said improving domestic economic fundamentals are likely to continue supporting the local currency. 

 Malcolm recommends selling U.S. dollars as he expects the currency to retreat to S$1.7900 by the end of September and S$1.7800 by the end of the year.

title: Emerging  FX  - Asian  forex  recover, Sing dollar lags.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 27 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies

 regained their composure late on Wednesday as the dollar backed 

 off against the yen. 

     Once again, the Singapore dollar lagged behind the other 

 regional currencies, though it managed to escape its day's low 

 point of 1.8510 to the dollar. 

     Claudio Piron, head of foreign exchange strategy at 

 Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said the Sing dollar also 

 coincidentally had the strongest correlation with the yen in 

 recent months. 

 On a three-month average, the Sing dollar has mimicked the 

 yen's movements 68 percent of the time compared with 63 percent 

 for the Thai baht, 43 percent for the Taiwan dollar and 33 

 percent for the Korean won, Piron said. 

 "There are three reasons for this, Singapore is a very open 

 economy. It's the most liquid market in the region. And it's 

 got deeper capital markets compared with the rest of the 

 region, and is a more 'freely-floating' currency

 notwithstanding the policy bands," he said, referring to the 

central bank's band in which the trade-weighted Singapore 

 dollar is allowed to trade. 

 Given that correlation, the Sing dollar has a rocky ride 

 ahead. The yen was expected to put up a fight later in the day 

 because of last minute yen orders ahead of fiscal year-end, but 

 the dollar was still holding its own even after a Federal 

 Reserve official called it a little overvalued.

 triggered.

 recent strong surge. 

 Analysts said a dollar/Sing at 1.8510 brought the

 secure debt rescheduling agreements during crucial talks with

 exporters and a steadier yen.

title: Emerging  FX  - Recovering yen helps, rupiah shines.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 26 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies took 

 advantage of the yen's bounce back late on Tuesday, with the 

 Indonesian rupiah standing out among regional currencies. 

     The Singapore dollar proved to be the laggard, suffering 

 from stop-loss dollar buying when key levels were triggered 

 during the course of the day. 

     The rupiah climbed to five-month highs of around 9,585, 

 aided by a sheer lack of dollar demand in the market as well as 

 slightly improving sentiment towards the currency as Jakarta 

 tries to tackle its many political and economic woes. 

 But dealers in Jakarta said the rupiah's comeuppance was 

 around the corner simply because local corporates need to buy 

 dollars to service foreign debt. 

 "This rally is very overdone. I think the genuine demand 

 (for the dollar) will be back and hit the rupiah," said a 

 foreign bank dealer in Jakarta. 

     Elsewhere, the yen's bounce aided some of the regional 

currencies such as the Thai baht, Korean won and Taiwan dollar. 

     However, analysts were skeptical that the yen could extend 

 its gains given the poor state of the Japanese economy and the 

 widely accepted view that the country may experience outflows 

 at the end of the month when the fiscal year finishes. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah rose to new five-month highs of 9,585, 

 continuing its recent steady progress. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said local corporates have just been 

 absent from the market, and that's helped the rupiah as they 

 are usually seeking dollars to meet debt obligations. 

 Some said the market was also buoyed by hopes for more 

 inflows into local markets, with the government expected to 

 secure debt rescheduling agreements during crucial talks with 

 the Paris Club next month. 

 However, charts showed the dollar/rupiah was very oversold 

 with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 26.658. This 

 could trigger a huge correction in the rupiah, especially if 

 the corporates return to the market to buy dollars. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar slipped through 1.8400 to hit lows not 

 seen since January amid talk it would be dragged along with the 

 yen to weaker levels after the Japanese fiscal year ends. 

 Dealers said stop-loss Sing dollar sales hit around 1.8427 

 sent it to a low of 1.8445, a level last seen on January 11 

 when it touched low of 1.8455. 

 But profit-taking on the dollar's sharp rise with offers 

 lined up beyond 1.8438 capped the Sing dollar's losses, helping 

 it bounce back to levels around 1.8425. 

 Market talk of the yen settling into a weaker 133-135 range 

 and recent data showing Singapore's economy still under 

 deflationary pressure encouraged players to sell the Sing

     The February consumer price index fell 0.6 percent on the 

 year but was up 0.3 percent from January. 

     There was little response to February manufacturing output 

 data, issued Tuesday, showing a drop of 11.3 percent on the 

 year versus January's 4.3 percent rise. The fall was mainly 

 attributed to plant closures for the Lunar New Year holidays. 

 Meanhwile, charts show the dollar overbought against the 

 Sing dollar with a 14-day relative strength index reading at 

 79.3, suggesting room for more profit-taking on the dollar's 

 gains.

 The Taiwan dollar stayed on the wrong side of 35 within a

title: Emerging  FX -Yen slide hurts north Asia  fx , not peso, baht.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 26 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies fell 

 early on Tuesday, succumbing to the yen's negative influence. 

     However, there was a difference in the extent of their 

 losses in relation to the yen, with some faithfully following 

 the Japanese unit and others dragged along reluctantly. 

     North Asian currencies and the Singapore dollar continued 

 to tag after the yen, which sagged on the market's assumption 

 of outflows from the economically frail Japan once the fiscal 

 year draws to a close this month. 

     In contrast, the peso and baht kept their yen-related 

 losses modest while the rupiah forged its own way higher. 

     The dollar hit a high of 133.46 yen before backing off to 

 trade around 133.06 yen on profit-taking. 

     Some said the yen could see more of a correction after 

 recent heavy gains. However, the dollar/yen's upward trend was 

 still intact. 

     Analysts said the mixed response of Asian currencies

 reflected the Japanese currency's diminishing importance in the 

 region, barring a complete, and highly unlikely, meltdown of 

 the yen. 

 "What happens to the US economy and to the Chinese renminbi 

 are even more important for the rest of Asia than what happens 

 to the yen," Standard Chartered Bank said in a research note, 

 adding the United States was Asia's biggest customer and China 

 its biggest competitor. 

     "Asia can cope with a slightly weaker yen if the US is 

 strong and the Chinese do not devalue," it said. 

     Ahead for the market was Singapore manufacturing data for 

 February, due around 0445 GMT. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won fell past a two-month low of 1,331.5 to the dollar,



and was trading around 1,333.3 -- a level last seen on January



24.



    While the weaker yen had some hand in driving the won



lower, a sell-off of local equities by foreign investors



masterminded the won's fall. Foreign investors dumped 222



billion won worth of stocks on Monday, a third day of net



selling.



    Net sales of Korean shares by foreign investors has



totalled 390 billion won in the past three days.



    Nevertheless Korea continued to see increasing signs of an



improving economy. Finance Minister Jin Nyum said earlier in



the day Moody's Investors Service was expected to raise the



country's sovereign rating by two notches to "A" by February



2003.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar was slightly down but was expected to



stay within its recent range around the level of 35 to the



dollar thanks to equity-related inflows and month-end dollar



sales by exporters.



    Dealers in Singapore said a softer yen and wariness over


central bank intervention was likely to keep its upside capped.



    The central bank had been active on both sides of the



market in recent sessions keeping the Taiwan dollar within a



narrow 34.95-35.05 range, dealers said.



    Foreign investors were net buyers of T$4.02 billion worth



of local stocks on Monday, taking their net buying over the



past five sessions to T$11.85 billion.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht edged down to around 43.44 to the dollar, compared



with late Monday's 43.38 on dollar demand from local corporates



and importers.



    Dealers in Singapore said despite a weaker yen players were



reluctant to pull the baht too low after some U.S. names were



spotted selling dollars around 43.45-43.50 range.



    They said some equity-related inflows were also supporting



the baht.



    Offshore players had been selling dollars since last Friday



when the central bank said it would keep its benchmark rates



higher than those of the United States.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar was down as speculators bought



dollars, betting the local currency would be dragged down with



the yen into a weaker range.



    Dealers said talk that the yen was heading for 133-135



range indicated the Sing dollar may have more downside. And



given recent inflation numbers, there was little hope the



authorities would resist a softer exchange rate.



Singapore manages its exchange rate against a basket of



trade-weighted currencies with the yen believed to be a



significant component.



The consumer price index fell 0.6 percent in February



against the same month a year earlier and was up 0.3 percent



versus January. Analysts said that indicated recent signals of



some life in the recession-hit economy were not strong enough.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah continued to gain thanks to optimism over



returning capital inflows ahead of a key Paris Club creditors



meeting next month.



The currency was around five-month highs, and dealers in



Jakarta said it could test the psychologically key level of



9,500 to the dollar - last seen on September 25.



Finance Minister Boedino told Reuters on Monday Indonesia



would seek to reschedule less than $5.5 billion in debt against



expectations of some $6 billion. That comment helped boost



sentiment towards the rupiah.



Despite the optimism over Jakarta's debt rescheduling and



its attempts to tackle graft, the government's handling of the



economy was still seen as shambolic.



The finance ministry and the central bank said on Monday



they were in dispute over the servicing of some $15 billion in



bonds, casting doubt on budget deficit figures for 2001 and



beyond.



The central bank governor was recently sentenced to three



years of jail for graft, but remains free and is still in



control of the bank.

The peso opened a touch softer and dealers in Manila saw

track movements in the dollar/yen, they said.

ahead of the long weekend.



Manila police have ordered tight security around churches

Monday. Eight such devices were found last week.

title: Emerging  FX  - Asian  currencies  ease with yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 25 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 easier late Monday as the yen slipped to fresh multi-week lows. 


    The yen        slipped through 133 per dollar amid talk



Japanese investors had started to send funds abroad ahead of



the new fiscal year starting on April 1.



    The Indonesian rupiah again managed to buck the trend,



hitting fresh five-month highs around 9,700, as Jakarta



expressed optimism over rescheduling $5.5 billion of its

Some equity-related inflows and month-end dollar sales by



exporters helped cap the downside for the Taiwan dollar and



Philippine peso but the won fell to two-month lows on fears of



outflows as foreign investors continued to sell Korean stocks.



After Wall Street's disappointing performance on Friday on



worries over corporate earnings, markets would be looking at



February durable goods and existing home sales data due later



in the day for confirmation that the U.S. recovery was on



course.



    Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was also due to



speak before a reception in Washington at 2200 GMT.

dollar, buoyed by investment-related dollar inflows and



optimism over Jakarta's upcoming Paris Club meeting.



   Dealers said the rupiah hit its highest levels since October



with dollar sales spotted from local players, including the

Boediono said creditor nations would agree to reschedule $5.5

The first payment by U.S. investment house Farallon for a

    TAIWAN DOLLAR

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; HKD Dlr Wet Blanket On Mkt
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Friday, after largely relinquishing their earlier gains as renewed jitters over the Hong Kong dollar's fate overwhelmed the support from a strong Japanese yen and growing optimism of a U.S.-led economic recovery, dealers said. 

 Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's markedly more upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy Thursday, compared with his comments made just last week, failed to sustain the recent upward momentum in Asian currencies. 

 "You would expect good sentiment on global reflation because of Greenspan's speech last night and the strength of the yen to help Asian currencies," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Instead, anxieties about the Hong Kong dollar peg and the unwinding of short yen positions against Asian currencies tossed a wet blanket on the market, he added. 

 The risk premium on holding one-year Hong Kong dollar forward shot up to 225-270 to the spot rate, compared with 160-170 late Thursday. 

 Dealers blamed the rise in Hong Kong dollar forward premiums to a report issued recently by U.S.-based consultancy Medley Global Advisors, questioning the future of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. currency. 

 The report stoked nervousness about a depegging of the Hong Kong dollar, in turn re-igniting fears of a competitive devaluation in Asia. Analysts, however, said that such prospects didn't appear imminent. 

 "The U.S. dollar was more biddish against Asian currencies because of the Hong Kong dollar peg rumor," said a senior dealer at a European bank. "Everybody just jumped onto the bandwagon; nobody wanted to be caught short in dollar/Asians." 

 The Singapore dollar retreated past the key S$1.8200 level against the U.S. currency, from its intraday high of S$1.8170. 

 Late Friday, the Singapore dollar was slightly weaker at S$1.8213, compared with S$1.8208 late Thursday. 

 The yen's continued rally overnight had propelled the Singapore dollar to as high as S$1.8135. 

 After posting its biggest single-day gain against the dollar in three-and-a-half years Thursday, the dollar was quoted at Y127.72 at 0920 GMT Friday, above Y126.99 in New York but well below Y129.91 in Tokyo late Thursday. 

 The yen has appreciated over 5.5% against the dollar the first four days of this week, climbing by 3.4% Thursday alone. 

 Recent U.S.-dollar purchases by a large Singapore bank left the market wondering if it was intervening on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore to keep the strength of the local currency in check. 

 But Jimmy Koh, the head of treasury research at Singapore's UOB Group, said such fears were "unwarranted." 

 Based on the bank's in-house model of the MAS' policy band, the upside limit on the Singapore dollar "could stretch to S$1.8040" based on the current levels of the yen and other Asian currencies, Koh said. 

 He said that with the yen in stronger territory, the Singapore dollar will likely trade between S$1.8100 and S$1.8300 for now. The U.S. dollar's rise to S$1.8250-S$1.8300 will provide opportunities for participants to get out of their long positions in the U.S. currency, he added. 

 The South Korean won ended barely changed against the U.S. dollar, but weaker against its Japanese counterpart - which continued to outperform the rest of the region's currencies. 

 Late dollar purchases by offshore participants and importers in South Korea pared the won's earlier gains, dealers said. 

 Expectations of increased dollar demand from foreign investors, who dumped some KRW230 billion worth of South Korean shares Friday, also contributed to the won's pullback against the dollar, Mohi-uddin at UBS Warburg said. 

 He added that foreign investors were selling shares of South Korean and Taiwanese companies, and shifting their funds into the Tokyo stock market, which has recently been rallying. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,314.3, steady compared with KRW1,314.5 Thursday. The dollar hit an intraday low of KRW1,306.5 Friday. 

 The yen was quoted around KRW10.29, higher than KRW10.17 late Thursday. 

 Propped up by the yen, the New Taiwan dollar finished at a two-month closing high against the U.S. currency. 

 Taiwan's central bank continued to intervene to keep a rein on the local currency's appreciation, buying an estimated US$250 million to US$300 million in the market, dealers in Taipei said. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.947, down from NT$34.989 Thursday. The U.S. dollar hit an intraday low of NT34.886. Dealings were valued at US$634 million. 

 The Thai currency was marginally stronger at 43.250 baht to the dollar, compared with THB43.275 late Thursday, but was off its new one-year high of THB43.110 reached early Friday. 

 Despite the baht's recent appreciation, Central Bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Friday the local currency "is not too strong," and that the current level is still competitive for the country's exports. 

 He said the central bank continues to monitor the baht's performance, but didn't make it clear if it had bought dollars in the market recently - as suspected by foreign exchange dealers. 

 The central banker's comments failed to push the baht higher. Instead, the baht retreated on worries about the future of the Hong Kong dollar peg, dealers said. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar ended at 50.97 pesos, relatively steady compared with PHP50.99 Thursday. The dollar opened at its intraday low of PHP50.90, but spiked toward PHP51 toward the close. 

 The Indonesian rupiah retreated to IDR10,035 against the dollar, compared with IDR9,945 late Thursday, as local corporations snapped up the U.S. currency following its slide to a fresh five-month low of IDR9,890 earlier in the day. 

 -By Netty Ismail, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4043; netty.ismail@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late On Yen; But Yen Vigor Unrivaled
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were stronger late Thursday, as the dollar took a drubbing in international foreign exchange markets, particularly against the yen. 

 The yen vaulted through the psychologically important Y130 threshold against the dollar to trade at two-and-a-half month highs, after dollar sales by foreign investors triggered a slew of stop-loss orders. 

 At 0900 GMT (4:00 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y129.32, below Y130.77 late Wednesday in New York. The dollar had shed more than a full yen during the overnight session. 

 The yen also chalked up gains against its other Asian counterparts, as the Japanese currency's vigor was unrivaled. 

 "During periods when the yen strengthens sharply against the dollar, one tends to expect the strengthening of Asian currencies to the dollar to lag," said David Simmonds, a regional currency strategist at Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank. 

 With the market having largely priced in expectations of an economic recovery in Asia, excluding Japan, later in the year, participants who had gone long Asian currencies against the yen in the last few months were now unwinding those positions; at the same time that they unloaded their short yen positions against the dollar. 

 "Markets have taken on board a strategy this year that Asian fundamentals are stronger than Japan's," Simmonds said, adding that this had led participants to build long positions in Asian currencies against the yen. 

 "The whole world has seen this theme and played this theme out for a long time," Simmonds said. "It's time for the market to shake out their positions." 

 The yen's strength was evident in the yen/won. 

 The yen rose to 10.17 won, from around KRW9.9 just two days ago, even as the South Korean currency strengthened against the dollar Thursday. 

 Still, given South Korea's more promising economic fundamentals vis-a-vis Japan's, Simmonds said he "would look to reestablish won-longs against the yen" at current levels. 

 Against the dollar, the won closed at KRW1,314.5, slightly stronger compared with KRW1,316.3 Wednesday. 

 The won was, however, off its intraday high of KRW1,309.0, as dollar demand from oil companies and short-covering in the U.S. currency by banks emerged, dealers said. 

 The market shrugged off the Bank of Korea's as-expected decision Thursday to keep its call rate target unchanged at 4% in March, as the economy shows signs of accelerated growth and inflationary pressures remain benign. The overnight call rate target has been maintained at 4% since late last year. 

 Late in the day, as the dollar collapsed below the key Y129 level, several Asian currencies extended their gains. At 0940 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y128.95. 

 As Asian currencies continue to receive a boost from the yen's gains and capital inflows in the region, some of the central banks - particularly in Taiwan, Singapore and Thailand - could become concerned over any excessive appreciation in their currencies. Since the anticipated economic recovery in the region has yet to take hold, it would be too early for the monetary authorities to allow their currencies to strengthen too much. 

 The yen lifted the New Taiwan dollar to a five-week closing high against the U.S. currency Thursday, although Taiwan's central bank had bought an estimated US$300 million in the last few minutes of trading to curb the appreciation of the local currency, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.989, down from NT$35.030 Wednesday. Dealings were valued at US$983 million, higher than US$602 million Wednesday. A dealer in Taipei said the central bank accounted for around half of Thursday's turnover. 

 As the baht climbed to a one-year high, the Thai central bank continued with its recent dollar-purchases to check its strength, although not aggressively, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at 43.275 baht, lower than THB43.515 late Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar was at S$1.8208 against its U.S. counterpart, stronger compared with S$1.8263. 

 With the Singapore dollar currently trading near the stronger end of the central bank's policy band, there's been ongoing jitters about intervention, dealers said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore guides the Singapore dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the city state's major trading partners and key competitors. In January, the MAS restored a tighter policy band. 

 "I don't expect the foreign exchange policy to change," said Simmonds at Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank. "The MAS wouldn't want to see the trade-weighted currency to trade through the strong end of the policy band." 

 Inspired by its regional peers, the Philippine peso cracked above the psychologically important PHP51.00 resistance level against the dollar for the first time in two-and-a-half months. 

 The dollar ended at PHP50.99, lower than PHP51.09 Wednesday. 

 The Indonesian currency was slightly firmer at 9,945 rupiah to the dollar, compared with IDR9,950 late Wednesday.
