title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late On Equity Inflows, Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Continuing foreign equity inflows into local stock markets and the yen's gains bolstered most Asian currencies late Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah's new found strength provided additional support to its Southeast Asian peers, although fears of intervention by the central banks in Singapore and Thailand stymied their currencies' rise. 

 The rupiah extended its climb toward IDR9,900 resistance, as interbank participants continued to sell U.S. dollars in anticipation of inflows from the Indonesian government's impending sale of its 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia, observers said. 

 The rupiah, trading at near five-month highs, hit an intraday high of IDR9,915 before retreating to around IDR9,950 late Wednesday. The rupiah was weaker at IDR9,980 late Tuesday. 

 Improving prospects for the privatization of state-held assets in Indonesia - which would underscore the government's commitment to economic reforms - helped thrust the rupiah through the psychologically important IDR10,000 threshold Tuesday. 

 "With corporate bids for debt repayment still much on the sidelines, the rupiah looks well positioned to test IDR9,800," Bank of America said in a research report. 

 The Thai currency strengthened to an intraday high of 43.490 baht to the dollar, thanks to strong foreign equity inflows and dollar sales by U.S. funds - as they simultaneously unloaded their dollar positions against the yen, dealers said. 

 But the baht subsequently pulled back past the THB43.500 level on market suspicions that the Thai central bank had bought dollars via two of its agent banks based in Singapore to check the baht's advance, market observers said. 

 In an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of Thailand's exports, the Thai central bank had been buying dollars in the last few days when the currency traded at THB43.55-THB43.60, said a dealer at a Thai bank. 

 "It's still in their practice to protect their exporters," he added. 

 At 0915 GMT (4:15 a.m. EST), the dollar was at THB43.515, lower than THB43.665 late Tuesday. 

 Against the Japanese currency, the dollar was quoted at Y131.84, below Y132.13 in New York and Y132.53 in Tokyo late Tuesday. 

 Market speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to check the strength of the local currency Wednesday provided a floor for the U.S. dollar around S$1.8250, observers said. 

 The U.S. dollar slid to an overnight low of S$1.8222 on long-liquidation, but subsequently bounced back on suspected intervention by the MAS, some dealers said. 

 A large Singapore bank bought a "significant amount" of U.S. dollars around S$1.8260 during the Asian session Wednesday, moderating the upward pressure on the Singapore currency despite the firmer yen and local stock market gains, said a dealer at a European bank. 

 Although some dealers said the Singapore bank was buying U.S. dollars on behalf of its corporate clients, jitters about central bankintervention led some to speculate that the Singapore bank was acting at the behest of the central bank. 

 The South Korean won closed at KRW1,316.3 against the dollar, little changed compared with KRW1,316.4 Tuesday. 

 The won strengthened to an intraday high of KRW1,313.7 earlier, before retreating as foreign investors turned net sellers of South Korean shares and onshore demand for dollars emerged when the U.S. currency traded below KRW1,315 support, said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 State-run banks, like Korea Development Bank, or KDB, were snapping up dollars on behalf of corporations and oil importers, said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 Some market participants also believe that South Korea's central bank had intervened through KDB, he added. 

 Expectations that the yen will remain rangebound - as foreign exchange participants attempt to defend their currency options positions - also limited the won's upside, said Mohi-uddin. 

 Market participants this week established "double no-touch options with barriers at Y131.50 and Y135.50," the strategist said, adding that these players will protect these levels to ensure that the options won't be exercised. 

 "External factors are not that bullish for the won," said Mohi-uddin. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed stronger on foreign equity inflows, but was off its intraday high as the central bank intervened to curb the local currency's appreciation, dealers said. 

 A Taipei-based dealer estimated that the central bank accounted for about half of Wednesday's turnover. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.030, slightly lower than NT$35.069 Tuesday. The New Taiwan dollar hit an intraday high of NT$34.995 Wednesday. 

 Trading volume was US$602 million, higher than US$458 million Tuesday. 


Buoyed by its regional counterparts, the Philippine peso closed at

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, But Off Overnight High; Tracks Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was higher against its U.S. counterpart late Wednesday, tracking a stronger yen, but was off its overnight high when local banks bought U.S. dollars on behalf of corporate clients, dealers said. 

 At 0845 GMT (3:45 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8263, down from S$1.8287 late Tuesday in Asia, but off its overnight low of S$1.8220 in New York. It traded between S$1.8250 and S$1.8285 in Asia Wednesday. 

 Dealers said liquidation of long U.S. dollar positions pushed the U.S. currency to a low of S$1.8220 the U.S. But it bounced off that level amid possible mild intervention on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore during New York time, said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The U.S. dollar opened higher in Asia Wednesday and rose steadily to an intraday high of S$1.8285 as local banks bought the currency on behalf of corporate clients. 

 However, U.S. banks and investment houses sold it back down after the U.S. dollar fell below Y132 in the afternoon, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar could edge lower overnight, especially if it loses more ground to the yen, dealers said. It is expected to find support at S$1.8220, then S$1.8200, with resistance expected at S$1.8300. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mixed late Wednesday after some bonds recovered from their early morning weakness, which had been due to an overnight fall in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said. 

 After the recent fall in prices, particularly in longer-term bonds, some investors were unable to resist picking up bargains, dealers added. 

 "The local market seemed to defy the U.S. Treasurys market. Our market proved to be quite resilient. Not only did they recover in the afternoon, but some even closed higher," a local bank dealer said. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was flat at 1.66% while the yield on five-year bonds was down two basis points at 3.08%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds slipped one basis point to 3.57% while the yield on 10-year bonds slipped one basis point to 3.80%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was flat at 4.24%.

title: Emerging  FX  - Higher, but rangebound.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 firm on Tuesday, but stuck in their recent ranges as the 

 dollar/yen dithered. 

     Given the economic events slated for this week, trading in 

 the dollar/yen kept to the safe side. Players idled on the 

 sidelines as they waited for the Japanese government to 

 announce its deflation-fighting package on Wednesday. 

     U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is also due to 

 appear before Congress for his biannual testimony on Wednesday. 

     On Thursday, the Bank of Japan's monetary board is due to 

 meet. 

     With the dollar/yen acting docile, regional currencies have 

 been in somewhat of a bind in terms of finding a new direction. 

     "We still like the regionals versus the yen ... but other 

 than that, everyone is still waiting for the dollar/yen to 

 move," a senior dealer at a European bank in Hong Kong said. 

     Players were trying to dig for cues on the local front, but 

 even there, they were coming up short. Equity-related flows 

 have influenced the direction of the regional currencies, but 

 not enough to push them out of their recent ranges. 

     As for data, Taiwan was set to issue its January M2 money 

 supply data. 

     Bangkok markets were closed for a one-day public holiday. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won slipped amid continued nervousness over further



possible equity sales by foreign investors.



    Foreign investors have been steadily selling local equities



for the past seven sessions. However, players were hopeful that



Wall Street's overnight gains and an early rise in the Korean



Composite Stock Price Index could reverse that trend.



Still, Singapore and Hong Kong dealers said there was also



some corporate demand that could keep the won on the backfoot.



They added there had been talk in the market that the



authorities were expressing more concerns over export



competitiveness at private meetings with banks, making players



wary about pushing the won higher.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar stuck around the higher end of its



recent range, close to the 1.83 level.



Since February 19, the Sing dollar has traded in a



relatively narrow range of 1.8250-1.8340 largely due to the



lack of interest and flows.



They added unless the dollar/yen breaks out of its current



range of 133-134, it was unlikely that the dollar/Sing was



going to make any radical moves.



THAI BAHT



Trading activity is subdued as offshore players were



reluctant to take fresh positions aggressively in the absence



of the onshore market.



    Thai financial markets are closed for a religious holiday



and will reopen on Wednesday.



    The baht was stuck in a tight 43.79-43.81 in early trade.



In the forward market, baht funding costs were mostly steady,



with the one-month rate quoted at 6/7 satang per dollar and the



tom/next rate at 0.04/0.09 satang.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah was held slightly down from late Monday levels



of 10,165 amid reluctance by interbank players to take fresh



positions on wariness over possible central bank dollar-selling


intervention to prop up the currency.



Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was spotted



checking rates in the currency market on Monday and some



dealers suspected dollar sales by state banks was on behalf of



the authorities.



Focus in the market is on the sale of the Bank Central



Asia, which has recently hit snags after some of the investors



bidding for the country's largest retail bank threatened to



pull out citing political reasons and a lack of transparency.



One foreign and several local companies separately have



said they were considering to pull out of the respective



consortium they were part of. In all four consortia are in the



race for up to 51 percent stake in the BCA.



Analysts say Jakarta's failure to to sell the bank would



hit foreign investor sentiment and the rupiah further worsening



the economic problems of the troubled country.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar rose slightly, taking heart in the



overnight gains on Wall Street, which lifted local stocks in



early trading.



As with Korea, Taiwan's bourse has been suffering from net



sales from foreign investors, which has worried the currency.



However, the market was hoping that the bourse's early gains



could mean that foreign investors become net buyers of local



stocks again.



Overall, the Taiwan dollar was not expected to move far



above or below the 35 level until there are clear signals as to



where the recession-hit economy was headed. Indeed, the market



was keeping its eye on key economic data due on Wednesday that



include January industrial production and export orders.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso market opened slightly firmer at 51.330 against



51.368 on Friday. The market is listless as players were still



reeling from a holiday on Monday, with no transaction done



until 0128 GMT.



Dealers expect the currency to move in a recent 51.30-51.40



as dollar demand for NDF settlements is offset by gains in the



regionals.



Apart from seasonal dollar demand for NDFs and hedging



purposes, dealers said the peso should be underpinned by



improved sentiment.



Analysts remain fairly positive on the ability of the



government to stay close to its fiscal targets. They also see



U.S. involvement as a net positive in maintaining political



stability.

title: Emerging  FX  - Dragged lower by yen, rupiah shines.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 19 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were on 

 the defensive late on Tuesday because of the stumbling yen. 

     After U.S. President George W. Bush left Japan for Korea, 

 the market threw aside its recent decorum, punishing the yen 

 for the Japanese government's failure to come up with fresh 

 ways to tackle its many economic problems. 

 Only the Indonesian rupiah defied the regional downward 

 trend, climbing some 0.20 percent higher thanks to the trickle 

 of equity-related dollar inflows from foreign funds. 

 Otherwise, regional currencies felt the gravitational pull 

 of the yen's fall past 133. But, as has been the trend since 

 late last year when the yen started on its decline to 

 three-year lows, losses in the regional currencies were modest. 

 The Thai baht did have to suffer through a bit of verbal 

intervention from the central bank, which said it would not let 

 the rate hurt exports. 

 "The market is really seeing this as a dollar/yen move. So 

 if the dollar/yen moves higher, why play it in the dollar/Sing 

 (dollar) or the dollar/baht? Just play it in the dollar/yen," 

 said the senior dealer at a local bank in Singapore. 

 Analysts have already taken note of this phenomenon, saying 

 the yen, and in turn, Japan, no longer casts such a long shadow 

 over the region, especially as many countries here are expected 

 to benefit from the long-awaited U.S. economic recovery. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The Indonesian rupiah rose above the 10,200 level helped by 

 equity-related inflows and as some major corporates sold 

 dollars for their seasonal needs. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said given the small size and the 

 illiquid nature of the currency market, the rupiah rose even 

 though some state banks were spotted buying dollars which 

 sparked rumours the central bank was in the market to beef up 

 its reserves. 

 Analysts said dollar/rupiah's failure to convincingly 

 breach the 10,250 level in the past several sessions would 

 further prompt interbank dealers to trim their dollar longs. 

 They said a test of the 10,000 level was possible in coming 

 days on the back of foreign inflows into the local stocks 

 market that has risen by about 19 percent year-to-date. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar followed the yen lower, flirting with 

 the 1.83 level on U.S. dollar short covering and U.S. dollar 

 demand from funds. 

     But greenback offers from a U.S. name near 1.83 helped the 

 local currency pare losses. 

     There had been talk earlier that the central bank might 

 have bought the U.S. dollar after one local bank was seen 

 bidding actively. 

     But some dealers dismissed such rumours, saying they saw no 

 need for the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene. 

     "We don't think this is due to the MAS as SGD is currently 

 trading well within its bands against its trade-weighted 

 basket," said a UBS Warburg report. 

     "Instead, we expect players may be manipulating the market 

 at present to squeeze USD shorts and so we remain wary of a 

 pull back toward 1.8330," the report said. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht gave up most of the gains it made in the past few



sessions after the central bank's verbal intervention prompted



some players to cover short dollar positions.



    Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on



Tuesday the baht was stable and the bank would not let it hurt



exports. The market took the remark to mean the central bank


would keep the baht soft to promote exports which is the



country's major growth engine.



"Moreover, some foreign banks bought back the U.S. dollar



because they believed the baht's recent appreciation was



overdone and that recent equity inflows might taper off soon,"



said a dealer at a European bank in Thailand.



Charts show the baht finally breaks out of its uptrend



channel dating back to January 23. However, a Fibonacci study



indicates 43.80 remains good support for the baht for now.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped in line with the regional currencies,



though it recovered from its day's lows of 51.33.



Dealers in Manila said the currency was slightly upset by



trade data that was issued earlier in the day. The National



Statistics Office said the trade surplus fell 61.1 percent in



2001 to $2.6 billion.



However, the data did reveal a bit of good news. Imports



fell in December 2001 on a year-on-year basis, but rose 5.1



percent month-on-month to $2.143 billion.



Moreover, sentiment towards the peso remained chipper, with



players hoping for more foreign funds inflows into the local



stock market as well as stronger economic growth this year.



KOREAN WON -2



The won was weighed down to around 1,321 from late Monday's



1,316 level by fresh losses in the local stock market which



raised the spectre of equity-related outflows.



Foreign investors were net sellers, for the third



consecutive day, of local stocks worth 48 billion won on



Tuesday.



Dealers said tapering off of foreign inflows in the stock



market had caught several interbank and offshore players short



of dollars. And covering of those positions could push the



dollar/won towards 1,325-1,330 range in coming days.



Those concerns overshadowed data showing consumer outlook



improved in January for the fourth consecutive month. The



consumer confidence index rose to 106.7 from 100.9 in December,



indicating higher household spending in the next six months.



    However, some export-related dollar sales helped the won on



the downside.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar ended the day lower on the weaker yen.



    Dealers in Singapore said some local corporates were



spotted offering dollars, though most in the market were



fretting over the yen's weakened state. Moreover, the local



dollar was hurt by net foreign investors' sales of some T$897



million in stocks.



They said Taiwan's very rich and very powerful central bank


was not seen in the market. The bank often intervenes on both



sides of the market to keep the rate stable, now especially



important as the island's economy struggles to get back on its



feet after being hit by its worst recession ever.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen weighs, U.S.-Japan summit disappoints.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies tracked the 

 yen lower in early trade on Tuesday as the market was 

 disappointed that no concrete steps were unveiled at the 

 meeting between President George W. Bush and Japanese Prime 

 Minister Junichiro Koizumi. 

     Trading is likely to be subdued, with financial markets in 

 the United States closed on Monday for a public holiday. 

     The yen, followed closely by most emerging Asian 

currencies, fell below the 133 level. Analysts expect the 

currency to move in a 130-135 range in the near term, and there 

 will be a search for official remark on any approach to these 

 extremes. 

 "The Bush-Koizumi meeting in a way is yen negative because 

 they did not say what the market had wanted to hear. That 

 should weigh on emerging Asian currencies as well, although the 

 downside is likely to be limited by recent capital inflows," 

 said a trader at a European bank. 

 On the data front, South Korea will publish its January 

 consumer outlook at 0300 GMT, and the Philippines will release 

 its trade balance data for December later in the day. 

     Taiwan will release fourth quarter current account balance 

 on Wednesday, and trade data on Thursday. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Sing dollar was easier on the back of U.S. dollar short



covering. There was talk of possible U.S. dollar buying on



Monday after one local bank was seen bidding aggressively.



    But some dealers dismissed such rumours, saying they saw no



need for the Monetary Authority of Singapore -- the city



state's de facto central bank -- to intervene at this point.



    "We don't think this is due to the MAS as the SGD is



currently trading well within its bands against its trade-



weighted basket," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist



at UBS Warburg, in his report.



"Instead, we expect players may be manipulating the market



at present to squeeze USD shorts and so we remain way of a pull



back towards 1.8330," he said.



Another dealer said the Sing dollar weakness was also



linked to demand for the U.S. dollar by funds and some



corporate players to invest in equities abroad.



KOREAN WON -2



The won succumbed to the downward pressure of the weaker



yen, with falls on the local stock market also depressing its



mood.



Overall, though, trading was subdued amid a dearth of fresh



leads. Analysts have noted that the onshore market may be long



on won, which meant there could be further downside for the


currency.



U.S. President George Bush arrives in Seoul late on Tuesday



from Japan for a visit, and is due to meet Korean President Kim



Dae-jung on Wednesday. The talks between the two leaders are



likely to centre on North Korea, which Bush dubbed as one of



the countries in an "axis of evil" along with Iraq and Iran.



    Washington's rhetoric was seen as undermining Seoul's



"sunshine policy" of rapprochement with the North.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht retreated below the 43.60 per dollar level to



reflect the yen's weakness as exporters held back on selling



the U.S. dollar.



    Dealers expect the baht to continue to be underpinned by



equity inflows. The semi-state run Thailand Opportunity Fund



said on Monday it planned to start investing an initial 3.6



billion baht in Thai stocks from this week.



The move is likely to attract more foreign investors into



the market where a number of blue chip stocks are still



considered cheap, they said.



    Charts show the baht is well-supported at 43.80 which



represents the dollar/baht's January 23-February 15 downmove.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah held steady within its recent range supported by



equity-related inflows and trimming of long dollar positions by



interbank players.



    Capping the upside for the rupiah were local corporates



buying dollars at around 10,200 level for import and debt



payment needs.



    Bank Indonesia said on Monday out of a total of $133



billion, the maturing foreign debt would total some $20 billion



in first-half 2002, adding pressure on the fragile rupiah, but



outstanding debt would continue to shrink in the coming years.



However, dealers said market sentiment has improved amid



growing optimism over the government's privatisation programme,



with the sale of a 30 percent stake in state-run Bank Central



Asia, Indonesia's largest retail bank, expected later in the



month.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar straggled along in familiar territory,



falling slightly on the back of the weaker yen.



Daily charts showed the local currency has been trading



within a wider range since December 21, when the central bank


let go of its usually dogged intervention to keep a stable rate



and allowed the Taiwan dollar to trade below the level of 35 to



the U.S. dollar.



Since then, the currency has fluctuated between 34.88-35.20



with the central bank appearing on both sides of the market to



temper any volatility.



Analysts expected the central bank to keep up its presence



in the market, perhaps allowing the currency to weaken given



the uncertain prospects for the Taiwan economy.



Unlike its North Asian counterpart Korea, Taiwan has yet to



show any firm signs of recovery. January exports fell by 1.4



percent year-on-year, damping hopes for a rebound.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso fell slightly, bruised by the yen's fall with



foreign banks buying the dollar/peso.



Dealers in Manila said the market was also perturbed by



news that the Philippine trade surplus fell to $503 million in



December compared with $1.259 billion a year ago. The country's



full year trade surplus for 2001 was $2.6 billion versus $6.691



billion in 2000.



Still, the peso's downside was expected to be limited



because of subdued corporate dollar demand and generally upbeat



sentiment about the peso and the country's economic outlook for



this year.



Dealers added the currency was expected to trade within a



range of around 51.17-51.27, with some local oil companies



looking to pick up dollars on dips past 51.20.

title: Emerging  FX  - Tracking yen in lacklustre holiday trade.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 down with the yen early Monday, although holidays around 

 the region were expected to keep trading subdued and ranges 

 narrow. 

     Japanese financial markets were closed for Monday for a 

 local holiday while Korea, and Taiwan were shut for the Chinese 

 New Year. Most Asian markets will be closed on Tuesday and 

 Wednesday. 

     The yen was probing lows hit last week around the 135 level 

 but analysts expected rangebound trade in Asian time zone due 

 to the holiday mood and a lack of cues from the Group of Seven 

 finance leaders' meeting in Ottawa over the weekend. 

     The G7 finance ministers and central bankers sounded 

 hopeful that the global economic downturn would be short, but 

 made only the most tepid reference to currency markets. 

     Markets had speculated that the world's industrialised 

 powers could discuss the Japanese currency, which has tumbled 

 sharply to three-year lows against the dollar. 

     Japan being a major trading partner and export competitor, 

 the yen's sharp losses of more than 15 percent since last 

 September has made authorities around the region sensitive to 

 their own exchange rate competitiveness. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar edged down from its late Friday levels



around 1.8310 with the market focused on the moves in the yen



for direction.



    Dealers said activity in the market was mainly due to



pre-holiday interbank position squaring and trading interest



was minimal. A range of 1.8330-1.8350 was expected for the day.



    Singapore currency market would be closed from Tuesday to



Wednesday and will resume trade on Thursday.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah touched a seven-week high of 10,230, a level



last seen on December 24, as interbank players trimmed their



long dollar positions ahead of the Tuesday holiday.



    Dealers in Singapore said fears of central bank

intervention, after aggressive dollar purchases by state banks



last week, had prompted players to square out of their long



dollar positions.



    Stop-loss dollar sales orders triggered along the way had



also aided the rupiah, they said.



    However, some local dollar demand was spotted around



10,225-10,230 which was expected to cap the rupiah's gains for



now.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht held its ground above 44.00 in a subdued market as



players were not willing to take fresh positions ahead of Lunar



New Year holidays.



    Although Thai financial markets are open during Lunar New



Year, a number of Chinese-Thai companies will be closed.



    Dealers said the baht was underpinned by dollar offers from



offshore names in Singapore and Hong Kong, and capital inflows



from a Japanese auto maker.



    Going forward, dealers expect the baht to retain its firm



tone, with charts showing 43.70 as its near-term resistance.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso was down in line with other regional currencies


and on local commercial demand for the dollar.



    Dealers in Manila said with holidays around the region and



absence of fresh local leads, most players would prefer to stay



out of the market.



    They expected the peso to linger within a tight range



around the 51.20 level for the day.



    Although financial market in Philippines would be open



through the week, dealers said trade would remain subdued due



to holidays in the region.

 - Singapore dealers say trading in the regional currencies

     - Indeed, Southeast Asian currencies are holding up rather

title: ANALYSIS-Asia c.banks cap  forex  gains, but not for long.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 30 (Reuters) - From Seoul to Bangkok, Asian central banks are out to make sure their currencies are not pushed too high by a positive turn in the region's economic outlook. 

 With the global economy stuttering back to life, Asian policymakers are anxious that strengthening currencies do not hamper their ability to compete in reviving export markets like Europe and the United States, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 "Nobody wants to miss out when the U.S. economy starts moving again. You don't want to be uncompetitive when the global demand cycle picks up," said Simon Flint, Bank of America's senior strategist in Singapore. 

 But as soon as the dollar peaks against the yen and the global recovery becomes more entrenched, most central banks are likely to allow their currencies to reflect their fundamental strength, the analysts said. 

 "These are currencies for economies that have seen strong productivity gains, they have been gaining export market share over the last decade. They should be appreciating over time," said James Malcolm, J.P. Morgan Chase's strategist in Singapore. 

 Given the region's exposure to global demand, analysts believe Asia, more than other emerging market zones, will benefit the most from an expected rebound led by the United States - its major export destination. 

 Recent data suggests most economies may have already hit a trough, while strong flows of money into Asian equities and moderating outflows from corporate debt repayments as interest rates fall are supporting most currencies. 

 The Korean won -2 and the Thai baht have gained more than four percent from their April 2001 lows against the dollar of 1,365.30 and 45.85 respectively. The Singapore dollar is up by over one percent and the Philippine peso by over half a percent since the start of 2002. 

 CONSERVATIVE BIAS 

 Still, with the yen sickly and doubts lingering over the strength of the U.S. recovery, central banks in the region are keeping up their guard and many are intervening to keep their currencies from appreciating too far. 

 "It is a conservative bias," Malcolm said. "We are in the very early stages of recovery, its tentative, a little bit too early to have a very strong view, so that sort of a cautious bias at least on the policymaker side is likely to continue for a little while." 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Monday the central bank had entered the market to maintain the baht's export competitiveness. He said the bank bought dollars recently to help boost the country's foreign reserves. 

 Analysts believe central banks in Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, through actual or verbal interventions recently, have also shown an explicit bias to keeping currencies capped within narrow ranges. 

 "If you had currencies completely freely floating they would have been strengthening much sharply against the yen and the dollar right now. The reason why they are not is that central banks are out there picking up dollars," said Peter Redward, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank. 

 TRADE-WEIGHTED WEAKNESS 

 Flint said the performance of the yen tended to be the biggest determinant of exchange rate policy as Japan was most Asian countries' major trading partner and competitor. 

 Given a stronger overlap of North Asia's export portfolio with that of Japan, authorities in Korea and Taiwan would be more vigilant against yen weakness, he said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore in a briefing to economists last month reportedly said volatility in the yen would impact its exchange rate management policy. 

 Singapore is the closest rival to North Asia's dominance in electronics exports. 

 "The low interest rate environment in a global recovery scenario suggests that currencies will be used more to keep monetary conditions loose and strengthen the recovery and we see that policy as being positive," said Redward. 

 There are risks to such an active exchange rate policy. 

 "If you create continuous expectations of exchange rate depreciations than you can have an unsettling effect on your domestic banking system, you can cause capital flight and losses of deposits," Flint said. 

 Analysts said that was probably the reason most central banks had not forced their currencies to follow the yen in lockstep in its recent slide against the dollar. 

 Malcolm said Bank of Korea was showing signs of breaking out of the old regime of mapping every yen move, when it did not intervene to stop the yen/won cross rate slipping above 10 won. 

 "We've been breaking through that and we're going to continue to move out of that range for the rest of this year. It does signal that they don't want to keep their currency super-weak to maintain a certain level of yen/won cross," he said. 

 The won last month touched a high of 9.90 against the yen, compared to a low of 11.24 in September.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen cheers,though equity losses sting.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose a tad 

 early on Tuesday, finding some solace in the steadier yen. 

     But they were held back by steep falls on Wall Street, 

 which dampened spirits on Asian bourses. The Dow Jones 

 Industrial Average lost 2.22 percent while the 

 technology-heavy Nasdaq slipped by 2.91 percent because 

 investors were growing more jittery about corporate accounting 

 practises. 

 Analysts, however, said most Asian currencies were expected 

 to continue strengthening in the longer term because of the 

 economic recovery in the United States - the largest consumer 

 of Asian exports. 

 For now, though, dealers in Singapore said there was little 

 interest in many of the regional currencies which meant that 

 they could find themselves trapped in their recent ranges for 

 some time. Interest in trading was also falling off ahead of 

 the Lunar New Year next week. 

 "The Singapore dollar for instance has proven itself to be 

 very frustrating. Even if you have a range you can't really 

 play it because there's no liquidity. Something drastic has to 

 happen to move it," said a European bank dealer. 

 On the events calendar, the Philippines released inflation 

 data for January set to be followed later by Taiwan, while 

 Korea was expected to issue its January producer price index. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won edged up, tracking the yen's gains and as interbank 

 players sold dollars in anticipation of higher demand for the 

 won by local corporates to pay Chinese New Year bonuses to 

 their employees. 

 Dealers in Singapore said recent losses in the stock market 

 were expected to cap the won's rise above the 1,305-1,310 

 range. 

 Meanwhile, Finance Minister Jin Nyum said Korea will 

 maintain a low interest policy in the first half of this year 

 as growth in exports and investment is not fast enough to spur 

 a full-fledged recovery. 

 Jin brushed off concerns that Korea's economy may show 

 signs of overheating, saying current economic and monetary 

 policies would be kept intact in the first half. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht lingered just above the 44 per dollar level aided 

 by equity-related inflows undetered by recent stock market 

 losses. Foreign investors have bought about 10 billion baht 

 worth of Thai stocks since the start of the year. 

 However, the upside was capped by fears of intervention by 

 the central bank that on Monday said it had bought dollars to 

 beef up foreign reserves and was prepared to intervene to stem 

 volatility in the currency market. 

 Dealers in Singapore said local corporate dollar bids were 

 expected around 43.90 while offers were lined up within the 

 44.05-44.10 range. 

 Underlining the growing foreign investor interest in Thai 

 stocks, ING Barings in a recent research report said it has 

 upgraded Thailand to overweight from neutral saying it is the 

 third cheapest market in Asia. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso rose against the dollar following the regional 

 trend but was expected to maintain a narrow 51.00-51.15 range 

 due to the lack of fresh leads and corporate interest. 

 Dealers in Manila said improving sentiment on the economic 

 outlook and some equity-related inflows were expected to 

 support the peso. 

 Inflation for January came at 3.8 percent on the year, down 

 from 4.1 percent in December. The data would cement hopes of 

 further rate cuts by the central bank that had recently said it 

 would continue to ease interest rates even after the U.S. ended 

 its easing cycle. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar drifted higher in its recent range of 

 around 1.8290-1.8400 per U.S. dollar, listlessly tagging after 

 the yen. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar was likely to trade up to 

 1.8290, but was unlikely to break that level given its failure 

 to do so last week. They added its downside was likely limited 

 around 1.8340. 

 As with some of the other regional currency markets, the 

 Sing dollar has been plagued by a sheer lack of trading 

 interest, especially ahead of the Lunar New Year. 

 Analysts said while the market was happy to sell the dollar 

 on rallies given the view that Singapore - with its key 

 electronics sector - would stand to benefit from the global 

 economic recovery, many were also playing it safe by buying the 

 dollar back on dips. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar held onto its gains above the 35 level 

 thanks to exporters' U.S. dollar sales. 

 The currency usually gets a boost ahead of the Lunar New 

 Year because local companies have to pay their employees 

 bonuses and to throw banquets for them. 

 However, the market was likely to remain well-behaved given 

 the central bank's looming presence in the market. The bank has 

 been active on both sides of the market to deter the Taiwan 

 dollar from straying too far from the 35 level. 

     Taipei markets will be closed between February 11-14, and 

 will reopen on the 15th. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was fenced in a fairly narrow range of around



10,310-10,320, with many players absent as Jakarta continued to



cope with the worst flooding seen in decades.



    Market players have been opting to stay at home rather than



brave the floods, which have affected many parts of the



Indonesian capital. Jakarta dealers have said trading has been



lacklustre as a result.



In the meantime, the government said its gross



international reserves were at $27.77 billion as of the fourth



week of January, the same figure as the week before. Before



rounding, there was a slight decrease of $3.3 million, which



the government owed to the repayment of foreign debts.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen spoils upbeat global economic outlook.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stumbled over 

 the yen early on Friday, though most resisted emulating the 

 yen's sharp losses as they have so far this year. 

     The dollar continued to hound the yen to three-year lows 

 after the market mulled over signs that the U.S. was indeed 

 recovering and decided to embrace optimism over the economy 

 whole-heartedly, especially as Japan struggled with political 

 and economic troubles. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill gave the dollar an 

 extra kick when he said he had no sympathy for U.S. 

 manufacturers fretting over the strong dollar. 

 Still, the dollar could face some resistance from Japanese 

 investors and companies seeking to repatriate ahead of the 

 fiscal year-end bookclosing in March. 

 Among the Asian currencies, the won was the most vulnerable 

 to waxing and waning of the yen's fortunes. However, gains on 

 Wall Street were likely to spillover to Asian bourses. 

 Indeed, many analysts have pointed out that regional 

currencies should rise if the U.S. - the biggest consumer of 

 Asia's exports - does rebound. However, they have hit a major 

 snag in the form of the weaker yen. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won gapped lower to open at 1,324 compared with 

 Thursday's close of 1,314.4, upset with the yen's weakened 

 state. 

 However, rises in the local stock market and foreign fund 

 inflows quickly served to counteract the yen's negative 

 effects. 

 Talks between Hynix Semiconductor and Germany's Infineon 

 Technologies were also likely to provide a boost to the won. 

 While an Infineon Japan spokesman said the talks were not 

 necessarily about a tie-up, some sort of cooperative agreement 

 could be possible. 


                             SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar drifted towards the weaker end of its



familiar range in early trade as it shadowed an ailing yen.



Dealers expected the Sing dollar to move between 1.8360 and



1.8460 against the dollar, edging softer in intraday trade.



Dollar buy orders from major banks were lining up around the



1.8380 level.



They said currency players who took short positions on the



dollar/Sing on Thursday were beginning to assume long dollar



positions.



But, capital inflows into the Singapore stock market, which



closed on a 10-month high on Thursday, should give the currency


a boost later in the day.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso tracked the regionals lower, opening at 51.30 to



the dollar compared with 51.235 at the close on Thursday. At



0125 GMT, the market turnover was $21 million.



But its downside was supported by improved sentiment after



key economic data beat forecast. The country's GDP grew 3.4



percent on the year in 2001 against a 3.075 percent growth



forecast by economists polled by Reuters.



Exporters and interbank players sold the U.S. dollar around



the morning low of 51.325 and dealers believed 51.350 should be



a good support for the local currency at this point.



THAI BAHT



The baht succumbed to the 44 level once again, with early



dollar bids on the back of the yen's falls driving it lower.



Singapore dealers described the buying as across-the-board,



but added it had lost some of its momentum around the 44.10



level as the yen regained some balance.



Still, while the baht was enjoying equity-related inflows,



the dealers expected to trade towards the 44.30 level - last



seen on December 28 - as the yen continued to struggle.



"There's no reason for a stronger baht. It's going to start



hurting their exports," said a European bank dealer in



Singapore.



The government said its current account surplus stood at



$1.022 billion at the end of December versus November's $556



million surplus.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah held steady around 10,300 to the dollar in



lethargic early trade as flooding paralysed the islands of Java



and Bali after three days of monsoons.



Dealers in Singapore said corporate demand for dollars



existed below the 10,300 level. They expect the rupiah to



weaken slightly against the dollar in intraday trade.



"The bottom line is that the dollar/rupiah still needs to



go up," a Singapore-based dealer at an American bank said,



adding that other regional currencies should also reflect a



bullish dollar.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar opened a touch easier at 35.032 against



the Thursday close of 34.980 on the back of a weaker yen which



the local currency tracked closely because Japan and Taiwan



compete in a similar export market.



However, its losses are likely to be limited by capital



inflows and seasonal dollar sales by exporters, especially



ahead of the Chinese New Year next month, dealers said.



    Foreign investors were net buyers of T$695 million



(US$19.86 million in local stocks on Thursday.



    "I don't thing it (the Taiwan dollar) will stray from its



recent range. It will be wedged between exporter dollar offers



and the yen as well as fears of central bank intervention,"



said a dealer in Singapore.



The central bank was rumoured to have bought around $80



million during the last minute trading on Thursday to curb the



local currency's appreciation.

title: Emerging  FX  - Take heart from recovery hopes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies

 retained their earlier gains on Thursday as market players took 

 the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady to 

 mean the world economy had bottomed. 

     The Fed ended its year-long easing campaign, keeping the 

 benchmark fed funds rate at 1.75 percent but warned there is 

 still a risk of weakness in the economy. 

     The dollar failed to find much support from the Fed's 

 decision, partly because Japanese officials have toned down 

 their rhetoric on the yen. 

     "It is the very weakness of the local asset market that 

 appears to have caused Japanese policy makers to tone down 

 their rhetoric for fear of a weakening currency coupled with 

 weakening equities and bonds causing investors to flee Japan en 

 masse," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS 

 Warburg. 

     "We continue to be short dollar/yen from 133.90 looking for 

 a return towards 130.00. We do note however that fundamentals 

 remain weak with banking shares and JGBs continuing to falter," 

 he said in a note. 

     The yen was hovering around 133.00 to the dollar. Charts 

 show the dollar/yen is trapped in a downtrend channel dating 

 back to January 28. 

     The Institute of International Finance forecast in its 

 latest report that private capital inflows into Asia should 

 pick up to $53.1 billion this year from around $44.4 billion 

 estimated for 2001. 

     SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

     The Sing dollar was among the best performing currencies, 

 advancing against the U.S. dollar in a sluggish market as it 

 tracked a more buoyant yen and was helped by investment flowing 

 into the stock market . 

     Dealers said a midday break of 1.8300 prompted some 

currency players to cut long dollar positions. But corporates 

 eager to buy cheaper dollars pushed the U.S. dollar/Sing back 

 near that level. 

     The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was rumoured to 

 be stepping in recently to slow the Sing dollar's appreciation, 

 which could hurt the export-driven recovery effort. 

      THAI BAHT 

     The baht was pushed higher by players betting the central 

 bank would allow the currency to appreciate on the back of a 

 steadier yen. 

     Dealers in Singapore said there were no signs of 

 dollar-buying intervention as the baht touched a 10-day high of 

 43.87 per dollar, aided by equity-related and export inflows. 

     But local commercial demand for the dollar and wariness 

 over central bank's recent interventions made most players 

 reluctant to push the baht higher. 

     The central bank upgraded its growth projection saying the 

 economy will grow 2-3 percent in 2002, against an October 

 prediction of 1-3 percent. The economy grew an estimated 1.5 

 percent in 2001. 

     INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

     The rupiah barely budged from its range around 10,300 

 level, with trading activity subdued as floods paralysed 

 transport and communications in Jakarta. 

     However, dealers in Singapore said the bias was for a 

 modestly stronger rupiah given a lack of commercial demand and 

 an improved economic outlook with lower interest rates. 

     The benchmark one-month SBI rate eased to 16.93 percent in 

 Wednesday's auction, from 17.09 percent the previous week. 

  KOREAN WON 

     The won ended the day slightly lower with the shaky yen 

 overshadowing foreign net purchases of 15 billion won worth of 

 local stocks. 

     Earlier in the day, the won was in an upbeat mood thanks to 

 growing relief over signs that the U.S. economy was indeed on 

 the mend and the infectious cheer in the stock market. 

     But the currency's fortunes began to sour, with 

 profit-taking driving the local stock market lower and the yen 

 taking a turn for the worse. 

     Singapore dealers added that genuine dollar demand from 

 importers also emerged around the 1,305 level. Charts also 

 showed the dollar/won had been on the verge of being overbought 

 with a 14-day relative strength index reading of around 35 on 

 Wednesday. 

     "It's obvious -- this is not a good level to sell at," said 

 a Singapore dealer at a European bank, noting that some players 

 had taken long-dollar positions ahead of the dollar's sharp 1.6 

 percent correction from January 23 to its present levels. Data 

 released earlier showed headline inflation rising in January by 

 2.6 percent year-on-year, which may signal the end of the Bank 

 of Korea's rate-cutting cycle. 

     TAIWAN DOLLAR 

     The Taiwan dollar was virtually flat from Wednesday's 

 34.985 close, caught between the battling influences of the 

 unsteady yen and gains in local stocks. 

     Trading was sluggish in the currency, and the range was a 

 tight 34.94-34.98. Singapore dealers said the central bank was 

 curbing the Taiwan dollar's gains in its regular attempt to 

 keep the exchange rate along the straight and narrow. 

     PHILIPPINE PESO 

     The Philippine peso closed at 51.235 against the dollar, 

 compared with 51.220 on Wednesday after spending the day in a 

 tight range between 51.21 and 51.26. 

     Trading was brisk, with $110 million changing hands. 

     Dealers in Manila and Singapore said the peso shrugged off 

 news the country's GDP grew 3.4 percent in the fourth quarter, 

 beating market and government expectations. 

     "The positive news has already been priced into the peso," 

 a Singapore-based dealer at an American bank said. 

     They said all the action was onshore, with corporates 

 buying dollars at the cheaper range to pay off debts.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mixed up between Fed and yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were torn 

 early on Thursday between the Federal Reserve's affirmation 

 that the U.S. economy was picking up and a stagnating yen. 

     The Federal Open Market Committee left interest rates 

 steady at the end of its two-day meeting. 

     While the decision to leave rates alone was widely 

 expected, U.S. stock markets were relieved to see the Fed 

 joining the ranks of those who believe the U.S. economy is on 

 the road to recovery. 

 "What it means is that the Fed has helped lay the 

 groundwork for the U.S. recovery with its previous cuts...that 

 could lead to some spillover buying of Asian stocks, which 

 would give some of the regionals some support," said Thio Chin 

 Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. 

     "But given how the yen and euro are struggling, the 

 dollar/Sing could reassert itself," she added. 

     The Fed's move to suspend its aggressive rate-cutting spree 

 gave the dollar a leg-up against the other major currencies. 

     The yen gave up some of its 0.64 percent gains on Wednesday 

 in early Asian trade, slipping beyond the 133 level. 

     The yen's fragility continued to dampen Asia's outlook, 

 which would have been brighter given the expected rebound in 

 the U.S., its largest export market. The Institute of 

 International Finance warned on Wednesday in a report that the 

 weaker yen threatened growth and capital flows into Asia. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won rose for the sixth day in a row as giddy spirits in 

 the local stock market dominated the mood in the market. 

 Korean shares were up one percent, taking heart 

 along with their U.S. counterparts the Fed's decision to sit 

 tight on rates amid signs that the U.S. economy was improving. 

 Exporters' dollar sales at month-end also gave the won a 

 boost, as did a report in a local newspaper that Kumho 

 Industrial Co. was likely to announce the sale of 

 its tire operations to a consortium led by U.S. private equity 

 fund, the Carlyle Group. 

 However, charts showed the dollar/won veering into 

 overbought territory with a 14-day relative strength index 

 reading of around 35 on Wednesday. That could bring some 

 support for the dollar in the near term. 

 Korea reported January inflation crept up 2.6 percent 

 versus a year ago and 0.6 percent from the previous month, in 

 line with expectations. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar bobbed around the middle of its recent 

 1.8300-1.8370 range in early trade as it looked for new 

 direction. 

 Dealers said the Fed's announcement had little effect on 

 the Sing dollar because the market had already factored in the 

 decision. They expected it to trade between 1.8320-1.8370. 

 The Sing dollar market continued to track the movements in 

 the dollar/yen. Still, the domestic dollar's upside was capped 

 by talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened to buy 

 dollars at 1.83 to prevent the currency from appreciating. A 

 strong Sing dollar would make exports, which account for about 

 70 percent of Singapore's GDP, less competitive. 

 Dealers said charts showed the dollar would be 

 well-supported around 1.8270, which it managed to avoid 

 breaking from December 6-December 14.. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht edged higher above the 44 per dollar level on 

 equity-related inflows and was further aided by the steadier 

 tone in the yen and other regional currencies. 

 But dealers in Singapore said most players still fear the 

central bank might start buying dollars around these levels to 

 cap the baht's rise. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said on Wednesday that 

 the budget deficit for fiscal year starting in October would be 

 cut to 175 billion baht from 200 billion baht this year. 

 He said Thailand could not rely solely on fiscal spending 

 to fuel economic recovery and more monetary measures would be 

 unveiled by the Bank of Thailand to kick-start growth. 

     The central bank had twice cut its benchmark 14-day repo 

 rate by a total of 50 basis points to 2.00 percent. 

     The bank is due to release its monthly economic indicators 

 for December and its quarterly report on inflation later in the 

 day. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah held on its range around 10,300 level with



trading activity subdued after heavy rains and floods paralysed



transport and communications in Jakarta.



    Dealers in Singapore said the rupiah is expected to trade



within 10,250-1,350 range for now but a lack of commercial



demand could push it higher.



    The benchmark one-month SBI interest rate eased to 16.93



percent in Wednesday's auction, from 17.09 percent in the



previous week.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The Philippine peso opened lower against the dollar while



the market waited for two key figures from the government.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Ctrl Bk Fears Cap Gains
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Concerns that the region's monetary authorities may step in and smother the appreciation of their respective currencies moderated the gains in Asian currencies late Wednesday, even as the yen bounced past the psychologically important Y133 threshold to the dollar, market watchers said. 

 The anemic performance of U.S., and in turn regional stock markets, also offset any potential boost coming from the yen, observers said. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average skidded 2.5% Tuesday amid fears that U.S. companies could fall victim to accounting problems like those that caused energy trading company Enron to go bankrupt. 

 "In the last few weeks there was a tug-of-war between a strong dollar/yen and equity inflows in Asia," said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at Singapore's UOB Group. "Now it's the other way around." 

 Portfolio inflows into the region's stock markets had helped cushion the blow on Asian currencies dealt by the weakness in the yen and the euro in recent sessions. 

 With Asian currencies having strengthened against their major trading counterparts, the region's authorities may now be anxious about keeping their currencies competitive, analysts said. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency remained supported above the psychologically important S$1.8300 level, as the threat of central bank intervention loomed, observers said. 

 The U.S. dollar slipped to an intraday low of S$1.8305, but had recovered to S$1.8326 at 0840 GMT (3:40 a.m. EST). The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8325 late Tuesday. 

 The trade-weighted Singapore dollar is trading at the stronger end of the monetary authority's policy band, analysts said. The Monetary Authority of Singapore - which uses the currency rather than interest rates as its primary monetary policy tool - guides the local dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and key competitors. 

 "The Singapore dollar has been hugging the strongest end of our estimate of the band," said Koh at UOB. "In fact, it has breached it slightly." 

 Koh estimates the upper boundary of the band at around S$1.8340, based on the assumption that the central bank has - earlier this month - narrowed the policy band to 1.5% on each side of the pivot point. 

 Although there were rumors in the last two days that the central bank had intervened to curb the strength of the Singapore dollar, some observers believe the MAS will unlikely stand in the way of a stronger currency. 

 They argue that the central bank would be wary of setting a psychological ceiling on the Singapore dollar, as the yen is widely expected to strengthen further on fund repatriation by Japanese institutional investors before the fiscal year-end in March. 

 Late Wednesday, the dollar was quoted at Y132.55, below Y133.31 late Tuesday in New York. 

 Some dealers also blamed the U.S. dollar's pullback against some of the region's currencies like the Singapore dollar and the South Korean won on long-liquidation of the U.S. currency ahead of the Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates. 

 After Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's encouraging assessment of the U.S. economy last week, markets have priced in expectations that the Fed will leave short-term interest rates unchanged when it concludes its two-day policy meeting later Wednesday. 

 Foreign equity outflows countered the upward pressure on the South Korean won from the yen's advance, dealers said. 

 Foreign investors unloaded a net KRW200.1 billion in shares Wednesday, contributing to a 3.2% plunge in the benchmark stock index, and in turn the won's slide to as low as KRW1,319.0 earlier in the day. 

 However, the yen's rebound and mounting expectations that South Korea's sovereign ratings might be upgraded - probably sooner rather than later - overwhelmed the yen's influence. 

 Reinforcing such optimism was an announcement by South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy Wednesday that a team of analysts from Moody's Investors Service Inc. will visit South Korea Feb. 25-28 for an annual review on the country's sovereign rating. In November, Moody's revised the outlook on South Korea's Baa2 ratings to positive from stable. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at KRW1,311.0, lower than KRW1,313.6 Tuesday. The U.S. dollar fluctuated between KRW1,310.5 and KRW1,319.0. 

 Some dealers said fears of intervention by the Bank of Korea kept the U.S. dollar buoyed above KRW1,310 support. 

 "There's a risk that if it breaks that level, people will sell the dollar down to KRW1,290," said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 Moderate intervention by Taiwan's central bank kept a rein on the local dollar's rise, dealers said. Apart from the yen, the New Taiwan dollar received a boost from heightened seasonal demand for the local currency ahead of the month-end and the Chinese New Year festivities around mid-February. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.985, down from NT$35.001 Tuesday. 

 The Thai currency was marginally firmer at 44.025 baht to the U.S. dollar, compared with THB44.040 late Tuesday. Fears of intervention by the Bank of Thailand - which dealers believe had been buying U.S. dollars in the last two days - kept the U.S. currency buoyed above THB44.000. 

 Bucking the trend in the region, the Philippine peso was slightly weaker as month-end corporate demand for U.S. dollars overpowered the support from the yen and foreign equity inflows into the local market. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at 51.22 pesos, slightly higher than PHP51.165 Tuesday. 

 The rupiah's gains Tuesday proved to be short-lived as Indonesian companies took advantage of the U.S. dollar's pullback to buy the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar was at 10,325 rupiah, higher than IDR10,295 late Tuesday. 

 The International Monetary Fund said Tuesday the economic challenges facing Indonesia are becoming more difficult as the government struggles to deliver promised reforms in the corporate and banking sectors. 

 Still, the IMF's board still agreed to excuse Indonesia's failure to satisfy a couple of conditions of its $4.5-billion IMF loan program. 

 The fund announced late Monday its approval of a $341-million loan installment for Indonesia, contributing to the brief surge in the rupiah.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen cheers despite stock losses.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies notched 

 higher late on Wednesday with the yen's gains providing 

 encouragement despite falls on the U.S. equity markets. 

     Trading was relatively subdued ahead of the U.S. Federal 

 Open Market Committee's rate announcement expected later in the 

 day. The market isn't expecting a rate cut, but was hoping for 

 a good prognosis on the U.S. economy from the Fed. 

 The market also remained largely focused on the yen, which 

 shot past the 133 level on a report in the Wall Street Journal 

 that U.S. auto giant General Motors was complaining to the Bush 

 administration about attempts to weaken the yen. 

 The Korea won saw the most volatile trade, opening lower at 

 1,319 before the yen's strength managed to pull it back towards 

 1,311, flat from Tuesday's close. The won has gained some 1.8 

 percent in a week, making it the region's leader in recent 

 sessions. 

 The other currencies paled in comparison, with many of the 

 Southeast Asian regionals merely trading in the higher end of 

 their recent ranges. But analysts said they expected that to 

 change in the long term because the U.S. recovery is expected 

 to show more signs of health. 

 "The other currencies really haven't taken off like the 

 yen. But that should change because we're expecting more good 

 U.S. data, which should be welcome news for the regionals," 

 said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in 

 Singapore. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 Despite a sell-off in local stocks on Wednesday, the won 

 managed to track the yen higher. The currency was also boosted 

 by capital inflows into the local bond market. 

 The won closed at 1310.90 to the dollar against 1318.50 at 

 the open and 1313.60 at the close on Tuesday. Foreigners 

 emerged as net sellers of Korean stocks, sending the benchmark 

 KOSPI index slipping 3.18 percent to close at 749.45. 

 The currency has gained around 1.80 percent in a week, 

 which is considered a sharp move in Asia's context, and dealers 

 said it should be top heavy going forward. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar rose alongside the yen, but the local 

currency was top heavy at around 1.8320 amid talk the central 

 bank might have recently stepped in to slow its appreciation. 

 Despite being rangebound in the past few sessions, the Sing 

 dollar has gained more than one percent since the end of last 

 year, making it the best performing Asian currency

 year-to-date. 

 Dealers say the next key level is 1.8300 where hefty 

 stop-loss U.S. dollar selling orders are lining up. Charts show 

 that a break above that level will take the Sing dollar out of 

 its recent consolidative phase, indicating further upside 

 ahead. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht edged above the 44 level aided by a steadier 

 regional tone and portfolio-related inflows. 

     But fears of central bank dollar-buying intervention and 

 commercial demand for the dollar capped its upside. 

     The market has been rife with talk that the Bank of 

 Thailand was seeking to buy dollars to increase its forex

 reserves and keep the baht's competitive edge. Singapore

 dealers said they believed the bank had repeatedly intervened

 above the 44 level. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said the Bank of 

 Thailand will raise this week its 2002 economic growth forecast 

 to 2-3 percent from 1-3 percent, saying the upbeat forecast was 

 based on the improving global economic outlook and the Thai 

 economy's better performance in the last quarter of 2001. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah held steady around 10,300, off its early 

 three-week high of 10,250 where local corporates were spotted 

 bidding for dollars. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said overall trading interest and 

 volumes were low as most of Jakarta was inundated by floods 

 after heavy monsoon rains that paralysed air, road and rail 

 transport. 

 The IMF issued a statement after its board approved the 

 latest $341 million instalment under the nation's $4.5 billion 

 loan programme, urging Indonesia to renew efforts to reform its 

 economy and take the needed steps to boost investor confidence 

 and reduce poverty. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The Philippine peso closed lower at 51.22 after meandering 

 in a familiar 51.17-51.25 range in the absence of clear 

 direction. 

 Trading was brisk with $136 million changing hands. 

 Dealers in Manila said most of the market action came from 

 corporates buying the greenback below the 51.20 level to pay 

 off dollar debts. The Philippine central bank was rumoured to 

 be also buying dollars at similar levels to pay their bills. 

 Marginal gains in the Philippine stock market on Wednesday 

 supported the peso, one of the most stable currencies in the 

 region. The main Manila index closed 0.21 percent higher at 

 1,301.11. 

 Dealers said gross domestic product data for the fourth 

 quarter of 2001 due on Thursday should offer the dollar/peso 

 market something new to chew on. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar rose above the 35 level in line with the 

 yen and won. 

 But its rise was much more tempered given the market's 

 wariness of central bank intervention. Taiwan's central bank

 has been on both sides of the market on a regular basis to 

 maintain a stable rate. 

     And dealers expected it to be even more keen to keep the 

 rate steady ahead of the Lunar New Year holidays.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Some Central Banks Check Gains
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies basked in the glow of the yen's rebound late Tuesday, although dealers believe the central banks in Taiwan, Singapore and Thailand had intervened to check the strength of their respective currencies, market watchers said. 

 In recent sessions, portfolio inflows had mitigated the pain on the New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht from the yen's slide to new 39-month lows versus the U.S. currency and the euro's weakness, analysts said. 

 Given the appreciation of these Asian currencies against their major trading counterparts, the region's central banks are probably concerned about the strength of their currency on a trade-weighted basis, they added. The authorities would need to maintain the price competitiveness of their exports. 

 The Singapore dollar was stronger at S$1.8325 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.8363 late Monday. 

 Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been bidding for U.S. dollars since Monday kept the unit buoyed above S$1.8300, even as the yen threatened to approach the Y133 psychological resistance level to the U.S. currency. 

 "Any further strength could push the Singapore dollar into more expensive area against the currencies of its trading partners," BNP Paribas said in a report. "This would run against the authority's current bias of maintaining a neutral Singapore dollar against its basket." 

 "We expect intervention to continue if portfolio-led Singapore dollar demand continues to push up the value of the local currency," the bank added. 

 At 0854 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at Y133.20, below Y133.50 in New York late Monday. The dollar was at Y133.86 in Tokyo late Monday. 

 In the Thai currency market, the dollar failed to stay below 44 baht, amid talk that the Thai central bank has been buying dollars sporadically via its agent banks in Bangkok and Singapore since Monday. 

 The central bank appeared to have bought dollars when the currency traded between THB43.990 and THB44.050, dealers said. 

 "The amount should be substantial," said a dealer at an Asian bank in Singapore. "They came in a few times and they're still there." 

 In fact, dealers believe that the Bank of Thailand has been curbing the strength of the baht almost daily in the last two weeks, in an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of the country's exports. 

 "We think that there has been a shift in policy thinking at the BOT from a focus on "stability" - through managing interest rate differentials and exchange rates (through the latter half of 2001) - to more conventional counter-cyclical 'growth-oriented' measures," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 "We expect the authorities to consciously guide the baht lower against its nominal effective basket, to boost exports," the bank said, adding that the dollar will likely be well supported around THB43.900 to THB43.950. 

 In Taiwan, the central bank reportedly bought U.S. dollars around NT$34.980, offsetting the pressure from the exporter U.S. dollar sales and the yen's rise, Taipei-based dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.001, marginally lower than NT$35.015 Monday. 

 The South Korean won closed at a two-week high, receiving an additional boost from dollar demand by foreign investors needing to settle their recent purchases of local shares, dealers said. 

 The won also gained from the unwinding of long dollar positions by foreign funds - triggered by the dollar's fall below the psychologically important KRW1,320 level - and jitters about the yen, with "dollar/yen hanging precariously above Y133," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "Offshore players are coming in and selling dollar/won for speculative reasons as well," noted Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Remarks by international ratings agency Fitch that there is room for an upgrade in South Korea's sovereign ratings also boosted sentiment toward the won. 

 "It helped sentiment - definitely," said Mohi-uddin. 

 The dollar ended at 1,313.6 won, down 0.6% from KRW1,321.3 Monday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah received a fillip from the International Monetary Fund's approval of a loan installment of $341 million for the country and its agreement to extend a $4.5-billion loan facility by a year to the end of 2003. 

 The rupiah also received another dose of good news - that a Standard Chartered Plc. (U.STA)-led consortium appeared to be the front runner in bidding for a stake in nationalized PT Bank Central Asia (P.PCA). 

 The Indonesian currency strengthened to 10,295 rupiah to the dollar from IDR10,390 late Monday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.165 pesos, down from PHP51.240 Monday. 

 Financial markets are awaiting the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates at the end of its two-day policy-setting meeting, which begins later Tuesday. 

 Markets have priced in expectations that the Fed will hold its overnight target rate steady at 1.75%, which would end a year-long streak of aggressive easing.

title: Emerging  FX  - Pulled back on their feet by yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies continued 

 their rise against the dollar late on Tuesday, spurred on by 

 the yen's gains. 

     With the Korean won leading the charge, the regional 

currencies have been steadily inching higher against the 

 greenback since late last week. 

     Still, dealers and analysts said the bearish sentiment 

 towards the yen despite its recent bounce and a lack of 

 interest in the regional markets was preventing Asian 

currencies from making more rapid advances. 

 Given the recent dramatic moves in the major currencies, 

 dealers said players were more interested in trading in the 

 majors, where the gains were bigger and the liquidity more 

 flush. 

 Peter Redward, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in 

Singapore, said central bank intervention was also holding back 

 some regional currencies. 

 "That's left the regional currencies in no man's land. With 

 the U.S. recovery underway, most of the regionals should be 

 strengthening. But then we've got central banks taking the 

 opportunity to build up their forex reserves," he said. 

 In recent weeks, most Asian central banks, with the 

 exception of Indonesia and Hong Kong, have reported a rise in 

 their forex reserves. 

 Besides regional developments, the market was also focusing 

 on the two-day Federal Reserve meeting which starts later in 

 the day. While most in the market are not expecting a rate cut, 

 they were waiting to see what the Fed might say about the 

 economy. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar managed to claw back some territory 

 from its U.S. rival, but was held in check by talk the central 

 bank may have been in the market to buy dollars. 

 Some dealers said the central bank was believed to have 

 bought a small amount of dollars around the 1.8315/20 level. 

 They, and others, said the central bank was probably keen to 

 cap the local dollar's gains given the still fragile yen and 

 the weaker euro, both of which are major components in the Sing 

 dollar's trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 News that Singapore Technologies and Hong Kong's Hutchison 

 Whampoa were seeking to take a combined 70-80 percent stake in 

 Global Crossing Ltd. also weighed on the local dollar. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was up on dollar sales by exporters for month-end 

 needs and on settlement of stock purchases by foreign investors 

 in the past two sessions in which they had picked up a net 449 

 billion won of local shares. 

 Dealers in Singapore said players were encouraged by the 

 correction in the dollar/yen that they believed had created 

 more room for the won to appreciate without resistance from 

 authorities. 

 Korean authorities have shown greater concern over the 

 won's competitiveness in the face of a near-term bearish 

 outlook for the Japanese currency given Korea's overlapping 

 export portfolio with Japan. 

 They said the yen's rebound overshadowed the steeper than 

 expected dip in industrial output for December. The won's 

 upside was expected to be capped around 1,310-1,305 for now, 

 but a steadier yen could allow the won to rack up more gains. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht advanced further against the dollar on the back of 

 the yen's rebound, but its gains were dented by talk of the 

central bank coming in to check prices. 

 The central bank has been in the market regularly lately to 

 pick up dollars below 44, either to top up reserves or to cap 

 the baht's gains against the backdrop of increased capital 

 inflows, dealers said. 

 "They (the central bank) were in the market to check rates, 

 but I'm not sure if they actually bought the dollar today," 

 said a local dealer. 

 Charts showed the dollar/baht was still trapped in a 

 downtrend channel, indicating more gains ahead for the local 

currency. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was firmer, reflecting the regionals' trend. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said corporate players were holding back on 

 dollar purchases on hopes the dollar would dip further. 

 The rupiah was also boosted by news of the IMF approving a 

 US$341 million instalment under Indonesia's $4.5 billion loan 

 programme, and extending the loan for a year. 

 Separately, the IMF said on Tuesday it was confident the 

 divestment of Indonesia's largest retail bank, Bank Central 

 Asia (BCA), would be well managed but said the sale should be 

 wound up swiftly. 

 In the money market, Bank Indonesia kept its intervention

 rates in the rupiah interbank money market unchanged at 15.125 

 percent for the overnight rate and 15.875 percent for the 7-day 

 rate. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar held steady but gave up its early gains 

 following a 2.68 percent fall in the local stock market and 

 dollar sales by a foreign bank suspected to be executing an 

 order placed by a foreign equity fund manager. 

 Dealers in Singapore said despite the yen's rebound and 

 some recent positive data flow, stock market losses and 

 wariness over the central bank's repeated dollar-purchase 

interventions has dampened market sentiment and could keep the 

currency in a tight range around the 35 per dollar level. 

 Foreign investors sold a net T$553.5 million of local 

 shares on Tuesday, following net sales of T$463.2 million on 

 Monday. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The Philippine peso was locked in a tight range of 

 51.16-51.23, ending the day at 51.165 as it tracked the yen and 

 regional currencies. 

 Trading was brisk with $134.2 million changing hands. 

 Dealers in Manila said bargain-hunting importers swooped in 

 to buy dollars when it fell below 51.20, while exporters wanted 

 to sell the greenback around 51.30. 

 Many importers hedged their dollar requirements in the 

 forward market just before 2002 and have been sitting on the 

 sidelines so far. But dealers said corporates may come back at 

 the right price. 

 Still, they expect the peso to be trapped in its familiar 

 range ahead of the Fed's announcement and economic data 

 including fourth quarter gross domestic product due on 

 Thursday.
