title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Recover Along With Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were stronger late Tuesday, as the Japanese yen's continued recovery offset the market's somber contemplation over the prospects of a U.S. economic recovery, observers said. 

 The yen's rise gained momentum after China issued its strongest warning yet over the yen's recent downdraft to three-year lows. 

 At 0900 GMT (4:00 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y131.20, below Y132.01 late Monday in New York. The yen hit a new three-year low of Y133.40 last Wednesday. 

 While reaffirming the country's pledge to maintain the stability of the yuan, People's Bank of China Governor Dai Xianglong warned that a further depreciation of the yen would increase the pressure on the yuan exchange rate and called on Tokyo to maintain the yen's stability. 

 While Dai ruled out China devaluing the yuan for now, he mentioned the risk of a weakening yen leading to "a domino effect of depreciations in Asia." 

 South Korea, too, reiterated its concerns over the yen. The country's Finance and Economy Minister Jin Nyum said Tuesday the government is currently collaborating with other neighboring countries to address "foreign exchange rate concerns," notably the weak yen, according to Yonhap news agency. He warned that it would be a "disaster" for the world economy if Japan moves to reflate its ailing economy through a weak yen policy. 

 Their expressions of concern over the yen came at the end of Japanese Prime Minister Juniro Koizumi week-long Southeast Asian tour, during which Japanese monetary officials have toned down their weaker yen rhetoric. Market observers now expect Tokyo to resume talking down the yen - albeit less aggressively for the short term. 

 "Generally, Asian currencies are in a correction phase together with the yen," said a senior dealer at a European bank. "We will see where dollar/yen will move from here, but Y130 will provide a very strong psychological support." 

 The Singapore dollar surged as market participants trimmed their long U.S. dollar positions, triggering stop-loss orders along the way, dealers said. 

 "There was long-liquidation by U.S. and U.K. funds," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 He warned, however, that the selling in the U.S. currency was overdone, and could provoke intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The central bank has, however, appeared to tolerate the currency's movements - at least for now. 

 "Based on the Singapore dollar trade-weighted index, it seems to me that the Singapore dollar is a bit too strong," the dealer said. 

 The U.S. dollar skidded to S$1.8253, down sharply from S$1.8383 late Monday. 

 The Thai baht's gains lagged behind those of the Singapore dollar and yen. 

 There were suspicions that the Thai central bank was checking the baht's strength, in part to maintain the competitiveness of the country's exports, dealers said. 

 Dealers believe the Bank of Thailand has been buying dollars daily since late last week via a Japanese bank in Singapore. 

 Late in the day, the dollar was fetching 43.870 baht, down marginally from THB43.900 late Monday. For most of the day, the dollar traded above THB43.900 - a level that the central bank appeared to have supported in recent sessions. 

 Apparently concerned over the competitiveness of its currency, Taiwan's central bank had also intervened to mitigate the upward pressure on the New Taiwan dollar from the yen's gains, foreign equity fund inflows and U.S. dollar sales by exporters, dealers said. 

 The central bank bought an estimated US$200 million during the day, a foreign bank dealer in Taipei estimated. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.999 - below NT$35.027 Monday - but off Tuesday's intraday low of NT$34.967. Trading volume was US$520 million, almost double that of US$282 million Monday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar ended at 51.255 pesos, down from PHP51.345 Monday. 

 Bucking the trend in the region, the South Korean won succumbed to heavy foreign equity fund outflows, dealers said. 

 As the won's movements decoupled from the yen's, the Japanese currency recovered above the psychologically important KRW10.00 mark for the first time in a week. The dollar was fetching KRW10.05 late Tuesday, up from KRW9.94 late Monday. 

 "U.S. funds were covering their yen/won positions - they've gone short in the cross since the end of last year and early this year," said a Singapore dealer. 

 Against the U.S. dollar, the won finished at KRW1,316.9, weaker than Monday's close at KRW1,312.3. 

 Foreign investors dumped some KRW294.2 billion in shares, sending the benchmark stock index reeling by 3.4% to a close of 718.64 points, its lowest finish since the end of last year. 

 Market participants who had bought currencies like the won, on hopes that the country is well-positioned to gain from a U.S. economic rebound, unwound their positions as such optimism faded, observers said. 

 "There was an unwinding of these reflation trades that were put on at the end of last year and early this year," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's cautious comments on the economy at the end of last week served as a reality check on the market, dashing hopes for a speedy U.S. economic recovery. In his downbeat assessment on the U.S. economy, Greenspan had emphasized the risks to growth and corporate profits. 

 Adding to the somber mood in Seoul's markets, South Korean Finance and Economy Minister Jin Nyum said Tuesday that it would be difficult for the country to see a genuine recovery in exports and capital investment during the first half of 2002, according to Yonhap News Agency. But he added that the government will nevertheless seek to attain a "reasonable" economic growth rate in the first half through fiscal and financial policies.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen drives regionals lower.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell under 

 the sickly yen's spell early on Wednesday, though the degree of 

 their losses has yet to match the yen's. 

     Compared with the yen's 0.29 percent decline from Monday's 

 levels in late Asian trade, the Singapore dollar has only ceded 

 0.11 percent and the Thai baht 0.18 percent. 

     Analysts say the chief reasons for the slightly more 

 subdued reaction from regional currencies to the yen this time 

 around are capital inflows, primarily into North Asia, and the 

 fact that most Asian currencies have corrected substantially 

 since the Asian financial crisis. 

 That said, they emphasise that the yen still wields huge 

 influence over regional currencies because it plays a 

 significant part in their trade-weighted baskets. Analysts 

 reckon the yen holds an 11-15 percent weighting in the 

 trade-weighted basket for the Sing dollar. 

 With little other fresh leads, the market was likely to 

 remain riveted on the yen's movements, and to whether Japan's 

 neighbours may express alarm. The currency received a drubbing 

 late on Monday after comments from senior Japanese officials 

 that the market interpreted as giving a green light for a 

 weaker yen. 

 Faced with an economy that has slipped into recession 

 again, Japan's government seems to be taking the option of 

 trying to export its way out of trouble, analysts say. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was wrestling with the 1.8500 level, 

 and found itself being defeated by the wobbly yen. 

 However, dealers said the Singapore dollar was able to 

 avoid its early morning lows of around 1.8525 because some 

 players were still trying to unload long dollar positions from 

 last week. 

 The currency has also been able to avoid more severe losses 

 because of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's decision last 

 week to narrow its trading band for the trade-weighted Sing 

 dollar. Analysts said they view that move as an indication of 

 renewed confidence in the city-state's economy and less 

 tolerance for exchange rate volatility. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won followed the shaky yen in its downward path, 

 gapping lower to 1,315.5 from Tuesday's close of 1,309.5. 

 But the currency continued to outperform the yen, with the 

 yen/won cross-rate at levels not seen since July 

 1999 and well below what many analysts had believed was the 

 government's threshold because of concerns over export 

 competitiveness. 

 The cross-rate's fall has prompted analysts to take the 

 view the government may be becoming more tolerant of a stronger 

 won against the yen because of capital inflows and a brighter 

 outlook for the Korean economy. 

 Indeed, a forex official from the Finance Ministry told 

 Reuters on Tuesday that while the government is monitoring the 

 won closely, it does not have a target for the yen/won rate and 

 respects market consensus. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar edged lower with the regional trend and 

 on talk that the central bank may allow the currency to weaken 

 further in line with the yen's recent losses. 

 The Taiwan dollar touched a low of 35.16 per dollar early 

 on, compared with 35.038 at the close of onshore trade on 

 Tuesday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said some support was expected from 

 equity-related inflows but overall the market would keep its 

 focus on moves in the yen. 

     A weaker yen raises competitiveness concerns as Taiwan 

 competes with Japan in several export markets. 

     Foreign investors were net buyers of T$5.9 billion of local 

 shares on Tuesday, taking net purchases in the past seven 

 sessions to T$33 billion. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah lingered around 10,430, wedged in between rising



dollar demand from local corporates and fears of central bank

intervention.



    Dealers in Singapore said suspected dollar sales by the


central bank through state banks on Monday had sparked rumours



the central bank would not allow the rupiah to slip beyond



10,500 per dollar.



    However, local corporates have kept the dollar supported



with strong bids at around 10,400, they said.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht found a toehold below the 44 level, tracking the



yen and the regionals lower. Dealers cited talk of the central



bank buying the U.S. dollar regularly recently to meet its



foreign debt requirement.



"I heard the central bank has bought regularly recently,



around $20-30 million each time. I don't think the objective is



to keep the baht weak but to meet its dollar debt requirement,"



said a dealer in Bangkok.



Otherwise, the baht should be well-supported around



44.15-44.20 where dollar selling orders are lining up, said



Bangkok and Singapore dealers.



The dollar gains are likely to be dented also by rising



baht funding costs. In the offshore market, the one-month



forward rate rose to 10/15 satang per dollar from around 8/10



satang late on Tuesday.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso was down tracking a weaker yen and other regional


currencies.



Dealers in Manila said the Philippine central bank was



rumoured to be selling dollars in early trading to prevent



volatility in the exchange rate.



They also said the intraday range for the dollar/peso was



expected to be about 51.60 to 51.75, with further possible



dollar-buying intervention by the central bank if the dollar



hits a high of 135 against the yen, which would prompt the bank



to further weaken the peso to maintain export competitiveness.



    Local corporate dollar demand has yet to emerge in the



market.



    Volume on the Philippine Dealing System was relatively thin



at around $23 million.

title: Asian  Currencies  Weaker Late As Yen Suffers Relapse
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The yen's relapse to a 39-month low flung Asian currencies to the weaker end of their recent ranges late Tuesday, ending their recent reprieve. 

 But the regional currencies' decline continued to trail behind that of the yen. 

Currencies of export-driven economies - in particular the South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar and the Singapore dollar - will likely continue to outperform the yen in coming months, amid expectations that they will be well positioned to gain from a U.S. economic convalescence. 

 "The problem is a Japanese problem; it's not an Asian problem," said a dealer at a European bank. "Now it's just a question of Asian currencies' competitiveness vis-a-vis dollar/yen." 

 Market watchers said there's a growing risk that the yen could slide past Y135 to the U.S. dollar, as Japanese officials appear to endorse a further weakening of their currency. 

 Renewed faith in Tokyo's tolerance for a weaker yen battered the yen to as low Y132.80 against the U.S. dollar - its weakest level since Oct. 6, 1998. At 0915 GMT (4:15 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was fetching Y132.54. 

 Japan's top currency spokesman, Vice-Finance Minister for International Affairs Haruhiko Kuroda, said early Tuesday that "current (market) conditions reflect a correction," from a previously too-strong yen, suggesting the currency had more room to weaken. 

 Japanese Economics Minister Heizo Takenaka said, after a meeting with U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill Monday, that "exchange rates should be left to market forces, but I don't think the current level doesn't reflect Japan's economic fundamentals." 

 Still, with foreign exchange participants holding long U.S. dollar positions against Asian currencies, the yen would need to drop much further before they would be enticed to push regional currencies beyond their recent lows. 

 "Maybe if dollar/yen goes to Y135 then everybody would sell Asian currencies again," said a senior dealer at a European bank. 

 Fears that monetary authorities in Asia won't tolerate excessive volatility in their respective currencies have also restrained U.S. dollar bulls, dealers said. 

 "For now, we think most of the authorities are still comfortable with the yen's level," said Philip Wee, a market strategist at DBS Bank. "What they don't want is volatility from the yen." 

 The Singapore dollar's movements, in particular, have been relatively tame despite the yen's gyrations, as the monetary authority's recent move to narrow the policy band within which it guides the trade-weighted Singapore dollar has stoked fears of intervention. 

 "The market doesn't dare speculate against the Singapore dollar too much for the time being," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.8495 against its U.S. counterpart, weaker than S$1.8407 late Monday. 

 In Seoul, the U.S. dollar closed at 1,309.5 won, up from Monday's close of KRW1,302.0. 

 The yen remained depressed below KRW10.00, despite the market's belief that South Korean authorities would prefer to keep the Japanese currency above that level to maintain the price competitiveness of South Korea's exports. With the South Korean economy expected to outshine Japan's, the yen was fetching KRW9.88. 

 U.S. dollar sales by foreign investors, who had snapped up South Korean shares in recent sessions, also kept a rein on the won's slide, dealers said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar closed at NT$35.038, higher than NT$34.943 Monday, in dealings valued at US$567 million. 

 Taiwan's central bank didn't appear too alarmed by the local currency's decline as it was stemmed by foreign portfolio inflows and was in line with the weaker currencies in the region, especially the won, dealers said. 

 The central bank - which regularly intervenes in the foreign exchange market - sold around US$150 million, but only to cushion the New Taiwan dollar's slide, dealers in Taipei said. 

 The Thai currency weakened to 44.070 baht to the U.S. dollar, compared with THB43.795 late Monday. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Tuesday the central bank won't use the baht as a tool to stimulate exports, signaling that it won't tolerate a further weakening of the currency. 

 He said the central bank's exchange rate policy must balance the need to keep its foreign exchange reserves strong to meet external debt repayments and the need to support export growth at the same time. 

 However, Pridiyathorn said the central bank wouldn't want to allow the baht to strengthen to the point at which it could hurt exports either, and that's why it decided last month to cut its benchmark interest rate. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the pressure on the peso from the yen was somewhat mitigated by persistent inflows of U.S. dollar remittances from Filipinos working overseas, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at 51.680 pesos, up from PHP51.500 Monday.

title: ANALYSIS-Asian  forex  expected to cruise in calm waters.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 8 (Reuters) - Punters should be rubbing their hands in glee at the prospect of more volatility in Asian currencies as 2002 kicked off with the yen bumping into fresh three-year lows. 

 But that's been far from the case as interest from speculators towards the regional currencies remains weak because of the intervening habits of regional central banks, said analysts and dealers. 

 "Every central bank in Asia manages its exchange rate very closely with the view of damping volatility," said Vincent Low, fixed income and regional currency strategist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore. 

 Analysts say the yen and the much anticipated U.S. recovery - last year's dominating factors in regional currency markets - will only fuel central banks' determination to head off volatility. 

 The weaker yen will prompt regional central banks, particularly in North Asia, to limit their currencies' upsides to maintain export competitiveness. But they will still be keen to keep their currencies from weakening too much as they wait for an economic rebound in the United States to take definite shape. 

 GLOBAL RECOVERY AWAITED 

 "Dollar/yen will put a cap on how much the won and Taiwan dollar can move up, and it's only when a global recovery is firmly entrenched that the Korean and Taiwan central banks will step out of the way," said James Malcolm, regional currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore. 

 Indeed, market players say the Monetary Authority of Singapore's recent decision to narrow the trading band for the trade-weighted Singapore dollar reflected a willingness to intervene more frequently in the market. 

 "There's not going to be the same degree of flexibility as they showed last year," said the head dealer at a foreign bank in Hong Kong, who added that he expected other Asian central banks to act the same way. 

 The MAS uses its trade-weighted Sing dollar to guide monetary policy. As a reaction to the city-state's severe economic downturn last year, the bank widened the trading band for the trade-weighted currency. Analysts say its decision to reverse that move reflects growing confidence over the economy. 

 Market players dubbed the yen and long-awaited U.S. recovery, now expected for the second half of this year, as the sources of possible volatility for Asian currencies. 

 While they unanimously agree that the markets will react violently if the U.S. recovery fails to materialise, they disagree over the extent to which a weaker yen will impact Asia. 

 Still, more and more people in the market are arriving upon the view that while the yen will determine the overall trend for Asian currencies, its influence was dwindling. The yen might fall to fresh three-year lows, but it will take some doing for Asian currencies to see their own record lows. 

 Even with Japanese authorities clearly advocating a weaker yen for the country to export itself out of trouble, analysts say an apocalyptic meltdown in the yen was unlikely because that would provoke strong objections from Japan's neighbours, especially China and Korea, which have already vocalised concerns at the end of last year. 

 "Nobody in Asia wants to give Japan an inch," said JP Morgan Chase's Malcolm, who has an end-June forecast for the yen of 138 to the dollar, a far cry from Asian financial crisis lows of nearly 150. 

 DELAYED CATCH-UP 

 Analysts also noted that the yen's current downtrend may amount to a long-delayed catch-up with the regional currencies. 

 "Since the Asian financial crisis, a lot of these currencies lost a huge amount of their value, and now the yen is finally catching up. You can say it's been overvalued all these years," said Thio Chin Loo, regional currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. 

 Furthermore, North Asian currencies have been enjoying a degree of stability thanks to the flood of capital inflows that began last year. Analysts say it's telling that the won, though weaker, is still outperforming the yen as reflected by the yen/won cross-rate, which has dipped to levels not seen since July 25, 1999. 

 To add insult to injury, even notoriously volatile currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso are expected to enjoy a more stable year compared with the yen because of the absence of their traditional foe - political instability.

title: Emerging  FX  - Sing, Taiwan dollars wilt, eyes on central banks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies shuddered as 

 the yen fell through key levels against the dollar on 

 Thursday, sparking fears central banks in the region may step 

 in to curb the pace of decline. 

     The Singapore dollar sank to a new 11-year low while the 

 Taiwan dollar slipped to fresh 15-year troughs as importers and 

 corporates scrambled to hedge their future dollar requirements 

 amid talk the yen could hit 135 level in days. 

     The yen slipped to a three-year low of 131.75 after 

 Japanese officials said its weakness was justified by 

 fundamentals, with more pressure coming from players seeking 

 settlements as Thursday was the last trading day for the year. 

     But dealers expected the yen and other Asian currencies to 

 regain some lost ground in the near future. 

     "Given the speed with which the dollar/yen has 

 moved....there is a possibility of a sharp retracement," said 

 Peter Redward, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist in 

 Singapore. 

     A weaker yen stirs up concerns across the region with 

 Korea, Taiwan and Singapore seen more vulnerable due to the 

 similarity of their exports and markets with those of Japan. 

     However, analysts said most central banks in the region 

 might see weaker currencies as less stimulating for exports and 

 more damaging for the real economy. Therefore, any intervention

 is likely for the sake of financial stability. 

SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was lower, although it managed to come off 

 its fresh 11-year lows on option-related purchases and fears of 

central bank intervention. 

 The local currency had earlier fallen to 1.8530 - its 

 worst level since June 30, 1990 when it hit 1,8540 - due to a 

 weaker yen and the country's bleak economic outlook. 

 Dealers said some banks were buying the Sing dollar to stop 

 the currency from falling to 1.8600 where their options would 

 be triggered. Apart from fears of intervention and the 

 option-linked buying, there is little else to support for the 

 local currency. 

 Recent economic data painted a gloomy picture, with its 

 non-oil exports shrinking 21.1 percent on the year in November 

 and its manufacturing output contracting 13.60 percent in the 

 same month. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at 15-year lows against the dollar, 

 weighed down by the yen and other regionals. It finished at 

 35.127, the lowest close since 35.140 reached on January 21, 

 1987, according to data from the central bank. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank surprised the market on 

 Thursday by announcing it would cut key interest rates by 

 another 0.125 percentage points. 

 Market participants had earlier speculated that the central 

 bank would keep the borrowing costs unchanged to support the 

 local currency against the backdrop of a weaker yen. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won tracked the yen down to a low of 1,331.0, the 

 lowest level since on April 16 when it hit a low of 1,334.0. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the yen's decline and talk of 

 further downside has sent importers and corporates seeking to 

 cover their dollar requirements. 

 Meanwhile exporters, who had sold dollars earlier for their 

 year-end requirements, were holding back to wait for more 

 attractive levels. 

 But the won's losses were trimmed by market wariness of 

 potential intervention after recent comments by government 

 officials against excessive currency weakness. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah eased to the wrong side of the 10,300, pushing a 

 three-week low of 10,350, as interbank players marked down the 

 local currency against the backdrop of weaker regionals. 

 But dealers in Jakarta said commercial demand for the 

 dollar from local corporates and importers tapered off ahead of 

 the year-end, which helped limit the rupiah's downside. 

     Bank Indonesia was not been in the market, but dealers do 

 not rule out the possibility if the rupiah falls further. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht sank to its one-month lows of 44.24 after the



weaker yen sparked short covering in the U.S. dollar among



interbank players, dealers said.



    But charts show the baht should be well-supported around



44.25 which represents the 50 percent retracement of the



dollar's October 25-December 13 downmove.



    The dollar's further gains should also be restrained by



higher baht funding costs offshore, with the one-month rate



firming up to 16/18 satang per dollar from 12/28 satang



earlier.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso closed lower at 51.49 against Wednesday's close of



51.32 after companies and exporters snapped up the U.S. dollar



to hedge for their future dollar requirements.



    Market turnover picked up, with $98.55 million traded



compared with $56.30 million on Wednesday.



    On the macro front, central bank governor Rafael



Buenaventura said on Thursday he expected annual inflation rate



to come in between 3.9 to 4.3 percent, which some analysts said



should provide room for further rate cuts.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen hurts, Sing dlr near 11-1/2-yr low.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were dragged 

 lower by the yen in early trade on Thursday, with the Singapore 

 dollar sliding towards its lowest level since mid-1990. 

     The Sing dollar fell to 1.8530 to the U.S. dollar during 

 Asian trading, a whisker away from the 1.8540 level hit on June 

 30, 1990. But it bounced back later on fears of potential 

intervention. 

 The yen, which is tracked closely by most emerging Asian 

currencies, dropped to a fresh three-year low of 131.40 to the 

 dollar due to speculation Japan wants a weaker yen to get 

 itself out of its economic mess. 

 The market seemed to ignore comments by a senior minister 

 that it was desirable for foreign exchange rates to move in a 

 stable manner. 

 A sharp weakening of the yen can arguably result in a loss 

 of export competitiveness for other Asian currencies, which 

 could spark competitive devaluation across the region. It would 

 also diminish demand from Japan for Asian goods. 

 Analysts said roughly 11 percent of exports from Asian go 

 to Japan, far less than 15 years ago but still a significant 

 portion. 

 Elsewhere in the region, Taiwan's central bank will hold a 

 quarterly monetary board meeting later in the day. The market 

 is betting the board will keep its rates steady to support the 

currency. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar managed to clamber off its lows, but the 

 downside risk against the U.S. currency remained due to the 

 weak yen and Singapore's gloomy economic outlook, dealers said. 

 Dealers said interbank players were in the market to cover 

 short U.S. dollar positions, but fears of intervention held 

 them back from pushing the Sing dollar too far too fast. 

 "Our synthesised basket of currencies suggests there might 

 be some form of intervention (if the Sing fell) below 1.8480. I 

 don't think the U.S. dollar will go much further from here," 

 said a senior dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 Another dealer said the Sing dollar was also supported by 

 option-linked buying as some banks were trying to stop the 

currency from falling to 1.8600 where their options will be 

 triggered. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht fell to a one-month low of around 44.12 on the 

 back of the sliding yen. The currency has since December 13 

 reversed its upward trend against the U.S. dollar which dated 

 back to October 25. 

 But dealers expected the local currency to be kept within 

 its recent range as most players had already squared their 

 positions for this year. 

 Baht funding costs in the offshore market were mostly 

 steady, with the one-month rate quoted at 12/28 satang per 

 dollar and the one-year rate at 100/250 satang. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won fell as low as 1,323, a level last seen on April 

 30, as the weakening yen prompted players to hedge their future 

 dollar requirements. 

 Dealers in Singapore said fears of central bank

intervention could provide some support to the won, but overall 

 the sentiment was in favour of the dollar. 

 Kim Yong-duk, deputy minister of the Finance Ministry's 

 International Affairs division, said on Wednesday that 

 authorities were concerned about the yen's steep fall and could 

 take action if necessary to stabilise the won. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar edged lower following the weaker tone of 

 the yen and the won. 

 Analysts believed the central bank may not cut its key 

 rates when it holds its quarterly meeting later in the day to 

 review monetary policy on concerns cheaper borrowing costs may 

 further hurt the currency. 

 The Taiwan dollar fell to a low of 35.20 last week, its 

 weakest since July 11 when it set a 2001 low of 35.30. It 

 touched a session low of 35.173 early on Thursday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said players were reluctant to take 

 aggressive positions and would be closely watching the central 

 bank's rate decision expected to be announced at a press 

 conference due at 0900 GMT. 

 Charts also showed the U.S. dollar was massively 

 overbought, with the 14-day relative strength index reading 

 99.169. This highlights the risk of a downward correction of 

 the U.S. dollar. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was down from late Wednesday levels as interbank 

 players beefed up their long dollar positions given the weak 

 regional bias. 

 But a lack of commercial demand for the dollar and a 

 trickle of inflows from overseas workers and exporters helped 

 limit the peso's losses. Turnover was thin, with only $27.50 

 million traded so far, dealers said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah slipped to the weak side of the 10,200 level, 

 weighed down by rising dollar demand by interbank players 

 worried about the yen and other regional currencies. 

     Dollar sales by exporters for year-end requirements and 

 some equity-related inflows were expected to limit the losses. 

     Dealers in Jakarta said players were reluctant to take 

 fresh positions in a lacklustre market thinned by holidays.

title: Singapore dlr pushing 11 = year lows, MAS eyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar was falling to precariously near 1.8540 - last hit on June 30, 1990 - on Thursday as the country's gloomy economic outlook and the sliding yen set off a new round of U.S. dollar short covering. 

 The currency fell to 1.8520 overnight before clawing back some gains in early Asian trading due to wariness of potential Monetary Authority of Singapore intervention. 

 "Our synthesised basket of currencies suggests there might be some form of intervention (if the Sing fell) below 1.8480. I don't think the U.S. dollar will go much further from here," said a senior dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 The losses were also exaggerated by thin trading volumes. 

 The yen, which carries substantial weight in Singapore's undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies, fell to a fresh three-year low of 131.33 to the dollar in early trade in Tokyo. 

 The Singapore market hardly drew any support from a better than expected manufacturing data on Wednesday. November production fell 13.60 percent on the year against a revised 20.60 percent contraction in October. 

 Although the figure came in better than the market expectation of a 21 percent decline, analysts said it was still a sharp year-on-year decline. 

 "It might be too early to assume the economy is bottoming out. There is not much good news out there to support the Sing dollar," said a dealer at a European bank.

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late, Revisits 11-Yr Low On Yen Weakness
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was down sharply against its U.S. counterpart Friday, after briefly revisiting its previous 11-year low, as the yen plunged to its weakest point in more than three years, dealers said. 

 Around 0930 GMT (4:30 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8374, up from S$1.8354 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.8360 and S$1.8435. 

 The U.S. dollar rose sharply in early Asian trading, underpinned by its strong overnight performance against the yen, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar rose further against the local dollar as stop-loss buying was triggered above the S$1.8400 mark, and as it popped through the Y129 mark against its Japanese counterpart. 

 The U.S. currency briefly touched S$1.8435 - the previous 11-year high against the Singapore dollar which it reached last month - in line with its broader gains against the yen and other Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 But the U.S. dollar pulled back slightly as commercial sell orders emerged in the afternoon session, dealers said. 

 Liquidity was thin and trading was muted as market participants wound down their dealings early ahead of the Christmas holidays. 

 Despite the U.S. dollar's sharp rise, dealers said they saw no indication of any intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to iron out excess volatility in the market. 

 "I think because the move has been slow, we haven't seen any sign of the central bank. It's been very gradual and has largely been in line with the other regional currencies," a senior European bank dealer said. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary-policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to retreat further as market participants in Europe and the U.S. are expected to take profit ahead of the weekend, dealers said. 

 Support for the U.S. dollar is expected at S$1.8350, with resistance at S$1.8450. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly lower late Friday, as sentiment was hurt by the crisis in Argentina, volatile U.S. Treasurys overnight and higher domestic interbank rates, dealers said. 

 Rates moved higher as liquidity in the system tightened ahead of the Christmas holiday season and on unconfirmed talk that rail operator SMRT Corp. needed funds to make payments on its bond issue to the Land Transport Authority, dealers added. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was up three basis points at 2.01% while the yield on five-year bonds was flat at 3.36%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds rose two basis points to 3.60% while the yield on 10-year bonds gained one basis point to 3.91%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was up five basis points at 4.29%.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mostly happily treading water.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies sat on 

 their hands late on Wednesday, happy to stay in their current 

 ranges while the dollar/yen treaded water. 

     Investors in Korea and the Philippines were starting to 

 turn their attention to their central banks, both of which have 

 meetings on Thursday. 

     Philippine inflation data issued earlier in the day pointed 

 the way towards more rate cuts. On the other hand, the Bank of 

 Korea was expected to keep its rate steady at four percent 

 despite the IMF's recent recommendation of another rate cut. 

 But for the most part, activity in the regional currency

 market was subdued with the Christmas holiday season 

 approaching. 

 Players were also lying low on the major currency markets, 

 though the dollar was well supported against the yen in light 

 of more dismal data from Japan. 

     The market was looking out for the U.S. non-manufacturing 

 NAPM index due later in the day. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won gathered some more gains thanks to stock inflows,



but still kept to its recent range.



    Foreign investors' equity-related flows have been the chief



driver behind the won's direction for weeks, with the market



shrugging off most economic news. They bought a net 202 billion



won of local stocks on Wednesday.



    Despite the heartened sentiment in Korea, the government



said it was too early to claim an economic recovery.



    Nevertheless, a recent Reuters poll showed 10 economists



unanimously expecting the central bank to hold its key



overnight call rate steady at four percent because of recent



encouraging signs for the economy.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar bobbed around its recent levels, caught



between equity inflows and fears over the central bank.



Dealers in Singapore said activity was thin with players



conscious the central bank was watching the market and ready to



step in to keep the local currency in check.



The central bank has been in the market on an almost daily



basis to maintain an exchange rate that is at once competitive



and stable. Analysts say the huge jump in its forex coffers of



around $5 billion to $121 billion reflects the level of


intervention that has been conducted.


SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar moved slightly higher in its recent



1.8310-1.8400 range after players decided to unwind their long



dollar positions when the greenback failed to break 1.8370.



The currency has been hostage to the major currencies,



particularly the yen. With the dollar unable to make much



headway against the yen, dealers say the market has not been



able to find the momentum to push the market either way.



THAI BAHT



The baht dawdled in paper-thin offshore trading, with the



onshore market closed for a public holiday. It will reopen on



Thursday.



Charts show the dollar/baht is still trapped in a downtrend



channel dating back to October 25, indicating the baht is



likely to retain its strength in the near term.



The pair's immediate resistance is seen at 44.25 which is



the 38.2 retracement of the dollar's October 25-November 30



downmove.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso traded in a 51.955-51.980 range in a quiet market,



with around $89 million transacted. Dealers in Manila said the



market was driven mostly by corporate dollar requirements and



seasonal inflows.



The market has largely priced in the possibility that the


central bank will cut interest rates by 25 basis points or cut



liquidity reserve requirements, or both, at its policy meeting



on Thursday.



But Philippine Socio-economic Planning Secretary Dante



Canlas said on Wednesday the central bank could cut benchmark



rates by up to 50 basis points.



His remark followed lower-than-expected inflation numbers.



Consumer prices in the Philippines grew 4.4 percent on the year



in November - their slowest pace so far this year. A Reuters



poll of 10 economists gave an average forecast of 4.73 percent.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah was caught in a tight range around the 10,480



level with dollar inflows from exporters matching demand from



local corporates in thin trade.



Dealers in Jakarta said interbank players were also



reluctant to take aggressive positions due to the low volumes



and ahead of the holiday season.



Chief Economics Minister Dorodjatun Kuntjoro-Jakti said the



government aims to push annual economic growth to 6-7 percent



in coming years, adding that poverty and unemployment would be



hard to cut if GDP growth remained at 3-5 percent.



    He said public consumption was expected to remain the major



driver for economic growth.



    Indonesia's statistics bureau said last month GDP growth



for 2001 would be at least 3.47 percent. The government also



forecast in the 2002 budget economic growth to swell to four



percent from 3.5 percent this year.

title: Emerging  FX  - Soft but helped by yen's rebound.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 lying low late on Tuesday but the yen's resilience to 

 another downgrade of Japan's sovereign debt helped limit their 

 downside. 

     The yen held steady in early European trade, off its early 

 lows and showing little lasting impact from a cut in Japan's 

 yen-denominated debt rating to Aa3 from Aa2 by Moody's 

 Investors Service. 

     The yen's rebound from overnight lows helped the Singapore 

 dollar bounce off its session low and capped losses in the won 

 and the Taiwan dollar. 

     Slowing equity-related foreign inflows, however, kept the 

 won and the baht under pressure while fresh data from the 

 Philippines and Singapore reinforced the negative view on 

 regional economies. 

     Analysts said traders of regional currencies will be 

 watching for U.S. economic data including the November 

 non-manufacturing NAPM index on Wednesday, weekly jobless 

 claims on Thursday and November jobs on Friday. 

     Most Asian economies need a U.S. rebound before they can 

 recover because of the large share of exports in their gross 

 domestic product, particularly to the United States. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won eased a touch because of local banks buying



dollars



 to pad their forex coffers, traders said.



    The currency was also scared off further gains by the



Korean authorities, who threatened to intervene if necessary.



    A Bank of Korea official told Reuters the bank would step



in to temper the market if necessary, denying a local newspaper



report that quoted an unidentified official as saying the bank



would remain out of the market as long as the won stayed



between 1,250-1,300.



Still, most analysts were of the view that the Bank of



Korea was taking an easier view than Taiwan on its currency's



rise, allowing the won to appreciate some three percent since



October 4 as equity-related inflows poured in.



    Foreign investors were net buyers of some 35.1 billion won



of local stocks on Tuesday.



    On the macro front, the market was starting to turn its



attention to the Bank of Korea's monthly rate-setting meeting



on Thursday. A recent Reuters poll showed 10 economists



unanimously expecting the central bank to hold its overnight



call rate steady at four percent because of evidence that the



economy was on the mend.



    Still, the IMF said Korea had further room to cut interest



rates to help spur economic recovery.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar kept close to its recent levels around



34.46, despite the opposing forces of a weaker yen and gains on



the local stock market.



    For weeks, the central bank has been keeping the exchange



rate stable to maintain export competitiveness while keeping



local confidence high. The Taiwan dollar has stuck to a tight



range of 34.4-34.6 since late September.



Analysts said the huge jump in Taiwan's forex coffers to



$121 billion was due to the central bank's near daily


intervention in the spot market.


SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar bounced off a low of 1.84 as the U.S.



dollar failed to make headway against the yen much beyond the



124 level.



Dealers said as the yen held out against the dollar,



players booked profits from the Singapore dollar's recent



gains.



    However, sentiment was weak on data that showed the



manufacturing sector shrank for the 10th straight month.



    Singapore's Purchasing Managers Index for November fell to



45.9 percent from 47.1 percent in October due to a drop in



order intakes as domestic demand weakened.



    Dealers said year-end corporate demand for dollars,



traditionally seen in December and early January, was expected



to cap any significant gains in the Singapore dollar.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    Fears of central bank intervention kept the rupiah within a



tight range, but local corporates were seeking dollars on



renewed doubts about the government's ability to meet its



fiscal deficit target.



Finance Minister Boediono proposed widening the 2001 budget



deficit target, a move seen contradictory to recent remarks



indicating the deficit would be well below the existing target.



THAI BAHT The baht edged below the 44-per-dollar



level as corporate and interbank traders covered their dollar



requirements ahead of a holiday on Wednesday.



Dealers in Bangkok said the softer yen and other regional


currencies further encouraged players to cover their short



dollar positions.



Financial markets in Thailand will be closed on Wednesday



to celebrate King Bhumibol Adulyadej's birthday. They will



reopen on Thursday.



Talk of more commercial banks cutting their interest rates



after Siam Commercial Bank cut its interest rates by



25 basis points on Monday also raised uncertainty about baht



liquidity.



Economists say there is room for the central bank to



further cut interest rates if it wants to, given the country's



tame inflation.



Thailand's headline inflation fell to 1.0 percent



year-on-year in November, its lowest level since February 2000,



thanks to fast falling oil prices and sluggish domestic demand.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped below 52 per dollar but found support from



inflows of remittances from overseas workers.



    Exports fell 13.5 percent on the year in October but came



in better than a 15 percent contraction officials had expected.



    That raised some cautious hopes that the decline in exports



was near a bottom. However, analysts said it was too early to



judge that and the slower fall could just be a blip.

title: Emerging  FX  - Helped by yen, hurt by U.S. data.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stuck to the 

 safety of recent ranges on Wednesday, unsure whether to cheer 

 the firmer yen or mourn the fall in U.S. consumer confidence. 

     The dollar retreated against the yen and euro after the 

 Conference Board said its index of consumer confidence fell to 

 an unexpected 82.2 in November from 85.3 in October - the 

 fifth straight month of decline. 

 Investors who were jubilant over the prospect of a U.S. 

 recovery in the second half of next year were taken aback by 

 the figure and held off dollar buying. 

 While that was good news for the yen and yen-sensitive 

 regional currencies, the fall in U.S. consumer confidence could 

 unnerve markets in Korea and Taiwan, two economies heavily 

 dependent on U.S. exports. 

 Rising hopes for a U.S. recovery and its spillover effect 

 in the region have inspired the recent rally in Asian 

currencies. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar finally mustered some strength thanks 

 to the firmer yen. 

 Since the beginning of the week, the Sing dollar has 

 notably lagged behind the other regional currencies, primarily 

 because of its shackles to the yen. However, with the yen 

 safely above 124, the Sing dollar was poised to win back ground 

 against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the market could be looking to test 1.83 if 

 the dollar/yen dips further. They added it was still slightly 

 long on the greenback, which could spur further unwinding of 

 long dollar positions. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won opened flat on Wednesday as investors took pause 

 from the recent strong rise both in the currency and stock 

 market. Fears of central bank intervention also dampened 

 sentiment. 

 The won opened at 1,265.2 to the dollar against the 

 Tuesday's close of 1,265.3. The KOSPI came off 1.46 

 percent, with foreign investors selling a net 37.3 billion won 

 worth of local stocks. 

 Dealers expect further gains for the won in the near-term 

 following what they believe would be a brief consolidation 

 because dollar demand for foreign debt repayment has dwindled 

 while more capital inflows into local stocks are expected. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was weighed by news of hostage taking and violence 

 in the southern city of Zamboanga which raised concerns over 

 the country's political and security stability. 

     Corporate players continued to buy dollars to settle their 

 contracts in the non-deliverable forward market. 

     Muslim gunmen freed 21 hostages early on Wednesday out of 

 more than 80 they seized following pitched battles with 

 Philippine troops. 

     But losses are likely to be trimmed by remittances from 

 overseas Filipino workers ahead of the Christmas holiday. 

     There are also continued expectations in the market that 

 the central bank will further lower overnight rates before 

 Christmas provided inflation remains subdued. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht rose to 44.00 overnight but failed to break the



key psychological level due to fears of central bank

intervention and dollar bargain hunting.



    But dealers said they had not heard of any intervention


during London and New York trading. Foreign names from


Singapore remained major buyers of the baht.



    The baht has risen steadily since October 25 and is still



trapped in the dollar's downtrend channel, indicating further



gains are possible.



    The one-month forward rate was quoted at 6/8 satang per



dollar in the offshore market and 2/2.5 satang onshore. The gap



between offshore and onshore rates was caused by the central



bank's regulations which restrict the amount of baht flowing



into overseas markets.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah shuffled around just below 10,400, relieved by



diminishing local corporate dollar demand.



The currency had little to cheer about. The government



posted on Tuesday a 16.5 trillion rupiah budget deficit for the



first 10 months of the year. While analysts say it might not



get worse, they added it was no cause for celebration as the



target was hit because of the reduction of much-needed



development spending.



The government is scrambling to plug its budget deficit, an



issue which has been a sore point between Jakarta and its



donors and lenders who have been frustrated by the slow pace of



reforms and privatisation.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar rose from its closing level on Tuesday of



34.468, though the market was slightly confused by which lead



to follow.



On the positive side, the yen was firmer. But the yen's



firmness was due to a dip in U.S. consumer confidence, which



has negative implications for Taiwan's exports.



A gain in the cabinet-level Council of Economic Planning



and Development's index of leading indicators rose in October



was another plus point.



Traders said another factor was market perception that the


central bank was unlikely to allow the Taiwan dollar to venture



far, especially ahead of key parliamentary elections.

title: FX  Asia: MAS May Put Brakes On Singapore Dollar Skid
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Singapore's economy is looking decidedly weak - indeed, the government thinks this year could see the nation's worst economic performance since independence in 1965. 

 So is this a good time to sell the local dollar? Even at 11-year lows the Singapore currency arguably has room to weaken further. After all, this country's economy relies heavily on earnings from exports, which are as vulnerable as ever amid the global economic and security uncertainty. 

 A weaker currency might ameliorate the problem to some extent. 

 There's just one problem: The Monetary Authority of Singapore probably doesn't feel all that inclined to let the currency slide much further. Many analysts suspect the local dollar has neared the limit - undisclosed by MAS - where central bank intervention becomes ever more likely. 

 The MAS allows the local currency to trade against a basket of currencies of major trading partners within a band. The list of currencies that make up the basket is confidential, although it isn't difficult to imagine that the dollar, euro and yen are the major components. 

 Far more difficult is gauging the boundaries of the band - also a closely guarded secret. 

 A major pastime of currency analysts here is to make educated estimates about the band's perimeters. 

 Earlier this week, as the U.S. dollar shot through key psychological resistance at S$1.8400 en route to an 11-year high of S$1.8430, the MAS remained sidelined, offering little opposition, verbal or otherwise, to the move. 

 Based on that, many now estimate that the top of band lies somewhere between S$1.8450 and S$1.8500, but no one really has more than a hunch. 

 Around 0700 GMT (2:00 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.8367, after having retraced somewhat on fears of MAS intervention. 

 As ever, planning foreign exchange strategy here requires powers of deduction worthy of Sherlock Holmes. 

 The latest round of Singapore dollar declines comes after the MAS announced last month that it would widen the trading band to cope with expected increased volatility in the wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. and the ensuing conflict in Afghanistan. 

 Analysts took the wider band to mean that MAS would allow the currency to weaken a bit more than previously was the case. 

 The last time the MAS is believed to have aggressively intervened was in July, halting the Singapore dollar slide at its previous 11-year low of S$1.8398. That was before the band was widened. 

 Based on this information, analysts say the upper tier of the newly widened band probably isn't much higher for the U.S. dollar than current levels. 

 "Even if you widen the band by 1.5 percentage points (on each side of the pivot point), you'll be looking at S$1.8460-70 as the limits. This is purely a 'guesstimate,' but anything higher than S$1.8450 could mean the limits of the band," said Jimmy Koh, head Of treasury research at United Overseas Bank Ltd. 

 Stealth is crucial for MAS. Ideally, it is uncertainty over the band alone that eventually slows currency moves in either direction. This saves the MAS from having to directly intervene in the market. 

 Irene Cheung, sovereign and currency strategist at ABN-Amro Bank, says she estimates the MAS band's limits to be around S$1.8450-S$1.8500. 

 "We're not far off from there. But as long as they (MAS) don't show their hand we won't know for sure where that band is," Cheung said. 

 Even though many are reluctant to test the resolve of MAS by pushing the U.S. dollar much higher, they aren't eager to sell the U.S. currency either. 

 Most expect MAS to maintain its current neutral monetary policy - inviting neither gains nor losses by the local currency against the basket - until the middle of next year. 

 The next policy review is scheduled in January. 

 The U.S. dollar has been rejuvenated by recent developments in Afghanistan as well as by a slew of highly encouraging economic data which seem to hint the economy may be ready to stabilize soon. 

 The persistently gloomy outlook for the Japanese economy has also boosted the U.S. dollar against its Asian counterparts as Asian currencies tend to take their lead from the yen. 

 "We expect the U.S. dollar to be generally well underpinned going forward especially on further optimism over the U.S. economy and the war on terrorism," DBS Bank Research said recently.

title: Singapore  Dlr Up Late On Fears Of MAS  Intervention

 Around 0836 GMT (3:36 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8381, down from S$1.8427 late Monday when it hit an 11-year low of S$1.8430. It traded in a range between S$1.8370 and S$1.8415.

 A Bank of America report said the U.S. dollar was in a consolidation phase against the local dollar, lacking any fresh trading direction. 

 "Interestingly though, there has again been no indication of central bank interest at these levels, which suggests the latter might not necessarily be uncomfortable with further Singapore dollar weakness," the report said. 

 However, the U.S. dollar is expected to resume its rise in overnight trading in London and New York, as the outlook for the U.S. dollar takes on a more positive tone on hopes the fighting in Afghanistan may be close to an end, dealers said.

title: WRAP:Singapore Dlr Weakens To 11-Yr Low,Testing MAS Band
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The U.S. dollar rose to an 11-year high against the Singapore dollar Monday just days after the government unveiled the latest in a series of grim economic indicators and said the near-term outlook is likely to remain dim. 

 In frenetic afternoon trading, the U.S. currency broke through key resistance at S$1.8398 and pushed all the way up to S$1.8432, last traded in June 1990. Many analysts said the trend toward a rising dollar is likely to continue, with next resistance pegged at S$1.8440 and then again at S$1.8500. 

 Around 1030 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.8432. 

 The Singapore dollar's decline is the result of concerns about deteriorating economic conditions here combined with uncertainty over monetary policy. The Monetary Authority of Singapore revised its monetary stance in July to a position calling for the currency to tread water against a basket of currencies, easing the bias from a policy that previously called for the local currency to strengthen gradually. 

 Last month, the MAS said it's widening the policy band to allow for more flexibility in managing the exchange rate, though the new band continues to be centered on zero percent appriciation of the Singapore dollar against the basket of currencies of its major trading partners. 

 "We have already entered a time of greater volatility in dollar/Sing," said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at Singapore's UOB Group. "The market is still trying to discover the MAS' threshold of tolerance." 

 The apparent lack of any intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore Monday gave credence to market talk that the central bank may be comfortable with a weaker local currency, especially if the yen and the euro continue to weaken. 

 The MAS declined to comment. 

 Indeed, some of the U.S.-dollar buying Monday was a result of the U.S. dollar's strength against the yen, a currency the Singapore dollar often tracks and one of the key components of the basket of currencies the local currency is measured against. 

 The dollar pushed up above Y123 Monday. 

 Many observers believe the MAS hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange markets since announcing, on Oct. 10, its decision to widen the undisclosed band in which it guides the trade-weighted Singapore dollar. At the time, market observers interpreted this move as a sign of tacit approval for a weaker Singapore dollar, which would help support exporters at a time when the city-state is grappling with the worst recession in its 36-year history. 

 In any case, with the MAS having widened its policy band, market participants are more willing to test the limits of the band, dealers said. 

 This is especially true as long as economic data continue to suggest the economy's recession is deepening. 

 Singapore's Ministry of Trade & Industry Friday released detailed third-quarter economic data that confirmed an economic contraction of 5.6%. Ministry officials also said they see no chances of a recovery anytime soon. 

 "Hopes of a recovery by the end of this year have evaporated" following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S., the ministry said. 

 Leading indicators point to further weakness. According to Singapore's trade and industry ministry, its composite leading indicator, which tracks economic activity three quarters ahead, declined 2.8% in the third quarter over the second quarter. The figure was, however, better than the 5.3% decline registered in the second quarter. 

 Business expectations surveys are also dismal. "Both manufacturing and services firms foresee worsening business prospects in the next six months," the ministry said. 

 Under the current economic environment, a weaker currency could be a plus, says Irene Cheung, currency strategist at ABN Amro Bank in Singapore who expects the U.S. dollar to rise to S$1.85 by the year's end.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Off Fresh 11-Year Low Vs US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was sharply weaker late Monday, after hitting fresh 11-year lows against the U.S. dollar following a decline by the yen, dealers said. 

 Around 0820 GMT (3:20 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8427, up from S$1.8361 late Friday. It traded between S$1.8355 and S$1.8430. 

 The U.S. dollar opened lower against the Singapore currency in Asia in very thin trading as the U.S. currency slipped on profit-taking by U.S. investment houses late Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar also showed little reaction to Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's naming of his new Cabinet, including the new Finance Minister, over the weekend. 

 Deputy Prime Minister, and Chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, Lee Hsien Loong, was named Finance Minister in place of Richard Hu. 

 The U.S. dollar then rose on buying by a large local bank and U.S. investment houses in line with its broader gains against the yen, dealers said. 

 ""They've been looking for dips to buy (U.S. dollars) and they started from S$1.8320. I think the U.S. dollar was looking very attractive just now," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The U.S. dollar reached its new 11-year high despite fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene above the key S$1.8398 mark, the previous 11-year high, to smooth out excessive volatility in the foreign exchange market. 

 The last time the U.S. dollar reached that level against the Singapore currency, the central bank was believed to have sold U.S. dollars aggressively in the market to prevent the Singapore dollar from falling too sharply. 

 However, after the MAS widened its policy band last month, market participants are more willing to test the limits of the band, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to rise further against its Asian counterparts, including the Singapore dollar, in overnight trading sessions on a more bullish outlook for the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to face initial resistance at S$1.8440, and next resistance at S$1.8500, with support at S$1.8320. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly higher late Monday, as bargain-hunting pulled prices up from their early morning lows, dealers said. 

 Bonds prices had tumbled earlier tracking falls in U.S. Treasurys late Friday and as planned corporate bond issues continue to cause concerns about oversupply, dealers added. 

 Singapore commuter rail operator SMRT Corp. is the latest company to seek financing through the debt market, having just priced its S$500 million issue earlier. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was down six basis points at 1.66% while the yield on five-year bonds was flat at 2.86%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was down two basis points at 3.17% while the yield on 10-year bonds was down one basis point at 3.55%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was down two basis points at 3.87%.

at 3.40% while the 10-year swap offer closed down three basis points at

The spread between two- and 10-year swaps was steady at 145 basis
points from late Friday.



In the interbank money market, rates were mostly steady although the

title: UPDATE 1-Singapore dollar falls past 1.84/dollar.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar slid past 1.84 to the U.S. dollar on Monday to an 11-year low on the back of a weaker yen, foreign exchange dealers said. 

 This was the lowest level since June 31, 1990 when the currency hit 1.8540. At 1008 GMT the Sing dollar was trading at around 1.8430 to the dollar. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore, the central bank, recently widened the trading band for the Sing dollar in a move the market saw as a tacit acceptance of A weaker currency. 

 Dealers said foreign banks scrambled to buy back the U.S. dollar to cover short positions after the stop near 1.84 was triggered. 

 But they highlighted the risk of central bank intervention if the local currency fell too far too fast because it is out of line with movements of other regional currencies. 

 "We've got lots of dollar buying orders from bank clients but I'm not sure exactly what the orders are linked to. My guess is that people are covering short positions due to a much weaker yen," said a senior dealer at a regional bank. 

 "But I will be very cautious at this point because the Sing dollar is falling at a much faster pace compared with its regional peers," he said. 

 The U.S. dollar hit a three-week high against the yen on Monday because of increasing worries about Japan's banking sector. 

 Dollar bulls were also reassured by progress in the U.S.-led military campaign in Afghanistan, although last week's growing optimism over the U.S. economy was dampened somewhat by grim industrial output figures released on Friday. 

 The Singapore dollar tracks the yen closely because the Japanese currency makes up a big chunk of Singapore's trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 FUNDING VEHICLES 

 Dealers say losses in the Singapore dollar are due partly to the fact that it is being used as a funding vehicle for some currencies, including the won. 

 JP Morgan suggested last week that clients go long of 1-month won/Sing dollar, saying the trade would earn 278 basis points if the dollar/won hits its target of 1,280 to the dollar and the U.S. dollar/Sing dollar hits 1.8350. 

 The rising won ended at 1,284.4 per dollar on Monday. 

 Dealers say the Singapore dollar is also used to fund U.S. dollar holdings due to a market view that the local currency might drop further because of Singapore's weak economic outlook. 

 BOND INTERVENTION? 

 There was also talk that the Sing dollar's declines might have been influenced partly by rumoured government's intervention in the local bond market to bring interest rates lower. 

 Market sources said the MAS might have been in the market to buy the five-year bond following the sell-off of the government bond on Friday, which was caused by moves in the U.S. Treasuries. 

 "It might have been indirectly linked to that although the impact should be very mild," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 "The MAS might have intervened to stave off volatility. But the move doesn't seem to have much of the impact on the money market which has been rather steady," he said.

title: Asia Markets-Korea shines, others flicker.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Korean assets commanded 

 centre-stage on Monday with some analysts voicing increasing 

 optimism over the country's financial markets. 

     Key Asian markets rallied despite a lacklustre Wall Street 

 on Friday on hopes for a U.S. recovery by the second half of 

 next year. The optimism helped boost the dollar's against most 

 regional currencies. 

     The Singapore dollar took a hit and a further reminder of 

 consolidation in banking came with job cuts at Merrill Lynch in 

 Asia. 

     Shares in Seoul closed up 2.55 percent with airline and 

 insurance counters leading the charge. Foreign investors, who 

 have been snapping up local stocks in recent weeks, were also 

 spotted buying stock market futures as well, providing more 

 cheer to the market. 

     The Korean won moved a bit more cautiously, anxious about 

 the weaker yen. Still, analysts have noted a steady uptrend for 

 the currency since October 4, when it touched a low of around 

 1,316 to the dollar. At 0902 GMT, it was quoted around 1,284. 

     The influence of foreign investment in Korean stocks, more 

 than worries about the yen, has held sway over the won. 

      Moreover, with Korean interest rates at four percent and 

 U.S. interest rates at two percent, the rate of return on the 

 won was attractive, traders said. 

     Dealers in Singapore said the market was wary of central 

 bank intervention around the 1,280 level, where they were last 

 suspected of intervening to head off the won's rise. Given 

 still gloomy global economic conditions, some analysts say the 

 authorities want to maintain the country's export 

 competitiveness. 

 But thanks to the resilience of Korea's domestic economy 

 combined with the equity-related inflows, others see the won 

 rising further. 

 "First of all you still have a very strong current account 

 surplus that is going to get even stronger because of the lower 

 oil prices. 

 "On top of that, after September 11, you had about $2.4 

 billion that left the country ... all coming back, and probably 

 more will come back," Dominique Dwor-Frecaut, director of Asia 

 Research at Barclays Capital in Singapore, told Reuters 

 Television. 

     She said the won could hit 1,250 to the dollar, but did not 

 give a time frame. 

     Stock markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and Taiwan also gained 

 ground thanks to rising hopes over the U.S. economy. 

     SINGAPORE DOLLAR SUFFERS 

     However, cheer that the U.S. economy would rebound next 

 year hobbled the other Asian currencies. 

     The Singapore dollar suffered the day's worst losses, 

 falling past the 1.84 level on the back of the weaker yen. 

     The currency has not seen levels past 1.84 since June 30, 

 1990, when it hit 1.8540, Reuters data show. 

     Dealers said a major U.S. bank was spotted actively buying 

 the dollar throughout the day. Others added the Sing dollar's 

 fall was caused when the authorities came into the government 

 securities market to buy bonds, keeping interest rates low. 

 Daily charts show the Sing dollar has been on a sharp 

 downtrend since September 17, shedding nearly six percent to 

 its current levels. 

 Analysts say the currency has been undermined by the 

 city-state's grim economic outlook, which many believed spurred 

 the Monetary Authority of Singapore to widen its neutral policy 

 band for the trade-weighted Singapore dollar recently. 

 The authorities use the trade-weighted Singapore dollar as 

 their main monetary policy tool because of the open nature of 

 the economy. Analysts say nearly 70 percent of the country's 

 gross domestic product comes from exports. 

 Confirming the dismal forecasts, government officials have 

 said repeatedly that the economy is unlikely to recover until 

 the second half of next year. 

 MERRILL LYNCH LAYS OFF STAFF 

 Singapore was not the only one in Asia feeling the pinch 

 from the global economic downturn. 

 U.S. investment banking giant Merrill Lynch has cut about 

 25 investment banking staff in Asia and will move its Asia 

 Pacific chief operating officer Ausaf Abbas to Japan following 

 the departure of two senior executives there, sources familiar 

 with the situation told Reuters. 

 On Friday, Merrill's New York office said around 2,600 

 employees, or nearly four percent of its workforce, had 

 accepted buyout packages. 

 Merrill is the latest U.S. brokerage house to have reduced 

 its staff in Asia. Salomon Smith Barney was expected to begin 

 cutting staff in its global investment banking division on 

 Tuesday, a person in the company's Hong Kong office said on 

 Friday.

title: Emerging  FX -Pare gains, dlr recovers from NY crash.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies pared gains 

 in early trade on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar, which had been 

 roiled by the crash of a passenger plane in New York, regained 

 some lost ground after it became clear the crash was likely an 

 accident. 

     The dollar/yen, closely tracked by the regional currencies, 

 had been sold down to its one-month low of 119.73 before it 

 crawled back above 120 during Asian trading as the incident 

 rekindled the horror of the September 11 attacks . 

     The American Airlines passenger jet, which was leaving New 

 York for Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, nose-dived 

 into residential homes in Queens shortly after takeoff from New 

 York's Kennedy Airport, killing up to 268 people. 

     There was no immediate indication of the crash's cause. 

     Otherwise, the regional currencies lacked a clear 

 direction, with players looking to local leads for trading 

 ideas. 

     The Indonesian rupiah was clouded by fears of fresh 

 violence in the eastern province of Irian Jaya following the 

 weekend killing of a rebel leader there. 

     The Thai baht defied the central bank's dollar buying 

intervention, drawing support from strong capital inflows 

 linked to a new share issue and stop-loss dollar sales. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah sank past 10,700 in early trade as jittery



corporate players continued to snap up the U.S. currency for



debt repayment due to fears of violence in Irian Jaya.



    A leading human rights group in Indonesia demanded an



inquiry, saying the death of a prominent Papua separatist



leader Theys Eluay was a well-orchestrated assasination.



    The concerns overshadowed optimism on fresh fund



disbursement from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).



    Finance Minister Boediono said on Monday he was optimistic



the IMF would disburse a new US$400 million loan to the country



this year.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Sing dollar was locked in a narrow range, with players



busy squaring positions ahead of a public and market holiday.



    Financial markets in Singapore will be close on Wednesday



for a national holiday and will reopen on Thursday.



    Dealers said some American names were buying back U.S.



dollars after they oversold the currency overnight in response



to the New York crash.



    The market awaits October trade statistics due on Friday.



Most players are keeping a low profile and carry only small



positions on books as annual book closing nears.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht retained its firm tone despite the central bank's



active dollar-buying intervention as foreign investors poured



in cash to buy shares of state-owned energy company the



Petroleum Authority of Thailand which will launch its IPO later



this week.



Dealers in Bangkok said the Bank of Thailand has been in



the market to curb the baht's rapid appreciation since Monday



from 44.45.



Despite the central bank intervention, the dollar/baht is



unlikely to rise above 44.55 in the near-term as the level



represents the 38.2 percent retracement of the pair's October



25-November 13 downmove.



KOREAN WON -2



The won drifted lower, disheartened by foreign investor's



selling of local stocks.



Dealers in Singapore said early losses in the local stocks



and heavy selling by foreign equity investors prompted currency


players to cover their short dollar positions.



The market was already cautious to the won's recent gains



following suspected dollar-buying intervention by the central



bank last Friday after it hit a high of 1,280.2, level not seen



since November 4.



Foreign investors were net sellers of 6.3 billion won worth



of local stocks early Tuesday. They bought a net 11 billion won



worth of local stocks on Monday, the eighth straight session



foreign investors had been net buyers.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar held steady early on, but dealers in


Singapore expected Monday's dollar-buying intervention by the


central bank and net selling of local stocks by foreign



investors to weigh down the currency.



Foreign investors were net sellers of 760.6 million Taiwan



dollars worth of local shares on Monday, after selling a net



332.9 million on Friday.



The central bank in recent sessions had repeatedly


intervened on either side to keep the Taiwan dollar from



straying far from the 34.50 level to protect its export



competitiveness.



Economists forecast third-quarter gross domestic product



(GDP) to shrink by an average of 4.27 percent on the year. The



government is due to issue the figures on Friday.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso edged lower on a lack of foreign exchange inflows



that dashed hopes of a steady rise in remittances from overseas



workers.



Suspected central bank intervention on Monday as the peso



slipped to a low of 52.10 would keep players from pushing the



peso too much too fast.



    However, dealers said local corporates fearing the peso may



slide lower were looking to buy dollars around the 52 level.
