title: Emerging  FX  - Holding ground, eye yen, c.banks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies held 

 their ground early Monday backed by a steady yen and on 

 expectations of subdued trade because of a holiday in the 

 United States. 

     Fears of intervention by Japanese authorities were expected 

 to cap the yen's gains, but analysts said market was short of 

 yen especially against the euro , limiting its downside. 

     With Wall Street's moderate gains on Friday, foreign 

 investors may continue to purchase equities in Korea and 

 Taiwan, supporting the Korean won and Taiwan dollar. 

     But suspected dollar buying by the central Bank of Korea on 

 Friday, to protect the won's export competitiveness, could 

 limit further gains. Similar intervention by Taiwan's central 

 bank was likely to keep Taiwan dollar's gains in check. 

     Southeast Asian currencies see the Singapore dollar likely 

 to stay pressured from the Asian Development Bank's report 

 saying Singapore's central bank needs to keep the exchange rate 

 weak. 

     The Thai baht was expected to follow the lead of the 

 Singapore dollar, while the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine 

 peso would focus on their domestic economic and political woes. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won was slightly lower as players covered their short



dollar positions after Friday's suspected intervention.



    Dealers in Singapore said the market was caught by surprise



as a state-run bank bought dollars halting the appreciation of



the won, which hit a high of 1,280.2 on Friday, not seen since



November 4 when it rose to a high of 1,278.5.



    The won's rise has been backed by equity-related inflows



with foreign investors purchasing a net 206 billion won worth



of local shares on Friday alone. It was the seventh straight



session foreign investors had been net buyers.



    The inflows and a steadier yen were expected to keep the



won's downside limited, the dealers said.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar steadied itself around 1.8250 against



1.8270 late on Friday, with the market unsure which direction



the currency would take.



    To the market's consolation, volatility in the dollar/Sing



has dropped, with charts showing the 10-day close to volatility



settling to levels of around four compared to seven in late



September.



Nevertheless, sentiment was still fragile because of the



city-state's struggling economy. On Friday, the Sing dollar was



bruised by an Asian Development Bank report that suggested the



authorities may have to intervene to weaken the currency given



the grievous state of the economy.



Underlining how badly the economy was doing, a local



newspaper reported over the weekend that Singapore's National



Wages Council may recommend severe wage cuts for the second



time in its 29-year history.



Dealers said a major local bank had been spotted steadily



buying dollars last Friday, and its activity was driving the



market's direction.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah held onto last week's gains, though the bid/ask



spread was unusually wide, indicating a reluctance to trade.



Players were still wary of possible central bank action



following last week's relatively huge intervention by the



authorities after the rupiah stumbled to 11,000.



Still, dealers in Jakarta see the central bank as the only



supplier of dollars. With little prospect of dollar inflows



from foreign investment, the rupiah's ambitions were likely to



be frustrated.



Daily charts showed the rupiah is likely to encounter



resistance around 9,900, which represents the 38.2 percent



Fibonacci retracement of the dollar/rupiah's rise from August



14-November 6.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar was expected to be supported by



equity-linked inflows with further boost to sentiment likely



from the World Trade Organisations's approval of the island's



entry.



Analysts believe the WTO's approval on Sunday, a day after



it welcomed China into the trade body, would increase economic



integration with the mainland which considers Taiwan a renegade



province.



China, despite chilly political relations, has been



Taiwan's major destination of exports and investment in the



past several years.



Dealers in Singapore said Friday's intervention by the


central bank that pulled the Taiwan dollar back to 34.50 from a



high of 34.455 should keep players cautious from seeking any



significants gains on the back of inflows.



THAI BAHT



With no fresh local leads, the baht was expected to keep



its focus on the Singapore dollar and moves in the yen.



Dealers in Singapore said tight baht liquidity and fears of


central bank intervention might keep the baht shy of the 44.50



level, but with the market short of dollars, gains for the baht



would be limited.



    Charts showed the dollar oversold with a reading of 25.90



on the 14-day relative strength index.



    One-month baht forwards were at 3/13 satang per dollar



compared to 6/10 on Friday.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso was bobbing around the 52 level, torn between the



country's poor fundamentals and hopes for dollar remittances.



    Dealers in Manila said the peso could get a hand from



dollar remittances from overseas Filipino workers ahead of



Christmas.



    However, some analysts say remittances for this year might



slow given the global economic downturn and the likelihood that



many overseas workers may have lost their jobs.



    Other analysts say the connection between a stronger peso



and dollar remittances was tenuous.



    The peso was still suffering downward pressure from



domestic economic woes. A local newspaper reported on Monday



that the budget deficit - one of the biggest concerns for the



government - may climb to 161 billion pesos by year-end, above



the target of 145 billion pesos because of the government's



failure to improve tax collection.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Ctrl Bks Cap Won, TWD Gains
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Friday, with intervention by the central banks in South Korea and Taiwan keeping a rein on the continued strengthening of their respective currencies, dealers said. 

 The Japanese yen's overnight bounce gave an added fillip to the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar, both of which have propped up by foreign portfolio inflows in recent weeks. In contrast, their Southeast Asian counterparts had wobbled on economic and geopolitical anxieties. 

 The yen rose as foreign exchange participants sold the euro for the yen. However, the market welcomed the half percentage point cut in interest rates by the European Central Bank Thursday. 

 At 0815 GMT (3:15 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y120.22, above Y119.99 late Thursday in New York. The dollar was at Y121.00 late Thursday in Tokyo. 

 As foreign funds investing in South Korean shares continued to sell dollars, the won extended its recent ascent to end at a nine-week high, dealers said. 

 But the central bank, in an apparent attempt to prevent the U.S. dollar from falling below 1,280 won, bought the U.S. currency, pulling the won - which has appreciated by about 1% in the past week - off its high, dealers said. 

 A state-run bank started to buy dollars when the U.S. currency hit an intraday low of KRW1,280.2; dealers believed the transactions were executed on behalf of the central bank. 

 The dollar finished at KRW1,283.1, lower than KRW1,281.1 Thursday. 

 Foreign investors bought a net KRW206.9 billion in shares Friday, helping to lift the benchmark stock index by 0.7%. 

 Taiwan's central bank signalled its resolve to prevent the local dollar from strengthening past NT$34.500 against the U.S. currency, buying an estimated US$100 million to US$200 million in the market, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at its intraday high of NT$34.500, slightly lower than Thursday's NT$34.510. 

 U.S.-dollar sales by banks and exporters had pushed the New Taiwan dollar to as high as NT$34.455 in the morning session, dealers said. 

 The central bank is widely expected to keep the New Taiwan dollar steady, and manage a gradual appreciation of the currency as the Dec. 1 legislative elections approach, dealers said. 

 But the New Taiwan dollar will likely weaken after the elections to reflect the island state's ailing economic fundamentals, market watchers said. 

 Uninspired by the yen's gains, the Singapore dollar slumped on short-covering of U.S. dollar positions by interbank participants, dealers said. Singapore banks were also believed to be buying U.S. dollars on behalf of corporate clients, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was also roiled by the Asian Development Bank's comments, in a report issued Friday, that the Monetary of Singapore might have to actively prevent the Singapore dollar from appreciating to cushion the slide in the city state's exports, Bank of America said in a note to clients. 

 The U.S. dollar was at S$1.8265, higher than S$1.8169 late Thursday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Sing dollar loses out as most others gain.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies gained 

 more ground on the dollar late on Friday, largely thanks to a 

 stable yen. 

     Only the Singapore dollar was the spoiler, stumbling past 

 the 1.82 level when local banks were spotted buying the 

 greenback on behalf of their corporate clients. 

     Some dealers also cited the Asian Development Bank's report 

 on Singapore that included a suggestion that the authorities 

 may have to weaken the Sing dollar, which it said had remained 

 persistently strong. 

 Overall, though, the ADB's growth forecasts did little to 

 damp the cheer in other regional markets where domestic factors 

 played a large role. 

 While rate cuts boosted hopes of a recovery in Taiwan, the 

 Bank of Korea's decision to keep its overnight call rate steady 

 fueled optimism in the won market that things weren't as bad as 

 they seem. 

 In Bangkok, the market was hopeful of dollar inflows ahead 

 of a share listing by the state oil firm PTT Plc. Even the 

 usually ailing rupiah found consolation as the central bank

 stepped in to intervene on its behalf. 

SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar bucked the regional uptrend, falling 

 past the 1.82 level while local banks bid for the greenback. 

 Dealers, however, said there was nothing unusual about the 

 dollar buying, and the banks were likely covering their short 

 dollar positions ahead of the weekend. Thin liquidity in the 

 market also exaggerated the moves. 

 Some in the market cited the ADB's report that recommended 

 that the authorities should weaken the currency further given 

 the massive decline in exports. Despite the Monetary Authority

 of Singapore's neutral policy stance on the trade-weighted Sing 

 dollar, and its recent move to widen the bands on the 

 trade-weighted Sing dollar, the ADB said it still saw the Sing 

 dollar appreciate in terms of its real exchange rate. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won enjoyed further gains, knowing that a stable won 

 and foreign investors' net purchases of local stocks were there 

 to help it along. 

 Still, its rise was held in check by dollar buying from a 

 state-run bank late in the day, which many believed was on 

 behalf of the authorities. Given Korea's export dependency, 

 analysts say the central bank is keen on keeping the exchange 

 rate competitive, yet stable. 

 After deciding to keep rates steady, the bank said on 

 Thursday the local forex market was likely to remain stable, 

 though it did warn of downside risks in Korea's growth 

 forecast. 

 Indeed, the Finance Minister, Jin Nyum, said the government 

 would lower its growth target for 2002 to four percent from 

 five percent. He also added the government would raise its 2002 

 budget by five trillion won. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar failed to hold onto its earlier gains 

 with the central bank making sure it did not stray too far from 

 the 34.50 level. 

 Still, it did manage to end at a four-month high of 34.50 

 despite the central bank's intervention. The Taiwan dollar has 

 been stuck in increasingly narrow ranges for the past several 

 months. 

 Dollar-selling on the non-deliverable forward market drove 

 the local dollar higher on the spot market, though the central 

 bank waded in to buy dollars. 

 Analysts say given Taiwan's poor economic prospects, the 

central bank is intent on keeping the rate stable to maintain 

 export competitiveness. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso held a narrow range around the 51.75 per dollar as 

 remittances from overseas workers outstripped demand for the 

 dollar. 

 But players were reluctant to push the peso too much either 

 way on talk of dollar bids lined up at around 51.60 level, 

 dealers in Manila said. 

 Doubts that the seasonal remittances, received annually 

 ahead of Christmas, would be lower than previous years also 

 held back most players from taking short dollar positions. 

     But on the downside dealers believe the central bank would 

 defend the peso at around 51.80 level. 

     The ADB expected GDP to grow at 2.7 percent in 2001, down 

 from an April forecast of 3.1 percent because of a 

 steeper-than-expected global slowdown. The government has a 

 target of 3.3 percent for 2001. 

     The ADB said growth in 2002 was expected at 3.0 percent, 

 down from a prediction in April of 4.2 percent. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht was stuck in a tight range around 44.50 supported



by expected buying of Petroleum Authority of Thailand's stock



offering by foreign equity investors.



    PTT is expected to raise up to 32 billion baht (US$719)



from its IPO by offering up to 920 million shares to the public



at 31-35 each during November 15-21.



    Dealers in Singapore said local corporate demand for the



dollar capped the baht's upside, while easing baht funding cost



in the offshore forward market also slowdown dollar sales by



offshore players.



    The one-month forward rate was steady at 6/10 satang per



dollar compared with 10/15 earlier this week.



    On the economic front, the government Thailand said it was



putting together a major package of measures, including tax



incentives, to lure foreign investors and encourage



multinational companies to set up regional headquarters in the



country.



Thai Deputy Prime Minister Somkid Jatusripitak told Reuters



the package would be ready in the next couple of months and



could be announced as early as January.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah firmed up to touch a session high of 10,340 on



repeated dollar sales by state-run banks which dealers in



Jakarta believed was on behalf of the central bank.



They estimated the central bank, Bank Indonesia, through



the state banks may have sold up to $20 million with total



turnover reaching slightly above $100 million near the close of



the day.



The rupiah was further supported by stop-loss dollar sales



triggered at around 10,400. But local corporates were seen



buying dollars around 10,350 capping further gains.



But overall most corporates were on the sidelines expecting



more donor aid commitments, after Thursday's $3.73 billion



pledged by the Consultative Group on Indonesia.



An International Monetary Fund mission is in Jakarta while



the talks with the Paris Club of donor nations are due next



week.



Indonesia's bank restructuring agency said it was



optimistic the sale of 51 percent stake of the country's



largest retail bank, Bank Central Asia, would go through by the



end of 2001 as planned.

title: CORRECTED-Emerging  FX -Up on firmer yen, Manila cuts rates.
text:
In Singapore datelined story with headline ...Emerging 

FX-Up on firmer yen; Seoul, Manila cut rates...please read in 

 the headline...Emerging FX-Up on firmer yen, Manila cuts 

 rates...(Removing erroneous reference in headline to rate cut 

 in Seoul). A corrected repetition follows. 

     SINGAPORE, Nov 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were higher 

 in late trade on Thursday, riding on the yen's coat-tails as 

 the U.S. currency retreated on the back of option-related 

 selling. 

 But the yen's gains were limited by fresh concerns over 

 Japan's banking system after shares in Asahi Bank and 

 Daiwa Bank - due to merge to form the country's fifth 

 largest banking group - plunged to new lows for the year, 

 sparking rumours the merger was failing. 

     Asahi later issued a statement saying the merger was still 

 on the cards. 

     Elsewhere, the Philippines' central bank cut overnight 

 interest rates by half a percentage point on Thursday, 

 exceeding market expectations of 25 basis points. 

     Governor Rafael Buenaventura said further cuts were likely 

 before the end of the year as inflation was likely to stay tame 

 and the U.S. Federal Reserve was likely to make more cuts. 

     The Bank of Korea, on the other hand, kept its key interest 

 rate target steady in November at a meeting on Thursday, but 

 economists speculated its next easing could be as early as 

 December. 

 It last cut rates by 50 basis points in late September. 

 Despite its patchy reforms, Indonesia managed to convince 

 donors to loosen their purse strings and pledge a fresh fund of 

 more than $3.5 billion for next year. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah held steady at around 10,500, in muted response 

 to a pledge of a fresh injection of $3.14 billion and $586 

 million by international donors because the news was largely 

 priced in. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said with an International Monetary Fund 

 mission still in the capital and debt negotiations with the 

 Paris Club of donor nations due next week, players would tend 

 to refrain from taking fresh positions. 

 The Consultative Group on Indonesia approved the aid 

 package but underscoring growing wariness over the government's 

 foot-dragging on economic reforms, the World Bank said $1.3 

 billion was conditional on a major boost in policy 

 implementation. 

 The chief dealer of a U.S. bank in Jakarta said the two-day 

 meeting in which Jakarta was repeatedly criticised by the 

 donors for failing to make progress on reforms would keep 

 overall sentiment glum. 

 Dealers said local corporate demand for the dollar was 

 still strong within a 10,450-10,500 range, but an upward breach 

 of 10,450 could push the rupiah up to levels around 

 10,250-10,300. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar failed to break free from its shackles, 

 and closed below 34.50 when the central bank stepped in to keep 

 it in line. 

 It spent much of the session above that level, hitting 

 34.42 for the first time since September 19 as hopes rose for 

 the island's maligned economy. 

 The market rallied around the Taiwan dollar after trade 

 data, which still recorded falls, came in better than expected 

 late on Wednesday. The currency also got an unexpected boost 

 from the central bank's 25 basis point cut in key rates. 

 Usually, a currency will be hurt by interest rate cuts 

 because of fears of capital outflows due to lower rates of 

 return. 

 However, because growth has been the main concern in Taiwan 

 and other parts of the region, the market was hoping the rate 

 cut would help spur the economy. 

 Dealers in Singapore said players had expected the central 

 bank to intervene on the U.S. dollar's behalf around 34.50, 

 which it has done in recent sessions. However, when the bank 

 failed to do so in early trade, the market quickly began 

 unwinding its long dollar positions. 

 They added the bank later bought the greenback around 

 34.42, and then more aggressively towards the end of the day. 

 The bank has been keeping the rate stable in order to hold on 

 to export competitiveness and keep domestic confidence intact. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar failed to hold onto its earlier gains 

 with the market covering its short U.S. dollar positions after 

 a major local bank was spotted buying. 

 Otherwise, dealers said trading was unremarkable, and there 

 was little talk attached to the dollar buying by the local bank 

 for now. 

 Stop-loss dollar buy orders were triggered when the 

 greenback rose above 1.8130 after languishing around levels of 

 1.8120 in early Asian trade. 

 The local dollar found some consolation in Singapore 

 Telecommunications' announcement that it would issue $1.5 

 billion in bonds, though the details of the issue are not 

 known. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won rose to an eight-week high after the Bank of Korea 

 announced it was keeping rates steady and expressed guarded 

 optimism about the economy. 

 The bank's Governor Chon Chol-hwan said he expected two 

 percent growth in the economy in the fourth quarter on the 

 year, and noted recent signs of improvement in the Korean 

 economy. 

 Still, he warned there were still near-term risks to 

 growth, and many analysts stuck by their predictions that the 

central bank will cut rates by at least 25 basis points in the 

 short term. 

 Nevertheless, the won's mood was buoyant, and continued 

 strong buying of local stocks by foreign investors also lifted 

 its spirits. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso rose on the back of remittances from overseas 

 workers to touch a session high of 51.74 where dollar bids from 

 importers and corporates capped further gains. 

 The central bank slashed key overnight interest rates by 

 half a percentage point, taking the borrowing rate to 8.25 

 percent and the lending rate to 10.5 percent. 

 Governor Rafael Buenaventura further cuts were possible 

 before the end of the year as inflationary pressure was 

 subsiding. He added that annual inflation was likely to be 

 below five percent in both November and December, falling from 

 a 12-month low of 5.4 percent in October. 

 With the rate cut already factored in, the peso showed 

 little response. The central bank said it was also 

 re-introducing a tiering scheme for overnight borrowing to 

 encourage banks to seek returns in government paper. 

 The scheme was withdrawn in August because of fears the 

 funds were being used to speculate against the peso. Seasonal 

 inflow of remittances ahead of Christmas has raised 

 expectations of the peso holding steady for sometime.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late; GDP Gives US Dlr Respite
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies wobbled in thin trading late Thursday, as the U.S. dollar found some respite from a smaller-than-expected contraction in the U.S. economy in the third quarter, dealers said. 

 The U.S. economy shrank at an annualized rate of 0.4% during the July-September period; economists had forecast a contraction of 1%. It was the first time since 1993 that the U.S. has experienced a quarterly economic contraction. 

 Anxieties ahead of the announcement of key U.S. economic data had restrained U.S. dollar bulls earlier this week, providing a floor to the region's currencies. 

 The slightly better-than-expected data revived the market's appetite for U.S. dollars, dealers said. 

 Trading volume in Asia's foreign exchange markets was thin, as activity started to show signs of slowing ahead of the year end, said a dealer a European bank. 

 As the honeymoon for Indonesian President Megawati Sukarnoputri came to an end, the local currency briefly floundered past 10,600 rupiah per U.S. dollar earlier in the day, its weakest level since the leader took office on July 23. 

 Just over 100 days into her rule, Megawati admitted Thursday in her address to the People's Consultative Assembly - the country's highest legislative body - that her government has achieved little since it was formed. 

 She also said the government's ability to repay its debt "has come close to a dangerous point." 

 But she didn't offer any concrete solutions, analysts noted. 

 The rupiah had soared by as much as 30% in the immediate weeks after Megawati came to power. Megawati formed a market-friendly cabinet, appointing a slew of technocrats to key ministerial positions, as she signaled her resolve to press ahead with economic reforms. 

 "Megawati's progress report was surprisingly negative," said Bank of America in a note to clients. 

 Still, a Jakarta-based dealer at a large European bank said the rupiah has priced-in the market's frustrations over her government's slow progress. 

 At 0940 GMT (4:40 a.m. EST), the rupiah had regained some of its footing to trade at IDR10,545, after sliding to as low as IDR10,640 earlier. 

 The central bank sold some U.S. dollars to stave off the pressure on the rupiah, "but it was not much - $10 million tops," said a Jakarta-based dealer at a European bank. 

 He added that the U.S. dollar was going through a downward correction, with interbank participants "very long" in the currency and customers showing little interest in buying U.S. dollars above IDR10,600. 

 Although market participants expect the U.S. dollar to trend higher toward IDR11,000 in the near term, the U.S. currency will likely first extend its downward correction to IDR10,400-IDR10,450, the dealer said. 

 The rupiah's fall added to the pressure on the Singapore dollar, which already hurting from the market's renewed appetite for the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Some dealers also blamed the Singapore dollar's weakness on market talk that Singapore Telecommunications Ltd. may have bought U.S. dollars to pay for its US$601 million purchase of a 22.3% stake in Indonesia's Telkomsel from Dutch telecommunications company Royal KPN. 

 Around 1000 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8272, higher than S$1.8166 late Wednesday. 

 Some dealers suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened late Wednesday to curb the appreciation of the local currency, helping set the firmer tone for the U.S. dollar Thursday. 

 Pressured by the regional currency slump, the Thai unit weakened to 44.705 baht per U.S. dollar, compared with THB44.685 late Wednesday. 

 In Seoul, U.S. dollar demand by offshore participants sparked short-covering in the U.S. currency, weighing on the South Korean won, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar finished at 1,298.0 won, up from KRW1,296.10 Wednesday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed steady amid lackluster trading, with the central bank slowing down in its intervention, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.529, little changed from Wednesday's close of NT$34.525. 

 Philippine markets were closed Thursday for a long religious holiday, and will re-open Monday.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late Vs US Dlr But Remains Pressured
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was steady against the U.S. dollar late Friday, but remained pressured by poor economic data and broad U.S. dollar strength. 

 At 0800 GMT (4:00 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8273, little changed from S$1.8274 late Thursday in Asia. It traded in a S$1.8238-S$1.8285 range Friday. 

 The Singapore dollar opened around S$1.8238 per U.S. dollar in Asia, down from its overnight high of S$1.8175 in New York. 

 The Singapore dollar's gains overnight was due to the U.S. dollar's blip lower on position adjustments, dealers said. Sentiment for the local currency remains fragile, they added. 

 Data published Friday showed Singapore's industrial output dived 22.3% on year in September, worsening from a 21.1% contraction in August. 

 Although the figure was slightly better than analysts' expectations generally, some players sold the Singapore dollar on the data. 

 The sharp fall in industrial production drew further attention to the country's exposure to the global slowdown, particularly the slackening in demand for electronics, a key export for Singapore, dealers said. 

 U.S. investment houses and local banks were selling the Singapore dollar, they added. 

 However, the Singapore dollar's losses against the U.S. dollar were limited by pre-weekend consolidation and central bank fears. 

 Dealers noted caution in the market as the Singapore dollar slipped to S$1.8285 against the U.S. dollar, amid rumors the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene near the local currency's intraday low, dealers said. 

 Nevertheless, dealers said sentiment toward the U.S. dollar remains strong, and it is likely to drift higher against the Singapore dollar overnight and early next week. 

 The Singapore dollar is expected to be supported at S$1.8300 against the U.S. currency and resisted at S$1.8200, according to dealers. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly higher, tracking U.S. Treasurys' gains overnight, and as local interbank rates stay pressured, dealers said. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was seven basis points lower at 1.67% as the newest issue of bonds, maturing February 2004, started trading, dealers said. The February 2004 bonds were auctioned at an average yield of 1.74% Thursday. 

 The yield on five-year bonds was down eight basis points at 2.55%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was down six basis points at 2.83% while the yield on 10-year bonds was down five basis points at 3.17%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was two basis points lower at 3.63%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web Site: 

http://www.mas.gov.sg/sgs("http://www.mas.gov.sg/sgs")


In the interest rate swaps market, swaps were mostly lower tracking
local bond yields.



The most liquid seven-year swap offer closed down five basis points at
2.96% while the 10-year swap offer also closed five basis points lower
at 3.26%.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late Vs US Dlr But Remains Pressured
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was steady against the U.S. dollar late Friday, but remained pressured by poor economic data and broad U.S. dollar strength. 

 At 0800 GMT (4:00 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8273, little changed from S$1.8274 late Thursday in Asia. It traded in a S$1.8238-S$1.8285 range Friday. 

 The Singapore dollar opened around S$1.8238 per U.S. dollar in Asia, down from its overnight high of S$1.8175 in New York. 

 The Singapore dollar's gains overnight was due to the U.S. dollar's blip lower on position adjustments, dealers said. Sentiment for the local currency remains fragile, they added. 

 Data published Friday showed Singapore's industrial output dived 22.3% on year in September, worsening from a 21.1% contraction in August. 

 Although the figure was slightly better than analysts' expectations generally, some players sold the Singapore dollar on the data. 

 The sharp fall in industrial production drew further attention to the country's exposure to the global slowdown, particularly the slackening in demand for electronics, a key export for Singapore, dealers said. 

 U.S. investment houses and local banks were selling the Singapore dollar, they added. 

 However, the Singapore dollar's losses against the U.S. dollar were limited by pre-weekend consolidation and central bank fears. 

 Dealers noted caution in the market as the Singapore dollar slipped to S$1.8285 against the U.S. dollar, amid rumors the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene near the local currency's intraday low, dealers said. 

 Nevertheless, dealers said sentiment toward the U.S. dollar remains strong, and it is likely to drift higher against the Singapore dollar overnight and early next week. 

 The Singapore dollar is expected to be supported at S$1.8300 against the U.S. currency and resisted at S$1.8200, according to dealers.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late On Yen; SGD Hardest Hit
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies floundered late Thursday as the yen slumped past Y123 to the dollar, and concerns over the region's deteriorating fundamentals continued to loom in the background, dealers said. 

 The South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar largely held their own, as persistent foreign equity fund inflows into their respective stock markets negated the pressure from the yen, dealers said. 

 At 0853 GMT (3:53 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y123.26, above Y122.90 late Wednesday in New York. The dollar was at Y122.60 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 "The market is still keen to buy dollars on any dip, in tandem with the global dollar picture," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The Singapore dollar was the hardest hit in Asia, temporarily sinking past S$1.8300 against its U.S. counterpart to hit an intraday low of S$1.8325 in earlier trading - its weakest level since July 19. 

 The weaker yen, euro and rupiah led participants to again probe the boundaries of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's widened policy band, pushing the local currency lower, dealers said. 

 Jitters surrounding the Nov. 3 general election - to be held in the midst of the city-state's worst recession in its 36-year history - had also cast a shadow on the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's announcement Thursday that Finance Minister Richard Hu will retire and won't stand for the coming election provided participants with an added "excuse" to sell down the local currency, said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 Still, policy continuity will likely be assured, as Health Minister Lim Hng Kiang, who's also second minister for finance, is widely expected to take over Hu's position. 

 When it became clear that the long-ruling People's Action Party, or PAP, was returned to power when nominations closed Thursday, the Singapore dollar recovered with the U.S. unit falling below the S$1.8300 level, dealers said. Opposition parties named candidates for just 29 of 84 seats in Parliament. 

 Fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore also helped the local currency regain its footing, dealers said. 

 "There were rumors that the authority was checking prices when the U.S. dollar was above S$1.8300," said a senior dealer at a European bank. "That made the market nervous and triggered some long liquidation." 

 But some dealers doubted the veracity of such rumors. 

 "Dollar/yen is at Y123," said a dealer at another European bank. "There's no reason for the MAS to intervene." 

 The market took the cue from a large local bank, which had sold the U.S. dollar when it traded around S$1.8320, dealers said. 

 Late Thursday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.8277, still higher than S$1.8262 late Wednesday, as the market's voracious appetite for the U.S. currency continued to keep it afloat. 

 Intermittent light dollar sales by state banks, believed to be acting on behalf of the Indonesian central bank, mitigated the pressure on the rupiah, which has been bruised by corporate demand for dollars, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at 10,250 rupiah, higher than IDR10,230 late Wednesday. 

 The regional currency slump, month-end corporate demand for dollars and security concerns, sparked by rumors of coup plots against the Philippine government, conspired to send the peso sliding past the psychologically important PHP52 mark to the dollar, dealers said. 

 The peso closed at PHP52.010, its weakest level since Aug. 9, compared with PHP51.945 Wednesday. Volume rose to $100 million from $85.3 million Wednesday. 

 Some dealers said the central bank likely sold as much as $50 million in the morning session, but stopped its dollar sales when it realized it was futile to fight the rising tide of corporate dollar demand. 

 However, central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura denied the monetary authority had intervened Thursday. 

 As it attempted to play catch-up with its weaker regional peers, the Thai currency's technical support at 44.850 baht per dollar finally gave way, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at THB44.880, higher than THB44.765 late Wednesday. 

 North Asian currencies continued to outperform their Southeast Asian peers, as foreign equity funds continued to flood into their respective stock markets, countering the onslaught from the yen, dealers said. 

 Taiwan's central bank bought U.S. dollars to curb the local currency's strength, dealers said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$34.545, unchanged from Wednesday. Dealings were valued at US$273 million. 

 Foreign institutional investors bought a net NT$3.63 billion worth of Taiwanese shares Thursday, the Taiwan Stock Exchange said. 

 In Seoul, the dollar finished at 1,297.0 won, after trading in a tight KRW2-range, marginally higher than KRW1,296.0 Wednesday. 

 Foreign investors bought a net KRW110.8 billion in Korean shares, extending their buying into an 11th straight session.

title: US Dlr Above S$1.83; First Time Since July 23 - Dealers
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar fell through a key support level early Thursday as the U.S. dollar rose above S$1.83 for the first time since July, amid gains by the U.S. unit against major currencies, dealers said. 

 Around 0140 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8308 from S$1.8257 late Wednesday. It has since reached a high of S$1.8313. 

 This is the first time since July 23, that the U.S. dollar has traded above S$1.8300, according to dealers. 

 "Right now all the U.S. names are buying," said a dealer in a Japanese bank. 

 The buying had been triggered by overnight gains in the U.S. dollar against major currencies, especially the yen. 

 However, market participants are treading cautiously at current levels as some fear the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to stabilize any sudden volatility in the local market. 

 Looking ahead, dealers said the overall sentiment remains bullish on the U.S. dollar against most Asian currencies, including the Singapore dollar. 

 Next resistance for the U.S. dollar is expected at S$1.8350, while support is expected at S$1.8270.

title: Emerging  FX -Bow to the dollar, but cautious.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies struggled 

 against a firmer dollar early on Tuesday in cautious trading 

 due to concerns over intervention by central banks, coupled 

 with uncertainties over the anthrax scare and the war in 

 Afghanistan. 

     The Singapore dollar was off but not far from its 

 three-month low of 1.8290 per U.S. dollar touched overnight. 

     Dealers said weighing down the Singapore dollar were 

 factors including speculation over local corporates' overseas 

 investment needs, pessimism over the economic outlook and the 

central bank's new-found tolerance with a weaker currency. 

 However, such tolerance was not expected by central banks 

 in Indonesia, the Philippines, and Taiwan and as such trading 

 interest was likely to be limited and ranges narrow in the 

 rupiah, peso and the Taiwan dollar. 

 Wariness over central bank policy is no less in Thailand, 

 but markets there will be closed Tuesday for the Chulalongkorn 

 Day. 

 Uncertainty surrounding the impact on the dollar from a 

 widening anthrax scare in the United States and the war in 

 Afghanistan, now in its third week, would also deter players 

 from seeking too much weakness in most regionals. 

 The frail yen, hit by gloomy industrial production data 

 seen as a proxy for the gross domestic product, would hurt 

 sentiment in the North Asian currencies. But the won and Taiwan 

 dollar might find some support in the Wall Street's rally 

 overnight. 

 In early Tokyo trading, the dollar held firm and was just 

 shy of its overnight highs against the yen, levels last seen in 

 mid-August. The euro was also off overnight lows but was 

 seen struggling due to growing pessimism over the German 

 economy. 

 Six leading economic institutions on Monday slashed their 

 2001 growth forecasts for Germany saying the euro zone's 

 largest economy was on the verge of recession. 

 Taiwan will release September jobless rate at 0300 GMT and 

 Singapore and Hong Kong will issue September consumer prices 

 data. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 Volatility marked the Singapore dollar's early trade as 

 funds speculating on its downside struggled against 

 profit-takers in dollars. 

 Dealers said with the dollar strengthening against both the 

 yen and the euro, the Singapore dollar was expected to stay 

 under selling pressure and could test the 1.8300 psychological 

 barrier. 

 The yen and euro are among the major components of the 

 trade-weighted basket of currencies used by the Monetary 

 Authority of Singapore to manage the exchange rate. 

 Analysts said a significantly weaker inflation number would 

 further raise expectations of a weaker currency. The consumer 

 price index in August rose 0.7 percent on the year, against 1.3 

 percent in July. 

 Trading range for the day was expected to be 1.8250-1.8300. 

 Charts showed the dollar in overbought territory with a reading 

 of 79.44 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 THAI BAHT 

 With local markets closed the baht held onto its recent 

 range of 44.65-44.80 in light offshore trade, impervious to the 

 weaker Sing dollar. 

 Dealers in Singapore said offshore players had shown little 

 interest in the baht after the Thai central bank implemented 

 stricter reporting rules on forex transactions. Their view was 

 that the bank could slap on more severe restrictions on trade. 

     And while the onshore market was still fairly liquid, 

 dealers said little speculative activity had been going on. 

     That said, dealers in Bangkok noted the baht had been 

 unable to strengthen much because many in the market were 

 anxious about the Thai economy's prospects. 


     TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar remained true to its sedentary ways of



the past month or so, with volumes in the market shrinking



steadily.



    Despite the island's struggling economy, the currency has



stabilised thanks to the central bank's determination to keep



it in line. Faced with a bank that boasts $115 billion in



reserves, many players have decided to sit on the sidelines for



the time being.



Still, the government was expected to issue more poor



economic data later in the day. The statistics bureau will



announce September's unemployment rate at 0300 GMT.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped to 51.80, though the central bank quickly



stepped into the market to prevent the peso from falling



further.



Turnover on the Philippine Dealing System has been



dwindling with players becoming increasingly frustrated by the



lack of flows and the central bank's dogged attempts to keep



the peso from slipping past 51.80.



With the Christmas season approaching, dealers in Manila



were expecting an increase in dollar remittances from overseas



workers, which should boost the peso. However, the market was



still perturbed by the Philippines' economic prospects.



The government conceded over the weekend that it might not



be able to sell its 10 percent stake in power firm Meralco by



the end of the year as planned. Analysts say this could make it



difficult for the government to reach its privatisation target



this year, which could widen the already large budget deficit.



KOREAN WON -2



The won softened in early trade with the market focusing on



the yen's weakness but a firm opening at the local stock market



was expected to cap the downside.



Dealers in Singapore said with the yen looking vulnerable



to more downside and with little hopes of a quick recovery in



domestic growth and exports the won was likely to probe weaker



levels in coming days.



An analyst at a U.S. bank said with the won now trading



below the 1,300-level, a test of 1,310 was possible on further



weakness of the yen.



To cushion the impact of the downturn, Seoul will unveil a



supplementary budget of $1.4 billion which comes on top of five



trillion won worth of extra spending already in the pipeline.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah was weighed down by local corporate demand for



dollars around the 10,000-level but fears of central bank

intervention kept the downside limited.



Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was expected to



step into the market to defend the 10,200-level. But a breach



of what has now become a psychological support level could



spark a steep fall of the rupiah, they added.



    The dollar was on the edge of the overbought territory with



a reading of 70.68 on the 14-day relative strength index.



    Worries about domestic political stability amid growing



anti-American sentiment against U.S. military action in



Afghanistan would also keep the players cautious.

title: Emerging  FX  - Better off being ignored.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies kept 

 modest gains late on Monday, though their composure was more 

 due to dimming trading interest rather than any change to the 

 region's economic health. 

     With uncertainty abounding in geopolitics as well as in the 

 global economy, more and more players have been favouring the 

 sidelines, dealers said. 

     Besides, investors were hardly likely to plunge into the 

 regional markets given how quiet the major currencies were. The 

 dollar barely budged from 121.00 yen the entire session as 

 concerns over anthrax reports in the United States were 

 balanced by wariness over possible Japanese intervention. 

     Low volumes plagued the Singapore dollar, which spent the 

 day swinging in a range of 1.8140-1.8225, ending near the low 

 end as some dealers took profits on recent hefty gains. 

     The market is eyeing Wednesday's release of non-oil 

 domestic exports for September which are expected to make grim 

 reading given how badly hit Singapore has been by the 

 electronics slowdown and the attacks on the U.S. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar managed to crawl back to the right



side 1.8200, taking heart from abating U.S. dollar bids.



    Dealers said a local bank that had been a big Sing$ seller



last week, so playing a leading role in its dive to 10-week



lows, had been quiet today. The let-upo in selling prompted a



general round of profit-taking on long U.S. dollar positions



and saw the Sing$ edge to $1.8150.



    Trading was choppy throughout the session, with thin



volumes aggravating the price movements. Many players decided



to hug the sidelines until fresh trading cues emerged.



    Unfortunately, there was little to boast about in the Sing



dollar's prospects with more bad economic news expected later



this week. September non-oil domestic export numbers (NODX) are



due on Wednesday, and a recent Reuters poll showed economists



on average expect NODX to fall by 14.6 percent in 2001.



    The dismal economic outlook has already prompted the


central bank to widen its preferred trading band for the Sing$,



a move which traders took as tacit acceptance of a weaker


currency.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht clawed back more ground as the market continued to



unwind long dollar positions after being caught short on baht



late last week.



    But the baht failed to break a key resistance level of



around 44.55 as players pessimistic about the country's



economic outlook were keen to buy dollar on dips.



    Bangkok dealers also attributed Friday's gains to one-off



maturing options and said the baht's fundamentals all pointed



downwards for the currency.



    They added the market was getting increasingly edgy over



the Bank of Thailand's refusal to lower interest rates. While



lower rates could hurt the baht, dealers and analysts believe



it is a necessary move to help boost Thailand's faltering



economy because it would help corporates refinance bad loans.



    The BOT, however, continued to disappoint their hopes,



steadfastly refusing to lower its benchmark 14-day repo rate



that was hiked by 100 basis points in July. It said earlier in



the day a visiting IMF delegation agreed with its rate policy.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso edged slightly higher in line with other regionals



higher amid paper-thin trading volumes as most players kept



away from the market.



    Dealers in Manila said wariness over intervention by the


central bank, which doggedly defended the 51.80 level last



week, has prompted most corporates and importers to stay out



and avoid getting caught on the wrong foot.



    However, Finance Secretary Jose Camacho accepted it was



difficult to prop up the peso.



    He said it might be difficult for the peso to stabilise at



50 to the dollar by year-end because low foreign exchange


inflows and the global tension following strikes on



Afghanistan.



President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo has said she hoped the



peso would stabilise at 50 to the dollar by the end of the year



after touching a six-month low of 54.70 in July.



Charts showed the dollar/peso overbought with 14-day



relative strength index reading at 76.86, indicating more room



for the dollar to correct downwards.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah idled in a narrow range around 10,000 per



dollar, with the local markets closed for a religious holiday.



Dealers in Singapore said there was no major activity



reported in the offshore spot market or in the Singapore-based



non-deliverable forward market.



    Rupiah's one-month NDF was quoted by a broker at



10,110.0/10,210.0 and three-month at 10,400.0/10,500.0.



    Dealers said rupiah's upside would remain capped by worries



about domestic political stability, with more street protests



reported on Monday following sporadic incidents of harassment



and assault on foreigners and tourists over the weekend.



KOREAN WON -2



A steady stream of foreign equity-linked flows lifted the



won, which closed a touch higher against the dollar to 1,296.9



against 1,299.3 on Friday.



Foregin investors were net buyers of 16 billion won worth



of stocks on Monday, after buying a whopping 500 billion won



worth last week.



Still, dealers said the won's upside was capped by



profit-taking from players nervous about events in Afghanistan



and the United States.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar chalked up miniscule gains to close at



34.549 from Friday's 34.550.



As with the won, the Taiwan dollar was boosted by steady



foreign investment in the local stock market, despite a two



percent drop in the TAIEX on Monday.



But central bank intervention kept the Taiwan dollar in



check. Given the dismal state of Taiwan's export-dependent



economy, the central bank has been actively buying U.S. dollars



in the market to keep the island's competitive edge.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mostly firmer as dollar fumbles.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies

 clambered onto firmer ground early on Monday after the dollar 

 suffered another blow to its confidence from poor economic data 

 and fears of more anthrax cases. 

     The exception was the Singapore dollar which softened again 

 despite being massively oversold following last week's slump to 

 10-week lows. 

     The respite elsewhere could also be cut short since Asia's 

 fortunes are largely tied to the fate of the U.S. economy. Data 

 reported on Friday showed U.S. retail sales fell by 2.4 percent 

 in September, which does not bode well for an economy fueled by 

 consumer spending. 

     And stores in the United States may have a tougher time 

 luring back consumers amid fears of biological warfare after an 

 anthrax case was reported in New York. 

     Toughening the odds for the regional currencies, the yen 

  was not providing much support. Though the dollar 

 wobbled against European currencies, it held its ground against 

 the yen thanks to wariness over intervention by the Bank of 

 Japan. 

SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore lost a battle to hold above $S1.8200 despite



pressure for a U.S. dollar correction, with manuy in the market



suspecting the local authorities want to see the currency lower



for economic reasons.



    Charts do show the dollar/Sing at its most oversold levels



since early July, with a 14-day relative strength index reading



of around 91.



    Dealers said a major local bank that had been bidding



aggressively for U.S. dollars was starting to sell back some of



those dollars. Analysts also warned higher local interest rates



or a stronger rupiah could also support the Sing dollar.



    But the prognosis for the Sing dollar was still poor as the



economy braces for a few more quarters of recession. The



government warned last week that the city-state's economy could



remain in recession during the first half of next year. It also



lowered it full-year 2001 gross domestic product forecast to a



three percent contraction.



    In response to the bleak economic outlook, the Monetary



Authority of Singapore said it was widening its policy band for



the currency, which the market took as tacit acceptance of a



lower currency.



    Dealers said the U.S. dollar was well-supported around



1.81, with many in the market posied to buy the U.S. unit on



dips.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso was expected to follow other regionals higher but



a lack of dollar inflows and economic worries were likely to



keep the rise limited.



    Dealers in Singapore said the peso's upside was expected to



be capped at around 51.65-51.70. On the downside the central



bank may step in again at around 51.80, the level it is



suspected to have repeatedly defended last week.



    Charts showed the dollar/peso overbought with 14-day



relative strength index reading at 77.31, indicating room for



profit-taking in the dollar.



    Secretary of Finance Jose Camacho after two days of talks



with Wall Street bankers, bond investors and ratings agencies



said on Friday the government is standing by its 2001 target of



3.3 percent gross domestic product growth despite the economic



shocks heaped upon it by the U.S. downturn.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht was steady at 44.70 wedged in between onshore



commercial demand for the dollar and trimming of long dollar



positions amid uncertainty about the local government's



monetary policy.



    Dealers in Singapore said offshore players were reluctant



to take any aggressive dollar/baht positions, despite repeated



denials by the central bank of any plan to cut its key interest



rates.



    The central bank also said it would announce within the



next two weeks whether it would go ahead with plans to issue



320 billion baht of bonds in October-December, to rollover debt



taken up by the central bank from bailed out and troubled



banks.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah trotted just above the 10,000 per dollar level,



with its upside capped on concerns about domestic political



stability.



    State media and tour operators said tourists and foreigners



are being harassed, and in the first of such incidents two



German tourists were punched and kicked after being mistaken



for Americans.



    But players were reluctant to push the rupiah too low on



fears of central bank intervention in support of the rupiah



just beyond the 10,000 level.



    The central bank last week confirmed it had intervened in



the currency market. The bank also said it would prefer to



support the rupiah through intervention, rather than by hiking



domestic interest rates.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won rose another notch against the dollar as the market



cheered the prospect of more foreign net purchases of local



stocks.



    Foreign investors bought a net 500 billion won worth of



Korean shares last week, helping the won close at its best



level since September 20 on Friday.



    However, the currency's gains could be limited if the Seoul



bourse takes Wall Street's losses on Friday to heart. The



benchmark Korean Composite Stock Price Index slipped 0.47



percent in early trade.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar crept higher to 34.546 against Friday's



close of 34.55, but the market remained wary of possible


central bank intervention to restrain the local dollar's gains.



    With the economy badly hit by the global electronics



slowdown, the authorities have been keeping the Taiwan dollar's



rise in check. Net purchases of local stocks from foreign



investors have buoyed the local dollar recently.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Singapore Dlr At 11-Week Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, with the Singapore dollar extending its slide to 11-week lows as the central bank apparently acquiesced to a weaker currency. 

 Foreign equity inflows helped support the South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar, which have recently been outperforming their Southeast Asian peers, burdened by economic and security anxieties, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso were firmer as their respective central banks mounted a continued defense of their currencies, which threaten to take a dive as domestic concerns persist. 

 The Philippine central bank appeared determined to prevent the dollar from rising beyond 51.800 pesos, while dealers believed its Indonesian counterpart was keen to keep the dollar below 10,000 rupiah. 

 The Thai baht was slightly lower, but, given the lack of trading interest in the currency, continued to trail behind the Singapore dollar's decline, dealers said. 

 While the other Southeast Asian currencies held their own, the Singapore dollar, being the most liquid currency, took the brunt of the region's woes. 

 Dealing another blow to the Singapore dollar was a New York Times article Wednesday that terrorists linked to Osama bin Laden's al-Qaeda group based in the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia were "likely the targets of future covert and overt American actions," dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar slumped past S$1.8100 overnight to as low as S$1.8160 against the U.S. currency. 

 "The Singapore dollar is used as a negative hedge," given capital restrictions in Malaysia, Philippines, Indonesia which limit the availability of dollars in these countries, said an Asian bank dealer. 

 In response to the report, however, Secretary of State Colin Powell said Wednesday that the U.S. is concentrating on its operations against Afghanistan and any actions against other nations are for the more distant future. U.S. ambassador to Singapore, Frank Lavin, added Thursday that U.S. military action in Southeast Asia is unlikely. 

 Without any evidence of intervention by the local monetary authority, the Singapore dollar extended its precipitous decline to an 11-week low of S$1.8251 against the U.S. currency Thursday, down from S$1.8068 late Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar has floundered on concerns over the severity of the city-state's economic slump and the central bank's move to widen its policy band to give it more flexibility in managing the currency. The Singapore dollar is guided within an undisclosed trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 Market participants continued to push the Singapore dollar lower, as they attempted to gauge the limits of the MAS' widened policy band, dealers said. 

 Persistent U.S. dollar purchases by a large Singapore bank, which helped thrust the currency through S$1.8200 Thursday, led some in the market to surmise that it was acting on behalf of the MAS. Some dealers, however, doubted such talk. 

 The Singapore bank turned a seller of U.S. dollars in late trading, causing the currency to retreat, but only temporarily. 

 Heavy dollar sales by exporters and a 2.7% jump on the Seoul bourse - following solid gains on Wall Street overnight - lifted the South Korean won, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,302.0 won, down from Wednesday's close of KRW1,306.7. 

 After leaving its call rate unchanged, South Korea's central bank hinted that its recent rate cuts might be sufficient for now, saying that the rate "had already been lowered considerably." 

 "After the rate decision, we believe that the won should be weakening from here," Bank of America said. "There has to be some stimulus from somewhere. The economy would certainly worsen if bond rates continue to rise and the won continues to strengthen." 

 In Taipei, the central bank bought an estimated US$20 million toward the close to counter a strengthening of the local currency from the 4.7% rally in the stock market, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.553, little changed from NT$34.555 Tuesday. The market was closed Wednesday for a national holiday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, dealers believed the peso continued to find reprieve from the central bank. 

 One Manila-based dealer estimated that the central bank sold around $50 million at PHP51.800. 

 The dollar ended at its intraday low of PHP51.750, from PHP51.791 Wednesday. 

 Volume rose to $75 million from $51.7 million Wednesday. 

 The market shrugged off the central bank's expected decision to leave its closely-watched overnight rates unchanged. 

 The Indonesian currency was stronger at 9,955 rupiah per dollar, compared with IDR10,005 late Wednesday. 

 The Thai currency was marginally weaker at 44.785 baht to the dollar, compared with IDR44.755 late Wednesday.

title: Emerg  FX -Sin$ gets sinking feeling as MAS stands aside.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The wobbly Singapore dollar 

 sank to its fresh 10-week lows in early trade on Thursday on 

 lingering concerns over the country's troubled economy 

 following dismal third quarter GDP data. 

     The currency fell a cent overnight to its lowest levels 

 since July 26 without any signs of central bank intervention. 

     On Wednesday the Monetary Austhority of Singapore widened 

 its preferred trading band for the trade-weighted Sing$, which 

 dealers took as tacit acceptance of further weakness as a 

 monetary policy stimulus. 

 Other regional currencies were rangebound as players kept 

 low profile ahead of fresh leads from central banks in Japan 

 and Korea, and key economic data from the U.S. 

 The Bank of Japan kicked off its two-day meeting on 

 Thursday, with analysts expecting it to maintain its official 

 daily target for excess funds in the money market and leave its 

 symbolic discount rate unchanged at 0.10 percent. 

 In Korea, central bank policy makers met this morning but 

 elected to keep rates unchanged, disappointing market hopes for 

 another easing. 

 Market participants also await Friday's double dose of 

 major data from the U.S. - consumer confidence and retail 

 sales. 

 They largely shrugged off the IMF's forecast on Wednesday 

 that Japan would slip into recession this year, Europe would 

 grow modestly and the U.S. should recover in first half of next 

 year, saying the view was fully priced in. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar got a brief reprieve after players, 

 especially one local name which had snapped up the U.S. 

currency recently, unwound long U.S. dollar positions. 

 But once that was done, the market quickly took to selling 

 the currency again sending it to $1.8190 and bringing losses in 

 the last month to five percent. 

 "The market is still pretty bullish on the U.S. dollar. 

 Having said that, I do expect some profit taking to continue 

 because the market has got ahead of itself in the past few 

 days," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "After a brief dollar correction, the Sing dollar is likely 

 to head further south. It might fall to 1.8190 soon and still 

 be consistent with the new MAS' policy band. Our year-end 

 target is 1.8300," the dealer said. 

 The market is focusing on a government's stimulus package 

 expected on Friday. Most analysts reckoned the package would 

 worth at least S$10 billion. 

     Singapore unveiled a S$2.2 billion stimulus package in 

 July. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won opened a touch firmer, drawing support from gains



in local stocks and a steadier yen.



    The Bank of Korea's decision to keep rates unchanged



disappointed some. Seven out of 10 respondents to a recent



Reuters poll expected the central bank to lower its target for



the short-term call rate by 25 basis points to an all time low



of 3.75 percent.



But rate cut hopes were dampened when a central bank


official said on Wednesday that the debt market had been



overreacting to U.S.-led raids on Afghanistan.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar was expected to stay underpinned by a



equity-related inflows and a steadier yen when local markets



open for trade after a national holiday on Wednesday.



Dealers in Singapore said foreign investors would continue



to settle their purchases of 9.43 billion Taiwan dollar worth



of local shares they had bought over a four-session buying



streak.



However, the central bank was expected to cap any



significant upside for the Taiwan dollar. The grim economic



outlook would also keep players cautious.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso edged down in light interbank trade but dealers in



Manila said a lack of dollar demand from importers and



corporates was expected to push it higher.



They said wariness over suspected central bank intervention


on Wednesday had sent most importers and corporates to the



sidelines.



Charts also showed the dollar heavily overbought with



14-day relative strength index reading at 80.67 indicating a



downward correction of the dollar/peso was due.



    The upside was however seen limited with dollar purchases



likely to emerge around 51.60-51.65 range.



    Meanwhile, Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said on Wednesday



that he is considering a bond issue guaranteed by the World



Bank as part of a plan to raise $1.4 billion in financing for



2002.



The new option is among several including an issue in



Singapore dollar. Philippines has already announced plans to



issue around $414.6 million in private placement of yen bonds



or a shibosai issue.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah was expected to stay supported around the 10,000



level amid wariness over dollar sales by state names.



Dealers in Singapore said concerns have also eased over the



protest rallies by Islamic radicals against the U.S.-led



strikes on Afghanistan.



But an unclear political and economic outlook, most players



would prefer to buy dollars at dips, they said. Dealers



expected a trading range of 9,900-10,100 for the day.



THAI BAHT



The baht edged lower taking cue from the Singapore dollar



and as dollar sales from exporters abated.



Dealers in Singapore said talk of strong dollar bids at



44.70 has also prompted players to beef up their long dollar



positions.



Capping the downside, exporters are expected to be back in



the market at around 44.85 per dollar level, while Wednesday's



suspected central bank intervention to support the baht would



also keep players wary of pulling the currency too low.

title: Asia Markets-Singapore GDP delivers blow to Sing$.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar teetered 

 close to 1.81 to the U.S. dollar on Wednesday after the 

 government issued a dire outlook for the city-state's economy. 

     The currency suffered another blow when the Monetary 

 Authority of Singapore later announced it was widening its 

 policy band for the trade-weighted Sing dollar. 

     Though the MAS added it would stick to its neutral policy 

 stance, the market took the step as tacit approval for a weaker 

 Sing dollar. Finance Minister Richard Hu reinforced that notion 

 when he said a wider band reduced the need for intervention. 

     Unlike most Asian countries, Singapore uses the 

 trade-weighted exchange rate as its primary monetary policy 

 tool rather than interest rates, since its economy is so open. 

 Around 70 percent of Singapore's GDP is derived from exports. 


    The Sing dollar        skidded to fresh 10-week lows of



around 1.8088 before profit-takers rescued it. The market had



been bracing for the news as aggressive dollar bids from a



local bank spurred talk that the data was going to be worse



than expected, forcing the MAS to tolerate a weaker currency.



    But the Sing dollar's prospects were not bright.



Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said its flash



estimate showed third-quarter gross domestic product shrank by



5.6 percent on the year and by an annualised 9.9 percent on the



quarter.



    Those figures could be revised downwards as they only



reflect the first two months of the quarter, before the



September 11 attacks in the United States.



    To make matters worse, the government said it had revised



its full-year GDP forecast to a 3.0 percent contraction, from a



previous target of 0.5-1.5 percent growth.



    Moreover, it said the 2002 outlook was "highly uncertain,"



and the first half could see another contraction. That would



mean six straight quarters of contraction.



    WHAT'S IN STORE FOR THE SING DOLLAR?



    After the MAS's announcement, analysts debated the merits



of the move.



    One camp of analysts argued that the MAS did its best in



finding a middle way between loosening and maintaining its



policy bias, which it only recently changed in July.



    The risk, they say, was that investors would demand a



higher rate of return from Singaporean assets if the exchange



rate weakened substantially.



    This camp also argues that Singapore's exports will not



necessarily benefit from a weaker exchange rate as global



demand remained sluggish. A weaker Sing dollar, they say, would



only translate into cheaper exports rather than more sales.



    The other camp, however, says the MAS was not being



flexible enough given size of the economic downturn.



    "They should have gone ahead and announced a depreciation



policy as well, rather than sticking to a zero percent



appreciation," said Rajeev Malik, an economist at JP Morgan



Chase.



    "The magnitude of the slump and the intense disinflationary



bias probably supports that."



    While analysts bickered over the wisdom of the MAS's move,



they also scrambled to adjust their estimates of the Sing



dollar's policy band and their dollar/Sing targets.



    The MAS does not reveal the exact composition of its



trade-weighted basket of currencies, nor its policy bands.



    Peter Redward, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in



Singapore, estimated that a widening would tack on another half



percentage point to the band. His current estimate for the band



is plus or minus three percent, which would have 1.8250 to the



U.S. dollar as the bottom of the band, and 1.79 in the middle.



"In terms of what this means for the bilateral exchange



rate for the dollar, a lot of it hinges on what happens to the



rupiah, the yen and all the other currencies that have a



material weighting in the trade basket," Manu Bhaskaran, Chief



Strategist at SG Securities in Singapore, told Reuters



Television.



"My best guess is that given that the yen is likely to



weaken, we're probably looking at anything between 1.85 and



1.90 even if the yen weakens a lot."



STOCKS EDGY



Singapore shares recovered some of their losses after the



GDP report's initial shock, with the benchmark Straits Times



Index only down 0.67 percent.



Elsewhere in the region, other key bourses slipped as



investors struggled with the lingering unease over the impact



and length of the U.S.-led military strikes in Afghanistan.



Tokyo stocks dipped below the key 10,000 level for



the first time this week as investors fretted over the grievous



state of Japanese banks. Shares in Seoul and Hong Kong



 also dipped following falls in U.S. technology stocks.



Markets in Taipei were closed for a public holiday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Rupiah slides to 10-week lows.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were 

 grappling with uncertainty in the wake of U.S. and British 

 attacks on Afghanistan, with the first inclination being to 

 mark down the Indonesian rupiah to a 10-week low. 

     Trading volumes were thin with Tokyo off on holiday and 

 dealers reported some proxy selling of the Singapore dollar as 

 one of the more liquid currencies in the region, taking that to 

 its lowest level in nine weeks. 

     "A lot of focus will be on how things unfold over the next 

 few days...the level of the joint attacks and any 

 counterattacks by the terrorists," said Lee Boon Keng, market 

 strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore. 

     "In the near-term, this could put some pressure on the 

 dollar But (the military operations) looked pretty 

 well-contained at this point," he said. 

     Dollar bulls were disappointed that there was no discussion 

 at the Group of Seven meeting of joint intervention in the 

foreign exchange market over the weekend. 

     The G7 finance ministers' words in their communique -- "We 

 will continue to monitor exchange markets closely and cooperate 

 as appropriate" -- merely mirrored those they have made about 

 the currency market in their past statements. 

     Elsewhere, South Korea's central bank said after an 

 emergency meeting on Monday it would intervene in the market in 

 case of volatility. 

Singapore is scheduled to publish its third quarter gross 

 domestic product data on Thursday. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar was hovering around 1.7900 per dollar



after hitting an early low at 1.7910.



    It was finding some support from a rise in the yen beyond



120.00 per dollar -- many regionals tend to track the Japanese


currency.



    "I think the initial reaction is to sell the dollar, but it



depends on what dollar/yen does. The market could be quite



volatile," said a European bank trader.



    He added there could be some dollar buying around 1.7750/60



from players caught short of dollars on Friday.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah slid past 10,000 in early trade as the market



feared the U.S. attacks in Afghanistan could spark protests



from Muslim hard-liners in Indonesia.



    Indeed, a Muslim extremist group called for a siege of the



U.S. embassy in Jakarta early on Monday. These groups are a



small, but vocal minority in Indonesia, which is the world's



most populous Muslim nation.



However, political analysts warn that President Megawati



Sukarnoputri, who has only been in office for two months, has



to strike a delicate balance between backing the United States



and appeasing radical Muslims.



Dealers in Jakarta said the market was also nervous that



these protests would give foreign investors another reason to



avoid Indonesia, which is struggling to piece together its



shattered economy.



The rupiah was quoted around 10,200 but the bid/offer



spread had widened out to a full 100 rupiah suggesting few



traders actually wanted to deal in the currency.



    "Even if the central bank intervenes, they can't do much



for the rupiah," said a European bank dealer in Jakarta.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won bounced in line with the yen, but the threat of


intervention kept the currency on its best behaviour.



    The government said before trading began on Monday the Bank



of Korea would intervene if it saw volatility in the domestic


foreign exchange market. The statement was issued after an



emergency meeting of economic ministers following news of the



U.S.-led attack on the Taliban.



THAI BAHT



The baht firmed at first as some offshore names sold the



U.S. dollar in a knee-jerk reaction to the attacks, but soon



lost the gains as the whole region suffered from risk aversion.



The U.S. currency's downside was supported by talk of the


central bank buying dollars below 44.60 to top up its reserve



and to repay IMF debt.



Otherwise, trade was thin as market participants were



reluctant to take fresh positions amid uncertainty following



the attacks on Afghanistan.



In the offshore market, the one-month forward rate was



quoted at 9/13 satang per dollar and the tom/next rate at 0/0.5



satang.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso edged up on wariness over central bank

intervention to stem exchange rate volatility.



Dealers in Manila said the peso rose as interbank players,



taking their cue from the yen, squared out of their long dollar



positions.



Corporates and importers also kept on the sidelines amid



fears any volatile moves in the peso would draw the central



bank into the market.



Dealers said there was some concern about a rally in front



of the U.S. Embassy in Manila against the bombing of



Afghanistan but few expected the protest to turn violent.



    A dealer at a U.S. bank said the peso was likely to stay in



a tight 51.50-51.60 range for the day.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar followed the yen's rise but players were



cautious ahead of trade data for September due later in the



day.



    Dealers in Singapore said worries about the direction local



stocks would take and fears the central bank may deter any



sharp move in the currency market would cap any significant



gains in the Taiwan dollar.



    The benchmark TAIEX         index was down 1.61 percent by



0122 GMT.
