title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Many Holding Dollar Longs
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Wednesday, with dollar bulls experiencing a resurrection as the region's grim fundamentals return to the forefront of investors' concerns, dealers said. 

 Anxieties over the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. had weighed on the dollar last month. But as panic in the market subsided, the dollar has gradually regained its footing. 

 The weaker yen exerted some pressure on the region's currencies Wednesday, dealers said. 

 At 0930 GMT (4:30 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y120.82, slightly up from Y120.81 late Tuesday in New York. The dollar was at Y120.35 late Tuesday in Tokyo. 

 But with many in the market already sitting on long dollar positions and as the threat of intervention by the region's central banks loomed, Asian currencies languished in rangebound trade, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar and the Thai baht were weaker, while the Indonesian rupiah, the Philippine peso and the New Taiwan dollar were slightly stronger. 

 Asian currencies showed a muted reaction to the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision Tuesday to cut the target for its benchmark federal-funds interest rate to 2.5% from 3%. 

 The rate cut was within expectations and isn't likely to provide an antidote to Asia's woes, analysts said. 

 Instead, a rebound in the region's exports would be needed to jump-start Asia's economies, analysts said. 

 "The way most of us have read the Fed's rate decision and the fiscal spending that's coming in the U.S. is that as far as the downturn is concerned it's becoming more real," said Philip Wee, a market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. 

 "Countries that have weathered the downturn so far have to reexamine their prospects, especially Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines," he added. 

 Including its emergency rate cut just before the U.S. stock markets reopened Sept. 17, the Fed has slashed rates a full percentage point since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, and by a whopping four percentage points since the start of the year. 

 Even though the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 1.3% Tuesday as the Fed left the door open to further rate cuts in the aftermath of the attacks, Asian stock markets displayed a lukewarm response. 

 "That's not a good confidence booster for the currencies in the region," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The Singapore dollar felt the brunt of the yen's weakness and on U.S. dollar demand by U.S. investment houses, which sent it reeling to its lowest level in almost two months, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar climbed to as high as S$1.7818, its highest level since Aug. 7. 

 The U.S. dollar, however, retreated below S$1.7800 late in the day as sales of the U.S. currency by local banks fueled speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore could have intervened to temper the sharp decline in the local currency in recent sessions, dealers said. 


Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7788, still higher
than S$1.7774 the previous day.
- - 03/10/01 10-04G



However, some dealers were skeptical on whether the Monetary Authority
of Singapore had defended the local currency, given that the local
currency still appeared stable against the currencies of its major
trading partners.



The weakness of the Singapore dollar and the yen weighed on the Thai
currency, which was at 44.760 baht a dollar, compared with THB44.690
late Tuesday.



The baht could succumb to further pressure as the Thai central bank
continued to resist the market's calls for it to lower interest rates,
market watchers said.



Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Wednesday there was no
immediate need to lower the country's interest rates to mirror the
latest policy easing in the U.S.



"Six months ago, they could do that because the outlook for the
economy wasn't that bad, but now, it's bad," said Wee at DBS Bank.



Suspected dollar sales by Indonesia's central bank helped push the
U.S. currency to below the IDR10,000 level late in the day, dealers
said.



But corporate demand for dollars kept the U.S. currency buoyed above
IDR9,900, dealers said.



Late in the day, the dollar was at IDR9,915, lower than IDR10,015 late
Tuesday.



Protests against possible U.S. military retaliation on Afghanistan for
the terrorist attacks in New York and Washington have sparked security
concerns and fears that this could drive foreign investors away.



Market observers are also worried that President Megawati's pledge to
support the U.S. in its war against terrorism might hurt her fragile
alliance with Muslim political parties.



"The market prices back the political risk premium whenever they see
the leadership being questioned," said Wee at DBS Bank.



On the Philippine Dealing System, the peso ended slightly higher as
dealers believed the central bank had supported the currency by selling
as much as $50 million to various banks at around PHP51.600.



Participants were wary of taking any major positions ahead of the
Philippine central bank's decision on its overnight rates at its weekly
board meeting Thursday. Although the central bank is under intense
pressure to lower rates, it finds it difficult to do so given
inflationary pressures.



The dollar closed at PHP51.575, down from PHP51.600 Tuesday.



The New Taiwan dollar resisted getting dragged by the tottering yen,
as the central bank bought and sold an estimated US$60 million to stave
off any currency volatility, dealers said.



The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.569, little changed compared with
NT$34.574 Tuesday, in dealings valued at a relatively thin US$260
million.



"Every central bank's game now is to temper the dollar's upside, but I
don't think they will fight the trend," said Wee at DBS Bank.



South Korean markets were closed Wednesday for a holiday and will
reopen Thursday.

title: Singapore Dollar Lower Late; Tracks Weaker Yen, Regionals
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar fell to its lowest level since Aug. 7 on Wednesday, tracking weakness in the yen and regional currencies, as banks bought U.S. dollars on concerns over Asia's economic fundamentals, dealers said. 

 Around 0910 GMT (5:10 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7784, up from S$1.7780 late Monday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7775 and S$1.7818. 

 The U.S. dollar opened little changed in Asia, but rose above S$1.7800 by midmorning in line with its rise to an intraday high of Y121. 

 Buying led by U.S. investment houses pushed the U.S. dollar to an intraday peak of S$1.7818, its highest level since Aug. 7. 

 However, the U.S. currency slipped below S$1.7800 in late afternoon trade on selling by local banks. This was interpreted by some market participants as probable intervention on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 "The selling wasn't very big, but the speculation is that it could have been to smoothen things," a dealer at a U.S. brokerage said. 

 Dealers said the currency market largely ignored the 50 basis point cut in the U.S. Federal Funds rate by the Federal Open Market Committee, as it had already been priced in. 

 Dealers expect the U.S. dollar to trade between S$1.7780 and S$1.7820 overnight. 

 Singapore government bond prices surrendered early gains to end unchanged Wednesday. 

 Bonds opened higher following the Fed rate cut, but retreated in the afternoon on profit-taking, dealers said. 

 "The 50 point cut was expected and had been priced in, so it was natural for some profit-taking to happen," a dealer at a local bank said. 

 The yields on two- and five-year bonds ended flat at 1.89% and 2.89%, respectively. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yields on seven-, 10- and 15-year bonds also ended flat at 3.14%, 3.38% and 3.73%, respectively.

title: Emerging  FX  - Calm now, but rough waters ahead.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Asian currencies clung onto 

 dry ground early on Wednesday with the market taking a moment 

 to consolidate after recent losses. 

     Little reaction as yet to the Federal Reserve's widely 

 expected 50 basis point rate cut on Tuesday, which took its 

 funds rate to 2.50 percent - the lowest level in nearly 40 

 years. 

 After announcing the ninth cut so far this year, the 

central bank said it was poised to act again to help cushion 

 the economy in the aftermath of the attacks in the U.S. 

 The dollar bounced against the yen immediately after the 

 cut, touching a high of 121.14 in overnight trade. 

 Profit-takers, however, later trooped out to drag it down. 

 Still, regional currencies, especially in Southeast Asia, 

 were quivering in fear of future falls given Asia's 

 vulnerability to a weaker yen as well as a damaged U.S. 

 economy. 

 Given these fears, central banks in Southeast Asia may 

 think twice before following the Fed's rate cut. Central banks 

 in North Asia, however, are widely expected to mimic the Fed's 

 move. 

 Hong Kong has already eased by 50 basis points and analysts 

 reckon South Korea, Taiwan and Malaysia may follow at some 

 point. 

 Southeast Asian currencies are also wrestling with domestic 

 concerns, with the Indonesian rupiah struggling to stay above 

 the 10,000 level amid anxiety that anti-American protests could 

 drive away badly needed foreign investment. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was trapped at 10,000 as the market despaired 

 over recent anti-American protests possibly driving away 

 foreign investors. 

 Indonesia has seen several small, but vocal anti-American 

 rallies held by fringe Muslim radical groups. While few 

 foreigners are actually leaving Indonesia, there is a growing 

 fear that a U.S. strike against the Taliban could produce a 

 backlash in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim 

 country. 

     Dealers in Jakarta said Bank Indonesia tried to cushion the 

 rupiah's falls on Tuesday, but only with limited success. 

     However, charts showed the dollar/rupiah was heavily 

 overbought, with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 

 83. If corporate dollar demand is less than expected, the 

 rupiah could enjoy a technical bounce. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar remained soft against the U.S. dollar, with 

 corporate players and local banks continuing to add to long 

 dollar positions against the backdrop of a weak yen and the 

 situation in Indonesia. 

     But the local currency drew some support from dollar profit 

 taking above 1.7780. 

     Charts show the U.S. dollar is slightly overbought, with a 

 reading of 74.3 on the 14-day relative strength index (RSI). 

 The overbought line is 70. This indicates the upside for the 

 dollar could be limited in the very near term. 

 UBS Warburg said in its note that the next key level for 

 the pair was 1.7795 as it marked the 200-day moving average, 

 and a break of this level would allow the dollar to trade 

 higher toward 1.7850 and then 1.7900. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht edged lower to 44.71 with some U.K. and U.S. names 

 heard buying the dollars. But exporters offers capped dollar 

 gains. 

 Dealers said trade was subdued as the market was digesting 

 the Fed's move overnight and monitoring how dollar/yen reacted 

 to the cut. 

     There were rumours the Bank of Thailand was in the market 

 on Tuesday to buy to dollars to repay IMF debt. 

     Baht funding costs were steady, with the offshore one-month 

 forward rate quoted at 8/13 satang per dollar and the 12-month 

 rate quoted at 110/135 satang. 

     Foreign investors sold net 142.70 million baht worth of 

 Thai stocks on October 2. 


    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar dipped, but decided not to stray too far



from the 34.50-34.60 range, where it has been since September



21.



    Trading interest in the spot market has dwindled, despite a



huge fall in local stocks on Tuesday. The central bank has been



in the market actively to keep the local dollar within a tight



range, and was spotted on Tuesday intervening on the currency's



behalf around 34.588.



However, Singapore dealers said the offshore



non-deliverable market has enjoyed active trade, with players



banking on a weaker Taiwan dollar in the months to come.



The September 11 attacks have squelched any hopes of a



quick recovery in Taiwan's economy, which was already seeing



its worst slowdown in years. The government has forecast the



island's first full-year contraction ever.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso held onto Tuesday's closing level of 51.60 as



players tested the central bank's resolve to defend the


currency.



Dealers in Manila said all eyes were on the central bank,



which has been trying to limit the currency's losses in recent



sessions. While there have been few fresh factors in the



market, the peso has come under attack given the grim picture



for the country's economic outlook and a simple dearth of



dollars.



There was a bit of a tussle over interest rates earlier in



the day. Philippine Soci-economic Planning Secretary Danta



Canlas said he expected the central bank to cut rates by at



least 25 basis points after the Fed's latest easing.



But central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura later said he



did not know if the bank's monetary board, which meets on



Thursday, would indeed cut rates. He added while the Fed's



decision would be taken into account, the board also had to



consider the exchange rate.



KOREAN WON -2



Financial markets in Korea are closed for a holiday, and



will re-open on Thursday.



    Because of the closure of local markets, trading on the



offshore non-deliverable market was minimal.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late; Hits 2-Mo Low On Weak Yen,Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar fell to its lowest level in nearly two months Tuesday, as a weaker yen and Indonesian rupiah triggered stop-loss U.S. dollar buying by banks and investment houses, dealers said. 

 Around 0840 GMT (4:40 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7780, up from S$1.7674 late Monday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7686 and S$1.7790. 

 The U.S. dollar opened higher against its Singapore counterpart in Asia, in line with its overnight rise above Y120. It rose above S$1.7700 in early trades dealt out of Sydney, and extended its gains once Singapore's currency market opened. 

 The U.S. dollar broke successive resistance levels at S$1.7730 and S$1.7750, and revisited its Aug. 8 intraday peak of S$1.7790 by mid-afternoon. This followed the U.S. dollar's rise above 10,000 Indonesian rupiah. 

 The rupiah weakened after the Indonesian Supreme Court Monday nullified a guilty verdict against ex-President Suharto's son, Hutomo Mandala Putra, in a land fraud case. It was the U.S. dollar's first foray above IDR10,000 since July. 

 However, the U.S. currency retreated from S$1.7790 amid fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to prevent the local dollar from sliding sharply. 

 Earlier, absence of any MAS action around S$1.7750 - the authority's last suspected intervention level - had emboldened market participants to push the U.S. dollar higher. 

 Dealers expect intervention fears to cap the U.S. dollar below S$1.7800 in overnight trading, with support at S$1.7740. 

 Singapore government bond prices rose Tuesday, mirroring overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys, as market participants positioned themselves for a likely 50-basis point cut in the U.S. federal-funds rate, dealers said. 

 The Federal Reserve's policy setting arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, is due to meet late Tuesday and is expected to cut rates again to boost the U.S. economy. 

 Local bond prices were also helped by softer interbank rates, which eased further amid flush liquidity in the banking system. 

 The yield on two- and five-year bonds ended down two basis points each at 1.88% and 2.89%, respectively. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was down three basis points at 3.13%, while the yield on 10-year bonds fell two basis points to 3.38%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds fell one basis point to 3.73%.

title: Emerging  FX -Hit multi-week lows,  intervention  abounds.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 12 (Reuters) -  Asian currencies sank to 

 multi-week lows in late trade on Tuesday, pulled down in part 

 by the yen which fell almost a full percent against the 

 dollar due to Japan's economic gloom and intervention fears. 

     Japan has sold the yen on seven days since September 17, 

 buying dollars and euros in the foreign exchange market to halt 

 the yen's rise, which Tokyo fears could hurt the fragile 

 domestic economy. 

     Keeping the market on its toes, Finance Minister Masajuro 

 Shiokawa warned on Tuesday that Japan was ready to conduct 

 further intervention if the dollar fell again. 

     "It's pretty clear the Bank of Japan and the Ministry of

Finance are not going to allow the yen to be strong. That 

 reverses concerns that the dollar/yen would continue to fall," 

 said Andrew Fung, head of Asian research at Rabobank. 

     But domestic concerns also weighed on regional sentiment. 


    The Indonesian rupiah        fell past 10,000 to the dollar



for the first time since July 31 on market worries that



festering anti-U.S. sentiment could scare away foreign



investment.



    The market is looking foreward to a rate cut from the



Federal Reserve when it meets later Tuesday, with analysts



seeing a good chance the Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea will



follow any easing.



    Financial futures markets have fully priced in a 50 basis



point cut in the Fed's main 3.00 percent funds rate, which



would take it to levels not seen since the early 1960s.



    However, most also suspect that no amount of monetary



easing will stop the U.S. from slipping into recession this



quarter, taking much of the rest of the world with it.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah sank past the 10,000 per dollar level as growing



anxiety over anti-American sentiment from a small, but vocal



Muslim minority gripped the market.



    Jakarta dealers said corporates chased the dollar to a high



of 10,120 amid fears that recent anti-American protests would



scare off foreign investors.



    Though Bank Indonesia managed to staunch the rupiah's



wounds by selling dollars, it could not pull it back from the



wrong side of 10,000. Volumes were thin, which made the



exchange rate more volatile and steepened the rupiah's fall.



    Indonesia's Finance Minister Boediono tried to calm the



market by calling the rupiah's losses temporary.



    But dealers said sentiment towards the rupiah had soured,



and hopes for a rebound were dimming.



    "Bank Indonesia is the only supplier of dollars now and



there's a huge demand for dollar out there. With these



protests, they're going to be the only supplier of dollars for



some time," said a European bank dealer in Jakarta.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Sing dollar hit a seven-week low before players took



profits on the U.S. currency near 1.7790 due to wariness of


central bank intervention.



Dealers said a steadier dollar/yen sparked rounds of dollar



short covering as the yen carries substantial weight in



Singapore's trade-weighted basket of currencies.



Charts show 1.7835 is the next resistance for the U.S.



dollar/Sing dollar as it represents the 50 percent retracement



of the July 16-September 17 dollar downmove.



THAI BAHT



The baht fell as far as 44.74 - its lowest level since



September 11 - as players took cues from dollar/yen.



Dealers said dollar buying intensified after stop-loss sell



orders were triggered at 44.65, before dollar profit taking



helped it from the lows.



News that Thai Petrochemical Industry failed to



make an interest payment due on October 1 due to liquidity



problems also dampened baht sentiment.



Meanwhile, the government said on Monday it planned to



issue 38 billion yen ($317 million) worth of samurai bonds with



a maturity of three to seven years around mid-November.



Proceeds are earmarked to refinance debts of state companies so



the money is not likely to be transferred into baht.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso ended a whisker away from the day low of 51.61



despite rumoured central bank intervention as interbank players



covered short dollar positions.



Dealers in Manila said the central bank was heard selling



around $30-50 million in the market to shore up the local


currency. The market turnover was $113 million compared with



$61 million on Monday.



The central bank has been keen to stabilise the peso given



the country's external debt obligations and large fiscal



deficit.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar bowed under the pressure of falling local



stocks and a pessismistic outlook for Taiwan's economy.



Dealers in Singapore said while volumes in the spot market



were thin, activity in the offshore non-deliverable forward



market perked up as investment houses hedged their Taiwan



dollar exposure.



Trading in the spot market was probably also subdued thanks



to the central bank's vigilance in preventing volatility in the



market, they added. The bank, which has over $110 billion in


forex reserves, was spotted offering dollars around the day's



high of 34.588.



"But given the dollar/yen's move and the dollar/Asians



move, offshore players figure it's just a matter of time before



the Taiwan dollar makes another move lower," said a European



bank dealer.

re-open on Thursday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Fri, Tracking Weaker Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were lower late Friday in line with a decline in the yen, after the Bank of Japan intervened once again in global currency markets to weaken the Japanese currency. 

 The Singapore dollar, the Korean Won, the Indonesian rupiah and the New Taiwan dollar all closed lower against the dollar, while the Philippine peso bucked the trend, getting a moderate lift from the gradual flow of remittances made by overseas Filipino workers. 

 Market activity was fairly subdued ahead of the weekend, with many traders reluctant to sell dollars due to widespread notions the BOJ will continue to boost the U.S. currency with intervention. Some traders also remained sidelined due to concerns the U.S. might launch a retaliatory strike in Afghanistan as part of its quest to punish the perpetrators of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York and Washington. 

 A late afternoon spurt of selling by Japanese banks and Hong Kong trading houses pushed the Singapore dollar lower. The U.S. currency touched a high for the session at S$1.7675 before ending at S$1.7662, up from S$1.7613 late Thursday. 

 "There was some selling toward S$1.77 from some large Hong Kong houses," one trader said. He added that he expects the U.S. dollar to meet firm resistance at that level in the coming sessions, with the immediate trading range likely to fall between S$1.7580 and S$1.77. 

 In Seoul, dollar demand from domestic banks and oil importers keen to take care of their dollar needs ahead of a five-day weekend pushed the won lower. Korean financial markets will be closed Monday and Tuesday for Chuseok, the Korean Thanksgiving, and on Wednesday for National Foundation Day. 

 The dollar finished at 1,309.6 won, up from Thursday's close of KRW1,306.4. 

 The tone for trading in most Asian currencies was set in Tokyo, where monetary authorities continued their relentless efforts to cap the yen's upside. The BOJ intervention appeared aimed at offsetting the effects of Japanese corporations repatriating dollar-assets to improve their balance sheets before closing their books at the Sept. 30 fiscal half year end. 

 The dollar strengthened initially against the yen following the BOJ intervention but later retreated to around Y118.90 late in the day, well off its Y119.75 high. 

 Some participants speculated that any further BOJ attempts to weaken the yen may meet with only limited success, as uncertainty in global financial markets is likely to discourage Japanese institutional investors from buying foreign assets. 

 "Given the global theme of risk aversion, it is extremely unlikely that we'll see any significant outflows of Japanese capital from October onwards," one trader said. 

 Although the BOJ was the only central bank in Asia that intervened Friday, the threat of intervention by other central banks in the region helped support some currencies. 

 The Thai baht weakened in light trade tracking the Singapore dollar, but fears of possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand limited its slide, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 44.385 baht, up from THB44.305 baht at the Asian close Thursday, after moving in a narrow range between THB44.33 to THB44.39. 

Central Bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula's comments Wednesday fueled speculation that the central bank remains ready to step into the market. He said the BOT would continue to prevent excess volatility in the baht's movements and would limit capital outflows. 

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso also was supported in part on notions the central bank might intervene. 

 Although the dollar spiked early on expectations of month-end corporate requirements, thin demand and the gradual inflow from remittances made by overseas Filipino workers helped the peso gain some lost ground. 

 The dollar closed at 51.32 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.365 Friday and well below Friday's intraday high at PHP51.395. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also ended lower as local companies continued to buy dollars amid fears the U.S. unit could rise amid growing anti-U.S. demonstrations. The dollar closed Asian trade at 9,710 rupiah, its intraday high, up from its close Thursday at IDR9,685. 

 Around 2,000 Muslims took to the streets of Jakarta Friday to protest possible U.S. retaliatory strikes against Afghanistan. Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim country, with around 90% of its 200 million population. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended nearly unchanged against its U.S. counterpart, coming off its earlier highs as market participants covered short U.S. dollar positions late in the session, dealers said. They also said the central bank was suspected of buying U.S. dollars to slow the local unit's rise. At 0800 GMT (4 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.549, nearly flat with Thursday's close of NT$34.548. 

 The market's focus next week will be directed toward Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which the U.S. central bank is increasingly expected to cut interest rates by 25-50 basis points. 

 Also, traders also will monitor how the yen reacts to release Monday morning of the Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan business sentiment survey. This will be one of the first reports to show how terrorist attacks in the U.S. on Sept. 11 affected business sentiment in Japan, a senior government official said Friday. 

 "The tankan survey will be studied very carefully," Eiji Kawade, vice minister of the Cabinet Office, said in a regular press conference. "The attacks may have heightened risk factors in various forms" in Japan's business environment, he said. 

 The Bank of Japan will be release the tankan at 2350 GMT Sunday, or 8:50 a.m. Monday JST.

title: Emerging  FX -Tries, and fails, to elude yen's shadow.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies wilted 

 late on Friday, taking their cue from the yen as it tried to 

 get back on its feet after yet another round of intervention by 

 the Bank of Japan. 

     The Bank of Japan waded into the market to buy dollars for 

 yen on Friday, the seventh day in two weeks it has intervened. 

 It also co-opted both the New York Federal Reserve and the 

 European Central Bank into selling yen for it during their 

 trading hours no Thursday. 

     Some had thought that officials were only trying to provide 

 Japanese firms a better rate at which to value their assets 

 ahead of the half-year bookclosing, which is today. 

     But, analysts say if the central bank continues to 

intervene next week, it would be a serious signal to the market 

 that it really intends to restrain the yen for the long term. 

     Still, with the U.S. economic outlook going from bad to 

 worse, the dollar did not make much headway against the yen 

 during Asian trade and struggled to hold around 119.00 . 

     All in all, regional currencies will likely suffer in the 

 coming sessions with a hobbled yen on one side and a damaged 

 U.S. economy on the other. 

     Markets in Korea, Taiwan, and Hong Kong will be closed on 

 Monday for public holidays. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar slipped slightly from levels seen late



Thursday in choppy trade as players took their cue from the



softer yen.



    But the local currency skirted further falls as a U.S.



investment house and some Japanese players shelled out to buy



Sing dollars.



    Dealers said the market was generally wary of testing the



dollar/Sing's upside after it corrected downwards from Monday's



1.5 percent gains. Many in the market feared the Monetary



Authority of Singapore may have intervened to rescue the local



dollar earlier in the week when it bumped against six-week lows



of 1.7750.



Still, dealers argued the only direction for the Sing



dollar in the medium term was down given the city-state's poor



economic health.



THAI BAHT



The baht was a touch easier in line with a weaker yen, but



the market was cautious to push the baht much lower due to



wariness of central bank intervention.



Few players were willing to take fresh positions ahead of



the Fed's meeting on Tuesday and the release of Japan's tankan



business sentiment survey on Monday.



News of the central bank easing some restrictions on baht



loans to individual non-residents and on foreign individuals



exchanging currencies, barely had any impact on the baht.



A central bank circular said foreigners with a valid work



permit for at least a year can each borrow up to five million



baht ($112,700) of consumer loans or baht-denominated bank



guarantees.



The central bank data released on Friday showed Thailand



posted a current account surplus of $1.1 billion in August and



a balance of payment surplus of $350 million.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso ended firmer at 51.32 to the dollar against 51.365



at the close on Thursday in a thin market, with only $72.95



million transacted.



The currency fell to an intraday low of 51.395 before



dollar profit-taking emerged amid talk the central bank might



still be defending the peso at 51.40-51.50.



The market barely reacted to news of the government



planning to raise 30-50 billion yen from the issue of shibosai,



a private placement of bonds in Japan, as it has not given the



timing for the issue.



Meanwhile, the country's value of production index rose



11.4 percent year-on-year in July, while the volume of



production index fell 2.1 percent.



KOREAN WON -2



The won was held hostage to the yen, closing at a 10-week



low of 1,309.60 compared with 1,306.4 on Thursday.



Players were focused on squaring positions ahead of a long



weekend holiday as the market will be closed October 1-3 for



the Chusok, or thanksgiving, holiday.



Bank of America said in a daily note that Korea's mild



inflation data in September and worsening consumer confidence



were pointing to lower interest rates and a higher dollar/won



in the near term.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



A struggling rupiah was bolstered by state banks who



managed to drag it away from early lows of around 9,715.



Jakarta dealers said local corporates were still on the



hunt for dollars, with the market nervous about reprecussions



at home of a possible U.S. strike on Afghanistan.



Fringe groups of Muslim radicals have been calling for a



holy war if the U.S. retaliates for the September 11 attacks



and have also threatened to take action against foreigners in



Indonesia.



While President Megawati Sukarnoputir has condemned the



attacks, she has not backed possible U.S. military action.



Political analysts say Megawati, whose hold on power is shaky



after two months, cannot afford to rile these groups.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar closed virtually flat from Thursday's



close of 34.548, after giving up earlier gains as the central



bank stepped in to steer it back in line.



Singapore dealers said the local currency opened higher



thanks to continued dollar sales by exporters ahead of



month-end. They added players both in the onshore spot and

title: Emerging  FX  - Tired of busy BOJ, but no rest ahead.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bowed to 

 the dollar in early trade on Friday following after the Bank of 

 Japan intervened yet again to to restrain the yen. 

     That made it seven days in eleven that it has intervened

 and followed a concerted effort on Thursday where the BOJ 

 called on both the European Central Bank and the New York 

 Federal Reserve to intervene on its behalf. 

 The effort nudged the dollar up to 119.45 yen after 

 an early dip to 119.00 and fed speculation the Ministry of

Finance would stay in the market today to provide Japanese 

 institutions with a better forex rate with which to value their 

 foreign assets. Today is the half-year bookclosing in Japan. 

     But that left open the question of whether Japan would 

 continue to intervene once bookclosing was over. 

     "If the authorities intervene again from Monday onwards, 

 then it will send a very strong signal suggesting that the 

 authorities have not been aiming to help firms window dress 

 their accounts but do indeed want the yen to weaken," said a 

 UBS Warburg note. 

     If so, then that will tend to limit the upside for regional 

currencies against the dollar. 

     Players were also reluctant to take new fresh positions 

 ahead of a busy schedule next week with the Fed widely expected 

 to cut U.S. interest rates further and Japan is due to release 

 its September tankan business survey. 

 Some analysts reckon the Fed is likely to slash borrowing 

 costs by another 50 basis points when its policy makers meet on 

 Tuesday, and that some in this region will follow with easings 

 of their own. 

 As for Japan, economists polled by Reuters predicted the 

 tankan survey due on Monday would show sentiment deteriorated 

 sharply because of the global economic slowdown and the attacks 

 on the United States. 

 Elsewhere in the region, Korea is due to publish its August 

 industrial output data at 0300 GMT and Thailand is releasing 

 its monthly key economic data at 0800 GMT. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar slipped from levels seen late Thursday 

 in Asian trade of around 1.7612, but shied away from 1.7700 in 

 a market wary of building long U.S. dollar positions for now. 

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar touched a high of 1.7689 

 overnight as buy orders sent players scrambling to cover their 

 short dollar positions. 

 However, the U.S. unit's gains were limited around 1.7750 

 - a level where many players suspected the Monetary Authority

 of Singapore may have intervened at earlier in the week. 

 They said the Sing dollar would likely enter a 

 consolidation phase, having recovered from Monday's losses of 

 around 1.5 percent. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won took its cue from the weakening yen and hit 1,311.5 

 per dollar early - its lowest level in more than two months. 

 But the won swiftly bounced off intraday lows on 

 expectations that exporters would offload dollars ahead of 

 quarterly book closings, as in recent sessions. 

     The market was gearing up for a likely cut in interest 

 rates if the Fed eases after its FOMC meeting on Tuesday. 

     The country's September consumer price index (CPI), the 

 broadest measure of inflation, was unchanged month-on-month 

 compared to a 0.5 percent rise in August, suggesting the Bank 

 of Korea still had leeway to ease credit further. 

     The ministry attributed the latest figures to lower prices 

 of agricultural and petroleum products. 

     On the year, CPI was up 3.2 percent in September versus 4.7 

 percent the previous month. 

     Meanwhile, core inflation -- which excludes noncereal and 

 fuel prices - rose 3.6 percent on the year, but was below the 

 BOK's upper target of four percent for the first time this 

 year. 

     All eyes will be on August industrial output data due at 

 around 0300 GMT. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah continued to languish below 9,600 to the dollar



despite news that the Paris Club of official creditors has



backed the second phase of a two-year debt rescheduling deal



with Indonesia.



Japan's Ministry of Finance said on Thursday the Paris Club



had contacted it and other creditor nations to say there was no



disagreement in approving the deal. Indonesian President



Megawati Sukarnoputri is in Japan on a state visit.



Jakarta dealers, however, said the agreement was long



expected. They added the market was more concerned with the



threat of a U.S. attack on Afghanistan following the September



11 tragedy and the possible reverberations it may have at home.



Though a minority, Indonesia's Muslim radicals have raised



fears of political instability with their calls for a jihad if



the U.S. retaliates.



Megawati condemned the attacks on the U.S. on Thursday, but



stopped short of declaring Jakarta's support if the U.S. does



take military action.



THAI BAHT



The baht retreated below 44.40, alongside the yen and other



regional currencies in early thin trade. But exporter dollar



offers above that level should provide a solid support for the



local currency.



Charts show 44.50 remained a good barrier for the dollar as



it represents the 61.8 percent retracement of the September



11-September 17 dollar downmove.



The market awaits economic data to be released by the Bank



of Thailand later in the day, including trade numbers, current



account balance and industrial production.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso opened lower at 51.39 to the dollar compared with



51.365 at the close on Thursday to miror weakness in the



regional currencies.



    But dealers in Manila expected the peso to hold at 51.50 on



fears of potential central bank intervention.



    On the macro front, the country's value of production index



rose 11.4 percent year-on-year in July, while the volume of



production index fell 2.1 percent, according to data released



earlier in the day.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar continued to steer a steady course thanks



to month-end U.S. dollar sales by exporters.



    Dealers said the central bank has been in the market to



keep the local dollar within a well-behaved range.



    Still, they said the Taiwan dollar would likely weaken in



the long term as the island's economy struggles through the



double shock of a likely U.S. recession and the electronics



downturn.



Taiwan's economics minister said on Thursday a



long-awaited recovery would be further delayed after the



September 11 attacks on the U.S. The government is projecting a



0.37 decline in 2001 gross domestic product - Taiwan's first



ever full-year contraction.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Banks Unwind Long US Dlr Positions
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was sharply higher late Thursday as banks unwound long U.S. dollar positions accumulated earlier this week, dealers said. 

 Around 0900 GMT (5 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7613, down from S$1.7690 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.7588 and S$1.7693, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar opened nearly flat and drifted lower through most of the day, before being sold down sharply against the Singapore dollar in late afternoon trading. 

Intervention by the Bank of Japan to weaken the yen briefly boosted the U.S. dollar against its Singapore counterpart, but the gains were short lived as local banks and interbank market participants resumed unwinding long U.S. dollar positions, dealers said. 

 Short of Singapore dollars, banks also sold yen and Thai baht crosses against the local currency, dealers added. 

 After having ended at S$1.7450 last week, the U.S. dollar surged to a seven-week high of S$1.7750 by early Wednesday and was viewed as overbought. Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have intervened Wednesday to stem the U.S. dollar's steep rise sent dealers scurrying to unwind the positions. 

 The U.S. dollar's fall below the S$1.7630 support level triggered stop-loss selling which pushed the currency to its intraday low of S$1.7588, dealers said. 

 Dealers expect the U.S. dollar to find support at S$1.7550 in overnight trading. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended higher tracking overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys. Softer interbank rates also helped lift bond prices, dealers said. 

 The yield on two-year bonds fell four basis points to 1.88% while the yield on five-year bonds was down two basis points at 2.91%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was down one basis point at 3.17% while the yield on 10-year bonds fell three basis points to 3.42%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds fell two basis points to 3.75%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site: 

http://www.mas.gov.sg/sgs("http://www.mas.gov.sg/sgs")

 In the interest rate swaps market, swaps were mostly lower in line with some local bond yields. 

 The most liquid seven-year swap offer closed one basis point lower at 3.29% while the 10-year swap offer also closed one basis point lower at 3.53%. 

 The spread between two- and 10-year swaps widened to 115 basis points from 113 basis points late Wednesday. 

 In the interbank money market, rates edged lower as DBS Bank joined the rate war, cutting its prime lending rate by 25 basis points to 4.75%, to become the cheapest lender in Singapore.

title: Emerging  FX -Mixed as domestic factors outweigh dlr/yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 mixed in late Thursday trade with domestic factors for once 

 outweighing the Bank of Japan's latest effort to weaken the yen 

 . 

     A move by dollar/yen above 118 per dollar following yet 

 more intervention by the Bank of Japan had a limited impact as 

 genuine corporate flows held sway in cautious Asian trade. 

     The most significant move of the day was seen in the 

 Singapore dollar which clawed back around 0.4 percent of its 

 recent losses, triggering speculation the monetary authorities 

 may have entered the market to limit volatility. 

     Dealers also had a wary eye on other central banks as talk 

 circulated the authorities in the Philippines might sell 

 dollars to shore up peso confidence if it fell to 51.40 levels. 

     Financial markets continued to await America's next steps 

 to avenge the attacks on New York's twin towers and the 

 Pentagon on September 11, fearing that a worse-case scenario 

 could spark a costly war. 

     Markets were also gearing up for next Tuesday's U.S. 

 Federal Reserve meeting as more rate cuts in the United States 

 were likely to prompt some Asian central banks to follow suit. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Sing dollar gained sharply as those who overbought the



dollar and Australian dollar in the past few sessions unwound



their long positions.



    A break above 1.7620 also triggered some stop-loss selling



in the U.S. dollar, but some bargain hunting emerged once U.S.


currency dropped to 1.7585.



    There was talk the central bank might have been in the



market to stave off volatility.



    "European and American names had sold the U.S. dollar quite



a bit today. There are rumours the MAS was on both ends of the



market to smooth out volatility, but we can't get a



confirmation on this," said a dealer at a European bank.



The Sing/Aussie cross had another wild session, with the



Australian currency sliding afresh to S$0.8570 after hitting a



high as S$0.8797 on Wednesday. The recent volatility in this



pair has stirred speculation of possible M&A flows.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah retained its weak tone as heavy corporate dollar



demand overshadowed news of Paris Club of creditors backing the



second phase of a two-year debt-rescheduling deal with



Indonesia.



It managed to bounce off intraday trading lows of 9,725 on



dollar profit-taking and offers from a state bank, but dealers



in Jakarta doubted if Bank Indonesia was behind sales.



"Of course, the Paris Club news is good news, but its



impact might be offset a bit by strong seasonal demand for the



dollar," said a dealer at one European bank in Jakarta.



"One onshore company placed a buying order of around $300



million and another around $100 million. That's a lot for a



thin market like this," he said.



Concerns over fresh violence also clouded the rupiah. A



hardline Muslim youth group warned on Thursday anyone backing



Washington's self-declared war on terrorism should leave



Indonesia or risk being forced out.



PHILIPPINE PESO



Corporate demand for dollars as month end approached and



negative sentiment towards the domestic economy weighed on the



peso although losses were limited amid talk the central bank


might intervene around the 51.40 to 51.50 level.



All eyes were on the central bank which decided to keep its



key overnight rates unchanged at its weekly policy-making



Monetary Board meeting.



The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that there



was still some room for monetary easing given that inflation



was likely to remain within official targets.



The central bank brought more gloom to the market after


central bank deputy governor Amando Tetangco told reporters the



country's annual imports would drop three percent this year as



manufacturers adjusted to slowing demand.



Bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Wednesday that



merchandise exports were expected to fall by 15 percent on the



year in 2001 due to a slowdown in the U.S. and Japan.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar eked out some gains despite the weaker



yen, falling local stocks and dismal economic fundamentals.



Singapore dealers said exporters' dollar sales ahead of the



month-end sent the local currency higher. They added trading



interest was lacklustre with volumes thin.



The cabinet level Council of Economic Planning and



Development said earlier in the day its index of leading



indicator rose 1.3 percent in August from the previous month to



94. However, it said the economy slowed that month, making it



the ninth month in a row of slowdown.



THAI BAHT



The baht sat pat in a tight range of 44.30-44.38 as players



remaind wary of possible central bank intervention.



Bangkok dealers said trading activity has been subdued



since a Japanese bank based in Singapore was spotted selling



dollars on Wednesday, sparking talk of intervention. However,



some dealers dismissed the rumours.



Offshore players were spotted buying dollars against the



baht on the back of the greenback's gains against the yen. But



those bids were met by offers from exporters.



    Baht funding costs in the offshore market rose slightly,



with the one-month tenor quoted at 7/9 satang per dollar.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won closed lower at 1,306.4 per dollar on Thursday



against 1,305.0 at the Wednesday's close on the back of a



weaker yen and dollar demand from importers.



    Sentiment was also dampened by the country's deteriorating



external account. The Bank of Korea said the nation posted a



current account deficit of $110.7 million in August - the



first deficit in 16 months.



But Vice Finance Minister Kim Jin-pyo told reporters he



expected a current account surplus of about $10 billion for



2001 and GDP growth of more than 0.5 percent in the third



quarter.

title: FX  Asia: Singapore Dollar Options Volatilities Rise
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column



SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Dollar bulls shouldn't be fooled into believing
that the Singapore currency's precipitous decline to near seven-week
lows heralds a reversal in the dollar-Sing dollar cross rate.


 "I think it's a bit premature," said Thio Chin Loo, a regional currency strategist at BNP Paribas. "The market is in a risk-reduction mode." 

 The U.S. dollar remains vulnerable to a knee-jerk selloff in the event of a military conflict, should the U.S. retaliate for the terrorist attacks in New York and Washington on Sept. 11., analysts say. 

 Further, with most economists expecting the terrorist assaults to drive the U.S. into recession - albeit a short one - and with Wall Street still shaky, the U.S. dollar is likely to continue tottering in the next few months even after knee-jerk selling in response to retaliatory raids runs its course, they add. 

 To be sure, recent activity in Singapore dollar trading would seem to defy this analysis, as the U.S. currency has been rebounding against the local dollar. This move gained momentum Monday, as the dollar jumped 1.5% during the global trading day to as high as S$1.7725 in New York trade, from around S$1.7460 at the start of the Asian trading day. 

 The U.S. dollar retreated to S$1.7643 around midday Tuesday on profit-taking by U.S. banks, dealers say. 

 "What happened last night was a little overdone," says a dealer at a European bank. 

 Indeed, the move Monday was exacerbated by special factors. Traders say a number of market participants were forced to buy U.S. dollars and sell Singapore dollars in the cash market because they weren't positioned for a sharp move in the options market. 

 When banks sell options, they delta hedge to limit their exposure. That is, as the probability that an option will be exercised - Delta - rises, option writers reduce options exposure with an offsetting position in the cash market. 

 Banks can also buy gamma, which reflects the rate at which delta changes, for this purpose. A long gamma position benefits from a sudden rise in volatility. 

 In this case, banks that had sold dollar call options and Singapore dollar puts were suddenly forced to cover that exposure, either by buying dollars or outright gamma. 

 "The market is short gamma," says Conrad Kwok, chief options dealer at Singapore's DBS Bank. "People are looking to sell vega and buy gamma." 

 Vega measures the change in an option's price in relation to the change in volatility. 

 Volatilities implied by one-month U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar options jumped Tuesday to around 6.25%/7.50%, from around 4.25%/5.75% Monday. 

 One-year options implied volatility of 5.50%/6.75% Tuesday, higher than 4.75%/6.50% Monday. 

 Volatility measures the expected range in the value of an asset over the period of the contract. Volatilities on currency options gauge the anticipated moves in the underlying currency, with a higher volatility implying a wider trading range. 

 The shift toward becoming risk averse has encouraged options writers to hedge exposure but hasn't spurred a major move by end users. One reason is the sudden costliness of these instruments. The steep fall in the Singapore dollar Monday has also pushed bid-offer spreads in volatilities far apart, making it difficult to trade and expensive for buyers. 

 "People have marked the vol curve higher, but not much is seen in the way of trading, at least in the broker market," said a currency options specialist at a U.S. bank. 

 "People don't want to pay such high vols to buy," he adds. "And they don't want to short vols because there's too much risk - right now, they could have a war or another round of intervention in dollar/yen which would affect the Singapore dollar." 

 The U.S. currency received an added fillip Monday after Japanese authorities intervened, buying dollars for yen even though Japanese markets were closed for a holiday, and the European Central bank bought euros against yen on behalf of Japan. The yen's decline added to the pressure on the Singapore dollar. 

 Speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had bought the U.S. currency late Friday, pushing it above S$1.7400, also made participants realize that it would be futile to push the U.S. currency much lower. 

 Though many foreign exchange participants are betting for a depreciation of the Singapore dollar to around S$1.8000 on a six-month horizon, the appetite for Singapore dollar puts has been measly, dealers said. 

 Whatever trades that were done, six-to-12 month maturity Singapore dollar put options with strike prices ranging from S$1.7800 to S$1.8500 were popular. 

 In the near term, analysts expect the Singapore dollar to stay resilient, finding support from the city-state's healthy current account surplus and the yen's strength even in the face of further possible rounds of intervention. 

 "The U.S. dollar's bounce is in response to actions of central banks and the market in risk reduction mode," said Thio Chin Loo, a regional currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 "Once military confrontation starts, investors will be prepared to put new positions by shorting the U.S. dollar," she adds. 

 Though Thio says the U.S. dollar could technically extend its rebound toward S$1.7850 resistance, and possibly as far as S$1.7975, "barring a breach of 1.8000, the bear trend is intact." 

 She adds that she expects the U.S. currency to eventually retreat to S$1.7200, and possibly form a base around S$1.7000. 

 The U.S. currency is then expected to rebound to S$1.8000 in about six months' time, with U.S. economic growth widely expected to resume in the first quarter of 2002, helped by aggressive interest rate cuts and a big boost in federal spending. 

 The threat of central bank intervention in the Singapore dollar has also ebbed, with the Singapore dollar now trading in the weaker half of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's policy band, providing some comfort to the authorities, some analysts say. The fallout of the attacks in the U.S. on the global economy is expected to aggravate demand for Singapore's exports. 

 The central bank had intermittently bought U.S. dollars to curb the appreciation of the local currency in the wake of the Sept. 11 attacks, as the Singapore dollar traded in the stronger half of the MAS' band. 

 "On a trade-weighted basis, the Singapore dollar has weakened about 2% in the last one week," says Jimmy Koh, the head of treasury research at UOB Group. "It's at the weaker half of the band, but well within the band, so there's no need for the MAS to do anything." 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary-policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners.

title: Asia Markets - Run for cover, nowhere to hide.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Asian stock markets crumpled 

 to their lowest levels in months on Friday, hit by worries over 

 exactly what kind of war America might wage against terrorism. 

     Sentiment had already been bruised by sharp losses on Wall 

 Street the session before and things turned brutal when 

 President George W. Bush declared the hour for military action 

 was approaching. 

     If a conflict were to erupt, scarring consumer sentiment in 

 the United States and elsewhere, the world could easily tip into 

 recession and bring even more pain to suffering Asian economies. 

     The prospective battle field also happens to be in Asia's 

 backyard, so threats of military action do not go down as well 

 here as they might in the United States. 

     With America rapidly deploying warplanes and aircraft 

 carrier groups to the Middle East and the Indian Ocean, Bush 

 told Taliban rulers in Afghanistan to surrender militant Osama 

 bin Laden and his followers or "share in their fate". 


    Singapore's Straits Times Index        and Hong Kong's Hang



Seng were the hardest hit after their markets gapped



lower at the open, fuelling heavy sales from the outset.



    Taiwan stocks ended at an eight and a half-year low while



the the Philippine market closed at a three-year trough.



    Heightened uncertainties spurred caution in the Asian bond



market as investors squared positions to avoid potential fallout



over the weekend.



    Spreads on Asian dollar bonds moved out by around 10 to 15



basis points (bps) after widening by some five to 10 bps in New



York overnight.



    DOLLAR THREAT LIMITED?



    Some analysts played down the threat of war, saying likely



events could have a limited impact on markets.



    "When we talk about war I think it is very important to



qualify the type of war that can happen...there is no declared



enemy," Dominique Dwor-Frecaut, director of research at Barclays



Capital, told Reuters Television.



    "Yes, the (U.S.) dollar could lose a bit of its safe haven



status but I don't think we are going back to a world war two



type of situation," she said.



    In the relatively illiquid Asian currency market, the



immediate focus remained centred on the yen , with



Japanese officials confirming the Bank of Japan (BOJ) had



unilaterally bought dollars to weaken the yen.



    The BOJ had already intervened to sell yen on Monday and



Wednesday.



    Moves to weaken the export-crimping Japanese currency helped



distance Asian regionals from their recent highs, calming fears



of intervention from the regional central banks at least for the



moment.



STILL ON INTERVENTION ALERT



However, despite the potential for Asian currencies to move



lower, some markets remained wary of possible central bank

intervention in the future.



Analysts said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was



likely to guide its currency lower given savage falls in the



city-state's exports recently.



The bank could also take a lead from this week's credit



easing by other central banks around the globe. Unlike most



Asian countries which adjust interest rates to tweak monetary



policy, Singapore favours its currency as a policy tool.



"We are seeing such a massive slowdown in Singapore, they



really do need to do something to try and ameliorate the impact



of the slowdown on the export side," said Andrew Fung, head of



treasury at Rabobank.



"So long as we're in this kind of behaviour where


intervention moves the yen by only 100 bps, then we will need



to see some intervention from the MAS," he said.



Otherwise, central banks were likely to keep a close eye on



the forex market, only intervening if their respective


currencies decoupled from the broader Asian trend, analysts



said.



The rupiah was a case in point given that it had fallen



substantially in recent days amid strong commercial appetite



for U.S. dollars as well as domestic factors.



Despite being export-dependant, particular weakness in the



rupiah compared to other currencies in Asia could give the wrong



signals to would-be investors and make it hard for corporates to



re-pay foreign debt.



"I'm not really sure whether one can characterise some Asian



central banks being at odds with what the BOJ is doing, apart



from Indonesia where movement in the rupiah has been out of line



with what was going on with dollar/yen," said Rabobank's Fung.

title: Emerging  FX -Jolted by BOJ, Bush speech digested.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies see-saw 

 once again as the yen first rises only to fall in the face of 

 apparent intervention from the Bank of Japan. 

     Yen had hit 7-month highs on the dollar around 115.85 

 following steep losses on Wall Street and mounting concerns 

 that the September 11 assault on the U.S. would push the global 

 economy into recession. 

 But the yen - tracked closely by regional currencies - pared 

 gains in early trade due to fears of potential BOJ 

intervention. And they did not have long to wait with the 

 dollar jumping to 116.87 yen on what dealers assumed was BOJ 

 buying. 

 If so this would be the third session this week that the 

 Jaspanese have intervened to try and limit the yen's gains, 

 though with limited success given the dollar started the week 

 around 118.00. 

 Activity was subdued overall in Asia as players watched 

 President George W. Bush giving a keynote speech to a joint 

 session of Congress, hoping for clues on what the U.S. will do 

 to punish the perpetrators. 

 Many also opted to take a wait-and-see stance ahead of a 

 fresh batch of data to be released by the U.S. and the region 

 next week. 

 U.S. consumer confidence data - a key leading indicator of 

 economic growth - are out on Tuesday. This will be the first 

 survey after the aerial attacks on the U.S. 

 The Bank of Thailand will release its key monthly economic 

 data including trade, balance of payment and industrial output 

 on September 28. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was trapped in a tight range early, 

 having rallied to 1.7375 from intraday low of around 1.7460 per 

 dollar hit the previous day. 

 But the Sing was barely changed compared to levels seen 

 late on Thursday when heavy U.S. dollar sales by at least one 

 U.S. name lifted the local currency of its lows. 

 One dealer from a European bank said the market was still 

 intent on offloading U.S. dollars, with the main market focus 

 centred on movements in dollar/yen. 

 But dealers expected potential gains on the Sing dollar to 

 be limited given the BOJ intervention and the possibility the 

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) might enter the market to 

 limit volatility. 

 There has been talk that the MAS may have made efforts to 

 guide the Sing lower this week following credit easing by many 

 central banks in response to last week's attacks on the United 

 States. 

 The Sing dollar, believed to have been trading at the 

 extreme strong end of its supposed trading range of late, is 

 one of Singapore's main monetary policy tools. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won came off overnight highs around 1,288 to stand at 

 1,295 in line with the yen with the upside was seen limited by 

 declines in domestic stocks. 

 By 0106 GMT, the benchmark KOSPI stock index was 

 down 2.74 percent at 467 points following continued falls on 

 Wall Street in the wake of last week's attacks. 

 Won sentiment was slightly boosted by expected month-end 

 dollar sales by exporters and confirmation that General Motors 

  would buy troubled Daewoo Motor. 

 General Motors said it would sign an MOU this morning to 

 take over two Daewoo Motor plants in South Korea with a final 

 deal expected by year's end. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won at 

 1,298.2/99.2 per dollar against 1,299.3/1,300.3 late on 

 Thursday. The six-month won was quoted at 1,302.0/03.0 against 

 1,308.5/09.5. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht retained its firm tone at 44.15 but the market 

 found few incentives to push it above 44.00 amid wariness of 

 BOJ intervention to curb the yen's appreciation. 

 In the money market, baht funding costs remained largely 

 steady in both offshore and onshore markets because there was 

 not much activity going on. 

 Meanwhile, the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) said it 

 had lowered the visitor arrival forecast to 9.68 million from 

 10.3 million in the wake of attacks in the U.S. 

     Revenues from tourists made a substantial contribution to 

 Thailand's foreign exchange incomes. 


    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso barely traded early around 51.24 as players were



glued to TV sets, listening to what President George Bush has



to say to a joint session of Congress.



    "The market is watching for clues on what he is going to do



as far as military retaliation is concerned," said a Manila



dealer.



    Bush said the evidence the U.S. has gathered all points to



Osama bin Laden's militant group and made a list of demands of



Afghanistan's ruling Taliban.



    The peso closed at 51.29 in on Thursday.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was marked up in thin early trade to 9,440 due



to a combination of firmer regionals and fears of local central



bank dollar-selling intervention.



    Bank Indonesia was rumoured to have sold the dollar at



around 9,550-9,600 on Thursday to shore up the rupiah.



    But its gains should be capped by persistent dollar demand



from onshore companies and lingering concerns over the fate of



$8.8 billion debt talk with Paris Club of creditors which has



been stalled since the attacks on the U.S.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Dlr Fails To Sustain Rise
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, after having recouped most of their earlier losses as the dollar remained wobbly against the yen despite the threat of intervention by Japanese authorities. 

 With little in the form of direction from the stable yen in early trading, most of the region's currencies fell under the sway of the Singapore dollar's swift decline, dealers said. 

 But the U.S. dollar failed to sustain its upward momentum, eventually succumbing to worries over the economic fallout of last week's terrorist attacks and uncertainty over the nature and extent of U.S. retaliation against the perpetrators of the assaults, dealers said. The dollar's fate is also tied to the performance of the U.S. equities market, which remains shaky. 

 "Everything should be sideways, at least between now and the end of the month," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 As the U.S. gears up for war, Islamic clerics Thursday urged terrorist suspect Osama bin Laden to voluntarily leave Afghanistan, where he and his followers have had sanctuary for five years, the Taliban news agency said. 

 The clerics' statement set no deadline for bin Laden to accept or reject the call, and it was unclear whether this would be enough to dissuade U.S. President George W. Bush from launching massive military strikes against Afghanistan. 

 Fears of central bank intervention, if not talk of actual intervention, also kept the market nervous, dealers said. 

 "Central banks galore," said the European bank dealer. 

 The Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah regained their footing after the central bank was suspected of having sold dollars to halt the depreciation of their respective currencies, dealers said. 

 Some dealers believed Taiwan's central bank bought U.S. dollars to prevent the local currency from strengthening with the yen. 

 There was also some talk - which many in the market played down, if not dismissed - that the authorities in Singapore and Thailand had intervened to weaken their currencies, dealers said. 

 Early in the day, the Singapore dollar floundered to S$1.7460 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.7417 late Wednesday. 

 U.S. dollar purchases by a large U.S. bank and investment houses based in Hong Kong propelled the currency, dealers said. The sharp jump fueled speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had bought U.S. dollars. 

 But profit-taking subsequently led to a retreat in the U.S. currency, dealers said. 


At 0935 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7416, little changed from
S$1.7417 late Wednesday.
- - 20/09/01 09-48G



The South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar teetered as foreign
funds bailed out of their equity markets, dealers said. The stock market
in Seoul slid by 1.3%, while the Taipei stock index skidded by 2.2%.



The New Taiwan dollar, however, found respite from U.S. dollar
purchases by the central bank late in the session, dealers said.



The New Taiwan dollar ended at NT$34.575 against the U.S. currency,
marginally weaker compared with Wednesday's close of $34.572. Trading
volume was US$279.0 million, less than half of Wednesday's US$719.0
million.



In Seoul, the dollar continued to face strong resistance around 1,300
won. The dollar finished at 1,297.5 won, slightly higher than KRW1,296.5
Wednesday.



Foreigners bought about $100 million worth of dollars and are expected
to buy more in the coming days as they have unloaded over KRW330 billion
in shares so far this week, a Seoul-based dealer said.



The Thai currency weakened to 44.220 baht per dollar, compared with
THB44.190 late Tuesday as U.S. banks snapped up dollars, dealers said.



The Indonesian rupiah rebounded, as reports of central bank dollar
sales prompted foreign banks to lock in profits, dealers said. Dollar
demand by local companies needing to repay their debt or fund their
import requirements earlier sent the Indonesian currency reeling to
9,735 rupiah against the dollar, dealers said.



Late Thursday, the dollar had retreated to IDR9,445, compared with
IDR9,630 late Wednesday.



On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.290 pesos,
down from PHP51.400 Wednesday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Soft as focus stays on BOJ  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Most regional currencies

 softened in early Thursday trade, with north asian currencies

 in particular looking to the yen for direction amid 

 fears of repeated central bank intervention. 

     Commercial dollar demand continued to dominate trading in 

 most Southeast Asian currencies, which were expected to remain 

 weak in any case due to shaky investor confidence. 

     The market was on high alert for Japanese intervention

 aimed at weakening the yen after the country's central bank

 bought dollars for yen on Wednesday for a second time this 

 week. 

     But dealers said most regional currencies had limited room 

 to move lower given that fears of a U.S. global recession had 

 heightened in the wake of last week's attacks. 

     News that the United States was sending more combat 

 aircraft to the Middle East drew a mixed response. Some were 

 relieved to know the U.S. was doing something but at the same 

 time worried at the potential for a military conflict, 

 particularly as this region is a lot closer to Afghanistan than 

 the U.S. 

     Added to that was nervousness as governments prepared to 

 slash growth forecasts and companies warned of more job cuts, 

 heightening the threat of recession. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar shed around half a percent to 1.7455



amid talk that local banks were off loading the currency.



    "There is no fundamentral news. The talk is that local



banks are selling Sing dollars but we cannot necessarily draw



conclusions from this," said a currency analyst from a European



bank.



    Dealers have given mixed accounts of possible intervention


by the monetary authority in recent days, with some saying it



was believed to have bought U.S. dollars in light of thee



recent credit easing by some central banks.



    Others have said they have no evidence of such moves.



    Despite appearing weak compared to its position last week,



the currency is still moving around the stronger end of its



assumed trading band and probably has room to drift lower,



according to dealers.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won weakened to 1298.0 on dollar demand from energy



companies keen to hedge against potential volatility in oil



prices following last week's attacks on the U.S..



    Japan's desire to stem relative strength in the yen also



weighed on the currency, dealers said.



    On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won at



1,300.6/01.6 per dollar, against 1,297.7/98.7 late on



Wednesday. The six-month won was quoted at 1,308.6/09.6 against



1,305.5/06.5.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso opened unchanged at 51.40 in the onshore market as



market participants were cautious amid rumours the central bank


was in the market to sell the U.S. dollar on Tuesday.



Dealers in Manila expected the peso to move in a tight



range as corporate dollar demand linked to settlements in the



non-deliverable forward market was countered by fears of


intervention.



    Activity was brisk, with $36.50 million transacted within



the first half hour of trading.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah remained at the wrong side of 9,500 per dollar



as the appetite for dollars, largely for genuine commercial



demand, continued to hold sway.



    Dealers said they expected the monetary authority to try



and guide the currency higher amid talk they had made efforts



to do this earlier in the week.



    "If the authorities had come in this morning at 9,550, the



rupiah may have strengthened to 9,500 but as always they were



too late," said a dealer from a European bank.



    "They probably wil be in later as they've made it clear



they want to defend the currency," he said.



    Indonesian President Megawati Sukarnoputri issued a



statement after meeting Bush in the U.S. on Wednesday,



condemning last week's attacks on the U.S. as "barbaric and



indiscriminate acts."



    Megawati also pledged to cooperate with the international



community in combating terrorism.



    Bush pledged at least $130 million in aid for judicial and



legal reform in Indonesia.



    Separately, the U.S. also said it would eliminate duties on



over $100 million of imports from Indonesia.



    U.S. officials hope she will take a strong stance against



the Islamic militants Washington believes were behind last



week's attacks.



    But several radical Indonesian Muslim groups have urged



Megawati not to cave in to pressure and vowed to launch a holy



war against the United States if Washington attacks



Afghanistan.



THAI BAHT



The baht was a shade softer at 44.30 but still within its



recent range as the market watched where the dollar/yen was



heading amid a dearth of strong domestic factors.



    Dealers said players were waiting to pick up the dollar at



44.00 and above, and to take profits below 44.20.



    Charts show 44.65 is a strong support for the baht in the



near term as it represents the 38.2 percent retracement of the



dollar's July 23-September 12 downmove.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar opened barely changed at 34.561 before



edging slightly lower, with the central bank expected to


intervene both ways to keep the currency steady.



    Dealers said the central bank was in the market on



Wednesday to curb gains in local currency.



    They said losses in local stocks and the country's bleak



economic outlook should keep the currency below 34.50 in the



near term.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Mkt Awaits Word On Bin Laden
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed against the dollar Wednesday as investors digested the latest developments in the U.S. effort to force the extradition of suspected terrorist Osama Bin Laden. 

 The dollar, which has suffered in recent weeks due mainly to the deteriorating U.S. economy, got a boost from the Bank of Japan, which intervened in the currency market for the second time this week in an attempt to weaken the yen. 

 The Singapore dollar, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah all tumbled against the U.S. currency. The Thai baht edged higher, while the South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar were little changed. 

 However, the outlook for the dollar over the medium term remains poor, analysts said, citing fears the U.S. economy may tip into recession and the difficulty the country will have in funding its ballooning current account deficit. 

 Last week's terrorist attacks in New York and Washington, and the threat of a U.S. military response have also hurt sentiment toward the dollar and U.S. stocks. 

 President Bush has demanded Afghanistan's hard-line Islamic Taliban government turn over Bid Laden, who is suspected of masterminding the attacks. Taliban leaders were considering whether to extradite Bid Laden or declare a holy war on the U.S. if it attacks Afghanistan. 

 An easing of tensions between the two sides Wednesday apparently soothed the markets and lent support to the dollar, said Thio Chin Loo, foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 "Today things were a little calmer than usual. Bush toned down his rhetoric and Afghanistan's leaders were more conciliatory," she said. 

 In Tokyo, the BOJ purchased dollars in the open market on behalf of the Ministry of Finance in an attempt to put a floor under the U.S. currency. 

 The move pushed the dollar from an intraday low of Y117.10 to a high of Y118.12. However, by late in the day the dollar had slipped to 117.54, down from Y117.94 late Tuesday in Tokyo. 

 Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa said Japan was in close contact with U.S. and European authorities when it intervened Wednesday, though Japan acted alone, and warned that the ministry was ready to take steps again if needed. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen lower after the BOJ intervention. But unlike the yen, it didn't rebound as the day wore on. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7417, up from S$1.7361 late Monday. The U.S. dollar drifted up to S$1.7420 before buying fizzled out. 

 Dealers said the reluctance to take fresh positions stemmed from uncertainty over how the U.S. might respond to last week's terrorist attacks. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended little changed as the central bank bought U.S. dollars shortly before the market closed to offset the local currency's early gains, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed at NT$34.572 against the U.S. dollar, compared with $34.575 Friday. The foreign exchange market was closed Monday and Tuesday due to a tropical storm. 

 The South Korean won also was barely changed from Tuesday's close. The dollar finished at KRW1,296.5 won, down slightly from KRW1,296.9 Tuesday. 

 The won fell in tandem with the yen after the BOJ intervened. Importer buying of dollars, which picked up in the wake of the BOJ's intervention, also weighed on the won. 

 However, the won managed to trim its losses as the yen climbed back later in the session. 

 The Indonesian rupiah weakened on corporate demand for dollars, but closed off its day lows as the central bank apparently sold dollars to help the local currency. 

 The dollar was quoted between 9,590 rupiah and IDR9,640 late Wednesday, much higher than IDR9,520 to IDR9,560 Tuesday. 

 The Philippine peso was pressured by corporate demand for dollars and losses in some regional currencies. 

 The dollar closed at PHP51.400 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP51.370 Tuesday. 

 The Thai baht drew support from foreign stock buying, but gains were capped by exporter dollar buying. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 44.190 baht, down from THB44.225 late Tuesday.
