title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Singapore Dlr Leads Rise
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies extended their recent ascent late Thursday, riding on the coattails of the Japanese yen's advance as the broad-based dollar retreat showed no sign of letting up, dealers said. 

 At 0920 GMT (4:20 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y119.32, below Y119.65 late Wednesday in New York. The dollar was at Y121.57 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 "The dollar is still weak globally, and this should support Asian currencies," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. "People are selling dollars on any rally in Asia." 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill's unconvincing defense of the dollar has heightened the ambiguity surrounding the Bush administration's commitment to a strong dollar policy, in turn supporting Asian currencies. 

 "There is no upside in talking about the dollar, except to say we have a continuing, continuous policy," Mr. O'Neill said in a CNBC interview Wednesday. "We've still got the same dollar policy." O'Neill didn't use the word "strong" to describe the dollar policy, contrary to the practice of the Clinton administration. 

 As the dollar continued to be clobbered, many Asian currencies, led by the Singapore dollar, surged to multi-month highs, ignoring the region's bleak economic fundamentals. 

 The appreciation of their respective currencies had prompted some of the region's monetary authorities to step in to slow the rise, in an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of their countries' exports, dealers believed. 

 Taiwan's central bank aggressively bought U.S. dollars, especially toward the close of trading, dealers said. The South Korean authority issued a warning against excessive gains in the won. Some dealers believed the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to slow the local currency's rise, though this was unconfirmed. 

 Talk of intervention failed to halt the Singapore dollar's rally, which gained momentum overnight, as participants continued to sell the U.S. currency. 

 The Singapore dollar surged to as high as S$1.7400 against its U.S. counterpart in late trade, before profit-taking in short U.S. dollar positions pushed the U.S. currency to S$1.7423. Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7534. 

 The South Korean won played catch up with the region's currency gains as trading resumed following a national holiday Wednesday. 

 But dollar purchases by the state-run Korea Development Bank and a warning by the finance ministry against "excessive market reaction to a specific currency's move" moderated the won's gains, despite the yen's rally, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,278.2 won, down 0.8% from Tuesday's close of KRW1,288.5. 

 The yen's strength and the local stock market's 1.4% jump thrusted the New Taiwan dollar through the NT$34.50 resistance level against the U.S. currency earlier in the day, dealers said. 

 But aggressive central bank intervention in the last 15 minutes of trading - which shored up trading volume to US$950 million from US$611 million - pushed the U.S. currency back above NTS$34.50, dealers said. The central bank accounted for more than half of the day's total volume dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at a seven-week low of NT$34.520, down from Wednesday's close of NT$34.570. 

 Overall, the central bank likely accounted for more than half of the total volume, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht gradually extended its recent gains, but continued to lag behind the region's rally, amid fears of central bank intervention and dollar demand by oil companies and importers, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at 44.555 baht, lower than THB44.905 late Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso ended unchanged, as remarks by a central bank official renewed fears of a further hike in the reserve requirement on bank deposits, helping the currency recoup its earlier losses, dealers said. 

Central Bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco said a hike in the liquidity reserve is an option "in case there is excess liquidity that can influence inflation, or trigger a weakening of the (peso)." 

 Some dealers suspected the central bank sold an estimated $50 million to $60 million to counter the pressure on the peso earlier in the day from corporate demand and short covering for dollars by banks. The central bank, however, denied intervening in the market. 

 The dollar closed at 50.950 pesos, unchanged from its level Wednesday. The dollar hit an intraday high of PHP51.160. 

 The Indonesian currency was firmer at 8,770 rupiah per dollar, compared with IDR8,825 late Wednesday.

title: Singapore Dlr Higher Late On Yen; MAS Rumored Buying Dlrs
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar rose sharply late Thursday as foreign banks and investors sold U.S. dollars in the wake of a soaring yen, dealers said. 

 The local dollar shook off several rounds of suspected intervention on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore aimed at smoothening its sharp rise, they added. 

 An MAS spokesperson wasn't immediately able to comment on the suspected intervention. 

 At 0821 GMT (4:21 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7430, down from S$1.7533 late Wednesday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7420 and S$1.7515. 

 The Singapore dollar opened higher compared with Wednesday's Asian close, in line with the yen's rise above Y120 per U.S. dollar and further gains in the euro, although it was off its overnight high around S$1.7400. 

 Dealers said U.S. dollar buying by local banks, suspected to have acted as MAS' agents, forced the Singapore currency to retreat from its overnight high. 

 The Singapore dollar opened around S$1.7470, rose to S$1.7440 in early trade, then fell sharply to S$1.7520 on the yen's brief slide to below Y120 per U.S. dollar. Local banks and a Swiss bank were the main sellers of Singapore dollars for U.S. dollars in this round, dealers said. 

 Then, during thin lunch-time trade, U.S. dollar sales by a European bank once again boosted the Singapore dollar to S$1.7440. This, again, attracted local banks to buy U.S. dollars. 

 In late afternoon trade, the Singapore dollar hit its intraday high of S$1.7420, tracking the yen's rise to Y119.29 versus the U.S. dollar. 

 Dealers expect the U.S. dollar to find support at S$1.7400 overnight, then at S$1.7350, while its upside is expected to be capped at S$1.7520. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly flat in thin trading and as interbank interest rates edged higher, curbing the market's appetite for bonds. 

 The yield on two-year bonds rose one basis point to 2.21% while the yield on five-year bonds was flat at 2.90%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yields on seven- and 10-year bonds were both flat at 3.31% and 3.58%, respectively.

title: Emerging  FX -Dollar fall enlivens Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies perked up in early trade on Friday, drawing strength from the dollar's losses against other majors. 

 Local factors also lent support. The peso was bolstered by news of the central bank raising liquidity reserve requirements to keep liquidity in check and defend the currency. 

 Dealers said the market was closely watching the trend of the dollar which had recently exhibited signs of fatigue, but it was too early to say if the U.S. currency was reversing course. 

 "A grim picture painted by the Fed's beige book is seeping in. The dollar seems to have recently displayed sensitivity to bearish data, news and lost its momentum," said a senior dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 "Now the question being asked by the market is this: If the U.S. economy is slow to react to rate cuts and tax packages, will U.S. policymakers soon turn a blind eye to dollar weakness? But I still think this is just a correction," he said. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso nudged up to touch a high of 52.84, against Thursday's low of 53.18 as commercial banks adjusted their positions after another hike in their reserve requirement. 

 The central bank on Thursday raised liquidity reserve requirements of commercial banks by two percentage points to 11 percent to mop up excess liquidity. The rise was in addition to a two percent hike on July 27. 

 Dealers in Manila said the move would suck about 12 billion pesos from the system in the next few days but with the import season at its peak, demand for the dollar was likely to persist. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar broke the key 1.7650 mark for the first time since March 19 in thin overnight trade, helped by a firmer yen and improved political situation in Indonesia. 

 Dealers said investors continued to pare long dollar positions early on Friday. 

 However, they expected the pace of the U.S. dollar decline against the local currency to be slow because most players had already unwound dollar longs quite actively ahead of the National Day holiday on Thursday. Charts show the Sing dollar is still in its upward channel against the dollar, dating back to July 17. 

 The government confirmed that the growth rate turned negative in the second quarter due to a sharp slowdown in electronics manufacturing and warned of worse ahead in the third quarter. 

 Second quarter GDP fell 0.9 percent on-year and 10.7 percent on an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won firmed up to touch a high of 1,278.5 on the back of a rising yen and a strong opening in the local stock market. 

 Dealers in Singapore said wariness over central bank intervention to slow the won's rise prompted players to square out of dollar shorts as the won broke through the 1,280 mark for the first time since June 1 when it touched a high of 1,277.5. 

 They said some state-run banks were spotted buying dollars, sparking rumours they were acting on behalf of the central bank. 

 Talk of brighter prospects of the sale of troubled Daewoo Motors to U.S. giant General Motors also buoyed overall sentiment. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah held on to its recent gains, hovering around 9,100 on euphoria over the new government, and support from a state bank, dealers said. 

 One state bank sold around $5 million into a thin market in early trade, sparking speculation Bank Indonesia might be behind the move. 

 President Megawati Sukarnoputri will swear in her new cabinet on Friday. Her choices of ministers won rave reviews from the market and media. 

 But strong rupiah gains are unlikely given the dollar is heavily oversold, with charts showing a reading of 7.2 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar edged up in line with a firmer yen but a bearish stock market outlook on poor July corporate sales and worries about economic growth prospects were expected to keep the upside limited. 

 Foreign investors were net sellers of T$2.19 billion worth of local shares on Thursday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said talk the central bank was likely to stall the Taiwan dollar's rise above 34.60 would also keep players cautious. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht nudged above 45.30 on the back of firmer regional currencies, but dealers saw its gains capped at 45.20 due to active corporate dollar demand. 

 The Bank of Thailand is yet to announce changes in forex disclosure rules, but the market has largely discounted the possibility they will be streamlined and more market-friendly. 

 Baht funding costs in the offshore market were mostly steady, with the tom/next rate quoted at -0.12/-0.06 satang per dollar, one-month rate at 3/12 satang and 12-month at 135/155.

title: Asian  Currencies  Steady To Up Late; Intervention  Fear Cap
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- -Intervention fears and some profit-taking helped curb the strength of Asian currencies Wednesday as worries that Japanese authorities would step in to check the dollar's decline helped support the beleaguered U.S. currency. 

 But with sentiment on the dollar remaining bearish, regional currencies were mostly steady to higher late in Asia, with the South Korean won chalking up a fresh six-month closing high - though off its intraday peak - in spite of verbal intervention by government officials. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,175.4 - its weakest close since July 25, 2002 - after trading between KRW1,171.0 and KRW1,176.8. The currency closed at KRW1,176.7 Tuesday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar firmed to a new two-month closing high amid modest inflows of foreign funds into the stock market, and offers from exporters and interbank players. 

 But dealers said bids for U.S. currency from the central bank and importers pulled it back from its intraday high. The dollar ended at NT$34.490, from NT$34.528 previously, after trading between NT$34.450 and NT$34.502. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened slightly within a tight trading range. The Philippine peso was also lower while the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah were little changed. 

 "It's still a weak dollar (story). The dollar has a lot of structural deficiencies," said Philip Wee, market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. With the U.S. budget and current account deficits, and the specter of a war in Iraq, "I can't see how it (the weak dollar picture) can change at this point," he added. 

 The dollar briefly dropped to a four-month low of Y117.55 overnight amid growing concerns about an imminent showdown in Iraq. The dollar also slid to its weakest level in more than three years versus the euro. 

 As of 0933 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y118.14, up from Y118.06 late Tuesday in New York, but weakening from Y118.75 in Tokyo. 

 Zembei Mizoguchi, Japan's new vice finance minister for international affairs, continued to warn markets the ministry is ready to act if needed to curb rapid foreign exchange movements. 

 "Excessive (foreign exchange) movements are unwelcome because they are bad for Japan's economy," Mizoguchi told reporters on his first full day in his new position. 

 Later, during a two-day visit to Australia, Japan's economy and banking minister Heizo Takenaka told reporters during a two-day visit he was carefully watching developments in the currency market, but said it was up to the market to determine the correct level for the yen. 

 Meantime, an official at South Korea's central bank said the monetary authority believes the won is appreciating too quickly but it won't make an official comment on whether, or when, it will intervene in the market. 

 "We are monitoring the market...and the won's appreciation does seem a bit fast," the official said. 

 His comments followed remarks to Dow Jones Newswires by an official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy earlier Wednesday that market participants shouldn't "underestimate the (South Korean) government's will to stabilize the foreign exchange market." 

 Kwon Tae-shin, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, wouldn't discuss when or how the government might act to stabilize the market. 

 "If we think there are speculative movements, then we should do some kind of smoothing operation," he said. 

 But dealers said the remarks from the officials didn't have affect trading very much. 

 "It (the verbal warning) comes out everyday, so I don't think it has a big impact on the market," said one dealer. 

 Still, in the near term, fears of intervention will likely keep market participants from pushing the dollar below KRW1,170, a support level that has held for the past six months. 

 "Everybody is a little bit scared of intervention," said a dealer. "They're very cautious and the dollar will keep trading between KRW1,170 and KRW1,175." 

 Elsewhere, traders said some agent banks of the Bank of Thailand were in the market when the dollar fell below 42.60 baht earlier in the day, though it was unclear if they were acting on behalf of the central bank to support the U.S. currency. 

 An offshore bank dealer said the agent banks were likely trading for themselves. 

 "There's no real proof it's on behalf of the BOT. The BOT only comes in when the market is very volatile," he said. 

 There was also some importer buying of the U.S. currency, which was quoted around THB42.65 late in Asia, from THB42.63 previously. 

 The dollar closed was flat at 8,875 rupiah for the second straight day as dollar short covering erased all the Indonesian currency's earlier gains. Intraday, the dollar traded between IDR8,860 and IDR8,880. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was modestly higher at S1.7348 late in Asia, from S$1.7335 Tuesday. During the Asian session, it moved between S$1.7300 and S$1.7350. 

 The dollar was also up against the peso, closing at PHP53.480 on the Philippine Dealing System, from PHP53.390 in the previous session. Intraday, it traded between PHP53.330 and PHP53.495.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  fears restrict gains.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Fears of intervention held back Asian currencies on Wednesday after they hit multi-month highs on heightened risks of war and rising pessimism on the U.S. economy. 

 The Singapore dollar and Korean won hesitated at six-month highs, the Thai baht failed to go past four-month highs and the Taiwan dollar stayed near two-month highs. 


The U.S. dollar hit a four-month low against the yen  and a fresh
three-year low against the euro        after weaker than expected U.S.
retail data and reports U.N. weapons inspectors found evidence Iraq had
smuggled arms-related goods.



But the dollar bounced back above 118 yen after the new Japanese Vice
Finance Minister for International Affairs, Zembei Mizoguchi, warned
Japan would take action against excessive forex moves.



"There remains a widespread perception in the forex markets that the
Bank of Japan will not be keen on seeing dollar-yen below 118 and
that's holding up the dollar up,"said Sameer Goel, strategist at Bank
of America, adding that the loss of momentum in the rallying yen had
reined in Asian currencies.



YEN A BIG FACTOR



"Most regional central banks think about their currencies in
trade-weighted terms and Japan is an important component in those
baskets. The markets would be comfortable driving Asian currencies
higher against the dollar as long as that is the trend which is
followed by the euro and yen," Goel said.



The Singapore dollar  hit a five-month high of 1.7297 per U.S. dollar
in offshore trade before giving up most gains.



But, given the U.S. dollar's lingering weakness, traders no longer
feared it was nearing the limits of the central bank's undisclosed
trade-weighted band, within which the currency is managed.



The Korean won             touched 1,171 per U.S. dollar but then pared
some of its gains after a finance ministry comment that the strength
was excessive.



"The current spot level is approaching 2002's (dollar) low of 1,165, a
support that is unlikely to be broken without a fight from Korean
officials, given lingering uncertainties in the external environment,"
JP Morgan said in a market commentary.



The Taiwan dollar  rose past a key resistance at 34.50 per U.S. dollar
to hit 34.45 and then stalled as traders anticipated central bankintervention. They said the authorities intervened the previous day.


INTERVENTION FEARS CAP BAHT



The Thai baht's gains were capped at the previous day's highs of 42.60
per U.S. dollar. Reports of central bank intervention to support the
dollar if it strengthened beyond 42.60 could not be confirmed. Traders
said the central bank normally intervened through other banks in
offshore markets.



The Indonesian rupiah  was relatively steady in a range of 8,860-8,875
per U.S. dollar, near a one-month high, as the currency market brushed
off ongoing protests against price hikes and focused on IMF aid
meetings next week.



Indonesia's international donors will meet on January 21-22 to discuss
fresh aid pledges with the government.



Jakarta-based traders said most of the dollar sales were by the bullish
offshore players.



"Rupiah is remarkably resilient below 8,900 as investor interest to

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: Singapore MAS Policy Likely Neutral
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Although Singapore's economic growth faltered somewhat in the second half of this year, the country's central bank isn't expected to switch to an easier monetary policy any time soon. 

 When it unveils its half-yearly policy plans next week, the Monetary Authority of Singapore is widely expected to stick to its current neutral stance. 

 Economists said that it will likely adopt this position, considering the current policy remains accommodative enough for an economy that has been growing by fits and starts, and which isn't expected to pick up speed till the second half. Inflation, meanwhile, is largely absent. 

 However, the local currency, the Singapore dollar, has appreciated against the U.S. dollar, and could pose some risks for the trade-dependent economy. 

 The local dollar's resurgence comes against a backdrop of a broadly weaker U.S. currency. In recent weeks, the U.S. dollar has weakened amid concerns over whether the current administration remains as committed to a strong dollar policy, as well as on fears related to the growing tensions between the U.S. and Iraq. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore will announce its policy stance at 0000 GMT Jan. 2. 

 The central bank implements monetary policy by weakening or strengthening the local currency in an undisclosed band against a basket of currencies of its major trading partners. 

 "An explicit depreciating policy risks instability and can be ruled out," Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said in a research report published Tuesday. 

 The MAS eased monetary policy to neutral eighteen months ago and has since then twice affirmed it. It has, however, adjusted the undisclosed band twice. 

 Allowing the Singapore dollar to trade within a broader range was taken as a signal to the markets that the MAS was more willing to tolerate a weaker local dollar, even though that wasn't considered an outright depreciation. 

 The Singapore economy contracted 2% last year. Despite a promising start in the new year, the economy continues to struggle to fully recover. The government expects gross domestic product growth to expand between 2% and 2.5% this year - sharply lower than earlier forecast. 


   3Q GDP Shrank Vs 2Q



"Throughout the whole of 2002, they (MAS) insisted they wouldn't use
the exchange rate to boost exports, I don't see why, now that things are
starting to look a little better, they would deviate from that
position," said Joseph Tan, an economist at Standard Chartered Bank in
Singapore.



A neutral stance also accommodates the government's view that the
economy will continue to recover next year, though that growth would
still be meek until the second half when the economy should begin to
pick up strength.



There were some fears earlier the economy could slip back into
recession following a quarterly contraction in the July-September
period, but recent data suggest otherwise. An unexpected 19%
year-on-year surge in non-oil domestic exports in November, for
instance, suggested the economy has regained some strength and that the
final quarter of the year will likely see GDP growing again.



Prices have begun to rise, after a period of persistent deflation. In
any case, inflationary pressures aren't a real concern at this time. In
November, the consumer price index, the most commonly used measure of
inflation in the republic, rose 0.2% over the year - the first
year-on-year rise since June. Indeed, the MAS doesn't expect the 2002
CPI to differ much from last year's rate by more than 50 basis points
either way.



"Things are starting to stabilize. We are seeing some signs of life. I
think all the talk of a double-dip recession has been over-hyped," said
Sim Moh Siong, economist at Salomon Smith Barney/Citicorp.



Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar has gained some 4.5% since October
against the U.S. dollar without apparently drawing any disapproving
growls from the republic's monetary authority. The MAS is believed to
have occasionally intervened to iron out any excessively sharp moves in
the Singapore dollar. It is believed to favor a weaker local dollar at
the moment to keep exports competitive.



But Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at United Overseas Bank Ltd.
(P.UOB), pointed out that on a trade-weighted basis, the Singapore
dollar has been flat, and that given the state of the economy, "could
very well underperform vis-a-vis the other regional currencies (by
year-end)."



Around 0745 GMT Thursday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7370
compared with S$1.7387, near the end of Tuesday's shortened Asian
trading session. Markets were closed Wednesday for Christmas.



Other analysts noted that even with the gains, the Singapore dollar
remains within the MAS's undisclosed policy range.



Other than the explicit policy statement, analysts would also be
scrutinizing the tone of MAS' statement, which usually accompanies the
policy announcement, for an update of the economic situation. Economic
data up to December should be available, giving the authority some
indication of whether the pickup in the economy in November has
continued - or stumbled again.



Emmanuel Ng, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said that
"they'll probably say (in the accompanying statement) that it (Singapore
dollar exchange rate) remains accommodative of the ongoing recovery."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Singapore dollar at 5-month high.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 24 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar  rose to a fresh five-month high on Tuesday, extending the previous day's yen-driven rally in thin holiday trade. 

 While verbal intervention by Japanese authorities and the mounting risk of a U.S-led attack on Iraq hemmed the dollar within a narrow 120.30-120.50 range against the yen, off an overnight one-month low of 119.83, the Singapore dollar continued rising after a brief corrective dip. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa said there is a need to keep watching purchasing power parity and currency rates, and that rapid moves in forex rates must be prevented. 

 Shiokawa has earlier said the yen should be at 150 to the dollar as per the purchasing power parity, which compares living standards among nations. 

 The Sing dollar hit a fresh five-month high of 1.7380 and quoted at 1.7380/90 after the morning's drop to 1.7412. 

 "This is quite surprising, given the market is quite worried about the trade-weighted band and intervention," a Singapore-based trader said. 

 "But I guess this is a result of stop-losses and thin liquidity." 

 Bank dealing rooms were thinly staffed on Christmas Eve, especially with regional markets in Indonesia and Philippines closed for the holiday. 

 Local markets have been wary of pushing the Sing dollar higher for fear it will become overvalued in trade-weighted terms just days before the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announces its twice-yearly review of monetary policy on January 2. 

 The Singapore dollar is up nearly three cents so far in December and has benefitted from a recent batch of healthier economic data and the yen's rise. 

 The MAS makes public its policy bias but never discloses the parameters of the band within which it guides the currency. It targets the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted nominal effective exchange rate and keeps the value within this secret band. 

 The last time the MAS issued a monetary policy statement was in July, when it reaffirmed its neutral policy stance on the Singapore dollar . The Thai baht  tailed the Sing dollar at a leisurely pace, hugging the 43 level. 

 Trading volumes were low but currency dealers waited for a likely hedging interest from oil importers after the risk of war and the prolonged strike in Venezuela pushed oil prices to a two-year high.

title: Informal MAS talks broach Sing dlr competitiveness.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 20 (Reuters) - Some economists consulted by the Monetary Authority of Singapore have floated the idea of a weaker Singapore dollar as an antidote to deflationary pressures, a local academic said on Friday. 

 Chen Kang, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University, said the question of a weaker dollar was discussed at informal talks he attended on Thursday at the invitation of Koh Yong Guan, the MAS's managing director. 

 "We did talk about this issue of a lower Sing dollar," Chen told a conference organised by the Institute of Policy Studies, a Singapore think tank. 

 "Some people mentioned that this could be an alternative... given the global environment of a deflationary situation," said Chen, head of the applied economics division at the university's business school. 

 "But the problem of how to do it is quite dangerous. If you try to lower the Sing dollar and the market pushes for it, there will be no end to it. So implementation is the most difficult part," he added. 

 Chen was speaking at the presentation of a report the IPS has submitted to the government on ways of revitalising Singapore's economy. 

 Asked to comment, the MAS said: "MAS has met with some economists from the private and public sectors to discuss recent economic developments and outlook for the economy. 

 "This is part of MAS's ongoing efforts to engage in public consultation and to enhance our surveillance of the economy. The discussion was informal and centred on macroeconomic issues, including monetary policy." 

 The Singapore dollar this week hit 1.7419 per U.S. dollar, the highest level since September 4, but dealers said the currency markets had been reluctant to push the currency higher for fear of provoking intervention by the MAS. 

 The MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, conducts monetary policy by targeting the exchange rate rather than interest rates to protect the small export-oriented economy from the disruption of major capital flows. 

 To run the policy, the MAS manages the value of the Singapore dollar against a weighted basket of currencies of its key trading partners such as the United States, Europe, Japan and Malaysia. 

 It targets the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted nominal effective exchange rate and keeps the value within a secret range or policy band. 

 Another speaker at the IPS conference said Singapore should actively consider the option of weakening the currency to boost the domestic sector of the economy. 

 Tan Kin Lian, chief executive officer of National Trades Union Congress's Income Insurance Cooperative Ltd, said the Singapore dollar had appreciated significantly in recent years against regional currencies. 

 "This is the main cause of our uncompetitiveness. Our customers in the region now find it too expensive to use our services," Tan said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Modest gains as dlr bows to war threat.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose marginally on Friday, benefitting as the U.S. dollar's weakened on heightening fears of a war against Iraq, but they lacked any real conviction in the move. 

 The dollar weakened to under 121 yen after the United States said Iraq was in "material breach" of the U.N. resolution on weapons inspections, raising worries of a war, although U.S. officials said an attack is not imminent. 

 The Singapore dollar was the main beneficiary of the U.S. dollar's weakness as the other regionals grappled with local factors. 

 Traders were also reluctant to take strong views on the yen, a dominant factor for the regionals, as confusion again reigned over what Japan's foreign exchange policy was. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa said the authorities were not thinking about intervening in the yen, after authoring a newspaper article saying the yen was overvalued and his ministry would take appropriate action if necessary. 

 Minutes of the Bank of Japan's November meeting also revealed Ministryof Finance calls for unsterilised intervention at a meeting last month, a move which could weaken the yen. 

 The Philippine peso stayed near the week's lows at 53.72-53.75, although fears the central bank would intervene curbed losses. Traders said the central bank had intervened earlier this week when the peso hit three-week lows. 

 Keenly awaited figures showed the budget deficit for the 11 months to November topping 200 billion pesos, but it may beat the 2002 target of 223 billion - although this has been revised up three times from an original target of 130 billion pesos. 

 Despite revenues beating their target for the first time this year, analysts remained bearish on the currency. 

 SING DOLLAR REINED IN, BAHT PRESSURED 

 The Singapore dollar rallied offshore to a 3-= month high of 1.7419 before Asian traders, concerned it will become too strong in trade-weighted terms and wary of Monetary Authority of Singaporeintervention, shaved some of the gains. 

 The MAS does not disclose the trade-weighted band it targets, but market estimates have the Sing at the strong end of the band. 

 "It is 0.25 percent away from the upper end of the band and there's always a risk that if this move is overdone the MAS will come in," Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS Warburg said. 

 The Korean won was slightly weaker despite the higher yen as onshore markets waited for the ruling party's president-elect Roh Moo-hyun to announce his policies. 

 Since winning Thursday's election, Roh has said he will make effort to stem the rises in consumer and property prices and has called for a mature relationship with the United States. 

 The won has not kept pace with the yen's rally from 125.70 two weeks ago, evidenced in the rising yen-won cross rate. 

 The cross rate is now quoted at 9.97, up from 9.61 at the start of December. Markets believe the Korean authorities are comfortable with a level of 10 to ensure the won's competitiveness. 

 "Although there are some big positives in Korea, the government is still, and quite legitimately, worried about competitiveness in a situation that's already quite bad for the external sector," Baweja said. 

 The Thai baht could not hold on to a high of 42.95 as offshore banks covered short dollar-baht positions in the final trading days of 2002. 

 A Bangkok-based trader said offshore banks had been selling dollars for more than two weeks hoping for baht appreciation, but local importers kept a lid on the upside. 

 The Taiwan dollar also to make gains, but closed just above Thursday's 34.885 close, as markets overcame a Standard & Poor's sovereign rating downgrade earlier this week. 

 The Indonesian rupiah held a familiar 8,875-8,890 range, awaiting foreign currency inflows from PT Astra International's rights issue and further bad loan sales by Indonesia's Bank Restructuring Agency.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Looking for direction, peso weak.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies struggled
for direction on Thursday as markets dithered over conflicting
signals on the U.S. dollar, with the Philippine peso setting a
three-week low ahead of a budget deficit update.
    After reclaiming 121 yen in early deals, the U.S. dollar
was largely unmoved in Asia as markets fretted over America's
build-up of troops in preparation for possible action on Iraq.
    The inertia was partly on account of Wednesday's White
House affirmation of its strong-dollar policy and the confusion
over which way Japanese authorities want the yen to head --
finance ministry rhetoric favours a weak yen but ruling Liberal
Democratic Party members have echoed the Bank of Japan's view
that a strong yen was not a bad thing.



    "The mood is clearly dollar-bearish, but because of all the
badgering by the Japanese authorities on the yen, there has
been little movement in regionals today," Sameer Goel,
strategist with Bank of America, said.
    The Philippine peso hit a three week low of 53.80 per
dollar in late trade, after the central bank governor denied
the bank had intervened to support the peso on Thursday -- talk
which had earlier helped the peso off its morning lows.
    Traders said the central bank was also thought to have
supported the peso on Tuesday and Wednesday. The peso has been
plagued by worries over the burgeoning fiscal deficit, and data
for the 11 months to November is expected on Friday.
     A government source told Reuters the deficit would be
around 200 billion pesos, close to the revised 223 billion
pesos or 5.6 percent of GDP target set for the whole year. The
original target was a full-year deficit of 130 billion pesos.
    "We are approaching the last trading day (of 2002) which is
December 27, so no one is taking aggressive positions and small
flows are causing exaggerated moves," a Manila-based trader
said.
    "I guess most traders will feel comfortable during this
holiday only if they go home with a slightly long dollar book,"
he said, referring to the persistent bearishness on the peso.
 
    Despite the gloom, the peso was little moved by data
showing a shrinking trade surplus and balance of payments.
    The trade surplus fell 24.7 percent in the January-October



period from a year earlier. The central bank said the balance



of payments in the nine months to September was in surplus by

BAHT STEADY, KOREA SHUT



A Korean market holiday for presidential elections thinned



regional trade, and the Taiwan dollar was spared further

The Singapore dollar stayed in a 1.7460-1.7470 range most

positions and fears of intervention saw it ease from an



offshore high of 1.7445 per dollar.



It struck a 3-= month high of 1.7420 this week, sparking



concern that it may overshoot the trade-weighted band it is



managed in, which could prompt intervention to cap its



strength.



 
    The Thai baht was lethargic around Wednesday's five-week

    The Taiwan dollar slipped early to a two-week low of 34.897

title: US Dlr Falls To S$1.7449 On Singapore Trade Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The U.S. dollar weakened against the Singapore currency, falling to levels not seen since since July 25, after a government report showed the island republic's trade performance in November far exceeded economists' expectations. 

 At 0502 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7430, sharply down from S$1.7462 immediately before the trade report was issued. 

 International Enterprise Singapore said non-oil domestic exports rose 19% on year to S$9.5 billion in November. The faster growth follows a 5.7% rise in October and tops the average forecast of 8.2% expansion by 10 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires. Individual forecasts ranged between a 6.5% and 10% expansion. 

 Tuesday's stronger-than-expected trade data were a huge relief for investors as the numbers suggest fourth-quarter gross domestic product might be given the boost it needs to see the city-state avoid a double-dip recession, economists said. 

 Singapore's GDP grew 3.9% on year in the third quarter but fell a seasonally-adjusted, annualized, quarter-on-quarter 10.1%. A second consecutive quarter-on-quarter contraction would push the economy into its second recession in a year. 

 While the trade data were the main factor that lifted the Singapore dollar earlier, traders also attributed the U.S. dollar's fall to its weakness against the yen. 

 Traders also said that the local dollar's sharp strengthening against the U.S. currency is unlikely to trigger any intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the island's central bank. 

 Compared with other Asian currencies, the Singapore dollar still looks weak on a trade-weighted basis, said a trader at an Asian bank here. 

 Using the exchange rate as its primary monetary policy tool, the MAS manages the value of the Singapore dollar against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 Some U.S.-dollar sell orders trickled into the market after the U.S. unit slipped below support at S$1.7460, with the trade data accelerating the decline, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar now has support at S$1.7430, then S$1.7400, they added.

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - A unexpectedly strong rise in
exports sent the Singapore dollar to its highest levels in over
three months on Tuesday, as most Asian currencies were lifted
off their early lows by a rebounding yen.
    The Singapore dollar rose to 1.7430 per dollar, last traded
on September 5, from an early low of 1.7493, after data showed
non-oil domestic exports had risen by 19 percent in November
from a year earlier, more than double the average market
forecast.
    Dealers said a sharp rise had been expected to follow the
hit exports took in October due to a lockout in U.S. West Coast
ports. The exports data followed Monday's unexpected rise in
October retail sales, which were up 1.8 percent on the year.
    Analysts said the upbeat data would support the Sing dollar
as it would douse expectations of the central bank shifting to
an easing stance in its monetary policy review in January.



    "Not even a small portion of the market is worried about a
widening (policy) band or a downright easing shift. Seems like
they are taking comfort in the numbers," said Bhanu Baweja,
currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore.
    The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the
currency against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of which
dollar, yen and euro are major components.
    In October 2001, the MAS widened its policy band to allow
larger exchange rate moves but said it would not seek an
appreciation of the Sing dollar on a trade weighted basis.
    Analysts believe the dollar's decline against the yen and
euro this year may have taken quite a bit of pressure off the
trade-weighted value of the Singapore dollar, and that is why
the MAS has not intervened to cap the nominal exchange rate
gains.
 
    "The Sing dollar hasn't gone beyond the band, it's still
about 0.4 percent from the stronger end," Baweja said.
    However, some dealers said the day's move was exacerbated
by the thin year-end conditions.
    BAHT, PESO OFF LOWS

resulted in heavy dollar sales from foreign banks.
    The Philippine peso hit a three-week low of 53.75 in early
trade, and the beleaguered currency proved unable to sustain
slight gains and weakened into the close.
    Dealers in Manila said a slowdown in dollar purchases from



local corporates and non-deliverable forward players helped the



peso after its opening losses, but sentiment was depressed



after a government source told Reuters the January-November



budget deficit was likely to be around 200 billion pesos.



Manila's inability to arrest a gapping budget deficit, now



forecast to hit 5.6 percent of gross domestic product this



year, has dented investor confidence. The peso is Asia's



weakest currency against the dollar this year, losing over four



percent.



The region's strongest currency in 2002, the Indonesian



rupiah, eased to back over 8,855 per dollar after it had



reached a three-month high of 8,805 on Monday.



Dealers in Jakarta said local players choose to book



profits on the rupiah's recent gains before any further



appreciation on the back of expected dollar inflows from state



asset sales.



The South Korean won hit its strongest since September 9,



encouraged by the yen's rebound. A finance ministry official



told Reuters the government was monitoring the rise of the won



closely.



The Taiwan dollar was off its early lows but worries over



outflows of foreign investment from local stocks capped its



gains.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Soft dlr helps, rupiah heads for 4-month high.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Dec 16 (Reuters) - The buoyant Indonesian
rupiah
 strengthened towards 8,800 per dollar on Monday, a break of
which would take it to four-month peaks and far from the gloom
that surrounded it after the devastating Bali attacks in
October.
    Most other Asian currencies also firmed against a broadly
weaker dollar, the friendless Philippine peso the exception,
with the Singapore dollar and Thai baht consolidating around
their respective three-month and one-month highs.
    The rupiah rose to around 8,805 per dollar, its highest
since September 9, supported by Sunday's part sale of telco
giant PT Indosat. Singapore's ST Telemedia will pay $634
million for a 42 percent stake in the state-run telecom.
    Dealers in Jakarta said while dollar demand from some local
corporates capped the rupiah and thin conditions deterred
aggressive moves, speculation over dollar inflows from the
Indosat sale kept the currency supported.



    "Players are betting that at least 20 to 30 percent of the
Indosat proceeds will flow into the market," said a dealer at
an American bank in Jakarta.
    He said that speculation could push the dollar beyond
8,800, and might have already halted some dollar purchases from
corporates who can afford to wait for cheaper dollars.
    The rupiah is Asia's best performing currency in 2002,
rising over 17.6 percent against the dollar, backed by steady
inflows from sale of state assets and repatriation of earnings
from exports due to higher yields at home.
    It has risen by almost seven percent from a six-month low
around 9,400 per dollar reached after the October 12 bombings
in Bali which killed almost 200 people, mostly foreign
tourists.
    SING, BAHT CONSOLIDATE
    Elsewhere, dealers said the yen's rally through 121 per
dollar aided sentiment in regional currencies, but gains for
some were capped by wariness of possible central bankintervention to protect export competitiveness.
    Although data from Singapore and Thailand bettered
forecasts, analysts said the economic outlook was clouded by a
lacklustre recovery in the United States -- export-driven
Asia's largest market.
    "Dollar weakness will support Asia regionals, but
uncertainty surrounding the U.S. economy will at best keep most
of them within ranges we have seen in the second half (of
2002)," said a senior dealer at a Singapore bank.
    Those concerns pulled the Singapore dollar off Friday's
three-month high of 1.7439 down to a session low of 1.7513 per
dollar. The Sing strengthened back through 1.75, but dealers
said fears of central bank intervention would cap gains.
 
    "Most players are booking profits on the Sing dollar to
preempt the risk of intervention," a European bank dealer said.
    She said unless the Sing dollar strengthens beyond 1.7450,
most players would feel safe in betting on a short-term
retracement in the dollar.
    The market largely ignored a surprising 1.8 percent annual



rise in October retail sales, which analysts associated with a



more buoyant stock market and higher visitor arrivals for the



month rather than any improvement in domestic consumption.



With the exception of a slight blip in July, Singapore's



retail sales have been in a downward spiral all year as the



rising numbers of jobless keep a tight hold on their wallets.



The Thai baht touched fresh one-month highs at 43.18, with



sentiment supported by the solid growth of gross domestic



product in the year to the September, despite a slowing in



quarterly pace of growth.



The National Economic and Social Development Board said the



economy grew 5.8 percent over the year, faster than the 5.6



percent growth forecast by analysts and the 5.1 percent

By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Dec 16 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah
hit three-month highs on Monday as a weaker U.S. dollar lifted
most Asian currencies, although the rapid gains raised
speculation that regional central banks may try to cap the
rises.
    The Singapore dollar was just off the three-month highs and
the Thai baht  neared one-month highs, supported by the
yen's  gains to around 120.5 per dollar, but traders said
further sharp rallies were unlikely as central banks were
expected to intervene to keep currencies competitive.
    "With the dollar likely to see trend weakness in the coming
months, there certainly will be pressure on the Asian regionals
to appreciate," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS
Warburg in Singapore.
    He said better than expected economic numbers and recent
investment inflows in equity markets had also helped sentiment
in the regionals.



    But with the economic outlook clouded by a lacklustre
recovery in the United States, export-driven Asia's single
largest market, currency strength would be under the close
watch of the region's central banks.
    "Having already allowed the Asian regionals to appreciate
strongly, Asian central banks would be weary of losing further
competitiveness in their export markets," Baweja said.
    Underscoring Baweja's view, the Singapore dollar stepped
slightly away from its three-month highs hit on Friday as
players speculated on possible intervention by the central
bank.
 
    The Singapore dollar        was around 1.7475 per dollar,
from 1.7743 in New York on Friday, last traded on September 6.
    Dealer said early U.S. dollar bids around 1.7450, on fears
of central bank intervention, prompted players to book profits
on the Singapore dollar's recent gains.
    Dealers said any impact from October's retail sales data
due at 0500 GMT and exports data on Tuesday was likely to be
moderate as weaker numbers have already been priced in.
    Players were likely to stay cautious as thin year-end
conditions could exacerbate price action, they said.

Dealers in Singapore said the market was now likely to aim

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  talk aids peso as GDP slows.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Sentiment on the bewildered
Philippine peso took another hit on Thursday after third
quarter economic growth data came below expectations, although
worries of central bank intervention stopped it from falling.
 
    Elsewhere, Asian currencies were a touch firmer in subdued
trade going into the U.S Thanksgiving holiday.
    The Philippine economy grew 3.8 percent year-on-year in the


 third quarter, down from 4.5 percent in the second quarter, as 

 a jump in manufacturing and services was held in check by flat 

 farm output. On a quarterly basis, the economy contracted 0.1 

 percent. 


 
    A Reuters poll of 10 economists had yielded an average
forecast of 4.0 percent year-on-year growth.
    Still, the peso held a tight 53.55-53.60 per dollar range,
clear of Monday's 16-month low of 53.86, thanks to talk of
central bank dollar sales, dealers in Manila said.
    "The market is looking to bid up the dollar but with the
central bank in the market players also know their
limitations," said a dealer at a local bank in Manila.
    He said the central bank sold about $5 million defending
53.60 per dollar, where the local market closed on Wednesday.
    "Basically, a token intervention through some foreign banks
to tell the market that it does not want the peso to weaken
further," the dealer said.
    Dealers suspect the central bank had been in the market



over the last week as since worries over a growing budget



deficit and slowing growth knocked the peso to its 16-month



lows. On Monday, the central bank denied it had intervened.



Some support for the peso was also expected after the



government said on Wednesday that it would issue up to five



billion pesos of dollar-linked three-year notes next week to



juggle its budget deficit financing requirements for the year.



Traders said other regional currencies were quiet, and a



lack of trading interest ahead of U.S. Thanksgiving holidays



was likely to keep their upsides capped.



"In the previous two, three days, we already had a



substantial amount of pre-holiday position squaring and now



people are not prepared to take substantial positions," said



Simon Flint, Bank of America's senior currency strategist in



Singapore.



 
    "In fact a lot of people would be rolling back risk
progressively as the new year approaches," he added.
    Flint said there was little impact on regional currencies
from the dollar and Wall Street's rally after U.S. data raised

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Ratings hurt peso, stocks buoy won.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Talk of intervention supported an unloved Philippine peso at 16-month lows on Monday, while the Korean won hitched on to a stock market rally to rise as the U.S. dollar stalled on another attempt to surge against the yen. 

 Ratings agency Fitch cut its sovereign ratings outlook for the Philippines to negative from stable, citing a loss fiscal credibility, and markets are worried that one of the major agencies will soon downgrade the country. 

 Traders said other Asian currencies were flat to slightly lower as the yen bounced off a three-week low of 123.19. 

 But they expect the U.S. dollar to stay strong this week on hopes of better economic data and stock market gains, which will allow it to benefit from the uncertainty over Japan's banks and the euro zone's troubles with growth. 

 "As U.S. markets slow for the long Thanksgiving holiday weekend, focus should shift to Japan's banking problem and Europe's less sanguine economic outlook," DBS Bank said in its market commentary. 

 "Our assessment is that the dollar should continue to expand on recent gains this week against the yen and euro, as well as Asian exchange rates, especially the peso," it said. 

 The Korean won rallied to 1,211 on a surge in foreign portfolio investments and the rise in its stock market to a two-month high. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped to over 1.77 per dollar early on, and then held a 1.7715-1.7721 range. Traders reported some light U.S. dollar bids from a local bank in the morning, followed by low trading volumes. 

 The Taiwan dollar closed weaker at 34.804 despite a rise in share prices, as markets fretted over the weekend resignations of pro-reform Minister of Finance Lee Yung-san and the Chairman of the Council of Agriculture. 

 Both the won and Taiwan dollar enjoyed relative strength against other regionals last week as their stock markets rallied on signs of a global recovery in the technology sector. 

 FOREIGN STOCK BUYING HELPS BAHT 

 The Thai baht stuck to the 43.35-43.40 range seen last week, even as its regional counterparts slid as foreigners turned buyers once again in its share market. 

 "Though dollar/baht was biased higher on the margin this morning, mostly in line with a higher dollar/yen from Friday's offshore session, the pair's gains were capped by continued good performance in the local stock markets," Bank of America said in its market commentary. 

 The Indonesian rupiah closed almost steady around 8,973-8,978 as hopes of further IMF funding and fresh foreign investment towards loan sales by the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency supported the currency. 

 Heavy local dollar demand had seen it weaken past 9,000 late last week. 

 "The generally lower levels of risk-aversion in global markets is providing a conducive environment for higher-yielders like the rupiah," Bank of America said. 

 The Philippine peso closed at a 16-month low of 53.85 despite suspected central bank intervention to defend the sliding currency in morning trade after the Fitch cut. 

 Markets have been worried that the widening budget deficit and downward revision in growth forecasts could lead to a sovereign rating downgrade. As well, traders reported heavy dollar purchases by a power firm. 

 The peso opened local trading at Friday's low of 53.85 and dipped to 53.86, its lowest since July 2001. Data on the local dealing system showed a high trading volume of $93.5 million on Monday morning, when the intervention was suspected, although volumes halved in afternoon trade. 

 Last week, the government announced the budget deficit to October exceeded the full-year target, and it set a new target - its fourth for 2002 - of 5.6 percent of GDP, about 220 billion pesos. title: Intervention  suspected after Philippine peso slips.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention by the Philippine central bank stemmed the peso's slide as it struck a fresh 16-month low following a rating outlook downgrade. 

 The peso dipped to 53.86 in morning deals and subsequently settled around Friday's low at 53.85, levels last seen in July 2001, amid heavy dollar bids. 

 "I believe the central bank has sold around 70-80 million dollars around 53.85," a Manila-based trader said. Other traders put the intervention at around half that estimate. 

 Data on the local dealing system showing an unusually high currency trading volume of $93.5 million on Monday morning, compared with Friday morning's $75.5 million, and at an average weighted rate of 53.843, supported the view that there had been intervention, the trader said. 

 The Philippine peso has been dogged by worries its widening budget deficit and downward revision in growth forecasts could lead to a sovereign rating downgrade. 

 Rating agency Fitch on Monday lowered its outlook for the Philippines to negative from stable. 

 Last week, the government said the budget deficit to October had exceeded the full-year target, and it set a new target - its fourth for 2002 - of 5.6 percent of GDP, about 220 billion pesos. It also cut the 2003 GDP growth forecast to 4.2-5.2 percent from 5.0-5.5 percent. 

 Fitch has a BB-plus long-term foreign currency rating on the Philippines. The country is rated BB-plus by Standard & Poor's with a negative outlook and Ba1 by Moody's Investors Service with a stable outlook.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Higher Late;Won,NT$ At 2-Mo High
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies firmed as the dollar lost ground against major rivals, particularly the yen, amid concerns about a U.S.-Iraq conflict and uncertainty about the U.S. economy. 

 Regional units were also beneficiaries of the hunt for higher yields after the U.S. Federal Reserve's larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate cut last week. 

 The Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar ended the day at two month highs, while the Thai baht hit levels unseen since September. 

 The Singapore dollar was hardly dented by Trade and Industry Minister George Yeo's comments that he isn't ruling out the possibility of a double-dip recession for the city state. 

 For the most part, trading ranges were tight and there wasn't much significant position-taking ahead of a U.S. holiday Monday. 

 Market players were also waiting for Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's views on the economy when he testifies before the Joint Economic Committee of Congress Wednesday, as well as a slew of U.S. economic data to be released this week. 

 Verbal intervention by Japanese government officials failed to curb the yen's strength in Asia. Nor did weak share prices and shaky economic data; the Nikkei 225 Stock Average briefly fell below its 19-year low during the session. 

 David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at The Royal Bank of Scotland, said markets remain concerned about why the Fed cut rates so sharply last week. 

 Some wonder if the decision reflects a greater worry about the economy than anticipated earlier. 

 Markets are also refocusing on Iraq after the United Nations approved resolutions that calls on the country to eliminate its weapons of mass destruction or face "serious consequences. 

 For now, though, markets are waiting to see how Iraq's response, and how the U.S. interprets that response, Simmonds said. 

 If there is conflict and oil prices jump, it would further threaten Asian economies that are already grappling with a slowdown in the U.S., he said. That should also curtail regional currencies' current strength, he added. 

 The dollar ended at 1,201.0 won, down from KRW1,207.4 Friday, and its weakest finish since Sept. 10. Intraday, it traded between KRW1,197.8 and KRW1,203.3. 

 Only demand from importers helped lift the currency back above KRW1,200 in the afternoon, traders said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency ended at NT$34.415, up from NT$34.505 Friday, and its lowest since Sept. 13, though bids from importers and central bank intervention helped cushion the fall. 

 After the market's close, Taiwan's central bank announced a 25 basis point rate cut, a move widely expected by analysts since the Fed slashed rates last week. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was quoted around S$1.7566 as of 1045 GMT, down from S$1.7615 late Friday. 

 The dollar opened at around S$1.7580 in Asia and slipped to S$1.7570 in the wake of its fall below 120 yen; it spent much of the session locked between S$1.7575 and S$1.7585. 

 Market participants said Yeo's bearish comments on the economy weren't a major surprise as most have already been expecting a weak economic performance in the second half. The government is widely expected to cut its full-year growth forecasts to 2%-3%, from 3%-4% currently. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar was quoted around 42.96 versus the Thai baht as of 1047 GMT, down from THB43.12 late Friday. 

 An Asian bank trader in Singapore said Thailand's central bankintervened via agent banks to curb the baht's rise when the dollar slipped to an intraday trough of THB42.94, it's lowest since Sept. 19. 

 "But with the U.S. holiday (Monday), nobody is taking new positions," he said. 

 Meanwhile, the Indonesian rupiah rose as offshore market players continued to liquidate long dollar positions as the probe into last month's deadly bombings in Bali progressed. 

 News that the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency sealed a pact Friday to sell a 51% stake in Bank Niaga to Malaysia's Commerce Asset-Holding Bhd. for around $114 million also lifted the market, dealers said. The deal is expected to bring capital flows into Indonesia. 

 The dollar closed at 9,145 rupiah, down from IDR9,190 Friday. 

 But the Philippine peso surrendered early gains as corporate demand for dollars emerged. 

 The U.S. currency ended at its intraday high of PHP52.960 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP52.880 Friday. 

 The dollar's closing level was different from the PHP52.910 initially posted on the system. 

 Metropolitan Bank & Trust Co., the electronic exchange's officer of the week, said the discrepancy was due to late mapping of the last transaction executed on the dealing system. 

 Some traders said the revision shouldn't stir negative reaction from market players since such incidents had happened in the past, and weren't an attempt to engineer the foreign exchange rate.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Regionals rally on weak dollar.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rallied
strongly on Monday as the dollar, weakened by economic woes and
fears of war, fell to two-month lows against the yen despite
verbal intervention by Japanese officials.
    The Singapore dollar, South Korean won, Taiwan dollar and
Thai baht hit levels last seen in September, while the
Indonesian rupiah traded at its strongest since before the Bali
bombings of October 12, and the Philippine peso was also near a
one-month high.
    After the local market had closed, the Taiwan central bank
lowered rates by 0.25 percent -- half the size of last week's
cut in the United States. The Taiwan move had been widely
expected.
    "A predominantly majors-inspired move with some markets
helped by the recent softening in oil prices and positive
equity flows," said David Simmonds, emerging markets strategist
at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore, of Monday's regional
gains.



    Simmonds said with the trade-weighted value of the dollar
easing, most players would be "comfortable in staying long Asia
against the dollar."
    The dollar hit 119.51 yen, it lowest since September 13, as
the market paid little attention to efforts by Japan's top
finance officials to talk the yen down. A widening U.S. current
account deficit, a possible war with Iraq, and higher interest
rates elsewhere have all eroded sentiment on the dollar.
    Analysts said that ahead of the Federal Reserve chairman
Alan Greenspan's testimony to a congressional committee on
Wednesday and key economic data at the end of the week, the
dollar was likely to stay defensive -- which would support
Asian currencies.
    "Signs that the Fed's easing could be working are perhaps
needed to trigger a period of pullback for the dollar, which is
looking oversold though markets remain biased to sell dollars
on any rallies," said Jimmy Koh Chew Teck, head of treasury at
UOB Bank in Singapore.
    The Singapore dollar touched 1.7544 per dollar, its
strongest since September 10, before paring some of those

target.

title: Indonesian rupiah drops 3.6 pct,  intervention  seen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah extended losses to 3.6 percent on Monday, despite suspected central bank intervention to cushion the slide, in reaction to the blasts on the resort island of Bali, dealers said. 

 At its weakest point, the rupiah hit 9,350 per dollar, a level last seen at the end of April. 

 The weekend blasts, which killed at least 183 people, drove the rupiah down to 9,250 initially from Friday's close of 9,005/9,015. 

 Dealers said Indonesian authorities were seen to intervene to buy the rupiah around 9,300 rupiah to the dollar. 

 "The market went short of dollars before the weekend and is still covering," a Jakarta-based dealer said. 

 He said Indonesia's Bank Restructuring Agency may also have sold some of the dollars it has been raising from sale of banks' bad loans. 

 No one has claimed responsibility for the bombs late Saturday night on Bali. The explosions ripped through packed nightclubs, popular with foreign tourists. 

 Fingers have been pointed to Osama bin Laden's al Qaeda network, blamed by the U.S. for the September 11 attacks on the United States. 

 Other regional currencies also weakened on Monday, especially the Philippine peso , fearing a spillover of the violence into the Philippines. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted up to 1.8020, a five-month low, before it recovered and the Thai baht was around 44, a level not seen since early February.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Tumble down, baht at 6-month lows.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuters) - The Thai baht fell to 

 six-month lows and the Singapore dollar closed in on 16-week 

 troughs on Monday as Asian currencies were pummelled by worries 

 over oil prices and the lockout in U.S. west coast ports. 

     Stumbling stocks and a weak yen added to the pressure, 

 sending the Taiwan dollar to 6-=   month lows, the South Korean 

 won to its weakest in 16 weeks and the Philippine peso to fresh 

 14-month lows. 

     "Risk aversion, weakness in global equities and increasing 

 worries on oil prices are likely to continue to weigh on Asian 

currencies," said Sameer Goel, market analyst at Bank of 

 America in Singapore. 

     World crude oil prices pushed past $30 a barrel after a 

 suspected terror attack on a tanker off Yemen. 

     Sunday's explosion on the French-flagged Limburg heightened 

 tensions surrounding the oil-rich Middle East, as the United 

 States presses for the removal of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein. 

     In the United States, talks to end a week-long management 

 lockout of west coast ports broke off without agreement late on 

 Sunday and without any schedule for the next round. 

     Some regional economists fear a prolonged lockout could not 

 only delay Asian exports, but losses to the U.S. economy - 

 estimated at $1 billion a day - would hurt a fragile U.S. 

 recovery just as Asia was gearing up for a surge in demand 

 ahead of the Christmas holiday shopping season. 

 Meanwhile, the yen slipped to a two-week low against 

 against the dollar, as the Nikkei stock average crumbled to a 

 fresh 19-year low, taking most Asian markets down with it. 

 BAHT SLIPS 

 The Thai baht slipped to 43.72, last seen on April 3, as 

 oil importers bought dollars. But fears of central bank dollar 

 sales, expected around 43.75, prompted some profit-taking. 

     Dealers in Singapore said they suspect the Bank of Thailand 

 did sell dollars beyond 43.60 last week to prop up the baht. 

     However, analysts believe any support would be temporary 

 and aimed at dampening volatility, given Thailand's dependence 

 on imported oil and its increased correlation to moves in 

 dollar/yen in recent weeks. 

     The Singapore dollar turned volatile after a quiet start 

 when it touched near one-week highs at 1.7795 per dollar. 

     Taking its cue from the yen, the Sing slipped to 1.7916, 

 just shy of the 16-week lows at 1.7925 it visited last week. 

     Dealers said the move gathered pace as stop-loss Sing 

 dollar sell orders were triggered beyond 1.7860. As the Sing 

 slipped past 1.7880, some locals were spotted covering short 

 U.S. dollar positions they had taken. 

 Ahead of the release of advance third quarter gross 

 domestic product estimates, due on Thursday, dealers said the 

 Sing dollar could ease further. 

 The Philippine peso ended onshore trade at 52.90 per 

 dollar, its lowest since August 10, 2001, weighed by a surge of 

 dollar buying from local corporates and speculative dollar 

 demand from offshore. 

     Dealers in Manila said they suspected the central bank was 

 in the market on Monday, including just before the local close. 

     However, the gloomy global outlook prompted Taiwan's 

central bank to loosen its grip a little and let the Taiwan 

 dollar ease through 35.0 per dollar. The central bank had 

 defended that level last week, trying to counter equity-related 

 outflows. 

 The currency touched a low of 35.089, last visited on March 

 21, before closing onshore trade at 35.069 as the market still 

 feared central bank intervention. 

 Dealers in Singapore said talk of some dollar sales by the 

central bank backed views in the market that the bank's 

 tolerance level has now shifted to around 35.10. 

 The Korean won ended onshore trade at 1,240.9, its lowest 

 since June 17, as market eyed more investment outflows by 

 foreign funds with the benchmark KOSPI down by over 3.5 

 percent. 

 Dealers in Singapore said given Korea's high dependence on 

 imported oil, corporates hedging against higher oil bills were 

 expected to keep the won under pressure. 

 Profit-taking in dollars just ahead of 1,241.0, the June 17 

 low, capped the downside, though dealers said any support would 

 be temporary.

title: Singapore Dlr Lower Late As Yen Weakens On Econ Concerns
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was lower in Asia late Friday tracking the yen's weakness as lingering concerns over Japan's economy helped to hold the otherwise weak U.S. currency from a free fall, traders said. 

 At 0915 GMT (5:15 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7493, up from S$1.7438 late in Asia Thursday. 

 A late afternoon rally pushed the U.S. currency as high as S$1.7508, breaking S$1.7500 psychological resistance for the first time this week. The U.S. dollar traded between S$1.7439 and S$1.7500 for the rest of the day. 

 The U.S. dollar's rally against the local currency was supported by speculative buying of the U.S. currency for yen in Asian trading, which was touched off by a mixure of fears that Tokyo stocks may open lower and rumors of stop-loss buy orders at Y118.80, traders said. 

 The U.S. currency opened in Asia at around S$1.7490, but was pressed down to about S$1.7440 mid morning. The pair hovered in a tight 10-point band between S$1.7449-S$1.7459 before speculative buying by a major local bank bid the U.S. dollar up, a local dealer said. 

 The general fear that a sharp fallout of the U.S. dollar against the local currency may trigger the Monetary Authority of Singapore's intervention is another factor that supported the U.S. dollar's rally, currency strategists said. 

 "The dollar has been on the bottom of the MAS trading band for two weeks. If it breaks out of it, we'll be talking about a new trading range. It also has to do with the sentiment," said James Malcolm, global foreign exchange strategist at JP Morgan. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary-policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 According to Malcolm, the current trading band is between S$1.7450-S$1.7880. 

 However, most traders continue to peg the U.S. dollar's near-term resistance at S$1.7500 in anticipation that a slew of negative factors will continue to weigh on the U.S. currency. 

 The U.S. employment data - due later in the global session and is generally expected to be weaker-than-expected - could send the U.S. stock markets south and spur another wave of U.S. dollar selling. 

 "If the (U.S.) dollar finishes off above today's high of Y118.60 in New York tonight, we can expect the Singapore dollar to open at a new trading level next week," said the dealer at a major foreign bank. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to find support at S$1.7440 overnight. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mixed Friday as some tenors shed their early gains due to profit-taking, dealers said. 

 Local bonds had opened on a stronger note before modest pre-weekend consolidation pared some of those gains, although the outlook for local bonds remains generally supportive, dealers added. 

 In a research report published Friday, JPMOrgan Chase Bank said bond-swap spreads are unlikely to stay low for much longer as interest rates come off their recent bottom. 

 "We recommend buying bonds against swaps, with the view that bond-swap spreads will gradually widen," JPMorgan said. 

 "We advise initially positioning at the short end, which is a more defensive trade, and moving to longer tenor swap spread wideners over the next couple of weeks," JPMorgan added. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was up one basis point at 1.22%, while the yield on five-year bonds was down two basis points at 2.35%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was also two basis points lower at 2.82%, while the yield on 10-year bonds was unchanged at 3.38%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was two basis points lower at 3.73%. 

 The above are pre-settlement closing bids obtained from dealers and are subject to minor changes. Historical bond yields and prices can be viewed at the Monetary Authority of Singapore's bond Web site: 

http://www.sgs.gov.sg("http://www.sgs.gov.sg")


In the interest rate swaps market, swap offers were mostly higher as
they tracked some local bond yields.



The two-year offer rose four basis points to 1.41%, while the
five-year swap offer rose one basis point to 2.50%. The 10-year offer
was up two basis points at 3.39%.



The spread between two- and 10-year swaps narrowed to 198 basis points
from 200 basis points late Thursday.



In the local money market, rates were mostly a little higher as
liquidity tightening modestly ahead of the weekend.



Dealers and analysts attributed the tightening to banks seeking
short-term funding in anticipation of stronger demand for home-loan
packages, especially amid the ongoing rate war between banks in
Singapore.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Bow to dollar strength.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso traded at 

 its lowest level since late 2001, the Taiwan dollar hit a 

 10-week low, and the Korean won and Thai baht touched two-week 

 lows as Asian currencies ceded ground to a rallying dollar on 

 Friday. 

     "The market was taken off guard by the dollar strength 

 overnight," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency strategist at 

 BNP Paribas. The dollar hit two week highs against the yen 

  and euro as recovering U.S. stocks boosted the 

currency. 

     Thio said market momentum was now in favour of the dollar 

 and it would be some time before Asian currencies found a 

 floor.     Dealers said position squaring ahead of the weekend 

 helped most currencies off their lows, while rumours of central 

 bank intervention aided the Philippine peso and the Taiwan 

 dollar. 

 The peso fell to an eight-month low of 52.37 per 

 dollar before steadying on the intervention talk, which was 

 denied by the central bank. 

     The Philippine central bank said it had not intervened and 

 would do so only in case of extreme volatility in the market. 

     Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the decline was 

 temporary, reflecting weakness across the region and reinforced 

 by negative domestic news, including Thursday's beheading of 

 two Christian preachers in the country's south by Muslim 

 extremists. 

 Manila dealers said sentiment was bearish on worries over 

 the budget deficit - which exceeded its 2002 target after just 

 seven months - and players simply used the comments to book 

 profits. 

 The Taiwan dollar fell to a 10-week low of 34.16 per 

 dollar, before talk of intervention helped it recover some 

 losses. 

 The Singapore dollar briefly touched 1.7601 per dollar, its 

 weakest since August 13, as the dollar strengthened. But dollar 

 sales by local corporates saw it recover later to around 

 1.7565. 

     A 0.4 percent fall in the July consumer price index from a 

 year earlier drew a muted market response. 


    The Thai baht        was around 42.28 per dollar, off an



early two-week low of 42.41. Dealers in Singapore said lack of



local factors and illiquid conditions had limited the downside.



    The Korean won        dropped to a two-week low of 1,204.8



before paring its losses. Dealers in Singapore said the won was



supported by inflows from settlement of export deals.



    The Indonesian rupiah        was down at 8,865 per dollar,



from late Thursday's 8,845. It hit a one-week low, but found



support in news that the bank restructuring agency has sold



$2.5 billion worth of non-performing loans.
