text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were easier 

 in early Friday trade as the dollar rose to two week highs 

 against the yen and euro , with the Philippine 

 peso hitting an eight-month low after disappointing budget 

 deficit data. 

     The dollar was lifted by another day of gains on Wall 

 Street and signs of improvement in corporate bond markets 

 following a flood of corporate issuance, easing concerns that a 

 credit crunch might hurt capital spending and the economy. 

     "Near term, market action should remain dollar positive as 

 dictated by the consistency and strength of recent moves," said 

 Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

     "The developments, such as declining risk aversion and a 

 reviving corporate bond market, on which these moves are 

 predicated are fundamental in that they constitute the dollar's 

 key drivers and should be watched closely," he added. 


    The Philippine peso        fell to an eight-month low of



52.30 per dollar as sentiment was depressed by Thursday's



confirmation that the 2002 budget deficit target of 130 billion



pesos had been exceeded in just seven months.



    The January to July deficit was 133 billion pesos, but the



government said it would stick with its full year forecast.



    Dealers in Manila said the market was likely to target



one-year lows beyond 52.50, but wariness over intervention and



overbought signals on the dollar was deterring players from



being too aggressive.



Charts showed the dollar/peso 14-day relative strength



index reading at 82.73, highlighting the risk of a correction



in the dollars' strength against the peso.



The Taiwan dollar fell to a 10-week low of 34.16 per



dollar, before bouncing back to 34.13 on talk of central bank

intervention.



    The Singapore dollar        slipped about half a percent to

    Dealers said some profit-taking in dollars, spotted around

strong offers are not expected before 1.7635, the August 13



low.



The July consumer price index is expected at 0500 GMT, but



dealers said the focus would stay on the yen and euro - both



major components of the trade-weighted basket authorities in



Singapore use to manage their exchange rate policy.



    The Thai baht        eased to 42.32 per dollar, from late



Thursday's 42.14, tracking losses in yen and other regionals.



    Dealers in Singapore said lack of local cues and illiquid



conditions were likely to keep the baht around 42.30-42.45.



    The Indonesian rupiah        was down at 8,865 per dollar,



from late Thursday's 8,845, although it drew support from news



the bank restructuring agency has sold $2.5 billion worth of



non-performing loans.



    The Korean won            eased past the 1,200 per dollar

    Dealers in Singapore said weak yen and wariness over



equity-related outflows after recent sale of local stocks by



foreign funds was weighing down the won. But inflows from



export deal settlements were expected to limit the losses.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Easier as dollar climbs on Wall St rise.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were easier 

 in opening Thursday trade, taking their taking cue from a 

 weaker yen which slipped back over 119 to the dollar. 

     Dealers said the dollar was drawing support from 

 stabilising U.S. stocks markets, after their rollercoaster 

 performance in past few weeks had raised global risk 

 perceptions. 

 On Tuesday, speeches by three U.S. Federal Reserve regional 

 presidents were seen as suggesting the economic recovery was on 

 track and there may not be need to cut interest rates. 

 "That rang a positive note to the ears of stock investors, 

 who seemed somewhat reassured by recovery hopes, sending stocks 

 rallying and thus providing support for the dollar," said Naomi 

 Fink, currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 


    The Nasdaq Composite Index         rose 2.37 percent and



the Dow Jones industrial average ended up 0.96 percent.



    J.P. Morgan Chase in a research note said the near-term



dollar rally would put most Asian currencies under pressure,



particularly the Singapore dollar, South Korean won and Taiwan



dollar, which are seen as more sensitive to moves in yen.



    Against this, there could be some support for regionals if



Asian stocks follow Wall Street's lead



    The Singapore dollar        touched a low of 1.7514 per



dollar early on before dollar sales from foreign names pushed



it back to around 1.7480, still down from late Wednesday's



1.7472.



Dealers said with speculative positions mostly liquidated



and given the lack of local leads, players were looking at



capital flows for trading cues.



A tight trading range was expected with dollar bids spotted



at around 1.7465 and talk of dollar offers around



1.7510-1.7520.



The Korean won was easier at around 1,194.0 per



dollar, from Wednesday's onshore close of 1,192.0, as local



interbank players tracked the yen's lead.



Exporter dollar sales and equity-related inflows were



protecting the downside, while second quarter gross domestic



product had little impact on currency trade.



South Korea's Q2 GDP grew 1.4 percent from the previous



quarter and was 6.3 percent higher than the same quarter a year



earlier - almost in line with the 6.4 percent forecast in a



Reuters survey of 10 economists.



The Taiwan dollar eased to around 34.04 per



dollar, after touching a low of 34.065, against Wednesday's



onshore close of 33.995.



Dealers in Singapore said Tuesday's central bank


dollar-buying intervention, suggesting authorities were in not



in favour of any currency strength at this moment, would keep



exporters cautious.



    The Thai baht        was down by about a quarter of a



percent from late Wednesday's 42.04 per dollar in thin trade.



    The bearish regional tone weighed down the baht, but dollar



sales by exporters and foreign names, and a reluctance to take



significant positions due to lack of liquidity was seen



limiting the baht's downside.



The Philippine peso eased beyond 52 per dollar on



low volumes as the market awaited budget deficit data now



expected later in the day.



The Indonesian rupiah eased to 8,845 per dollar,



from late Wednesday's 8,825, on dollar purchases from local



corporates and foreign banks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Reined in by Taiwan independence talk.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slipped on 

 Monday morning as Taiwan's talk of independence from China and 

 more worries about the impact of a slower U.S economy on the 

 region's export-reliant countries turned the market jittery. 

     Taiwan President Chen Shui-bian's controversial remarks 

 that Taiwan and China were really separate countries knocked 

 the Taiwan dollar and the TAIEX share index in 

 early trade, drawing more attention than the U.S. economic 

 troubles. 

     A second factor weighing down currencies was the Japanese 

 yen's failure to make significant headway against the 

 dollar, despite depressing U.S. manufacturing and employment 

 data and falling stocks, as currency traders waited for Japan 

 to release its leading economic index later in the day. 


    The Singapore dollar       , Philippine peso         and



Taiwan dollar erased early gains, while other



regionals were mostly steady.



    "Talk about the Taiwan independence comments and the



possibility of negative reaction from China is weighing on



Asian currencies," said Peter Redward, currency strategist at



Deutsche Bank.



    Taiwan's Chen told a gathering of pro-independence



activists in Tokyo during a video conference on Saturday that



he supported legislation for a referendum, a move certain to



anger Beijing.     Redward said those tensions would keep



Taiwanese assets under pressure, but regional impact would be



limited unless there was military action by China.



    The Taiwan dollar fell to 33.80/90 per U.S. dollar from a



close of 33.72, supported lightly by hopes authorities would


intervene to cushion sharp moves.



    The Singapore dollar failed to hold on to brief gains above



1.75 in the morning on concerns it was getting too close to



being overvalued in trade-weighted terms.



    Analysts say Singapore's highly export-dependent economy is



most at risk within the region if growth in the United States,



Asia's biggest export market, slides further.



    The Indonesian rupiah        was steady around its previous



close at 9,075/85, but traders expected it to lose ground to



the dollar since it had failed to respond to a run of positive



news, gaining just 0.6 percent last week.



    Indonesia's Bank Restructuring Agency has recently managed



to sell non-performing loans, some to foreigners. As well, PT



Telekomunikasi Indonesia closed a deal to sell a cellular unit



to Singapore's SingTel for $429 million.



    "The telecom sale, the loans auction and falling



inflation...none of that has been reflected in the currency or


forex reserves. Besides, Jakarta equities remain under



pressure," Redward said, adding he expected to see the rupiah



weaken towards 9,500 per dollar soon.



    The Thailand baht        was steady, hugging the 42 per



dollar level, barely changed from Friday's close at 42.10 and



pinned down by fears of intervention.



    Last week, Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra



reprimanded the central bank for letting the baht swing



sharply.



    The Philippine peso        was marginally weaker at



51.32/39 compared with Friday's 51.27 per dollar close.



    The Korean won        was dragged down by weak stocks, to



be at 1,186 from Friday's 1,184.3 per dollar, although traders



said exporters had a bullish view on their currency and were



eager to sell overseas earnings quickly.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Dulled by weekend,  intervention  worries.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed 

 bag in Friday trade, although a listless Japanese yen, the 

 approaching weekend and fears of intervention kept most from 

 rising much. 

     Regionals started the day firmer after weak U.S. economic 

 numbers undermined the dollar, but fears of intervention wiped 

 out gains in the Thailand baht and the Korean won 

 . 

     Traders were also unwilling to initiate positions before 

 the weekend with key U.S. unemployment numbers due later on 

 Friday, particularly after having seen two sets of dismal data 

 on growth and manufacturing this week. 

     "This is typical behaviour ahead of the weekend," Sameer 

 Goel, markets strategist with Bank of America, said. 

     "Given Asia's dependence on the United States, people are 

 also wondering if regional currencies should be supported or 

 hammered if the United States does not do well." 

     Adding to that uncertainty were fickle equity markets, Goel 

 said. 


    The Singapore dollar        spent most of Friday in a



1.7540-1.7570 range, firmer than the previous day's close at



1.7598 and with bullish traders seemingly daunted the fact that


currency was close to being over-valued in trade-weighted



terms.



The Korean won rose up to 1,176 before the concerns



that won had appreciated too much compared with the Japanese



yen , which could threaten export competitiveness and



invite intervention, weighed and pulled it back to the day's



lows around 1,185.



The won was also driven down by market talk that flows from



SK Telecom, which recently raised funds overseas through



American Depositary Receipts, are drying up.


Intervention fears were largely responsible for keeping the



Thailand baht too narrowly bound. It gained briefly,



spiking above 42 per dollar, but soon settled around Thursday's



close at 42.13.



The finance ministry said on Friday there was no plan to



fire the central bank governor, although earlier this week



Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra hauled up the central bank


for letting the baht swing sharply.



The Philippine peso slipped to 51.30 by close, after



trading most of the day in a tight range of 51.10/15 per dollar



despite talk of heavy foreign inflows from Philippine

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Sharply On Dlr Short-Covering
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The dollar surged against Asian currencies Monday as a runaway correction smashed through technical resistance levels and investors rushed to cover short positions. 

 "The focus has shifted (from the U.S. dollar's long-term current account-related problems) to the fact that equity weakness in the U.S. ripples out to Asian equities - that U.S. growth, if undermined, can hit Asian growth," UBS Warburg currency strategist Bhanu Baweja told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 Most analysts remain convinced that a long-term bear trend for the dollar will reassert itself due to the difficulties the U.S. is expected to have funding its current account deficit, as foreigners reduce purchases of U.S. assets from levels seen in recent years. 

 But the long-term trend counted for nothing Monday. 

 "We are not convinced that the U.S. dollar is out of the woods yet. However, we would not advise standing in front of a runaway train," United Overseas Bank's Treasury Research department said in its daily note. 

 The train went out of control after the dollar closed in Tokyo Friday at Y117.73 to the dollar. By late Friday in New York, the dollar had climbed to Y118.94. Asian currencies were already in for a beating Monday, but the regional trendsetter slipped further. By 0922 GMT (5:22 a.m. EDT) the dollar was at Y119.32. 

 The magnitude of the dollar's recent correction against Asian currencies surprised the UOB team, but they don't expect a further recovery in the dollar unless U.S. equities markets can sustain some of the stability they saw late last week. 

 Technical analysts said the dollar broke above medium-term downtrend lines on its charts against all East and Southeast Asian currencies except the Japanese yen, signaling an end to a rally in regional currencies that began in April. 

 Uncertainty helped Asian currencies to recover in the afternoon, however, as tests of long-term downtrend lines lie ahead and exporters sold dollars heavily to take advantage of attractive levels. 

 Against the South Korean won, the dollar ended Monday at KRW1,200, off a high of KRW1,209 but up from a close Friday at KRW1,190.4. 

 The won's corrective decline of KRW29.1 Friday and Monday comprised the biggest two-day loss since late March 2001. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was also substantially weaker, but the central bank reversed its role in recent interventions to sell the U.S. dollar Monday and slow the local currency's rise. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.894, up from a previous close of NT$33.689. 

 Dealers expect a test of NT$34.00 if the yen - a regional trend setter - continues to fall. 

 Dollar buying by Indonesian corporate debtors ahead of the end of the month reinforced the regional trend, pushing the U.S. unit to an intraday high of 9,280 rupiah from a close Friday at IDR9,150. 

 The rupiah came off lows to close at IDR9,225 to the dollar, however, on profit-taking and suspected central bank intervention to slow the local currency's decline. 

 The Philippine peso ended at PHP51.53 to the dollar, up from PHP51.30 at Friday's close. 

 Sentiment toward the peso was battered by both the general sell-off in Asian currencies and expectations that the government will have to sharply increase its budget deficit target. 

 The U.S. dollar came off an early intraday high of PHP51.93, however, on profit-taking by banks and selling by exporters. The Philippine central bank said it wasn't in the market Monday, as it was useless to intervene when all regional currencies were falling sharply. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. dollar was quoted late Monday at S$1.776, up from S$1.7589 late Friday. 

 The break of S$1.765 was a major bullish signal for technical chart analysts. 

 But dealers warned that the rise took place in thin volume, as investors in the export-dependent city state waited for clearer direction on the U.S. economy and equities markets. 

 An Asian bank dealer in Singapore said the U.S. unit's rise looks overdone, but if it holds above S$1.76 in London and New York overnight Monday, it's likely to test S$1.78 in Asia Tuesday. 

 The baht finished at THB42.39 to the U.S. dollar, down from a close Friday of THB41.82. 

 Short-covering after the dollar broke decisively through a technical resistance level - at THB42, on a downtrend line from April - pushed the U.S. unit to an early intraday high of THB42.50, it's highest level since June 6. 

 Dealers said resistance was strong at the high, and some players took profits on the dollar's sharp gains when regional currencies stabilized in the afternoon. 

 Heavy selling in Thai equities last week also hurt sentiment toward the baht Monday. 

 Analysts said U.S. funds have been selling Asian equities to lock in profits on this year's gains. 

 But UBS Warburg's Baweja said the selling can't continue to be as strong a factor into the medium term. 

 UBS Warburg's core long-term view is that the U.S. dollar will gradually weaken, but that the U.S. economy won't perform too badly, Baweja said. 

 He expects a modest recovery in capacity expansion in the U.S. in the latter part of the year, which will help Asian exports and currencies. 

 The U.S. dollar should weaken due to current account problems in the long term, however, because you are not going to see a substantial rebound in the U.S. stock market, he said.

text:
SINGAPORE, July 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were 

 volatile on Thursday, as the dollar's renewed weakness, 

 uncertain foreign investment flows and the narrow movements of

     The dollar fell across the board, even dipping below parity

     Asian currencies firmed initially and later see-sawed as

     Traders said they expected the yen's movements to be

     "To the extent that the yen is not expected to deviate much

currencies," said Jan Lee, currency strategist with Hypo-und 

 Vereinsbank AG. 

     "We expect a multi-week equity markets consolidation and 

 Asian currencies may be ranged for a week or so." 

     With expectations that the yen will strengthen

title: Asian  intervention  seen slowing, not halting,  fx  gains.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 19 (Reuters) - Asian central bankers may know the financial market maxim - never try to catch a falling knife - but that has not stopped them from buying the ailing dollar to keep a lid on gains in their own currencies. 

 As the U.S. dollar has plunged against regional currencies in recent weeks, central banks in Seoul, Taipei and Bangkok have stepped into currency markets to sell their own currencies. 

 Policymakers are typically tight lipped about their reasons for intervening, but currency analysts say it is more likely directed at slowing regional currencies' gains against the dollar than halting them. 

 "In all of these countries, and this goes for Japan as well it's not so much about levels, it's more about the pace of appreciation which could be damaging to business confidence," said James Malcolm, JP Morgan Chase's currency strategist in Singapore. 

 "So what they (central banks) are trying to do is to hold back the market from getting carried away," he added. 

 The story in any case is about dollar weakness rather than regional currency strength. 

 The dollar has been hobbled by doubts over the U.S. ability to fund a gapping current account deficit while Wall Street swoons to multi-year lows on accounting scandals. 

 CAPITAL FLOWS 

 "So the real story has been the capital flows. The flight out of the dollar has been the flight into Asian assets," said Micheal Spencer, Deutsche Bank's chief economist in Hong Kong. 

 He said large enough external surpluses and strong capital inflows would continue to pressure regional currencies higher. 

 Malcolm said central banks would continue to offset some of that pressure but eventually; "they will begin to take their foot off the pedal a little bit." 

 In Taiwan, where the central bank has an almost daily presence in the market, foreign reserves rose to an all-time high of $148.242 billion at the end of June, representing an increase of $8.421 billion from the end of May. 

 The Taiwan dollar strengthened below 33 per dollar this week to its strongest levels in 14 months. It has risen by about six percent so far this year. 

 NOT TOO SCARED 

 Analysts said intermittent comments, contravening with the spirit of these interventions, confirm that Asian governments in general may not be too averse to some modest currency gains against the background of broad dollar weakness. 

 Thailand's Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Sunday the baht could strengthen to levels beyond 40 per dollar, sending the currency to its highest level in two years. 

 And the Bank of Korea's Governor Park Seung said the won might remain strong for a while and efforts to curb it would have limited impact. 

 Park's comments were quickly watered down by statements from other officials to deter the market reading too much into them. 

 NOT EXPENSIVE YET 

 Naomi Fink, UBS Warburg's currency strategist in Singapore said the difference of opinion among finance officials, to some extent, stems from the uncertainty over the yen which has also soared in past weeks. 

 The yen has risen 15 percent against the dollar since early April despite bouts of Japanese intervention to buy dollars and sell yen. 

 "It seems the uncertainty over where Japanese policymakers would put a cap on the yen has spread to the region," she said. 

 Although the correlation has withered in recent years, Asian policymakers keep a close track of the yen, as Japan is both a competitor and a major market for most of these economies. 

 The dollar has lost over 13 percent of its trade-weighted value since the start of the year, as it plunged recently to 17-month lows against the yen and around 2-= lows against the euro . 

 Asian currencies have followed suit, but analysts said they have underperformed the yen and euro, meaning trade-weighted gains have been moderate and impact on export competitiveness modest.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;  Intervention  Steadies US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The struggling U.S. dollar stabilized against Asian currencies Thursday with the help of foreign exchange market intervention by monetary authorities in South Korea and Taiwan. 

 The U.S. dollar finished Asian trading hours little changed against the won, New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht, after falling to multimonth lows against all four a day earlier. The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso weakened. 

 However, any strengthening of the U.S. dollar is likely to be short lived because the underlying sentiment in global markets continues to be biased heavily against the U.S. currency, analysts said. 

 U.S. dollar buying by state-run Korean banks saved the U.S. currency from posting a new low against the won. The state run banks swung into action after the U.S. dollar fell to around 1,172 won early in the session after closing a 19-month low of KRW1,179.4 a day earlier. 

 Traders said they believed state-run banks bought around $500 million on behalf of the government. The move helped the U.S. currency rebound to close at KRW1,179.5. 

 A senior Bank of Korea official later hinted at the government's involvement in the round of U.S. dollar buying, saying it is "natural" for the government to take actions to stabilize exchange rates "when market participants lose their balance." 

 Governments in Korea, Taiwan and Japan have all intervened either directly or indirectly in foreign exchange markets recently to slow the rise of their currencies. 

 Authorities have expressed concern that rapid appreciation of their currencies could undermine the price competitiveness of their exporters in global markets. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked its north Asia counterparts to remain steady against the U.S. dollar. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7502, compared with S$1.7505 late Tuesday. 

 An announcement by the Monetary Authority of Singapore that it will maintain its neutral policy on the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis for the balance of 2002 had little immediate impact on the currency. 

 However, over the longer term it means there will be room for the currency to continue appreciating against the U.S. dollar, analysts said. 

 JP Morgan is targeting the U.S. dollar to fall to S$1.72 by the end of September and S$1.70 by the end of December. 

 Investors favor countries with positive cash flows like Singapore during times of stock market volatility and heightened risk aversion, said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 Singapore's large current account surplus, healthy foreign reserves, and balanced budget are all supportive of the local currency because they make Singapore less vulnerable to volatility in global capital flows, she said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$33.284 compared with NT$33.282 Wednesday. 

 The central bank, which regularly intervenes in the market to smooth out volatility, bought around US$700 million throughout the day, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar would have substantially eclipsed its 14-month high set Wednesday if not for the central bank's actions to prop up the U.S. dollar, one trader said. 

 Against the rupiah the U.S dollar broke through the key IDR9,000 resistance level for the first time in six sessions. 

 A 1.4% decline in the main index of the Jakarta Stock Exchange and U.S. dollar short covering weighed on the rupiah. 

 At the end of Jakarta trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at a two-month high of IDR9,125, up from IDR8,915 late Wednesday. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, was rumored to have sold the U.S. currency to try to keep the rupiah below 9,000 per U.S. dollar, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar traded in a narrow range against the baht, finishing the session at THB41.160, compared with a 22-month low of THB41.150 Wednesday. 

 Thailand's Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik said the recent strength in the baht against the U.S. dollar hasn't harmed export growth, which is expected to be sustained in June. 

 Adisai told reporters that the country's exports will remain competitive as the baht strengthens along with other currencies in the region against the weak U.S. dollar. 

 He said exports were estimated to rise by between 3.5% and 4.2% in June from a year ago.

title: Singapore Dlr Steady Late;Mkt Watches NE Asia,Ignores MAS
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was little changed against its U.S. counterpart late Thursday after the local currency was shaken and then revived by events in Northeast Asian markets. 

 The Singapore dollar surrendered early gains after reports of South Korean intervention to strengthen the U.S. dollar unsettled local players. However, late-session gains by the Japanese yen revived the local currency to late Wednesday's level. 

 The local dollar, however, didn't specifically react to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's widely anticipated decision to keep it's currency-centered monetary policy in neutral gear to aid the Singapore economy's recovery. 

 At 0825 GMT (4:25 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7502, compared with S$1.7505 late Tuesday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7490 and S$1.7535 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened slightly higher around S$1.7513 in Asia but, after an initial lull in trading, drifted to an intraday low of S$1.7490 in line with its early losses against the yen. 

 Subsequently, following reported intervention by the South Korean government to cap the won's rise, the U.S. dollar reversed direction against its Singapore counterpart and rose to an intraday high of S$1.7535. 

 The South Korean government Thursday bought $200 million in the foreign exchange market through state-run banks, in a bid to support the falling U.S. currency, Yonhap Infomax newswire reported, citing traders. 

 The U.S. dollar's fell to around KRW1,172 early in the session, after closing Wednesday at a 19-month low of KRW1,179.4, after the Korean government indirectly intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the U.S. currency. 

 However, the U.S. dollar's rally against the Singapore currency ran out of steam around midday and it subsequently retreated to trade in a tight S$1.7500-S$1.7510 range for most of the afternoon. 

 The U.S. dollar's retreat against the Singapore dollar in the afternoon followed a fresh bout of weakness in the U.S. currency against the yen. The U.S. dollar fell to in intraday low of Y117.33 from an early high of Y117.93. 

 The U.S. dollar didn't react much to the MAS statement. However, analysts said that central bank's neutral policy stance means that while the Singapore dollar will remain steady against its trade-weighted currency basket and therefore continue to rise against the U.S. dollar in line with strength in the yen and euro. 

 The cyclical recovery in Singapore's economy and the bearish outlook for the U.S. currency could result in the U.S. dollar falling to S$1.7000 by the year-end. In late March, the U.S. dollar rose as high as S$1.8500. 

 Dealers said that the U.S. dollar appears to be consolidating around the S$1.7500 for now, and expect it to trade between S$1.7480 and S$1.7530 overnight in London and New York. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended higher Thursday, tracking overnight gains in U.S. Treasurys. Dealers said the MAS' semiannual monetary policy statement had a negligible impact on bond prices. 

 A local bank dealer noted that bond prices have mostly risen this week but Thursday's trade volume was smaller than that of recent sessions. That suggests market participants' appetite for bonds may be running out, which could result in profit-taking in coming sessions. 

 The yield on two-year bonds fell three basis points to 1.37% while the yield on five-year bonds fell eight basis points to 2.73%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds fell eight basis points to 3.23%, while the yield on the 10-year bonds fell five basis points to 3.78%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds fell six basis points to 4.07%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Step back on  intervention  fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 11 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 down in late Thursday trade as players trimmed their short 

 dollar positions, fearing intervention by Japanese authorities 

 to cap the yen's recent gains. 

     Dealers said with U.S. weekly jobless claims due later in 

 the day and the June retail sales numbers and University of 

 Michigan consumer sentiment survey on Friday, players who were 

 extremely short of dollars scrambled to cover those positions. 

     "The market finally decided to take a breather whether the 

 Japanese authorities intervene or not. They just wanted to 

 lighten up and start afresh," said a dealer at a European bank. 

     He said a fresh round of verbal warnings by South Korean 

 authorities followed by dollar purchases by state banks and 

 with no surprises in Singapore's monetary policy review, 

 players saw no incentive to push regionals any higher. 

     Dealers said although the dollar, may get a brief reprieve, 

 risk-aversion in U.S. assets, with its bearish implications, 

 was very much intact. 


    The dollar rose a quarter percent against the euro



to around 98.62 cents and was steady versus the yen at 117.50



at 0728 GMT.



    The Singapore dollar        fell to a session low of 1.7535



per dollar, from late Wednesday's 1.7490, after it failed to



break 1.7480, its highest level of the day. It managed to



recover some losses and was around 1.7500 by 0808 GMT.



    Dealers said interbank players and local corporates were



the main buyers of dollars. They said some foreign names were



also seen covering their short dollar positions.



    Earlier in the day, the Monetary Authority of Singapore



said it would maintain its stance of zero appreciation in the



nominal effective exchange rate for the second half of 2002 in



view of a benign inflationary environment.



    The policy announcement follows Wednesday's surprisingly



strong second quarter gross domestic product growth data, which



had pushed the Singapore dollar to a 9-=   month high of



1.7457.



    The Korean won         -2 slipped to a session low of



1,183.5, off a fresh 20-month high of 1,171.5. It took its cue



from dollar sales by state-run banks after a barrage of verbal



warnings against the won's gain were made by central bank and



finance officials, including Finance Minister Jeon Yun-churl.



Eyeing the onslaught by the Korean authorities, the central



bank in neighbouring Taiwan also stepped up its physical


intervention and weighed down its dollar to a low of



33.29, from early high of 33.21.



However, equity-related inflows and dollar sales by



exporters helped the Taiwan dollar end onshore trade at 33.284,



compared to 33.282 on Wednesday.



The Thai baht eased to a session low of 41.175, off



an early high of 41.08, as offshore players trimmed their short



dollar positions.



However, the sentiment was supported by a consumer survey



that showed confidence in June rose for the ninth straight



month after plunging in September in the wake of the attacks on



the United States.



The Philippine peso ended onshore trade at 50.33,



from a session high of 50.185, as interbank players followed



the regional tone and commercial dollar demand rose.



The Indonesian rupiah eased to a five-week low of 9,040,



from around 8,900, as local corporates continued to buy dollars



for debt payment needs and some offshore players were also

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Touch fresh peaks but cautious.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 9 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies held 

 their ground around multi-month highs in late Tuesday trade as 

 the dollar slipped to levels just shy of parity with the euro 

  and to a nine-month low against the yen . 

     Still dealers said with most players now short of dollars, 

 they were cautious over pushing regional currencies too far, 

 too soon amid fears of intervention by authorities. 

     "Though players are cautious, but a breach of last week's 

 lows (against the dollar) suggest they are ready to rebuild 

 short dollar positions," a senior dealer at a bank in Singapore

 said. 

     Japan's Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa stoked 

intervention fears by clarifying his weekend comments that had 

 tripped the dollar off a technical recovery. 

     Later a Korean finance ministry official expressed concerns 

 over the won's -2 rise to a 20-month high of 1,181.9 

 and said the government would intervene whenever needed to 

 stabilise the foreign exchange market. 

     The Finance Ministry also said it would sell 500 billion 

 won in foreign exchange stabilisation bonds on July 10. 

     The won ended onshore trade at 1,182.2 per dollar, against 

 Monday's close of 1,191.40. Backed by a resilient economy and 

 foreign investment inflows, the won has gained slightly over 

 eight percent year to date. 

 The Taiwan dollar rose to 33.364 per dollar, a 

 level not seen since May 22, 2001, encouraged by the won's 

 performance and Monday's surprising rise in June trade numbers. 

 Dealers in Singapore said a lack of aggressive intervention

 by the central bank was seen by the market as a signal that 

 authorities would tolerate currency strength on the back of 

 improving economic fundamentals. 

 Taiwan's June exports rose 9.0 percent on the year, the 

 strongest in 16 months, while imports expanded at the fastest 

 pace in 19 months at 11.2 percent. 

 In the Southeast, the Thai baht rose to a 22-month high of 

 41.30 per dollar, on the back of dollar sales by exporters and 

 settlement of local stock purchases by foreign investors. 

 The Singapore dollar breached the 1.7600 per dollar 

 level to touch a nine-month high of 1.7590, amid speculation 

 ahead of second quarter growth numbers, due on Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso ended onshore trade at a 

 one-week high of 50.29, against its previous close of 50.47, 

 tracking other regional currencies and a lack of dollar demand 

 from local corporates. 

 However, the Indonesian rupiah failed to sustain its gains 

 from opening levels this morning, despite the general bullish 

 regional tone. 

 Weighed down by local corporates' dollar purchases for debt 

 repayment needs, the rupiah languished around 8,900 levels, 

 against 8,890 in late Monday trade.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Multi-month highs hit as dollar wobbles.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 9 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies firmed 

 to multi-month highs early on Tuesday as the dollar, hobbled by 

 U.S. corporate accounting controversies, looked vulnerable to 

 further losses against other major currencies. 

     Dealers said with long dollar positions mostly wiped out on 

 Monday, most players in regional currencies were now looking to 

 position themselves short of dollars, showing a general lack of 

 confidence on the greenback. 

     "With the August 15 deadline for (U.S.) corporate 

 executives to vouch for the accuracy of their firms' financial 

 statements approaching, we expect further disclosures of 

 controversial accounting practices to dampen the outlook for 

 the dollar," said Naomi Fink, currency strategist at UBS 

 Warburg in Singapore. 

Intervention wariness helped the dollar off a nine-month 

 low of 118.32 yen hit in early Sydney trade and stay 

 flat at 98.83/86 cents against the euro , but doubts 

 persisted. 

     Lee Boon Keng, treasury market strategist at DBS Bank, said 

 120 yen has become a new resistance level for the dollar 

 as Japan continues to pour out evidence of a cyclical recovery. 

     The latest number backing that view was Japan's machinery 

 orders for May released on Monday. A 0.2 percent on-the-month 

 rise surprised economists who had expected a 2.8 percent fall. 

     Surprising Taiwan trade data on Monday also reinforced the 

 view that recovery in other Asian economies was gaining 

 traction. 

     Taiwan's June exports rose 9.0 percent on the year, the 

 strongest in 16 months, while imports expanded at the fastest 

 pace in 19 months at 11.2 percent. 

     Responding to those numbers and to gains in the yen and 

 Korean won -2, the Taiwan dollar jumped to a 

 fresh 13-month high of 33.371 per dollar. 

     Dealers in Singapore said central bank intervention capped 

 the rise and pulled the Taiwan dollar back to around 33.395. 

 But dollar sales from exporters were expected to keep the 

currency supported, they added. 

     WON TESTS FRESH HIGHS 

     The Korean won, also backed by equity-related inflows, rose 

 to touch a high of 1,185.4, a level not seen since December 12, 

 2000. 

     Dealers in Singapore said exporters and offshore players 

 were selling dollars as foreign investors continued to buy 

 local stocks for the fourth consecutive session. 

     However, repeated verbal warnings by authorities 

 threatening action against excessive gains in the won kept 

 players cautious and capped further gains. 


    In the southeast, the Singapore dollar        breached the



1.7600 per dollar level to touch a nine-month high of 1.7590.



    Dealers said speculation of better-than-expected second



quarter growth numbers, due on Wednesday, was fuelling the



rally. But with the market now short of dollars, gains were



expected to be limited.



The Thai baht touched a high of 41.35 per dollar, a



level not seen since September 12, 2000, as dollar sales by



offshore players gained momentum.



Dealers in Bangkok said several U.S. and European banks



were spotted selling dollars, prompting local players to take



fresh short dollar positions.



    However, rumours of central bank dollar purchases were



expected to keep the baht's gains limited from these levels.



    The Philippine peso        also gained in line with other



regional currencies, rising to a one-week high of 50.38 per



dollar, but talk of corporate dollar bids at 50.30-50.35 was



likely to cap further gains.



The only detractor of the regional trend was the Indonesian



rupiah , which eased to around 8,900 from late Monday's



8,890 on dollar purchases by local corporates and state-run



banks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Firmer on weak dollar, won shines.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 8 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 firmer in late Monday trade following news of more inflated 

 accounting at U.S. firms and on a surprising lack of dollar 

 support in fresh comments by Japan's finance minister. 

     Dealers said most players opted to bail out of long dollar 

 positions they had taken in response to last week's upward 

 correction in the greenback against the yen and euro 

 . 

     That and signs of renewed interest among foreign investors 

 in local stocks helped the Korean won -2 strengthen to 

 a fresh 19-month peak and the Singapore dollar and Thai 

 baht to one-week highs. 

     "All eyes are now fixed on whether the dollar/yen breaches 

 its June 28 low (of 118.30) which will trigger a fresh round of 

 dollar sales," said a senior dealer at a European bank in 

 Singapore. 

     Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa's comment on the weekend 

 that world financial authorities believed a weakening of the 

 dollar was in progress pressured the U.S. currency which Tokyo 

 itself had repeatedly propped up in the past several sessions. 

     Further weighing down the dollar was news late on Friday 

 that Houston-based energy firm Reliant Resources Inc 

 had erased $7.9 billion in revenues and the Wall Street Journal 

 Europe Monday report that drugs giant Merck & Co 

 recorded billions in revenue that were never collected. 

     WON BREACHES 1,200/DLR 

     The won breached 1,200 to levels not seen since December 

 17, 2000, largely ignoring the Finance Ministry's verbal 

intervention and dollar sales by some state-run banks early in 

 the day. 

     A senior Finance Ministry official said authorities were 

 concerned about the impact of the won's appreciation on the 

 economy and exports and vowed to take active steps to stabilise 

 the currency market. 

     Dealers in Singapore said offshore players sold dollars 

 encouraged by the third consecutive session of local stock 

 buying by foreign investors. 

     The won touched a high of 1,191.2 per dollar, before easing 

 back slightly to 1,191.4 at the close of the onshore trade. 

 That was up 1.13 percent against Friday's close of 1,204.90. 

     Dealers said a test of higher levels around 1,180 was 

 expected in coming sessions though interbank players were 

 cautious on fears of the oft threatened physical intervention

 by authorities.

    The Singapore dollar        strengthened by about half a



percent to a one-week high at 1.7628 per dollar, against late



Friday's 1.7720.



    Dealers said dollar's decline versus the yen and euro and

players covering short Sing dollar positions.



    Talk of dollar bids around 1.7625, the Sing dollar's

around 1.7636.



    Dealers said gains from these levels were likely to be



limited ahead of second quarter economic growth estimates due



on Wednesday and the central bank's mid-year policy review and



macroeconomic analysis on Thursday.



    The Thai baht        was at one-week highs around 41.40,



against late Friday's 41.62 on dollar sales by exporters and



offshore players.



    Dealers in Bangkok said dollar supply was mostly from



Singapore and Hong Kong names.



    The Indonesian rupiah       , however, bucked the firmer



regional trend, as some local names were spotted bidding

percent to 8,890, against late Friday's 8,845.



Dealers in Jakarta said talk of the central bank selling



dollars to defend the 8,900 level, helped the currency bounce



off an intraday low of 8,925.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -In cautious mood, but uptrend intact.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - Fears of Japan's 

 dollar-buying intervention held Asian currencies back on 

 Monday, but their bullish tone was intact as the U.S. dollar 

 faced unrelenting pressure over disillusionment with U.S. asset 

 markets. 

     Trading volumes were thin as several centres -- South 

 Korea, Thailand and Hong Kong -- were closed on holiday. They 

 will resume trading on Tuesday. 

     Japan monetary authorities on Friday defended the dollar in 

 the foreign exchange market, using the European Central Bank

 and the U.S. Federal Reserve as its agents in overseas markets. 

     Even the country's better-than-expected "tankan" corporate 

 sentiment survey report on Monday barely lifted the yen. 

     At 0935 GMT, the dollar traded around 119.85 yen and 

 $0.9912 to the euro . 

     Despite the U.S. unit's pull back here and there, the 

 market  still favoured the regional currencies, with most 

currency strategists keeping their long Asia/dollar positions. 

     "I can see the Asian currencies continue to appreciate in 

 the next nine to 12 months," said P.K. Basu, regional 

 strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Singapore, adding 

 he did not expect this round of the dollar's decline to hurt 

 export-dependent Asia. 

 "Given the fact that inflation is very tame across Asia, 

 the regional currencies are still pretty cheap on a real 

 effective basis," he said. 

 "Asia's exports are benefitting from recovery in global 

 demand. And since Asian countries primarily compete with one 

 another, the fact they are all appreciating together doesn't 

 really hurt any single exporter," he said. 

 SING $ RETREATS 

 The Sing dollar stepped back, shedding around a 

 quarter of a percent on the back of the yen's losses. It was 

 trading at around 1.7663 to the dollar in late trade. 

     But its firm tone remained in place, with recent economic 

 data pointing to gradual but solid recovery. 


    The Thai baht        was flat in the offshore market,



giving up its earlier gains in sympathy with most other



regional currencies.



    But it is still trapped in the uptrend channel against the



U.S. dollar. Charts shows the baht is being overbought,



suggesting further upward moves could encounter some profit



taking.



PESO EYES BUDGET



The peso ended slightly weaker at 50.43 compared with 50.42



in the previous session, with the market focusing on fiscal



data due out later this week.



"We advise investors to brace for a poor outturn," said a



Salomon Smith Barney report. "The deficit for the first five



months of the year will likely breach the 100 billion peso



deficit mark, or less than 30 billion shy of the full-year



target with seven months still to go."



The currency managed to clamber off its intraday lows of



50.53, drawing mild support from news that the central bank had



successfully raised $675 million from five-year syndicated loan



facility as the loan will lengthen the central bank's foreign



debt maturity profile.



The Taiwan dollar came off, ending its



eight-session appreciation streak due to hefty local central



bank intervention. The currency ended at 33.568 to the dollar



compared with 33.560 at the open and 33.558 at the close on



Friday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Regionals firm, WorldCom knocks dlr.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 26 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were firmer 

 on Wednesday as the revelation about accounting irregularities 

 at the U.S. telecommunications giant WorldCom added to 

 the dollar's woes. 

     WorldCom said on Tuesday it had uncovered improper 

 accounting for almost $4 billion in expenses, marking the latest 

 case of accounting irregularities to hit U.S. companies. 

     The Bank of Japan has intervened repeatedly in the market on 

 Wednesday to support the U.S. currency, with dealers estimating 

 it might have poured at least $4 billion into the market to slow 

 the yen's gains. 

     But the move did not do much for the dollar as concerns over 

 Corporate America -- confidence in which is crucial in 

 attracting inflows to finance U.S. gaping current account 

 deficit -- seemed to have taken the teeth out of the 

intervention. 

     "There is a lot of bad news about U.S. companies. All in 

 all, it doesn't look pretty," said Claudio Piron, currency

 strategist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

     "In term of dollar yen, intervening at this level is like

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; BOJ Action Little Help To Dlr
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar's slide against Asian currencies picked up steam Monday as attempts by Japanese authorities to bolster the U.S. currency against the yen had little impact on the rest of the region. 

 Most Asian currencies remained at multi-month highs amid growing investor distaste for the dollar, which has come under pressure from falling U.S. stock prices, Middle East tensions and the large U.S. current account deficit. 

 Only the Philippine peso, hampered by concerns the government will overshoot its fiscal deficit target, fell against the dollar. 

Foreign exchange market intervention by the Bank of Japan on behalf of the Ministry of Finance did succeed in lifting the struggling dollar briefly from a seven-month low of around Y121 to a daily high of Y122.80. 

 Authorities bought an estimated $2 billion to $3 billion to prop up the dollar, marking their fifth market intervention in a month. But within minutes market players pushed the dollar back down to Y122, and near the end of Asian trading it had slipped to Y121.30. 

 "The jump in dollar/yen was only momentary," said Naomi Fink, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 While fears of further BOJ intervention may make some players wary of pushing the dollar lower, the fact remains in such an environment of global weakness intervention can do little more than slow the pace of the dollar's decline, Fink said. 

 And most Asian currencies will continue to capitalize on the dollar's fragility, with the South Korean won, Thai baht and Singapore dollar poised to gain the most, she added. 

 The won gave up some of its gains Monday in tandem with the yen's intervention-inspired fall, but still had enough momentum to finish at an 18-month high against the dollar. 

 The dollar closed at 1,213.5 won, below KRW1,219.4 Friday. It was the won's strongest finish since KRW1,209.2 on Dec. 19 2000. 

 The dollar had fallen as low as KRW1,210.7 in early trading before verbal intervention by the South Korean government and the subsequent action by Japanese authorities pulled the U.S. currency higher. 

 The won often tracks the yen because of the similarities between South Korean and Japanese exports and export markets. 

 The Thai baht posted a 21-month high, raising concerns the central bank may step into the market to curb the currency's strength. 

 The dollar's broad weakness and improving prospects for the Thai economy fueled baht buying, traders said. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at THB41.800, down from THB41.990 late Friday. It was the baht's best performance since September 2000. 

 The Taiwan dollar powered to a 13-month high despite aggressive intervention by the central bank to slow the local currency's appreciation. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.772, compared with NT$33.855 Friday. It was the New Taiwan dollar's strongest close since NT$33.495 on May 25, 2001. 

 The market was full of U.S. dollar sellers, but there were few buyers. The central bank worked hard to keep the dollar bid, buying about $2 billion on a day where the volume of all transactions totaled $2.65 billion. 

 "It was mostly the central bank in there today," said one dealer at a foreign bank in Taipei, noting that both exporters and offshore players were selling the greenback. 

 The Singapore dollar finished Asian trading at a nine-month high. Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.765, down from S$1.772 late Friday. 

 Despite the U.S. dollar's sharp fall, market participants said the move wouldn't likely draw the attention of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The central bank is more likely to tolerate a strong Singapore dollar when other Asian currencies are strengthening as well, they said. 

 The MAS doesn't intervene very often, but has done so in the past when the Singapore dollar had strayed outside of an undisclosed trading band that measures the local currency on a trade-weighted basis. 

 The U.S. dollar's recent slide has probably pushed the lower range of the trading band to S$1.7500, according to a report from United Overseas Bank. 

 The Indonesian rupiah capitalized on regional dollar bearishness and positive sentiment surrounding the country's loan program with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at IDR8,595, down from IDR8,630 late Friday. 

 The IMF late last week announced it was disbursing the next US$358 million of loans to Indonesia as part of a $5 billion assistance package. 

 However, the IMF warned that a recent government decision to declare bankrupt the local affiliate of Canadian insurer Manulife showed the country's legal system needs further reforms. 

 In Manila, lingering fiscal concerns and sluggish U.S. dollar inflows weighed on the peso. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.35 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP50.32 Friday. 

 "The peso should be hovering just above PHP49 against the dollar, but the market is pricing in the budget deficit," one trader said. 

 The government recently reported that its budget deficit reached PHP82.69 billion for the first four months of the year, a pace that would put it significantly over its full-year target.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Hits 9-Mo High On US Dlr Weakness
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar surged to a fresh nine-month high late Monday on the U.S. dollar's persistent weakness against its major counterparts and regional currencies, dealers said. 

 At 0855 GMT (4:55 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7656, down from S$1.7720 late Friday in Asia. It traded between S$1.7643 and S$1.7715. 

 In Asia Monday, the U.S. dollar opened weaker, extending the losses it suffered in New York late Friday, when it dropped below S$1.7700 amid more losses in the U.S. stock market, dealers said. 

 The U.S. currency broke immediate support at S$1.7685 in early Monday trading as local banks and U.S. investment houses kept up with their U.S. dollar sales. The outlook for the U.S. currency continues to worsen, dealers said. 

 However, despite the U.S. dollar's sharp fall, market participants weren't too concerned that the move would draw the attention of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, mainly because the U.S. dollar was broadly weaker against other Asian counterparts at the same time. 

 In a research report published Monday, United Overseas Bank said it doubts the MAS would be uncomfortable with the U.S. dollar's inherent weakness against the Singapore dollar and reckons the MAS' undisclosed lower limit for the U.S. dollar to have slipped to S$1.7500. 

 The U.S. dollar at one point Monday bounced higher against the Singapore dollar, albeit briefly, when Japan intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the U.S. currency against the yen. The U.S. dollar shot up to Y122.76 from Y121.02. 

 The U.S. dollar soon tumbled again against other currencies, including the Singapore dollar, which touched a fresh nine-month low of S$1.7643, when Europe-based players joined in the U.S. dollar selling in favor of a strong euro late in the Asian trading day, dealers said. 

 Overnight, the U.S. dollar is expected to test lower, "unless they (BOJ) intervene again," said a dealer at a Japanese bank. 

 Barring that, the U.S. dollar may head toward its next support at S$1.7600. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds were mostly higher Monday, in tandem with gains in U.S. Treasurys late Friday, and as local interbank rates stayed weak, dealers said. 

 Most tenors had started the local session higher and held up through the day, though volumes tapered off slightly, in the wake of the heavy flows seen last week, dealers added. 

 Some dealers said the political uncertainty in Malaysia following Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's flip-flop over resigning dissipated early in the session. 

 Mahathir announced before a national television audience Saturday that he was quitting but changed his mind about an hour later after entreaties from leaders of United Malays National Organisation, or UMNO, the dominant political party in Malaysia's ruling coalition. Mahathir then left Sunday on a previously unannounced 10-day vacation. 

 The yield on two-year bonds ended five basis points lower at 1.39%, while the yield on five-year bonds fell 10 basis points to 2.66%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds fell nine basis point to 3.15% and the yield on 10-year bonds fell six basis points to 3.58%.

title: SGX Nikkei 225 Futures End Up; BOJ  Intervention  Lifts Mkt

 At 0651 GMT (2:51 a.m. EDT), the dollar was quoted at Y121.74, above Y121.12 late Friday in New York, but still below Y123.36 late Friday in Tokyo. 

 A weaker yen against the dollar is often considered beneficial for Japan's export-oriented economy. 

 BOJ's intervention triggered some short-covering in the futures market, dealers said, adding that if prices continue to rise, more short position holders will probably be forced to close their contracts. 

 Nikkei September now faces resistance at 10,550, with support at 10,000, dealers said.

SINGAPORE, June 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies kept their 

 strength as more rumblings in the Middle East added woes to the 

 wobbly dollar, which was still languishing near its multi-month 

 lows against the euro and the Swiss franc . 

     The dollar sank anew after a Palestinian suicide bomber in 

 Jerusalem killed seven people and wounded about 35 at a bus 

 stop. News that the U.S. Secret Service briefly evacuated the 

 White House after an aircraft flew into restricted airspace a 

 few miles away from the president's residence also unsettled 

 the market. 

     Although the U.S. currency managed to recover some lost

 vulnerable as investors still questioned the valuations of the 

 U.S. assets. 

     "Most of my clients almost universally take a bearish view 

 on the dollar and U.S. assets which, relative to other markets, 

 are still expensive," said a fund manager at one U.S. firm in 

 Singapore. 

     "U.S. companies will need strong growth to justify the 

 current prices. Although there is evidence the U.S. is 

 recovering, the quality of its growth is not going to be that 

 fantastic," he said. 

     Economists said Asia should benefit if investors shift 

 their investments from the United States to seek better 

 risk-adjusted returns. 

     "Perhaps the cash portions (of investments) have gone up 

 significantly, because apart from Thailand, we haven't seen

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Won Ends Dn On Ctrl Bk Talk
text:
OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Friday, with comments by several central bankers in the region indicating different levels of comfort with the dollar's recent weakness. 

 The Korean won fell against the dollar as the market struggled to interpret remarks by the Bank of Korea, while the Thai baht finished firmer thanks to equities-related inflows and the central bank's reassurance it was comfortable with the baht's strength. 

 The rupiah, Singapore dollar, Taiwanese dollar and peso were mostly flat late, although the central bank governor in the Philippines said he thought the peso should trade higher. 

 Friday's trade continued to be muted with many participants distracted by key World Cup matches, and volume in many markets was thin. 

 Early in the session, Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung said that the recent weakening in the dollar against the won has reduced the need for an interest rate hike in Korea, a comment some took to indicate the central bank would tolerate a stronger won. But Park also said the central bank will have to buy dollars in the market if the U.S. currency's drop versus the won is "excessive" - suggesting the bank won't let the won strengthen much more. 

 The market eventually chose to focus on the latter interpretation after a spate of afternoon dollar-buying by state-run banks spurred a round of dollar short-covering, pushing up the dollar to 1,236.1 won, above Wednesday's finish at KRW1,233.6. South Korean markets were closed Thursday for a holiday. 

 In Singapore, the dollar dipped against the local currency after Moody's Investors Service announced a surprise upgrade of the nation's ratings. The dollar hit an intraday low of S$1.7835 after Moody's raised Singapore's foreign currency country ceilings for bonds and deposits, as well as the government's foreign currency rating, to Aaa, its highest grade, from Aa1. 

 The ratings agency said that the upgrade reflects continued strengthening of the country's external financial position over the past several years. Although Singapore's fiscal surplus has declined recently, Moody's said the government has very large holdings of financial and other assets and no foreign debt. 

 With the U.S. dollar having retreated significantly from a high of S$1.7945 Monday, market participants were wary of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to weaken the local dollar. 

 These concerns prompted foreign and local banks to buy U.S. dollars, lifting the currency above S$1.7860. 

 The dollar closed at S$1.7865, unchanged from levels a day earlier. 

 In Thailand, the dollar finished at 42.175 baht, down from THB42.265 Thursday. Capital inflows for foreigners' portfolio investments continued to weigh on the U.S. currency, a Bangkok dealer said. 

 But Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said late Friday he isn't concerned about the baht's strength. "There is nothing serious about the baht's recent strength. It moves up and down. That's normal," he told reporters. 

 The market wasn't affected much by the governor's comments, as they confirmed existing policy and were identical to comments of central bank officials issued repeatedly in recent weeks as the baht has slowly strengthened. 

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso closed flat amid a dearth of fresh incentives. The dollar closed at its intraday high of PHP50.470, little changed from PHP50.465 Thursday, as a recent rally by the U.S. currency appeared to be running out of steam. 

 The peso's downside was supported by comments from the country's central bank chief, who said the dollar should fall below PHP50.00 given the strong foreign-exchange inflows and expectations of a sizable balance-of-payments surplus this year. 

 "The dollar should be below PHP50 and around PHP49," said Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura. 

 Traders said they expect the dollar to move between PHP50.15 and PHP50.50 in the coming week. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended stronger against its U.S. counterpart on U.S. dollar selling by exporters - although the rise was capped by central bank intervention, dealers said. 

 At 0800 GMT (4:00 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.112, down from NT$34.121 Thursday. 

 One dealer said the central bank's U.S. dollar bids totaled around US$150 million. 

 The Indonesian rupiah ended steady in range-bound trading, but is expected to head higher next week following gains in local stock prices in the last four sessions, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 8,740 rupiah, little changed from its close at IDR8,745 Thursday. 

 Dealers said that dollar demand from local companies to pay maturing offshore debts offset dollar offers from foreign banks, leaving the dollar range-bound. 

 Local companies are saddled by around $60 billion of foreign debts, which they borrowed before the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis. Most Indonesian companies only managed to get a three-year rollover on the payment of the debts, which means some of them started making repayments last year. Offshore debt payments occasionally weigh on the rupiah.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; BOJ  Intervention  Fears Persist
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Concerns that Japanese monetary authorities might intervene in foreign exchange markets to prop up the dollar against the yen kept a lid on all Asian currencies Wednesday. 

 The intervention fears were heightened after the Bank of Japan bought dollars against the yen Tuesday for the fourth time in two weeks in an attempt to control the yen's recent rise. 

 The BOJ acted on behalf of the Ministry of Finance, which has expressed concern that excessive yen strength could undermine the country's fragile economic recovery. 

 While most analysts agree that no amount of government intervention can reverse the negative sentiment toward the dollar in global markets, the $20 billion spent by the MOF so far has been successful in stinging market players who have taken short positions in the dollar against the yen and other Asian currencies. 

 "The market is afraid of more MOF intervention. The dollar is likely to stay supported for now, which will indirectly cap Asian currencies gains," said Jimmy Koh, head of Treasury research at United Overseas Bank in Singapore. 

 The dollar has fallen by about 7% against both the yen and euro since March as global investors have shifted capital away from the U.S. into markets in Europe and Asia looking for better returns. 

 The dollar's fall against its major counterparts, combined with an improving outlook for Asian economies, has pushed most regional currencies to multi-month highs in recent trading sessions. 

 Following the dollar's bull run over the past few years, many analysts say U.S. government authorities would welcome a gradual weakening of the currency because it would help U.S. manufacturers become more competitive in global export markets. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at 124.30 yen, up from Y123.99 late Tuesday in New York. The euro was at $0.9374, down from $0.9395 late Tuesday in New York. 

 The South Korean won backed off an 18-month high to finish the day weaker after officials from both the Bank of Korea and Ministry ofFinance and Economy made public statements expressing their concern over the currency's strength. 

 The dollar traded as low as 1,218.7 won at midday as exporters sold the currency aggressively. The dollar bounced back after the jawboning to close at KRW1,224.3, up from KRW1,220.1 Tuesday. 

 Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung warned that the won's recent appreciation was hurting the competitiveness of South Korean exporters. He said the central bank would take unspecified measures to counter the won's appreciation against the dollar if the domestic currency's rise hurts the economy. 

 Echoing the central bank governor's comments, an official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy said the government was "greatly concerned" about the negative impact on the economy from the won's appreciation. 

 The Philippine peso came under pressure from the yen weakness and continuing concerns over a political dispute that has split in the Senate leadership. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.800 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP50.430 Tuesday. 

 The defection of a government-allied senator means the opposition now controls 12 of the upper house's 24 seats. There were concerns that the split could delay passage of key reform bills needed to push the economy forward. 

 "Jitters over the situation in the Senate and its impact on the government's economic agenda continue to hound the market," said a trader with a local bank. 

 The Indonesian rupiah fell sharply, triggering speculation that the currency's recent rally to a nine-month high may be near its end. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at IDR8,900, up from IDR8,650 late Tuesday. 

 The decline "reaffirms our position that the risk-reward has turned against the currency, with the market over-stretching its optimism on Indonesian assets," Bank of America said in a note to clients. 

 A string of failures in the country's economic reform program in recent weeks, including last week's decision to cancel an auction of a 51% stake in Bank Niaga due to low bids, raised concerns about the sustainability of the rupiah rally, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar finished a touch weaker, affected only marginally by the yen's decline. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.097, compared with the previous close of NT$34.093. 

 "You saw the yen weaken a bit, but on the other hand most players still think that the Taiwan dollar has more room for appreciation, so the two factors balanced each other out," a foreign bank dealer in Taipei said. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped as the decline in regional currencies prompted foreign and local banks to cover their short positions in the U.S. dollar. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7945, up from S$1.7836 late Tuesday. 

 The Thai baht also followed other regional currencies lower, with a lack of domestic developments to drive trading. 

 The dollar was quoted at 42.51 baht in late Asian trading, up from THB42.31 late Tuesday.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Higher Late;Only Peso, Rupiah Fall
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Ongoing concerns about the U.S. economy and stock markets pushed the dollar lower against most Asian currencies Tuesday. 

 Only the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah failed to take advantage of the dollar's global weakness. 

 Most other regional currencies continued to trade at multi-month highs, with the South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar posting their best performances in 17 months and one year respectively. 

 The dollar opened the Asian trading day on the defensive, with overnight declines in U.S. equity markets underscoring the negative wave of sentiment weighing on the currency. 

 "The weakening bias in the U.S. dollar persists, with the new week kicking off in an increasingly familiar manner," BNP Paribas said in a note to clients. 

 Sizable declines in both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nasdaq Composite Index overwhelmed a report from the Institute for Supply Management that showed the U.S. manufacturing sector grew robustly in May. 

 In Seoul, a new round of verbal intervention by South Korean authorities briefly halted the won's rise, but the currency continued its climb shortly thereafter as exporters resumed their dollar sales. 

 The dollar finished at 1,220.1 won, down from Monday's close at KRW1,226.3, and its lowest level since December 2000. 

 Concerned that the won was appreciating too rapidly, the Finance Ministry issued a statement that it was concerned about market "uneasiness" and would take necessary action. 

 "No one believes what the government says anymore," said a dealer at a local bank. "Unless there's some actual dollar purchase by the government, the market isn't likely to react." 

 The South Korean government has repeatedly threatened action in the foreign exchange market over the past three weeks, but has yet to take any concrete steps. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.093, down from NT$34.139 Monday. It was the Taiwan currency's strongest finish since last June. 

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar's decline will likely slow as it reaches the NT$34.00 support level. The central bank is also expected to support the U.S. currency to prevent it from falling to sharply. 

 The peso came under pressure following negative news regarding the country's budget deficit, and a brewing political storm in the government. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.430 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP50.360 Monday. 

 Reports that tax collections for May were lower than expected fueled ongoing concerns that the government may not be able to meet its budget deficit target for the year. 

 The government has already overshot its budget target for the first quarter. 

 Sentiment toward the peso also was dented by what many termed as a "senate coup" staged Monday, when opposition lawmakers wrested the leadership of the chamber from senators allied with President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's government. 

 The defection of a government-allied senator has given the opposition control of 12 of the chamber's 24 seats. 

 "The market is concerned that such political events might backlash on the government's economic agenda," said a trader with a local bank. 

 The Indonesian rupiah weakened slightly after market participants booked profits following the local currency's recent rally, traders said. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at IDR8,650, up from IDR8,540 at Monday's close. 

 The rupiah rallied to nine month high Monday due to investor optimism regarding the country's debt restructuring effort, and economic outlook. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen and other regional currencies higher. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7836, down from S$1.7878 late Monday. 

 The market has been reluctant to sell the U.S. dollar more aggressively for fear the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene in the market to support the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The baht also moved in tandem with its regional peers with little in the way of domestic news to drive trading. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 42.31 baht, down from THB42.38 late Monday.

SINGAPORE, May 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies held on to 

 their gains on Thursday, but regional bulls lacked the resolve

     "But the yen could strengthen rapidly if it gets into the

currency strategist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo. 

     Despite doubts about the economic recovery in the U.S. -- a 

 major market for Asian exports -- most regional currencies were 

 largely underpinned by improving domestic economies. 


    The Singapore dollar        rose past 1.7900, but it failed



to rise beyond 1.7880 where corporates and some local players



ambushed the local currency.

that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) would intervene


to rein in its gains as the Sing dollar was not out of sync



with other regional currencies.

Minister Jeon Yun-churl told a gathering of economists that



authorities were discussing appropriate steps regarding the



won.



    The won has been having a ball lately, gaining 4.50 percent

with data showing a strong pick up in industrial output -- a



key barometer for exports performance.



    Analysts suggested that the Bank of Korea could become more



aggressive in tightening monetary policy now that exports might

engine.



    "When export is strong, it does not make sense for Korea to



continue to leverage up just to keep the economy going at a



double speed," said Andie Xie, regional economist for Morgan



Stanley in Hong Kong.



    "A more sensible approach is to increase interest rates



aggressively to slow down household credit," he said.



    The central bank bumped up the key overnight rate target to



4.25 percent from a record low of four percent in early May in



a pre-emptive move aimed at deflating a potential credit



bubble.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Mostly firm, but off early highs.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 28 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 firm late on Tuesday, aided by a steadier yen , but gains 

 were capped with the market wary of interventions and awaiting 

 consumer data from the United States. 


    Those concerns pulled the Korean won         -2 down to



1,237.5 per dollar at the close of onshore trade, from a fresh



17-month high of 1,225.5. The Taiwan dollar was also



off its new 11-month high of 34.275 to end onshore trade at



34.309.



    While analysts said dollar losses could be limited by



actual or feared central bank interventions, the near-term



outlook for the greenback was bearish.



    "Japanese stocks remain attractive to investors looking for



the next big thing, especially while the US market is not so



hot while the rest of Asia is booming," said Marshall Gittler,



head of Asian currencies at Bank of America in Tokyo.



    The dollar managed to stay almost a yen above last



Wednesday's lows of around 123.50 when the Bank of Japan


intervened to prop it up, but down from late Monday's 124.86.



    The dollar was also within sight of eight-month lows



against the euro .



    CAUTIOUS GAINS



    Dealers in Singapore said concerns over verbal and actual


interventions in the yen and other North Asian currencies was



sending markets in Southeast into bouts of dollar short



covering, given that most players were extremely short of



dollars.



Those concerns pulled the Singapore dollar off its



early session high of around 1.7900, even after a surprise rise



in April manufacturing production data that confirmed a



tentative rebound was gaining momentum.



The first quarter business receipts index however shrank



1.7 percent on the year, larger than the previous quarter's 0.3



percent drop, showing the services sector may still lag.



The April manufacturing production index rose 8.1 percent



year on year beating forecasts of minus one percent to plus



three percent.



Dealers said Singapore dollar eased to levels around

on. It was still higher from late Monday's 1.7083.



The Indonesian rupiah stalled at around 8,845 per

.



Two out of four consortia were qualified on Monday to buy



the 51 percent stake, but authorities say their bids should



meet price expectations for the sale to proceed.



The qualifying consortia are led by Australian and New



Zealand Banking Group Ltd and Malaysia's second



largest lender, Commerce Asset-Holding Bhd .



The Financial Sector Policy Committee was due to review on



Wednesday the sale process, seen as a key gauge of investor



sentiment and the government's commitment to reform.



PESO STRUGGLES AT 50



The Philippine peso poked above the 50-per-dollar
