title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Southeast track won, Taiwan dlr gains.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies firmed up 

 early on Tuesday, taking their cue from a steadier yen and 

 local factors, though lingering fear of intervention by 

 Japanese authorities against their currency was expected to 

 limit gains. 

     The Korean won hit a fresh 17-month high and the Taiwan 

 dollar rose to 11-=   month peaks. 

     Dealers in Singapore said players in Asian currencies, 

 including the yen, would be less aggressive ahead of consumer 

 data from the United States. 

     But if April personal income and spending numbers and May's 

 conference board consumer confidence index support the dollar, 

 dealers said that would be taken only as an opportunity to sell 

 the greenback. 

 "Given the current bullish sentiment towards the yen, any 

 rebound of the dollar would be unsustainable, and should be 

 taken as an opportunities to sell the dollar," a senior dealer 

 at a Singapore bank said. 

 He said historically, over the last decade, bounces in the 

 Japanese economy accompany equity-related inflows which in turn 

 push the yen higher and snuff out the economic recovery. 

 "The Japanese authorities are well aware of this fact but 

 how far they are prepared to go (to limit the yen's gains) is 

 still a matter of speculation," said the dealer, whose bank 

 forecast the yen would hit 120 per dollar in a few weeks' time. 

 NORTH LEADS 

 The bullish view on the yen coupled with growing optimism 

 that most regional economies in Asia would outperform other 

 emerging markets have been supporting sentiment in regional 

currencies and other Asian assets. 

 Dealers said recently the North Asian currencies were 

 getting an extra boost from month-end dollar sales by 

 exporters. 

 The Korean won hit a fresh 17-month high at 1,226 per 

 dollar, up more than a percent from late Monday's 1,233.8 and 

 shrugging off recent verbal intervention by the authorities. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the market was more focused on 

 April industrial output numbers due on Wednesday and May 

 consumer price data on Friday. 

 The Taiwan dollar, cheering the release of positive 

 economic data, rose to 11-= month highs at 34.275 per dollar, 

 from late Monday's 34.375. 

 Taiwan said late on Monday the index of leading indicators 

 for April rose for the seventh straight month to a 20-month 

 high. 

 Dealers in Singapore said equity-related inflows were also 

 backing those gains although dollar purchases from the central 

 bank were seen capping gains for now. 

 SOUTHEAST TO CATCH UP 

 In the southeast, the Singapore dollar and Thai baht jumped 

 in an attempt to catch up with the gains in the north as trade 

 resumed there after a long weekend. 

     Both Singapore and Thailand were closed on Monday for local 

 holidays. 

     The Singapore dollar rose to levels just shy of 1.7900 per 

 dollar, from levels around 1.7980 on Friday, following gains in 

currencies of export rivals Korea and Taiwan. 

     But some profit-taking and local commercial dollar demand 

 pulled the Sing dollar back to levels around 1.7930. 

     April industrial production data due later in the day was 

 expected to confirm a tentative rebound is gathering momentum, 

 after recent strong export figures for April. 

     The Sing dollar is still some way from its 7-1/2-month high 

 of 1.785 hit last Wednesday before physical intervention

 against the yen prompted players to cover their short dollar 

 positions. 

 The Thai baht strengthened to a session high of 42.60 

 before some profit-taking by local interbank players pulled it 

 back to levels around 42.70, though that was still higher than 

 last Friday's 42.82, before the market's long weekend. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the Thai market would track gains 

 in the Singapore dollar and other regionals, though fears of 

 potential dollar purchases by the Bank of Thailand and talk of 

 local dollar bids around 42.50-42.60 was likely to limit the 

 upside. 

 Buyers of the Indonesian rupiah kept their fingers crossed 

 ahead of an expected announcement of the winner of a 

 majority-stake in the state's Bank Niaga. 

 The level of final bids by the two bidders left in the race 

 could send an important signal about investor confidence. If 

 the bids are at too great a discount to the market price of the 

 bank's shares, Indonesian authorities might abandon the 

 auction. 

     The rupiah hit a peak of 8,845 per dollar, a level last 

 seen on September 12. 

     The Philippine peso also gained to test the 50 per dollar 

 level, encouraged by the gains in the other regionals. It hit a 

 session high of 50.08, from late Monday's 50.53.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Won Hits 17-Month High
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar continued their assault against the U.S. dollar Monday, advancing to fresh 17-month and 11-month respective highs. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also gained on the dollar, while the Philippine peso slipped. Trading in the Singapore dollar and Thai baht was limited because markets in Singapore and Bangkok were closed for public holidays. 

 The yen wasn't much of a factor in Asian currency markets as it was trapped in a narrow range against the dollar due to the Memorial Day holiday in the U.S. Monday. 

 In Seoul, verbal intervention by South Korean officials had only a minimal impact on the won as it strengthened to its best finish against the dollar since December 2000. 

 The dollar ended at 1,233.8 won, down from KRW1,243.2 Friday. 

 Finance Minister Jeon Yun-churl said that while the appreciation of the won basically reflects South Korea's economic fundamentals, the government is concerned over the speed of the currency's appreciation. 

 The won has appreciated 8% against the dollar since mid-April. 

 The won dropped back after Jeon's comments, but the retreat was brief because few market players believe the government will actually intervene to support the dollar. 

 "Our government has no intention to buy U.S. dollars in the market," said Gin Lee, head of foreign exchange sales trading at BNP Paribas in Seoul. "Intervention will be very difficult because of worries about inflation." 

 Allowing the won to strengthen tends to reduce the cost of imported goods and keeps inflationary pressures from building. 

 Dollar selling was widespread, with exporters dumping the U.S. currency the most aggressively, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar edged higher in thin trading, closing at its highest level against the U.S. dollar since June 2001. 

 The dollar closed at NT$34.375 compared with NT$34.414 Friday. 

 With Singapore markets closed during Asian hours and with the U.S. holiday, turnover was thin, one dealer said. 

 Many participants were also sidelined because of fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the dealer added. However, the central bank, which intervenes on a regular basis to stave off market volatility, was relatively inactive. 

 The Philippine peso fell to a four-week low against the dollar amid dollar short-covering by banks and rising corporate demand for the U.S. currency. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.530 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP50.350 Friday. 

 Traders said some banks opted to cover their short-dollar positions on growing perceptions that the central bank won't move to support the peso. 

 The rupiah strengthened despite market talk that efforts to sell PT Bank Niaga may have hit rocky ground. 

 The dollar closed at 8,880 rupiah, its intraday low, versus IDR8,950 at Friday's close. 

 Indonesian officials remained quiet over the fate of PT Bank Niaga, a small bank that has become the latest test of the country's resolve to fix its broken banking system. 


Jakarta set Monday as the deadline for final bids for Niaga from four
shortlisted investors. Market speculation swirled that Indonesia is
likely to reject the bids as being too low and reopen the bidding.

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was weaker Friday as concerns of central bank intervention weighed on sentiment after another wave of U.S. dollar buying by the Bank of Japan late Thursday sent the yen sliding, dealers said. 

 Around 0825 GMT (4:25 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7990, up from S$1.7965 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.7980 and S$1.8010 intraday in thin trading. 

 The U.S. currency opened around S$1.8005 in Asia but dropped sharply as U.S. banks took advantage of the overnight U.S. dollar rise to take profits, dealers said. 

 But trade thinned after the U.S. dollar fell below S$1.8000 support, triggering fears that such a drop might force the hand of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Market participants were also less inclined to try and initiate fresh positions, especially ahead of a long weekend in Singapore and the U.S. 

 Singapore's financial markets will be closed for a religious holiday Monday, while markets in the U.S. will be closed for the Memorial Day holiday. 

 "It's been a lot quieter today. Earlier on, many people, mostly U.S. banks, were just taking profit, but now that's eased," a Japanese bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said the volatile movements of the U.S. dollar against its regional counterparts during the week had hurt market participants, especially with the intervention action, so many were just staying on the sidelines, waiting for the weekend. 

 Looking ahead, the U.S. dollar is expected to continue to be thinly traded against the local dollar as market participants adjust positions. Support for the U.S. dollar is expected at S$1.7950 and resistance at S$1.8030, dealers said. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended mixed late Friday in light trading, with many market participants staying on the sidelines ahead of the long weekend, dealers said. 

 Local bonds fell marginally in early trading, tracking modest falls in U.S. Treasurys overnight, but most tenors managed to recoup part of their losses on bargain-hunting, dealers added.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Flinch on BOJ threats, data eyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 24 (Reuters) - Asian currencies ended the 

 week on a jittery note, after the Bank of Japan sent the market 

 a multi-billion dollar message that they are not going to take 

 the yen's rapid rise sitting down. 

     The BoJ bought dollars to rein in the yen on Wednesday and 

 Thursday for the first time since September, forcing traders to 

 cover short positions. 

     Some dealers estimated the central bank spent $2-3 billion 

 on the first day and $1-2 billion on the second, while others 

 said it could have spent $5-6 billion on the first round 

 alone. 

  Dealers said Asian currency markets were now pretty squarish 

 and most were reluctant to be aggressive on either side of the 

 fence ahead of a long Memorial Day holiday weekend in the U.S. 

     "The BOJ will have little difficulty in supporting the 

 dollar through the long U.S. holiday weekend, but how they 

 behave after Monday should also shed light on their 

 determination to hold current levels," said Ron Leven, currency

 strategist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo. 

     The market was trapped between wariness of Japanese central 

 bank intervention on one side and traders wanting to sell the 

 dollar on heightened fears of terror attacks in the U.S. 

     Fresh violence in Israel and Japanese exporters with 

 substantial dollars to sell above 125 yen were also seen 

 keeping pressure on the dollar. 

     The market is watching out for a raft of data, starting 

 with U.S. first quarter gross domestic product figures due 

 later on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters expect GDP to be 

 revised up to 6.0 percent from 5.8 percent. 

     Next week, Taiwan is scheduled to release its leading 

 economic indicator which analysts said was likely to confirm a 

 pick up in activity. 

     The Philippines publishes its first quarter gross domestic 

 product data on May 31. A Reuters poll predicted the economy 

 had grown around 3.6-5.0 percent in that period, compared with 

 the government's target of 3.8-4.2 percent.

finishing at 50.35 to the dollar -- its worst closing level



since May 2 -- compared with 49.84 in the previous session.



Trading was brisk, with $220.50 million transacted.



    Dealers in Manila said corporate players, especially oil



companies, piled in to buy dollars on views that perhaps the



BoJ's latest intervention might be providing a floor for the



dollar.



    "The market was pretty short in the first place. The BoJ's


intervention just provide participants with an excuse to adjust



their positions," said a dealer.



    "And the central bank's remarks on the peso did not help



either."



    Philippine central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said



on Friday the peso's slide to 50 was not worrisome and that the



bank had not intervened.



    BAHT, SING DOLLAR SOFT



    The Thai baht        and the Singapore dollar        were



also weaker as players pared short dollar positions, fearing



they might get caught on the wrong side of the market when they



return from a long weekend holiday.



    Financial markets in Thailand and Singapore will be closed



on Monday for a religious holiday. They will reopen on Tuesday.



    The baht languished around 42.85 late on Friday, with



exporters holding off dollar offers on speculation the dollar



would rise further from here.



    The Sing dollar trimmed early losses on the strength of the



euro and the Indonesian rupiah - its major



trading partners - but failed to pull back into positive



territory.

with 1.8010 earlier in the day.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; BOJ  Intervenes  Again
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed in narrow trading ranges Thursday as market participants remained cautious of further U.S. dollar buying by Japanese authorities to curb the yen's strength. 

 The Bank of Japan and Ministry of Finance intervened in the currency markets for the second straight day, following through on the MOF's threat to "take action when necessary" to keep the currency pair in line. 

 Japanese authorities pulled the trigger when the U.S. dollar fell through the Y124 level after the Asian session had closed and movements were largely being driven by trading in London. The U.S. dollar shot up to Y124.90 within minutes after the intervention. 

 The U.S. dollar had traded in a tight Y124-124.15 range during Asian hours as fears of possible MOF intervention hung over the market. Most other regional currencies were similarly rangebound. 

 "The market will continue to be wary of the BOJ, with expectations that it may have to act again in the current dollar-heavy environment," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. 

 After a long period of strength, the U.S. dollar has languished over the past few months as flat corporate profits in the U.S. have sent investors looking for better opportunities in Asia and elsewhere. 

 The South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar and Indonesian rupiah strengthened. The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso finished marginally weaker, while the Thai baht was unchanged. 

 The won hit another 15-month high on investor optimism over South Korea's economic recovery. The country is pegged to be Asia's top performer this year as structural reforms have boosted economic efficiency and turned a current account deficit into a surplus. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at 1,246.1 won, down from Wednesday's finish at KRW1,247.2. The U.S. dollar traded between KRW1,245.8 and KRW1,250.0.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; BOJ Checks Yen Strength
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Currency market intervention by Japanese authorities to check the yen's strength helped the dollar gain modestly against most Asian currencies, although analysts said the dollar's weakness is likely to persist in the near term. 

 The surprise intervention by the Bank of Japan boosted the dollar by more than one full yen in afternoon trading and helped the beleaguered U.S. currency regain some of its recent losses across Asia. 

 The dollar finished higher against the Singapore dollar, Thai baht, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah. The South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar shrugged off the dollar's bounce to post 15- and 11-month highs, respectively. 

 The BOJ intervened on behalf of the Ministry of Finance, which had expressed concerns that excessive yen strength could derail the country's nascent economic recovery. 

 The yen has appreciated nearly 8% since the end of March, hitting an seven-month high of Y123.51 per dollar Wednesday. Some traders estimated that the BOJ bought at least US$1 billion, sending the dollar from Y123.70 to a high of Y125.10 in a matter of minutes. 

 "Recent movements of exchange rates have been too rapid," Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa said in a prepared statement following the intervention. 

 "We will continue to closely monitor the market and take appropriate action as necessary." 

 The dollar held relatively firm for the balance of the session, finishing Asian trading hours at Y124.90, compared with Y124.07 late Tuesday in New York. 

 However, the pressure that the dollar is experiencing in global currency markets is expected to continue, given investors' concerns about U.S. assets and the resulting flow of capital out of U.S. markets. 

 Data compiled by UBS Warburg showed that net outflows of equity-related capital for the week ended May 17 totaled US$277 million, the fifth net outflow in six weeks. The Asia-Pacific, meanwhile, enjoyed its largest inflows since mid-February. 

 "This is troubling news for dollar bulls given the U.S.'s need for capital inflows to fund its current account deficit. It also explains the recent dollar weakness," UBS Warburg said in a report. 

 The U.S. current account deficit stands at 4.2% of gross domestic product and US$1 billion in capital inflows is required each day to finance the shortfall. 

 The yen's retracement triggered some short covering of dollars against the won, not enough to keep the South Korean currency from barreling to its strongest finish since February 2001. 

 The dollar ended at 1,247.2 won, compared with KRW1,254.6 Wednesday. 

 Government officials repeated warnings to market players about excessive currency movements, keeping the possibility of intervention fresh on their minds. 

 Vice Minister of Finance and Economy Yoon Jin-Shik said the government was "greatly concerned" about the won's rise. Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung later added that while there was no need for intervention at the moment, the central bank was prepared to do so if the won appreciated too sharply. 

 The government has made such statements in recent days every time the won strengthens by more than 0.5% against the dollar, Roger Yip, foreign exchange strategist at Bank of America noted. 

 Because the warnings have been somewhat effective, the authorities have not felt the need to actually intervene, Yip added. 

 The yen's fall and sporadic U.S.-dollar buying by importers dealt a brief setback to the New Taiwan dollar. 

 "But the outlook for the yen and NT dollar remains bright in the near term because Japan's intervention will likely only be temporary and foreign equity funds are continuing to flee the U.S. to Europe and Asia," a local bank dealer said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.393, compared with NT$34.415 at the previous close. It was the strongest close for the New Taiwan dollar since June 2001. 

 The Taiwan central bank lowered a key open market rate, sending a signal that it remains cautious about the economic recovery and that it is worried the strength of the New Taiwan dollar could threaten exports. 

 Analysts said cutting the offered rate on the central bank's daily 14- and 28-day negotiable certificates of deposit and CDs effectively loosens monetary policy although it didn't act through its usual policy instruments. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened along with the yen following the BOJ's intervention. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7940, up from S$1.7930 late Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar slipped to a low of S$1.7865 in early trading but recovered as market players became concerned that the Monetary Authority of Singapore's might intervene to halt the U.S. currency's slide. The U.S. dollar rise accelerated later in the day following the BOJ's intervention. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it was not overly concerned that movements in the currency markets would derail Asia's economic recovery. 

 With global inventories being replenished and demand for information technology products beginning to recover, "this momentum is unlikely to be significantly affected by short-term volatility in currency markets," the MAS said. 

 The peso relinquished its early gains as traders scrambled to cover short-dollar positions after the Japanese government intervened to stall the yen's advance. 

 The dollar closed at its intraday high of 49.79 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP49.465 Tuesday. 

 The dollar's close was also a dramatic reversal from its opening level of PHP49.25 - a 14-month low. 

 The rupiah surged to an eight-month high in early trading, but gave up its gains later in the session, partly due to the yen's decline. 

 The dollar opened on the defensive and quickly fell through 9,000 rupiah on its way to a low of IDR8,905, its weakest performance since last September. 

 The dollar then climbed steadily through the session to finish Asian trading at IDR9,055, up from IDR9,030 late Tuesday. 

 "The fact that the dollar didn't stay below IDR9,000 for a long time reflected that people aren't yet fully comfortable with holding excessive dollar-short positions below that level," a dealer said. 

 Investors may be getting ahead of themselves with their exuberance over Indonesia's privatization program, said Sameer Goel, currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 While progress on reforms may help the rupiah strengthen over the near term, investing in Indonesia still carries considerable risks, he said. 

 "Investors should be cautious. The rupiah will likely be weaker by the end of the year rather than stronger," Goel said. 

 The baht succumbed to the yen's late session weakness. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at 42.810 baht, up from THB42.670 late Tuesday. 

 Corporate dollar buying for debt repayments also weighed on the baht.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down As Yen Pulls Back
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies backed off from recent rises, taking the tone from a falling yen Tuesday and as stock markets around the region tumbled. 

 Lingering concerns over intervention by some regional central banks added to the pressure on local currencies, prompting investors to cover their U.S. dollar short positions. 

 However, near-term sentiment toward the dollar remains bleak, and traders expect Asian currencies to resume their upward move after a short period of consolidation. 

 Only the Indonesian rupiah ended the day higher as investors bet the government will forge ahead with the sale of shares in several state-owned companies and assets controlled by the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency. 

 Comments from the International Monetary Fund - that Indonesia's macroeconomic situation has improved in recent weeks, reflected in the stronger currency, declining inflation, and lower interest rates - also aided the rupiah. 

 The IMF added it made "good progress" during initial discussions with Indonesia aimed at reaching a new loan agreement under the fund's $5 billion program for the country. 

 The U.S. dollar closed lower at IDR9,030, compared with IDR9,050 Monday. 

 For most of the other regional currencies, however, the yen's fortunes held sway. 

 A flurry of comments by Japanese policymakers voicing increasing discomfort over the yen's recent surge knocked the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar off their multi-month highs against the U.S. currency. 

 At 0903 GMT (5:03 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at Y125.65, above Y125.36 late Monday in New York. The dollar was at Y125.78 late Monday in Tokyo. 

 Rumors the Monetary Authority of Singapore was in the market aided the Singapore dollar's decline, while lingering concerns over similar action by the Taiwan central bank also pressured the New Taiwan dollar. 

 South Korea, Hong Kong, Taiwan Shares Down 

 In Seoul, South Korea's central bank governor Park Seung made it clear the won's recent rally against the U.S. dollar wasn't welcome. He didn't elaborate but there are concerns the won's persistent strength could erode export competitiveness. 

 Indeed, shares of Korean exporters fell Tuesday on those concerns as well as on weaker DRAM prices - Korea's exports are driven by DRAM products, traders said. 

 "Today there was good demand for dollars (against the won), but I don't think it's permanent," said a trader. 

 Sentiment over the won, however, remains positive as investors continue to expect the Korean economy to grow faster than earlier anticipated. 

 The government is due to announce first quarter gross domestic product data Wednesday. A survey of 10 economists by Dow Jones Newswires expect the economy to grow 4.9% on year in the first quarter or a seasonally adjusted 1.2% on quarter. The government predicts a slightly slower 4.7% year-on-year expansion, and follows a 3.7% rise in the fourth quarter of last year. 

 The U.S. dollar finished higher against the won, at KRW1,254.6, following four sessions of decline. The dollar ended at KRW1,253.6 Monday. 

 It isn't just the won which has surged on optimism over the economy. The Singapore dollar, which has benefited from the island nation's increasingly bullish economic outlook, returned some of its recent gains Tuesday on the yen's retreat. Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7930, up from S$1.7910 late Monday. 

 Rumors that the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market Monday to slow the local dollar's rise did the rounds again. Some dealers suspected the MAS bought the U.S. dollar yesterday after it fell through support at S$1.7920. 

 Such market talk isn't surprising as the issue of the country's export competitiveness remain on the government's agenda and joblessness continue to tick higher. 

 Meanwhile, the New Taiwan dollar also ended lower as traders covered their short positions in the U.S. dollar. The U.S. currency finished at NT$34.415, up from NT$34.412 at Monday's close. 

 Taiwan shares fell for the fourth consecutive session Tuesday, hit by a selloff on Wall Street. But dealers said the focus of the forex market remains on the yen, whose uptrend is expected to stay in place. 

 The Philippine peso finished lower largely on the yen, and also after a power outage hit the capital and the rest of the main island of Luzon. 

 "The dollar moved up as some traders speculated that something bad may happen," said a trader, referring to the flurry of coup rumors that often accompany power outages in the Philippines - a throwback from a number of coup attempts during the presidency of Corazon Aquino in the late 1980s.

title: Asian  intervention  habit seen fading on recovery hopes.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 17 (Reuters) - Asian policymakers are well known for trying to steer foreign exchange markets. 

 From setting up currency pegs to direct intervention, central bankers from Bangkok to Seoul have a well-deserved reputation for manoeuvring to keep their currencies at preferred levels. 

 Thus, it comes as no surprise the recent weakness in the U.S. dollar, and especially since early April, has spurred central banks to intervene to temper strength in their currencies. 

 But foreign exchange analysts say the bout of intervention may soon fade, reflecting growing optimism about an economic recovery,twinned with the relative weakness in the region's currencies against those of other major trading partners - Europe and Japan. 

 UNDERPERFORMED YEN 

 "Some of these Asian currencies have underperformed the yen and euro as they rallied, making sure that on a trade-weighted basis they haven't really gone up," said David Simmonds, Salomon Smith Barney's currency strategist in Singapore. 

 Trade-weighted exchange rates show the value of a currency against a weighted basket of currencies of its trading partners. 

 Though Simmonds believes central banks will keep the markets on their toes with verbal threats, the chances of actual interventions are small. 

 "Most central banks are reasonably relaxed with the recent gains," he added. 

 This view was underlined on Friday when the Monetary Authority of Singapore said the local dollar's recent strength had not pushed it out of the central bank's actively managed policy band, used to keep the currency competitive. 

 "Although the Sing dollar had appreciated...the Sing dollar is still within the band," MAS senior director Khor Hoe Ee said. 

Currency players saw the comments as a green light for the currency to further appreciate and took the Singapore dollar to a seven-month high. 

 VERBAL NOT REAL 

 It may take time, though, to wean policymakers completely off the intervention habit. 

 A South Korean finance ministry official, also on Friday, said Korea was ready to rein in the won's sharp rise, although most analysts saw that as an effort in micro manage market expectations rather than a real threat and the won rose to a new five-month peak. 

 The warning followed remarks from Commerce Minister Shin Kook-hwan that he expected the won to strengthen to 1,250 per U.S. dollar in the second half of 2002 versus around 1,265 now. 

 Dealers said with the yen/won cross almost unchanged at around 9.8 Korean won since early April, there was scant chance of any market intervention. 

 In a region where exports account for about half of the total gross domestic product and foreign investment is seen as one of the major drivers of growth, maintaining exchange rate competitiveness is a top priority for policy-makers. 

 UNDERVALUED VS DOLLAR 

 Geoffrey Barker, chief economist of HSBC in Hong Kong, said that on an inflation-adjusted basis most currencies were still 15 to 20 percent undervalued against the U.S. dollar. 

 "There is no doubt that the rise in currencies so far does not leave them expensive," he said. 

 Simmonds, meanwhile, said that while the trade-weighted yen is still down by about five percent over the last 12 months, it has gained some 3.5 percent in the recent rally against dollar. 

 The euro in the same period has gained about 2 percent in trade-weighted terms. 

 On the same scale and period, most Asian currencies have only slightly appreciated. In fact, several of them are weaker from levels where they were 12 months back, with the Taiwan dollar down six percent and Singapore dollar off about three percent. 

 In contrast, on a nominal basis the Taiwan dollar is up by about five percent since May 2001 and the Singapore dollar has gained more than one percent.

title: Emerging  FX  - Squeezed as overweight market trims fat.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies pared some of 

 their recent gains on Wednesday as players covered short dollar 

 positions after strong data and stabilising equity markets in 

 the United States left dollar bears feeling exposed. 

     But strategists cautioned the dollar's rebound should not 

 be taken as a sign of a turnaround yet as U.S. assets, a key 

 ingredient to the dollar's strength, remain generally weak. 

     "I've never been that bearish about the dollar. But that 

 said, I don't really have signals in place that I'm looking for 

 to be able to pound the table and say 'go out to buy the dollar 

 today'," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at Lehman 

 Brothers. 

     The Singapore dollar retreated to 1.8075 after surging to a 

 seven-month high of 1.7980 in the previous session, as players 

 bought back U.S. dollars on fears of central bank intervention

 and as the dollar rebounded. 

Singapore's economic recovery is still fragile and many in 

 the market are convinced it is unlikely the central bank would 

 allow the currency to appreciate sharply. 

     The Indonesian rupiah came off intraday lows of 9,310 after 

 the central bank painted a bright economic picture for the 

 second quarter, but the good news failed to jolt the currency

 into positive territory due to strong corporate demand for 

 dollars. 

     It said in a statement obtained by Reuters that the country 

 was likely to grow by 3.5-4.0 percent in the April-June period 

 on the back of domestic demand, with the balance of payments 

 outlook also improving. 

     "The main theme today is still the dollar's movement 

 against majors and short covering. The numbers from the central 

 bank look good, but I don't think people are completely 

 surprised by them,"  said a rupiah non-deliverable forwards 

 dealer in Singapore. 

     DOLLAR'S REBOUND 

     The bruised dollar clambered off its multi-month lows 

 against majors and Asian currencies, thanks to strong U.S. data 

 which showed first quarter productivity was up 8.6 percent on 

 an annualised basis -- its fastest pace in almost 19 years. 

     The U.S. currency also drew support from news that Cisco 

 Systems Inc -- the world's biggest maker of equipment that 

 powers the Internet -- reported its quarterly profits more than 

 tripled last year's results and beat Wall Street estimates. 

     Rumours that the Bank of Japan was in the market overnight 

 to check rates also boosted the dollar. 

     It rose to a one-week high against the yen to around 

 128.50. The Japanese currency is closely tracked by the 

 regional currencies. 

     KOREAN WON, BAHT 

     The won 2 flinched, closing at 1,285.40 against  Tuesday's 

 close of 1,279.50, which had been its highest since 

 mid-December. 

     Wariness of potential central bank dollar-buying 

intervention and foreign demand for the dollar in the wake of 

 recent selling in local stocks weighed on the currency. 

     But its downside was limited by news that the government 

 was stepping up its privatisation drive, which raised hopes for 

 more capital inflows. 

     The Thai baht was a whisker away from the 43 level which it

 year to US$10.876 billion, as it was pretty much in line with 

 market consensus.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; Dollar Rebounds Across Region
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A rebound against the yen helped the dollar break its string of losses against several regional Asian currencies Wednesday. 

 The dollar finished Asian trading hours above 128 yen for the first time in six sessions, inspired by a strong report on first-quarter U.S. labor productivity released overnight and a bullish earnings report from computer-networking equipment maker Cisco Systems Inc. after the close of markets in New York. 

 A possible Moody's Investor Service downgrade of Japan's sovereign rating, and a new round of jawboning from Ministry of Finance officials also kept the yen under pressure. 

 Haruhiko Kuroda, vice finance minister for international affairs, repeated the MOF's now familiar refrain suggesting that the ministry may intervene to cap the yen's strength if it appreciates too far against other currencies. 

 Late in Asian trading the dollar was quoted at Y128.55, up from Y127.70 late Tuesday. 

 The dollar's strength flowed through to other foreign exchange markets in the region, beating back a number of currencies that had hit multi-month highs against the dollar recently. 

 The U.S. dollar gained on the New Taiwan dollar for the first time in 17 sessions as the yen's fall encouraged short-covering in the U.S. currency. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.588, up from NT$34.565 Tuesday. 

 The U.S. currency also garnered some support as the result of a slowdown in the closing of U.S. dollar deposit accounts by Taiwanese investors. The central bank's apparent goal of keeping the U.S. dollar above NT$34.50 gave depositors incentive to hold onto the U.S. currency. 

 The South Korean won fell against the dollar for the first time in five sessions. 

 The dollar ended at 1,285.4 won, up from Tuesday's close at a four-month low of KRW1,279.5. 

 The dollar lost ground early in the session as exporters sold the U.S. currency as part of their normal trading activities, but recovered later on short covering on the back of the yen's fall. 

 However, the won is likely to outperform the dollar and yen in the months ahead as a result of South Korea's strengthening economy, according to Bank of America. The bank is forecasting the dollar to fall to KRW1,180 and the yen to KRW9.5 by the end of the year. 

 The Philippine peso's fall broke a string of 10 straight sessions of gains against the dollar. 

 The dollar closed at PHP49.820 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP49.640 Tuesday. 

 "This is a healthy correction for the peso," said a trader with a local bank, noting that the Philippine currency is likely to resume its advance against the dollar in the near term because remittance and portfolio investment inflows remain strong. 

 The central bank left its overnight rates unchanged at its board meeting Wednesday, in line with the current neutral stance of the U.S. Federal Reserve. The central bank's headline overnight borrowing rate is 7%, the lowest in a decade. 

 The Singapore dollar fell in line with the yen and other regional currencies. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8092, up from S$1.8023 late Tuesday. 

 The U.S. currency also benefited from worries about possible Monetary Authority of Singapore intervention on behalf of the U.S. dollar.

text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were on a 

 roll on Tuesday, holding strong gains against the dollar, 

 although some paused in late trade ahead of a U.S. Federal 

 Reserve meeting later in the day just in case there was a 

 surprise rate rise. 

     The market expects the U.S. central bank to keep its 

 federal funds rate steady at 1.75 percent for now, given recent 

 poor economic data and disappointing corporate earnings. 

     "Our view is that the dollar will continue to weaken, and 

 that meant Asian currencies are going to continue to strengthen 

 against the dollar on a trend basis," said Peter Redward, 

currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.

     Buying of local currencies was also slowed by concerns of 

central bank intervention to cap gains against the dollar,

     The Singapore dollar strengthened past the key 1.80 level

 the Monetary Authority of Singapore might have been buying

interest rates, which make it more attractive to hold. The Bank



of Korea on Tuesday surprised the market with a 25 basis point



rate hike.

fears of intervention.

It hit multi-month lows against the yen, the euro and the Swiss



franc, on doubts over the U.S. economic outlook, shaky asset



markets and poor corporate earnings.

    Some analysts see the dollar's slide as part of much-needed



correction, and expect it to regain ground in the medium term.

    "And with so much having been loaded into the pipelines,

title: Wall Street weighs on Asia stocks, dollar glum.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - Wall Street's losses cast a pall over Asian stocks on Tuesday, with Tokyo worst off after a four-day break, while the dollar hit fresh multi-month lows against the yen, euro and Swiss franc. 

 Spot gold extended Asian gains to open at 26-month highs of $312.40/312.90 a troy ounce in Europe as London traders returned from Monday's holiday to a weaker dollar, reinforcing the metal's safe haven appeal. 

 Escalating intervention warnings from Japanese officials brought only a temporary reprieve to the dollar, which reached two-month lows on the yen and seven-month troughs on the euro and Swiss franc. 

 The dollar was quoted at 126.85/91 yen at 0650 GMT. 

 A near universal expectation that the Federal Reserve would stand pat on interest rates made Tuesday's policy meeting a non-factor, with softer U.S. data in recent weeks suggesting the central bank might not tighten till the second half of the year. 

 Asian dollar bonds rallied as investors rushed back to buy higher yielding regional credits, which offered handsome bargains after the recent weakness in spreads. 

 But South Korea's central bank surprised markets with a quarter point rate hike, its first rise since October 2000, sending stocks lower and major sovereign yields sharply higher. 

 The Bank of Korea said its move was aimed at curbing inflation pressures but it came earlier in the year than economists expected and counter to government claims on Sunday that no rise was imminent. 

 TOKYO TRIPS 

 Tokyo's Nikkei share average fell 2.03 percent or 234.97 points to 11,316.04, led by steep falls in high-tech shares as traders returned from the Golden Week break to face a 2.14 percent fall in the U.S. Nasdaq, its 12th down day in the last 14 trading sessions. 

 "A U.S. economic recovery is an important prerequisite for a "V"-shaped earnings recovery here. However, as last week's jobs data suggested, the U.S. recovery may not be as strong as we had hoped," said Masayoshi Yano, an investment information manager at Tokai Tokyo Securities. 

 "Also, another important pillar in that recovery scenario is a softer yen, but it is actually firming." 

 The Japanese currency's immediate upside was blocked by option-related dollar bids around 126.50/60 yen and talk a Japanese public fund may be supporting the dollar. 

 Expectations of a downgrade when Moody's Investors Service completes its review of Japan's credit rating next week also gave yen bulls some pause. 

 Although the Japanese Finance Ministry's unease with the yen's rise was largely ignored, traders avoided pushing the dollar below 1.5800 Swiss francs fearing protests by the Swiss National Bank. 

 Asian regional currencies also made limited headway in the face of intervention fears, with the Singapore dollar backing off early seven-month highs amid rumours the central bank might have bought dollars to slow its rise. 

 STOCKS SAG 

 Elsewhere, Seoul shares posted their third consecutive decline, with the Korea Composite Stock Price Index falling 0.06 percent to 826.34 as investors gave a thumbs-down to the central bank's pre-emptive rate hike. 

 "There has been consensus that interest rates will be raised but I think the timing was not appropriate given that uncertainties are growing about economic growth," said Kim Jin-sung, an analyst at Kyobo Securities in Seoul. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 0.21 percent or 24.18 points at 11,712.90 at 0645 GMT, off its early lows on hopes for a sustainable domestic recovery in the second half. 

 In Singapore, the Straits Times Index was just 0.05 percent or 0.86 point at 1,721.19 percent at 0646 GMT, while Taiwan's weighted TAIEX stood out with a 0.38 percent rise to finish at 5,663.98 as bargain-hunters emerged after Monday's 4.5 percent slump to a two-month low.

title: Singapore dollar hits seven-month high.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar strengthened on Tuesday past the key 1.8000 level for the first time since October last year, after a firmer yen encouraged investors to add the local currency to their positions and cut losses on the U.S. dollar. 

 A U.S. name and one major European bank were seen actively selling the U.S. currency versus the Sing, dealers said. At 0110 GMT, the Sing dollar was trading at 1.7998 to the dollar. 

 The Sing dollar tends to track the yen because of heavy trade flows between the two countries. Singapore's central bank monitors the currency's progress against a trade weighted basket of currencies in a managed float. The yen is believed to account for 15 percent of the basket. 

 The Sing dollar, which has gained almost three percent so far this year from 1.8515 to the dollar, has been on a steady upward trend against the U.S. currency since early April.

Currency strategists were divided over whether Singapore's central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), would intervene at current levels to meet its aim of a stable currency. The MAS actively intervenes to stave off excessive volatility. 

 Some strategists expect the MAS to buy U.S. dollars soon, based on a view that the Singapore's economic recovery is still too fragile to warrant a strong currency and the 1.8000 level was a line of defence for now. 

 Others argued the central bank was likely to leave the market alone for now because the Sing's dollar gains are in line with other currencies in the region. 

 "I don't see the MAS coming into the market before 1.7900, and that's almost another 100 points to go," said Peter Redward, currency strategists at Deutsche Bank in Singapore. 

 "In this environment where the yen and the euro are rising and Asian currencies are rising, I think the MAS will be cautious about intervening too aggressively," he said. 

 U.S. DOLLAR BLEAK 

 The Asian rises reflected a falling U.S. dollar across the board. It hit multi-month lows against the yen, the euro and the Swiss franc, thanks to a sinking feeling over the U.S. economic outlook, shaky asset markets and poor corporate earnings. 

 Wall Street stocks sank on Monday, with the Dow Jones industrial average shedding almost 200 points as pessimism deepened. 

 But some analysts see the dollar's slide as part of much-needed correction, and expect the currency to regain ground in a medium term. 

 "The market is way too short of the dollar now, therefore a strong upside potential is there," said a senior dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 "And with so much having been loaded into the pipelines, the U.S. economy should recover well this year. Its productivity is still high. I think the market is just looking for an excuse to take profits," he said.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Gains Muted By Yen Fall
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar weakened against most Asian currencies Tuesday, but a late session rally against the yen helped the U.S. currency trim its losses in the region. 

 The dollar jumped nearly one full yen in the last hour of Asian trading, providing the U.S. currency with at least a temporary respite from its recent downward slide against Japanese unit. 

 Dealers dismissed any speculation that the move may have been engineered by the Bank of Japan, saying it was more likely a result of the dollar having been oversold against the yen in recent sessions. 

 The dollar hit an intraday low of Y126.75 early in the Asian day without attracting much attention. But a bounce back above this level late in the session triggered a round of dollar buying that caught many market players off guard. The dollar quickly shot up to Y127.60 as players were forced to buy back the U.S. currency to cover their short positions. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at Y127.70, up from Y127.16 late Monday in New York. 

 The dollar weakened against other Asian currencies, but closed well off its intraday lows. 

 The South Korean won, Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Philippine peso all strengthened. The New Taiwan dollar and Indonesian rupiah were unchanged. 

 Investor sentiment continues to run against the dollar globally due to concerns about the strength of the economic recovery in the U.S. and questions over the outlook for U.S. corporate profits. 

 Central bankers in Asia don't appear overly concerned about the strength of their currencies against the dollar, said Jimmy Koh, head of Treasury Research at United Overseas Bank. 

 While the regional currencies are gaining on the dollar, on a trade-weighted basis most regional currencies remain fairly competitive against each other, he said. 

 "You may see some central banks trying to slow down the rate of appreciation of their currencies, but they're not in the market trying to put a cap on them," Koh said. 

 The Philippine peso advanced to a 13-month high against the dollar amid weak demand for the U.S. currency. 

 The dollar closed at PHP49.640 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP49.775 Monday, but off its intraday low of PHP49.440. It was the dollar's weakest finish since March 2001. 

 The Philippine central bank governor appeared to give his blessing to the move, acknowledging in a radio interview that analysts were predicting the dollar could fall as low as PHP48-PHP49 in the near term. 

 The Singapore dollar briefly touched a seven-month high against the U.S. dollar before falling back on concerns of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the yen's late slide. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8023, down from S$1.8047 late Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar fell through the key psychological S$1.8000 mark against the Singapore currency early in the session on its way to an intraday low of S$1.7988, its weakest performance since mid-October last year. 

 The won strengthened for the fourth straight session to yet another four-month high against the dollar. 

 The dollar finished at 1,279.5 won, down from Monday's close at KRW1,281.2. The dollar traded as low as KRW1,276.6 during the session. 

 Bank of America currency strategist Frank Gong said the dollar is likely due for some consolidation given its recent losses against the won. The won has gained 4% against the dollar since closing at a one-year low of KRW1,332.0 in mid-April. 

 The baht extended its recent gains against the dollar. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at 42.875 baht, down from THB42.950 late Monday in offshore trade. The baht wasn't traded onshore Monday because markets in Bangkok were closed for a holiday. 

 The dollar fell to a 14-month intraday low of THB42.81 in afternoon trading before recovering slightly in line with the U.S. currency's late rebound against the yen. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was unchanged against the U.S. dollar, snapping a string of 15 straight gains. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.656, unchanged from Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar was weaker for most of the session, but gained late in the session on the back of the weaker yen. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was unchanged as dollar bids from local companies offset dollar selling by foreign banks still bullish on the rupiah. 

 The dollar closed unchanged at 9,280 rupiah after trading in a tight range of between IDR9,275 and IDR9,290.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, But Off 7-Mo High On MAS Concerns
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar strengthened Tuesday, briefly touching a seven-month high against the U.S. dollar, before slipping back on concerns of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Around 0825 GMT (4:25 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8023, down from S$1.8047 late Monday. It traded between S$1.7988 and S$1.8028 intraday. 

 The U.S. currency opened around S$1.8005 against the local currency in Asia, hurt by persistent selling on U.S. dollar rallies in favor of its stronger regional counterparts, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar subsequently slumped below the key psychological S$1.8000 mark against the Singapore currency and proceeded to its intraday low of S$1.7988, its weakest since mid-October last year. 

 However, sellers became spooked when local banks bought U.S. dollars heavily, bringing it back up above S$1.8000, and sparking fears they may be acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary-policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners. 

 Although the possible MAS action couldn't be confirmed, market participants took on a more cautious note, and the U.S. dollar soon recouped part of its overnight losses, as local banks continued their purchases. 

 Looking ahead, the U.S. dollar is expected to trade in a tight range against the Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies ahead of the meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee, later Tuesday. 

 Support for the U.S. dollar is expected at S$1.7950, with resistance likely at S$1.8050. 

 Singapore government bond prices were mostly higher late Tuesday, as domestic interbank rates stayed weak, keeping the costs of borrowing low, and as investors remained confident the FOMC will keep U.S. interest rates steady, dealers said. 

 Local bonds opened higher, defying the overnight drop in U.S. Treasurys, though trading volumes were still relatively small, with some market participants preferring to wait on the sidelines until after the FOMC announces its decision late Tuesday, dealers added. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was down two basis points at 1.54%, while the yield on five-year bonds slipped one basis point to 2.91%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yield on seven-year bonds was two basis points lower at 3.53% while the yield on 10-year bonds was down one basis point at 3.87%. 

 The yield on 15-year bonds was flat at 4.37%.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; US Dlr Under Siege
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies extended their recent uptrend late Thursday, as the U.S. dollar remained under siege and many of the region's stock markets regained their footing, dealers said. 

 The dollar suffered another blow after U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill's remarks overnight heightened speculation that Washington was backing away from its commitment to a strong dollar policy. 

 After a sharp yen-and-half plunge overnight, the dollar fell for most of the Asian session as traders pondered the implications of O'Neill's failure to state clearly that the U.S. stands by a strong dollar, in his high-profile Congressional testimony Wednesday. 

 After briefly dipping below Y127 earlier in the day, the dollar clambered to Y127.26 at 0950 GMT, but was still below Y127.44 late Wednesday in New York and Y128.56 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 The near-term direction of Asian currencies would depend on whether the U.S. dollar would crack key levels against its other major counterparts, namely the euro's resistance at $0.9100 and the U.S. dollar's support of Y126.50 against the yen, said Thio Chin Loo, a senior regional currency analyst at BNP Paribas. 

 As most Asian currencies remained buoyed at multi-month highs, speculation of central bank intervention made their rounds in the Thai, Singapore and Philippine foreign exchange markets. 

 But it was only in Taiwan's currency market where dealers felt unequivocal about the central bank's presence. 

 The Philippine peso surged to its strongest level in almost a year, boosted in part by relief that antigovernment protests passed off peacefully Wednesday and the prospect of U.S. pension fund Calpers reversing a decision to pull investments out of the country, dealers said. 

 California Public Employees' Retirement System, or Calpers, pulled out of four Asian emerging markets in February due to stricter investment guidelines, but Manila lobbied successfully for reinclusion. 

 The Philippine central bank's denial that it had bought dollars to damp the peso's rally also emboldened participants to push the local currency higher, dealers said. There was talk in the market that the central bank had bought around $25 million at PHP50.50 to boost reserves earlier Thursday, but died down when the U.S. dollar continued its downward spiral, dealers in Manila said. 

 In fact, central bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco said it was possible for the dollar to extend its slide to PHP50 soon, although he didn't provide a timeframe. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.20 on the Philippine Dealing System - its lowest close since May 17, 2001 - down 0.7% from PHP50.54 Tuesday. 

 Worries that antigovernment demonstrations by supporters of ousted leader Joseph Estrada and leftist groups May 1 would be marred by violence kept support for the dollar well buttressed at PHP50.50 in recent trading days. 

 Despite fears that the region's central banks might curb the appreciation of their respective currencies, analysts said they are likely to tolerate some strength - provided the currencies are stable on a trade-weighted basis. 

 As the Seoul stock market climbed 2.1%, the South Korean won closed at a fresh four-month high of KRW1,288.0 against the dollar, compared with KRW1,294.0 Tuesday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar muscled through NT$34.700 resistance to close at a four-and-a-half month peak against its U.S. counterpart as it found additional support from U.S. dollar sales by exporters, dealers said. 

 U.S. dollar purchases by Taiwan's central bank - up to an estimated US$400 million - and a 3.3% plunge on the Taipei bourse failed to salvage the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.645, lower than NT$34.717 Tuesday. Dealings totaled US$698 million. 

 The Thai currency strengthened to 43.150 baht to the dollar, compared with THB43.225 late Tuesday. 

 There was market talk that the Thai central bank bought dollars via banks in Thailand when the U.S. currency traded at the day's low of around THB43.100. 

 "But we didn't really see anything," said a dealer at an Asian bank in Singapore, adding that there was little justification for the central bank to intervene since the baht was merely adjusting to the recent gains in the yen and the Singapore dollar. 

 "The baht should be at a comfortable level at the moment," the dealer said. 

 Thailand's business sentiment improved significantly in March, rising above the 50-point level for the first time in 14 months, indicating that the businessmen who were surveyed by the central bank expect future business conditions to improve. 

 The central bank's Business Sentiment Index - based on a survey of businessmen at medium-to-large firms - was at 53.5 points in March, up from 49.9 in February and 49.2 in January, it said in a monthly report posted on its Web site. 

 A reading below 50 points means that most respondents expect future business conditions to worsen. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.8094 against the U.S. currency, marginally stronger compared with S$1.8097 late Tuesday. The benchmark stock index closed 0.9% higher. 

 Financial markets in the Philippines, Taiwan, Singapore, Thailand and South Korea were closed Wednesday for Labor Day. 

 The Indonesian currency was steady at 9,340 rupiah to the dollar, compared with IDR9,335 late Wednesday.

authorities who are concerned about export competitiveness.



The recent net sale of local stocks by foreign equity



investors in most Asian markets, part of which could end up



chasing dollars, was also likely to offset any gains from the



usual month-end dollar sales by exporters.



Mohi-uddin said central banks of Singapore and Thailand

gains, while equity-related dollar outflows have already



started to weigh down the Korean won and the Thai baht.

dollar positions ahead of economic data for March and revised


central bank macro targets due later on Tuesday.

    A weak exports outlook is likely to strengthen fears of


central bank intervention that has kept the baht in a narrow



43.10-43.20 range in the past several sessions. The baht has



gained over two percent year-to-date.



PESO PERKY, RUPIAH QUIET

    The comment sent local players scrambling to cover their

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Stock Selloff Curbs Rise
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies hit fresh multi-month highs late Monday as the U.S. dollar remained on the defensive - particularly against the yen - in international foreign exchange markets. 

 However, the selloff in regional equity markets - weighed by losses on Wall Street - and fears of central bank intervention kept a rein on the strength of Asian currencies, preventing them from breaking key resistance levels, observers said. 

 "The yen would appreciate and outperform Asian currencies because the central banks want to maintain some measure of competitiveness," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Earlier in the day, the dollar slipped to as low as Y127.65, having shed three yen in just a week. Trading was thin Monday with Tokyo markets closed. 

 At 0900 GMT (5:00 a.m. EDT), the dollar had reclaimed some ground and was quoted at Y127.83, compared with Y127.80 in New York, and Y128.79 in Tokyo late Friday. 

 The yen's gains helped push the Singapore dollar to six-and-a-half month high, the South Korean won to a four-month peak, the New Taiwan dollar to a fresh four-month high and the Philippine peso to seven-month high. The Thai baht rode on the coattails of its regional cousins. 

Foreign exchange participants were increasingly nervous about the prospects of a collapse in the U.S. currency, although some analysts ruled out such a possibility. A further slide in the dollar against the yen could extend the recent rally in Asian currencies. 

 The U.S. dollar index, trading around 114.93, was approaching key long-term trendlines, a break of which could end the currency's long period of strength. 

 "It is actually a very fine call now," said Mohi-uddin at UBS Warburg. 

 "The dollar is at a very critical juncture at the moment, but I don't think the dollar will collapse just yet," he said. "The corporate bond market is still attracting inflows, and European fundamentals are lagging those of the U.S." 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency opened at S$1.8020, its weakest level since Oct. 10 last year, after having been sold off in New York trade Friday. 

 U.S. dollar purchases by Singapore and U.S. banks helped the currency regain its footing, dealers said. 

 The U.S. currency's rebound also led some in the market to surmise that the Monetary Authority of Singapore could have intervened to curb the local currency's strength, although some observers dismissed such speculation, dealers said. 

 "Though we think the Singapore dollar is at the stronger end of the (policy) band, we are skeptical that it is strong enough to attract the attention of the authorities," Bank of America said in a report. The MAS guides the Singapore dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and key competitors. 

 Late in the day, the Singapore dollar was stronger at S$1.8067, compared with S$1.8097 against its U.S. counterpart late Friday. 

 Month-end dollar sales by exporters provided an additional fillip for the South Korean won, dealers said. 

 The won finished at KRW1,293.6 against the dollar, stronger than Friday's close of KRW1,297.6. The won hit an intraday high of KRW1,289.0. 

 Short-covering in U.S. dollar positions emerged late in the day after the local currency failed to sustain its break below KRW1,290, dealers said. 

 Net sales of some KRW208.6 billion worth of South Korean shares by foreign investors somewhat restrained the won's rise, although it failed to reverse its trend. 

 Helped in part by exporters' dollar-sales, the New Taiwan dollar finished at NT$34.730 against the U.S. currency, stronger compared with NT$34.769 Friday. 

 Intermittent U.S.-dollar purchases by Taiwan's central bank and foreigner equity sales of a net NT$5.22 billion worth of shares on the Taiwan Stock Exchange Monday helped put a lid on the local currency's gains, dealers said. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the peso closed at PHP50.630 to the dollar, compared with PHP50.823 Friday. 

 "The dollar managed to break below its long-standing support at PHP50.80 this morning on expectations of more inflows from overseas remittances, as well as positive sentiment following reports of U.S. pension fund Calpers is likely to review its decision to pull out of the Manila stock market," Bank of America said in a report. 

 Philippine Finance Secretary Jose Isidro Camacho said Friday that U.S. pension fund Calpers was prepared to review its decision to divest its equity holdings in the country. The California Public Employees' Retirement System, or Calpers, decided in February to pull out of four Asian emerging markets due to stricter investment guidelines. 

 The Thai currency was firmer at THB43.205 to the dollar, compared with THB43.260 late Friday. 

 Left out in the cold, the Indonesian rupiah retreated after having priced in news that the International Monetary Fund had agreed Friday to unlock an additional $347 million in loans to the country. 

 The fund said the Indonesian government has broadly fulfilled the conditions of a $4.6 billion IMF loan aimed at rebuilding the economy. 

 The Indonesian currency was quoted at IDR9,325 to the dollar, compared with IDR9,300 late Friday.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Singapore Dollar Soars
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies continued to rally Friday as global sentiment toward the dollar was damped by concerns over the U.S. economic recovery and disappointing corporate earnings. 

 The yen set the tone for the region, trading below Y129 per dollar for the second day in a row. 

 The Singapore dollar was among the stronger regional currencies in Asia, breaking through key resistance levels on its way to a six-month high. 

 The Singapore dollar powered its way through the psychologically important threshold of S$1.8100 per U.S. dollar on its way to an intraday low of S$1.8070. It was the U.S. dollar's poorest showing since last October. 

 The U.S. dollar recovered somewhat to finish Asian trading at S$1.8097, down from S$1.8120 late Thursday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah also gained on the dollar. The South Korean won was unchanged and the Thai baht edged lower. 

 Most of the currencies remained near multi-month highs against the dollar reached earlier in the week following a round of weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data. 

 The disappointing U.S. data, along with continuing negative corporate news and concerns about the sustainability of the enormous U.S. current account deficit, are likely to keep pressure on the dollar in the near term, analysts say. 

 "This shift in sentiment is set to continue for some time, making us cautious on the dollar," UBS Warburg currency strategist Mansoor Mohi-uddin said in a research report. 

 However, the dollar weakness isn't the "start of a collapse" and the UBS Warburg's report predicts the U.S. currency will continue its upward trend over the longer term. 

 The U.S. current account deficit, which covers trade in goods and services as well as investment earnings, has become a major concern for the dollar. The U.S. must attract an estimated $1 billion a day from abroad to finance the shortfall, which stands at about 4% of gross domestic product. It is those capital inflows that have helped underpin the dollar. 

 The fear is that if foreigners lose interest in U.S. assets, and the inflows dry up, the dollar will undergo a rapid and sizable downward correction. 

 A recent study by the Federal Reserve of 25 episodes of large adjustments in the current account deficit of developed countries showed that the shortfalls usually began to reverse once they exceeded 5% of GDP. The adjustments were typically accompanied by a 10% to 25% fall in the exchange rate. 

 An increasingly rosy outlook for the Singapore economy this year compared with more modest expectations for the U.S. are working in the local currency's favor, dealers say. 

 However, it will be difficult for the Singapore dollar to appreciate significantly going forward, analyst say. Recent moves in the Singapore dollar have probably resulted in its shift to the stronger half of a trading band used by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to guide the currency. 

 Any further movement toward the band's limit could prompt the MAS to intervene in the market to cap the Singapore dollar's strength, analysts said. 

 There was some speculation in the market Friday that the MAS may have intervened, but many analysts dismissed this. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed at a four-month high as the yen's rise inspired U.S. dollar selling by Taiwanese exporters. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.769, compared with NT$34.783 Thursday. 

 Offshore and local banks' short-covering of U.S. dollar positions and central bank intervention combined to lift the U.S. currency from its intraday low of NT$34.741. 

 In Seoul, a mix of offsetting factors left the won unchanged from its four-month high a day earlier. The dollar closed at KRW1,297.6. 

 Foreigners' net sales of KRW279 billion in local shares convinced some foreign exchange players to build long-dollar positions. But the rising yen prompted others to shed the U.S. currency. 

 In addition, exporters sold dollars as part of their regular month-end book balancing. 

 With no fresh leads to drive peso trading, the Philippine currency tracked the yen and other regionals higher. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.823 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP50.835 Thursday. 

 The rupiah strengthened modestly as sentiment continues to improve toward Indonesia's debt restructuring efforts. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at IDR9,300, down from IDR9,360 a day earlier. 

 Moody's Investor Services raised Indonesia's sovereign outlook to positive from stable this week due to the country's successful $5.4 billion debt rescheduling with the Paris Club of creditors earlier this month. 

 Corporate demand and dollar short-covering kept the U.S. currency firm against the baht. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at THB43.260, up from THB43.210 late Thursday.

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar rose to a six-month high against the U.S. dollar Thursday, as local and foreign banks sold the U.S. currency in line with its broader decline against Asian units, dealers said. 

 Around 0907 GMT (5:07 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8126, down from S$1.8190 late Wednesday, but off its intraday low of S$1.8108 - its lowest level since mid-October. Trading volume was moderate to heavy. 

 The U.S. dollar opened around S$1.8160 in Asia and fell through the day on selling led by local banks. Market participants unwound long U.S.-dollar positions in line with the currency's decline against the yen and other Asian units. 

 The U.S. dollar fell below Y129 to an intraday low of Y128.77. 

 In late afternoon trading, U.S.-dollar selling by U.S. banks and investment houses pushed the currency below an important 200-day moving average support at S$1.8121 to hit an intraday low of S$1.8108. 

 However, the U.S. dollar quickly bounced off its low as participants feared the currency had been oversold and cautiously bought it back to ward off possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to prevent the currency from sliding too sharply. 

 Technical analysis shows the U.S. dollar's intraday fall to below the key support at a 200-day moving average is very bearish, as it seems to signal an end to the medium-term sideways consolidation that has prevailed since November. 

 This is the first time since October that the U.S. dollar has fallen below its 200-day moving average against the Singapore dollar. 

 Analysts say the U.S. dollar is now appears to be initially targeting a decline to S$1.8070, but a drop below that level is quite possible if it continues to slide against the yen. 

 The U.S. dollar's upside is expected to be capped at S$1.8170, dealers said. 

 Singapore government bonds extended their recent rally Thursday, tracking gains in U.S. Treasurys overnight and on expectations inflation and interest rates in Singapore will remain low this year as the economy recovers gradually and the Federal Reserve keeps U.S. rates on hold at least until August. 

 Dealers said shorter-dated bonds were also boosted by an expected supply shortfall as S$3.28 billion of one- and five-year paper maturing May 14 and May 15 will be replaced only by S$2.20 billion worth of one-year Treasury bills to be issued next week.

title: Emerging  FX  - Edging higher, U.S. dollar defensive.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were 

 firmer across the broad on Thursday after the U.S. dollar was 

 put on the defensive by bleak economic data and the Federal 

 Reserve's "beige book", which pointed to muted recovery. 

     But after trading around their multi-week highs for a 

 while, most currencies found themselves a bit top heavy, with 

 bargain hunters gradually snatching back dollars. 

     "The market is focused on the U.S. growth story, which 

 doesn't look very good at the moment," said Thio Chin Loo, 

currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. 

     "Meanwhile other countries such as the Euroland have come 

 up with some good numbers. That gives some thoughts to the 

 market that perhaps they should diversify from the U.S. dollar 

 to other currencies," said Thio. 


    The Sing dollar        was among star performers, rising by



a quarter of a percent as those economic concerns prompted



traders to liquidate long dollar positions.



    But dollar buying from some U.S. names and U.S. dollar



demand linked to hedging activities by local firms capped the



Sing dollar's gain at 1.8125 -- its five-month high.



    The Thai baht        was higher, briefly breaking above its



week high of 43.20 only to retrace on fears of cental bank


intervention and concerns over recent selling of local stocks



by foreign investors.



    It drew support from news that the government had raised



its economic growth forecast for 2002 to 3.6 percent from 3.4



percent seen in March, although some economists see the number



as too optimistic.



    U.S. ECONOMY STUTTERS



    The dollar was clouded by durable goods and new home sales



data which showed the U.S. economy has lost steam after growing



at a speedy pace earlier this year.



    Buying orders for costly manufactured goods dropped 0.6



percent in March while new homes sales fell 3.1 percent in the



same month, selling at an annual rate of 878,000, below the



forecast 882,000 pace.



    But dealers said what upset the market most was the Fed's



beige book which is its anecdotal summary of economic



conditions across the country.



    The report said the labor market was still "slack" and



manufacturers' plans to invest in new equipment were "limited."



    WON, PESO RISE



    The won, which trailed the yen closely, made good gains. It



was trading around 1,299 to the dollar at 0300 GMT compared



with 1310.0 at the open and 1,307.0 at Wednesday's close.



    Dealers in Singapore said barring central bank

intervention, the won might close above 1,300 for the first



time since December 19.



    The Philippine peso        lurched higher on the regionals'



coat tail as interbank players bought the local currency to



cover short positions.



    "But we do expect some corporate players to buy the dollar



at around 50.80," said a local dealer.



    At 0300 GMT, the peso was trading around 50.82 with $54



million transacted so far in the onshore market. It closed at



50.895 on Wednesday.


Currency strategists expect appreciation in the regional


currencies to slow from here given recent foreign selling in



local stocks, which prompted concerns over potential outflows.



    Foreign investors sold a net 299.38 million baht ($6.92



million) worth of Thai shares and 60.50 billion won ($46.67) in



Korean shares on Wednesday.



    "Given what is happening in the U.S. equity market, I think



the stock markets around the region will find their tops pretty



soon. If the stocks take a breather, the dollar/Asians should



find a floor - meaning Asian currencies will come off," said



BNP's Thio.
