title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;  Intervention  Jitters Grow
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Tuesday, as the inexorable rise of several currencies to multi-month highs in recent sessions heightened jitters about central bank intervention, dealers said. 

 Still, except for Taiwan's central bank - which intervenes regularly to curb any excessive currency volatility - there wasn't any solid evidence that the other monetary authorities in Asia had bought U.S. dollars to check the appreciation of their respective currencies. 

 DBS Bank said in a research note that the region's central banks "appeared to have relaxed their rigid currency stance" due to growing confidence over exports, easing worries about a tottering yen and the cost-push pressures on inflation as a result of higher oil prices. 

 "Overall, we believe that central banks want to keep domestic interest rates low for as long as possible to put the recovery on a sound footing," said DBS Bank's market strategist, Philip Wee, 

 "Growing official talk of improving exports and capital inflows suggest that policymakers may not mind modest currency appreciation, which would not only help curb imported inflation but also be useful in reflecting the recent improvement in investor confidence," he added. 

 But Wee and other analysts warned that the yen remains the wild card - even though the Japanese currency is expected to extend its recent uptrend in the near term. 

 "The market trend is fairly bullish for Asian currencies, but there's always the yen risk," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 For now, however, Mohi-uddin expects the yen to strengthen further toward Y128.50 against the dollar, and in turn continue to bolster the rest of the region's currencies. 

 At 0905 GMT (5:05 a.m. EDT), the dollar was quoted at Y129.95, marginally higher than Y129.89 late Monday in New York, but lower than Y130.08 late Monday in Tokyo. 

 The U.S. currency's bounce off its morning low of Y129.76 in Asia Tuesday helped lift the U.S. dollar off its intraday lows against the currencies of Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. 

 "It shows that the market is a bit short of U.S. dollars against Asian currencies and that the yen is still important," said Mohi-uddin at UBS Warburg. 

 The Singapore dollar lost ground after hitting a fresh six-week high of around S$1.8120 in early trade on aggressive U.S. dollar sales by U.S. banks and Hong Kong-based funds. 

 A large Singapore bank had bought U.S. dollars at the currency's intraday lows, giving some semblance of intervention by the local monetary authority, although some dealers said this was unlikely. 

 Technically, observers said it made sense to pick up the U.S. currency around that level, with the 200-day moving average - which acts as critical support - hovering around S$1.8122 on the charts. 

 Late in the day, the U.S. dollar was higher at S$1.8191, compared with S$1.8177 late Monday. 

 Fears of intervention by the Bank of Korea also contributed to the won's slight pullback from its intraday high, dealers said. 

 Still, the won ended stronger at a three-month peak of KRW1,306.3 against the dollar, compared with KRW1,308.8 Monday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed at a four-month high, even after relinquishing the bulk of its earlier gains after the central bankintervened - buying an estimated US$200 million in the market - and banks covered their short positions in the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 U.S. dollar sales by exporters and foreign equity fund inflows helped shore up the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed at NT$34.810 against the U.S. currency, stronger compared with NT$34.845 Monday. The New Taiwan dollar hit an intraday high of NT$34.760. 

 Trading volume for the session totaled US$695 million, nearly half of Monday's US$1.201 billion, as the central bank's aggressive intervention discouraged foreign exchange participants. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 50.960 pesos, little changed from PHP50.970 Monday. 

 Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Tuesday the bank's closely watched overnight rates may have already bottomed, but added that monetary authorities can hold the rates steady until November. 

 Buenaventura is trying to dispel market speculation that the central bank may soon tighten monetary policy due to rising inflationary pressure. Inflation in March rose to 3.6% on year after falling to a two-year low of 3.4% in February. 

 The Indonesian currency was weaker at 9,435 rupiah to the dollar, compared with IDR9,255 late Monday, on short-covering in the U.S. currency and corporate demand for dollars, dealers said. 

 The rupiah was indifferent to Standard & Poor's as-expected downgrade of Indonesia's sovereign ratings to "selective default," as it was a technical move following the government's recent debt rescheduling with the Paris Club of official creditors. 

 The Thai currency was slightly weaker at 43.360 baht to the dollar, compared with THB43.260 late Monday. 

 The baht shrugged off the central bank's decision to leave its key 14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 2% at its regular monetary policy meeting Monday.

title: Emerging  FX  -  Currencies  dither on  intervention  fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 23 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies took 

 a step back from multi-week gains late Tuesday as dollar-buying 

intervention fears prompted players to cover their short dollar 

 positions. 


    Analysts said despite a firmer yen       , holding strong



above 130 level, a slight trade-weighted appreciation of the



dollar was seen as raising chances of intervention aimed at



capping exchange rate gains.



    The dollar trade-weighted index        rose to a high of



116.82, up from late Monday's 116.49. The United States is the



biggest export market for most Asian economies.



    "Some of these regionals have come quite far, quite quickly



and now there is a bit of a sense of some restraint creeping



in," said David Simmonds, Salomon Smith Barney's strategist in



Singapore.



    Simmonds said the latest economic data indicated, at best,



a gradual recovery in most regional economies and the U.S., but



there is lingering suspicion on the yen's recent run up.



    "So from this stage onwards both policy makers and markets



are likely to look for some restraint...though there might



still be some more room for gains in some of the currencies,"



he said.



    WEAK BIAS



    The Taiwan central bank was already spotted in the market,



as usual, capping Taiwan dollar's gains after it got



near four-month highs at around 34.76 per dollar, backed by



continuing equity-related dollar inflows.



    The Thai Baht        was slightly weaker on dollar-buying


intervention fears exacerbated after the central bank kept its



14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 2.0 percent, signalling it



favours a relatively weaker baht to boost growth and exports



over loose monetary conditions.



    The baht eased to around 43.30 per dollar from late Monday



's 43.25.



    SINGAPORE RUMOURS



    In Singapore, dollar offers from two local banks sparked



rumours they were acting on behalf of the central bank after



the Singapore dollar strengthened to five and a half



month highs around 1.8125.



However most dealers said they found no evidence supporting



the rumours and argued intervention risks were low unless the



Sing dollar challenges 1.8100 level.



Technical analysts said the market would need fresh impetus



to take out a strong 200-day moving average dollar/Sing support



at around 1.8123. But a convincing breach of that level could



send the Sing dollar to levels beyond 1.8100, they added.



MORE PATIENT



Analysts said the Bank of Korea was expected to be more



patient as a stronger won -2 may induce some monetary



tightening, need to keep a lid on inflationary growth.



The won touched a high of 1,303.9, a level not seen since



January 7, as offshore players and exporters offloaded dollars.



However, concerns over equity-related dollar outflows pulled it



back to late Monday's levels around 1,306.



DIFFERENT REASONS FOR RUPIAH



For different reasons, the Indonesian rupiah also



eased beyond the 9,300 per dollar level after hitting fresh



seven month highs around 9,240 early on.



Dealers in Jakarta said a rupiah liquidity squeeze due to a



corporate tax payment deadline forced players to cover their



short dollar positions.



However, the widely-expected sovereign credit rating



downgrade to "selective default" by Standard & Poor's had



little impact on the rupiah.



Dealers said S&P had been telegraphing the move for weeks,



linking it to a recent $5.4 billion foreign debt rescheduling



deal with the Paris Club of creditor nations under which some



private loans would also be affected.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; NT$ Hits 4-Month High
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Several Asian currencies posted near-term highs Monday as prospects for economic recovery in the region continued to damp the dollar's popularity. 

 The New Taiwan dollar and Indonesian rupiah recorded their best performances so far this year. The South Korean won, Singapore dollar and Thai baht also strengthened, but the Philippine peso tumbled following a bomb explosion that killed 14 people Sunday in the southern part of the country. 

 The Taiwan central bank tried to keep a lid on the New Taiwan dollar's rise by intervening in the foreign exchange market, but the local currency still managed to power its way to a four-month closing high against its U.S. counterpart. 

 Foreign inflows to the local stock market, which surged to NT$35 billion last week, have been helping fuel demand for the New Taiwan dollar. 

 Although the normally interventionist central bank has eased its activity in the market in recent days, it jumped in and bought U.S. dollars when the currency fell through several key support levels on its way to an intraday low of NT$34.757. 

 The central bank bought an estimated US$600 million to US$700 million, dealers said. 

 The intervention helped the U.S. dollar recover some of its losses to close at NT$34.845, down from $34.898 Friday. It was the New Taiwan dollar's best finish since Dec. 20 when it closed at NT$34.756. 

 For most of this year the central bank has managed the New Taiwan dollar in a fairly tight trading range in an effort to keep the country's exports competitive with the likes of Korea and Singapore, said James Malcolm, foreign exchange strategist at JP Morgan. The pair has traded roughly between NT$35.10 and NT$34.90. 

 But with signs of economic recovery beginning to lift other currencies in the region, Taiwan's central bank is apparently more willing to let the local currency strengthen against the dollar, he said. 

 "Going forward we expect authorities to become more comfortable with letting the currency go higher," he said. 

 JP Morgan is forecasting the U.S. dollar to weaken to NT$34.50 by the end of June and NT$33.50 by the end of the year, Malcolm said. 


   The rupiah powered to its best finish since last September,
continuing a rally that began last month with the government's
successful sale of its 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia.



The dollar closed at 9,255 rupiah, down from IDR9,340 Friday.



With political stability and economic reforms helping reduce the risk
sometimes associated with Indonesia, investors are becoming more
attracted by the high yields Indonesian assets have to offer, JP
Morgan's Malcolm said.



He said he expects the rupiah, which has already appreciated by 10% to
12% so far this year, to strengthen to about IDR8,500 per dollar by the
end of the year.



The won ended at a three-month high, but came off its intraday peak on
late afternoon dollar demand.



The dollar finished at 1,308.8 won, down from Friday's close of
KRW1,312.3. It was the dollar's weakest finish since closing at
KRW1,302.0 Jan. 7.



Demand for the dollar from corporations and offshore players pulled
the U.S. currency off its morning low, sparking short covering at
KRW1,307, said dealers.



The Singapore dollar rose to a six-week high, benefiting from the U.S.
dollar selling going on elsewhere in the region.



Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8177,
down from S$1.8221 late Friday.



Heavy selling briefly pushed the U.S. dollar to a six-week low of
S$1.8160 in mid-afternoon trading, but it bounced off the low amid fears
the local monetary authority might intervene do prevent the Singapore
dollar from strengthening too rapidly, dealers said.



The peso was unable to overcome negative sentiment associated with a
series of bomb explosions in the south.



The dollar closed at 50.970 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up
from PHP50.890 Friday.



A series of bombings Sunday in General Santos, one of the largest
cities in the southern Philippines, killed at least 14 people and
injured around 45 others.



Another explosion occurred in General Santos early Monday, prompting
President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo to order a state of emergency in the
city.



The Thai baht tracked other Asian currencies higher.



Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 43.260 baht, down from THB43.310
late Friday.

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- After having been trapped in watertight ranges for months, the U.S. currency's fragility against the yen and foreign equity inflows finally set the New Taiwan dollar free, propelling it to a four-month closing high Friday, dealers said. 

 Other Asian currencies, too, retained their recent strength, as the U.S. dollar remained on the defensive in international foreign exchange markets. 

 But their gains were somewhat restrained by the yen's inability to make much more headway, as caution reigned ahead of this weekend's Washington meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the Group of Seven industrialized nations. 

Foreign exchange traders are seeking clues from finance ministers on whether they will tolerate a weaker yen - as part of Japan's efforts to revive its ailing economy, participants said. 

 "We have no idea where the general dollar is going, especially against the yen," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 At 0930 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y130.29, above Y129.86 in New York, but below Y130.61 in Tokyo late Thursday. 

 The South Korean won and the Singapore dollar - which had been leading the region's advance in the past few sessions - turned instead to the New Taiwan dollar for direction Friday. 

 Foreign banks sold the U.S. currency against the New Taiwan dollar on the offshore non-deliverable forward market, amid persistent foreign equity inflows into Taipei and following the U.S. dollar's temporary slide below Y130. 

 "The morning's moves were very speculative," said a dealer in Singapore. 

 The New Taiwan dollar muscled through key resistance at NT$34.900 against the U.S. currency. 

 The U.S. currency's closure below that level signals Taiwan central bank's willingness to allow the local currency to appreciate further - albeit in a controlled fashion - if the yen trends higher and portfolio inflows persist, observers said. 

 Still, the central bank did aggressively intervene to check on any excessive strength in New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 In the last 15 minutes of trade, US$372 million changed hands, pulling the New Taiwan dollar off the NT$34.858 level against the U.S. dollar, dealers in Taipei noted. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed at NT$34.898 against its U.S. counterpart, stronger than NT$34.940 Thursday. The New Taiwan dollar touched an intraday high of NT$34.838. 

 Trading volume more than doubled to US$1.41 billion - the highest daily volume since early August - from US$632 million Thursday. 

 Charts suggest that the U.S. dollar may be entering a weaker medium-term range of NT$34.70-NT$34.90. 

 Judging by bearish daily oscillators, the U.S. currency could test immediate support at NT$34.79 - which marks a 50% retracement of its move up in December - with the permission of the central bank, that is. 

 Bank of America believes Taiwan's central bank will continue to maintain its vigil on the local currency - even as it allows it to appreciate slightly. 

 "The Taiwanese authority is not very sure about this recovery," said Bank of America's Hong Kong-based analyst, Steven Cheung. "It wants to wait for a solid recovery, which will probably take place in the second half, before allowing the currency to appreciate dramatically." 

 Foreign institutional investors bought a net NT$2.14 billion of shares on the Taiwan Stock Exchange Friday, the exchange said. For the month to date, foreign institutional investors have bought a net NT$38.03 billion of shares. 

 The South Korean currency found support from foreign equity inflows and the yen to close at a three-month high, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 1,312.2 won, down from KRW1,313.2 Thursday. 

 Foreign investors were net buyers of KRW130.9 billion of South Korean shares, as they extended their buying spree since Tuesday. 

 Tracking the yen and the New Taiwan dollar, the Singapore dollar climbed to a five-week high of S$1.8188 against its U.S. counterpart, before relinquishing part of its gains, dealers said. 

 At 1000 GMT (6:00 a.m. EDT), the Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.8226, stronger than S$1.8235 late Thursday. 

 Following the Singapore dollar's inexhorable rise of late, fears of intervention by the local monetary authority have crept in, dealers said. 

 "There's a feeling that if the U.S. dollar falls further to S$1.8150, it could attract the attention of the authority because the slide has been sharp recently," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 50.890 pesos, down from PHP50.940 Thursday. 

 The Thai currency was at 43.329 baht to the dollar, slightly firmer compared with THB43.310 late Thursday.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Hits 5-Wk High As Regionals Rise
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar hit a five-week high against the U.S. dollar Friday before partially surrendering its intraday gains as market participants squared positions ahead of a meeting of finance ministers and central bank chiefs of the group of seven industrialized nations over the weekend. 

 Around 0835 GMT (4:35 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8221, down from S$1.8250 late Thursday. It traded between S$1.8188 and S$1.8240 intraday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened slightly lower against its Singapore counterpart, but fell steadily until mid-afternoon on persistent selling by U.S. investment houses and European banks in line with its broader weakness against the yen and other Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar's decline below Y130 pushed it below the key level of S$1.8220, which triggered stop-loss selling of the U.S. currency against the Singapore dollar. Another set of stop-losses were triggered when the U.S. dollar fell below S$1.8200, pushing it to its intraday low of S$1.8188, its lowest level since mid-March, dealers said. 

 However, the U.S. dollar bounced back above S$1.8200 as its sharp decline prompted market participants to cover their short positions amid fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to stem the U.S. currency's sharp slide. 

 Squaring of U.S. dollar positions against Asian currencies ahead of the meeting of finance ministers and central bank chiefs of the group of seven industrialized nations over the weekend also helped the dollar regain some lost ground against the yen, Singapore dollar and other Asian units. 

 Dealers said they expect the U.S. dollar's upside to be capped by profit-taking on moves toward S$1.8250, while MAS intervention fears and potential corporate buying will likely support it initially at S$1.8180 and then at S$1.8150. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds rose in a day of active trading as market participants bought bonds on expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve may put off rate hikes until August, and domestic rates in Singapore would remain weak though the year. 

 Participants also bought bonds ahead of two large issues maturing next month. Dealers said S$2.50 billion worth of one-year treasury bills mature May 14, followed by S$750 million worth of five-year bonds May 15. 

 The one-year bills likely will be replaced by a new one-year issue scheduled for May 2, dealers said. 

 However, participants were covering for an expected shortfall arising from the maturity of the five-year bonds. The next bond issue won't take place until July 1, when the government issues new 10-year paper. 

 The yield on two-year bonds was down four basis points at 1.63%, while the yield on five-year bonds slipped three basis points to 3.05%.

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  forex  ride yen's coattails higher.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose 

 early on Wednesday, riding on the yen's coattails. 

     Concerns about the Middle East, where the Israeli army 

 reported its highest number of casualties so far in its 

 conflict with the Palestinians, hounded the dollar. Investors 

 ran for the safe cover of other major currencies because of 

 worries that U.S. involvement in the Middle East and rising oil 

 prices could hamper the country's economy. 

 But the gains in regional currencies were modest because of 

 local developments and most of Asia's susceptibility to any 

 rises in oil prices, not only from the Palestinian-Israeli 

 conflict but also from the possibility that the United States 

 may strike at Iraq in the next stage of its war on terror. 

 "East Asia ex-Japan is particularly sensitive to oil price 

 fluctuation. The region imported six million barrels per day in 

 2000. Each dollar increase in oil price would amount to 0.1% of 

 GDP in extra cost," said Andy Xie, chief economist at Morgan 

 Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong, in a research note. 

 Malaysia and Indonesia are Asia's only net oil exporters. 

 On the local front, advance figures for Singapore's first 

 quarter gross domestic product showed the economy shrank more 

 than expected by 2.6 percent on the year. But analysts said the 

 city-state's recovery was still on track. 

     Taiwan will issue its March exports and trade balance data 

 at 0800 GMT. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won opened slightly lower before creeping up on the



back of the yen's rebound. It kicked off a trading session at



1,330.60 compared with the Tuesday's closing of 1,329.60, but



later rose to 1,328.60.



The currency was top heavy due to recent foreign selling of



local stocks which sparked concern of outflows. In April, net



foreign equity outflows from Korea was recorded at $1.9 million



as of April 3.



Concerns over the lingering Middle East conflict and its



potential impact on oil prices also weighed on the won because



Korea is a major net oil importer.



Although the yen/won cross has risen to around



10 from around 9.8 last week, some strategists continue to



suggest that clients stick to short yen/won positions as the



pair is likely to fall to around 9.0-9.5 by mid-year.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar is trading higher, drawing support from



gains in the yen which the currency closely trails, and hopes



for more inflows into the equity market.



    The local currency opened at 34.952 from 34.982 at the



close in the previous session.



    According to JP Morgan, net equity inflows into Taiwan as



of April 3 were US$1.5 million. The inflows in the first



quarter were recorded at US$2.02 billion.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar lost some ground after first quarter



gross domestic product data failed to impress the market.



    Local banks and interbank players bought U.S. dollars at



around 1.8350 pushing up the Sing dollar to 1.8370, but dealers



expected the currency to remain rangebound.



    First quarter Singapore GDP figures fell towards the bottom



end of forecasts validating long dollar positions, dealers



said.



    Advance figures were down 2.6 percent on year. The market



had expected a contraction of between 1.8-2.5 percent. The



economy shrank 6.6 percent in the fourth quarter last year.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht edged higher with gains in the yen and other



regionals giving the market confidence that the central bank


would not intervene to cap its rise.



    Moreover, dealers in Singapore said foreign names were



still spotted selling dollars as the baht strengthened beyond



the 43.50 per dollar level.



    The baht had recently seen upside pressure on equity and



investment related inflows with sentiment buoyed by hopes of



economic recovery.



    But with exports still struggling the central bank has



repeatedly hinted that it would like to keep the baht at



relatively weaker levels.



    PHILIPPINES PESO



    The peso poked above the 51 level aided by thin demand for



dollar, a lack of fresh leads and a firmer regional bias.



    Dealers in Manila said dollar bids by local corporates were



expected to be lined up around 50.80-50.90 level while offers



were expected around 51.10.



    They said with no strong enough fresh factors the peso may



continue to stay within a tight range around the 51 per U.S.



dollar level for the day.

    The rupiah lost its footing against the U.S. dollar, and



was clinging to the 9,600 level.



    After several sessions of steady gains, the rupiah ran into

    Still, charts showed the dollar/rupiah consolidating around

    Indeed, dealers in Jakarta said many players were looking



to sell the dollar on rally with sentiment towards the rupiah



still upbeat ahead of key Paris Club talks on Thursday and

Jakarta is seeking to reschedule $5.5 billion in debt due

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Rupiah Hovers Near 6-Mo High
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were stronger Monday with the rupiah continuing to hover near a six-month high as investors bet Indonesia's creditors will agree to lenient terms this week for the country's debt rescheduling. 

 The Singapore dollar, South Korean won and New Taiwan tracked a stronger yen, while financial markets in Thailand and the Philippines were closed for public holidays. 

 The rupiah strengthened to near a key level of IDR9,500 per dollar early in the session amid optimism that the government will be given some breathing room on debt repayment and build on recent successes in its privatization plans. 

 Late in Asian trading the dollar was quoted at IDR9,525 down from IDR9,560 at Friday's close. It was the rupiah's best performance since last September. 

 An agreement by the Paris Club group of creditor nations to roll over an estimated $5.5 billion in Indonesian debt maturing between now and 2003 would also clear the way for the International Monetary Fund to press ahead with its Indonesian aid package. The creditors are slated to meet Thursday and Friday in the French capital. 

 For the first time, creditors are likely to allow Indonesia to delay repayment of interest on its debt, as well as principal. In two previous Paris Club reschedulings, creditors only agreed to push back principal payment deadlines. 

 "The debt rescheduling is key for Indonesia's projected 2.5% (of GDP) deficit target compared to 3.7% last year," Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said in a research report. 

 Dealers said the rupiah garnered additional support from comments by visiting U.S. Trade Representative Robert Zoellick over the weekend expressing his support for President Megawati Sukarnoputri's efforts to reform the economy and help in the global fight against terrorism. 

 The won benefited from the yen's rise, despite heavy demand for dollars by foreigners who recently sold shares in the South Korean stock market. 

 The dollar ended at 1,328.2 won, down from Thursday's close of KRW1,330.5. Markets in Seoul were closed Friday for a public holiday. 

 The yen rose against the dollar Monday as uncertainty about how events in the Middle East would unfold prompted some players to sell the U.S. currency. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was at Y131.27, below Y131.65 in New York late Friday. 

 Foreigners snapped up dollars against the won Monday after being net sellers of local shares for four straight sessions. On Monday, they unloaded KRW263.3 billion in shares, pulling down the main stock index by 1.9% to 900.69. 

 The New Taiwan dollar strengthened against the U.S. dollar to its best finish in more than three weeks. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.978, down from NT$34.999 Thursday. Dealings were valued at US$534 million, down from US$629 million Thursday. The market was closed for a public holiday Friday. 

 The local dollar's rise was slowed by the Taiwan central bank, which bought more than US$200 million in the session, mostly in the final minutes of trading. The central bank routinely intervenes to prevent excessive volatility in the New Taiwan dollar. 

 The Singapore dollar's rise was tempered by concerns that the central bank might be reluctant to allow it to appreciate to sharply, dealers said. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8349, down from S$1.8358 late Friday. 

 News that Dutch electronics giant Philips Electronics will move its regional headquarters from Singapore to Hong Kong, caused worries over Singapore's competitiveness to resurface. That, in turn, prompted concerns among market players that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to keep the local dollar competitive against its regional peers.

title: Emerging  FX -Stumble on weak yen, U.S.-China woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies buckled under a heap of negative factors, ranging from a weaker yen, U.S.-China tensions over a U.S. spy plane, and increased risk aversion towards the region as the global economy cooled on Wednesday. 

 Analysts said the dollar remained a preferred currency despite sustained losses in U.S. equities, a sharp decline in U.S. interest rates, and easing oil prices. 

 "Longer-term structural optimism for the U.S. economy triumphs for now over shorter-term cyclical pessimism with respect to the value of dollar," said a Salomon Smith Barney report. 

 It suggested that investors continue to stay long of dollars against the regional currencies. 

 The yen retained its bearish tone after a much-hyped package of emergency measures for Japan's ailing economy was delayed. Dealers said the dollar might consolidate briefly around this level before moving higher toward 127 yen. 

 The standoff between Washington and Beijing over a U.S. spy plane and its crew also kept the market nervous. 

 China has adopted a hardline, blaming the U.S. for Sunday's mid-air collision between the spy plane and a Chinese fighter over the South China Sea, demanding an apology and holding on to the 24 crew. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar trailed off to lows of 1.8158 in quiet afternoon trade, with sporadic U.S. dollar bids countered by unwinding of long positions. 

 There was renewed talk of Singapore's Changi airport looking to buy Sydney Airport after the Australian government said last week it would complete the sale in the second half of 2001. The Sydney Airports Corp has said its book value is A$3.25 billion. Dealers said prospects of further capital outflows related to more M&A activities were handicapping the Sing dollar. 

 A disappointing 1.2 point dip in Singapore's Purchasing Manager's Index in March reinforced concerns about the slowing economy, analysts said. The figure represented the second month of contraction since January 1999. 

 However, one currency strategist said the downside was well supported at 1.8180 and then 1.8230, levels where she said the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in London on Monday, when the Sing dollar fell to decade lows. 

 She said her calculation showed the Sing dollar nominal exchange rate was bobbing out of the policy band, which the MAS uses to manage the economy. 

 "Bears think they can pressurise the Sing forever, but stop and think about it. This is way out of the band," she said. 

 "I think the MAS is waiting for a big jump (in dollar/Sing) to intervene in the market again." 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won slid to a fresh 30-month closing low of 1,365.2 as the yen stumbled past 126, despite the Korean government's pledges to introduce measures aimed at stabilising the currency. 

 Dealers said trading was initially cautious as the market remained wary over central bank intervention. The Bank of Korea was rumoured to have intervened via state banks on Tuesday. 

 However, the won later succumbed as the dollar gained more ground on the yen and foreign investors sold a net 177.4 billion won worth of stocks. 

 Authorities said earlier they were working on a package of measures to stabilise the market. They also repeated warnings that they were watching the market closely. 

 On the offshore non-deliverable forward market, one-month dollar/won was at 1,358.5/59.5 against 1,344.5/45.5 late Tuesday and the three-month was at 1,362.5/64.5 against 1,347.3/48.3. 

 THAI BAHT The baht turned tail to hit fresh three-year lows of 45.47, despite official efforts to talk it up. 

 Local banks joined a selling spree with banks in Singapore and foreign banks in Bangkok, dealers said. 

 The market had been wary about possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand after talk circulated authorities sold U.S. dollars via a Singapore-based bank at 45.40 late on Tuesday. 

 But bears regained confidence in trouncing the baht after Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said the BOT had not intervened to support the baht. 

 He said the baht's weakness was caused by external factors and it did not suggest the Thai economy was not sound. The central bank said the baht has been too volatile versus regional currencies and that it was ready to act. 

 "They are trying to find ways to slow the pace of the decline," a currency analyst said. "They don't mind the decline. They mind the pace of the decline." 

 He said firmer offshore baht funding costs provided the only solace for the baht. The one-month forward rate stood at 50/70 satang per dollar against 50/60 earlier. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah hit a three-week low of 10,600 as demand for dollars from local corporates spiked despite sporadic intervention by Bank Indonesia. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said with an increase in the flow of bad news from the economic front, in addition to currency weakness across the region, most corporates were staying long of dollars. 

 A dealer at a European bank said the central bank pumped in about $25 million and finally succeeded in defending the 10,600 mark and propping it up to 10,560. 

 The dealer said early intervention had little impact as the bank sold dollars in small amounts, at different levels. 

 Governor Sjahril Sabirin said BI would continue intervening as the rupiah would get worse without the intervention. 

 Meanwhile chief economics minister Rizal Ramli warned the 2001 budget deficit could overshoot the target of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product to slightly over five percent. 

 The defence minister said violence could get worse if political tensions do not ease. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso eased to a low of 50.17, not seen since mid-January, as importers chased the dollar up expecting more pressure from other regional currencies in the coming days. 

 Dealers in Manila said most exporters were holding back their earnings while importers were trying to lock in their dollar needs before the peso slipped lower with the regional downturn. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said support for the peso was likely to come in at around 50.20 while its upside was capped at 49.80. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar tripped over the weaker yen, but resisted the 33 level thanks to wariness over central bank intervention. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was speculated to be selling dollars when the Taiwan dollar edged to 32.995. But they added the market was expected to test that level again, especially if the yen showed further weakness. 

 Outflows from foreign investors also hobbled sentiment towards the local dollar as Taiwan stocks closed lower for the fourth straight session. Foreign investors sold a net T$5.132 billion in Taiwan shares on Tuesday. 

 Taiwan was also coping with anxiety over the stand-off between the U.S. and China over a U.S. surveillance plane. China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and has been perturbed by the Bush administration's more openly pro-Taiwan stance and possible U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

title: Asian  currencies  find calm before brewing storm.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 3 (Reuters) - Government rhetoric and a firmer yen gave Asian currencies some respite from their recent losses on Tuesday, but analysts warned the worst was yet to come. 

 Japanese officials expressed concern over the swift decline of the yen to Monday's 2-= year low of 126.84 to the dollar, forcing dollar bulls to retreat for now. 

 Authorities in Seoul and Bangkok also tried to ward off further losses in their currencies through verbal, and in the case of Korea, actual intervention. 

 However, the Singapore dollar, Korean won, and Thai baht remained mired at lows not seen since 1998, though the Sing dollar did recover from an 11-year low of 1.8235 to the dollar touched in overnight trading. 

 And with the yen expected to resume its slide towards 130 per dollar, Asian currencies were expected to again be taken lower. 

 Besides the fragile yen, analysts said the other major bugbear regional currencies were facing was investor risk aversion, which has gripped the market recently. 

 "Risk aversion is bad news for Southeast Asian currencies where investors are faster at getting out of positions when things look ugly," said Rebecca Patterson, regional currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore. 

 THE "C" WORDS 

 Since the start of the year, the Sing has shed around four percent of its value, while the won has lost around five percent and the baht over three percent. 

 The rapid fall of regional currencies has sparked some talk of another currency crisis. 

 But analysts are quick to stamp out such talk, pointing to important differences between current circumstances and the events that led up to the 1997 Asian crisis. 

 "A lot of these countries basically have current account surpluses, which are narrowing, in contrast to '97/'98, and they've built up their foreign exchange reserves. Inflation is actually pretty moribund as well," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 Despite public consternation over the weaker regional currencies, the market has begun kicking around the idea that Asia is engaged in "competitive devaluation". 

 "You can call what's going on competitive devaluation. It's not incorrect. The move in the won, peso, baht, and even the Taiwan dollar, they're keeping up with the yen," said JP Morgan Chase's Patterson. 

 Analysts said with the yen headed lower and sentiment towards the region headed the same way, regional central banks were unlikely to spend precious foreign exchange reserves defending their currencies. 

 Artificially propping up a currency at a time of regional weakness could also harm export competitiveness. 

 SINGAPORE TO REVISE GROWTH 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore said in a quarterly report it would revise down its 5-7 percent growth target for 2001 because of the slowdown in the U.S. and electronics industry, but would not announce the new target until next week. 

 The announcement came against the backdrop of a substantially weaker local dollar and speculation the MAS would switch its current tightening bias to a neutral stance in recognition of deteriorating external factors. 

 Some analysts doubted the central bank would make such a shift, as it views exchange rate policy as a weapon against imported inflation rather than a tool for export competitiveness. 

 However, others said such a shift had already taken place as the Sing dollar has weakened against its trade-weighted basket of currencies, without strong resistance from the MAS. 

 "It's safe to say there is minimal risk that a tighter monetary policy will be pursued as it's completely at odds with fundamentals because the threat is to growth not to inflation," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank. 

 While a formal policy shift would be a significant change for the MAS, some analysts doubted whether it would affect the market, given the way the Sing has weakened in the past week. 

 "Even if they come out now and say that they've moving to a neutral policy stance I don't think it will have much of an impact because it's there already in the price," said UBS Warburg's Mohi-uddin.

title: UPDATE 1-Singapore dlr falls past Asian crisis low.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 2 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar buckled under 1.8150 to the U.S. dollar on Monday, falling beyond lows last seen during the Asian financial crisis. 

 It hit a low of 1.8165 in afternoon trade, down 0.7 percent from its late Friday levels of around 1.8030. It has lost more than four percent since the end of last year. 

 Dealers said the breach of 1.8150, last hit on January 8, 1998 according to Reuters data, exposed the Singapore dollar to a decline towards decade-lows beyond 1.8300. 

 Its drop on Monday came amid further weakness in the yen and the Thai baht. There was no sign of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), dealers said. 

 "I don't think they'll (the MAS) come in at this point. Sentiment is just too weak for the Sing dollar," said a chief dealer at a European bank. 

 After falling through 1.8100 psychological support in early trade, the Singapore dollar won a mild respite before extending its decline as European markets opened and the yen revisited 30-month lows around 126.65 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the market had grown increasingly bearish amid reduced prospects for the Singapore economy, the fragile yen and euro and anticipation of further merger and acquisition related outflows. 

 But they said the Singapore dollar was by no means isolated in its troubles and the fall owed much to an inevitable spillover effect from other regional currencies. 

 Some analysts said the Singapore unit's recent fortunes foreshadow tougher times ahead for regional currencies. 

 "I think what is going on with the Sing dollar is an illustration of how difficult things will be for the region," said Simon Flint, senior currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 "The Sing is an exemplar of an actively managed currency, and the authorities are clearly concerned about lower global demand." 

 However, Flint pointed out that the weakness in the Singapore dollar had been aggravated by the Singapore Telecommunications Ltd purchase of Australia's Cable & Wireless Optus , which has sparked widespread demand for dollars amid speculation SingTel had yet to fulfil its requirements. 

 Flint said the trade-weighted Sing had actually only fallen by 1.5-2 percent. 

 Chia-Liang Lian, economist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore, said the Sing dollar was being weighed down by corporate demand for U.S. dollars. 

 "We are having a bit of overshooting here due to real corporate demand related to specific purposes as opposed to speculative nature," he said. 

 "But we do expect some pullback (in dollar/Sing) once that corporate demand slows," he said, adding that he was sticking to his mid-2001 forecast of 1.80 for the Sing dollar. 

 The MAS uses the Sing dollar as its main policy tool, managing it against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies. Analysts say the basket includes the U.S. dollar, the euro, the yen and other regional currencies.

title: Emerging  FX  - Sagging yen casts shadow.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies came under renewed pressure on Monday as the yen struggled at fresh 30-month lows, raising expectations of further weakness across the region. 

 The Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" survey, showing business sentiment had worsened, coupled with conflicting comments from Japanese finance officials pulled the yen down to lows of around 126.65 against the dollar. 

 The euro also fell to new lows for the year below $0.8750 against the dollar. 

 The Singapore dollar fell past its Asian crisis lows of 1.8150 while the baht was beaten down to lows not seen since March 1998. 

 The only exception was the rupiah which held steady at 30-month lows, drawing support from modest dollar sales by state banks, usually active on behalf of the Indonesian authorities. 

 Other central banks and governments in the region only attempted to slow the declines through verbal intervention. 

 With the yen believed to be still far from a bottom despite its over nine percent decline since the begining of the year, most regional currencies were likely to see further downside. 

 "The yen weakness looks irretrievable and at the moment, that is the key catalyst for weakness in all the regional currencies," said Jan Lee, chief strategist at HypoVereinsbank. 

 A chief dealer at a European bank said pessimism over Japanese economic performance and uncertainty about the euro zone monetary policy had fuelled safe-haven flows to the dollar. 

 He said even U.S. equity gloom was helping the dollar, as investors were repatriating funds from other markets to cover their losses. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar remained downcast after hitting lows of 1.8165 to the dollar against the backdrop of a weakening yen and corporate demand for dollars. 

 Dealers attributed much of its drop to the yen, with offshore parties out of London aggressively bidding up dollar/Sing in afternoon trade. 

 They said solid buying interest for the U.S. dollar was still intact, most of which they reckoned was genuine demand related to M&A activities. 

 The apparent lack of any official intervention also generated speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore might have opted to keep out of the market given persistent demand for dollars. 

 "Of course this is a 39-month low and very weak, but relative to what? The yen is falling way faster than the Sing dollar," a European bank dealer said. 

 "They (authorities) can control how the Sing fluctuates but they can't do anything about the yen, or other currencies." 

 The Sing dollar is managed against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies, believed to include the yen, euro and regional currencies. 

 Some analysts believe the MAS has already shifted its stance to neutral from a tightening bias, given deteriorating external demand, despite its statement last week that short-term fluctuations did not affect its policy stance. 

 THAI BAHT The baht was beaten down to 36-month lows around 45.20 weighed by weaker regional currencies and the uncertain economic picture at home. 

 It was kept from falling further after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said he had asked the central bank to monitor baht movements to determine if there was any speculation behind its decline. But dealers saw the respite as short-lived. 

 Adding to the gloom, a business confidence survey by the Bank of Thailand showed Thai companies were less optimistic about the economic outlook for the second month in a row in February. 

 On the political front, Thailand's Constitutional Court begins hearing a graft case against Thaksin on Tuesday. 

 If the court upholds a ruling Thaksin would face a five-year ban from politics. Thaksin said he would not attend the first day of the hearing. He is due to address the country and unveil an economic stimulus package in the evening. 

 The only support the baht found was extremely tight offshore liquidity, brokers said. Baht funding cost in the offshore market jumped, with the one-month forward rate at 65/75 satang per dollar against 30/50 earlier in day. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won ended at a near 30-month low despite repeated verbal intervention by the authorities. 

 Dealers said its weakness was mainly due to the yen's breach of 125 after the release of the BOJ's tankan survey of business sentiment. The won has been tied to the yen for several weeks as Korea and Japan compete on the same key exports to the U.S. 

 Investors in Korea have been fretting over the speed of the yen's drop. Dealers in Singapore said dollar bids in the offshore non-deliverable forward market have also pressured the currency. 

 Both the Finance Ministry and the Bank of Korea warned the market that they were watching it closely, reiterating that the won's sensitivity towards other currencies was not desirable. 

 However, dealers said the authorities were not spotted intervening, though state banks had sold dollars on Friday. 

 Analysts said the authorities were unlikely to actually intervene, as Korea needs to keep its competitive edge in the face of slowing external demand. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso gapped down at the open and dipped to a session low of 49.83 from Friday's close of 49.51. 

 But profit-taking on dollar longs and a lack of dollar demand from local corporates provided some support at around the 49.80 level, helping the peso close at 49.77. 

 Dealers in Manila said the peso was likely to trend lower in line with other regionals with next psychological support seen at the 50 figure. 

 But charts showed the dollar might pull back a bit before testing 50 as it was deep in overbought territory with a reading of 91.53 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 The central bank said commercial banks' non-performing loan ratio increased to 16 percent of total loans at the end of January from 15.10 percent in December. 

 It said it expected annual inflation in March to be between 6.5 percent and 7.0 percent. A Reuters poll earlier showed an average forecast of 6.8 percent, almost flat from the 6.7 percent rise in February. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR The Taiwan dollar stayed soft after hitting three-month lows of 32.965, due to the falling yen and a slide in Taiwan equities. 

 The benchmark TAIEX fell 3.3 percent, led by a sell-off in electronics shares. 

 "I think the Taiwan dollar should fall further because in real terms it is still overvalued compared with the won and the yen," a senior European bank trader in Hong Kong said. 

 The Taiwan dollar has lagged losses in the yen and won, which are down more than nine percent and five percent respectively since the end of last year. 

 He said the Taiwan dollar was targeting a major psychological support of 33.00, a break of which would open the way to last year's lows of 33.20. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 Despite the yen-inspired falls in other regional currencies, the rupiah held steady on early dollar sales by state banks. 

 Jakarta dealers said state banks pumped in a small amount of only $5 million but that proved enough to deter dollar-starved local corporates wary of further central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the suspected intervention also worked as overall trading volume was low, with less than $50 million dealt. 

 However, sentiment was negative on lingering political uncertainty and on negative news flow from the economic front. 

 Finance minister Prijadi Praptosuhardjo warned the 2001 budget deficit could be wider than the expected 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, because of a weak rupiah, high domestic interest rates and low world oil prices. 

 An official from the statistics bureau said 2001 annual inflation could exceed the 7.2 percent forecast in the budget. The bureau earlier announced March annual inflation growth at 10.62 percent, up from 9.14 percent in February. 

 Trade data also painted a dismal picture showing the February surplus shrank to $1.70 billion from $1.82 billion in January as exports eased and imports were flat.

title: Emerging  FX -Cower as dollar keeps the upper hand.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 30 (Reuters) - Dollar bulls came out in full force late Friday, chasing Asian currencies lower while the yen and euro flailed. 

 With the end of the Japanese fiscal year around the corner, the yen was flung to 22-month lows in a rumour-wracked market. In late Asian trade, the dollar rose above 125 yen for the first time since October 1998. 

 The euro recovered slightly from 15-week lows amid rumours of possible European Central Bank intervention later in the day. 

 All this cast a pall over already struggling regional currencies. The Singapore dollar suffered the brunt of the regional weakness, as both the euro and yen make up a substantial chunk of its trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 In North Asia, the won and Taiwan dollar retreated with the yen, prompting verbal and actual intervention by their central banks. Southeast Asian central banks also let the markets know where they stood on the latest bout of regional weakness. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore said late Thursday short-term volatility would not affect its current policy bias towards tightening and the Bank of Thailand said it would let the market determine the baht's level. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar lurched lower to 1.8033 in the afternoon as funds and investment houses kept bidding up the U.S. dollar. 

 The latest drop brought its loss to more than four percent since the beginning of the year and put it within striking distance of 1.8150, a level last seen in January 1998. 

 Dealers attributed the fall to the fragile yen and euro, with more weakness expected despite some speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore might have intervened late on Thursday. 

 Persistent dollar offers from local banks around the 1.8030 level on Friday fanned speculation they may be acting on behalf of the MAS, after the central bank reiterated on Thursday that it would intervene if needed to curb excessive exchange rate moves. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won scrambled away from the day's low of 1,331 - a level not seen since October 1998 - as dollar sales by state banks spurred speculation of intervention by the authorities. 

 Dealers in Singapore cited state bank dollar sales around the 1,328 won level. Government officials have repeatedly expressed dismay over the won's falls, and threatened to take action in recent days. 

 For the past several weeks, the yen has been the dominant influence on the won's direction as Korea and Japan compete on key exports. 

 Dealers said offshore bidding interest in the dollar on the non-deliverable forward market was fairly strong across the board. At 0800 GMT, the six-month won was at 1,335.8/36.8, and the one-year was at 1,342.8/43.8. 

 On the macroeconomic front, March inflation rose 0.6 percent on month, and 4.4 percent on year, higher than forecasts of 0.3 percent on month and 4.1 percent on year. 

 While the market shrugged off the data, analysts said it had muted hopes for a rate cut when the Bank of Korea holds its next monthly monetary policy meeting on April 6. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar drooped with the weaker yen and won, but was helped off its intraday low of 32.898 by the central bank. 

 The central bank's rate cut of 12.5 basis points on Thursday also damped sentiment towards the local dollar, though the move was widely expected. 

 The cut brings the bank's discount rate and accomodation with collateral rate to 4.125 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the bank was spotted in the market in early trade, though they added the amount was not significant. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, dealers said dollar bids were focused in the one-month and three-month rates, which were at 0.070/90 and 0.200 /230, respectively. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 Players in Jakarta momentarily forgot troubles at home only to realise the currency woes plaguing the region, driving the rupiah back to the wrong side of 10,400. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said local corporate dollar demand was strong despite the end of the first quarter, as customers were concerned with the general weakness throughout the region. 

 Bank Indonesia sold dollars around 10,410/20, though dealers estimated the amount to have been only around $20 million. 

 On the brighter side, Jakarta issued new guidelines to improve transparency over corporate debt restructuring with the help of key donors such as the World Bank and IMF. 

 The move raised hopes that differences between the IMF and Jakarta could be narrowing, paving the way towards the eventual resumption of the Fund's $5 billion lending programme. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was within a whisker of fresh three-year lows of 45.00 as the yen past 125.00 against the dollar. 

 Bankok dealers said both offshore and onshore players were rushing to buy the U.S. dollar after Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Sinawatra echoed recent comments by officials that the government would not intervene to support the currency. 

 Shinawatra also said the baht should not fall much further. 

 Thai central bank chief economist Atchana Waiquamdee said earlier the bank would let the market decide the appropriate level for the baht. 

 Offshore baht funding costs remained firm, with the one-month forward rate at 30/50 satang per dollar against 38/48 late Thursday. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended domestic trade at its session low of 49.51 per dollar, weighed by weakness in regional currencies. 

 Dealers said corporate dollar demand prevented it rising above 49.27, but dollar profit-taking limited its downside. They said a convincing break of 49.50 would put the dollar on track for further gains towards 49.70. 

 Amid a dearth of fresh local leads, the fiscal position remained a focal point with Finance Secretary Alberto Romulo saying the government would pursue fiscal consolidation to achieve a budget surplus between 2004 and 2006. 

 On Thursday, the government said it was targeting a lower budget deficit of 120.6 billion pesos next year, or about 2.8 percent of gross national product, against this year's 145 billion or 3.8 percent of GNP. 

 But analysts remain concerned about its likely success in lowering the deficit given the difficulties of revenue collection in the Philippines. 

 Separately, National Treasurer Sergio Edeza said the Bureau of Treasury hoped to offer 150 billion pesos worth of Treasury bonds to small, individual investors this year to finance the government's budgetary needs.

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late; Gives Up Early Gains As Yen Falls
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar tracked the yen lower late Friday, surrendering early gains on suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Around 0851 GMT (3:51 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.8036, up from S$1.7995 late Thursday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar opened lower and quickly fell to an intraday low of S$1.7953, on selling by local banks suspected to be acting on MAS' behalf. 

 Dealers said these banks had also capped the U.S. dollar's rise in London overnight after the European Central Bank decided to leave interest rates unchanged. 

 Late Thursday, the MAS declined to comment on the Singapore dollar's fall to a fresh 38-month low of S$1.8040. However, it repeated its statement issued Monday to Dow Jones Newswires that any short-term volatility in the Singapore dollar "will not" affect its declared, moderately tight monetary policy stance or the undisclosed band within which it manages the currency. The MAS manages the foreign exchange rate as its primary policy tool, it doesn't set interest rates. 

 However, the U.S. dollar recovered quickly against the local unit on the back of the U.S. unit's rise above Y125. It rose to an intraday high around S$1.8036, but further gains were capped by fears that the MAS or its agent banks would again intervene, dealers said. 

 Dealers said they expect the U.S. dollar to test immediate resistance around S$1.8045-50 near-term if the yen weakens further. 

 A Bank of America research note said that, despite recent suspected intervention, the MAS may have loosened its monetary policy stance a tad. 

 However, research issued by the government-linked DBS Bank earlier Thursday said the MAS hasn't changed its policy stance to neutral from a moderate tightening bias. 

 DBS, which often acts on behalf of MAS in the foreign exchange market, "reminded" investors that Singapore doesn't use a weak currency to boost exports and that domestic price stability is a "pivotal" policy objective. 

 Singapore imports almost everything it needs, including water. 

 A weaker Singapore dollar also hurt government bonds, which were sold amid light trading. 

 Interbank money market rates edged higher in the wake of a weaker local currency. Interest rate swaps were also driven higher by weakness in the currency and bond markets. 

 The yield on the 10-year bond ended three basis points higher at 3.66%, and the seven-year bond yield also rose three basis points to 3.49%. 

 The yield on the five-year government paper rose one basis point to 3.10%. The two-year bond ended at 2.43%, up three basis points. 

 These are pre-settlement closing bids and are subject to minor changes. 

 Historic bond yields and prices can be viewed at the MAS Web site (https://secure.mas.gov.sg/dataroom/dataroom_findbindex.htm l). 

 In the interest rate swaps market, the most liquid seven-year swap offer was at 3.57%, up six basis points from late Thursday. The 10-year swap offer rose seven basis points to 3.79%. 

 The spread between the two- and 10-year swaps was 107 basis points, from 106 basis points Thursday.

 An analyst at a U.S. bank forecast that the Sing will test 1.8150, a low hit on January 8, 1998 according to Reuters data, within two weeks.

 The baht was bruised after hitting fresh lows at 44.75, its lowest since March 1998, in tandem with the falling Sing. 

 The latest upset was also caused by Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak, who said the government may cancel guarantees on foreign bank deposits. 

 Adding insult to the baht's injury, he said he was not concerned about the weak baht and the government would not intervene in the market. 

 He said the weakness of the baht and regional currencies was caused by the slowdown of the U.S. and Japanese economies. 

 "It just cheered up the (baht) bears," a Bangkok dealer said. 

 Jatusripitak also said he had asked foreign banks in Thailand to increase deposit rates and cut lending rates to help boost the Thai economy. 

 The harried baht failed to even draw much support from firmer baht offshore funding costs. The one-month forward rate rose to 38/48 satang per dollar from 15/18 late on Wednesday. 

 Analysts said the baht was not likely to escape the weaker yen and the Sing, and would break 45.00 within a few weeks. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was steady after state banks sold about $11 million and corporates waited for parliament's response to President Abdurrahman Wahid's rejection of its censure. 

 "Most of our customers are holding back as they are not sure if the power struggle between the President and Parliament is over or another censure is on its way," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta. 

 Wahid's critics said another censure would be issued by parliament, moving closer towards an impeachment vote. 

 Adding to the uncertainty was the IMF's position on whether it would send a review team to Jakarta, a step towards resumption of lending withheld since last December. 

 The IMF's senior Indonesian representative John Dodsworth said he was optimistic a team would arrive next month. Earlier, an IMF spokesman in Washington said it was too early to set a date for sending a mission. 

 Dealers said the market was waiting for IMF's formal decision on whether to resume lending. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso fell, but was off a session low of 49.45 helped by dollar inflows from exporters and overseas workers. 

 The dollar/peso was also overbought, with a reading of 86 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 As widely expected, the central bank left its key overnight rates unchanged at its weekly policy-making meeting. 

 Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank would be watching for domestic inflation data and moves by the Federal Reserve. 

 The overnight borrowing rate now stands at 10.0 percent and the lending rate at 12.25 percent. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 Verbal intervention from the authorities failed to help the won, which hit a day's low of 1,319.7. 

 Investors fretted over the yen's outlook, which has been the main force behind the won. Dealers also said the market was disappointed by lacklustre month-end dollar sales by exporters. 

 A Bank of Korea official said the won's "instability" could affect the economy, adding the bank was monitoring the market. 

 Later, a Finance Ministry official echoed the warning, saying the government was worried about the won's movements. 

 But dealers said the market, while cautious, was more likely to react to these comments if actual intervention followed. 

 February industrial output rose slightly more than expected, expanding 0.6 percent on month and 8.6 percent on year. The data had little impact on the market. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar retreated with the yen and won, with the market focusing on the central bank's monetary board meeting. 

 Gains on the local bourse failed to give the local dollar much of lift, as investors remained more concerned about the yen's direction. 

 The central bank was widely expected to cut rates by 12.5 basis points, bringing its discount rate and accommodation with collateral rates to 4.25 percent and 4.625 percent, respectively.

title: UPDATE 1-Singapore MAS says no change in policy stance.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 29 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Thursday short term volatility in the local currency will not affect its policy stance, contrary to speculation it would shift to a neutral from tightening bias. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped past the psychologically key 1.8000 mark against the U.S. dollar for the first time since January 12, 1998, raising speculation the MAS would intervene. 

 "In the short-term, merger and acquisition activities by local companies may cause volatility in the Singapore dollar," it said in a statement in reply to Reuters' queries. 

 The MAS said M&A activities did not affect the fundamentals of the Singapore economy. 

 "Therefore, any short-term volatility in the Singapore dollar will not affect MAS' policy stance on the Singapore dollar, or the policy band," it added. 

 The Singapore dollar had been struggling under a barrage of bad news from the weaker euro to the Singapore Telecommunications Ltd proposed purchase of Australia's Cable & Wireless Optus . 

 SingTel is 78 percent owned by the Singapore government. 

 In February, the central bank restated its stance that it would maintain its current monetary policy and continue to allow a gradual, modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis. 

Currency dealers said on Thursday the Sing dollar had moved below the policy band in their simulated trade-weighted currency baskets, heightening the risk of intervention. 

 MAS reiterated that it would intervene if necessary to dampen excessive Singapore dollar exchange rate movements, including movements arising from the funding of corporate M&A activities. 

 The central bank also said: "Apart from the bank counterparties which MAS deals with for its money market and foreign exchange operations, MAS does not transact foreign exchange with any other commercial entity." MAS said that it manages the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies and not against the U.S. dollar or any other bilateral exchange rate.

title: Singapore MAS Declines To Comment On SGD Fall To New Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore late Thursday declined to comment on the Singapore dollar's fall to a fresh three-year low. 

 In written reply to questions, the central bank said it had nothing further to add to a statement issued Monday to Dow Jones Newswires, in which it said: "We do not comment on specific market movements in the Singapore dollar." 

 Monday's statement also said that the MAS believes any short-term volatility in the Singapore dollar "will not" affect its declared, moderately tight monetary policy stance or the undisclosed band within which it manages the currency. 

 "Any short-term volatility in the Singapore dollar will not affect MAS' policy stance on the Singapore dollar, or the policy band," the central bank had said. 

 The MAS also reiterated Monday that it will intervene, if required, "to dampen excessive Singapore dollar exchange rate movements," but failed to carry out its threat, encouraging some speculators to drive the currency lower all week. This triggered stop-loss buying by banks and local companies who had been expecting the MAS to arrest the local dollar's descent. 

 The Singapore dollar's plunge to another 38-month low, without opposition from the central bank, fueled speculation that the MAS may have subtly eased its monetary policy stance from moderately tight to neutral. 

 The U.S. dollar crested psychological resistance at S$1.8000, hitting a high of S$1.8040, as market participants tested the central bank's resolve to carry out its oft-repeated threat to intervene if currency moves become too volatile. 

 This was the Singapore dollar's lowest level since January 1998 - the depths of the Asian financial crisis - when it touched S$1.8170. 

 However, it recovered by late afternoon, as jittery bankers and investors sold U.S. dollars amid interventions fears. Light U.S. dollar selling by two local banks during Asian trading also aided the Singapore dollar's recovery, but the selling wasn't aggressive enough to suggest that it was at the MAS' behest, dealers said. 

 At 1519 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8000. 

 Following is the full text of the MAS statement issued Monday, which it repeated late Thursday: 

 "We do not comment on specific market movements in the Singapore dollar. MAS manages the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, and not against the U.S. dollar or any other bilateral exchange rate. 

 "Over the medium to long term, we expect the trade-weighted Singapore dollar exchange rate to reflect the fundamentals of the Singapore economy. In the short term, M&A activities by local companies may cause volatility in the Singapore dollar. But these M&A activities do not affect the fundamentals of the Singapore economy. Therefore any short term volatility in the Singapore dollar will not affect MAS' policy stance on the Singapore dollar, or the policy band. 

 "As MAS stated in its press answer on 5 March, MAS will intervene if necessary to dampen excessive Singapore dollar exchange rate movements, including movements arising from the funding of corporate M&A activities. 

 "Apart from the bank counterparties which MAS deals with for its money market and foreign exchange operations, MAS does not transact foreign exchange with any other commercial entity."

title: FX  ASIA:Singapore Dlr Hits New Lows Amid MAS Easing Talk
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column



SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar plunged to another
38-month low Thursday without opposition from the central bank, fueling
speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have subtly
eased its monetary policy stance from moderately tight to neutral.


 The U.S. dollar crested psychological resistance at S$1.8000, hitting a high of S$1.8040, as market participants tested the central bank's resolve to carry out its oft-repeated threat to intervene if currency moves become too volatile. 

 The Singapore dollar hit an all-time low of S$1.8170 in January 1998. 

 If indeed the MAS has changed track, it would amount to a reversal of its standing policy that it expects the local dollar to reflect the Singapore economy's fundamentals, which remain strong. The central bank reiterated that stance as recently as Monday. 

 However, the Singapore dollar recovered by late afternoon, as jittery bankers and investors sold U.S. dollars amid interventions fears. Light U.S. dollar selling by two local banks also aided the Singapore dollar's recovery, but the selling wasn't aggressive enough to suggest that it was at the MAS' behest, dealers said. 

 At 0740 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7998. 

 Analysts and dealers say that the MAS' reluctance to defend the local dollar even though its recent decline has outpaced that of the yen points to a rethinking of its declared policy of facilitating a gradual and modest appreciation of the trade-weighted currency. 

 The MAS manages the Singapore dollar exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and competitors. It maintains the trade-weighted exchange rate within an undisclosed band. 

 The Singapore dollar has "been out of the band for about two weeks now," says Rebecca Patterson, a currency strategist with J.P. Morgan in Singapore. 

 "It the MAS sees the move caused by things outside its control, and because Singapore's growth is also weakening, it could be that it's moving towards a more neutral policy stance," she adds. 

 In fact, Patterson says that despite the central bank's "rhetoric" about a strong local dollar, the MAS has remained neutral this year. This likely explains the Singapore dollar's descent from S$1.7318 at the beginning of this year. 

 Notions that the MAS might have changed its tune - at least for the time being - were supported Thursday by research published by government-linked DBS Bank Ltd. In a research note, DBS said that the Singapore dollar's decline suggests a "more flexible" MAS policy may be in play in view of low inflation and slowing growth in exports. 

 Inflation eased to 1.3% on year in February from 2% in January. 

 After having expanded at a rapid 9.9% last year, Singapore's economy is expected to grow at a slower pace this year. Analysts say growth could come at the lower end or below the government's 5% to 7% forecast range, as a slowing U.S. economy and global electronics downturn take their toll on exports. 

 Analysts at Citibank/Salomon Smith Barney and Bank of America said they expect the MAS to formally switch to a neutral policy stance within the next three to six months. 

 Though a comment from the MAS wasn't immediately available, the head of research at DBS Bank cautioned against interpreting the central bank's current flexible stance as a policy change. 

 "The MAS has always said that it is not in Singapore's long term interest to have a weak currency to compete globally," said Fong Cheng Hong. 

 "We (Singapore) are not China. We don't have a huge resource base. So our companies need to increase productivity and move into high end products with high margins to stay ahead. Also, we are heavy importers, so a stronger Singapore dollar will always be in interest of our long term stability," she said, adding that "I think this (outlook) has not changed." 

 Fong attributes the local dollar's recent slide to a weaker euro and merger and acquisition outflow related to Singapore Telecommunication Ltd.'s (P.SGT) successful bid for Australia's Cable and Wireless Optus (A.CWO) valued at up to A$17.2 billion. The euro has slipped from US$0.9298 on March 1 to around US$0.8866 currently. 

 MAS' reluctance to intervene, says Fong, reflects its pragmatism as intervention would likely be an unwise move in the face of strong market forces. 

 "If you watch the MAS (actions) over the past 10 years, you will see that they come in only when conditions are right, says Fong. 

 This means that speculators need to watch out for the MAS lurking in the wings once the euro and yen show signs of recovery. Fong expects the Singapore dollar to recover to S$1.77-S$178 by end-June and around S$1.72-S$1.75 by end December. 

 While most analysts expect the Singapore dollar to recover by the end of the year if the local economy's strong fundamentals kick in on the back of a U.S. recovery, some also believe that the Singapore dollar has yet to hit a bottom. 

 Recent research issued by Bank of America and ABN Amro Bank forecast the Singapore dollar will slide to S$1.82 by June, a level not seen since June 1990.
