title: Emerging  FX  - North Asia dismayed, baht bounces.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 22 (Reuters) - North Asian currencies had few good tidings on the Friday before Christmas as sentiment soured over domestic woes. 

 Most markets in Asia will be closed for Christmas on Monday, with Taiwan also shut for Constitution Day. This report will resume on Tuesday, December 26. 

 Concerns over slowing growth in the U.S. and Japan loomed over the region, but weighed especially hard on North Asian markets. Both Korea and Taiwan are viewed as being particularly exposed to the technology sector's slowdown. 

 In Seoul, some 16,000 unionised bank workers took to the streets to protest government-led restructuring efforts. 

 Korean markets have been fretting over the possibility that ongoing labour unrest may delay progress in much needed reforms. 

 Authorities in Korea and Taiwan moved in to support their sagging currencies with verbal and actual intervention. Dealers also noted that thin markets across the region distorted otherwise small bids and offers. 

 Southeast Asian currencies fared a little better, with the Thai baht's unexpected year-end star turn extending for another session. But analysts were divided as to whether it would last next year, with some pointing out that pre-holiday markets were not a reliable barometer of sentiment. 

 Others said this could be a turning point for the baht, and other Southeast Asian currencies that have been troubled by a year of political turmoil and shaky signs of economic recovery. 

 The euro was the only real winner, defying long-term bears with its climb against the yen and dollar. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was rescued from a day low of 1,237.5 after state banks entered the market to sell around $150 million to support the ailing currency. 

 A dealer in Singapore said there was also talk of the central bank intervening directly in the market at 1,233. 

 The won - which has lost around eight percent of its value since the start of this year - was weighed by problems both at home and abroad. 

 Protracted declines in the Nasdaq raised concerns over the global tech sector. At home, Kookmin Bank and Houseing and Commercial Bank unions went on strike despite the government's promise not to force the two to merge. 

 Analysts said the strike underlined difficulties faced by the government in pushing ahead with much-needed reforms. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar sagged anew as the stock market reversed early gains to hit a fresh 57-month low on heavy selling triggered by rising margin calls after the TAIEX's seven-session losing streak. 

 Buying by state funds and microchip foundry United Microelectronics' announcement that it would buy back 400 million shares between December 27, 2000 and February 26, 2001 helped the TAIEX finish just 0.12 percent lower. 

Central bank intervention also cushioned the Taiwan dollar's fall, but dealers expected further declines as Thursday's weaker than expected industrial output for November had only confirmed the picture of a slowing economy. 

 The central bank's toughened stance on forex trading kept players cautious amid rumours it had temporarily barred several foreign and local banks from trading in forwards. 

 A central bank official declined to comment on the rumours, but said the bank would punish commercial banks found to have broken the rules, noting that this could include a suspension. 

 Active dollar buying in the non-deliverable forward market, which has pushed six-month NDF rates to more than T$1 over the spot price, has pressured Taiwan's exchange rate despite frequent support from the central bank. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht marched higher, flirting with resistance at 42 to the dollar on the back of dollar offers from funds and interbank players, with gains exaggerated by a thin pre-holiday market. 

 The currency repeatedly failed to break the 42 barrier, which represents a 62 percent Fibonacci retracement of the dollar's August 23-November 21 upmove. 

 "A few funds are selling dollars through local banks, prompting some interbank players to trim long dollar positions. And the market is so thin, hence the magnitude of its rise," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Bangkok. "Players are also cautious to build fresh long dollar positions at this point given it's the year-end and the central bank is monitoring trade closely ahead of the election," he said. 

 There was a vague rumour the central bank was in the market to sell dollars, but a number of dealers dismissed it as unlikely. The bank had itself denied such talk on Wednesday. 

 "If the government needs to do anything at all in the market, they'd probably buy rather than sell the dollar because they need to repay IMF loans," said another Bangkok dealer. 

 Charts show that if the 42.00 level is breached, the baht will face another strong resistance at 41.50 which is the 38 percent retracement of the dollar's broad rise between January 3 and November 21 this year. 

 Political developments are likely to take the limelight next week, with the National Counter Corruption Commission expected to rule on cases against Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai, political front runner Thaksin Shinawatra, and Deputy Prime Minister Banyat Bantadtan of false declaration of assets. Analysts believed Chuan is likely to be cleared, while cases against Thaksin, who is tipped to be the next prime minister, and Banyat, are more serious. If they are found guilty, they will be banned from politics for five years. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar found a toehold above 1.7300 in a thin afternoon market, with one British name seen buying the local currency actively. 

 It had briefly dipped to the day's low of 1.7350 on dollar bids from a local bank before offers from other banks and a few local companies reversed its course. The Sing dollar was also buoyed by the perky euro, believed to be a substantial component in its trade-weighted basket. 

 Gains were well-capped at 1.7260, indicating players were cautious the central bank might step in to curb a sharp rise. 

 The government is expected to release November consumer price data at 1030 GMT on Saturday. 

 Analysts expect mild inflation ahead for Singapore. A Reuters poll of 10 economists forecast inflation at 1.41 percent on average for 2000 and 2.01 percent in 2001. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah dragged its feet the wrong side of 9,350 for most of the day, sandwiched between dollar bids from corporate and offshore players and offers from state banks in a thin pre-holiday market. 

 Traditional year-end inertia was worsened by caution ahead of a central bank meeting with local and foreign bank dealers. 

 A Bank Indonesia official said deputy governor Miranda Goeltom would meet with dealers around 0630 GMT. 

 The topic of discussion was unclear, though traders in Jakarta said it was likely to focus on a credit facility for forex loans to banks and the corporate sector. 

 Separately, central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said the bank did not want to raise interest rates excessively, adding that it was difficult to predict the rate trend early next year because of a variety of uncertainties. On Wednesday, the bank's benchmark SBI certificates were hiked to 14.53 percent, continuing a gradual uptrend of recent months that has sparked some worries about the impact on the embattled corporate sector. 

 The market was unimpressed by Finance Minister Prijadi Praptosuhardjo's forecast on Thursday, that gross domestic product growth could reach 5.5-6.0 percent next year, exceeding the state budget target of five percent. 

 A research note from SEB Merchant Banking described the finance minister as "ambitious and optimistic" in his assessment. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 Trade in the peso was moribund with domestic players keen to square up before the Christmas weekend. 

 The peso managed to poke above the 50 per dollar mark, but remained well within Thursday's already narrow band, on meagre end-year volume of $57.9 million. 

 Chartists said narrowing price action in dollar/peso had created a constricting triangle on the daily chart and a break to the upside was likely soon. 

 Analysts expect the peso to weaken again in early 2001 as the prop of overseas worker remittances subsides, and the market re-focuses on political and economic turmoil within the country. 

 Even data showing the sixth straight month of growth in production indices for October failed to excite peso traders. 

 The value of production index surged 31.7 percent year-on-year while the volume of production index leapt 21 percent on higher output from oil refiners, food manufacturing and electrical machinery. 

 Economists attributed the rise to seasonal pre-Christmas rises in production and said output was likely taper off in November and December.

text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar reached a 15-week high against the U.S. dollar Friday, despite fears that the de facto central bank might again enter the market to weaken the local currency. 

 Trade was thin ahead of the weekend and holidays period, adding to the market's volatility. 

 Around 0830 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7275 down from S$1.7312, late Thursday in Asia. 

 The Singapore dollar was benefitting from the U.S. dollar's weakness against the euro, the Australian and the New Zealand dollars also, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar gained despite fears of another intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which, traders suspect, bought U.S. dollars late Thursday at around S$1.7270. 

 In the bond market, the yield on Singapore government bonds was unchanged ahead of the holiday season amid very light trading. 

 Bond prices have risen in recent months and banks are comfortable holding bonds at current levels at least until the end of the year. 

 The yield on the 10-year paper was 4.11%, the seven-year bond yield was 3.81% and the five-year bond yield at 3.48%, all unchanged. 

 In the money market, the overnight offered rate rose to 5.5% from 2.75%. Demand is usually high ahead of the weekend and holidays.

title: Emerging  FX  - N.Asia gloomy, baht, Sing dlr buoyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies went separate ways in late trade on Thursday, driven by year-end needs and local factors. 

 The Korean won and Taiwan dollar, whose performance has been linked closely to their stock performance, led regional losers as another savaging on Wall Street sent local bourses reeling. 

 The Thai baht stole the limelight, gaining more than one percent at one point on the back of big dollar offers from a major global fund believed to be covering short baht positions. 

 Asian markets had little reaction to U.S. president-designate George W. Bush's choice of Treasury Secretary. Bush on Wednesday gave the important portfolio to Paul O'Neill, head of the world's largest aluminium company. 

 Although O'Neill won a glowing endorsement from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts are still digesting whether his manufacturing background would lead him to favour a lower dollar as a boost to U.S. exports. 

 The euro jumped to four-month highs against the dollar for the second consecutive day on Thursday, cashing in on growing concerns about a rapid slowdown in the U.S. economy. The yen climbed off its 16-month lows of around 113.15 on dollar profit taking. Chartists said if the dollar could hold above 113, the next target could easily be 115. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht made strong gains as one global fund was believed to be buying the unit aggressively in the past few days in relatively thin trade to cover short positions. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said the fund sold around $200-300 million through one European bank alone. 

 A break above 42.50 - which had not been pierced since October 10 - also prompted exporters and other players to sell the dollar to guard against further losses. 

 But the baht pared earlier gains in the afteroon on news that Thai banks made little or no progress restructuring their billions of dollars in bad loans in November, dealers said. 

 Three of the country's top banks actually reported small increases in their levels of non-performing loans (NPLs) - loans yielding no income for at least three months. 

 Baht funding costs nudged up, with one-month forward rates quoted at -2/1 satang per dollar from -3/-1 satang earlier. The overnight interbank rate was soft at 1.75-2.50 percent. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar followed the baht higher, though trading was extremely thin leaving it vulnerable to any shifts. 

 "It's just the year-end situation with the market not really willing to hold on to any (U.S.) dollars. But they're caught short now and then," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 With few players in the market, a local bank's U.S. dollar selling in early trading brought the Sing dollar to a high of 1.7255. But dealers said some U.S. dollar buying interest emerged around these levels. 

 Dealers also pointed out that with the euro as well as regional currencies firmer, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was less likely to intervene as the Sing has not appreciated too much against its trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah saw its gains from earlier in the week slip away as onshore and offshore players bought back dollars. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said several onshore interbank players were caught short, having held off on buying dollars as state banks and the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency sold off the currency earlier in the week. 

 However, neither the state banks nor IBRA came into the market to sell dollars, spurring others to take advantage of the relatively cheap levels. 

 Dealers added that foreign banks onshore bought around $30-$50 million, as dollar bids gathered momentum after it breached 9,275. 

 The market shrugged off Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid's denial of an impending cabinet reshuffle amid media reports that several ministers were expected to quit over disappointment with his leadership. Wahid's over one-year old administration saw a cabinet reshuffle in August. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso withstood the government's downward revisions to growth forecasts for next year and the latest twists in President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial, ending at 50.045, little changed from Wednesday's 50.058 close. 

 Volume was light at $88.5 million and trade confined to a tight 50.045-50.105 range. Chartists said the narrowing price action in the dollar/peso had created a constricting triangle on the daily chart, with a break to the upside likely soon. 

 Analysts too have said the peso is likely to head south again in the new year, once the prop of seasonal remittances from overseas workers disappears and the country's political and economic woes return to centrestage. 

 Socio-economic Planning Secretary Felipe Medalla said gross domestic product was expected to be between 3.0-3.5 percent next year if the impeachment process was concluded in the first quarter. The government had previously predicted 3.5 percent growth next year, down from an earlier 4.0-4.5 percent forecast. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar sank to a 22-month low against the U.S. dollar on Thursday despite central bank intervention, depressed by hefty Nasdaq-inspired losses in local stocks. 

 Dealers in Taipei said the central bank was believed to have intervened at $T33.175 which the dollar repeatedly failed to breach. 

 But analysts said the intervention was likely to be aimed at curbing volatility and not at boosting the currency because Taiwan would need a weak currency to support its slowing economy. 

 Data from the island's economics ministry on Thursday showed that export orders had slowed in November from October despite reaching a traditional peak season for mainstay electronics products. 

 However, year-on-year growth of 14.72 percent still exceeded analysts' expectations. A Reuters poll of 10 economists yielded an average forecast of a 13.09 percent rise. 

 Taiwan's industrial output also rose a slower than expected 1.63 percent on year in November due to sluggish domestic consumption. The government forecast five percent output growth in 2001, below its 2000 forecast of over eight percent growth. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won closed at a 21-month low, spooked by the stock market's recent declines and a planned bank strike on Friday. 

 Unions of six banks involved in merger plans were expected to start a general strike on Friday, which union officials said could cripple operations of 30 percent of the banking sector. 

 The government declared the strike illegal and vowed stern action if it went ahead, but union leaders showed little sign of backing down, setting the stage for what could be the biggest confrontation between labour and government since the crisis. 

 It said nearly 6,000 riot police would be mobilised to counter the planned strike. 

 Data released on Thursday showed the seasonally adjusted jobless rate rose to 4.1 percent in November, up from 3.9 percent in October but down from 4.9 percent the year before. 

 The won's drop to its lowest level since March 17, 1999 spurred a verbal warning from a forex official, but dealers said there was no sign of actual intervention.

title: Emerging  FX -SE Asia cheers in dozy, holiday trade.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies were firmer early Thursday, benefiting mostly from pre-holiday unwinding of long dollar positions in thin markets, and slightly from global dollar weakness. 

 The dollar and yen have been groaning under the weight of growing pessimism over the Japanese and U.S. economies, making Europe a more attractive investor destination for now. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the recent dollar sell-off had helped Southeast Asian markets a bit as any dollar sales in illiquid markets would mean a big shift in the exchange rates. 

 And sticking to the trend in recent weeks, North Asian currencies were smarting from their economies' exposure to the U.S. and the Nasdaq's misfortunes. 

 Downgrades of tech heavyweights Cisco Systems and International Business Machines sent U.S. blue chips and tech shares far south, with the Nasdaq dropping 7.12 percent. 

 Some analysts say Southeast Asian currencies have steadied in recent sessions due to low liquidity and easing demand for dollars from local corporates. 

 They point out that the political risk situation in Indonesia and the Philippines has not changed. And in Thailand, it could worsen if the front-runner of the January 6 polls Thaksin Shinawatra is indicted by the country's anti-graft watchdog. 

 Other analysts also note that markets in Southeast Asia have priced in much of the bad news already and have been predominantly long on dollars. 

 Players in these markets recently have been unwinding stale long dollar positions, giving these currencies a boost. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar reaped the benefits of a stronger euro, briefly breaching the 1.7300 mark in early trading. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar was likely to extend its gains as Southeast Asian currencies slowly inched higher. 

 They added that the Monetary Authority of Singapore was not seen as intervening in the market to cap the local dollar's gains as the Sing dollar had not appreciated excessively against its trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 Chartists say the Sing dollar needs to break resistance of 1.7275, which it touched on November 3 and 6, but has not breached since early September, before seeing further gains. 

 That area also cuts in near the 62 percent Fibonacci retracement of the U.S. dollar's broad August 10-November 24 rally. It has almost entirely retraced its steep run-up through November. 

 However, on the 14-day Relative Strength Index chart (RSI), the U.S. dollar was skimming the 30 level, with any move below that level indicating it is oversold. INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah slipped back the weak side of 9,200 despite early dollar offers from onshore and offshore names, and from state banks which were spotted selling from 9,200. 

 Although some players stepped in to buy the U.S. unit on dips, the bids were broadly outnumbered by offers, dealers said. 

 "It's not clear if the state banks sold dollars on the central bank's behalf. Some were seen unwinding long U.S. dollar and Sing dollar positions against the rupiah," said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "One U.S. fund was also heard selling dollars through onshore banks," he said. 

 Chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said on Wednesday Indonesia's approval of new foreign investment projects reached $14.6 billion in the first 10 months of this year, a jump of 35.2 percent from the same period last year. 

 A total of 1,286 foreign investment projects were approved in that period compared with 1,164 in the same period a year ago. 

 Charts show the dollar/rupiah, which had burst into overbought territory on many occasions since September 12, is just a whisker away from oversold territory with a reading of 33.23 on the 14-day RSI. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht nudged higher in early thin trade, supported by dollar offers from interbank players seeking to cut losses and exporters. 

 Despite the baht's recent rapid gains, dealers said it was likely to be capped in the near-term at 42.50 - a barrier it has failed to break since October 10. 

 The IMF's bullish comments about the economy on Thursday were likely to provide further support to the baht. 

 The Fund Thailand's external vulnerability had been much reduced since the 1997-1998 crisis and four to five percent growth was achievable next year if confidence returns after the January 6 election. 

 It also expressed support for the central bank's accomodative stance given tame Thai inflation. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won skipped past its support level of 1,220 to hit a year low of 1,223.4 per dollar in early trading as local sentiment was sideswiped by the Nasdaq's losses. 

 Skittish investors have been wringing their hands over the downturn in the electronics sector, which makes up a bulk of Korea's exports. 

 Moreover, trouble at home in the form of labour unrest and the government-led corporate and financial restructuring has depressed local investors' spirits in recent weeks. 

 However, Singapre dealers said the move downwards happened in a thin market, meaning the rate was vulnerable to any shift. 

 They added that the market was extremely cautious given that state banks sold off dollars heavily at 1,220 on December 1, sparking talk of central bank support. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said offshore players were targeting 1,280 before year-end were behind the dollar buying. 

 He added that there was no sign yet that the central bank would intervene in the market, though he expected it to send out a verbal warning later in the day. 

 Some traders also mentioned that players were trying to push dollar/won up in the hope of triggering option positions with a strike price of 1,300, but activity in the options market was very light overall. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar buckled as local stocks took a tumble following further losses on the Nasdaq. 

 The currency finally gave into mounting pressure of falling stocks and softer currencies in Taiwan's two biggest competitors, Korea and Japan, on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the central bank eased its determined defence of the local dollar at the 33.10 on Wednesday, but added that it had been detected in the market on Thursday trying to cushion the Taiwan dollar's fall. 

 Some dollar buying in the non-deliverable forward market by offshore parties has also turned up the pressure on the spot market. 

 Longer-dated tenors in the NDF market were all higher, with the six-month Taiwan dollar NDF at 1.0/1.1, the nine-month at 1.07/1.12 and the one-year at 1.12/1.25. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso yawned through a sluggish session in the morning, with interbank players as major participants. The first deal worth around $1.0 million was taken at 50.50. 

 Dealers said the currency was likely to trade in a narrow range in the near-term amid a dearth of trading incentives. 

 "People are already in holiday mood. They intend to celebrate their Christmas and they don't care what else is going on in the world," said a local dealer. 

 Political problems were also expected to be put on a slow burner for now. The impeachment court decided earlier this week to take a break starting next week on President Joseph Estrada's corruption trial, ensuring the outcome of the trial will not be known until next year. 

 Supreme Court Chief Justice Hilario Davide said the trial would resume on January 2.

title: Singapore Dlr Higher Late, Tracks Baht, Rupiah; Bonds Dn
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was slightly higher against its U.S. counterpart late Wednesday, fluctuating in a narrow range in tandem with the Indonesian rupiah and the Thai baht. 

 Around 0840 GMT (3:40 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7330, down from S$1.7335 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar opened slightly higher in line with its overnight gains, but its losses against the baht and the rupiah pushed it lower against the Singapore currency as well. 

 Dealers said currency moves were largely flow driven and somewhat exaggerated in a thin year-end market. 

 Dealers said that the U.S. dollar's fall below support at S$1.7330 was short-lived given fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to buy U.S. dollars. The MAS is believed to be uncomfortable with the U.S. dollar's rapid decline against the local currency in recent weeks. 

 Dealers expect the U.S. dollar to mostly trade in a S$1.7330-S$1.7380 range in the near term. However, if the U.S. dollar does stay below S$1.7330, dealers expect it will be strongly supported at S$1.7300. 

 In the bond market, prices of longer-dated Singapore Government Securities ended slightly lower amid thin trading. 

 The longer bonds were bid lower, but few trades took place because of a lack of selling interest, dealers said. 

 Bond prices have risen in recent months and banks are comfortable holding bonds at current levels, at least until the end of the year.

 In the money market, the overnight offered rate edged higher to 2.625% from 2.5625% late Tuesday, but was within its normal trading range. However, term rates remained steady amid ample liquidity in the banking system.

title: Emerging  FX  - Steady early on, but concerns linger.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly steady early on Friday, taking some respite from overnight declines in the U.S. dollar against the euro and the yen. 

 Subdued year-end trading, weekend squaring of long dollar positions and fears of central bank intervention could also provide support to some of the regional currencies. 

 But growing evidence of a slowing U.S. economy and Thursday's fall on Wall Street amid worries about corporate earnings were likely to cap any gains. 

 Sentiment in Asian currencies is already weighed by domestic political worries, slow pace of corporate and financial restructuring and on an expected slowing of growth and exports amid peaking global demand. 

 Profit warnings from financial giants Chase Manhattan Corp and J.P. Morgan pulled the Dow Jones industrial average down 1.11 percent while a cut in revenue forecast by software leader Microsoft wiped 3.34 percent off the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite Index . 

 With the victory for Republican George W. Bush in the presidential race already discounted, markets returned their focus to the gloomy corporate earnings outlook and impact from a slowing economy. 

 The U.S. Labor Department said on Thursday its Producer Price Index, a key measure of inflation at the wholesale level, inched up only 0.1 percent, following a 0.4 percent increase in October and matching market expectations. 

 The core PPI, that excludes more volatile food and energy prices, was unchanged from the prior month after a decline of 0.1 percent in October. 

 Markets would be watchful of U.S. November consumer prices due Friday. 

 But analysts said the flat core rate suggested receding threat of inflation and could prompt the Federal Reserve to shift its policy stance to neutral in its December 19 meeting. 

 The euro poked higher in early Tokyo trade, closing in on the $0.8974 major resistance mark against the dollar and was at around four-month highs against the yen. 

 The yen gained from dollar profit-taking in late New York trade, coming off its new 16-month lows against the dollar but was still perched around the 112 mark. 

 However, analysts said the overall dollar strength remained intact while the yen was likely to remain broadly weak which should keep most of the Asian currencies under pressure. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was likely to come under renewed pressure on the back of another fall in technology stocks in the U.S. 

 Adding more woe to the U.S. technology sector, U.S. software giant Microsoft Corp. said on Thursday after the market's close that it would miss its quarterly earnings and revenue targets due to the global slowdwon, lower personal computer sales and less corporate spending. 

 Investors on the tech-dominated Korea stock market were likely to continue pulling out of local tech stocks as Korea braced for a more dramatic slowdown than expected. 

 Another setback in the country's corporate and financial restructuring also hit local sentiment as Kookmin Bank announced on Thursday it had suspended merger talks with Housing and Commercial Bank . 

 Concerns over the reforms have been dragging local investor sentimemt lower in recent weeks. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won was at 1,201/2 and the three-month was at 1,201/2. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was supported by fears of central bank intervention and expectations of higher interest rate triggered by a recent spike in inflation. 

 Bank Indonesia has repeatedly warned the market recently that it was ready to supply dollars to ease downward pressure on the rupiah. 

 The central bank also said on Wednesday the inflation rate for this year was expected to be 9-10 percent, the first official indication the figure could reach double digits, prompting some to speculate the central bank might have to hike rates soon. 

 But the rupiah's gains could be capped by another rumour that the IMF would delay the next disbursement of loans to Indonesia because the government missed a number of key reform commitments, dealers said. 

 "The talk in the market now is that the funds will not be blocked but it will be delayed. It won't be disbursed in December," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 However, a senior IMF official told Reuters in Jakarta earlier this week that its $5.0 billion assistance programme to Indonesia was not under threat and the next letter of intent paving the way for future loans was being drawn up. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 Market players were set to test the Taiwan dollar's support of 33.10, but were likely to meet with stiff resistance from the central bank. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore had said the bank was believed to have made up 50 to 70 percent of the daily total volumes in the onshore foreign exchange market this week. 

 Dealers in Taipei have, however, noted that foreign institutional investors have bought a net total of T$13.614 billion of local stocks over the past eight sessions, lending some support to the local dollar. 

 But sentiment towards the local dollar remains poor as the key technology sector was expected to see slowing growth in the new year. Microsoft's profit warning was likely to send new jitters through Taiwan's retail investor-driven stock market. 

 Dealers in both Hong Kong and Singapore have said the market believed that only the central bank's intervention was propping up the local dollar in the face of slowing growth, ongoing problems in the banking sector, and doubts over government policies. 

 They also have said higher rates across the board in the NDF market accurately reflected the sentiment, as the spot rate has not been allowed to move according to market forces. 

 Short-term NDF rates have also risen recently as U.S. dollar buying continues in the market. The one-month Taiwan dollar NDF was at 0.32/37 and the three-month was at 0.510/610. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was driven up by tight liquidity in the market which forced players to unwind long dollar/baht positions. 

 Although some participants sold forward contracts on rally to cash in on recent gains, baht demand and hence its funding cost, remain high, particularly in the offshore market. 

 The one-month forward rate in the offshore market rose to 10.7/20.7 satang per dollar in early trade compared with -7.0/-3.0 satang last Friday. 

 The onshore rate of the same tenor edged up to -4/-2 satang from -4.5/-4.0 satang late on Thursday. 

 The bankruptcy court is expected to reconvene on Friday to decide on a landmark $3.8 billion debt restructuring plan for Thai Petrochemical Industry Plc . 

 The delay was caused by a petition by TPI founder and chief executive Prachai Leopairatana, who is bitterly opposed to the debt plan, to replace the judges presiding over the case. 

 The restructuring deal involves converting nearly $800 million in unpaid interest to a 75 percent stake for creditors which include Thailand's largest commercial bank Bangkok Bank . 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was supported on profit-taking in U.S. dollars led by some foreign banks, but dealers said fears of U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) at around 1.7350 were likely to cap gains. 

 Dealers have cited local banks buying U.S. dollars on behalf of the MAS to temper recent gains in the Sing that pushed it to a five-week high of 1.7300 last Tuesday. 

 Analysts said the MAS had not changed its policy of "gradual appreciation" of the Sing against the undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies that it uses to manage the exchange rate. 

 But it appeared the authority might be concerned about the Sing dollar appreciating excessively against the basket, given the recent declines in the yen, won and the Taiwan dollar. 

 Japan, Korea and Taiwan are competitors of Singapore's major exports. 

 But dealers said overnight gains in the euro, which also had a significant weighting in the basket, could prompt the MAS to ease off its pressure on the Sing dollar. 

 Another factor that could help the Sing dollar was an early announcement by Taiwan's United Microelectronics Corp which said it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Infineon Technologies AG to jointly invest US$3.6 billion to build a 12-inch wafer plant in Singapore. 

 Infineon is a microchip unit of Germany's Siemens . 

 On the macro front, October retail sales data is expected at 1030 GMT. The September retail sales index rose 16.9 percent on the year, and was up 5.5 percent over August 2000. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso moved in a narrow range on the wrong side of the 50 to the dollar mark in early trade ahead of a widely expected central bank decision to cut key overnight rates. 

 Dealers said most players were expecting the central bank to cut its overnight borrowing and lending rates by another 50 basis points, after lowering them by a total of 100 basis points in the past two weeks. 

 But a deeper cut could result in volatile moves, they added. 

 "The market is already pricing in slowing down of overseas workers' remittances to normal pace by the end of this month. In this situation a bigger cut can result in a sharp fall of the peso," a dealer at a European bank in Manila said. 

 Remittances from overseas workers usually peak ahead of the Christmas holidays. 

 The central bank had hinted earlier in the week it was ready to trime overnight rates by another 50-100 basis points. The overnight borrowing rate now stands at 14 percent and the lending rate at 16.25 percent. 

 The rates were jacked up by four percentage points when the peso slid to 51.95 to the dollar at the height of the political scandal surrounding President Joseph Estrada. 

 Dealers said the market was likely to trade within a range of 50.00-50.50 on low volumes in the absence of any surprises as most players were on the sidelines ahead of the holidays and as Estrada's impeachment trial drags on.

title: Emerging  FX  - Choppy waters lie ahead.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 14 (Reuters) - North Asian currencies were under pressure late on Thursday, but analysts said the rest of the region would soon feel the heat from slowing external demand. 

 Technology-driven stock markets in Taiwan and Korea slipped on the back of the Nasdaq's fall as investors fretted over the prospect of dwindling earnings in the technology sector. 

 Major currency markets shrugged off the official concession by Democrat presidential hopeful Al Gore and focused on the Japanese economy, which was showing signs of floundering. 

 Japan's Economic Planning Agency said the country's gross economic product during the July-September period fell 0.3 percent on quarter under an old calculation method. 

 A report in major Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun that said the agency was likely to make such a revision had been weighing on the yen earlier in the day. 

 The yen suffered another blow from data showing Japanese corporate bankruptcies rose for the 13th straight month in a row. 

 On top of the weaker yen and slowing U.S. economic growth, regional markets are also facing a slew of homegrown political and economic problems. 

 And analysts warn that with slowing external demand, Asia's domestic developments will take centre stage. "As global support for Asian economic growth subsides, the internal stories have moved front and center," said Merrill Lynch in its latest monthly publication on the regional economic outlook. 

 While Northeast Asia faces doubts over corporate and financial reforms, as well as political uncertainty in Taiwan's case, the Philippines, Thailand and Indonesia remain challenged by "the most difficult domestic economic and political stories," it added. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso slipped to the wrong side of 50 as unexpected local corporate demand for dollars emerged in a fairly illiquid market. 

 Dealers in Manila said the market had assumed most local companies had already filled their dollar requirements ahead of year-end. However, they said the dollar buy orders were small, and the peso stayed within a tight range of 49.95-50.15. 

 They also said the market was starting to price in another 50 basis point cut in the central bank's key overnight rates. The bank hinted earlier in the week it was ready to take the overnight rates down another 50-100 basis points, having cut a total of 100 basis points in the past two weeks. 

 While dealers said the peso was unlikely to react to a 50 basis point cut, it may buckle a little more if the bank lowers rates by 100 basis points. The overnight borrowing and lending rate were jacked up four percentage points when the peso slid to 51.95 to the dollar at the height of the political scandal surrounding President Joseph Estrada. 

 Dealers said the market was sluggish as most investors sit out on the sidelines ahead of the holidays and as Estrada's impeachment trial continues. 

 But problems in the economy continued to loom over markets. Finance Secretary Jose Pardo said earlier in the day the government had secured a $200 million loan to help bridge the country's huge budget deficit. He later retracted that comment, saying he had made a mistake. 

 The budget deficit for full year 2000 is expected to come in between 110 billion and 120 billion pesos against an earlier target of 62.5 billion pesos. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The U.S. dollar failed to extend gains beyond 1.7400 despite talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened overnight to curb the local currency's recent sharp rise. 

 A rise above 1.7400 was met promptly by dollar profit taking from corporate and interbank players, dealers said. 

 "I guess the market is a tad long on dollars and players are unwinding their positions," said a dealer at an Asian bank in Singapore. "But I don't think market players will push (the Sing dollar) above 1.7350-1.7370 where the MAS was rumoured to have intervened." 

 In the money market, the one-month forward rate was slightly firmer at -55.5/-54.5 while the six-month rate was quoted at -299/-294. 

 On the macro front, the government said the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 2.5 percent in September, down from 3.5 percent a year ago. 

 It said overall employment ws expected to grow in 2001 but at a slower pace, given that economic growth was likely to moderate next year. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won weakened past the 1,200 mark on a fall in the local equity market amid worries about tech-sector earnings, declines in the yen and on growing evidence of a slowing U.S. economy. 

 But dealers said some reprieve was likely from an expected overnight relief-rally on Wall Street after the five-week-long dispute over the U.S. presidential polls came to an end. 

 "There may be a relief-rally in U.S. stocks and that could provide some support...but judging by the reaction markets have given so far, it isn't going to be anything big or lasting," a chief dealer of a European bank in Singapore said. 

 Japan is Korea's closest export competitor while the U.S. is its biggest export market. The export sector, dominated by electronics, accounts for a large portion of Korean GDP. 

 The won was hit early after Korea's largest commercial bank Kookmin Bank said it had suspended merger talks with Housing and Commercial Bank in the face of worker protests and the threat of a strike by unions. 

 Analysts said the suspension highlighted impediments to Korea's corporate and financial restructuring drive. 

 Investors fear slowing growth and exports would test the government's resolve to go ahead with tough reforms already facing opposition from traditionally strong labour unions. 

 In the non-deliverable forward market, three-month NDFs firmed to 1,201/1,202 and six-month forwards to 1,201.5/1,202.5. Both were at 1,194/95 earlier in the day. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar firmed on the back of heavy intervention by the central bank. 

 Dealers estimated that the bank spent around $250 million in the early part of the session to keep the local dollar above the 33.10 level. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore said the market was speculating that the bank's dollar selling activity had accounted for 50 to 70 percent of the daily turnover during the week. 

 The U.S. bank dealer said there was U.S. dollar buying interest on the NDF market in the three-month and six-month tenors, adding that buyers included "everybody who doesn't believe the CBC (Central Bank of China)." 

 Three-month Taiwan dollar NDFs were at 0.58/61 and the six-month stood at 0.77/80. 

 Craig Chan, currency strategist at ING Barings in Hong Kong, said the central bank had little choice but to let the currency depreciate as Taiwan faces slowing exports and economic growth. 

 He said higher NDF rates reflected offshore investors' belief that the spot rate was not trading according to market forces, and they would ease when the spot Taiwan dollar was allowed to depreciate. 

 In addition to concerns over slowing growth, investor sentiment towards Taiwan has been battered by worries over increasing bad loans in the banking system. Analysts said the government had been unable to effectively address the problem. 

 Moreover, a weaker yen was also pressuring the local dollar. The cross rate between the yen and Taiwan dollar has crept up and stood at 3.3979 late Thursday. Analysts said the higher cross rate reinforced the view that the central bank would allow the local dollar to depreciate. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht perked up, riding a liquidity squeeze and caution about the central bank's vigilance in enforcing forex trading rules regarding baht credits to offshore players. 

 Baht funding costs ticked up in both offshore and onshore markets, with one-month offshore forwards quoted at 7.0/17.0 satang per dollar, up sharply from around -7.0/-3.0 satang late last week. 

 Onshore rates of the same tenor rose to -4.50/-4.0 satang from -5.50/-5.0 satang earlier. 

 The market is likely to focus on a bankruptcy court ruling on Thai Petrochemical Industry's $3.8 billion debt restructuring deal on Friday after repeated delays. 

 "If it's delayed again or if the court rules in favour of TPI, the baht will be hit. But the impact now might be limited given the market is being driven by year-end liquidity. People are also cautious about the central bank's close monitoring," said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "But after the New Year holiday, when people return from vacation and when political uncertainty is heightened ahead of the elections, this factor will add heavily to the baht's downward bias," he said. 

 On the political front, Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai narrowed the gap on front-runner Thaksin Shinawatra ahead of the January 6 general election, but a large chunk of voters remain undecided. 

 The poll by ABAC, a Bangkok university, showed telecoms tycoon Thaksin still in front, backed by 28.2 percent of 4,177 Bangkok respondents compared with 29.9 percent in the previous poll in October. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah traded in a narrow range for most of the day with the downside capped by sporadic dollar-selling by state banks, suspected to be acting on behalf of the central bank. 

 "It has been a very quiet day and even customer flows were very small and whatever pressure those flows created was absorbed by state banks," a dealer at a European bank in Jakarta said. 

 The dealer said state banks were spotted selling dollars at different levels from 9,440 to 9,410 and could have contributed over 10 percent of about $150 million turnover in the market. 

 "In the absence of most players, small amounts of dollar sales from state banks tend to force players to square long dollar positions," the dealer said. 

 He said with holidays approaching, the market was likely to get thinner and calmer by the day. 

 Dealers said the market ignored a survey published by state-owned Danareksa Research Institute showing consumer confidence grew almost nine percent in Indonesia last month. 

 The monthly survey of 1,724 respondents said the consumer confidence index increased 8.8 percent to 56.8 from October, but pointed out that this did not reverse the downtrend in the index over the past six months.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Won Back On Downward Track
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar advanced decisively against the South Korean won Thursday, while other Asian currencies finished mixed during regional trading hours. 

 Resisting the dollar's upward movement were the New Taiwan dollar, Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht, which strengthened modestly. 

 The won continued its downward slide after rallying against the dollar earlier in the week. The U.S. currency closed above the psychologically important KRW1,200 level for the first time in six sessions. 

 A softening yen, lower local share prices and onshore dollar demand by banks and importers combined to pressure the won, dealers said. 

 The dollar's uptrend against the won "remains intact," UBS Warburg said in a note to clients, noting that the U.S. currency is in high demand by offshore participants in the market for non-deliverable forward contracts. 

 At the close of trading the dollar was quoted at 1,202.0 won, up from KRW1,193,8 at Wednesday's finish. 

 The Philippine peso weakened slightly, but finished within its trading range of recent weeks. 

 Although investor concerns about political stability in the Philippines has kept pressure on the peso, the currency is likely to remain wedged between 49.3 and 50.5 per dollar until there is a clearer idea of the outcome in President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial on corruption charges, DBS Bank said in a research report. 

 The dollar closed at PHP50.085 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP49.975 and the end of trading Wednesday. 

 Philippine prosecutors and lawyers for Estrada Thursday grappled over the issue of whether to admit into evidence bank documents, including a PHP142 million check allegedly used to buy a mansion in Manila used by an Estrada mistress. 

 An expected central bank cut in short-term interest rates of between 50 and 100 basis points Friday should have little impact on the peso, DBS said. 

 The U.S. dollar rose against its Singapore counterpart after suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in offshore markets overnight to restrain the local currency's recent appreciation. 

 Near the end of Asian trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7392, up from S$1.7374 late Wednesday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened stronger and short-covering by Singapore-based market participants and companies pushed the currency to an intraday high of S$1.7410 in early trading. 

 However, the U.S. currency eased below the S$1.7400 level on subsequent selling by some U.S. investors. 

 The New Taiwan dollar benefited from central bank support and squaring of U.S. dollar long-positions by corporations. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.077, compared with NT$33.081 the day before. 

 The central bank allowed the U.S. dollar to venture as high as NT$33.130 in the morning session before intervening to cap it at NT$33.100 in afternoon trading. The central bank sold a total of US$150 million to support the local dollar, dealers estimated. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was supported by dollar selling by state banks, but dollar demand by local companies limited the rupiah's gains. 

 After falling to an intraday low of IDR9,400, the dollar closed at IDR9,430 in Asian trading, down slightly from IDR9,450 late Wednesday. 

 State banks, most notably Bank Mandiri (D.MAN) and Bank Rakyat Indonesia (P.RKI), actively sold the dollar. Dealers believed they were selling on behalf of the central bank to ease the pressure on the rupiah. 

 The Thai baht edged higher as the threat of an offshore swap squeeze on the currency kept speculators out of the market. Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted at THB43.495 in late Asian trading, down from THB43.625 late Wednesday. 

 The dollar could get a boost against the baht Friday if Thai Petrochemical Industry PCL's (H.TPE) debt restructuring plan is further delayed or HSBC Holdings PLC's (HBC) bid to buy several nationalized banks fails.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late On Yen Fall; Won Hard Hit
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Japanese yen's slump to its lowest level this year dealt a blow to most Asian currencies late Wednesday, with the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar feeling the brunt of the pain, dealers said. 

 While all the other regional currencies were weaker, the Indonesian rupiah bucked the trend, thanks to support from local state banks, dealers said. 

 A weaker-than-expected quarterly tankan survey of business sentiment by Bank of Japan and a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that all but sealed the election of George W. Bush as the next U.S. president sent the yen reeling to a year low of Y112.55 against the dollar, dealers said. 

 Around 0750 GMT (2:50 a.m. EST), the dollar was at Y112.43, up sharply from Y111.47 late Tuesday in New York. 

 The U.S. Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Florida Supreme Court to order a manual recount of thousands of ballots, likely sounding the death knell for Vice President Al Gore's presidential hopes. 

 "The weaker yen hit sentiment toward the Korean won and the Taiwan dollar," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Strong gains on the Seoul bourse early Wednesday initially failed to counter the downward pressure on the won, which yielded to an offshore assault from the non-deliverable forward market, dealers said. 

 "Despite foreign equity purchases and a nearly 3% rally in the Kospi stock index, the Korean won attached itself to the yen and headed lower," said Peter Redward, a currency strategist at Deustche Bank. 

 He noted, however, that the dollar failed to make a sustainable break through the psychologically important KRW1,200 level. 

 After pulling back from around the 1,200 won mark on long dollar liquidation, the U.S. currency was at KRW1193.30, up from KRW1,190.30 Tuesday. 

 Heavy intervention by Taiwan's central bank, which accounted for close to half of the session's volume, helped alleviate the stress on the local dollar coming from the floundering yen, dealers said. 

 After languishing closer to NT$33.09-NT$33.10 against the U.S. currency most of the day, the New Taiwan dollar ended slightly firmer as the central bank stepped up its defense of the currency toward the close of the session, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$33.081, down marginally Tuesday's close of NT$33.088. Trading volume was US$535.5 million. 

 The dollar's gains against the yen and the euro, combined with onshore dollar demand cast a shadow on the Singapore dollar and the Thai baht, dealers said. Offshore interest in the latter currency remained sparse following the Thai government's recent crackdown on speculative trading in the baht. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was at S$1.7374, up from S$1.7347 late Tuesday. 

 Suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore Tuesday around S$1.7320, to curb the local dollar's recent strength, also contributed to the reversal in the local dollar's recent ascent, dealers said. 

 Mohi-uddin at UBS Warburg said this should keep the U.S. dollar supported above S$1.7300, since the MAS policy is for a gradual appreciation of the local currency. 

 DBS Bank said in a report Wednesday that the de facto central bank may find it "more acceptable in the current environment, to have the U.S. dollar near or even above S$1.7400, instead of S$1.7300." 

 The Singapore bank said that before the Singapore dollar can resume its recent rise, the euro must follow through on its recent rebound above US$0.88, the dollar needs to fall below Y110 and sentiment must improve for "politically troubled" currencies, such as the Indonesian rupiah and the Philippine peso. 

 In the Thai currency market, the dollar edged up to 43.625 baht, from THB43.520 late Tuesday. 

 The Philippine peso closed lower in thin trade, with the market cautiously tracking President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial. 

 The dollar closed at PHP49.975 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP49.850 at the previous close. 

 Resisting the downward pressure from its regional peers, the rupiah was stronger, thanks to dollar selling by state banks, believed to be acting on behalf of the central bank. 

 The dollar was at 9,440 rupiah, down from IDR9,510 late Tuesday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Firmer, but pitfalls remain.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were generally a touch firmer late Thursday but analysts warn the slight gains may be deceptive with many risks still lurking. 

 Slower U.S. growth, political uncertainty, and stalled corporate and economic reform are all affecting regional markets. 

 The impeachment trial of President Joseph Estrada began late Thursday in Manila, where the markets have buckled under the recent political uncertainty and signs of a flagging economy. 

 Thailand will hold a general election on January 6, and doubts persist over the future of Indonesia's president. 

 For the time being, central bank intervention or unwinding of long dollar positions ahead of the year-end in illiquid markets will give regional currencies a temporary boost. 

 The firmer yen and stronger euro also gave regional currencies a lift. 

 Looking ahead, the market will be closely monitoring U.S. jobs data and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Friday. Greenspan hinted at an end of monetary tightening cycle earlier in the week. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar spiked up to post a high of 1.7340 in late trade on what dealers said was dollar/Sing selling by some American banks. 

 But strong demand for the U.S. dollars from local corporates below the 1.7350 mark pulled the Sing back to around 1.7360-70, still better than its day's low of 1.7430. 

 Some dealers attributed the sharp move to unwinding of long U.S. dollar positions in response to Wednesday's measures by Monetary Authority of Singapore to encourage foreign investors to invest or issue debt in local fixed income market. 

 The MAS said banks could now lend to non-residents for investment in the country, saying the move would help broaden investor base for Sing dollar assets. 

 It also allowed banks to make transactions in Singapore dollar currency options with other banks and financial institutions in Singapore. 

 "Sell on rumours and buy on news, that is how the market played the MAS announcement but some players might have been caught long or short," chief dealer of a European bank said. 

 He said the MAS announcement has disappointed those who were betting on broader liberalisation of Singapore's exchange rate policy. 

 Singapore manages the exchange rate against an undisclosed trade-weighted currency basket and in the past several months has repeatedly indicated its desire of an appreciation of the Sing against that basket. 

 But dealers said realisation in the market was growing that the measures were positive in the long-run. 

 Other dealers said low trading volumes exaggerated the move. 

 "Remember half of the market participants are on year-end holidays so the volume is thin and that exaggerates any move," a dealer said. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won strengthened on exporters' dollar-selling in otherwise thin, dull trade. 

 Dealers said moves in the currency are often exaggerated in illiquid markets, and there has been little interest in the won market with the lack of fresh incentives and year-end approaching. 

 As expected, the Bank of Korea kept its key overnight rate at 5.25 percent. Central bank governor Chon Chol-hwan said it would consider cutting interest rates when inflationary pressures ease and financial markets stabilise. 

 Chon also warned of an economic slowdown given shrinking exports earnings. According to Rebecca Patterson, a currency strategist at JP Morgan, that isn't the end of the challenges Korea faces. 

 "The market has priced in to a degree slowdowns in both Korea and the U.S. But we have more room to go. This isn't over, in Korea we're going to get more restructuring hiccups, more labour union strikes, and confidence, if you look at consumer or business surveys, is tanking," she said. 

 JP Morgan recently revised its won forecast to 1,270 by the end of the first quarter next year. 

 Patterson also noted that given a more competitve export sector, Korean authorities are also keeping a close eye on the yen/won cross-rate, seeking a range of 10.25-11.50. It stood at 10.81 late Thursday. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was steady in late trade despite a rash of bad news for the island's economy. 

 Dealers said foreign-equity related inflows and exporters boosted the local dollar. But analysts have said the currency will weaken as economic growth slows. 

 Taiwan's November trade surplus came in far below expectations, falling 45.6 percent on year to US$774.6 million. The Ministry of Finance later said it expected full year 2000 exports to grow slower than previously expected due to a global economic slowdown. 

 The data comes on the heels of a revision of Standard & Poor's outlook for Taiwan to negative from stable because of delayed economic reforms as the political impasse between the president and legislature drags on. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank said its foreign exchange reserves dipped in November to US$108.231 billion due to an increase in private foreign currency deposits. Analysts said bank's defence of the local dollar might also have had something to do with the fall. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht shuffled towards the higher end of a narrow 43.49-43.65 range in line with firmer regionals. 

 But dealers in Bangkok said volumes were negligible, with only a few local corporates and banks in the market. Offshore players continue to shy away from the baht market following the central bank's clampdown on speculation. 

 However, analysts expect the baht to see further weakness in the run-up to the election and in its aftermath. 

 "The new government will likely be even weaker than the current. You have an economy that is slowing, reforms that are going slowly, and yields which are still low," JP Morgan's Patterson said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was helped up, after it hit a day low of 9,635, by state-run banks which dealers said were active on behalf of the central bank. 

 "It was basically the state banks...yes they were selling dollars on behalf of the central bank. They were selling dollars all along from 9,620 to 9,570," said chief dealer of a U.S. bank in Jakarta. 

 He said some dollar supply, close to rupiah's lows, was also seen coming from exporters. 

 Talk of central bank intervention sent Jakarta-based foreign banks and Singapore-based players scrambling to unwind their long dollar positions. 

 But dealers said importers and local corporates took advantage of the easing dollar and came in to support the dollar at around 9,550 level. 

 Dealers said as soon as the market senses lack of state banks' support, the rupiah would be back beyond the 9,600 level. 

 Dealers said the market was closely watching developments surrounding the controversial revamping of the central bank. 

 They said the Parliament that would go into recess from Saturday has yet to approve proposed changes in central bank laws aimed at making the bank more accountable and empower government to sack the institution's top officials. 

 The proposed changes have come under criticism as an attempt to bring under government control an institution that is guaranteed wide-ranging independence under existing laws. 

 The central bank governor on Wednesday resumed control of his office after nearly six months detention on charges of corruption. 

 Sjahril Sabirin's release from house arrest and his return to the central bank has raised fears of fresh rift between President Addurrahman Wahid and the bank. 

 Indonesia's chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said on Thursday changes to the central bank laws are expected to be approved by the parliament in January or February. 

 He also said all members of the board of governors should resign when the changes stand approved. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso edged down in late trade but moved in a tight range through most of the day with most players stayed away from the market as the impeachment trial against President Joseph Estrada began. 

 Dealers said the other factor that kept players cautious was Friday's weekly meeting of the central bank's monetary board. 

 The central bank has hinted earlier in the week of a cut in excessively high key domestic interest rates to help boost weakening economic growth. 

 Dealers said a cut in rates was widely expected, after a 50 basis point cut earlier in the week. 

 "But the uncertainty is on how deep the cut will be. So people are taking a cautious view," a dealer at a European bank in Manila said. 

 Some dealers said the central bank taking advantage of a relatively quite day was buying dollars to replenish its reserves.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mostly easier, North Asia worst hit.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and Taiwan dollar were expected to stay in the limelight in Asian currency markets on Thursday after recent substantial losses. 

 Dealers said the dollar's strength against major currencies, bolstered by better-than-expected third quarter gross domestic product numbers, would also weigh on the regional currencies. 

 There had been some speculation that U.S. third quarter GDP growth would fall below two percent, but the figure came in at 2.4 percent, though it was still the slowest pace of growth in four years. 

 Concerns over a domestic loan scandal in Korea, Nasdaq-inspired losses in local stocks and jitters over the corporate sector and economic outlook are weighing against the won. 

 In Taiwan, dealers expected some technical rebound after the local dollar hit a 19-month low of 33.20, but any reprieve could be brief as pressure from political and banking sector worries rose. 

 Southeast Asian currencies, on the other hand, were relatively subdued. 

 The Philippines' financial markets are closed for Bonifacio Day, and will resume trading on Friday. Dealers expected offshore trade to be thin in the light of political uncertainties. 

 The Thai baht was also expected to have a subdued session as offshore players remained cautious although onshore banks had cleared gridlock in the past week. 

 The problem was triggered by banks scrambling to pare credits to offshore counterparties down to the central bank's limit of 50 million baht, just before the central bank stepped in to strictly enforce existing curbs and imposed a hefty penalty on those who violated them. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was holding just the right side of 33 per dollar and some dealers said they suspected the central bank was defending the unit. 

 With the Nasdaq hitting its lowest close in over a year, Taiwan's heavyweight technology stocks were under assault, though buying from government-linked funds kept the benchmark index cushioned. 

 Losses in the stock market and an expected slowdown in Taiwan's economic growth have been weighing on the Taiwan dollar. 

 It slid to its lowest since April 1999 on Wednesday, when the central bank stepped back from its defence of the 33 level. 

 Analysts say the bank has little choice but to allow a steady depreciation in order to compete amid slowing exports demand. 

 Some dealers said with the more pessimistic forecasts for Taiwan's economy, offshore players have been actively buying dollars in the non-deliverable forward market. 

 One-month dollar/Taiwan dollar NDF points were at 0.23/27 while six-month NDFs were at 0.43/47. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah slipped past the 9,500 per dollar level to lows last seen on November 21 on active corporate demand for dollars. Its losses were exaggerated by thin trading volumes and dealers expected it to trade in a 9,500-9,600 range on Thursday. 

 A convincing break of 9,570, which has been repeatedly tested but not breached since October 1998, would expose the rupiah to severe declines, chartists said. 

 The market seemed to have ignored a rosy forecast by the government which on Wednesday revised the 2001 target for growth to five percent from the original forecast of 4.5 percent. 

 But it also revised up its 2001 inflation forecast to 7.2 percent from 7.0 percent earlier. 

 In the banking sector, the government said on Wednesday it would issued so-called staple bonds on December 8 which banks can swap with their recapitalisation bonds, some of them at a higher rate. 

 The move is to stimulate investor interest and help calm fears of looming fiscal trouble when the recapitalisation bonds - whose rates are too low to encourage a secondary market - start to mature in a few years. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar eased in line with regional currencies, though dealers said the market was reluctant to test the 1.7600 level due to intervention fears. 

 They also said local banks sold the U.S. dollar around the 1.7564 level overnight, pushing the Sing dollar to a high of 1.7539. 

 The Sing dollar is managed against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, and often moves in line with regional currencies. A weaker yen and baht specifically were weighing on the Sing dollar. 

 Despite fears of intervention by the powerful Monetary Authority of Singapore, analysts said the Sing dollar would grind lower as regional currencies and the euro remained fragile.

title: Emerging  FX -Weak bias persists, won wins reprieve.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Friday, with some winning a reprieve from recent losses, though domestic political uncertainties and a hazy economic outlook still held sway. 

 With U.S. markets closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, firm DRAM prices and a rise in Nasdaq futures helped most Asian equity markets post gains and supported their currencies. 

 The Korean won, battered in the past few days, saw the most volatile session in the region. 

 It slid through the 1,200 psychological support and later, helped by stock market gains and some positive news on the political front, made its way back up wiping out the early losses. 

 Analysts said more weakness was expected in the coming months as growth and exports were likely to slow down throughout the region, while political unease in several countries was likely to stretch well into the first quarter of next year. 

 A broadly stronger U.S. dollar was also likely to keep the regionals under pressure. 

 The dollar held near nine-month highs against the yen and close to one-month highs against the euro . 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won rebounded from a 13-month low of 1,207 on profit-taking on a heavily overbought U.S. dollar and on news of an end to the political stalemate delaying a key reform bill. 

 Dollar/won came off from overbought levels of 94.5, not seen since January 1998, on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 Dealers said the profit-taking in dollars got a further boost after the main Korean opposition party decided to end a parliamentary boycott and support a government bill for 40 trillion won in public funds for financial sector reforms. 

 A 3.21 percent rise in the KOSPI on the back of technology stocks also helped sentiment in the forex market. 

 But analysts said worries about the fate of the restructuring drive amid threats of a nationwide labour strike on December 5 would cap won gains. 

 And the troubled Daewoo Motor was again facing insolvency after it failed to convince its labour union to agree on job cuts as part of a rehabilitation plan. 

 "The Korean won remains vulnerable given the backdrop of corporate and financial restructuring uncertainties and heavy dollar buying by oil importers," said Standard Chartered in a weekly research note. 

 The bank cut its six-month forecast for the won to 1,380 from 1,150 and said a break of 1,200 would set it on track for a near-term test of the 1,230-1,250 area. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The Thai baht failed to firmly break through 43.50 resistance, though dollar selling from U.S. investment banks rescued it from a low of 43.97. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said the selling pressure on the dollar from offshore players caught short on the baht to fund forward positions was still evident. However, they added that pressure was expected to taper off next week. 

 One-month offshore forwards were at 7.0/15.0 satang to the dollar at 0819 GMT against 5.0/10.0 satang earlier in the day. 

 With importers' dollar-buying keeping the dollar buoyed, a dealer at a local bank in Bangkok said 43.40 was strong resistance for the baht. 

 He added that with currencies buckling in North Asia, as well as the weaker yen, the baht was likely to fall towards the 44 level in the short term. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was holding comfortably away from the 33 level, with a little help from the central bank. 

 The currency opened stronger after closing at a 19-month low on Thursday, but then quickly headed south. Dealers in Singapore said the central bank came into the market in full force at 32.99, hauling the Taiwan dollar back onto its feet. 

 They added that given the heavy intervention, estimated at $150-$250 million, local players in Taipei decided to take profit on the dollar's rise. 

 But analysts say the cards are stacked against the Taiwan dollar. Besides negative external factors such as a slowing U.S. economy, a downturn in the electronics cycle and a weaker yen, Taiwan is dealing with a raft of domestic woes. 

 Among them are political squabbling between the DPP president and the KMT-dominated parliament and rising bad loans. 

 Standard Chartered said it now expected the Taiwan dollar to hit 35 in the next six months, though the central bank was likely to draw a line in the sand around 33 in the near term. 

 Third-quarter gross domestic product data was expected later on Friday. Analysts polled by Reuters expected third quarter GDP to have expanded by 6.29 percent on the year. SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was back near its day lows of 1.7592 per dollar again after rebounding earlier to around 1.7560 on dollar profit-taking and a large Sing dollar order from a U.S. bank. 

 Dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence despite the Sing dollar's overnight decline past a longstanding support of 1.7575/80 where the Monetary Authority of Singapore is believed to have intervened in the past. 

 Analysts said recent weakness in the yen, euro and regional currencies, which are believed to be components in Singapore's trade-weighted basket, might be making the authorities more tolerant of a weaker Sing dollar. 

 UBS Warburg said in a daily research note that Singapore's consumer price index for October had also posted a lower than expected 1.8 percent year-on-year rise, suggesting inflation was not a pressing concern. 

 "...fears about the MAS intervening to bolster the Sing dollar (and hence monetary policy) seem unjustified at present. As such we look for dollar/Sing to reach 1.7600-1.7650 before the MAS comes in," it said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah fought shy of the 9,500 per dollar level, tracking a tight range between 9,440 and 9,480 amid a lack of fresh leads. 

 The saga over the recapitalisation and board reshuffle at the central bank remained in focus, with players awaiting parliamentary approval of changes to laws governing the bank. 

 Chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said on Thursday that the proposed changes were needed to restore accountability and credibility and were not an attack on the bank's independence. 

 He said the government should have reformed Bank Indonesia before granting it independence a year ago, given its performance record in the aftermath of the crisis. 

 BI deputy governor Achjar Iljas, one of only two deputies who did not resign from the board last week to pave the way for a reshuffle, said the bank needed the backing of parliament and the government to clear the aura of scandal surrounding it and solve its massive debt woes. 

 Analysts said uncertainty over the central bank's role and leadership would only undermine the rupiah if it persisted. 

 Standard Chartered Bank said in a that a break of the 9,570 support, which has been tested but held since October 1998, would establish a 24-month inverted head and shoulders pattern, creating a new weakening trend. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended flat at 49.39 to the dollar in the onshore market after touching a day low of 49.73. 

 Dealers said a lull on the political front ahead of the formal start of President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial had lowered trading interest. 

 "The market is moving on flows alone. There is very little trading interest and even interbank deals are very few," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Manila. 

 Dealers said inflows from overseas workers were supporting the peso while bouts of dollar buying by corporates and foreign banks were capping the upside. 

 They said the dollar purchases by foreign banks were believed to be on behalf of the central bank, which is seen as replenishing foreign reserves spent in defending the peso last month. 

 The Philippine central bank in its weekly monetary board meeting decided not to change key overnight rates, saying the decision to cut rates hinged on November inflation numbers and stability of the peso. 

 November inflation data is due on December 5. 

 The central bank jacked up its overnight rates by four percentage points last month saying it was a temporary measure in defence of the peso.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late On Korean Won Declines
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was lower against the U.S. dollar in late trading Wednesday, tracking developments in the Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar///./// 

 Around 0845 GMT (3:45 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7570, up from S$1.7552 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar had hit a high of S$1.7570 in intraday trading for the second straight day - its highest level since Oct. 31 when it touched S$1.7578. 

 But the small gains turned into losses when the Korean won hit a new year low, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar's recent push toward the S$1.7600 level stirred speculation in the market that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might be prepared to intervene on behalf of the local currency. 

 But analysts said the MAS would probably tolerate the Singapore dollar at current levels because the yen and other regional currencies have also weakened against the U.S. dollar. 

 Yields on Singapore government securities were mixed in light trading, dealers said.
