title: Emerging  FX  - Off recent lows, but outlook bearish.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies managed 

 to stay off their recent lows late on Thursday helped by lack 

 of fresh leads and some technical leverage but analysts said 

 the outlook broadly remains bearish. 

     Mixed equity markets offered little help and firm oil 

 prices, hefty losses in U.S. markets and political worries in 

 the  Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand and Taiwan dampened 

 sentiment. 

     The Korean won probed its eight-month low while the Taiwan 

 dollar lurched slightly higher from 16-month lows it hit on 

 Wednesday. Fears of central bank intervention in both markets 

 kept players on guard. 

     Analysts said overall the region was suffering from lack of 

 investor confidence which deteriorated at a faster pace 

 recently on a worsening global environment. 

     "We are suffering a confidence crisis. Basically we have a 

 weak external environment and a weak domestic environment," 

 said Craig Chan, currency strategist ING Barings in Hong Kong. 

     Chan said high oil prices, volatile U.S. markets and fears 

 of global slowdown in growth led by the U.S. had exposed 

 structural weaknesses in Asian corporate and financial sectors. 

     "We don't see anything that's really going to turn around 

 from now until probably after the first quarter of next year. 

 Domestically there's not going to be anything to impress the 

 markets," he said. 


    The euro	  on Thursday sank to new lows against the



dollar and the yen in Tokyo trade, but clawed off the lows on



fears of intervention.



    The yen	 , helped by euro weakness, managed to keep



the dollar below the 108 level.



    World oil prices held firm on concerns about low U.S.



inventories ahead of the winter.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won rebounded to close unchanged at around its



five-month low after hitting an eight-month trough earlier in



the day.



    Dealers said fears of central bank intervention prompted



players to square their long dollar positions as the currency


reached the 1,142.9 level in the afternoon, its lowest since



February 25.



Analysts said foreign funds' selling in the equity market,



already off by about 50 percent from the 1999 close, weighed on



sentiment.



"Korea is suffering from lack of confidence because



basically we ourselves underestimated the time in which



confidence would be restored in Korea in terms of



restructuring, and that obviously has hit the equity market,"



ING Barings' Chan said said.



Chan said high oil prices and an expected slowdown in



growth of electronic exports was likely to hit Korea's



strongest positive - trade surplus.



    He said the other hit to the surplus was likely to come



from the foreign investment front.



    "There is still excess supply of dollars, it's true from



the balance of payments perspective. But the point is,



portfolio outflows have recently accelerated at such a pace



that obviously it must hit FDI (foreign direct investment) and



the current account surplus," he said.



THAI BAHT



The baht regained some lost ground as selling pressure



eased after a sizeable dollar/baht option expired on Thursday,



dealers in Bangkok and Singapore said.



Dealers said one foreign entity had hedged against its



investment in Thailand by buying an option offering a strike



price of 44 baht per dollar.



"The baht had been under selling pressure in the past few



days partly because of this option. Now, that it expired



without reaching that level, the pressure was off," said a



dealer at a major European bank.



"Some dollar/baht option deals barely affect the market,



but I heard this one was around $200 million...sizeable enough



to move the market," he said.



The baht was also lifted by central bank supportive



remarks, saying the unit would not fall to 44 per dollar and



that it had seen no speculation.



    But the bank again defended its low interest rate policy



which it regarded as crucial in sustaining economic recovery.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Sing dollar stayed clear of its overnight low of



1.7580, as fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of


Singapore (MAS) kept trading tame.



    However dealers said the Sing dollar would likely fall in



the next few sessions as the U.S. dollar continued to tower



over regional currencies.



    They also said the MAS could wait for the rate to shoot up



to 1.76 before intervening in the market, but that no one was



willing to start testing the authority.



     "There's no reason for the Sing dollar to move higher. The



non-oil exports data was dismal, and all the regionals are



down," said a dealer at a European bank.



    Singapore's non-oil domestic exports in September recorded



growth of nearly 12 percent, but below analysts' average



expectation of an 18 percent rise.



    A clean break by the U.S. dollar of 108 against the yen or



further falls in the euro could be a trigger for the Sing



dollar to move lower, he added.



     TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar was hovering above its 16-month closing



low as jitters in the island's stock markets spilled over to



the foreign exchange market.



    After easing its defence of the Taiwan dollar in the



previous session, Taiwan's central bank was back in action on



Thursday. Dealers said it intervened at the opening, pushing



the currency down to 31.50. The move caught many players by



surprise, said a dealer at a U.S. bank.



    Dealers estimate the central bank spent around $200 million



in its intervention on Thursday.



    Meanwhile, the third quarter earnings of Taiwan



Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. , the world's



largest dedicated microchip foundry, beat expectations.



    The company also said its outlook for 2001 remained



positive, which may help calm the nerves of local retail



investors who have been fleeing Taiwan's equity markets.



    Heavy stock losses, triggered by gloomy predictions of a



slowdown in the tech sector and eroding confidence in the



government, have been weighing on the Taiwan dollar.



    INDONESIA RUPIAH	



    The rupiah continued to ignore the downtrend in regional


currencies, and clung to its recent range of 8,800 to 9,000.



    The currency is expected to remain in that range for the



next several sessions. Local companies seeking dollars



dominated trading, as they have for the past few weeks.



    Dealers said they didn't expect any real movement in the



rupiah until the end of the month, when many local companies



had to repay foreign debts.



    News that the Consultative Group on Indonesia had agreed to



lend $5.3 billion to Jakarta failed to move the rupiah. The aid



package was widely expected, and thus already factored into the



market, dealers said.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso retained its bearish tone, hovering around its



record low of 49.00, after the central bank said previously it



had not decided on further measures to prop up the ailing


currency.


Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Thursday



he hoped the pressure on the peso would ease in the next 30-90



days, referring to the forthcoming election in Thailand which



has had unsettling effect on the baht.



Analysts said further downside risks remained intact due to



lack of investor confidence even though the Philippine economy



has performed relatively well this year.



"What is clear is that the peso's weakness is likely to be



fought aggressively due to the debt servicing and sentiment



implications of a weaker peso," said Steve Brice, treasury



economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore.



"In the short-term, the authorities are likely to use



measures that have already been employed - higher interest



rates, tighter reserves requirements and currency intervention


- but more aggressively," he said.



Brice added if those measures failed to stop the peso from



weakening, the market should not rule out more drastic measures



such as capital controls or debt moratorium.

 Despite fears of intervention, analysts said the Monetary Authority of Singapore will likely tolerate some weakening of the local currency, as it maintains a neutral policy stance for the rest of the year. 

 The MAS, which rarely comments on its actions in the foreign exchange market, will likely step in to smooth out any excessive movements in the Singapore dollar, but any intervention isn't expected to be aggressive for the rest of the year, analysts said. 

 Some analysts expect the U.S. dollar to rise to S$1.7600 soon if the MAS sits on the sidelines. 

 Trading in Singapore government bonds was subdued, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Weaker, Led By NT Dlr Drop
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 


   TOKYO -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were weaker late Wednesday,
with the New Taiwan dollar dropping to a new 16-month low late in the
session after the central bank withdrew active support for the local
currency in the foreign exchange market.


 Bucking the downtrend was the Indonesian rupiah, which rose slightly after sovereign donors agreed to provide Jakarta with US$4.8 billion in budget aid for 2001 to plug a fiscal deficit expected to amount to 3.7% of gross domestic product. 

 After spending an estimated US$800 million during the day to defend the New Taiwan dollar, the Central Bank of China - the local central bank - late in the session loosened its grip on the currency, allowing it to fall briefly to NT$32.500 against the U.S. dollar. Traders said the move appeared to signal a shift by the central bank to easier monetary conditions in a bid to stave off a deepening liquidity crunch. A massive outflow of capital from the equities market has tightened liquidity for some sectors of the economy. 

 "It (the central bank) had to do something soon or the economy would likely have landed very, very hard," said a U.S. bank trader in Singapore. 

 The Taiwan Index of stock prices, or Taiex, plunged 4.7% Wednesday to 5,432.23, its lowest close in four and a half years. The index is down 36% so far this year and has plummeted 47% from its high for the year set in February. 

 Simmering political concerns in several Asian nations and a savage drop overnight in prices of U.S. semiconductor issues combined to undermine many stock markets in the region Wednesday. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange's semiconductor index fell 9.4% in a reaction to fresh profit warnings. 

 The U.S. dollar ended domestic trade in Taipei at NT$32.383, up from NT$32.260 a day earlier and marking its highest close since June 1999. 

 The South Korean won slid to its lowest levels since May in early trading, although it managed to pare those losses after the stock market staged a spectacular rebound late in the day following the announcement of stock-supportive measures by the South Korean government. 

 The dollar initially rose as high as KRW1,141.50, its highest level since May 24, as the Korea Stock Exchange buckled at the outset of trade, shedding close to 5% during the morning. But the South Korean currency rebounded smartly at the end of the day, pushing the dollar down to KRW1,136.7 at the close. That was still a higher close for the dollar compared with KRW1,133.20 late Tuesday. 

 The South Korean Ministry of Finance and Economy said that it will support the stock market by providing 1 trillion won in funds to local investment-trust companies through Seoul Guarantee Insurance Co. The government also said it will ease regulations on corporate stock buybacks to help companies support their stock prices. 

 Korea's stock index ended the day 0.3% higher. 

 In Manila, the Philippine peso suffered in response to news that the International Monetary Fund had decided to cancel $300 million in loans to the nation because of Manila's failure to meet fiscal targets attached as conditions for the loan program. That, coupled with a fresh bout of political jitters after opposition politicians submitted an impeachment resolution against President Joseph Estrada, pushed the dollar as high as PHP48.700. 

 The peso later regained some of those losses, with the dollar closing at 48.570 pesos, up from PHP48.300 at the previous close. 

 The impeachment complaint against Estrada accused him of accepting millions of dollars in bribes from gambling operators. 

 "We have yet to see an easing of the political concern. It deepens day by day, mainly due to uncertainties," said a trader from another local bank. 

 "The political scandal is only adding to the gridlock" over the peso, which continues to suffer from concerns over how the government will make up for its lack of funds to cover the gaping fiscal deficit, said Desmond Supple, head of research at Barclays Capital in Singapore. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped late Wednesday as it succumbed to the weakness of its regional counterparts, but the U.S. dollar remained capped below S$1.7570 as market participants were wary of provoking another round of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The de facto central bank was said to have defended the Singapore dollar through several banks between S$1.7560 and S$1.7580 against the U.S. currency last Friday. 

 In late trading, the dollar was at S$1.7560, up from S$1.7533 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 In Bangkok, the dollar rose sharply against the baht after the central bank indicated it remains unconcerned about the weakening of the local currency. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said that the current level of the baht is good for exports and isn't worrisome, as the amount of Thai private sector foreign debt is "very low." 

 "Therefore the low baht will not increase the debt burden of the private sector," he said, adding that there is no need for the BOT to raise benchmark interest rates. 

 Late in the day, the dollar was trading at 43.705 baht, up from 43.365 baht a day earlier. 

 Bucking the overall trend, news that international donors meeting in Tokyo had agreed to go through with the fresh loans to Jakarta - although widely expected - buoyed the rupiah. The dollar stood at 8,875 rupiah in late Asian trading, down from IDR8,895 late Tuesday.

title: MAS Likely To Tolerate Some Singapore Dlr Weakness
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore will likely tolerate some further weakening of the local currency as it maintains a neutral policy stance for the rest of the year, according to analysts. 

 Nonetheless, traders are uneasy about pushing the Singapore dollar much lower, as it hovers near the levels that provoked a suspected intervention by the MAS last week. 

 The MAS, which rarely comments on its actions in the foreign exchange market, would likely step in to smooth out any excessive movements in the Singapore dollar, the analysts say, but any intervention isn't expected to be aggressive. 

 "As long as inflation is contained, they will let it (the Singapore dollar) go," says an economist at an Asian bank, who expects an inflation rate of 1.6% this year. The MAS expects inflation to remain below 2% for the year. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary-policy tool in seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. 

 The Singapore dollar is guided within an undisclosed trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and has remained relatively stable against these currencies. 

 Despite having signaled its preference for a relatively stronger Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis in the coming year, the MAS won't be in a rush to shift to a tightening bias this year, analyst say. 

 "We don't really see any significant pressure on the authority to shift to a tightening stance" for the rest of the year, says David Simmonds, a regional currency strategist at Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank. 

 Higher oil prices, the increasingly cloudy prospects of the electronics industry and political instability in some Southeast Asian countries will continue to cast a shadow over other regional currencies, which in turn will weigh on the Singapore dollar, analysts say. 

 And the pressure from North Asia is also building up. The South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar, which earlier this year stood out as bastions of stability, have recently buckled under the pressure of drooping local equity prices and a surge in oil prices, analysts say. 

 The euro too remains shaky after hitting a record low of $0.8438 last month. 

 "The MAS will have to wait for the dust to settle first before they do anything," says the economist at an Asian bank. 


   Fears Of Intervention Keep US Dlr Below S$1.7570



Fears of intervention by the MAS have kept the U.S. dollar below
S$1.7570 Wednesday, the level that traders speculate could provoke such
a move.



Around 0830 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7560, up from S$1.7533
late Tuesday.



The MAS was suspected of having defended the Singapore dollar through
several banks last Friday above S$1.7560 against the U.S. currency, as
the local unit fell to its lowest level in almost 25 months.



Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg,
says he expects further intervention by the MAS if the U.S. dollar rises
to S$1.7578, the high last Friday before the reported intervention
supported the Singapore currency.



Market participants have been fearful of testing the resolve of the
MAS after it said in late July that it was prepared to allow for a
gradual and modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar against the
currencies of its major trading partners over the coming year to ward
off incipient inflationary pressures.



Since then, the Singapore dollar has appreciated about 1.2% relative
to the currencies of its top-12 major trading partners, as the euro and
other Asian currencies experienced sharp falls against the U.S. dollar,
says the Asian bank economist.



Against the U.S. dollar alone, however, the Singapore dollar has
weakened about 0.6% since the end of July.



Some analysts say it will only be a matter of time before the
Singapore dollar slides to S$1.7600 against its U.S. counterpart, which
was last tested in September 1998, at the height of the regional
financial crisis.



And if the MAS continues to sit on the sidelines, the Singapore dollar
will hit this level "very soon," says the Asian bank economist.



Looking farther ahead, Simmonds of Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank
expects the U.S. dollar to trade around S$1.7500 in a month's time and
around S$1.7400 and S$1.7500 in the next three months, after the bank
lowered its forecasts on the Singapore dollar last week.

title: ANALYSIS-Philippine peso no Pied Piper for regional  FX .
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 17 (Reuters) - With its deepening political crisis and floundering markets, the Philippines is putting up a tough fight for Indonesia's ranking as the least sought-after investor destination in Asia. 

 The peso's almost daily slide to new lows has soured already poor sentiment for other Asian currencies in recent weeks, but analysts see little basis for a widespread knock-on impact. 

 However, with no shortage of domestic worries and the grim backdrop of high oil prices and jittery U.S. stocks, investors have ample reason to stay away from Asia generally, they say. 

 "These currencies obviously are still correlated. But people are not saying that if the Philippine peso goes to 50, by default the baht has to go to 46," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. 

 "That may actually happen, but one doesn't lead to the other. There are domestic factors in Thailand that would lead to the baht weakening, and domestic factors in the Philippines." 

 The peso was hovering around 48.44/50 to the dollar at 0530 GMT, off Monday's all-time low of 49.00, as the threat of another massive interest rate hike held the market in check. 

 The central bank said on Tuesday it had not yet decided on a further tightening after raising overnight rates by 400 basis points and hiking bank reserve requirements twice in the past two weeks. 

 FUTILE EFFORTS? 

 Higher rates and repeated central bank intervention have done little to support the peso as jitters about President Joseph Estrada's gambling payoff scandal stoke pessimism about an ever-expanding fiscal deficit and slowing economy. 

 Estrada, facing calls for his resignation from the predominantly Catholic country's powerful clergy, has said he was ready to face impeachment action over the scandal. 

 Manila markets continue to head south as the saga unfolds, and analysts say the central bank's efforts to shore up the peso have assumed an increasingly desperate tone. 

 "We think the central bank has misjudged market sentiment... Just by imposing higher interest rates, what little foreign investor interest there is around the region may be scared away from the Philippines," said Stanchart's Brice. 

 Analysts say the peso's weakness is being driven by domestic corporate and retail buying of dollars and higher interest rates are only likely to hurt the fragile economy. 

 A number of banks have slashed their end-year peso forecasts in the wake of its sharp drop against the dollar and no sign of a let-up in the gloom. 

 Barclays Capital and JP Morgan are among the more bearish, with an end-2000 forecast of 52. Citibank expects the peso to reach 50.5 on a one-month horizon and Stanchart is looking at 50 over the same period. 

 BAHT EXPOSED 

 So far, the Thai baht has tended to be most susceptible to weakness in the peso as traders link the two currencies due to similarities in their economies. 

 The baht was quoted at 43.33/36 at 0530 GMT, well off Friday's 28-month low of 43.68. 

 But apart from some shared difficulties on the political front, large fiscal deficits and similar status on the technology chain, the Thai economy is more than twice the size of the Philippines in terms of gross domestic product. 

 And Thailand has more than its own share of problems, with elections looming and investors still concerned about the slow pace of financial sector restructuring. 

 Low interest rates and the Thai central bank's hands-off exchange rate policy have also made the baht a prime funding currency, analysts say. 

 "What we have seen in the last several weeks are investors who want to have some short exposure to the region are looking around and finding that negative carries are very high in Indonesia and the Philippines," said Rebecca Patterson, currency strategist at JP Morgan. 

 "The baht is the one outlier. You have lower yield and you have a central bank that has a track record of not intervening nearly as much as the Monetary Authority of Singapore. So I think investors are going to continue using the baht as their vehicle to short," she said.

title: Asia Markets - Revived by Nasdaq, still vulnerable.
text:

    SHORT BAHT



    The weakness in the peso is likely to also drag the Thai



baht lower, with most strategists still recommending their



clients short the baht.



    They said its low yield and the Thai central bank's



hands-off policy made the baht an attractive funding currency.



    "What we have seen in the last several weeks is investors



who want to have some short exposure to the region and are



looking around and finding that negative carries are very high



in Indonesia and the Philippines," Patterson said.



"The baht is the one outlier. You have lower yield. And you



have a central bank that has a track record of not intervening


nearly as much as the Monetary Authority of Singapore," she



said.



    Patterson suggested clients continue to take long Korean



won positions against the baht.



    Salomon Smith Barney, which just revised its three-month



baht forecast to 45 from 44, also suggested that clients long



the dollar against the baht.



    "In terms of positioning, we maintain the view that long



dollar is advisable against Thai baht on a one- to three-month



horizon," said David Simmond, currency strategist at the bank.



    KOREA AT BOTTOM



    Some analysts believed Korean stocks were looking



attractive again, with return on equity (ROE) improving. The



KOSPI has shed around 46.49 percent since the end of



last year.



"We look at corporate balance sheets and corporate ROE to



see whether or not we have seen the return on equity (come



back) in Korea. Actually we find that it has improved



dramatically," said Sadiq Currimbhoy, equity strategist at



Merrill Lynch.



"I have a sense that the market is very oversold. And the



fact we are seeing the return on equity improve going forward,



that means the market is forming a bottom," he said.



Currimbhoy said the country's largest cellular phone



service SK Telecom would be one of a few



telecommunications stocks that would drive the market high up



from its bottom.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; 6th Straight Loss For Peso
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies turned in a mixed performance Monday, with threats of a presidential impeachment in the Philippines continuing to keep the peso on the defensive. 

 The peso slumped for the sixth straight session as President Joseph Estrada braced for possible impeachment proceedings amid allegations he received millions of dollars in gambling kickbacks. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah avoided the peso downdraft and posted marginal gains. In North Asia, the South Korean won strengthened, while falling stock prices pushed the New Taiwan dollar to a 14-month low. 

 Against the peso, the dollar soared to an intraday high of PHP49.000 in early trading before the central bank intervened to support the local currency. The dollar gave up some of its gains, but still managed to close at a new record high of PHP48.670, up from 48.500 late Friday. 

 Estrada, who has denied receiving "even a cent" from illegal gambling, Monday challenged his political opponents to "go ahead with their impeachment." 

 The House of Representatives must investigate any impeachment charges against Estrada. If it finds the charges substantial, it sends them to the Senate, which conducts a trial and decides a verdict. 

 The peso will continue to face selling pressure in the fourth quarter due to the corruption saga, potentially losing another 2% of its value, DBS Bank said in a note to clients. 

 The Thai baht was helped by improving sentiment for regional currencies and forecasts that third quarter earnings at Thai banks will be the best since the Asian financial crisis, traders said. 

 Near the end of Asian trading, the dollar was quoted at THB43.195, down from THB43.575 late Friday. 

 Still, overall market sentiment toward the baht will remain bearish due to political risks associated with general elections, expected in December or early January. 


    The New Taiwan dollar tumbled to 14-month low against the U.S.
dollar as share prices on the Taipei exchange fell to a 20-month low
in late trading.



The U.S. dollar closed at NT$31.990, up from the previous close of
NT$31.920.



The Weighted Price Index of the Taiwan Stock Exchange fell 4.2% as
investors took profit on the bourse's early gains and offloaded tech
shares.



The rupiah rebounded ahead of a meeting of Indonesia's international
donors this week in Tokyo. Indonesia is seeking $4.8 billion in new
funding in 2001 to help bridge its widening budget gap.



The Indonesian currency also got a lift from the strengthening
Singapore dollar and Thai baht, dealers said.



Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at IDR8,875, down from IDR8,922
late Friday.



Dealers said offshore participants unwound their dollar positions, but
dollar bids from state banks prevented the U.S. currency from falling
sharply.



The Singapore dollar was buoyed by the strength in other regional
currencies and by improved sentiment following the Nasdaq's Friday
rebound.



Market players also remained wary of testing the resolve of the
Monetary Authority of Singapore, which is suspected of intervening to
support the local currency Friday after the U.S. dollar rose to the
S$1.7560-S$1.7580 range.



The U.S. dollar was at S$1.7515, in late Asian trading down from
S$1.7545 late Friday.



The South Korean won tracked the Seoul stock market higher.



The dollar finished at 1,127.40 won, down from Friday's close of
KRW1,128.60.



After ending Friday at its lowest finish since February 1999, the
benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index, rose 25.50 points, or
4.86%, to end Monday at 550.10, following a rebound Friday in the Nasdaq
Composite Index and a decline in crude-oil prices.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Baht, Nasdaq Rebound
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was stronger late Monday, finding reprieve from a firmer Thai baht and a rebound on Nasdaq last Friday, as tensions in the Middle East appeared to ease, dealers said. 

 Suspected moves by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in defending the local currency last Friday, at around S$1.7560 to S$1.7580 against the U.S. dollar, also made market participants wary of pushing the Singapore dollar lower, dealers said. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said the MAS has probably drawn a line at S$1.7560. 

 Around 0830 GMT (4:30 a.m. EDT) Monday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7515, down from S$1.7545 late Friday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar had opened at an intraday high of S$1.7535 at the start of Asian trading, but it pulled back to as low as S$1.7505 as the Thai baht rebounded, dealers said. 

 But the Philippine peso's decline to yet another historic low against the U.S. dollar helped the U.S. currency recover some of its lost ground to around S$1.7520, where it lingered most of the day, dealers said. 

 The Philippine currency skidded to a new record low of PHP49 against the U.S. dollar Monday, amid concerns over President Joseph Estrada's hold on power following accusations that he received kickbacks from illegal gambling operations. 

 Despite reports of intervention last Friday, the Monetary Authority of Singapore will likely allow a moderate weakness in the local currency if regional currencies continue to slide, analysts said. The Singapore dollar has been relatively stable compared with the currencies of its major trading partners, they added. 

 "If the regional currencies weaken, there is probably some room to tolerate some Singapore dollar weakness, but not excessively," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank. 

 The government's policy is "probably in neutral mode, with bias towards tightening next year," he added. 

 Yields on benchmark Singapore government bonds were mostly unchanged from late Friday's levels. 

 The yield on the 10-year bond was quoted at 4.41%, unchanged from Friday, while the seven-year paper was one basis point lower at 4.05%. 

 In the interbank market, bids for the overnight rate fell rose to 2.3750%, from 2.7500% on Friday. 


Trading in the money market was subdued amid a dearth of market-moving

title: MAS seen allowing Sing easing despite buying talk.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar's rise from near 25-month lows on Friday sparked talk of central bank intervention, but analysts said regardless of whether it had happened, authorities would tolerate a lower local currency. 

 "They are not averse to a slightly weaker Sing at this time. They just don't want a one-way trade," said Vasan Shridharan, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. 

 Dealers said local banks were seen selling the U.S. dollar near a high of S$1.7575, spurring talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The local bank sales sent the dollar to near S$1.7515 and it was quoted at S$1.7523 late on Friday. 

 "Given the current (weak regional currency) environment, I believe they probably had to come in," said Song Seng Wun, economist at GK Goh Securities. 

 "We ought to have seen the dollar at least at S$1.76," he said, noting falls by the Philippine peso, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah. 

 The three are believed to be in an undisclosed basket of trade-weighted currencies the MAS uses to manage the exchange rate. The U.S. unit makes up some 20 percent of the basket. 

 The 1.76 level to the dollar was last seen during the Asian currency crisis in September 1998. 

 MAS SMOOTHS 

 A MAS spokeswoman said the central bank does not comment on market speculation, but the central bank has said it occasionally does intervene to smooth out excessive volatility. 

 Song said the MAS could allow the Sing dollar to fall to 1.80 to the U.S. unit if declines in regional counterparts continued. 

 The Singapore dollar touched an Asian crisis low of 1.8150. Of Asian currencies affected, it is among the closest to its nadir on a percentage basis. 

 Analysts say the MAS would see limited benefit in trying to aggressively push the Sing dollar higher and noted its relative inaction since July, when it said it was prepared to allow a gradual appreciation. 

 The comments gave an upward jolt to the Singapore dollar that has subsequently been erased. 

 Shridharan, said the weakening occurred because authorities were less worried about inflationary pressure now than in July, while the spectre of a global slowdown had become more menacing. 

 "If you look at recent comments, they don't reckon oil as big a problem as other nations," he said. 

 "The possibility of a global slowdown has been a concern and that possibility has increased." 

 He said the Sing's upside was limited to near 1.7480. 

 GROWTH NOT AN ISSUE 

 Singapore's robust economic growth outlook, officially pegged at near nine percent in 2000 and 5-7 percent next year, is also not forcing the MAS' hand. 

 "Growth is not the primary consideration in monetary policy," said P.K. Basu, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 "It's basically within the range they want it to be... (The Sing's) remained fairly stable against the trade-weighted basket." 

 But Basu said inflation would be an issue for the MAS and a tightening could be expected if the consumer price index continued to see higher month-on-month growth. 

 CPI rose 0.5 percent month-on-month in August and in July. 

 He pegged a year-end rate of 1.72 to the U.S. dollar.

title: Sing dlr docile as  intervention  talk haunts market.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar shuffled along in a narrow range in Friday afternoon trade as fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore left many traders on the sidelines. 

 Dealers said local banks had been seen selling U.S. dollars around the early high of S$1.7575, spurring talk of intervention by the authority. 

 An MAS spokeswoman declined to comment on the speculation, but the quasi central bank has said in the past it would intervene to smooth out any excessive volatility. 

 "I doubt people will be aggressive (in selling Singapore dollars) for a while," said a dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 It was quoted at 1.7533/43 against the U.S. dollar at 0713 GMT, little changed from its late Thursday levels. 

 However, dealers said the local dollar should come under renewed attack as a tricky combination of sinking equities and rising oil prices continued to drag down regional currencies. 

 Over the past two weeks, the Singapore dollar has been weakening alongside the Thai baht and Philippine peso, which are under intense pressure due to domestic political turmoil. 

 In addition, increasing violence in the Middle East has sent crude oil rocketing to prices not seen in 10 years. Most Asian countries, with the exception of Indonesia and Malaysia, are net importers of oil. 

 The MAS said in July it was prepared to allow a gradual, modest appreciation of the Sing dollar on a trade-weighted basis, reminding the market that containing inflation remained a key objective. 

 DBS Bank said in a report the Sing dollar should strengthen to around 1.72 by the end of the fourth quarter, citing strong economic figures, the MAS's desire to cap inflation, and an expected soft landing of the U.S. economy. 

 But the head of treasury at a local bank said a slowdown in the United States was still worrisome for regional economies. 

 With U.S. technology companies issuing profit warnings in recent weeks, he said a possible softening of electronics demand would hurt Singapore's economy, and in turn, its currency. 

 He said the Sing dollar could touch lows of around 1.76, not seen since September 4, 1998, by the end of the year.

title: Intervention  talk keeps Sing dlr from 25-month low.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Talk of intervention helped the Sing dollar rebound from close to a 25-month low of 1.7600 on Friday, but dealers said violence in the Middle East and weakness in other regional currencies would keep the unit under pressure. 

 Dealers said some local banks were spotted selling U.S. dollars around the early high of S$1.7575. 

 The move sparked talk of intervention, and sent players scrambling to cover their short Sing positions, leaving dollar/Sing bid at around 1.7520 at 0235 GMT. 

 "There were some local banks selling U.S. dollars, so it could be on behalf of the authorities," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept to its policy of not commenting on its market operations. 

 "It is Monetary Authority policy not to comment on market rumours," an MAS spokeswoman told Reuters. 

 But the central bank had said in the past that it would intervene to smooth out any excessive volatility. 

 It was last believed to have intervened in the foreign exchange market when the Sing dollar fell to 22-month lows in July. 

 The central bank jolted markets soon after by saying it was prepared to allow a gradual, modest appreciation of the Sing dollar on a trade-weighted basis, reminding traders that containing inflation remained a key objective. 

 The Sing dollar's latest bout of weakness came amid declines in other regional currencies, with the Philippine peso skidding through a series of record lows and the Thai baht at a 28-month trough. 

 Dealers said the fear of intervention would keep players cautious for now, but they expected some spillover from markets panicking around the world on the prospects of the Middle East situation turning into a wider conflict. 

 "Whenever there is talk of war people go for U.S. dollars. So I would say there are more chances of dollar/Sing moving up," the European bank dealer said. 

 Oil prices jumped to decade highs in near-panic trading on Thursday, rocking global markets after violence escalated in the Middle East and peace efforts hit the wall. 

 Technical analysts said the Sing dollar's next support was at 1.7600, a level not seen since September 4, 1998.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Late; Peso Again Leads Falls
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Friday the 13th lived up to its reputation. 

 An escalation of violence in the Middle East rocked global equity markets, ignited a savage oil price rally, and drove all Asian currencies lower. Faced with severe downward pressure, most regional central banks either intervened, or threatened to step into the market to support their local currencies. 

 The Philippine peso led the decliners again, falling for a fifth straight session on a deepening political scandal surrounding allegations President Joseph Estrada received millions of dollars in payoffs from illegal gambling operators. 

 Political instability has triggered capital flight this week from the Philippines, prompting the central bank Thursday to increase its overnight interest rates four percentage points, lifting the headline rate to 15%. 

 Although the peso ended the week at Thursday's all-time intraday low against the dollar of PHP48.500, the rate hike has at least stabilized the currency, which has fallen 6% during the past four weeks, and 17% so far this year. 

 Rising crude prices also hurt the peso. 

 The Philippines like most Asian economies - including South Korea, Thailand and India - is heavily dependent on oil imports for its energy needs. 

 So a surge in oil prices on fears supplies might be interrupted if violence in the Middle East escalates into an all-out war between Jews and Arabs is particularly damaging for the currency. 

 An apparent bombing of the U.K. embassy in Yemen early Friday crystallized those concerns, and some analysts said this could be a precursor to concerted attacks on Western interests. 

 The dollar ended at PHP48.500, up from PHP47.700 at Thursday's close. 

 The Singapore dollar was weaker despite apparent intervention early in the day by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to support the local dollar. 

 Traders said the MAS bought Singapore dollars against its U.S. counterpart through a number of local banks at around S$1.7570, pushing the local currency up to around S$1.7520. But the effect was short-lived as weakness in the peso and rupiah, and a 2.7% fall in the benchmark Straits Times Index of local stock prices knocked the Singapore dollar from its intraday highs. 

 A dealer at the European bank said: "The Sing dollar is surrounded by bad news. No matter what authorities do, sentiment is still weak and won't just change overnight." The MAS intervened a number of times above S$1.7500 in recent months to curb weakness in the local currency, which was inspired at that time by falls in the rupiah due to political problems in Indonesia. 

 The U.S. dollar late was at S$1.7550, up from S$1.7523 a day earlier. 

 In neighboring Indonesia, the central bank said it is considering whether to intervene in the market to support the rupiah, which hit a 10-week low early in the day of IDR9,030 against the dollar. 

 "We will need to evaluate what caused the rupiah weakness before we make a direct move in the market," said Bank Indonesia senior official Achjar Ilyas. 

 Bank Indonesia Acting Governor Anwar Nasution has previously said the central bank would defend the rupiah at IDR9,000, arguing that beyond this level it is grossly undervalued compared to economic fundamentals. 

 The dollar was at IDR8,955, up from IDR8,940 late Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, Bank of Thailand acknowledged for the first time there are signs of speculation against the baht in the foreign exchange market, activity that as a general rule might prompt a central bank to intervene. 

 Chetthavee Charoenpitaks, assistant central bank governor, told reporters the Bank is closely monitoring movements in the market, but declined to comment on whether the central bank plans to intervene to support the baht. 

 The baht hit a 28-month low Friday of THB43.68 against the dollar, and late in the session was at THB43.580, down from THB43.295. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won sank as local stock prices slumped 1.9%. 

 The dollar ended trade in Seoul at KRW1,128.5, up from KRW1,122.10 late Thursday. While in Taipei, the New Taiwan dollar dropped sharply to finish the week at NT$31.650 against the U.S. currency, down from NT$31.300 a day earlier.

title: Singapore ST Index Open 3.3% Lower On Wall St Losses
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The shock wave from the violence in the Middle East that ravaged Wall Street is sweeping through Asia, including Singapore, Friday. 

 In early trading, the Straits Times Index broke past the 1800-point support level and fell 3.6%, or 66.86 points, to 1798.99. 

 The DBS-50 index, which gives greater weighting to the largest stocks and excludes foreign-currency issues, was down 3.25%, or 19.96 points, to 612.76. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market early Friday through a number of local banks to buoy the local currency, which has been dragged down by weakness in the baht and peso, traders said. 

 They said the de facto central bank stepped into the market and bought Singapore dollars around the S$1.7560/U.S. dollar level, pushing the local currency up to around S$1.7525. 

 In the bond markets, the yield on the benchmark government 10-year bonds and the seven-year bonds are also higher at the open, dealer said. The 10-year was bid at 4.43% while the yield on the seven-year was at 4.07% from 4.05% Thursday. 

 The turmoil was expected. The killing of two Israeli soldiers by a Palestinian mob Thursday led to a forceful retaliatory attack by Israeli forces on Palestinian targets. 

 Around the same time, an explosion ripped a gaping hole in the 9,100-ton U.S. Navy destroyer USS Cole, killing six members of the crew, injuring 35, leaving 11 missing, and putting Yemen at the center of what appeared to be a terrorist plot against the U.S. 

 Wall Street - where sentiment was already fragile - fell sharply. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 3.6% lower at 10034.58, and the Nasdaq shed another 3% to 3074.68. Crude oil prices rose to a 10-year high on fears of a disruption in supplies as winter approaches in the northern hemisphere. 

 In Asia-Pacific trading, the Nikkei 225 was down 2% and South Korea's Kospi index plunged 6% at one point. 

 In Singapore, the STI briefly fell below the 1800-point level. At 0128 GMT it was at 1813.20, down 2.8%. 

 Selling in Singapore was across the board. A total of 317 stocks were down, 20 were up, and 45 were unchanged. 

 Singapore Airlines, which has one of the strongest fuel hedging policies of any airline, was down 4.2%, or 70 cents, to S$15.70, on trade of 400,000 shares. 

 Among technology stocks, Venture Manufacturing was down 70 cents, or 4.8%, to S$14, on trade of 478,000 shares. Chartered Semiconductor shares plunged 8.3%, or 65 cents, to S$7.20, on trade of 2.1 million shares. 

 Among banks, DBS Group Holdings was down 2.1%, or 40 cents, to S$18.30, on trade of 1 million shares. United Overseas Bank shed 40 cents, or 3.3%, to S$11.90, on trade of 379,000 shares. 

 However, Singapore Technology Engineering was up 2%, or 5 cents, to S$2.51, on trade of 259,000 shares. 

 The government-linked defense conglomerate reported after market close Thursday a net profit of S$201.3 million for the nine months to Sept. 30, up 39% on-year. 

 Oil-related stocks also gained. Singapore Petroleum Co. was up 6.5 cents, or 7.8%, to S$0.90, on trade of 260,000, while Keppel Fels Energy was up one cent to S$1.17, on trade of 192,000 shares.

the persistent political instability in the Philippines was



driving investors away from the country.



    "It's not the impeachment risk as such, but political risk



keeps coming up," she said.



    The heightened political risk in the Philippines has hit



foreign direct investment inflows. According to Patterson, for



the year to September, the Philippines had net inflows of $584



million in announced foreign investment, compared with



Thailand's $1.68 billion in the same period.



    This factor, along with the country's widening budget



deficit, have been weighing heavily on the peso.



    Dealers also said the market has been ignoring the central



bank's attempts to shore up the peso, including its currency


risk protection programme.



    However, the dollar's rise may be capped this session



around 47.10, as there are stops around that level.



    KOREAN WON

In addition to the Nasdaq's fall, the 10.1% drop in the

Dealers added that the market was keeping an eye on GM

in Singapore said.

was likely to remain rangebound on a lack of market-moving



news.



    "The flow of news has been quite down in the past few days,

    The analysts said thin volume in the market suggested major

    Indonesia will be seeking around $4.8 billion in fresh aid

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Peso Hits Record Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies weakened late Tuesday, with the Philippine peso feeling the brunt of the pain as it tumbled to a fresh record low. 

 Renewed strength in crude oil prices overnight - fueled by mounting concerns over escalating strife in the Middle East and a cold snap that hit the U.S. Northeast - combined with the languid performance on Asian bourses to push the currencies lower, dealers said. 

 Bucking the downtrend were the Singapore dollar and the Indonesian rupiah. 

 The rupiah, which benefited from spiking oil prices, stayed mostly flat throughout the day, while the Singapore dollar recovered most of its early losses by late in the day, climbing to around Monday's levels by late trade. 

 The Philippine peso moved into uncharted waters again for the second time in a week, skidding to its lowest level in history against the U.S. dollar, on the region's weakness and heightened political anxieties. 

 The dollar closed at 46.890 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Monday's close of PHP46.550. 

 The dollar hit an intraday high of PHP46.900. 

 Fears of potential impeachment proceedings against President Joseph Estrada, following allegations that he and his family received kickbacks from illegal gambling operations, continued to unnerve market participants, dealers said. 

 Governor of northern Ilocos Sur province Luis Singson, Monday alleged Estrada received more than PHP400 million from illegal gambling as well as PHP130 million from his province's tax revenues. 

 The allegations are the most serious yet against Estrada, who assumed the presidency in 1998, and have triggered discussions of impeachment proceedings. 

 "The attempt to get impeachment proceedings initiated will create far more political risks," said Simon Flint, an analyst at Bank of America. 

 With the government already burdened by a budget deficit that has already exceeded its yearly target and a prolonged insurgency in the south, it will only be a matter of time before the dollar breaks above PHP47, analysts said. 

 "We're pretty bearish on the peso," Flint said. "It's a question of whether they (the authorities) can short-circuit the overwhelmingly negative market sentiment and negative political fundamentals." 

 News that Philippine oil companies will be able to acquire up to $300 million a month under a currency risk protection program, aimed at easing the recent heavy dollar demand which has depressed the peso, has failed to provide any reprieve for the beleaguered currency. 

 Dealers said they were disappointed that users of the facility will have to pay market rates for their funds, and won't receive any subsidy from the central bank. 

 "It turned out to be a major letdown," a U.S. bank dealer said. "Initially, people thought they could take up their hedging activity at a subsidized rate, but it turned out that they could only take it at the market rate." 

 The Thai baht continued to fall on higher oil prices, a weak euro and rising political tensions ahead of the country's general elections, expected later this year, dealers said. 

 Around 0935 GMT (5:35 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at 42.875 baht, up from THB42.585 late Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar was unaffected by robust economic data released earlier in the day, and yielded to the pressure from its regional counterparts and the weak euro, dealers said. 

 The Ministry for Trade and Industry Tuesday raised its economic growth forecast for 2000 to around 9%, from a range of 7.5% to 8.5% previously. 

 The U.S. dollar climbed to as high as S$1.7525 before retreating late in the day to S$1.7502, little changed from S$1.7498 late Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar's sharp intraday rebound had initially raised speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened. A local bank, which normally intervenes on behalf of the MAS, was selling the U.S. currency around S$1.7520, dealers said. 

 But dealers said the selling was just part of normal trading activity. 

 With the U.S. dollar trading above the S$1.7500 level, the de facto central bank may tolerate a slight weakness in the local currency, an economist at a local bank suggested. 

 "Inflation remains extremely benign," the economist said. 

 Also, despite weakness against the U.S. dollar, the Singapore dollar has appreciated by about 1.5% against the currencies of its major trading partners since late July, when the de facto central bank signaled its preference for a stronger local currency, the economist said. 

 He added that the U.S. dollar will likely trade between S$1.7300 and S$1.7600 for the rest of the year, "with bias toward the upside." 

 In South Korea, the dollar finished at 1,119 won, up from Monday's close of KRW1,117. 

 Against the Indonesian currency, the dollar was at 8,825, little changed from late Tuesday. 

 Taiwan financial markets were closed Tuesday for a national holiday.

title: Asian  currency intervention  threat remains alive.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Concerted intervention by leading industrialised nations to boost the ailing euro last week is giving Asian central banks a break, but analysts said it might be a matter of time before they feel the need to act on their currencies. 

 There have been signs recently, explicit or subtle, that some regional central banks might be wringing their hands over high oil prices and sliding currencies. 

Currencies across the region, which trended downward for several weeks on concerns over the impact of oil prices and the euro, rebounded slightly following Friday's surprise intervention by the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations. 

 But analysts dismissed the market reaction as knee-jerk. With sentiment for the dollar remaining strong and more people betting against Asian currencies due to political and economic uncertainty, they could soon head towards levels that would prompt the authorities to react. 

 "They might not need to be in the market at this point. But I would not rule out the possibility," said Chia Woon-Khien, chief analyst at SEB Merchant Banking in Singapore. 

 "Normally, there are three conditions that prompt central banks to act - when currencies drop below certain target levels, when the pace is out of synch with others in the region, and when domestic factors lead to speculative actions. These risks are still very prominent," she said. 

 TAIWAN AND THE PHILIPPINES 

 Taiwan's central bank, frequently in the market for smoothing operations, has been particularly vigilant in the past few weeks to support the currency which is hurt by outflows and poor sentiment brought about by uncertainty over the tech sector. 

 Last Monday alone, dealers estimated its intervention accounted for a third of the day's $689 million turnover. 

Forex dealers in the Philippines said the central bank might have spent around $250 million to $300 million during the first half of this month to defend the peso. 

 The bank says it has not been in the market since last week, but adds it does not rule out the possibility in the future. 

 BAHT'S MIXED SIGNALS 

 In Thailand, government officials have sent mixed signals to the market recently on currency intervention. 

 While one minister said the authorities might resort to short-term market intervention if excessive volatility in the baht hurt the economy, another senior minister said there was no need to prop it up. 

 Contradicting remarks notwithstanding, there have been signs the authorities are growing concerned about the macro picture. 

 Some economists forecast that if the baht fell below 43 per dollar, the government's inflation target of 2.5-3.0 percent for this year could be breached. 

 "Last week, the central bank was in the market to check for rates and monitor who's involved in major transactions. I think they were quite edgy," said a European bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 "I don't pay attention to what officials say. Before the central bank intervened in May when the baht was around 39, they had said the same thing. With political uncertainty intensifying, the intervention risk is very much there," he said. 

 Thailand is expected to hold an election later this year. 

 The Bank of Thailand has adopted a hands-off policy on the baht since floating it in July 1997. But it has intervened in the market occasionally to smooth out volatility. 

SINGAPORE'S IMPORTED INFLATION 

 Worries about potential intervention kept the Sing dollar above the key psychological 1.7500 level after briefly dipping below that mark on Friday for the first time since July 24. 

 Singapore manages its dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, using the exchange rate as a tool to fight inflation in its open economy. 

 With inflation as measured by price of imported manufactured goods surging to nearly 10 percent, some analysts reckon the government might soon act to curb inflation before it reaches consumer prices. 

 "These are rates which have triggered policy actions on the currency in the past," said David Carbon, strategist at Pacific Asset Management. 

 "Authorities in recent weeks have begun reminding the public and financial markets that pre-crisis currency policies remain the order of the day, and fighting inflation with currency appreciation will be pursued as and when the need arises," Carbon said in a recent report.

title: ANALYSIS-G7 action on euro won't help Asian  currencies  much.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The Group of Seven's concerted intervention to support the euro will give Asian currencies some breathing space against the dollar, but any positive impact will not last long, analysts said. 

 It was the first combined central bank action since 1995, when the dollar hit a record low on the mark and a post-World War Two low on the yen. 

 Friday's intervention took a thin market completely by surprise, particularly as any action on the euro was expected after this weekend's G7 meeting, not before. 

 "The initial impact will be long-dollar liquidation and I wouldn't be surprised to see things like dollar/sing down below 1.74 on Monday, the baht and the won should benefit but there won't be too much in the rest," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas in Singapore. 

 Such long dollar liquidation is seen being much lighter in the Philippine peso, Indonesian rupiah and Taiwan dollar because there has been less speculative position-taking. 

 While an initial knee-jerk is on the cards, the euro's reaction to the intervention - estimated at $2-5 billion - was not spectacular. 

 After jumping some five percent against both the dollar and yen to just over 90 cents and nearly 96 yen, it came right back to end in New York on Friday around 87.70 cents and 95 yen. 

 "Given the (euro) market sold off so aggressively after the intervention suggests people don't believe it's the end of a trend," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 STRONG DOLLAR 

 "Unless that sentiment changes it's not going to do much for regional currencies at all...the key everyone is looking for is an end to the strong dollar environment and we certainly don't seem to have seen that yet." 

 Fund managers would seem to agree and were not too impressed with the central banks' action. 

 Asked on Friday about the intervention they continued to believe there were a number of major economic factors still favouring U.S. markets over euro-zone assets. 

 "I've told our asset allocation committee to keep calm and keep in mind that intervention in the past has never been one way," said Charles Van Vleet, a senior portfolio manager at Credit Suisse Asset Management in New York. 

 "Intervention alone rarely works unless you change other policy variables such as monetary and fiscal policy also in line." 

 Also, Europe has had a very bad press of late with newspapers full of pictures of blockaded roads as lorry drivers and farmers bought some countries to a virtual standstill in protest over soaring fuel prices. 

 The subsequent perceived panic in Europe's political circles can only serve to turn investors off, analysts said. 

 DANISH REFERENDUM 

 Events next Thursday could further undermine the euro-zone in the eyes of investors when Denmark holds a referendum on whether to join the euro. 

 Opinion polls show the anti-euro camp at 46 percent with the pro-euro camp at 43 percent and analysts are warning a 'no' on Thursday could weaken the euro. 

 On top of all this, the United States is maintaining its strong dollar stance. At the G7 meeting in Prague on Saturday U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest and said the global effort to boost the euro did not conflict with Washington's strong dollar policy. 

 "A strong dollar is in our national interest and that will continue to be our policy," Summers said. 

 All this means the dollar will keep the pressure on Asian regional currencies, particularly those like the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah where political and social factors are making matters worse. 

Currencies like the South Korean won and Taiwan dollar will also continue to be affected by stock market outflows. 

 Given the Nasdaq shed 0.66 percent on Friday any knee-jerk move higher for the won and Taiwan dollar is likely to be limited by easier stocks because of the Nasdaq drop. "If Summers is saying the U.S. still has a strong dollar policy then nothing has changed," Paribas' Thio said. 

 "It's very difficult for the U.S. to reverse its strong dollar policy at this point given the forthcoming election. After all, it's worked very well for them."

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Intel Adds To Won Woes
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies had weakened late Friday, after a profit-warning from U.S. semiconductor giant Intel Corp. sent many regional bourses reeling, dealers said. 

 The warning dealt the hardest blows to the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar, given the importance of semiconductor chips for these countries' exports, analysts said. The increasingly pessimistic outlook on the semiconductor sector has exacerbated the short-term prospects of these currencies, which have recently been weakening on other domestic concerns. 

 But heavy intervention by Taiwan's central bank kept a rein on the New Taiwan dollar's decline, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar wasn't unscathed. The U.S. dollar briefly crossed above the critical S$1.75 resistance as the local stock market index skidded to a four-month low on Intel's announcement. 

 Intel said late Thursday it expects its third-quarter revenue to fall below previous expectations, primarily because of weaker demand in Europe. 

 The won, which had already been weakening on falling prices of computer chips, one of South Korea's biggest export items, skidded to as low as KRW1,134.90 to the dollar minutes after the open on Intel's warning. 

 The dollar finished at KRW1,134.70, higher than Thursday's close of KRW1,128.10, as the local stock market tumbled 7.2%. 

 The won, has been on a steep decline since last Friday, when Ford Motor Co. said it had aborted its bid for Daewoo Motor. The currency is poised to extend its downward spiral in coming weeks, currency watchers said. 

 The dollar is poised to test its upside target of KRW1,140 soon, they added. 

 But Thio Chin Loo, a foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas Group, said a lot of the bad news has already been priced in the won, which is expected to trade between KRW1,120 and KRW1,140 against the dollar in the short term. 

 "If stability returns to the stock market, the dollar will trade at the lower end of its trading range," she said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$31.295, up from Thursday's close of NT$31.263, in dealings valued at US$428 million. 

 Dealers said the central bank sold around US$150 million throughout the day to stem the New Taiwan dollar's losses, but it failed to overcome the pressure from heavy foreign equity fund outflows, which contributed to a 4.5% plunge on the local stock market. 

 The slump in regional foreign exchange markets dragged the Philippine peso to a new record closing low while the Philippine Central Bank's stayed absent from the local market, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 46.155 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP45.995 Thursday and just off its intraday high of PHP46.165. 

 The peso's weakness had sparked debate about pegging the currency, but such a move appears unlikely. 

 Opposing a senior lawmaker's call that the central bank at least consider a peg, Finance Secretary Jose said Friday the government opposes capital controls and has no plans to implement a peg to stabilize the peso. 

 Elsewhere, the selloff on the Singapore bourse and the fall in other regional currencies accelerated the Singapore dollar's descent in late trading, dealers said. 

 With no signs of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore as the U.S. currency cracked above the crucial level of S$1.75, market participants pushed the U.S. dollar to S$1.7523 around 1000 GMT (6:00 a.m. EDT), up from S$1.7460 late Thursday, dealers said. 

 The de facto central bank is believed to have defended the local currency on July 24 at around S$1.7515 against the U.S. dollar. 

 With the Thai currency hitting fresh 27-month lows, the psychological support level of 43 baht to the dollar is expected to give way next week, dealers said. 

 The dollar had climbed to THB42.945, from THB42.67 late Thursday. 

 Strong onshore dollar demand; expensive oil prices and mounting political anxieties ahead of the country's general elections, expected later this year, continued to pressure the baht, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian currency weakened to 8,805 rupiah against the dollar, from IDR8,792 late Thursday. 

Currency watchers are waiting to see if the weekend meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations will come up with concrete measures to salvage the euro, which has consistently been falling to new lows against both the dollar and the Japanese yen.

title: Emerging  FX  - Sit tight as market awaits fresh cues.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies sat pat 

 in their recent ranges early on Tuesday with fading local 

 factors forcing the market to await fresh cues. 


    The yen        failed to provide much guidance, as



attention on the major currency market was more focused on the



euro .



    Investors were keeping an eye on preliminary second quarter



U.S. productivity data due later on Tuesday to gauge how weak



the economy may be.



    While the recent bailing out of long U.S. dollar positions



against the Singapore dollar and North Asian currencies has



tapered off, investors were not yet keen on rebuilding their



long U.S. dollar positions. That could leave regional


currencies trapped in familiar territory.



In the long term, analysts say the U.S. dollar should



resume its climb against the regional currencies as Asia's



recovery depends on the U.S. picking up first.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar declined to make any drastic moves,



and was expected to consolidate around the 1.7800-1.7850 range.



Dealers said with activity on the dollar/yen subdued, the



market found little motivation to test the dollar/Sing in



either direction.



Charts showed the dollar/Sing was in oversold territory,



with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 28.741,



indicating the Sing dollar had room for downwards correction.



THAI BAHT



The baht was locked in a narrow range as most players were



done with dollar unwinding linked to Prime Minister Thaksin



Shinawatra's court victory on Friday.



Dealers said the currency was trapped between dollar bids



from oil firms and importers at 45.30 and offers from U.S.

    Given a dearth of fresh leads, the market was awaiting the


central bank's new forex regulations which are expected soon.



    Baht funding costs eased slightly, with the tom/next rate



quoted at -0.20/0.15 satang per dollar in both the offshore and



onshore markets.

opening and as players covered their short dollar positions



amid talk the central bank may intervene to cap the won's rise.


Singapore dealers said the market was also cautious ahead



of the Bank of Korea's monetary policy meeting on Thursday with



analysts divided on whether key interest rates will be lowered.



    The BOK last cut its overnight call rate by 25 basis points



to 4.75 percent in July as inflationary pressure seemed to



ease.



    The won's downside was expected to be limited on



export-related inflows and settlement of stocks bought by



foreign investors last week.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar edged down in subdued trade ahead of the



July trade data due at 0245 GMT.



    Singapore dealers said sentiment towards the currency also



took a hit from a weaker Nasdaq close, which would put pressure



on the local stock market. Foreign investors sold on Monday a



net T$22.74 million worth of local stocks.



A Reuters poll showed economists expect July exports to



fall 23.7 percent on the year and imports to shrink by 32.9



percent.



    Inflation data issued on Monday sparked hopes the central



bank may further lower key interest rates.



    The consumer price index in July rose 0.11 percent on the



year while wholesale price index fell 0.22 percent.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso barely moved from Monday's local close of 53.22,

dollars.

"While the market may not have high hopes, there are still

title: UPDATE 1-Sing dollar rises above 1.80, first since May 24.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 26 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar strengthened to 1.80 against the U.S. dollar for the first time since May 24 on Thursday, aided by a simmering of the Indonesian political crisis. 

 Dealers said U.S. funds and local banks were dumping their U.S. dollar positions amassed during the height of Indonesia's political crisis and the economic turmoil in Argentina. 

 "The market has found the situation in Indonesia is stabilising so there is an expectation the rupiah will strengthen to 9,000," a European bank dealer said. 

 The Indonesia rupiah hit 11-week highs around 9,800 on Wednesday, as the market reacted positively to Tuesday's sacking of Wahid Abdurrahman as president. 

 Dealers said funds might also be reassessing their favourable view toward the currency in recent months in light of poor corporate earnings from the U.S and little sign the U.S. economy will recover soon. 

 The U.S. dollar has also recently slipped against the yen and euro as the market wondered whether a change may be afoot in the long-standing strong dollar policy. 

 But U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill has repeated his commitment to the policy. 

 Dealers said heavy U.S. dollar sales from funds triggered stop-loss orders at 1.8090-1.8100 and 1.8050, pushing the Singapore dollar to highs around 1.7998 from 1.8169 late on Wednesday. 

 The European bank dealer added interbank players also started trimming long U.S. dollar positions on fears of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 This in turn opened the floodgates for more U.S. dollar selling. 

 But dealers said the Singapore dollar would have trouble clearing resistance around 1.7980 as players were looking to buy dollars on dips and added it would correct back to around 1.8050. 

 "The dollar is unquestionably a buy at these levels, but I think the market is going to take some time to settle after the violent move today. A lot of people have got burnt today and quite badly," said a local bank dealer. 

 Charts showed the dollar is oversold with a 14-day relative strength index reading at 15.67. 

 Dealers noted the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been intervening both in the spot and money markets last week to support the local currency after it changed its policy stance earlier this month to neutral from tightening. 

 The Singapore dollar had been under pressure given the country's deteriorating economic fundamentals, losing around 3.5 percent since January. It touched an 11-year low of 1.8398 on July 12. 

 The city state is now technically in recession after advance second-quarter GDP fell 10.1 percent on an annnualised quarter-on-quarter basis. The government has slashed its economic growth forecast for 2001 to just 0.5-1.5 percent from 3.5-5.5 percent.

title: Emerging  FX -Sluggish as market begs for fresh cues.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies trod familiar ground late on Wednesday as the market rooted around for fresh trading cues. 

 Singapore dealers said with the yen failing to give much direction and Hong Kong markets closed due to a typhoon, most players were content to hold their fire for now. 

 However, the market was still keeping close tabs on the dollar/yen following U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill's repeated committment to the strong dollar policy. 

 On the local front, the Singapore dollar shrugged off the government's off-budget measures to shore up the economy. 

 And the initial euphoria over Indonesia's peaceful change of power settled down, as players in Southeast Asian currency markets woke up to what little attention global investors are actually paying to the country. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar settled around the 1.8160 level after hitting a high of 1.8153 when foreign funds were dumping their dollar longs. 

 Dealers said the market was wary that the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene as they have been suspected of doing since it announced a change in its Sing dollar policy on July 12. 

 But dealers said there was no sign of the central bank on Wednesday, and players were unwinding their dollar positions with the aim of building them up again around 1.8150. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah kept within 9,800-10,000 for most of the session, only briefly weakening to touch a session low of 10,075. 

 Jakarta dealers said sporadic dollar offers from state banks kept most players on the sidelines but strong dollar demand was spotted around 9,800. 

 Overall the market was in a wait-and-see mood pondering as the new government and economic team took shape. 

 The central bank said it was too premature to lower domestic interest rates on the back of the recent rupiah spike and would wait another couple of weeks before making a decision. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was stuck in a tight 1,306.8-1,310.4 range in cautious trade ahead of June current account balance and industrial output and first half trade data due on Friday. 

 Singapore dealers said exporters' dollar inflows limited the won's downside while uncertainty about the yen and a weak local stock market capped gains. 

 A Reuters poll showed economists expect industrial production to shrink for the third consecutive month in June, with an average forecast of a 0.4 percent fall mainly on sagging exports. 

 Dealers said weak economic numbers were likely to pressure the won towards the 1,320 mark, seen last on April 30. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was wedged in a tight 45.69-45.76 range in lacklustre trade with players reluctant to take aggressive positions on worries over new currency trade reporting rules. 

 The central bank has said stricter rules, aimed at discouraging speculation by foreigners holding baht bank deposits, would be placed for the governor's approval this week. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Thailand had no plans to impose capital controls or return the baht to a fixed exchange rate and had no intention to raise domestic interest rates. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 Trading on the peso moved sluggishly with players complaining about the dearth of fresh factors. 

 However, Manila dealers said sentiment towards the peso was still hobbled by the country's poor economic fundamentals and bleak external environment. 

 "The attitude around here is hoard dollars while you can," said a local bank dealer in Manila. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank would likely keep overnight rates steady, but may consider raising commercial bank's reserve requirements. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar crept higher as a bounce in local stocks fuelled hopes of foreign investment equity-related inflows. 

 But given how poorly Taiwan's economy is doing, the central bank capped the local dollar's rise to around 34.80 to keep its export competitiveness. 

 Taiwan saw some badly needed good news on the macroeconomic front. June M2 money supply grew by 6.01 percent on year, compared to May's 5.61 percent growth, which was a record low. That pick-up hinted at an increase in investment and lending.
