title: Emerging  FX -Mixed on Indonesia, steady yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed bag early Monday as the southeast Asia markets warily eyed developments in Indonesia while the northen markets followed the yen's lead. 

 Caution prevailed as the Indonesian parliament meets to impeach President Abdurrahman Wahid in defiance of his declaration of a state of emergency early Monday. 

 The rupiah jumped to 10,400 after the Supreme Court ruled that Wahid's declaration was illegal. 

 A peaceful impeachment of Wahid could lead to a further rally in the rupiah, but analysts said that may have been already priced in while the risk of violence and weak economic fundamentals will cap significant gains. Volumes in either case will be tiny, they said. 

 Early losses in the Singapore dollar, the most liquid currency in Southeast Asia, reflected those worries. 

 The yen was slightly off its New York highs. But lingering doubts over the strong dollar policy's fate despite President George W. Bush's assurances during the weekend's Group of Eight summit was expected to keep the currency under pressure. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah bounced to 10,400 from 11,125 as the market betted that President Wahid would soon be kicked out of office. 

 Jakarta dealers said local and foreign banks unloaded dollars as moves against Wahid gathered steam. But volumes were extremely thin, which exaggerated the move higher. 

 The bid/ask spread was wide, indicating players are reluctant to trade. Dealers added, however, local corporate clients may emerge around these levels to snap up dollars given their debt servicing needs. 

 Bank Indonesia said forex and monetary policy remained unchanged after the state of emergency. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The market jerked the Singapore dollar lower in reaction to the Indonesian political crisis. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar slipped past the 1.8300 mark in Sydney in early trade, but was saved by players looking to take quick profit on the dollar. 

 They added the market was eyeing the yen's direction for trading cues. 

 But caution dictated the market with talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened on behalf of the local dollar on Friday during London and New York trade. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso slipped on local corporate dollar demand, though dealers hesitated in testing the central bank's resolve in defending the currency. 

 Manila dealers said the central bank was viewed as keen on capping the peso's losses ahead of President Gloria Arroyo's State of the Nation address. 

 The bank said over the weekend it was considering stiffer penalties against speculators, who the government has blamed for the peso's recent losses. 

 Dealers said a dearth of dollars along with poor economic fundamentals and local corporate dollar needs have driven the peso lower. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht sank as corporate players and offshore names continued to bid for dollar amid weakness in regional currencies. 

 Dealers said dollar offers from exporters around 45.80 helped limit the baht's losses, but a decisive break below 45.85 could lead to 46.00, a level not seen since March 1998. 

 Thailand's foreign reserves fell to $31.5 billion as of July 13, below the minimum of $32-34 billion suggested by the IMF. 

 Baht funding costs in the offshore market were easier, but remained high, with the one-month forward rate at 19/27 satang per dollar and the 12-month tenor at 175/215 satang. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won tracked the yen's fall with poor sentiment in the local bourse and equity-related outflows likely to weigh on it. 

 Analysts said with the view on the Korean economy still bearish, players would continue to buy dollar on dips. 

 The Korea Development Institute last week cut its 2001 GDP forecast to 4.0 percent from 4.3 percent, saying exports will remain sluggish due to the global slowdown. 

 The central bank urged financial institutions to lower their lending rates to spur investment activity. Finance Minister Jin Nyum said on Monday the government will boost spending in the second half and hoped to see an impact in the fourth quarter. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar edged up but was close to the 35 mark in cautious trade after the central bank was spotted intervening on both sides on Friday. 

 However, dealers said the market's direction would be set by June export orders and industrial output numbers due 0230 GMT and June jobless rate due 0300 GMT. 

 A recent Reuters poll showed economists on average expected June export orders to fall by 16.88 percent on year, and industrial output to slip by 9.21 percent on year.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Tracks Asian  Currencies ' Gains
text:

title: MAS Lee Says To Guard Against Singapore Dlr Speculation
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore will continue to "guard against destabilizing speculation in the Singapore dollar," MAS Chairman Lee Hsien Loong said Friday. 

 "The MAS' primary objective over the medium term is to maintain price stability and the purchasing power of the local currency," Lee told participants at a conference marking the MAS' 30th anniversary. 

 By pursuing foreign exchange policy through a "managed float" of the Singapore dollar, the MAS can buffer the effects on the economy of short-term financial volatility, and avoid sustained currency misalignments that could damage the export sector, Lee said. 

 "Managing the float requires us to lean against the wind at times, but provided our exchange rate policy is aligned with economic fundamentals, and our ability and determination to counter destabilizing speculation is not in doubt, we need to intervene less than might be expected." 

 Until recently, the MAS didn't reveal its view of the Singapore dollar exchange rate, or its policy intentions. But the MAS has adopted a more transparent approach to help the market and general public understand the MAS policy stance better, Lee said. With less uncertainty, policy implementation will be more effective, he added. 

 The MAS was suspected of intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the Singapore dollar earlier this week. 

 Market watchers said the central bank was probably demonstrating its resolve to defend the Singapore dollar, even though it shifted its monetary policy on July 1 to a neutral position from a bias toward a gradual appreciation of the local currency. 

 With the market heavily long in U.S. dollars, it was even more compelling for the MAS - which has been making its presence felt recently - to step in, market watchers said. 

 Regarding banking regulation, Lee said the MAS is adopting a "risk-focused, consolidated approach" to supervision. 

 "We will place more emphasis on understanding and evaluating an institution's risk management systems and internal controls," he told conference participants. 

 On the subject of corporate governance, Lee said the MAS will continue to push for higher standards, particularly on enhancing the independence of boards and institutionalizing professional management. 

 "But this must be phased in judiciously. We cannot impose these standards in a vacuum without regard to the institutional and cultural realities in our corporate sector."

title: Asian  Currencies  Higher Late; Yen Gives Region A Lift
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies finished higher across the board against the U.S. dollar Thursday, enjoying support from a firmer yen. 

 Comments by President George W. Bush that the strong dollar was hurting U.S. exports gave traders an excuse to sell the dollar against the yen in Asia. 

 The comments don't, however, change the consensus view that the dollar will continue to appreciate against the yen as Japan's economy continues to experience difficulties, analysts added. 

 The dollar fell to Y123.25 late Thursday after trading as high as Y124.40 a day earlier. 

 The Philippine peso got an additional boost from a second straight day of suspected central bank intervention to support the currency, which has suffered from weak economic fundamentals and local corporate demand for dollars. 

 Traders said they believed the central bank sold dollars in the spot market, but it was denied by monetary authorities. 

 The dollar closed at 53.20 pesos, down from PHP53.74 at the close Wednesday. 

 Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura denied the monetary authority had intervened in the currency market Thursday and attributed the peso's gains to new measures that the central bank and the Department of Finance plan to implement. 

 The New Taiwan dollar gained on the back of the rising yen. The U.S. dollar closed at NT$35.015, down from Wednesday's close of NT$35.027. 

 Dealers reported some squaring of long U.S. dollar positions in the afternoon session as the yen strengthened. 

 Taiwan's main stock index recovered from an intraday decline of 3.7% to finish down just 0.7%. Government funds were suspected of buying shares to support the market. 

 However, pressure to sell the New Taiwan dollar is likely to continue as investor confidence erodes amid Taiwan's worsening economic situation, BA Asia said in a research report. 

 Taiwan's central bank is likely to mount a strong defense of the local currency around the level of NT$35.2 per U.S. dollar, BA Asia said. 

 The dollar gained ground against the won in early trade, but slipped later as the yen strengthened. 

 The dollar finished at 1,305.8 won, down from Wednesday's close of KRW1,311.7. 

 A trader at a foreign firm in Seoul said there was heavy dollar-selling from domestic banks at the KRW1,306 level. 

 The Indonesian rupiah edged higher on guarded optimism that President Abdurrahman Wahid will be ousted. 

 The dollar closed at 11,240 rupiah, down from IDR11,270 Wednesday. 

 Wahid is viewed by some as a weak and effective leader who is a liability to Indonesia's economic recovery. 

 The country's highest legislative body has said it plans to impeach Wahid early August, citing his poor leadership and alleged involvement in two financial scandals. 

 The Thai baht also moved higher, but corporate demand for dollars and pessimism over the outlook for Thailand's economy supported the U.S. currency. 

 The dollar was quoted in late trade at 45.715 baht, down from THB45.790 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 Although the bias in the market remains generally in favor of the dollar, comments from the Bank of Thailand that it was monitoring the local currency should prevent the U.S. currency from rising too sharply, analysts said. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen higher. Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8281, down from S$1.8319 late Wednesday. 

 Fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore around S$1.8300 also supported the local currency, dealers said.

title: Emerging  FX  - Find cheer as dollar sulks.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 19 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies lurched towards firmer ground early Thursday as the market pounced on the dollar following remarks from President George Bush and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan. 

 Bush ushered dollar bears into the market by telling reporters the strong dollar threatened U.S. exports but Teasury Secretary Paul O'Neill later said the U.S. still backed its long-standing strong dollar policy. 

 The dollar found little solace in Greenspan's semi-annual congressional testimony as the Fed chairman warned the U.S. economy faced a range of hurdles and more interest rate cuts may be needed. 

 A Reuters poll showed primary dealers unanimously expecting another 25 basis point cut when the Fed next meets on August 21. 

 Double click or for the full poll. 

 But the bounce regional currencies were enjoying may be short-lived as Asia's economic fortunes are bound to the U.S. Wariness over central bank intervention is holding players back from properly trouncing the regional currencies, dealers said. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso took a gasp of air as players unwound some of their long dollar positions after talk on Wednesday the central bank was intervening through two foreign banks. 

Singapore dealers said the dollar/peso was due for a slight correction, with its 14-day relative strength index showing the dollar in overbought territory since June 15. Its reading on Thursday was 85. 

 But dealers said they were still looking to snatch up dollars on dips, given the gloomy economic outlook for the Philippines coupled with the dearth of dollars. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 President Bush's dollar comments lifted the won to 1,302 in New York. The currency opened at 1,305 in the onshore market on Thursday, against the Wednesday's close of 1,311.7. 

 But gains were expected to be capped by Greenspan's cautious outlook on the U.S. economy, which is a major market for Korean exports. 

 Dealers said 1,300.00 should remain a solid barrier for the won to crack as players are likely to buy the dollar on dips to that level. 

 The one-month won in the non-deliverable forward market was quoted at 1,314/1,315 and three-month at 1,319/1,320. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The Thai baht was off its overnight low of 45.81 on the back of a firmer yen, but the upside was limited by hedging activity and political concerns. 

 Consitutional court judges denied reports by local media the court may deliver a verdict in Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's graft case as early as next week. 

 "It's every one's guess what the outcome would be, and the market is reluctant to pare long dollar positions," said a dealer in Bangkok. 

 "Also, investors people are quite active in hedging against baht losses despite high swap points. That added selling pressure to the currency," he said. 

 The baht remained trapped in the dollar's uptrend channel dating back to June 26. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar extended gains to 1.8280 having popped above 1.83 overnight for the first time in more than a week. 

 Dealers said interbank players liquidated their long dollar positions, triggering some stop-loss U.S. dollar selling orders at 1.8300. But they emphasised there was no particular catalyst for the latest Sing dollar rise besides the steadier yen and said it might resume its downtrend after pulling back to around 1.8265-50. INDONESIAN RUPIAH The rupiah held onto gains at two-week highs around 11,265, as banks liquidated their dollar long positions in thin trading. But Jakarta dealers said the outlook was not so rosy given concerns about rising political tension. President Abdurrahman Wahid said he would declare a state of emergency and call early elections if his enemies try to oust him. 

 Top legislators are calling for bringing forward impeachment hearings against President Wahid from the scheduled date of August 1. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar trading around the key psychological level of 35.00, underpinned by the dollar's retreat against the yen and wariness of central bank intervention. 

 The currency opened slightly higher at 34.983 against the Thursday's close of 35.027 before dipping to 35.025. 

 Dealers expected the central bank to continue to defend the currency to keep it around 35.00 amid downward pressure from the ailing domestic stock market, and poor economic outlook.

title: Asia Economy Watch: Singapore Barometer Of Asia's Health
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column



HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Singapore is Asia's canary in the coal mine.
The government's frank economic warnings sent shivers through the region
but also spurred thinking about finding an escape route.


 The Singapore government last week not only announced preliminary figures that suggest it entered a recession for the second time in three years, but officials rubbed salt in the wound by predicting conditions will worsen. 

 "The extent of the slowdown has exceeded what was expected at the beginning of the year, and so has the risk of a more protracted downturn," the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in a statement. 

 So much for inspiring confidence. 

 But Singapore's news is important partly for the solutions the government has promised it will apply to relieve the pain, including a dip into its coffers. 

 Asian policy makers have for much of this year done little more than repeat the hopeful wisdom of notables like Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan that the U.S. economy will see growth by late 2001. 

 But it's now apparent Asia's bounce will come later. Singapore's statements last week reinforce views that any recovery will be mild, and will start later than it does in the U.S., requiring official action. 

 The timeliness and reliability of Singapore data help make the bear story a more believable one. Singapore is among the Asian economies most closely tied to the critical electronics cycle, and it will soon be more widely apparent that Asian exporters aren't getting many fresh orders from U.S. purchasing managers. 

 Dong Tao, chief regional economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Hong Kong, said "in the next three months we're going to see massive bad news from Asian countries." 

 He said markets are prepared for weak - even recessionary - gross domestic product performances. But markets aren't expecting exports in some countries to slide by 25% to 35% from last year, which he predicts. 


   Many Expect 3Q To Be Asia's Weakest This Year



Fears Asia is returning to the dark days of the 1997 financial crisis
will undoubtedly rise, and hurt confidence. Many analysts expect the
third quarter to be Asia's weakest this year.



"How you feel about this crisis is going to be very, very bad," Tao
predicted. "This is going to prompt Asian governments to take action."



In this vein, Singapore also bears watching.



To contrast with its bare-knuckles message last week, the government
announced proactive ways official Singapore would ease the pain. Its
steps, to various degrees, are likely to be matched elsewhere in Asia.



Singapore's steps included announcing a policy change regarding its
currency. Analysts believe it has tacitly embraced a beggar-thy-neighbor
strategy.



The central bank's shift to a "neutral" level on the Singapore dollar
had the psychological impact of a broker withdrawing a "buy"
recommendation on a stock. Although the central bank tried to put a
floor on the currency with intervention, the Singapore dollar's fall to
11-year lows helped prompt heavy selling of other Asian currencies and
analysts expect weakness to persist as a way to keep export prices as
attractive as possible.



An alternative way to ease the pain, interest-rate reductions, is a
policy tool few in Asia have the ability to use. And Singapore
authorities offered no signals they will ease credit in coming months.



Most notably, the Singapore government also said it would announce
late this month a package of financial "pump priming" measures that it
hopes will inject some confidence into the economy.



Analysts expect the government - with one eye on a parliamentary
election due by August 2002 - to bring forward infrastructure works,
reduce some fees, and possibly slice a bit off the 16% of salaries that
it mandates employers save for workers.



Fiscal steps are another area where analysts expect to see other Asian
governments follow the Singapore example. Indeed, South Korea has also
announced plans to step up some major construction projects and
government-linked companies will do the same.



But these won't be economic saviors, so much as politically smart
moves. "It would be hard to stand idly by with the economy in recession,
but neither do we think higher government spending will have much
impact," Deutsche Bank AG economists wrote last week about Singapore.



It's got to be remembered that Singapore also has the most ability
among Southeast Asian countries to dip into its reserves for spending,
according to Daniel Lian, a Morgan Stanley & Co. economist.



"We expect good but not maximum fiscal support from the government,"
he told investors last week.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen, weak outlook hurt Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, July 17 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies headed south in late trade on Tuesday as fears of further monetary easing in Japan and the less-than-rosy economic oulook across the region kept the U.S. dollar in favour. 

 The yen came under some pressure when two senior ministers - Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa and Economics Minister Heizo Takenaka - argued there was more that monetary policy could do to support the economy. 

 Their comments reinforced expectations of a further easing from the Bank of Japan which could come at the expense of a weaker yen. 

 Elsewhere in the region, there was no shortage of bad news. 

 In Singapore, long considered Southeast Asia's oasis, non-oil exports fell a worse than expected 16.9 percent on-year in June. 

 Just a day earlier, Thailand downgraded its export growth target to minus 1.2 to zero percent from a previous forecast of 9.46 percent growth. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar braved through June's dismal non-oil export figures as the market remained on its toes over central bankintervention. 

 Dealers said players were reluctant to test 1.8375/80, being mindful of talk that local banks were seeking to offer dollars around 1.8390. Those offers spurred speculation they were acting on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 However, dealers added that given the grim outlook for the economy, offshore players were opting to stay long of dollars, and were looking for opportunities to buy on dips. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso hit a fresh six-month trough of 53.95 but avoided a damaging break of 54 thanks to fears of possible intervention. 

 Dealers saw a U.S. bank offering around $10 million in the morning at 53.95, spurring talk it was acting on behalf of the authorities which might want to defend the psychological 54 mark. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank had not intervened in the forex market on Tuesday. He added the peso was not totally out of line with other currencies and the bank would not adjust interest rates to support it. 

 Dealers said dollar demand from oil companies and manufacturing importers seeking to hedge against further peso weakness was still robust and the peso should breach 54 in the near term. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah endured a listless session, shackled in a tight range as players focused on rising political tension and developments over the possible release of a frozen $400 million loan from the IMF. 

 The IMF said it was still aiming to release the loan next month, adding a change of government would not delay the disbursement. 

 Legislators said parliamentary debate on controversial central bank law changes had been scheduled to resume early on August 16. The IMF has raised concerns that parts of the proposed law changes could undermine the central bank's independence. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar lingered around the 35 mark, pressured by a weaker yen and a grim economic outlook but supported by fears of central bankintervention. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was not spotted in the market but local corporates and interbank players continued to offload their U.S. dollar longs. 

 Despite modest gains in the local stock market, foreign investors were net sellers of local stocks and settlement of those transactions would continue to pressure the Taiwan dollar. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht stuck to levels around 45.75 wedged between dollar demand from importers and corporates and trimming of dollar longs by offshore players. 

 Dealers in Singapore said U.S. and Singapore names were spotted offering dollars just above 45.80 while local demand was strong around 45.65-45.70. 

 Uncertainty over the central bank's interest rate policy, fears of intervention and of tougher reporting rules has prompted offshore players to book profit on any dollar gains. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said to help hasten economic recovery his government planned to standardise Thai time with regional economic financial centres Singapore and Hong Kong. 

 He said the measure was part of a 28-point economic stimulus package approved by his cabinet late Monday. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was steady in slow, offshore trade. Markets in Seoul were closed for a public holiday, and will re-open on Wednesday.

text:
SINGAPORE, July 17 (Reuters) - Domestic woes and 

 Argentina's economic crisis ruffled Asian currencies early on 

 Tuesday, with the wobbly yen providing more distress. 

     "Risk aversity is pretty high right now. All in all it's a 

 pretty dire environment and the slowness of the U.S. recovery 

 is not helping much. Investors are on the defensive," said a 

 dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 He added the region's dependence on its exports coupled 

 with the still-sluggish U.S. economy left most Asian countries 

 with little choice but to accept weaker currencies. 

 Singapore will release June non-oil export figures at 0530 

 GMT, which analysts expect to show another slump due to the 

 electronics downturn. 

 The market was keeping tabs on the latest developments in 

 Argentina, where the government is seeking support for an 

 austerity plan to prevent a debt default. 

 Investors were also focused on Federal Reserve Chairman 

 Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony on Wednesday and U.S.

 later Tuesday, and consumer price data on Wednesday. 

     Markets in Seoul were closed for a public holiday.

    The peso slid to fresh six-month lows of 53.84, but trading



remained thin with only $2 million transacted by 0137 GMT.

banks placed arbitrage orders between the spot and

    Dealers said the peso would breach 54 soon but fears of

    Dealers said local banks were interested in selling dollars



around 1.8390, sparking talk that they may be acting on behalf



of the Monetary Authority of Singapore.



    But they added local corporate dollar demand for hedging



purposes provided firm support for the dollar around 1.8355.



    June non-oil exports due out later in the day were expected



to extend their sharp decline, and could dampen the Sing



dollar's prospects further.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht ground lower alongside the yen and other regional


currencies, but high baht funding costs and fears of central



bank intervention helped limit the downside.



    Dealers said there was talk the central bank might have



entered the market to shore up the baht around 45.70 on Monday.



However, with regional currencies heading south, they added



they did not expect the central bank to be aggressive.



There was no shortage of negative news on the local front.

Dealers said the market was also eyeing developments over

title: WRAP:Singapore Ctrl Bk Eases Policy In Wake Of Recession
text:
OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Recession-hit Singapore is starting to pull policy levers to soften the blow dealt to its trade-dependent economy by the slowing U.S. economy and, in particular, a sharp drop in global electronics demand. 

 A day after the government promised a package of measures aimed at helping to cut business costs and curb rising unemployment, the Monetary Authority of Singapore Thursday surprised the currency market by shifting to a neutral exchange rate policy from a previous tightening stance. 

 It was the first time the central bank eased its policy bias since January 2000, when it changed to a policy of allowing a gradual and modest appreciation of the trade weighted Singapore dollar from a policy of allowing the currency to weaken during the Asian crisis, MAS officials said. 

 "Against the backdrop of a weaker external economic environment and a more protracted global electronics downturn, near-term growth prospects for the Singapore economy have turned significantly weaker while inflationary pressures are subsiding," Tharman Shanmugaratnam, MAS' managing director said. 

 "MAS has therefore shifted to a neutral exchange rate policy stance, with a policy band centered on a zero percent appreciation" of the trade weighted Singapore dollar, he added. 

 The policy shift took financial markets by surprise, with the Singapore dollar plunging to S$1.8398, yet another 11-year low against the U.S. dollar. However, the local currency subsequently recovered after the central bank apparently intervened in the currency market. 

 MAS declined to comment on whether it had intervened. 

 Prices of longer term Singapore government bonds rose as investors switched to safe-haven instruments. 

 However, the stock market took the news in stride, with prices rising marginally partly in response to higher Nasdaq futures. 

 "This (policy shift) caught a lot of us by surprise, but they (MAS) had no choice, the economy was falling off the cliff," said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at United Overseas Bank Ltd. 

 Julian Jessop, an economist with Standard Chartered Bank, said the MAS' move was surprising in view of the risk of the knock-on effect that a weaker Singapore dollar could have on regional foreign exchange markets. However, the move wasn't "shocking" given the bleak economic data issued this week. 

 At 0634 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8357, up 5.9% from S$1.7340 at the end of 2000. 

 Bhanu Baweja, an economist with research firm IDEAglobal, said he was surprised, "not so much by the policy itself as by the fact it (MAS) is now willing to openly admit it's moving to a neutral to loosening stance." 

 Indeed Singapore's economic prospects are grim. The change comes a day after the government said it's preparing an off-budget package of measures to help businesses and workers ride out the recession. The specific measures will be announced in late July, possibly July 25, when Parliament reconvenes. 

 Earlier this week, the government issued advance, or flash, estimates showing that Singapore's economy contracted at an annualized pace of 10.1% in the second quarter from the first quarter. Coming after the 11.3% annualized quarter-on-quarter drop in the January-March period, the latest data mean that Singapore is now in recession by conventional standards - two consecutive quarters of GDP shrinkage. 

 "The economy is technically in a recession," the MAS said in its biannual policy statement. 

 The MAS uses the Singapore dollar exchange rate as its main monetary policy tool and, unlike other central banks, doesn't set interest rates which are market determined. Inflation control is the sole declared objective of MAS' monetary policy as Singapore imports almost everything it needs, including water. 

 It manages the Singapore dollar exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and competitors. It maintains the trade-weighted exchange rate within an undisclosed band. 

 Shanmugaratnam said the MAS has switched to a neutral policy stance for the second half of the year, and the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is currently in the "lower half of the new (neutral) band." 

 The MAS' decision to switch to a neutral policy bias from July 1, he said, is consistent with its objective of keeping inflation low in the medium term. He said the MAS usually views the medium term as three years, but sometimes its internal models for the medium-term view run up to five years. 

 The central bank noted that inflationary pressures are subsiding as oil prices soften. 

 Singapore's consumer price index is expected "to trend down for the rest of the year, coming in within the 1%-1.5% range for 2001 as a whole." 

 Singapore's consumer price index grew at an average of 1.8% from January through May, down from a peak of 2% in the fourth quarter, although the MAS' measure of underlying inflation was still relatively high at 2.3% in the first five months of this year, it said. 

 Shanmugaratnam said the central bank will stick to the neutral stance throughout the second half of this year, and review the policy bias at the end of the six-month period. 

 In the light of the policy change, analysts expect the Singapore dollar to gradually weaken to S$1.85 to the U.S. dollar in coming weeks, as regional currencies succumb to a further slowing in their economies. 

 UOB's Jimmy Koh noted that Shanmugaratnam's statement that the currency is in the lower half of the new policy band, implies its downslide will likely be limited for now, "unless you see weakness in regionals, yen or euro." 

 Deutsche Bank strategist Peter Redward said with the recession and falling export and import prices, there is room for the Singapore dollar to fall to S$1.85, as the trade-weighted currency falls "to the bottom of the trading band in coming weeks." 


"By our estimates, the currency is now just below the middle part of
the band," he said.

title: Singapore stocks close firmer, techs up on Nasdaq.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 12 (Reuters) - Singapore stocks ended a touch higher on Thursday on a lack of market-moving news but technology shares firmed modestly in line with the Nasdaq's gains. 

 The benchmark Straits Times Index ended up 0.69 percent at 1,672.81 points. Turnover was 486 million shares against Wednesday's 341 million. 

 There was little impact from the central bank's announcement that it had shifted to a neutral exchange rate policy in line with the sharp downturn in the city state's trade-driven economy. 

 The Singapore dollar sank to fresh 11-year lows near 1.84 to the U.S. dollar after the Monetary Authority of Singapore announcement but bounced back after intervention by the central bank, foreign exchange dealers said. 

 It was at 1.8335/45 at 0945 GMT. 

 The electronics sector index jumped 2.21 percent with help from Motorola Inc and Yahoo! , both of which posted quarterly results that edged ahead of analysts' consensus estimates. 

 Some traders said the MAS shift could help export-oriented firms, especially technology companies, expecting a weak local currency to boost exports. 

 But more argued that a slightly weaker Sing dollar would barely help to counter the electronics sector's high inventory levels and the global slowdown. 

 Lingering worries over the local economy should keep the market weak, although no major movements were expected after dismal growth numbers on Tuesday and gloomy government projections on Wednesday. 

 "The bearish data has been factored into the market pretty much. Investors in Singapore are bearish but they are prepared for the worst outcome," said Nicholas Yeo, an investment manager at Aberdeen Asset Management. 

 "The market is at its oversold levels now." 

 Trade Minister George Yeo told parliament on Wednesday unemployment was likely to worsen in the second half, when economic growth may come in between minus one and plus one percent. 

 This came one day after Singapore slipped into recession with anaemic second quarter gross domestic product data. The government also revised its growth forecast for 2001 to 0.5 to 1.5 percent from 3.5 to 5.5 percent. 

 Top net gainer Venture Manufacturing rose 2.36 percent to S$13.00, followed by OCBC Bank which gained 2.56 percent to S$12.00. 

 Yeo remained conservative on the tech and banking sectors, expecting more earnings warnings from tech firms and little growth room for banks. 

 NatSteel Ltd was one of the biggest net losers with a fall of 2.75 percent to S$1.06. 

 The diversified steel miller said on Thursday it would post a loss in the first half of the year and lay off about a fifth of the workers at its Singapore steel plant due to continued weakness in the local construction sector. 

 This came after its unit NatSteel Broadway warned on Wednesday its interim results would be crimped by the global electronics downturn. 

 The contract manufacturer rebounded five cents to end at S$2.41 after sinking to a four-week low on Wednesday. 

 Despite earnings warnings, market watchers expect to see activity in small and medium-sized electronics firms amid merger and acquisition speculation. 

 Top active Fu Yu Manufacturing , a plastic injection moulder maker, surged 31.46 percent to S$0.585 in hectic volume of 52.5 million shares, buoyed by rumours it would be acquired by a global electronics contract manufacturer.

title: UPDATE 2-Singapore dlr move pragmatic due to recession.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 12 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank made a pragmatic and surprise shift to a neutral exchange rate policy on Thursday as the city state's trade-driven economy slides into recession. 

 The move, designed to keep the Singapore dollar steady on a trade-weighted basis rather on a gradually appreciating trend, effectively is an easing of the central bank's monetary stance. 

 "This is pragmatic given the sharp slowdown. The economy is already in recession and the second half will still be in recession," said ABN AMRO Asian currency strategist Gerard Teo. 

 "They announced it saying this is the stance now - it doesn't mean they did not change it earlier." 

 The Sing dollar hit 11-year lows near 1.84 to the U.S. dollar after the announcement but bounced back sharply after the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) intervened in the market. 

 By 0830 GMT, the currency was quoted at 1.8359/69. 

 WEAK ECONOMY PROMPTS CHANGE 

 While most central banks use interest rates as their main tool, the MAS tightens or loosens monetary conditions in the economy primarily by steering the value of the local dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 The MAS had maintained a bias of gradual and modest appreciation of the currency on a trade-weighted basis since early 2000 as the region came out of the Asian financial crisis. 

 But it said it was making the change against the backdrop of a weaker external economic environment and as near-term growth prospects for the Singapore economy turned gloomier. 

 "Economic activity slowed much more in the first half of 2001 than was expected, causing market sentiment to shift against the Singapore dollar," Tharman Shanmugaratnam, managing director of the MAS, told a news conference. 

 "MAS has therefore shifted to a neutral exchange rate policy stand, with a policy band centred on a zero percent appreciation of the S$ Neer (nominal effective exchange rate)." 

 The central bank said it would continue to guide the S$ Neer within the policy band and stood ready to intervene to dampen excessive volatility. 

 SURPRISE AT SHIFT 

 "The shift to a neutral stance wasn't priced in by many people. Some banks were still calling for a no change, although we were thinking they would shift," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. "I think it really opens up 1.85 now." 

 The central bank said inflationary pressures were subsiding and it expected inflation as measured by the consumer price index to trend lower to the 1.0-1.5 percent range for 2001 as a whole. 

 Shanmugaratnam said the Sing dollar's slide was due partly to concerns of a weakening economy but also to a stronger U.S. dollar. Strong demand for the U.S. dollar to fund mergers and acquisitions by local corporations contributed to the weakness. 

 But Shanmugaratnam noted that the current slowdown reflected a decline in demand, not an erosion of competitiveness. 

 "There is no reason for any persistent weakening of the Singapore dollar," he said. 

 GDP TO WEAKEN FURTHER 

 Analysts said the shift in monetary stance ought to ease the impact of the downturn on Singapore's manufacturing economy. 

 "When you have a slowdown, all competing economies' exchange rates are also depreciating so you really cannot be standing still," said Eddie Lee, strategist with Vickers Ballas. 

 But the exchange rate has also become less of an issue among manufacturers than before as they are more concerned about price competition, productivity and other costs, Lee said. 

 Dismal advance second quarter growth data on Tuesday fuelled fears the city state was heading for tougher times. 

 Singapore entered a recession as gross domestic product contracted 0.8 percent on year in the April to June quarter and dropped 10.1 percent on an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis. 

 The poor data prompted the government to revise its growth forecast for 2001 to 0.5 to 1.5 percent from 3.5 to 5.5 percent. 

 "I am slightly surprised but the (MAS) decision is well justified by the recent economic data," said Julian Jessop, global markets economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 "We suspect they have been allowing the Sing dollar to depreciate on a trade-weighted basis so 1.86 should be a reasonable cap for now." 

 (With reporting by Joyce Liu and Sonali Desai).

title: UPDATE 1-Sing dlr bounces off 11-yr low on  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, July 12 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar bounced back sharply from a fresh 11-year low around 1.84 as the central bank intervened in the market, dealers said. 

 The Sing dollar lost half a cent immediately after interbank players scrambled to sell following the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) surprise shift in stance to neutral from tightening in its half-yearly policy review statement. 

 "The shift to neutral stance wasn't priced in by many people... they have intervened at 1.84," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 The MAS had maintained a bias of gradual and modest appreciation of the currency on a trade-weighted basis since early 2000 as the region came out of the Asian financial crisis. 

 The MAS does not reveal the make-up of the trade-weighted basis. 

 Dealers said the central bank sold the U.S. dollar aggressively through local banks, pushing the Sing dollar back to 1.8345. 

 When contacted by Reuters, the MAS said it did not normally comment on its market operations. 

 The MAS said in its policy statement it was ready to intervene to dampen excessive volatility. 

 "But the MAS has said that the Sing dollar has already shifted down to the lower half of the band, so if it hits the bottom end, we can expect the MAS to come in to support the Sing dollar," BNP's Thio said. 

 "Still if you think that the rest of the Asian currencies, the euro and the yen will stay weak then on a trade-weighted basis, the Sing dollar should continue to depreciate on a nominal basis. Certainly the first target is 1.85 for us. We think that should be achieved quite shortly." 

 Dealers said fears of more intervention limited further declines for the time being but many were still looking to buy U.S. dollars on dips from 1.8300 and 1.8330. 

 "We are moving our view on the Sing dollar to 1.86 (from 1.84) in the next three months," said Julian Jessop, global markets economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 The Sing dollar has been under sustained downward pressure since the start of the year on persistent fears of ebbing growth as a slowing global economy eats into exports. 

 Advance GDP growth fell 0.8 percent year-on-year in the second quarter and dropped 10.1 percent on an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis, leaving the city state in a technical recession. 

 In its policy review statement, the MAS said inflation pressures were subsiding with the consumer price index to head lower to 1.0-1.5 percent for 2001. 

 Singapore's CPI rose 1.9 percent in May from a year earlier but fell 0.4 percent compared with April.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late, Off 11-Year Low Vs US Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was slightly higher against the U.S. dollar late Wednesday after a roller coaster ride, rebounding from 11-year lows. 

 Suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and profit-taking helped the local dollar recover from two dips, amid gloomy prospects for the economy in the second half of the year, dealers said. 

 At 0954 GMT (5:54 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.8359, down from S$1.8370 late Tuesday. The U.S. dollar traded between S$1.8340 and S$1.8376, a fresh 11-year high. 

 The U.S. dollar opened lower against the Singapore currency, and drifted higher to a pre-lunch peak of $1.8370, before falling to S$1.8340 on suspected intervention by the MAS via its agent banks. 

 In the afternoon, it surged to S$1.8376 after Trade and Industry Minister George Yeo told Parliament that the economy is expected to continue contracting in the third quarter, and that overall growth in the second half is likely to be flat from a year ago. 

 Yeo and Manpower Minister Lee Boon Yang said unemployment would worsen in the second half of this year, and that around 20,000 job losses are expected in 2001. 

 The government will announce a package of measured aimed at softening the blow dealt to employers and workers alike by the current recession, Yeo said. 

 The U.S. dollar retreated from its 11-year peak on profit-taking by market participants. 

 Looking ahead, however, market participants are looking to the MAS' biannual policy review Thursday to provide direction to the market for the near term. 

 Dealers said they expect the central bank to continue intervening in the currency market to smoothen volatility, and expect the U.S. dollar's upside to be capped between S$1.8375 and S$1.8380 overnight, with the next resistance level at S$1.8400. 

 The U.S. dollar expected to find support S$1.8330. 

 Prices of Singapore government bonds ended higher, amid bleak prospects for the local economy this year, and on tumbling equity prices in both the U.S. and Singapore, dealers said. 

 The yield on two-year bonds ended down two basis points at 2.16%, while the yield on five-year bonds fell one basis point to 2.92%. 

 At the longer end of the curve, the yields on seven-year and 10-year bonds were down two basis points each at 3.30% and 3.59%, respectively.

 Singapore's worsening economic outlook has hammered the local dollar, sending it to 11-year lows. 

 Advance, or flash, gross domestic product estimates issued Tuesday were worse than economists had expected, accelerating the Singapore dollar's fall. 

 Singapore's economy contracted an annualized 10.1% in the second quarter from the first quarter. After an 11.3% annualized quarter-on-quarter drop in the January-March period, Singapore meets the conventional definition of a recession - two back-to-back quarters of economic contraction on a quarter-on-quarter basis. 

 The Singapore government consequently slashed its 2001 GDP growth forecast to 0.5%-1.5%, from April's 3.5%-5.5% estimate. 

 Market participants expect the government to provide hints on an expected stimulus package to help resuscitate the economy when Parliament meets later in the day. 

 As well, most economists expect the MAS to reaffirm its policy of allowing a gradual, modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar against the currencies of its major trading partners and key competitors, when it announces the results of its biannual policy review Thursday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Depressed as outlook worsens.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were easier late on Tuesday with the Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar hitting new multi-year lows, depressed by poor economic data. 

 The yen also gave up some of its gains, but still managed to keep its distance from late Friday lows around 126. 

 But that was not enough for Asian currencies battered by slowing economies at home and abroad, and with little to suggest the slowdown had hit bottom. 

 The Sing dollar saw new 11-year lows after the government slashed its 2001 growth forecast as the economy shrank for the second straight quarter raising fears of a full-blown recession. 

 The Taiwan dollar fell to 34-month lows as second quarter export and import declines hit record levels. 

 Analysts said the poor data had raised fears Singapore may announce a radical shift in its monetary policy at a review due Thursday, which would have consequences for other regionals especially the baht, rupiah and the peso. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar sank to fresh 11-year lows beyond 1.8370 on disappointing growth numbers. 

 Advance second quarter GDP data showed falls of 0.8 percent on-year and 10.1 percent on an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis, leaving Singapore in a technical recession. 

 The government slashed its 2001 growth forecast to 0.5-1.5 percent from 3.5-5.5 percent, adding to the gloom. 

 Dealers said European banks and U.S. investment banks were early sellers of the Sing dollar, with a further selloff by local banks pushed it to levels not seen since July 1990. 

 They cited sporadic corporate U.S. dollar offers at around 1.8370 but said players were looking to buy dollars on dips. 

 Analysts said the dismal GDP data raised the prospect of the MAS shifting its bias to neutral from tightening at its mid-year policy review on Thursday. 

 Dealers also focused on a parliamentary sitting on Wednesday when the government might raise the prospect of fiscal stimulus to counter the downturn. PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso came under pressure from weaker regional currencies, but avoided a damaging break of 53.10, 5-= month lows hit last week. 

 Manila dealers said telecom companies bought dollars near 52.85 with scattered dollar bids by importers lining up around 52.90 in otherwise thin trading. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said he did not expect the peso to deteriorate to between 55 and 60 in the next several months as predicted by some investment banks. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht held on to levels around 45.50 amid fears of central bankintervention but the regional weakness, especially the Singapore dollar's fall kept the dollar well bid around 45.40. 

 Dealers in Singapore said foreign players were trimming dollar longs while local corporates and importers were bidding for dollars. 

 But caution prevailed after the Bank of Thailand confirmed on Monday it had intervened last week to shore up the baht. 

 Dealers said speculation about Thailand's commitment to a managed float had also kept foreign players cautious, despite repeated assurances by Thai officials they would stick to the current regime. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar touched a low of 34.759 with bearish trade data cementing views the authorities would guide the exchange rate lower to cushion the ailing economy. 

 Dealers said the central bank gave up its defence of the 34.50 level late Monday and had since only conducted smoothing operations to slow the pace of the Taiwan dollar's decline. 

 June trade numbers showed exports shrinking 16.6 percent on the year, slightly better than market forecasts while imports contracted by a worse than expected 25.2 percent. 

 For the second quarter exports declined 17 percent and imports were down 22.8 percent on the year. Both were record quarterly declines. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won gave up its early gains as the yen came under pressure and as foreign investors continued to offload local stocks, raising concerns some of the sale proceeds may be converted into dollars. 

 Foreign investors sold a net 81.6 billion won worth of shares on Tuesday after sales of 285 billion in the past two sessions. 

 Dealers said the falling Taiwan dollar and Singapore dollar also pressured the won. Taiwan and Singapore compete with Korea in several export sectors including electronics. 

 The won has failed to strengthen past the 1,290 level since June 12 but hopes of heavy investment flows in the second half have kept it in an overall uptrend since April 4, when it touched a low of 1,365.30. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah kept well within its week-old 11,225-11,375 per dollar range, with mild corporate dollar bids driving activity in a very thin market. 

 Political and economic worries continued to cloud the outlook, with the market shrugging off news Jakarta had reached agreement on almost all fronts with a visiting IMF mission. 

 Chief economics minister Burhannudin Abdullah said talks on controversial changes to central bank laws, the main sticking point in negotiations, had been deferred as sufficient compromise had been reached before the mission's arrival last Thursday. 

 Chartists said the rupiah could be headed for further losses if the dollar broke out of a constricting triangle dating back to early April on the weekly chart, and continued its uptrend. 

 Bank Indonesia said the IMF expected it to further tighten monetary policy during certain periods, but added it would do so only if such a move would not hurt economic growth.

title: Asia Markets-Earnings woes dog region, typhoon blasts HK trade.
text:
HONG KONG, July 6 (Reuters) - Earnings fears sent Asian 

 asset prices sagging to a lower close with Hong Kong stocks 

 suffering a particularly soggy end to the week after Typhoon 

 Utor blew shut the territory's financial markets on Friday. 

     The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong cancelled all trade on 

 Friday as the heavy tropical storm lashed the south China coast 

 and kept the bond, gold and money markets shut. 

     Malaysian equities shone through an otherwise gloomy day as 

 the benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index climbed an 

 impressive 1.6 percent to mark its highest close in three 

 months. 

     Fears of central bank intervention helped restrain dollar 

 bulls in Asian currency markets although the Japanese yen's 

  sustained losses below 125 pointed to a bearish outlook. 

     Tokyo stocks skidded for the third straight day with the 

 benchmark Nikkei 225 finishing 2.4 percent off at a

 high-tech bellwethers after profit warnings abroad rekindled 

 nagging earnings worries at home. 

     MALAYSIA STOCKS SHINE THROUGH 

     Malaysian stocks extended a recent run-up as comparatively 

 cheap valuations continued to attract investors back to one of 

 the year's worst-performing markets in Asia. 


    The benchmark Composite Index         ended up 1.6 percent



on the day -- it's highest close since April 3 -- and 5.7



percent higher over the course of the week.



    The Malaysian stock market had been one of regional



laggards this year -- down 7.8 percent so far -- but at current



levels, it is trading around 12 times earnings for 2001, below



an average of 20 times in the past 10 years.



    "Malaysia is not drop-dead gorgeous but attractive enough



to warrant some interest in it," said Johan Tazrin Ngo, who



helps manage 80 million ringgit ($21 million) at Kenanga



Investment Management.


CURRENCIES CRUNCHED BY DOLLAR STRENGTH



    The Singapore dollar hit fresh 11-year lows of 1.8285 on



hedge fund selling but quickly bounced back on wariness of


intervention following rumours the Monetary Authority of


Singapore (MAS) had stepped in in overseas trade on Thursday.


Intervention talk also echoed in the peso and rupiah



markets, while Taiwan's central bank was active again in



defending the 34.50 per U.S. dollar mark.



    In the region, next week's major events include Singapore's



preliminary second-quarter growth data on Tuesday and the


central bank's monetary policy statement on Wednesday.



    Some market players said the Sing dollar's weakness was



largely in line with the yen and other regionals and estimated



that levels around 1.8325 would be a threshold for the MAS.



    Some economists argue GDP figures, due on Tuesday, would



likely show another downturn, prompting the MAS to shift its



bias to neutral from tightening to weather the slowdown.



    "Next week there will be a big announcement coming out from



the MAS and I wouldn't be surprised if the MAS was to subtlely



signal to the market that there would be a bias towards a less



restrictive monetary stance," Steve Xu, regional economist at



SG Securities in Hong Kong said.



    "Therefore dollar against Sing is likely to reach S$1.85,"



Xu told Reuters Television.



    He said the Taiwan dollar and the Korean won were also



facing pressure from the overwhelming strength of the



greenback.



    "In the near term, we suspect three economies -- Taiwan,



Korea and Singapore because they do not have an external debt



overhang - are going to devalue their currencies quite



sharply," he said.



The Taiwan dollar ended off lows after the central bank and



exporters offered dollars when the local currency was just a



whisker away from the key psychological support of 34.50.



"I suspect the Central Bank of China in Taiwan will



engineer a one-off devaluation very soon, probably to around



the 35-36 level against the dollar," Xu said.



SEOUL STOCKS DOWNCAST



South Korean shares underperformed the region on Friday



with the benchmark KOSPI sinking 2.5 percent as



technology shares were hit hard by profit warnings from global



tech giants such as Britain's Marconi and U.S. Advanced



Micro Devices (AMD) .



Chipmakers such as Samsung Electronics and Hynix



Semiconductor suffered after microchip maker AMD



warned its fiscal second-quarter earnings would be a fraction



of what Wall Street had forecast.



ASIAN BOND TRADE BLOWN OUT



Asian dollar bond spreads drifted slightly wider on Friday



as trade was all but blown away in Hong Kong by Typhoon Utor,



which kept financial markets closed and dealing rooms silent.



"There's nobody trading here today. The market is



officially closed so it's pretty quiet. It may pick up when



London opens later," a dealer at a U.S. bank in Hong Kong said.



"As it is stands, we're probably a few basis points wider

Recent issues were quoted wider after overnight trade, with

over Treasuries.



Philippine Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said in a



statement on Friday the government had mandated Credit Suisse



First Boston as its sole book runner for its forthcoming $500



million sovereign bond issue.

title: Emerging  FX  - Cushioned by  intervention  fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 6 (Reuters) - Fears of central bank intervention helped restrain dollar bulls in Asian currency markets on Friday although the yen's sustained losses below 125 pointed to a bearish outlook. 

 The Singapore dollar hit fresh 11-year lows of 1.8285 on hedge fund selling but quickly bounced back on wariness of intervention following rumours the Monetary Authority of Singapore had stepped in in overseas trade on Thursday. 

 The Thai baht was well-supported offshore after the central bank was rumoured to have sold at least $100 million in both spot and forward markets to shore up the currency the previous day. Thai markets were closed on Friday. 

Intervention talk also echoed in the peso and rupiah markets, while Taiwan's central bank was active again in defending the 34.50 per U.S. dollar mark. 

 The market will be focused on the U.S. June jobs report due out at 1230 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters forecast nonfarm payrolls fell 44,000 in June after May's 19,000 drop. 

 In the region, next week's major events include Singapore's preliminary second quarter growth data on Tuesday and the central bank's monetary policy statement on Wednesday. 

 THAI BAHT 

 Baht trading was thinned by a holiday in Thailand, but the currency held above 45.40 after Thursday's rumoured intervention pushed baht funding costs in the offshore market sharply higher. 

 The one-month forward rate shot up to 41/49 satang per dollar from around 10/14 satang earlier this week, making it expensive to hold the dollar. 

 The baht was also supported by a Financial Times report quoting Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula as saying he intended to manage the baht more actively. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar suffered a volatile session, stumbling to fresh 11-year lows of 1.8285 before bouncing back to 1.8250 as a U.S. bank and a local bank took profits on their dollar longs ahead of the weekend. 

 Fears of possible intervention did exist but some said the Sing dollar's weakness was largely in line with the yen and other regionals. They estimated levels around 1.8325 would be a threshold for the MAS. 

 Some analysts argue GDP figures, due on Tuesday, would likely show another downturn, prompting the MAS to shift its bias to neutral from tightening to weather the slowdown. 

 "With the economy contracting sharply and inflation low, the MAS is likely to have a bias for a weaker Sing dollar," Ron Leven, chief Asian currency strategist at Lehman Brothers said in a research note. He expects the Sing dollar to reach 1.90-1.95 in the first quarter of next year. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso kept to a narrow 52.92-52.94 range in listless trade, with volume of only $73.5 million against Thursday's $111.06 million. 

 Manila dealers said companies were still looking to buy dollars as the peso's stumble to 5-= month lows of 53.10 on Wednesday encouraged corporate treasurers to hedge their dollar requirements for the second half of 2001. But both banks and corporates became cautious after central bank officials asked them to use the non-deliverable forward market to cover future dollar needs. 

 The Philippines' gross international reserves rose to $14.58 billion at the end of June from $14.44 billion a month before. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar ended off lows after the central bank and exporters offered dollars when the local currency was just a whisker away from the key psychological support of 34.50. 

 It was pressured by a weaker yen and there was also no shortage of negative news to worsen its outlook. 

 Economists polled by Reuters predicted June exports fell an average 18.95 percent on the year to US$10.03 billion and imports slid even further by 22.79 percent to $8.91 billion. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won kept steady around 1,295 on expected foreign direct investment flows and hopes Thursday's rate cut by the central bank would help the economy bottom out later in the year. 

 Data from home and abroad also helped sentiment, including the U.S. NAPM non-manufacturing business survey which showed economic activity may be turning around.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen saps regionals, baht shines.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were dragged lower in late trade on Thursday as the yen's sustained losses beyond 125 heightened concerns about competitive devaluation and capital outflows. 

 Only the Thai baht bucked the trend, racking up good gains after rumours of central bank intervention sent players stumbling to cover short baht positions. 

 The yen was weighed by comments by Japan's top financial diplomat Haruhiko Kuroda on Wednesday that he would not resist a weaker yen as long as it reflected fundamentals. 

 Investors fear a weaker yen could jeopardise Japan's ability to absorb imports from the rest of Asia, make its exports cheaper in other markets, and prompt some Japanese lenders to recall their loans from Asian debtors. 

 Meanwhile, the euro hit seven-month lows against the dollar on expectations the European Central Bank would leave rates unchanged later in the day despite evidence of slowing growth. 

 The market is likely to closely watch the U.S. June employment report due on Friday for clues on where the U.S. economy is heading. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht bounced sharply from a low of 45.70, its worst level since April 27, as talk of intervention spurred short covering. 

 Dealers in Singapore and Bangkok said a major Japanese bank and a U.S. bank which often deal on behalf of the Bank of Thailand were seen selling dollars at around 45.60-65, fuelling speculation the central bank was behind the move. 

 But assistant BOT governor Chettavee Chareonpitaks declined to comment on whether the central bank would intervene to help support the baht, or on market talk it had been selling dollars. 

 However, he said the baht's fall was in line with regional currencies and it was likely to fall further if the yen kept declining. 

 The baht had come under pressure from offshore sales after a senior BOT official said on Wednesday the bank would probably not require commercial banks to reveal the identities of offshore parties trading the baht, as planned earlier. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO The peso kept a softer tone to end just above 53 having slipped to 5-= month lows of 53.10 on Wednesday. 

 Manila dealers said a U.S. bank and a European bank sold around $15-20 million from 53.0 pesos, fanning talk they were acting on behalf of the central bank. 

 They also reported talk the central bank had asked its auditors to carefully monitor transactions of at least eight local and foreign banks in Manila. 

 But dealers said most of the dollar buying was by importers and trading houses looking to hedge their requirements for the second half of 2001. 

 The central bank left key interest rates unchanged in a widely expected move. The overnight borrowing rate stands at 9.0 percent and the lending rate at 11.25 percent. 

 Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said the peso's weakness was temporary. Economic Planning Secretary Dante Canlas said he expected inflation to rise to an annual 6.8 percent in July from 6.7 percent in June due to some volatility in the exchange rate. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was dragged lower by a weaker yen and a bearish euro which are believed to be substantial components in Singapore's trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 It dropped to an intraday low of 1.8260, and some believe it is just a matter of time before it retests 11-year lows of around 1.8270 touched on May 9. 

 The market awaits the Monetary Authority of Singapore's review of monetary policy expected this month. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah drifted to 11,360 as sentiment was hurt by a weaker tone in regional currencies. 

 Jakarta dealers spotted a state bank selling $2-3 million at 11,355 and 11,352, but the rupiah's upside was limited. 

 Senior IMF officials arrived in Indonesia on a mission aimed at reviving a stalled $5 billion loan programme. 

 The programme has been deadlocked for more than six months over Indonesia's foot-dragging on economic reforms and controversial central bank law amendments. The team is expected to remain in Jakarta for up to 10 days. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was easier in line with the yen but took the Bank of Korea's widely expected quarter percentage point interest rate easing in its stride. 

 The central bank lowered its overnight call rate target to 4.75 percent after a cut of similar proportion in February. 

 With the cut already factored in, dealers said uncertainty over whether monetary easing would be followed by a weaker won policy kept players from taking aggressive positions. 

 Economists were divided over whether the BOK, caught between a sagging economy and inflation levels close to the bank's ceiling, would lower borrowing costs further in coming months. 

 The won was also cushioned by expected inflows in foreign investment, but concerns over the yen, a grim economic outlook and equity-related dollar demand capped the upside. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was weighed by the yen and as local stock market losses raised concerns foreign investors may convert the cash generated by recent selling to U.S. dollars. 

 But the central bank was again active, capping the Taiwan dollar's fall at around 34.49, dealers in Singapore said. 

 Consumer prices contracted for the second successive month. The June CPI shrank 0.16 percent on the year, after an 0.21 contraction in May. 

 Analysts said with little room left for further monetary easing, declining inflation would raise expectations Taiwan may ease its grip on the exchange rate to spur growth and exports.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late, But Off Low; Tracks Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was lower against the U.S. dollar late Thursday, but off its intraday trough, as it tracked a weaker yen, dealers said. 

 Around 0832 GMT (4:32 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.8256, up from S$1.8243 late Wednesday. It traded between S$1.8244 and S$1.8263 Thursday, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar rose to near its 11-year high of S$1.8267 set on May 8 as the U.S. currency surged to Y125.59. 

 Dealers noted that trading was fairly light, due to fears of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in the market. Such concerns emerged after the U.S. dollar broke key resistance at S$1.8250. 

 Dealers said there was unconfirmed talk that the MAS checked rates, but there were no signs of action by local banks and other banks that usually act on behalf of the de facto central bank in the foreign exchange market. 

 Local and U.S. banks were the most active buyers of U.S. dollars against the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 Dealers added that the Singapore dollar may well retest its recent 11-year low against the U.S. dollar, with the U.S. currency expected to drift higher overnight and over the next few days. 

 In overnight trading, support for the U.S. dollar is expected at S$1.8230, and resistance at S$1.8280, dealers said.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late On Yen; Thin Trading, Tight Range
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was lower late Wednesday, as it tracked a weaker yen in thin, range-bound trading, dealers said. 

 At 0820 GMT the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8243, up from S$1.8212 late Tuesday. It traded between $1.8228 and S$1.8243. 

 The local dollar opened lower, in line with a weaker yen which came within striking range of the Y125 mark against the dollar but succeeded in staying above it. 

 Local banks were active buyers and sellers of U.S. dollars though the day, and some U.S. names were also seen buying the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 "Generally there was some buying on dips, but trade has basically been thin," a dealer said. 

 Dealers said that market sentiment toward the local currency was also hurt by talk that the Singapore government may cut its 3.5%-5.5% growth forecast for 2001 when it issues an advance estimate of growth in the second quarter on July 10. 

 Trading is expected to continue to remain light overnight with U.S. markets being closed for Independence Day. 

 Support for the U.S. dollar is expected around S$1.8230, with resistance at S$1.8250. 

 "I don't think there will be any great attempt to take it higher," the dealer said. 

 The S$1.8250 resistance is expected to hold as market participants expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene at or above that level. 

 Prices of benchmark Singapore government bonds ended mixed in a directionless market, dealers said. 

 Dealers said market participants are looking to U.S. unemployment data, due Friday, for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will need to cut rates further. Also awaited is next week's issuance of Singapore second quarter growth data and an expected revision of the 2001 growth forecast, they added.

 SINGAPORE, July 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies kicked off the the first trading session of the third quarter on Monday on a bearish note as the market watched out for economic data from their biggest export markets. 

 The yen dipped to around 125 to the dollar even though the Bank of Japan's tankan business sentiment survey came in pretty much in line with market expectations. 

 The main diffusion index for large manufacturers fell to minus 16. A Reuters survey had shown a median forecast of minus 16, with forecasts ranging from minus 11 to minus 25. 

 However, the fall in planned capital investment for business year 2001/02 was only 1.3 percent from the previous year and against a forecast of a 4.8 percent decline. That raised hopes of a possible recovery later in the year. 

 In the U.S., the key NAPM index for June is slated for 1400 GMT Monday and is expected to rise to 42.8 from 42.1 in May. 

 That would suggest a slower rate of decline of activity in a sector which comprises one-fifth of the overall economy, though a NAPM reading under 50 still indicates industrial activity is shrinking.

 The won eased in line with the yen, and as players preferred to stay long of the dollar ahead of a revised economic policy for the second half to be announced at 0300 GMT. 

 However, dealers in Singapore said expected foreign investments and equity-related inflows were likely to underpin the downside, keeping the won within a near-term range of 1,290-1,310. 

 Hopes of investment inflows and fear of central bank intervention has kept the won in an uptrend channel against the dollar since it touched a low of 1,365.30 on April 4.

 The baht hovered around the lower end of its recent 45.04-45.41 range as a weaker yen dragged down most regional currencies.

 The report raised hope that a new pact would lead to resumption of the Fund's frozen $5 billion programme. The country desperately needs the Fund to release a $400 million loan delayed since last year to win investor and donor confidence. 

 Dealers said they expected players to take some profits on the dollar because of the report, but the rupiah's upside was likely to be capped at 11,250 due to lingering political uncertainty. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar stumbled to seven-week lows of 1.8241 after some Australian banks bought the U.S. dollar due to a weaker yen. 

 Dealers said fears of possible intervention did exist but some now reckon the absence of the authorities might mean they were tolerating the weaker currency to weather the slowdown. 

 Charts showed the dollar is overbought against the Sing dollar, with a 14-day relative strength index reading at 73.97, indicating some scope for short-term correction.

title: Emerging  FX  - Fed cut boon countered by yen softness.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies drew little support from the Federal Reserve's 25-basis-point cut overnight as hopes for possible recovery in the U.S. were clouded by concerns over Japan's economic outlook. 

 Dealers said the market took the Fed's cut to mean that the easing cycle may be nearing an end, but it was pretty much in line with market expectations. 

 "This can be taken as good news, but I don't expect any big reactions from the regional currency market this time," said Syetarn Hansakul, economist at WestLB. 

 "At the end of the day, the market will look at how the cut would translate into the U.S. ability to take more exports from Asia. Our view is that we might very well be at the bottom, but when we are going to take off from here is a question. Japan's bleak economic picture will also limit the upside," she said. 

 The yen slipped to the wrong side of 124 following weaker-than-expected Japanese industrial data which showed a 1.2 percent month-on-month decline in May, compared with an average forecast of a fall of 0.4 percent. 

 Players were cautious ahead of Bank of Japan's (BOJ) policy meeting later in the day amid speculation the central bank was likely to decide against easing its super-loose policy further. 

 The market will also watch out for Korea's May current account data due out at 0300 GMT and Taiwan's central bank policy meeting on Thursday. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was stuck at around 1,300, wedged between exporter dollar offers and equity-linked dollar buying. Players warily eyed the yen ahead of the BOJ policy meeting later in the day. 

 Dealers in Singapore said players were also reluctant to take aggressive positions ahead of the May current account data due 0300 GMT. June consumer prices and May industrial output are due on Friday. 

 Foreign investors were net sellers of local stocks worth about 140 billion won in the past two sessions. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar slipped to 1.8230 from 1.8196 in thin morning trading, with some European and local banks looking to buy dollars at 1.8200. 

 The recent run of gloomy data reinforced view the economy was indeed weakening and fanned speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) would shift its monetary policy to neutral from tightening at its policy review in July. 

 But many analysts believe the current stance is neutral in reality. Dealers said the Sing dollar would retest 1.8267, 11-year lows hit on May 9 in the near future. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht weakened alongside the yen, hovering around 45.20 in a thin market as players braced for key monthly economic data due out on Friday. 

 But the downside was underpinned by foreign investment in local stocks and comments by the central bank that it aimed to keep the baht stable, indicating its willingness to intervene on both sides. 

 Onshore baht funding costs eased slightly as demand for funds ahead of mid-year tax payment subsided. The one-month forward rate dipped back into discounts at -2/1 satang per dollar. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was dragging its feet around 11,400 on political worries, but with few players interested in pulling it lower amid fears of central bank intervention. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the rupiah would stay within a narrow range with the market focused on government efforts to appease the International Monetary Fund. 

 A renewed threat to impose emergency rule by President Abdurrahman Wahid has reignited worries over political stability but dealers said possible resumption of lending by the IMF could help the rupiah. 

 The government has indicated it was prepared to delay controversial changes to the central bank laws while the IMF said the move would result in resumption of talks with Jakarta. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso edged down to 52.32 from 52.29 late on Wednesday. 

 Manila dealers said importers were keen to buy dollars from 52.20, but fears of intervention offered support at around 52.50. 

 Manila dealers expect the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged when its monetary board meets later in the day, following the bank's comment it would keep them steady unless the Fed cuts by 100 basis points. 

 The overnight borrowing rate stands at 9.0 percent and the lending rate at 11.25 percent. 

 Jitters persisted after the military said late on Wednesday soldiers shot dead four Muslim rebels in the south but failed to locate any of more than 20 Filipino and U.S. hostages held by them for weeks. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar weakened, weighed by expected equity-linked U.S. dollar demand and ahead of the central bank's quarterly board meeting widely expected to track the Fed's move. 

 Foreign investors sold a net 889.43 million Taiwan dollar worth of local stocks on Wednesday, and dealers in Singapore said the sale proceeds would be chasing U.S. dollars in the currency market. 

 Expected rate cut by the central bank has also sparked speculation it may allow the Taiwan dollar to ease into a weaker range of 34.50-35.00.
