title: Asia Markets-Stocks shadow U.S. slide,  currencies  sag.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 9 (Reuters) - Asian equities ceded ground 

 on Monday as bleak job numbers and corporate profit warnings in 

 the United States fanned fresh fears about the outlook for 

 Asian economies. 

     The Nasdaq Composite Index slid 3.6 percent and the Dow 

 Jones Industrial Average shed 1.3 percent on Friday, leaving 

 stocks in Japan, Singapore and Malaysia as major casualties. 

     Japan's benchmark Nikkei average fell four percent, with 

 additional home-grown pessimism emerging from a disappointing 

 emergency stimulus package unveiled on Friday and a dip in 

 March domestic wholesale prices, fuelling doubts about Japan's 

 ability to shake off anaemic growth. 

     Singapore's Straits Times Index was the region's worst 

 performer, falling as much a five percent at one point to 

 breach the key 1,600 mark for the first time in two years. 

     Concerns about slowing export demand knocked Malaysia, with 

 the benchmark Composite Index losing 4.17 percent. 

Currencies also eased back against the U.S. dollar. The yen 

 lapsed a full yen to 124.94 yen from 123.82 on Friday. 

     Dealers said regional currencies drew marginal support from 

 wariness about possible intervention by central banks. 

SINGAPORE BRACED FOR GDP RELEASE 

     Those fears kept the Sing dollar from revisiting decade 

 lows of 1.8235 hit last week, allowing it to hang around 1.8150 

 over the course of the day. 

     The market was even more wary of possible intervention

 after Singapore's second finance minister was quoted at the 

 weekend as saying the authorities would continue to defend the 

 Sing dollar if it became too volatile. 

 The market is waiting with bated breath for a revised 

 growth forecast for 2001 and preliminary growth figures for the 

 first quarter due out on Tuesday. 

 A Reuters poll predicted the government would trim its 

 official forecast for 2001 growth to between four to six 

 percent, from its current estimate of five to seven percent. 

     This compares with growth of 9.9 percent last year, which 

 was mainly due to buoyant electronics exports. 

     Dealers said bleak numbers could confirm the need for the 

Monetary Authority of Singapore to shift its monetary stance to 

 neutral from tightening. 

     Speculation was intense the MAS might have already shifted 

 its monetary stance given recent steep falls in the Sing dollar 

 amid a lack of aggressive intervention. 

     But some said the MAS may not need to do so as it manages 

 its exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of 

currencies, most of which crumpled against the dollar in line 

 with the weaker yen. 

 "The Sing dollar can actually gain competitiveness without 

 having to shift that much, because it is managed on a very 

 broad-based basket," Chia Woon Khien, regional strategist at 

 Dresdner Bank Ag told the Reuters Television. 

 If the U.S. dollar rose to 130 yen and other Asian 

currencies moved 50-75 percent of that proportionately, she 

 said the Sing dollar would appreciate in relative terms, given 

 that the Malaysian ringgit - also a major component in its 

 trade-weighted basket - is pegged against the greenback. 

     "So I don't think there is need to panic on the dollar/Sing 

 that it would shoot past 1.85," Chia said. 

     INDONESIA AND THE IMF 

     Indonesia saw both its currency and stocks wallow despite 

 growing hopes a long-awaited mission by the International 

 Monetary Fund would help its limping economy. 

     The visit should pave the way for disbursement of a $400 

 million loan delayed by the IMF since late last year and 

 trigger a $5.8 billion debt restructuring deal with the Paris 

 Club of official creditors. 

 But analysts cautioned about expecting too much from the 

 visit and said there were still many lingering economic 

 concerns such as controversial central bank law changes. 

 An independent panel reviewing planned reforms to central 

 bank laws completed its work on Sunday but no details of its 

 findings have been released. 

 The government said on Monday it agreed in principle with 

 the results of the independent panel's review of planned 

 reforms to the central bank law.

title: Emerging  FX -Steadier, but bleak U.S. data weighs.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies regained their composure in early trade on Monday as players cashed in on recent dollar gains, but a weak yen and poor U.S. employment data kept them vulnerable to downside risks. 

 The U.S. March jobs report showed a decline of 86,000 in non-farm payroll jobs versus an expected increase of 58,000 jobs. The unemployment rate matched expectations for a rise to 4.3 percent but was the highest since mid-1999. 

 Dealers said the numbers stoked fears of a U.S. recession and that worry was likely to weigh on currencies of Asian countries whose growth depends a great deal on exports to the U.S. 

 "I see medium-term softness for the regional currencies which can be attributed to both internal and external factors. Firstly, you need the U.S. to be confident about itself before Asia can be confident about its outlook," said Philip Wee, currency strategist at DBS in Singapore. 

 "And you cannot blame the U.S. or the yen alone. Asian countries seem to have missed the opportunity to reform. And unless they push harder for it, their currencies would continue to be pressured," he said. 

 In the region, Singapore is scheduled to release a flash estimate of its January-March economic growth, along with its revised forecast for growth domestic product in 2001 on Tuesday. 

 Economists polled by Reuters forecast the economy grew 5.9 percent in the first quarter and are predicting growth on average of 4.6 percent in 2001, hurt by a slowdown in the U.S. and global technology demand. 

 Philippine markets are closed for a national holiday. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won steadied with the help of the firmer yen and wariness over central bank intervention. 

 State banks were spotted selling dollars heavily on Friday, pulling the won off the day's low of 1,358.5. 

 The Bank of Korea was believed to be behind the dollar selling. The bank kept rates steady at its monthly policy meeting on Friday, citing growing inflationary pressures due to rising consumer prices and a weakening currency. 

 However, while the market was erring on the side of caution following Friday's activity, analysts said the BOK was unlikely to step up its intervention if the yen headed south again. 

 "But while intervention risks have undoubtedly increased, the authorities are aware that their FX reserves can quickly begin to fall ... Moreover, the authorities will not want to hurt the competitiveness of Korean exporters," said a UBS Warburg report. 

 It also noted the Korean authorities had allowed the won to weaken against the yen. The yen/won cross rate was at 10.78 at 0030 GMT. 

 The Finance Ministry announced on Saturday the government would redo its marcroeconomic targets, adding it would also curb hikes in public service charges that have been blamed for the increase in inflation. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was steady in early trade in line with other regionals and on wariness of central bank intervention but dealers said local corporates were likely to chase the dollar up to test 10,900 again. 

 The market will also keep an eye on the IMF mission which is due to begin a much-awaited review of Jakarta's performance on agreed targets under a funding programme. 

 Differences with the IMF on proposed changes to laws governing the central bank became more obvious when Attorney-General Marzuki Darusman said on Saturday the IMF was overstepping itself by insisting Article 75 be dropped. 

 Article 75 stipulates that the whole board of Bank Indonesia resign once the new law takes effect. 

 The controversial changes to central bank law are among the the major reasons the IMF has withheld disbursement of a $400 million loan tranche since December. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso held steady in light offshore trade with markets in Manila closed for the Valour Day holiday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the peso was likely to stay under pressure in the near term with exporters and overseas workers holding back dollars due to the weaker regional outlook. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said at the weekend commercial banks should aim to build up their loan-loss provisions to cover more than 60 percent of bad loans. 

 At end-January, commercial banks' non-performing loan ratio rose to 16 percent of total loans from 15.1 percent in December. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar posted some gains as the market kept a close eye on the yen's moves, but Taipei dealers said its upside was being capped by the central bank, which was spotted buying dollars on Friday. 

 Analysts said inflation data issued on Friday showed room for looser monetary policy, meaning the local dollar could weaken further. Consumer prices rose a tame 0.44 percent on year in March against February's 1.02 percent on year fall. 

 Taiwan's central bank has cut rates repeatedly since December, citing relatively subdued inflation. 

 With external demand slowing, analysts said the bank was seeking to boost the domestic economy while maintaining the competitiveness of Taiwan's exports. 

 "With the economy sluggish and Asian competitor currencies devaluing substantially, the CBC (Taiwan central bank) will have to let the Taiwan dollar adjust as well in order to maintain economic growth," said UBS Warburg in a research note. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing bounced half a cent to 1.8120 in early trading from Friday's lows of 1.8184, thanks to the firmer yen. 

 Dealers said bears were reluctant to push the Sing dollar lower given its four-percent loss since the beginning of the year, due to concerns about possible intervention. 

 Such fears were rekindled after media reports quoted Singapore's second finance minister Lim Hng Kiang telling reporters at the weekend ASEAN meeting the authorities would continue to defend the Sing dollar if it became too volatile. 

 But dealers said U.S. names were eager to bid up dollar/Sing, with large orders around 1.8110-30. 

 The market is keeping a wary eye on a revised growth forecast for 2001 and preliminary growth figures for the first quarter due out on Tuesday. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was looking vulnerable at 45.60, not far from fresh 37-month lows of 45.72 hit in light offshore trade on Friday when Thai markets were closed. 

 Bangkok dealers said both onshore and offshore banks were looking to bid dollar/baht up, with 45.50 seen as good support. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said late on Friday the central bank should not allow speculation in the baht and he did not think the currency would reach 47 or 48 to the dollar. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak added to a string of official warnings, saying on Sunday he expected volatility in the baht to be short-lived. 

 He added interest rates could ease soon if the national asset management company can resolve bad loan problems. The benchmark 14-day repo rate currently stands at 1.5 percent. 

 The AMC plans to take over a portion of 1.7 trillion baht in non-performing loans from banks and push ahead with restructuring. 

 Offshore baht funding costs were still firm with the one-month forward rate at 40/45 satang per dollar against 30/40 late on Friday.

title: ASEAN: MAS To Defend Singapore Dlr If Needed - Minister
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore will continue to defend the local currency if it becomes too volatile, Singapore's second finance minister, Lim Hng Kiang suggested Sunday. 

 "The MAS has put a statement on the Singapore dollar - that statement still remains effective," Lim said, when asked by Dow Jones Newswires if the government is concerned by the Singapore dollar's fall to an 11-year low earlier this week. 

 Earlier this week, the Singapore dollar fell to an 11-year low of S$1.8230 against its U.S. counterpart as the Japanese yen slumped and as traders speculated that the MAS would ease the moderately tightening bias of its monetary policy. Late Friday in Asia, the Singapore dollar was hovering around S$1.8184. 

 The de facto central bank recently reiterated that it would intervene, if necessary, to dampen excessive fluctuations of the Singapore dollar, including movements arising from the funding of corporate merger and acquisition activities. 

 Lim was speaking to reporters at the fringes of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations finance ministers' weekend meeting.

title: Asia Markets - Nasdaq gives stocks some lift,  currencies  glum.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - Asian stocks danced to the 

 Nasdaq's upbeat tune on Friday in early trade, but lost some 

 energy as the day wore on and doubts developed about whether 

 U.S. gains would be sustained. 

     Most closed firmer but well off their highs. 

     Regional currencies stumbled alongside the yen after 

 euphoria surrounding a new Japanese economic package quickly 

 fizzled out. 

     Tech-heavy Korean and Taiwan markets rose after the Nasdaq 

 jumped 8.92 percent or 146.20 points to close at 1,785.00 

 overnight -- its biggest percentage gains ever. 

     U.S. market sentiment had been boosted by news Dell 

 Computer Corp stood by its first-quarter targets. 

     The Korean Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) ended 2.54 

 percent or 12.53 points higher at 506.22. Taiwan's TAIEX gained 

 2.02 percent on the Nasdaq's rally and signs of easing 

 U.S.-China tensions. 

 Japan's stocks closed off their intraday's high after a 

 long-awaited emergency economic package designed to boost the 

 country's growth and stock market came in short on detail. 

 "The package looks fairly solid - it just left too many 

 questions unanswered to warrant a broad-based advance," said 

 Nobuaki Kurisu, chief fund manager at Sumisei Global Investment 

 Trust Management. 

 The next event for market focus is the all-important U.S. 

 job report to be released later in the day, for a clue to U.S. 

 economic health and the prospect of further rate cuts by the 

 Federal Reserve. 

 Economists polled by Reuters expected the March jobs report 

 to reveal a higher unemployment rate, up to 4.3 percent from 

 the current 4.2 percent rate where it has been lodged all year. 

CURRENCIES SINKS, INFLATION FEARED 

 Asian currencies buckled under the yen's renewed weakness, 

 with the Indonesian rupiah leading the losers due to persistent 

 corporate dollar demand. 

 But central bank intervention underpinned some of the 

currencies. Dealers said the Korean central bank sold the 

 dollar through state banks while Bank Indonesia was spotted 

 selling the U.S. currency directly to cap the rupiah's fall at 

 10,930. 

 The move came after the Monetary Authority of Singapore was 

 rumoured to have intervened in the market on Monday and the 

 Bank of Thailand suggested earlier this week that it had been 

 in the market to stave off baht volatility. 

 Analysts expressed concerns sustained declines in these 

currencies could worsen the already bleak growth prospect of 

 the region as they increased risk of inflation. 

 "This stops people from placing a one-way bet on the 

 direction of inflation and interest rates in the region," said 

 David Fernandez, head of Asian sovereign research at JP Morgan 

 Chase. 

 "The market right now is taking currency weakness seriously 

 and it's time to be cautious as hopes that central banks would 

 continue to cut rates to boost the economy will have to be put 

 on pause," he said. 

 WEAK YEN COULD HIT PEGS 

 There has been concern in the market that the yen's 

 sustained weakness could raise the spectre of competitive 

 devaluation among Asian pegged currencies such as the Malaysian 

 ringgit, Chinese yuan and Hong Kong dollar. 

 The yen has depreciated by around 10 percent year this 

 year. While other free-floated currencies can fall in tandem 

 with the yen, these pegged currencies have not, making them 

 look overvalued. 

 "There has been yet again rhetoric about pressure on the 

 Hong Kong economy via price and output adjustments witnessed in 

 1998, and about how the Chinese renminbi peg stands in the face 

 of persistent yen weakness," said Lian Chia Liang, analyst at 

 Merrill Lynch. 

 China managed to hold the yuan steady against the dollar 

 despite Asian financial crisis which saw the yen falling past 

 140 in summer 1998. Investors are questioning if the country 

 would be able to do the same this time. 

     Yan Haiwang, deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, 

 said on Friday that a devaluation of the yuan was impossible. 

     "I have never thought about devaluing the yuan and it is 

 quite impossible for that to happen," he told an economic forum 

 attended by finance and central bank officials from Japan and 

 China.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen weighs,  central bank  fears help.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies came under renewed pressure on Friday as the yen's three-day winning streak against the dollar ran into some resistance. 

 The yen stumbled as a much-awaited economic package by the Japanese ruling coalition failed to impress the market, but renewed jawboning boosted it in late trade. 

 The Finance Ministry's Haruhiko Kuroda said it was hard to justify recent moves in the dollar/yen as there had been no big change in Japan's fundamentals and that Japan would take action in currency markets if current trends continued. 

 Most regional currencies opened higher on the back of the yen's overnight gains but a reversal of those gains sparked covering of short dollar positions. 

 But central banks in Korea and Indonesia intervened while the fear of that in Singapore kept the won, rupiah and Sing dollar off recent lows. 

 With Bangkok closed for a holiday, the baht was not so lucky and slipped to a fresh 37-month low in offshore trade. 

 Analysts said central bank threats and actions could temporarily ease some pressure on the currencies but the outlook remained weak on slowing growth and exports. 

 Fresh trading cues were likely to emerge from the U.S. March employment report due at 1230 GMT. 

 Economists polled by Reuters on average expect a higher unemployment rate, up to 4.3 percent from February's 4.2 percent. They also forecast 58,000 new jobs were created outside the farm sector in March, compared with 135,000 in February. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar kept a soft tone as the yen eased. 

 Dealers said local banks placed sizeable U.S. dollar orders in the afternoon, which pushed it down to session lows of 1.8184. 

 But the market turned wary as the Monetary Authority of Singapore was suspected to have defended that level late on Wednesday. This allowed the Sing dollar to avoid a damaging break of 1.8200 which would expose it to decade lows of 1.8230 hit on Monday. 

 But the market saw no signs of aggressive action by the authorities, which again spurred speculation the MAS had already shifted its monetary stance to neutral from a tightening bias. 

 The MAS has said it would review its monetary policy in the middle of the year. 

 Dealers said the market would focus on a revised growth forecast for 2001 and preliminary growth figures for the first quarter due for release on Tuesday. 

 The government estimates the economy will grow between five to seven percent this year, but economists suspect worsening external conditions could slow growth to as low as 4.8 percent. 

 THAI BAHT 

 Offshore players took advantage of a holiday in Bangkok to push the baht to a 37-month low of 45.72. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the dollar crawled higher in ultra-thin trade, which exaggerated the impact of relatively small deals. They added U.S. names were spotted buying up dollar/baht when the yen fell past 125. 

 "With Bangkok on holiday, that means no Bank of Thailand. So you might as well take adventage of that," said a dealer at a European bank, referring to the central bank's suspected intervention to shore up the baht earlier this week. 

 Charts showed the dollar/baht had wandered deeply into overbought territory with a reading of 84.863 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 Offshore baht funding costs were still firm at 41/52 satang per dollar against 40/50 satang late Thursday. 

 KOREAN WON -02 

 The won was propped up by the Bank of Korea as it tried to track the yen's retreat against the dollar. 

 Dealers estimated the central bank had directly sold about $150-200 million at around 1,358 won in late morning trade, intervening again in the afternoon. 

 Both times the won rose to around its session high of 1,339.9 where importers and offshore players were seen buying dollars. 

 Hong Kong dealers said the intervention, which came after weeks of verbal threats and recent state bank dollar sales, was not as aggressive as expected, given the $1.5 billion average daily turnover in the won market. 

 They said fears the central bank was probably testing the depth of the market and might come in more strongly later, kept players cautious. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was firmer, but did not venture very far from Thursday's close of 32.979 as the yen wavered. 

 For the past several weeks, the Taiwan dollar has been tracking the yen closely as Taiwan and Japan compete on electronics exports. 

 Consumer inflation data showed a slight 0.44 percent on-year rise in March against February's 1.02 percent fall. Analysts said the slight rise meant inflation was still benign and may provide more room for the central bank to cut rates. 

 On the Taiwan dollar NDF market, the six-month rate was at 0.560/610 and the one-year was at 0.850/900. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah dipped to a near four-week low of 10,930 as early dollar buying by some state and foreign banks sent local corporates scrambling for dollars. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the central bank pumped in around $10-30 million from around 10,930 all the way to 10,850, but they added that local corporate demand for dollars was strong in the 10,750-10,800 range. 

 The market was unimpressed by news an IMF review mission would start its work in Jakarta on Wednesday as conditions of the visit had been met. 

 Dealers said the market was likely to wait for a formal resumption of IMF lending before pushing the rupiah higher. 

 However, Bank Indonesia governor Sjahril Sabirin said he expected the IMF visit to help boost sentiment in the rupiah which could give the central bank room to lower interest rates. 

 The mission's visit should pave the way for a new $400 million loan from the IMF which has been delayed since late last year due to a dispute between Jakarta and the Fund over key reforms. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended at 50.200, slightly below its Thursday close after hitting a session low of 50.50 in line with weakness in other regional currencies. 

 Dealers said oil importers and some foreign banks were seen bidding the dollar up in early trade but inflows from overseas workers ahead of a long weekend capped the peso's downside. 

 Manila's financial markets will be closed on Monday for the Day of Valour.

title: WRAPUP 2-Asia stocks mixed, eyes Fed action next week.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 12 (Reuters) - Asia's stock markets turned in a mixed performance on Friday following solid gains on Wall Street, but investors were cautious ahead of a widely-anticipated rise in key U.S. interest rates next week. 

 "Sentiment is not too positive and people are quite cautious ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday," said Alex Wong, research manager at OSK Securities in Hong Kong. 

 In foreign exchange markets, the yen was trading below its early intraday peak but was clinging to gains helped by a recovery in Japanese stock prices. 

 Tokyo's Nikkei average finished up 2.82 percent at 17,357.86 after four straight losing sessions. 

 Tokyo traders said overall sentiment was cautious because of potential volatility next week when the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets. 

 Australia's S&P/ASX 200 index also staged a rebound following recent losses, closing 1.28 percent up at 3,034.8. 

 Hong Kong stocks were firmer following a losing streak since May 3. The Hang Seng Index was up 1.50 percent at 14,709.72 by 0705 GMT. 

 Wall Street rallied overnight after a government report showed U.S. retail sales fell 0.2 percent in April - the first decline in almost two years. 

 The closely watched data might ease pressure on the Fed to keep tightening interest rates in a bid to cool the economy. 

 Before the data, analysts forecast the Fed would hike U.S. rates by 50 to 75 basis points, even after the expected increase in rates next week. 

 Fed-watchers now turn to U.S. April Producer Price Index data due later on Friday, with the PPI expected to post a 0.2 percent drop and core-PPI - which strips out volatile food and energy prices - seen gaining 0.1 percent. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.72 percent to end at 10,545.97 on Thursday, while the technology heavy Nasdaq rose 3.39 percent to 3,499.58 after enduring three consecutive sessions of steep losses. 

 Taiwan's TAIEX ended up 2.52 percent at 8,560.44 in cautious trade, while South Korea's KOSPI fell 2.53 percent to 740.30. 

 And Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur Composite index was off 0.76 percent at 913.72 in mid-afternoon trade. 

 TOKYO STOCK RALLY LIFTS YEN 

 The yen extended overnight gains against the dollar and the euro after Japanese stocks rebounded. 

 Ken Landon, a senior currency strategist at Deutsche Bank, said Wall Street's recovery had reduced concern about investors pulling money out of Japan to cover their U.S. positions. 

 "The dollar should stablise around 107 yen and again try the 110 level," Landon said. 

 Dealers said the dollar's retreat to a low of 107.65 yen was also driven by technical factors as many traders, caught with long positions after the dollar's quick decline from Thursday's high of 110.08 yen, sought to sell on rallies. 

 Heavy demand for yen in cross trade, particularly against the euro and sterling, was also weighing the U.S. currency down. 

 Dealers were unsure if the dollar's setback was a correction after the recent rally or a shift in the dollar's uptrend. 

 "It's really difficult to predict direction at the moment after it touched the long-targeted 110 yen," a trust bank dealer said. 

 Around 0715 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 108.19/29 yen compared with 108.45 yen in U.S. trade late on Thursday. 

 Dealers said a Fed rate rise of less than 50 basis points would hurt the dollar. 

 The euro was holding above 90 U.S. cents but had no clear direction in Tokyo after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on Thursday. 

 Around 0715 GMT, the euro was trading at $0.908/13 versus $0.9013 in late U.S. trade. 

 The euro/yen was at 97.51/59 against 97.71 yen in late U.S. trade. 

 Dealers said the European currency was expected to remain under downward pressure after European officials failed to offer any indication they would intervene to support the ailing currency.

title: Singapore Dlr Ends Up, Supported By Fear Of MAS Action
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended moderately stronger against the U.S. dollar on Friday as dealers hesitate to sell the currency for fear of provoking central bank intervention. 

 Around 0935 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7245, down from Thursday's close of S$1.7265. 

 The Singapore dollar gained despite a steep drop in the Indonesian rupiah. South Asia's currencies often move in tandem. 

 The stability of the Singapore currency Friday was a testament to the effectiveness of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which intervened in support of the currency on Thursday, analysts said. 

 While the MAS may allow the currency to weaken somewhat if the region's other currencies continue to soften, it's not likely to allow the U.S. dollar to climb much above S$1.7350, said Patrick Bennett, currency strategist at Warburg Dillon Read. 

 "I think if we go to S$1.7350 they will step in again," Bennett said. 

 The Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies are under pressure from expectations that the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee will raise its key interest rate by 50 basis points when it meets next week. 

 Although the rate hike appears to be inevitable, investors are now starting focus on the possibility that rates will continue to rise in the U.S. after next week's FOMC meeting. 

 As rates rise, higher yielding U.S. investments start to look more attractive. In addition, stock market volatility in the U.S. is prompting foreign investors to reduce positions in emerging markets. 

 In Singapore's local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered unchanged at 0.125%. The three-month rate was offered at 3.0625%, also unchanged.

title: Asian  Currencies  Under Pressure Late From Rupiah's Slide
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah continued to weaken Friday on a series of misstatements by senior policymakers, putting pressure on currencies in other Asian markets. 

 In late trading Friday, the U.S. dollar briefly surged past the level of IDR8,700, its highest point since Sept. 27, after the governor of the central bank said he would intervene to support the rupiah only "if it will be effective." 

 The statement by Sjahril Sabirin was widely interpreted as a sign of weakness by traders already inclined to sell the currency following a statement on Thursday by Indonesia's top economic official, Kwik Kian Gie, who said he couldn't recommend his country to foreign investors. 

 The Thai baht and the Philippine peso were dragged lower by the rupiah. Regional currencies had already been weakened by expectations of an impending rise in interest rates in the U.S., where the Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to hike its key federal funds rate by 50 basis points when it meets Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar, meanwhile, was higher in late trading Friday following reports that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to defend the currency on Thursday. The Thai baht, while lower, also gained support from reports of central bank intervention the previous day. 

 Around 0845 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at IDR8,485, up from IDR8,375 late Thursday but off its intraday peak. 

 Against the baht, the U.S. dollar was at THB38.845, up from THB38.815 late Thursday. 

 The dollar also rose to PHP41.475 from PHP41.430. The peso continued to suffer from the Muslim insurgency in the southern province of Mindanao, where rebels are holding foreign hostages, said Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Among southeast Asian currencies, only the Singapore dollar gained ground following Thursday's intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The U.S. dollar fell to S$1.7243 from Thursday's S$1.7265. 

 Traders hesitated to bid the U.S. dollar above the level of S$1.7300 for fear of provoking a further round of intervention by the MAS, analysts said. 

 "If selling intensifies to the levels we have seen, I'm sure they will step back in," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 But across southeast Asia, currencies are likely to weaken further on expectations that U.S. rates will continue to rise even after next week's Fed meeting. And a volatile U.S. stock market is adding to the uncertainty, prompting investors to withdraw funds from relatively risky emerging markets, analysts said. 

 Analysts said the supply of U.S. dollars had all but dried up in Indonesia, with exporters withholding the currency from the market in the expectation that the rupiah will fall even further. 

 Patrick Bennett, currency strategist at Warburg Dillon Read, said the market is waiting for a stronger stance from the Indonesian central bank. 

 "They don't want to come in just to provide liquidity to the market," Bennett said. "Nothing that's being said is dissuading anyone from holding on to these dollars." The central bank, he said, "Needs to come out and say something stronger." 

 Analysts said the rupiah would continue to weaken as the market starts to wonder how long Kwik would stay in his job. Some observers said the dollar could quickly jump to IDR9,000 or beyond. 

 "The markets will remain very cautious in Indonesia," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore. "There clearly will continue to be talk and speculation about a further cabinet reshuffle." 

 Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid, however, said he had no plans to replace Kwik, calming the markets somewhat. He blamed the weakening currency on the anniversary of 1998 ethnic riots, saying local businesses were holding on to their U.S. dollars for fear of unrest. 

 In South Korea, the U.S. dollar rose to KRW1,114.5 in late trading, up from KRW1,109.10 on Wednesday. Thursday was a holiday in Korea. Friday's closing level was the weakest for the won since April 17, when it touched KRW1,115.30 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said, however, that the won was unusual among Asian currencies in that it would gain against the dollar if authorities tighten monetary policy in response to surging economic growth. 

 The Taiwan dollar got a boost from a stock market rally. The U.S. dollar ended trading at NT30.739, down from Thursday's close at NT30.752. The central bank also supported the currency, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Under Pressure Early, But Trading Stable
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies remained under pressure early Friday as the prospects for tighter U.S. monetary policy underpinned the dollar. 

 Analysts say the bias toward the U.S. currency in global markets probably will be retained at least through next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which policy makers are expected to raise short-term interest rates by a half percentage point. 

 However, trading in Asian currencies was relatively stable after a session Thursday that saw heavy volatility and rumored central bankintervention. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered around the 8,400 rupiah to the dollar level as poor investor sentiment and negative comments Thursday by the country's Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie weighed on the currency. 

 At 0110 GMT (9:10 p.m. EDT Thursday), the dollar was quoted at IDR8,400, up slightly from IDR8,375 late Thursday. 

 The Singapore dollar edged up after hitting a 13-month low a day earlier. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7246, down from S$1.7265 late Thursday. The U.S. currency had risen to S$1.7351 Thursday before the Monetary Authority of Singapore was reported to have intervened on the Singapore dollar's behalf. 

 Dealers said the continuing preference for U.S. dollars should keep the pair in a trading range of S$1.7250-$1.7290 Friday. 

 The Thai baht resumed its downward slide after being propped up a day earlier by technical factors. The currency got a boost Thursday when foreign banks that bet on a decline in the baht were forced to pull back due to the rising cost of funding their long-dollar positions through offshore swaps.

title: Emerging  FX  - Browbeaten by dlr, c.banks jump in.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 11 (Reuters) - Hefty losses in regional 

 stocks and the prospect of higher U.S. rates put Asian regional 

currencies on the defensive late on Thursday. 

     The fall was more pronounced in the rupiah and the baht 

 which hit their 2000 lows as flustered importers and corporate 

 players scurried to buy dollars. 

     Central banks in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand were 

 heard intervening in the market to prop up their sliding 

currencies, but no official confirmation was available. 

     "Regional currency sales were broad-based. There's talk 

 that central banks were in the market today - Singapore, 

 Indonesia and Thailand," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at 

 Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

     "The dollar offers were mostly done through offshore banks. 

 But there's no confirmation on this," he said. 

     Analysts said Asian currencies would retain their weak tone 

 in the near-term against a backdrop of continued dollar 

 strength. 


    The dollar briefly rose above the 110 yen	  barrier as



a sharp fall in Tokyo shares overshadowed confidence in Japan's



economic recovery.



    The benchmark Nikkei	   closed 4.63 percent off on



Thursday, ending below 17,000 points for the first time since



September 27, 1999.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    A stream of dollar bids from offshore and corporate players



sent the rupiah reeling to 8,420 -- its lowest level since



September 29.



    Although talk of central bank intervention and sporadic



dollar profit-taking lifted the unit from its day low, market



sentiment remained glum.



    Dealers said any rebound could be temporary as corporate



dollar demand remained high and exporters were opting to park



their dollar receivables offshore amid political and economic



uncertainties.



THAI BAHT



The baht struggled to stand above the key 39.00 level where



the central bank was rumoured to have intervened.



Dealers said it was likely to slip back below the level



again soon due to sustained dollar demand from both offshore



and corporate players.



"If the central bank declares that it had indeed intervened


and that it hates to see the baht below 39, then market



participants might perhaps hold their baht sales for a while,"



said a dealer at a European bank.



    "But I don't think sellers would be deterred much by the



market talk," she said.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar staged a mild rebound amid market



rumours that the central bank had intervened to defend it after



it fell to 13-month lows against the U.S. dollar.



    Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was



spotted selling dollars fairly aggressively from the 1.7350



level downwards, pushing the Sing dollar back to the firm side



of 1.73.



There was also talk that the MAS had drained liquidity in



local money markets, pushing short-term interbank rates to



their highest since the last quarter of 1998 on Wednesday.



An MAS spokeswoman said the bank does not comment on its



actions in the market. The central bank has said in the past



that it intervenes in forex markets to smooth sharp moves in



the exchange rate.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso was at the lower end of its intra-day range,



offering few buying incentives as investors opted to wait for



the expected increase in U.S. interest rates next week.



The unresolved armed conflict in the southern Mindanao region



also weighed on sentiment, dealers said.



On the macro front, the country's gross international



reserves were $15.8 billion at the end of April, down from



$15.99 billion the previous month, a central bank official



said.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar took its cue from the weaker yen and a



near 2.5 percent drop on the stock market, which pushed the



benchmark TAIEX to its lowest close in 2000.



Dealers said worries about the scale and impact of the next



Fed rate hike and hefty overnight losses on the Nasdaq



were depressing Taipei markets.



The Taiwan dollar's plight was worsened by the central



bank's failure to defend the T$30.72 level, where it has been



seen recently, though dealers said the bank was in the market



intermittently over the course of the day.



The central bank has been in the market of late and dealers



said its moves were aimed at eliminating market expectations of



a depreciation of the Taiwan dollar amid political



uncertainties.



KOREAN WON -2



The Korean won was quoted lower in thin offshore trade,



with local markets closed for Buddha's birthday.



    Finance Minister Lee Hun-Jai said Korea's GDP this year



would probably exceed an originally forecast six percent.



    He also said inflation this year would be within the



originally estimated three percent, while a strong export



performance would yield a continued trade surplus.



    Over the medium term, South Korea's GDP would be around six



percent and inflation below three percent, he added, without



specifying the time period.

title: Singapore  Dlr Ends Higher; MAS  Intervenes  To Buy US Dlrs
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The central bank intervened to shore up the Singapore dollar on Thursday after the currency fell to its lowest level in 13 months. 

 Around 1000 GMT, at the close of local trading, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7267, down from S$1.7301 late Wednesday. 

 The U.S. dollar touched a high of S$1.7355 before the Monetary Authority of Singapore stepped in to buy the U.S. currency for Singapore dollars, dealers said. 

 That was the highest level for the U.S. dollar since it hit S$1.7357 on April 8, 1999. 

 The Singapore dollar was dragged down by the Indonesian rupiah, which plunged following remarks by Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie, who said his country faces too much instability and social unrest to appeal to investors. 

 Expectations that the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee would raise interest rates by 50 basis points at its May 16 meeting also weighed on the Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies. 

 The intervention by the MAS came as a surprise. Most dealers had said the central bank would allow the currency to drift lower because of the dollar's recent strength against the euro, the yen and other currencies. 

 But one dealer said the MAS intervened to calm the markets in the wake of "panic selling" of the rupiah and wasn't trying to determine the exchange rate against the U.S. dollar. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 2.125%, up from 1% on Wednesday. The three-month rate was offered at 3.0625%, up from 3%.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Panic Selling Hurts Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah was driven sharply lower by panic selling Thursday, prompting Singapore monetary authorities to intervene in foreign exchange markets to prevent their currency from being swept along, dealers said. 

 The rupiah had been pressured all week by concerns over Indonesia's political and economic outlook, a softer yen, and prospects for higher U.S. interest rates. But it was dealt another blow Thursday by shocking comments from the country's top economic minister questioning the wisdom of investing in Indonesia. 

 Indonesia faces too much instability and social unrest to appeal to investors, Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires. 

 "I never talk about foreign investment and things like that because I'm realistic enough; if I were a foreign investor, I wouldn't come to Indonesia," he said. 

 "The law enforcement is not there. But not only that, the whole thing is so confusing. How can you come here?," he asked. 

 The rupiah reacted negatively, falling to nearly a seven-month low against the dollar. The dollar touched 8,430 rupiah in intraday trading, the strongest it has been against the Indonesian currency since hitting IDR8,492 on Oct. 14, 1999. 

 Near the end of Asian trading, the dollar was quoted at IDR8,375, up from IDR8,203 late Wednesday. 

 "Kwik is apparently unhappy with President Wahid's decision to appoint two advisors to oversee the activities in his ministry," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 "It's difficult to see any respite for the (rupiah), especially after it broke through key resistance at 8,200. Neighboring currencies are in for a rough ride as well," Wee said. 

 The Philippine peso, New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht also traded lower for most of the day before the latter two currencies recovered somewhat in the afternoon. 

 In the case of the Singapore dollar, dealers said the rebound was at least partially driven by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which entered the market late in the afternoon to halt the currency's slide. 

 The MAS has a policy of not commenting on its monetary actions. 

 Dealers said the MAS' action was driven more by its desire to show the market that it has control over its currency than any significant concern about the currency's value relative to the U.S. dollar. 

 The dollar has risen significantly against the euro, yen and other world currencies on expectations that Federal Reserve policy makers will raise short-term interest rates by a half a percentage point next week. 

 Because the dollar strength is broad-based, and not aimed specifically at the Singapore dollar, it is of less concern to the MAS, analysts said. 

 "They (MAS) were just trying to send a message to the market," a dealer at a foreign bank said. "There was so much panic in the market today...they just wanted to prevent undue volatility," he said. 

 The MAS intervened after the dollar hit a 13-month high of S$1.7351, dealers at three different foreign banks said. The MAS sold dollars all the way down to the $1.7250 level, they said. 

 Late in Asian trading, the dollar was quoted at S$1.7265, down from S$1.7301 late Wednesday. 

 The Thai baht spent most of the day battling poor sentiment spurred by the expected U.S. rate hike, stock market outflows and concerns over the pace of debt restructuring in Thailand. 

 At its high point, the dollar broke through a key THB39.00 resistance level for the first time since November 1999. 

 But the dollar reversed course in the afternoon after offshore players, who held long dollar positions through swap contracts, took profit on the dollar's rise, dealers said. 

 Late in the session the dollar was quoted at 38.815 baht, down from THB38.915 late Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso closed lower on prospects for a widening interest rate differential with the U.S., as well a rebel uprising in the southern part of the country. 

 The dollar closed at 41.430 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Wednesday's close at PHP41.370. Earlier in the session, the dollar rose to a 19-month high of PHP41.440. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended lower Thursday following a 2.5% drop in the local stock market index. Foreign institutional investors, who helped boost the local currency in recent months, sold a net NT$3.09 billion worth of Taiwan shares Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$30.752, compared with it's previous close at NT$30.697. 

 Markets in South Korea were closed for a holiday.

title: Singapore Straits Times Index Ends Down 2.6% To 2003.72
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Singapore shares closed sharply lower Thursday on a host of factors, pushing the Straits Times index below the 2000 points level for the second time since April 17. 

 The 5.6% decline in the Nasdaq and the 1.6% fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average overnight were key triggers to the selling Thursday. The U.S. declines added to already strong worries about the impact of a sharply higher interest rate hike in the U.S., which is Singapore's key trading partner. 

 The Federal Reserve is set to revise the federal fund rate when its rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets May 16. Market participants expect a 50 basis point hike. 

 Also adding to market concerns was the Singapore dollar's sharp decline against the U.S. dollar Thursday - to S$1.7351, triggering an intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The Singapore dollar fell following a sharper decline in the Indonesian rupiah after Indonesian Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie told Dow Jones Newswires that Indonesia isn't yet stable enough politically to honestly invite foreign investors to invest. 

 The statement comes at a time when the Singapore government is encouraging local companies to invest in Indonesia. Some companies such as Cycle & Carriage have already done so. 

 The benchmark Straits Times Index fell 53.50 points, or 2.6%, to 2003.72. The DBS-50 index, which gives greater weighting to the largest stocks and excludes foreign-currency issues, fell 16.34 points, or 2.5%, to 647.29. 

 The Straits Times index hit an intraday low of 1986.57 points - the lowest since April 17 when it sank to 1981.29 in intraday trading. 

 Volume was estimated at 548.5 million shares, compared with 488.4 million shares Wednesday. Decliners led advancers 280 to 64, with 102 stocks unchanged.

title: Emerging  FX  - Strong dollar smothers regionals.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 10 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 were easier on Wednesday, as investor appetite for dollars 

 showed no signs of letting up amid expectations of an 

 aggressive Fed rate hike next week. 

     The rupiah fell through 8,100 to the dollar to its weakest 

 levels since mid-October in early morning trade, hit by fresh 

 offshore dollar buying on concerns over the country's political 

 stability and economic progress. 


    The dollar kept its firm stance against the yen	 ,



helped by commercial demand and buying interest from Japanese



trust banks looking to unwind earlier hedge positions.



    The ailing euro	  held most gains against the dollar



in morning trade after hitting a high of 90.80 cents overnight



on wariness of possible intervention by European authorities.



    The euro got a boost overnight when French Finance Minister



Laurent Fabius reminded markets that currency market


intervention was a weapon at Europe's disposal.



    But underlying bearish sentiment for the euro remained, as



doubts about actual intervention still lingered.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah looked set to test the psychological 8,200



support on a combination of U.S. rate fears and concerns over



the country's political stability and economic progress.



    "The rupiah is most likely to maintain its weak tone for a



while," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore.



    "Uncertainties about the peaking of U.S. interest rates in



terms of timing and magnitude and lack of foreign interest in



(Indonesia) should limit investment inflows into the country.



And that is bearish for the rupiah," he said.



Dealers said its upside would be capped at 8,050-8,100



where active bargain hunting on the dollar was expected. THAI



BAHT



The baht dipped through a key support of 38.60 on strong



dollar demand from local firms seeking to repay or refinance



foreign debts in the face of rising international interest



rates.



Dealers said baht bids against the Singapore dollar had



slowed the fall, but would not be sufficient to stop it. Some



reckoned the unit could test the next support of 38.80 later on



Wednesday.



Analysts believe the widening differential between local



and the U.S. interest rates suggests significant capital



outflows will continue for the rest of this year.



    Thailand's private foreign debt was estimated at around $36



billion in February.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso tracked the regionals lower in light trade, but



dealers reckoned the downside should be limited by central bank


support.



    The peso was likely to be wedged in a narrow range and



trading would remain light until the central bank releases its



grip on the market, dealers said.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won started the day weaker against the dollar as



players looked to buy the U.S. unit as it strengthened against



the yen.



    "Dollar sentiment is strong this morning as Asian


currencies, including the yen, appeared weaker versus the U.S.



unit," said a foreign bank dealer.



    Another dealer said the overhang and the bearish sentiment



were pushing the regionals lower.



    Seoul dealers said they expected dollar/won to move in a



tight range between 1,109.5 and 1,110.5 for the day.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar was dragged down by other regionals



and the yen though dealers were cautious of possible



dollar-selling intervention by the Monetary Authority of


Singapore (MAS).



    "People are expecting the MAS to come in to prop up the



Sing," said one dealer at a European bank.



    But he saw no reason for the MAS to intervene at this level



as other regional currencies were generally weak. He expected



the Sing dollar to test the downside of 1.74 next week.



    Traders expected a narrow range of 1.7260-1.7310 on



Wednesday with a focus on moves in the yen and the embattled



rupiah.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    Lacking fresh incentives, the Taiwan dollar remained



trapped in a range with markets warily eyeing the inauguration



of President-elect Chen Shui-bian on May 20.



    Chen, a member of the pro-independence DPP (Democratic



Progressive Party), said on Tuesday he would neither provoke



the island's giant communist neighbour nor give in too much.



    In Beijing, Tang Shubei, a top Chinese negotiator with



Taiwan, pressed Chen to embrace the mainland's cherished "one



China" principle. Tang warned that Taiwan's new administration



would "create extremely grave new problems" if it failed to



adhere to the "one China" policy.



Standard and Poor's MMS said in a report the Taiwan dollar



was poised to test the downside but was not likely to fall



beyond 30.80 even if any sudden cross-strait tension erupted.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late As Mkts Brace For US Rate Hike
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies slumped Wednesday as the dollar continued to build momentum ahead of next week's expected interest rate hike in the U.S. 

 Local factors, such as political uncertainty in Indonesia and a hostage crisis in the Philippines, also weighed on individual Asian currencies. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to its lowest level in nearly a year, while the Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht tumbled to their lowest levels in roughly seven and five months, respectively. 

 The dollar held steady against the yen, remaining above a key Y109 support level. 

 The Federal Open Market Committee, the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy setting arm, is widely expected to boost short-term rates by a half a percentage point when it meets on May 16. 

 "Going forward, most regional currencies will weaken across the board as we move closer to the FOMC meeting," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 A recent spate of strong economic data in the U.S. has boosted market expectations that the Fed will have to tighten credit aggressively to keep the economy from overheating. 

 The Singapore dollar dropped sharply in the first hour of regional trading and remained pressured throughout the day. The currency hit it's low point near the close of local trading when the U.S. dollar rose to S$1.7308, its highest level since May 27, 1999 when it touched $1.7317. 

 Near the end of regional trading, the U.S. dollar slipped back to S$1.7301, up from S$1.7250 late Thursday. 

 Such levels in the past would have surely triggered intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to support the local currency. But analysts say recent weakness in the yen and euro means the MAS probably has developed a higher tolerance for U.S. dollar appreciation against the Singapore currency. 

 The rupiah also wilted under prospects of higher U.S. rates. Additionally, the slide was exacerbated by lingering uncertainty about the government's ability to bring about economic reform. 

 Late Wednesday the dollar was quoted at 8,203 rupiah, up from IDR8,070 late Tuesday. Wednesday's closing level was the highest for the U.S. currency since Oct. 15, 1999, when it reached IDR8,260 in intraday trading. 

 In Manila, concern over a hostage crisis and fighting between government and Muslim rebel forces in the southern Philippine region of Mindanao added to the gloomy sentiment for the peso. 

 The dollar closed at 41.370 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP41.279 late Tuesday. 

 Traders said relatively thin demand for dollars and some banks taking profits on recent gains in the U.S. currency helped relieve pressure on the peso. 

 The Thai baht ended lower as dollar selling by local exporters failed to offset a surge in the U.S. currency.

title: Singapore Dlr Ends At 11 Mo Low As US$ Surges In Asia
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended at its lowest level in almost a year Wednesday as the U.S. unit continued to gain against most Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 "Everyone wants to be long (on U.S.) dollars," a dealer at a U.S. bank said. "The regionals seem to be weakening across the board. I don't think it will end here." 

 Around 0850 GMT (4:50 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7302, up from S$1.7250 late Tuesday. The U.S. dollar was at its highest level since May 27, when it reached S$1.7317. 

 Dealers said, however, that the threat of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore was slowing the local currency's decline. 

 Local banks, which often act at the behest of the MAS, were reportedly offering to sell the U.S. currency for the Singapore dollar at the level of S$1.7300. 

 Even so, some dealers added, Singapore's de facto central bank is likely to allow the currency to weaken somewhat further if the U.S. dollar continues to rise in anticipation of higher U.S. interest rates. 

 "I see no reason for any action if U.S. dollar keeps strengthening across the board," the bank dealer said, adding that "S$1.74 is quite a sensible level to me." 

 Hedge funds and investment banks are buying the U.S. dollar cautiously for fear of drawing intervention. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.00%, down from 3.00% late Tuesday. The three-month rate was offered at 3.000%, down from 3.0625%.

title: Singapore  Dlr Ends Lower;  Intervention  Threat Limits Loss
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended lower Tuesday against the U.S. dollar as the U.S. unit continued to gain ground on world markets, but the threat of central bank intervention limited the local dollar's losses. 

 Around 0920 GMT (5:20 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7242, up slightly from S$1.7237 late Monday but down from an intraday peak of S$1.7261. 

 The U.S. dollar was at Y109.13, up from Y108.89 late Monday in Tokyo. 

 With U.S. dollar rising above Y109, many market participants had expected the Singapore dollar to be weaker. But the danger of action by the Monetary Authority of Singapore limited its losses, they said. 

 Because the MAS has intervened to sell U.S. dollars above the level of S$1.7200 in the past, there was a reluctance to bid the currency much higher, traders said. 

 "The market is quite cautious around this level," said a trader at a European bank. 

 One trader said the MAS, acting through local banks, was offering to sell the U.S. dollar at the level of S$1.7260, although that couldn't be confirmed. The MAS didn't actually buy the currency, the trader said. 

 Despite the MAS offers, the U.S. dollar may yet move up against its Singapore counterpart if it continues to gain against the euro, yen and other Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 "I don't think MAS is going to intervene too aggressively yet," a dealer said. "They just want to avoid panic selling of Singapore dollar assets." 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered unchanged at 3.000%, while the three-month rate was offered at 3.0625%, up from 3.000%.

title: Singapore  Dlr Weaker Midmorning; No MAS  Intervention  Seen

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar is weaker against the U.S. dollar at midmorning Monday following the footsteps of the softer yen. 

 At 0225 GMT (10:25 p.m. EDT Sunday), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7235, up from S$1.7214 late Friday. 

 The Singapore currency is expected to remain under pressure Monday, with the U.S. dollar finding resistance around the S$1.7250 level, a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 In the absence of any other market-moving news, the Singapore dollar reacted primarily to the falling yen, traders said. The yen hovered around the Y109-to-the-dollar level after hitting a two-month low of Y109.61 to the dollar last week. 

 Trading volume was relatively light as market participants kept an eye on activity in the Tokyo markets, which had been closed for three sessions for the Golden Week holiday. 

 The weakness in the yen and euro means the Monetary Authority of Singapore probably has a higher tolerance for U.S. dollar appreciation against the Singapore currency, analysts at Standard Chartered Bank said. 

 In the past, the MAS has intervened when the U.S. dollar rose above S$1.7200. The equivalent level Monday on a trade-weighted basis would be S$1.7600, according to Standard Chartered. 

 "That said, we look for authorities to try to limit Singapore dollar weakness to the S$1.7400 level," Standard Chartered added.

title: Emerging  FX  - Heartened by dollar's retreat.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 5 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 generally well-supported in late trade on Friday after the

     Most banks and businesses managed to shield themselves from 

 the "Love Bug" computer virus which wreaked havoc in e-mail

bank.

The market is focused on U.S. non-farm payrolls data, due

are likely to be at their May 16 policy meeting.

Dealers said better prospects for the IMF's delayed $400



million loan were positive for the rupiah but the sacking of

province cast doubt over its prospects.



"On the macro perspective, over the next six months or



towards the year-end, I'm looking for a weaker rupiah, probably

    But continued caution over intervention by the Monetary

    The won fell against the dollar on Thursday, weighed by the

    The market will reopen on Monday.

    The peso tracked the baht lower, with interbank and

    The market barely drew support from slightly lower than

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late In Holiday-Thinned Trading
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are mixed against the U.S. dollar late Friday in trade thinned by holidays in Japan, South Korea and Thailand. 

 The dollar took a break from its recent rise against the yen, giving support to some regional currencies. Late in the local trading session it fell toward Y107 after peaking earlier this week at a two month-high of Y109.61. 

 A decision overnight by the Bank of England's monetary policy committee to leave interest rates at 6% triggered heavy sales of sterling, particularly against yen, which helped keep the Japanese currency firm during the Asian session. 

 Most traders, however, were on the sidelines awaiting the issue tonight of U.S. non-farm payrolls data for clues on the likely scale of interest rate action by the Federal Reserve. 

 Further evidence of a tighter labor market would fuel expectations of aggressive monetary tightening, and likely push the dollar higher against Asian currencies. 

 Expectations for the jobs report center on a 310,000 rise in employment in April after a 416,000 rise in March, and a fall in the jobless rate to 4.0% from 4.1%. 

 The federal funds rate is 6% now, but analysts expect it will be lifted to 7%, or more, by year-end to keep inflation in check. Most expect the Fed's policy-making arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, to hike the fed funds rate 50 basis points when it next meets May 16. 

 The Singapore dollar, which often tracks the currency of Japan - a key trading partner - rebounded with the yen after posting a nine-week low Thursday against the U.S. dollar. 

 Late in the day, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.7190, down from S$1.7240 a day earlier. 

 "It's tracking the dollar-yen movement," a dealer at a U.S. brokerage said. "But trading is pretty listless with a lot of traders out for the holidays," he added. 

 Speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to support the local unit around S$1.7250 - as traders say it did in recent months - also helped it rise. 

 The Thai baht, however, failed to benefit from the strengthening yen in offshore trade. 

 Foreign speculators took advantage of low baht liquidity, due to the holidays in Japan and Thailand, to buy dollars in the hope of making profits in the short-term. 

 Thai Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtan attempted to soothe jittery financial markets, saying the baht's weakness likely will be only temporary. 

 Pisit, speaking to reporters on the sidelines of an Asia Development Bank annual meeting in Chiang Mai, said the baht's decline Thursday to a five-month intraday low against the dollar at THB38.560 was "something of a surprise." 

 Exports and other economic indicators are doing well, meaning the baht is out of kilter with fundamentals, he said. 

 The dollar was at 38.455 baht from THB38.425 a day earlier. 

 Elsewhere, the New Taiwan dollar rose slightly, helped by a 3.3% jump in local stock prices. The U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$30.648, compared with NT$30.699 at the previous close. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso were barely changed. 

 Late in the day the dollar was at 7,967 rupiah, down from IDR7,975 late Thursday, and unchanged at 41.280 pesos. 

 Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the monetary board next week will "most likely" leave the overnight borrowing rate unchanged at 9% after inflation came in at lower-than-expected 3.7% year-on-year in April. 

 However, a 50-basis-point hike in the U.S. may force a response from Philippine monetary officials for fear of sharp decline in the local currency. 

 The South Korean won didn't trade because of a government holiday. The dollar ended Thursday at 1,111.0 won.

title: Singapore Dlr Ends At 9-Week Low As US Dlr Surges
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar fell to its lowest level in nine weeks late Thursday as the U.S. dollar surged on world currency markets. 

 Around 0935 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7240, up from S$1.7186 late Wednesday. 

 Traders said the Singapore dollar's weakness was a reflection of the U.S. dollar's strength against world currencies, particularly the euro. 

 In coming trading sessions, the level of the Singapore dollar will be tied closely to the fate of the euro, traders in Singapore said. 

 The U.S. dollar broke decisively through a level of resistance at S$1.7200. That is the level at which the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been considered likely to intervene in support of the local currency. 

 However, traders said that intervention is now unlikely because of the U.S. dollar's generalized strength against the euro, yen and other Asian currencies. 

 "There is tremendous (U.S. dollar) strength across the board," said one trading desk chief for a European bank. "It's unbelievable." 

 Given U.S. dollar strength, the MAS may allow the Singapore currency to fall to between S$1.7300 and S$1.7400 to the U.S. dollar, said a dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 Another dealer predicted that the U.S. dollar could soon rise above S$1.7250, taking out stop-loss orders along the way. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 2.3750%, up from 2.2500% late Wednesday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.6875%, up from 2.5625%.

title: Singapore Dlr Slightly Down Late On US Dlr Strength
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar drifted lower in sluggish dealing late Wednesday in reaction to U.S. dollar strength against world currencies. 

 The Singapore dollar approached the key level of S$1.7200 to the U.S. dollar, but dealers said it wasn't likely to break through it. 

 In recent weeks, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been suspected of intervening in the market to keep the U.S. dollar from rising above S$1.7200. 

 Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said the MAS is concerned that sustained Singapore dollar weakness could raise the cost of imported components for local industries. 

 Around 0855 GMT (4:55 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7184, up from S$1.7165 late Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar is gaining against the euro, yen and other world currencies on expectations the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee will raise rates aggressively when it meets May 16. 

 Higher U.S. interest rates make U.S. dollar-denominated securities more attractive and lure foreign investment from countries where interest rates are lower. 

 On the Singapore dollar money market, longer-term rates also moved higher on expectations that U.S. rates would be raised, while the overnight rate fell slightly. 

 The overnight rate was offered at 2.2500%, down from 2.3750% late Tuesday, while the three-month rate was offered at 2.5625%, up from 2.5000%.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; S&P Downgrade Hurts Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly higher late Tuesday, buoyed by a rebound in most regional bourses after a hammering a day earlier. 

 A recovery on Wall Street Monday after record points losses in major indexes Friday helped lift regional stocks and currencies with the exception of Jakarta equities and the rupiah, which both sank after Standard & Poor's Corp. downgraded Indonesia's credit rating. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average Monday rose 276.7 points to end at 10,582.5, while the technology-laden Nasdaq jumped 217.9 points to 3539.2. 

 Jakarta stocks and the rupiah fell after S&P cut its long-term foreign currency issuer credit rating on Indonesia to SD, or selective default, from CCC+, and lowered its short-term foreign currency issuer rating to SD from C. 

 While the downgrade was expected after the government last week rescheduled $5.8 billion worth of sovereign debt with the Paris Club of creditors, there was a "knee-jerk" response in financial markets, says a rupiah trader in Singapore, who declined to be named. 

 Syetarn Hansakul, East Asia analyst at WestLB, said the downgrade doesn't reflect sudden negative risks emerging. 

 "The original (Paris Club) loans are technically in default until banks are officially notified of the rescheduling, which will be done soon, therefore we expect rupiah weakness to be temporary," she said. 

 "Once the facts are clarified, the rupiah should head toward 7,600." 

 The dollar late in the day was quoted at 7,725 rupiah, up from IDR7,670 a day earlier. The JSX Composite Index fell 0.5% to 526.7 from 529.3. 

 Among the other Asian currencies, the Singapore dollar was the standout performer as it surged to a two-month high late in the day against its U.S. counterpart at S$1.6970, up from S$1.7055 late Monday. 

 Traders said heavy buying of the Singapore currency by European banks pushed it through the psychological level of S$1.7000 against the U.S. dollar. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which market participants say intervened last week around S$1.7200 to support the local dollar, may be promoting a stronger currency in a bid to control inflation in the wake of much stronger than expected consumer price index data from the U.S. Friday. 

 It may also be providing liquidity to offset a spate of recent foreign acquisitions by companies including Singapore Airlines and Singapore Telecommunications, know as SingTel, traders say. 

 A 0.6% rise in the benchmark Straits Times Index of share prices to 2,010.7 after an 8.7% slump Monday also aided the Singapore dollar. 

 Elsewhere in the region, a 5.6% jump in the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, to 747.3 after an 11.6% fall a day earlier lifted the won. 

 Buying of South Korean bonds after a statement Monday by the Bank of Korea - the nation's central bank - that it wouldn't tighten monetary policy also aided the currency, according to market participants. 

 "Some institutional investors expanded their bond buying," said Kim Il-soo, a broker at Hyundai Securities Co. 

 The yield on three-year corporate bonds ended down seven basis points to 9.97% while the yield on three-year government bonds ended 11 basis points lower at 8.93%. 

 At the close of trade in Seoul, the dollar was quoted at 1,110.4 won, down from KRW1,113.8 late Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$30.517 against the New Taiwan dollar from NT$30.555 previously. Against the Philippine peso, it closed at 41.175 pesos from PHP41.190 and against the Thai baht, it ended at 37.870 baht, down from THB37.885 previously, on solid stock market gains in each country.

title: Singapore  Dollar Higher On Reports Of MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar jumped to its highest level against the U.S. dollar in nearly two weeks Friday following reports of intervention by local monetary authorities. 

 The rally began Thursday and a number of dealers said they believed it was the result of the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervening on behalf of the local currency. 

 The MAS, as a matter of policy doesn't comment on its foreign exchange activities. 

 Dealers said the MAS began selling dollars at about the S$1.7195 level, which was near the top of the recent trading range for the two currencies. 

 The alleged MAS action in turn put pressure on market players who had taken long U.S. dollar positions, dealers said. The ensuing dollar selling pushed the U.S. currency to an intraday low of S$1.7108 Friday, the lowest level since S$1.7103 on April 3. 

 "I doubt anyone will go long with the U.S. dollar now," a dealer at a foreign bank said. "The MAS is sending a message." 

 By the close, the U.S. currency recovered slightly to S$1.7115, down from $1.7152 late Thursday. 

 Some analysts said the timing of the supposed MAS intervention was puzzling, since the Singapore dollar didn't appear to be unusually soft. 

 But there was also speculation that the MAS did it as a preemptive move to head off what it may have perceived as a trend toward a weaker Singapore dollar. The timing was calculated, the theory goes, to take advantage of the long U.S. dollar positions. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 3.2500%, up from 1.8750% late Thursday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.4375%, up from 2.3750%.

title: Asian  Currencies : Stock Sell-Off Weighs On Won, S$ Rises
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won tumbled under the weight of a stock market sell-off Friday, while the Singapore dollar spiked up on reports of intervention by local monetary authorities. 

 Elsewhere in the region, currencies were lower in light trading. 

 South Korea's Kospi index plunged 4.7% Friday as stocks across Asia moved lower in the wake of Wall Street's recent downturn. 

 The won fell to its lowest level in more than a week as foreign investors pulled their money out of stocks, dealers said. 

 Opinion was divided over what impact Thursday's general elections in South Korea would have on the market. Some analysts said the ruling party's failure to secure a majority could potentially slow the pace of reform in corporate restructuring. Others, however, said the fallout would be minimal. 

 Late Friday, the dollar was quoted at 1,111.00 won, up from KRW1,108.00 Thursday. 

 The Singapore dollar jumped to its highest level in nearly two weeks, continuing a rally that began Thursday. A number of dealers said they believed the Monetary Authority of Singapore got things started by entering the market and selling dollars at about the S$1.7195 level Thursday. 

 Players who had taken long U.S. dollar positions were forced to unload the currency, pushing it to an intraday low of S$1.7108 Friday. That was the lowest level since it was S$1.7103 on April 3. 

 "I doubt anyone will go long with the U.S. dollar now," a dealer at a foreign bank said. "The MAS is sending a message." 

 By the close, the U.S. currency moved to S$1.7115, down from S$1.7152 late Thursday. 

 Some analysts said the timing of the supposed MAS intervention was puzzling, since the Singapore dollar didn't appear to be unusually soft. 

 But there also was speculation that the MAS did it as a preemptive move to head off what it may have perceived as a trend toward a weaker Singapore dollar. The timing was calculated, the theory goes, to take advantage of the long U.S. dollar positions. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also felt the pressure of declining share prices. The island's main index fell 2.98%, and has now dropped 7.4% over the past four sessions. 

 Dealers also said sentiment toward Taiwan stocks and the currency are still being negatively affected by tensions with mainland China. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S dollar was quoted at NT$30.461, up from NT$30.380 at the end of the previous session. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained in relatively good shape one day after the government reached an agreement with the Paris Club group of creditor nations to reschedule $5.8 billion worth of sovereign debt. 

 The debt rescheduling, almost $2.2 billion of which is slated to take place this year, is contingent upon the successful completion of an International Monetary Fund review by June 5 at the latest, an IMF official said. 

 The IMF is optimistic it can resume lending to Indonesia by late-May, after delaying its latest $400 million loan disbursement over Indonesia 's failure to keep pace with its reform program. 

 At the close of trading in Jakarta, the dollar was at IDR7,623, up from IDR7,600 late Thursday. 

 The Philippine peso moved lower in thin trading amid corporate demand for U.S. dollars. Declines were limited, however, following a favorable assessment of the Philippine economy by the IMF. 

 The fund said Thursday it was confident that the Philippines will be able to meet its growth target of four to five percent this year and set the stage for "rapid growth" in the next five years. 

 The dollar was quoted at 41.168 pesos at the close of trading, up from 41.155 the previous session. 

 The Thai baht lost some ground in light offshore trading as markets in Bangkok were closed for a public holiday. Dealers said the baht selling was typical before a weekend. 

 The dollar closed at THB37.965, up from THB37.900 late Thursday.
