title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Paris Club Hopes Buoy Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday in lackluster trade as many financial market participants hugged the sidelines ahead of key U.S. inflation data. 

 Activity was also restricted by a holiday in Thailand and a parliamentary election in South Korea, where financial markets were shut for the day. 

 U.S. producer price index and consumer price index data - slated for release Thursday and Friday - will be watched closely for clues as to how much further the Federal Reserve needs to up interest rates to keep inflation in check. 

 Higher U.S. rates may place downward pressure on Asian currencies, particularly those - such as the Singapore dollar - which have yields below the Fed funds rate, which now stands at 6%. 

 The Indonesian rupiah ended firmer on expectations the Paris Club of creditors will later Thursday agree to restructure $2.1 billion of Indonesian sovereign debt maturing this year. 

 "There is a high hope that Indonesia will get much of the debts rescheduled on favorable terms," said Syetarn Hansakul, an analyst at WestLB. "Positive news on this front could push the rupiah toward IDR7,500 (against the dollar)," she added. 

 Around 0920 GMT (5:20 a.m. EST), the dollar was at IDR7,600, down from IDR7,620 a day earlier. 

 Sentiment remains bullish toward the won on expectations incumbent President Kim Dae-jung will retain enough parliamentary support to push through further economic reforms. Voting has ended and exit polls show Kim's Millennium Democratic Party holding a slight lead. 

 Kim's party faces the challenge of maintaining control of the 273-seat assembly as recent opinion polls had it trailing by about 10 seats. But many analysts believe the first-ever summit between the two Koreas, announced Monday, has tipped the scale toward the ruling party. 

 The dollar ended Wednesday at 1,108.0 won, down from KRW1,109.4. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the New Taiwan dollar fell sharply as foreigners dumped local stocks after another sharp selloff in the Nasdaq Composite Index, and a fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. 

 The Taiwan stock index ended down 2.5% at 9662.60, while the New Taiwan dollar finished the session at NT$30.380 to the U.S. dollar from NT$30.303 a day earlier. 

 The Singapore dollar rose slightly, helped by rumors the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened late in the day to prop up the currency around S$1.7200 against the U.S. dollar. 

 The U.S. currency was at S$1.7145 late, down from S$1.7180 previously. 

 With Thai markets closed, the baht rose in thin offshore trade. The dollar ended at 37.900 baht, down from THB38.020 late Wednesday.

text:

 Late in the day, the dollar was quoted at Y105.50, down sharply from Y106.66 a day earlier and Y106.99 late Tuesday in New York. 

 Brighter economic prospects for Japan augur well for the currencies of its regional trading partners, as demand for their exports is likely to rise. 

 The BOJ in its April report card on the economy said improvement "is becoming distinct" on a rosier outlook for business investment. It added that recovery has started in some areas of private demand. 

 This was a notch up from the BOJ's previous report, in which it said the economy had "started to improve" but clear signs of a self-sustained recovery in private demand were yet to be seen. 

 Yen strength pushed the Singapore dollar, the South Korean won, the New Taiwan dollar, and the Thai baht higher late Wednesday. The Philippine peso was lower, but off its intraday lows on the late afternoon comment from Hayami. 

 On the eve of an important South Korean parliamentary election, the won rose slightly as foreign capital inflows into the local stock market offset dollar-buying by the state-run Korea Development Bank. 

 Financial markets hope incumbent President Kim Dae-jung will retain enough parliamentary support to push through further economic reforms, but Kim's Millennium Democratic Party faces the challenge of maintaining control of 273-seat assembly as recent opinion polls have it trailing by about 10 seats. 

 However, with up to 40% of voters still undecided, many analysts agree the first ever summit between the two Koreas, announced Monday, tips the scale toward the ruling party. 

 The dollar ended at 1,108.0 won, down from KRW1,109.4 previously. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the New Taiwan dollar rose on heavy buying by exporters to end at NT$30.303 from NT$30.307 late Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar, which weakened steadily this week on planned foreign acquisitions by Singapore companies such as Singapore Airlines and Singapore Telecommunications, rose slightly, helped also by expectations the Monetary Authority of Singapore will intervene to support the currency if it falls further. 

 Traders say the MAS intervened April 5 around the S$1.7225 level. 

 The U.S. currency was at S$1.7180 late, down from S$1.7205 a day earlier. 

 The baht was also a touch higher late, buoyed by a 24% jump in Thai exports to $5.90 billion from a year earlier, and 51.2% on-year growth in auto sales in the first quarter. 

 The dollar was at 38.020 baht, down from THB38.040 a day earlier. 

 The Indonesian rupiah, however, ended unchanged at 7,620 rupiah against the dollar as traders await the outcome of a meeting Wednesday and Thursday of the Paris Club of creditors. Financial markets expect it will agree to roll over $2.1 billion of Indonesian sovereign debt maturing this year. 

 In Manila, the dollar rose to 41.175 pesos from PHP41.120 as local banks appeared to test a central bank pledge to allow market forces to determine the exchange rate. Traders suspect the central bank will intervene to support the peso if it trades below PHP41.200.

title: Asian  Currencies  Little Changed Early Ahead Of G7 Meeting
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are little changed against the U.S. dollar in early regional trading Wednesday, as market participants remain cautious ahead of this weekend's meeting of the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations. 

 Trading is relatively light with market participants apparently reluctant to go too far out on a limb given the uncertainty over what G7 leaders may say about exchange rates, dealers said. 

 There is speculation in the currency markets that the G7 countries could offer a statement expressing their concern over the strength of the yen. That talk already has translated into support for the dollar, with the U.S. currency rising above 107 yen in overnight trading for the first time in more than two weeks. 

 The Indonesian rupiah edged downward, but remains well above the six-month low hit last week. The rupiah has been boosted by optimism that the Paris Club donor nations may reschedule $2.1 billion in foreign debt when the group meets beginning Wednesday.

title: Singapore Dollar Sapped By Investments In Foreign Assets
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- What's good for companies like Singapore Airlines Ltd. (P.SAL) is bad for the Singapore dollar - at least in the short run. 

 Singapore Airlines shares rose 3.3% Tuesday on news that it had bought an 8.3% stake in Air New Zealand for NZ$141.3 million (NZ$1=US$0.4974). 

 But the Singapore dollar weakened on expectations that Singapore Airlines and other local corporations would have to sell the currency to finance foreign acquisitions. 

 The Singapore Airlines deal is the latest in a string of acquisitions by cash-rich local companies seeking to expand beyond the tight confines of the island-state. 

 In recent months, Singapore Airlines paid GBP600.25 million for 49% of Virgin Atlantic Ltd., and Cycle & Carriage Ltd. (P.CYC) took 23% of Indonesian auto maker PT Astra International (P.ASI) for US$310 million. 

 Such news "does have an impact on the Singapore dollar just now," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank. "There are likely to be further outflows relating to international mergers and acquisitions." 

 Late Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7197, up from S$1.7165 late Monday. Many foreign exchange dealers say the U.S. dollar would be stronger still if not for the threat of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 News of the deals has pushed down a currency that just a few months ago had been expected rise sharply on the back of Singapore's robust economic growth. Some analysts had predicted that the local dollar would strengthen to S$1.55 to the U.S. dollar by year's end. 


       More Outflows Expected On More M&As



More money yet is expected to flow out of the country, creating a
demand for U.S. dollars and other foreign currencies.



Singapore Airlines is in talks to buy another 16.7% of Air New Zealand
from its principal shareholder, Brierley Investments.



Singapore Telecommunications Ltd. (P.SGT) is in talks to buy stakes in
Malaysia's Time Engineering and two of its subsidiaries in a deal
estimated to be worth 2.1 billion ringgit (US$1=MYR3.80).



And on Tuesday, Indonesia's Bank Restructuring Agency said it had
talked to the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation about
taking part in the planned initial share offering of PT Bank Central
Asia (P.PCA).



Chia Hsin-Li, Asian markets strategist at J.P. Morgan, says the market
tends to overreact to news of foreign investments.



In some cases, like that of Singapore Airlines, the company may
already have a stock of U.S. dollars, so the transaction doesn't move
through the foreign exchange market. In others, companies quietly
accumulate foreign currency for months before an announcement is made.



Even so, the overall effect is to weaken the Singapore dollar,
analysts say, because the investments create demand for foreign
currencies.



There are other reasons for the Singapore dollar's weakness, of
course. One is the strength of the U.S. dollar against the euro and the
yen, which lifts the currency against the local dollar as well.



Another is the low level of interest rates in Singapore, making the
Singapore dollar a favorite funding currency for plays on other regional
foreign exchange markets, like South Korea.



Analysts add that the Singapore dollar is a tightly managed currency,
and that the MAS guides it within a band against a trade-weighted basket
of currencies, including the dollar, euro and yen.



"Ultimately, the level of the Sing is determined by monetary policy
imperatives," said Simon Flint, currency economist at the Bank of
America.



On the one hand, the MAS wants to maintains the currency at a level
that keeps exports competitive. But on the other hand, it wants to avoid
imported inflation through an overly weak currency.



At the moment, most analysts say, there's little incentive for the MAS
to tighten monetary policy because inflation is well under control at an
annual rate of 1.3%.



-By Christopher Wellisz; 65/ 421-4802;
christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com

title: Singapore Dlr Ends Lower On Foreign Acquisitions,Weak Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended lower Tuesday on yen weakness and news of foreign investments - actual and potential - by Singapore companies, dealers said. 

 After inching up for most of the day, the U.S. dollar briefly breached the sensitive S$1.7200 level, above which the Monetary Authority of Singapore is considered likely to intervene. 

 However, the U.S. currency fell back without MAS intervention. Around 0835 GMT (4:35 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7197, up from S$1.7165 late Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar was weakened by news that Singapore Airlines had taken an 8.3% stake in Air New Zealand, paying NZ$141.3 million (NZ$1=US$0.4974). 

 Singapore Airlines is also in talks to acquire an additional 16.7% of Air New Zealand. 

 Singapore's currency weakens on such news on the expectation that corporations like Singapore Airlines will have to sell the local currency to finance acquisitions. 

 Other foreign investments are in the works. Singapore Telecommunications is in talks to buy stakes in Malaysia's Time Engineering and two of its subsidiaries in a deal that analysts say could be worth MYR2.1 billion (US$1=MYR3.80). 

 In addition, local newspapers reported Tuesday that the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation had been asked to bid for a stake in Indonesia's Bank Central Asia. Later in the day, Indonesia's Bank Restructuring Agency confirmed that GIC had been asked to make a bid. 

 Such news "does have an impact on the Singapore dollar just now," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank. "There are likely to be further outflows relating to international mergers and acquisitions," he said. 

 A weaker yen also contributed to the Singapore dollar's decline Tuesday, because the yen constitutes a large part of the basket of currencies against which the Singapore dollar trades, dealers added.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Singapore Dlr Slides On M&A
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are mixed late Tuesday as the spotlight remains on the yen, which continues to weaken against the dollar and the euro ahead of a weekend meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations. 

 Traders expect the G7 will again express shared concern about a strong yen, and perhaps the weak euro, but with joint intervention extremely unlikely, the impact on currency markets may be minimal. 

 But for now, the weaker yen, along with planned foreign acquisitions by Singapore companies, pushed down the Singapore dollar toward levels where traders say the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened last week. 

 The U.S. currency was at S$1.7205 late, up from S$1.7165 a day earlier, and near the recent MAS intervention level of S$1.7225. 

Singapore companies often need to sell the local dollar in the spot currency market to finance foreign acquisitions. 

 National carrier Singapore Airlines Ltd. (P.SAL) confirmed Tuesday it has bought an 8.3% stake in Air New Zealand (A.AIZ) for an undisclosed amount, and remains in negotiations with Brierley Investments Ltd.(A.BRY), along with Qantas Airways Ltd. (A.QAN), to purchase a further 17% of the carrier. 

 Singapore Telecommunications Ltd. (P.SGT), or SingTel, recently detailed plans to buy a stake in Time Engineering Bhd.(P.TEN) of Malaysia for more than 2.2 billion ringgit ($1=MYR3.80), while the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) - the government's investment arm - may be considering taking a "significant stake" in Bank Central Asia (P.PCA) of Indonesia through an initial public offering. 

 Singapore's Business Times newspaper reported the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency approached GIC about taking a stake. 

 None of the parties referred to were immediately available for comment. 

 IBRA owns 92.8% of BCA, and wants to sell 30% of the bank in an IPO to raise around US$200 million. 

 In neighboring Indonesia, the rupiah continued to recover from a six-month low last week amid market optimism that the Paris Club of creditors will agree to roll over $2.1 billion sovereign debt maturing this year. 

 The International Monetary Fund's endorsement Monday of the debt restructure, and an Indonesian newspaper report Tuesday that quoted Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie saying Japan has pledged to roll over its $1.6 billion share of the debt buoyed investor sentiment. Paris Club creditors and Indonesian officials will meet Wednesday and Thursday in Paris. 

 The dollar late in Asian trading was quoted against the rupiah at 7,615 rupiah, down a touch from IDR7,660 late Monday. 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht was lower as market participants squared positions before markets close Thursday and Friday for the Songkran Festival. 

 The dollar was at 38.040 baht from THB38.000 a day earlier. 

 In Manila, the peso dropped to 41.120 pesos against the dollar from PHP41.100 previously. Traders cited ongoing question marks over President Joseph Estrada's leadership, and a fall in the baht for the peso fall. 

 In North Asia, the dollar ended flat against the won at 1,109.4, and a touch higher against the New Taiwan dollar at NT$30.307 from NT$30.300 after the Central Bank of China, Taiwan's central bank, sold the local currency aggressively in the domestic foreign exchange market. 

 The intervention lifted the dollar from an intraday low of NT$30.265, a new 30-month high for the Taiwanese currency.

title: Singapore  Dlr Higher Late After Reported MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar moved higher late Thursday, a day after the central bank reportedly intervened in the market to prop up the currency. 

 A local bank was seen selling U.S. dollars against the Singapore currency late in late Asian trading Wednesday in a move that had all the markings of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 The action triggered dollar selling in the London market, pushing the U.S. currency down from a one-month high of S$1.7240 to levels around S$1.7120. 

 Dollar demand pushed the U.S. currency back up to S$1.7140 near the end of the trading day, but it was still down from S$1.7185 the late Wednesday. 

 The MAS apparently was uncomfortable about the decline in the Singapore dollar against the trade-weighted basket of currencies it uses as a benchmark, analysts said. 

 "If you use that calculation, the currency basket was slightly overshooting their usual tolerance," said Alison Seng, an analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 The market will retain a bias for U.S. dollar demand in the near-term, she said, based on expectations that Singapore companies will continue selling the local currency in order to acquire foreign companies. 

 Furthermore, concerns over the political and economic situations in Indonesia and Thailand will weigh on the Singapore dollar, she said. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.5000%, up from 1.2500% late Wednesday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.3125%, up from 2.2500%.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed; Singapore Dlr Up After MAS Action
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies had a mixed day Thursday. With regional markets in Thailand and Indonesia closed for holidays, activity was muted. 

 The Singapore dollar ended local dealings significantly higher, after the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the market during London trading hours Wednesday, selling U.S. dollars in support of the local currency, according to dealers. 

 Over the preceding days market players in Singapore had built short positions in the U.S. currency in anticipation of MAS intervention to maintain the exchange rate within its intended trading band. 

 Those positions became the target of speculative traders in London, who pushed the U.S. currency higher hoping to cause a cascade of U.S. dollar purchases, as stop-loss orders to liquidate their short positions were triggered. 

 The attempt was partially successful, driving the dollar up to levels around S$1.7225 Wednesday in London before the MAS entered the market. 

 The intervention pushed the U.S. dollar rapidly below S$1.7150, a level from which the exchange rate barely deviated through Asian trading Thursday, as market participants remained nervous of provoking further official action. 

 Dealers didn't rule out a further effort to trip stop-loss orders above the S$1.7200 level, although they said a second attempt was unlikely in the immediate short term. 

 Late Thursday in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7156, down from S$1.7185 at the same time the day before. 

 Other Southeast Asian markets were quiet Thursday. Fear of official intervention to support the Philippine peso kept the dollar below its six-month high of PHP41.200. 

 At the close of local trading the U.S. currency was quoted against the peso at PHP41.120, down from PHP41.130 the previous day. 

 With markets in Jakarta and Bangkok closed for local holidays, offshore volumes in the rupiah and the baht were extremely thin. 

 Sentiment toward the rupiah remained poor, however, after the International Monetary Fund last week postponed the disbursement of its latest tranche of assistance funding. The delay has raised market fears that Indonesia may fail to clinch an agreement at its April 12 meeting with the Paris Club of sovereign creditors. 

 Analysts at Standard Chartered Bank warned the Indonesian currency remains vulnerable after falling to its lowest level since mid-October on Wednesday, when the dollar was bid up to hit IDR7,800. 

 Analysts at Bank of America added that a deal on debt restructuring is urgently needed, together with a resumption of lending to Indonesia. 

 "The rupiah is likely to retain a weak tone in the short term, due to consistent corporate demands for dollars to repay debts," they wrote in a research note, which cautioned that the dollar may rise to IDR8,000 "earlier than expected." 

 Near the end of Asian hours the dollar was quoted in the offshore market at IDR7,785, unchanged from late the previous day. 

 Against the baht the dollar was slightly higher at THB38.135, up from THB37.995 the day before. 

 "The dollar is still looking bid," commented one broker. 

 In North Asia the New Taiwan dollar ended a touch lower as foreign investors unloaded local stocks, partly in response to technology sector volatility and partly on fears that the government is to begin to liquidate its holdings of local equities. 

 At the close the U.S. dollar was at NT$30.469, up marginally from NT$30.465 the day before. 

 The South Korean won gained ground, however, with the dollar easing to close at KRW1,112.00, down from KRW1,113.70 Tuesday. The Seoul market was closed Wednesday for a holiday.

title: Singapore  Dlr Higher After Monetary Authorities  Intervene
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar is higher midmorning Thursday following intervention by local monetary authorities overnight to halt a decline in the currency against the U.S. dollar, dealers and analysts said. 

 Economic fundamentals remain positive for the Singapore dollar, analysts said, noting Wednesday's selling of the currency was more technical in nature. 

 A Monetary Authority of Singapore spokesman said it is the agency's policy not to comment on interventions in currency markets. 

 Dealers, however, said the MAS entered the market Wednesday in London and New York after a drop in the Singapore dollar triggered stop loss orders that threatened to push the local currency to its lowest level for the year. 

 The Singapore currency, which had fallen during Asian trading hours, continued its decline in London as market participants looked to cover their short positions in U.S. dollars. Once the U.S. currency rose to S$1.7189 the stop loss orders were triggered and the unit quickly jumped to S$1.7225, prompting the MAS to step in, a dealer at a U.S. brokerage said. 

 "They didn't want the Singapore dollar to hit a new low for the year based on technical selling," he said. 

 At 0230 GMT (10:30 p.m. EDT Wednesday) the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7148, down from S$1.7185 late Wednesday in Asian trading. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank said he expected the pair to trade in a range of S$1.7135 to S$1.7180, with concerns over further MAS intervention limiting the topside.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed,  Singapore  Dlr Up On  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies are lower in early trading against the U.S. dollar Thursday, except for the Singapore dollar, which is higher in the wake of intervention by the local monetary authority. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore entered the market Wednesday in London and New York, dealers said, after a decline in the Singapore dollar triggered stop loss orders that threatened to push the local currency to its lowest level for the year. 

 The Singapore currency, which had fallen during Asian trading hours, continued its decline in London as market participants looked to cover their short positions in U.S. dollars. Once the U.S. currency rose to S$1.7189 the stop loss orders were triggered and the U.S. unit quickly jumped to S$1.7225, prompting the MAS to step in, a dealer at a U.S. brokerage said. 

 "They didn't want the Singapore dollar to hit a new low for the year based on technical selling," he said. 

 At 0130 GMT (9:30 p.m. EDT Wednesday) the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7145, down from S$1.7185 late Wednesday in Asia. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank said he expected the pair to trade in a range of S$1.7135 to S$1.7180, with concerns over further MAS intervention limiting the topside. 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah were lower in offshore trading as markets in the two countries were closed for holidays. The Philippine peso and Korean won also were lower. 

 Continuing concerns that Indonesia may not be able to meet International Monetary Fund deadlines for reform ahead of a key Paris Club meeting of creditors weighed on the rupiah, dealers said. 

 The dollar was quoted at 7,790 rupiah, up from IDR7,785 late Wednesday. Dealers said they expected little activity in the rupiah trading Thursday because of the market closure. 

 The Philippine peso edged lower amid market anxiety over President Estrada's leadership. 

 The dollar was quoted at 41.155 pesos, up from PHP41.130 late Wednesday. Market participants may be reluctant to push the dollar much higher in the near term because of concerns the central bank might intervene in the market, a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won slipped from levels two days ago. Markets were closed in Korea Wednesday for a holiday. 

 The dollar was quoted at 1,113.6 won, up from KRW1,113.4 late Tuesday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was slightly higher. The U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$30.471, down from NT$30.45 late Wednesday. 

 Markets were closed in Thailand for a holiday, but the baht slid lower in offshore trading. The dollar was quoted at THB38.075, up from THB37.995 late Wednesday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Sturdy despite  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, April 3 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 looking generally brighter in early Monday trade despite 

intervention on the yen	    and on the won	   .



    The yen was pushed to around 102.00 per dollar -- its



highest rate in nearly three months - on Friday amid rising



expectations of economic recovery in Japan but had slipped by



early Asia on news Japanese Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi had



been hospitalised.



    The Japanese Government later said Obuchi had suffered a



stroke and was in intensive care.



    The yen later eased to 105 per dollar on the intervention.



    Finance Ministry International Bureau head Zembei Mizoguchi



also confirmed the Bank of Japan (BOJ) had intervened in the



market early and reiterated that abrupt currency movements were



undesirable.



The BOJ's quarterly "tankan" business sentiment index for



major manufacturers came in within market expectations in



March, at minus nine and up from minus 17 in December.



KOREAN WON	



Heavy dollar buying from the open believed to have been



orchestrated by the authorities knocked the won off fresh



28-month highs of around 1,104 per dollar.



    The won had been propelled higher at the open by exporter



dollar sales by exporters and the yen's bullish tone.



    South Korea March imports rose 52.8 percent to $14.22



billion year-on-year while exports climbed 25.3 percent to



$14.6 billion, according to the commerce ministry.



    The trade account came in at a provisional surplus of $382



million, representing an 83.8 percent decline from a $2.35



billion surplus in March 1999.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    Although little changed compared to its close on Friday,



the rupiah was still looking weak at around 7,600.



    Dealers said the market was awaiting government action to



fulfil pledges made to the IMF to secure the IMF's next $400



million loan payment and persuade creditors to reschedule the



country's debt at a Paris Club meeting on April 12.



Chief economics minister Kwik Kian Gie has said the country



has until April 12 to complete 42 tasks from its latest letter



of intent to the IMF, including starting legal action against



uncooperative debtors, clamping down on on corruption and



recapitalising state banks.



    Dealers say the dollar is likely to remain well bid and



that the rupiah will find support at around the 7,500 level.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar was well bid at the upper end of its



recent 1.71 per dollar range on the back of renewed yen



strength.



    Dealers said it would be advisable to sell on any sustained



dollar move higher if the yen remains firm.



    The island's Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for March



rose 4.3 percentage points to 62.5 percent month-on-month on



the back of higher order and output growth. The manufacturing



index hit its highest level since June 1999.



Singapore's PMI has been above 50 percent since January



last year, indicating 15 months of expansion in the



manufacturing sector.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso was supported by strong January-February exports



which rose 9.1 percent year-on-year to $5.62 billion.



Investors were also cautious about aggressively selling the



peso after Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said on



Sunday the central bank may intervene in the foreign exchange


market if necessary to ensure the peso's stability.



He said the unit should strengthen to 40.90 mark "very



soon" as the central will not let the currency "get out of



control."



The currency was also heartened by news of a sharp rise in



remittance from overseas Filipino workers in 1999. More than



five million overseas workers sent home $6.794 billion last



year, a 38 percent rise from the previous year.



THAI BAHT	



The baht hovered around the upper end of the recent range,



underpinned by tight baht liquidity during tax payments and



holiday season as well as strong economic numbers released on



Friday.



    The market awaited March consumer prices and whole sale



prices numbers to be released by Commerce Ministry at 0400 GMT.



    Salomon Smith Barney said despite high oil prices, the



March inflation should remain tame.



    "While costs have risen due to higher oil prices, we expect



the still sizeable output gap to continue to put a cap



inflation," it said in a report.



    The market will also watch closely domestic political



developments following the resignation of powerful Interior



Minister Sanan Kachornprasart who was accused of false asset



declarations last week. He denied any wrongdoing.



TAIWAN DOLLAR	



The Taiwan dollar was well bid in early offshore trade



though little activity was expected with domestic forex and



stock markets shut for a one-day Women and Children's Day



holiday.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Late;Follows Rupiah Lower In Quiet Trade
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar, searching for direction in listless trading, was lower late Wednesday, following the Indonesian rupiah lower. 

 However, declines in the local currency against the U.S. dollar were limited as investors remain generally bullish on the Singapore economy and the prospects for continued growth. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7158 late Wednesday, up from S$1.7145 Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar opened the day on the defensive against the U.S. dollar, but recovered somewhat after its initial decline. The pair traded in a fairly narrow range for he balance of the day. 

 The main culprit in the drop in the Singapore currency was the faltering rupiah in neighboring Indonesia. The rupiah came under pressure when the release of its next loan installment from the International Monetary Fund was delayed. 

 The U.S. dollar touched an intraday high of S$1.7172 but market participants were reluctant to bid it up higher on fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene in the market to support the local currency, a trader at a Japanese Bank said. 

 The pair are expected to trade in a range of S$1.7130 to S$1.7190 in the near term with the latter representing the likely trigger point for MAS action, he said. 

 The longer-term outlook for the Singapore dollar remains bullish, traders said, with expectations the government will take in several billion dollars from the sale of telecommunications licenses beginning April 1. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.8750%, up from 1.6259% late Tuesday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.5333%, up from 2.3125%.

title: Bk Of America Lowers S$ Forecast To S$1.60/USD By Yr-End
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Bank of America on Tuesday revised its forecast for the Singapore dollar exchange rate downward to S$1.60 to the U.S. dollar by year-end from S$1.51 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The recent weakness of the Singapore dollar has confounded a number of forecasts, including that of the Bank of America. The U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7168 late Thursday, up from S$1.6655 at the end of last year. 

 Bank of America had argued that incipient inflation, along with sustained economic recovery, would prompt Singapore's central bank to tighten monetary policy by allowing the Singapore dollar to appreciate. 

 The exchange rate is the Monetary Authority of Singapore's sole monetary policy tool. A stronger Singapore dollar stifles inflation by reducing prices of imported goods. 

 The MAS recently revised the January annual inflation figure downward to 0.9% from 1.5%, based on a reweighted basket of consumer goods and services. In February, the inflation rate, based on the new basket, rose to an annual 1.3%. 

 With inflation on a lower path than previously expected, the pressure to tighten monetary policy has eased, Bank of America said in a report. 

 "The latest CPI number suggests there is little pressure for monetary tightening at present," the report says. 

 But the report also cites recent rumors that the MAS has intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the Singapore dollar. "This suggests that the present period of looseness may have run its course," the report says.

title: Singapore Dollar Gives Up Gains To End Little Changed
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended little changed in calm dealing Tuesday after giving up intraday gains, dealers said. 

 At about 0835 GMT (3:35 am EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7156, up marginally from S$1.7152 late Monday and higher than an intraday low of S$1.7121. 

 The Singapore currency started out strong, maintaining its momentum from Monday, when rumors of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore propelled it upward against the U.S. dollar. 

 Dealers also reported a smattering of Singapore-dollar purchases by investors putting money into the local equities market. 

 Seeking to take advantage of its gains, some participants sold the U.S. dollar short early in the day, only to be caught flat-footed by a larger order to buy the currency, dealers said. 

 One dealer identified Citibank as the buyer, but a dealer there declined to comment. 

 Later in the day, the Singapore dollar continued to inch downward, following the path set by the Indonesian rupiah, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar is likely to stay within its recent range of between S$1.7100 and S$1.7200, dealers said. 

 However, one dealer said that the U.S. dollar could test S$1.7200, the recent ceiling, if the euro weakens to US$0.95 in European trading later Tuesday. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.625%, unchanged from late Monday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.3125% down from 2.375%.

title: Singapore Dollar Ends Higher On Buying By Large Fund
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar ended stronger Monday after a large offshore fund sold U.S. dollars for the local currency, dealers said. 

 At about 0940 GMT (4:40 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7135, down from S$1.7149 late Friday and from a peak Monday of S$1.7191. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened early Monday following Friday's announcement that a Singapore-led consortium had won a bid to buy a US$506 million stake in Indonesian auto-maker PT Astra International. 

 But during the lunchtime break, the U.S. dollar suddenly dropped nearly half a Singapore cent in thin dealing. Some dealers said they suspected that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in the foreign exchange market to keep the currency from depreciating too quickly. 

 However, other dealers said that a major offshore fund had sold U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars in several transactions parceled out among local banks, possibly to buy equities on the Singapore Exchange. 

 "A large fund let go of some (U.S.) dollars," a dealer said. 

 Indeed, share prices on the stock market ended up 3.3% on Monday, boosted by program buying of blue-chip shares by foreign funds. Stock market dealers said bank and property shares had been oversold and were viewed as bargains. 

 Dealers said they were surprised by the timing of the lunch-time foreign exchange transaction, since thin liquidity exaggerated the speed of the Singapore dollar's gains. One dealer estimated the size of the transaction at US$200 million. 

 In addition, dealers said, the foreign exchange transactions associated with the Astra deal had already been completed, releiving the selling pressure on the Singapore dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar is likely to trade in a range S$1.7050 and S$1.7150 Tuesday, dealers said. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.6250%, down from 1.875% late Friday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.375%, down from 2.4375%.

title: Singapore Dlr Down Midmorning; Astra Sale,Indus Output Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar is lower against its U.S. counterpart midmorning Monday on news that a Singapore-led consortium will take a controlling stake in Indonesian automaker PT Astra International. 

 Weaker-than-expected data on industrial output, announced Sunday, also weakened the Singapore dollar, analysts said. 

 Around 0310 GMT (10:10 p.m. EST Sunday), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7180, up from S$1.7149 late Friday. 

 The Indonesian government announced late Friday that a consortium led by Singapore's Cycle & Carriage Ltd. will take a stake of nearly 40% in Astra for US$506 million. 

 Capital outflows associated with the transaction have weakened the Singapore currency, analysts said. Some suggested that a portion of the total sum remains to be exchanged into U.S. dollars, meaning the currency could weaken further. 

 Industrial data for February also sapped the currency. Manufacturing output rose at an annual rate of 9.4% in February, down from 28.2% in January. 

 Analysts said, however, the Singapore dollar is likely to be supported by the threat of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The MAS is concerned about volatility on the foreign exchange market and also worries that a persistently weak Singapore dollar could spark inflation, said Simon Flint, an economist at the Bank of America in Singapore. 

 Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said the U.S. dollar was unlikely to rise above S$1.7200.

title: Asian  Currencies :  Intervention  Saps Won;  Singapore  Dlr  Down
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won has been pushed down on dollar-buying by a state-run bank in early trading Monday, but observers say the authorities have resigned themselves to a stronger currency on the back of a resurgent economy. 

 The new Taiwan dollar is also gaining in early dealing Monday, propelled by continuing flows of foreign capital into the equity market. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Singapore dollar has been weakened by disappointing industrial production figures and by news that a Singapore-led consortium has taken a controlling stake in Indonesian carmaker PT Astra International. 

 The Indonesian rupiah, meanwhile, is little changed, although some analysts say the currency is likely to gain as a result of the Astra sale, which will pump US$506 million into the state's coffers. 

 In Korea, U.S.-dollar buying by the state-run Korean Development Bank has pushed the won lower. In addition, reports that Korea Asset Management Corp. will buy US$1.95 billion of Daewoo Group foreign debt have also weakened the won. 

 However, analysts say that the Korean currency's climb is inevitable as economic growth continues to pick up speed. 

 "The appreciation pressure on the won has been intensifying over the past few trading days," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore. "There is little doubt in my mind that that pressure will prevail." 

 Simmonds said the Korean authorities have resigned themselves to a stronger won and will seek to maintain an orderly appreciation. 

 "There is an acceptance that the fundamentals justify - indeed, probably demand - a stronger currency in a short period of time," he said. 

 Around 0150 GMT (8:50 p.m. EST Sunday), the U.S. dollar was trading at 1,109.80 won, up from KRW1,108.70 late Friday in Asia. 

 The Taiwan dollar is also expected to continue climbing as more money flows into the stock market and concerns ease about the March 18 presidential election, which saw the victory of an opposition party that has espoused formal independence from China. 

 With the victorious Democratic Progressive Party moving toward abandoning its pro-independence stance, worries about strained relations with China have eased and investors have focused again on Taiwan's fast-growing economy. 

 Taiwan's central bank has maintained a strong grip on the currency, though, and will likely slow the rate of its appreciation and keep it within a tight trading range, observers say.

title: Asian  Currencies  Stronger As Won Hits Post-Crisis High
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Sustained foreign investor interest in South Korean assets coupled with inward trade flows Wednesday to drive the won to its highest level since November 1997. 

 Most other Asian currencies also gained. Only the Thai baht slipped as traders unwound long positions established over the last week in anticipation of heavy foreign direct investment flows into Thailand. 

 The continued run-up in the won prompted repeated verbal interventions from Korean finance officials, anxious that the currency's rapid appreciation will dent the country's export sector. 

 Twice during the session the Ministry of Finance and Economy issued statements calling the won's rise "worrisome." The government is watching the market closely and is ready to take measures to slow the won's rise, the ministry warned. 

 Threats of intervention did little to damp the enthusiasm of won bulls, who noted comments from Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai stressing Korea's continued need for foreign investment. Further equity investment in Korean companies will help stabilize the country's highly leveraged corporate sector, Lee told reporters. 

 His remarks helped fuel heavy won purchases, which pushed the dollar down to KRW1,112.70 in intraday trading, the lowest the U.S. currency has seen since November 27, 1997. 

 Although state-run banks were spotted buying dollars during the day, most market participants believe the government's intention is merely to slow, rather than to halt or reverse, the won's appreciation. 

 At the close the dollar was at KRW1,112.90, compared with KRW1,116.40 the previous session. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also rose Wednesday, building on gains made the previous day, as investor sentiment continued to recover from the sell-off preceding and immediately following the weekend's presidential election. 

 At the close of trading in Taipei, the U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$30.711, down from NT$30.738 the day before. At $413 million, transaction volumes were less than one third the level seen during Monday's hectic session. 

 In Southeast Asia the Singapore dollar strengthened and the baht slipped back as dealers unwound long baht positions in the cross market. 

 "Over the last two days trading has been driven by a lot of talk about acquisitions, but most of it was on a preemptive, speculative basis," said a dealer at one U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 Market players, who earlier in the week had bought baht for Singapore dollars on rumors that Singapore Airlines was in talks to buy a stake in Thai Airways and that HSBC was looking to acquire Bangkok Metropolitan Bank, moved to close out their positions Wednesday, pushing the Singapore dollar up and the baht down. 

 Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore was closely watching exchange rates also helped to boost the Singapore currency, as traders covered their short positions, afraid of possible intervention to lift the Singapore dollar. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted against the Singapore currency at S$1.7138, down from S$1.7191 the previous day. Against the baht the dollar was at THB37.830, up from THB37.820. 

 The rupiah strengthened a touch, but traders said the currency was still being capped by dollar demand from Indonesian corporations. Toward the end of Asian dealing the dollar was at IDR7,441, down from IDR7,461 Tuesday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the peso ended higher, with the dollar dropping to PHP40.895, from PHP40.963 the day before.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen meddling sours regional mood.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 15 (Reuters) - Heavy yen	


intervention by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) weighed on regional


currencies late on Wednesday despite a brief respite for the 

 baht and peso. 

     The baht and peso edged higher after Thailand's bankrupcy 

 court ruled in favour of creditors in a landmark case involving 

 Thailand's biggest debt defaulter, Thai Petrochemical Industry 

 (TPI)   . 

     In the major currency market, the spotlight trailed on 

 dollar/yen after it jumped more than one percent to a high of 

 105.75 on the BOJ intervention. 

     The central bank last intervened a week ago, selling yen 

 for dollars to weaken the Japanese currency, which has 

 appreciated 6.4 percent against the dollar since February 22 

 amid optimism over Japan's recovery. 


    The euro	    was steady against the dollar and at the



top of its intraday range against the yen following the BOJ



moves.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht soon surrendered a 0.2 percent gain, sparked by



news of that Thailand's Bankruptcy Court had found TPI



insolvent and ordered it to be restructured.



    The court also ruled that TPI's chief executive officer be



the interim planner for the company while creditors met to pick



their own planner to revamp the company.



    Analysts had expected a ruling in favour of TPI to hurt



Thai markets and investor perception of the government's



commitment to bankruptcy reform.



    The baht's rise was thwarted by confusion over whether


central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul had threatened to



resign due to a bitter dispute with the cabinet.



    A cabinet source told Reuters Chatu had said he would step



down if proposed changes to the Bank of Thailand (BOT) Act were



approved without alterations ensuring the bank's independence.



    But the director of the BOT's legal department later denied



that Chatu had threatened to quit.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The won was off intraday highs of 1,115 per dollar after



the yen was swiped off recent peaks, calming fears of won


intervention by the Korean authorities.



    South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy said it was



ready to take action to cap the won's rise against the dollar



and that it was not desirable for the won to appreciate in line



with the yen.



Dealers said the market had been reluctant to sell dollars



below 1,116/1,117 on Wednesday and that range-trading was



expected on Thursday.



    A Reuters poll showed that South Korean GDP was expected to



grow 6.8 percent in 2000 and 6.0 percent in 2001.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah slipped in line with other regional currencies


after trading in a tight 7,390-7,440 range.



    The rupiah market has come under slight pressure recently



amid worries the International Monetary Fund might again



suspend its loan programme to the country if key players in a



Bank Bali  banking scandal are not brought to justice.



Though the IMF warned lending might be halted the previous



day, Jakarta dealers expressed confidence the matter would be



resolved.



    Indonesian GDP was seen rising 3.86 percent in 2000 and



4.95 percent in 2001, according to a Reuters poll.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso was off an intraday high of around 40.7 seen after



the baht steadied on the back of the TPI court ruling.



    But sentiment remained weak due to concerns over likely



U.S. rate hikes, a domestic stock manipulation scandal linked

 The Singapore currency enjoyed a firm tone for most of the week as market participants unwound long U.S. dollar positions against the backdrop of a brighter yen.

If the dollar should fall through to the S$1.7000 level, however, the Monetary Authority of Singapore would be prepared to intervene in an attempt to maintain an orderly ebb and flow of the local currency, traders said.

title: Asia Markets - Regionals aloof to euro woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The euro's breathless descent 

 to fresh life lows against the dollar had traders in Asia 

 transfixed on Monday, though most regional markets remained 

 impervious to the single currency's plight. 

     Thin trading conditions and hedge selling of euro/yen by 

 Japanese institutional investors triggered stop-loss sales, 

 taking the euro to a record low of $0.9390, a 3.6 percent drop 

 on the day. 

     Fears of central bank intervention pushed it up to $0.9655 

 by 0900 GMT while euro/yen was at 105.29 after falling as far 

 as 102.45, within a whisker of its life low of 102.05. 

     Analysts said there was little in the way of fresh factors 

 behind the move -- just a growing conviction the European 

Central Bank won't hike rates, coupled with Friday's 

 unexpectedly strong U.S. GDP numbers. 

     REGIONALS COOL TO EURO SHOCK 

     Regional currencies held their ground in the face of the 

 euro's drop, merely extending their early gains as the yen 

 headed higher against the dollar. 

     Analysts said this was hardly surprising, given that Japan 

 and the United States are Asia's main export markets. 

     They said the impact of the euro's moves was more likely to 

 be felt through the yen. 

     "The significant decline we've seen in euro/yen has brought 

 some incremental decline in dollar/yen and that can be manifest 

 in some renewed regional currency strength against the dollar," 

 said David Simmonds, regional currency strategist at Citibank. 

 The yen's rise drove the Korean won through the 1,130 per 

 dollar barrier, but authorities were quick to express unease 

 with its strength and intervene indirectly through state-run 

 banks. 

 Even the Singapore dollar, managed against a trade-weighted 

 basket believed to include the euro, took its cue from the 

 firmer yen and some robust economic data. 

 Singapore's industrial output rose 26.8 percent on the year 

 to January after December's 7.2 percent rise. It was up 17.3 

 percent in January on a three-month moving average basis. 

 Evidence that Singapore's recovery was indeed on track 

 despite some poor export numbers last week, coupled with strong 

 chart support at 1.7120 would limit the Sing dollar's downside 

 in the near term, analysts said. 

 But some pointed out that its rise could also be capped 

 despite a pick-up in inflation and strong domestic 

 fundamentals. 

 Barclays Capital said Singapore was unlikely to face a 

 monetary tightening until late in the second quarter, or 

 beyond. 

     "Despite the strength of recovery, the government remains 

 concerned that the base of recovery is narrow and relies on 

 strong export growth and a recovery in private consumption..., 

 which in turn was driven by a rally in the local stock market," 

 it said in a weekly report. 

     WALL STREET GNAWS AT ASIA STOCKS 

     Most Asian stock markets headed south in the wake of Wall 

 Street's losses on Friday, as investors worried that 

 unexpectedly strong U.S. growth would spur aggressive interest 

 rate hikes. 

     The Nikkei 225 lost nearly 0.5 percent due to the yen's 

 rise. 

     Korea's KOSPI closed at its lowest in four months, with key 

 telecom shares worst hit. 

     Manila shares were also down a hefty 4.13 percent as 

 worries about U.S. rate hikes were compounded by a perception 

 of growing cronyism in the administration of President Joseph 

 Estrada. 

 Hong Kong shares lost out despite gains in China Telecom, 

 with investors still focused on merger talks between Pacific 

 Century CyberWorks (PCCW) and Cable & Wireless HKT Ltd. 

     C&W HKT said a deal between its parent, Britain's Cable & 

 Wireless Plc, and PCCW could be reached within 48 hours. 

     CHINA GROWTH ON TRACK 

     China affirmed its 1999 GDP growth forecast of 7.1 percent 

 and said it was looking for an even better performance this 

 year. 

     The State Statistical Bureau said the economy grew at a 6.8 

 percent pace in the fourth quarter year-on-year to give a 7.1 

 percent rate for the full year. 

     It said retail sales rose 6.8 percent year-on-year, while 

 industrial output steamed ahead by 8.5 percent. 

     Fixed asset investment was up 5.2 percent but foreign 

 direct investment dropped 11.4 percent. 

     Despite the strong growth, prices continued to drop. The 

 consumer price index fell 1.4 percent year-on-year. 

     Growth this year was expected to at least match the 1999 

 rate, and possibly surpass it, thanks to strong exports, the 

 government's commitment to active fiscal policy and its plan to 

 pour money into the poorer western hinterland.

title: Singapore dlr believers tested by trade picture.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar looks set to remain pressured by a weak yen and euro in the near-term, having defied forecasts of a strong rise early in the year. 

 "We still maintain that dollar/yen will go up, and the Sing dollar will follow that," said an analyst at a European bank. 

 "The issue with the yen is not so much a direct impact on the Sing dollar, more that Asia is a major trading bloc," he said, adding that Singapore's major export rivals - Korea and Taiwan - also tended to be influenced by yen weakness. 

 The euro's soft tone was also weighing on the Singapore dollar as Europe is the country's most important non-oil export market after the United States, he said. 

 Analysts said the authorities seemed fairly relaxed about the Singapore dollar's slide since the start of the year. 

 Dealers said they suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to smooth out sharp swings in the exchange rate, but they did not sense unease with the Sing dollar's overall trend. 

 "The Singapore dollar is considered a cheap funding currency because of the low interest rates. But MAS does not want it to become internationalised," an analyst at a European bank said. 

 Singapore has gradually liberalised the use of its currency in equity and debt markets, but the authorities have resisted internationalising it due to the small, open economy. 

 Chartists expected the U.S. dollar to meet resistance at S$1.72, with a second, stronger band at S$1.74. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.7095 at 0700 GMT. Economic data out this week have been below expectations, knocking the currency down to around 1.7150 from 1.7020 late last week. 

 Gross domestic product (GDP) data released on Thursday were at 5.4 percent for 1999, a shade below preliminary numbers of 5.6 percent, but had limited impact on the Singapore dollar. 

 The currency did take a knock from export data, showing a 7.6 percent rise on the year to January compared with December's 25 percent jump. 

 Analysts attributed the poor performance to a supply glitch in the global electronics industry, while the government said it was mainly due to Y2K factors. 

 "The GDP figures were lower than expected, but the disappointing non-oil export figures before that took away most of the bite," an analyst said. 

 "The interesting point to note is that in a survey of manufacturers, they said price competition was the number one obstacle to getting export orders." 

 This added weight to the argument that there would be a more relaxed exchange rate policy, he said. 

 But most analysts maintained their bullish long-term forecasts for the Singapore dollar on expectations of solid growth this year. 

 "The direction over the medium term is still for Singapore dollar strength to 1.50 by year end," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. ((Sarah Cheung, Asia forex desk (65) 970-3841;fax (65) 870-3787; e-mail asia.forex@reuters.com)).

title: Brunei Turmoil Seen Having Little Effect On Singapore Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Charges of financial mismanagement against Prince Jefri of Brunei should have little, if any, impact on the Singapore dollar, analysts said Friday. 

 Although Brunei's currency is pegged to the Singapore dollar, the news of the charges Thursday doesn't appear to be of much concern to foreign exchange traders, the analysts said. 

 "This should not have any material impact on the Singapore dollar," said Song Seng Wun, economist at G.K. Goh Research in Singapore. 

 "Both economies are seeing recovery with increasing exports in Singapore and higher oil revenues for Brunei," he added. 

 The Singapore dollar has been falling in recent sessions against the U.S. dollar, hitting a five-month low in overnight trading Thursday. 

 At 0440 GMT (11:50 p.m. Thursday EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7130, barely changed from S$1.7136 late Thursday. 

 Gerard Teo, economist at ABN Amro Bank, agreed that the events in Brunei aren't registering on the radar screens of foreign exchange traders. 

 "The key thing driving the Singapore dollar is the (U.S.) dollar-yen relationship. The Singapore dollar is falling in line with other regional currencies," he said. 

 And the Singapore central bank, for the time being, doesn't appear to be in any hurry to intervene in support of the Singapore dollar, he added. 

 "So far, we've seen no shift in their neutral policy," he said. 

 The Brunei government said Thursday it had started legal proceedings against Prince Jefri, freezing his assets and accusing him of improper use of state funds. Prince Jefri is the younger brother of the sultan of Brunei. 

 The Brunei dollar is pegged to the Singapore dollar on a one-to-one basis. The two currencies move in virtual lockstep in foreign exchange markets. 

 -By Alan Yonan Jr.; 65-421-4859; alan.yonan@dowjones.com

title: Emerging  FX -Sour as dollar/yen creeps higher.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Overnight strength in the 

 dollar after reassuring comments by U.S. Fed Chairman Alan 

 Greenspan weighed on regional currencies, but the Singapore

title: Asian  Currencies  Under Pressure; Won Falls To Six-Wk Low
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies came under pressure on Thursday as the recent weakness of the yen combined with souring sentiment toward local markets to drive regional currencies lower against the U.S. dollar. 

 Only the New Taiwan dollar held its own, as the Taiwanese central bank stepped into the market to support the local currency, anxious to iron out any unwelcome volatility following the upsurge in political tensions with mainland China. 

 In Seoul, the won continued to weaken in response to the yen's slide and a deterioration in South Korea's trade balance. 

 "The yen is an important factor," said Steven Xu, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. "Korea targets its exchange rate on a cross-basis against the yen, and the long-term target is KRW10." 

 With the dollar/yen exchange rate testing five-month highs, the won has come uncomfortably close to that level recently. Only in the last few trading sessions has the Korean currency begun in earnest to play catch up with the yen's fall. 

 Thursday saw the dollar trade as high as KRW1,141.00 against the won, its highest level in six weeks. According to traders, much of the dollar-buying was executed by Korean oil exporters, underlining fears that the current high crude oil prices will damage the trade balance of Korea, which is heavily dependent on energy imports. 

 Last week, South Korea announced a surprise $1.4 billion trade deficit in the first two weeks of February, sharply souring investor sentiment. Despite official reassurances that the country will still record a surplus for the month as a whole, that shock partly accounts for a selloff in local blue-chip stocks, which dragged down the main board Kospi index by 1.5% on Thursday, in turn weighing on the currency as foreign investors retreated. 

 At the close of Seoul trading Thursday, the dollar was quoted at KRW1,140.50, up from KRW1,135.30 the previous day. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the New Taiwan dollar ended unchanged following purchases of the local currency by the central bank. 

 Analysts said that despite the heightened tensions with Beijing, foreign investors in Taiwan were mostly standing firm, reassured by the Taiwan government's pledge to support local stock prices and by the structural strength of Taiwan's economy. 

 At the close, the U.S. dollar was flat against the New Taiwan dollar at NT$30.785. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Singapore dollar ended local trading lower after a large customer purchase of U.S. dollars against the Singapore currency was worked through the market during European hours on Wednesday, propelling the U.S. currency up through the S$1.7100 level. 

 Pointing to the current spate of foreign investments by Singapore companies, including a $240 million Hong Kong property purchase on Thursday by Singapore's Pidemco, dealers said the U.S. dollar is likely to test higher against the Singapore currency over the short term. 

 "The MAS isn't in the market, so it could test S$1.7200," said one trader at a local bank, referring to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which typically intervenes to maintain the exchange rate within an undisclosed target range. 

 Late Thursday in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7134, up from S$1.7083 early in European trading the previous day. 

 The Thai currency also lost ground, after baht liquidity in the offshore market eased following a funding squeeze on Wednesday. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted against the baht at THB38.190, up from THB38.030 the day before. 

 The rupiah came under selling pressure late in the session as fears over the frail health of Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid unsettled local markets, after the head of state canceled his schedule of meetings Thursday. Toward the end of local trading, the dollar was quoted against the rupiah at IDR7,885, up from IDR7,445 late Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso suffered in line with the regional trend and a downturn in the Manila stock market. At the close, the dollar was at PHP40.870, up from PHP40.700 the day before.

title: Asian  FX intervention  risky as rates rise - Merrill.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 22 (Reuters) - Asian central banks face a growing dilemma as they try to rein in appreciating currencies against a backdrop of gradually rising short-term interest rates, Merrill Lynch said in a research report. 

 The policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets to buy dollars and then sterilising the interventions - or mopping up the domestic currency injected into the system - would become increasingly untenable as interest rates headed higher, Merrill's February Asian strategy report said. 

 Growing trade surpluses and capital inflows bolstered Asian currencies last year, prompting central banks to buy an estimated $65 billion in dollars in the spot market. 

 The fact that base money went up only slightly suggested that the operations had been mostly sterilised, Merrill said. 

 While this policy could continue in a context of low inflation and large external surpluses, it noted that the Bank of Korea's recent decision to raise key overnight rates revealed that inflation was not the only consideration in a monetary tightening. 

 "The BOK stated that there was no inflation threat in sight, but wanted to narrow the spread between short and long rates; it is likely concerned over banks' excessive reliance on short-term credit." 

 Despite the still-benign inflation environment in most of Asia, Merrill said interest rates were set to climb as more central banks used monetary policy to address any banking sector imbalances that might pose risks to macroeconomic stability. 

 And the resulting rate hikes could in turn weigh, given that much of Asia's early asset price recovery was driven by domestic institutions flush with central bank-infused liquidity. 

 With foreign funds set to continue buying into the Asian recovery, central banks were likely to either step up their forex sterilisation efforts or allow their currencies to strengthen. 

 "Either option would be unwelcome - sterilisation gets more expensive and ineffective as interest rates rise while currency appreciation at a mature stage of recovery has always been a difficult option to pursue," it said. 

 But Merrill added that Asian currencies with flexible exchange rate regimes remained greatly undervalued against the dollar despite recovering substantially from their 1998 lows. 

 It said the rupiah and ringgit were 33 percent and 27 percent undervalued respectively, while the Thai baht and Philippine peso were more than 20 percent undervalued. 

 Even the Korean won, whose dramatic gains have drawn frequent official comment and intervention, was nearly 15 percent below its fair value, while the Singapore and Taiwan dollars were some eight and nine percent undervalued. 

 Merrill said its study computed nominal effective exchange rates based on the top 10 trade partners of individual countries in 1999, using the pre-crisis first half of 1997 as a base. 

 It then worked out the real effective exchange rates and used trends in these to derive the fair value of individual currencies against the U.S. dollar.

title: Singapore Dollar Gains Late On Back Of Euro
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar strengthened slightly against the U.S. dollar late Monday as it tracked gains in the euro and the yen. 

 Around 0908 GMT (4:08 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7067, down from S$1.7085 late Monday. 

 "The market is cooling down after two days of buying pressure" that boosted the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar, a dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar is linked to a trade-weighted basket of currencies, which is thought to include the dollar, the euro and yen. 

 Generally, a change in the U.S. dollar against one of the other major currencies mirrors the U.S. dollar's performance against the Singapore dollar. 

 Late Tuesday, the U.S. dollar gave up ground against the yen, falling to Y111.24 from a peak of Y111.71 early in the day. The euro rose US$0.9990, up from US$0.9873 late Monday in Europe. 

 On Monday, the Singapore dollar dropped sharply after the release of figures showing that export growth in January was far lower than expected. 

 Some dealers, however, said the Singapore dollar had been oversold, and that some participants Tuesday were buying back the local currency. 

 Fear of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore also eased some pressure on the Singapore dollar, dealers said. The MAS is said to intervene to smooth volatility. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 2.1875%, up from 1.500% late Monday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.375%, up from 2.250%.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Won Makes 27-Mo High
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly lower against the U.S. dollar late Friday, although the South Korean won bucked the trend to end sharply higher as funds continued to pour into the Korean stock market. 

 But overall, it was a day of U.S. dollar strength fueled by another record close on the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite Index. 

 The Nasdaq Composite Index jumped 2.8% Thursday to a new all-time high close of 4,485.63. This was the second record in the past three sessions, and it helped the dollar retain its overnight gains against the yen and euro. 

 The South Korean won ended trading in Seoul at its highest level to the dollar in nearly 27 months as foreign investors purchased won to pay for recent and future purchases in the local stock market. 

 The dollar finished at KRW1,115.30 won - its lowest close since Nov. 26, 1997 - down from KRW1,120.80 a day earlier. 

 Foreign investors bought a net KRW142.4 billion of Korean shares Friday, lifting their net purchases for the week to KRW822.53 billion. 

 The heavy dollar-selling pressure overwhelmed periodic attempts by state-run Korean Development Bank to shore up the dollar. 

 Although a decision Thursday by the Bank of Korea to raise its one-day call rate by 25 basis points triggered a round of won buying, analysts say it may eventually reduce upward pressure on the currency. 

 Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in a report said the rate hike will limit upward pressure on the won because the government has used its recent appreciation to stem inflationary pressure from rising import prices. 

 Traders said they expect the dollar to continue sinking next week as foreign funds that poured into the Seoul stock market late this week enter the currency market. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended little changed against its U.S. counterpart despite a rise in local share prices to a near 10-year closing high, and unexpectedly strong exports data. Intervention by Taiwan's central bank, in which it bought U.S. dollars, prevented the local dollar from rising. 

 The Central Bank of China wants to keep the New Taiwan dollar as weak as possible to ensure that its exporters remain competitive. 

 At the end of trading in Taipei, the dollar was at NT$30.613, little changed from late Thursday. 

 Trading volumes in other regional currencies were down as Tokyo markets were closed Friday for a Japanese holiday. 

 In late trading in Jakarta, the dollar was quoted at IDR7,300, up marginally from IDR7,295 late Thursday as traders locked in profits on long rupiah positions. 

 Positive political and corporate developments, particularly a shakeup in the management of Indonesian automaker Astra in preparation for its sale, helped fuel the rupiah's recent rise from IDR7,700. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar was down against its U.S. counterpart, but well off its intraday low on news that Singapore Telecommunications Ltd. (P.SGT) may face competition in its bid to merge with Cable & Wireless HKT (HKT). 

 Pacific Century CyberWorks Ltd. (H.PCW) said it is considering investing in the unit of Cable & Wireless PLC (CWP). 

 When Singtel announced its merger plan, the local currency fell as traders expected the company would need to sell Singapore dollars and buy sterling to pay Cable & Wireless for some of its stake in the Hong Kong company. 

 Traders expect the weakness in the Singapore dollar will continue to be limited to S$1.7000. They say the Monetary Authority of Singapore likely will intervene at that level to curb the slide of the local currency. MAS bought Singapore dollars last week between S$1.7000 and S$1.7100. 

 The U.S. dollar late Friday was trading at S$1.6935, up from S$1.6912 late Thursday, but below an intraday high of S$1.6977. 

 Against the Thai baht, the U.S. dollar was trading at THB37.475, up from THB37.365 a day earlier, while the dollar ended trading in Manila at PHP40.450, up from PHP40.385 late Thursday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Higher Late Ahead Of Lunar New Year
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are higher in late Asian trading Friday, although a number of markets were closed for a lunar New Year holiday. 

 Regional currencies were buoyed by the rupiah, which rose as fears of a military coup arising from a standoff between Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid and powerful Security Minister General Wiranto receded. 

 A rise in the local overnight interest rate after authorities decided Thursday to tighten the money supply also helped the currency. 

 There is a growing belief in financial markets that Wiranto will resign from the Cabinet without fuss when Wahid returns to the country on Feb. 13. 

 Traders took heart from comments by Indonesian Defense Minister Juwono Sudarsono, which appeared to indicate Wahid is softening his line on Wiranto and will negotiate a graceful exit for the former military chief. 

 Sudarsono said he passed on to Wiranto a request from Wahid for him to step down immediately, but indicated nothing may happen until the president returns. 

 The dollar is at IDR7,520, down from IDR7,660 late Thursday and a four-month high of IDR7,700 earlier that day. 

 The Singapore dollar rose sharply on the back of the stronger rupiah, a rise in local stock prices, and ongoing fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which sold U.S. dollars earlier this week. 

 The Straits Times Index rose 9.6 points, or 0.4%, to 2,258.9. 

 Late in the day, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6870, down from S$1.6955 previously. 

 Elsewhere, the baht rose strongly against the U.S. dollar in line with the stronger Indonesian currency and a higher yen. 

 Analysts say the baht may rise further on the back of more corporate restructuring and foreign investment, both of which helped lift Thailand out of a severe recession. 

 Citigroup and IDEAglobal.com economists expect the baht to breach 36.000 against the dollar by the end of the year. 

 "The capital account should support the baht. We expect capital inflows," said Citigroup economist Anusorn Tamajai. 

 Still, Anusorn warns the currency may come under pressure during that period, especially "when the government and corporates pay external debts." 

 Last September, the dollar rose above THB40 amid a round of corporate foreign-debt repayment. 

 In late trade, the dollar is at THB37.500 down from THB37.680 late Thursday. 

 The peso also ended the week higher at PHP40.535 to the dollar from PHP40.680 a day earlier. 

 The South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar markets were closed due to holidays in South Korea and Taiwan. The U.S. dollar ended Thursday at KRW1,129.9 and NT$30.775.

 This would scuttle talk of a possible military coup, which has weighed on the rupiah for a number of weeks. Wahid demands Wiranto step down after a government report implicated him and other military officials in atrocities last year in the former Indonesian province of East Timor.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Early; IDR Hurt By Political Concerns
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are lower against the U.S. dollar early Wednesday as another strong night on Wall Street helped the U.S. currency to a four-month high against the yen, and a new all-time high against the euro. 

 In addition, political concerns are weighing on the rupiah as a showdown between Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid and Security Minister General Wiranto looms. 

 Wahid, who was in London overnight for meetings with the U.K. government, again called for Wiranto to quit his Cabinet post after a government report blamed him and other top officers for atrocities in East Timor last year. 

 Wiranto has declined to respond to calls for him to resign, which some observers interpret as a sign he will seek to remain in the Cabinet. 

 This would add to tension between the administration and disgruntled elements of the military, and likely spark renewed talk of a possible military coup, although Wahid dismissed such speculation as "hogwash." 

 However, there should be some good news for the Indonesian economy and rupiah later Wednesday. The Consultative Group for Indonesia, which comprises the main foreign donors to Indonesia, is expected to pledge around $4.5 billion in new loans to Jakarta to help it finance its budget. The CGI is holding its annual meeting Tuesday and Wednesday in Jakarta. 

 In early Asian trade, the dollar was quoted at 7,470 rupiah, up slightly from IDR7,450 late Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar is weaker against its U.S. counterpart, weighed down by the rupiah and proposed foreign acquisitions by local companies such as Singapore Airlines S$1.6 billion buy of a 49% stake in Virgin Atlantic. 

 Traders said they expect the U.S. dollar will test above S$1.7000. 

 "The market wants to see if the MAS will step in to buy Singapore dollars as they did on Monday at S$1.7100," said a U.S. bank trader. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore is believed to have intervened in the market Monday to slow the steep decline of the local currency. 

 U.S. currency was quoted against the Singapore dollar at S$1.6985, up from S$1.6955 at Tuesday's close. 

 The won opened weaker in Seoul at 1,129.0 against the dollar from KRW1,126.6 at Tuesday's close, with traders citing dollar buying by state banks. The dollar ended higher Tuesday on buying by the state-run Korea Development Bank and net selling of local stocks by foreign investors. 

 Elsewhere, the U.S. currency was at 37.515 Thai baht, up slightly from THB37.505 late Tuesday. 

 Domestic trade in Taipei and Manila is scheduled to commence at 0100 GMT. 

 The New Taiwan dollar edged higher Tuesday to close at NT$30.681 against the U.S. dollar from NT$30.699 a day earlier, while the peso ended Tuesday at 40.550 pesos from PHP40.572 at Monday's.

title: Singapore Dlr Falls To 4-Mo Low Late On Corp US$ Orders
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar plunged to a four-month low against the U.S. dollar late Friday on aggressive U.S. dollar buying by DBS Bank on behalf of corporate customers, dealers said. 

 At about 0830 GMT (3:30 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7023, up from S$1.6892 late Thursday. 

 DBS Bank foreign exchange dealers were unavailable for comment, but a dealer at a U.S. bank estimated that DBS bought US$1 billion in the market. 

 Traders said DBS could be buying on behalf of Singapore Airlines Ltd., which recently announced it was taking a stake in Virgin Airways, or Singapore Telecommunications Ltd., which is in merger talks with Cable & Wireless HKT. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said the Singapore dollar is almost certainly trading outside its accepted trade-weighted band, and he expects the Monetary Authority of Singapore to step into the market to prop up the local currency. 

 "I'm a little surprised they haven't been in yet," he said. 

 Such a move would be highly unusual for the MAS since it usually intervenes in the markets by selling Singapore dollars in a bid to preserve export competitiveness. 

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar will probably retreat next week, especially as players square their positions on the last day of the month on Monday. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.875%, up from 1.750% late Thursday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.3125%, down from 2.4375%.
