title: Singapore Dlr Ends Unchanged, But Up From Intraday Lows
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar bounced back from intraday lows to end virtually unchanged late Thursday as institutions locked in gains from long U.S. dollar positions. 

 At about 0810 GMT (3:10 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6892, compared with S$1.6891 late Wednesday. Early Thursday, the dollar hit an intraday high of S$1.6933. 

 Dealers said U.S. and Hong-Kong based institutions liquidated long U.S. dollar positions at the level of about S$1.6930, lifting the local currency. 

 In addition, dealers said, local banks sold the U.S. dollar on behalf of commercial clients, sparking rumors of intervention in support of the Singapore currency by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The MAS generally works through local banks when it intervenes in the foreign exchange market. However, the rumor was met with some skepticism, since the MAS is said to have intervened recently to weaken the Singapore dollar, rather than strengthen it. 

 Investors sold the U.S. dollar as it approached its long-term resistance level of S$1.7000. That level should remain an effective cap on the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 On the other hand, political uncertainty in Indonesia and the prospect of an interest rate hike in the U.S. when the Federal Open Market Committee meets next month will limit the downside for the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Thursday's dealing also saw unwinding of long Thai baht positions against the Singapore dollar. Some players had sold Singapore dollars for baht to take advantage of relatively higher interest rates in Thailand. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 1.750%, down from 1.875% late Wednesday. The three-month rate was offered unchanged at 2.4375%.

SINGAPORE, Jan 24 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 were mostly lower in early trade on Monday in a knee jerk 

 reaction to the Group of Seven nations' weekend statement that 

 they share Japan's concerns about the strong yen. 

     Dealers said they expected trade to be choppy in the run up 

 to the Federal Reserve's policy meeting on February 1 and 2. 


    The yen	    gained ground after retreating against the



greenback in early Tokyo trade as buyers squared long positions



in disappointment over the dollar's failure to sustain a rally.



    Over the longer-term, the yen is seen supported by



foreigners' investment in Tokyo stocks and buying by Japanese



exporters, dealers said.



    "There was some dollar buying in early trade. But I don't



think the dollar's rise would be sustained. There was no pledge



of possible coordinated action to check the yen's rise, only



sympathy," said a dealer at a major European bank.



Some dealers said recent losses in the Dow Jones index



could put the dollar on firmer footing against the regionals in



the near-term as it could mean lower foreign inflows into local



equity markets.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



The rupiah pierced the 7,300 level as further fighting



between Christians and Moslems in the spice islands broke out



over the weekend.



"Fundamentally, the rupiah should not be this bad because



the upward trend since end-December has not been threatened," a


currency analyst said.



There was also unrest on the island resort of Bintan, near



Singapore, where Indonesian police and military forces



dispersed demonstrators, injuring 13 people.



The analyst noted that the protests in Bintan for the past



week were over land rights claims by villagers and were



isolated from religious riots in the rest of the country.



    However, he said dollar/rupiah could head for 7,400, with



reasonable support seen at 7,250.



    Finance Minister Bambang Sudibyo was quoted by local press



over the weekend as saying the central bank did not need to be



recapitalised after all.



    Sudibyo was quoted by the Jakarta Post as saying an



accounting adjustment showed Bank Indonesia actually had 100



trillion rupiah in assets.

    The won was lower against the dollar as banks, which had



bought dollars believing the won might be hurt by news of a



merchant bank's suspension, reversed course as market sentiment



appeared little changed, dealers said.



On Friday, the Financial Supervisory Commission ordered



Nara Investment Banking Corp , which had been



staggering due to its large exposure to the ailing Daewoo Group



, to halt operations for three months from on



Saturday.



    A local bank dealer said market players bought dollars



after the news but the impact was shortlived.



    Underlying market sentiment was still betting on the won



strengthening as foreign investors kept up their interest in



direct and equity investment in Korea, he said.



    Dealers said the market was also cautious about dollar



holdings as they believed the authorities would continue to


intervene to prevent volatility.


SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    Local bank buying of U.S. dollars and technical factors



weighed on the Sing dollar while a clash between police and



protesters on the neighbouring Indonesian island of Bintan



unsettled sentiment.



Chartists said dollar/Sing was well entrenched in an upward



channel from Jan 4 and that 1.6850 was seen as a strong



resistance level.



If touched, the U.S. dollar was likely to slip as the



channel looked a little over-extended. Support was seen at



around 1.6775/80.



One analyst said local banks had been seen supporting the



U.S. dollar again with a view to keeping it between the 1.67



and 1.69 level in the medium term, to keep exports competitive.



Developments on Bintan, where Singapore has investments,



were keeping players slightly wary though there seemed to be no



real effect on flows as yet, he said.



THAI BAHT	



The baht edged down on importer dollar demand. The unit is



expected to move in a narrow range in the near-term due to



modest commercial demand.



Rating agency Fitch IBCA says Thai commercial banks appear



on track to return to profitability this year, but some -



including top banks like Bangkok Bank  and Siam



Commercial Bank  - are likely to need to make further



provisions against loan losses.



Some analysts said the worst was over for Thai banks after



they reported massive losses for 1999 last week, blaming the



poor results on huge loan losses provisionings.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso tracked the baht lower due to commercial demand



for the U.S. dollar, dealers said.



    The market showed little immediate reaction to positive



January-October current account data released on Monday.



    The central bank said the Philippines posted a hefty



current account surplus of $5.55 billion in the first ten



months of 1999, exceeding the full-year target of $1.67



billion.



It also cut its overnight lending rate to 11 percent from



12 percent. The bank had raised its lending rate to 12 percent



last month when it opened a facility to meet banks' immediate



cash requirements for the Y2K cross over.



TAIWAN DOLLAR	



The Taiwan dollar was slightly firmer and well within the



parameters of a recent range carved out by the central bank.



The firmer yen and expected inflows by foreign equity funds



were expected to drive gains in the local currency but the


central bank was expected to cap any significant upside.



December unemployment figures were expected at 0300 GMT but



a local newspaper quoted the Statistics Office as saying the

an all-time record high of 2.92 percent for all of 1999.

title: Emerging  FX  - Boosted as U.S. inflation fears fade.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly 

 firmer in early Monday trade after more evidence that U.S. 

 inflation was looking tame pushed the Dow to yet another record 

 closing high. 

     That was seen as giving regional stocks and sentiment in 

currencies a boost. 

     Eagerly awaited Consumer Price Index data for December came 

 in at a less than anticipated 0.2 percent, compared to 

 expectations for an average 0.3 percent increase according to a 

 recent Reuters poll. 

 Dealers said that had underpinned hopes the U.S. Federal 

 Reserve might stop at a 25 basis point rise when it meets on 

 February 1 and 2. 

 Wall Street's fortunes pushed the dollar to its highest 

 levels against the euro in 1-weeks on Friday but failed to 

 have any visible impact on dollar/yen which sagged. 

 By early Asia, dollar/yen was a shade easier on sporadic 

 selling by U.S. operators but its downside was seen supported 

 near 105.50 yen. 

     The euro remained pressured but was off lows seen on Friday 

 while follow-through sales also weighed on euro/yen. 

     U.S. markets are closed Monday a partial market and public 

 holiday for Martin Luther King day. The foreign exchange market 

 remains open.

as players sold dollars offshore and the market remained



positive over a pre-weekend cabinet re-shuffle.

title: Emerging  FX  - Weaker, eyeing Wall Street.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Most Asian regional 

currencies were softer late on Friday as players adjusted 

 positions, awaiting Wall Street's reaction to remarks by 

 Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan. 

     Greenspan told the Economic Club of New York late on 

 Thursday that the Fed is intent on defusing mounting imbalances 

 between supply and demand, and will support higher borrowing 

 costs to take some heat out of the U.S. economy. 

  The market was divided, with some dealers expecting U.S. 

 financial markets to take Greenspan's comments in stride as 

 they confirmed an already discounted 25-basis-point rate hike. 

     "But there are others who think the remarks might signal 

 the possibilities of the Fed opting for a 50 basis point rate 

 hike in February rather than 25 as earlier expected," said a 

 dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

     "This led to some profit taking and position adjustments 

 ahead of the weekend. That said, there were no drastic moves in 

 the market. Trade is normally thin on Friday," he said. 


    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The won bucked the trend, rising on the new finance



minister's market-friendly comments.



    Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai on Friday stressed the



importance of market forces in restructuring the corporate



sector. He also said the government would shun intervening in



the market unless it was volatile.



    But further upside for the won could be limited given that



the dollar is edging toward oversold territory against the won



on the 14-day relative strength index.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah wilted against the dollar, with 7,300 seen as a



solid support near-term but dealers said 7,100 could be a



strong resistance for now as investors are expected to buy



dollars near that level.



 Sentiment was dampened by tensions between Moslems and



Christians in the spice islands.



    Indonesia's military said on Friday it would send hundreds



of crack troops to the islands to quell widespread violence.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso was wedged in a narrow range in listless trade.



    The Philippine central bank's policy making Monetary Board



decided to keep overnight rates steady next week.



    Dealers said so long as the peso does not weaken beyond 41



per dollar, Philippine authorities should be able to keep



interest rates low, at least until the next U.S. Federal Open



Market Committee meeting on February 1 and 2.



TAIWAN DOLLAR	



The Taiwan dollar edged lower after the stock market failed



to sustain its recent momentum.



Recent aggressive dollar-buying interventions by the


central bank had pressured investors to slow down their



greenback selling, traders said.



The demand for the local unit also dwindled as investors



retreated from the market to await Wall Street's reaction to



the hawkish remarks made by Greenspan.

The downside could be limited as the US dollar is

But 1.6550 was expected to be a strong barrier for the Sing

intervening to buy U.S. dollars at that level, dealers said.

currency could hurt Thailand's trade surplus.

title: POLL - Asia  currencies  seen strengthening in 2000.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Robust global growth and a 

 gradual pick-up in inflationary pressures should see most Asian 

currencies reaching for higher ground this year. 

 A Reuters poll of 92 economists and dealers across Asia 

 found that regional currencies are set to ride a wave of 

 investment and asset inflows, leaving the worst of the crisis 

 far behind. 

 As inflation picks up alongside rising imports, employment 

 and consumer demand in the second half, central banks are 

 expected to allow their currencies more leeway to appreciate. 

 "The authorities may be approaching a policy crossroad in 

 managing the current economic cycle," said Chia-Liang Lian, 

 fixed income stategist at Merrill Lynch. 

 "Specifically, central banks could acquiesce to stronger 

currencies if balance of payments inflows continue unabated 

 amid maturing economic recoveries," he said. 

 The Australian and New Zealand dollars are expected to make 

 strong headway thanks to rising commodity prices, while the 

 Korean won, which gained 5.4 percent in 1999, is seen surging 

 some 10 percent by the end of 2000. 

 Marginal gains are predicted for the Thai baht and 

 Philippine peso, which lost about three percent each against 

 the dollar last year amid worries about public and private 

 sector debt. 

 As much of the upside for regional currencies is likely to 

 be driven by foreign portfolio flows, analysts warn that any 

 rout on Wall Street could shake confidence in markets across 

 the Pacific. 

 AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR 

 Higher commodity prices, driven by a pick-up in world 

 growth, are expected to propel the Australian dollar to levels 

 not seen since November 1997. 

 Analysts see the Aussie gaining over five percent to end 

 the year at US$0.7023 against the current US$0.6660, supported 

 by an expected rise in official interest rates. 

 Tax reforms encouraging investment which start in July and 

 the Olympic Games in September should keep the Aussie supported 

 in the second half, but its rise could be slowed by a large 

 trade deficit, yen strength or if commodity prices fail to 

 rally. 

 NEW ZEALAND DOLLAR 

 The region's other commodity currency, the New Zealand 

 dollar, looks set to soar this year, with analysts predicting 

 an average five percent rise in the first half and a near 10 

 percent gain over the course of the year. 

 The kiwi lost about 0.5 percent against the U.S. dollar in 

 1999, but analysts said its prospects should improve with the 

 economy now on the verge of sustainable expansion. 

 Expectations of a series of interest rate hikes this year 

 could also bolster the kiwi, but New Zealand's large current 

 account deficit remained a worry, analysts said. 

 KOREAN WON 

 Official forecasts of growth in excess of seven percent 

 this year and robust foreign direct and equity investment 

 should help the won extend its blistering rally. 

 Interbank dealers and economists expected the won to gain 

 over five percent by the end of June and some 10 percent by 

 end-2000, from about 1,135 currently. 

 Analysts said the won was undervalued due to heavy 

intervention by Korean authorities, who are anxious to keep 

 exports competitive, but the government is likely to relax its 

 grip on the exchange rate to curb inflationary pressures. 

 Only a worsening of Daewoo's debt crisis could pose a 

 serious threat to the won uptrend, if it spurred an exodus from 

 Korean asset markets, analysts said. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 Singapore's sound fundamentals and signs of a pick-up in 

 inflation should see the local dollar appreciate steadily 

 through the year, with analysts predicting a five percent gain 

 from the current 1.67 per U.S. dollar by year end. 

 Most houses did not foresee a significant build-up in 

 domestic price pressures but some cautioned that the island 

 remained highly vulnerable to external shocks like a dramatic 

 rise in oil or commodity prices. 

Singapore's central bank is believed to have intervened in 

 recent months to cap the Sing dollar, which is managed against 

 an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 But Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was quoted as saying the 

 island had never depended on a weak currency to stay 

 competitive. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 Taiwan's return to pre-crisis growth rates and a seemingly 

 unstoppable stock market are expected to lift the tightly 

 controlled Taiwan $1.2 percent to 30.36 by year-end. 

 Analysts expected its rise to be muted by the central 

 bank's frequent interventions -- part of an unspoken policy of 

 protecting exporters. 

 Taiwan's expected entry to the World Trade Organisation in 

 the second half could see the local dollar benefit from foreign 

 investment flows, though some analysts expected a shrinking 

 trade surplus to weigh on the currency. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso should strengthen marginally this year, thanks to 

 strong growth in exports, remittances from Filipinos working 

 overseas and U.S. dollar loan proceeds. 

 But worries about the ballooning budget deficit and growing 

 political risk could limit foreign investment flows. 

 "Although the current account will be very strong, I think 

 because of the domestic political uncertainty with regards to 

 liberalisation and charter change, the Philippines will not 

 outshine the rest of the region," said Chan Chia Lin, head of 

 Asian economic research at ABN Amro Bank in Singapore. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht is expected to move in a stable range near its 

 current level, supported by a pick-up in capital inflows as 

 Thailand's economic outlook improves. 

 Analysts said Thailand could make further headway in 

 repaying foreign debt in the first half, while foreign 

 portfolio flows were likely to improve further into the year. 

 They expected the baht to remain on the weaker side of 37 

 per dollar on average, but strengthen slightly from its 37.52 

 level at the end of 1999. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 Indonesia's huge debt overhang and the uncertain fate of 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid's infant government will keep the 

 rupiah a risky buy this year. 

 An improved economic picture is likely to be offset by a 

 jump in imports and foreign debt repayment, as well as worries 

 about communal violence. 

 Analysts expect the rupiah to be near current levels by 

 mid-year, with an average forecast of an over seven percent 

 rise to 6,685 per dollar by end-December. 

 MALAYSIAN RINGGIT Malaysia is not expected to abandon its 

currency peg of 3.80 ringgit to the U.S. dollar before June, 

 but half of the research houses polled saw the government 

 re-examining its exchange rate policy beyond mid-2000. 

 This could result in an adjustment of the fixed rate or a 

 move to a managed float, with the undervalued ringgit seen 

 appreciating by about 3.8 percent to 3.66 per dollar by 

 year-end. 

 Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has said the ringgit peg 

 will remain until there is a global agreement on a new 

 financial framework that would prevent speculative attacks on 

currencies.

title: Singapore Dollar Weakens Sharply Late On Selling By Funds
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar dropped sharply in late afternoon trading as European funds sold the currency for U.S. dollars, traders said. 

 About 0918 GMT (4:18 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6738, up from S$1.6684 late Thursday. 

 Traders were surprised by the sudden late afternoon move, which saw the U.S. dollar break out of a range of S$1.6710-S$1.6720 in which it had been trading for most of the day. 

 "There's a lot of interest to buy," said a dealer at a European bank. "Everybody's on the same side." 

 The dealer said there was only one major seller, a French institution. 

 The sharp move on the Singapore dollar was out of step with other regional currencies, which were generally stable against the U.S. dollar. Usually, regional currencies move in tandem. 

 Some traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to buy U.S. dollars, as they had done twice earlier in the week, but others said there was no clear evidence of intervention. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar could weaken further in the course of the European trading day, in large part because participants generally don't want to hold short U.S. dollar positions over the weekend. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 0.500%, up from 0.125% late Thursday. The three-month rate was offered at 2.375%, unchanged.

title: Singapore MAS Seen Smoothing  Forex  Volatility
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Recent central bank intervention to weaken the Singapore dollar has been aimed at smoothing volatility and discouraging speculation rather than influencing the exchange rate, analysts said Thursday. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened late Wednesday to buy U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars, said traders, who pointed out the move marked the second time this week the MAS has intervened to support the U.S. unit. 

 But the MAS action puzzled some observers because it came at a time when the Singapore dollar was falling against the U.S. currency - a trend that the central bank should have welcomed. In the past, the MAS has intervened to subdue a strengthening Singapore dollar. 

 "From the fundamental point of view there is no compelling reason to tinker with the exchange rate," said Friedrich Wu, chief economist at Development Bank of Singapore. "They are fairly comfortable at this level of S$1.6600 to S$1.6700" to the U.S. dollar, he said. 

 In the absence of reasons to influence the exchange rate, observers said, the MAS was most likely acting to prevent sharp moves in the currency. "It might just be smoothing fluctuations in the market given that dollar-Sing has been a bit choppy of late," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 Other participants added that Singapore's monetary authority may have been trying to discourage what it considers to be undue speculation in the Singapore dollar. 

 The authority frowns on offshore use of the Singapore currency for purposes not related to trade or direct investment. 

Intervention During London Hours When Trade Is Thin



Late Wednesday, during London trading hours, traders said the
authority bought U.S. dollars in several transactions between S$1.6650
and S$1.6690.



The authority, which generally acts through Singapore banks,
intervened during London hours when liquidity is thin and the exchange
rate more volatile, they added.



On Monday, the MAS bought U.S. dollars at the level of S$1.6600,
dealers said, at a time when the Singapore dollar and other Asian
currencies were already weakening in response to declines in local stock
markets. The MAS intervention accelerated the Singapore dollar's
downward move.



MAS spokesman Toh Yong Chuan declined to comment on Thursday, saying
the authority generally doesn't discuss reports of market intervention.



The MAS doesn't target a specific U.S. dollar exchange rate for the
Singapore dollar. Instead, it guides the Singapore dollar against a
basket of currencies the island-state's most important trading partners.



Although the MAS doesn't reveal the structure of the basket, the U.S.
dollar is thought to represent about 20%, with the yen close behind at
about 16%.



Generally, the MAS intervenes to subdue the Singapore dollar if the
currency's gains against the U.S. dollar aren't offset by declines
against the yen or other currencies in the basket, analysts say.



The MAS uses the Singapore dollar exchange rate in order to juggle two
policy objectives.



On the one hand, it wants to keep the exchange rate competitive in
order to promote economic growth. On the other, it's wary of an overly
weak currency that would fuel inflation in the form of higher prices for
imported goods.



But with exports rising and economy growing at a healthy clip, there's
no particular need to weaken the Singapore currency. If anything,
analysts say, a mild upturn in inflation suggests that the authority
will allow the local dollar to strengthen.

christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com

title: ANALYSIS - Asia  FX intervention , old habits die hard.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currency markets are facing more intervention this year, with many governments unwilling to leave domestic currency values to the forces of supply and demand despite signs of solid economic recovery. 

Foreign exchange analysts say that in light of rising inflationary pressures such intervention may cause more problems than it resolves, and question whether in the long run it can be successful in stopping currency gains that reflect economic fundamentals. 

 Recent interventions by South Korea and Taiwan show the reluctance of some Asian governments to stay away from the forex markets, analysts say. 

 "They are likely to continue with their King Canute policy," said Marshall Gittler, head of the global currency risk group at Bank of America in Hong Kong, referring to a Viking king of old who thought he was powerful enough to hold back the tide. 

 OLD HABITS DIE HARD...IF THEY DIE AT ALL 

 The Bank of Korea jumped into the market on the first trading day of 2000 to rein in the won as it surged to its highest level in two years on the back of a strong tide of capital inflows. 

 It has been curbing the won's rise although most analysts believe the currency is undervalued. The latest Citibank forecast said the won should rise to 1,050 per dollar by the second quarter and 1,000 in the fourth. 

 Dealers are on a sustained won intervention vigil, especially after President Kim Dae-jung said in a New Year message that Korea's usable foreign reserves would rise to $100 billion by the end of 2000, around 35 percent up on their end-1999 level. 

 IT'S NOT JUST SOUTH KOREA 

 Elsewhere, the Central Bank of China, Taiwan's central bank, was also in the market last week to curb the local dollar's rise. 

 And there were rumours the central bank of Singapore, one of the region's most efficient economies, stepped in to stem the domestic currency's gains. 

 There was no official denial of intervention but Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was quoted as saying Singapore has never depended on a weak currency to stay competitive. 

 JAPAN LEADS INTERVENTION BINGE 

 The most glaring example of government intervention in Asia would of course be the Bank of Japan, which has intervened in currency markets some 14 times since June to check the rising yen. 

 The most recent intervention on January 4 - Japan's first trading day of the new year - took the dollar from around 101.46 yen to highs of around 103.17 yen. 

 The dollar has since strengthened to above 105 yen, taking some heat out of the yen's extended rise, at least for now. 

 Japanese finance officials issue almost daily warnings about the economic risks of an excessively strong yen, but analysts have increasingly begun to question their arguments - as well as their success rate. 

 Given that dollar/yen once rose above 160 in April 1990 and fell as low as 79.70 in May 1995, last year's 101-125 range looks fairly stable. 

 And if the strong yen merely reflects a higher assessment of Japan's economy, it should not be causing such concern. 

 Deutsche Bank argues Japanese macroeconomic variables have historically been strongest in years following a yen rise, which is in some ways equivalent to a tax cut. 

 "Japanese corporate profits are decidedly better when the yen is strong," the bank said in a report. 

 "Corporate profits on average rose by 11 percent during 

  years when the yen strengthened against the dollar...and fell 

  by five percent in years when the yen was weak," it said. 

INTERVENTION COULD WORK, BUT... 

 Analysts said Asian governments' desire to control their currency markets was not entirely unjustified, given that the aim was to stave off volatility and support the key exports sector. 

 But sometimes the line between effective and useless intervention could be very thin. Badly executed intervention can distort the market and raise false expectations. 

 "In theory, intervention does have some benefits. Currencies tend to overshoot and companies cannot handle such volatility," said Supavud Saicheua, head of economics and strategies at Merrill Lynch in Bangkok. 

 But he added that governments might not know where best to draw that line in the sand. 

 "Before the crisis, the Bank of Thailand thought the baht should be at 25 to the dollar and kept defending it at that level," he said. 

 "The result was disastrous." 

 SOMETHING HAS TO GIVE 

 The bottom line is that Asian governments cannot expect to have the best of all worlds: a strong economic recovery and subsequent capital inflows do not gel with a policy of keeping the currency soft and interest rates low. 

 To deliberately keep currencies weak to boost exports might not be a viable option at this juncture and may actually be unnecessary, given that much depends on global demand. 

 "Intervention can work short-term," said Chan Chia Lin, head of research at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore. 

 "It can give you the best of both worlds - weak currencies and low interest rates. But given the vigour of the recovery, it might not be viable," she said. 

 "Export demand is being driven more by the economic recovery and global demand rather than having competitive currencies."

title: Asian  Currencies  Stabilize; Market Retains Bullish Outlook
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies stabilized late Friday, after suffering sharp falls for two consecutive days, raising hopes that the sell-off that soured trading in the first week of the new year may have played itself out. 

 Although the Singapore dollar ended Asian dealing hours a touch lower, the Thai baht inched upward and the South Korean won and the Philippine peso closed appreciably higher. 

 "The dollar is close to topping out against a lot of the regional currencies. Even on a short term outlook, we're fairly bullish," said Steve Brice, a treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 Other analysts backed this view, saying the sell-off in Asian stock markets responsible for propelling the slide in regional currencies appeared close to an end. 

 "The short term jitters which originally caused the equity market correction have been sufficiently priced in," said Vincent Low, regional foreign exchange and interest rate strategist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore. 

 "Once equity markets are on a firmer footing, the turnaround story will continue and Asian currencies will resume strengthening," he concluded. 

 Some dealers fretted that even if regional stock prices do level out and recover over the coming week, renewed weakness in the Japanese yen ahead of next weekend's G8 summit meeting in Japan could drag Asian currencies lower. 

 Brice at Standard Chartered dismissed the fears, however. 

 "The time is long past that the yen's movements were a huge influence on regional market sentiment," he said. 

 Nevertheless, dealers suspected that with the yen heading lower, the Monetary Authority of Singapore would be prepared to covertly intervene in the market to suppress any Singapore dollar appreciation, maintaining the local currency's trade-weighted valuation. 

 "I don't think the authorities would be too happy to see the Singapore dollar strengthen," said one trader at a foreign bank in the city. "We are seeing strong (U.S. dollar) bids at S$1.6620 from local banks now. I don't think the (U.S.) dollar will go below S$1.6600. 

 Late in Asian dealing the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.6621, well below its earlier intraday high of S$1.6672, but still above S$1.6615 late Thursday. 

 Among other Asian currencies, the Thai baht edged a touch higher, with the U.S. dollar easing to THB37.3750 late in Asian trade from THB37.3950 the previous day. Traders said that solid offers at THB37.7000 should cap any dollar advances in the near term. 

 The South Korean won also closed higher after recovering from a sharp early fall that drove the currency to its lowest level in over a month. 

 An early rash of dollar-buying propelled the U.S. currency upward to touch an intraday high of KRW1,156.00, its highest since the first week of December. 

 The dollar soon fell back on profit-taking, however, after Minister of Finance Kang Bong-kyun reiterated the country's high growth and low inflation outlook for 2000 while reassuring markets that the Seoul government has no intention of raising interest rates in the foreseeable future. 

 By the close the dollar had dropped to KRW1,138.00, down from KRW1,146.50 the day before. 

 In other markets, the Philippine peso closed higher after as market volatility eased following the surprise resignation Wednesday of Finance Secretary Edgardo Espiritu. 

 Although uncertainties remained ahead of the appointment during the weekend of a new economic coordinating council, market participants took a broadly positive view of the naming of Trade Secretary Jose Pardo as Espiritu's replacement. 

 By the close, the dollar had fallen back to PHP40.330, from PHP40.550 at the end of Thursday's session. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed lower, but dealers attributed the fall to sustained U.S. dollar-buying by the local central bank rather than to negative investor sentiment. 

 Against the Taiwanese currency, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$30.860, up from NT$30.854 the previous day. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also ended the day down. With local markets in Jakarta closed Friday and Monday for the Eid al Fitr religious festival, offshore dealing was thin. Concerns over political developments in Indonesia supported the U.S. dollar, which ended Asian hours at IDR7,175, up from IDR7,165 late Thursday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Soggy as stocks slide.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Hefty losses on Asian stock 

 markets in the wake of Wall Street's slump dented regional 

currencies on Wednesday, with the recent star performers -- the 

 Korean won, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar -- among the worst hit. 

     Analysts said it was too early to view the declines on 

 Asian bourses as anything more than profit-taking after recent 

 heady gains, but investors were likely to keep a close eye on 

 movements on the Dow Jones index and the high-tech Nasdaq. 


    The yen	    was pressured in late Asian trade as



euro/yen reached new six-week highs amid growing bullishness



about the single European currency.



    The euro	    reached new seven-week highs after piercing



a strong barrier around $1.0340-50.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht was dragged off its recent six-month highs as



major European and U.S. names bought the dollar to settle



mismatched forward contracts.



    A near-six percent drop on the SETI and corporate dollar



demand also weighed on the baht, but dealers expected exporter



dollar offers to limit its downside to 37.30.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar was depressed alongside its regional



counterparts and on the back of a near-six percent drop on the



Straits Time share index.



    Dealers cited rumours that the local central bank had been



in the market on Tuesday, buying U.S. dollars around the 1.65



level to slow the Sing dollar's recent rise.



    A Monetary Authority of Singapore official declined comment



on the intervention rumours. The central bank traditionally



says it intervenes in the market to smooth sharp moves.



    Trade and Industry Minister George Yeo said recent



fluctuations in the Sing dollar were due to "normal



volatility".



    Dealers said the currency's upside could be limited for now



as players would remain wary of the MAS, but most expect it to



rise in the months ahead as inflation picks up in Singapore.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The won ran into a brick wall as the Kospi suffered its



biggest ever one-day drop, spurring offshore dollar buying and



short-covering by banks.



    Foreign investors sold a net 112.8 billion won worth of



stocks on Wednesday.



    Finance Minister Kang Bong-kyun said GDP growth this year



might exceed seven percent -- compared with a previous forecast



of five to six percent -- if external conditions improve.



    He also said the government would not expand money supply



ahead of the April general elections.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	


Central bank moves to temper a rapid rise in the Taiwan



dollar helped pull it around 0.5 percent lower despite the



local stock market's bravado in the face of losses elsewhere.



    The TAIEX	     was the only regional bourse to rack up



gains after Wall Street's falls overnight, in stark contrast to



declines of more than five percent in many key markets.



    Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was expected to



stop the currency firming above the T$30.00 per dollar level.



    Consumer price index data for the year to December came in



lower than expected, at 0.14 percent. Analysts surveyed in a



recent Reuters poll had forecast an average rise of 0.72



percent.



That put full-year inflation for 1999 at just 0.18 percent



- its lowest level since 1986 and far below forecasts made a



year ago.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso shed nearly one percent as the baht hovered around



the 37 per dollar level and as corporate demand for dollars



picked up.



    Traders in Manila said they expected the peso to remain



below 40 per dollar during the year.



    Inflation remained tame in December, with consumer prices



rising only 4.3 percent year-on-year.



    The monthly inflation rate for 1999 hit an average 6.6



percent, with the government saying the monthly rate should



average 6-7 percent in 2000.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    Jitters over the financial health of the country's central



bank, Bank Indonesia, lingered in what traders described as a



still thin market.



    The rupiah lost more than one and a half percent but was



still trading the right side of 7,200 per dollar.



    A recent audit into the bank suggested its financial



position was so problematic it might need to be recapitalised.



    Finance Minister Bambang Sudibyo has said the government



might issue bonds to recapitalise it and that it may sell some



of them overseas.

title: Singapore dlr fluctuations normal - trade minister.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Singapore's trade and industry minister George Yeo said on Wednesday recent fluctuations in the Singapore dollar were due to "normal volatility". 

 "It's just normal volatility," he said, declining further comment on the currency. Yeo was speaking to reporters at the sidelines of a conference in Singapore. 

Foreign exchange dealers had said there were rumours in the market that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had been intervening on Tuesday, buying the U.S. dollar around the S$1.65 level to slow the Singapore dollar's recent rise. 

 A MAS official on Tuesday declined comment on the intervention rumours. 

 The central bank traditionally says it intervenes in the market to smoothe sharp fluctuations. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar's upside could be limited now as players would remain wary of the central bank, but most expect it to appreciate in the months ahead as inflation picks up in Singapore. 

 At 0320 GMT, the Singapore unit was trading at S$1.6550/60 to the dollar.

title: Emerging  FX  - Lose lustre as stocks take a hit.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Sharp falls across key 

 regional stock markets took the shine off most Asian currencies


on Wednesday, with the recently high-flying baht	    taking



one of the heaviest hits.



    Heavy overnight losses on Wall Street knocked the wind out



of key Asian stock markets, but analysts reckoned it provided



an excuse to take profits after recent sharp gains and did not



represent a significant shift in sentiment.



    They said the appreciative trend in regional currencies


remained.



    A more than three percent fall in Japanese stocks also



played its part in pressuring the yen	   .



    Dealers in Tokyo said upside for dollar/yen was limited



though as solid bids by some Japanese investors were detected



below 103.



    New Zealand markets re-opened for their first day of trade



after their extended new year break.



    On the economic indicator front, Taiwan was due to release



closely watched December consumer price index (CPI) data at



0300 GMT while the Philippines published inflation data for



December 1999 at 0100 GMT.



THAI BAHT	



The baht slid as major European and U.S. names bought the



dollar to settle mismatched forward contracts.



    Importers were in the market to take advantage of the



baht's recent gains, dealers said.



    "The Dow's fall overnight will also ease the upward



pressure on the baht because funds might slow down investments



in the stock market for now while monitoring the situation,"



said a Singapore-based dealer.



    "And technically, the baht has been heavily overbought



lately. So, some selling is to be expected," he said.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar lost some ground in line with a heavy



drop on the Straits Time share index.



    Dealers cited rumours that the local central bank had been



in the market on Tuesday, buying U.S. dollars around the 1.65



level to slow the Sing dollar's recent rise.



    The Monetary Authority of Singapore does not comment on


interventions, but has said that it intervenes in the market to



smooth sharp moves.



    Dealers said the Sing dollar's upside could be limited for



now as players would remain wary of the MAS, but most expect it



to rise in the months ahead as inflation picks up in Singapore.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    A more than four percent fall in domestic stocks weighed on



the won, forcing it to open at around 1,125 per dollar.



    It had closed at 1,122 the previous day on the back of fat



gains in the KOSPI -- its highest levels in almost two years.



    Dealers in Singapore said they expected it to trade in a



1,120-1,130 range for the rest of the day partly due to the



sell-off in stocks.



    But they said the bullish mood in equities remained intact



and the KOSPI's drop was being driven by profit-taking, as with



the rest of the region.



     TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar bucked the regional uptrend and held on



to its firmer tone.



    It was bid at around 30.50 per dollar early, above its



close of T$30.6 the previous day and way above its recent



string of 25-month highs around the T$31.39 level.



    Singapore dealers said fundamentals remained strong for



Taiwan and that an overnight glitch on Wall Street would not



have any lasting impact.



    One dealer with a European bank said it was seen heading



towards 30.00 per dollar near-term but that the central bank


would probably enter the market to slow its rise at around the



30.20 mark.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso lost ground in line with other regional


currencies and especially the baht, which it tends to track as



both markets compete in similar export markets.



But it was still the right side of 40 per dollar after



closing at a 17-week high of 39.77 on the back of capital



inflows from foreign funds the previous day.



Dealers said dollar/peso was likely to firm further if



dollar/baht headed back towards the 38 per dollar level and



that it would also take its cue from the mood in stocks.



CPI rose 4.3 percent in the year to December 1999 against



an annual 3.9 percent rise in November. Economists polled by



Reuters had expected the figure to come in at 4.35 percent.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



The rupiah lost around two percent in thin early trade as



players continued to monitor the financial health of Bank



Indonesia, the country's central bank.



    A critical state audit of the bank last week suggested its



finances were so problematic it might need to be recapitalised.



    All eyes were on domestic stocks after they hit six-month



highs the previous day, with players waiting to see the



reaction to Wall Street's falls.

title: Singapore Dollar Weaker Late On Stock Market Sell-Off
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar is weaker against the U.S. dollar late Wednesday following a hefty drop in stock prices, dealers say. 

 At about 0850 GMT (3:50 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6567, up from S$1.6535 late Tuesday. 

 The Straits Times Industrial Index plummeted more than 5.5% Wednesday, taking its lead from a 3.2% decline in the Dow Jones Industrial Average the previous day. 

 The equity market sell-off reversed the Singapore dollar's strong upward trend, which saw it hit an intraday high of S$1.6465 against the U.S. dollar Tuesday. 

 But dealers say the local currency's reversal is temporary since the stock market correction has run it's course and heavy capital flows are seen entering Asia in the new year. 

 An analyst at a U.K. bank said strong economic fundamentals as well as renewed stock market strength will put upward pressure on the Singapore dollar in the near term. 

 He said, however, that fears of a U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore will support the U.S. dollar at S$1.6500. 

 This week, he said the U.S. dollar will trade between S$1.6500 and S$1.6600. 

 In the local currency money market, the overnight rate was offered at 0.125%, down from 0.250% late Tuesday, while the three-month rate was offered unchanged at 2.4375%.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mood bullish, Taiwan dlr jumps.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 4 (Reuters) - The mood was bullish for Asian 

 regional currencies on Tuesday as some domestic markets 

 re-opened for their first day of trade this year. 

     Dealers in Singapore said the focus was on regional stock 

 markets after key indices that had resumed trade the previous 

 day hit record highs. 


    The Taiwan dollar	    jumped more than one percent as



foreign funds soaked up stocks on that market's first trading



day.



    Financial markets also re-opened in Japan, South Korea, and



Thailand, with Indonesian stocks also resuming activity.



    Only New Zealand's markets were still closed and were set



to re-start on Wednesday.



    The yen	    was steady despite wariness of possible Bank



of Japan yen-selling intervention. Dealers in Tokyo said fund



repatriation by local banks, now that Y2K had been a non-event,



could lend it support.



The Philippines expected November export numbers at 0100



GMT while Thailand was slated to release consumer price and



wholesale price data at 0400 GMT.



TAIWAN DOLLAR	



Fresh momentum in domestic stocks helped push the Taiwan



dollar above T$31 per dollar during its first day of domestic



trade after the new year break, representing new 25-month



highs.



But dealers in Singapore said they were aware of the


central bank's interventionist hand anywhere above the T$31



level for the local unit.



    Traders in Taipei said the Taiwan dollar had also drawn



inspiration from bullishness in the yen.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    Speculative offshore dollar sales pushed the won above its



1999 high of 1,125.0, sparking moves by the monetary



authorities to temper its rise.



    A central bank official said the authorities had entered



the local market to buy dollars.



    Traders in Singapore said the won's direction would depend



on the appetite for domestic stocks -- Asia's top performer in



1999 -- as trade got underway.



    One analyst from a European bank said the Bank of Korea was



likely to condone a stronger won as the year progressed,


intervening less frequently in order to keep inflation at bay.



    THAI BAHT	



    The Thai baht shed some of Monday's steep gains, which were



driven by offshore players unwinding long dollar positions



after a smooth crossover to the new year.



    Dealers said the baht should appreciate in the medium-term.



But some consolidation was expected this week as the dollar was



already deep in oversold territory with a reading of 13.65 on



the 14-day relative strength index (RSI).



The onshore market resumed activity on Tuesday and players



were awaiting the release of consumer and wholesale price data



at 0400 GMT.



The market will also watch closely the Bank of Thailand's



plan to revamp its monetary policy. The central bank recently



submitted a draft to the Ministry of Finance.



The draft seeks greater independence in pursuing an



inflation-targetted monetary policy. It is expected to



publicise details of the plan on January 20-21.



    It will take months for the draft to be passed into law.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    Capital inflows into the stock market jolted the Singapore



dollar higher against the U.S. dollar.



    Some analysts expected the blue-chip Straits Times Index



   to head toward 2,700 by late January from around 2,500



now.



    Dealers said although the currency could rise to the



1.50-1.60 level by the end of this year, the government is



likely to be cautious and unwilling to allow to rapid an



appreciation.



PHILIPPINE PESO (PHP=)



The peso edged up against the dollar as players continued



to unwind long dollar positions they kept from late last year



due to concerns over potential millennium computer glitches.



    Sentiment was also boosted by robust trade data released by



the National Statistics Office (NSO) on Tuesday.



    Philippine exports in November reached $3.073 billion, up



18.8 percent from a year ago. In January-November, exports



reached $32.089 billion, up 19 percent from $26.973 billion in



the same period in 1998.



But dealers reckoned any rise in the peso would be gradual



as foreign funds were likely to concentrate on big stock



markets such as those in Singapore, Hong Kong and South Korea



first.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



The rupiah was a shade weaker, with Singapore dealers



saying trade was thin as investors continued to monitor



political and economic developments in Indonesia in the new



year.



    Concerns about the precarious financial situation of



Indonesia's central bank weighed on the currency.



    Several analysts were upbeat on the rupiah's prospects on



the basis that it has been undervalued and that economic growth



this year should underpin its firmer tone.



    One analyst from a U.S. bank said dollar/rupiah was likely



to trade between 6,850 and 7,300 in the next couple of weeks



and slip to around 6,500 later in the year.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late But Off Highs On Suspected MAS Move
text:

title: Malaysia PM: Govt May Take Over Clob Shares If Necessary
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said Thursday the government will take over the frozen Malaysian shares which once traded in Singapore, if the issue is not resolved. 

 "If necessary, we'll take over the shares," Mahathir said, adding that the government may also extend the nominee status given to Singapore's Central Depository Pte Ltd. 

 "If the Ministry of Finance takes over the Clob shares, the shares will still be owned by the investors," Mahathir said. 

 "We will have to redeem or compensate them for the shares," he added. 

 The Malaysian shares, estimated to be worth about 17 billion ringgit ($1=MYR3.80), were previously traded over the counter on Singapore's Central Limit Order Book, or CLOB, system, until Malaysia banned trading in these stocks as part of the capital controls it imposed in September 1998. 

 But Mahathir added that the decision to extend the deadline depends on the Ministry of Finance. 

 He said that Clob shareholders "should be happy" to accept the many "reasonable offers", while blaming Clob shareholders for battering the Kuala Lumpur stock market during the financial crisis. 

 Last week, a newly registered Singapore company, Collective Custodial Services, proposed taking custody of the Clob shares and then selling them over a 12-month period on the KLSE. The company will charge a 2% fee, the reports said. 

 It is the first such proposal from a Singapore company to end the deadlock. 

 Other proposals from Malaysian parties have involved selling the shares to them at heavily discounted prices. 

 Mahathir added that the Clob shareholders "have been dilly-dallying". 

 "I think that is not right," Mahathir said, adding that the Clob shares have appreciated by about 200% since September 1998. 

 Mahathir declined to comment on the remarks Tuesday by the Monetary Authority of Singapore that it hopes the Malaysian government won't intervene in the fate of the Clob shares. 

 Mahathir said the Malaysian stock market should continue to rise next year as the business climate is favorable and companies are doing well. 

 As such, he said the key stock index may hit 1000 points as early as next year. 

 Wednesday, the benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index closed at 804.74 points. 

 Mahathir also said the Malaysian economy is expected to grow more than 4.0% this year. 

 In October, the government raised the 1999 official GDP forecast to 4.3% from 1.0% earlier. 

 "Next year should be better," Mahathir said, adding the economy has been insulated from short-term capital flows with the capital control measures in place. 

 "Currency traders can no longer fiddle around with the currency," he said. 

 When Malaysia imposed capital controls in September 1998, it prohibited offshore trading of ringgit, effectively pegging the Malaysian currency at MYR3.80 to the dollar. 

 The policy was crafted to allow Malaysia's economic planners to pump more liquidity into the recession-hit economy without undermining the stability of the currency. 


The ringgit can now only be exchanged on the current account for
trade-related purposes.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lifted By Investor Buying In Thin Mkts
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies strengthened Thursday, lifted by moderate capital inflows in conditions of thin market liquidity. 

 The Singapore dollar, however, ended Asian trading hours lower after customers bought U.S. dollars to hedge their currency exposure ahead of the year's end. 

 Government threats of intervention to slow the won's rise and aggressive dollar-buying by state-owned banks once again failed to damp buoyant market sentiment toward the South Korean currency. 

 Despite a warning from the Finance and Economy Ministry saying it's prepared to act to check the won's appreciation, along with sizable dollar purchases executed by the Korea Development Bank and the Korea Exchange Bank, investors chose rather to focus on the positive news to emerge from Seoul. 

 Boosting won sentiment, the Korea Development Institute said it expects GDP to expand by 13% year-on-year in the fourth quarter bringing the growth rate for 1999 as a whole to 10.1%. 

 For 2000, the KDI raised its forecast economic growth rate to a robust 7.8%, from 5.8% previously. 

 The institute also predicted that the inflation rate will rise to 3.2% next year from 0.8% this year, reinforcing market beliefs that the authorities will allow the won to appreciate in order to damp inflationary pressure, in preference to raising interest rates. 

 Won bulls were further encouraged by news that foreign direct investment has hit a record $15.2 billion so far this year, while the completion of the sale of Korea First Bank to U.S. investors, although not expected directly to affect the exchange rate, was also seen as a positive sign. 

 By the close of local trading, selling pressure had pushed the dollar down to KRW1,130.70 from KRW1,131.50 the previous day, despite the South Korean government's efforts to support the U.S. currency. 

 Investor buying also lifted the New Taiwan dollar on Thursday, as offshore portfolio managers chased Taiwanese technology stocks following the rise of the U.S. Nasdaq Composite stock index to yet another record high. 

 An surge of selling hammered the U.S. dollar early in the session, prompting the central bank to enter the market to buy dollars in order to support the U.S. currency. 

 Even so, the U.S. dollar still finished sharply lower, ending at NT$31.626, down from NT$31.662 at Wednesday's close. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Philippine peso rose strongly lifted by year-end remittances from expatriate Filipinos and confirmation that the Development Bank of Singapore has acquired a $700 million stake in Bank of the Philippine Islands. 

 By the close of trading in Manila, the dollar had slumped to PHP40.190, from PHP40.405 the previous day. 

 The Thai baht also strengthened, with the dollar slipping to THB37.42 late in Asian hours, down from THB37.53 late on Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar, however, ended weaker after dropping sharply in afternoon trading. 

 The abruptness of the fall, which saw the U.S. dollar rise to S$1.6700 from levels around S$1.6650 within a matter of minutes prompted speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore was intervening in the market through domestic banks to weaken the local currency. 

 The idea was dismissed by one Singapore bank trader, who attributed the local currency's sudden dip to commercial hedging ahead of the year's end. 

 "Around S$1.66 is a good level to hedge," he said, adding that market illiquidity had exaggerated the extent of the move. "It only takes $50 million to move the market at the moment," he explained. 

 Toward the end of Asian dealing, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.6695, up from S$1.6660 late the day before. 

 The rupiah ended Asian hours almost untraded. Late in Asia the dollar was quoted against the Indonesian currency at IDR7,080 compared with IDR7,095 the previous session.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed But Market Retains Bullish Outlook
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies had a mixed day Friday, but most market players reaffirmed their bullish view of regional markets. 

 In North Asia the South Korean won closed just fractionally higher despite actual and verbal intervention by local authorities. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Singapore dollar nudged upward on portfolio inflows, extending gains made over the previous two days. 

 The Thai baht, however, closed marginally lower as profit-taking pared its recent gains. 

 The Indonesian rupiah closed flat, while the Philippine peso and the New Taiwan dollar both lost ground. 

 In Seoul, the Finance and Economy Ministry issued what is fast-becoming its customary early morning threat to act to suppress an appreciating won. 

 "The government stance that won's rise is never desirable to the country's economic recovery is unchanged," the ministry said in a statement. "The government will take proper measures anytime." 

 But other news Friday from South Korea only served to reinforce the market's impression that ultimately the authorities are fighting a losing battle in their attempts to check the won's rise. 

 Data released Friday showed that South Korean corporate bankruptcies fell in November to their lowest level since June 1991. 

 Meanwhile, government officials confirmed that the country currently has no need to draw on further funds available under the International Monetary Fund's 1997 rescue package. 

 "South Korea is seeing a lot of flows coming in, but the market remains wary of intervention. Personally I don't see a rapid (dollar) move to KRW1,100 in the near term," said Syetarn Hansakul, regional treasury economist at West LB in Singapore, forecasting that the U.S. currency will remain locked in a KRW1,125 to KRW1,135 range until the year's end. 

 At Friday's close the dollar was at KRW1,130.30, down slightly from KRW1,131.30 Thursday, with light purchases from state-run banks early in the session. 

 In Southeast Asia the Singapore dollar strengthened on portfolio inflows to the local stock market, a trend that is likely to accelerate in 2000, according to Thio Chin Loo, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas in the island republic. 

 Traders and investors have long remained wary of buying into the Singapore dollar too aggressively, lest they trigger intervention from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which has been keen to guard the currency's competitiveness. 

 But with economic growth rates robust and the global electronics cycle swinging upward, the authority's stance may change in 2000, argued Thio. 

 "The MAS is very likely to tolerate a stronger Singapore dollar in the New Year," she said. 

 Late Friday in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted against the Singapore currency at S$1.6725, down from S$1.6775 the previous day. 

 Profit-taking saw the Thai baht ease from the four-month high set late Thursday, but dealers reported continued interest to buy the currency from smart money investors attempting to front-run January's anticipated portfolio inflows.

title: Asian  Currencies  End Mostly Down; Rush To Buy Dollars
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies dropped steeply during local trading hours Monday as dollar-supportive intervention by the Bank of Japan triggered an end-of-the-month rush to acquire the U.S. currency. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and the Thai baht both finished Asian dealing down compared with levels seen Friday, as dollar-buying by local corporations in Bangkok and Jakarta dominated trade. 

 Dollar-buying also weighed on the Philippine peso, while the sharpness of the Singapore dollar's decline led dealers to believe that the Monetary Authority of Singapore was intervening against the local currency. 

 The South Korean won, however, held its own, strengthening against the U.S. dollar as the country's strong economic performance continued to attract heavy inflows of foreign investment funds into the Seoul stock market. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also edged higher. 

 The Bank of Japan's action Monday to support the dollar and arrest the yen's appreciation sparked an early round of dollar-buying against the Southeast Asian currencies. 

 Heavy bids were seen from customers in Bangkok and Jakarta as regional corporations hastened to acquire dollars lest the U.S. currency appreciate further before their debt service obligations fall due at the end of the month. 

 Fearing a liquidity crunch ahead of the New Year, customers also bought dollars to meet December's debt payments, exaggerating the decline in the regional currencies, traders said. 

 "Local corporations are buying in a last ditch attempt to get dollars before the month's end," said a dealer at one U.S. bank in Singapore. "And they are buying for December too. Demand is extra big this month." 

 Toward the end of Asian trading hours the dollar had been pushed higher to trade against the baht at THB39.0350, up steeply from THB38.7650 late on Friday. 

 Against the rupiah the U.S. currency had risen to IDR7,320, up from IDR7,200 Friday as fears of trouble in the restive provinces of Aceh and Irian Jaya further fueled demand. 

 Against the Philippine peso, the dollar rose to close at PHP40.935, up from PHP40.835 at the end of Friday's session, despite a rise in government debt yields at the weekly auction. 

 The weight of bids to buy the U.S, dollar against the Singapore dollar forced some market participants to conclude that the Monetary Authority of Singapore was covertly intervening in the market, acting through local and locally-active foreign banks to push the Singapore currency lower. 

 Dealers suggested that the MAS was keen to emphasize its grip on the local currency's exchange rate after it relaxed Friday a number of restrictions governing foreign banks' access to the fledgling Singapore dollar debt market. 

 "The authorities have bought a lot" of U.S. dollars, said one trader. "They want to make it clear that the new regulations are not meant to internationalize the local currency." 

 The MAS has repeatedly bought U.S. dollars over recent months in order to block any unwelcome appreciation of the Singapore dollar, which may threaten the competitiveness of the island republic's exports. 

 Late in Asian trading Monday, the U.S. dollar was being quoted at S$1.6765, up from S$1.6710 Friday. So heavy was the buying Monday that one dealer at a Japanese bank in Singapore suggested the U.S. dollar was likely to be pushed to a six-week high above S$1.6800 in the near term. 

 The South Korean won strengthened as Korean asset markets continued to attract heavy fund inflows of around $50 million a day from foreign investors. 

 Won bulls were further encouraged by comments made over the weekend by the country's trade minister, Han Duck-soo, who said the won's strength hasn't damaged South Korean export competitiveness. 

 Some observers interpreted the remark as a sign that Seoul's hard line on won appreciation may be softening.

text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Dollar buying by the Korean 


authorities tempered the won's	    recent bull run on


 Friday, while the Singapore government's moves to tweak 

 restrictions on the local currency failed to have any immediate 

 impact. 

     Elsewhere, currencies held on to their easier bias partly

yen	    looked set to revisit recent highs amid growing



bullishness about Japan.



    The euro grabbed the limelight, falling to all time lows



against the yen		 and hovering near 4-month lows



against the dollar below $1.0150.



    Traders in Tokyo said the already bearish euro had suffered



after European Central Bank board member Eugenio Domingo Solans



said the bank had no intention of intervening.



    SOUTH KOREAN WON	



    Dollar buying by the monetary authorities and expectations



they would curb any won rise kept dollar/won in a tight range



despite won purchases by foreign stock funds.



    The market was kept on tenter-hooks from early on, after



the government expressed "deep concern" over the won's strength



and said it was ready to take action.



    But Seoul traders said the dollar was unlikely to hold onto



its gains due to more expectations for foreign stock purchases,



dollar sales by offshore players and month-end export deals.



    Traders saw a 1,152-1,162 range for Monday.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    Disappointment over a sharp sell-off in stocks weighed on



the Taiwan dollar after institutional investors turned net



sellers in the TAIEX	   on jitters over relations with



China.



But last minute central bank intervention cushioned the



Taiwan dollar's fall, showing players the authorities were



staying true to their pledge to defend the exchange rate at any



sign of trouble.



Unsubstantiated rumours of Chinese military deployment off



Taiwan sent already bearish stocks reeling to a close of



7,595.44, down nearly four percent.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



Plans unveiled by the government to liberalise the use of



the Sing dollar to bolster local capital markets had no



discernible impact on the currency, with analysts saying the



move would only have longer-term results.



The government announced a relaxation of rules governing



foreigners' use of the Sing dollar for bond, equity, interest



rate and repurchase agreement transactions.



Analysts said the moves fell short of internationalising



the currency, partly because no move had been made to ease



existing limits on Sing dollar swap trade.



"In the long-term, (the policies) could create more demand



for the currency. But it's not a key issue determining the Sing



dollar right now," said Anand Aithal, regional strategist at



Goldman Sachs in Singapore.



THAI BAHT	



The baht slipped on corporate dollar demand as debtors were



spooked by the yen's bullish trend and rushed to repay debt on



fears it could rise further.



    The baht's fall was somewhat amplified by thin volume,



dealers said.



    The Bank of Thailand said on Friday it planned to peg



monetary policy to inflation targets and thereby stabilise the



baht and manage the economy.



    Under the new system, the central bank would set an



inflation target for two years.



    A national monetary policy comprising central bankers and



independent experts would then change interest rates to keep



inflation within the target.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso drooped as market participants continued to cover



short dollar positions.



    The currency took third quarter growth figures in its



stride as they were mostly in line with the market



expectations.     June-September GDP growth came in at 3.1



percent year-on-year versus 3.6 percent in the second quarter.



    On the ballooning fiscal deficit, a concern among



investors, Socio-economic Planning Secretary Felipe Medalla



said the government must adopt a tighter fiscal policy next



year.



Medalla said the government should keep the deficit below



62.5 billion pesos next year as the gap this year could be as



high as 90 billion pesos.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



Persistent demand for dollars ahead of year-end pushed the



rupiah to around 7,200, with dealers expecting pressure to



remain due to Y2K worries and political uncertainties.



They said the market's focus was still on separatist



pressure in the province of Aceh, with some analysts fearful of



possible disintegration in Indonesia if the country breaks



free.



    The government has decided not to impose martial law and to



try and resolve differences through dialogue.



    HONG KONG DOLLAR	



    The government released GDP data showing the economy grew



4.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, well above



market forecasts of two to four percent growth.



    It also revised its 1999 growth forecast to 1.8 percent



from 0.5 percent previously.

title: DATA VIEW: Singapore GDP Growth May Bolster  Currency
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Singapore's economic growth maintained its brisk annual pace of 6.7% in the third quarter, prompting some economists to predict the central bank will allow the currency to strengthen. 

 GDP growth was unchanged from the second quarter and slightly below the 6.9% average forecast of economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires. But it was strong enough to prompt the government to raise its full-year 1999 growth forecast to the top end of its 4% to 5% range. 

 The Singapore dollar gained slightly on the news. At 0152 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6670, down from S$1.6697. Share prices, which generally look to Wall Street for direction, opened lower in response to worries that U.S. inflation could rise on higher oil prices, but have bounced back. 

 The benchmark Straits Times Index is up 10.95 points at 2239.81. 

 Simon Flint, currency strategist at Bank of America in Hong Kong, said strong growth coupled with a slight increase in inflation will prompt the Monetary Authority of Singapore to allow the Singapore dollar to strengthen. 

 The consumer price index rose at an annual rate of 0.9% in the third quarter, up from just 0.1% in the second quarter. 

 In the past year, the MAS has tried to nurture economic recovery by intervening in the currency market to keep the Singapore dollar from rising to a level that would hurt exports. 

 The central bank conducts monetary policy in Singapore by guiding the exchange rate rather than interest rates. A stronger currency would make imported products cheaper, putting downward pressure on inflation. 

 "As growth is restored you'll see a tightening of monetary policy and hence an appreciation of the Singapore dollar," Flint said. 

 Rising oil prices will push up the inflation rate next year, Ho Meng Kit, the deputy secretary of the Ministry of Trade and Industry, said Thursday. 

 Singapore likely will see inflation between 1% and 2% next year, up from a forecast inflation rate of 0.5% in 1999, Ho said. 

 Manufacturing output continued to lead economic growth, rising by 16.7% in the third quarter, compared with a gain of 14.5% in the second quarter. 

 Electronics sector output jumped by 26%, driven largely by exports of telecommunications equipment and semiconductors, the ministry said. But the disk drive segment continued to languish as major producers moved operations to lower-cost countries. 

 Analysts say lagging disk-drive exports are being replaced by rising shipments of specialty chemicals and pharmaceuticals. 

 The construction industry remained weak, with output falling by 15.6%, an even steeper decline than the 13.3% drop in the second quarter. Contracts awarded in the third quarter, an indicator of future activity, fell by 44%. 

 Economists and policymakers said the overall outlook for Singapore's economy remains good as growth stays steady or accelerates in its major export markets - the U.S., Japan and the European Union. 

 Friedrich Wu, chief economist at the Development Bank of Singapore, said manufacturing investments, an indicator of future activity, rose by 22% in the third quarter. 

 He predicted growth this year would exceed the government's 5% forecast and would come close to the top of the 4.5% to 6.5% range that the government expects in 2000.

title: Asian  Currencies : Won Soars To 4-Mo High; Rupiah Tumbles
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Soaring market sentiment drove the South Korean won to its highest level in over four months Thursday, prompting central bank intervention to suppress the currency's rise. 

 Asia's other regional currencies fared less well, as market concerns over Aceh's calls for independence plunged the rupiah to its lowest level since Indonesia's presidential elections three weeks ago. 

 The nervousness spilt over to affect other South East Asian markets, dragging the Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Philippine peso lower. 

 Sentiment toward South Korea, already riding high after a long-expected liquidity crisis failed to materialize, was further boosted Thursday when ratings agency Standard & Poor's Corp. upgraded the country's sovereign ratings, citing the strength of its economic recovery. 

 The upgrade triggered heavy buying of the local currency, which briefly pushed the dollar to a four-month low of 1,169.70 won before the Bank of Korea stepped into the market to buy dollars in a rare direct intervention. 

 "Continued strong portfolio capital inflows from abroad and a good supply of dollars to the market from local exporters have led to intense appreciative pressure on the won in the last few days," explained David Simmonds, Asian currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore. 

 "Not surprisingly, we have seen official intervention at these levels," added Simmonds. "Government sensitivity to the role of the export sector as the key driver of economic growth is still strong." 

 By the end of trading in Seoul, the central bank's intervention had lifted the dollar from its earlier lows. But closing at KRW1,173.10, the U.S. currency remained well below Wednesday's close of KRW1,180.00. 

 Although the South Korean authorities won't attempt to reverse the won's appreciation over the long term, further intervention to slow the pace of the currency's rise is probable in the near future, warned Simmonds at Citibank. 

 With the market already heavily long in the won, and investment inflows unlikely to continue at their current pace, the Korean currency's advance is set to be erratic, he said. 

 Investment inflows and exporters' sales of U.S. dollars also lifted the New Taiwan dollar Thursday. At the close of dealing in Taipei, the U.S. currency was quoted at NT$31.745, down from NT$31.754 the previous day. 

 In Southeast Asia, the market's growing concern that calls for independence by the North Sumatran province of Aceh could evolve into a fresh Indonesian crisis triggered heavy buying of dollars against the rupiah. 

 Market participants who went long in the rupiah at the time of Indonesia's presidential elections three weeks ago anticipating a major post-election rally were seen buying dollars to cover their positions. 

 In conditions of thin market liquidity, the buying rapidly pushed the dollar above the 7,000 rupiah mark to reach IDR7,150 late in Asian trading, up over IDR250 compared with IDR6,897 late the previous day. 

 The rupiah's fall soured sentiment toward other currencies in the region, dragging the Thai baht, the Singapore dollar and the Philippine peso all lower. 

 Dealers also cited Thailand's political backdrop as a reason to sell the baht, saying an opposition no-confidence motion tabled for next month was deterring foreign investment in the country. 

 Late in Asian trading, the dollar had risen to 39.0450 baht, up from THB38.9600 the day before. 

 The Singapore dollar also slipped in line with the regional trend, with some traders suggesting that market participants caught long in the rupiah were attempting to hedge their exposure by selling the Singapore dollar short. 

 Toward the end of Asian interbank dealing, the U.S. currency was quoted against the Singapore dollar at S$1.6763, up from S$1.6723 the previous day. 

 The Philippine peso also closed down, with the U.S. dollar rising to end trading in Manila at 40.323 pesos, up from PHP40.270 at Wednesday's close.

title: Asian  Currencies  Open Higher As Rupiah Rally Continues
text:

 With the rupiah enjoying a honeymoon period among foreign exchange traders and international investors, many market players are predicting the currency will make further gains over the short term, with the U.S. dollar falling as low as 6,500 rupiah.
