title: Asian  Currencies  Give Up Early Gains To End Mixed Vs Dlr
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Early gains in Asian currencies were whittled away late in regional trading hours to leave regional markets mixed on Monday. 

 The Thai baht, the Singapore dollar, and the Indonesian rupiah all advanced strongly in early trading, only to succumb to profit-taking later in the day. The Philippine peso also slipped in late trading to end the session lower. 

 In North Asia the Korean won strengthened modestly, while the New Taiwan dollar ended unchanged. 

 The dollar's fall against the yen and the euro, impelled by Friday's fall in U.S. equity prices, was the chief reason cited for the U.S. currency's early decline against Asian regional currencies. 

 "The dollar's bias is to the downside across the board," said Thio Chin Loo, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore, as the U.S. currency softened during morning trading. 

 Nevertheless, the market hesitated to sell the U.S. currency down too aggressively, leading some traders to conclude that any further dollar losses would be limited. 

 "Regional markets have been led by the baht, but the (dollar against the) baht is looking oversold now," said one trader at a European bank in Singapore. 

 In early Asian trading the U.S. currency was sold down to test an intraday low against the baht of THB39.0800 before rebounding as traders bought dollars back again to take profits from their short positions. 

 Towards the end of Asian interbank dealing, the buying had pushed the dollar as high as THB39.3300, higher than THB39.2600 late Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar also fell against the Singapore dollar during the Asian morning, although the fear of provoking dollar-supportive intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore deterred traders from pushing the U.S. currency below an intraday low around S$1.6720. 

 With the U.S. currency seen as well supported above S$1.6700, position liquidation lifted the U.S. dollar in afternoon trading, to leave the currency pair quoted at S$1.6754 late in Asian hours, down from S$1.6777 late Friday. 

 Trading in the peso followed a similar pattern, with the U.S. currency opening down, only to recover to end the session higher, at PHP40.440, up from PHP40.330 at Friday's close. 

 The rupiah, however, managed to hold onto most of the ground it gained, although it failed to extend the advances made in early trading. 

 Dealers in Jakarta and Singapore reported interest to buy the local currency coming from offshore players seeking to establish long-rupiah positions in expectation of an extended rally should opposition leader Megawati Sukarnoputri capture the presidency in Wednesday's elections. 

 The rupiah's gains were limited, however, by firm dollar-buying interest which supported the dollar at the IDR7,800 level. 

 Late in Asia the dollar had recovered from its earlier low to trade at IDR7,865, down from IDR8,050 Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Strengthen; Rupiah Flat Despite Unrest
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies strengthened robustly against the U.S. dollar during local trading hours on Friday, despite lingering fears that worsening unrest in Indonesia could generate increasing regional contagion. 

 The rupiah itself closed local trading flat compared to levels seen late Thursday, having rallied strongly from its earlier intraday low. 

 Market attention throughout Asia remains closely focused on the political process in Jakarta ahead of Indonesia's presidential election next Wednesday. 

 Early dealings on Friday saw the rupiah sold down steeply on fears of violent protests following President Habibie's so-called "accountability speech" late Thursday. 

 But, as on Thursday, the Indonesian currency's fall was arrested by rupiah purchases executed by a handful of European banks acting in both Singapore and Jakarta. 

 Traders in both centers said the banks were positioning themselves long in the rupiah in anticipation that an election victory for opposition leader Megawati Sukarnoputri would trigger a sharp rally in the rupiah toward the end of next week. 

 The rupiah-buying drove the dollar off its early high of IDR8,200, back down to IDR8,050 before trading in Jakarta ground to a halt as many dealers left the city center early, anxious to avoid running foul of street demonstrations protesting against Habibie's candidacy. Late Thursday in Asia, the dollar had also been quoted at IDR8,050. 

 In other regional markets, the Thai baht gained more ground on the U.S. dollar as a liquidity squeeze in the offshore market forced a number of players to buy baht in order to cover short forward positions. 

 Offshore baht liquidity has been hard to come by since last week when the Bank of Thailand tightened restrictions governing nonresidents' access to baht funding. 

 Friday saw offshore tomorrow/next forward rates rise to a premium of 0.15 sen over the spot rate according to one Singapore dealer, in stark contrast to the discount of 0.02 sen quoted in the onshore market. 

 The baht's rise was reinforced by an inflow of foreign funds associated with Friday's recapitalization of Thai Farmers Bank, which is expected to have raised up to $300 million from offshore investors. 

 By late in Asian trading, the U.S. dollar had slipped to THB39.26, down from THB39.42 the day before. 

 The U.S. currency also eased against the Singapore dollar, although fears of Monetary Authority of Singapore intervention to block excessive local currency appreciation supported the U.S. dollar above S$1.6750. 

 Late in local trading hours, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6777, down from S$1.6805 late Thursday. 

 The Philippine peso closed flat, with the U.S. dollar ending domestic trading in Manila unchanged from Thursday at PHP40.330. 

 The South Korean won closed higher, aided by Friday's rise in the yen and boosted by a late rush of pre-weekend position squaring, despite dollar purchases executed by state-run banks. 

 At the Seoul close, the U.S. dollar was trading at KRW1,206.00, down from KRW1,208.50 at the end of Thursday's session. 

 Active central bank participation in the Taipei foreign exchange market helped to hold the new Taiwan dollar within a narrow trading range. 

 At the close of trading Friday, the U.S. currency was at NT$31.769, down fractionally from NT$31.771 the previous day.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Asia up, Colombia set to drop.
text:
LONDON, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies firmed on Monday as players sold dollars after taking a closer look at comments on the yen from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial powers. 

 Colombia's newly floated peso was expected to tumble on the first trading day after the scrapping of its old currency band, while the surging world gold price helped lift the South African rand sharply higher. 

 A weekend G7 statement expressed concern over the potential impact of the strong yen on the global economy, and triggered rumours the Bank of Japan might agree to ease credit in return for international cooperation to halt its currency's climb. 

 The dollar reached a day's high of 106 yen on that view, but on closer scrutiny players decided the G7 statement contained little concrete sign of action on the yen and the dollar slipped back to around 104. 

 "There was no agreement on coordinated intervention or policy change," said Callum Henderson, currency strategist at Citibank in London. 

 "Reassessment of that statement caused dollar/yen to fall and that provided a perfect excuse for profit-taking on long dollar positions in a number of exchange rates." 

 The volatile Indonesian rupiah showed the sharpest move against the greenback, strengthening past 8,400 in thin trade after grazing 8,900 late last week during clashes between students and security forces. 

 Jakarta was quiet after President Habibie delayed signing the controversial new security law that sparked the riots. But analysts said the calm was unlikely to last as student groups have vowed to continue their protest until the law is scrapped. 

 They said the rupiah's stronger tone owed more to last week's tough parliamentary report saying seven top officials, including the central bank governor and the finance minister, should face swift legal action over the Bank Bali scandal. 

 The Thai baht, which has led regional currency weakness over the past couple of weeks, firmed back through the key barrier of 41 to the dollar, helped by rumours in Singapore that the Bank of Thailand intervened in the forward market late last week. 

 But analysts saw further medium-term weakness as a heavy burden of non-performing loans continued to weigh on the Thai banking sector and players nervous of the millennium bug became increasingly wary of emerging Asian assets. 

 "Medium-term technicals point to 43.50 in perhaps a six-month frame," Henderson at Citibank said. 

 The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso were also significantly firmer. 

 COLOMBIA PESO'S SLIDE SEEN LIMITED 

 Colombia's peso was expected to slip when American markets opened later on Monday, after the central bank scrapped its trading band and crawling peg system on Saturday. 

 But most analysts said the slide should be limited as the currency was not drastically overvalued, and was likely to bounce back towards current levels later in the week. 

 The peso closed on Friday at 1,994.49 to the dollar, and most analysts saw it tumbling on Monday to between 2,000 and 2,200. 

 "It depends how the Americans view it, but it won't be there for long - it'll come back a bit towards the end of the week," said Mike Noone, Latin America economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank in London. 

 The move to a free float followed persistent market attacks on the band, and was announced one day after Colombia clinched an agreement with the International Monetary Fund for a $7 billion international loan package. 

 The central bank had haemorrhaged more than $400 million in reserves last week alone to try to defend the band. 

 Elsewhere, the rand firmed to hover around 6.0 to the dollar after world gold prices soared on Sunday's news that 15 European central banks had agreed to cap gold sales. The metal was fixed in London at $281.70 a troy ounce, its highest since early May, against Friday afternoon's $270. 

 Analysts said the rise had a strong emotional impact on the spot rand market, although gold accounts for less than one-fifth of South Africa's export earnings. 

 Comments by Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni on the need for caution on further monetary easing after last week's prime rate cut also supported the currency, analysts added. ((Gill Tudor, London Capital Markets +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, gill.tudor@reuters.com)).

title: ASIA MARKETS - Ease on yen wobbles, U.S. rate fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Jitters over possible 

 Japanese intervention pressured the yen and other regional 

currencies on Thursday, as Asian stock markets bowed to fears 

 of another U.S. interest hike. 

     News that Japanese Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa was 

 meeting Bank of Japan governor Masaru Hayami to discuss 

 monetary policy stoked fears intervention could be imminent, 

 propping the dollar up briefly against the yen. 

     Chin Loo Thio, currency strategist at Paribas, said in a 

 daily report the dollar was technically unlikely to find a 

 bottom until September 29, the end of the first half of Japan's 

 fiscal year. 

     "Once September is over, the need for yen purchases may 

 decline as both Japanese exporters and investors complete their 

 hedges," she said. 

     RUPIAH SLIPS BACK BEYOND 8,000 

     The rupiah eased to the wrong side of the 8,000 per dollar 

 level as players maintained their wait-and-see approach to the 

 smouldering Bank Bali scandal and plans to move a U.N. peace 

 keeping force to East Timor. 

     Some dealers in Jakarta said fears the U.N.'s presence 

 could heighten animosity in the bloodied territory were 

 overwhelming relief over the impending arrival of foreign 

 troops. 

     Sentiment was also weak due to comments by the central bank

 that an audit into the Bank Bali scandal had been unfair and 

 that loan delays by the World Bank and the IMF could harm the 

 economy. 

     And central bank governor Syahril Sabirin warned that Bank 

 Indonesia could take legal action against 

 PricewaterhouseCoopers, which conducted the audit. 

     "The currency is underpinned by quite tight monetary policy 

 in Indonesia but politically, the threat is still great," said 

 Kate O'Donoghue, regional economist at Barclays Capital Asia. 

     "Volatility will be on the cards for quite some time," she 

 told Reuters Television. 

     PESO RISK RETURN SEEN WORTHY DESPITE DEFICIT 

     The peso was placed under added pressures by prospects of a 

 widening budget deficit one day after the IMF agreed to a 10 

 billion peso increase to this year's fiscal shortfall. 

 Socio-economic planning secretary Felipe Medalla said next 

 year's deficit was also likely to overshoot the 40 billion peso 

 target by about 10 billion pesos. 

 But analysts remained upbeat on the Philippines. 

 "The Philippines' chronic fiscal deficit has made them 

 develop a healthy T-bill market so we are still quite bullish 

 on the peso. The economy is suffering more from cyclical 

 problems than from structural ones," Barclays Capital's 

 O'Donoghue said. 

     "We see the peso offering value and we would certainly be 

 looking to buy it at these levels," she said. 

     THAILAND RULES OUT INTERVENTION ON BAHT 

     The baht hovered near its year lows, pressured as the yen 

 came off its high, but the government said it had no plans to 

 step in. 

     Thai Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtam said current 

 baht levels were okay and the government had no plans to 

intervene. 

     "The baht should be dictated by market forces. The current 

 level of the currency is okay. There is no irregular movement 

 so far," he told reporters in Bangkok. 

     KOSPI SLIDES AMID LIQUIDITY FEARS 

     Korean stocks slid more than three percent partly due to an 

 uptick in domestic interest rates triggered by liquidity fears. 

     The benchmark three-year Treasury bond yield crossed the 

 9.5 percent mark amid fears Daewoo's financial troubles could 

 spark a run on investment companies in November, when more 

 redemptions of beneficiary certificates are to be allowed. 

     Investment trusts hold 75 percent of the 30.75 trillion won 

 ($25.8 billion) in Daewoo's bonds and commercial papers. 

     Some analysts said the direction of the KOSPI -- which has 

 yielded dollar-based year-to-date returns of over 88 percent -- 

 depends on future government handling of Daewoo's problems.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Unscathed by early yen  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Japanese efforts to tame the 

 volatile yen on Friday were largely shrugged off by Asian 

 regional currencies, while stocks were mixed amid a spate of 

 domestic factors. 

     Most regional currencies remained firm despite early 

 dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Japan, with most of 

 the day's trade dominated by short-covering of local currency

 positions ahead of the weekend. 

     "Movements on the yen really haven't been the key driver 

 behind currencies like the rupiah, Thai baht and Philippine 

 peso just now," said David Simmons, regional currency

 strategist at Citibank in Singapore. 

     "Only the won and the Singapore dollar (have) seen some 

 movement in line with the yen," Simmons told Reuters 

 Television. 

     RUPIAH JUMPS ON POSITION SQUARING 

     The rupiah bounced back to levels seen at the start of the 

 week as players who had gone long of dollar/rupiah amid the 

 escalating violence in East Timor closed off their positions 

 ahead of the weekend. 

     Players adopted a wait-and-see stance as violence in East 

 Timor showed few signs of abating and as international threats 

 to delay financial aid to Indonesia were stepped up. 

     Thousands may have died in the wave of killing and arson in 

 East Timor, much of it blamed on rampaging pro-Jakarta militia, 

 in the days since the territory's vote for independence was 

 announced. 

     The rupiah's thin trading environment was likely to mean 

 continued volatility in the currency, analysts said. 

     "It's a pretty stressful experience when ones sees the 

 rupiah gyrating between 7,900 to 9.000 and most of the way back 

 again," said Citibank's Simmons. 

     "But I am sure there will some pockets of demand for U.S. 

 dollars on these sorts of dips, on the back of the continued 

 uncertainties," he said. 

     PESO NUDGES BACK THROUGH 40 LEVEL 

     The Philippine peso pared losses seen earlier this week, 

 firming to the right side of 40 per dollar. 

     But the peso -- which has lost heavily against the dollar 

 amid fears over East Timor -- soon edged back to levels 

 encouraged by the central bank as the regional mood brightened. 

     Philippine central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said 

 earlier in the day that the peso should revert to the 39 per 

 dollar level as regional tensions eased. 

     "There is no reason for the peso to go beyond that level," 

 he said, referring to the 40-per-dollar level. 

     Buenaventura also threw water over his earlier hints that 

 the central bank might adjust its overnight floating rate to 

 woo investors into Treasury bills. 

     He said the policy-making Monetary Board had opted to keep 

 its key overnight rates steady at a weekly meeting. 

     THAI Q2 GDP SEEN HIGHER 

     The baht was firmer ahead of expected capital inflows 

 arising from Standard Chartered Bank's acquisition of 

 Nakornthon Bank. 

     Thailand's economy grew about eight percent over the year 

 to the second quarter of 1999, according to a government think 

 tank. 

     A senior finance ministry official quoted the National 

 Economic and Social Development Board as saying Thailand's 

 second quarter performance might raise growth for 1999 to about 

 six percent against a 9.4 percent contraction in 1998. 

 MALAYSIA PUT ON POSITIVE RATING OUTLOOK 

 Malaysian stocks were unimpressed by an upgrade in the 

 country's credit outlook by ratings agency FITCH IBCA. 

 Fitch put Malaysia on rating alert positive which could 

 lead to a sovereign upgrade and said the country was ahead of 

 its Asian neighbours in restructuring its banks and corporate 

 debt. 

 Fitch now sees Malaysia's economy expanding as much as five 

 percent this year, after a contraction of 7.5 percent last 

 year. 

     Malaysia's short and long term foreign currency is rated at 

 BBB minus.

title: Singapore Exch-Rate Stance -2: Eased During Crisis
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore's "neutral" exchange-rate stance remains unchanged despite recent volatility on Asian currency markets, the spokesman for the Monetary Authority of Singapore said Thursday. 

 "Our neutral exchange-rate stance remains unchanged," MAS spokesman Leong Sing Chiong told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 Leong was responding to a question about the recent decline of the Singapore dollar against the U.S. dollar, which has been widely attributed to fallout from the plunge in the Indonesian rupiah. 

 He declined to comment on whether the MAS, the de facto central bank, would intervene in the foreign exchange market to stabilize the Singapore dollar exchange rate. 

 The MAS guides the Singapore dollar exchange rate within an implicit trading band against a trade-weighted basket of foreign currencies. 

 During the Asian financial crisis of 1997 and 1998, the MAS widened the band to give the Singapore dollar exchange rate more flexibility as markets became volatile and Asian currencies depreciated substantially. 

 As Singapore and other Asian economies started to recover, the MAS narrowed the band again and shifted its exchange-rate stance back to "neutral" against the trade-weighted basket. 

 The Singapore dollar has been slipping in recent weeks after reaching a seven-month peak of S$1.6639 Aug. 10, largely as a result of the sharp slide in the rupiah. 

 Violence in East Timor following a referendum in favor of independence from Indonesia has aroused international condemnation and concerns that economic aid may be suspended. The dollar breached the key IDR9,000 level midmorning, before it fell back to IDR8,970. 

 At 0326 GMT (11:26 p.m. EDT Wednesday), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6935, up slightly from S$1.6930 late Wednesday.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Weaker yen, Timor pressure regionals.
text:
1000 GMT - Most regional currencies were easier in late 

 Asian trade as worries over East Timor persisted and as the yen 

 held on to its weaker bias. 

     The yen was seen pressured by some position-squaring ahead 

 of Japan's April-June GDP numbers due on Thursday. 

     A Reuters survey on Wednesday showed that economists had 

 lowered their GDP forecasts after capital spending data for 

 Japanese companies for the same period showed a larger than 

 expected decline. 

     Japan's GDP number, due on Thursday, is now forecast to 

 contract about 0.35 percent compared with the previous quarter. 

     Bank of Japan Governor Masaru Hayami said on Wednesday that 

 a recent rise in the yen and in Tokyo stocks was largely due to 

 foreign buying. He also said that forex movements would 

 eventually return to previous levels if excessive. 

 *** The rupiah was lower despite government intervention as 

 martial law and a shoot-on-sight curfew in East Timor showed no 

 signs of halting the widespread violence. 

 Indonesia's central bank governor Syahril Sabirin said the 

central bank was intervening to prop up the currency but 

 admitted that it was having little impact. 

     He said the government's currency target was still in the 

 range of 6,000 to 7,000 to the dollar. 

     Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downing said that 

 only U.N. peacekeepers could restore order in East Timor, where 

 militias have massacred hundreds since locals voted for 

 independence last week. 

 But Indonesian State Secretary Muladi ruled out accepting 

 foreign peace-keepers, saying the country would have to deal 

 with the problem alone until the vote for independence is 

 ratified by Indonesia's highest legislative body at its October 

 meeting. 

 Indonesia's parliament is expected to receive preliminary 

 results on possible insider dealing in Bank Bali shares next 

 week. 

 Indonesia's Supreme Audit Agency and PriceWaterHouse 

 Coopers had said on Tuesday that they had discovered evidence 

 of irregularities in their investigation of a fee payment by 

 Bank Bali to a ruling Golkar party official. 

 *** Worries over East Timor also weighed on the baht, as 

 some players switched out of regional currencies into the 

 dollar, traders said. 

 A central bank official said on Wednesday that the 

currency's drop to levels not seen since October 1998 was 

 largely due to the weakening yen and the Finance Ministry's 

 comments condoning a weaker baht. 

     Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi also said the 

 baht's present levels were good for exports. 

     *** The peso fell to its lowest close in 10 months, 

 pressured by weakness in regional currencies and in line with 

 the baht. 

     Manila dealers said the central bank's plan to change its 

 overnight borrowing scheme to make Treasury bills more 

 attractive also weighed on sentiment. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said he might 

 adjust the central bank's floating rate for overnight borrowing 

 to encourage banks to invest in T-bills. 

     Buenaventura said he saw no need for dollar-selling 

intervention or for interest rate readjustments to prop up the 

currency.	"This is more of a knee-jerk reaction to the



Thai baht problem," he said, adding that the peso was likely to



return to the 39 level once volatility in regional currencies


faded.



    *** The won ended lower as players built up dollar



positions amid regional jitters.



    Seoul traders said the currency was likely to trade in a



tight range against the dollar on Thursday.



    Revised International Monetary Fund predictions for South



Korea's GDP growth were ignored.



    According to preliminary data published on the Dutch



finance ministry's web site, the IMF raised its forecast for



South Korea's annual GDP growth to 6.5 percent from 2.0



percent.



*** The Taiwan dollar softened with the yen, slipping as



T$31.864 per dollar before late intervention by the central



bank propped it up.



    *** The Singapore dollar was easier, weighed down by the



troubles in East Timor.



    Singapore's close trade, investment and political ties with



Indonesia mean its markets often suffer with signs of trouble

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Mixed amid wary yen, rupiah wobbly.
text:
0200 GMT - Regional currencies were looking mixed in early 

 trade, with the dollar slipping against the yen on speculative 

 sales. 

     But the market was cautious about selling the greenback too 

 aggressively below 111 yen due to lingering concerns over 

 possible yen-selling intervention by the Bank of Japan. 

     Japan's Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs 

 Haruhiko Kuroda said in Singapore on Sunday that the yen's 

 premature appreciation was undesirable. 

     Kuroda was attending a meeting of Manila Framework member 

 countries to discuss Asia's economic crisis. 

     Separately, Japan's former Vice Minister for International 

 Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara told Japanese television on Sunday 

 that the United States and Japan would discuss the weak dollar 

 at a G7 deputies meeting in September. 

 *** The rupiah was weaker amid lingering concerns about the 

 Bank Bali scandal and as voting in East Timor's independence 

 referendum got underway. 

 The IMF said on Sunday that the next disbursement of funds 

 for Indonesia depended on satisfactory settlement of the Bank 

 Bali case. 

 Indonesia has promised an independent audit of its central 

 bank in the wake of the scandal which centres on payment of a 

 large fee by Bank Bali to a firm run by an official of the 

 ruling Golkar party to recover loans from the Indonesian Bank 

 Restructuring Agency (IBRA). 

 All eyes are also on the U.N.-organised independence vote 

 in East Timor on Monday. President Clinton has warned 

 Indonesian President B.J.Habibie that ties with Washington 

 would be seriously damaged and that foreign aid could be 

 curtailed if the recent violence escalates. 

 *** The won was easier after posting solid gains against 

 the dollar in late Friday trade as banks unwound dollar 

 positions after accepting export-linked documents from Daewoo 

 Group companies. 

 On Sunday, South Korea reported a 33.1 percent annual jump 

 in industrial output for July compared with a 14.0 percent 

 decline a year earlier. 

 July production was also 2.3 percent higher than in June. 

 The rise was spurred by growing demand for goods both 

 domestically and internationally, especially for automobiles 

 and semiconductors. 

 *** The Philippine peso was holding up ahead of a 

 government auction of Treasury bills which should show if a 

 decision to allow yields to rise will boost the faltering 

currency. 

 The government said on Friday it would allow Treasury bill 

 yields to rise to help restore the premium on local interest 

 rates after last week's U.S. rate hike. 

 Shrinking interest rates spreads and uncertainty over the 

 domestic rate outlook pushed the peso to nine-month lows last 

 week. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Friday 

 the decision to allow higher T-bill rates had reduced the need 

 for the central bank to hike overnight rates or bank reserve 

 requirements. 

 *** The Singapore dollar was a shade easier in light trade. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Sunday that 

 the currency should reflect underlying economic fundamentals as 

 the best way to detract speculative pressures. 

 Singapore operates a managed float system, keeps its 

currency within a certain band to make sure exports remain 

 competitive. 

 The Singapore dollar rose to a seven-month high against the 

 dollar at around 1.66 in early August, with some traders 

 suspecting intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore

 (MAS) to stem its gains.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Mixed as yen slips in cautious trade.
text:

 investors remained keen to buy the Japanese currency. 

     But the market was cautious about pushing it up 

 aggressively ahead of a weekend meeting of deputy finance 

 ministers and central bankers of the 14 Manila Framework member

title: FOCUS-S'pore rates seen benign after hike in U.S.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Singapore interest rates are likely to remain benign in the medium-term despite a 25-basis point hike in the U.S. on Tuesday, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was expected to continue with its intervention policy in the foreign exchange market to keep the Singapore dollar competitive, which in turn would induce liquidity in the system, they said. 

 "It's a fact that capital inflows are coming back again as the stock market recovers," Vincent Low, fixed-income strategist at Merrill Lynch, said. 

 "The MAS would keep the currency from appreciating and therefore, its intervention will probably keep interest rates capped, or even on a downward bias," Low added. 

 The MAS had intervened in the foreign exchange market in the last couple of days to prevent the Singapore dollar from appreciating too much against the U.S. dollar. 

 The move had increased liquidity in the banking system and resulted in interbank rates falling. 

 Some said there was no reason for the Sing dollar to have strengthened to 1.67 recently against the U.S. dollar as it was not warranted on a trade-weighted basis. 

 By 0710 GMT on Wednesday, the Singapore dollar was trading around 1.6918 against the U.S. dollar. 

 The benchmark three-month interbank rate softened to 2.375 percent at Wednesday's fixing from a high of 2.625 percent about two weeks ago, the highest since mid-January 1999. 

Currency dealers said the rates were trending up on nervousness in the Asian financial markets, fears of a U.S. rate hike and tension in North and South Asia. 

 Cheong Kwok Mun, analyst at GK Goh, said Singapore interest rates were unlikely to move up in line with U.S. rates. 

 The city-state was just coming out of a recession unlike the U.S., which had been booming for several years. 

 On Tuesday, the U.S. Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate for overnight loans between banks and the less-used discount rate by a quarter percentage point each. 

 It also kept an open-minded or "neutral" position on the interest rate outlook, reassuring investors who had feared the central bank might lean toward additional increases in borrowing costs by adopting a formal tightening "bias." 

 The Fed had also nudged rates higher at its most recent meeting on June 30. Tuesday was the first time in more than five years the Fed had boosted rates at two consecutive meetings. 

 Low said Merrill's view was that there would not be anymore rate hikes for the rest of the year. 

 "The pressure point has been released already. I think it ought to benefit the stock market," he said, adding Singapore's economic recovery was likely to gather momentum. 

 Merrill raised its forecast for Singapore's GDP growth to 6.3 percent in 1999, up from 4.4 percent previously.

title: Asian  Currencies  Weaken; Singapore Dlr Down To Month Low

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Risk aversion ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting coupled with the dollar's overnight run-up against the yen pushed Asian regional currencies lower Tuesday. 

 Among the biggest falls was that of the Singapore dollar, which dropped to its lowest level so far this month, propelled in part by sales executed by the local monetary authority, according to dealers. 

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso fell to a nine-month low during intraday trading, despite verbal intervention by central bank officials aimed at supporting the currency. 

 Talk in the Singapore market Tuesday morning centered around rumors that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in the foreign exchange market the night before, buying U.S. dollars during New York trading hours to weaken the local currency. 

 The MAS is said by traders to have bought U.S. dollars on a number of occasions recently, in pursuit of its efforts to enhance Singapore's export competitiveness. 

 From a low Monday night of around S$1.6720, the U.S. dollar rose steadily to hit an intraday high of S$1.6912 Tuesday in Asia, as both U.S. and Singapore banks bid heavily for the U.S. currency. 

 According to a trader at one U.S. bank it was "highly likely" that the MAS had intervened in the market to initiate the move. 

 Nevertheless, the principal reason for the U.S. currency's rally was a growing aversion to risk ahead of the FOMC meeting later Tuesday, he said.

text:
The Bank of Korea Thursday forecast that exports would rise by 7% in the second half on a year-on-year basis, bringing the overall increase in export volume for 1999 to 3%. 

 The good economic news failed to buoy the won, however, as local banks continued to buy U.S. dollars in order to meet government requirements on loss provisioning for foreign assets. 

 The early provisioning requirement is just one of a number of measures introduced by the government in recent months to preserve Korea's export competitiveness by countering the trade and capital inflows pushing the won higher. 

 By the end of local dealing, the U.S. currency had been pushed higher, to close at 1,203.50 won, up from KRW1,198.70 at the previous close. 

 Positive sentiment also failed to lift the Singapore dollar. After rising strongly in early Asian trading, with the U.S. dollar dropping to a fresh six-month low at S$1.6750, the local currency was pushed sharply lower by aggressive U.S. dollar buying from Singapore banks. 

 Most dealers assumed that the purchases were executed on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, as the buying pushed the U.S. currency right up to levels above S$1.6900. 

 U.S. dollar sellers emerged at the high, however, and the U.S. currency settled back to S$1.6857 toward the end of Asian trading, up from S$1.6810 at the same time the day before. 

 Despite the suspected intervention, many dealers remain relatively positive on the Singapore currency, reasoning that with the yen, the euro and other Asian regional currencies relatively strong, the MAS should allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate against the dollar, in order to maintain a neutral trade-weighted exchange rate.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lifted By Yen, Easing Regional Concerns
text:
- 

 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--A combination of the yen's strength, abating concern over the tensions between China and Taiwan, relief at South Korea's handling of the Daewoo Group's near collapse, and improving economic fundamentals lifted Asian currencies Thursday. 

 The Thai baht, the Indonesian rupiah and the New Taiwan dollar all finished Asian trading hours higher. 

 The Singapore dollar, however, ended down following suspected central bank intervention. The South Korean won closed lower, in response to government-directed dollar purchases by local banks. 

 But overall sentiment toward the region has improved markedly since a week ago, when withdrawal of funds by foreign investors spooked by the cross-strait squabble and Daewoo's cash crisis forced many Asian currencies to multiple-month lows. 

 "On the whole, the economic recovery is very much intact," explained Thio Chin Loo, global currency strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore, saying investors had been greatly reassured by unexpectedly strong industrial production numbers released this week by both South Korea and Singapore. 

 "There are very strong reasons why Asian currencies should strengthen further from these levels," she said. 

 In South Korea, the government announced that industrial output surged by 29.5% year-on-year in June, the biggest rise in over 10 years. Coming on top of a 21.7% increase in May, the rise was attributed to a combination of rising export volume and resurgent domestic demand.

title: US Dlr/MAS -2: US Dlr At S$1.6900
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Monetary Authority of Singapore is believed to have entered the currency market to shore up the sagging U.S. dollar, pushing it above the key S$1.6800 level Thursday morning. 

 At 0230 GMT (10:30 p.m. Wednesday EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6900, sharply higher than S$1.6775 about half an hour earlier and S$1.6820 late Wednesday. 

 Dealers say local banks are buying U.S. dollars, which is believed to be at the behest of the MAS. 

 Officials at the Monetary Authority of Singapore could not be reached immediately. MAS rarely confirms individual interventions, saying only that it intervenes from time to time to smooth market volatility. 

 The U.S. dollar has been trading the past few days at six-month lows against the Singapore dollar in line with its weakness against the yen.

title: Asian  Currencies : US Dlr Dragged Lower By Tumble Vs Yen
text:
- 

 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The dollar's tumble against the yen dragged the U.S. currency lower against Asian regional currencies during local trading hours Wednesday. 

 In southeast Asia, the dollar weakened against the Singapore dollar and dropped sharply against the Indonesian rupiah. Heavy sales of the U.S. currency were also seen against the Thai baht, despite the closure of markets in Bangkok for a holiday. 

 In North Asian markets, the dollar dropped steadily from its opening high against the Korean won, slipping once again below the KRW1,200 level. 

 The U.S. currency also softened against the new Taiwan dollar and the Philippine peso. 

 Further unwinding of Asian cross currency trades funded through short positions in the Singapore dollar was credited with driving much of the run-up in the Singapore dollar. 

 Although the Singapore currency failed to surpass the six-month high it touched briefly Tuesday, traders generally expected it to push higher in coming sessions. 

 "The U.S. dollar's trend is still down," said one trader at a Singapore bank. 

 Given the weakness of the U.S. currency against the yen, the Monetary Authority of Singapore is unlikely to intervene aggressively to support the U.S. dollar, he said, adding that the U.S. currency could easily slide all the way to S$1.6700 over the short term.

title: INTERVIEW-S'pore sees 1999 GDP forecast revised up.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Singapore's economy enjoyed better-than-expected growth in the second quarter of 1999 and an upward revision in full-year growth is coming, the nation's deputy prime minister and central bank chief said on Wednesday. 

 "The second quarter has turned out better than we had expected," Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told Reuters Television in an interview. 

 "We had a very good quarter and I think we have to recognise this and make a realistic forecast for what we expect for the year," he said. 

 GDP for 1999 is currently forecast between zero and two percent higher than last year. The Singapore government is expected to announce a new forecast on National Day, August 9. 

 Singapore's total manufacturing output surged 18.4 percent during the 12 months to June, the government said on Monday. 

 Exports for June showed 7.5 percent annual growth. 

 In July, Singapore announced changes in the way it calculated gross domestic product and revised down growth estimates for 1998 and the first quarter of 1999. 

 GDP for 1998 is now seen 0.3 percent higher than in the previous full year, rather than 1.5 percent, while the first quarter is estimated 0.8 percent higher than a year earlier, rather than 1.2 percent. 

 But the deputy prime minister said he did not think the changes would be significant to the overall 1999 figure. 

 "It affects only the financial sector. It may make a half a percentage point (difference) or so," Lee said. 

 He said that when an earlier 1999 growth forecast of minus one to plus one percent was made in November last year, it reflected an overall sense of uncertainty. 

 "Minus one to plus one really meant 'we can't say, we don't know, this is a stab in the dark,'" Lee said. 

 "Then we had a fairly good first quarter so we revised it up (to the current range). Now we've had an even better second quarter, so we revise it up again." 

 Singapore has been criticised as being too conservative in its growth forecasts, but Lee said this was to avoid having to make revisions downward later. 

 "We are conservative on what we publicly commit to being certain of delivering. I think that is a sensible, sober approach," he said. 

 Singapore's equity market had steamed ahead until early July as investors sensed an improving economic outlook, but Lee said the rally had exceeded the improvement in the underlying economy. 

 "The change in the stock market far exceeded the change in the fundamentals. Maybe it was a bit undervalued before, perhaps it's a bit overvalued now, probably a mix of both," he said. 

 The Singapore stock market has tumbled more than seven percent since reaching a record high of 2,247.43 on July 5. The key Straits Times Index ended at 2,077.65 on Wednesday. 

 Lee also said he was "very comfortable" with the Singapore dollar level on a trade-weighted basis. 

 "On a trade weighted basis, we are very comfortable, so I don't think that anything important happened yesterday." 

 The Singapore dollar rose to a six-month high on Tuesday of around 1.6755 per dollar before edging back. 

 Some traders suspected that the MAS had intervened to stem the currency's gains.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Strong yen supports Asian  currencies .
text:
HONG KONG, July 28 (Reuters) - The strength of the yen 

 underpinned the Asian currency markets on Monday sending the 

 regionals all slightly higher. 

     While most stock markets took their cue from the higher Wall 

 Street finish overnight to resume recent rallies, lead by Korean 

 investors who seem to have shaken off their Daewoo jitters. 

     BULLS RETURN TO KOREAN ASSET MARKETS 

     Early demand for the Korean won saw the currency break 

 through the 1200 level to the dollar drawing verbal intervention

 from the authorities. 

     Korean finance ministry officials said they were closely 

 monitoring the market, and state banks were seen active buyers of 

 dollars. 

     In addition to the yen the won is getting a boost from signs 

 the Daewoo crisis might be moving toward a better outcome after 

 the creditors stepped in yesterday to take control of the 

 restructuring process. 

     Korea's KOSPI ended up around 1.7 percent after being as much 

 as four percent higher during the day.  But analysts doubt all 

 the bad news is out yet for the Korean corporate sector. 

     "Is Daewoo the only case in Korea where you have a severe 

 need for restructuring? I don't think so," said Andrew Dermot 

 Fung, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in 

 Singapore. 

     SINGAPORE DOLLAR STRENGTHENS AS ECONOMIC OUTLOOK IMPROVES 

     The Singapore dollar pushed through the 1.69 level overnight 

 to a low of 1.6815 in the Asian day. 

     There were rumours of intervention in the market by the 

Singapore authorities, though the currency does have a tendency 

 to track the yen. 

     But analysts and the authorities point out that the economy 

 is improving sharply as well. 

     Singapore's economy enjoyed better-than-expected growth in 

 the second quarter of 1999 and an upward revision in full-year 

 growth can be expected, the nation's deputy prime minister and 

central bank chief said. 

 "The second quarter has turned out better than we had 

 expected," Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told Reuters 

 Television in an interview. 

 GDP for 1999 is currently forecast up or down one percent on 

 last year. The Singapore government is expected to announce a new 

 forecast on National Day, August 9. 

 Singapore's total manufacturing output surged 18.4 percent 

 during the 12 months to June, the Economic Development Board said 

 on Monday. 

 INDONESIA LOOKS FOR STRONGER RUPIAH 

 Elsewhere Indonesia's economics minister Ginandjar, in Paris 

 for the Consultative Group meeting of international donors, was 

 again talking up the rupiah. 

 He said the government is comfortable with a dollar-rupiah 

 level around 6,500 and sees improvement to around 6,000 as a good 

 move. 

     However, Ginandjar hastened to add there would be no 

intervention to support such a move. 

     ASIA NEEDS TO BOOST DEMAND - WORLD BANK 

     Asia must focus on the restoration of demand and although it 

 is clear the crisis has bottomed out, the region is far from full 

 recovery, according to World Bank chief economist Joseph 

 Stiglitz. 

     "The real focus ought to be on the restoration of aggregate 

 demand in these countries," he told Reuters Television. 

     "While exchange rates have stabilised and clearly the crisis 

 has bottomed out, most of the countries are nowhere near recovery 

 in terms of fundamentals of output, employment and real wages." 

     He said there was still a lot of room for stimulating demand. 

     Stiglitz indicated he favoured a continuation of relaxed 

 monetary policy in the crisis countries, although he said there 

 was room in those recovering more quickly to bear higher rates. 

     "In general for the region as a whole the fact is the 

 recovery is nowhere along so far that one can be complacent." 

     REGIONAL STOCKS ALL RALLY 

     The Dow's strong one percent gain overnight set the stage for 

 a good day around the region. 

     In Singapore the Straits Times index shot up by 3.6 percent, 

 boosted by some strong results from DBS Land on Tuesday. The 

 company unveiled a 174 percent rise in interim profits.

title: Singapore  Dollar Stronger Late;  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar strengthened against the U.S. dollar late Tuesday, but has fallen off a six-month high on suspected intervention by Singapore's monetary authority. 

 At 0950 GMT (5:50 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6880, weaker than S$1.6973 late Monday, but higher than its intraday low of S$1.6797. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is believed to have bought U.S. dollars Tuesday through local banks to arrest the Singapore dollar's rapid climb. 

 The authority rarely comments on its daily activities, but admits to controlling large movements in the market. 

 Before the MAS reportedly stepped in, stop-loss orders triggered at the S$1.6850 level carried the U.S. dollar through support at S$1.6800, dealers said. 

 They also noted an MAS report that said currency flows in and out of a country shouldn't be regulated had suggested to market players that the de facto central bank was easing its grip on the market, imbuing participants with confidence in pushing the Singapore dollar higher without being caught short U.S. dollars by an MAS intervention. 

 The U.S. dollar's steep descent against the Singapore dollar began late Monday, following both the yen's sharp rise and the bullish industrial production figures for Singapore showing June total manufacturing output rose 18.4%. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said the positive figures point to strong economic growth, which will put pressure on the MAS to yield on its monetary policy. 

 On the local money market, the interbank overnight rate was offered at 1.250%, down from 1.625% late Monday in Asia, while the three-month rate was offered at 2.1875%, down from 2.3750% late Monday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Rally; Singapore Dlr Touches 6-Mo High
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The continued strength of the yen helped other Asian currencies to rally against the U.S. dollar during local trading hours Tuesday. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Singapore dollar and the baht both rose strongly against the U.S. currency. In North Asia, the Korean won firmed as local markets recovered from the sell-off seen in recent days. 

 The yen's overnight rally, coupled with unexpectedly strong industrial production numbers for June, pushed the Singapore dollar higher to touch a six-month high briefly during Tuesday's trade. 

 Spooked by the yen's overnight rise, traders moved to unwind short positions in the Singapore dollar against other Asian currencies. 

 Interbank dealers soon jumped on the trend, selling the U.S. dollar short in an attempt to trigger stop-loss orders below S$1.6800. The sales did briefly push the U.S. currency to a six-month low at S$1.6780, but at that level local banks emerged, aggressively bidding the U.S. dollar back up above S$1.6800. 

 "They looked quite determined," remarked an interbank trader, echoing the market's belief that the bids had been executed on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The MAS seldom intervenes openly, although last month the authority did admit buying U.S. dollars to arrest an overly rapid appreciation of the local currency. 

 As Asian interbank trading drew to a close, the U.S. dollar had been pushed up from its earlier low to trade at S$1.6850. Late Monday the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.6973.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX - Currencies  in thrall to Fed.
text:
LONDON, July 27 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies

 recovered slightly on Tuesday after Monday's losses, but were 

 still held in thrall by the second part of Federal Reserve 

 Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on 

 Wednesday, analysts said. 

     However, Asian currencies saw a recovery as a result of 

 gains on the region's stock markets, with the Korean won firmer 

 after creditors stepped in to take over the restructuring of the 

 ailing Daewoo conglomerate, said Callum Henderson, emerging 

 market currency strategist at Citibank. 

     The Korean won firmed to 1203 bid to the dollar, up from 

 1208 in early London trade on Monday. 

     But it is Greenspan who holds sway. 

     "Overall the environment remains pretty jittery," said 

 Henderson. "Since the U.S. is basically the provider of global 

 liquidity, that automatically weighs on emerging markets." 

     East Asian currencies benefited from some strength in the 

 Singapore dollar, which posted sharp gains on Monday. 

     Some analysts said they suspected Singapore authorities had 

intervened to support the currency. 

     The Taiwan dollar was aided by central bank intervention on 

 Monday and closed unchanged on Tuesday. The currency was trading 

 at 32.230 in London. 

     Standard Chartered said in a note to investors that the 

currency looked capped at 32.30 and an "apparent easing of 

 tension with China, combined with injections of funds, is 

 resulting in interest rates adopting a marginally softer bias". 

     Stanchart believes that some of the bearishness on emerging 

 market assets as a result of the Fed testimony has gone too far. 

     "However, as concerns about the Fed appear overdone, 

 pessimism about regional markets appears to be exaggerated," the 

 bank said. 

     In eastern Europe, the picture was somewhat similar to Asia, 

 with currencies posting some gains after the Fed-inspired 

 selloff in global markets on Monday. 

     The Polish zloty opened at 6.10 percent above parity against 

 its basket of euros and dollars and was trading a tad weaker 

 than its domestic opening price of 4.0516 to the euro and was at 

 4.0591 bid to the euro by 1000 GMT. 

 "As recent comments about a higher current account deficit 

 are still being digested, we expect the zloty to stabilise 

 around the six percent level," said Mark Rall, currency

 strategist at HypoVeriensbank. 

     Rall expects the Czech crown to appreciate to around 36.50 

 to the euro in coming days from 36.669 now.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late; Mkt Unwinds Long US Dlr Positions
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar has strengthened against the U.S. dollar late Tuesday as market players unwind their long U.S. dollar positions on the apparent easing of tensions between China and Taiwan, dealers said. 

 At 0845 GMT (4:45 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6972, down from S$1.7052 late Monday in Asia and from S$1.6995 earlier Tuesday. 

 A dealer at a European bank said traders who had gone long the U.S. dollar last week as friction between China and Taiwan intensified were now adjusting their positions. 

 "There's a lot of unwinding of cross-currency hedges put on last Friday," he said. 

 He said that although there is momentum to push the Singapore dollar stronger against the U.S. dollar, fear of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore is likely to keep it from strengthening above S$1.6950 against the U.S. currency. 

 On the local money market, the interbank overnight rate was offered at 1.125%, down from 2.250% late Monday in Asia, while the three-month rate was offered at 1.875%, down from 2.125% late Monday.

title: Dollar revives in Asia after overnight mugging.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 20 (Reuters) - The dollar was looking a bit healthier by midday in Asia after an overnight shakeout which led traders to speculate on possible European Central Bank intervention and surprised them by the Bank of Japan's absence. 

 It perked up as short-term players booked profit on the yen's overnight surge to five-week highs, with traders in Asia still wary of the BOJ despite a Japanese holiday. 

 But most analysts dismissed the likelihood of the BOJ intervening in thin Singapore and Hong Kong markets. 

 "To be sure during a Tokyo holiday you could have a big impact because the market's thinner. But are you influencing the people who are going to be moving the market?" said Andrew Dermot-Fung, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. 

 "The answer has to be no... The big risk is if they intervene during a Tokyo holiday, then London comes in and says, 'Thankyou very much,' and we're back to where we were," he said. 

 The dollar stood at 118.57/60 yen at 0455 GMT against its New York close at 118.15/25 yen. The euro was at $1.0294/04 against $1.0307/12. Euro/yen was at 122.21/3.21 against 121.73. 

 Some analysts said the BOJ could also be signalling tolerance of a wider trading range for dollar/yen. 

 "Overall I think they are happy in a range of 115-125 and I think they have to be more flexible. To defend the 120 yen level in a stubborn way is difficult against the market," said Karl Broecker, head of treasury at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg. 

 Broecker told Reuters Television the BOJ was likely to step in and check prices if the dollar fell below 117.50 yen, but added that this was likely to be aimed at stabilising the market. 

 Further gains in the dollar were, however, blocked by offers left by Japanese exporters and investors below 119 yen. 

 Analysts noted that the euro's overnight bounce had also removed pressure on the euro/yen exchange rate - a major source of concern for Japanese officials. 

 "Japanese exporters need to sell euro/yen more than they need to sell dollar/yen. They went into European assets at the end of last year and that really hasn't paid off," said a senior trader at a European bank. 

 The BOJ has intervened repeatedly to block the yen's rise against the dollar and euro in the past month, with much official fretting that a strong yen could smother Japan's infant recovery. 

 The euro won a reprieve overnight amid speculation the ECB had stepped in to stem the seven-month-old unit's embarrassing slide towards parity with the dollar. 

Intervention talk was fuelled by ECB Vice President Christian Noyer's comment on Monday that the euro is now being watched much more closely than before. 

 No official confirmation was available and there was also talk of large hedge fund orders in a market severely short of euros, but analysts said covert central bank action could not be ruled out. 

 "The action, if it was taken, was in a very sensitive way. Simply an open intervention would have failed and this would be a blow in the face of the ECB. But getting the market wrong-footed helped to engineer this recovery (in the euro)," said Broecker. 

 He noted that expectations of a strong German Ifo business climate index for June should also give a boost to the euro. Analysts in a Reuters poll predicted a rise in the headline western Germany index to 91.1 from 90.4 in May. 

 But few were willing to bet on the euro's rebound being more than a mild respite and dealers said its near-term prospects remained shaky. 

 "The economists are saying the ECB could hike rates soon, European growth could pick up soon, but soon is not something we trade on," said one. 

 Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas, agreed that it was too early to call a reversal in the euro's overall downtrend. 

 "I wouldn't be convinced that the euro has turned around until it closes above $1.05," she said.

title: Asian  Currencies : New Taiwan Dollar's Risk Premium Mounts
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The risk premium on the New Taiwan dollar mounted steeply Wednesday, as political tensions across the Taiwan strait deepened. 

 Although central bank intervention limited the extent of the local currency sell-off in the Taipei market, dealers in the offshore market responded to the crisis by aggressively bidding up the premium on non-deliverable U.S. dollar/New Taiwan dollar forwards. 

 With market attention focused squarely on the escalating tensions between Taiwan and China, currencies elsewhere in the region enjoyed a day of relatively quiet trading. 

 The South Korean won was pushed lower by government-directed dollar purchases, but the Thai baht, the Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar all edged higher. The Indonesian rupiah softened. 

 Massive intervention by the Taiwanese central bank, which was estimated to have sold well over $250 million in the U.S. currency, managed to nudge the New Taiwan dollar only a fraction higher as deteriorating sentiment and a steep 4% slide in the local stock market weighed heavily on the local dollar. 

 The sell-off was prompted by an escalating war of words between Taipei and Beijing. Relations between the two governments took an abrupt turn for the worse after Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui told a German radio station that island aims to conduct dealings with the mainland on a state-to-state basis, explicitly claiming for Taiwan a statehood status that China refuses to recognize. 

 The New Taiwan dollar sell-off drove the U.S. currency to an intraday high of NT$32.330 Wednesday before the Taiwanese central bank stepped into the market and began selling U.S. dollars. By the end of the trading session the U.S. currency had been driven back down to a level of NT$32.272, a touch below Tuesday's closing level of NT$32.275.

title: ASIA MARKETS-China-Taiwan brouhaha rattles stocks.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 14 (Reuters) - Regional stocks took a bit of 

 a pasting on Wednesday with Taipei and North Asia markets badly 

 mauled by concern over the mounting tension between Taiwan and 

 China. 

 Taipei stocks reeled to close nearly four percent lower as 

 the political punch-up with China over the scrapping of Taiwan's 

 one-China policy sent stocks lower for a second day. 

 "It's obviously a huge concern and as we look forward, 

 sentiment is likely to remain poor," said Steve Brice, regional 

 treasury economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 "Whether we see any official intervention for stocks seems 

 reasonably unlikely, they were looking for a moderation of the 

 stock market rise anyway." 

 TAIPEI TOTTERS 

 Taiwan's weighted index dropped through the psychologically 

 important 8,000 level and broke below some important chart 

 levels. 

 Traders said the stand-off with China was undoubtedly the 

 main driving force behind the slide but investors were using it 

 as an excuse to take profits, particularly in technology issues. 

 Taiwan authorities are quite capable of intervening directly 

 in the markets and the finance ministry did not rule this out. 

 "The government has a tool in hand," finance minister Paul 

 Chiu said. "The tool is stabilisation fund. We do not rule out 

 the possibility of using it when necessary." 

 In 1996 when China staged "war games" in the Taiwan Straits 

 around election time in Taiwan, the markets sagged alarmingly 

 but the authorities moved in aggressively to prop them up. 

 TAIWAN WOES RATTLE NORTH ASIA STOCKS 

 The Hang Seng was not immune to the China/Taiwan situation, 

 giving up nearly three percent, with China plays sharply lower 

 on fresh concern about a devaluation of the yuan after an 

 apparent softening of the central bank's line on the subject. 

 But analysts do not see a move by China anytime soon. 

 "There won't be any immediate Chinese devaluation," said 

 Bill Overhalt, Asia strategist at Nomura International in Hong 

 Kong. 

 "The Prime Minister is concerned about a combination of low 

 interest rates, a lot of fiscal stimulus and a potential 

 devaluation sparking off another round of inflation." 

 "They are going to hold tight and see how the other policies 

 play out first." 

 More foreign cash flowed out of the Seoul stock market which 

 extended its two day losing streak. 

 THAI STOCKS FRET OVER BANK EARNINGS 

 Thai markets were jittery over forthcoming bank earnings 

 with financial issues leading the stock market lower. 

 Thai commercial banks are seen reporting further heavy 

 quarterly losses next week but some of the larger institutions 

 could see a return to profitability next year. 

 Sector analysts expect the banks to post a combined loss of 

 60 billion baht ($1.62 billion) for the April-June period, their 

 seventh hefty quarterly setback since the baht's devaluation. 

 This compares with an actual 46 billion baht net loss the 

 previous quarter and a 104.4 billion baht loss for the period 

 from October to December last year. 

 But consumer confidence seems to be picking up in Thailand, 

 with a survey showing that 24.3 percent of Thais expected their 

 incomes to improve in the next six months. 

CURRENCIES HAVE FIRMER BIAS 

Currencies had a firmer bias but the Korean won bucked the 

 trend as banks continued to suck up dollars for loan loss 

 provisioning. 

 This has been overshadowing the market ever since the 

 government advanced the deadline for banks to cover overseas 

 loan losses to the end of September in a move expected to drain 

 around $2 billion dollars from the market.

title: Singapore Dlr Slightly Weaker Early;Moving In Tight Range
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is slightly weaker early Tuesday against the U.S. dollar after moving in a very narrow range overnight. 

 At 0140 GMT (9:40 p.m. Monday EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6995, higher than its level of S$1.6980 in late Monday trade in Asia. 

 Dealers said trade in the local currency has been sluggish following the Monetary Authority of Singapore's intervention in the market last week. 

 "There's been no incentive to trade after the intervention," a dealer at a Japanese bank said. 

 He said that while traders are wary of taking the Singapore dollar higher on fears of intervention, commercial selling of the U.S. dollar above S$1.7000 is keeping trade mired in a tight range. 

 "Corporate demand (for the Singapore dollar) is capping the upside of the (U.S.) dollar," he said. 

 The dealer said the U.S. dollar is likely to track a course between S$1.6850 and S$1.7250 for the rest of the month. 

 On the local money market, the interbank overnight rate was offered at 2.000%, down from 2.125% late Monday in Asia, while the three-month rate was offered at 1.9375%, up from 1.875% late Monday.

title: Asian  Currencies  -3: NT Dlr Strengthens To 5-Mo High
text:
The Singapore dollar, too, edged higher Monday. But following the Monetary Authority of Singapore's intervention in the market last week to arrest the appreciation of the local currency, market players were tentative buyers. 

 Late in Asian trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6980, down from S$1.7000 at the same time Friday. 

 Although there is interest from investment funds to sell the U.S. dollar at S$1.7000, bids at S$1.6950 from local banks and speculative players should support the market in the short term, said dealers.

 Despite near-daily central bank intervention to check the local currency's rise, the New Taiwan dollar is set to appreciate further over the medium term, according to analysts at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 In a research note issued Monday afternoon they said that the Central Bank of China, Taiwan's central bank, has little option but to sanction a mild appreciation of the local currency.

title: Asian  Currencies  Weaken As Investor Sentiment Cools
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies ended local trading hours lower across the board Friday, weakening against the U.S. dollar for the third day in a row as foreign investor sentiment toward local stock markets showed signs of cooling. 

 The majority of analysts kept a brave face, however, maintaining their bullish view towards regional markets despite Friday's selloff. 

 "I think this is a nice, healthy shakeout of some of the more speculative positions," said Andrew Fung, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 Although some foreign investors were bailing out of regional stocks and currencies, worried that local markets may be overheating, any selloff would merely represent a buying opportunity for the longer-term investors Asia needs to help fund economic recovery, said Fung. 

 "As we see more positive economic numbers coming out, we will see long-term investors stepping in to take advantage of any dips in the market," he predicted. 

 Other market watchers broadly agreed, but warned that the selloff may drive Asian currencies lower still over the coming week, before they can establish a firm bottom. 

 Much of the swing in sentiment toward the regional currencies has been propelled by the slide in the Singapore dollar since the local monetary authority intervened in the market late Tuesday to support the U.S. currency.

title: =Asia Fund View: CMG First State Sees Stk Rally Extending
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's stock markets have been on the rise since late last year, prompting some to wonder whether a reversal may be in the offing. But, CMG First State Investments Singapore expects the region's bourses to continue their upward trend. 

 "The opportunities for Asia, we feel, are long haul," said Kim Teo, chief executive officer for the fund manager, Thursday. "Asian markets have been very productive, but we feel that it's not a short-term blip." 

 For CMG First State Investments Singapore, Asia remains the most attractive investment region despite the fact that stock markets from Korea to the Philippines have gained between 30% and 75% since January. 

 That's the main reason the company relaunched its two Asian equity funds last week even though the sharp region-wide rally is almost eight months old. 

 The two funds - one investing broadly in the region, the other investing in Singapore - were previously managed by Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management, which was acquired in May by Australia's Colonial group. CMG First State Investments, of which Nicholas-Applegate is now a part, is Colonial's fund management arm. 

 While there is a chance that the bourses could retreat in coming months, post-crisis changes in many regional markets are expected to translate into real economic benefits that will help prolong the rally, said associate director Yeo Boon Hong. 

 "I think generally Asian markets will continue to benefit from the reforms and restructuring in 1997 and 1998," Yeo said. "If you think of those years as building years, we should be able to see sustained earnings recovery in 2000." 

 Increasing paid-up capital of companies, lower and falling interest rates, reduced corporate debt and a gradual revival of earnings are among these changes, he said. 


Moreover, Asian companies have started to pay greater attention to
return on equity and enhancing shareholder value, themes that are
helping to underpin stock market gains, Yeo said.
             Liquidity Not Expected To Dry Up



In Singapore, for instance, the return on equity for companies in
general is between 5% and 10%. While the level is similar to that in
1996, when the benchmark Straits Times Index was also hovering just
above the 2000 mark, Yeo said the situation is now different. While the
return on equity was on its way down in 1996, it is now headed upward,
he said, justifying the Singapore bourse's strong advance.



Some have expressed concerns that liquidity will begin to dry up now
that stock prices in some Asian countries are well above their
pre-crisis levels, but Yeo disagreed.



The flow of money - overseas and local - which has been the primary
driver of regional stock gains, is in no danger of ebbing, he said.



Citing recent market intervention by the Monetary Authority of
Singapore and the Bank of Korea to depress their local currencies, Yeo
said the moves suggest fund flows into Asia remain strong.



"I believe liquidity will be here, and going forward that will be
supported by earnings growth," he said. "So, we're fairly optimistic on
Asian markets."



Gains are likely to remain broad-based, Yeo said, but as individual
markets are at different stages of reform, he said he especially favors
the stock markets of South Korea, Singapore and Thailand.



The restructuring process has been most prominent in South Korea,
where the paid-up capital of many companies has doubled this year, and
where the stock market is at a 40-month high, Yeo said.



South Korea, blazing the trail for markets in the region, is up around
78% so far this year. Singapore's Straits Times Index is up about 55%,
and Thailand has gained around 40%.



While the gains seem unusually steep, and may suggest further
increases will be hard to come by, Yeo suggested there's still room for
the markets to climb given the return of investor confidence.



"You must keep the market's rise in perspective," he said. "The
markets were very oversold; they were disliked and disowned. But, there
has been a drastic change in sentiment."

title: Asian  Currencies  -3: Position-Squaring Saps Baht, Peso
text:
Purchases of the U.S. currency against the baht by U.S. and European banks that went short the U.S. dollar last week were blamed for depressing the Thai currency to its lowest level since early June. 

 The banks moved to exit their trades after the U.S. dollar held firm above Y122 and after Wednesday's admission by the Monetary Authority of Singapore that it had intervened to support the U.S. currency against the Singapore dollar. 

 "They saw the baht wasn't going to go very far and so they covered their positions, pushing the dollar higher," explained the head trader at a Thai bank. 

 Late in Asian trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at 37.0400 baht, up from THB36.8850 the day before. With dollar selling interest seen emerging from Bangkok at the dollar's highs for the day, dealers said the U.S. currency would struggle to climb above THB37.10 in the near term. 

 Continued position-squaring was also behind the weakening of the Philippine peso, as the currency dropped to its lowest level since early April. 

 Traders said foreign investors who had bought the peso for its high yield have exited their positions as successive interest-rate cuts in the Philippines and last week's U.S. interest-rate hike have narrowed the positive carry available on the peso. 

 At the close of local trading Thursday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at 38.440 pesos, up from PHP38.300 the day before.

 About 0145 GMT (9:45 p.m. EDT Wednesday), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6987, up from S$1.6960 in late Wednesday trade in Asia. 

 "The dollar-yen is firmly above Y122 and this is exerting some influence" on the Singapore dollar a dealer at a U.S. bank said.

 Singapore's benchmark Straits Times Index tumbled 1.4% Wednesday, correcting from a rally last week that had pushed shares to their all-time highs. 

 Stock market bullishness had lent support to the local dollar, and so its retreat helped drag it down, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the market is also still smarting from the acknowledged intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which stepped into the currency markets late Tuesday to quell excessive Singapore dollar strength. 

 "The market was caught very long on Singapore dollars," the dealer at a U.S. bank said. "There's some position adjusting." 

 He said that although these factors were conspiring to weaken the Singapore dollar Thursday, the medium-term outlook is for a bullish Singapore dollar.

title: ASIA MARKETS- Currencies  ease, KOSPI breaches 1,000.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - Most Asian markets were in a 

 consolidation mode on Wednesday, as currencies finished 

 slightly weaker and stocks wilted toward the end of trade. 

     KOSPI ENDS ABOVE 1,000, FIRST IN NEARLY FOUR YEARS 

     But South Korea's KOSPI went against the region's easier 

 trend, closing above 1,000 points for the first time in 45 

 months. 

     Brokers said retail fund buying prompted institutions to 

 load up on stocks. 

     Analysts said it could take some time before the index 

 settles comfortably above 1,000. Some expect it to consolidate 

 before firming further. 

     The central bank said it expected the economy to grow an 

 average 6.8 percent year-on-year in 1999 and 7.2 percent in the 

 second half. 

     The outlook was even more bullish than the Ministry of

Finance and Economy's recent forecast of five to six percent 

 growth year-on-year for both periods. 

     "If (Koreans) continually revise their growth figures, 

 they're also going to have to expect to intervene more 

 frequently in the market as people become more bullish about 

 the economy," said Andrew Dermot-Fung, treasury economist at 

 Standard Chartered. 

 The won extended its losses as interbank operators bought 

 dollars to meet new foreign exchange loan-loss provisioning 

 rules. 

 The government has directed local banks to complete 

 building up the provisions by the end of September, three 

 months earlier than scheduled. 

SINGAPORE DOLLAR WEAKER, WARY OF INTERVENTION

 The Singapore dollar was still weaker after the central 

 bank intervened on Tuesday to curb its rise. 

 In its annual report on the economy the central bank said 

 prospects for the second half of the year onwards were good, 

 but also warned it was too early to conclude it was "totally 

 out of the woods." 

     "Major uncertainties lie ahead," said an official in the 

 annual report. 

     The comment followed an earlier statement by the deputy 

 prime minister that the government would make an upward 

 revision to its 1999 GDP growth forecast, since the economy was 

 growing faster than expected. 

 Standard Chartered's Dermot-Fung said the Monetary 

 Authority of Singapore was doing well in taking a cautious 

 stance on economic outlook. 

 "One of the things that we are seeing in regional equity 

 markets is that retail investors are being very optimistic," he 

 said. 

 "It seems to reflect a view that once the recovery is in 

 place, we will get back to very strong growth levels. And 

 clearly that is not going to be the case and I think MAS is 

 actually doing well by trying to tone down people's expectatons 

 of what the economy will look like in the post-crisis era." 

 Singapore shares fell although brokers said there was no 

 specific news that could have led to the fall, except for 

 on-going talk of credit curbs on retail punters. 

 TAIWAN TRADE FIGURES BOOST SHARES 

 Stronger than expected June trade figures lifted Taiwan 

 stocks, wiping out early losses on recent credit-tightening 

 moves. The index closed 0.18 percent higher at 8,470.07. 

 Taiwan's June exports were up 8.2 percent year-on-year, and 

 imports were a solid 5.2 percent higher after several months of 

 flat of negative year-on-year change. 

     Both figures exceeded market expectations, giving off 

 strong signs of recovery. 

     THAI FINANCIAL SHARES PULL DOWN INDEX 

     Thailand's stock index weakened as downward momentum and 

 worries about the financial sector induced more selling. 

     Brokers said rumours that the government may close down 

 more ailing finance companies were used as an excuse to take 

 profits from recent gains in the financial sector.
