title: FOCUS-S'pore MAS narrows  FX  band,upbeat on economy.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said economic prospects were positive for the second half of 1999 and beyond, adding it would revert to a pre-crisis forex rate policy band as regional currency volatility had died down. 

 "Prospects for a sustained economic recovery into the second half of 1999 and beyond are good," MAS managing director Koh Yong Guan said at the release of the central bank's annual report on Wednesday. 

 "The external environment is expected to be favourable and the policy measures taken in 1998 in response to the economic slowdown are beginning to take effect," he said. 

 The typically conservative central bank warned, however, that Singapore's economy was not totally "out of the woods" as major uncertainties lay ahead. 

 "There are risk factors to watch out for, particularly a sharp correction in the U.S. stock market, a weakening of the Japanese yen, and rising protectionist pressures," Koh said in the report. 

 Koh declined to peg any levels for Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate for the year, but said economic data indicated that a revision of government forecasts slated for August would likely be a change "on the upside". 

 Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, also chairman of the central bank, said in parliament on Tuesday that the economy was recovering faster than expected and the government would revise the growth forecast in August, when full economic results for the second quarter became available. 

 The government's 1999 GDP forecast currently sees growth of between zero to two percent, but some economists told Reuters the actual figure could be as high as four percent for the year. 

 Koh added that the central bank, which broadened the trading band for the Singapore dollar last year in response to the Asian financial crisis, would return the band to the pre-crisis width. 

 He said the move was not an indication by the central bank that it would tolerate a stronger Singapore dollar but was more in response to the stabilising of currency markets. 

 "The widening of the band last year did allow for a greater appreciation of the Singapore dollar than would otherwise have been the case..., conversely it cannot be that narrowing of the band is aimed at the strengthening of the Singapore dollar," said MAS Deputy Managing Director Tharman Shanmugaratnam. 

 Singapore does not publish information about the band. 

 MAS officials, traditionally tight-lipped about the bank's action in forex markets, confirmed on Wednesday that the central bank had stepped into the market on Tuesday to dampen a surge in the Singapore currency against its U.S. counterpart. 

 "Just as we intervened on the downside last year when people were unduly pessimistic, so too we have to intervene on the upside," said Yeo Lian Sim, MAS assistant managing director of capital markets. 

 At 0705 GMT on Wednesday, the Singapore dollar was trading at 1.6967/77 to the U.S. unit. It reached a high of 1.6870 in thin overnight trading, a high not seen since mid-April. 

 Koh said MAS was maintaining its current neutral exchange rate policy stance as the Singapore economy was "still operating below potential" and the inflation outlook was benign. 

 "At the moment the economy is recovering nicely so we have set a neutral policy path," said Khor Hoe Ee, the central bank's senior executive director, economics. 

 "But once the economy has recovered fully and it seems to be overheating then we of course have to react, but we don't see that as a risk at the moment." 

 The central bank had said in its report that overall consumer price index inflation was expected to be zero percent in 1999.

title: MAS move to delay, not defeat Singapore dollar rise.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar ignored a rare admission by local authorities on Wednesday that they had intervened and the market is convinced the currency will soon head higher. 

 Analysts said the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) confirmation of its intervention would discourage players from pushing the local dollar up too abruptly, but it showed limited downside given gains in regional currencies. 

 "With growth and inflation returning to positive territory and the rapid stock market turnaround threatening to fuel more consumer price gains, the argument for a depreciating Sing dollar is rapidly deteriorating," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas. 

 The Singapore dollar stood at 1.6968/78 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade, little changed from its early levels after the MAS knocked it from an overnight high of 1.6870. 

 The MAS said it had stepped in on Tuesday to curb the Singapore dollar's gains because the speed of its rise was unwarranted and seemed at risk of getting ahead of the economy. 

 It rose sharply on Tuesday after the government said the economy was recovering faster than expected. 

 The Singapore currency has strengthened less than three percent from its 1999 trough of 1.7390 to the U.S. dollar, compared with gains of 3.5 percent to 40 percent in other Asian currencies. 

 Even the stolid Taiwan dollar, which is frequently reined in by its central bank, has gained 3.5 percent from its year low of 33.72 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Singapore and Taiwan compete closely in export markets. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar was likely to trade in a 1.69-1.70 range for the time-being, with a raft of offshore dollar offers above 1.70 limiting its declines. 

 "Offshore players who are unwinding some of their carry trades have good interest to sell (dollars) above 1.7000," said a senior regional currencies trader at a European bank. 

 The Singapore dollar has been under pressure as traders took advantage of low domestic interest rates to use it as a funding tool for carry trades, positioning themselves long Philippine peso/short Sing for instance. 

 But Thio at Paribas said such trades now looked less attractive as interest rates were on the decline throughout Asia. 

 "These are slowly being reversed. And because the Sing dollar has been a laggard in terms of appreciation, it could now perform better than the others," she said. 

 Analysts said the intervention appeared aimed at slowing the pace of the Sing dollar's rise, rather than trying to reverse it. 

 Thio said a target of 1.6850 remained intact for the near term, and the Sing dollar should strengthen to 1.65 further down the road. 

 The MAS also said it would now tighten its exchange rate bands to levels it maintained before the Asian crisis sparked huge volatility in currency markets. 

 Singapore maintains a tight currency regime, managing its exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of currencies and within a band. It does not publish information about the basket or the band. 

 Analysts said the decision to narrow the band suggested greater confidence in the stability of financial markets, but added that it could also be a warning that more intervention was likely. 

 "While there is the expectation that the recovery process is in place and that is helping to dampen volatility, there are still some major risks out there," said Andrew Dermot-Fung, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. 

 "They have brought (the band) back to pre-crisis levels, which would suggest that they have a slightly increased tendency to intervene in the market if volatility does not die down," Fung told Reuters Television.

title: FOCUS-S'pore economic recovery prospects good - MAS.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - Singapore's central bank said on Wednesday prospects for the domestic economy in the second half of the year onwards were good, but it was too early to conclude it was "totally out of the woods." 

 "Major uncertainties lie ahead," Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) managing director Koh Yong Guan said in the bank's annual report, released on Wednesday. 

 "There are risk factors to watch out for, particularly a sharp correction in the U.S. stock market, a weakening of the Japanese yen and rising protectionist pressures," he said. 

 The robustness of the U.S. economy, signs of recovery in Japan and an increase in production and exports from many crisis-hit economies were encouraging signs, the bank said. 

 Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, who is also MAS chairman, said on Tuesday the government would revise its 1999 gross domestic product growth forecast in August as the economy was growing faster than expected. 

 The official forecast is for growth of zero to two percent. The economy grew at 1.2 percent during the first quarter. 

 "Prospects for a sustained economic recovery into the second half of 1999 and beyond are good," Koh said in a statement. 

 "The external environment is expected to be favourable and the policy measures taken in 1998 in response to the economic slowdown are beginning to take effect," he said. 

 In its outlook for the economy, the MAS said there were signs that some sectors were bottoming out but cautioned that recovery was not across the board and that downside risk was apparent in industrialised nations and those emerging from the crisis. 

 The MAS said it remained vigilant on the Singapore dollar and confirmed that it had intervened to curb a rise in its value against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday. 

 "It seemed the (currency's) move was not warranted and it seemed the speed of the movement was going ahead of the economy," Yeo Laim Sim, MAS assistant managing director of capital markets, told reporters. 

 She said further action would depend on moves in the foreign exchange markets and their impact on the trade-weighted basket of currencies against which MAS manages the Singapore dollar. 

 The Singapore dollar was traded at 1.6900 to the U.S. dollar late on Tuesday, compared with 1.6970 a day earlier. At 0550 GMT on Wednesday, it was traded at 1.6970/80. 

 The bank said it would tighten its exchange rate bands to levels it had maintained before Asia's economic crisis struck. Koh did not disclose details of the bands. 

 Last year, MAS eased its exchange rate policy to cushion the economy from the crisis and facilitate recovery. Since early this year, the trade-weighted value of the Singapore dollar has been back at pre-crisis levels. 

 The MAS said it would ensure exchange rate policy remained conducive to a sustained non-inflationary recovery. It maintained its inflation forecast for 1999 at zero percent.

title: MAS confirms  intervention  to curb S'pore dollar.
text:
SINGAPORE - July 7 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Wednesday the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday to curb the rise of the Singapore dollar. 

 "Yes, we have intervened, just as we intervened on the downside last year when people were unduly pessimistic, so to we have to intervene on the upside," said Yeo Lian Sim, MAS assistant managing director of capital markets. 

 "It seemed the move (in the currency) was not warranted and it seemed the speed of the movement was going ahead of the economy," Yeo told a news conference. 

 She declined to give details on the extent of the intervention. 

 Yeo said further action would depend on moves in the foreign exchange markets and their impact on the trade weighted basket of currencies against which the Monetary Authority manages the Singapore dollar. 

 MAS officials added that they were not concerned about the value of the yen against the U.S. dollar. 

 The Bank of Japan has been intervening sharply to keep yen strength on a tight leash, as the currency has been buoyed by signs of domestic economic recovery in Japan. 

 "We are all very comfortable with the yen at its current exchange rate," Khor Ho Eee, senior executive director of economics at the MAS, told reporters.

title: Singapore  Dlr Dn Late After Tue  Intervention , Quiet Wed
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is lower late Wednesday compared with a day earlier, after the Monetary Authority of Singaporeintervened during Tuesday's European session, then admitted the intervention Wednesday. 

 About 0920 GMT (5:20 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6960, up from S$1.6880 late Tuesday in Asia just ahead of the intervention, but down from its overnight peak of S$1.7005. 

 The rare admission Wednesday and the unusually late market action Tuesday kept the Singapore dollar in a tight trading range during Wednesday's Asian session. 

 The MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, said Wednesday it bought U.S. dollars Tuesday to stem excessive Singapore dollar strength. Yeo Liam Sim, MAS assistant managing director for capital markets, wouldn't reveal the size of the purchases, but said it was "sufficient" to serve its purpose. 

 "We intervened, and we consider that we did a good job yesterday," Yeo said. 

 Traders and analysts said the intervention indicates the MAS is not likely to allow the U.S. dollar to fall below S$1.69, and was also a reaction to obvious speculative positions being built up. 

 The intervention triggered short covering by players betting the Singapore dollar would appreciate, especially as the economic outlook brightened. 

 Market participants are wary of testing the MAS resolve again, and the U.S. dollar is seen caught in a narrow range of about S$1.6960 to S$1.6990. 

 Adding to the sense of caution, the MAS also said Wednesday it was switching to a narrower exchange rate policy band, suggesting it would tolerate less fluctuation of the local currency when measured against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 While the switch will still allow the Singapore dollar to shift in line with other regional currencies, it could make the MAS quicker to intervene if it feels the currency's moves aren't supported by fundamentals, watchers said. 

 On the local money market, the interbank overnight rate was offered at 1.750%, up from 0.875% late Tuesday in Asia, while the three-month rate was offered at 1.8125%, up from 1.6825% late Tuesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down On  Intervention , Position Squaring
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Intervention, the threat of intervention and position liquidation combined to drive Asian currencies lower against the U.S. dollar during local trading hours Wednesday. 

 Although most observers retain their fundamentally positive outlook on Asia's economic recovery, foreign exchange dealers are becoming less sure that improving growth prospects will translate into further short-term currency appreciation. 

 Sentiment towards the Singapore dollar took an especially hard knock after the Monetary Authority of Singapore made a rare admission, confirming it had intervened in the foreign exchange market late Tuesday to weaken the local currency. 

 Elsewhere, the authorities in South Korea reiterated their determination to rein in the appreciation of the won, driving that currency sharply lower. 

 Fears that the Bank of Thailand may follow the example of the MAS and the Bank of Korea and enter the market to buy U.S. dollars helped to push the baht down, although the baht found firm support at the floor of its recent range. 

 The Philippine peso was sold off too, although dealers attributed that move to the continued liquidation of long positions in the local currency in reaction to narrowing interest rate spreads.

title: Asian  Currencies  Open Dn;  Intervention  By MAS Suspected
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies have opened down against the U.S. dollar early Wednesday, following what brokers believe to have been overnight intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

title: Singapore Dollar Higher Early, Watching For MAS Action
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is higher in early Asian trading Tuesday, but a sharp move is unlikely as the market remains wary of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 About 0100 GMT (9 p.m. Monday EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6940, down from S$1.6990 late Monday in Asia. 

 Continued economic optimism and a generally bullish stock market have given the local currency an upward bias, but at these levels, traders are watching for signs that MAS will step in to cap the Singapore dollar's strength. 

 Traders also report foreign banks selling U.S. dollars in early Tuesday action, putting more upward pressure on the Singapore dollar. 

 "I think MAS will be in somewhere on the low side of S$1.69," a trader at an Asian bank in Singapore said. "It is probably the only country in the world that is trying to discourage people from taking up the stock market and strengthening the currency." 

 Although Singapore officials have repeatedly denied using the currency as a trade tool, the market believes MAS is working to keep the Singapore dollar from strengthening too much and eroding the country's export competitiveness. 

 Also, officials have stressed that while there are signs of recovery, the country is not yet in the clear, and belt-tighening measures taken to counter last year's recession must stay in place. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong repeated this message in a magazine interview released Tuesday in which he says the local stock rally has overstated the recovery. 

 The Singapore dollar's strength is seen capped around S$1.6930 to the U.S. dollar Monday, while orders should hold any weakness to around S$1.6980, traders said.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Take Fed move in their stride.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 2 (Reuters) - Asian markets welcomed on 

 Thursday the U.S. Fed's decision to implement a small rate hike 

 and move to a neutral stance on future policy, but their 

 attention was quickly focused on bullish domestic developments. 

     The Asian markets' reaction was also muted by holidays in 

 Hong Kong and Taiwan -- two of the most U.S. interest 

 rate-sensitive markets in Asia -- and in Thailand. 

     KOREA'S RECOVERY ACCELERATES, STOCKS CELEBRATE 

     South Korea outperformed the region once again, helped by the 

 U.S. interest rate move, positive economic news and a decision by 

 one of the big chaebol to seek receivership for an unprofitable 

 auto unit. 

     Seoul's KOSPI closed at a 37-month high of 919.98 points, up 

 4.19 percent on the day. 

     South Korea said it expected the economy to maintain healthy 

 growth of five to six percent year-on-year in the second half of 

 1999 and for the whole of 1999. 

     In its second-half policy review, the Ministry of Finance and 

 Economy also forecast GDP would expand seven percent in the 

 second quarter after posting a 4.6 percent rise in the first 

 quarter. 

 The ministry predicted the country's consumer price index 

 (CPI) would rise about two percent year-on-year in 1999, against 

 7.5 percent the previous year. 

 "The CPI will rise more or less in the second half on the 

 back of the economic recovery, but for the year it is forecast to 

 stabilise at around two percent," the ministry said. 

 It also said South Korea's total external liabilities were 

 projected to fall below $139 billion by the end of 1999, after 

 payments on $10 billion to $14 billion worth of loans were made 

 during the year. 

 News that Samsung was willing to seek receivership for its 

 debt laden auto unit rather than sell it to the Daewoo Group was 

 also seen an encouraging sign of chaebol restructuring. 

 KOREAN WON SET TO STRENGTHEN 

 In the currency market the central bank was not sighted on 

 Thursday after Wednesday's buying of dollars, but analysts said 

 the positive economic number would see the won head higher. 

 "We could well see the Korean won breach the 1,150 level," 

 said Daniel Lian, Asian strategist at Barclays Capital in 

Singapore. 

 "The Bank of Korea is already poised to intervene at this 

 level, and in the last three or four days they are able to 

 convince the market not to test the level. 

     "But I think further down the road we could see Korean won 

 trading below the 1,150 level," Lian said. 

     SINGAPORE SHARES ROCKET TO NEW HIGHS 

     Singapore's red-hot share market closed up 2.17 percent, at a 

 new record finish of 2,214.75, breaking through significant 

 resistance around 2,200. 

     The close broke a week-old record and is being attributed to 

 the return in massive numbers of small retail investors. 

     MALAYSIA POSTS ANOTHER BIG TRADE SURPLUS 

     Malaysia completed a 19-month streak of consecutive trade 

 surpluses when it released May numbers. These revealed a surplus 

 of 6.4 billion ringgit with January to May imports up 3.2 percent 

 and import levels still down 5.2 percent over the same period. 

     "Export growth is robust. Import growth has been constrained, 

 so overall the trade picture is very bullish," Lian said. 

     Malaysian shares did well on the news, ending up 2.98 percent 

 at 835.31.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed; Fed Move Seen Broadly Positive
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies had a mixed day Thursday. Although the Singapore dollar pushed up through a key resistance level in response to renewed investment flows into the local stock market, both the South Korean won and the Indonesian rupiah ended Asian trading hours weaker. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to raise its federal funds target rate by 25 basis points had little impact on trading, as this rise had long been discounted by regional markets. Less widely expected, however, was the Fed's subsequent reversion to a neutral monetary policy bias - a development interpreted as broadly positive for Asian currencies. 

 "Market sentiment favors stronger regional currencies. Flows into local stock markets should cap the dollar," a trader at a U.S. bank in Singapore said. 

 The Singapore dollar benefited the most from this effect Thursday, as sales of the U.S. dollar by local banks pushed the U.S. currency below the S$1.7000 level at which many dealers had expected the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene to weaken the local currency. 

 A trader at a Singapore bank indicated that the MAS had shifted its sights, and that support would now emerge at around S$1.6950, although a further U.S. dollar selloff is probable in European trading hours. 

 Late in Asian trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6975, down from S$1.7003 Wednesday.

title: Singapore Dlr Choppy Late; Brunei Report Damps Fed Move
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar fidgeted sharply in late Thursday trade in Asia, but remained stronger compared with levels a day earlier. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve's decision Wednesday to return to a neutral monetary stance form a tightening bias has given the Singapore currency strength against the U.S. dollar by deflating any immediate hope of further rate cuts in the U.S. 

 However, that sentiment was buffeted in midafternoon trading by a large corporate order to buy U.S. dollars, and news of a forthcoming report by Asiaweek magazine that Brunei's foreign reserves have almost been deleted. 

 About 0800 GMT (4 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.6975, down from S$1.7003 in late Asian trade Wednesday. About an hour earlier, it had peaked momentarily at S$1.7047. 

 Traders said the spike was caused by an order from a Singapore-based company to buy U.S. dollars and by news of the upcoming magazine report on Brunei. 

 Asiaweek reportedly estimates in this week's edition that Brunei's foreign reserves have fallen to US$5 billion from US$30 billion. A summary of the story was released ahead of publication. 

 "Brunei stories always effect Singapore, but it's kind of a muted effect," one trader said, noting the Singapore dollar movement was relatively small. 

 Brunei and Singapore have pegged their dollars at parity since 1967 by mutual agreement, and bad economic news for Brunei tends to put pressure on the Singapore dollar. 

 Although the market is watching out for intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore at these levels, traders said there is so far no sign of the authority moving to curb Singapore dollar strength.

title: Asian  Currencies  Little Changed But Sentiment Strong
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Most Asian currencies ended little changed against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, as expectations of an increase in U.S. interest rates damped activity in local markets. 

 Although the majority of analysts and traders believe a 25-basis point rise in the U.S. federal funds rate target is unlikely to have a significant impact on Asian economies, dealers still trimmed back open positions in the regional currencies just in case the Federal Reserve surprised them. 

 Underlying sentiment toward the regionals remains strong, however, and most traders expect further local currency appreciation in the second half of the year. 

 The growing belief that regional economic recovery is gathering steam helped push the Singapore dollar slightly higher Wednesday. 

 Although the Singapore currency's gains were moderate - the market didn't test the S$1.7000 level at which traders believe the Monetary Authority of Singapore is prepared to intervene to support the U.S. dollar - many dealers believe the local currency is set to rise further over the longer term. 

 "I favor the (U.S. dollar's) downside from here," said the head of foreign exchange trading at one of Singapore's big four banks. "The range is intact for the moment, but if the economic data continues to come in positive, it will confirm that Singapore is getting out of the woods and we should see the Singapore dollar strengthen." 

 After recent data releases showed a 16.4% increase in manufacturing output and a 15.5% rise in non-oil domestic exports for May, the chance the Singapore dollar will weaken is "limited" according to the Singapore bank trading chief, who said the U.S. currency would find a solid ceiling at S$1.71. 

 Late Wednesday in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7003, down from S$1.7044 toward the end of Asian trading hours the previous day.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Asia balancing act,Europe quiet.
text:
LONDON, June 23 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies kept up their balancing act on Wednesday, caught between investor bullishness and central bank concern over exports. 

 Central European currencies were quiet, with the Polish zloty tipped to test resistance at five percent above its basket parity and the Czech crown becalmed ahead of Thursday's central bank board meeting. 

 Most Asian currencies were slightly softer from late New York levels, with central banks divided on how to cope with the regionals' recent surge. 

 The Bank of Korea intervened again to buy dollar/won, and analysts said there was talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to curb Singapore dollar strength. 

 But the baht hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Bank of Thailand said it would not intervene to restrain the currency's rise. 

 "Their currencies are strengthening to the extent that some are definitely starting to impinge on export growth, or even cause export contraction," said Callum Henderson, emerging market currency strategist at Citibank in London. 

 "They seem to be trying to intervene and as a result continuing to offer the market good opportunities to sell into any rallies." 

 But he noted that Taiwan's central bank stopped intervening to damp down the Taiwan dollar a couple of weeks ago, and was now acting only to smooth out market moves. 

 "You could argue that one by one the Asian central banks have seen the writing on the wall and are giving up," he said. 

 Analysts said emerging Asian currencies were still showing little correlation with movements in dollar/yen, which firmed back through 122 in the London morning. 

 "This is largely a reflection of the strength of Asian currencies, and the underlying demand for them," analysts at Banque Paribas said in a briefing note. 

 "As authorities' confidence in the economic recovery improves, gradual currency strength will be tolerated." 

 The won was slightly weaker on the day after the Bank of Korea waded back in to buy an estimated $350 million. 

 The baht also lost some ground after rating agency Moody's slammed Thai banks, saying the sector was still in deep crisis. The Philippine peso tracked the baht lower, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah tried to press on towards 6,500 to the dollar but got stuck around 6,700 as profit-taking trimmed earlier gains, despite upbeat comments by central bank Governor Syahril Sabirin that he would be happy with a stable range of 6,000-6,500. 

 In Europe, the zloty edged up to around 4.8 percent above its basket parity from Tuesday's 4.7 percent. 

 Analysts said the currency, which has gained two percentage points against the basket in June alone, would soon test five percent amid expectations that the $1 billion privatisation of Pekao bank would bring in large foreign inflows. 

 Data showing Poland's gross domestic product grew by 1.5 percent in the first quarter of the year had no immediate impact on the currency. Analysts said the figures were close to expectations and were already discounted.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Won off on  intervention , rupiah gains.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 23 (Reuters) - Regional currencies shrugged 

 off the yen's softer bias on Wednesday, while the South Korean 

 won was dragged to a lower close on intervention aimed at 

 protecting South Korean exports. 

     Asian shares finished mixed. Singapore shares gained more 

 than two percent and Korean shares nearly one and a half 

 percent, while Thailand and Taiwan shares declined by more than 

 one percent. 

     KOREAN WON CLOSES WEAKER ON LAST MINUTE INTERVENTION

     The South Korean won finished weaker against the dollar 

 after verbal and physical intervention by the central bank. 

     Dealers said the Bank of Korea stepped in to buy dollars at 

 both the opening and the closing of trade. The won finished at 

 1,162.8, compared with Tuesday's 1,159.4. 

     A finance ministry official said the government would take 

 steps to rein in the won, saying its appreciation was 

 undesirable when the yen was continuing to depreciate against 

 the dollar. 

     Catherine Tan, managing analyst for Asian currency at 

 Thomson Global Markets in Singapore, said the intervention

 would not likely have a lasting effect. 

     "Eventually the government is not going to win the fight 

 against the market sentiment due to the huge influx of funds," 

 she said. 

     A weaker yen is perceived to be a potential threat to 

 Korea's export manufacturers, as it would boost Japan's export 

 competitiveness. 

     RUPIAH HEADED EVEN STRONGER, SAYS INDONESIAN C.BANKER 

     The Indonesian rupiah continued to shine after yesterday's 

 move through 7,000, inching towards 6,500 to the dollar as 

 overseas money continued to flow in. 

Central bank governor Syahril Sabirin told reporters that 

 the rupiah could strengthen to 6,000 to the dollar, saying he 

 would be happy with a stable range of 6,000 to 6,500. 

     "I cannot predict what the level is, but the possibility 

 for strengthening is there," he said before a meeting with 

 President B.J. Habibie. 

     "We have calculated that the level of 6,000-6,500 is okay 

 for exports," he said. 

     MALAYSIAN Q1 GDP EXPECTED TO SHOW CONTRACTION 

     Malaysian first quarter GDP, due at 1030 GMT, is expected 

 to show a contraction of 1.6 percent year-on-year in the first 

 quarter. 

     Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on June 9 that GDP 

 shrank by that amount, but that GDP was likely to expand in the 

 second quarter. 

     But even the first quarter GDP growth figure given by the 

 prime minister would compare favourably with the 8.10 percent 

 contraction in the final quarter of last year. 

     TAIPEI STOCK RALLY HALTS, CURRENCY DEALERS SIDELINED 

     Taiwan released unemployment figures for May, which showed 

 a 2.84 percent rate, up from April's 2.75 percent. The rise was 

 sharper than most market expectations. 

     An official said the June jobless rate may be even higher, 

 and might exceed three percent in July and August before easing 

 back in September. 

     But he said that since unemployment numbers were a lagging 

 indicator, the latest figures should not be interpreted as a 

 negative sign for the country's economic recovery. 

     Taipei shares finished lower for the first time in four 

 days, as profit-taking in the heavily weighted electronics 

 sector halted the market's rally. 

     The Taiwan dollar closed unchanged, with investors stepping 

 to the sidelines as they detected some central bank moves to 

 limit its upside.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late, Won Resumes Downward Trend
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, with the South Korean won resuming its downward spiral after a two-day pause. 

 Persistently high oil prices, which hit a 10-year peak overnight, a slide in the Korean stock market and lingering concerns over the fallout of Ford Motor Co.'s aborted bid for Daewoo Motor conspired to push the won lower, dealers said. 

 Concerns over high oil prices also contributed to the Thai and Philippine currencies' descent to fresh lows since 1998, when the countries were mired in the regional financial crisis. 

 Bucking the region's weakness, the Singapore dollar and the New Taiwan dollar were slightly firmer. The Indonesian rupiah was little changed. 

 In the South Korean market, the dollar rose to 1,128.10 won from Wednesday's close of KRW1,124.80, ending the won's two-day rebound. The dollar jumped to an intraday high of KRW1,131.80 at the start of trading. 

 After tumbling to a 16-week closing low Monday on the Daewoo fiasco, currency watchers are betting that the won could weaken further toward KRW1,140 to KRW,1,150 against the dollar in coming weeks. 

 The scuttled Daewoo deal has aroused concerns over whether this would hurt foreign capital inflows into South Korea, analysts said. 

 But analysts are preserving their longer-term bullish forecasts on the won, amid expectations of a gradual shift to a tighter monetary policy and the country's strong balance-of-payment position. 

 "I'm not looking for excessive weakness in the won," said Chi Lo, regional head of research and senior economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 Chi said while he expects the dollar to hover around KRW1,130 at the end of the year, it will likely fall to KRW1,045 in 12 months' time. 

 The Thai currency recovered slightly after hitting a 27-month low of 42.77 baht to the dollar in early trading. Strong onshore dollar demand; spiking oil prices and mounting political anxieties ahead of the country's general elections, expected to take place in the fourth quarter, helped extend the baht's recent losses, dealers said. 

 Despite dollar profit-taking and exporter selling of the U.S. currency, onshore demand for dollars remained solid as most corporates and state enterprises need to meet their debt repayment ahead of the Thai fiscal year-end and Japanese half-year book closing, dealers said. 

 Reported remarks by a cabinet minister that the authorities may resort to short-term market intervention to prop up the baht if it is "unusually volatile" kept a reinon the baht's decline. 

 But few market participants took the nebulous warning too seriously, especially since recent remarks by senior officials suggested that the authorities are likely to tolerate the baht's current weakness. 

 Abhisit Vejjajiva, a minister in the Prime Minister's Office, was quoted as saying that the central bank would likely adjust its policy if the exchange rate were to hurt inflation and economic growth. 

 "It's not a very clear-cut statement," said a chief dealer at a European bank. 

 With no concrete signs of intervention by the central bank, most market pundits remained confident that the U.S. currency could strengthen to the psychologically important level THB43 as early as next week. 

 Tracking the baht's descent, the Philippine peso ended at a new 32-month closing low of PHP45.995 against the dollar, compared with PHP45.910 Wednesday. 

 For the first time since January 1998, the dollar muscled its way through the psychological resistance level of PHP46 to hit an intraday high of PHP46.04 in early trading. 

 Despite suspicions from some traders that the central bank lightly intervened over the morning, the authority insisted it wasn't in the market, and attributed the peso's losses to an "overreaction" to falls in other regional currencies, especially the baht. 

 Given the raft of problems that have been undermining the peso - including a ballooning budget deficit and waning confidence in President Joseph Estrada's administration - many dealers expect the peso to depreciate further to PHP46.50 to the dollar. 

 In Taipei, last-minute heavy central bank intervention salvaged the New Taiwan dollar, which had earlier in the day languished on demand for the U.S. currency from importers and the regional curreny markets' weakness, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$31.263, down from Wednesday's close of NT$31.274. 

 Profit-taking in the U.S. currency and fears of central bankintervention helped buoy the Indonesian rupiah and the Singapore dollar, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Baht Extends Fall
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The relentless fall in the Thai baht dragged most Asian currencies lower late Wednesday, as the respite in the region earlier in the day proved to be short-lived, dealers said. 

 Investors continued to fret about the extent of damage persistently high oil prices would have on the region's economic growth and inflation. 

 "The market is still trying to come to terms with how much high oil prices will hurt Asian markets," said Vasan Shridharan, a treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. "The three countries which will be most hurt are Thailand, the Philippines and Korea." 

 Indeed, worries about expensive oil prices continued to pressure the South Korean won. The won ended firmer, but it had relinquished most of its earlier gains, which were inspired by a Nasdaq-driven rebound on the Seoul bourse. 

 Elsewhere, central bank intervention countered the downward pressure from foreign fund outflows, helping keep the New Taiwan dollar steady. 

 In contrast, Southeast Asian central banks opted to stay on the sidelines as their currencies, led by the Thai baht, extended their southward trek, dealers said. 

 Dollar profit-taking by U.S. names earlier in the day had provided some reprieve for Southeast Asian currencies, but the grim political outlook in the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand continued to haunt the market, dealers said. Concerns over the effect of rising oil prices on the Thai and Philippine economies also cast a pall on the baht and the peso, respectively, they added. 

 The Thai baht's slide to its lowest level since late July, 1998, accelerated the fall in the currencies of its other Southeast Asian neighbors late Wednesday. 

 Comments by Thai central bank Assistant Governor Chetthavee Charoenpitaks late Wednesday that the local currency should be trading in a range of THB40 to THB42 to the dollar failed to deter participants from pushing it below the key THB42.50 support level. 

 With no mention of actual, or planned intervention in the foreign exchange market, the U.S. currency rose to as high as THB42.63, and was trading THB42.590 around 0900 GMT. 

 Despite Charoenpitaks' remarks, the Thai central bank is likely to tolerate the baht's current trading range, unless it weakens too sharply, said Standard Chartered Bank's Shridharan. 

 But "they'll be mindful of any one-way trajectory of the baht" and a rapid depreciation, which could hurt Thailand's debt servicing, he added. 

 With the baht remaining depressed below THB42.50 at the end of the Asian trading day, the dollar could rise "very quickly" to THB42.75 to THB42.80 this week, a Thai bank dealer said, adding that a break above those levels could propel it toward the next upside target of THB43.20. 

 In Manila, the dollar closed at a record closing high of 45.910 pesos on the spot market, up from Tuesday's close of PHP45.875. 

 The dollar is poised to test the psychological resistance level of PHP46 if the central bank doesn't show any sign of intervention, dealers said. The dollar had reached an intraday high of PHP45.950. 

 News that government forces rescued two French hostages held by Muslim rebels on Jolo island boosted the peso in early trading. But persisting domestic economic concerns which have undermined the peso for months - including worries over a ballooning budget deficit - subsequently overshadowed the good news. 

 The Indonesian currency slipped to 8,785 rupiah to the dollar, from IDR8,695 late Tuesday, as President Abdurrahman Wahid's decision to fire deputy commander of the Indonesian armed forces, Gen. Fachrul Razi, is expected to arouse further political controversy. The move came hot on the heels after Wahid sacked the national police chief Monday, following a bombing in the Jakarta Stock Exchange building last week which killed 15 people. 

 Unable to escape unscathed from the region's woes, the Singapore dollar weakened to S$1.7462 against the U.S. currency, from S$1.7455 late Tuesday. 

 The euro's fall to a fresh record low also weighed on the Singapore dollar, but fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore tempered the local currency's slide, dealers said. 

 The euro was trading at $0.8462 after hitting a new all-time low of $0.8465 in Asian trade Wednesday. 

 Elsewhere, the South Korean won ended higher, extending Tuesday's rebound, as the local stock market leapt 6.1% following the surge on the Nasdaq, dealers said. Dollar-buying in the non-deliverable forward market and short-covering in the U.S. currency by local and foreign banks had, however, wiped out most of the won's earlier gains, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,124.80 won, down from KRW1,125.80 Tuesday. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$31.274, barely changed from the previous close of NT$31.275. 

 Taiwan's central bank accounted for more than a quarter of the day's volume, which was valued at US$486.5 million, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Won Bears Brunt Of Sell Off
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won continued to lead the downward spiral in Asian currencies late Monday, as the bloodbath on the Seoul bourse and doubts on the country's debt restructuring efforts triggered a wave of panic selling in the local currency, dealers said. 

 Reflecting the international strength of the U.S. dollar, better-than-expected economic data out of Thailand and Singapore even failed to provide much reprieve for those local currencies, dealers said. 

 "It's not just the Asian currencies that are weak, but all the other emerging currencies as well," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. "The dollar is strong globally and oil prices are high, affecting many emerging markets." 

 Like the rest of the Asian currencies, the Thai baht and the Singapore dollar caved in to the gloom pervading the region's foreign exchange and stock markets. 

 The Thai currency collapsed below the psychologically-important support level of 42 baht against the dollar to hit a 25-month low. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency threatened to test the key S$1.7500 psychological resistance mark, but retreated on fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 The South Korean won felt the brunt of the selling frenzy in Asian foreign exchange markets, as the local stock market posted its second-biggest daily drop this year, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,131.40 won, up from Friday's close of KRW1,119.90 and its highest close since June 1, when it ended at KRW1,132. 

 The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index plunged 8.1% to end at 577.56, its lowest finish since March 10, 1999, when it ended at 569.27. 

 Ford Motor Co's announcement last Friday that it won't make a final bid for struggling Daewoo Motor continued to worry investors, as it cast doubts on South Korea's efforts to restructure its debt-ridden industries, market observers said. 

 Market sentiment was also bruised by escalating crude oil prices and falling dynamic random access memory chip prices, which have reinforced the bleak outlook for the semiconductor industry, dealers said. 

 The dollar had jumped to as high as KRW1,138 in intraday trading, but profit-taking in the U.S. currency and dollar-selling by exporters, especially after the stock market closed, helped the won recoup the bulk of its losses, dealers said. 

 "The won rebounded quite impressively, but the market is still shaky," said Suktae Oh, a Seoul-based economist at Salomon Smith Barney/Citibank. "The market will restore some of its stability, but at higher levels than maybe about two weeks ago." 

 The dollar will likely consolidate between KRW1,120 and KRW1,130 in the short term as panic-selling in the won dies down, said Suktae Oh. 


With the won's steep decline largely sentiment-driven, "everybody
would agree that this would not be a foreign exchange crisis," Oh said.

title: Rupiah rebounds, possible c.bank  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah rebounded in late trade on Thursday on speculation the central bank had intervened to prop up the ailing currency. 

 "We assume the central bank is selling dollars through the state banks," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 By 0930 GMT the local unit had clawed back to 8,565/8,595 against the dollar from 8,835/8,855 in early trade when it was still reeling from a massive car bomb explosion at the Jakarta stock exchange building that killed 15 people the day before. 

 Apart from some limited profit taking, dealers - who earlier tipped the market would test 9,000 against the dollar - otherwise struggled to explain the market's about turn. 

 "It must be due to central bank intervention...the only other reason is that Singapore has been very long dollars for the past three days and when the market started to turn they started selling," another dealer said. 

 "Now it will be fairly hard to touch 9,000," he added. 

 The market shrugged off news late on Thursday of more bomb threats made against key buildings in the capital. 

 State-owned Bank Mandiri told Reuters it received two threats after lunch. The Surabaya stock exchange office in Jakarta received four threats. 

 The market also paid no attention to the resumption of the graft trial of former President Suharto on Thursday. The former autocrat did not appear due to ill health. 

 Despite the rupiah's recovery, Wednesday's explosion, which was the latest in a series to hit key targets in the capital, is likely to further dent investor confidence. 

 Market sentiment has also been dampened by the murder of three U.N. aid workers in the West Timor border town of Atambua last week which has angered the international community.

 Fears the international community would isolate Indonesia if it fails to quell the violence in West Timor had also cast a shadow on the rupiah. 

 Earlier in the day, economics chief Rizal Ramli attributed the rupiah's losses to the diplomatic fallout from last week's killings of United Nations workers in West Timor and a weakening of regional currencies, adding that the weakness was temporary. 

 But the Indonesian currency won't likely find any respite in the short term, with many participants in Singapore betting that the beleaguered currency would spiral lower toward IDR8,800-IDR8,900, dealers said. Banks in Singapore were pushing the rupiah lower, they added. 

 And despite the looming threat of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the city-state's strong economic fundamentals, the Singapore dollar wasn't spared from the slump in the region. 

 The U.S. dollar climbed to S$1.7445, from S$1.7390 late Tuesday. The U.S. dollar is expected to face stiff resistance around S$1.7450, dealers said. Even if it breaks that level, stop-loss selling expected around S$1.7480 will likely curb the U.S. currency's rise, a European bank dealer said. 

 Despite the bearish undertone, some analysts warned against pushing the Singapore dollar and some of the other Southeast Asian currencies much lower at current levels. 

 "We are wary of the market getting too ahead of itself," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg, adding that any good news could prompt the market to liquidate their long dollar positions. 

 In Manila, intervention by the Philippine central bank limited the peso's losses. The dollar ended Wednesday at 45.69 pesos, up from PHP45.60 Tuesday. 

 Elsewhere, the New Taiwan dollar closed at an eight-month low, thanks to U.S. dollar-buying in the non-deliverable forward market and volatility on the local bourse, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$31.112, up from Monday's close of NT$31.095. Financial markets were closed Tuesday for a national holiday. Wednesday's finish was the lowest level since Dec. 30, 1999, when the New Taiwan dollar closed at NT$31.395.

title: Emerging  FX  - Trapped in ranges, eyeing rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 stuck in ranges in early Wednesday trade, feeling the 

 conflicting effects of the still strong yen and 

 lingering political concerns in Indonesia and the Philippines. 

     Most units were barely changed compared to levels seen late 

 the previous day, with only the rupiah looking vulnerable 

 around 8,380 per dollar. 

     Political and economic concerns also kept the peso within 

 arm's reach of recent 30-month lows. 

     The yen held firm around 106 per dollar on confidence 

 Japanese markets would benefit from continued growth in Japan. 

     Analysts said an a lower than expected 0.7 percent fall in 

 July industrial production month-on-month did not detract from 

 recovery hopes. 

     The spotlight trailed on the euro, sterling and Swiss 

 franc 

 after they slid against the dollar and yen overnight amid 

 speculation the European economy had passed its peak. 

 Sterling extended its losses in Tokyo trade, hitting a 

 seven year low against the dollar on expectations rates would 

 be kept on hold. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah recouped part of its early losses but remained 

 shaky amid caution towards the country's new economic team and 

 parliamentary probe into Wahid-linked scandals. 

 New chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said he had 

 indicated to IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer 

 some conditions in the current of intent might not be 

 applicable. 

 Ramli said the new government wanted to first study the 

 letter, signed on July 31, and that this was the reason Jakarta 

 had asked the IMF to postpone a board meeting this week. 

     The basis of the meeting was to be discussions for a new 

 cash injection for Indonesia. 

     Dealers said trade was thin and the mood volatile though 

 strong rupiah support was seen around 8,420 points. 

     Singapore's United Overseas Bank said in a research note it 

 advocated buying on dollar dips to 8,100/200. Its end-2000 

 target was 8,500 to 8,800 per dollar. 


    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso clung to levels of around 45 per dollar despite



news the economy had grown a faster-than-expected 4.5 percent



year-on-year in the second quarter.



    Dealers said the government's widening budget deficit and



concern over a Moslem insurgency in the south continued to dog



sentiment.



    In the spotlight was the latest kidnapping of an American



by Abu Sayyaf guerrillas who still hold six Europeans and a



Filipino hostage.



    Six Western hostages have been released by the rebels over



the last two days.



    Separately, the central bank said the better-than-expected



GDP data did not warrant cutting its widely watched overnight



borrowing rate which currently stands at 10 percent.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht dipped alongside the rupiah in early trade, with



onshore parties bidding actively for dollars.



    Dealers said the market seemed to have finally reacted to



news of the government allowing the state-owned power firm EGAT



to raise 5.3 billion baht from the local bond market to



refinance its foreign debt.



The move would further add pressure to the baht as the



company is expected to enter the market in the near future to



buy yen and dollars to repay its debt.



"They are unlikely to buy all in one go, and I doubt if



they have to cover the whole amount in the forex market. But



still, this is a big amount and it will definitely weigh on the



baht," said a dealer at a European bank.



On the macro front, the central bank will publish key



monthly economic data on Thursday and the Commerce Ministry



will release price data on Friday.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar lost some ground in early trade as



foreign names bid for the U.S. currency after the rupiah



faltered.



    The unit move in a narrow 1.7204-1.7220 band, with dealers



anticipating range-trade ahead.



    While the rupiah only makes up a small proportion of the



local unit's nominal effective exchange rate in terms of its



trade weighted index, sentiment can be affected due to



Singapore's strong trade and investment ties with Indonesia.



    Most analysts remain bullish on Singapore's economic



outlook, and expect a gradual appreciation of the currency.



    SEB Merchant Banking forecast in its latest report that the



Sing dollar would move to 1.69 by end-2000 and 1.63 by



mid-2001.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won flirted with a fresh 16-week closing high at the



open as dollars from exporters and foreigners keen to buy local



stocks filtered through.



    Seoul dealers said exporters were unloading dollars to meet



end-month won fund demands and that foreign investors were seen



buying into KOSPI stocks.



    Foreign investors have been net buyers of 1.5 trillion won



worth of Korea stocks so far this month.



    Despite a recent protest by some local and foreign dealers



against frequent central bank intervention, the authorities



were seen defending the 1,108 per dollar level.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar was underpinned by foreign fund inflows



and demand from local parties covering their month-end



positions.



    Players were reluctant to push the Taiwan dollar much lower



given the recent central bank intervention to shore up the



unit, dealers in Singapore said.



    On Tuesday, foreign funds bought a net T$719 million in



Taiwan stocks on Tuesday against net selling of T$172 million



on Monday.

title: Sing dlr extends gains despite  intervention  talk.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar extended gains in afternoon trade on Thursday, briefly piercing the key 1.7100 level despite talk the central bank was in the market to rein in its sharp appreciation. 

 Dealers said injured dollar bulls stumbled into the market to cover short Sing dollar positions after it was strongly boosted by robust growth data and the central bank's comment it saw the currency appreciating over the next 12 months. 

 "There were bouts of profit taking on the Sing dollar which helped slow down its pace...but only a bit. At one point, it breached 1.7100," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 "There are lots of stop-loss orders above that level. So, I reckon it would move much higher once the 1.7100 level is convincingly broken," he said. 

 At 0623 GMT, the Sing dollar was quoted around 1.7115/1.7125, its best levels since a May 2 high of 1.7085, according to Reuters Graphics data. 

 Singapore posted robust year-on-year GDP growth of 8.0 percent for the second quarter, bringing growth for the first half to 8.8 percent. 

 Some analysts said they did not see much further upside for the Sing dollar because the authorities were likely to step in to smooth sharp moves. 

 The U.S. dollar was also looking oversold against the Sing with a reading of 19.5 on the 14-day relative strength index, below the 30 oversold mark. 

 "The Sing dollar had been unjustifiably weak for a while because investors used it as a funding currency. Now a lot of them are being caught short," said Fong Cheng Hong, head of treasury research at DBS Bank in Singapore. 

 "But going forward, I think the pace of appreciation should slow down a bit. The rise is a bit overdone, and I wouldn't be surprised if the central bank comes in to smooth it out." 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore has said in the past that it does not comment on its market operations, but does intervene in forex markets to curb volatility.

title: POLL-Singapore dlr seen rising to 1.70 by end-2000.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar	  is



expected to rise to 1.70 against the U.S. dollar by end-2000


 and to 1.67 by the middle of next year, a Reuters poll showed 

 on Thursday. 

     But forecasts were wide ranging with the 10 economists 

 polled on the Sing dollar's outlook for this year seeing it 

 between 1.66 and 1.74. Six economists polled on its outlook in 

 mid-2001 expected it to be in a 1.63 to 1.70 range. 

     The Sing dollar, which had plummeted to 22-month lows 

 before comments from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) 

 last week that it would allow the currency to gradually 

 appreciate, has been steadily climbing. 

     It was off its highs by midday on Thursday after breaching 

 the 1.7280 technical barrier overnight. 

     At 0555 GMT, it was quoted at 1.7258/65. 

     In announcing its willingness to allow a stronger Sing 

 dollar, the MAS said consumer price inflation was expected to 

 edge up slightly to one to two percent over the next two years 

 as the labour market tightened and higher commodity prices 

 filtered through. 

 Cindy Chua, economist at Kay Hian, expected the central 

 bank comments to be realised by a currency appreciation to 1.71 

 by year-end, adding the US dollar in general would also lose 

 some of its recent strength. 

 But JP Morgan economist Tan Tzu Ping, who forecast an 

 end-2000 level of 1.73, said the MAS was only sending a signal 

 and actual upward pressure on the currency would not be coming 

 soon. 

     "You're likely not to see an immediate change. The comments 

 were a warning shot across the bow," he said. 

     The MAS intention to use the Singapore dollar to stamp out 

 inflationary sparks comes amid a still fragile Southeast Asian 

currency environment. 

     That climate was linked to a generally lower level seen for 

 the Singapore dollar at the end of the year and at mid-2001. 

     A similar poll taken on May 19 had produced average levels 

 of 1.66 and 1.64, respectively. 

     "Our 1.73 (forecast) does assess the region as more 

 volatile, and while these currencies are not heavily weighted 

 for the Sing... On the risk and policy side, there have been 

 negative repercussions," said Morgan's Tan. 

     Until the MAS comments, the market had believed Singapore

 authorities were relaxed about currency decline, and previous 

intervention had been seen as simply a smoothing exercise. 

     The strength of the U.S. unit against the yen and euro, all 

 believed to be in the undisclosed basket of trade-weighted 

currencies the MAS uses to manage the exchange rate, was also 

 seen as key to the Singapore dollar's performance, analysts 

 said. 

     The underlying good performance of the economy will also 

 tend to lend support to the local dollar. 

     "We are seeing some gradual firming of the Sing dollar 

 because the underlying economic fundamentals are still very 

 good," said Kaan Quan Hon, economist at DBS Securities.

title: Bk Indonesia's Nasution Denies Singapore Helping Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Acting Bank Indonesia Governor Anwar Nasution late Tuesday denied that Singapore authorities have sold dollars recently to help the rupiah. 

 Market participants said they had seen evidence that the Government Investment Corp., the Singapore government's investment arm, has been selling dollars for rupiah in recent weeks. 

 Last week, Nasution told reporters that the central bank was cooperating with Singapore and other countries in the region to make sure banks didn't break rules governing maximum forward contracts allowed in rupiah. 

 But such cooperation didn't mean Singapore was selling dollars to help the rupiah, Nasution told reporters. 

 "The Asian currency market is a very liberal market," he said. "I don't think Singapore would intervene on behalf of us. Of course not," he added. 

 GIC's rupiah-buying may be linked to a possible investment in Indonesia in the near future, market participants have speculated. 

 Nasution reiterated that Bank Indonesia's increased supervision of forward trading didn't amount to capital controls. 

 "We're only checking. It's not capital controls," he said. 

 The acting governor also said the central bank will "take any measures that we need to take" to stop a slide in the rupiah. 

 Bank Indonesia can raise interest rates, and sell foreign reserves in the market, to stop speculative attacks on the rupiah, he said. 

 However, Nasution added that interest rate hikes alone won't help the rupiah if the political situation remains unstable. 

 A more stable political situation would also help encourage local exporters to bring dollar earnings back into rupiah, he added. 

 The rupiah has lost almost 30% in value since the start of the year, amid tensions within President Abdurrahman Wahid's coalition government. The dollar closed Tuesday in Asia at IDR8,965. 

 Investors remain loath to hold rupiah ahead of Wahid's state of the nation speech next Monday, which marks a major political test for his 10-month-old administration. 

 Although Wahid is unlikely to face impeachment, the session will form a rallying point for opposition, which blame the president for trying to consolidate his power over the coalition.

title: Asia Markets-Chilled by Nasdaq, Nikkei breaches 16,000.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Hefty losses on the U.S. 

 Nasdaq overnight took a toll across most Asian stock markets on 

 Friday. 

     The exception was Taiwan, boosted by state fund buying. 

     Shares in Tokyo fell sharply with the benchmark Nikkei 

 average ending below key 16,000 support for the first 

 time since May 1999 as major tech issues were bruised. 

     Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said he was not worried 

 about movements in the Japanese stock market but declined to 

 comment on the Nikkei's drop under 16,000. 

     Economic Planning Minister Taichi Sakaiya, however, said 

 the Bank of Japan should take into account recent falls in 

 stock prices when deciding whether it should end its zero-rate 

 policy. 

     In South Korea, the KOSPI suffered a near five percent drop 

 as foreign selling rocked blue chips SK Telecom and 

 Samsung Electronics . 

     Most Asian currencies failed to cling to Thursday's gains 

 as players opted to cover their dollar positions ahead of the 

 weekend. 

     SING DOLLAR UPSIDE LIMITED 

     The Singapore dollar was rescued from 22-month lows after 

 an official from the Monetary Authority of Singapore said on 

 Thursday it was prepared to allow a gradual appreciation of the 

currency given the country's strong fundamentals. 

     It traded comfortably off a 1.7515 trough hit on Monday but 

 analysts said the rebound was not likely to last too long. 

     Chartists said the Sing dollar could breach 1.7300 

 convincingly next week, with 1.7240 seen as a strong 

 resistance. 

     "In the immediate term, dollar/Sing is going down as charts 

 indicate it's under a downward correction here," said Eric 

 Chong, technical analyst at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

     "But the recent (dollar/Sing) fall is a bit overdone. 

 Therefore, on a longer term view, the dollar is still on the 

 uptrend," he added. 

     On the fundamental front, any gains will be hampered by 

 lingering political uncertainty in the region, especially ahead 

 of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) in Indonesia where 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid will be called on to account for 

 his turbulent first year in office. 

 THAI BAHT BEARISH 

 Despite the Sing dollar's rebound, which has helped other 

 regionals, the embattled Thai baht came under renewed pressure 

 after the central bank said it would only intervene to support 

 the currency in case of excess volatility. 

 Bank of Thailand (BOT) deputy governor Tanya Sirivedhin 

 said: "We would not intervene unless there were signs that 

 there is really some excessive volatility taking place". 

 The baht erased most of Thursday's gains in early trade as 

 dealers poured cold water on a local press report the BOT had 

intervened in London markets to support it. 

     Bangkok newspaper The Nation said the central bank had 

 bought dollars as the baht hit a 10-month low of 41.36. 

     On the sidelines of a regional central bank conference in 

Singapore, Tanya told Reuters she was unaware of any 

intervention as reported by the Nation. 

     "I've been here in Singapore so I don't know if anything 

 like that took place," she said, but added that she would be 

 rather surprised if it had. 

     The baht now looked poised to test the 41.36 level hit on 

 Wednesday as the the authorities seemed to have given a green 

 light for it to weaken further, analysts said. 

     KOREA REFORM 

     Analysts are upbeat on South Korea's economic recovery on 

 the back of strong exports and the booming high-tech sector, 

 but there are still concerns over debt-laden financial firms 

 and slowing restructuring among major conglomerates. 

 The Finance Ministry said it would ask creditors of the 

 country's second largest conglomerate Daewoo Group to 

 draw up final plans by September for reforming or selling off 

 its 12 core affiliates. 

 In a statement issued after a meeting of economic-related 

 ministers, the ministry said creditors would be asked for final 

 reform plans for dozens of non-Daewoo firms also under debt 

 workouts by the end of the year. 

 Analysts warned of the risks of slowing reform but pointed 

 out that a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy would prod the 

 government to be more aggressive. 

 "I think there's definitely a reform fatigue going on right 

 now. It's coming through because there's slight amount of 

 complacency due to the fact that the economy is so strong," 

 said Dilip Shahani, senior treasury economist at HSBC Markets 

 in Hong Kong. 

 "We believe that as the U.S. economy slows down, this 

 reform fatigue will turn into an urgency. As that urgency comes 

 up, the government will be able to push through the final 

 phases," he said.

title: Singapore Dlr Unlikely To Gain Much More On MAS Remarks
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar jumped Thursday on news that the central bank was prepared to allow the currency to appreciate, but it's unlikely to gain much more in the near term, analysts said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore "is prepared to allow a gradual and modest appreciation of the Sing dollar on a trade-weighted basis in the coming year, in line with the strengthening of economic fundamentals," Managing Director Koh Yong Guan said. 

 The Singapore dollar rose sharply on the remarks. The U.S. dollar fell to S$1.7341 from S$1.7413 shortly before the statement, which came at around 0355 GMT at a news conference to unveil the MAS annual report. Around 0820 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7377. 

 However, the Singapore dollar's rise may be over for the time being, analysts said. "I doubt we'll see markets get too carried away on the strong side for the Singapore dollar," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore. 

 Simmonds and other analysts said they had expected the MAS to move toward a tighter policy stance some time this year to fight any sign of incipient inflation. Although the MAS has signaled its intent, it's not clear when the move toward a tighter policy will come. 

 Quoting Koh's remarks, Simmonds said that "'modest' and 'gradual' are important words." 

 In the next one to three months, Simmonds said, he expects the U.S. dollar to remain at the level of S$1.7300 to S$1.7400, rather than the S$1.7400 to S$1.7500 he forecast earlier. Simmonds's six-month target remains unchanged at S$1.6900-S$1.7000. 

 Analysts said that despite Singapore's strong fundamentals - the economy is expected to expand between 5.5% and 7.5% this year - regional uncertainty will continue to weigh on the Singapore dollar. The woes of the Indonesian rupiah, in particular, are dragging down the Singapore dollar. 

 "Our forecast is that the Singapore dollar will strengthen to around S$1.7300 by the end of the year," said Chia Hsin-li, market strategist at J.P. Morgan & Co. She called Thursday's gain in the Singapore dollar a "knee-jerk reaction" and not the start of a trend toward appreciation. 

 Thursday's statement comes days after the MAS was said to have intervened directly in the foreign-exchange market to support the Singapore dollar. Dealers said the MAS sold U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars at the level of S$1.7515 on Monday, sending the U.S. dollar sharply lower. 

 At Thursday's news conference, MAS Director Koh tacitly acknowledged the intervention. "It's no secret that we intervene in the market from time to time when speculation and speculative elements bring the Singapore dollar out of line," he said. 

 The MAS uses the currency, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary policy tool, seeking to maintain brisk growth and low inflation. The Singapore dollar is guided within a trading band against a basket of currencies of Singapore's major trading partners. 

 Koh said the MAS was prepared to allow a stronger Singapore dollar as a way of keeping inflation in check. Although inflation is expected to remain benign at between 1% to 2% this year, higher wages and commodity prices could produce inflationary pressures, he said. 

 Although the Singapore dollar has been vulnerable to movements in the more volatile rupiah, "We don't see any fundamental reason why that should be the case," said Khor Hoe Ee, MAS's senior executive director for economics. "Indonesia is doing well" despite the recent steep decline in the rupiah, he said. 

 Analysts say that the recent MAS intervention was a sign that the Singapore dollar is already nearing the weaker limit of its trading band. As a result, foreign exchange traders were unwilling to bid up the U.S. dollar more. 

 "Basically the timing couldn't have been better," Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said of Thursday's MAS statement. "Players were caught long on U.S. dollars," forcing them to sell, he said. 

 -By Amit Prakash and Christopher Wellisz, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-421-4800; christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com; amit.prakash@dowjones.com.

title: Singapore MAS/IDR Link -2: Investors More Discerning
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- There is no fundamental link between the levels of the Singapore dollar and the Indonesian rupiah, even though both currencies tend to move in tandem, a senior official of the Monetary Authority of Singapore said Thursday. 

 "We don't see any fundamental reason why that should be the case," Khor Hoe Ee, senior executive director for economics, said of the parallel movements of the two currencies. 

 Because of Singapore's trade and investment links with other countries in southeast Asia, "It's natural that when investors look at Singapore they also look closely at what happens in the region," he added. 

 But he said that fundamentally, "Indonesia is doing well," despite the recent steep decline in the Indonesian rupiah. 

 He said investors are starting to separate economic fundamentals from market sentiment. "Investors are much more discerning than they have been before," he said. "They will make a distinction between what happens in the financial markets and what happens in the real economy." 

 Observers have been surprised by the sensitivity of the Singapore dollar to movements in the rupiah, saying that the economic links between the two countries aren't particularly strong. 

 The two countries don't compete for the same export markets, and Singapore investment in Indonesia has been modest. Singapore investments in Indonesia in 1997 came to just US$3.1 billion, less than 10% of the total USR$36 billion of outward investment. 

 MAS officials declined to discuss whether the MAS had responded to a recent appeal by the Indonesian central bank for help in shoring up the level of the rupiah. 

 However, MAS Managing Director Koh Yong Guan tacitly acknowledged that the MAS had intervened in the foreign exchange market in recent weeks to shore up the Singapore dollar. 

 "It's no secret that we intervene in the market from time to time when speculation and speculative elements bring the Singapore dollar out of line," he said. 

 -By Christopher Wellisz, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-421-4802; christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com

title: REPEAT:Singapore MAS Sees Incipient Inflationary Leaning
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore is prepared to allow a modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar in relation to the currencies of its major trading partners, its managing director said Thursday. 

 Although inflation remains benign for the time being, the MAS is concerned by signs that it may rise in the future, Managing Director Koh Yong Guan said. 

 "MAS is, therefore, prepared to allow a gradual and modest appreciation of the Sing dollar on a trade-weighted basis in the coming year, in line with the strengthening of the (country's) economic fundamentals," Koh said at a news conference to present the MAS annual report. 

 The Singapore dollar rose within minutes on Koh remarks. 

 At 0415 GMT (12:15 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7375, down from S$1.7415 immediately before Koh's remarks were reported. 

 Consumer price inflation was zero in 1999, and rose modestly to an on-year level of 0.8% in June. For the year as a whole, the MAS expects inflation to come to between 1% and 2%. 

 But as Singapore's economy continues its brisk recovery from the Asian financial crisis, it will start reaching the limits of its capacity, and inflationary pressures will build, he said. 

 "We expect the remaining slack in the economy to be taken up within the next 12 months," he said. "As the labor market tightens further, wage pressures will begin to emerge." 

 In addition, rising world commodities prices will contribute to increases in the prices of imported goods, he said. 

 MAS said the gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar would "contain any incipient inflationary tendencies without exerting undue pressure on our competitiveness." 

 Koh declined to specify a level to which the MAS may be prepared to allow the currency to appreciate. 

 The MAS uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary policy tool. A stronger exchange rate reduces inflationary pressures by lowering the cost of imported goods in this trade-dependent economy. 

 The Singapore dollar trades against a basket of currencies of the country's major trade partners and is allowed to fluctuate within a band established by the MAS, which doesn't reveal the width of the band. 

 "As always, the exchange rate will be allowed to move flexibly within the policy band without undue or excessive fluctuations," the MAS said in its annual report, released Thursday. 

 Koh tacitly acknowledged that the MAS has intervened to support the Singapore dollar in recent weeks. "It's no secret that we intervene in the market from time to time when speculation and speculative elements bring the Singapore dollar out of line," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar has weakened considerably against the U.S. dollar this year, in part, the MAS said, because of the demand for the U.S. currency by Singaporean corporations making acquisitions abroad. But the Singapore dollar has gained against other currencies. 

 Khor Hoe Ee, senior executive director for economics, said the current level of the Singapore dollar is "appropriate" on a trade-weighted basis. 

 He added: "The Singapore dollar at the moment is within the band we have set and we are comfortable with it." 

 -By Christopher Wellisz, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-421-4802; christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com
