title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Baht Near 10-Mo Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were lower late Wednesday, as the Thai baht dropped around 1% in intraday trading, hitting its lowest level in almost 10 months. 

 The baht, which has lost more than 2% of its value against the dollar this week, is expected to weaken further after breaking below 41 baht to the dollar, analysts said. 

 The baht's relentless slide dragged the Philippine unit below support at the 45 peso-mark against the U.S. currency Wednesday. 

 Caution kept trading volumes in the Singapore and Indonesian currencies thin, amid fears of intervention by local authorities, dealers said. The Singapore dollar was slightly higher, while the rupiah was almost 1% weaker. 

 Elsewhere, the New Taiwan dollar was steady, while the South Korean won ended slightly firmer. 

 The dollar's strength against the Japanese yen and a lack of selling pressure in the U.S. currency, apart from profit-taking late in the day, pushed the baht through one support level after another. 

 Around 0859 GMT, the dollar was at THB41.140, up from THB40.925 late Tuesday. The dollar had risen to THB41.340 earlier, its highest level since September 29, 1999. 

 The Thai central bank indicated no intention of halting its sharp depreciation. And contrary to expectations, Thai exporters didn't unload their dollars around THB41 and are likely to hold out until the U.S. currency rises to THB41.50, dealers said. 

 Panic buying by local importers and stop-loss orders from offshore participants after the Thai currency sank below support at 41 baht to the dollar contributed to the baht's slide, dealers said. 

 Dealers also blamed the uncertainty over continuity of economic policies and reform efforts ahead of Thailand's general elections later this year. 

 Thailand's inflation report issued late Tuesday, which confirmed that the country's interest rates will remain depressed for some time, is also expected to keep the baht under pressure, analysts said. 

 Indeed, the dollar looks set to climb further to its next upside target of THB41.500 as early as Thursday, before heading higher, a dealer at an Asian bank said. 

 "The baht has a target which everyone is looking at now, and that is THB42," says Alison Seng, an analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS International. 

 The Philippine peso fell to a fresh 30-month low, tracking the Thai baht's fall. The peso is expected to test new post-crisis lows over the next few months, analysts said. 

 The dollar pushed through the PHP45 resistance level to close at PHP45.070, up from Tuesday's close of PHP44.755. 

 The dollar had touched an intraday high of PHP45.195 in intraday trade, its highest level since early January 1998, breaking above the 30-month high of PHP44.140 it had hit two weeks ago. 

 On the domestic front, concerns that the government will overshoot its budget deficit target this year and the country's sluggish economic growth continued to unnerve investors, currency watchers said. 

 Standard Chartered Bank expects the peso to decline further to PHP46 by the end of the third quarter, foreign exchange strategist Steve Brice said. 

 Dollar-selling by Indonesian state banks and profit-taking in the U.S. currency by offshore participants had recouped part of the rupiah's losses, dealers said. 

 The dollar had climbed to as high as IDR9,150 in early trading, but retreated to IDR9,070 around 0905 GMT. 

 Similarly, steady U.S. dollar selling in Singapore by local banks - which traders said might have been executed on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore - helped the Singapore dollar to recover, resisting the pressure from its Southeast Asian counterparts. 

 The U.S. dollar was at S$1.7428, down from S$1.7452 late Tuesday. 

 The Taiwanese central bank was also present in the foreign exchange market, albeit in a relatively more overt manner, selling around US$200 million Wednesday to stabilize the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. A rebound in the local stock market also buoyed Taiwanese currency. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$31.061, barely changed from NT$31.063 late Tuesday. 

 The South Korean won edged up as local banks liquidated their long-dollar positions following the U.S. currency's strength earlier in the day, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,115.30 won, down slightly from Tuesday's close of KRW1,115.60.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Thai Baht Hits Fresh 9-Mo Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were weaker late Tuesday, as the Thai baht continued its downward spiral to hit fresh nine-month lows. 

 The poor sentiment on the baht, which is expected to slide further, weighed on the other Southeast Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 In North Asia, a slump in their respective local stock markets dented the New Taiwan dollar and the South Korean won. 

 Asian currencies were also adjusting to the U.S. dollar's strength against the yen, which had again tested the Y109 support level to the dollar Tuesday. 

 The baht - the latest target for investors already bearish on most Southeast Asian currencies - fell to its lowest level since Oct. 1, 1999, when it tested the psychologically-important support level of 41.000 baht to the dollar. 

 In late Asian trading, the U.S. currency was traded at THB41.000 in currency brokers, and was bid at that level by some participants in the Singapore interbank market. However, offshore profit-taking and dollar-selling by exporters limited the dollar's strength. 

 Around 0750 GMT (3:50 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at THB40.925, up from THB40.805 late Monday. 

 The baht is down 5.8% against the dollar since early June amid uncertainty over the continuity of economic policies and reform efforts ahead of Thailand's general elections later this year. The weakness in Southeast Asian foreign exchange markets has also hurt the Thai currency. 

 This week technical and option-related dollar-selling, the depressed stock market and local dollar demand by importers and debtors have triggered the baht's sharper-than-expected decline, dealers said. 

 The Thai central bank's apparent tolerance over the baht's weakness gave investors the added impetus to push the beleaguered currency lower. 

 Deputy central bank Governor Pakorn Malakul reiterated Tuesday that the baht's fall is due mainly to the U.S. dollar's rise against regional currencies, and that it hasn't seen any unreasonably speculative or abnormal activity in foreign exchange market. 

 Some analysts expect more gloom for the baht in the short term. 

 "I really don't think we have seen the worst," said Syetarn Hansakul, treasury economist at WestLB Research. "With the next week or so, it can go in the direction of THB42.00 (to the dollar)." 

 The Indonesian rupiah was jolted out of its narrow trading range after President Abdurrahman Wahid abruptly canceled a news conference he was scheduled to give late Tuesday. 

 The dollar climbed above the psychologically-important 9,000 rupiah level to trade at IDR9,025 around 0920 GMT, up from IDR8,903 late Monday. 

 Lingering uncertainty over Wahid's political fate ahead of Indonesia's national assembly meeting next month had also prompted some offshore participants to start building up long-dollar positions again. Sentiment, however, remained cautious amid fears Bank Indonesia would defend the local currency. 

 Many traders expect strong dollar demand to emerge around IDR8,800 to IDR8,850, but fears of central bank intervention will likely cap the U.S. currency around IDR9,200 in the short term. 

 The bleak outlook for the baht and the rupiah stung the Philippine peso. The dollar was at 44.750 pesos, up from Monday's close of PHP44.60. 

 The Singapore dollar was slightly weaker, as the pressure from the strength of the U.S. currency was offset by fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Market participants were wary of pushing the Singapore dollar lower, following the de facto central bank's suspected intervention Monday. The intervention pushed the U.S. dollar down from its brief rise to a 22-month high of S$1.7515. 

 The U.S. dollar was at S$1.7452, up marginally from S$1.7441 late Monday. 

 In South Korea, the dollar finished at 1,115.60 won, up from Monday's close of KRW1,114. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency ended at NT$31.063, up from NT$30.046 late Monday. 

 The fall in the local stock markets had hurt the South Korean and Taiwan currencies. 

 Investors are, meanwhile, awaiting U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony on monetary policy later Tuesday to the House Banking Committee. His speech isn't expected to be different from the version he delivered to a Senate panel last week. However, investors are keeping a close watch on other comments that could emerge in response to questions posed from the House panel following his address.

 The rupiah was largely stable as the Indonesian currency took a backseat following last week's roller-coaster ride when President Abdurrahman Wahid refused to explain to Parliament the reasons for the sacking of two ministers. /// 

 ///The Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar were also down late Monday.

 The Thai baht was pushed to its weakest level since Oct. 1, 1999, partly due to a 3.6% slide in the key index on the Thai stock market to below the psychologically-important 300 mark. 

 Around 0810 GMT (4:10 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at 40.805 baht, up from THB40.315 in Asian trading last Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Rupiah Recovery Aids Region
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Tuesday, with the beleaguered Indonesian rupiah regaining some ground as investors unwound their long-dollar positions, dealers said. 

 The rupiah's recovery helped lift the Thai baht, the Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar off their intraday lows in late trading. 

 Around 0745 GMT (3:45 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at 9,365 rupiah, down from IDR9,520 late Monday. 

 Those liquidating their long-dollar positions had probably given up waiting for the U.S. currency to break above IDR9,570 to IDR9,600, dealers said. The dollar had touched those levels last week, but rapidly retreated thereafter. 

 Fears that Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid would be impeached have waned, providing some reprieve for the rupiah, currency watchers said. 

 "There's also a feeling maybe the Indonesian authorities are considering alternatives to limit the rupiah's losses," said Steve Brice, foreign exchange strategist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 State banks were said to have defended the rupiah Tuesday and local interest rates are expected to climb higher this week. 

 Political uncertainties, however, remain high and the rupiah's respite will likely be short-lived. Some analysts still predict that the rupiah will resume its downtrend toward the psychologically important IDR10,000 mark to the dollar ahead of the People's Consultative Assembly session in mid-August, when Wahid's performance will be reviewed. 

 "We'll still see a firmer dollar going forward," said Brice. 

 Strong corporate demand for the U.S. currency around IDR9,250 to IDR9,300 will likely provide strong support for the dollar, he added. 

 The mood is also cautious ahead of an expected showdown between Wahid and the Indonesian parliament Thursday over his controversial sacking of two ministers earlier this year, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht - which briefly touched a nine-month low of THB40.375 to the dollar on offshore dollar demand earlier in the day - recouped some of its losses, thanks to the rupiah's rebound and dollar-selling by local exporters, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at THB40.255, up slightly from THB40.225 late Monday. 

 The Philippine peso moved in tandem with the baht and the rupiah. The dollar was at PHP44.545, down from Monday's close of PHP44.590, and way below Tuesday's intraday high of PHP44.660. 

 The U.S. currency had also pulled back against the Singapore dollar but remained well-bid despite the rupiah's recovery and suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore late Monday, dealers said. 

 Some investors appeared to be holding short positions in the U.S. dollar versus the Singapore currency that they needed to cover, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar was at S$1.7462, down from S$1.7489 late Monday, the level it was trading before the de facto central bank stepped in. 

 After having allowed the local currency to drift lower in the past two weeks, the MAS, which rarely comments on its actions, was rumored to have defended the Singapore dollar around the S$1.7470 to S$1.7490 range to the U.S. currency late Monday, dealers said. 

 Fears of another intervention will likely cap the U.S. dollar around S$1.7500 in the short term, currency watchers said. 

 A 2.5% slide in the local stock market and the grim outlook for most Asian currencies depressed the New Taiwan dollar to its lowest level in almost eight months, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$30.960, up from Monday's close of NT$30.912. 

 The South Korean won closed slightly lower following a government bond issue and amid fears of intervention by local monetary authorities, dealers said. 

 The government warned last week it was prepared to intervene to prevent the won from appreciating too sharply. 

 The dollar finished at 1,113.5 won, up from Friday's close of KRW1,112.90. South Korean markets were closed Monday for a national holiday. 

 The ministry sold KRW800 billion in five-year won stabilization bonds, at an average yield of 8.13%, through an auction earlier Tuesday. The market had expected an average yield of 8.20%.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Rupiah Set To Tumble Further
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Wednesday, with the Indonesian rupiah plummeting to a 21-month intraday low against the dollar before recovering some of its losses. 

 After pressuring the Philippine, Thai and Singapore currencies through key support levels earlier this week, investors preyed on the rupiah on Wednesday. 

 The dollar pierced through the psychologically important 9,500 rupiah mark in afternoon dealings, climbing as high as IDR9,505, its highest intraday level since mid-March, 1999. The last time the dollar was above IDR9,500 at the close of Asian trading hours was in October, 1998. 

 Panic dollar buying by local corporates that needed to service foreign debt obligations and persisting doubts over President Abdurrahman Wahid's hold on power and economic reforms cast a pall on the rupiah, currency watchers said. 

 A local newspaper report quoting Bank Indonesia acting governor, Anwar Nasution, as suggesting that the central bank was largely powerless in halting the rupiah's slide also contributed to the beleaguered currency's fall, dealers said. 

 But the dollar failed to convincingly breach above IDR9,500 as dollar profit-taking by offshore players set in. 

 Market talk that the Indonesian central bank has invited foreign treasury heads for a meeting Thursday, fueling speculation the central bank may be considering ways to strengthen the rupiah, in part helped recoup some of the rupiah's losses, dealers said. 

 Around 0915 GMT, the dollar was at IDR9,420, up from IDR9,338 late Tuesday. 

 Market pundits are betting that the dollar will likely march higher toward IDR10,000 over the coming week on speculative buying interest. 

 "IDR9,700 to IDR9,800 will be the next crucial area," said Steve Brice, strategist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 The Singapore dollar strengthened in late trading but remained below S$1.7400 after tracking the Indonesian rupiah, dealers said. Fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene when the U.S. dollar climbed to around S$1.7440 fueled profit-taking in the U.S. currency, they added. 

 Around 1000 GMT, the U.S. currency was at S$1.7413, down from S$1.7433 late Tuesday. 

 After sinking below THB40 against the dollar Tuesday, the Thai baht remained depressed below that level after the Thai central bank governor gave the green light for the currency to weaken further, dealers said. 

 Thai central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said Wednesday that the recent baht weakness has been in line with regional currencies, and added that it is in an appropriate range relative to currencies of Thailand's export competitors. He said there was no need for the central bank to defend the baht for the time being. 

 The dollar was at THB40.085 late Wednesday in Asia, up slightly from THB40.045 the previous day. 

 The Philippine peso rebounded slightly, thanks to dollar profit-taking by offshore players after the U.S. currency touched an intraday high of PHP45.095, dealers said. The dollar Tuesday hit a 30-month high of PHP45.150. 

 The dollar closed at PHP44.640 Wednesday in the Phlippine Dealing System, down from Tuesday's close at PHP44.820. 

 Elsewhere, the South Korean won ended Seoul trading higher as foreign investors bought the local currency to invest in the local stock market, and as Tuesday's bank strike ended after the government hammered out a compromise with the bank union, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,115.60 won, down from Tuesday's KRW1,116.50 in thin trading. Traders said they expect the dollar to trade in the KRW1,113 to KRW1,116 range Thursday. 

 A 1.2% slide in the Taiwan stock market weighed on the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. The U.S. dollar closed at NT$30.862, up from NT$30.842 Tuesday.

title: Sing dollar breaks key support, falls limited.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 11 (Reuters) - The faltering Singapore dollar broke key psychological support to hit 16-month lows on Tuesday as analysts predicted more declines in the weeks ahead. 

 In early trade, the Sing dollar, which has recently hovered in a tight range, breached 1.7400, a level that had been widely expected to trigger central bank intevention to curb further falls. 

 "There's a lot of talk, certainly technically, that 1.74 is a very key level," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "That's why the authorities have been protective about levels..." 

 But despite the breach of key support and heightened speculation, there have been no signs of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), dealers said. 

Singapore manages its currency against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket. 

 Analysts said the Sing dollar now looked poised to test the next key target at 1.7500 as the MAS was probably not too concerned with the recent softness. 

 The fall was mostly due to weakness in other Southeast Asian currencies, battered due to domestic political and economic uncertainty, analysts said. 

 "We would have to ask the Thais, the Filipinos, the Indonesians. Primarily, it is really those currencies which are directing the Sing dollar at this point," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at G.K. Goh Research. 

 But players saw the currency gradually stabilising given healthy economic fundamentals coupled with low inflation. 

 "Clearly with the economic growth here, there's nothing to be massively fuelling the weaker Sing," said Kevin Ralph, first vice president of strategic trading at Sanwa Bank in Singapore. 

 Singapore's second quarter gross domestic product data, released on Monday, pointed to a stronger-than-expected 7.7 percent growth in the second quarter compared to the same period the previous year.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Lower; Rupiah Takes Biggest Dive
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A slew of negative political and economic news pushed most Asian currencies sharply lower Wednesday, with the Indonesian rupiah taking the biggest tumble. 

 An overnight bomb blast at the Indonesian attorney general's office, along with continuing political turmoil affecting President Abdurrahman Wahid's government, triggered rupiah selling that pushed the currency to its lowest level in nearly 16 months. 

 On Wednesday, a second, unexploded bomb, was found at the attorney general's office and police evacuated the building while the device was removed. 

 The beleaguered rupiah started out the trading day on the defensive, after having hit a historic low the day before. Near the end of Asian trading Wednesday, the dollar was quoted at 9,305 rupiah, up from IDR8,600 Tuesday. It was the rupiah's weakest performance since March 12, 1999 when it slipped to IDR9,505 per dollar. 

 And with no resolution to Indonesia's political turmoil in sight, the rupiah is in store for continued selling pressure that could conceivably push it to IDR10,000 per dollar, analysts said. 

 "The rupiah was hit by panic-selling," a trader at a European bank said. "People were scrambling to get their hands on dollars," he said. 

 There were no injuries in Tuesday night's bombing in Jakarta. 

 No one claimed responsibility for the bomb blast, but Indonesia's police chief didn't rule out the possibility that one of former President Suharto's sons was involved. 

 Senior government ministers have accused Suharto's supporters of inciting riots on the Maluku islands in an attempt to destabilize Wahid's nine-month-old government. 

 Economic Minister Kwik Kian Gie, meanwhile, said the rupiah's fall had nothing to do with the country's economic fundamentals. He predicted that the currency will strengthen to IDR7,000 per dollar after the annual session of the People's Consultative Assembly in early August. 

 In the Philippines, ongoing concerns over low local interest rates, political unrest in the southern island of Mindanao, and fears that the economy is slowing, kept sentiment firmly against the peso. 

 The dollar closed at a 21-month high of 43.690 pesos, up from PHP43.535 the previous day. The trading session was abbreviated because of heavy rains that caused flooding in some parts of Manila. 

 With the dollar climbing as high as PHP43.695 in intraday trading, dealers said they expected it to breach the PHP43.700 in the next trading session. 

 Falling regional currencies also pulled the Singapore dollar lower. Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7370, up from S$1.7327 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 "The rupiah, baht and peso are all affecting the Singapore dollar even though its fundamentals are good," said Steven Brice, currency strategist for Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 While the Singapore dollar approached lows it reached last week, dealers said it was unlikely the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene to support the local currency, with sentiment so strongly in favor of the U.S. dollar. 

 "It (intervention) would be like standing in front of a truck," an Asian bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The South Korean won ended lower Wednesday amid worries about an upcoming strike at local banks and continued weakness in Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The dollar finished at 1,117.20 won, up from Tuesday's close at KRW1,115.30. 

 "I don't see the strike as catastrophic for the won," Brice said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Weaker: Wahid Comments Help IDR
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly weaker late Tuesday, as market-soothing words from Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid helped stabilize the embattled rupiah. 

 Wahid called a news conference to refute reports that he was targeting opposition lawmakers as part of an investigation into corruption and riot-inciting in Indonesia. 

 Comments Wahid had issued over the weekend regarding the investigation were misinterpreted, he said. 

 "They (legislators) will be questioned only as witnesses. My other statement was twisted for political purposes," Wahid said at the news conference. 

 The rupiah, which had touched an almost 16-month low of 9,000 to the dollar in early trading, staged a modest recovery after Wahid's comments to finish the day at 8,600, unchanged from Monday's close. 

 Wahid nonetheless acknowledged that the political infighting and sectarian violence in the Maluku islands is taking its toll on the currency. 

 "The rupiah weakness is because the market knows that the problem faced by Indonesia is very complicated, that there is disharmony among the people of Indonesia," he said. 

Currency dealers said the rupiah will remain under pressure until Indonesia's political and economic situation improves. 

 They said market participants are concerned that continuing turmoil will prevent Indonesia from implementing reforms necessary to stay in the good graces of the International Monetary Fund and keep its economic expansion on track. 

 "We are worried that if this political mudslinging doesn't end or get better, confidence in Indonesia will be severely eroded and the IDR could be headed toward the 10,000/USD level in one month's time," said Syetarn Hansakul, economist at WestLB Bank in Singapore. 

 The Philippine peso, which also is suffering from negative investor sentiment, also traded lower against the U.S. dollar. 

 The dollar climbed to a 21-month high of 43.600 pesos in intraday trading as the narrowing differential between U.S. and Philippine interest rates prompted investors to shift their holdings to dollars. 

 By the close, the dollar edged back to PHP43.535, up from PHP43.530 at Monday's finish. 

 Traders said concerns that the government may overshoot its budget deficit target and the unresolved crisis in southern Mindanao also weighed on the peso. 

 The South Korean won declined on the heels of a weaker yen and fears of a strike next week by employees at local financial institutions, traders said. 

 "Plus the won has been outperforming other Asian currencies in the last few days so there is now some profit-taking," said Frank Gong, currency strategist at Bank of America in Hong Kong. 

 The dollar closed at 1,115.30 won, up from KRW1,113.80 a day earlier. 

 The won also took a hit from a drop in the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, which closed down 16.68 points, or 2%, to 818.53. 

 The softer yen and falling stock prices put pressure on the New Taiwan dollar as well. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$30.822, up from NT$30.812 late Monday. 

 The U.S. unit dropped early in the session but reversed course after the Taiwan stock prices began to falter. Declines in the New Taiwan dollar were limited by the central bank, which was seen selling small amounts of U.S. dollars throughout the day. 

 The Thai baht closed slightly higher Tuesday as investors took profit on the back of the dollar's recent strong performance, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 39.355 baht, down from THB39.362 at the Asian close Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar finished lower as corporate dollar buying kept the U.S. dollar well bid, dealers said. 

 Late Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7327, up from S$1.7317 late Monday in Asia. 

 Market participants were reluctant to push the U.S. currency much higher because of fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene at levels above S$1.7340, a dealer at a European bank said.

text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Investors expressed a general distaste for Asian currencies Monday, with the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso bearing the brunt of the selloff. 

 Offshore selling of the rupiah was sparked by President Abdurrahman Wahid's comments over the weekend that he plans to crack down on legislators suspected of fomenting unrest in Indonesia, dealers said. 

 When markets opened Monday morning the rupiah immediately began declining against the U.S. dollar. By the end of the trading day the dollar had climbed to 8,940 rupiah, up from IDR 8,753 late Friday and the highest level in nearly 10 months. 

 Wahid's comments highlight the stress being placed on Indonesia's political system as Wahid attempts to restore economic growth and prevent separatist violence from tearing the country apart. 

 Cabinet Secretary Marsillam Simandjuntak, expanding on Wahid's comments, said Monday the president has suspended parliamentary immunity for at least 10 legislators being investigated. 

 He wouldn't say what the politicians were being investigated for, but there was speculation that Wahid's political rivals and critics were among those being investigated. 

 "What's happening to the rupiah has to do with the fact that Wahid is going after the legislators," said Vincent Low, currency strategist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore. 

 "It looks like there may be a standoff with parliament and that is causing concerns," he said. 

 The Philippine peso, under pressure on a number of fronts, fell to a 21-month low of 43.580 per dollar during intraday trading before staging a modest recovery in late trading. The dollar closed at PHP43.560, up from 43.230 late Friday. 

 Traders attributed the peso's decline to a host of factors, including a regional bias in favor of the dollar, low local interest rates, budget deficit concerns and rising oil prices. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura went on television as the peso was falling and said he wasn't overly concerned about the currency's decline. 

 "It's still at a comfortable level at the moment," he said, adding that the peso's level should be "market determined." 

 He said the central bank would only intervene to head off speculative activity, which didn't appear to be occurring. 

 The U.S. dollar gained some ground against the Singapore currency, but remained below levels that would cause concern to local monetary authorities, dealers said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore was rumored to have intervened to support the currency late last week when the U.S. dollar rose to S$1.7380, its highest level in more than a year. 

 Near the end of trading Monday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7315, up from S$1.7271 late Friday. 

 "The current level shouldn't unduly alarm authorities," Low said. 

 The Thai baht also came under pressure as players took long-dollar positions amid declines in other regional currencies. 

 Offshore banks sold dollars against the baht, pushing the U.S. currency to 39.362 baht at the close, up from THB39.220 late Friday. 

 The dollar could move to test its year-high of THB39.470 against the baht Tuesday, one trader said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar came under pressure amid weakness in the yen. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$30.812, up from NT$30.794 late Friday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar opened higher, but lost momentum in the afternoon following a weaker yen. The Taiwan currency often tracks the yen because Taiwan competes directly with the Japan export market. 

 The South Korean won was the sole gainer among the Asian currencies, moving higher following the release of stronger-than-expected trade data for June.

title: Singapore MAS Action Not Expected To Signal Policy Shift
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore surprised the foreign exchange market by apparently intervening to support the currency, but the move didn't signal a fundamental shift in policy, analysts and traders said Friday. 

 The suspected intervention started late Thursday in New York trading hours and then continued early Friday morning in Asia, pushing the Singapore dollar to its strongest level in two weeks against its U.S. counterpart. 

 Late Friday in Asia, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7277, down sharply from its overnight peak of S$1.7380 and Thursday's Asian close of S$1.7344. 

 The move likely was a signal that the MAS wouldn't tolerate a sharply weaker currency, rather than a fundamental shift away from its neutral monetary policy stance, which is meant to encourage non-inflationary growth, economists and traders said. 

 The MAS declined to comment. "As a policy we don't usually comment," a spokeswoman for the MAS said. 

 The purpose of the MAS action, said a strategist at a European bank, is "not to try to change the trend but to create an awareness of where the tolerance levels are." 

 In recent months, the MAS has maintained a neutral policy on the Singapore dollar, meaning that it wants the currency to remain stable against a basket of the currencies of its biggest trading partners. 

 With the help of a stable currency and an inflation rate that remains low, the MAS can continue to nurture Singapore's export-led economic recovery. 

 A tighter policy - meaning a stronger currency - could derail the recovery, while a looser policy could spark inflation by raising the price of imported goods. 

 Although the Singapore dollar, like other currencies around the world, has weakened against the U.S. dollar, it has gained against the euro and some of the other currencies that make up the basket, economists said. 


           Surging US Dlr Creates Dilemma For MAS



However, the surging U.S. dollar has created a dilemma for the MAS,
economists added. With interest rates low in Singapore and high in the
U.S., it has become easy to make money by borrowing Singapore dollars
and selling them for the U.S. currency.



Investors who made such bets were protected from losses by the MAS's
policy of keeping the Singapore dollar from weakening too much.



"Clearly, the temptation is to buy (U.S.) dollars against Sing given
that you've got the MAS protecting your downside," said the European
bank strategist.



The accumulation of long U.S. dollar positions threatened to overwhelm
the Singapore currency, pushing the U.S. dollar beyond what some
observers say is a key technical level of S$1.7400.



That represents the U.S. dollar's last peak against the Singapore
dollar in March 1999. Technical analysis suggests that pushed beyond
that level, the U.S. dollar would quickly shoot up to the previous peak
of S$1.7900, said Steve Brice, Treasury economist at Standard Chartered
Bank.



"It would be a key signal to the market that they are willing to let
the Sing weaken against the (U.S.) dollar," Brice said.



While the apparent MAS intervention doesn't signal a shift in policy,
it has prompted renewed speculation as to where the Singapore dollar is
likely to head from here.



Several traders said the U.S. dollar is likely to weaken further in
coming days as long positions are liquidated. But they add that the U.S.
dollar will find support at about S$1.7220 and then resume its ascent.



The Singapore dollar will weaken as the interest-rate differential
with the U.S. continues to widen and the Indonesian rupiah weakens
further in response to political uncertainty in Jakarta, some analysts
argue.



Continued investment abroad by big Singapore companies could also add
to the downward pressure on the currency as money flows out of the
country. Some traders cited as a possible factor reports that two
Singapore banks are in the running to buy the Hong Kong assets of Chase
Manhattan Bank.



On the other hand, the euro's sharp recovery in the past two days
could be a signal that the U.S. dollar's glory days are over, and
therefore cap its gains against the Singapore dollar, said David
Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore.



"The rally of the euro tends to put a little bit of a ceiling" on
expectations that the U.S. dollar will rise to S$1.7400 or beyond,
Simmonds said.



-By Christopher Wellisz, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-421-4802;
christopher.wellisz@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; But S$ Bucks Trend
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- While most other Asian currencies drifted lower late Friday, the Singapore dollar defied the downward pressure, thanks to suspected intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Domestic political and economic anxieties had stung the Thai baht, the Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah, dealers said. 

 The MAS - which declined to comment Friday on its rumored actions - was said to have sold U.S. dollars when the U.S. currency climbed to a high of S$1.7380 in overnight trading. This pushed the U.S. currency back down to its recent trading level around S$1.7340, dealers said. 

 The de facto central bank defended the local currency again around the level of S$1.7330 to S$1.7340 early Friday. Stop-loss orders were triggered when the U.S. dollar sank below S$1.7300, sending the U.S. currency reeling to below the S$1.7380 support level, dealers said. 

 "We do have a market that was caught long," said Alison Seng, an analyst at market consultants Standard & Poor's MMS International. 

 Economists said the intervention doesn't herald a shift in the central bank's monetary policy, which is to allow the Singapore dollar to remain broadly stable against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 Instead, the MAS probably wanted to put the market on notice that it wouldn't tolerate a significantly weaker Singapore dollar, several economists said. 

 Bank of America said it expects the U.S. dollar's next support level of around S$1.7250 to S$1.7260 to hold, ahead of a move back to S$1.7300. 

 Strong corporate U.S. dollar demand - needed to fulfill the recent string of overseas acquisitions - and expectations the Indonesian rupiah will weaken further will continue to weigh on the Singapore currency, analysts said. 

 Worries over the narrowing differentials between U.S. and domestic interest rates hammered the Philippine peso, dealers said. A lower-than-expected domestic oil price hike, however, helped the peso recoup some of its intraday losses, they added. 

 The dollar closed at 43.230 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Thursday's close of PHP43.170. The dollar rose to an intraday high of PHP43.320 earlier in the day, its highest level since hitting PHP43.400 May 25. 

 The 55-centavo per liter oil price increase, lower than the expected PHP1.30 per liter, helped the peso recover some of its losses. Earlier Friday, central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said an increase of PHP1.30 would have been inflationary. 

 In Thailand, political uncertainty, amid heightened fears of an early election, weighed on the baht. 

 Around 1000 GMT, the dollar was at 39.205 baht, up from THB39.165 late Thursday. 

 Mounting concerns over Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid's hold on power and whether the country could meet its economic reform deadlines by the middle of next week, which would pave the way for the disbursement of funds by the International Monetary Fund, weighed on the rupiah, dealers said. 

 Dollar-selling by Jakarta retail investors, however, capped the U.S. currency's ascent around the IDR8,745 to IDR8,755 level, dealers said. A lack of offshore buying interest, with the rupiah having moved within narrow ranges recently, also stymied the dollar's rise, they added. 

 The dollar ended Asian trading at IDR8,753, up slightly from IDR8,735 late Thursday. 

 Dollar-demand by corporates that need to meet their debt repayment schedule and the political uncertainty will likely push the dollar higher to IDR8,800 next week, dealers said. 

 The South Korean won barely moved against the U.S. dollar as short-covering of dollars by local banks offset month-end dollar selling by local exporters, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,115 won, nearly flat from Thursday's close of KRW1,114.90. 

 The New Taiwan dollar finished higher, bolstered by inward flows that could mean foreign investors are preparing funds to buy stocks at the start of the third quarter. 

 The U.S. dollar finished lower at NT$30.794, compared with Thursday's close of NT$30.808.

title: Singapore  Dollar Up Late After Suspected MAS  Intervention

 Around 0826 GMT (4:26 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7271, down from S$1.7344 late Thursday in Asia. 

 Traders said, the Monetary Authority of Singapore first intervened in New York trading hours after the U.S. dollar shot up to S$1.7380, pushing it back down to its recent trading level of about S$1.7340, traders said. 

 Then, late Friday morning, the MAS was back in the market, selling U.S. dollars for Singapore dollars at S$1.7330, traders said. 

 However, the central bank expectedly declined to comment on the suspected intervention. "As a policy we don't usually comment," an MAS spokeswoman said. 

 The suspected intervention came as a surprise, since the MAS has stayed aloof from the foreign exchange market for weeks, allowing the Singapore dollar to drift lower against its U.S. counterpart. 

 Economists said, however, that the intervention doesn't signal a shift in the central bank's monetary policy, which is to allow the Singapore dollar to remain broadly stable against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

 "Neutrality with regards to the trade-weighted Singapore dollar policy remains in place," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Citibank. 

 Like many regional currencies, the Singapore dollar is lower against the U.S. dollar. But it is stronger against the euro and some other currencies, leaving it broadly unchanged in recent months. 

 Rather than signal a shift in policy, the MAS wanted to put the market on notice that it wouldn't tolerate a significantly weaker Singapore dollar, several economists said. 

 With interest rates in Singapore remaining low and those in the U.S. expected to continue rising, investors have been selling the Singapore currency against the U.S. dollar and earning money on the interest rate spread. 

 The accumulation of such long U.S. dollar positions has threatened to push the U.S. dollar to levels that the MAS could no longer tolerate, analysts said. 

 In particular, the MAS doesn't want to see the U.S. dollar rise above S$1.7400, the currency's last peak in March 1999, said Steve Brice, currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 If the U.S. dollar does break through S$1.7400, it could then rise to the previous peak of S$1.7900, Brice said. "They are just aware that this is a key technical level and if they do go through, it would be that much harder to pull back," Brice said. 

 Traders said the U.S. dollar is likely to drift lower in the short term as profitable long positions are liquidated for fear of further intervention. But several traders said the U.S. currency is likely to find support again around S$1.7220 and start rising again from there.

title: Emerging  FX  - Narrowly mixed again...on Fedwatch.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 27 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 were narrowly mixed in early business with local factors having 

 some influence, although volume was low ahead of the Fed. 

     The two-day Federal Open Market Committee begins its 

 two-day meeting later on Tuesday. 

     A Reuters poll of all 29 primary dealers of U.S. Treasuries 

 showed none expected short-term rates to be changed this time, 

 but most saw a rise in August. 

     The Fed funds target rate is currently 6.5 percent and a 

 decision from this meeting is expected around 1815 GMT on 

 Wednesday. 

     The yen slipped overnight on rumours rating agencies were 

 ready to downgrade Japan's sovereign debt. 

     But the major rating houses said no action had been taken 

 after Japan's elections returned the ruling coalition to power, 

 albeit with a sharply reduced majority. 

     But yen bulls still happy and are looking for a strong 

 tankan next week to set the scene for an end to the zero 

 interest rate policy soon. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Sing dollar was slightly weaker despite strong



industrial output data on Monday.



    Manufacturing output was up 20 percent in May on the year,



boosting hopes the government's growth forecast of 5.5 percent



to 7.5 percent this year will be met.



    The data was not expected to have a major impact on the



Sing dollar as the market had already had a preview through



strong exports in May, dealers said



    They saw a tight range of 1.7300-1.7375 on fears of



possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore


ahead of the 1.74 level.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar opened slightly lower after the central



bank announced on Monday to raise key interest rates by 0.125



percentage points, meeting market expectations, to curb



inflation and stabilise financial conditions.



Effective Tuesday, the discount rate will rise to 4.75



percent from 4.625 percent previously while the accomodation



with collateral rate will climb to 5.125 percent from 5.00



percent.



In addition to fighting inflation, dealers said the cut was



also aimed at playing catch-up with the United States, which



has raised rates by 1.75 percentage points since June 1999.



    Dealers said they broadly expected a T$30.760 to T$30.830



range.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    Tracking regionals, the peso adopted a cautious stance



ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting.



    Under the new tiering scheme, a 10 percent rate was set for



the first five billion pesos placed overnight, 8.5 percent for



the second five billion and seven percent for funds in excess



of 10 billion pesos.



It had previously borrowed at a straight 10 percent.



Traders said banks would have to bring down their peso



deposit rates in line with the new tiering scheme, which in



turn might drive depositors to shift to dollar assets.



The peso was expected to touch an initial support at 42.95



to the dollar in coming days, and later aim to break the 43



psychological support.



KOREAN WON -2



The won was slightly firmer as hefty dollar offers by



exporters outpaced demand from importers.



Dealers said exporters sold dollars for won to meet



month-end financial demand locally. Moreover, the unit was also



underpinned by the prospects for a trade surplus in June.



    Local dealers said the country's trade surplus will likely



be at least $1.0 billion in June.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah was wedged in a tight range with little



direction as the market was dominated by range trading.



    European and Australian banks were head selling dollars to



take profits while American names bid on dips.



    Dealers said the rupiah was unlikely to convincingly break



above 8,500 as concerns over its political and economic



upheavals kept long-term buyers on the sidelines.



    "It's a very thin market to start with. Players are likely



to take profits on the dollar at around 8,700 and buy it back



once it approaches 8,600," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in



Singapore.



    "The market is watching the Fed as there are few fresh



leads from the domestic front to trade on," he said.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht was a touch firmer. Standard and Poor's MMS said



some players who accumulated the dollar in early May when it



was below 38.00 were selling to square positions ahead of



half-year book closings.



    Dealers said the baht should also be underpinned by light



capital inflows into Thailand's fixed income market.



    They said the baht should be trapped in a tight



39.00-39.130 range this week.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Early; Downside Bias Expected
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are narrowly mixed early Tuesday, and are likely to trade at the lower ends of their trading bands ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting, dealers said. 

 While the Federal Open Market Committee is widely anticipated to keep interest rates steady at its two-day meeting, which starts later Tuesday, the market's focus has shifted to the FOMC's next meeting in August. The Fed is expected to resume its tightening cycle then, analysts said. 

 The Fed, which has raised rates by a total of 175 basis points over the past year, is expected to announce Wednesday that there are still inflationary risks for the U.S. economy, analysts said. 

 "Traders will likely take a defensive stance and (are) prone to take profits on gains on the regionals, thus we see a slight weakening bias of the regionals versus the U.S. dollar," said Syetarn Hansakul, an economist at West LB Research. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is being buoyed by news of a civil state of emergency declared in the eastern Maluku islands to halt fierce fighting between Muslims and Christians that has left scores dead in recent days. 

 Around 0130 GMT (9:30 p.m. EDT Monday), the dollar was at 8,680 rupiah, unchanged from late Monday's level. The dollar is expected to find support around IDR8,660 on dollar-buying by local corporates and face resistance around IDR8,725, "unless we see more social tension," said a chief dealer at a European bank. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency has declined to S$1.7332 from S$1.7344 late Monday. The U.S. dollar is expected to remain in its recent range of S$1.7310 to S$1.7360, as lingering fears the Monetary Authority of Singapore might intervene around S$1.7350 contribute to cautious trading, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht is steady at 39.130 baht versus the U.S. dollar. The U.S. currency will likely be hemmed in around THB39.050 to THB39.250 in the absence of market-moving incentives, dealers said. 

 In South Korea, the dollar was at 1,118.50 won, marginally higher than KRW1,118.10 at Monday's close, and is expected to trade at KRW1,117 to KRW1,119. 

 The dollar has edged up to 42.945 pesos from Monday's close of PHP42.910, on an effectively lower Philippine central bank overnight borrowing rate, dealers said. The central bank replaced Monday its single-rate borrowing system with a three-tier system. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was at NT$30.785, down slightly from NT$30.797, as the market shrugged off an expected 12.5-basis-point increase each in two key interest rates by Taiwan's central bank late Monday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Shuffle along, Fed in focus.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 26 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 continued their recent narrowly mixed performance on Monday 

 with Japan's election containing no real surprises and keeping 

 dollar/yen within a narrow range. 

     The ruling coalition managed to hang onto its majority in 

 the Lower House although voters made their feelings clear by 

 handing Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori's ruling bloc a sharply 

 reduced majority. 

     It won 56.5 percent of seats against the two-thirds it held 

 before the election. 

     With the election out of the way the next big focus is the 

 Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. 

     While Fed officials do not yet seem convinced the U.S. 

 economy is slowing the majority in the market do not expect the 

 Fed to move this time. 

     The Fed funds target rate is currently 6.5 percent. 

 However, there are a few who believe Greenspan might want to 

 send a strong message to the fresh stock market bulls and as no 

 change is so widely expected this would be a golden 

 opportunity. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was wedged in a narrow range, with demand for 

 dollars in non-deliverable forwards (NDF) trading kept its 

 upside capped in early trade. 

 Dealers expect the unit to move in a 1117-1125 range this 

 week and it is currently below its 14-day moving average of 

 1116.3. 

     The market is likely to watch closely banks' debt data 

 which the government said it would disclose by the end of June. 

     South Korea's finance ministry recommended that commercial 

 banks should put aside more than three trillion won ($2.86 

 billion) in additional provisions against non-performing loans 

 (NPLs). 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah nudged up on a technical rebound as players took 

 profits from recent dollar gains. 

     But the reprieve would be short-lived as corporate demand 

 for dollars remained robust, dealers said. 

     Indonesia's slowly improving macro economic picture was 

 clouded by political problems which held the government back 

 from taking necessary steps to repair the badly-damaged 

 economy, dealers said. 

 The International Monetary Fund said on Friday Indonesia's 

 economy was "pretty good" but stressed that the government 

 should speed up its recovery programme and sell off more assets 

 if it wanted to lure more foreign investments. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso tracked the regionals higher while the market 

 digested news about the central bank's new tiering scheme on 

 overnight borrowing rate. 

 The central bank said on Monday that the first five billion 

 pesos worth of funds placed overnight with the agency would 

 receive a 10 percent rate and the second five billion pesos 

 would receive 8.5 percent. 

 Funds in excess of 10 billion pesos would receive seven 

 percent while overnight lending rate would stay unchanged at 

 12.25 percent, it said. 

     The move effectively cut the borrowing rate from the 

 previous 10 percent, it said. 

     Dealers said the news was likely to have limited impact on 

 the peso which looked set to test 42.93 in the near-term. 

     "Most players still look to buy dollars on dips. I don't 

 think the peso will be able to break 42.70 in the near-term 

 because that's the level where the market expects dollar 

 bargain hunters to emerge," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was flat in thin early trade and most companies 

 had closed their books for the first half of the year. 

 The market seemed to be digesting news that the main 

 opposition New Aspiration Party (NAP) would resign en masse on 

 Wednesday to force an early election, dealers said. 

     Some dealers said the news was unlikely to fluster the 

 market because an election must be called by November anyway. 

     Moreover, a spokesman for the Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai 

 said the government would still be able to push through next 

 year's budget by September. 

     Dealers expected the baht to move in a narrow range pending 

 the Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates on Wednesday 

 and the release of central bank's monthly economic data on 

 Friday. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar retained its weak tone due to demand for 

 the U.S. dollar from local companies seeking to investment 

 abroad, dealers said. 

 But players were reluctant to sell the unit aggressively on 

 fears of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of 

Singapore. 

 Some dealers said the Sing dollar should remain trapped in 

 a range of 1.7300-1.7375 as the authority would probably step 

 in ahead of the 1.74 level. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was easier as recent consolidation in 

 local stocks dampened demand for the unit. 

 But the downside should be limited due to the stronger yen. 

 The Taiwan dollar is typically affected by movements in the yen 

 because Taiwan and Japan compete in the similar export markets. 

 Dealers said they expected the Taiwanese central bank to 

 hike rediscount rate by 25 basis points in its policy board 

 meeting on Monday. 

 "Justification is based on the recent rise of inflation to 

 1.6 percent in May and to catch up with U.S. interest rates," 

 SEB Merchant Banking said in a report. 

 "However, with leading index dipping for three straight 

 months and inflation largely an imported phenomenon, we rather 

 think the central bank will keep rates on hold until the second 

 half," it said.

 Trading is expected to remain subdued as market participants are hesitant to open up new positions as the half-year end approaches, dealers said. 

 Caution is also prevailing ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting beginning Tuesday, dealers said. While the Fed is widely anticipated to leave interest rates unchanged, some market participants have already priced in the possibility of a 25-basis-point hike, dealers said. 

 The Japanese yen's stability, after the Liberal Democratic Party-led coalition retained power in elections for Parliament's lower house Sunday, has provided little incentive for Asian currencies to snap out of their recent trading ranges, dealers noted.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Down Early; Rupiah Breaks Key Support
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies are lower early Thursday, with the Indonesian rupiah accelerating late Wednesday's slide after Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin was detained, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar muscled its way through the 8,700 rupiah level - which had proved a tough level to crack in recent weeks - to IDR8,728 at 0115 GMT (9:15 p.m. EDT Wednesday). The last time the dollar was around this level was in mid-May. 

 The latest twist in the politically-charged feud between President Abdurrahman Wahid's government and Bank Indonesia's Sjahril has scared investors. 

 Shahril has been detained for his alleged involvement in the Bank Bali scandal. 

 Dealers said Sjahril's detention comes as a surprise given newly enacted laws that stress the central bank's independence and could hamper the progress of the country's financial reforms. 

 "The market's losing confidence," a dealer at a U.S. bank said. "There's no policy consistency." 

 The dollar could test IDR8,750 later in the day, although this could be stymied by Bank Indonesia's moves to defend the rupiah and the relatively modest interest to buy dollars at higher levels, dealers said. 

 The weaker rupiah has weighed on the Singapore dollar, the Thai baht and the Philippine peso, dealers said. 

 A confluence of factors has also pushed the U.S. currency to break a key resistance level against the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 Having broken above S$1.7350 resistance, the U.S. dollar is likely to test S$1.7380-S$1.7390 later Thursday, dealers said. 

 At 0135 GMT, the dollar was quoted at S$1.7350, up from S$1.7347 late Wednesday. Earlier, the dollar risen to a high of S$1.7362, but retreated on profit-taking and fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. 

 Strong U.S. dollar demand linked to DBS Bank's recapitalization of unit DBS Thai Danu Bank, Singapore Power's A$2.1 billion acquisition of Australian power transmission company GPU PowerNet, and a reclamation project on Jurong Island have weighed on the Singapore currency, dealers said. 

 However, the MAS' plan to introduce new legislation that forces Singapore's banks to separate their non-financial activities from their core bank and finance business has had little impact on the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar has broken resistance at 39.200 baht, but isn't expected to test the next resistance level at THB39.300 as offshore selling in U.S. dollars will likely cap the U.S. currency around current levels, dealers said. 

 The dollar was quoted at THB39.240, up from THB39.175 late Thursday. 

 In Manila, the dollar was quoted at 42.970 pesos, up from Wednesday's close at PHP42.830. 

 Unscathed by the regional market's weakness, the South Korean won has been buoyed by the 2% rally on the local bourse. The dollar was quoted at 1,118.80 won, down from Wednesday's close at KRW1,119.10.

title: Emerging  FX  - Rupiah bounces, others rangebound.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 1 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah	



stole the show in late trade on Thursday as talk the government


 might be exploring some form of capital control prompted 

 players to cover their short positions. 

     Other Asian regional currencies shuffled along, driven by 

 commercial demand and moving within their recent ranges. 


    The yen	  retreated to six-week lows against the euro



 and its lowest level since May 19 against the dollar



on worries about the health of Japan's financial sector.



    Such fears were triggered after mid-sized Japanese insurer



Daihyaku Mutual Life announced its closure, which spurred fears



of more such bad news.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah gained almost three percent as players, spooked



by the capital controls talk, rushed to cover short positions



in thin offshore markets. Jakarta was closed for a holiday.



    Singapore dealers said foreign banks in Asia and London



actively covered short rupiah positions against the U.S. dollar



and the Singapore dollar after Horst Koehler, the new IMF



chief, said controls on capital movements were not "taboo", but

Analysts said the IMF's apparent softening in stance might

title: Singapore Dlr Ends Up Late; Gives Up Most Intraday Gains
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar gave up most of its intraday gains but managed to end slightly higher against its U.S. counterpart in quiet trading Wednesday. 

 Around 0850 GMT (4:50 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7335, down from S$1.7345 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Early in the day, the Singapore dollar gained along with other regional currencies on the back of rallies in Asian stock markets, which were sparked by Tuesday's 7.94% jump on the Nasdaq Composite Index. 

 Regional currencies were also buoyed as exporters sold U.S. dollars in time for month-end bookkeeping, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar briefly dropped below the level of S$1.7300 before starting to climb again on the back of gains against the yen, dealers said. 

 Local banks started selling the U.S. currency at the level of S$1.7345, pushing it back down again, dealers said. The selling sparked rumors of central bank intervention. 

 Although the Monetary Authority of Singapore generally acts through local banks, dealers said there was no evidence of intervention. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar is likely to remain vulnerable to movements in Indonesia and elsewhere because of the island-state's increasingly close economic links to its neighbors. 

 "There is no reason for me to tell anybody to put his money into Sing dollars," said a trading desk chief at a European bank. "Sentiment is very weak."

title: Emerging  FX  - Treading water, rupiah comes to.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 little changed in late trade on Tuesday, though the Indonesian 

 rupiah managed to pull off its lows after the central bank

 governor denied rumours of his resignation. 

     Assurances by Indonesian economic ministers that the IMF 

 was likely to release a delayed $400 million loan in June as 

 Jakarta had met all its economic reform targets also lent some 

 support to the currency. 


    Activity in G7 currencies was dominated by the euro	 ,



which rose to five-week highs against the dollar on



expectations the European Central Bank would raise interest



rates at its next meeting and on supportive comments from



European officials.



    The yen	  regained lost ground against the dollar,



bolstered by bullish economic data and an upbeat OECD report.



 The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development



(OECD) projected that Japan will grow 1.7 percent in this



calendar year, up from its previous forecast of 1.4 percent



growth.



    It said in its semi-annual report that Japan's economy was



on a cyclical recovery path with deflationary pressures easing,



but warned that the country should continue to aim at



sustaining the recovery given uncertainties over economic



prospects.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah fell near a May 12 low of 8,770 on reports the


central Bank Indonesia governor Sjahril Sabirin planned to



resign as early as Tuesday in connection with the high profile



Bank Bali scandal.



    But it managed to claw back some losses after the bank



denied the reports. A recovery in the stock market also helped



improve sentiment, dealers said.



    Onshore dollar demand took the lead as most offshore



dealers remained sidelined due to the U.S. Memorial Day holiday



on Monday.



    Chief economic minister Kwik Kian Gie said the recent



decline in the rupiah was driven by psychological factors and



was not in line with economic fundamentals.



    He also expressed confidence that the IMF would proceed



with the disbursement of a delayed $400 million loan tranche.



     PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso ended lower as most players kept a cautious stance



due to lingering concerns over the domestic political



situation.



    Dealers said the market was unmoved by first quarter GDP



data that showed the economy growing 3.4 percent year-on-year,



broadly in line with expectations.



    The peso hit an intraday low of 42.90 before recovering



near the close.



    "It was pretty quiet," one dealer said. "It was only range



trading...the low volume also suggests that most of the players



are very cautious."

over the domestic political situation.

    KOREAN WON	   -2

    Dollar buying in the non-deliverable forward market



overseas prompted late short-covering, limiting the won's



upside, dealers said.



    "In early trade, the currency market traced the movement of

    Fears of foreign equity funds selling local stocks and



uncertainty over Taiwan-China relations also dampened sentiment



for the local currency.

title: Singapore Dlr Slightly Weaker Late In Quiet Range Trading
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar is slightly weaker against its U.S. counterpart, reflecting weakness on other regional currencies, in quiet, range-bound trading on Tuesday. 

 Around 0850 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7345, up from S$1.7336 late Monday in Asia. 

 Although the Singapore dollar weakened slightly, it remained well within its recent trading range, showing that it has managed to insulate itself from wild swings in other Asian currencies like the peso and rupiah, dealers said. 

 With the U.S. dollar stable against the yen and weakening slightly against the euro, traders are no longer convinced it will continue to rise against the Singapore dollar, one said. 

 In addition, the market is unwilling to push the U.S. dollar higher against the Singapore dollar for fear of provoking intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, one dealer added, even though there have been no recent reports of the MAS checking prices. 

 However, some dealers say the Singapore dollar could remain sensitive to strong movements in the rupiah, which has been weakened by reports of sectarian violence in Indonesia and doubts about the direction of economic reform. 

 If the U.S. dollar moves above IDR8,800, "The pressure will be on the Sing," one dealer said. 

 But barring any major turbulence in Indonesia, most dealers say the U.S. dollar is likely to continue trading in its recent range of S$1.7300 to S$1.7350.

title: Singapore Dlr Dips To 13-Month Low, Regains Ground Late
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar weakened Wednesday amid wider turmoil in regional stock and currency markets, briefly falling to its lowest level in more than 13 months before regaining some ground, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar rose to an intraday high of S$1.7363, its highest point since April 5, 1999, before slipping back to S$1.7358 around 0820 GMT (4:40 a.m. EDT). Late Tuesday in Asia, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7318. 

 Like other regional currencies, the Singapore dollar has been weakened by declining share prices and concerns that interest rates in the U.S. will continue to rise, making Asian assets relatively less attractive. 

 But the Singapore currency is being bolstered by the country's political stability and sound economic fundamentals, even as currencies like the Philippine peso are punished. 

 "It's quite resilient," a dealer said of the Singapore currency. "It has stabilized. I'm not sure we will go further (down) from here." 

 Dealers added that the threat of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, though unlikely, is forcing buyers of U.S. dollars to move cautiously. 

 "A lot of people are buying (U.S.) dollars on the dips," a dealer said. "They are testing the S$1.7365-70 level" to see if the MAS intervenes. 

 Local Singapore banks did sell U.S. dollars near the day's peak, the dealer said, but added that it was unlikely that the banks were acting at the behest of the MAS. The de-facto central bank generally intervenes by placing orders through local banks. 

 Another dealer said that the U.S. dollar isn't likely to move above Wednesday's peak. "A lot of people are happy to sell dollars around those regions," the dealer said. 

 In fact, some players appear to be betting on MAS intervention, and have sold the U.S. dollar short. Stop loss orders on those short positions could propel the U.S. dollar higher if it breaches S$1.7370, dealers said.

title: Singapore Dlr Lower; Pressured By Peso, Inflation Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A swooning Philippine peso pulled down the Singapore dollar in its wake early Wednesday along with other regional currencies. 

 Around 0245 GMT (10:45 p.m. EDT Tuesday), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7352, up from S$1.7318 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 The peso fell to its lowest point since October 1998, pressured by various factors such as the recent bombings in Manila and the Muslim insurgency in the south. At 0200 GMT, the U.S. dollar pushed past the psychological 42.50 peso level. 

 The Singapore dollar's woes were compounded by plunge in local share prices and surprisingly low inflation data for April, which suggest that a tightening of monetary policy isn't in the offing. 

 Data released late Tuesday show that annual inflation in April came to 1.1%, down from 1.2% in March. As a result, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has no incentive to favor a stronger currency, said Simon Flint, an economist at the Bank of America. 

 "In the foreseeable term it's hard to see them tightening monetary policy," Flint said. The MAS uses the exchange rate, rather than interest rates, as its primary monetary policy tool. 

 Stocks are down sharply early Wednesday. The Straits Times Index is off 2.96%, or 55.63 points, at 1850.15 points. 

 Dealers said, however, that the Singapore dollar is showing greater resilience to the regional market turmoil than other currencies. A dealer at a U.S. bank said there are few long U.S. dollar positions against the Singapore dollar. 

 As a result, intervention by the MAS to support the currency is unlikely, the dealer said. "They won't intervene anytime soon," he said. "The market isn't long enough on dollars." 

 Even so, participants are likely to tread carefully for fear of provoking intervention, dealer said, adding that the U.S. dollar is unlikely to move above S$1.7370 Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso has been hammered by a spate of bombings in Manila and the hostage crisis in southern Philippines. There are also concerns about cronyism in the government.

title: Singapore Dollar Ends Lower As Regional  Currencies  Weaken

SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar was dragged down by other regional currencies to end lower Tuesday as stock markets fell across most of Asia. 

 Around 0955 GMT (5:55 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7318, up from S$1.7277 late Monday in Asia. 

 Expectations that interest rates will continue to rise in the U.S., together with declines in Asian stock markets, have pushed down local currencies as foreign investors liquidate their holdings and buy U.S. dollars. 

 In Singapore, the Straits Times Index fell 1.25%, or 24.10 points, to end at 1905.78 points, in reaction to interest-rate worries and declining stock prices in the U.S. 

 Dealers said they expected the Singapore dollar to continue weakening in coming days. Further declines could provoke intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore at the level of S$1.7350, one dealer said. 

 "I think people will be cautiously buying on dips," the dealer said. "I think you will see regional currencies weakening across the board." 

 If the U.S. dollar breaches S$1.7350 without drawing intervention, stop-loss orders above that level could quickly propel it to between S$1.7400 and S$1.7500, dealers said. 

 Local economic data isn't expected to help the Singapore dollar, which lately has been reacting largely to other regional currencies, such as the Indonesian rupiah. 

 Inflation data for April is due to be released at 1030 GMT on Tuesday. However, inflation is likely to remain under control, meaning that the MAS will have no incentive to tighten exchange-rate policy, Citibank said in a research report. 

 Citibank said it expects annual inflation in April to remain unchanged at 1.2%. "An inflation rate below 2% is healthy and should not trigger any sustained policy tightening," Citibank said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down On Stock Market Falls;Peso Hits 19-Mo Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The drubbing on regional stock markets continued to push Asian currencies lower late Tuesday. 

 However, while a recovery in the yen provided a mild respite for some currencies in late trading, faltering investor confidence in the Philippines sent the peso reeling to a fresh 19-month low. 

 The peso will likely remain frail as long as the conflict in the southern island of Mindanao between government military forces and Muslim rebels remains unresolved and bombings in Manila continue to raise concerns over national security, market observers said. 

 "It's difficult to envisage any significant improvement in the short term," Bank of America strategist Simon Flint said. 

 The dollar closed at 42.370 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up 46 centavos from Monday's close of PHP41.915. 

 Earlier in the session, the dollar climbed to a fresh 19-month high of PHP42.375, its highest level since hitting PHP42.560 Oct. 23, 1998. 

 Market players expect more gloom for the peso. 

 "I wouldn't be surprised if the dollar hits PHP43 to PHP44, or even PHP46 this year," a dealer at an Asian bank said. 

 Some analysts expect the central bank to step in soon to prop up the peso, despite Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura's remarks Tuesday that the authority isn't intervening on the spot market to help support the peso and will continue to allow the local currency to remain "market-determined." 

 Buenaventura said the central bank didn't intervene Tuesday to defend the ailing local currency by selling dollars on the spot market. 

 Analysts, however, said the central bank can only provide temporary reprieve for peso. 

 "We are afraid the country needs more drastic solutions to help mend the peso weakness," said Syetarn Hansakul, an analyst at WestLB Research. 

 The dollar has breached every resistance level pegged by traders in daily spot market trading since April 24, following the abduction of 21 Western and Asian hostages from a Malaysian diving resort by Philippine Muslim rebels. 

 Philippine Finance Secretary Jose Pardo said Tuesday he believes the weak peso is a "serious concern" because it could erode the economic gains due to strong imports earlier in the year. 


Separately, Buenaventura said further raising the overnight borrowing
rate, which stands at 10%, remains an "option" to preempt another U.S.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Early On Stock Mkt,Domestic Woes
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies are weaker against the dollar early Tuesday, pressured by declining regional stock markets, dealers said, adding that the Philippine peso and South Korean won have been rendered particularly vulnerable by domestic political and financial woes. 

 While most Asian currencies are expected to be confined to narrow trading bands in the absence of a clear short-term trend, the peso has resumed its rapid descent, dealers said. 

 The dollar rose to a fresh 19-month high of 42.05 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Monday's close at PHP41.915. 

 A bomb blast last Sunday in the country's largest shopping mall has reinforced fears of political instability and concerns over national security, threatening the country's mediocre economic growth prospects and President Joseph Estrada's administration. An unresolved conflict in the south between government military forces and Muslim separatists has also damped investors' confidence in the country. 

 A trader said the dollar is set to climb further to PHP42.20 later in the day, but the Philippine central bank could step in at that level to prevent a further slide. 

 But Philippine Finance Secretary Pardo hinted earlier in the day that the central bank may not be very keen to intervene at this stage. While Pardo said the weak peso is a "serious concern" because it will affect the country's level of imports for the rest of the year, he added that the central bank will defend the local currency only "if it becomes absolutely necessary." 

 The slide in regional bourses has cast a pall on most Asian currencies, following the volatility in the U.S. stock market overnight, dealers said. 

 "The forex market is taking a back seat, following what is happening on the equity market," a dealer said. 

 In New York Monday, the Nasdaq Composite Index plummeted as much as 6.4% to a year-low of 3172.65 before recovering a bulk of its losses to end just 0.8%, or 26 points, lower at 3364. The Dow Jones Industrial Average pared a 250-point loss to close 0.8%, or 84.30 points, lower at 10542.55. 

 Against the Korean won, the dollar has climbed to 1133.90 won, the highest intraday level since it hit KRW1135.50 on Feb. 29. The dollar had closed at a 12-week high of KRW1130.60 Monday. 

 Looming potential problems at South Korean financial institutions due to ongoing concerns about needed reforms at investment trust companies and debt restructuring have weighed on the won, dealers said. 

 But signaling its intention to expedite reforms of investment trust companies, South Korea's Finance and Economy Ministry will complete the planned injection of KRW4.9 trillion in public funds into ailing Korea Investment Trust Co. and Daehan Investment Trust Co. by end June, instead of September, as previously planned, the local Yonhap News Agency reported Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar has weakened in sympathy with its regional counterparts, dealers said. 

 At 0245 GMT (10:45 p.m. EDT Monday), the U.S. dollar is quoted at S$1.7340, up from S$1.7277 late Monday. 

 However, the Singapore dollar's fall will likely be tempered by fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may intervene to defend the currency if it declines too steeply, dealers said. 

 "There's talk the authorities will cap it," a dealer said. "But looking at the regional currencies across the board, I doubt it...It's not a Singapore dollar problem." 

 Even if the de facto central bank were to intervene, it will unlikely be aggressive, the dealer added. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the U.S. dollar is quoted at 8495 rupiah, up from IDR8318. 

 The dollar has also strengthened against the Thai baht, and was quoted at 39.18 baht compared with THB39.00 late Monday. 

 The Thai baht is poised to weaken further, but will likely face psychological resistance at THB39.50-THB40, dealers said. 

 Fears the central bank may defend the ailing currency around that level will likely cap the U.S. dollar's strength, dealers said. 

 In Taiwan, the U.S. dollar has risen to NT$30.736, from its Monday's close at NT$30.709, following a 1.6% slide in Taiwan stocks, dealers said. 

 The central bank is, however, expected to remain active in market to maintain the local currency's stability, some dealers said.
