title: Merrill sees Thai cenbank tolerating weaker baht.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 16 (Reuters) - Despite its recent rumoured interventions, Thailand's central bank is unlikely to be overly concerned about the baht's weakness as long as inflation does not overshoot its targets, Merrill Lynch said. 

 The Bank of Thailand has projected a 2.5-3.0 percent inflation rate for 2000 against 0.3 percent in 1999. 

 "Our baht forecast rests mainly on domestic inflation," said Suvavud Saicheua, head of Thailand economics at Merrill Lynch in a note to clients. 

 "As long as inflation does not exceed four percent, we believe that the Bank of Thailand can tolerate some baht weakness," he said. 

 The report said the central bank is likely to leave interest rates unchanged for the next 12 months to keep Thailand's economic recovery on track despite growing prospects for more aggressive interest rate increases in the U.S. 

 This means it will have to be more tolerant of a weaker baht. 

 "Recent Bank of Thailand intervention to push the baht back below 39 per dollar does not imply a baht target in our view. Rather, it suggests that the BOT would like to increase the cost of speculation against the baht," Supavud said. 

 "The three percent baht depreciation from 1999 would push inflation up by only 1.0-1.5 percent in our estimation...," he said, citing factors including declining food prices. 

 The baht was quoted at 39.26/31 per dollar at 0527 GMT, down some 4.6 percent from its end-1999 level of 37.45, based on Reuters Graphics data. 

 Merrill said it was sticking to its recently revised forecast of 39 baht per dollar for the fourth quarter and the rest of 2001, although occasional weakness beyond this level could not be ruled out. 

 Merrill lowered the forecast earlier this month from a previous projection of 38.00 per dollar.

title: Indonesia Must Weigh Downside Of  Currency Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Of the Southeast Asian nations considering central bank intervention to shore up their faltering currencies, Indonesia may well be at the head of the queue. 

 But such meddling in the market is never without its costs, and Indonesia probably would suffer the harshest side effects by doing so, analysts say. 

Currencies across the region have been trending downward for several weeks in the face of broad-based dollar strength associated with rising interest rates in the U.S. In the case of Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, the pressure has been exacerbated by a host of local factors weighing on the currencies. 

 For Indonesia, the road has been perhaps the roughest, with the currency experiencing wild swings amid growing investor uncertainty about the Jakarta government's ability to push through reforms and keep the economic expansion on track. 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid and his top advisors haven't helped matters by issuing confusing statements about exactly what the government was prepared to do to keep the rupiah from falling further. 

 Wahid's latest jawboning Tuesday appeared to provide some stability for the currency as the dollar fell to about 8,500 rupiah after trading as high as IDR8,720 earlier in the day. 

 "I have asked the finance minister to persuade state banks to help (boost the rupiah)," Wahid said at a news conference. 

 "I have also asked Bank Indonesia to take necessary action to stop the rupiah weakening," he added, in a clear effort to prod intervention by the supposedly independent central bank. 

 But with limited foreign currency reserves, the central bank would be limited by the amount it could spend defending the rupiah, said Steve Brice, treasury economist for Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 With a huge debt level more than 100% of GDP, Indonesia can ill afford to squander its reserves in what would likely be an ill-fated attempt to stop a stampeding market, analysts say. 

 Such a move also would go against the advice of the International Monetary Fund, which has been providing the discipline keeping Indonesia on the path to reform, Brice added. 

 "The IMF has been keeping Indonesia pointed in the right direction. The only way we'll see the rupiah strengthen is through a massive change in international investor confidence that comes with continued reform," he said. 

 Other possible quick fixes available to Indonesia, such as capital controls or a currency board, also would do more harm than good because they would take the pressure off the government to stick with the tough IMF-prescribed reforms, Brice said. 

 John Dodsworth, the IMF's Indonesia representative, made the institution's position clear in comments Monday. 


"We don't think the government should spend the money on defending an
exchange rate when it has so many other choices to spend the money on,"
he said in Brussels.
  - - 16/05/00 09-38G



In contrast to Indonesia, government officials in Thailand and the
Philippines probably are not overly concerned about the recent
depreciation of their currencies, analysts said.



They might even quietly invite a certain amount of slippage to help
the competitiveness of their exports, as long as inflation remains under
control, analysts said.



Merrill Lynch's forecast for the Thai baht rests mainly on the
performance of domestic inflation.



"As long as inflation does not exceed 4%, we believe that the Bank of
Thailand can tolerate some baht weakness," said Supavud Saicheua, head
of Thailand economics for Merrill Lynch.



Thailand, which last week became the first financial crisis victim to
emerge from IMF oversight, was rumored to have supported the baht
through central bank intervention when the dollar rose above the
THB39.000 level.



But the central bank's motivation needs to be carefully examined,
Supavud said in a research paper.



"We believe the BOT's intervention in the foreign exchange market to
push the baht back below 39 per dollar does not signal an attempt to
defend the baht at that level," he said. It appeared to be more of an
effort to prevent excessive volatility and deter speculators from
attacking the currency, according to Supavud.



The Bank of Thailand's main objective is to keep the Thai economic
recovery from stalling, and to do so it needs to keep interest rates low
and the baht competitive against other regional currencies, he said.



The Philippines similarly probably will tolerate a certain amount of
peso depreciation to keep its economic expansion moving forward, Brice
said. The currency has been under pressure lately from expectations of
higher U.S. interest rates and government fighting with separatist
rebels in the southern Philippines.



The dollar closed Tuesday at 41.630 pesos, its highest level since
late October 1998.



Economic fundamentals, including the Philippines' improving budget
situation, should be encouraging investment there, Brice said.



"Unfortunately for the authorities, the market is not looking at
that," he said.



The central bank will probably remain on the sidelines as long as the
depreciation of the peso occurs in an orderly fashion, Brice said.



"If the dollar hits 42 pesos over the coming week I don't think they
will be worried at all."

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Lower Late; Rupiah Off 7-Mo Low

 The Indonesian rupiah was slightly weaker, but well above its intraday low. 

 Fears of intervention by Indonesia's central bank and state banks lifted the currency, which has plunged as much as 9% over the past week. 

 It rallied sharply from a near seven month-low after Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid urged the central bank and state-run banks to support the flagging local currency. 

 Syetarn Hansakul, an analyst with WestLB, said "Wahid's intervention comment today helped lend some support but may not be enough if U.S. FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) impacts negatively tomorrow." 

 It is also unclear if Wahid could order the central bank, which in theory works independently from the president, to defend the local currency, analysts said. 

 Wahid also instructed Finance Minister Bambang Sudibyo to review the economic projections in this year's budget, which appear too optimistic. The government had based the budget on an exchange rate of 7,000 rupiah to a dollar. 

 The U.S. currency late in the local session was at 8,545 rupiah, marginally up from IDR8,541 late Monday, but well below its intraday high of IDR8,730.

 The FOMC is widely expected to raise short-term interest rates by half a percentage point in an effort to slow rapid U.S. economic growth to a more sustainable rate. 

 As the market has largely factored in a hike of this magnitude, some analysts say they expect a "relief rally" in Asian currencies in the short term if this occurs. 

 The extent of the rate hike is expected to be influenced by U.S. inflation data, to be released before the FOMC meets. 

 The looming U.S. rate hike and a domestic political crisis embattling Philippine President Joseph Estrada's administration dragged the Philippine peso to a 19-month low. 

 The Estrada administration has been widely criticized for its handling of the country's hostage crisis. 

 The dollar's gains were, however, capped at 41.640 pesos as banks that were long on dollars opted to take profit at this level before repurchasing the U.S. currency at a lower rate, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at PHP41.630 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from of PHP41.560 Monday. 

 Philippine central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Tuesday that while the peso should strengthen after jitters over the Fed's rate decision subside, it will likely remain above PHP41 to a dollar in the near term. 

 Buenaventura reiterated that the central bank is prepared to provide dollar liquidity to the market if necessary, but this hasn't been needed yet. 

 The South Korean won ended little changed against the U.S. dollar as afternoon dollar selling by local banks offset earlier dollar buying by overseas players in the non-deliverable forward market, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,114.60 won, barely changed from Monday's close at KRW1,114.70. 

 Bucking the regional weakness, the Singapore dollar was slightly stronger as participants locked in profits on some long U.S. dollar positions ahead of the FOMC's meeting, traders said. 

 Around 0950 GMT (5:50 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7280, down from S$1.7296 late Monday in Asia. 

 A 50 basis-point U.S. rate increase will be neutral for the Singapore dollar, traders said, adding that they expected the U.S. unit to continue trading in a range of between S$1.7250 and S$1.7350. 

 However, the outlook for the likely level of the Singapore dollar has been clouded by the expectation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, would intervene at the upper end of that range.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Early Ahead Of Expected US Rate Hike
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are lower against the dollar early Tuesday on the eve of what most analysts expect will be an aggressive interest rate hike in the U.S. 

 Local factors, such as political turmoil Indonesia and concerns over debt restructuring in Thailand also weighed on regional currencies, dealers said. 

 The Federal Reserve's policy making committee is widely expected to raise short-term interest rates by a half percentage point later Tuesday in an effort to slow rapid U.S. economic growth to a more sustainable rate. 

 Such a move would represent a tightening of policy for the Fed, which has limited its rate hikes to a quarter point since it began its latest round of tightening last June. 

 The strengthening dollar has taken its biggest toll on Indonesia and Thailand, where corporations that have high levels of dollar-denominated debt want to get their hands on the U.S. currency before interest rates rise. 

 The dollar opened higher against the rupiah and continued to gain ground in early trading. At 0145 GMT (9:45 p.m. EDT Monday), the dollar was quoted at 8,715 rupiah, up from IDR8,541 late Monday. Dealers expect a trading range of IDR8,500-IDR8,800 Tuesday. 

 Against the baht, the dollar was quoted at THB39.315, up from 39.250 late Monday. 

 "Corporates are frantically trying to get their hands on dollars," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 The Singapore dollar moved precipitously close to the 1.7350-per-dollar level that dealers said could trigger intervention by local monetary authorities. 

 The U.S. dollar touched S$1.7333 within the first hour of trading before falling back to S$1.7314, up from S$1.7296 late Monday. Short-covering spurred by expectations of higher U.S. rates pushed the U.S. dollar up overnight in London and New York trading, dealers said. 

 U.S. dollar appreciation above S$1.7350 probably will be limited by concerns of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, dealers said. The MAS was said to have entered the market last week to sell U.S. dollars when the currency rose above that level. 

 The peso was lower on U.S. interest rate jitters, hitting its lowest level in nearly seven months. 

 The dollar was quoted at 41.615 pesos after closing at PHP41.560 Monday. Continued gains could push the dollar to PHP41.700, dealers said. 

 The dollar's rise against the New Taiwan dollar likely drew central bank intervention in early trading, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; Rupiah Casts Pall Over Region
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The foundering Indonesian rupiah Monday cast a pall over regional Asian currencies already under pressure from what analysts say is an impending hike in U.S. interest rates later this week. 

 The rupiah has taken a pummeling in recent weeks amid growing investor skepticism about the Indonesian government's ability to push ahead with reforms and keep the economic recovery on track. 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid said Monday he had no plan of action to keep the currency from falling further, but added he would be discussing the situation with his economic ministers in the coming days if the weakness persists. 

 An outbreak of rioting in the streets of Jakarta's Chinatown over the weekend provided the latest impetus for market players to dump the rupiah. 

 Late Monday, the dollar was quoted at 8,541 rupiah, up from IDR8,485 late Friday. 

 The currency had been pushed to seven-month low of IDR8,768 to a dollar at one point last Friday following a confusing barrage of comments by Indonesian policy makers. Wahid helped the currency rebound at the day's end by saying the government was prepared to act if the currency remained weak. 

 That sparked speculation that he was prepared to impose some type of capital controls, but on Monday he said his comments were misinterpreted. 

 The Singapore dollar couldn't escape the gravitational pull of the falling rupiah. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7296, up from S$1.7243 late Friday. 

 Although the Singapore dollar mimicked the rupiah, its swings were far more moderate, and its losses were capped by expectations that the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene above the level of S$1.7300. 

 Some analysts said there was a chance that the Singapore dollar and rupiah could get a boost if investors move to liquidate their long U.S. dollar positions ahead of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting in the U.S. 

 Market players have been snapping up U.S. dollars on expectations that the FOMC will raise short-term rates by a half percentage point, and that it likely will continue raising rates later in the year. 

 The Philippine peso also suffered under the weight of the expected narrowing of interest rate differentials with the U.S. 

 Profit-taking by banks long on dollars capped the U.S. currency's gains, however, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 41.560 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Friday's close at PHP41.500. 

 Concerns over the conflict in southern Mindanao between Muslim rebels and government troops, as well as questions on the stability of the banking industry, have been brushed aside for the time being, traders said. 

 The South Korean won slipped to its lowest closing level against the U.S. dollar in nearly eight weeks on dollar buying by overseas players in the non-deliverable forward market. 

 The dollar closed at 1,114.70 won, up from KRW1,114.50 on Friday. It was the highest close for the U.S. dollar since March 21 when it reached KRW1,116.40. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended weaker on concerns over relations with China and the ailing stock markets in Taiwan. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$30.767, up from NT$30.735 Friday. Trading was light as many market participants were sidelined, awaiting President-elect Chen Shui-bian's inauguration speech Saturday, hoping for clues on future relations with China, dealers said. 

 Rupiah weakness weighed on the Thai baht, which breached the a key support level of 39.200 to a dollar. Lack of liquidity in the rupiah forced some dealers to sell the baht in a proxy move. 

 In late trading the dollar was quoted at 39.250 baht, up from THB38.845 late Friday.

title: No need to change Singapore dollar policy - govt.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 11 (Reuters) - Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Wednesday the government saw no reason to change its policy on the Singapore dollar. 

 "Our currency is not on autopilot. There is a trade weight which we monitor, but we exercise judgement in deciding how closely to follow (it) over the short-term," Lee told parliament. 

 He was replying to parliamentary questions on whether Singapore would devalue the Singapore dollar due to the sharp depreciation of other currencies in Southeast Asia. 

 "I don't see ourselves having to make major adjustments to our policy as a result of regional currency movements," he said. 

 Singapore's de facto central bank, The Monetary Authority of Singapore, intervenes from time to time to adjust the value of the Singapore dollar on foreign exchange markets. 

 The government says its policy is mainly guided by the value of the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of international currencies.

title: Singapore Dollar A Touch Higher In Choppy Pre-Budget Trade

title: FOCUS - Asia  currencies  off highs as Sing dlr fizzles.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies remained firm but were off their highs in late Friday trade as the Singapore dollar subsided after the country's 1998 budget failled to deliver any major tax cuts. 

 But traders were reluctant to commit themselves aggressively due to possible weekend developments, including an ASEAN finance ministers meeting in Jakarta expected to address the proposal of using regional currencies for intra-ASEAN trade. 

 "We could see totally different levels when we come in on Monday so I don't think people want to carry positions over the weekend," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The U.S. dollar's decline against the yen and gains in several Asian stock markets following Wall Street's bullish performance helped regional currencies stay on positive ground. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped back through the 1.62 level to the U.S. dollar in thin overseas markets as Finance Minister Richard Hu concluded his budget speech without any mention of a widely-sought corporate tax cut. 

 Hu announced a series of tax concessions for the financial sector, but added that Singapore's tax rates remained competitive and no major tax changes were to be made against a backdrop of lower revenues and rising development expenditure. 

 He said Singapore should see a budget surplus of S$2.7 billion, or 1.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1998, compared with an average surplus of 3.8 percent of GDP in 1996 and 1997. 

 The Singapore dollar reached early highs of 1.6100/10 to the U.S. dollar on stop-loss U.S. dollar sales sparked by expectations of a pro-business budget. 

 It was also lifted by Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's comment that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) would maintain confidence in the domestic dollar by intervening in foreign exchange markets when necessary. 

 Lee told parliament fears of a sharp fall in the rupiah dragging down the Singapore dollar were hypothetical at this stage and "the weight of the rupiah in our basket is small". 

 Talk of MAS intervention kept the Singapore dollar from strengthening through the 1.61 level in early trade, but dealers said it was likely to target the 1.60 level soon. 

 The Malaysian ringgit tracked its neighbour's moves, benefitting further from gains in Kuala Lumpur stocks and news the government was raising the ceiling on foreign share ownership in telecommunications companies. 

 News Standard and Poor's Corp had lowered its ratings on six Malaysian banks failed to dampen sentiment, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah rose through the 9,000 per dollar level on U.S. dollar sales by U.S. investment houses in the wake of the Singapore dollar's early rise. 

 But dealers said worries about unrest ahead of the presidential elections and uncertainty over Indonesia's plans to stabilise its rupiah via a currency board system would limit gains to the 8,500 level. 

 The Thai baht made way for investor and corporate dollar demand after failing to firm above the 42.50 per dollar level. Dealers said the market was largely unmoved by economic data showing a $1.03 billion trade surplus and a $1.18 billion current account surplus for December. 

 The Philippine peso firmed with its regional counterparts and as foreign funds flowed into stock and fixed income markets. The central bank said it was planning to cut banks' reserve requirements by three percentage points and raise liquidity reserves by the same amount to nudge bank lending rates lower. 

 In north Asia, the Taiwan dollar ended firm on the yen's strength and confidence over the appointment of new central bank governor Perng Nai-fan, known for his tough stance against speculators. 

 Perng said after his swearing-in on Thursday that he favoured "dynamic stability" in the foreign exchange market but would intervene in the face of abnormal factors -- echoing his predecessor Sheu Yuan-dong's stance. 

 The South Korean won finished above the psychological 1,645 level to the dollar on month-end export deals and a surging stock market. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was firm while forwards rebounded after the Hong Kong banks' association left deposit rates unchanged at its weekly review meeting. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) was heard offering longer-dated funds on Friday, though it said it had not been interfering in money markets to add liquidity and push down interest rates.

title: Present Singapore exchange rate policy fine - Hu.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Friday he though the country's present exchange rate policy was fine and he was comfortable with the current level. 

 Hu was speaking on a television programme discussing the budget he presented on Friday. 

 "I think our present exchange rate policy is fine," he said in response to a question about whether the policy was appropriate. 

 Asked if he was comfortable with the present level, he said, "Yes." 

 Hu noted Deputy Prime Minister and Monetary Authority of Singapore Chairman Lee Hsien Loong had commented on exchange rate policy in parliament earlier in the day. 

 Lee said Singapore would maintain confidence in its currency by intervening in the foreign exchange market when necessary. 

 Lee also said the depreciation of regional currencies relative to the Singapore dollar would have some impact on the country's export competitiveness, but it should be limited. 

 He said in most product categories Singapore was not competing directly with the countries which have seen sharp depreciation in their currencies. 

 Singapore exchange rate policies are not mechanically driven by trade weights, Lee said. 

 "MAS exercises judgement in managing the exchange rate, and takes into account exceptional market factors."

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  up on Singapore budget hopes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose on Friday, inspired by the Singapore dollar's upbeat tone ahead of the country's 1998/99 budget, but dealers said trade was cautious due to uncertainties elsewhere in the region. 

 The U.S. dollar's decline against the yen and gains in several Asian stock markets following Wall Street's bullish performance also helped regional currencies keep their footing. 

 But traders remained wary of possible announcements from an ASEAN finance ministers meeting in Jakarta. 

 Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the proposal of using ASEAN currencies for trade within the group would be discussed at the Saturday meeting. 

 In Singapore, mounting expectations of a pro-growth budget, along the lines of Hong Kong's well-received budget last week, sparked stop-loss U.S. dollar sales, pushing the Singapore dollar to highs of around 1.6100/10. 

 Finance Minister Richard Hu will begin his budget speech in parliament in the afternoon, but most major announcements are expected after the stock market closes at 0900 GMT. 

 "A lot of stop-losses were triggered around 1.6180 and 1.6150. I think the market was caught a bit long but it seems the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) was around near 1.6100," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, intervenes in foreign exchange markets to iron out sharp moves in the Singapore dollar. It does not comment on these operations. 

 The Singapore dollar was also lifted by Deputy Prime Minister and MAS chairman Lee Hsien Loong's comment that the MAS would maintain confidence in the domestic dollar by intervening when necessary. 

 Lee told parliament fears of a sharp fall in the rupiah dragging down the Singapore dollar were hypothetical at this stage and "the weight of the rupiah in our basket is small". 

 Dealers said the government's newly announced measures to develop the fund management industry and bond market were also supporting the Singapore dollar as they would generate further demand for the domestic currency. 

 "I think 1.6220/30 would be a good area to sell dollar/Sing. We should ideally see 1.60," a European bank dealer said. 

 "We're not going back to 1.70 unless 1.64 breaks," she said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit tracked it's neighbour's rise, helped further by gains in Kuala Lumpur stocks and news the government was raising the ceiling on foreign share ownership in telecommunications companies. 

 But dealers expected its rise to be capped by dollar demand near the 3.60 level. 

 The Indonesian rupiah rose through the 9,000 per dollar level on U.S. dollar sales by U.S. investment houses in the wake of the Singapore dollar's rise. 

 But dealers said worries about unrest ahead of the presidential elections and uncertainty over Indonesia's plans to stabilise its rupiah via a currency board system would limit gains to the 8,500 level. 

 Singapore's Lee said the Indonesian government had not yet made a decision on the proposed currency board system. 

 The Thai baht edged higher in slow trade as the market awaited key economic data, including central bank reserves, due later in the day. 

 The Philippine peso continued to benefit from a lack of dollar demand, but dealers said its uptrend could hit resistance next week when oil companies are expected to begin buying dollars again. 

 In north Asia, the Taiwan dollar slipped back below the T$32.00 level to the U.S. dollar as the yen shed some of its gains, but its fall was limited. 

 Dealers said confidence over the appointment of new central bank governor Perng Nai-fan, known for his tough stance against speculators, was supporting the Taiwan dollar. 

 Perng said after his swearing-in on Thursday that he favoured "dynamic stability" in the foreign exchange market but would intervene in the face of abnormal factors -- echoing his predecessor Sheu Yuan-dong's stance. 

 The South Korean won rose above the psychological 1,645 level to the dollar on month-end export deals and a surging stock market. 

 President Kim Dae-jung said he would appoint an acting prime minister if talks with the opposition majority failed over the nomination of Kim Jong-pil, whose involvement with past military dictatorships has raised resistance. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was firm and forwards reversed course to rise due to fading expectations of a prime rate cut by local banks. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said it had not been interfering in money markets to add liquidity and push down interest rates, as rumoured. 

 James Lau, executive director (external) of the HKMA, told a news conference recent market liquidity was due to tax payments coming due.

title: Singapore  says MAS will  intervene  when necessary.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Singapore will maintain confidence in its currency by intervening in the foreign exchange market when necessary, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Friday. 

 Answering questions in parliament, Lee, who is also Chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said "the MAS will maintain confidence in the Singapore dollar by intervening in the foreign exchange market when necessary".

 Dealers said the government's newly announced measures to develop the fund management industry and bond market were also supporting the Singapore dollar as they would generate further demand for the domestic currency. 

 "I think 1.6220/30 would be a good area to sell dollar/Sing. We should ideally see 1.60," a European bank dealer said. 

 "We're not going back to 1.70 unless 1.64 breaks," she said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit tracked it's neighbour's rise, helped further by gains in Kuala Lumpur stocks and news the government was raising the ceiling on foreign share ownership in telecommunications companies. 

 But dealers expected its rise to be capped by dollar demand near the 3.60 level. 

 The Indonesian rupiah rose through the 9,000 per dollar level on U.S. dollar sales by U.S. investment houses in the wake of the Singapore dollar's rise. 

 But dealers said worries about unrest ahead of the presidential elections and uncertainty over Indonesia's plans to stabilise its rupiah via a currency board system would limit gains to the 8,500 level. 

 Singapore's Lee said the Indonesian government had not yet made a decision on the proposed currency board system. 

 The Thai baht edged higher in slow trade as the market awaited key economic data, including central bank reserves, due later in the day. 

 The Philippine peso continued to benefit from a lack of dollar demand, but dealers said its uptrend could hit resistance next week when oil companies are expected to begin buying dollars again. 

 In north Asia, the Taiwan dollar slipped back below the T$32.00 level to the U.S. dollar as the yen shed some of its gains, but its fall was limited. 

 Dealers said confidence over the appointment of new central bank governor Perng Nai-fan, known for his tough stance against speculators, was supporting the Taiwan dollar. 

 Perng said after his swearing-in on Thursday that he favoured "dynamic stability" in the foreign exchange market but would intervene in the face of abnormal factors -- echoing his predecessor Sheu Yuan-dong's stance. 

 The South Korean won rose above the psychological 1,645 level to the dollar on month-end export deals and a surging stock market. 

 President Kim Dae-jung said he would appoint an acting prime minister if talks with the opposition majority failed over the nomination of Kim Jong-pil, whose involvement with past military dictatorships has raised resistance. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was firm and forwards reversed course to rise due to fading expectations of a prime rate cut by local banks. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said it had not been interfering in money markets to add liquidity and push down interest rates, as rumoured. 

 James Lau, executive director (external) of the HKMA, told a news conference recent market liquidity was due to tax payments coming due.

title: FOCUS-Hopes of G7  intervention  lift Asia  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 19 (Reuters) - The fate of Indonesia and its neighbours rests solely on this weekend's meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven (G7) nations, dealers said on Thursday. 

 Asian currencies were mostly firmer on strong hopes the G7 would issue a communique announcing a concerted currency intervention to prop up the beleaguered Asian units. 

 The communique is also expected to include a rupiah-stabilising alternative to Indonesia's proposed currency board system, which had been under heavy international criticisms. 

 "There is an optimism at large that the G7 will come out with strong measures to resolve Asia's crisis and this has to, must, include an alternative to Indonesia's currency board," said a senior dealer with a European bank. 

 "Because if they do not, and Indonesia goes, Asia will be destabilised and we will head for a global recession," he said. 

 This G7 hope was fuelled by a Japanese report that there would be an intervention, a measure advocated by Japan and aimed at restoring confidence in Asia and notably the rupiah, which had lost over 70 percent of its value. 

 On Thursday, the rupiah was firmer, hitting a high of 8,600 as confusion reigned over its planned currency board system. 

 "The rupiah bearishness has been capped at 10,000 over the last few days because no one wants to short rupiah at this level in case the currency board is implemented," said a dealer with a local bank. 

 "There is still a lot of nervousness over Suharto's intentions although it now appears more likely the proposal might have to be shelved," the dealer said. 

 Indonesia faces mounting international pressure on its currency board proposal. 

 Singapore's Straits Times newspaper said on Thursday it should abandon plans for the board. 

 German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a news conference in Jakarta that Indonesia did not presently fulfill the criteria for the currency board and that there was not an alternative to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reforms. 

 Asian currencies firmed in tandem with the rupiah. 

 The Malaysian ringgit strengthened to 3.7200/7500 on offshore demand as players scrambled to sell the greenback. 

 "There is strong selling in the dollar/Malay. Stop losses were triggered at 3.75 and good interest to buy the ringgit at 3.71 to 3.73 by two major American players," said the senior dealer with a European bank. 

 The sale of dollar/Malay triggered sales in dollar/Sing. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar was very likely to test 1.6200 when London starts trading later Thursday. 

 "There is a lot of squaring of dollar positions ahead of the G7. The threat of the central bank intervention is very real now," said a dealer. 

 "If 1.62 is broken, the Sing dollar could look to test 1.60/65. And that is very possible," he said. 

 Earlier on Thursday, Singapore's Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said if the Singapore dollar was widely held, it would be more vulnerable to speculative attacks even though Singapore could fend this off with its huge reserves. 

 "As a small and open economy, we can't afford this," Lee told parliament. 

 He said the government was reviewing specific adjustments to the use of the Singapore dollar, particularly in the capital markets. 

 Fund selling ahead of the G7 gave the Thai baht a boost to 44.00/200 compared to 45.25/45.55 on late Wednesday. 

 Reports of Waigel saying the baht's current level did not reflect its true fundamentals also lifted the baht, dealers said. 

 Taiwan dollar got an added boost from a soaring stock market, which mirrored Wall Street's record close on Wednesday. 

 South Korean won was unchanged as dollar unwinding limits the dollar's rise. 

 Bucking the regional trend was the Hong Kong dollar as the sharp drop in local interest rates following the release of a better-than-expected fiscal 1998/99 budget proposals.

title: FOCUS-Asia  currencies  cool to Indonesia debt halt.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's proposal of a voluntary freeze on corporate debt servicing caused few ripples in Asian currency markets on Tuesday as most banks had already wound down for Lunar New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr holidays. 

 The freeze on foreign currency debt servicing, effective immediately, would allow time for borrowers and lenders to work out new arrangements to restore debt payments as soon as possible, said Radius Prawiro, appointed by Indonesian President Suharto to oversee the debt crisis. 

 Prawiro said a steering committee of international bankers from Indonesia's main creditor countries, led by senior officials from Standard Chartered Bank and UBS, and a committee of borrowers would form a framework to manage the massive private sector debt. 

 Analysts said the move had been widely expected by the market as some Indonesian companies had already stopped servicing their debts following the rupiah's 80 percent drop in value against the U.S. dollar since July. 

 "It is a necessary measure that provides some breathing space for the Indonesian economy. In the long-term, it is a step in the right direction," said Andy Tan, general manager of MMS/Standard and Poor's in Singapore. 

 "In the short term, it could cause more confusion and will probably create some selling pressure on the currency. But a lot depends on the details," he added. 

 But the rupiah showed little reaction to the news, edging up to 12,000/12,100 per dollar against 12,500/13,500 late Monday. 

 "This would amount to a moratorium, which is what's been feared. That's why we stopped trading the rupiah. Nobody's touching it at all today," said a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore. 

 "The whole day's been very quiet. It's ranged between 12,100 and 13,500 and not much has been dealt within that," he said. 

 Some Singapore dealers said the Indonesian central bank had been intervening to prop up the rupiah in the face of persistent dollar demand in a thin market. 

 But any gains were expected to be short lived. 

 "Even if there's joint intervention over the holidays, we'll only see a temporary correction in the rupiah. A lot still needs to be done and it will take a long time before people get back their confidence," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Jakarta dealers said the rupiah had strengthened briefly after the central bank raised rates on its certificates for all maturities and announced reforms to the banking sector. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar gained ground as Indonesia's announcement prompted players to unload some of their long dollar positions. 

 "In the event of a moratorium, there'll be no need for dollar buying against Asian currencies. So it's a speculative move, those guys who are long are just throwing back (their dollars)," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit firmed to 4.3850/950 per dollar at 0520 GMT from 4.5300/600 late on Monday. The Singapore dollar rose to 1.7335/85 against 1.7535/65 earlier. 

 The Thai baht strengthened to 54.40/55 per dollar onshore against 54.70/90 late on Monday as exporters unloaded dollars in a thin market. 

 Dealers said trading was subdued due to holidays elsewhere in the region, although Thai markets are not closed for the Lunar New Year. 

 The Philippine peso was quoted at 43.00/60 to the dollar against Monday's 43.08 close as dollar demand dwindled ahead of holidays in the region. 

 The central bank raised its call money rate -- a benchmark for interbank call loan trading -- to 14 percent from 12 percent. 

 The Hong Kong dollar slipped to HK$7.7445/65 to the U.S. dollar from Monday's 7.7438/58 close, but it was expected to find support at 7.7480 despite soft interbank rates. 

 The Indian rupee firmed to 38.420/450 to the dollar against a previous 38.70/73 close on exporter dollar sales after a long weekend. 

 Markets in Taiwan and South Korea were closed for the Lunar New Year.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  wind down for holidays.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Asian currencies traded sluggishly on Monday as activity dwindled to position adjustment ahead of the Lunar New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr festivities throughout the region. 

 The dollar's loss of face against major currencies due to mounting concern about a sex scandal involving U.S. President Bill Clinton also gave bruised Asian currencies some relief. 

 "The dollar is quite well offered at the moment. It looks like Clinton's helping the Far East currencies a little bit," a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore said. 

 The dollar briefly fell below 125 yen in early trade and extended its losses against the mark and Swiss franc amid allegations of misconduct by Clinton and a British newspaper report that the G7 nations were likely to agree next month to boost the yen. 

 Even the Indonesian rupiah, which has led the fray in recent sessions, showed signs of stability, though dealers said its undertone remained weak due to the unresolved issue of massive corporate debt. 

 The rupiah was a shade firmer at 12,250/13,250 to the dollar at 0840 GMT against an opening at 13,500/14,500. 

 Some Singapore dealers said Bank Indonesia was seen intervening in the market around midday, pushing the rupiah to a high of 13,000 to the dollar. 

 But trade was very subdued, with many players reluctant to take positions after key Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said on Sunday Japan planned some measures with the IMF this week on Indonesia's financial crisis. 

 Concerns over mounting private debt and political problems have haunted the market and sent the rupiah to a historic low of 17,000 last week. 

 "The market's been more or less stable today because no one dared to do anything ... Japan didn't give any details, which makes the market a bit nervous," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said trading was also hampered by ambiguity over the maturity of the spot date due to the impending Eid al-Fitr holiday, which ends the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan. 

 The Thai baht was at 54.65/75 to the dollar onshore against 54.60/75 late on Friday as the market awaited details of talks between Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and the IMF on a possible review of Bangkok's bail-out terms. 

 Tarrin said on Friday the IMF and Thailand were in broad agreement on technical changes to the programme to make it more flexible, but he declined to detail the changes. 

 The Malaysian ringgit whipped around in a thin market, receiving a slight boost from the dollar's weakened stance. 

 The Singapore dollar sagged to 1.7570/1.7620 to the U.S. dollar from 1.7515/65 four hours earlier. Dealers said it was likely to keep to a 1.7450-1.7650 range in the short term. 

 The market shrugged off comments by Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong on Sunday that, barring shocks, Singapore was not expected to slide into a recession. 

 The Philippine peso recovered from a weak start as corporate demand for the dollar subsided and the market absorbed Friday's news of a central bank plan to increase dollar liquidity by entering into swaps with banks. 

 In north Asia, the Korean won ended at 1,688 to the dollar from Friday's 1,745 close on exporter dollar sales and hopes of a speedy conclusion to Korean debt talks in New York. 

 Finance Minister Lim Chang-yuel said talks with international creditors were likely to be concluded in February. 

 The Taiwan dollar shed early gains to importer dollar demand and finished at T$33.996 against a previous 33.925 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar dipped to HK$7.7443/63 per U.S. dollar from Friday's 7.7400/20 close and forwards firmed amid jitters about insolvencies at local brokerage firms.

title: Asian  currencies  sag,  intervention  supports rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Depressed Asian currency markets largely ignored Indonesia's revised, IMF-endorsed 1998/99 budget, driving the rupiah to seek refuge in the arms of the central bank. 

 Dealers said the budget, which included a forecast of zero economic growth, inflation at 20 percent and a rupiah rate of 5,000 to the U.S. dollar, contained no surprises and left the market anxious about the unresolved issue of corporate debt. 

 "The market is not focusing so much on the budget revisions. It's just a theoretical exercise. What they want to see is how the government is going to cope with the debt restructuring," said the head of regional currencies trading at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "Up to now, they haven't offered anything and if nothing is done, the rupiah will not be able to stabilise at all," he said. 

 Dealers said intervention by Bank Indonesia in a very thin market, characterised by spreads as wide as 1,000 rupiah, was practically the only thing keeping the rupiah out of the depths. 

 The Indonesian central bank was believed to have sold dollars for rupiah at the 14,000 level and its repeated rate checking in Singapore and Jakarta kept traders on their toes. 

 "The market's very nervous of pushing dollar/rupiah higher. But if we don't see a retracement to 12,000 by Monday, there could be another sharp plunge in the rupiah," the dealer said. 

 "The demand for dollars from Jakarta is still very strong." 

 Banque Paribas said emergency Indonesian action to deal with the country's private sector debt crisis might be on the cards. 

 "What this implies for the currency market is that liquidity will likely dry up as the currency overshoots to unbelievable levels, and wide spreads could see offers reach 20,000," it said in a daily commentary. 

 Indonesia's troubles continued to weigh on other Asian markets, but the effect was more muted as activity wound down ahead of next week's holidays for the Lunar New Year and Islam's Eid al-Fitr. 

 Dealers began to view the rupiah more as an isolated disaster. 

 The Philippine peso, an island of relative calm in recent sessions, succumbed to mounting pressure from the region and fell far enough to trigger a market rule that effectively suspends trading for the day. 

 Manila traders said no central bank presence was detected and even foreign banks, which were actively selling dollars recently, had stopped doing so. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was weak at 4.5100 to the U.S. dollar, against 4.5325 late Thursday, but activity was confined to a subdued range with dollar bids around 4.45/50. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped to 1.7635 to the U.S. dollar, against Thursday's 1.7500, but dealers said it looked well supported around 1.7700 for the time being. 

 "There's ringgit/Sing selling from the 0.3900 level and also flight-to-quality buying (of the Singapore dollar) from Indonesia," a dealer said. 

 The Thai baht dipped to 54.65 to the dollar onshore from 54.45 on Thursday as the market awaited details of talks between Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and the IMF on a review of Bangkok's bailout package. 

 IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer said the talks, which features measures to accelerate Thailand's economic reforms, went well, but he gave no details. Tarrin said he would issue a statement on Friday. 

 In north Asia, the Seoul won outshone its regional counterparts, firming to 1,745 per dollar versus Thursday's 1,760 close on strong cash demand ahead of the Lunar new year festivities. 

 But dealers said its rise would be blocked by dollar demand from importers and banks with month-end debt servicing needs. 

 The Taiwan dollar sagged below the T$34.00 level from Thursday's 33.706 close as worries about the region triggered dollar demand from importers ahead of the new year break. 

 The Hong Kong dollar slipped to HK$7.7430 from a previous 7.7385 close as local interest rates eased. 

 The Australian dollar held above a support level of US$0.6560 but failed to make much headway due to fears about the rupiah. 

 The Indian rupee firmed to 38.65 per dollar as the impact of the central bank's measures to tighten liquidity overshadowed the potential contagion effect of other Asian currencies.

title: Intervention  will help rupiah near-term - analysts.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention is the right step for Indonesia to take and will help halt the rupiah's slide, but only in the near-term, analysts said. 

Intervention has certainly come at the eleventh hour, given the rupiah's 60 percent slide since the turn of the year, but will help arrest the meltdown because volume in dollar/rupiah is so tiny at the moment. 

 "It's not a long-term answer, but with spreads as wide as we are seeing in dollar/rupiah, it won't take much to move it by 600 or 1,000," said Chiang Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 Spreads in dollar/rupiah have been as wide as 1,000 rupiah when trading has become highly erratic. 

 On Thursday there were bids from brokers for rupiah at levels of 16,500 and 17,000 to the U.S. dollar, but it was unclear now much business was being done at these levels, dealers said. 

 The rupiah opened around 11,000 but quickly started to fall, and Singapore traders reported dollars going through at 15,000 in early business. 

 It was then Bank Indonesia entered the market, selling dollars at 13,500 rupiah, then again at 14,000. 

 Late in the day the central bank said it would step up forex intervention if need be and would soon draw on an existing $2.0 billion stand-by loan facility and partly use it to defend the currency. 

 "The government of Indonesia will do its utmost to stabilise the rupiah's value against the dollar," a senior government official said. 

 After that, the central bank was in again at 12,000 in late trading. 

 Dealers said with spreads so wide and trading volume so thin, any central bank buying of dollars would have a significant impact. 

 "Immediately the offer (on dollar/rupiah) gets hit, it jumps up by the spread," said one trader. "So with very little, they will be able to move it in 1,000 roop (rupiah) jumps. And that will continue to work as long as volume remains as tiny as it is." 

Intervention is certainly not the complete answer for Indonesia, but something has to be done to stop the rot in the rupiah and intervention is a way of buying time, analysts said. 

 "It won't provide long-term stability but they have to buy time given the extent of the rupiah's fall," CIBC's Yao Chye said. 

 "Long-term solutions have to be addressed and would have to include a debt restructuring programme." 

 Indonesia has around $140 billion total external debt, of which around $66 billion is in the hands of the private sector. 

 Dealers noted there had been talk in the market of dollar/rupiah going to 20,000 by the end of the week, but that looked highly unlikely if the central bank kept up its intervention.

title: Chronology of the Asian financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 15 (Reuters) - President Suharto of Indonesia and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director, Michel Camdessus, signed an agreement on Thursday to strengthen economic reforms. 

 The following is a chronology of the financial crisis that has rocked Asia. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso all slump, as confidence in the region rapidly deteriorates. Around this time the Singapore dollar starts a gradual decline. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates to IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Oct 6 - Rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 6 - Russia and London Club sign agreement rescheduling roughly $33 billion of debts over 25 years with seven years grace, dated from December 1995. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. The Hang Seng index plunges 23.34 percent to 10,426.30 by Thursday's close, after 13,601.01 the previous Friday. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump rapidly in value. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea. Two days later the Central Bank of Korea announces that it received $5.22 billion. 

 1998 

 Jan 6 - Indonesia unveils its 1998/99 budget projecting an increase of 32.1 percent growth in revenue and expenditure over the current budget and a four percent economic growth rate. 

 But the rupiah loses half its value against the dollar over five-day period, breaking through the 10,000 to the dollar level, before a slight recovery. 

 Freefall is triggered by perceptions that budget not tough enough to meet IMF-mandated austerity measures and by market talk that Jakarta might declare debt moratorium. 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 10 - Indonesia's President Suharto comes under increasing international pressure to adhere to IMF conditions. He calls the delay or review of 15 big infrastructure projects. 

 Jan 11 - The IMF's first Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer arrives in Jakarta for talks about the IMF's programme and how to move ahead with it. 

 Jan 14 - IMF Managing Director Camdessus heads for Jakarta. Stopping off in Singapore he says the IMF is asking Indonesia to sign a new letter of intent committing itself to implementing further IMF reforms. 

 Jan 15 - Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement  strengthening economic reforms.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  hunker down for Indonesia.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies sat relatively tight during a moribund session as the market awaited the outcome of what is being seen as make or break talks between the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Indonesia. 

 Towards the end of last week analysts and traders had been looking seriously at the chance of Indonesia calling a debt moratorium but most are now cautiously confident this week's talks will yield some solid action and see economic and banking sector reforms finally put in place. 

 The bloodied rupiah was basically steady around the 8,400 per dollar level against the opening 8,800 as traders opted to stay out amid widening spreads. Although this was weaker than Friday's 8,000 close it was well above last Thursday's dive below 10,000. 

 President Suharto on Monday met IMF Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer and will on Wednesday have talks with Managing Director Michel Camdessus. 

 U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers was due in Jakarta late on Monday to add weight to international pressure for Indonesia to reform. 

 The IMF said Monday's meetings with Suharto were "very, very good." 

 "Early indications are that talks are progressing well," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 "Although the outlook for the regional currencies would hinge on developments in Indonesia/IMF/U.S. talks, a debt moratorium in Indonesia has been averted for now as well as capital controls and a fixed exchange rate regime." 

 While a number of Asian currencies were  steady, the Thai baht plumbed new depths, sinking below 55.00 per dollar with traders unimpressed by the central bank's measures to curb currency speculation. 

 The Bank of Thailand said late on Friday it would step up scrutiny of foreign exchange markets and threatened to impose severe penalties for trading violations. 

 "There's been unwinding of long rupiah/baht positions. And the baht has also weakened after Friday's capital controls because not much action was taken," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The baht was at 56.20 to the dollar onshore against 54.00 late on Friday with the offshore rate at 56.00 against 53.00. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was softer at 4.6700 per dollar from 4.60 late on Friday, but dealers said its decline was being capped by dollar sales from U.S. funds above 4.70. 

 They said activity was subdued as the central bank stayed out after three straight days of intervention last week. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped to 1.7980 to the U.S. dollar from 1.7700 late Friday as domestic interbank rates eased. Overnight rate fell below 10 percent from highs of 36 percent last week, spurring speculation the authorities had added liquidity to the system in an effort to shore up the sagging stock market. 

 But any extra liquidity did little for the Straits Times Industrials index which closed 8.75 percent lower after dropping 23 percent last week. 

 "The stock market's been battered for the last three sessions. If it goes on like this, there'll be a lot of defaults and bank shares especially will be affected," a dealer said. 

 "I think the (Monetary Authority of Singapore) is monitoring the situation closely and will continue to put back liquidity to ease the crunch," he said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was steady around Friday's 7.7430 close, but local interest rates and forwards rose sharply. 

 Dealers said the market appeared to be gearing for another attack on the Hong Kong dollar peg as the territory's stock market came under intense pressure. 

 The Hang Seng Index lost over 11.0 percent at one stage after Peregrine Investments, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, went into liquidation. 

 "If the stock market continues to plunge, the pressure will be high to lift the peg," a dealer in Singapore said. 

 "If they're able to hold it for six months and the regional currencies stabilise, the speculators will get badly burned because of the carry costs," he said. 

 "But the funds are very much enriched by the Asian currencies fall, so they have a lot of firepower. It will be interesting to see whether the Hong Kong dollar can hold up." 

 Elsewhere, the South Korean won firmed to 1,735 per U.S. dollar from Friday's 1,810 close on foreign fund inflows to the stock market, and the Taiwan dollar weakened to T$34.480 per U.S. dollar against a previous T$34.100 close as the yen shed some gains. 

 The Philippine peso traded sluggishly at 43.650 to the dollar against Friday's 44.30 close.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  bide time for Indonesia.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bided their time on Monday as traders nervously looked for signs that Indonesia planned to deal more effectively with its financial crisis after last week's confidence-shaking budget. 

 Most currency markets withstood the waves of selling in stock markets across Asia as dealers awaited the outcome of talks between Indonesian leaders and IMF officials and the arrival of a U.S. team led by Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers. 

 But there was little optimism. 

 "These visits have created some uncertainty, so the market is just awaiting developments out of Indonesia. But I think the currencies will resume their weakening after the visits," the head of trading for regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was practically static around 8,300/8800 to the dollar at 0525 GMT against its opening 8,700/900 as traders opted to stay out amid widening spreads.

 International Monetary Fund First Deputy Managing Director described his meeting with Suharto as encouraging, but provided no specific details. 

 Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said the outcome of the IMF talks would be announced on Thursday. 

 Jakarta stocks rose nearly three percent as spirits improved with the IMF talks signalling the start of an international effort to persuade Jakarta not to backtrack on its commitment to reforms tied to a $43 billion IMF-led bailout. 

 Dealers said the market was also awaiting Summers' arrival in Jakarta on Monday, where he was expected to urge Indonesian leaders to push ahead with the reform process. 

 Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, the Thai baht ploughed new depths, crumbling through the 55.00 per dollar level onshore as players remained unimpressed by the central bank's measures to curb currency speculation.

 The overnight rate fell back below 10 percent from highs of 36 percent last week, spurring speculation the de facto central bank had added liquidity to the system in an effort to shore up the sagging stock market.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currency  traders frozen with fear.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Asian currency trading was practically petrified on Friday as activity shrank amid mounting panic about the potential outcome of Indonesia's financial debacle. 

 Dealers said liquidity had dwindled in Southeast Asian currencies as spreads widened amid fears that Indonesia was on the verge of declaring a debt moratorium or introducing trading curbs on the rupiah. 

 The Indonesian currency has lost nearly half its value against the U.S. dollar in the last six trading days. 

 "There's not much trading going on. Everything is customer- or commercially-driven at the moment," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "In the rupiah, the interbank market doesn't exist anymore. Yesterday, the spread was about 100 rupiah. Today, it's 500-1,000, so it's practically impossible to trade," he said. 

 Financial markets were rife with rumours about street demonstrations in Jakarta and the health of President Suharto. Both were denied by military and government officials. 

 There was also talk of intervention by the U.S. Federal Reserve to support the rupiah overnight and the immediate release of the second $3.0 billion tranche of IMF loans to Indonesia. But neither could be confirmed. 

 "These are all baseless rumours. The only true one was that there was a rush on basic commodities. I think Singapore players have built up extensive long dollar positions," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 Dollar sales by state banks in Jakarta and follow-through selling by Singapore operators helped the rupiah rebound more than 30 percent to 7,900 per dollar from its opening around 10,500/11,500. 

 News that U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers would soon visit Indonesia and other Asian countries also helped calm Indonesian markets. 

 Summers, who has called on Jakarta to step up efforts to convince markets it is committed to IMF-sponsored economic reforms, would travel to the region to consult on the economic situation, said White House press secretary Mike McCurry. 

 He said in a statement Clinton had spoken to Suharto and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong by telephone and underscored the importance of the region to the United States. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit firmed to 4.6200/300 to the dollar from lows of around 4.7800, following intervention by the central bank and calming words by the country's leaders. 

 Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim both said Malaysao would not seek help from the IMF. 

 Mahathir said Kuala Lumpur had sufficient reserves to defend the ringgit and that depositor funds were safe. 

 Malaysia also announced a trade surplus of 700 million ringgit for November compared with a 500 million ringgit deficit the year before. 

 But dealers said the ringgit would remain under pressure from corporate demand for the dollar and weakness in regional currency and stock markets. 

 The Singapore dollar also showed a slightly healthier tone amid higher domestic interbank rates and talk of overnight intervention by the de facto central bank. 

 Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in thin overseas markets to defend the Singapore dollar after it fell to a more than seven-year-low of 1.8160 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The MAS does not comment on its market operations. 

 The Thai baht recovered from record lows in onshore and offshore markets as traders turned cautious ahead of the announcement of new measures to curb speculation in the currency, expected later on Friday. 

 It was at 53.60/80 to the dollar onshore against 53.70/54.00 in early trade. The offshore rate was at 52.00/53.00 against 54.10/60 earlier. 

 But dealers remained sceptical about the potential benefits of the new measures and said that sentiment for the baht remained weak amid further credit ratings downgrades. 

 "We don't expect much really because it is quite difficult to limit the speculators. What we really need is foreign inflows. Also it takes time to do these things and you need laws and regulations. It doesn't just happen," a dealer said. 

 The Philippine peso firmed to 44.595 to the dollar against a previous 44.92 close on a market perception that the central bank was providing dollar liquidity indirectly. 

 Police said they would shut down 130 money changers in Manila's main tourist district, accusing them of hoarding dollars and contributing to the peso's decline. 

 North Asian currencies were relatively shielded from the mayhem elsewhere, mainly due to the yen's relative strength against the dollar. 

 The Taiwan dollar was at T$34.03/13 to the U.S. dollar against Thursday's T$34.325 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at HK$7.7435/55 against Thursday's HK$7.7455 close. Forwards also backed off a bit. 

 The South Korean won was at 1,800/05 to the dollar against a low of 1,815 as the positive impact of news that global bankers had reaffirmed short-term financing for the country was countered by jitters about Indonesia. 

 The Austalian dollar was much higher at US$0.6404/09 from morning levels of around 0.6320/25, as a big buy order sparked rumours the Reserve Bank had intervened. A central bank spokesman said the bank's policy was never to comment on market rumours or its operations. 

 The rumours also boosted the New Zealand dollar to US$0.5705/15 from an opening 0.5673/80.

title: Singapore Dlr/Late -2: Speed, Not Level, Seen Worrying MAS
text:
About midday, MAS, the country's effective central bank, warned it would take 'decisive' action against speculative attacks targeting its currency, reminding the market that it intervenes occasionally 'to ensure orderly movements' on the market. 

 But the authority noted its policy doesn't focus on 'any single currency,' but rather a trade-weighted basket. In this regard, the Singapore dollar has remained stable, 'notwithstanding the currency turmoil,' it added. 

 'MAS would carry more weight than the other central banks because it has the ability to act,' said one dealer in Singapore. 'But at the end of the day, I would think that their concern is not so much the right value for the Singapore dollar, but the speed at which it is depreciating.' 

 While the MAS statement may have reminded market participants that they're being watched, exchange rates remained stable immediately after the statement was released. The Singapore dollar turned higher only after the Bank Negara intervened. 

 In the local money market, the overnight rate on Singapore dollar deposits was quoted at 10.000%-11.000%, from 5.000%-5.500% earlier in the day. 

 The 3-month interbank rate was at 9.500%-10.500%, from 8.000%-8.500%.

title: Singapore MAS/Comments/Analysts -2: Sort Of Moral Suasion
text:
Earlier, as reported, the MAS, the country's effective central bank, said Wednesday it's ready to stop any speculative attacks against the Singapore dollar. 

 MAS said in the statement that it occasionally intervenes in the currency markets 'to ensure the orderly movement' of the Singapore dollar exchange rate consistent with its policy and economic fundamentals. 

 'We do not publicize our exchange rate operations,' it said, but warned, 'The MAS stands ready to act decisively against any speculative attack on the Singapore dollar.' 

 Commenting on the statement, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken regional economist Chia Woon Kien said, 'The contents (of the MAS statement) are not new but it is a message to the market that the MAS isn't sleeping. A lot of other (regional) central banks appear to be quiet.' 

 'The (MAS) message just underscores Singapore's macroeconomic policy. But it's sort of a moral suasion to the market that maybe the Singapore dollar has risen too fast in too short a period,' said a regional economist at a major U.S. investment bank here. 

 Economists also said that the MAS statement also showed that the de facto central is trying to find the appropriate approach to reminding the market about its macroeconomic policies, given that it generally keeps a low profile. 

 At a time when most central banks in the region lack the funds to support their currencies or the stamina to defend them, the MAS' comments appear to err on the side of caution while at the same time attempting to deliver its message, economists added. 

 Rising domestic interest rates could have been another key factor in motivating the MAS statement Wednesday, said one economist. The continued rise in the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar is likely to exert an upward pressure on interbank money market rates, eventually resulting in higher domestic lending rates and braking economic growth, he said. 

 Key interest rates have already been hiked twice in the past month.

title: Singapore/Malaysia Ctrl Bk -2: Traders See No Sign Of MAS
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Foreign exchange traders in Singapore said Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, was seen in the market buying ringgit against the U.S. dollar midday Wednesday in Asia. 

 A dealer said the central bank was selling dollars beginning at 4.7000 ringgit (MYR) to MYR4.6000. Immediately before the reported intervention the dollar was at a record high of MYR4.8825.

 Still, the Singapore dollar strengthened considerably in tandem with the ringgit's move, with the U.S. dollar trading at S$1.7755, down from S$1.7915 20 minutes earlier.

title: Monetary Officials Provide Respite For Malaysia, Singapore  Currencies
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Officials in Malaysia and Singapore burst a speculative bubble Wednesday, sending some Southeast Asian currencies up against the U.S. dollar in late Asian trading. 

 But traders said that even as speculators retreated under the pressure from authorities, demand for dollars remains robust and regional currencies are likely to remain under selling pressure. 

 "It doesn't take much to shake (speculators) out of the trees," a currency dealer in Singapore said. The official who did most of the shaking was Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who said Malaysia's ringgit is "grossly undervalued in an environment of highly unstable market conditions." 

 Anwar confirmed that Bank Negara, the country's central bank, has intervened to support the currency. 

 Late in the Asian session, the ringgit, which traders said was a focus of speculative pressure, was almost 7% stronger against the U.S. dollar compared with its intraday low, and the Singapore dollar had gained more than 2%. 

 At about 6 a.m. EST, the U.S. dollar was trading at 4.5755 ringgit, down from a record 4.8800 ringgit earlier in the day, but up from 4.3400 ringgit late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Setting the stage for Anwar's remarks and Bank Negara's intervention, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, or MAS, which serves as the country's central bank, warned that it "stands ready to act decisively against any speculative attack against the Singapore dollar." 

 The MAS's managing director, Koh Yong Guan, also reminded markets that the agency intervenes "from time to time" in order to "ensure orderly movements" on the currency market. The MAS emphasized that it manages the currency against a trade-weighted basket of currencies "and not against any single currency." 

 While the Singapore dollar has weakened against the U.S. dollar, the German mark and the British pound, the MAS said, the currency has risen against the ringgit, the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah. "Overall, on a trade-weighted basis, its value has remained stable, notwithstanding the (regional) currency turmoil," the MAS said. 

 The Singapore dollar didn't react immediately to Koh's comments, but traders said the remarks gave the market food for thought. The MAS "would carry more weight than the other central banks because it has the ability to act," a dealer in Singapore said. "But at the end of the day, I would think that their concern is not so much the right value for the Singapore dollar, but the speed at which it is depreciating." 

 In late trading, the U.S. currency was at 1.7529 Singapore dollars, down from an intraday high of S$1.7930, its highest level since late March 1991, but above S$1.7375 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Some traders said that with underlying demand for U.S. dollars still robust, Wednesday's scant show of strength isn't likely to be sustainable. "The tough thing for the central banks is that as soon as they take their foot off the gas, it will go back up again," one trader said of the U.S. currency. 

 Traders said the sharp round of weakening early in the Asian day was triggered by Indonesian President Suharto's budget message late Tuesday. Disappointment with Indonesia's 1998-99 budget sent the rupiah to a record low against the U.S. dollar before the currency rebounded. Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was changing hands at 8,000.00 rupiah, down from its intraday high of 8,425.00 rupiah but up from 7,350.00 rupiah late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Thailand's baht, meanwhile, closed at an all-time low at 53.10 baht to the U.S. dollar in trading in Bangkok compared with 52.15 baht late Tuesday. At Wednesday's closing level, the baht is down 51% since the Thai government abandoned its fixed foreign-exchange system last July 2. 

 Elsewhere in Asia, South Korea's won closed at 1,745 won to the U.S. dollar, down from 1,742 won late Tuesday in Asia, while the Philippine peso ended at a new low of 46.50 pesos to the dollar compared with 45.46 pesos Tuesday. But the Hong Kong dollar climbed to HK$7.7360 to the U.S. dollar, up sharply from HK$7.7500 late Tuesday, amid speculation Asia's central banks may pull together a massive joint intervention effort later in London and New York.
