title: FOCUS-Nervous Asian  currencies  pull out of depths.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Southeast Asia's ravaged currencies limped tentatively out of the depths in late Wednesday trade as fears of concerted central bank action halted a mad scramble for dollars. 

 Speculation Japan might ask the United States to help it prop up the sagging yen pushed the U.S. dollar below 133 yen ahead of a meeting between U.S. and Japanese monetary officials, injecting a note of caution in other Asian currency markets. 

 "The market is actually quite worried there might be some concerted intervention in the dollar/yen and that all the regional central banks will come in as well," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Earlier, most currencies in Southeast Asia headed relentlessly lower due to heavy dollar demand from companies and investors amid poor liquidity and wide spreads. 

 "It's moving in big figures these days. I come in in the morning and don't recognise the levels. I go for lunch and the same thing happens," said one senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore. 

 The bloodletting on the currency markets spilled over, yet again, into Asian bourses and several stock indices fell through key support levels. Oil markets and many commodities were also savaged by the rapid fall of regional currencies. 

 But the Malaysian ringgit recovered in late trade as players liquidated long dollar positions after Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed the central bank had intervened in the currency markets to defend the ringgit. 

 It was at 4.5600/700 at 1100 GMT after falling to a low of 4.8800 in morning trade. 

 Dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia had sold dollars for ringgit at various levels. 

 The central bank said in a statement that Malaysia's total debt amounted to $45.2 billion or 42 percent of its Gross Domestic Product. 

 It said short-term debt at the end of June accounted for 30 percent of total external debt outstanding, in contrast with a ratio published by the Bank of International Settlements of 56 percent, which had earlier spooked the market. 

 The Singapore dollar was also sharply higher at 1.7500/50 to the U.S. dollar after falling to a more than seven-year low of 1.7940 earlier. 

 Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, had intervened to stem the domestic currency's sharp drop. 

 The MAS said in a written response to questions from Reuters that it stood ready to "act decisively against any speculative attack on the Singapore dollar". 

 "The MAS intervenes in the foreign exchange market from time to time to ensure orderly movements of the Sing dollar exchange rate ... We do not publicise our exchange rate operations," MAS managing director Koh Yong Guan said in the statement. 

 Late rumours that the MAS had asked forex traders in certain banks work to late on Wednesday also spurred some short-covering in the Singapore dollar, dealers said. The MAS declined comment. 

 The Indonesian rupiah perked up a bit to 7,900/8,000 to the dollar from an early low of 8,450, but dealers said it remained shaky amid disappointment over Indonesia's 1998/99 budget, unveiled on Tuesday. 

 Analysts said Jakarta's projections of four percent economic growth, inflation at nine percent, the rupiah at 4,000 to the dollar and an increase in tax revenue would be difficult to achieve given the depth of Indonesia's crisis. 

 A Washington Post report that International Monetary Fund officials had called Indonesia's economic crisis worrisome and faulted Jakarta for failing to follow through on pledges to restructure the economy also dented the rupiah. 

 The Thai baht recovered from below the 53.00 level to the dollar in domestic and offshore markets in late trade after Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the government would announce new measures to curb currency speculation on Friday. 

 The baht was at 52.85/53.15 to the dollar onshore against 53.10/30 six hours earlier and 52.05/35 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate was at 52.50/53.00 against 54.10/30 earlier. 

 The Philippine peso ended weak at 45.35 to the dollar but off its opening low of 46.50. The central bank raised the overnight borrowing rate to 12 percent from 11 percent in a bid to curb speculation. 

 Manila traders said the rate hike had little impact, but the peso received some support from a plan under which commercial banks would offer non-deliverable forwards from 0500 GMT. 

 This will help companies hedge dollar-denominated debts against further falls in the peso without having to buy dollars now. 

 North Asian currencies continued to look jaundiced with the Taiwan dollar faring the worst. 

 It fell through a 10-year support of T$34 to the U.S. dollar within minutes of opening and ended at T$34.400 against Tuesday's T$33.755 close in the face of mayhem elsewhere in Asia. 

 Dealers said the previously stolid currency was likely to head for the T$35 level unless other Asian currencies saw a sustained rebound. 

 Taiwan announced a rare trade deficit of US$80.1 million for December, reflecting civilian aircraft imports, against a surplus of US$1.078 billion in December 1996, the Finance Ministry said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar clung to the 7.75 support level against the U.S. dollar and forwards jumped amid jitters in other currency markets. 

 Traders said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was seen offering short-dated funds to ease rates in an effort to boost the sagging stock market. 

 The South Korean won was relatively unscathed but fell off its highs of 1,680 to the dollar as expectations of importer dollar demand near the 1,600 level eclipsed foreign fund inflows to the stock market. 

 It ended at 1,745 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,742 close. 

 The Australian dollar ploughed 11-year-lows, weakening to US$0.6316, before rebounding to 0.6372/77 from 0.6345/50 late on Tuesday. 

 The New Zealand dollar also recovered to US$0.5680/87 against 0.5622/29 six hours earlier.

title: Singapore dollar traded at a low of 1.7850.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 7 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar continued its beating of some Asian currencies, sending the Singapore dollar trading to a low of 1.7850 early on Wednesday, dealers said. 

 "Sentiment stays weak and the weaker regionals are not helping. They will inevitably weigh on the Sing," said one dealer, referring to the free-fall of the Indonesian rupiah towards an unchartered territory of 8,000 level. 

 "It is likely to remain weak as we hear more about the difficulties some Asian countries will have in meeting the the International Monetary Fund bailout terms," he said. 

 At 0135 GMT, the Singapore dollar was quoted firmer at 1.7730/80 to the greenback. 

 The dollar's gains were capped by profit-taking orders when dollar/Sing hit 1.7850, dealers said. 

 "There was a lot of interest, but today's spread is wider than the past few days. Moves tend to be exaggerated," said another dealer. 

 Dealers said it was unclear if Singapore's de facto central bank, The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), intervened but noted the presence of several local banks.

title: Asia base metal trade hammered by  currency  blight.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 6 (Reuters) - The Asian base metal trade was pounded on Tuesday by imploding regional currencies with business in the region practically at a standstill. 

 "The Asian currencies have been murder. There's not going to be any buying out of this area," a senior dealer for a Western metal trading house said. 

 Southeast Asian currencies tumbled like dominoes on Tuesday, with most touching fresh record lows as they were steamrolled by the rampant U.S. dollar. 

 The Indonesian rupiah crashed to a historic low of 7,400 to the dollar, the Thai baht slid to 52, the Malaysian ringgit plumbed fresh depths of 4.20 and the Philippine peso sank to a record 44.35. 

 Even the Singapore dollar dipped to 1.7420 from the previous 1.7020/30 despite rumours the de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, would intervene in the market. 

 "It's absolutely crazy. Base metal business, especially in Southeast Asia, is at a standstill," the aluminium dealer of a European trading company said. 

 "The problem now is finding somebody here to buy the stuff," a dealer added. 

 Aluminium purchases in Indonesia, estimated at around 100,000 tonnes last year, may slide below 50,000 tonnes in 1998 and may even go lower. 

 "It's even getting worse. Who knows when all this will end," one exasperated trader said. 

 Dealers said it was difficult to quantify immediately the impact of renewed turmoil in the area's financial markets on base metal demand, but the outlook in the region is grim. 

 "The atmosphere here is doom and gloom. All you're hearing about are cancelled construction contracts. The Chinese are not buying. No one is picking up any forward material in copper," one said. 

 One European dealer said he had received reports that buyers in South Korea were shipping out large quantities of the red metal, putting copper prices under further pressure. 

 "They're shipping it out very aggressively. That is putting a lot of pressure on copper prices," he said. 

 In Asian trade, three-month copper was quoted by the trade at 0400 GMT at around US$1,698/703 a tonne, slightly below the last trade on the London Metal Exchange on Monday of $1,702. 

 "Many consumers here are struggling to survive," one trader said. "They cannot afford to import at the moment. If they have to pay for their purchases in U.S. dollars, it's going to kill them." 

 Base metal traders said many of their customers scampered for the sidelines to ride out the crisis. 

 "Business is very, very slow. People are still trying to learn to cope with the situation," one said.

title: Singapore  Late-AM: US$ Down;  Intervention  Fears Cap Rise
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar is slightly lower but expected to be steady in late-morning Singapore trading Monday from levels around 0215 GMT in Tokyo, amid moderate volumes. 

 Although market players in Singapore are upbeat about the prospects for the dollar, most fear that central bank intervention will cap the U.S currency's rise, especially against the yen, for now. In addition, willingness by market players to take profits around Y132.50 is seen capping the dollar's rise, they said. 

 'Central bank intervention seems to be a concern and some comments this morning seem to have taken the sting out of the dollar (versus the yen),' said the chief dealer at a major European bank here. As reported earlier, Haruhiko Kuroda, head of the ministry's international finance bureau, told a group of reporters he 'doesn't accept' a further weakening of the yen. 

 A treasury economist at a U.K. bank here said the 'Bank of Japan's resolve to limit the yen's weakness' will cap the dollar's rise for the short term. The higher end resistance for the dollar is seen around Y133.30, said the economist. 

 Apart from fears of central bank intervention, dealers said market players are ready to take profits if the dollar rallies. 'We're not sure is Europe or New York will want to take the dollar higher. They themselves want to lock in some of their profits around Y132.50,' said a senior dealer at a Japanese bank here. 

 Looking head, the dollar is seen well supported at Y129.70-.90 against the yen. Against the German currency, the dollar is seen holding between DM1.7970 and DM1.7820 for the rest of Asian dealings, said dealers. 

 Around 0255 GMT, the dollar is at Y132.29, down from Y132.40, quoted at both 0215 GMT and late Friday in New York. The U.S. currency is at 1.7974 marks, down from DM1.7995, and down from DM1.8045 in New York Friday. 

 Sterling is at $1.6435, a touch higher than $1.6433 at 0215 GMT and above from $1.6407 late Friday in New York. The mark is quoted at Y73.57, steady from Y73.58 around 0215 GMT, but up from Y73.37 in New York late Friday.

 Traders said the U.S. dollar seems to have reached decisively above S$1.7000 in early trading Monday, with S$1.7100-S$1.7150 watched as the next target.

title: Singapore Dlr Lower Early Vs U.S. Dlr, Seen Breaking S$1.70
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is weaker against the U.S. dollar in early Asian trading Friday as the currency braces for another push lower. 

 About 0200 GMT (9 p.m. EST Thursday), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6910, up from S$1.6845 in late Asian trading Wednesday. The market was closed for the New Year's Day holiday.

 The dealers noted overall negative sentiment for Southeast Asian currencies, emphasizing the Singapore dollar's drop against the U.S. dollar has lagged behind that of its sibling currencies.

He also noted the Singapore dollar's decline since July 1 has been less than half that of the Philippine peso, the Malaysia ringgit, the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah. 

 But unless there's a exaggerated move on the foreign exchange market, traders said its unlikely that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's effective central bank, will intervene to protect the S$1.7000 level.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  idle on New Year's eve.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Asian currency traders sat on their hands on Wednesday as holidays in several centres, including Tokyo, severely inhibited trade on New Year's Eve. 

 The South Korean won remained prey to year-end dollar demand from importers and companies scrambling to meet debt payments. It ended at 1,695 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,590 close. 

 But dealers said sentiment was boosted by news the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had approved payment of $2 billion to Seoul under an accelerated schedule to ease South Korea's credit crunch. 

 Foreign commercial and investment banks also pledged on Tuesday to roll over billions of dollars of short-term debt, giving South Korean banks an extra month's breathing space. 

 The won's weakness was limited to the 1,800 level against the dollar as a result of all the good news, but there was no consensus among dealers over the won's longer-term prospects. 

 "If more foreign lenders roll over loans to Korean companies and provide fresh loans, the currency market could improve quite quickly in January," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul. 

 Selling orders were also placed around 1,800 won for three-month non-deliverable forwards in overseas markets. 

 But some dealers remained pessimistic. 

 "Right now things look slightly better for Korea. But there's still a lot of bad news that's not filtered through. I think the won will be in worse trouble next year," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Taiwan dollar shed its early gains and slipped to T$32.638/698 to the U.S. dollar at 0800 GMT from Tuesday's T$32.600 close as exporter sales of the U.S. dollar were offset by importer demand in an otherwise slow year-end market. 

 Taiwan central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said Asia's financial turmoil would affect Taiwan in 1998, but the government would press forward with financial reforms. 

 He told an annual year-end news conference the central bank would keep its target zone for the overnight interbank rate at 6.5-7.0 percent and would only intervene in the foreign exchange market in the face of abnormal or speculative factors. 

 The Hong Kong dollar edged up to 7.7472/82 against the U.S. dollar from Tuesday's 7.7493/03 close. 

 Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah remained soft, hitting lows of around 5,800 to the dollar in subdued offshore trade with Jakarta foreign exchange markets closed for book squaring. 

 Singapore dealers said Jakarta banks were updating screen prices at lower levels than the actual traded rates in an effort to suppress the rupiah's decline. 

 "They're trying to window-dress the rate down. We even saw a quote of 4,800/6,000 for $10 (million). But there's nearly no market here," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said they had not seen any sign of actual intervention by Bank Indonesia in Singapore markets and the rupiah would struggle to rise above the 5,000 level after Tuesday's interventions failed to boost it. 

 An Indonesian court's decision to postpone the liquidation of Bank Jakarta, one of 16 banks ordered closed by the government in November as part of economic reforms, was expected to be poorly received by the market once trading resumed. 

 The bank is part-owned by Probosutedjo, President Suharto's half brother. 

 The Thai baht was very thinly traded as many participants were out after the government changed the New Year's market holiday to January 2 from December 31. 

 The baht slid to 47.60/48.20 to the dollar onshore against 47.05/15 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate was at 46.80/47.30 against 46.20/46.70. 

 The Bank of Thailand projected the government would post a current account deficit of $4 billion, or 2.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), for 1997, a government spokesman said. 

 Akapol Sorasuchart also said Thailand's GDP was expected to grow at 0.3 percent in 1997 and contract by 0.7 percent in 1998. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from a brief dip below the 1.68 per U.S. dollar level after Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the economy grew at 7.6 percent in 1997, above the government's higher-end forecast of seven percent. 

 Goh said in a New Year message the Singapore dollar should remain strong and imported inflation should be subdued in 1998. 

 But he added that next year would be more difficult for Singapore as trade would be hit by slowing growth in neigbouring countries. 

 The Malaysian ringgit also pulled off its early lows to stand at 3.8600/700 to the dollar in very thin trade against 3.8710/910 four hours earlier. 

 Philippine markets were closed for a holiday.

title: FOCUS - Asia  currencies  hit by seasonal dollar demand.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies yielded to commercial demand for dollars in otherwise uninspired trade on Tuesday as activity wound down for the end of the year. 

 The South Korean won shed early gains and fell sharply on dollar demand from importers and for year-end interest payments on foreign debts. 

 Dealers said news that major U.S., European and Japanese lenders were planning to roll over loans to South Korean banks had been largely priced in by the market. 

 "All the good news is already factored in. And there's still a lot of corporate demand for dollars," said a Japanese bank dealer in Singapore. 

 Even intervention by the central bank and reports that banks in the U.S., Europe and Japan were considering extending new credit to Seoul of as much as $10 billion failed to lift the won in late trade. 

 "What we want to see and hear more than anything else is an immediate inflow of real foreign hard currency into the market," a local bank dealer in Seoul said. "If not, all news will be just an empty announcement." 

 Seoul traders said the Bank of Korea sold dollars at 1,640 won in a clear attempt to cap the dollar's surge. 

 But the won closed weak at 1,590 to the dollar against its opening 1,220 and Monday's 1,395 close. 

 It had opened sharply higher as some local banks tried to push the dollar down in an attempt to reduce their foreign currency losses before book closing. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended higher at T$32.600 to the U.S. dollar against Monday's T$32.686 close, boosted by bargain-hunting interest in an otherwise slow market. 

 The Hong Kong dollar ended near its day low on consistent year-end demand for the U.S. dollar while forwards remained firm in line with higher domestic interbank rates. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Indonesian rupiah stayed soft but was off its lows against the dollar amid fears of central bank intervention. 

 "Dollar/rupiah is the most well bid of all the dollar/regionals. But the market is on the defensive because of Bank Indonesia. There's talk they'll intervene today or tomorrow," the Japanese bank dealer said. 

 The central bank sold dollars for rupiah at the 5,300 level late on Monday. 

 Dealers said companies had placed dollar buying orders at various levels on expectations the central bank would intervene again to boost the rupiah for the year end. 

 They said short-dated swaps recovered above par as operators began boosting their rupiah reserves. 

 The Indonesian forex market will be closed on Wednesday for book-closing and on Thursday for the New Year holiday. Trading will resume on Friday.

title: New round of Singapore rate hikes begins, more seen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 29 (Reuters) - A second round of prime rate hikes began in Singapore on Monday and analysts said they feared there could be further rises which would hurt the economy. 

 "My feeling is that there are quite high risks of another round" of prime rate hikes, said Eddie Lee, regional economist at Vickers Ballas. 

 Lee said Asia's economic crisis could drive Singapore banks to raise rates again in the next three to six months after OCBC Bank said on Monday it was raising its prime rate to seven percent from 6.5 percent with immediate effect. 

 OCBC lifted its prime rate by 50 basis points on December 2. Other banks followed suit and were expected to do so again in the next few days, the analysts said. 

 They said OCBC's new move was not surprising given the firmness in interbank rates, which surged to 10 percent earlier this month and are now around seven percent. 

 "Basically, you could see another 50-100 basis points as long as interbank rates stay at these levels," said Maminder Singh of Nomura Securities. 

 Further rate rises could hurt a Singapore economy already feeling the chills from the regional financial crisis which has swept through Southeast Asia and is now engulfing South Korea, the analysts said. 

 "The problem is most things are already slowing and the last thing you want is for interest rates to move up sharply," Singh said. 

 "A 100-point hike is already very tough on consumers, especially on those with housing loans. Persoanlly I wouldn't want to see higher prime rates from here," said Lee. 

 A key question was whether the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, would intervene if prime rates continued to rise, the analysts said. 

 "We did expect them to put more money into the system to sort of help the interbank market, but that would also weaken the Singapore dollar," Singh said. 

 The MAS was not expected to intervene at this stage, but there could be greater pressure to do so later on, Singh said. 

 The analysts said prime rates would remain stable at best in the near term. 

 "Overnight rates have come down very sharply. There is a chance that at least over the next month things would stabilise for a while, but you really want to watch what happens in the currency market," said Lee. 

 Lim Chung Chun, head of research at ING Baring, said interbank rates could soften only in the second half of 1998. 

 He thought banks might not raise prime rates more than 100 basis points in the meantime. 

 Singh at Nomura said rates were unlikely to ease as the interbank market was expected to remain tight for the next three to six months. 

 He said banks were looking at firm interbank rates as a longer-term trend and so were unlikely to cut back prime rates. 

 Lee said even if interbank rates came off, banks would hold prime rates steady and take advantage of the wider margins. 

 "They might as well have some cushion," he said.

title: More blues in store for Singapore dollar-analysts.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Singapore's long resilient dollar will remain prey to the weakness plaguing Asia's frazzled currencies, but its fall should be far more dignified, analysts said at the weekend. 

 They said it was likely to resume its gradual descent to keep up with the much worse-hit currencies of its neighbours as Asia's six-month-old crisis showed no signs of ending. 

 "The current corrective phase is technically inclined. The fundamental picture hasn't changed," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 "The Singapore dollar could easily hit 1.70 by year end and 1.80 by the first quarter," she added. 

 While once practically unimaginable, these levels are still a far cry from the more bearish forecasts of 2.00 and 2.10 that dealers were calling for when the Singapore dollar dived to six-year lows of 1.7175 early last week. 

 Shrinking liquidity in Asian currency markets and a perception Singapore's dollar had to fall further for Singapore to remain competitive with its neighbours induced a selling spree. 

 The normally static currency lost nearly seven percent in three trading days. 

 "We were hearing people saying the market was thin in other currencies so the Sing dollar was the only thing they could sell, which is ridiculous," said an analyst who declined to be identified. 

 But apparent intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the yen's recovery against the U.S. dollar and higher domestic interbank rates helped the Singapore dollar recover to around 1.66 in late Asian trade on Friday. 

 Analysts said more was almost certainly in store despite a rare statement from the MAS, the de facto central bank, that it saw no reason for the Singapore dollar to weaken given strong domestic economic fundamentals. 

 Singapore officials have said previously they were not concerned about the currency's slide against the U.S. dollar, leaving the exchange rate to market forces while other Asian central banks scrambled to shore up their currencies. 

 Analysts said the MAS comments highlighted Singapore's dilemma as a highly trade-dependent, exposed economy. 

 "On the one hand, there's the real threat of competition from the closer exporter countries like Malaysia, Taiwan. On the other hand, they would be concerned about import inflation," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken. 

 "And the bigger concern is the stability of the financial markets. Just like Hong Kong, they would not want a Sing dollar that's going to be spinning downwards because it would affect a lot of investment interests in this country," she said. 

 But with genuine U.S. dollar demand from companies seeking to cover import requirements or for debt payments, the Singapore dollar was likely to remain under pressure. 

 "Companies are hedging their positions up to six months down the road," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at I.D.E.A. 

 He said the Singapore dollar had actually strengthened on a trade-weighted basis and given the relatively muted threat of imported inflation, government emphasis would be on curbing upward pressure on domestic interest rates. 

 "We expect the authorities to start providing liquidity for the market because to keep a firm Sing dollar via high interest rates would kill the economy. The property market is already extremely weak," he said. 

 Interbank rates came off highs of 10 percent on Friday on talk the MAS had been injecting funds in the interbank system.

title: FOCUS-Yen rebound props up calmer Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Asian currencies extended their gains on Thursday, lifted by the yen's resurgence against the U.S. dollar in very thin year-end markets. 

 Talk of fresh intervention by the Bank of Japan after its repeated dollar-selling operations on Wednesday knocked the dollar off its fragile perch above 127 yen and weakened the U.S. currency across the board, dealers said. It recovered slightly to stand at 127.47/57 yen at 1008 GMT. 

 But Asian currencies were expected to make only limited headway in the face of lingering corporate demand for dollars to meet year-end payments. 

 In the Philippines, the peso perked up on the central bank's new measures to boost dollar liquidity, but traders said the bank's failure to intervene aggressively in foreign exchange markets pulled the peso off its highs. 

 It ended at 39.69 to the dollar after rising to 39.00 in early trade against Wednesday's 39.77 close. 

 The central bank was seen selling dollars at 39.50 pesos and 39.40 pesos after buying an estimated $1.5 million in opening deals, traders said. 

 They generally welcomed the central bank's efforts to counter a shortage of dollars by agreeing with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) to provide up to $150 million in the spot market daily. 

 The central bank will also enter into non-deliverable forward contracts with banks whose clients are unhedged. 

 BAP president Deogracias Vistan said Philippine banks sold nearly $50 million to the central bank on Thursday to help lift the peso. 

 Volume in the peso-dollar market totalled $195 million. It had shrunk to less than $10 million in recent days due to the shortage of dollars. 

 Manila shares were also heartened by the peso's recovery. The main stock index ended 2.74 percent up at 1,846.09 points. 

 The Indonesian rupiah burst through the 5,000 level against the dollar for the first time since Monday as Jakarta companies unloaded dollars, sparking offshore sales in very thin markets. 

 It was quoted at 4,800/900 to the dollar, a near 11 percent gain from its opening of 5,300/5,500. 

 Dealers said fears of concerted intervention by the central banks of Indonesia, Japan and Singapore in support of the rupiah after the Bank of Japan's dollar/yen sales also lifted the unit. 

 Indonesian President Suharto's first public appearance, in apparent good health, since doctors advised him to rest put the rupiah on relatively solid footing early in the day. 

 Suharto, attending a graduation parade for military academy cadets, called for national resilience to overcome the country's economic and financial crisis. 

 The Singapore dollar strengthened towards 1.66 to the U.S. dollar against levels of 1.6735/75 late on Wednesday as discouraging noises from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and high domestic interbank rates curbed a selling frenzy. 

 Dealers said they did not detect the MAS behind Thursday's U.S. dollar sales. 

 But they remained wary of testing the de facto central bank's resolve after apparent interventions on Tuesday and Wednesday and a statement that it saw no reason for the domestic currency to weaken given Singapore's sound fundamentals. 

 Vague rumours the government intended to liberalise the use of funds from Singapore's state savings scheme for the purchase of private property also lifted the Singapore dollar in late dealings, though dealers were largely dismissive of the talk. 

 "Basically they're looking for excuses to sell dollar/Sing and the market is exaggerated because the volume's very thin," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar's gains were expected to be capped by U.S. dollar demand near 1.65. 

 The Malaysian ringgit whipped around in thin markets, firming to 3.7833/933 to the dollar from 3.8000/9000 five hours earlier. Dealers said its gains were blocked by corporate dollar demand near 3.77 ringgit, while the stock market's firm tone limited declines. 

 The Thai baht bounced higher as exporters sold dollars following the baht's recovery in offshore markets where players unwound long dollar positions. 

 The Bank of Thailand's downward revision of its 1997 current account deficit forecast and its projection of a rise in foreign reserves to $29 billion at the end of 1997 from $26.3 billion at the end of November also helped the baht. 

 It rose to 45.00/10 to the dollar onshore against 47.10/30 late on Wednesday. The offshore rate was at 43.75/44.25 against 45.80/46.30. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended sharply up at T$32.200 to the U.S. dollar from Wednesday's T$32.520 close as players booked profit on the subsiding U.S. dollar.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  take heart as yen surges.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies calmed down a bit on Wednesday as the dollar dropped dramatically against the yen following the Bank of Japan's unexpected -- and repeated -- interventions and news of a massive Japanese income tax cut. 

 The dollar lost what had looked like a firm grip above the 131 yen level and fell as low as 125.85 yen in Tokyo trade. 

 But no one was prepared to predict the end of its reign over Asian currencies just yet. 

 "Overall, sentiment in the whole of Asia is still very fragile so what we're seeing today may just be a technical rebound. I think the dollar demand is very real," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at I.D.E.A. 

Currencies in Southeast Asia, where the region's economic crisis had its beginning, had a much better day. 

 The Philippine peso reversed course, the Singapore dollar recovered from a heavy fall, the Malaysian ringgit moved higher and the Indonesian rupiah stopped falling. 

 The peso bounced to 39.904/937 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after hitting an all-time low of 41.60 earlier. 

 Manila traders said the central bank was seen selling dollars heavily at various levels in an effort to counter dollar demand amid shrinking supply. 

 News the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) and the central bank had agreed to set up a dollar pool to cover the requirements of oil companies and other corporations helped boost the peso, they said. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the bank had also agreed to enter into non-deliverable forward contracts with dollar borrowers to ease demand in the spot market. 

 The Singapore dollar also staged a recovery as talk of intervention in overnight trade and possibly early on Wednesday by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, spooked the market. 

 It was quoted at 1.6885/915 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after firming through the 1.6800 level against a morning low of 1.7010. 

 "The MAS was in in London last night. When dollar/Sing got to a high of 1.7175, they were in selling," a senior regional currencies trader said. 

 "I heard they were in again through some local banks this morning. But then again, other local banks were bidding on the other side," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure and dived through the key 1.70 level in thin London trade on Tuesday, reaching lows not seen in over six years. 

 The sharp drop meant the once static currency had lost nearly seven percent in three trading days as poor year-end liquidity exaggerated movements. 

 Dealers and analysts said it remained in a downtrend but the market was likely to avoid the 1.70 level for the time being. 

 "They (the MAS) don't mind a weaker Sing. In fact, they'd welcome it for now, but not too fast," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit also pulled back from its lows on the yen's rebound and on talk of foreign inflows to the stock market. It was at 3.8300/400 to the dollar against 3.8825/925 late on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the thin market was keeping the ringgit volatile, with small volumes causing wild gyrations. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 5,450 and 5,600 to the dollar all morning as spreads narrowed to 50/100 points amid dwindling interest. 

 Dealers said the dollar maintained a firm undertone against the rupiah, which gained little mileage from news that President Suharto would attend a public function on Thursday. 

 Worries about his health have sent the rupiah spiralling to new lows in the past week. 

 The Thai baht was little changed at 47.80/48.00 to the dollar onshore against 47.60/48.10 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate stood at 46.65/85 against 46.90/47.20. 

 Dealers said they expected the baht to have a steadier day as regional currencies should gain from the yen's rise. 

 In north Asia, the South Korean won slipped for the first time this week due to dollar buying for importer settlements due early next week. 

 The won was at 1,505/10 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,425 close, but dealers said its decline would be limited by fears of central bank intervention. 

 The Taiwan dollar continued to be driven by external factors, firming to T$32.644/669 against Tuesday's T$32.820 close as traders watched the yen rebound. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was protected from weakening through the 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar by thin year-end conditions and the yen's rise. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority did not appear to have intervened in the foreign exchange market, but it was seen offering three-month money in early trade. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said the ringgit's ability to hold above the 3.93 per dollar level for the second time on Tuesday suggested i 

 The Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar had the most volatile morning, both rebounding sharply against the U.S. dollar 

 Asian currencies posted fresh losses on Tuesday as persistent dollar demand and dwindling trading volumes sparked fresh carnage in foreign exchange markets. 

 Only the South Korean won defied logic, surging nearly 16 percent to highs of 1,350 against the dollar after the central bank decided late on Monday to scrap its 10 percent trading band. It ended at 1,425.0 against Monday's 1,563.9 close. 

 Dealers said the won was benefitting from expectations of heavy dollar inflows under the IMF's $57 billion bailout scheme for South Korea, which had moved players to unwind long dollar positions built during the won's near 50 percent drop last week. 

 The government's decision to float the won, as requested by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), sell off one or two troubled banks and push forward with a $10 billion sovereign bond issue boosted Korean financial markets on Tuesday. 

 But dealers said sentiment could quickly turn negative if more of the pledged IMF loans were not disbursed soon. 

 The won was also expected to face selling pressure from importers seeking dollars towards the weekend. 

 Its improved fortunes gave the Taiwan dollar an opening boost, but it soon shed the gains in the face of strong U.S. dollar demand from importers. 

 Taipei traders said there was also concern about the previously sturdy Singapore dollar's sharp falls, which triggered renewed fears of a competitive depreciation in the Taiwan dollar. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at T$32.820 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest close since November 1987, against Monday's T$32.746 close. It hit a low of T$32.950. 

 Dealers said the central bank appeared to have intervened in the last minute of trade in a bid to keep its dollar above the psychological T$33 level. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remained on the cusp of the key 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar, but forwards eased in the wake of the won's rebound. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was heard buying the local dollar via a major commercial bank to limit the U.S. dollar's rise. 

 Southeast Asian currencies were off their lows but remained weak and weary as companies scrambled to buy dollars to meet loan payments amid shrinking liquidity and widening spreads. 

 "There's just a lack of liquidity in the market. There are very few interbank players around so if you're buying, the whole world knows you're buying," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore. 

 "Given the widening spreads, the pace of depreciation is much faster. People are just extremely bearish on the region," he added. 

 Dealers said transaction volumes had fallen sharply as players sought to limit their exposure to growing market volatility towards the year end. 

 "In the middle of the year, people would trade something like 20 to 50 (million) dollars. But lately because of the volatility and the fact that the big figure changes so fast ... positions have been reduced to one to two (million) dollars," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered in late trade as attempts to test the 6,000 level failed, causing a pullback in the currency which was reinforced by central bank intervention. 

 It was at 5,500/600 to the dollar at 1020 GMT after Bank Indonesia sold dollars at 5,700, dealers said. The rupiah hit an early record low of 5,980 to the dollar. 

 Dealers said it remained fragile on lingering worries about President Suharto's health despite clear signs he was gradually resuming work after a period of rest and corporate difficulties in meeting debt payments. 

 They said liquidity had practically dried up and spreads of 200 or 300 points were exacerbating the rupiah's moves. 

 The Thai baht's abrupt recovery from a record low of 49.35 against the dollar sparked speculation of central bank support. 

 Bangkok dealers said exporters sold dollars around the 48 baht level, but the Thai unit remained weak at 47.50/48.00 to the dollar against 47.30/90 late on Monday. 

 Offshore baht was at 46.90/47.20 against 46.90/47.40. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda appealed to Thais to refrain from speculating against the baht and said the government would use the limited resources at hand to defend it. 

 The Philippine peso ended at a record low of 40.214 to the dollar against a previous 38.853 close despite intervention by the central bank. Further falls were only prevented by the activation of volatility bands. 

 Poor market liquidity -- total turnover was a mere $9.5 million -- did little for the peso's condition and dealers expected more declines. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the peso would only recover if people stopped speculating against it. 

 Dealers attributed the peso's steep drop to panic buying of dollars by firms with dollar exposures and importers hedging future dollar requirements. 

 A slowdown in remittances from overseas contract workers was also contributing to the shortage of dollars. 

 The Singapore dollar fell within a hair's breadth of the key 1.70 level to the U.S. dollar, but fears of central bank intervention pulled it back from the edge, dealers said. 

 It was at its weakest in more than six years at 1.6935/55 to the U.S. dollar at 1020 GMT after hitting a low of 1.6995. Late on Monday it was at 1.6835/65. 

 There was no consensus among dealers about the likelihood of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) selling U.S. dollars above the 1.70 level, or over whether it was behind a spurt of dollar sales that pushed the Singapore dollar up to an early high of 1.6660. 

 "I think they were in at least once or twice this morning, but it didn't really help because dollar/Sing is still biddish," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 I.D.E.A.'s Koh was skeptical about the MAS intervening given the sharp falls in other regional currencies. 

 "The authorities have affirmed again and again that they look at the Singapore dollar, not just against the U.S. dollar, but on a trade-weighted basis," he said. 

 The MAS declined to confirm rumours about an intervention. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered as players took profit on the dollar's gains after the rupiah rose on Bank Indonesia's intervention. 

 It firmed to 3.8825/925 to the dollar against 3.9025/125 late on Monday.

title: Singapore dollar slide seen slowing.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Apparent central bank support helped lift the Singapore dollar from six-year lows against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, but dealers and analysts expected more weakness in the once sturdy currency. 

 It firmed above the 1.68 level to the U.S. dollar, partly due to talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, had sold U.S. dollars above S$1.70 to stem the decline. 

 Dealers said MAS commments that it saw no reason for the Singapore dollar to weaken given the country's strong economic fundamentals further boosted the Singapore dollar to 1.6720/70 at 1005 GMT against 1.6935/55 late on Tuesday. 

 Some dealers said the MAS had also intervened in thin London markets overnight when the Singapore dollar succumbed to mounting pressure and dived to a low of 1.7175 per U.S. dollar. 

 "The MAS was in in London last night. When dollar/Sing got to a high of 1.7175, they were in selling," said a senior regional currencies trader. 

 "I heard they were in again through some local banks this morning. But then again, other local banks were bidding on the other side," he said. 

 The previously stolid Singapore dollar had lost nearly seven percent in three trading days as market participants sold it on a perception that it needed to fall for Singapore exports to remain competitive regionally. 

 But the MAS's comments on Wednesday, and the yen's steep drop against the U.S. dollar, gave dealers cause to suspend their selling spree. 

 "As Singapore's economic fundamentals remain sound, we see no reason why the Singapore dollar should weaken," the MAS said in a written response to questions from Reuters. 

 "The MAS intervenes in the foreign exchange market from time to time to iron out short-term fluctuations. We do not publicise our exchange rate operations," it said. 

 Singapore government officials have said previously during months of Southeast Asian currency turmoil that they were not concerned about the domestic dollar's slide against the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the MAS comments highlighted Singapore's dilemma as a highly trade-dependent economy. 

 "I think they're a bit ambivalent, because on the one hand there's the real threat of competition from the closer exporter countries like Malaysia, Taiwan. On the other hand, they would be concerned about import inflation," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken. 

 "And the bigger concern is the stability of the financial markets. Just like Hong Kong, they would not want a Sing dollar that's going to be spinning downwards because it would affect a lot of investment interests in this country," Chia said. 

 Dealers and analysts agreed there was a basis for the Singapore dollar to track declines in neighbouring currencies, though at a slower pace, in the short term. 

 "We expect more weakness. It's at current levels only because of MAS intervention," said an analyst at a foreign bank who declined to be identified. 

 She said the intervention was aimed more at smoothing moves in the exchange rate. "I don't think there is a level they're defending." 

 She said the Singapore dollar was likely to reach 1.75 to the U.S. dollar by March. 

 Most dealers expected the Singapore dollar to slide below the 1.70 level again in the weeks ahead. 

 "They (the MAS) were concerned because it moved so fast. But I don't think they'd mind if dollar/Sing moved slowly up to test 1.72, especially if the Malaysian ringgit goes back below 3.90," a U.S. bank dealer said.

title: FOCUS-Asian stocks battered by Korea, but HK rises.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 12 (Reuters) - Asian stock markets continued to be battered by fallout from the financial crisis in South Korea, but contrarians enjoyed pointing out rises in Hong Kong and Taiwan. 

 Korea's economic woes tended to dominate sentiment throughout Asia. But some markets had doemstic travails of their own, and this included Jakarta, where news that President Suharto had cancelled a trip to Malaysia next week prompted a currency and stock market rout. 

 A poor day in the region was guaranteed after the Dow Jones industrial average fell 129.80 points, or 1.6 percent, to 7,848.99 overnight. 

 Investors there were perturbed by further warnings from U.S. companies that Asia's problems were having a direct impact on their bottom lines. 

 The last thing sentiment needed was another corporate collapse in Korea -- but it got one. 

 Dongsuh Securities Co Ltd, one of Korea's leading brokerage houses, filed for court receivership -- the latest in a series of corporate collapses. 

 As if this wasn't enough, the Korean won initially performed its now habitual routine of plunging its 10 percent limit down on the foreign exchange market. 

 In fact, the won later benefited from central bank intervention and ended the day slightly firmer at 1,710 to the dollar against Thursday's close of 1,719.8 and the limit low of 1,891.4. 

 But the regional currencies dealer at a European bank in Singapore doubted the intervention would work in the future. "The Korean central bank hasn't got enough dollars to stop the currency hitting 2,000 in a very short time," he said. 

 The Seoul stock market duly took its cue from the gloomy scenario. It opened more than six percent down, failed to recover, and ended more than seven percent down. 

 The composite stock index closed at its lowest level in a decade at 350.68, a fall of 7.07 percent. 

 Park Young-chul, chief trader at Hyundai Securities, called the collapsing market a "tragedy". 

 "The market is cut loose from the normal framework. There are no rules applying...right now," he said. 

 The dubious honour of the regions biggest percentage decline belonged to Jakarta. 

 Stocks there -- which had already been affected by Korea's malaise -- were sent into a tailspin by an announcement that Presiden Suharto would not after all be attending next week's Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Kuala Lumpur. 

 Earlier this week, stocks and the Indonesian rupiah had been sold heavily on rumours that the 76-year-old leader was seriously ill, or even dead. 

 But it was then announced he would attend the meeting and prices perked up. 

 Today's news of his non-attendance came as a body-blow. 

 At one stage, the Jakarta stock index was off more than nine percent. It ended at 365.85, down 7.64 percent. 

 The rupiah also plunged, crashing through the 5,000 level. In late trading it was quoted at a staggering 5,150.00 to the U.S. dollar compared with yesterday's finish of 4,505.00. 

 One currencies trader at a bank in Singapore said, "This news is disastrous for Indonesia. They told us he (Suharto) was well and now they say he's not going to KL (Kuala Lumpur)." 

 "Can you believe one guy was quoted as saying Suharto can't travel long distances. Well, he's just come back from South Africa. How far is KL from Jakarta, two hours (flight)? He's ill. Sell," he said. 

 Markets in Tokyo, Manila, Singapore, Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur all fell. 

 But Hong Kong and Taiwan bucked the trend, manging to eke out gains. 

 In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index closed at the day's high of 10,614.66, a gain of 1.87 percent. Dealers said this reflected a technical rebound after three days of losses. 

 Taiwan dealers went bargain-hunting and the weighted index ended 1.54 percent higher at 8,393.27.

 They said the low for the rupiah was 3,940 in Singapore and 3,935 in Jakarta. Spot rupiah was at 3,938/48 at 0515 GMT, compared with an opening of 3,800/15. The previous low for the rupiah was 3,865 on October 6.

 "If that happens, I think the rupiah is going to overshoot again because of stop-loss selling," one chief treasurer said. 

 He said the central bank was seen checking one-week swap prices, but had not intervened yet. Dealers said cheap swaps at the short-end had also made long dollar holdings attractive. 

 They said the market was very thin, which favoured the central bank stepping in. They, however, said the central bank appeared to be reluctant because of a slump in the region. 

 Dealers said operators were also seen buying dollars following comments by Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad in Malaysia that concerted intervention by Indonesia, Singapore and Japan had been put on hold because the entire region was in a slump. 

 Dealers said the underlying tone remained weak for the rupiah and for currencies in the region. 

 The rupiah ended firmer in New York overnight at 3,800/10 and the more positive tone extended to the opening in Jakarta before falling afoul of regional woes. 

 One Japanese bank dealer said the market was so thin that people only needed small volumes to move the whole market. 

 One Singapore-based dealer said he was worried about entering the market at current levels because the rupiah appeared to be oversold. However, the whole region was in a slump, he added.

title: Indonesia In Talks With Singapore On Aid For Companies
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia is holding talks on redirecting money pledged by Singapore to defend the rupiah into assisting Indonesian companies suffering from high interest rates and a liquidity squeeze, a senior official of the Indonesian central bank confirmed. 

 But the official said the amount of money to be used hasn't been agreed upon and "still under negotiation." 

 "The exact amount of money we hope to use is still uncertain, and our Finance Ministry is discussing the issue with Singapore," the official said. "It's still uncertain." 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore has intervened in the currency markets several times to defend the rupiah since Indonesia reached agreement with the International Monetary Fund in October. Separately, Singapore has pledged $5 billion toward the IMF's rescue package for Indonesia. 

 Singapore officials have said the amount of money to be spent on supporting the rupiah is undetermined. They have also made clear that the $5 billion pledge is contingent on Indonesia fulfilling the terms of its IMF program. 

 Indonesian Minister of Industry and Trade Tunky Ariwibowo last week that the government was seeking to use Singapore money to help small-scale and export-oriented companies with liquidity in the current environement.

title: FEATURE - Cash plus confidence make Singapore safe haven.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Don't go to Singapore if you're looking for second-hand Rolex watches at knock-down prices or Mercedes convertibles from bankrupt investors. 

 As the 'For Sale' signs go up on the condominiums of Bangkok and Hong Kong, Singapore has remained an island of relative calm in the financial storm raging across Asia. 

 True, the Singapore dollar has depreciated by about 13 percent against the U.S. dollar and the stock market has lost about a quarter of its value this year. 

 The great property boom of the early 1990s is also over and modest price falls have stopped speculators making a fortune buying apartments from the blueprints and reselling them before completion. 

 But the economy has remained almost unscathed by the turmoil that has rocked banks from Tokyo to Jakarta this year. 

 And it is likely to stay that way. Even pessimistic forecasters say Singapore economic growth may slip only a point or two next year from the 7-10 percent range of recent times. 

 Economists argue the keys to Singapore's remarkable stability are cash and confidence: it has no foreign debt and its tightly regulated financial sector inspires trust. 

 "Singapore just doesn't have the potential for the kind of balance of payments crisis seen elsewhere in the region," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at Barclays Capital Group. 

 "And the regulatory environment is very firm. In the past the Singapore authorities have been criticised for being overly cautious in the regulation of the financial sector. Their approach has been fully vindicated by what has happened now. The banking sector is stable," Supple said. 

 Exploiting its location at the crossroads of Asia, Singapore has nurtured a busy entrepot trade since independence in 1965. 

 Next to the world's most active shipping route between the South China Sea and the Indian Ocean, Singapore has one of the world's busiest ports and has used this to develop a financial sector now among the top four foreign exchange markets. 

 Bequeathed a solid infrastructure by its former British colonists, the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) of patriarch Lee Kuan Yew has built up huge foreign exchange reserves which topped Singapore $118 billion (US$74 billion) in September. 

 And through a compulsory government-controlled savings scheme, it has encouraged a high level of domestic savings, which have then been used to avoid borrowing abroad. 

 Singapore is now the world's sixth largest capital exporter and has an annual current account surplus of US$16 billion. 

 Singapore's critics, and there are many, say the PAP, which won 81 of the 83 parliamentary seats at the last election in January 1997, runs the country like a corporation. 

 They say it only pays lip service to democracy, stifles the press and regards citizenship as something that can be bestowed or removed like a company which can hire or fire its workers. 

 PAP stands for "Pay And Pay", they say, citing the numerous government levies and indirect taxes such as charges of up to S$70,000 (US$44,000) for the right to buy a car. 

 But Lee, prime minister from 1959 to 1990 and still in cabinet as senior minister, shrugs off critics who call the Singapore style of government authoritarian or autocratic, a label he rejects. 

 "If I ran a Western-style democracy and took a straw poll and went according to the poll, we would have come to grief," he told Reuters in an interview this month, describing his experiences as prime minister. 

 And with direct and corporate taxation rates low and excellent communication links to the rest of the region, Singapore is the first choice for many multinational companies. 

 Business leaders say the government's conduct during the continuing economic turmoil has been admirable. 

 By contrast with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, whose trenchant attacks on speculators in the financial markets have sent funds scurrying to sell the Malaysian ringgit, Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has soothed markets. 

 "I take the view that you can't fight the market," Goh told reporters in Tokyo in August. 

 Although the de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, does intervene in currency markets from time to time, it appears to be content to let the Singapore dollar find its own level. 

 Economists say that level is probably within a few percent of where it is at the moment at 1.59 to the U.S. dollar -- not much changed from around 1.40 at the beginning of the year. 

 "Both from a macro-economic point of view and from a corporate point of view, the country is doing quite well," said Bruce Gale, analyst at Political & Economic Risk Consultancy. 

 "It has very large foreign reserves to defend the currency if it wanted to and no one can pull out their funds because there is no debt." 

 Singapore has also been partly insulated from the current regional crisis by its mix of industries. 

 On top of its finance and business sectors, which account for about 28 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), Singapore's commerce, entrepot, transport and communications industries provide another 31-32 percent of output. 

 Only 26 percent of GDP is manufacturing and more than half of this is in electronics or related industries, which sell most of their wares to developed economies. Sales from this sector to the region tend to be of semi-finished goods. 

 The global electronics industry slumped in 1996, trimming GDP growth back a little, and it may slow again in 1998 or 1999, but there has been modest growth this year in the sector. 

 Singapore is reluctant to say so, but most economists argue it could teach the rest of the region a few tricks. 

 "What has characterised all the countries that have been battered in the crisis, is that they are massive capital importers," said Supple. "If you are a capital importer, you are vulnerable to a flight of capital." 

 "A country cannot grow just by borrowing from abroad. Financing excessive growth leads to escalating foreign debt and widening current account deficits. Singapore is an example of how that should be avoided," he said. 

 Manmindar Singh, senior economist at Nomura Securities in Singapore agreed: "If there is a lesson it's this: 'You should only finance what you can afford.'"

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Yamaichi Securities said on Monday it would shut down, setting off a government offensive to assure world markets that Japan's biggest financial failure since World War Two was not a sign of a breakdown in the country's financial system. 

 Yamaichi's failure was the latest development in a string of financial crises across Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils an austerity plan and complete revamp of its finance sector as part of IMF-suggested policies for a rescue package. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits an historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 19 - The South Korean won hits an all time low of 901 to the dollar. The currency has been sliding gradually during the year. On January 1 it stood at 842. 

 August 20 - The IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Oct 2 - Won slips to 913.50 on news Ssangbang Wool faces a debt default. Corporate defaults have been one of the reasons for the won's fall. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 28 - The won's fall accelerates. It ends at 953 despite central bank intervention. 

 Oct 30 - The won -- which has a 2.25 percent daily trading band -- hits its lowest permitted level of 984.70. 

 Oct 31 - The IMF package for Indonesia is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - The won will "never, never, never" breach the psychologically important 1000 barrier a Korean central bank official says. 

 Nov 2 - Indonesia announces the liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks under the IMF economic reform programme. 

 Nov 4 - Thailand's government collapses as Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh resigns. The baht rises to 38.75 from 40.95 on the unpopular premier's departure. 

 Nov 7 - The markets are now openly speculating Seoul will have to go to the IMF to help defend the won. The won ends at 979.90 and traders are targetting the 1000 barrier. 

 In Thailand, opposition Democrat leader Chuan Leekpai says he will form the new government. 

 Nov 9 - Chuan is appointed new Thai premier. 

 Nov 10 - The won closes at 999.00 to the dollar. 

 Nov 17 - South Korea cracks. The central bank announces it will no longer defend the 986 level to the dollar. The won immediately falls its daily limit down to 1008.60. 

 Nov 18 - The Korean central bank suggests to the finance ministry that Korea should seek an IMF bailout loan. The won is at its 1012.80 daily limit low.

 Nov 21 - Finance ministry official announces that Seoul is discussing details of a bailout package with the IMF worth $20 billion.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Friday it was talking to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about emergency loans. 

 This was the latest development in a string of financial crises across Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils an austerity plan and complete revamp of its finance sector as part of IMF-suggested policies for a rescue package. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits an historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 19 - The South Korean won hits an all time low of 901 to the dollar. The currency has been sliding gradually during the year. On January 1 it stood at 842. 

 August 20 - The IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Oct 2 - Won slips to 913.50 on news Ssangbang Wool faces a debt default. Corporate defaults have been one of the reasons for the won's fall. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 28 - The won's fall accelerates. It ends at 953 despite central bank intervention. 

 Oct 30 - The won -- which has a 2.25 percent daily trading band -- hits its lowest permitted level of 984.70. 

 Oct 31 - The IMF package for Indonesia is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - The won will "never, never, never" breach the psychologically important 1000 barrier a Korean central bank official says. 

 Nov 2 - Indonesia announces the liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks under the IMF economic reform programme. 

 Nov 4 - Thailand's government collapses as Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh resigns. The baht rises to 38.75 from 40.95 on the unpopular premier's departure. 

 Nov 7 - The markets are now openly speculating Seoul will have to go to the IMF to help defend the won. The won ends at 979.90 and traders are targetting the 1000 barrier. 

 In Thailand, opposition Democrat leader Chuan Leekpai says he will form the new government. 

 Nov 9 - Chuan is appointed new Thai premier. 

 Nov 10 - The won closes at 999.00 to the dollar. 

 Nov 17 - South Korea cracks. The central bank announces it will no longer defend the 986 level to the dollar. The won immediately falls its daily limit down to 1008.60. 

 Nov 18 - The Korean central bank suggests to the finance ministry that Korea should seek an IMF bailout loan. The won is at its 1012.80 daily limit low. 

 Nov 19 - Korean finance minister Kang Kyong-shik resigns to take responsibility for the financial turmoil. South Korea also widens its daily band limit on the won to 10 percent. 

 Nov 21 - Finance ministry official announces that Seoul is discussing details of a bailout package with the IMF.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  sink, battered by won.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies sank deeper on Wednesday as the South Korean won again hit its daily limit and a new low just as the country's finance minister resigned. 

 Thailand's political uncertainties, which took centrestage in Asia's currency market in recent weeks, have been upstaged by South Korea's beleaguered won and an ailing Malaysian stock market. 

 Early Wednesday, the won dived to a new low of 1,035.50 to the U.S. dollar against Tuesday's 1,012.80 on news Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik had resigned amid a looming financial crisis. 

 The replacement of Kang by Trade Minister Lim Chang-yuel did little to lift sentiment, dealers said. 

 Also weighing on sentiment was a more than four percent plunge in Malaysia's stock market as foreigners bailed out of the peninsula on fears of more financial troubles. 

 After breaking its key 3.45 level to the dollar, the Malaysian ringgit proceeded to break 3.46. On Tuesday, it was trading around 3.4090/190. 

 Malaysia and the won sent fresh tremors throughout the regional currencies, many of which are expected to test even lower levels within the week. 

 "It is very likely some of the regionals will test lower levels later this afternoon and this week," said a dealer with a European bank. 

 He expected the ringgit to test 3.50 to a dollar during the week now that 3.46, the previous low, had been tested. 

 "Dollar/ringgit is likely to go higher from here because most is real capital outflow from the Kuala Lumpur stock exchange since yesterday. The ringgit has to weaken more," said the dealer at a European bank. 

 After testing 3,500 to the dollar, the Indonesian rupiah was quoted at 3,490/00 at 0445 GMT. 

 Outlook for the rupiah was hazy, with many dealers unwilling to venture a forecast. 

 "It is difficult becasue the market is worried about concerted central bank interventions," said a dealer in Singapore. 

 Dealers said the forward market could be under attack by Bank of Indonesia since it came in on Tuesday to drain liquidity from the tom/next market. 

 "But today, the tom/next came in quite tight and then backed off. It will depend on the forward markets," the dealer said. 

 In Jakarta, tom/next swap was at 0.2/0.3, while in Singapore, tom/next was at 0.1/0.6. 

 The Thai baht slid past the key 40 per dollar level and was trading around 40.250/350 in the onshore market at 0445 GMT. 

 Dealers in Singapore were expecting it to test 40.750 later on Wednesday. 

 "We see customers interested to buy below 40 figure. Eventually it will trade back around 40," a dealer said. 

 In the offshore market, the baht was quoted at 39.780/880. 

 The Singapore dollar was also not spared the contagion effect. It was poised to test 1.6000 to the dollar after hitting a low of 1.5965, where most deals were done in the morning. 

 Elsewhere in Asia, the Taiwan dollar broke 32.000 to the greenback and hit a low of 32.426 compared to Tuesday's 31.770 close, and the Philippines peso hit its first volatility limit of 35.422 to the dollar.

SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar sank to a low of 1.5900/20 to the U.S. dollar in late morning trade on Tuesday after Singapore's senior minister Lee Kuan Yew said the level of the local dollar was a matter for the markets to decide. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar was also battered by keen selling of the ringgit/Sing by U.S. players. 

 "Lee's comments made some impact but the Singapore dollar also weakened because of the Kuala Lumpur stock market is bad. Some U.S. players are selling the ringgit/Sing," said a dealer with a local bank. 

 At 0345 GMT, Malaysia's key composite stock market index was down 5.74 percent at 628.99. 

 In an interview with Reuters, Lee said the relative strength of the Singapore dollar, which has fallen far less against the U.S. currency than some other Asian currencies, would have a negative impact. 

 "That's going to be a real problem for us because they are much cheaper than us now...they have gone down by 25 to 35 to, in the case of the Thai baht, about 40 percent against the U.S. dollar and we've only gone down barely 10 percent," Lee said. 

 But he said the level of the Singapore dollar against the other currencies was a matter for the markets to decide. 

 At 0345 GMT, the Singapore dollar was quoted around 1.5890/10. 

 Dealers said they were watching to see if Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which had been absent so far, would intervene later.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  uninspired as dollar drops.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies softened on Thursday while the Indonesian rupiah found itself torn between its central bank and companies seeking dollars. 

 Dealers said IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus's calming words about Southeast Asia's efforts to pull out of months of economic turmoil were largely ignored by the market. 

 Camdessus, on a tour of Southeast Asia, said he believed Asia would quickly rebound from its current crisis and should be able to return to high rates of economic growth. 

 He said Thailand had passed its first IMF review while Hong Kong and Malaysian banks were unlikely to face a crisis. 

 He also said Malaysia was in solid economic condition, though its current account gap was still on "the higher side". 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah was pushed to a high of 3,355 to the dollar in early trade on talk Bank Indonesia had sold dollars above the 3,400 level in Jakarta and Singapore markets. 

 But there was no official confirmation of the intervention and no clear sign the central banks of Japan and Singapore were involved in the operation, as was the case twice last week. 

 The rupiah drifted lower on dollar demand from offshore parties, especially Japanese companies, in afternoon trade. It was quoted at 3,400/10 to the dollar at 1010 GMT amid vague talk Bank Indonesia had checked rates above the 3,400 level again. 

 "We heard BI had been checking rates for the third time but I'm not sure if they actually sold dollars," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "I don't think BI coming in alone would scare the market. It's unlikely they'll have that much effect unless they come in with the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)," she added. 

 The Japanese finance ministry and the MAS declined to comment on whether the BOJ had taken part in the intervention. 

 Other Asian currencies looked soft but dealers said the market lacked energy as many players were winding down for the end of the year and the dollar's abrupt drop against the yen on talk of BOJ intervention also dominated interest. 

 In Thailand, the baht was steady but weak at 38.70/80 to the dollar against 38.55/65 late on Wednesday. The offshore rate was at 38.30/31 against 37.999/00. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting the announcement of Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai's new cabinet. Chuan was due to present his cabinet list for approval to King Bhumibol Adulyadej later on Thursday. 

 Dealers said the baht did not react to comments by the IMF's Camdessus that the Fund had no plans to make changes to Thailand's economic programme. 

 In Bangkok, Supachai Panitchpakdi, expected to be named deputy premier in charge of economic affairs in the new cabinet, appeared to echo the IMF chief's statements. 

 He said Thailand did not intend to renegotiate the terms of the IMF-led $17.2 billion economic bailout package. 

 The Singapore dollar eased to 1.5795/10 to the U.S. dollar against 1.5746/66 on Wednesday on buying of the Malaysian ringgit/Singapore dollar cross. 

 "There's been some ringgit/Sing buying going through. There's talk that the cross might go to 50 cents but I think it has to break 48.20 first," a European bank dealer said. 

 The ringgit was at 47.70/89 Singapore cents at 1010 GMT. 

 Across the border, the ringgit showed little sign of stirring out of the range it has established against the U.S. dollar in recent sessions, hovering around 3.3000/100. 

 The Philippine peso ended lower at 33.93 per dollar against a previous close of 33.43 on dollar short-covering and offshore dollar demand. 

 Dealers said the central bank intervened to sell about $4 million at 33.98 pesos in late trade, but further falls were expected to be capped by inflows from overseas contract workers. 

 In north Asia, the Korean won ended up at 986.70 to the dollar as the central bank kept to its staunch defence, selling dollars at 988.00 won in opening trade while repeating its daily words of support. 

 "Our stance to maintain the won steadily stronger has not changed," said Lee Eung-baek, chief of the central bank's foreign exchange division. 

 The Bank of Korea has moved its defence line up by one won to the dollar for each of the last two days, steering the embattled currency away from the 1,000 level eyed by the market. 

 But its actions have taken their toll on the money market where the overnight call loan rate hit a yearly high of 14.90 percent on Thursday. 

 Seoul traders said the market was awaiting a government package of measures to stabilise financial markets. 

 The Taiwan dollar slid to T$31.105 against its previous T$30.992 close on jitters about the weak yen and won. 

 After the market close, the central bank said there was no change in its monetary policy for the time being and it reserved the right to intervene in forex market when needed. 

 The Hong Kong dollar ended lower at 7.7320/40 to the U.S. dollar from Wednesday's 7.7300/10 close as interest rates eased. 

 Dealers said liquidity improved after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) clarified its rules on borrowing from its discount window. 

 On October 23, the HKMA had said it would levy penal rates on "repeated borrowers" at the window, making banks wary of tapping the facility and leading to a liquidity crunch. 

 The HKMA said on Thursday repeated borrowers are licensed banks which have borrowed through the facility on eight occasions in any period of 25 days or on four consecutive days in which the window is open.

 "There's been some ringgit/Sing buying going through. There's talk that the cross might go to 50 cents but I think it has to break 48.20 first," a European bank dealer said.
