title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  tread water as won recovers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies remained in well-worn territory on Tuesday as the stricken Korean won managed to stave off further attacks with the help of its central bank. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Korea stepped in to rescue the won from the brink of the psychological 1,000-to-the-dollar level in opening trade and later lowered its intervention level. 

 The won ended at 989.90 to the dollar after the central bank sold dollars aggressively at 999.90 won and then at 989.00 won. 

 The Bank of Korea backed its action with strong verbal support, discouraging heavy won sales for the time being. 

 A central bank official said the bank would strenuously support the won's "Maginot Line" of 1,000. 

 "We will absolutely defend the 1,000 won level to the dollar," a central bank official said. "To this end, we will implement stronger measures." 

 Singapore dealers said the central bank's efforts had caused won non-deliverable forwards to come off their highs as well. 

 "The reason the forwards are moving to the left is because people are probably saying that the spot Korean won is not going to pass 1,000 anytime soon. They think the central bank is not going to let it," said one dealer. 

 But not everyone was convinced. 

 "Any strengthening in the won would be a correction. I don't foresee any help for the won in the short term," a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore said. 

 Korea's overnight call loan rate shot to a yearly high of 14.50 percent as merchant banks, saddled with bad debts following major bankruptcies, sought hard cash to buy dollars. 

 The government said it would soon announce a financial stabilisation package, including relief for the troubled banks. 

 Elsewhere in north Asia, the Taiwan dollar ended weak but off its lows on the won's recovery and speculation the central bank had intervened to defend the Taiwan dollar at the T$31 level to the U.S. dollar. 

 It ended at T$30.992 against Monday's T$30.985. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar's direction would continue to be driven by the won's moves due to intense competition between the two territories in key export markets. 

 "The only reason for the Taiwan dollar to cross 31.00 is if the won goes past 1,000," a Singapore dealer said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar eased to 7.7315/45 to the U.S. dollar from 7.7295/10 at Monday's close, but dealers said there was little impact on the interbank market from Monday's run on International Bank of Asia. 

 However, some dealers said they expected borrowing costs of smaller banks to rise after the incident. Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said Hong Kong authorities would help International Bank of Asia meet its obligations. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Thai baht slid to 37.90/38.10 to the dollar onshore from 37.10/37.30 late on Monday as initial euphoria over the appointment of new Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai faded. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting details of Chuan's new cabinet and concrete steps to rehabilitate the financial sector. 

 Chuan was quoted in an interview with a Thai newspaper as saying he expected to be able to revitalise confidence in the immediate term to halt capital flight from Thailand and solve liquidity problems. 

 "People are just waiting to see what the new man is going to do and how the government is going to shape up," said one dealer. 

 Dealers said the baht's direction would also hinge on the ability of the government and private sector to persuade foreign creditors to roll over $21-$30 billion of short-term debt due by the end of this year. 

 The offshore baht rate eased to 37.84/94 to the dollar from Monday's 37.20/35 as unwinding of long dollar forward positions abated. 

 But dealers said the baht could head higher as the remainder of the positions, established when the baht came under speculative attack six months ago, matured by the end of the week. 

 The Philippine peso rose to close at 33.82 to the dollar from a previous 34.27, after breaching its first volatility band at 34.74 and hitting a high of 34.48. 

 Manila traders said the peso was boosted by large inflows from overseas contract workers repatriating their wages and talk a Hong Kong firm might have moved some funds to Philippine-based banks to buy shares in a local beer and food conglomerate. 

 After the market close, central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the peso's depreciation had been "over-exaggerated" and it was likely to correct in line with economic fundamentals. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 3,310 and 3,330 to the dollar, trapped between corporate dollar demand and fears of concerted central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the government's pledge on Monday to close 16 unhealthy banks despite potential political fallout had boosted support for the rupiah. 

 Joint interventions by the central banks of Japan, Singapore and Indonesia to buy the rupiah last week had also helped stabilise the currency for the time being. 

 The Malaysian ringgit edged up to 3.2960/60 to the dollar from Monday's 3.3150/250, but activity was confined to a very narrow range, dealers said. 

 A Standard & Poor's report saying it did not see Malaysia facing the same problems as Indonesia and Thailand helped prop up the ringgit, dealers said.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  muted as won enjoys respite.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies tracked familiar ground on Tuesday as traders waited for the shaky Korean won to slide through a key support level. 

 The Bank of Korea's aggressive intervention in opening trade rescued the won from the brink of the 1,000 to the dollar level, but dealers said its reprieve was likely to be short-lived. 

 "The focus is more on the won. There was very aggressive selling (of the dollar) by the Korean central bank and that brought the won back from 999 to 989 but there are still fears about it," the head of Asian currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 The won was at 988.50/9.30 to the dollar at 0450 GMT after firming to 986.0 against an opening at 999.90. 

 The central bank's move to back its action with strong verbal support also kept traders on guard. 

 "We will absolutely defend the 1,000 won level to the dollar," a central bank official said. "To this end, we will implement stronger measures." 

 The won's recovery boosted Seoul stocks as well with the composite index adding 0.53 percent to 528.12 points. 

 In Thailand, the baht slipped to 37.40/60 to the dollar from 37.10/37.30 late on Monday as initial euphoria over the appointment of new Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai faded. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting details of Chuan's new cabinet and concrete steps to rehabilitate the financial sector. 

 Chuan was quoted in an interview with a Thai newspaper as saying he expected to be able to revitalise confidence in the immediate term to halt capital flight from Thailand and solve liquidity problems. 

 "Prime Minister Chuan will have to move fast to capitalise on the positive sentiment the public has for him," a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 Dealers said the baht's direction would also hinge on the ability of the government and private sector to persuade foreign creditors to roll over $21-$30 billion of short-term debt due by the end of this year. 

 The offshore baht rate also eased to 37.30/60 to the dollar from Monday's 37.20/35 as unwinding of long dollar forward positions abated. 

 But dealers said the baht could head higher as the remainder of the positions, established when the baht came under speculative attack six months ago, matured by the end of the week. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 3,310 and 3,330 to the dollar, trapped between corporate dollar demand and fears of concerted central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the government's pledge on Monday to close 16 unhealthy banks despite potential political fallout had boosted support for the rupiah. 

 Joint interventions by the central banks of Japan, Singapore and Indonesia to buy the rupiah last week had also helped stabilise the currency for the time being. 

 "The 3,350 level is very well resisted and also well monitored at the moment," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit edged up to 3.3035/135 to the dollar from Monday's 3.3150/250, but activity was confined to a very narrow range, dealers said. 

 A Standard & Poor's report saying it did not see Malaysia facing the same problems as Indonesia and Thailand helped prop up the ringgit, dealers said. 

 "The S&P report had an impact though not very much. It pushed dollar/ringgit down to 3.30 from around 3.32," another European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Philippine peso firmed to 33.60/99 to the dollar from Monday's 34.27 close on easing corporate dollar demand and expectations of fund inflows from overseas contract workers. 

 Sentiment was also helped by the government's decision to appeal for a reconsideration of last week's Supreme Court decision declaring oil deregulation unconstitutional. 

 In North Asia, the Taiwan dollar continued to mirror the won's moves on expectations it would have to undergo a competitive depreciation if the won fell further. 

 The Taiwan dollar firmed to T$30.957/999 after slipping to T$31.010/030 against Monday's T$30.985 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was steady at 7.7290/00 to the U.S. dollar while interbank rates remained firm.

text:
"With the authorities on top (of the U.S. dollar against

   With the U.S. dollar trading above 3,300 rupiah, traders

title: SE Asia  Currencies  Mixed Early; Mkt Nervous Of  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (DOW JONES)--Southeast Asian currencies are
mixed in early trading Friday, with the Indonesian rupiah
and Singapore dollar both lower against the U.S. dollar,
while the Malaysian ringgit and the Thai baht are up from
levels seen late Thursday.
   Activity in the market is subdued, with traders saying
the only notable order flow consists of sales of U.S.
dollars against the Thai baht, sourced largely from Hong
Kong.
   While the overall sentiment toward regional currencies
is still negative, market participants are hanging back,
nervous of further central bank action following the
concerted interventions of recent days.
   At 0200 GMT (9 p.m. Thursday EST) the U.S. dollar is
quoted at 3,310 rupiah, up from 3,280 rupiah late Thursday,
and "approaching the intervention zone," according to one
trader at a U.S. bank in Singapore.
   Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency is at
S$1.5755, up from S$1.5690 late Wednesday.



   Although the market is looking for the Singapore dollar
to drop further, in line with other regional currencies, in
the short term its fall is due to commercial interest to
sell U.S. dollars, traders say.
   At the same time the U.S. dollar is at 3.3147 ringgit,
down a touch from 3.3150 late the previous day.
   Against the Thai currency the U.S. dollar is trading at
38.95 baht in the offshore market, below 39.3650 baht at the
close of Asian trading Thursday.

title: FOCUS-Asia  currencies  mixed on Thai hopes,won woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mixed on Friday as traders veered between growing optimism of an opposition victory in the fight for Thailand's leadership and fears the South Korean economy was nearing crisis point. 

 Most Southeast Asian currencies were relatively steady, but North Asian markets showed signs of strain due to Seoul's difficulties and signs the Hong Kong dollar might face another speculative assault. 

 In Thailand, the baht bounced to 37.85/38.05 to the dollar at 0510 GMT against 38.90/39.10 late on Thursday as players unwound long dollar positions on expectations the baht would surge if the opposition Democrats succeeded in wooing smaller parties necessary to forming a parliamentary majority. 

 Thai stocks also jumped, with the composite SET index rising 4.64 percent to 500.52 points. 

 The baht was also up offshore at 38.42/52 to the dollar against 39.30/39.60 on Thursday, but Singapore dealers said investment houses were keen to pick up dollars on the way down. 

 "They still haven't decided who will take over. I'd think Chuan (Leekpai) would be good for the country but he's not a friend of Chavalit (Yongchaiyudh), so that could be difficult," a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore said. 

 Democrat party leader Chuan Leekpai and Chatichai Choonhavan, head of the Chart Pattana Party, are in a fierce contest to succeed Chavalit as prime minister. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped to 3,300/10 to the dollar in slow trade as players remained wary of further coordinated central bank intervention. 

 A legal challange by President Suharto's second son Bambang Trihatmodjo, who has filed a law suit following the government's closure of Bank Andromeda, which he part owns, also kept players cautious. 

 "The market is slow as players are staying sidelined, closely watching the government's stance over Bambang's legal challange," another dealer with a European bank said. 

 State Secretary Murdiono, however, said the government stood by the decision to close 16 privately-owned banks and said it was still legally effective. 

 Dealers said sentiment for the rupiah remained weak but fears the central banks of Japan and Singapore might add their weight to any intervention by Bank Indonesia would limit its declines to 3,340 to the dollar. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) confirmed that it had bought rupiah with the Bank of Japan and Bank Indonesia twice this week. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was at 3.2950/50 to the dollar, but talk of dollar offers by local banks around the 3.3300 level would cap its declines, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5710/20 to the U.S. dollar, with dollar offers seen at 1.5770. 

 The Philippine peso traded sluggishly at 34.74/84 to the dollar against Thursday's 34.83 close. Traders said the central bank's dollar offers at 34.95 pesos were shielding the peso. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won came under fire again, falling to new lows despite the central bank's dollar sales at the 975 won and 980 won levels in early trade. 

 Talk that Korea would be forced to turn to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for assistance as it dealt with a string of corporate defaults and shrinking foreign reserves continued to swirl around the market despite government denials. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus backed Seoul's efforts to reassure investors. 

 "South Korea has taken, during recent months, courageous measures to prevent dangers. These measures...have produced the desired effect and in particular have contributed to a significant reduction in external imbalances," Camdessus said. 

 But dealers and analysts remained gloomy about the won. "Everybody is talking about the won reaching 1,000 to the dollar. They're saying the Bank of Korea is almost bankrupt after all these interventions," said one. 

 A senior Bank of Korea official denied newspaper reports that its foreign reserves may already be too depleted for a continued defendce of the won. 

 "The reports were much exaggerated and based on market rumours, some of them ill-intended," the official told Reuters. 

 Official figures put foreign reserves at $30.5 billion at end October, about 2.5 times Korea's monthly imports. 

 The won's woes depressed the Taiwan dollar as players worried that further depreciation in South Korea -- a key industrial rival -- would undermine Taiwan's export competitiveness. 

 The Taiwan dollar was at T$30.888/927 against Thursday's T$30.700 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar edged up to 7.7295/15 to the U.S. dollar from Thursday's 7.7315/25 close. 

 Forwards and interbank rates firmed on fears of a speculative attack even as Camdessus praised Hong Kong's recent defence of its dollar and said the IMF "strongly endorses" the government's commitment to the peg to the U.S. dollar.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  eye Thai politics, weak won.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mixed on Friday as traders veered between growing optimism of an opposition victory in the fight for Thailand's leadership and fears the South Korean economy was nearing crisis point. 

 Most Southeast Asian currencies were relatively steady, but North Asian markets showed signs of strain due to Seoul's difficulties and signs the Hong Kong dollar might face another speculative assault. 

 The Thai baht, on firm ground for much of the day, was buoyed further after opposition Democratic Party leader Chuan Leekpai said he had the support of enough members of parliament to form a new government. 

 The news came as a relief to Thai markets after days of wrangling between the Democrats and the Chart Pattana Party, whose leader Chatichai Choonhavan was also a front runner in the race to replace outgoing Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh. 

 "Before the news, dollar/baht was trading around 39.00. It just dropped 50 pips on the news," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. "But I don't know how long this enthusiasm can last," he added. 

 He said the baht was facing resistance from dollar demand offshore at 38.00 baht and at 37.50 baht onshore. 

 It stood at 37.90/38.10 to the dollar onshore at 0930 GMT against 38.90/39.10 late on Thursday. The offshore rate was at 38.00/50 against 39.30/60 previously. 

 Thai stocks also gained on the news, with the composite SET index up 3.08 percent to 493.04 at 0931 GMT. 

 Chuan, a former prime minister, was expected to be more effective in implementing economic reforms pegged to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) $17.2 billion loan package. 

 "We are aware of the immediate needs of the public, that they want up to help shore up the economy," Chuan said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah traded sluggishly as players kept a wary eye on simmering political tensions from the government's efforts to overhaul the financial sector by closing down 16 unhealthy banks. 

 An outburst by one of President Suharto's sons and court challenges by two banks linked to members of his family raised questions about the government's commitment to pushing through banking reforms. 

 However, State Secretary Murdiono said after meeting Suharto the government stood by its decision to close the privately-owned banks and that it was still legally effective. 

 Dealers said fears of further coordinated central bank intervention also kept the rupiah petrified around the 3,290/00 level to the dollar, little changed from 3,280/90 on Thursday. 

 They said sentiment for the rupiah remained weak but fears the central banks of Japan and Singapore might add their weight to any intervention by Bank Indonesia would limit its declines to 3,340 to the dollar. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore confirmed it had bought rupiah with the Bank of Japan and Bank Indonesia twice this week. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was at 3.2950/50 to the dollar, but talk of dollar offers by local banks around the 3.3300 level would cap its declines, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5665/85 to the U.S. dollar, with dollar offers seen at 1.5770. 

 The Philippine peso ended steady at 34.85 to the dollar after Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the government might seek a reconsideration of a Supreme Court order declaring oil industry deregulation unconstitutional. 

 News of the court order dampened the peso earlier this week. De Ocampo said the government was considering delaying its exit from the IMF programme after the Supreme Court decision. The Philippines is scheduled to exit from 35 years of IMF supervision in December. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won came under fire again, ending at new lows of 979.90 to the dollar despite central bank dollar sales at the 975 won and 980 won levels in early trade. 

 Seoul's composite stock index closed at 515.63 points, down a record 6.9 percent. 

 "It's like a ping-pong game. The won gets hit and foreigners dump shares, and thus the won gets hit further," said SEOULBANK dealer Lee Jong-ho. 

 Dealers said the won was floundering as financial institutions had difficulty borrowing funds overseas after Moody's and Standard and Poor's credit rating agencies downgraded South Korean banks and debt ratings. 

 Fears Seoul would be forced to turn to the IMF for help as it dealt with a string of corporate defaults and shrinking foreign reserves continued to swirl around the market despite government denials. 

 "I think the won will continue to be weak. There are a lot of internal problems in South Korea. Companies are dealing with liquidity problems and the central bank doesn't have enough reserves to defend the currency," a Singapore dealer said. 

 "The pessimism is not necessarily justified but a lot of people are building positions to attack the won. Sentiment is bearish and market is just trying to make up stories," he said. 

 A senior Bank of Korea official denied newspaper reports that its foreign reserves may already be too depleted for a continued defence of the won. 

 Official figures put foreign reserves at $30.5 billion at end October, about 2.5 times Korea's monthly imports. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus backed Seoul's efforts to reassure investors, saying South Korea has taken bold steps to reduce external imbalances in recent months. 

 The won's woes depressed the Taiwan dollar as players worried that further depreciation in South Korea -- a key industrial rival -- would undermine Taiwan's export competitiveness. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at T$30.952 against Thursday's T$30.700 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was little changed at 7.7300/20 to the U.S. dollar from Thursday's 7.7315/25 close. 

 But forwards and interbank rates firmed on fears of a speculative attack even as Camdessus praised Hong Kong's recent defence of its dollar and said the IMF "strongly endorses" the government's commitment to the peg to the U.S. dollar.

title: SE Asian  Currencies  Boosted By Further Rupiah  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The central banks of Indonesia
and Singapore again waded into regional foreign exchange
markets on Thursday to halt the rupiah's slide against the
U.S. dollar.
   The intervention, which took place in thin afternoon
trading, forced the embattled Indonesian currency up by 2.5%
within a matter of minutes. And as with Monday's tripartite
action by Bank Indonesia, the Bank of Japan and the Monetary
Authority of Singapore, other regional currencies rose in
parallel, with the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore
dollar strengthening sharply.
   Traders' estimates of the sums spent in the operation
varied widely. Some said that, given the illiquidity of the
market, no more than $200 million worth of rupiah had been
bought. Others said the central banks spent as much as $1
billion.



   Many market participants suspected that, as on Monday,
the Bank of Japan also took part in the intervention, but
while the Monetary Authority of Singapore confirmed its own
participation, a spokesman for the Japanese central bank
declined to comment on the issue.
   The strategy behind the recent joint interventions, say
many analysts and traders, is not necessarily to punish
speculators and drive them out of the market, but rather to
maintain the rupiah within a stable trading range.

title: FOCUS-Central banks act again to help rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Talk of coordinated central bank intervention to support the Indonesian rupiah helped most Southeast Asian currencies recoup early losses on Thursday. 

 Dealers said regional currencies reversed track after the Indonesian rupiah jumped to around 3,260 to the dollar from its lows of 3,330 in afternoon trade. 

 The move triggered strong speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened to buy rupiah with Bank Indonesia in a move similar to Monday's joint intervention which also included the Bank of Japan (BOJ). 

 The MAS later confirmed it had intervened in concert with Bank Indonesia and the BOJ, but gave no further details. 

 Dealers were unsure of the amount of the interventions, but they said the market remained on edge for further such moves amid vague rumours that Malaysia and Brunei had also been involved in the operation. 

 "It was kind of a sudden move. One minute dollar/rupiah was at 3,340, the next minute it was at 3,260...when the central banks hit the market, the next move was very fast," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst at I.D.E.A. 

 "Normally, Bank Indonesia comes in in excess of $80-$100 million. But the MAS could have intervened in a bigger amount because the Singapore market is large," he said. 

 On Monday, Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu and Japanese Finance Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the day's intervention was aimed at correcting what they called the excessive depreciation of the rupiah and they would act again if needed. 

 Traders estimated the three central banks sold between $300 million and $500 million on Monday. 

 The rupiah was at 3,280/90 to the dollar at 1030 GMT on Tuesday against 3,330/40 six hours earlier. 

 "There are dollar bids coming in around 3,270/80, but it depends on their intentions. If they want to really push the dollar lower, they could come in again," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was also near its day highs at 3.2950/50 to the dollar against 3.3200/300 earlier. 

 Dealers said Bank Negara's agent banks were selling dollars for ringgit, sparking speculation the central bank was taking advantage of the dollar's downturn against regional currencies to shore up the Malaysian currency. 

 The ringgit had weakened earlier on news Kuala Lumpur had approved a start next year to work on a 10 billion ringgit landbridge with Thailand, raising questions about Malaysia's commitment to cutting its current account deficit. 

 The Singapore dollar popped above 1.5700 to the U.S. dollar on rumours oil-rich Brunei was selling U.S. dollars above that level. But it slid back to 1.5720/40 by 1030 GMT, little changed from its midday levels. 

 Even the Thai baht firmed to 38.70/39.00 per dollar onshore but remained weak offshore at 39.30/60 as players awaited the outcome of talks between political parties to choose a successor to outgoing Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh. 

 Former prime ministers Chuan Leekpai and Chatichai Choonhavan were touted as front-runners for the post, but conflicting Thai media reports left the market reluctant to act. 

 "At the moment, nobody even knows who the actual prime minister is," the head of regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 Bangkok dealers said the baht was receiving some support from exporters on a belief that it would strengthen if Chuan, leader of the Democrat Party, became prime minister. 

 Dealers said the health of 69-year-old King Bhumibol Adulyadej also remained a source of concern. 

 "If something happens to the King, that will undermine investor confidence again. He's the only one who can have some impact on the political scene," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The Philippine peso ended weak at 34.830 to the dollar against Wednesday's 34.74 close as sentiment soured after the Supreme Court declared oil deregulation unconstitutional. 

 The Korean won ended weak at 975.00 to the dollar against Wednesday's 969.7, despite repeated dollar sales by the central bank and reassurances by officials. 

 The central bank's failure to defend the 970.00 won level, previously a trigger-point for intervention, earlier sparked rumours overseas of an impending devaluation, causing the won to weaken in the non-deliverable forwards market. 

 But an official at the Bank of Korea strongly denied the rumours, saying the central bank's "will to stabilise the foreign exchange market is as firm as ever". 

 A senior Finance Ministry official also denied talk that South Korea would seek emergency loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 "Our financial markets are not in serious danger. We have no plan to request emergency loans from the IMF," said Choi Joong-kyong, director-general of the ministry's financial cooperation division. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was steady at 7.7315/25 per U.S. dollar, paring its early gains, but dealers said fears of another speculative attack on the currency were mounting as forwards firmed, pushing interest rates up. 

 Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said he expected interest rates to fall once the government succeeded in defending the local dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 He said the government's policy of defending the peg "will never change". 

 The Taiwan dollar ended lower at T$30.700 from Wednesday's T$30.451 close, under pressure from the U.S. dollar's overnight surge to six-month highs against the yen. 

 The Australian dollar lost more than half a cent after the Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane highlighted the dangers financial strife in Asia held for exports. It was at $0.6991/96 from an early $0.7035/40.

title: Indonesia rupiah stronger on joint  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 6 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah strengthened against the dollar in late trading on Thursday following concerted intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia, dealers said. 

 The rupiah rose to a high of 3,250 in Singapore and 3,270 in Jakarta from 3,340 before settling at 3,280/3,300 at 0930 GMT, compared with an opening of 3,320/40 on Thursday. 

 The MAS said it had intervened in foreign exchange markets on Thursday to buy the rupiah in concert with Bank Indonesia and the Bank of Japan (BOJ). 

 "We confirm that we have," as MAS spokesman told Reuters.

title: Singapore MAS confirms buying rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Thursday it had intervened in foreign exchange markets to buy the Indonesian rupiah. 

 "We confirm that we have," as MAS spokesman told Reuters. 

 He declined to specify the amount of the intervention or provide any further details. 

 The rupiah jumped to highs of around 3,260 to the dollar from lows of 3,330/40 on talk the MAS and Bank Indonesia had intervened in foreign exchange markets in the afternoon. 

 Dealers said the Indonesian central bank had intervened in Jakarta markets while MAS bought rupiah in Singapore. 

 "It was kind of a sudden move...I suppose the liquidity was thin and when the central banks hit the market, the next move was very fast," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst at I.D.E.A. 

 "They entered at a key technical resistance (for the dollar)," he said. 

 Dealers were unsure of the amount of the intervention. 

 "Normally Bank Indonesia comes in in excess of $80-$100 million. But the MAS could have intervened in a bigger amount because the Singapore market is large," Ishak said. 

 On Monday, the MAS and the Bank of Japan intervened to buy the rupiah in Singapore foreign exchange markets in concert with Bank Indonesia. 

 Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu and Japanese Finance Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in separate statements the intervention was aimed at correcting what they called the excessive depreciation of the rupiah. 

 They said both central banks would be ready to act in the market when necessary in the future. 

 Traders estimated the three central banks sold between $300 million and $500 million on Monday.

title: FOCUS - Korean won woes weigh on Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Worries about a possible devaluation of the Korean won, Thailand's political troubles and the illness of its king and Indonesia's long road to economic recovery depressed Asian currency markets on Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise to six-month highs against the yen worsened the plight of regional currencies, but dealers said there was no sign of panic selling and many institutions were winding down for the year-end. 

 The South Korean won fell through the 970 level to the dollar, previously a trigger-point for central bank support, sparking rumours overseas of an impending devaluation. 

 But a Bank of Korea official said the central bank had no plans to devalue the won or widen its 2.25 percent trading band. "Our will to stabilise the foreign exchange market is as firm as ever," the official said. 

 The central bank intervened to sell dollars at 975 won, cushioning further declines in the won for the time being. 

 "The dollar will trade mostly under 975 won level, but if the central bank doesn't intervene, the dollar could rise to 980 won," a dealer in Seoul said. The won was at 975.30/5.30 at 0445 GMT against Wednesday's close at 969.70. 

 The central bank official said the bank did not concentrate exclusively on maintaining one level for its interventions. "Watching the dollar/yen movement and adjusting our markets accordingly is important for stability as well." 

 Korea's dwindling foreign reserves and stricken financial sector have triggered growing speculation it might need to seek help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 In Thailand, the baht lost its footing as the market awaited the outcome of talks between political parties to choose a successor to outgoing Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh. 

 Former prime ministers Chuan Leekpai and Chatichai Choonhavan are touted as front-runners for the post, but conflicting Thai media reports left the market reluctant to act. 

 "At the moment, nobody even knows who the actual prime minister is," the head of regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 Bangkok dealers said the baht was receiving some support from exporters on a belief that it would strengthen if Chuan, leader of the Democrat Party, became prime minister. 

 The baht was at 39.10/20 to the dollar onshore against 38.90/39.20 late on Wednesday. Offshore baht was at 39.20/40 against 39.00/25. 

 Dealers said the health of 69-year-old King Bhumibol Adulyadej also remained a source of concern. 

 "If something happens to the King, that will undermine investor confidence again. He's the only one who can have some impact on the political scene," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped to 3,330/40 to the dollar from 3,300/10 late on Wednesday, but dealers said activity was confined to a narrow range between dollar demand and fears of aggressive central bank intervention. 

 "The market seems stuck with short-covering at the 3,330 level from Singapore and selling interest from Jakarta at the 3,340 level," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 Singapore dealers said players were having trouble pushing the dollar above the 3,400 rupiah level due to fears of a repeat of Monday's coordinated intervention in forex markets by Japan, Singapore and Indonesia. 

 The IMF's approval of a $10 billion loan package as part of a massive international bailout for Indonesia had no impact. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus praised Jakarta's efforts to reform the economy, but said slower growth and higher inflation would be unavoidable over the next two years. 

 The Malaysian ringgit weakened to 3.3200/300 to the dollar from 3.2750/850 late Wednesday on news Kuala Lumpur had approved a start next year to work on a 10 billion ringgit landbridge with Thailand. 

 "The market is asking how serious is Malaysia in trying to cap its current account deficit. This kind of news certainly doesn't help," a dealer with a European bank in Singapore said. 

 The government recently announced a delay in several large infrastructure and construction projects in a move to slow down the economy and cut the current account deficit. 

 The Singapore dollar looked soft but was off its lows of 1.5795 to the U.S. dollar on a flight-to-quality from Thailand. 

 But dealers said it was likely to weaken again alongside its neighbours, with forwards seen moving to the right. 

 The Philippine peso recovered a bit after falling through the 35 to the dollar level in early trade, but dealers said sentiment remained poor after the Supreme Court's decision to declare oil deregulation unconstitutional. 

 The Hong Kong dollar firmed to 7.7300/20 from 7.7325/35 on Wednesday as the wide interest rate spread with the U.S. dollar attracted players seeking a higher yield. 

 Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said he expected interest rates to fall once the government succeeded in defending the local dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 He said the government's policy of defending the peg "will never change". 

 Hong Kong interest rates have risen in recent months as investors positioned for a possible attack on the peg and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority moved to discourage speculation. 

 The Taiwan dollar eased to T$30.640/710 from Wednesday's T$30.451 close, under pressure from the U.S. dollar's overnight surge against the yen.

title: Singapore Aid Policy -2: Singapore Dlr Affected
text:
Since the Thai baht was floated in July, the Singapore dollar has fallen 8.5%. 

 'No matter how good Singapore's policy making is, it will still be held hostage to the policy mistakes of neighboring countries,' said Malik. 'The currency crisis shows that Singapore is guilty by association'. 

 Singapore's Foreign Ministry didn't immediately respond to questions on the switch of policy on foreign aid. 

 But Singapore's politicians have admitted that, despite the country's huge foreign exchange reserves and healthy economy, that the city state hasn't been untouched by the regional crisis. 'Growth will be slightly slower, but nothing to be alarmed about,' Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was quoted as saying last week. 

 Manmindar Singh, economist at Nomura Singapore, said financial aid from Singapore could help restore confidence to the southeast Asian region as a whole. 

 Indeed on Monday, the rupiah rallied strongly on news of details of the IMF package for Indonesia and after the Monetary Authority of Singapore joined the central banks of Japan and Indonesia in intervening to support the rupiah. 

 That boosted the Singapore dollar and the Singapore stock market as well. 

 This higher profile in the Southeast Asian rescue packages has been accompanied by a higher profile for Singapore internationally. Singapore agreed earlier this year to contribute about US$470 million to a new emergency IMF funding mechanism known as the 'New Arrangements To Borrow,' which is expected to total US$50 billion. 

 Impetus for the NAB came after the 1995 bailout for Mexico, which sparked concerns that the IMF might need to raise extra funding quickly, particularly in situations where the U.S. was less motivated to act separately. 

 The NAB will replace an old IMF emergency program that included contributions only from the Group of 10 (G-10) leading industrialized nations. 

 Singapore has also expressed interest in Japan's controversial idea of creating an 'Asia Fund,' though officials have stressed that the facility should be made subordinate to the IMF. 

 Singapore's Goh has also stressed bilateral aid for Indonesia will be contingent on the reform measures agreed with the IMF.

title: INTERVIEW- Nicholas-Applegate sees more Asia pain.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Shaky Southeast Asian financial markets are likely to face more pain in the months ahead as their economies get on the road to difficult but much-needed reform, a fund manager said on Tuesday. 

 Kim Teo, managing director of Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management Asia, said currency and stock markets were enjoying a technical recovery, but the worst was not over. 

 "We think the reaction we are seeing in the markets is more a technical bounce from an oversold position," Teo told Reuters. 

 Japan and Singapore's coordinated intervention in foreign exchange markets on Monday to support the Indonesian rupiah with Bank Indonesia helped to calm nerves. 

 But Teo said there were more rocky times ahead as Indonesia and Thailand moved to restructure their economies to meet the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) conditions for assistance. 

 "The medicine has been paid for but it has to be taken, which means there will be further pain ahead," Teo said. 

 The IMF arranged a US$17.2 billion international loan package for Thailand in August and announced a US$23 billion multilateral aid package for Indonesia last week. 

 Teo said the Indonesian economy was unlikely to achieve the government's target of five to six percent economic growth this year. 

 "The restructuring itself would cause economic contraction to some extent...Perhaps we're looking at zero to two percent instead of five percent," he said. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's announcement on Monday that he would resign had been well received by currency markets, but it remained to be seen how his successor would cope with unpopular economic decisions, Teo said. 

 Singapore, which has been relatively cushioned from its neighbours' troubles, would see some impact on company earnings in the first quarter of next year, he said. 

 "Although Singapore is very well placed, there will still be a slowdown because of the hinterland that it services and the investments into the surrounding region which Singapore companies have been doing," Teo said. 

 He said the benchmark Straits Times Industrials stock index was unlikely to rally beyond the 1,800 points level. The index stood at 1,706.36 at 0821 GMT, up 0.14 percent. 

 Teo said Nicholas-Applegate was more bullish on North Asia, with the exception of South Korea. 

 He said the recent depreciation of the Taiwan dollar had been very helpful for the island's export industry. 

 The Taiwan dollar has slithered to 10-year lows of around T$31 to the U.S. dollar after the central bank abandoned a watertight defence of the T$28.50 level on October 17. 

 "We're still optimistic on China and Hong Kong. We think the (Hong Kong dollar) peg will remain where it is," Teo said. 

 He said Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng Index was likely to head back for the 13,000 level after tumbling below 9,000 last week. 

 "(Asian) currencies will remain weakish but certainly not at the near panic collapses we've seen. I think it will be a lot more orderly in the next one to three months."

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  gain as baht cheers up.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The Thai baht greeted Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's promise to resign with gusto on Tuesday, bringing cheer to most Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The baht made a strong start after Chavalit's surprise announcement late on Monday, sparking predictions that the rally was overdone and would soon fizzle out. 

 But official assurances that political changes would not hurt implementation of IMF-backed economic reforms and news of government spending cuts kept the baht well bid through the day. It ended at its day high of 38.60/80 to the dollar onshore, more than five percent above late Monday levels of 40.90/41.00. The offshore rate was at 38.40/50 at 1040 GMT against 39.85/40.35 previously. 

 "It seems the market is quite receptive to Chavalit's resignation," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said spirits were further lifted by announcements that the government would lop another 18 billion baht from 1997/98 spending, on top of a previous 100 billion baht cut. 

 Thai stocks also rallied with the composite SET index adding 6.9 percent to end at 478.33. But currency traders remained conservative about the baht's potential for more gains. 

 "I just can't see dollar/baht continuing to come off. I can't see the baht strengthening much further than 37.50/38.00," one said. 

 And while Chavalit's decision to resign removed some of the market's immediate gloom, Thailand still faced a long, arduous road in rehabilitating its economy, analysts said. 

 "A change of leadership obviously means something has to be done and decisions which have to be taken are not going to be popular," said Kim Teo, managing director of Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management Asia. 

 Teo said Southeast Asian markets were in for more pain in the next six to 12 months as Thailand and Indonesia moved to restructure their economies in line with IMF requirements. 

 "The reaction we are seeing in the markets is more a technical bounce from an oversold position," he said. "Currencies will remain weakish but certainly not at the near panic collapses we've seen," he added. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah continued to rise on appreciation of the government's efforts to reform the economy in response to a massive IMF-led international aid package. 

 Dealers said the scramble caused by tighter liquidity after three central banks intervened on Monday to buy the rupiah lifted forward rates in early trade. 

 The value of concerted dollar sales for rupiah in Singapore on Monday by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia was estimated at $300 to $500 million, senior Japanese traders said. 

Singapore dealers said Bank Indonesia had intervened again on Tuesday to sell dollars. 

 "They sold quite a few times even around the low of 3,210. I don't think it was really big amounts but they tried to cap (the dollar) above 3,270," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The rupiah was at 3,260/70 to the dollar against its New York close at 3,205, sharply up from its Monday Asian close at 3,300/10. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5555/75 to the U.S. dollar, off its highs of 1.5450 after active U.S. dollar buying by local banks below the 1.5500 level. 

 Dealers said there were rumours the dollar purchases were on behalf of the MAS, which was believed to be buying back dollars after Monday's intervention to support the rupiah. 

 Malaysia's ringgit was at 3.2675/775 to the dollar against 3.2600/700 late on Monday. 

 Dealers said selling was expected after the ringgit's recent bounce, but they saw a further test of the 3.20 per dollar resistance. 

 The Philippine peso ended higher at 34.84 to the dollar from a previous 35.14 close. The central bank offered dollars at 34.85/90 pesos but found no takers. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the policy-making Monetary Board would discuss by how much to lower the overnight lending rate at a regular meeting on Wednesday. The rate is at 16.125 percent. 

 Even the Taiwan dollar and South Korean won perked up on Tuesday. The Taiwan dollar ended sharply up at T$30.730 against Monday's 10-year low of T$31.245. 

 Dealers said investors took profit on U.S. dollar gains after the central bank said on Monday the Taiwan dollar had lost too much value. 

 On Tuesday, the central bank said the Taiwan dollar's recent depreciation made Taiwan remained "extremely competitive" against South Korea and Singapore in global export markets. 

 The South Korean won ended at 961.00 against Monday's 969.90 close after the central bank poured an estimated $300 million into the market to support it. 

 Only the Hong Kong dollar slipped as traders unwound long positions on a belief that the premium of Hong Kong dollar interest rates over U.S. rates would wane. 

 Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said last week that domestic interest rates were likely to ease in the short term.

title: FOCUS-SE Asian  currencies  upbeat as baht revives.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - An impressive early rally by the Thai baht after Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said he would resign boosted Southeast Asian currencies on Tuesday. 

 The markets reacted positively to the news, although early buying of the beleaguered baht cooled somewhat on uncertainties surrounding efforts to reform the economy, dealers said. 

 "A lot of U.S. investment funds tried to push dollar/baht higher, but it seems there were very good offers around the 39.50 level," a dealer with a local bank said. 

 The baht was quoted at 39.20/30 per dollar in the onshore market against 40.90/41.00 late on Monday. Earlier, dollar/baht fell to 38.90 in a knee jerk reaction to Chavalit's resignation promise. 

 Dealers said, however, concerns on the political situation would cap gains in the short term. "The market is still not too confident that Thailand will have a quick recovery, like Indonesia," said one. 

 Indonesia's efforts to reform its economy in response to a massive IMF-led aid package continued to lift the rupiah. 

 Dealers said the scramble caused by tighter liquidity after three central banks intervened on Monday to buy the rupiah lifted offshore and forward rates against the U.S dollar. 

 The value of concerted dollar sales for rupiah in Singapore on Monday by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia was estimated at $300 to $500 million, senior Japanese traders said. 

 The rupiah traded in a narrow range between 3,205 and 3,265 against the U.S. dollar with an upward bias firmly in place. At 0445 GMT, dollar/rupiah was at 3,215/00 against its New York close at 3,205. 

 Malaysia's ringgit came off its highs on profit taking after recent sharp rises with dollar/ringgit slipping to 3.2730 per U.S. dollar against 3.2600/700 earlier. 

 Dealers said selling was expected after the ringgit's recent bounce but that they saw a further test of the 3.20 per dollar resistance. 

 The Singapore dollar drifted lower to 1.5588/90 with one dealer citing rumours of central bank buying of dollars against the Sing below the 1.55 level. 

 Others said they had expected the Singapore dollar to rise after Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitzuzuka said that Monday's joint intervention would bring currency stability to Southeast Asia. 

 They felt Singapore's currency, already in a more positive posture than other regionals, would make further gains. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was slightly weaker at 7.7360/70 against the U.S. dollar, but forwards firmed in line with regional forwards like the rupiah. 

 The interbank rate was slightly higher at Tuesday's fixing, while overnight rates also climbed, dealers said. 

 The Philippine peso rose to 34.70 against the U.S. dollar compared with 35.10/20 on Monday. Rates hit a high of 34.55 and a low of 34.95, with the central bank pegging its selling price at 34.85/90. 

 The Taiwan dollar climbed on profit taking on the  U.S. dollar. Comments from the central bank that Taiwan's dollar had already lost too much value also helped its recovery to T$30.737 against Monday's T$31.245. 

 The South Korean won traded at 958.00/000, underpinned by the central bank's determination to curb rises in the dollar. 

 The Bank of Korea poured about $300 million into the market to support the local unit, dealers said. The bank sold dollars at 970 won in spot trading early.

title: Asian  Currencies  -3: Won Hits 5.5-Mo High; NT$ Higher
text:
Elsewhere the South Korean won (KRW) leapt to its highest level since early January after local wire services reported remarks by Finance Minister Kang Bong-kyun that "the government doesn't favor direct intervention in the currency market." 

 After two months of consistent dollar buying by state-run banks and, more recently, the Bank of Korea, traders in Seoul interpreted the remarks as implying that the government was backing away from its policy of suppressing the won to safeguard export competitiveness. 

 In response Korean exporters holding U.S. dollar revenues rushed to convert them into the local currency, pushing the dollar to an intraday low of KRW1,156.50, the lowest it has been offered since January 8. 

 By the end of local trading, the U.S. dollar had recovered slightly, closing at KRW1,159.40, down from KRW1,165.50 at Monday's close. 

 The new Taiwan dollar continued to grind higher in the face of dollar purchases by the local central bank, setting a fresh four-month high in intraday trading. 

 At the close the U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$32.32.348, down fractionally from NT$32.349 the day before. 

 Had it not been for the intervention of the central bank, the U.S. currency could easily have fallen below NT$32.000, said dealers. 

 In Southeast Asia, fear of central bank action helped support the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar and the Thai baht (THB). 

 Toward the end of Asian dealing, the U.S. currency was quoted against the Singapore dollar at S$1.7065, down a touch from S$1.7090 late Monday but still above the level of S$1.7000 at which the market fears intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 Against the baht the U.S. dollar held firm through Asian trading, only to drop sharply in European hours, falling below the THB36.6000 level at which some dealers had expected the Bank of Thailand to enter the market. 

 Around 0930 GMT the U.S. currency was quoted at THB36.5850, down from THB36.8900 late in Asian trading Monday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the U.S. dollar ended trading against the Philippine peso at PHP37.855, down from PHP37.910 at the previous close.

title: Singapore Dollar Stronger Late; Following Bullish Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar has climbed against the U.S. dollar in late Asian trading Tuesday, riding on the coattails of the bullish Indonesian rupiah, dealers said. 

 At 0940 GMT (5:40 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7090, weaker than S$1.7117 late Monday in Asia. 

 The Indonesian rupiah rose to its highest level since October, as foreign investors return to the country, encouraged by falling inflation and a peaceful campaign ahead of last week's parliamentary election. 

 "There's a total reassessment of the whole regional risk," a dealer at a European bank said, noting that Indonesia was now benefiting from the resurgence of investor inflows that its neighbors have seen in recent months. 

 Because of it's greater liquidity, the Singapore dollar often acts as a proxy for the rupiah. 

 Dealers also said the absence of intervention by the Bank of Japan in the currency market Tuesday had also supported the Singapore dollar. 

 The BOJ's Monday intervention, its third in as many days, was aimed at capping the yen's rise against the U.S. dollar in order to maintain Japan's export competitiveness. 

 The dealer at the European brokerage said the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de-facto central bank, would closely watch the rupiah's advance in order to determine an appropriate level for the Singapore dollar. 

 In recent months, the MAS has been following a policy of gradual depreciation for the Singapore dollar, but restored confidence in the rupiah could lead the MAS to yield on its stance, the dealer said. 

 He said he expected the U.S. dollar to weaken below the key support level of S$1.7000 later this week if the rupiah continued its rally. 

 On the local money market, the interbank overnight rate was offered at 0.875%, up from 0.125% late Monday in Asia, while the three-month rate was offered at 1.625%, unchanged from late Monday.

title: Asian  Currencies  -2: Correlation With Yen Breaks Down
text:
Toward the end of local hours the U.S. dollar was quoted against the Singapore dollar at S$1.7251, down from S$1.7317 the previous day. 

 Against the Thai baht (THB), the U.S. dollar was at THB37.0650, down from THB37.1100 late in Asia on Thursday. 

 The recent breakdown of the long-standing correlation between regional currencies and the yen has left traders with little idea which direction markets are likely to take over the coming week. 

 "You can't take the yen as a guideline any more," complained one dealer, adding that market players would be closely watching local central banks for their trading cues. 

 "The important thing for the authorities around the region is to stabilize their currencies," he said. While central bankers may be prepared to tolerate moves of a couple of percentage points either side of current exchange rates, he argued that they would intervene to check any extreme fluctuations. 

 Other dealers agreed, saying that they would be wary of indirect intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore should the U.S. dollar fall to levels approaching S$1.7150. Equally, the authority would be likely to check any rapid appreciation toward S$1.7350, they added. 

 The baht is thought likely to be similarly range-bound in coming sessions, with the U.S. dollar continuing to trade in a THB37.05 to THB37.15 band.

title: Asian  Currencies  -3:  Intervention  Rumors Rife In Mkts
text:
Against the Singapore currency, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6998, up from S$1.6984 in late Asian trading Tuesday. 

 While regional currencies have seen marked appreciation, the Singapore dollar has seen less upward pressure because it is being used to fund regional carry trades. 

 "The interest rates are so low in Singapore that people are going short Singapore dollars to fund purchases in baht, rupiah or (Philippine) peso - currencies with higher yields," a trader at a Japanese bank in Singapore said. "Without this element, the Singapore dollar would be much stronger." 

 Traders also said rumors abound that the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been actively intervening in the market through local banks, in an effort to keep the U.S. dollar at or near S$1.70. 

 The U.S. dollar was also trading at 36.7350 Thai baht, unchanged from late Asian trading Tuesday. Despite the inactivity in the market, traders said central bank intervention - as in Singapore and South Korea - has become a fact of life in Thailand. 

 "Governments are concerned that their currencies don't strengthen too quickly, especially as funds pour into their domestic stock markets," said a currency strategist at a U.S. investment house. 

 The Bank of Thailand is thought to be using a number of foreign banks in Singapore as a quiet avenue for buying U.S. dollars. "It's a lucrative business for the foreign banks. They keep their mouths shut and get to keep tabs on what one of the largest players in the market is doing," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "Big advantage." 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the U.S. dollar was trading at 37.585 pesos, down from PHP37.610 late Tuesday. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was at NT$32.732, down from NT$32.735 Tuesday.

title: Singapore  Dollar Higher Early; No Sign Of MAS  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is drifting higher against the U.S. dollar in thin trading early Tuesday, traders said. 

 They said the Monetary Authority of Singapore and local banks are, for the moment, taking a laissez-faire approach to the Singapore dollar's strength, letting the market determine the direction of the U.S. dollar. 

 "There are no signs of intervention at the moment," a trader at a U.K. bank in Singapore said. 

 At 0145 GMT (9:45 p.m. Monday EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.6984, down from S$1.6999 in late trading Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar has been falling gradually against the Singapore dollar during the past three or four sessions, traders said. 

 "The bulk of U.S. dollar selling appears to be done, and we should see some consolidation within a range today," said a trader at a U.S. investment house in Singapore. 

 He expects the U.S. dollar to move between S$1.6950 and S$1.7035 during the session. "The MAS looks comfortable with the strength of the Singapore dollar, given that the region looks stable at the moment. It appears that the central bank will let the (currency) drift higher as long as the pace isn't too quick." 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to continue sliding this week unless regional news stirs up the markets, traders said. 

 "We should see S$1.6850 by the end of the week," a trader at a Japanese bank in Singapore said. 

 In the local-currency money market, the overnight offered rate on the Singapore dollar was 0.875%, up a touch from 0.75% Monday. The three-month rate was 1.50%, slightly up from 1.4375% late Monday.

title: SE Asian  Currencies  -3: S$ Stronger; US$ Support At S$1.70
text:
The Singapore dollar edged slightly higher Wednesday, although the U.S. dollar remained above the S$1.7000 support level below which many traders believe the Monetary Authority of Singapore would intervene to support the U.S. currency. 

 At the local close, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7005, down from S$1.7058 late Tuesday in Asia.

title: FX  Asia: Regional  Currencies  Seen Nearing Top Of Bull Run
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian regional currencies are unlikely to keep pace with an extended run-up in the yen, as market players fret that local central banks will step in to brake, or block entirely, any further appreciation. 

 A sell-off in the U.S. dollar against the yen overnight Tuesday and early Wednesday in Asia drove a sharp rally in the regional currencies. The Singapore dollar, for example, gained 1.5% against the U.S. currency as offshore players were forced out of their long U.S. dollar positions by the yen-induced rise of the local currency. 

 But although dealers in Asia expect renewed selling to drag the U.S. dollar as low as Y118 when European markets open later in the day, market participants believe that the U.S. currency is close to finding a bottom against its Asian regional counterparts. 

 "Regional central banks have made it clear that they don't want their currencies to strengthen, so you can expect intervention to stand in the way," warns Ron Leven, Asian markets strategist at J.P. Morgan in Singapore. 

 As investor funds pouring into Asia in recent weeks have boosted local currencies, regional markets have seen a barrage of dollar-supportive verbal intervention from monetary authority and finance ministry officials from around the region. In Taiwan and South Korea, the authorities have actually entered the local markets, buying U.S. dollars in an attempt to forestall the rise of the New Taiwan dollar and the won. 

 "Asian governments don't want their currencies to strengthen dramatically. Given that the recovery in regional economies is uncertain and by no means entrenched, they still want to have competitive currencies," explains Thio Chin Loo, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 Technical Analysts See Dollar Nearing Bottom 

 While fear of intervention is a major factor, it is not the only reason traders and analysts believe the Asian currencies are approaching the top of their run. 

 The U.S. dollar is fast approaching key technical support levels against the regional currencies, which dealers think are extremely unlikely to be breached. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, many dealers are eying the U.S. currency's 200-day moving average at S$1.6925, a level they say should provide solid support for the U.S. dollar. And even if that is breached, they believe the market will certainly balk at pushing the U.S. dollar below its long term upward trend line at S$1.6870, given the slow pace of economic recovery the island is thought likely to see. 

 The U.S. currency's floor against the Thai baht (THB) is more difficult to call, especially in the short term. With Thai markets closed for much of this week, trading in the baht is likely to be thin and whippy, warn dealers. 

 Nevertheless, Wednesday morning saw the U.S. dollar bottom out at THB37.5100, as traders shied away from pushing the U.S. currency down through the THB37.5000 level at which the Bank of Thailand intervened to support the dollar in March. 

 If the central bank declines to defend that level, however, traders and analysts agree that the authorities would have little hesitation in entering the market to buy U.S. dollars if the U.S. currency threatened to drop below the THB37.00 mark. 

 Similarly, market participants believe the U.S. dollar's potential losses against the Philippine peso are limited, after the U.S. currency dropped to a low of PHP38.060 on Wednesday morning from PHP38.295 at the close of trading the previous day. 

 "The Philippine government has clearly indicated that it is not comfortable with the peso stronger than PHP38.00" to the U.S. dollar, says Cliff Tan, foreign exchange and interest rate strategist at Warburg Dillon Read in Singapore. "The authorities don't want the external sector, which has been the economy's only piston of growth, to fall into recession." 

 North Asian currencies also have little scope to strengthen further from current levels over the short term, according to analysts and traders. 

 Although the South Korean won rose more than 0.5% Wednesday morning, with the U.S. dollar hitting a low of KRW1,215.00, dealers say the U.S. currency is likely to encounter solid support at levels between KRW1,200 to KRW1,210. 

 Government-directed buying of U.S. dollars by the state-run Export-Import Bank, coupled with forthcoming repayments of foreign currency debt obligations, will draw a line under the U.S. currency's decline at KRW1,200, agree analysts and traders. 

 In Taiwan, market participants believe the central bank is likely to support the U.S. dollar at NT$37.75, and subsequently at NT$37.50, should fund inflows force a retreat from the first level. Beyond that, however, the central bank would be "very unhappy indeed" according to one trader. 

 Few analysts are attempting to pick levels for the dollar against the Indonesian rupiah (IDR), however. With the dollar barely straying beyond an IDR8,000 to IDR9,000 band this year, and little capital flowing either in or out of the country, there are no trends to whet the market's appetite. Although some market observers predict the rupiah may fall in advance of Indonesia's June 7 parliamentary elections, others argue that the central bank's reserves are more than sufficient to offset any likely outflows.

title: FX  Asia: Fall In Singapore Reserves May Have Been Euro Bet
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--A US$1.76 billion drop in Singapore's foreign reserves has some people wondering whether the authorities have discretely intervened to support the local currency. But others speculate that the drop could suggest that the Monetary Authority has lost heavily by banking on a strong euro. 

 Falling reserves, some analysts argue, are clear evidence that the MAS, an organization famed as much for its opacity as its plentifully stuffed coffers, has quietly sold U.S. dollars over the past month to help the Singapore dollar. 

 If that's true, they contend, then the market consensus that the U.S. currency is set to retest its 1998 high of S$1.80 is far wide of the mark. 

 But intervention is not the only possible explanation for the dip in Singapore's foreign reserves. If market whispers are correct, toward the end of last year the MAS bought heavily into the strong euro story then being touted by so many single-currency bulls, and converted a healthy portion of its reserves into shiny new euros. 

 Since then of course, the European single currency has lost some of its luster, dropping 7.7% against the U.S. dollar from its launch. That, along with February's the slide in the yen, is more likely to account for the missing US$1.76 billion, say skeptics. 

 Singapore's foreign exchange reserves fell 2.4% to US$72.38 billion at the end of February, from US$74.14 at the end of January, according to figures released last Thursday. 

 "This shows that the MAS is determinedly selling foreign currency. It is as clear a signal as it is possible to get that the MAS is aggressively defending current levels," says Prasenjit Basu, a regional economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Singapore. 

 Over the same period the Singapore dollar slipped by 2% against the U.S. currency, with the U.S. dollar rising to end February at S$1.7250 compared S$1.6900 at the end of January. 

 Even though the Singapore dollar still fell, Basu believes intervention was necessary to ensure a controlled, gradual depreciation of the local currency. 

 With Singapore dollar short term interest rates consistently below 2% over the last two months, the Singapore dollar has become the funding currency of choice in Asia's foreign exchange market. Those who are able have sold the Singapore dollar short to fund long positions in currencies including the Thai baht and the Philippine peso, as well as in the U.S. dollar. 

 To offset the demand to sell the local currency, says Basu, the MAS has been forced to sell U.S. dollars in the foreign exchange market. 

 And this willingness of the MAS to part with some of reserves indicates that market players have been overly pessimistic in their forecasts for the Singapore dollar's exchange rate, he argues. 

 "I disagree with the consensus year-end forecast of S$1.85. The Singapore dollar won't go much further than S$1.76," to the U.S. dollar, Basu says. The U.S. currency hovered around the S$1.72 level Tuesday, down from S$1.7260 late in Asia Monday. 

 Valuation Effects Thought Most Likely To Explain Fall 

 Other analysts, however, question whether Monetary Authorityintervention could have caused the hole in Singapore's foreign reserves. 

 "I don't think the exchange rate moves in February warranted a US$1.7 billion intervention," says one. "Valuation effects are a more convincing argument." 

 With a current account surplus running at around $15 billion and with its enviable status as a net creditor nation, Singapore's trade and investment flows are not feasible explanations for the drop in foreign exchange reserves. But valuation effects, the drop in the U.S. dollar value of the reserves caused by the depreciation of other reserve currencies, are a possible cause. 

 But valuation effects could only be the explanation if the Monetary Authority was holding a relatively large proportion of its reserves in the euro and the yen, which depreciated by 3.2% and 3.3% respectively against the U.S. dollar during February. 

 Assuming that the reserves are split solely between U.S. dollar, euro and yen, that would mean over two thirds of Singapore's foreign reserves would have to have been held in euro and yen-denominated instruments to account for their 2.4% decline in U.S. dollar terms. 

 Few observers believe the MAS would hold anything like that proportion of its reserves in currencies other than the U.S. dollar. Nevertheless, sources familiar with the workings of the authority say that dollar, euro and yen are not held in the roughly 45%-40%-15% split current trade relationships would imply. 

 "The composition of the reserves is not cast in stone," says one knowledgeable source. "The MAS is just like any other fund manager. It forecasts rates of return and makes its allocations accordingly." 

 If the Monetary Authority called this year's foreign exchange market wrongly, it would hardly be the only one. Nevertheless requests for official comment elicited no response on Tuesday morning. 

 The MAS, an organization whose press officers have been known to respond to media enquiries with a terse "No comment, and that's off the record," was remaining characteristically tight-lipped.

title: SE Asian  Currencies  Stronger Late Vs Dlr As Yen Moves Higher
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)-- Southeast Asian currencies were generally stronger against the U.S. dollar in late, choppy trading Thursday, as the yen found new footing against the U.S. currency and the specter of central bank intervention weighed heavily on regional markets. 

 Traders in the Singapore dollar, Thai baht and yen markets were especially cognizant of central banks, as well as their U.S. dollar-buying agents, keeping close watch on the strength of the respective currencies. 

 As the U.S. dollar fell below Y111 and headed toward a key resistance level at Y110, traders wondered aloud when Japan's central bank would make its presence felt. Japanese politicians and exporters have been voicing concerns about the detrimental effects of a strong yen, leaving the market poised for a massive yen-selling exercise by the central bank. 

 "This week has been remarkable in the sense that the majors have been so volatile," one currency strategist a U.S. investment bank said. "There are no real themes to be found in the yen, euro and U.S. dollar. Even people who are bearish on the yen aren't really taking positions because market liquidity is poor and currency movements have been too whippy." 

 As the yen has strengthened, the Singapore dollar has weakened against the U.S. dollar, leaving traders convinced that the republic's currency has now finally decoupled from the movement of the yen. 

 "The Singapore government is actively supporting the U.S. dollar because the Singapore dollar has room to depreciate," said a currency strategist at a U.K. bank, noting that the Monetary Authority of Singapore let the republic's currency slide by 10% in 1986 during the last recession.

title: Singapore Dollar Lower Late But Some See US$ Dn To S$1.60
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar slipped back in Asian trading on Friday from levels seen at the height of the yen's rebound against the U.S. dollar on Thursday.

title: Singapore dollar rides crest of yen surge.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar was among the biggest beneficiaries of the yen's spectacular overnight rise as hedge funds and investors who had been selling it as a proxy for Asia cut their short positions, dealers said on Thursday. 

 Singapore's currency, recently a victim of its own liquidity as trade in the other Southeast Asian currencies withered, gained over two percent from late Wednesday levels in line with the dizzying drop in dollar/yen. 

 It stood at 1.6400/20 to the U.S. dollar at 0240 GMT after briefly firming above the 1.6400 barrier, compared with about 1.67 late on Wednesday. 

 The dollar was holding above 120 yen in Tokyo morning trade after tumbling to a 12-month low of around 118.95 yen overnight as hedge funds, unwinding short yen positions, took the view that Japan would implement new measures to revitalise its banking system. 

 "The Sing is just riding on the back of the yen's movement. I reckon there are still a lot of sellers who missed the boat last night, but we should see more consolidative trading today," said the head of foreign exchange at an Asian bank. 

 He said the the Sing dollar was likely to face some resistance around 1.62 per U.S. dollar and should trade in a range of 1.62 to 1.67 in the next few days. 

 Analysts said hedge funds and interbank players had been shorting the Singapore dollar as liquidity dwindled in the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah and after Malaysia imposed stringent controls on the ringgit. 

 "Relative to the rest of the Asian currencies, it's very easy to run a short position in the Sing dollar because interest rates are rather low," said Chiang Yao Chye, head of Asia-Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 "That's been a very popular trade for some time and a lot of these short-Sing/long-dollar positions are just getting out. As long as dollar/yen drops further, you're going to see more of that," he added. 

 Dealers said there was no sign of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to slow the local currency's rise as it was in line with the overall trend for Asian currencies. 

 "With the yen strengthening by nearly 10 percent, and the Sing is only up by some two to three percent, I don't think the MAS is uncomfortable," the dealer said.
