title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from a Group of 15 summit in Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements put further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 July 2 - World Bank approves $1 billion loan disbursement to Indonesia, another $6 billion to arrive from international donors. 

 Japan Prime Minister Hashimoto and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party agree to adopt bridge bank system to tackle the country's massive bad loans. 

 July 4 - Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi hints at permanent tax cuts. 

 July 8 - Hashimoto vows to seek permanent tax cuts and an overhaul of the tax system, but reveals no details. 

 July 9 - South Korea announces its intention to double this year's budget deficit in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 July 12 - The ruling LDP is trounced in Upper House elections, winning only 44 seats, well short of a majority and 17 less than the 61 it had held prior to the election. 

 South Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission imposes involuntary restructuring on conglomerates, or chaebols, directing eight banks to pick about 16 chaebols for the exercise. 

 July 13 - PM Hashimoto announces his resignation and cancels planned official visits to France and the United States. 

 July 14 - Tens of thousands of South Korean workers down tools to protest against wage cuts and layoffs, part of the massive corporate restructuring programme. 

 July 15 - IMF approves immediate $1 billion loan payment to Indonesia. 

 July 16 - Striking Korean workers return to work, but warn of further protests if necessary. 

 Indonesia revises 98/99 budget to reflect the deteriorating economy, assuming a rupiah/dlr rate of 10,600. 

 Foreign governments announce their agreement to reschedule the country's $54.4 billion in sovereign debt. 

 July 20 - Protests begin at Hyundai's factory in Ulsan, striking workers pitch tents. 

 July 23 - Record 7.0 percent unemployment in South Korea, with more than 1.5 million unemployed. 

 July 24 - Obuchi wins 225 votes out of 411 in LDP voting to become LDP president and, almost certainly, prime minister. 

 July 29 - Moody's Investors Service warned that it may downgrade credit ratings of Thai banks due to poor results. 

 July 30 - Parliament formally names Obuchi prime minister; he then announces his new cabinet. 

 August 3 - Thailand unveils 25 point plan to salvage its economy at the start of two weeks of talks with the IMF. The plan includes measures to create jobs and stimulate the economy, and is later endorsed by the IMF. 

 Indonesia launches debt rescheduling agency to aid the country's debt-ridden companies. 

 August 6 - New Japanese prime minister Obuchi announces a plan to vary tax cuts according to existing tax brackets, and says he will ask parliament to approve cuts worth more than six trillion yen ($41.3 billion). 

 August 14 - The Hong Kong government intervenes in the local stock market, buying stocks to squeeze out investors accused of playing the currency and interest rates against the stock market. The Hang Seng Index soars 8.47 percent. 

 August 17 - Russia effectively devalues the rouble and declares a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt. The next day, Asian markets slide. 

 Thousands of Hyundai Motor workers rally near the South Korean company's main factory complex in Ulsan, suspending production in protest over layoffs. Police stand ready for action. 

 August 25 - Hyundai workers return to work after a union-brokered agreement to limit number of layoffs. 

 August 26 - IMF approves $1 billion loan to Indonesia. 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest point loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 IMF approves $900 million loan payment to South Korea. 

 Sept 1 - Malaysia imposes new foreign exchange controls to contain speculation and restrict capital flows. The IMF warns that the move may undermine investor confidence. 

 Sept 2 - Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking off a rally in Asian markets. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. Police state that Anwar is under investigation over allegations made in a banned book, "Fifty Reasons Why Anwar Cannot Become Prime Minister". 

 Sept 3 - South Korean riot police storm plants owned by Mando Machinery Corp., the country's largest auto-parts producer, to end a strike over planned mass layoffs.

title: ANALYSIS - Govt action in Asia rings alarms.
text:
By Valerie Lee SINGAPORE, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The intervention by some Asian governments to support their stock markets and fend off speculators has received the thumbs-down from most analysts, who say governments should keep clear of markets or risk getting their fingers burned. 

 Investors gave a clear signal late last week, taking profit after sharp rallies in markets in Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Taiwan earlier in the week on talk of official intervention. 

 At the close of trade on Friday, several Asian markets had surrendered the week's gains with Malaysia's key Composite Index tumbling 7.69 percent as investors cashed out. 

 "Obviously, investors will be disappointed because they hate surprise elements and if the governments try to manage the market it is not taken very positively," said Nilesh Jasani, a regional strategist with SG Securities in Singapore. "The alarm bells always go off a bit when you hear about governments propping up the markets because you are never quite sure where the real floor is," said Peter Douglas, Director of Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore. 

 Analysts said government-backed buying of shares would bring out sellers eager to liquidate their holdings at the expense of the regional authorities. It could also hurt the long-term investor outlook for the markets involved, as risk premiums for these markets would rise, they added. 

 "What is more, you are not addressing the real issues, you are just swirling money around in the economy," said Kevin Gin, a director with Kleinwort Benson Securities. "It's taking money from out of one pocket and putting it into another," he said. 

 In recent weeks, several Asian governments either stepped into their battered share markets as buyers or announced their intention to use public funds to stimulate markets that are drastically weaker than they were before the Asian financial crisis flared up a year ago. Hong Kong started things, repeatedly intervening in stocks and future markets after leader Tung Chee-hwa said the government would step in if speculators attacked the Hong Kong dollar and pushed interest rates higher while holding short stock positions. 

 In Malaysia, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said last week that a fund that subsidises the annual pilgrimages of Malaysian Muslims to Saudi Arabia might intervene to buy shares on behalf of the government. 

 Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the huge Employees' Pension Fund (EPF), could also step in. 

 Taiwan also said its securities watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission, was drafting various proposals to stabilise the stock market. 

 Investors said the Hong Kong intervention might succeed as the government was not committed to defending a specific level on the key Hang Seng share index. But the win would not come without a price. "It is not coming cheap. What it means is that the government is not going through the mechanism of the currency board," said a European investment house strategist, who declined to be named. 

 "It is going outside it, which means that risk premiums on Hong Kong in future will go up," he said, adding that the country's reputation as perhaps the freest financial market in Asia had been compromised. 

 Another issue was also whether or not the regional authorities had deep enough pockets to sustain their support of the markets as sellers continue to emerge, analysts said. 

 "...the market will cap any artificially generated boost to the asset markets," London-based research house I.D.E.A. said in its regional markets focus on Friday. 

 "In the near-term, some caution may be evident in shorting the indices and the currencies but over a longer time frame (bearish) fundamentals are seen winning through," it said. 

 But at least one investor said regional authorities were entitled to take protective measures. 

 "A government has a social objective at the end of the day. If you are a government, you have been elected, you have a social objective and if investors are getting unreasonable you have to act," said Jean Paolo Guarnieri, a director with Salomon Brothers Asset Management in Hong Kong. 

 "All this excitement from investors against the government intervention is a little bit naive. When you deal in foreign exchange markets around the world, for example, the central bank is always there....the objective of the central bank is not always mercantile," he said.

title: Singapore  central bank  selling own  currency  - traders.
text:
SINGAPORE (Reuters) - It would seem rather odd for a Southeast Asian central bank to be selling its own currency after more than a year of market turmoil and grinding currency depreciation. 

 But that is what foreign exchange traders say the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has been doing in the last couple of weeks. 

 They say local banks, which often act on behalf of the central bank, have been spotted buying the U.S. dollar each time the Singapore dollar shows signs of strengthening. 

 "Every time the dollar/Sing drops too much, the local banks are in to support it," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 "Singapore needs to not have too strong a currency because of export competitiveness," she added. 

 But analysts say that although there are compelling arguments for a weaker Singapore dollar, including the oft-mentioned export competitiveness concern, the MAS is highly unlikely to actively depreciate the local currency. 

 "I don't buy the idea that the government is out there trying to depreciate the Singapore dollar to 1.80 or even 2.00 (to the U.S. dollar)," said Daniel Lian, head of Asian markets research at ANZ Investment Bank. 

 "If there's any activity (buying of dollar/Sing), the volume has been extremely light. I don't think they're in a mood to sharply depreciate the Sing dollar," he added. 

 An MAS spokesman said the bank does not comment on its intervention operations. 

 The Singapore dollar stood at around 1.72 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade on Friday. It has not strengthened above the 1.70 level since July 21. 

 Most analysts attributed the apparent MAS purchases of U.S. dollars to routine smoothing of sharp moves in the currency market or to the bank adjusting its own portfolio. 

 "The argument of trying to replenish reserves at the margin makes more sense because if you're trying to weaken the currency, you would typically catch it on a weakening trend," said Paul Alapat, senior economist at Indosuez W.I.Carr. 

 "The direction would be to tolerate some weakness in the currency in line with its trading partners and to that extent the Singapore dollar has some catching up to do," he said. 

 ANZ's Lian said the 1.66-1.75 region would be a suitable trading range for the Singapore dollar unless other Asian currencies, including the yen, fell sharply. 

 But given the Singapore dollar's relative resilience compared with the currencies of its export rivals and a benign domestic inflation scenario, analysts say there is potential for more depreciation. 

 The Singapore dollar is down by about 17 percent against the U.S. dollar since the start of the Asian crisis last July, while the Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht have lost between 35 and 40 percent.

title: Singapore MAS: Mkt Forces Will Determine S$ Value - Report
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Monetary Authority of Singapore, or MAS, will continue to allow market forces to determine the value of the Singapore dollar, but will intervene to counter unwarranted speculation, according to a report in the Business Times' weekend edition. 

 The MAS, which is Singapore's de facto central bank, said the value of the Singapore dollar is determined by market forces, and at the same time, by maintaining a trade-weighted exchange band, according to the article. (US$1=S$1.6210) 

 The article quoted an MAS official as saying: "We manage the exchange rate against a basket of trade-weighted currencies of our major trading partners, because that's the best way to preserve our purchasing power. We allow a band within which the trade-weighted exchange rate can fluctuate." 

 The MAS' policy goal is to achieve sustained non-inflationary growth, the article said. 

 Even if the exchange rate moves out of the band, the MAS official said intervention wouldn't be automatic, the article said. 

 The band is adjusted according to how the MAS perceives inflation, adding that as long as the exchange rate stays within the band, the MAS wouldn't influence it, the article added. 

 The MAS will only intervene to support the Singapore dollar if the exchange rate moves too sharply because of unwarranted speculation or if its movement is inconsistent with MAS' view of the fundamentals, the article said. 

 The article quoted the MAS official as saying the monetary authority wouldn't intervene "if the outlook for the region suddenly worsens. It's not our job to support what is not sustainable on a fundamental basis."

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late On Yen Rally; MAS Rumors Brake Gains
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar made dramatic gains against the U.S. dollar Thursday, spurred on by joint intervention in the dollar/yen market by the U.S. and Japan overnight. 

 However, rumors that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in the market in the morning by buying U.S. dollars at S$1.6550 effectively put a lid on Singapore dollar bullishness, according to Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist with Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 A trader with a Japanese bank in Singapore said market players were spooked when they saw a big local bank buying U.S. dollars. "Some rushed to buy U.S. dollars after they saw that," he said. 

 However, a trader at a domestic bank in Singapore expressed doubt that the MAS had actually intervened. 

 "It was probably a commercial buyer," the trader said. "The market is very nervous and it looks cheap right now for corporates to buy U.S. dollars." 

 Traders also cited political uncertainties in Indonesia and Malaysia as reasons to buy the U.S. dollar against the Singapore currency.

title: CORRECTED-FOCUS-Asian leaders applaud yen  intervention .
text:
In SINGAPORE story headlined "FOCUS-Asian leaders applaud yen intervention" please read in 13th paragraph....Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency...instead of....China's state-run Central News Agency... (correcting reference). 

 A corrected story follows. 

 By Jason Szep 

SINGAPORE, June 18 (Reuters) - Coordinated U.S.-Japan intervention to support the troubled yen won loud applause on Thursday from Asian leaders, lighting a flicker of hope in the otherwise gloomy region. 

 Official reaction was fast and most hoped fresh yen strength would help give Japan better footing to pull Asia out of its economic mess. 

 "We are glad to see that the exchange rate of the Japanese yen is picking up," said China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong. 

 He was quoted by China's official Xinhua news agency as telling Asian bankers in Beijing that a devaluation of the Chinese yuan was not necessary. 

 Other Asian leaders and central banks joined in the praise for the dollar sales, with many hoping that a firmer yen would help prevent China from abandoning promises not to devalue the yuan, a move that would push Asia's financial crisis to new depths. 

 "I am glad to see that the Japanese yen rebounded yesterday after strong intervention," Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa Tung told reporters during a visit to New Zealand. 

 "The key is now for Japan to move forward," he said, adding that the revitalisation of the Japanese economy "will have a great deal of impact on us all". 

 Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was happy with the impact of the intervention on the market. 

 "I am happy with the fact that the joint intervention was appreciated by the market," he told reporters. 

 Some dealers estimated the Bank of Japan and the New York Federal Reserve spent up to $6 billion to boost the yen, which rallied to about 136 to the dollar from about 142. The yen remained fairly steady in early Asian trade on Thursday but remained under pressure amid concerns over further interventions. 

 Stock prices surged on Wall Street and in Asia in reaction to the intervention, which also gave regional currencies a much-needed boost. 

 "The move will help stabilise Asian financial markets," said Taiwan's Finance Minister Paul Chiu. 

 "And after the foreign exchange rates stabilise, it will also be positive to our economy and financial markets," Chiu was quoted late on Wednesday by Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency as saying. 

 Some officials said the move should help take pressure off China, which has seen its exports plunge as the yen crumbled. 

 "It was especially meaningful because the recent depreciation of the yen was increasing pressure on the Chinese yuan, whose depreciation will have a strong shock throughout Asia," said a senior official at the central Bank of Korea. 

 The head of the Thai central bank's banking department, Tassana Rachatapoh, said the intervention provided some reprieve to the baht, which jumped in early trading to 40.00-41.00 per dollar from 43.00/43.12 on Wednesday. 

 "This is a move in a right direction. If the yen keeps plunging, the impact would be enormous," Tassana said. 

 "But at the end of the day, Japan will need to sort out the fundamental problems, which include the troubled financial institutions. However, we welcome the move which should help lift the sentiment near-term," she added. 

 New Zealand Prime Minister Jenny Shipley described the concerted support of the yen "helpful". 

 "Japan is such an important trading partner that whatever is happening there will affect not only our trading position, but also our currency," she said. 

 "So what has happened overnight is helpful, but I will only personally have real confidence in whether or not we are going to find our way out if we see the sorts of reforms undertaken in Japan that not only I but very many other APEC leaders have discussed on many occasions in the recent past." 

 Jean-Michel Severino, World Bank vice president for East Asia and the Pacific, who said on Tuesday that Asia was plunging into depression, described the intervention as positive. 

 "It's a very positive step forward," he told reporters in Sydney. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Singapore growth seen hurt by Asia economic woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 16 (Reuters) - Singapore's economic growth is expected to slip more than forecast because of Asia's economic crisis and could contract if the turmoil got worse, an official of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Tuesday. 

 "We're in the process of reviewing the growth rates for the year," Khor Hoe Ee said. 

 Khor, director of the economics department at the de facto central bank, told a seminar that a review of Singapore's 1998 growth forecast was expected to show a smaller rate of growth for 1998 than the current official projection of 2.5 to 4.5 percent. 

 "We expect that we'll come out at the lower end of that range. If we're lucky we'll stay there," he said. 

 Several economists have said that Singapore faced a likely recession due to the regional crisis. Even those who are more optimistic feel the official forecast is too high. 

 "If the external environment became more adverse, then I think it's not unfair to say the economy could dip into negative," Khor added. 

 But he said there was confidence about the soundness of the economy and some sectors were still faring well. 

 If the Japanese economy revived and the European economy continued to strengthen, boosting Singapore exports, there was a fair chance Singapore's economy would turn around, he said. 

 Despite the economic slowdown, there were still pockets of strength, such as in growth of semiconductors. 

 Electronics account for about 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports. 

 Further, the government's promise to stimulate the economy with off-budget measures if second quarter figures showed significant decline would also help alleviate problems. 

 He said off-budget measures could be announced around the time the economic review was finalised. That is expected within a month. 

 Asked what kind of reserves Singapore had used during the recent financial turmoil, when it intervened in currency markets, he said: "Like all central banks we do intervene in the forex markets, but our attention has been directed at smoothing out the volatility." 

 He said the Singapore dollar's exchange rate depended on market conditions. 

 "We operate flexibly, I would say, with a band in which we allow the exchange rate to fluctuate. And as long as it fluctuates within that band, we don't really intervene," he said. 

 However, it was unrealistic for the Singapore dollar to remain high when regional currencies were weakening, he said. 

 The Singapore dollar exchange rate is managed against a basket of currencies. It has fallen around 18 percent against the U.S. dollar since the start of Asia's crisis a year ago. 

 "We believe our fundamentals are a lot stronger than most countries. The underlying tendency for the exchange rate is to appreciate over time rather than depreciate," Khor said.

title: Singapore dollar level dictated by market - Hu.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 2 (Reuters) - Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Tuesday the level of the Singapore dollar was decided by the market. 

 "We don't defend the Singapore dollar. The Singapore dollar level is market-dictated," Hu told reporters on the sidelines of a news conference launching a new bank product. 

 He said the "MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) only goes in to intervene to avoid large fluctuations". 

 "No one can successfully defend the currency at unrealistic levels indefinitely," Hu said. 

 Asked whether Singapore exports, which are showing signs of slowing, could influence the government's idea of where the currency rate should be, Hu said: "That has never been an issue."

title: Japan reserve policy won't soon be altered by euro.
text:
TOKYO, May 11 (Reuters) - Despite euphoria at the impending birth of the euro, Japan's monetary authorities say they do not intend to jump at the chance to boost holdings of the new European currency soon after its debut in January 1999. 

 Japan, holder of the world's largest foreign reserves, is cautious about making snap decisions to reshuffle components of its reserves, now denominated in U.S. dollars. 

 "The euro will be officially launched with 11 European nations. However, there's much uncertainty along the way as to how the euro will fare, what character it will possess and how the unified European financial market will look," said a senior official at the Ministry of Finance. 

 "Japan will take steps after all these factors become clearer," he said. 

 The European Union (EU) held a landmark summit on May 1 and 2 in Brussels, agreeing to launch the single currency in January 1999 with 11 members, and appointing the first president of the European Central Bank (ECB). 

 One monetary source said sound macroeconomic policy in European nations would be in the interests of the Japanese government, while integrated European financial markets free from currency risks could benefit Japanese firms operating there. 

 But he and analysts said there was uncertainty over whether tight monetary and fiscal policy by European nations would be maintained in concert after the euro was introduced. 

 Germany and the Netherlands could favor tight monetary policies, while Spain and Italy may not accept them, depending on the economic situation. 

 Still, some foreign central banks already see the euro in a positive light. Taiwan's central bank said last week it would shift one billion marks into euro holdings immediately after it was launched. 

 Japanese private investors have been shifting some investment into European bonds and equities in the belief that the euro will have a smooth launch, while trying to avoid excessive exposure to U.S. asset markets, currency dealers said. 

 Regarding the possibility of Japanese authorities' increasing euro holdings, however, Taisuke Tanaka, strategist of global foreign exchange at Credit Suisse said: "In the short-term period it isn't possible. But on a long-term horizon it is." 

 Some monetary sources agreed. 

 "If Japan comes to realise that stabilising the euro is important to the stability of the yen, Japan would hold it or increase euro holdings to prepare for cases of concerted currency intervention," said the monetary source. 

 Analysts estimated over 90 percent of Japan's $205.758 billion reserves outstanding was denominated in U.S. dollars, and the rest was in European currencies such as the mark and sterling. 

 Japan also began holding the Indonesia rupiah last November as a result of concerted intervention with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank Indonesia. 

 The action, aimed at propping up the value of the rupiah against the dollar, was based on Japanese authorities' judgment that Asian currency stability would be important to Japan's economy and firms operating there, monetary officials said. 

 Some analysts said European currency holdings by the Finance Ministry were likely to be converted into the euro automatically after 1999. 

 But most said no shift to the euro at the expense of the dollar would take place because of wider economic and political relations with the United States. 

 Credit Suisse's Tanaka said: "Besides economic relations with the United States, political incentives could influence Japan to hold the bulk of reserves in the dollar." ((Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3 3432 1396 tokyo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Singapore Dollar Ends Down, But Up From Intraday Low

title: Dollar slips on yen in Asia while dlr/mark steady.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 5 (Reuters) - The dollar slipped around a yen in early Asian trading and extended the loss later, but volume was low in the absence of the Tokyo market and selling pressure was light, dealers said. 

 Dollar/yen was coming down even in the face of a still firm mark/yen which was still well above the 74.50 yen level and expected to perk up to the 75.00 level soon. 

 "Mark/yen is still the best risk reward trade as far as we are concerned on a medium term basis," said Steve Brice, Regional Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 But he noted there was some concern about BoJ intervention, although probably not at these levels, and the very fact that a lot of investors are long mark/yen could mean any negative news from Germany or positive news from Japan could see it snap back. 

 Dollar/yen's slip certainly did not represent a huge shakeout and it bounced nicely at 132.60 and 132.50 would almost certainly hold if it tests the downside again, dealers said. 

 Traders said there is a good chance that Europe will buy dollar/yen back up again from the sub-133 level. London traders return to their desks today after Monday's holiday. 

 There is good technical resistance at 133.50, where knock-out options exist, dealers said. 

 The mark has shrugged aside the compromise deal on the European Central Bank head and dollar/mark was holding steady around the New York close of 1.7790/95. 

 Traders said that technically, the mark rally has good reason to stall and it is approaching strong resistance levels. 

 The Australian dollar held steady after March retail sales data came in much in line with expectations at up 0.7 percent. 

 This followed a 1.0 percent drop in February and while analysts had seen this as an aberration there were some jitters after Monday's news of a record monthly trade deficit. 

 Analysts said today's 0.7 percent rise together with elements of the trade data which showed some semblance of growth means the authorities are likely to hold hard on monetary policy. 

 The dollar was at US$0.6419/24 against US$0.6411/16 ahead of the data. 

 The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets today to discuss monetary policy but a Reuters poll showed that just 30 percent of economists surveyed expected an easing. 

 Governor Ian Macfarlane's semi-annual policy statement and testimony before a parliamentary committee is later this week. 

 Official Australian interest rates currently stand at 5.0 percent and were last cut by 0.5 point on July 30, 1997.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  end mixed on domestic news.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 4 (Reuters) - Regional currencies turned in mixed performances in subdued holiday-affected trade on Monday as the focus shifted to domestic developments around the region. 

 These included the aftershocks of the May Day riots in Korea, deepening concern over the future of Thailand's Central Bank governor and news of another sharp rise in Indonesian inflation. 

 "Overall market players are sidelined just waiting to see what happens in Indonesia, " said Kenneth Cheng chief Asian analyst at MCM Asia Pacific. 

 Late in the day Indonesia reported a jump in its year-on-year inflation to 44.9 percent in April from 39.1 percent in March. 

 "It's in line with the trend. I think we're looking at hyperinflation numbers here," Cheng said. 

 But the Indonesian government earlier on Monday announced sharp hikes in fuel electricity and transport prices, which will feed into inflation in the coming months, and the army came out warning students about further anti-Suharto riots. 

 The rupiah has so far remained fairly stable as most market players are reluctant to get too involved. 

 In Thailand pressure was building on the central bank governor all day with rumours of his imminent resignation sweeping the markets. The news finally came near the close of trading when the Central Bank chief, Chaiyawat Wibulswadi, announced he was going on May 5. 

 The baht had been slightly weaker all day in anticipation of the news. 

 The South Korean won was an early target of sellers as concerns over labour instability continue to plague the currency. On Friday over 20,000 workers and students staged widespread rioting in the capital Seoul. 

 The riots led to condemnations by the government but also sparked a large sell off in Korean shares with the KOSPI index shedding some 3.6 percent on the day and putting further pressure on the won. 

 The Philippine peso bucked the trend to rise by over two percent on the day as foreign banks sold U.S. dollars for peso when it struck the 40 .39 level. 

 Some traders suspected the Central Bank might have had a hand in the action prompting firm denials from the Bank. 

 It said it had undertaken no intervention in the forex market on Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar strengthened slightly on reports the Monetary Authority is continuing to look at the details of Singapore dollar internationalisation, one analyst said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS-Regionals propped up but rises cappe.
text:
0500 GMT - Asian currencies stuck at early levels, see-sawing between strong yen and demand for cheap dollars from U.S. funds. 

 * The Indonesian rupiah firms slightly after the central bank raises its rupiah deposit rates by four percentage points. 

 * Dealers say the market failed to react to Bank Indonesia governor Sjahril Sabirin's overnight comment that he does not see another interest rate hike in the near term. 

 Sabirin told Reuters in an interview late on Thursday Bank Indonesia was following a dual policy to strengthen the rupiah - through interest rates and economic reform measures to boost confidence. 

 He also said fair value for the rupiah was at 5,000-6,000 to the dollar and he saw the Indonesian economy starting to rebound in the first quarter of next year. 

 * In Thailand, the Labour Ministry says the number of unemployed has jumped to 2.03 million, exceeding end-year projections, from 1.8 million at the end of 1997. 

 * The baht remains caught between offshore dollar sales and demand from importers and other companies. 

 * News of Bangkok Bank's new share issue at 93 baht per share is welcomed by the market, though most dealers say it has been largely priced in. 

 Thailand's top bank raised more than $1.0 billion on Thursday with the 440 million new share offering. 

 * The share issue is expected to generate offshore demand for the baht and dealers in Singapore say there is talk the Government of Singapore Investment Corp (GSIC) has been buying the baht in recent sessions. 

 A GSIC spokeswoman declines to comment on the rumours. 

 * Taiwan's central bank says foreign reserves fell to US$83.615 billion at end March from $84.011 billion at end February. 

 Dealers say the fall could be due partly the central bank's quiet defence of the Taiwan dollar. 

 * The central bank also says broad M2 money supply grew 8.13 percent year-on-year in March after rising 8.51 percent in February. 

 * The Taiwan dollar remains above the T$33 level to the U.S. dollar on the yen's strength. 

 * Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit looks weak after failing to extend its gains much despite the stock market's rally on news of the merger between RHB Bank and Sime Bank. 

 * Interest is dampened by news Bank Negara Malaysia is to provide a 12-month guarantee against unforeseen liabilities of Sime Bank. 

 * "The inability of the ringgit to strengthen reflects investor concern over the Malaysian banking industry as a whole," said Banque Paribas strategist Thio Chin Loo. 

 "The lack of transparency over bank asset problems despite central bank assurances is unlikely to be improved in the near term and investors are expected to remain wary of further surprises around the corner," she said in a daily report. 

 * The ringgit is seen trading a 3.73-3.80 range to the dollar, with fears of central bank intervention limiting its decline. 

 * The Singapore dollar tracks a now familiar 1.58-1.60 range to the U.S. dollar, with activity largely driven by cross play against the ringgit. 

 * The Philippine peso remains weak after falling to 38.79 per dollar in early trade as dealers buy dollars to square their positions before leaving for a weekend foreign exchange conference. 

 * The South Korean won gains from the yen's strength, but its rise is expected to be determined by the size of expected import deals. 

 * Finance Minister Lee Kyu-sung says South Korea urgently needs to lower interest rates no later than May. 

 Lee says in an advance copy of a speech that high interest rates threaten to push many economically viable companies into bankruptcy, which would lead to rising unemployment. 

 But he implies that any move to lower interest rates would only be with the blessing of the IMF.

title: FOCUS-Strong Singapore dollar soothes Asia  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, March 27 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies lurched higher in late Friday trade as the Singapore dollar suddenly burst out of a drowsy range on rumoured buying by the Brunei Investment Agency. 

 Talk that Brunei, whose currency is pegged to the Singapore dollar, had bought a large amount of Sing dollars, pushed the currency through the 1.59 barrier against its U.S. counterpart, to a high of 1.5850. 

 "I think the market was just caught by surprise and a lot of stops were triggered. Everything seemed so quiet in the morning," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Apparent central bank intervention near the U.S. dollar's highs thwarted a further rise in the Singapore dollar, but dealers said it would now target the 1.56 level. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervenes in foreign exchange markets to smooth sharp moves in the exchange rate. It does not typically comment on these operations. 

 The Singapore dollar's rise also lifted the Malaysian ringgit out of its lethargy, taking it to a high of 3.57. 

 But traders said the ringgit's rise was being blocked by dollar bids below 3.55 per dollar, making the 3.50 level an increasingly difficult target amid anxiety about Thursday's riots at an immigration deportation centre in Malaysia, in which nine people were reported killed. 

 "If we fail to see 3.50 broken next week, the ringgit could be in for a very messy stretch," a senior European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz said the ringgit was expected to strengthen but probably not return to its previous level around 2.50 per dollar. 

 She said she did not want to see interest rates rise because this would raise costs for industry. 

 Elsewhere, Indonesia's debt problems remained in the spotlight as the market awaited details of how Jakarta planned to deal with $74 billion worth of corporate debt and when the IMF might release its next instalment of cash to the country. 

 The head of the IMF team in Jakarta, Hubert Neiss, said Indonesia's formula to resolve the debt crisis relied heavily on a model used by Mexico in the early 1980s. 

 Under that programme, the Mexican government assumed the foreign exchange losses of companies' loans but not the loans themselves. 

 Neiss told reporters after a meeting with Indonesian officials that he needed time to respond to the proposal and various other plans were also being discussed. 

 Key Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said there was no consensus on Indonesia's corporate debt at the Manila framework meeting of finance and central bank deputies from the Asia-Pacific region. 

 He said international banks had yet to agree on a delay in the repayment of Indonesian corporate debt. 

 Bank Indonesia managing director Miranda Gultom said in Tokyo Indonesia was still reviewing proposals to stabilise the rupiah, including a trading band and a managed floating exchange rate, after shelving plans for a currency board. 

 The rupiah dipped slightly in late trade, but remained underpinned by Bank Indonesia's sharp rate hikes early in the week. 

 Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the city-state would launch a bilateral trade financing scheme with Indonesia. 

 He said the trade guarantee should be backed by at least US$2 billion, which would come from Singapore's pledge to the IMF rescue package for Indonesia. 

 The plan follows what Goh described as a lack of interest from Group of Seven nations in his original proposal for a multi-lateral trade financing scheme. 

 The Philippine peso rebounded sharply from a weak open due to dollar inflows to the local stock market and a lack of corporate dollar demand. Traders said it could soon target the 36 level to the dollar. 

 The central bank said it expected the current account deficit to fall to 3.2 percent of gross national product this year, from 4.9 percent in 1997. It said the current account deficit stood at $4.303 billion by the end of 1997. 

 The Thai baht remained sandwiched between dollar demand from domestic firms and offshore sales, keeping it in a tight band, though dealers said the market continued to target the 35 level. 

 The IMF's Thailand representative, Reza Moghadam, said the baht's recent appreciation would help in servicing its debt and reduce inflationary pressures. 

 He also praised the government's progress in implementing economic reforms and said Thailand could have more funds if necessary. 

 The South Korean won strengthened as traders unwound dollar positions after the World Bank approved a $2 billion loan to the country. 

 The Hong Kong dollar dipped fractionally while forwards softened after the Hong Kong Association of Banks said deposit rates would be cut by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent. 

 Standard Chartered Bank and Hang Seng Bank said they would cut their prime rates by 25 basis points from Monday. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Malaysia offered to defend baht, says Thai minister.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, June 6 (Reuter) - Malaysia offered to defend the baht during a recent speculative attack on the Thai currency, Thailand's Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan revealed on Friday. 

 "There have been offers from countries (of the region), including Malaysia, but we have not used the facilities," he told a news conference. 

 Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, has not commented on whether the Thai government had sought its help to defend the baht during a sharp attack on the currency in mid-May. 

 But the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it intervened in the market, along with the Bank of Thailand, to help the baht during the recent assault on the currency. 

 Central banks in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have an ongoing pact to defend each other's currrencies in times of such crises. 

 "There has been some manipulation, some attack on our currency," said Amnuay, visiting Kuala Lumpur on the invitation of Malaysia's acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. 

 "The situation has calmed down and stabilised," he said. 

 Amnuay said Malaysia had gone through a similar currency turmoil in 1993 and "we can learn from experiences of Malaysia". 

 Since the assault on its currency, Thailand has introduced capital controls which have decreased foreign investors' access to the baht. 

 But Amnuay declined to give any details of the situation or how long the controls, under which overseas currency swaps have been stopped, will remain in place. 

 "It is not the place or time to discuss our plans," he said when asked if the country would formalise an exchange policy with other countries in the region.

title: Asian top 7  forex  reserves match G7 - Singapore.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 30 (Reuter) - The foreign exchange reserves of the top seven Asian countries are equal to those of the Group of Seven industrialised nations, Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu told a conference on Friday. 

 "The aggregate reserves of the top seven Asian countries matches that of the G7 countries," Hu told the annual conference of the International Securities Market Association (ISMA). 

 Hu's comments follow the recent speculative attack against the Thai baht in which the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) -- of which Hu is chairman -- intervened to help defend the currency. 

 Many Asian central banks have repurchase pacts between each other which enable them to defend another country's currency using that country's holdings of U.S. Treasury securities as collateral. 

 Hu noted Singapore is the fourth most active foreign exchange trading centre in the world. "Daily turnover in Singapore's foreign exchange market averaged US$130 billion in 1996." 

 "Of this, only about six percent actually involved trading in the Singapore dollar," he added. 

 Turning to the prospects for Asia, Hu said the ongoing economic liberalisation in China, India and Indo-China is expected to unleash the next wave of economic growth in Asia. 

 "A recent World Bank study indicated that the Asian economies will expand at an average rate of 7.2 percent annually over the next 10 years, which is almost three times that of the industrialised countries," he said. 

 Hu said Asia's full growth potential can be realised only if there is efficient access to capital. 

 "Large infrastructure investments will cause demand for funds to exceed domestic savings in many countries. This will compel the Asian economies to look within and beyond the region for surplus capital," Hu said. 

 He said that over the next decade Asian financial markets will have to modify their traditional role of channelling funds from the developed economies. 

 "The key challenge for Asia in the next decade is therefore to sustain the healthy development of its financial markets, which is critical to fostering continued macro-economic growth of the region," he said. -- Singapore newsroom 65-8703080

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah shrugs off campaign unrest.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 26 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah firmed in slow Monday morning trade despite news of widespread violence surrounding the country's election campaign. 

 Dealers said the unrest on the last campaign day for the May 29 poll, which included the deaths of at least 142 people in the South Kalimantan capital of Banjarmasin, did not affect the foreign exchange market. 

 Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,440.0/41.0 at 0405 GMT against an opening of 2,440.0/42.0. 

 "I suspect operators have gone long on the dollar in the spot market. They also have gone long in forwards," one dealer in Singapore said, adding that a U.S. public holiday was hampering trade as well. 

 Dealers said participants seemed to have factored in the risk of violence in the run-up to the general election, keeping the market relatively stable despite sporadic riots. 

 "I think operators are looking for good levels to sell," the dealer in Singapore said, adding that there was no reason for forwards to go higher because of cheap tom/next swaps. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said the dollar was looking supported around 2,440.0 but its upside would be capped around 2,445.0/47.0 ahead of the election. 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht had a very subdued morning as players in both domestic and offshore markets awaited the announcement of new monetary measures from the central bank's press briefing, due to begin at 0400 GMT. 

 "Most players were reluctant to take new positions this morning as they are eagerly waiting for the central bank's new measures," a dealer at a foreign bank in Bangkok said. 

 Thai Bankers Association president Olarn Chaiprawat said on Sunday that he expected the Bank of Thailand (BOT) to give a strong signal for a domestic interest rate cut on Monday. 

 Olarn said the central bank was also likely to come up with new measures to formally separate the offshore and onshore foreign exchange markets. 

 The baht/dollar forex market has been informally divided into offshore and local markets since the central bank moved to cut off offshore players' access to the baht when the currency came under speculative attack almost two weeks ago. 

 The U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said the offshore market was unlikely to be much moved by news of a cut in the BOT's discount rate, as interest in the baht had been severely dampened by the creation of a two-tier market. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit firmed a few notches on the back of the dollar's drop against the mark, but activity remained largely subdued in the absence of fresh leads. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said the market was focusing on the French elections, where losses for President Jacques Chirac's coalition were causing a sell-off in the dollar/mark. 

 Dealers said there was good dollar buying interest from Kuala Lumpur parties around the 2.4990 ringgit level. 

 Further south, the Singapore dollar gained some ground from corporate selling of the U.S. dollar but fears of central bank intervention capped the domestic unit's rise, dealers said. 

 "There was (U.S. dollar) selling interest from corporates from the 1.4310 level this morning and it touched a low of 1.4290/95 but local banks are still bidding around there," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 He said wariness of central bank support for the U.S. unit would limit its downside to around 1.4280 for the time being. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, typically intervenes in forex markets through major local banks to stem any sharp moves in the Singapore dollar.

title: Asian  central bank  officials discuss the baht.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 25 (Reuter) - Asian central bank officials met in Bangkok on Saturday and the top item on their agenda was the recent speculative attack against the Thai baht, central bank sources said on Sunday. 

 The Bank of Thailand issued a one paragraph statement about the meeting which read in part, "The meeting has contributed to strengthening the cooperation among the central banks and monetary authorities in the region and enhancing the stability of the regional financial markets." 

 But foreign exchange traders contacted by Reuters said it was obvious the main topic of conversation amongst the officials would have been the Thai baht. 

 "The meeting would have been a post mortem about the events of the week before last. They'll have looked at what they did right and what they did wrong," the head of foreign exchange trading at a European bank in Singapore commented. 

 A central bank offcial from one of the banks attending the meeting declined to specifically say what had been discussed, but added, "Look at the timing and draw your own conclusion." 

 On May 14 and 15 the baht was the subject of a massive attack by speculators who had decided that the combination of a high current account deficit, economic woes and rumours of instability in the cabinet were good reasons to sell the baht. 

 The Bank of Thailand -- with the aid of other Asian central banks -- was able to fend off the attack. 

 Since the so-called 'Tequila Crisis' of 1994 when the Mexican peso was savaged by speculators, Asian central banks have been signing bilateral repurhase pacts between each other in which they agree to help defend their currencies against speculative attacks. 

 The first real test of these repurchase pacts came with the foreign exchange market's assault against the baht. 

 The usually secretive Monetary Authority of Singapore confirmed it had intervened to defend the baht while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, although not confirming it officially, was also highly visible in intervening. 

 The Thai central bank said this weekend's gathering was part of the regular meeting of the Executives' Meeting of East Asia and Pacific (EMAP) Central Banks. 

 But the head of trading at the European bank said, "Regular it may be, but the location is a bit of a coincidence. They're sending a message to the speculators." 

 He added, "The message is pretty simple. It's along the lines of 'You're not taking Thailand on, you're taking all of us on.'" 

 The meeting was attended by senior central bank officials from Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Indonesia, China, Hong Kong and Thailand. 

 The head of Treasury at a U.S. bank in Singapore told Reuters he had not been aware of Saturday's meeting. "I think its hugely significant. They may say its under the auspices of EMAP, but...they would, wouldn't they." 

 "A lot these (central) bankers are worried that what happens to Thailand today could happen to them tomorrow. This sort of gathering of the clans will give them confidence," he added.

title: S.E. Asia Central Bks/Baht -2: Tighter Monetary Policy
text:
The Bank of Thailand was joined by the other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in supporting the Thai central bank in its defence of the currency, Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said early Friday. The Monetary Authority of Singapore described the intervention as 'effective'. 

 But the sources said the coup de grace of the banks' operations was the squeeze in short term interest rates engineered Thursday and Friday in Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines. 

 'I'm less impressed with the intervention and more impressed with the rise in Thailand's interest rates,' said the senior foreign exchange trader at a U.S. investment bank, speaking on condition of anonymity. '(The Bank of Thailand) dried up liquidity to punish the speculators,' he said. 

 Overt measures by the Bank of Thailand - urging domestic banks not to lend baht to offshore counterparties at rates less then 1,000% - ensured that many speculators who wanted to liquidate short positions in the Thai currency could do so only at an unacceptable cost. 

 Bank Negara has also pushed up short-term interest rates to defend the ringgit, though it was quick to deny suggestions Friday that it was penalizing offshore players in the ringgit swaps market. Bank Indonesia issued a similar denial Friday. 

 And the Philippine central bank jacked up its overnight interest rates in stages to 20% by Friday from 12% Wednesday, steadying the Philippine peso by the end of the day. 

 Regional currency dealing rooms were frantic Friday as liquidity in the forward and swap markets evaporated. 

 'The (local) banks were quoting such ridiculous spreads... basically Thailand and Malaysia were barricading their capital accounts (from offshore players),' said Chia Wooh Khien, treasury economist at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (South East Asia) Ltd. in Singapore. 

 The sources agreed the effect of sharply higher short-term interest rates in Malaysia and Thailand had much the same effect Friday as a temporary imposition of exchange controls. 'This hasn't been a natural market,' said StanChart's Van der Wath.

title: Southeast Asia Mkts Fall Seen Linked To Hedge Funds
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)--The recent heavy selling of Southeast Asian stocks is seen linked to foreign hedge funds that are also active in regional currency markets, fund managers and dealers say Friday. 

 But while hedge funds sold regional stocks, Asian funds managed from within the region were mainly on the sidelines, say fund managers. 

 Asian markets tumbled Thursday after heavy speculative attacks on Thailand's baht Wednesday unsettled regional currencies and stock markets. 

 The selldown sent regional benchmark stock indexes falling between 1.4% and 3.4% Thursday. Malaysia was worst hit, followed by the Philippines, two markets where there are the most concerns about a Thai-like situation developing. Thailand in recent years has become victim to overbuilding in the property sector that led to a slump that exposed its banks to bad loans. 

 Most Southeast Asian markets stabilized Friday in tandem with the retreat of currency speculators, suggesting further that the activity of hedge funds in the currency and stock markets was linked, market watchers say. 

 'Who were the main sellers? U.S. hedge funds. We executed some orders for them,' says a dealing vice president at a European brokerage house. 

 'They might be shorting the markets at first. But later, they were selling stocks to fight the currency front. Hedge funds often leverage one instrument against the other,' he says. 

 After launching fierce attacks on the baht Wednesday, many hedge funds were stung Thursday when the Bank of Thailand jacked up short-term interest rates. The bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore also intervened by selling dollars for baht.

title: =Southeast Asia Mkts Fall Seen Linked To Hedge Funds
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The recent heavy selling of Southeast Asian stocks is seen linked to foreign hedge funds that are also active in regional currency markets, fund managers and dealers say Friday. 

 But while hedge funds sold regional stocks, Asian funds managed from within the region were mainly on the sidelines, say fund managers. 

 Asian markets tumbled Thursday after heavy speculative attacks on Thailand's baht Wednesday unsettled regional currencies and stock markets. 

 The selldown sent regional benchmark stock indexes falling between 1.4% and 3.4% Thursday. Malaysia was worst hit, followed by the Philippines, two markets where there are the most concerns about a Thai-like situation developing. Thailand in recent years has become victim to overbuilding in the property sector that led to a slump that exposed its banks to bad loans. 

 Most Southeast Asian markets stabilized Friday in tandem with the retreat of currency speculators, suggesting further that the activity of hedge funds in the currency and stock markets was linked, market watchers say. 

 'Who were the main sellers? U.S. hedge funds. We executed some orders for them,' says a dealing vice president at a European brokerage house. 

 'They might be shorting the markets at first. But later, they were selling stocks to fight the currency front. Hedge funds often leverage one instrument against the other,' he says. 

 After launching fierce attacks on the baht Wednesday, many hedge funds were stung Thursday when the Bank of Thailand jacked up short-term interest rates. The bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore also intervened by selling dollars for baht.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht recovers but still vulnerable.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 15 (Reuter) - The Thai baht recovered some ground on Thursday as players turned wary of selling it down after the previous day's joint intervention by the central banks of Thailand and Singapore. 

 "The hedge funds are still buying the rumours the same as yesterday but the force is lesser now since the Bank of Thailand and other banks came in," a Siam Commercial Bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 Dealers said activity had subsided in the spot baht market but forwards were shooting up due to a severe shortage of funds after Wednesday's aggressive baht sales by speculative funds. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.790-25.840 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against 25.910/25.940 earlier and 26.330-26/430 late on Wednesday. The Bank of Thailand (BOT) set the mid-rate at 25.81. 

 "Everybody's hitting the forwards. I think they're just squeezing the short-term liquidity. Tom/next is at 65/100 -- it's like trading the one-year," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said there had been no signs of central bank intervention on Thursday. 

 "They (the BOT) have informed banks in Thailand not to quote to offshore parties for tom/next. There's no need for them to intervene," another Singapore-based dealer said. 

 "Everybody's just trying to fight for survival, they're just scrambling for funds," he added. 

 Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Thursday that Thailand had been and would continue to be successful in defending the baht. 

 "We have support from all our friends," he told reporters as he left a seminar in Tokyo. 

 The BOT and Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said in a statement on Wednesday that they had taken joint action to stem excessive speculative activities in the baht. 

 It was the first joint action confirmed by the two central banks. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah remained under pressure after being aggressively sold overnight on false rumours of unrest in Jakarta during the campaign for the May 29 election. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,438.50/39.50 at 0415 GMT after finding some support at the 2,439.0 level, compared with an opening of 2,433.0/44.0. 

 Swap rates rose broadly on foreign buying, dealers said. 

 They said a carry-forward effect from Wednesday, coupled with the ongoing jitters in the Thai market, hit the rupiah, triggering more stop-loss dollar buying. 

 The rupiah tumbled to a low of 2,445 in London overnight on false rumours of violence and arson at a police station in Jakarta, but it later recovered to 2,435. 

 Dealers said stop-loss limits were triggered in Singapore and London late on Wednesday after the rupiah was hit by the rumours. 

 One major local bank dealer said swap points jumped in early Thursday trading as offshore operators were squeezed on the forward side. 

 "Offshore players going long on dollars have to buy swaps for hedging or to get the rupiah financing, driving swap rates up across the board," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit staged a partial recovery but continued to look vulnerable after foreign funds dumped the currency on Wednesday due to spillover fears over Thailand. 

 "Today the market is caught a bit long so they're selling dollars but it looks supported around 2.5160," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said players would also be wary of pushing the ringgit down again after Bank Negara's aggressive intervention in London markets overnight. 

 "Negara was in aggressively around the 2.5250 level yesterday in London. They probably sold more than $1 billion," he said. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore pegged the amount sold by the Malaysian central bank at around $700 million. 

 The ringgit was at 2.5176/86 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against 2.5240/50 at close of Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday. It had fallen to as low as 2.5260, its lowest level since January 3. 

 The Singapore dollar was firm in the face of its neighbours' woes, but dealers said potential "safe-haven" flows to the currency were being dampened by fears of MAS intervention. 

 "The MAS has been supporting the (U.S) dollar at the 1.4320 level. I don't know why they want to hold it here since the dollar/yen has come off so much," a U.S. bank dealer said.

title: Asian repo pacts seem to have survived first test.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 15 (Reuter) - The first real test of a series of agreements between Asian central banks to help each other defend their respective currencies appears to have been successful, economists and traders said on Thursday. 

 "The symbolic importance (of the central banks' intervention) should not be understated. It's hugely significant," Desmond Supple, a senior analyst at BZW in Singapore, told Reuters. 

 The Thai baht has been battered by huge sell orders in the last two days from investors and speculators concerned over the future direction of the economy and the currency. 

 But on Wednesday afternoon, the Bank of Thailand (BOT) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, confirmed they had intervened to defend the baht. 

Foreign exchange traders reported that other Asian central banks such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had also intervened to defend the baht. But apart from the MAS, confirmation from other central banks was not forthcoming. 

 In the last 18 months, central banks in Asia have been signing up reciprocal repurchase agreements between each other. 

 The 'repo pacts' give participants instant access to cash for use to defend their currencies. Under the pacts the central bank receiving the assistance will put up U.S. Treasury securities as collateral. 

 "One's always wondered if these pacts actually mean anything. After yesterday I rather think they do," said the head of Treasury at a European bank in Singapore. 

 He said the intervention amounts concerned were not necessarily the major factor. "The fact, that of all people, the MAS was prepared to ... be identified with intervention is crucial. They're being seen helping someone out," he said. 

 The Treasury head also noted the Bank of Japan had said it would be prepared to intervene in the financial markets to help support the baht if it were asked to by the Thai authorities. 

 "The agreement is there, although it is not a thing we would activate unless we were asked by Thailand," a Bank of Japan (BoJ) official told Reuters. 

 "Here we've got the BoJ saying they'll defend the baht. Okay it's not with their own money, but when you've got the BoJ on your side is that helpful or not?" the Treasury head said. 

 BZW's Supple noted that even after news of the MAS's and the BOT's intervention had hit the market, some participants had continued to sell the baht. 

 But he added, "The market should realise they're not just taking on the Bank of Thailand." 

 Said the Treasury head; "Thailand's got over US$30 billion in its warchest. Under the repo agreements there's maybe another US$300-400 billion spare (cash) floating around." 

 He added; "These (repo) agreements make a difference. If the fundamentals are wrong, then fine, kick the hell out of the market. But if you're punting (speculating) then you have to accept you're taking on other central banks."

title: Thailand says regional  intervention  supported baht.

BANGKOK, May 15 (Reuter) - Several Asian central banks on Thursday cooperated with Thailand by jointly intervening to defend the embattled baht against speculative attacks, Thai deputy central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said.

title: Thailand/Singapore/Central Banks-4: Deemed Ineffective
text:
Data released by the Bank of Thailand in late April showed the economy at its lowest ebb in years: Manufacturing activity in February slowed to a five-year low, and private-investment activity dwindled to a four-year low. Imports and exports fell to their lowest levels in more than two years.

'We're not sure how much the authorities bought but the way the intervention is done doesn't seem to be effective,' the chief of regional currencies at a Japanese bank in Singapore said. 'The currency is now 20 pts above the intervention level. It seems the market is having the upper hand.' 

 He and other analysts, who also asked not to be named, suggested that the intervention was unsuccessful because the two banks had not been aggressive enough. 'Maybe they lack dollars,' the currency chief at the Japanese bank said, referring to the Bank of Thailand. 

 A senior official at the Bank of Thailand declined to comment on that observation. 'We don't comment on money market operations,' he said. At the end of March, Thailand's foreign reserves stood at $38.1 billion, unchanged from February. 

 So far in May, the dollar has finished outside the central bank's trading band as often as it has finished within the band, four occasions. Some currency experts said that may have tempted speculators to attack the baht. 

 'Because we've been trading above the fixing, the market perception is there's a built-in fault in the fixing,' said Robin Cheung, chief dealer for emerging-market currencies at Hong Kong & Shanghai Banking Corp. in Hong Kong. text:
SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuter) - The Thai baht recovered from Friday morning lows by midday after the Bank of Thailand (BOT) denied market rumours of a band widening and intervened in spot and forward markets to stem the currency's decline. 

 Dealers said the rumours, that the BOT planned to widen the dollar/baht trading band, emerged in London markets overnight and prompted a sell-off in the baht. 

 The baht was quoted at 26.013/26.018 to the dollar at 0510 GMT after the BOT intervened in Singapore forex markets to sell the dollar at 26.025 baht, dealers said. The Thai unit fell to to a low of 26.090 in early trade. 

 Paiboon Kittisrikangwan, the central bank's division chief in charge of money and foreign exchange markets, told Reuters the Bank of Thailand had no plan to change the exchange rate mechanism. 

 "A lot of U.S. investment houses were trying to attack the baht and buy dollars yesterday and it's been quite hectic today as well," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 Dealers said the dollar's sharp drop against the majors on Friday also helped the baht rebound, but it was still trading well above the central bank's mid-rate of 25.99. 

 "People were reluctant to take many long dollar positions due to a weakening of the U.S. unit abroad and the central bank's intervention in the Singapore market," a dealer in Bangkok said. 

 But sentiment remained bearish and dealers said the baht could be vulnerable to further declines against the backdrop of continued weakness on the stock market and worries about the stability of the finance sector. 

 Elsewhere, regional currencies benefitted from the dollar's sharp fall against the yen as fears of a rate hike in Japan gained ground while the likelihood of a further U.S. tightening appeared to recede. 

 A speech by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan late on Thursday was viewed as signalling that the U.S. central bank might hold back from further rate hikes for the time being. 

 Greenspan said he expected economic growth to slow later this year and next, but that the central bank would need to act if that did not prove to be the case. 

 "People took it as a sign that there won't be any immediate rate hike. That's why the market sold dollars and it has also turned quite bearish recently," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The dollar was quoted at 122.75/85 yen at 0510 GMT in Tokyo against its opening 123.15/18. 

 The rupiah rose amid steady money market liquidity though overall activity remained slow. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said the rupiah maintained a bid tone after strengthening to a high of 2,427.0 on Thursday in Singapore and New York while Jakarta was closed for a holiday. 

 Spot rupiah was traded at 2,428.50/29.50 at 0510 GMT against an opening of 2,429.0/30.0. 

 A local bank dealer said the dollar briefly touched an early high of 2,430.0 before it was sold down on weakness in major offshore markets, where players brushed aside the heated campaign for Indonesia's general elections on May 29. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit rebounded on the dollar's fall but a lack of participation kept it confined to a tight range. 

 "Ringgit sentiment for the short-term has changed due to weak dollar/majors," a dealer with a Malaysian bank said. "A lot of dollar selling is expected at above 2.5100." 

 Dealers said the ringgit's upside could, however, be limited due to political concerns after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said he would grant full powers to his deputy Anwar Ibrahim and go overseas for two months later in May. 

 The Singapore dollar showed signs of strengthening beyond the 1.4400 level against the U.S. dollar for the first time in more than three weeks. 

 "Dollar/Sing could come off to 1.4380 depending on how far dollar/yen comes off. The market is still long dollar/Sing and ringgit/Sing," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 He said several stop-loss sell orders for the U.S. dollar appeared to be building below the 1.4410 level. The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4412/22 at 0510 GMT. 

 -- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662-652-0642) and Sonali Desai in Singapore
