title: Bank of Thailand  intervenes  to sell dollars.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuter) - The Bank of Thailand intervened in Singapore foreign exchange markets on Friday to sell dollars at 26.025 baht after the Thai unit came under intense pressure on rumours it denied of a band widening, dealers said. 

 The baht was quoted at 26.012/26.017 to the dollar at 0330 GMT after falling as low as 26.090 earlier, dealers said. 

 They said the Thai central bank had also intervened earlier in the swap market, offering the six-month and one-year swaps. 

 The rumours, that the Thai central bank planned to widen the dollar/baht trading band, emerged in London markets overnight and prompted a sell-off in the baht. 

 "A lot of U.S. investment houses were trying to attack the baht and buy dollars yesterday and it's been quite hectic today as well," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said the baht had calmed down somewhat after the central bank's denial of the rumour and its intervention. But the currency was still trading well above Friday's mid-rate of 25.99 per dollar. 

 "We should trade between 26.000 and 26.030 for the rest of the day," another dealer said. 

 Paiboon Kittisrikangwan, the central bank's division chief in charge of money and foreign exchange markets, told Reuters the Bank of Thailand had no plan to change the exchange rate mechanism. 

 "Rumours about any change in the exchange rate mechanism, including band-widening, are utter nonsense," he said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah stable as new year begins.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 1 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah made a slow start to the new financial year on Tuesday, remaining steady amid flush liquidity after a four-day break. 

 Dealers said trading was slow, with some Japanese players establishing new positions by selling outrights. 

 "There is not much activity except some players trying to pull April 1 hoaxes that the central bank would hold a press conference this afternoon," a dealer in Singapore said. 

 Bank Indonesia said there was no press conference scheduled on Tuesday. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said earlier rumours of a band widening after the financial year end had failed to materialise and the market was largely neutral. 

 Dealers said there was some light selling in dollars but it could also be attributable to operators establishing fresh positions with the start of a new fiscal year. 

 "I hear some Japanese names in the market opening new positions but volumes are not significant," one said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,400.00/1.00 at 0400 GMT against an opening of 2,400.50/1.50. 

 In Malaysia, fresh buying by Japanese and U.S funds boosted the ringgit. 

 "Funds are selling both dollar/Sing and dollar/ringgit," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 He said this was part of the traditional Japanese funds outflow into Southeast Asian currencies at the beginning of their new financial year on April 1. 

 "This should continue through this month. But it will be matched, I think, by Malaysian corporate demand for the dollar," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said Malaysia was expected to buy a Boeing 777 this month and also raise funds for the Bakun hydroelectric project in the eastern Sarawak state. 

 Further south, the Singapore dollar firmed as U.S. names sold the U.S. unit and players remained wary of pushing the Singapore dollar down after the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened for the first time in months last week. 

 "I think dollar/Sing should be sold on rallies for it to come down to 1.4300 before seeing new highs. This is just a correction after it was overbought to 1.4520/30," said a European bank dealer. 

 She said dollar/Sing was likely to be supported around 1.4410 for the day and face resistance at 1.4450/55 and 1.4480. 

 The Singapore dollar dropped to an 18-month low last week on heavy selling by offshore funds following reports, later denied, that Malaysia had decided to freeze new ties with Singapore. 

 The Thai baht firmed on the dollar's decline against major currencies but ample domestic liquidity continued to prevent strong gains in the baht. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.955-25.960 to the dollar at 0400 GMT against 25.976-25.981 on Monday. The Bank of Thailand fixed the mid-rate at 25.96 against 25.97 on Monday. 

 The overnight interbank rate edged higher to 7.50-8.00 percent early from 5.75-6.00 late on Monday on higher demand for funds, dealers said. 

 But they said any upside in the interbank rate would be curbed by the entry of Government Pension Funds (GPF) worth a total of about 80 billion baht ($3 billion) launched last week, which will enter the market in stages.

title: Singapore dollar recovers on Malaysia denial.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 27 (Reuter) - The Singapore dollar bounced back in late Asian trade on Thursday as players were heartened by a Malaysian denial of reports Kuala Lumpur had decided to suspend new bilateral ties with Singapore. 

 After falling to an 18-month low of 1.4528/30 against the U.S. dollar overnight after news reports said the Malaysian cabinet had decided to freeze ties with its neighbour, the Singapore dollar rebounded sharply to 1.4425/35 in late trade. 

 Dealers said the currency was boosted after lunch by a Malaysian government statement that no decision had been made to freeze ties with Singapore. 

 "The statements released have been very confusing but it clearly shows there are no thoughts of freezing the ties," said a European bank dealer. 

 The Malaysian news agency Bernama said late on Wednesday the cabinet had decided to freeze new official dealings, including granting of contracts to Singapore firms, over Singapore elder statesmen Lee Kuan Yew's comment that Malaysia's Johor state was "notorious for shootings, car-jackings and muggings". 

 Dealers said talk of U.S. dollar sales by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) near the highs of 1.4525/30 in early trade sparked the Singapore dollar's initial recovery. 

 "Local names were offering good amounts (of U.S. dollars) at 1.4525 this morning and also in London time so it gave the impression that the authority might be behind these offers and made the market very nervous," the dealer said. 

 He said the amount of dollars sold might not have been substantial, but players were deterred from pushing the U.S. dollar higher by the apparent presence of the de facto central bank, which had not been felt in recent months. 

 "They haven't come in and stopped the depreciation of the Sing from 1.4100 to the current level. It's the first time the central bank has been rumoured to be in so it really made the market nervous," he said. 

 He said the Singapore dollar's recovery was also reinforced by stop-loss U.S. dollar sales below the technical support level of 1.4470. 

 "We're testing another low of 1.4420," he said, adding that a breach of that level could take dollar/Sing back down to 1.4370/75. 

 "I think people realise that anything above 1.4500 is very dangerous. And most of the funds who've been long dollar/Sing as well as ringgit/Sing would be happy to take profit at those levels," he said. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar was to hit the 1.4500 level in the medium term as it had been under pressure from heavy fund flows into the higher-yielding Malaysian ringgit since the beginning of the year. 

 The Singapore dollar has depreciated some two percent against the US dollar since the start of the year. 

 Dealers said talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) helped the Singapore dollar recover from an 18-month low of 1.4525/30 to the U.S. dollar in early trade. 

 -- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)

title: Malaysia, Singapore spat hits  currencies .
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, March 27 (Reuter) - The ringgit and Singapore dollar fell sharply on Thursday, becoming the first victims of reports that Malaysia has decided to freeze ties with the island nation, dealers and analysts said. 

 The Malaysian national news agency Bernama's reports late on Wednesday pushed the Singapore dollar to an 18-month low and halted the Malaysian ringgit's steady rise against the dollar, they said. 

 Malaysian cabinet ministers were quoted by Bernama as saying that all official dealings, including granting of contracts to Singapore firms, were being frozen. 

 The row was sparked by Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew's remarks in a court affidavit that Malaysia's Johor state was "notorious for shootings, car-jackings and muggings". 

 But, Malaysia's Works Minister S. Samy Vellu said on Thursday afternoon there was no freeze on deals with Singapore, only suspension of cultural and sports agreements. 

 "The market just reacted to Malaysia's decision. People sold both Sing dollar and ringgit," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 On Thursday morning, the Singapore dollar hit a low of 1.4528/30 a dollar from around 1.44 on Wednesday morning, while the ringgit slipped to a low of 2.4880/85 a dollar against 2.4770/80. 

 A dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore said there was heavy selling from Japanese and Hong Kong-based funds, although the two currencies later found support. 

 They recovered in early afternoon trading, partly on profit-taking and squaring up of positions ahead of the Good Friday holiday, and partly on talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), dealers said. 

 They said the defacto central bank of Singapore was said to have bought the Singapore dollar around 1.4520/25. There was no confirmation available from MAS, which does not usually comment on its currency operations. 

 At 0650 GMT, the Singapore dollar was at 1.4458/68 and the ringgit was at 2.4801/06. 

 "Many U.S funds were selling (dollars) at the high levels and the dollar has also come off against other major currencies, which carried some weight," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. 

 "Dollar/Sing has not seen these levels since September 1995. This is totally new ground," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur. 

 "Now people are talking about 1.46 and maybe 1.47. I don't know, it could go up there. This incident has just helped those who were bullish dollar/Sing," said the U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 But, near-term the statement by Samy Vellu was expected to aid the currencies in a further recovery, he said. 

 "The market will do a reverse if Malaysia announces all is well," he said. The market was uncertain but many felt that given the close economic links, Malaysia and Singapore could resolve the issue, he added. 

 "This rise in dollar/ringgit is inducing Malaysian exporters to come out and sell," said the head of dealing at a European bank in Kuala Lumpur. 

 He said the exporters' perception was to use this situation to sell the dollar, as the ringgit was still headed for higher ground once this issue was resolved, he said. 

 -- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)

title: Singapore dollar seen heading for two-year low.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 20 (Reuter) - The normally unflappable Singapore dollar is set to plumb lows not seen in over two years against the U.S. dollar as the city-state struggles in an export slump and funds flood into the Malaysian ringgit. 

Foreign exchange dealers said the Singapore dollar fell to a low of 1.4443 from just below 1.4400 to the U.S. dollar on Thursday after the government announced an unexpected drop in non-oil domestic exports for February. 

 They said the move put the Singapore dollar, which has weakened steadily since starting the year just shy of 1.4000, firmly on track to 1.4500, a level not seen since February 1995. "The market has been building up for dollar/Sing to test 1.4500 and ringgit/Sing to test 0.5850 for a few months, so we're almost there," said a U.S. bank dealer. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4438/48 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade on Thursday. The ringgit was at a 30-month high of 58.30/36 Singapore cents against 55.37 at the beginning of the year. 

 The Trade Development Board said Singapore's non-oil domestic exports fell 7.9 percent year-on-year in February. A Reuters survey of 16 economists earlier in the week produced a average forecast of a 1.5 percent rise. 

 Dealers and analysts said massive fund flows into the higher yielding Malaysian ringgit, backed by the country's positive economic outlook, were the driving force behind the Singapore dollar's weakness against the U.S. dollar. 

 Daniel Lian, chief strategist, Asian bond and currency, at NatWest Markets, said the market had pushed the ringgit to a level that was technically bullish, helping perpetuate long positions. 

 "In the past few weeks, we have seen another few yards (billions) of long ringgit positions being added to the market both on the ringgit/sing crosses and versus the U.S. dollar," Lian told Reuters Financial Television. 

 He said the exchange rate could consolidate around the 58.30/40 region for a while but an eventual push to 60 Singapore cents was likely this year. 

 Expressions of unconcern by Singapore authorities about their dollar's fall against the U.S. dollar have also contributed to its descent, analysts said. 

 "The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) did not intervene when we were at 1.4300 and now we have decisively broken into territory that nobody expected dollar/sing to be traded to," Lian said. 

 P.K. Basu, director of regional macroeconomics at Union Bank of Switzerland, said sluggish export growth, coupled with subdued inflation, had led to a marginal shift in Singapore's unstated policy of maintaining a strong currency against the U.S. dollar. 

 He said domestic factors as well as the U.S. dollar's strength against the major currencies had led to a "policy response from Singapore authorities aimed at weakening the Sing dollar against the strong U.S. dollar". 

 But Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at research firm I.D.E.A., said Singapore was unlikely to condone any sustained weakness in its dollar. 

 "I think 1.4500 is quite overdone because the government still basically favours a long-term uptrend on the Sing dollar to curb imported inflation," Ong said.

title: Singapore dollar hit by ringgit demand,thin market.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 11 (Reuter) - Flush money market liquidity, thin trading conditions and the Malaysian ringgit's return to favour combined to drag down the Singapore dollar against its U.S. counterpart on Tuesday, forex dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.4160/70 to the dollar in late Asian trade after hitting a low of S$1.4165 against its opening below S$1.4100. 

 A U.S. bank dealer said the Singapore dollar's decline was sparked by a New York-based fund buying into the ringgit/Sing cross in early trade, lifting the rate from an opening 0.5660/65. 

 "I think it was just people going into carry trades again because if you short dollars against the ringgit, you can make on the swap points," he said. 

 He said the original move seemed to be driven by funds establishing new positions but it had caused other players to follow suit. 

 Ringgit/Sing was quoted at 0.5685/91 in late afternoon trade, close to its target of 0.5700, not seen since July 1996. 

 He said the U.S. dollar faced a temporary top around the S$1.4165/70 level, but it could easily reach S$1.4200 within the week. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar's slide was exaggerated by thin market conditions and stop-loss U.S. dollar buying above S$1.4130. 

 "Also liquidity's been very flush today because funds have returned to the system over the holidays so that's undermined some support for the Sing dollar," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International. 

 Dealers said there was no indication of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, despite the domestic unit's relatively steep fall, partly because it was in line with the U.S. dollar's strength against major currencies. 

 They said the market had also gone short on the U.S. dollar before a four-day break to mark the Chinese and Moslem new years on expectations the Singapore dollar would gain sharply as it did during the same period last year. 

 "There was a lot of talk that there'd be a big sell-off in dollar/Sing like the year before. So I think a lot of people squared up their positions ahead of that. Now they're just getting back in and going short Sing, long a high-yielding currency such as the ringgit," said a chief dealer at a Hong Kong-based bank. 

 -- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)

title: ASIAN EXOTICS -Baht hit by dollar rise,weak stocks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 6 (Reuter) - The Thai baht came under renewed pressure from a surging dollar/yen and poor sentiment on the local stock market, dealers said on Thursday. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.971-25.976 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against 25.927/25.933 late on Wednesday. The Bank of Thailand (BOT) fixed the baht/dollar mid-rate at 25.90, its lowest level since June 1990, and against 25.89 on Wednesday. 

 "There were very active bids for dollar this morning. Sentiment on the baht was relatively weak following the stock market plunge yesterday," said a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 The Thai SET Index lost nearly three percent on Wednesday, partly on reports of an interest payment default by a major property company, brokers said. 

 "News on interest payment default by a property firm also triggered concern in the foreign exchange market about positions of commercial banks and finance companies," said another senior dealer at a local bank. 

 "Banks and finance companies have large loan exposure to the property sector," he said. 

 Dealers said the government's reduction of its 1997 trade deficit forecast to 413 billion baht from 595 billion earlier did not help sentiment. 

 A senior dealer with a Thai bank in Singapore said there had been no sign of intervention by the BOT on Thursday despite the fact that the baht was trading outside the central bank's band. 

 "I don't think they will come in until we all go on a long weekend. Without the Hong Kong and Singapore players around, they can determine where they want the rate to be," he said. 

 The Thai overnight interbank rate shot to a new six-month high of 19.00-20.00 percent in early trade due to strong demand for funds for the Lunar New Year and the central bank's reserve requirement on Friday. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar remained weak but had recovered from its low of S$1.4145 to the U.S. dollar after the previous day's sell-off by a large U.S. fund. 

 Dealers said activity was very subdued with most banks preparing to close early on the eve of a four-day break for the Chinese and Moslem new years. 

 "There's buying interest in dollar/Sing at 1.4120 and selling at 1.4140. It'll depend on the dollar/majors, but I prefer the upside," said a European bank dealer. 

 He said there was also a lot of corporate buying interest for the U.S. dollar below S$1.4100 and a breach of the S$1.4150 resistance would put it on track for S$1.4200. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit was similarly afflicted by two-way trading interest and thin market conditions, but dealers said it was likely to remain underpinned by buying interest in the ringgit/Sing cross. 

 "We're capped in a range but it looks like the market is more keen to buy the ringgit/Sing since this is what both central banks want," said the European bank dealer. 

 The Thai bank dealer said the dollar was likely to be well supported at its previous resistance of 2.4900 ringgit. 

 Dealers said the ringgit could be in for some volatility in a thin holiday market. Malaysian banks are closed from Friday through Tuesday for the festivals. 

 "If 2.48 to 2.50 range is broken, a lot of stops would break on both sides," said another European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was relatively stable as activity dwindled in the spot market due to the absence of offshore parties and ahead of holidays in Jakarta. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,376.50/77.00 at 0415 GMT against an opening of 2,377.5/78.0. 

 The Jakarta foreign exchange market will be closed for Eid al-Fitr on February 10 and 11 inclusive, while the stock market will be closed from February 7 to 11 inclusive. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the focus was on the swap market, with foreign players seen heavily short-covering in short-term swaps. 

 "Offshore players are maintaining long dollar positions as they anticipate the central bank might be forced to buy dollars in the near future," said a local bank dealer. 

 He said an intervention from the bank would result in fresh rupiah injection which might drive swap rates down. This would cause players to establish short positions in long-term swaps in advance while covering them with short-term commitments.

title: Singapore Dlr Up But Off Early Highs After Fin Min Comments
text:

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals sag as dollar roars ahead.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 29 (Reuter) - The U.S. dollar's relentless climb to a 47-month high of 122 yen in Asian trade dominated activity in most regional currency markets on Wednesday. 

 The dollar was quoted at 121.83/88 yen in Tokyo at 0445 GMT after rising above 122 yen earlier. 

 Only the typically stoic Singapore dollar stood its ground against the U.S. unit, boosted by a newspaper report quoting the city-state's finance minister saying he expected the currency to appreciate this year. 

 In an interview published by the Financial Times in its Wednesday edition, Richard Hu was quoted as saying some strengthening of the Sing dollar would be desirable to keep inflation down. 

 Dealers said market participants reacted to the report by unwinding long Malaysian ringgit/Sing dollar positions. 

 But they said active buying of the U.S. dollar around the S$1.4060 level by local banks sparked speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, causing players to back off. 

 The de facto central bank typically intervenes in forex markets through local banks. 

 "Some people suspect that our authorities might be down there picking up (the U.S. dollar) because they can't have the Sing that strong either," said a senior dealer at an Asian bank. 

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar was likely to remain above S$1.4060 for the day but would have trouble rising above a large number of sell orders around S$1.4100. 

 "I don't think the article will have an impact over the medium term...the trend of the ringgit/Sing is still higher," said a Japanese bank dealer. 

 He said the cross was likely to stay supported around 0.5620 and face resistance at 0.5660 for the day. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah was also relatively firm as players remained concerned about a possible liquidity squeeze. 

 Some Jakarta dealers said the early liquidity concern was exaggerated. 

 "I don't think liquidity is tight. It's merely that people are rushing to square overnight swap positions which triggered overnight money to increase," one dealer said. 

 A local bank dealer said offshore operators were seen entering the local market late on Tuesday, buying up tom/next swaps to a high 0.65/0.70 points. 

 "But local operators could not square the entire exposure, while some were speculating for a lower rate on Wednesday as overnight money fell to 10.0 percent late on Tuesday," he said. 

 "As everybody moves to cover his short position early this morning, rates are being driven up. I think short-term rates will decline later because there is sufficient supply at present," he added. 

 Dealers said overall sentiment on the rupiah remained firm as operators focused on a possible tightening in the money market on month-end factors, the lunar new year and the Eid al-Fitr celebrations in early February. 

 The local bank dealer said a temporary slowdown in the central bank's rupiah depreciation policy and weekly swap costs of some 3.5 points caused operators to go short in dollars. 

 The Thai baht slid against the dollar as the U.S. unit's surge forced the Bank of Thailand to fix the baht/dollar mid-rate at a 6-1/2-year low of 25.86. It was at 25.81 on Tuesday. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.890-25.895 to the dollar at 0445 GMT against 25.845-25.865 late on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said dollar/baht forward positions were being bought up, partly on concern about some Thai economic data due to be released on Thursday. 

 "With all the buying of dollars, the market needs to unwind its outright positions now. People took these positions early and failed to hedge them. They're now feeling the pinch because what they gain on interest may not cover the loss in terms of the exchange rate," said the Asian bank dealer in Singapore. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit came under pressure from the rising dollar/majors and from players unwinding their ringgit/Sing positions. 

 But dealers said it was unlikely to weaken beyond 2.50 to the U.S. dollar for the day as market sentiment still favoured the Malaysian currency. 

 "I don't see dollar/ringgit going much higher even with the strong dollar/majors...Of all the regional currencies, Malaysia has got the best fundamentals at the moment," said the Singapore-based dealer.

title: Singapore dollar gains seen capped for time being.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 29 (Reuter) - Comments by Singapore's finance minister favouring a stronger Singapore dollar are unlikely to have a sustained impact in the face of a surging U.S. dollar and relatively subdued inflation, economists said on Wednesday. 

 In an interview in the Financial Times' Wednesday edition, Finance Minister Richard Hu was quoted as saying some strengthening of the Singapore dollar would be desirable to keep inflation down. 

 "Some degree of appreciation is desirable from our point of view because we import 70 percent of all the goods we consume," Hu said. 

 The local currency started just below S$1.4100 to the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning and rose to S$1.4060 on the back of the report. 

 But forex dealers said active buying of the U.S. unit by local banks around the S$1.4060 level sparked speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). 

 The MAS, the de facto central bank, typically intervenes in forex markets through major local banks to stem any sharp moves in the domestic currency. 

 The local unit was quoted near S$1.4080 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade. 

 "It was more a knee-jerk reaction. It's just the speculative traders who would jump on this," said a senior dealer at a Thai bank in Singapore. 

 "If the dollar/majors choose to climb like this, they've got no choice but to let the Sing dollar weaken because an ultra-strong Sing would be bad for investment here and for our exports," he added. 

 The U.S. dollar surged to 122.60/70 yen in late Asian trading against a New York overnight close of 120.95/21.03. 

 The Singapore dollar appreciated by a subdued 1.2 percent against the U.S. dollar last year after posting a near-three percent rise in 1995. 

 "As long as inflation is not threatening, (the authorities) would be quite happy to see a stable Sing dollar," said Lim Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. 

 He said inflation was expected to be higher this year than in 1996, but was unlikely to climb above three percent, reducing the need for the authorities to endorse a sharply stronger Singapore dollar. 

 While Singapore's sound economic fundamentals inevitably led to an appreciation of the currency over time, Lim said the scope for such rises looked limited. 

 "Against the background of a surging U.S. dollar, the Singapore dollar will struggle to achieve many gains at the moment," said Desmond Supple, senior economist at independent research firm I.D.E.A. 

 While the Singapore dollar has remained relatively steady against the U.S. unit, it has strengthened sharply against the Japanese yen over the past year, he said. 

 The Singapore dollar's 18 percent appreciation against the yen since the end of 1995 had helped control import prices as Japan is Singapore's largest supplier of imports.

text:

 "Dollar/ringgit came down quite rapidly over the new year and I think those who had gone short want to cover back because they're afraid the central bank might say it's been too rapid a rise for the ringgit," said a Japanese bank dealer in Singapore. He said players were likely to return to the ringgit towards the 2.4850-2.4900 levels.

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar looked supported around S$1.4030/40, where bidding by local banks had generated some talk of central bank intervention.

 The Indonesian rupiah calmed down after a volatile overnight session, which saw it fall sharply in London markets on fears that a much-expected band widening would fail to materialise as the central bank raised its fixing again on Monday. 

 Some dealers said spot rupiah fell to a low of 2,383.0 in London overnight while others said the low was 2,379.0.

 Offshore operators started speculating heavily last Friday that the central bank was set to widen its band.

 The Thai baht slipped in line with the dollar's firmer tone against the majors, but dealers said its weakness was limited by some selling of the dollar.

title: INTERVIEW-UOB sees long way to "international" S$.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuter) - The head of Singapore's United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB), said on Friday he did not expect a speedy relaxation of rules curbing trading of the Singapore dollar on currency markets. 

 UOB chairman and chief executive Wee Cho Yaw told Reuters the Singapore economy was too small to allow active speculation in its currency. 

 "I don't see any benefit to Singapore if the Singapore dollar is internationalised. I don't see the reason for it," Wee said in an interview. 

 UOB has a large treasury operation which is active in a range of regional currencies against the U.S. dollar. 

 But, like its competitors, it is restricted by the size of Singapore dollar loans it can make and is discouraged by Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), from speculating in the currency. 

 The MAS scrutinises all large trades in the local currency and regularly intervenes in the market to adjust its value. 

Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu has said several times in the past year that he plans to gradually relax the rules on international trading of the Singapore dollar. 

 He says he wants to boost the city-state as a regional centre for financial services and also encourage the trading of shares in foreign companies on Singapore's stock market. 

 But he has given no time frame for relaxing the rules and has not said how the MAS plans to do it. 

 Wee said the Singapore dollar, which has appreciated steadily against the U.S. dollar and most other major Western currencies over the past few years, could be vulnerable to manipulation if it were traded freely on global foreign exchange markets. 

 "The Singapore dollar market is so small, if someone manipulated the Singapore dollar I think it would be a big problem. We are not a big economy," he said. 

 He said he thought it would take a long time for the Singapore government to make any changes. 

 Asked how long it would take, Wee said: "I don't know. It is up to the government. But to me it is of no benefit at all." 

 Wee said UOB's treasury activities had suffered recently from volatility in forex markets. 

 "Over the past year I think our forex business was not very good ... I think 1995 was the best. I think 1996 will be worse. There was more volatility in the (forex) market. People were reading it wrongly," he said, but declined to give details.

 But Jakarta dealers said short-term swaps rose on overseas buying, possibly driven by speculation or short-covering ahead of the weekend.

 * Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar confined to range trade with lingering fear of central bank intervention capping Sing dollar's rise. 

SINGAPORE, Sept 6 (Reuter) - The Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah were hurt by devaluation rumours, apparently started by Singapore players in late morning trade on Friday. 

 Dealers said there was little obvious rationale behind the rupiah rumours, but Thailand's looming political crisis, the downgrade of short-term currency debt rating by Moody's and market talk of financial defaults at Thai brokerage houses had made the baht very vulnerable. 

 Desmond Supple, regional economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore told Reuters Financial Television the baht rumour was just the most recent in a stream of periodic devaluation rumours. 

 "The baht's going to remain susceptible to these given that we are seeing a slowdown in short-term capital inflows to Thailand while at the same time, the current account deficit remains high," Supple said. 

 Thai stocks continued to be sharply sold on lingering rumours of financial problems at Thai finance and securities houses, despite denials by the firms themselves and by the Bank of Thailand. 

 Thai stocks fell by 2.27 percent with the index hitting a 35-month low amid forced selling. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said the flight of capital from Thai stocks would keep the baht under pressure. 

 "People are still suggesting buying the dollar because the corporates in Thailand are doing the same thing, so they might know something we don't," said another Singapore dealer. 

 The baht weakened to 25.341-25.346 to the dollar at midday from 25.322-25.332 late on Thursday. 

 In Indonesia, spot rupiah fell to a low of 2,348.75 in early trade. It was quoted at 2,347.25/47.75 at midday against an opening of 2,346.50/47.00. 

 A Singapore dealer said the rumours of a rupiah devaluation were clearly without basis but gave short-term speculators a chance to capitalise on the situation.

 A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said the relatively ample money supply, which kept short-dated swap rates low, also seemed to have created room for speculation on a weakening in the rupiah. 

 "Some offshore players took the chance to speculate on the rupiah because of the cheap swap rates. They have no problem to finance dollar purchases," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit traded in a tight band but was expected to come under some pressure from overseas investors. 

 "Nothing much is happening. There is some pressure on ringgit, but I think it will trade in the 2.4960/10 range," said a foreign bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur.

 Dealers said the presence of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had not been detected despite earlier expectations that the de facto central bank would intervene to curb the Singapore dollar's strength. 

 "This is a continuation of the liquidation of long (U.S. dollar) positions people built up over the last three weeks when the gloomy projections about Singapore's economy started to surface," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International. 

 Tan said the Singapore dollar was also benefitting from weakness in the ringgit/Sing cross as interest rates softened in Malaysia.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Political jitters weigh on baht.
text:
* Thai baht falls on offshore concern about stability of Thai government after third largest party in ruling coalition threatens to leave. 

 * Indonesian rupiah under pressure amid ample liquidity as overseas operators await political developments. 

 * Singapore dollar gives up some overnight gains as players turn wary of possible central bank support for U.S. dollar at S$1.4110/20. 

 * Malaysian ringgit continues decline on dollar short-covering and unwinding of ringgit/Sing positions. 

 SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuter) - The Thai baht fell prey to overseas concern about the stability of the Thai government on Wednesday after the third largest party in the ruling coalition threatened to leave the administration. 

 The baht fell to 25.289-25.292 to the dollar at midday from 25.275-25.278 late on Tuesday. The Bank of Thailand fixed the mid-rate at 25.27 to the dollar against 25.26 on Tuesday. 

 "There are a lot of calls (from offshore) about the political situation," said a swap market dealer in Bangkok. "Buying (of forward dollars) is quite strong, but not panicky." 

 Meetings were being held on Wednesday morning to consider the future of Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's government. 

 "There's been some buying of dollars out of U.S. houses in the morning but nothing much because Bangkok is not really reacting," said a Singapore-based dealer. He said some players in Bangkok felt Thailand would be better off with a different leadership due to the scandals plaguing Banharn's government. 

 Another Singapore dealer said she would favour selling dollar/baht on any moves up to 25.30/32, despite the political doubt, as Thai interest rates still offered an attractive yield. 

 Value added tax payments and outflows of foreign funds due to the uncertainty tightened domestic money market liquidity, pushing the Thai overnight interbank rate to 14.00-14.50 percent in early trade from 13.00-13.25 late on Tuesday. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah lost some ground as local players sold the currency amid high liquidity. 

 "The falls are relatively small as foreign operators are not active yet due to worries of possible political uncertainties," said a Japanese bank dealer. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,340.50/41.50 at midday, compared with an opening of 2,339.00/40.00. 

 Dealers said foreign operators were awaiting outstanding police and court hearings in August involving Megawati Sukarnoputri, the ousted opposition leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party. 

 Megawati, who is to be questioned in connection with the recent riots in Jakarta, has filed a lawsuit against the government and the military for backing a rebel congress which ousted her as leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party. 

 The Singapore dollar gave up some of its overnight gains as traders turned wary of central bank intervention after London players pushed it to a high of 1.4115 to the U.S. dollar. 

 "Even though dollar/Sing is looking soft, it's very tough to sell it at this level," said a European bank dealer, adding that the U.S. dollar was likely to hold above S$1.4110. 

 "This has always been the intervention level so the market gets wary when it reaches here," he said. 

 Although the presence of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had not been clearly detected, dealers said the market would be reluctant to push the Singapore dollar above its overnight high. 

 The MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, tends to intervene to support the U.S. dollar if the Singapore dollar shows signs of appreciating too sharply. 

 "I would favour a sell on any uptick to the 1.4140 region to see it going lower to 1.4100/10," said another European bank dealer. 

 Across the border, the Malaysian ringgit came under further pressure from continued unwinding of the ringgit/Sing cross and a lack of fresh buying incentives. 

 Dealers said the slight fall in local interest rates was also making the ringgit less attractive, especially against the Singapore dollar. Players have favoured the cross for its yield in recent months. 

 The ringgit was at 2.4950/55 to the dollar at midday against 2.4935/45 at close of Kuala Lumpur on Tuesday. 

 "I would buy dollar/ringgit on any dips for a test of the 2.4990 level," said a Singapore dealer, adding that this could provide a temporary cap to the dollar. 

 On the money market, interbank rates were mostly steady but remained under pressure ahead of fresh maturities which are expected to further expand liquidity.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht calms down as rates soften.
text:
* Thai baht firm but activity subdued as domestic interest rates subside following central bank measures to ease liquidity. 

 * Indonesian rupiah holds steady but seen rising as confidence returns among offshore investors. 

 * Malaysian ringgit lacks direction in thin market ahead of May trade data. 

 * Singapore dollar stays encased in recent range as players remain wary of pushing it higher. 

 SINGAPORE, Aug 2 (Reuter) - The Thai baht remained on solid ground but saw limited interest on Friday as domestic interest rates subsided from their recent heady levels. 

 The Thai overnight interbank rate was steady at 13.00-14.00 percent in early trade after falling sharply from Thursday's high of 25.00-26.00 percent following the central bank's measures to ease tight liquidity. 

 "The money supply continues to improve this morning. There are more banks offering funds in the market," said a local bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 The Bank of Thailand injected 10 billion baht into the system through the bond repurchase market and intervened in swap markets in Hong Kong and Singapore to bring down swap interest rates on Thursday. 

 The central bank also said it would allow finance firms and banks to borrow funds from the central bank through guaranteed instruments in the repurchase market. 

 The bank previously only accepted government and state enterprises' bonds as guarantees for borrowing in the bond repurchase market. 

 Liquidity had come under intense pressure in Thailand due to heavy outflows of foreign funds following the central bank's downward revision of its 1996 growth forecast last week. 

 A dealer with a Singapore-based bank said there had been no sign of Bank of Thailand intervention in the swap market on Friday. "People already sold everything yesterday. Once the market has cooled off, I don't think the central bank would come in," she said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah held steady as fears of the recent political turmoil fade, prompting expectations of a renewal of overseas investor confidence. 

 "Offshore operators seem to be reducing dollar holdings. Some may start to establish short dollar positions," said a dealer in Jakarta. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,343.25/44.25 at midday, compared with an opening of 2,345.0/47.0. Its high was 2,342.75. 

 A European bank dealer said the dollar was well supported at 2,340.0 and some operators were seen trying to break the 2,342.0 support level but had failed. 

 "Operators are also looking at this weekend. If nothing major happens, I think we are going to see the rupiah strengthening further," another foreign bank dealer said. 

 Jakarta was calm on Friday morning although troops were still seen guarding strategic points in the city in the wake of last weekend's riots. 

 The stock and foreign exchange markets made a strong recovery on Thursday after fears of a confrontation between troops and opposition activists eased. 

 The Malaysian ringgit continued to track narrow ranges, showing no clear direction in a thin market as players awaited May trade data. 

 "There is virtually nothing happening. No one seems to know what will really move the market," said the head of foreign exchange dealing with a foreign bank in Kuala Lumpur. 

 Dealers said it was widely believed Malaysia would report a trade deficit for May this year. 

 "The trade figures may provide some excitement, but going by past trend, it may be a 'sell on rumour, no action on fact' situation," a dealer with a European bank in Singapore said. 

 Across the border, the Singapore dollar was similarly afflicted by a lack of interest. But dealers said the U.S. dollar would remain well supported at S$1.4130 partly due to a perception that the central bank would support that level. 

 "In the past few days, the market went there (the 1.4130 level) and bounced up very fast," said a dealer with a European bank. She said Singapore authorities were likely to stem an appreciation of the currency due to signs of slower economic growth following an unexpected decline in June non-oil exports. 

 She said dollar/Sing would remain well contained in a range of 1.4130 and 1.4170 for the day.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit ranges, market awaits data.
text:
* Ringgit rangebound but volatility expected as traders await Malaysia release of key February trade data in afternoon. 

 * Singapore dollar seen capped at 1.4000 to dollar where market pegs next Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) intervention. 

 * Baht edges up in profit-taking after Friday panic sales. 

 * Dollar-rupiah trades to bottom of band on tight rupiah liquidity. 

 SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuter) - Regional currencies were traded moderately in the morning but the dollar-ringgit is poised for a volatile afternoon with the release of key trade data today. 

 Malaysian Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told reporters on Tuesday that the country had chalked up a trade deficit in February but added the actual figure would be released when Parliament meets this afternoon. 

 "We've seen a pretty good range of trading in the dollar-ringgit this morning, but everyone is waiting for the numbers," said one dealer with a U.S.bank in Singapore. 

 Dealers have been speculating on a figure of between 500 million and 1.5 billion ringgit after 1.1 billion in January. 

 "Anything outside these figures could see the market move either way," said a regional currency dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore. At 0430 GMT, the ringgit was trading at 2.4935/45. 

 But another dealer in Singapore said, "Whatever the figure, the market seems to have largely discounted it. It is a buy on rumour, sell on fact situation." 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht firmed in early trade on the back of tight liquidity but market expectations are for heavy buying of dollars from the Bank Of Thailand to tighten liquidity and dollar demand from offshore players. 

 Dealers said, however, the baht, which fell on Friday following comments from a central bank official about the standing practice of pegging it to a fixed dollar-denominated basket of curencies, will remain under pressure. 

 "There's still concern over the official's comment," said a dealer with a U.S. bank in Bangkok. 

 The Indonesian rupiah fluctuated against the dollar in active early trading, dealers said, adding that tight liquidity caused offloading of value-today dollars. 

 One European bank dealer said the downside of the dollar appeared to be limited because it was already at the lower end of the central bank's floor rate. 

 "Should the dollar-rupiah dip below the central bank's floor rate, we can expect bank Indonesia to flood the market with rupiah funds,' said one currency strategist's report. 

 The Singapore dollar remains capped at the 1.4000 level against the U.S. dollar, pressured by market expectations for central bank dollar-buying at the level. 

 "For today resistance should be 1.4020/25," said one economist, adding, however, that the MAS may shift its preferred U.S.-Singapore dollar fluctuation band to a highe level at 1.4020/25.

title: Japan/Bilateral Repo Accords -3: HK Welcomes Accord
text:
Hong Kong set up repo agreements with Australia, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. 

 In a statement after the agreement Thursday with Japan, Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong central bank, said, the latest accord 'would enhance cooperation between Asian central banks in their efforts to maintain currency stability. This would also improve liquidity of foreign exchange reserves of central banks.' 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said that entering in the secured agreements with central banks whose credit standings are generally higher than those of the private sector banks would improve liquidity with minimal risk. 

 The Asian monetary authorities have been in close contact since the Mexican peso crisis a year ago prompted them to begin discussing means of providing each other liquidity when necessary to ensure currency market stability. 

 Japan had expressed interest in joining the arrangements but hadn't until now formalized any agreement. In an effort to promote currency market stability, however, it announced an agreement in February with monetary authorities of Hong Kong and Singapore under which Hong Kong and Singapore could intervene in dollar-yen trading in their markets on behalf of the Bank of Japan.

title: Japan signs repo pacts with seven Asian nations.
text:
TOKYO, April 25 (Reuter) - Japan banded together with seven Asian partners on Thursday in a drive to provide liquidity and help stabilise foreign exchange markets in the region. 

 Japan's monetary authorities said they had signed a set of bilateral accords called repurchase agreements, or "repo pacts", with Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, that went into effect on Thursday. 

 The pacts give participants access to immediate cash -- for use to defend their currencies against excessive volatility -- by selling their holdings of U.S. government securities to a pact partner on a temporary basis with a promise to buy them back later. 

 Asian countries began mulling such arrangements after the 1994 Mexican peso crisis raised the spectre of similar speculative attacks on currencies in the fast-growing Asian economies. 

 The dollar jumped after the announcement, trading at just above 107 yen in Tokyo mid-afternoon trade after closing at around 106.56 yen in New York on Wednesday. 

 But currency dealers said that while the pacts would certainly provide some support for the dollar in the short term, they were unlikely to be a long-term factor. 

 "For now, its greatest value is to emphasise the cooperative relationship between Asian monetary authorities," one dealer said. 

 A Finance Ministry official told reporters the arrangements were meant to increase cooperation and were not specifically aimed at boosting the dollar. 

 In November, Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand -- mindful of the potential economic damage that currency volatility can inflict -- signed similar agreements. 

 The Philippine central bank then said it would do so with Indonesia and Singapore, adding to the bilateral accords it forged last year with Hong Kong, Malaysia and Thailand. 

 In February, the Finance Ministry unveiled a pact allowing Japan's central bank to ask its counterparts in Singapore and Hong Kong to intervene on its behalf in dollar/yen trade in their markets, a move that some in the ministry were keen to portray as a step toward closer Asian currency cooperation. 

 Japan's Finance Ministry said in its statement announcing the pacts on Thursday that Japan's monetary authorities believed the latest moves would "further enhance mutual cooperation amongst Asian monetary authorities". 

 Japanese officials have said regional currency mechanisms like the repurchase pacts would be useful supplements to the leading role played by Washington and Tokyo in stabilising the key dollar/yen exchange rate and to that played by the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit brushes aside deficit woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 9 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit was untouched by a sharp rise in the January trade deficit and remained rangebound on Tuesday amid growing market hopes of an interest rate hike. 

 Dealers said the announcement by Malaysia late on Monday of a 1.1 billion ringgit trade deficit in January had little impact as the market was already short ringgit. 

 "The figure was largely discounted by the market. The interest rate hikes are seen as positive for the Malaysian economy," said a dealer with a Singapore bank. 

 Malaysia is widely rumoured to be planning interest rate hikes through a combination of a hike in banks' statutory reserve requirements and open market intervention by Bank Negara. 

 The ringgit was at 2.5320/30 to the dollar at midday against 2.5319/25 at the close of local markets on Monday. 

 The Thai baht eased to 25.273-25.278 to the dollar against 25.247-25.250 late on Friday on a firmer dollar abroad and offshore demand for the American unit, dealers in Bangkok said. 

 Thai money and foreign exchange markets were closed for a public holiday on Monday. 

 "The dollar is about to test 108 yen again," said one currency dealer. "Singaporean banks are actively buying dollars (against baht) this morning to cover their dollar short positions." 

 A daily market commentary by consulting firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore said the baht could suffer following reports that the Bank of Thailand was considering changes to its foreign exchange management system in the face of continuing inflows of short-term capital. 

 The Thai overnight interbank rate rose to 6.25-6.50 percent in early trade on Tuesday from 5.00-5.25 late on Friday on higher commercial bank demand for funds after a long weekend. 

 The Indonesian rupiah edged lower on selling by some Japanese fund managers, dealers in Jakarta said. 

 One U.S. bank dealer said big players seemed to have driven spot dollar up to 2,332.5 from its early low of 2,330.5. 

 "Even Singapore operators are scared of them. They have to follow the big players from Japan," he said. 

 He said there was no fundamental reason for the move but Japanese fund managers appeared to have triggered early dollar buying despite counter selling from local players. 

 Dealers said liquidity was relatively ample but U.S. fund managers seemed to be supporting the rupiah due to its attractive yield. 

 "There is not much direction in the market. The signals are a bit mixed," one said, adding that swap rates were a bit high although liquidity was ample. 

 The Singapore dollar was locked within a 10-point band in thin trade, with wariness of central bank support for the U.S. dollar limiting the local currency's upside. 

 A European bank dealer said dollar/Sing was being supported by commercial buying interest around the 1.4050 level, while sell orders around 1.4060 were capping gains. 

 Dealers said U.S. dollar purchases by local banks, which normally intervene on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), was too light to shift dollar/Sing out of its range. 

 "They are not really pushing the price. I would say they are not acting on behalf of the MAS," said a senior Japanese bank dealer. 

 Rumours that the central bank would step in to support the U.S. dollar on any moves towards S$1.4040 have kept the market from pushing up the Singapore unit in recent weeks.

title: Singapore will not use  currency  to boost exports.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 29 (Reuter) - Singapore, which sees exports growing as robustly this year as in 1995, will not need to manage its currency to stimulate its export market, finance minister Richard Hu said on Friday. 

 In a wide-ranging interview with Reuters Financial Televison, Hu said the contribution of exports to Gross Domestic Product in 1995 was 66 percent, "a shade lower than in 1994." 

 He said that in 1996 the export contribution will be "similarly strong." 

 "Given we don't see a problem of a decline in exports, there is no need to utilise...an exchange rate stimulus," Hu said, speaking just before the launch of RFTV in Singapore on Friday. 

 Hu said Singapore has a completely open economy without capital and foreign exchange controls, and any attempt to keep the Singapore dollar artificially weak to sustain export growth would result in price and wage inflation. 

 "Our policy is to maintain sustainable growth with low inflation," he said, adding that monetary policy has been successful over the last decade and the Singapore dollar has appreciated against most major currencies during the period. 

 "In particular against the US dollar we have appreciated 33 percent," Hu said. 

 The finance minister said Singapore's policy was also not to manage the local currency to support any particular sector of the economy. 

 "(The Singapore dollar) has been floating since we lifted all foreign exchange controls in 1978. The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervenes periodically in forex markets to erase any spikes in exchange rates," Hu said. 

 Hu said Singapore is unlikely to be adversely affected by the growth of other financial centres regionally as it is a "sophisticated financial centre with a full range of sophisticated financial products". 

 In a speech at the launch of RFTV, Hu said as at the end of February this year, 142 commercial banks and 79 merchant banks were operating in Singapore while 20 new fund managers started operations here, bringing the total number to 140. 

 Hu said Singapore's financial industry grew by 7.3 percent in 1995 against 1994. 

 The republic's foreign exchange market grew by 43 percent in daily average volume terms to US$105 billion, maintaining Singapore's position as the fourth largest foreign exchange market in the world. 

 Hu said fund managers in Singapore managed total funds of Singapore $90 billion in 1995, an increase of 37 percent over the S$66 billion in 1994 while the total amount of loans syndicated grew by 15 percent to S$11.5 billion in 1995 from S$10 billion in 1994. 

 The Singapore minister said the location of Reuters regional operations in Singapore was an important contribution to the development of the city state as an international financial centre. 

 He said presently 23 news wire agencies and 19 foreign television, radio and satellite broadcasters have set up bases in Singapore. -- Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)

title: Currency  agreements send useful signal--Hu.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 19 (Reuter) - Recent currency repurchase agreements among some Southeast Asian monetary authorities will send a useful signal to the market, Finance Minister Richard Hu was quoted as saying. 

 In an interview in Tuesday's Straits Times, Hu said the agreements would show the widening pool of ready credit available to maintain currency stability in the region. 

 Hu said the Monetary Authority of Singapore's recent agreement to intervene in the foreign exchange market on behalf of the Bank of Japan was another "small first step" to help maintain an orderly currency market. 

 But the Straits Times also quoted Hu as saying problems arising from the volatility of the yen/US dollar rate should be resolved by Japan and the United States. 

 Hu said there had been no request at a Sunday meeting of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) finance ministers that Singapore or any economy use its reserves to prevent another round of yen appreciation. 

 "There is an understanding among member economies that such an intervention is beyond APEC," Hu was quoted as saying.

title: Singapore Dlr Wallows In Tight Range Vs U.S. Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar wallowed in a narrow trading range against the U.S. dollar Monday, dipping slightly from intraday highs in late trading. 

 The U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.4065 around 0805 GMT, up from an intraday low of S$1.4063 around 0444 GMT, but down from S$1.4070 at its Asian opening. 

 Dealers said trading volumes were thin, with the market looking ahead to Taiwan's presidential election March 23 and its impact on the strained relations with China. 

 A dealer with a German bank said 'big banks have just been playing around inside the trading range' for both the U.S. dollar and Malaysian ringgit against the local currency. 

 'The Singapore dollar is not moving anywhere,' he said. Dealers said the market is still wary of possible Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) intervention around S$1.4050 after the de facto central bank's intervention last month to support the U.S. currency.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit falls on speculative sales.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 11 (Reuter) - Regional currencies were softer on Monday following the U.S. dollar's strong gains after the release of a sharply higher-than-expected U.S. non-farm payrolls report. 

 The dollar gained ground in Tokyo after rising in New York on Friday on news that February payrolls had risen by 705,000, more than double the level projected by economists. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit slid on dollar buying by a large Japanese speculator in early morning Sydney. 

 "The Japanese buying was purely speculative, but it triggered several stops," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 He said the action had ceased in late morning Kuala Lumpur and the ringgit was likely to remain in a range for the day. 

 "The market is looking at the seven percent tender from (Bank) Negara as being indicative that Negara is not going to follow dollar interest rates," said a chief dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia said it intervened in the interbank market to borrow for three-month deposit at 7.0 percent, unchanged from the last time it intervened in response to a massive speculative attack on the ringgit. 

 The Singapore dollar held firm despite the U.S. dollar's rise and a sharp drop on the local bourse following the Dow's plunge on Friday due to the payrolls report. 

 Dealers said the domestic currency was being bolstered by ringgit/Sing cross sales and possible nervousness over China's missile tests near Taiwan. 

 "The residual Sing strength at the current levels is possibly still a part of the Taiwan factor," said the U.S. bank dealer. "But it's hard to justify an investment in the Singapore market where you get neither a return on the money market and a potential downward move in equities," he added. 

 A European bank dealer said Taiwanese funds were more likely to invest in Singapore property than in the foreign exchange or stock markets. "It's the most stable and there's only one way property can go," he said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah dipped amid ample liquidity during early trade but showed little discernible trend, Jakarta dealers said. 

 A foreign bank dealer said some players were seen trying to test the high side of the dollar, but the market had no firm direction with major volume coming from offshore. 

 The central bank kept its intervention rate at 2,303/2,369 and the conversion rate at 2,303/2,347 on Friday. 

 The dollar's firmer tone put pressure on the Thai baht, which fell to 25.230-25.239 against 25.215-25.218, despite tightened money market conditions. 

 The Thai overnight interbank rate rose to 7.00 percent in early Monday trade from 6.50-6.75 late on Friday. 

 "The money supply tightened slightly as some banks were short of funds after the weekend," said one foreign bank dealer in Bangkok. "But I don't think the interbank rate will rise much today. The funds in the market remain plentiful." 

 The central bank fixed the mid-rate at 25.24 to the dollar versus 25.21 on Friday. 

 The one-month swap premium rose to 6.50/7.00 satangs in early trade from 6.25-6.75 late on Friday on talk that the Thai central bank was studying a plan to impose a tax on dollar swap for baht transactions, dealers said. 

 "That talk prompted heavy swap transactions. They think that it is better to buy now to avoid any possible loss if such a tax were to be really imposed," one currency dealer said.

title: Singapore/Budget/Market Impact -2:  Currency  Concerns

Analysts estimate that a cut in the corporate tax rate to 26% from 27% could add 1.5 percentage points to their forecasts of corporate earnings growth of around 18.5% in 1996. 

 The budget will also confirm the strength of state finances. Economists forecast the surplus for the 1996 fiscal year will be near $10 billion (Singapore) against a government estimate a year ago of S$5.75 billion. 

 Yang Sy Jian, economist At Kay Hian James Capel Ltd., said one remedy the government might consider in the budget to offset the 'contractionary' impact of the surplus is to top up individual Singaporeans' contributions to the Central Provident Fund (CPF), a state-run pension fund. 

 The strength of state finances feeds the Singapore dollar's strength against the U.S. dollar, which is a good reason for government to cut taxes, some economists said. 

Intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de factor central bank, propped up the dollar when it dipped below S$1.4000 last week. The U.S. currency has lost 0.6% in value against the local unit since the end of 1995. 

 The U.S. dollar has proved steady this week against the local currency, trading at S$1.4075. 

 Economists noted the MAS, which uses exchange-rate policy as its key monetary policy tool, will be anxious to curb any further appreciation in the Singapore dollar in 1996. 

 Foregoing tax revenue by easing the fiscal burden on companies, and encouraging consumer demand for imports through lower personal taxation - especially when government forecasts inflation to remain a low 1.7% in 1996 - would be ways for government to help curb the Singapore dollar's upward momentum, said UBS Global Research economist Chia Woon Khien.

title: Singapore dealers shrug off  currency  pact with BOJ.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 22 (Reuter) - Singapore and Hong Kong's pact to intervene in currency markets on behalf of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will boost forex liquidity in both centres but do little to keep speculators at bay, foreign currency dealers said on Thursday. 

 "It will be effective for a while. Then the market will get smart to it and realise it's basically all from the same source. These days there's nobody too big for the market," said a U.S. bank trader.

 A dealer with a British bank said the agreement was no different from similar pacts between the Bundesbank and the Federal Reserve, and the BOJ's own agreements with other central banks.

title: Japan  currency  pact amounts to little - analysts.
text:
LONDON, Feb 20 (Reuter) - Hong Kong and Singapore's agreement to intervene on the Bank of Japan's behalf is of limited significance and will only lend modest support to the dollar, financial analysts said on Tuesday. 

 "There is little exceptional or substantive in this agreement," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan. 

 "The Asian central banks have not agreed to use their own reserves to support the Bank of Japan but merely to act on its behalf," he added. 

 He also noted that Japan already has similar agreements with a host of other central banks, including the Federal Reserve, but this did not stop dollar/yen falling below 100.00 last year. 

 But the announcement of the agreement -- coming as it did alongside aggressive BoJ intervention -- did give the dollar a boost, pushing it up two and half pfennigs/yen to around 1.4600 marks and 106.50 yen. 

 "The timing of the announcement was impeccable. Not only was it a holiday but it was when the dollar had fallen to 103-yen and at a time when the market had the potential to move the most," said Jiro Nagato, senior dealer at Sumitomo Bank. 

 Even if the timing of the announcement was aimed at giving dollar/yen a bit of a boost, the Bank of Japan itself was pouring cold water on the idea that the pact was aimed to rein in the yen. 

 A BoJ spokesman said Japan started discussions with Singapore and Hong Kong last year and the decision about the timing of the announcement was made last week and was regardless of market conditions. 

 Analysts said the impact of the BoJ buying and the pact was probably greater than it otherwise would have been because it had got the market speculating about G7 dollar intervention. 

 "Possibly one difference that BoJ intervention through Singapore or Hong Kong will have from intervention through the Bundesbank or Fed is disclosure," said Steve Barrow, economist at Chemical Bank. 

 He said very often when the BoJ intervenes through a G7 central bank the central bank involved is keen to tell the market that it is acting on behalf of the BoJ. 

 "Whether this will be the case when the BoJ go through Singapore or Hong Kong remains to be seen," he said. "If they keep quiet it might keep the market guessing and possibly make the intervention more effective." 

 There was certainly more talk of G7 intervention in the European market on Tuesday with traders speculating about the likelihood of a show of strength. 

 "They missed a golden opportunity late last week to get the dollar higher and now we are in a new lower trading range it will be more difficult to get it higher if they want to," said one trader. 

 "Maybe they will and maybe they won't. It's a tough one to call but people are ready for it and it's been the main topic of conversation in the dealing room this morning," she added. 

 Aside from possible intervention, the market will be closely watching Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to congress. 

 His report on the current state of the U.S. economy is due to start at 1500 GMT and given the current confusion about growth his words will be carefully picked over. 

 "Greenspan cannot be too downbeat about growth prospects but he is sensitive to market concerns and may therefore seek to offer encouragement to easing hopes by again highlighting the real economy's current sluggishness," said Tim Fox, currency economist at Credit Suisse. 

 At 1140 GMT the dollar was 105.68/73 yen and 1.4510/15 marks, having drifted down gently from 106.08/17 and 1.4561/67 at the European opening. 

 It closed on Monday after a quiet session, with most of Asia and the U.S. on holiday, at 103.80/85 yen and 1.4428/38 marks.

title: Forex  pact not aimed at halting strong yen-BOJ.
text:
TOKYO, Feb 20 (Reuter) - Japan's decision to ask other Asian monetary authorities to intervene in the currency market on its behalf was not aimed as a measure to halt the strengthening of the yen, a senior Bank of Japan official told reporters on Tuesday. 

 He said Japanese, Singaporean and Hong Kong authorities started discusssing the cooperative ties last year and decided last week to make the announcement at the beginning of this week regardless of market conditions. 

 He said that a recent shift towards a stronger yen was due to change in the market's view of interest rates. 

 Although the markets had expected interest rates to stay low for some time, recent moves, such as Germany's decision to keep its rates unchanged and Japan's announcement that its economic conditions were headed for a gradual recovery had changed sentiment. 

 He said there was a need to determine whether this shift in the markets reflected economic fundamentals. 

 He added that if this was the case, the central bank would have to accept it. He said he wanted to hear Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments to Congress later today to determine whether the currency trend reflected fundamentals. 

 The central bank was also watching Germany's money supply data, to be released later this week. 

 The official said the currency pact, under which the Japanese central bank will ask Hong Kong and Singapore to intervene in dollar-yen trade on its behalf in their markets, was agreed upon in order to strengthen cooperative ties with Asian countries. 

 He explained that Singapore and Hong Kong markets tend to lead market sentiment, and asking other monetary authorities to intervene for Japan will help in keeping secrecy. He added that another reason was that local traders know their markets best.

title: U.S. hasn't objected to Asian  forex  plan - MOF.
text:
TOKYO, Feb 20 (Reuter) - Japan has not received any objections from the United States or other countries concerning its agreement with Hong Kong and Singapore on dollar-yen intervention, which was announced earlier on Tuesday, a senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official told reporters. 

 The pact allows the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to ask its counterparts in Singapore and Hong Kong to intervene in dollar-yen trade in their markets on Japan's behalf. 

 Earlier, the MOF unveiled a pact allowing the BOJ to ask its counterparts in Singapore and Hong Kong to intervene in dollar/yen trade in currency markets on its behalf, adding that a similar arrangement had existed for some years between Australia and Japan. 

 "You would have to ask the Federal Reserve about their reaction, but we have not received any objections from the U.S." or other countries, the official said. 

 The official also said that the arrangement with Hong Kong and Singapore would increase the effectiveness of Japan's intervention in those currency markets, which previously had to be carried out through private banks. 

 "It does increase the effectiveness of intervention," he said. "Intervention through central banks can be massive and quite effective." 

 The official also said the ministry's Advisory Council on Foreign Exchange would discuss "some possible deregulation" concerning foreign exchange at its meeting set for February 27, including "some regulations with regard to foreign exchange regulations imposed on securities companies". 

 But he did not elaborate, and said he could not predict the outcome of those deliberations at this point.

 The dollar, which fell as low as 103.58 yen on Monday in overseas markets, jumped above 106 yen after the official announcement was made.

 Japan is keen to prevent its fragile economic recovery from being derailed by a strong yen, as it was last year after the dollar dropped to a postwar low of 79.75 yen last April. title: Singapore dollar seen likely to remain safe haven.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 28 (Reuter) - The inflow of funds from neighbouring countries will continue to boost the Singapore dollar this year despite government concern about its safe haven appeal, dealers and economists said at the weekend. 

 "I think the Sing dollar will continue to be the strongest currency in the region," said a strategist at a large U.S. bank, citing Singapore's low inflation rate, large foreign exchange reserves and healthy trade as factors underlying investor confidence. 

 The Singapore dollar's secure position was thrown into relief late last week as investors sold the Malaysian ringgit aggressively against the Singapore dollar due to growing concern over a delay in the release of Malaysia's October trade data. 

 The sell-off, which pushed the Singapore dollar to a high of 1.4165 against a surging U.S. dollar, prompted intervention by the central banks of Singapore and Malaysia. 

 Some dealers attributed the Singapore dollar's gains late last week partly to nervousness about a possible Chinese attack on Taiwan. 

 Economists said uncertainty in the economic or political climate of neighbouring countries would continue to benefit the "Asian greenback", although it was expected to appreciate at a slower pace this year. 

 The Singapore dollar hit an all-time high of 1.39 to the U.S. dollar last April as investors dumped the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah in a panic over emerging economies after the Mexican peso crashed. 

 Soon after the peso crisis, Finance Minister Richard Hu said Singapore would not hesitate to curb sharp rises in its currency prompted by a sudden inflow of funds. 

 "Singapore has attracted its share of safe haven money ... If this persists for any length of time, it causes asset inflation and you got to balance it," Hu said. 

 Most economists said the Singapore dollar would appreciate to about 1.38-1.40 to the U.S. dollar by year end, but there was no immediate consensus on its shorter term outlook. 

 "My guess is that the authorities would be willing to accept a one to two percent appreciation of the Singapore dollar over the course of the year," said Andy Tan, general manager of MMS International. 

 He said the currency's strength over the past three years had helped keep a check on inflation in import-dependent Singapore. 

 But he said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, was likely to intervene if the currency showed signs of rising to 1.35 to the U.S. unit. 

 Tay Mei Yuen, economist at Crosby Securities, said Singapore's slowing growth and concerns about export competitivenes suggested a slower rate of appreciation for its dollar. 

 Tay said the U.S. dollar was likely to reach S$1.38 by the year end and that the Singapore dollar would appreciate by only 0.5 percent on a trade weighted basis. 

 "I don't think the authorities are targeting merely the U.S. dollar, although that is the intervention currency. The U.S. dollar's going up now but the yen is coming down, and Japan is one of our top export partners," she said.

title: George Soros seen behind ringgit sales - dealers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 25 (Reuter) - The shadow of billionaire American investor George Soros was glimpsed behind a continued attack on the Malaysian ringgit in favour of the Singapore dollar on Thursday, forex dealers said. 

 The ringgit recovered slightly after Bank Negara Malaysia intervened to sell the U.S. dollar at around 2.5640 in the morning. It was quoted at 2.5605/15 in late afternoon trade. 

 "There's no confirmation. But I do think it's the only fund with big enough pockets to fly so aggressively in the face of the central bank of Malaysia," said a dealer with a U.K. bank. 

 He said the nature and location of the activity mirrored movements last week, when Soros was also believed to be behind an attack on the ringgit before Bank Negara effectively raised interest rates. 

 The Hungarian-born Soros is considered one of the world's most successful hedge fund managers. 

 The U.K. bank dealer estimated Soros' Quantum Group of funds had probably sold about one billion ringgit over the past two days. 

 The Singapore dollar's status as a safe haven and its relative lack of volatility made it an obvious choice for an investor speculating in Asian currencies, he added. 

 Sentiment for the ringgit has turned bearish due to growing anxiety about Malaysia's trade figures. 

 The Singapore dollar benefited from its neighbour's woes for the second straight day on Thursday, firming to around 1.4168/78 to the U.S. dollar in late afternoon trade, despite the greenback's strong tone against the major currencies. 

 Chia Woon Khien, Union Bank of Switzerland's economist for Singapore and Malaysia, said she would not rule out the possibility of Bank Negara raising interest rates again. 

 "It's understandable that the ringgit would weaken given that the U.S. dollar has gained a lot of ground in the last couple of days. But I don't think they (Bank Negara) like the way the market has been speculating," she said. 

 The ringgit made a sharp but short-lived recovery last week after Bank Negara raised three and six-month deposit rates by an average 25 basis points. 

 Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had not intervened to curb the Singapore dollar's rise on Thursday, but it was expected to step in if the U.S. dollar showed signs of slipping below S$1.4150/60. 

 "There's no really fundamental reason for the MAS to want to allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate in this fashion," Chia said.
