title: Ringgit sales bolster Singapore dollar --dealers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 24 (Reuter) - The Singapore dollar held its own despite the U.S. dollar's sharp rise against the major currencies on Wednesday, as investors sold the Malaysian ringgit in favour of its calmer neighbour. 

Forex dealers attributed the Singapore dollar's resilience and ringgit sales to growing anxiety about Malaysia's delayed trade figures and disappointment over Bank Negara's failure to raise interest rates again. 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4210/20 to the U.S. dollar in late afternoon trade, after firming to 1.4188 earlier. 

 "We have been waiting for the release of Malaysian trade data for a few weeks now. And it really reduces investor confidence if they don't release the figures on time," said the head of global currency trading at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 He said a large European bank had been actively selling the ringgit in the past few weeks, possibly in an effort to transfer funds out of Malaysian stocks to the Singapore bourse. 

 "People really feel that unless (Malaysian interest) rates rise substantially,the ringgit is vulnerable, especially against the Singapore dollar," he said, pointing to Singapore's high current account surplus as a reason for confidence in its dollar. 

 The ringgit staged a sharp recovery late last week after Bank Negara raised three and six-month deposit rates by an average 25 basis points. 

 On Wednesday, the Malaysian central bank accepted slightly higher bids at its borrowing for three-month deposits, but players failed to react to what they saw as a cosmetic move. 

 "It wasn't a big increase. I think the market's looking for a proper increase in the rates," said a dealer with a U.K. bank. 

 But dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, had intervened on two occasions to prevent the Singapore dollar from firming beyond S$1.4200. 

 "They were just putting a bid at the (1.42) figure level. They were not really pushing it up higher," said a dealer, adding that the MAS was expected to provide strong backing for the U.S. dollar at S$1.4180. 

 The MAS's presence is normally detected through activity by one of Singapore's major local banks. 

 Dealers said the U.S. dollar's gains were likely to be capped at around S$1.4250 in the near term, despite its rise against the Deutschemark and Japanese yen. 

 "Singapore enjoys a huge current account surplus and that will always create pressure for the Singapore dollar to appreciate," said Andy Tan, general manager of MMS International. 

 According to the latest figures, Singapore's current account surplus for third quarter 1995 stood at Singapore S5.76 billion, compared with S$4.61 billion in the second quarter. 

 Dealers said selling of the U.S. dollar against the Singapore unit by Brunei's national investment agency had abated by mid-week. 

 -- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)

title: Sterling's surge a mystery to  forex  markets.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuter) - The identity of the trader or financial institution whose purchases of sterling sent the British currency sharply higher against the U.S. dollar overnight remained a mystery on Wednesday. 

 But foreign exchange dealers in Singapore and Tokyo agreed that the impact of the orders was boosted by skimpy Christmas holiday volumes. 

 The pound sterling rose to $1.5595/05 at the close of New York trade on Tuesday, up from $1.5435/45 at Friday's U.S. close. It was quoted at around 1.5555/62 in mid-afternoon in Singapore on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said sterling's rise in New York was propelled by a series of stop-loss buying orders between $1.5450 and $1.5550 in thin market conditions. Stop-loss orders are instructions to buy or sell which operate only when a given price is reached. 

 "At this time of year, it doesn't take a very large amount to move sterling by this magnitude," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 He said the purchases could have come from a trader trying to buy up the British currency before the end of the year, with an eye to selling it off later. But he said sterling was likely to be vulnerable to profit-taking after its overnight rise against the dollar and mark. 

 Tokyo dealers said the rally was probably sparked by speculative buying by Middle East operators, while one U.K. bank dealer said there were rumours of a purchase by Swiss-based funds or Singapore monetary authorities. 

 A local bank dealer in Singapore said it was unlikely that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the city-state's de facto central bank, was behind the sterling purchases. 

 "I don't think the MAS would intervene in sterling. They only come in during the day if they need to, and usually they intervene in the Sing (Singapore dollar) market," she said. 

 Dealers said the MAS tended to prop up the U.S. dollar against its Singapore counterpart when the latter showed signs of strengthening too sharply. Its presence was normally seen through activity by major local banks, they said. 

 The local bank dealer said the purchases could have come from a large hedge fund trying to guard against the uncertainty surrounding U.S. budget negotiations, which have kept the U.S. government partially shut for a second consecutive week. 

 She said sterling had been overbought after Tuesday night's move and was unlikely to strengthen above $1.5620 during Asian or European trade. 

 But a foreign exchange manager at a U.K. bank in Singapore said sterling's move was too small to suggest that an institution or central bank was trying to sell off U.S. assets out of concern about the budget stalemate. 

 "I would not have classified sterling as having a safe haven status. If people were to move out of the U.S. dollar, the first (currency) that would make a big gain should be the Swiss franc. But it has dropped about 30 points since yesterday," he said.

title: INTERVIEW - Singapore comfortable with strong dlr.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 22 (Reuter) - Singapore is comfortable with the appreciation of the local dollar against major international currencies, Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Friday. 

 "For the time being, Singapore is comfortable with the present rate of appreciation," Hu told Reuters in an interview. 

 "It is quite stable this year after a rapid run-up last year," he said. 

 "The value of the Singapore dollar is market driven," he said, adding that it was driven basically by Singapore's strong fundamentals. 

 Hu said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, intervenes only to ensure there are no large fluctuations due to market manipulations. 

 The local currency has appreciated by 2.88 percent against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of this year. It rose five percent aginst the Japanese yen and almost four percent against the British pound over the same period. 

 Asked about the impact the growing strength of the local currency had on higher operational costs, Hu said the government recognised the appreciating Singapore dollar had created some problems for the manufacturing and service sectors. 

 "But there were two sides to the coin," he added. 

 Although a strong Singapore dollar raised the selling price of goods produced locally, it reduced the costs of manufacturing and service inputs, he said, adding that approximately 70 percent of Singapore's manufaturing inputs were imported.

title: U.S. Dlr Flat Vs. Singapore Dlr; Seen In Thin Ranges
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-DJ)--The U.S. dollar has hardly changed against the Singapore dollar from early Asian dealings Friday, after staying in a thin 9-point range. 

 Traders said the lackluster sentiment on the dollar against the Singapore currency continued to persist as it stayed in the familiar range of S$1.4110 to S$1.4150. 

 Market players said they are reluctant to sell the dollar below S$1.4100 for fear of intervention by the authorities. The Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's de facto central bank, was seen recently buying the dollar at S$1.4080-85. Its presence was not noted Friday.

title: S'pore dollar rise capped by  central bank  -- dealers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 10 (Reuter) - Gains in the Singapore dollar are seen capped at 1.41 to the U.S. dollar in the near term due to fear of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), foreign exchange dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.4112/22 against its U.S. counterpart at the close of local trading on Friday compared with the opening of 1.4107/12. 

 The local dollar remained trapped in a very tight range against the U.S. dollar during Asian trading despite the greenback's weakness against major currencies. 

 Dealers said the S$1.41 level is seen as a crucial support for the U.S. unit. 

 A U.S. bank dealer said the MAS was believed to have bought the U.S. dollar when it fell to S$1.4095 in New York earlier this week. 

 The MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, traditionally does not comment on interventions. 

 "As long as dollar/yen remains above 100, I think they might still continue to provide support at 1.41," the dealer said. 

 A European bank trader said the MAS was unlikely to try to push for a higher U.S. dollar. 

 "It is just a smoothening process. They don't want people to get too speculative on either side," the trader said. 

 He said the U.S. dollar's topside is seen at around S$1.42 for the time being. 

 But dealers said the MAS was expected to give up the support level of S$1.41 if the U.S. dollar drops below 99 yen. 

 "If the dollar is really coming down in a big way, I don't think the central bank here will go against market forces," said another European bank trader. 

 The Singapore dollar hit a record high of 1.3912 earlier this year. -- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)

title: U.S. Dlr Down Vs. Singapore Dlr Despite MAS Buys At S$1.4210
text:

As long as the dollar is below 100.00 yen and 1.4200 Deutsche marks, it is going to depress the U.S. dollar against the Singapore dollar, said a dealer at a Singapore bank. 

 Market players said that the Malaysian ringgit is likely to stay in ranges against the Singapore currency in the near term, after big swings both ways since last week. The ringgit is seen holding between S$0.5600-40 in the short term, said dealers.

text:

title: Singapore  Forex  Survey -4: Volume Below Expectations
text:
The volume was below the expectations of many market observers, some of whom had even expected Singapore to overtake Tokyo as the busiest foreign exchange center in Asia. Senior bank executives said the MAS has been citing a figure of U.S.$110 billion as the average daily volume for 1995 up to July. 

 But the Bank of Japan's survey, also released Tuesday, showed Tokyo still far in the lead, with 34% volume growth pushing its turnover to U.S.$161.4 billion in April 1995. 

 In advance of the figures, some traders and economists in Singapore said they were wary of the survey representing the markets accurately because of its timing. Most of the Asia-based trading in the U.S. dollar against the Japanese yen takes place in Tokyo, and the dollar sank to its post-World War II low against the yen during that period amid heavy central-bank intervention, traders noted. 

 Traders also noted that Singapore is a more diversified market. In its 1994-95 annual report, the MAS reported that dollar-mark and dollar-yen transactions made up 27% and 23% respectively of the market's total volume. And senior market observers now estimate that trading in the 'regional currencies' - primarily the Malaysian ringgit, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah - makes up about 20% of market turnover. 

 Speaking before the MAS release on Tuesday, Y.S. Wong, the head of regional financial markets for Citibank in Asia-Pacific, said that, regardless of the volume data, he views Singapore as Asia's most vibrant market. 

 'Singapore no doubt right now is the most active - I don't know about the largest - interbank foreign exchange center in Asia, no question about it.'

title: S'pore will slow its dollar's rise when necessary.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuter) - Singapore will act to slow its currency's rise when necessary, but its basic value is determined by the market, a government minister said. 

 Trade and Industry Minister Yeo Cheow Tong told Parliament: "The Singapore dollar will continue to increase as long as we continue to have strong economic growth...The private sector should bear this in mind when planning business operations." 

 Yeo said the value of the Singapore dollar is determined by the international foreign exchange market. "It would be impossible for the Singapore government to artificially set the value of the Singapore dollar." 

 Yeo said the Monetary Authority of Singapore "will continue to intervene to slow down the pace of the increase when necessary." 

 He said that in the first five months of this year, the Singapore dollar has appreciated by 11 percent against the U.S. dollar but depreciated by five percent against the yen and six percent against the Deutschemark year-on-year. 

 He said the government is making a study on the impact of the appreciation of the Singapore dollar on different industries, which will be completed in several months.

title: S'pore MAS says profits cut by  intervention  - paper.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 29 (Reuter) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) reported a sharply lower profit in 1994 as a result of intervention to check the Singapore dollar's rise, the Straits Times said, quoting an MAS spokesman. 

 The paper said the strong local dollar had also led to a depreciation in the value of MAS foreign currency reserves. MAS made a profit of Singapore $288.20 million in 1994 against S$1.13 billion in the previous year after providing for contingencies. 

 The paper added the lower profit arose from the foreign exchange intervention by Singapore's de facto central bank. 

 In addition, the value of MAS's U.S. dollar-denominated reserves declined over the year when they were converted back into Singapore dollars. 

 Last year, the Singapore dollar rose by about 10 percent against the greenback. 

 The paper, quoting the spokesman, said that given Singapore's strong balance of payment surplus and huge inflows of capital, the currency would have risen even more against the U.S. dollar were it not for MAS intervention. 

 "But the official made it clear the level of trading would not be a constraint on MAS monetary policy," the paper said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Firm as dollar weakens further.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 26 (Reuter) - Asian exotics continue to maintain a firm tone as the dollar continued to be battered by the yen and mark, local forex traders said. 

 "The dollar is in big bad trouble. I think the market was caught long," said the head of regional currencies with a European bank. 

 "The (dollar) plunge is still fresh -- barely 36 hours. We can still see it go lower," he added. 

 The Malaysian ringgit opened firmer against the dollar on offshore demand, dealers in Kuala Lumpur said. 

 "Buying orders are mostly from Singapore and Hong Kong. Interbank dealing is thin," said a local bank dealer. 

 He said given the dollar's bearish sentiment and Malaysia's strong economic fundamentals, the ringgit could test the 2.4500 resistance level soon. 

 However, a senior forex trader with a Singapore bank said the market was still short on dollar/ringgit. 

 "The market is trying to sell dollar/Malay lower. It's going to be pretty much in a range as the market still wants to buy dollar on dips, especially around 2.4600," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar was also slightly firmer against the U.S. unit in quiet trade, said Singapore dealers. 

Intervention by the central bank was keeping the strong local dollar in check at around the 1.3900 level. 

 "The authorities were heard overnight in London and New York at 1.3900. This morning they are here buying dollar/Sing again," said a dealer with a European bank. 

 He said the Singapore dollar would continue to be bid with the U.S. unit drifting lower eventually. 

 The Thai baht also continued to firm against the dollar in early trade hovering around 24.640/650. 

 The midrate was fixed at 24.66. 

 A dealer in Singapore said there was good commercial selling of dollars for the baht. "Some of the money is also going into the Thai equity market. 

 The baht is expected to strenghten further against the dollar ranging between 24.60-24.70 next week, dealers in Bangkok said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah edged higher against the dollar in early trade on active offshore buying of rupiah from Singapore, dealers in Jakarta said. 

 Dollar sentiment remaines weak, but some support is seen at around 2,227.00, said one foreign bank dealer. 

 Another dealer said operators might cover their positions later ahead of the weekend leading to a light recovery in dollars. 

 Dealers expect the spot rate to range between 2,226.00/2,233.00 rupiah next week. 

 One foreign bank dealer said the dollar would be under pressure due to month-end and tax payments factor. 

 "But it might be difficult to break 2,227. It's too close to the central bank's lower limit which was fixed at 2,220.0 on Wednesday," he added.

title: Singapore economy unaffected by strong S$ - minister.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 25 (Reuter) - The recent strengthening of the Singapore dollar against the U.S. currency will not affect the outlook for the domestic economy, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told Parliament. 

 "Overall, the value of the Singapore dollar has remained little changed measured against a basket of currencies of Singapore's major trading partners and competitors," Lee said. 

 "The recent exchange rate movements are thus unlikely to have a significant impact on the Singapore economy as a whole," he said. 

 In the period from March 1 to April 30 the U.S. dollar depreciated by 3.8 percent against the Singapore dollar. In the same period, the Yen appreciated by 10.4 percent against the local currency, Lee said. 

 Lee said among local companies, exporters to the U.S. faced pressure on margins due to the weak greenback, but exporters to Europe and Japan were expected to benefit. 

 "The MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) will continue to intervene whenever necessary against exchange rate movements which are not supported by fundamentals," he said. 

 Lee added that the Government of Singapore Investment Corp (GIC), which manages Singapore's oficial foreign exchange reserves, had not suffered any major losses as a result of the exchange rate movements.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Taiwan dlr plunges, others steady.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 22 (Reuter) - The Taiwan dollar plunged against the U.S. dollar in mid-morning but other Asian currencies were steady in quiet trade, dealers said. 

 The Taiwan dollar tumbled on strong month-end U.S. dollar demand, falling to T$25.9250 after 105 minutes of trade, against Saturday's T$25.7280 close. 

 Dealers in Taipei said Saturday's news of Taiwan's first-quarter balance of payments deficit triggered expectations of more Taiwan dollar falls. "Seeing that the central bank has not entered to stop the rate's plunges as it said it would, month-end U.S. dollar demand just emerged heavily," one said. 

 The Taiwan dollar was quoted around 25.8155/00 at midday. 

 In other currencies, the U.S. dollar's firmness against the yen and mark was seen supporting it against the Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit. 

 The dollar managed to stay above 87.00 yen at midday after a New York close at 86.80/90. 

 The Singapore dollar was quiet and range-bound against the greenback. It opened at 1.3937/40 and firmed to 1.3926 in late morning. At midday it was quoted around 1.3920/30. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said the Monetary Authority of Singapore would probably intervene if the Singapore dollar firmed above 1.3915. 

 "It's a level where they've intervened in the past," he said. The authority does not normallt comment on interventions. 

 The Singapore dollar should trade in a range of 1.3915/70 this week, the dealer said. 

 The ringgit gained slightly against the dollar in thin early trade as players awaited fresh leads before taking positions, dealers in Kuala Lumpur said. 

 "There's some ringgit buying from Singapore but otherwise, not much interest is seen," said one dealer. He said the lack of activity also reflected the dollar's uncertainty against major currencies. 

 At 0415 GMT, the ringgit was trading at 2.4625/35 to the dollar against 2.4655/65 at Friday's close. 

 A Singapore dealer said foreign funds still wanted to sell the ringgit for U.S. dollars. "It's trending softer towards the top of 2.46, but I don't see it coming below 2.4600 for the short term. This week it will probably be 2.4600-2.4700." 

 The Thai baht was marginally firmer against the dollar in active early trading at 24.755-24.765, from Friday's 24.76. 

 But in Singapore trading, "the baht is surprisingly quiet, with nothing going on after last Friday's announcement of dissolution of parliament," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. "The market doesn't seem to be too concerned about the political ramifications. They expect it will be business as usual." 

 The Singapore dealer described the Indonesian rupiah as "pretty dead." 

 "It's been around 2,229 all morning. Liquidity is a touch easier in the market. It's a very quiet morning. There's no discernible trend in anything. 

 "There's still investor interest coming in to sell dollars and buy the rupiah, but because of the easier liquidity situation, the market is tending to support the dollar at these levels. It's basically a Mexican standoff." 

 Rupiah was quoted at 2,228.75/9.50 at midday.

title: Hu says MAS keeps rein on Singapore dollar - paper.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 17 (Reuter) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has been intervening actively in the currency market in recent months to stem the tide of money seeking refuge in Singapore, Finance Minister Richard Hu said in an interview with the Business Times. 

 "Singapore has attracted its share of safe haven money, which of course exerts upward pressure on the Singapore dollar, and the MAS has had to intervene quite actively to support the U.S. dollar, not to allow the Singapore dollar to rise too rapidly," Hu told the paper. 

 However, Hu discounted the idea of having to take drastic action soon to curb the Singapore dollar's rise. 

 "It hasn't reached that point yet," he said. "This is an unusual period because of the yen, but we don't expect the appreciation to continue indefinitely. The main impact isn't on the U.S., it's a Japanese problem," he said. 

 Hu said Singapore has to continue to curb the local currency's appreciation and the consequence of this was that it drives liquidity up and depresses interest rates. If this persists, it causes asset inflation, Hu said, adding that there was a need to balance the two effects. 

 He said Singapore would only use negative interest rates and foreign exchange controls as a last resort because of fears that meddling with such controls may hurt Singapore's reputation as a financial centre.

title: Asian exotics seen doubtful of US dlr 'recovery'.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuter) - Dealers of Asian exotic currencies doubt that the U.S. dollar has temporarily bottomed at around 86.00 yen and are unimpressed with Washington's efforts to drum up central bank support for the greenback. 

 The dollar's longterm weakness "will not change until the U.S. changes monetary policy", said Ian Clague, managing director of global trading at Chemical Bank in Singapore. 

 "The pure fact of the matter is that monetary policy is too lax in the U.S. The Japanese have done what they can to alleviate the strength of their currency, but really the source of the problem is with the U.S." 

 Clague said the U.S. must confront its huge budget and trade deficits in order to put the dollar on the path to permanent recovery. 

 Asian exotic currencies firmed against the dollar, led by a high-flying ringgit, which was buoyed by domestic election news. The ringgit opened firmer and is expected to track a wide range between 2.4900 and 2.5100 today. 

 Dealers in Kuala Lumpur said buying interest was chiefly from offshore interbank players, although corporate buyers were also seen buying the ringgit against the dollar. 

 "I know the ringgit looks like a one-way trend at the moment, but there is some possibility that Bank Negara might smooth the rise," said Clague. 

 The Singapore dollar was locked in at 1.4055/57 early on, but was still within striking distance of its historic high of 1.4030 on March 8. 

 "So far dollar-Sing has not reacted fully to the rise in the yen and the ringgit," said Clague. "I think Singapore interest rates should rise, and the reduction in the volume of intervention by Monetary Authority of Singapore also means there should be less liquidity in the money market."

title: Asian  currencies  firmer, eye on Fed  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, April 3 (Reuter) - Exotic Asian currencies firmed against the U.S. dollar but stayed within tight bands as players waited to see if the dollar's slide would be halted by U.S. Fed intervention in Asian time, dealers said. 

 They said sentiment for the dollar remains bearish despite the moves by the BUBA to cut German interest rates and by the BOJ to support the dollar against the yen. 

 "The main points of interest this morning are (Indonesian) rupiah and (Thai) baht," said Ian Clague, managing director of global trading at Chemical Bank in Singapore. 

 He said the dollar's weakness against the yen and mark prompted a 10-satang increase in the dollar/baht midrate from Friday. 

 For the rupiah, the market is watching to see if Indonesia's central bank will intervene if the currency continues to trade at the top end of its band. 

 In early Thai trade, the baht firmed against the midrate and traded in a narrow band in morning dealings on offshore selling of the dollar, dealers said. 

 Spot baht ranged 24.635-24.640 to the dollar, up from an earlier 24.635-24.655, said a Citibank dealer. 

 The midrate was fixed 10 satang higher at 24.64 to the dollar from Friday when the baht ended at 24.64-24.65. 

 There was some baht traded at value today at 24.62875, he said. 

 The swap market was thin and mainly corporate demand was sending premiums higher, said dealers. 

 Clague said the market interpreted the midrate increase as "quite positive." 

 "That increases confidence in the basket system," he said. 

 For the rupiah, Clague said that central bank intervention could well be triggered at the 2,235.00 level. 

 "On Friday night we were trading above the central bank band, so there was some expectation of intervention this morning, that hasn't happened so far. But it's still a strong possibility, because we're still trading right at the top level of the band." he said. 

 "The forwards are now discounting devaluation of the rupiah of over eight percent next year against an official target that looks like three or four percent. So we may have an announcement of that target and perhaps see some intervention in the forwards," Clague said. 

 In early Jakarta trade, the rupiah hovered below the central bank lower limit following early offshore dollar buying, dealers said. One private bank dealer said Singapore players became nervous after the dollar lost more ground against the yen. 

 "They dumped the rupiah and pushed up spot dollar, which hit 2,235.50 before the Jakarta market opened," the dealer said. 

 But relatively tight money market liquidity urged local banks to unwind their dollar positions, keeping spot rupiah at 2,234.00/34.50 against the dollar at mid-morning. 

 Value tomorrow was last quoted at 2,233.50/34.00. 

 For the Singapore dollar, dealers said activity was quiet, although the unit firmed against the greenback to 1.4088/98 around midday. The Singapore dollar's all-time high, reached last month, is 1.4020/30. 

 The Malaysian ringgit is seen in a range of 2.5200 to 2.5260 on Monday, dealers said. "There is some speculation that the reserve requirements of Malaysian banks might be raised," said Clague. "Bank Negara are looking for ways to reduce their liquidity in the money market, and this would be one way to do it."

title: BOJ has been buying dlrs via Singapore - traders.
text:
TOKYO, March 14 (Reuter) - The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has started using a new method of currency intervention of having a limited number of banks here discreetly buy dollars through U.S. and European banks in Singapore, traders here said. 

 The tactic, which is in addition to ordinary dollar-buying intervention in the Tokyo market, is seen aimed at the banks in Singapore which apparently handle the orders of overseas hedge funds, a major driving force in the foreign currency market. 

 "The method is helping make the BOJ's action less visible in Tokyo, while leaving people here the impression that the dollar's bottom is strangely solid," said a Tokyo bank trader. 

 The BOJ customarily does not comment on its intervention. 

 The central bank has also occasionally bought dollars directly through banks in Singapore, or checked dollar/yen rates as a step preceding intervention, Tokyo traders said. 

 "The BOJ now seems keen to get to grips with the activity of overseas hedge funds, since Japanese investors' influence in the foreign exchange market has waned," said one currency manager. Hedge funds are highly leveraged investment trust funds, generally backed by a number of wealthy individuals. 

 Tokyo bank traders said the BOJ has been using its new method since last week, but volume so far has not been large. 

 The traders said the dollar's plunge against the yen last week apparently prompted the BOJ to adopt the method. 

 BOJ buying through this method tends to take place when the dollar is pushed down after a round of stop-loss sales, they said. 

 The dollar has hovered around 90-92 yen since it plunged to a new global low of 88.75 yen last Wednesday.

title: Asian exotics up on U.S. dlr, but can't catch yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 8 (Reuter) - Most Asian exotic currencies have risen sharply against the weak U.S. dollar, but in many cases they have failed to keep pace with the rising Japanese and German currencies. 

 The strength of the yen and the mark means that on a trade weighted index (TWI) basis some Asian currencies are weakening, giving already strong economies an extra stimulus and raising the prospect of imported inflation, economists said. 

 "If the dollar doesn't bounce back there's definitely a risk of overheating in some Asian economies," said Bernhard Eschweiler, head of emerging markets research at J.P. Morgan in Singapore. 

 The two economies most at risk at present are Singapore and Malaysia, but Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia may also have to adjust economic policies if the the dollar's weakness is sustained, the economists said. 

 The Singapore dollar soared to an all-time high against the greenback to S$1.4040/50 despite sporadic intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), dealers said. 

 The slide in the dollar versus the yen, coupled with a fear of Thai baht devaluation, made the Singapore dollar a safe haven in Asian currencies, said a dealer. 

 The fear of a Thai devaluation "caused a lot of players to cover their short Thai baht (positions) and park their funds in Sing, which has become like a safe haven for the Asian currencies," a dealer said. 

 In Malaysia the ringgit traded to a two-year high against the dollar, cracking the 2.54 ringgit level in early trade. 

 The Malaysian currency rose to a high of 2.5383/93 ringgit in early Asian dealings, spurred by interbank dollar selling from both Singapore and Malaysia, foreign exchange dealers said. 

 The ringgit's key upside target is currently at 2.4800 ringgit, they added.

 They said the rupiah would probably hover around the central bank ceiling, fixed at 2,197/2,227 rupiah on late Wednesday. 

 "The dollar is still considered a safe-haven currency whenever players become jittery with the rupiah," one private bank dealer said. 

 Dealers in Taipei said the plunging U.S. dollar against the Japanese yen and the mark will continue pushing the Taiwan dollar up in the near term despite expected quarter-end U.S. dollar commercial demand later this month. The Taiwan dollar soared to T$26.000 at one stage in early afternoon. 

 "The T$26.00 level is only a short-term resistance for the Taiwan dollar. It will climb over that level sooner or later," said one dealer at a foreign bank. 

 Most dealers did not expect major central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market during the Taiwan dollar's appreciation as a higher Taiwan unit will help to ease domestic inflationary pressure and lower import product prices, they said. 

 "The central bank may buy some U.S. dollars if the Taiwan dollar rises too quickly, but just to smooth the market and not to support the American currency," said a second dealer. 

 The Taiwan dollar may test the next resistance at T$25.80 in the near term, dealers said. 

 In Bangkok dealers expect the Bank of Thailand (BOT) to continue its policy of steadying the rise of the baht against the dollar should the dollar continue to fall in overseas markets. 

 Dealers at both foreign and local banks in Thailand said overseas talk of a baht devaluation was "all rubbish". 

 The baht is expected to range in the high 24.70s and low 24.80s to the dollar over the next week. Today the baht traded 24.73-24.74.

title: FOCUS-SE Asian  currencies  leap as optimism returns.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies leapt on Monday as Indonesia's early efforts to reform its economy in response to a massive IMF-led aid package sparked hopes the region might be headed for a turnaround. 

 Asian stock markets, particularly Hong Kong and Singapore, also benefitted from the rosier mood, rising substantially. 

 The Indonesian rupiah led Asian currencies higher, shooting to a high of 3,240 to the dollar, a gain of more than nine percent from its opening around 3,540/55 after Japan and Singapore said they had intervened to support the rupiah. 

 In separate statements released in Singapore, the two Finance Ministries said the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in Singapore foreign exchange markets with Bank Indonesia. 

Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said in a statement the MAS bought Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar in concert with the other authorities. 

 "Singapore's participation in this joint intervention reflects our confidence in the macroeconomic policies of the Indonesian government," it said. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the operation was "aimed at correcting excessive depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah," and the three authorities would be ready to act again when necessary. 

 Dealers said the rupiah, which opened on an upbeat note, sharply extended its gains after the intervention was confirmed. 

 "The market was already very happy with the package...It was very timely to come in and strike while the iron was hot," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 She said Japan and Singapore had probably intervened in "token amounts" with Indonesia selling the bulk of dollars, but the move caught players off-guard in a market severely thinned by a Japanese holiday. 

 Singapore and Japan said on Saturday they were each ready to extend US$5.0 billion to Indonesia to supplement resources organised by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 Indonesia could receive upto US$40 billion in financial aid from multilateral agencies and individual countries provided it meets strict IMF conditions to rehabilitate its economy. 

 Analysts saw Monday's joint intervention as aimed at curbing a further loss of confidence in Indonesia, especially in the face of Thailand's persistent woes. 

 "I guess regional central banks felt they could have done more in the case of Thailand. They didn't and things got worse, so if they didn't do anything aggressive now, they'd never turn it around," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in Singapore. 

 "Indonesia's case was also slightly less problematic so they were more willing to commit their money and the market was more willing to believe in their commitment," she added. 

 The Indonesian government liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks, some of them linked to President Suharto's family, was welcomed by currency and stock markets. 

 "Indonesia has helped a lot. They've taken firm actions, unlike the Thais," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 In August, the IMF organised $17.2 billion in aid for Thailand and on Monday the Thai baht was the only Southeast Asian currency to fall, plagued by political uncertainties and delays in implementing financial sector reforms. 

 The baht was at 40.90/41.000 to the dollar onshore at 1005 GMT, off a low of 41.00 against Friday's 40.70/41.00. It was firmer offshore at 40.20/40 against 40.60/90 previously. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh came under fresh pressure to resign on Monday as a key coalition partner, former prime minister Chatichai Choonhavan, quit his advisory post. 

 The market shrugged off expressions of confidence in the baht's long-term stability fromFinance Minister Kosit Panpiemras, whot urged Thais to refrain from buying foreign currencies unless absolutely necessary. 

 The Singapore dollar remained near its highs at 1.5525/55 to the U.S. dollar against an opening below 1.5740. Singapore's benchmark stock index ended the day with a hefty 7.83 percent rise to 1,703.95 points. 

 "It looks like dollar/Sing has seen a top at 1.5970. If it rallies to 1.5700/40 now, I'd favour a sell," another European bank dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit surged to a high of 3.2500 against 3.4070/180 late on Friday. 

 Comments by U.S. financier George Soros also fuelled buying of Southeast Asian currencies, dealers said. He told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) he believed the world's financial turbulence was over and called for international regulatory coordination to head off further storms. 

 "What he says goes," said the U.S. bank dealer. 

 The Philippine peso ended up at 35.14 to the dollar against Friday's 35.42 close on gains in other regional currencies and the central bank's early interventions to sell $500,000. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said he would meet commercial bank presidents to discuss ways to cut bank lending rates and reduce volatility in the peso. 

 The Taiwan dollar ploughed new depths, ending at T$31.245 to the U.S. dollar amid widespread expectations of long-term depreciation as the central bank remained out of view. 

 After the market closed, the central bank cited an external index showing the Taiwan dollar had lost too much value, but vowed to let the market determine its exchange rate. 

 The South Korean won ended weak at 969.9 to the dollar against 964.60 on Friday despite central bank interventions. 

 A Bank of Korea official told Reuters on Saturday the battered won would "never, never, never" breach the psychological 1,000 to the dollar level. 

 "That was a dangerous statement. It immediately made the won go to 970 today: never say never," said a Singapore dealer. 

 The Australian dollar received a boost from a firm set of retail sales data, swinging sentiment against a rate cut. It firmed to $0.7129/34 from an early $0.7007/12.

title: Emerging market  foreign exchange  - global snapshot.
text:
LONDON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies were mixed on Friday as the dust began to settle on global markets, though most units looked set to complete the week well off troughs set during the turmoil. 

 Indonesia's financial rescue package, organised by the International Monetary Fund, stole the limelight in Asia. While the rupiah held firm after the announcement, Jakarta stocks reacted negatively. 

 Analysts said the full extent of the international package was yet to be made public, but it now looked likely to exceed $20 billion. 

 "It's pretty clear now this is going to be a massive package," said Carlos Daurignac, emerging markets strategist at Credit Agricole Indosuez. "The danger, however is we get a buy-the-rumour/sell-the-fact reaction from the rupiah and the stock market reaction was worrying in this respect." 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht continued to spiral lower to record lows, but central bank intervention managed to stabilise the South Korean won. 

 In central Europe, the Czech central bank took the market by surprise and raised its key interest rates. 

 The crown was a touch softer against the mark after the hike, but analysts welcomed the move as a pro-active step. It showed the authorities were not willing to depend on foreign exchange reserves alone to defend the currency. 

 The following is a brief snapshot of a selected group of emerging market currency moves overnight. 

 ASIA 

 * Indonesian rupiah firms 1.0 percent against the dollar from Thursday, although still slightly weaker from last Friday. Market concerned about negative stock reaction to IMF package and there are jitters about durability of a wave of new carry trades put on the rupiah in recent weeks. 

 * Final details of IMF package still awaited, but reports show IMF committing $10 billion and Asian Development Bank $3.5 billion. With bilateral deals from Singapore, Malaysia, Japan and Australia, whole package could exceed $20 billion. 

 * Onshore Thai baht spirals lower, down 2.8 percent from Thursday, but off new record low set at 41.97 per dollar. Investors fret about unstable political situation. Thai central bank says it has net foreign currency commitments of $23.9 billion. 

 * South Korean won stabilises, little changed from Thursday and off record low of 984.70 set yesterday. Central bank steps up intervention to sell dollars. 

 * Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar both a touch firmer, while Philippine peso and Indian Rupee slightly softer from Thursday. New Taiwanese dollar little changed 

 EASTERN EUROPE 

 * Czech crown a little weaker versus mark despite surprise Czech central bank rate hike, pushing two-week repo rate to 14.8 percent versus 14.5 percent. 

 * Volatile Polish zloty hovering about 2.32/2.35 percent versus currency basket compared with minus 2.12/2.91 percent at the open. Zloty little changed at 3.5000/5200 per dollar, but slightly firmer at 2.0245/10 per mark from Thursday's close. 

 * Hungarian forint opens unchanged versus basket at 1.90 percent above parity, slightly firmer versus mark at 112.83. 

 * Slovak crown softer at 0.3 below parity versus target basket compared with 0.02 percent on Thursday. Little changed versus mark 

 * Russian rouble firmer versus dollar from Thursday at 5900/5905 Russian central bank official said rouble liquidity on interbank market fell sharply on Friday as speculative hard currency demand dried up. 

 LATIN AMERICA 

 * Mexican peso rises 3.1 percent from Thursday's close amid easing in global market turbulence 

 * Brazilian real firmer at 1.1015/40 per dollar after speculative pressure Thursday forced central bank to almost double its key monthly interest rate to defend currency. Government aide said $4-$5 billion spent on defending real this week. 

 AFRICA 

 * South Africa's rand firmer at 4.8150, local dealers cite profit-taking on short rand positions 

 * Kenyan shilling little changed at 63.80 per dollar.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  hold up as bourses dive.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies held their ground for most of Tuesday as the U.S. dollar fell out of favour after Wall Street's historic drop overnight. 

 Wide spreads and thin volumes exaggerated volatility, but dealers said most Asian currencies kept their cool after an expected sell-off on the back of diving regional stock markets failed to materialise. 

 Still, there was little respite for frightened investors as stock markets from Karachi to Sydney reeled from the impact of the Dow's 554-point drop, its biggest single-day point loss. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index, which sparked mayhem in global stock markets last week, ended the day almost 14 percent down after hitting a 26-month low of 8,775.88 while other Asia-Pacific bourses posted drops of between four and 12 percent. 

 The dollar, fragile after the Dow's plunge, fell sharply against the mark and yen during Asian hours, prompting players to reduce their dollar holdings against regional currencies too. 

 "Instead of selling regional currencies due to the fall-off in the stock markets, people were buying them and selling the U.S. dollar instead because the Dow has fallen," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at research firm I.D.E.A. 

 "But we're not sure whether this will be sustainable. We see more pressure building up," she added. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was at 3.4150/250 to the U.S. dollar at 0930 GMT after diving to a record low of 3.4600 earlier. 

 Talk that a large Singapore investment house had recommended buying the ringgit below the 3.40 to the dollar level helped prop up the ringgit, dealers said. 

 "There were good names selling dollar/ringgit at 3.40/41. I think the market's long of dollars," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "I think the topside in the dollar/regionals has been seen. I would prefer to sell on rallies," she added. 

 But others said the ringgit remained vulnerable to further weakness towards the 3.50 level. The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index ended down 6.64 percent to 647.32. 

 The Korean won skidded through a series of record lows, closing at 957.60 to the dollar, the day's lowest permitted level and nearly two percent off Zits previous close at 939.90. 

 Pressure on the won mounted after Moody's Investors Service downgraded Seoul's foreign currency ceiling for short-term debt. 

 The central bank's hands-off stance after it intervened aggressively in spot and forward markets early, to no avail, exacerbated the won's woes, dealers said. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at a 10-year low of T$30.80 against Monday's T$30.510 as players were spooked by stock market sales. 

 The Philippine peso ended slightly higher at 35.15 to the dollar after the central bank sold dollars through the day. 

 Manila traders said the central bank's efforts helped shield the peso from the stock market's traumas. The main share index lost 6.31 percent to end at a new four-year low of 1,740.18. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the bank had asked commercial banks to cooperate in curbing speculation against the peso and to look at ways to lower interest rates. 

 Philippines Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said there was no need to panic over the fall in Asian stock markets, describing it as a "corrective" drop, not a long-term trend. 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered to 3,610/20 to the dollar from an early low of 3,775. Dealers said the central bank was seen checking prices and some said it intervened selectively to smooth rates as it had did in the past few days. 

 Moody's downgrade of the outlook for Indonesia's foreign-currency country ceiling to negative from stable had no sustained impact as players awaited news on an IMF aid package. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5780/95 to the U.S. dollar after touching a low of 1.5950. Dealers said there was talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in the forward market, supporting three-month swaps. 

 "It looks like the MAS is expecting and also accepting a weaker Singapore dollar. I wouldn't be surprised to see it at 1.60 or even 1.62 to the U.S. dollar," a local bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar was helped by a newspaper report that one of Singapore's Big Four banks, Overseas Union Bank (OUB), had raised short-term deposit rates by as much as two percentage points. 

 An OUB spokeswoman told Reuters the bank had not changed the board rates for any of its Singapore dollar deposits. She said the rate rise for short term deposits mentioned in the newspaper report "was a special quotation for a client for a special amount". 

 The Thai baht slipped to 39.10/20 to the dollar onshore against 38.45/38.55 late on Monday as importers sought dollars while exporters held back from selling them in the face of the market turmoil. The baht was at 38.95/05 to the dollar offshore. 

 The Hong Kong dollar dipped to 7.7310/50 to the U.S. dollar from 7.7285/35 five hours earlier as interest rates eased after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) added liquidity to the interbank system to counter pressure on the stock market. 

 Traders said the HKMA offered overnight money at six percent, one-week money at 12 percent and three-month at 13.5 percent. 

 Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said his government was optimistic about the stock market, blaming Tuesday's drop on plunging overseas markets. He also said the Hong Kong dollar was likely to stabilise as currency speculators had retreated. 

 The Australian dollar pulled back from a 46-month low of US$0.6820 as rumours of Reserve Bank intervention unnerved a very short market. 

 The Aussie dollar's rebound helped the New Zealand dollar recover from a three-year low of 0.6145.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  shaky as market looks north.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies trickled lower in subdued trade on Monday as North Asia's nervous markets hogged the limelight. 

 Dealers said players remained concerned about a fresh speculative assault on the Hong Kong dollar despite its relative stability and lower overnight interest rates. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at 7.7280/30 to the U.S. dollar at 0445 GMT against 7.7280/90 late on Friday. The overnight rate was at seven percent compared with Friday's high of 50 percent. 

 The blue chip Hang Seng Index ended the morning down six percent at 10,475.53 as nervous investors unloaded holdings after Wall Street failed to take its cue from a recovery in global stock markets on Friday. 

 "The market seems quite orderly this morning, but I think funds still want to attack the Hong Kong dollar. Look at what's happening to the Korean won," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The beleaguered won dived to a record low of 942.00 to the dollar as heavy speculative dollar buying overwhelmed the central bank's early efforts to stem the won's fall by selling dollars at 929.90 won, dealers said. 

 The won was at 940.10/20 against Friday's close at 929.50. 

 Dealers said worries about corporate debt defaults and foreign fund outflows from the stock market were fuelling dollar buying. The composite stock index was down 2.01 percent to a year low of 537.43. 

 South Korean President Kim Young-sam urged economic ministers to introduce measures to stabilise the financial markets. 

 In Southeast Asia, the staid Singapore dollar saw the biggest move, hitting an early low of 1.5920 to the U.S. dollar after opening near its late Friday levels of 1.5780. 

 Dealers attributed the drop, driven by U.S. hedge funds, to bullish sentiment for the U.S. dollar and weekend reports quoting Singapore leaders. 

 Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew was quoted as saying Singapore had allowed its dollar to go down and wanted it to be at a competitive level. 

 Finance Minister Richard Hu was quoted as saying the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervenes in the market occasionally to prevent wild fluctuations, but lets the market determine the Singapore dollar's level. 

 Dealers and analysts said there was nothing new about the comments but they gave players an excuse to buy the U.S. dollar. "I don't know why the market took this as an excuse, but they're basically quite bullish on dollar/Sing for the time being, ready to take it to 1.60," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5865/85 at 0445 GMT, off its recent low of 1.5970 seen last week. 

 "The bias remains on the upside for dollar/Sing unless the regionals make a strong recovery, and also the Hong Kong dollar," said Alison Seng, an analyst as MMS Standard & Poor's. 

 The Thai baht was steady at 38.45/55 to the dollar onshore and 38.62/72 offshore following the appointment of a new Finance Minister, Kosit Panpiemras. 

 The market largely shrugged off Kosit's promises to try to stop the economy from sliding further by maintaining strict fiscal discipline. 

 But dealers said the dollar's upside looked capped for the time being as the market welcomed the removal of some political uncertainty and exporters were keen to sell dollars at 39 baht. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was weak at 3.3850/900 to the dollar against 3.3700/800 late on Friday, but a lack of fresh factors and fears of dollar sales by Bank Negara's agent banks limited its falls. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was wedged between Jakarta banks' dollar orders around 3,560 rupiah and offers near 3,590/600, as players continued their wait for an announcement about the IMF's assistance package for Indonesia. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad was quoted by the Kompas newspaper as saying he could not say when negotiations would be completed. 

 Dealers said the underlying tone remained biddish for dollars but the IMF package and the threat of possible central bank intervention slowed demand and kept the market cautious. 

 The Philippine peso recovered to 35.150/350 to the dollar after the central bank sold dollars at 35.50 pesos in early trade to curb pressure on the peso.

title: Singapore: MAS To Let Mkt Decide S$ Value - Report

title: FOCUS-SE Asian  currencies  cold to Hong Kong bounce.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies remained downtrodden on Friday as most regional stock markets failed to follow Hong Kong's startling recovery with the same enthusiasm they showed for its descent. 

 The dollar maintained its favoured position against Asian currencies, but its rise was limited by pre-weekend position squaring in a generally calmer market, dealers said. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index ended almost seven percent up at 11,144.34 points, reversing an early drop and regaining some poise after Thursday's historic losses shook markets worldwide. 

 The Hong Kong dollar steered clear of the 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar, believed to be a trigger point for official intervention. It was at 7.7260/10 to the U.S. dollar at 0945 GMT against 7.7065/15 late on Thursday. 

 Overnight rates slumped to a week low of six percent from Thursday's highs of 300 percent after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) was seen lending overnight money aggressively. 

 Hong Kong's Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa voiced confidence in winning the war against speculators. 

 "We are determined to defend the dollar peg," Tung said after returning to Hong Kong from a visit to Europe. "We are trying to beat off speculative attacks on our dollar. We will succeed in that." 

 He said interest rates would remain high only in the short term. The Hong Kong dollar jumped on Thursday as a liquidity squeeze, believed to have been engineered by the HKMA, sent short-term interest rates soaring. 

 Dealers and analysts remained divided on the sustainability of the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar, but most agreed that a complete removal of the peg would further shake confidence in fragile Asian markets. 

 "They may shift it a bit to 8.00 or 8.20 to the U.S. dollar but they won't give it up completely. It's done well for them," said a senior regional currencies trader at a Singapore bank. 

 Hong Kong's peg to the U.S. dollar has been held steady at 7.80 since the link was established in 1983. 

 In Singapore, overnight interest rates came off Thursday's heady levels of 50 percent but remained relatively firm at 10-15 percent. Dealers said there was no sign the central bank was intervening in the spot or money markets after Friday's spike up in short-term rates triggered speculation of intervention. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5800/20 to the U.S. dollar after swinging between a high of 1.5675 and a low of 1.5835. Dealers expected it to head for the long-awaited 1.60 level next week, alongside renewed selling of other regional currencies. 

 The Malaysian ringgit had an even more volatile day, hitting an early record low of 3.4330 to the dollar and later firming to 3.3300 on pre-weekend covering. It was at 3.3725/75 to the U.S. dollar at 0945 GMT. 

 Dealers attributed the early drop to thin market volumes and vague talk that Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had said Malaysians would have to tolerate a dollar/ringgit rate of 3.60. 

 But the dollar's rise was capped by fears of dollar sales by agent banks of Bank Negara Malaysia. 

 The baht slid as Thai markets resumed trading after a holiday that shielded them from the worst of the fallout from Hong Kong on Thursday. 

 But political uncertainties and Standard and Poor's downward revision of Thailand's long-term foreign currency and baht-denominated debt ratings kept the baht heavy at 38.50/60 to the dollar onshore against 37.95/38.25 late on Wednesday. It was at 38.80/90 offshore against Thursday's 37.65. 

 The market was awaiting the announcement of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's new coalition cabinet, but sceptical that it would be able to cure the country's economic ills. 

 The Indonesian rupiah firmed in late trade after the central bank sold dollars to take advantage of the momentum from dollar sales by offshore funds, dealers said. 

 The rupiah was at 3,575/60 but trade was subdued as players remained on tenterhooks for details of an IMF-led assistance package. 

Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said talks with the IMF-led team continued on Friday and an announcement would be made once they were concluded. 

 The Korean won ended weak at 929.50 to the dollar after hitting a record low of 930.00 despite the central bank's efforts to prop it up. Dealers blamed the won's drop on heavy foreign selling of stocks, which saw the composite index down 5.49 percent to 570.91. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at T$30.362 after hitting a low of T$30.550, triggering apparent intervention by the central bank. 

 The market earlier ignored central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong's comment that the Taiwan dollar would rise in the mid-term and would be "reasonable" at T$28.5-T$28.6. 

 "What currency is he talking about?" asked one dealer. 

 The central bank said foreign reserves fell to US$85.752 billion at end September from US$87.793 billion a month before, mainly due to the bank's massive defence of the Taiwan dollar.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - A dramatic week on the Hong Kong stock market, with a savage fall followed by a partial recovery, is the latest development in a string of financial crises across East Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate financial impact in the Philippines, where the overnight rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 14 - Vietnam, bowing to months of pressure on its dong currency, doubles the permitted trading range to 10 percent either side of the daily official rate. 

 Oct 17 - Malaysia presents a belt-tightening budget to try to stop the economy sliding into recession. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. The Hang Seng index plunges 23.34 percent to 10,426.30 by Thursday's close, after 13,601.01 the previous Friday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the U.S. dollar at an official rate of 7.8 to one. After the turmoil in Southeast Asian markets, the heat is on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Oct 24 - The Hong Kong stock market makes a partial recovery, climbing 6.89 percent to 11,144.34, but this still leaves the market 25 percent weaker than it was at the start of October.

title: Singapore Dollar Down But Seen Supported In Short Term
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)-- The Singapore dollar is down against the U.S. dollar in mid-morning trading Friday, compared with its level late Thursday. 

 The Singapore currency fell from Friday's open, tracking the Malaysian ringgit, which dropped sharply on a local newspaper report which quoted Malaysian finance minister as saying no interest rate rises were foreseen. 

 Despite being dragged down by the ringgit's fall, the Singapore dollar's potential to drop further is limited in the short term, say traders. 

 With overnight interest rates on the Singapore dollar still at abnormally high levels following Thursday's liquidity squeeze, market participants are selling the ringgit against the Singapore dollar in order to pick up yield, say traders. 

 Coupled with fear of further Monetary Authority of Singaporeintervention in the spot market or tightening in the money market, the positive carry versus the ringgit is helping to buoy the Singapore dollar, say traders. 

 'If Singapore dollar interest rates stay where they are for much longer, the ringgit will come under serious pressure,' said a trader at a major Singapore bank. 

 At 0250 GMT (10:40 p.m. EDT Thursday) the U.S. dollar is quoted at S$1.5797, up from S$1.5790 at the close of Asian trading Thursday. In the short term, say traders, the U.S. dollar is unlikely to rise above S$1.5850.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Stock market blues hit regionals.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Most Southeast Asian currencies stumbled lower on Thursday as Hong Kong's collapsing stock market triggered shock waves across most of Asia. 

 Declines in currencies were led largely by funds fleeing regional stock markets in the face of enduring pessimism about Asia's prospects for a recovery, dealers said. 

 The normally resilient Singapore dollar led the fray, dropping to a 46-month low of 1.5970 to the U.S. dollar in morning trade before talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) pushed it back up to 1.5850. 

 It firmed further to 1.5740/70 at 0450 GMT. 

 "The Singapore stock market was down nearly 100 pips so a lot of funds were pulling out of the Sing dollar," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 "But then the overnight interest rate went as high as 50 percent and dollar/Sing collapsed all the way from 1.5950 to 1.5860," he said. 

 The benchmark Singapore stock index ended the morning session down 5.43 percent at 1,637.66. 

 Dealers said the MAS was probably behind the money market liquidity squeeze, jacking up short-term rates and making it painfully expensive to run a short position. 

 "Local banks were offering U.S. dollars on the way up above the 1.5950/60 level, but it's more the squeeze in liquidity that's doing the job," the dealer said. 

 He said the Singapore dollar could strengthen towards 1.57 to the U.S. dollar, and possibly head higher in the near term, as the interbank market had been caught long. 

 But dealers said the Singapore dollar was likely to head towards 1.60 and possibly 1.65 in the not-too-distant future. 

 "People realise that Singapore cannot escape the currency turmoil in the region and it may take another three to four months to settle," a European bank dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was held hostage to its neighbour's fortunes, sliding to 3.4150 to the dollar before recovering to around 3.3550/650. 

 "U.S. funds are still buying the dollar. The retracement was shallow, so we should see dollar/Malay testing new highs," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. "It may try 3.45/46 first, but people are already looking at 3.50-3.60." 

 Malaysia's diving stock market and a U.S. investment bank's recommendation to steer clear of regional currencies also did not bode well for the ringgit, dealers said. 

 Sun Bae Kim, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs, said on Wednesday that Asian currency volatility was likely to continue over the near term and advised investors to refrain from "bottom fishing" despite the oversold situation. 

 The key Kuala Lumpur stock index was down 4.70 percent to 696.78 at the midday break. 

 The Philippine central bank sold dollars at 34.50 pesos to prop up the currency after the local stock market lost over four percent. 

 Manila traders said the central bank might have sold about $10 million, taking advantage of a market that was long on dollars. The peso firmed to 34.35/55 against an opening 34.73. 

 The Indonesian rupiah continued to hold its ground in the face of mayhem elsewhere, benefitting initially from a rumour that Indonesia would receive massive financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 "There were rumours that the IMF would extend $25 billion to Indonesia," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Jakarta dealers said the rupiah was also boosted early by overnight U.S. fund buying. 

 The rupiah was at 3,640/50, little changed from its late Wednesday levels of 3,660/70. 

 The Thai baht was subdued at 38.990/39.090 to the dollar in offshore markets against 38.45/55 late on Wednesday. Thai markets were closed for a holiday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar, blamed for the latest crisis in Asian currency markets, rose to 7.6100/50 per U.S. dollar from an opening at 7.7410/20. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) was squeezing liquidity to ward off speculative attacks on Asia's last U.S. dollar-linked currency as the stock market went into a free-fall, losing over 14 percent at one point. 

 The blue chip Hang Seng Index ended the morning down 9.35 percent at 10,549.47 points. 

 Overnight rates shot to 250 to 300 percent by noon, compared with about 6.0 percent on Wednesday morning. 

 The HKMA also said it might levy penal rates on a case-by-case basis to discourage repeated borrowings from its liquidity adjustment facility. 

 The Taiwan dollar shed its early gains, slipping to T$30.350/398 against Wednesday's T$30.211 close.

title: Focus-Thai worries weigh on SE Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies were pummelled to fresh lows on Wednesday as Thailand's mounting political crisis looked set to throttle prospects of an economic recovery before it could even get off the ground. 

 Even the Hong Kong dollar, which has Asia's strongest link to the U.S. dollar, faced growing pressure despite efforts by the territory's officials to shore up confidence. 

 In Thailand, street protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh entered their third day as the baht tumbled towards the 40 level to the dollar in both domestic and offshore markets. 

 It recovered to 38.05/30 per dollar onshore and 38.50/60 offshore at 1015 GMT from lows of 39.80 and 39.90 earlier, partly due to market talk that a favourable candidate had agreed to accept the finance ministry portfolio. 

 Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya's decision to resign after an impending cabinet reshuffle had prompted concern Thailand might not meet the conditions for a $17.2 billion loan package arranged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), dealers said. 

 Bank of Thailand governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi attributed the sell-off in the baht to political factors and said the central bank would let the market determine its level. 

 The cabinet reshuffle is expected to be finalised this week and should show some major changes, a minister with the powerful Chart Pattana Party told Reuters on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the baht's decline might be limited for the time being, but the market remained determined to test the 40 level and possibly push the baht lower. 

 The Malaysian ringgit also caved in to worries about Thailand and lingering disappointment with Malaysia's efforts to address its problems in its 1998 budget. 

 It skidded to 3.43 to the dollar, eclipsing its previous record low of 3.4080, but later recovered to 3.3880/980. 

 Dealers said the central bank might have been checking rates when the ringgit fell through 3.40 and Kuala Lumpur banks were active dollar sellers above 3.41/42. 

 The Singapore dollar slithered to a fresh 42-month low of 1.5885 to the U.S. dollar, over two percent below its Tuesday low of 1.5740. 

 Dealers said the haemorrhaging stock market did not help the currency, with the benchmark index falling 2.23 percent to close at a new year low of 1,731.68. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore was believed to have checked rates and possibly intervened sporadically, but this only smoothed the Singapore dollar's decline. 

 The Indonesian central bank's intervention helped pull the rupiah back to 3,645/55 to the dollar from a day low of 3,700. 

 Dealers said the currency was holding up relatively well as players focused on the outcome of talks between Indonesian authorities and the IMF. 

 Further north, the Hong Kong dollar slipped to 7.7497/02 to the dollar from 7.7475/85 late on Tuesday. 

 Fierce selling of Hong Kong stocks did little to bolster sentiment as the blue chip Hang Seng Index lost a whopping 765.33 points or 6.17 percent to end at 11,637.77, its lowest in 13 months. 

 Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said the currency was backed by huge foreign reserves and sound fundamentals, echoing Financial Secretary Donald Tsang's early comments. 

 Tung said Hong Kong would not pursue a competitive devaluation of its currency amid steep declines in other Asian currencies and that rates may have to rise in the process of defending the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Dealers did not expect Hong Kong to surrender its 14-year peg to the U.S. dollar easily but they noted that defending it would drain reserves. 

 "The pressure is quite immense this time because the stock market is really performing badly...and all the countries around Hong Kong have already surrendered to this pressure," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Taiwan dollar closed firmer at T$30.211 against T$30.615 on Tuesday as investors booked profit on the dollar's sharp rise since the central bank stopped defending the Taiwan dollar last Friday. 

 The Korean won was propped up by the central bank's continuous dollar sales between 922 won and 916 won to the dollar. The won closed at 915.0 against Tuesday's 924.40.

title: Thailand woes send new SE Asia  currency  shockwaves.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Southeast Asia currencies came under renewed selling on Tuesday after mounting political unrest in Thailand, and dealers said they saw no immediate reprieve for regionals yet. 

 "Everyone is buying dollars. They see more downside for most regionals and there is more pain to come," said a dealer with a U.S. institution. 

 Bears took the reigns again on renewed political uncertainties in Thailand after the resignation of its Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya on Monday sparked street protests calling for Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to step down. 

 "The anti-Chavalit protests and demostrations are coming at a bad time when the country is trying to regain investors' confidence. Any resignation is going to send the baht tumbling and regionals as well, due to the close links Southeast Asia has," said another dealer with a U.S. institution. 

 The Thai baht sank to a record low of 38.40 to the dollar in the onshore market as investors offloaded the currency. It was quoted at 38.500/650 at 0955 GMT. 

 In the offshore market, the baht was at 38.650/750. 

 "I think people are just panicking now. They are just buying at any price. I think we should stop around 39 but it is uncharted territory," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 The Indonesian rupiah's upside was capped by the gloom spreading from Thailand. 

 Spot rupiah was at 3,630.00/0.00 against the dollar, a day after the central bank eased rules to improve liquidity. 

 Dealers said the rupiah was mixed as some offshore players absorbed the news by selling dollars, while others interpreted it as a chance for further rupiah weakening. 

 "It's quite a mixed picture. But it creates a two-way market. We see some offshores are cashing out from dollars on anticipation of increased supply due to a cut in the reserve rate," one U.S. bank dealer said. 

 "But others look at the danger of increased rupiah supply which could trigger increased hedging activities. I don't know which factor is going to emerge stronger," he added. 

 Bank Indonesia on Monday reopened its short-term securities (SBPUs) facility and cut foreign exchange reserve requirements for banks to three from five percent. 

 Dealers said the rupiah was capped by the potential outcome of negotiations with an International Monetary Fund (IMF)-led team for an economic aid package. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said on Monday in France that IMF talks with Indonesia were extremely constructive and he hoped for an important deal soon. 

 A bearish cloud continued to hover over the Malaysian ringgit, with dealers expecting it to test 3.4000 to a dollar in the next one to two weeks. 

 "There is still more downside room for the ringgit. The post-budget excitement is over and regional gloom, led by Thailand, has taken over again," said the dealer with a Japanese bank. 

 At 0955 GMT, the ringgit was at 3.3340/9 to the dollar. 

 A survey of 18 dealers and research houses in Singapore and Malaysia on Monday forecast the ringgit to end the year at a median 3.37 to a dollar. 

 The Singapore dollar, typically deemed a safe-haven in times of crisis, fell to a 42-month low of 1.5740 to the U.S. unit. 

 "I see (dollar/Sing) buying from the local boys, the Americans, the inter-bank London parties and even Hong kong funds. Everyone is buying the dollar against the regionals," said a dealer with a foreign institution. 

 Dealers said selling was triggered in the morning out of Sydney on concerns over the extent of Singapore banks non-performing loans (NPLs). 

 Dealers said about S$30-S$40 million could have been sold in Sydney at around 1.5680, the previous year low, and stops were triggered all the way up to 1.5740. 

 Some dealers said there could have been some intervention by Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), buying the local currency at 1.5750. 

 Dealers said the market expects the Singapore dollar to test 1.60 to the greenback within a week. 

 North Asian currencies were not spared the Southeast Asian woes. Hong Kong dollar, South Korean won and Taiwan dollar sank in tandem. 

 The Hong Kong dollar sank under selling pressure and was at 7.7475/85 to the greenback. Dealers said continued weakness on the blue chip Hang Seng stock index depressed the currency. 

 The won reached a historic low of 924.90 to the dollar, triggering two central bank interventions to cushion its plunge. The won was spooked by fears of financial market turbulence following a chain of corporate defaults, bad debt and foreign investors' exodus, dealers said. 

 "The dollar is likely to rise to 930 this month and 940 in november or December. I cannot rule out the possibility of 950 by the end of this year," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 The Taiwan dollar too tumbled against the greenback as investors grew nervous ahead of the summit meeting between China President Jiang Zemin and U.S. President Bill Clinton. The Taiwan dollar was at 30.530/630 to the dollar at 0430 GMT.
