title: Dollar/Sing hit by strong fund buying - dealers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Strong buying of the U.S. dollar against most Asian currencies sent the Singapore dollar on a roller-coaster ride on Tuesday, dealers said. 

 "I see buying from the local boys, the Americans, the interbank, London parties and even Hong Kong funds. Everyone is buying the dollar against the regionals," said a dealer with a foreign institution. 

 At 0850 GMT, the Singapore dollar was quoted at a 42-month low of 1.5740/50. 

 "The market could be caught short. So there is lots of short-covering on the back of the regional currency troubles, especially after the baht eased," said a dealer with a local bank. 

 "Basically, the Sing dollar had been quite strong against the rest of the regionals. I think funds are trying to see if dollar/Sing can play catch up," said a dealer with a U.S. house. Some dealers said there could have been some intervention by Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), buying the local currency at 1.5750 to a dollar. 

 "This cannot be confirmed. But from the way the local banks were selling the dollar against the Sing at 1.5745/50 initially and then at 1.5770/80, there seems to be some support," a dealer said. 

 Dealers said the market expects the Singapore dollar to test 1.60 to the U.S. within a week. 

 "Dollar/Sing is still healthy against the rest of the Asian currencies. Looking at the crosses, ringgit/Sing is at 0.47 but I think it would be more comfortable at 0.48/0.49," said the dealer with a local bank. 

 Dealers mostly shrugged off the strong nominal 15.8 percent year-on-year growth in Singapore's September non-oil domestic exports announced on Monday. 

 "I think we are not looking at fundamentals at the moment. The market just wants to buy the dollars. And the Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) plunge of over one percent gave more momentum to that buying," said the dealer with a U.S. bank. 

 The STII ended 1.32 percent or 23.70 points down at 1,771.22 on Tuesday.

title: Key dates in Southeast Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuter) - Indonesia's announcement on Wednesday that it will seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund was the latest development in Southeast Asia's financial crisis. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 May 16 - Thailand says foreign speculators will have to "pay the price" for their attacks by buying back the baht from the more expensive swap market. 

 Again the Philippines is affected. The overnight rate is hiked seven percentage points to 20 percent and the central bank sells more dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines. There, the central bank had cut the overnight rate in the morning to 12.75 percent from 13 percent. But after the resignation announcement it jacks it back up to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. The IMF backs the move and Managing Director Camdessus says he would recommend the IMF board approve the Philippines' request for an extension of its Extended Fund Facility (EFF). 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Singapore dollar hits 32-month low of 1.4738 to the dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. 

 August 27 - Brunei adds $500 million more to Thailand's bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 2 - A falling equity market helps push the Philippine peso to a record low of 30.90 to the dollar. 

 In Jakarta, the rupiah ends at 3,045. 

 Sept 3 - Indonesia announces measures to revive investor confidence in the country, including scrapping a 49 percent limit on foreign purchases of shares at initial public offerings and a hike in luxury taxes. 

 The package has little impact on the rupiah. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. A controversial measure to ban short selling in 100 key stocks will also be withdrawn. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Sept 22 - The forex market gives its answer to Mahathir. The ringgit tumbles more than two percent to end at 3.1220 to the dollar. 

 Sept 30 - Ringgit fall continues. Mahathir says in Chile that 1998 Malaysian economic growth would slow due to the falling ringgit. It hits a low of 3.2150. 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. Dealers are now talking of the possibility of Indonesia having to go to the IMF for help. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals firm on  central bank  fea.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies regained their footing on Tuesday as traders turned cautious about buying the dollar too aggressively amid growing talk of central bank intervention in very thin markets. 

 Bank Indonesia, which stepped in to sell dollars when the rupiah slumped to an all-time low of 3,850 per dollar on Monday, was believed to have intervened again on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the central bank had sold dollars in small amounts, pushing the rupiah to a high of 3,475 against its opening 3,600/50. 

 But persistent dollar demand from underhedged domestic companies and offshore funds jumping on the bandwagon pushed the rupiah back down to 3,640/50 by 0455 GMT. 

 The rupiah's overnight gains after State Secretary Murdiono said the government would take steps to stabilise the rupiah, while remaining committed to free foreign exchange flows, also helped sentiment. 

 The Philippine central bank also stepped in to prop up the peso as it fell prey to pent-up dollar demand from foreign banks, diving to a record low of 35.981 per dollar. 

 Manila traders said the central bank's dollar sales from the 35.85 peso level helped turn the tide, pushing the peso back up to 34.65/75 by 0455 GMT. 

 The reimposition of a volatility band added to the market mayhem as the peso twice breached its limits before the central bank intervention, leading to trade suspensions. 

 The Bankers Association of the Philippines, which operates the electronic forex dealing system, decided late on Monday to reintroduce the band due to the peso's recent volatility. 

 It calls for a 30-minute recess if the peso moves outside a two percent limit. Upon resumption of trading, the band is narrowed to one percent and trading can be suspended two more times before being stopped for the rest of the day. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit recovered sharply amid rumours in Singapore that the central Bank Negara Malaysia was intervening to support the unit. 

 But Malaysian dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence and most attributed the ringgit's rise to commercial demand and buying of the unit against the Singapore dollar. 

 "U.S. names were said to be buying about $200-$300 million in ringgit/Sing," said one Singapore dealer. 

 Dealers said the market was also plagued by fears Malaysia might implement a two-tier market, similar to Thailand's system, after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for further curbs on currency trading. 

 There was confusion on foreign exchange markets when the format on a Reuters currency quotation page was mistakenly changed early on Tuesday. The changes gave the impression a two-tier market had been created in the ringgit, rupiah and peso. 

 This mistake was subsequently corrected to reflect global consolidated contributions. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from its lows around 1.5470 to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's move, but its gains were capped by buying of the ringgit/Sing cross. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting discussion in parliament, later in the day, about the impact of the Southeast Asian currency crisis on Singapore's economy and whether steps were being taken to address it. 

 The Thai baht showed a firm bias on growing optimism about the government's finance sector reform package, due to be announced on October 15. 

 "It is a very narrow bid and offer, I think people are looking into the future for October 15 and some people think the news will come out positively," a local bank dealer in Bangkok said. Onshore baht was at 36.60/65 to the dollar while the offshore rate was at 35.65/75.

title: FOCUS-Thai baht gleams in S.E. Asia  currency  gloom.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 25 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies lost their footing again on Thursday as persistent demand for cheap dollars from companies and hedge funds thwarted rises. 

 There was no sign of massive selling of regional currencies, but dealers said their failure to extend the gains of the last two days prompted players to reverse track amid continued uncertainty about economic and political developments. 

 The Thai baht alone was insulated from the region's gloomy performance, extending its recent rise as sentiment brightened after the IMF's endorsement of Bangkok's efforts at implementing reforms to help stabilise the economy. 

 Dealers said sentiment for the baht appeared to improve markedly following the World Bank/International Monetary Fund meeting in Hong Kong this week. 

 "Actually there were lots of kind words and positive views about Thailand coming out of that meeting," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Bangkok. 

 The baht was at 35.70/80 to the dollar onshore at 0445 GMT against 36.20/30. Offshore it was at 34.85/95 against 35.15/25. 

 Bangkok dealers said dollar selling by offshore players in the past few days was prompted promptly by market talk that Thai authorities may remove a two-tier baht system soon. 

 The head of regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore said dollar sales were also being fuelled by hedge funds closing outright positions taken in mid-May, when the baht first came under speculative attack. 

 Thailand then tried to defend its currency by separating its domestic baht market from offshore markets. 

 "But the underlying sentiment is still positive for the dollar. Corporates and funds will buy any dip below the 34.50 baht level," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit slid to 3.0610/60 to the dollar from 3.0400/50 late on Wednesday, but dealers said dollar selling interest from companies and hedge funds above the 3.0800 level would limit its decline for the time being. 

 At the same time, the dollar would be well sought on declines towards the 3.00 ringgit level after aggressive overnight buying by hedge funds near 3.02 ringgit. 

 The head of trading at a foreign bank in Kuala Lumpur said sentiment was also affected by rumours that finance firm MBf Capital was in financial trouble. 

 "I think foreigners are using MBf news to buy dollars again," he said. He said the rumour was being used despite clarifications by the central bank and the company. 

 MBf Holdings, the parent company of MBf Capital, called a news conference for 0600 GMT to reassure investors after a run on deposits on Wednesday, triggered by rumours -- emphatically denied by MBf -- the group's chief executive officer had died. 

 The Singapore dollar traded in a subdued range with the focus on the ringgit/Sing cross. It has been weak since falling below the crucial 0.5000 level for the first time last week. 

 "A lot of people are looking at 0.4800 as the medium-term target for ringgit/Sing. But in the longer term, the fundamentals suggest it should be at 0.5200 or 0.5300," the European bank dealer said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped to 3,022/27 from an opening 3,012/17 as ample money market liquidity spurred corporate dollar purchases, dealers said. 

 A local bank dealer in Jakarta said the dollar appeared to be capped by selling out of Singapore at the 3,030 level. 

 In Seoul, central bank intervention in forward markets pulled the won back from a record low of 914.90 to the dollar, but there was still heavy importer dollar demand, dealers said. 

 The Taiwan dollar remained rock solid around T$28.601/602 as market turnover soared on the central bank's intensified defence of it after cutting commercial bank reserve requirements. 

 The central bank said its foreign exchange reserves fell to US$87.793 billion at the end of August from US$88.77 billion a month before. Analysts attributed the drop to the bank's vigorous defence of the Taiwan dollar.

title: Singapore Dollar Drifts Lower Late In Quiet Market
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is fractionally lower against the U.S. dollar in late Asian trading Thursday, compared with its level earlier in the day. 

 But the Singapore currency is stronger against the Malaysian ringgit, as the ringgit slipped against the U.S. dollar. 

 At 1000 GMT (6:00 a.m. EDT) the U.S. dollar is quoted at S$1.5173, slightly higher than S$1.5170 in morning trading Thursday and up from S$1.5165 late Wednesday. 

 Throughout Thursday the Singapore dollar has traded in a tight band against the U.S. currency, with the U.S. dollar ranging between a high of S$1.5185 and a low of S$1.5155, both of which were seen in early morning trading. 

 Trading was subdued Thursday, with most activity consisting of market participants buying the Singapore dollar against the ringgit, said traders.

title: Singapore Dollar Down Mid-AM In Line With Other Regionals
text:

title: FOCUS - Sturdy Singapore dollar turns volatile.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 29 (Reuter) - The chaos rampaging through Southeast Asian markets pulled the usually unflappable Singapore dollar off its perch on Friday, before talk of heavy U.S. dollar sales by oil-rich Brunei brought it bouncing back. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a 38-month low of 1.5375 to the U.S. dollar in early trade as the Malaysian ringgit, the Thai baht and Indonesia's rupiah dived to uncharted depths. 

 But it staged a sharp rebound to 1.4960 in the afternoon on talk the Brunei Investment Agency (BIA) had sold U.S. dollars in large amounts for the Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar -- at 1.40 to the dollar in early January -- was at 1.5050/1.5100 at 0900 GMT and dealers said the currency, long a regional safe haven in times of trouble, was likely to remain volatile. 

 Dealers estimated the BIA had sold at least $200-300 million against the Singapore dollar in thin Friday afternoon markets. 

 A currency strategist at a European bank said the BIA had sold around $150 million through his bank. The extent of the move suggested they had sold far more, probably through a number of channels, he added. 

 "We spoke with them this morning and they seem to be very concerned about the erosion of the Singapore dollar," he said. 

 The Brunei dollar is pegged to Singapore's under a currency interchangeability agreement. 

 "Brunei has always been a net seller of dollars against the Singapore dollar even prior to the (regional currency) crisis," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst at independent research firm I.D.E.A. 

 "But the market was stunned because they don't normally enter in the ringgit," he said. 

 But the move was likely to provide little more than a temporary respite as investor confidence in Malaysia remained badly damaged after Kuala Lumpur's unexpected move on Wednesday to stop short-selling of major stocks, he said. 

 "For Singapore, it's more a competitive depreciation rather than anything else," he said. 

 A surge in Singapore's overnight interbank rate to highs of seven to eight percent, coupled with the speed of the Singapore dollar's recovery, sparked some speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in the market or squeezed short-term liquidity to boost the currency. 

 But most dealers remained unconvinced the de facto central bank would try to defend its dollar aggressively in the middle of regional currency turbulence. 

 "I don't think it's the MAS. The ringgit/Sing is too low and they won't be happy with it continuing to depreciate because then the Sing would be too strong," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The ringgit has fallen to all-time lows against the Singapore dollar, in line with its almost eight percent depreciation against the U.S. dollar in the past week. 

 Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong added to the fray by saying central banks could not control exchange rates if the markets believed currencies were overvalued. That pulled the Singapore dollar off its afternoon highs. 

 "You can't fight the market," Goh told a news conference on the final day of a visit to Japan. 

 He said the Singapore dollar had lost only one percent of its value against a basket of currencies of major trading partners during the regional currency crisis, despite falling five percent against the U.S. dollar.

title: S.E. Asian  currencies  lose more flavour.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 29 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies lost yet more flavour on Friday, with players piling into the U.S. dollar as stock markets crumbled across the region. 

 Rapidly dwindling investor confidence sent the Malaysian ringgit, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah further into uncharted territory. The Singapore dollar hit a fresh 38-month low. 

 Weakness in the Philippine peso, Hong Kong dollar and South Korean won was muted by fears of central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the latest bout of selling was triggered by large U.S. hedge funds dumping the ringgit on growing fears of a trade deficit in July and investor panic after Kuala Lumpur's unexpected move to stop short-selling of major stocks. 

 But they said the malaise had spread as regional stock markets slumped, spurring dollar demand from companies, investors and portfolio managers. 

 The ringgit hit an early low of 2.9650 to the dollar against 2.8840/90 at the close of Asian trade on Thursday -- a drop of almost three percent in less than 24 hours. 

 "People are talking about all sorts of levels for the ringgit now. But I think the closest resistance (for the dollar) is at 3.00," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The ringgit was at 2.9530/80 to the U.S. dollar at 0435 GMT. The Kuala Lumpur stock index fell to a low of 777.96 in morning trade, but staged a recovery to 811.17 at midday, 1.01 points below its previous close. 

 "There's a lot of panic building up and the market's overshooting now. I'm quite convinced that in one month's time, dollar/ringgit will be at 2.75, not at 3.00," a European bank dealer said. The ringgit last traded at 2.75 on August 21. 

 The Thai baht, the trigger for the mayhem in regional currency markets that began in May, was pulled to a new record low of 34.49 to the dollar onshore. 

 "I think it's become a regional factor right now. People lack confidence in the regional currencies, including the baht," a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 Dealers said volatility in regional currencies and continued economic and political uncertainty in Thailand spurred strong dollar demand from importers and foreign loan borrowers seeking to hedge their positions. 

 The baht was at 34.20/30 to the dollar onshore and at 34.15/30 offshore at 0435 GMT. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained below the key 3,000 level to the dollar all morning, hitting a low of 3,070 before tight domestic liquidity prompted a partial recovery. 

 Overnight rupiah rose to 80 percent and overnight swap was hovering around 18/19 points. The rupiah was at 3,005/15 at 0435 GMT against 2,930/35 late on Thursday. 

 The Singapore dollar bounced back from a low of 1.5375 to the U.S. dollar, sparking speculation of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 "There was no real reason for the U.S. dollar to go back down to 1.5250, so as usual the market will talk about the central bank, but we didn't see the usual central bank parties selling," a dealer said. 

 She said buyers would snap up the U.S. dollar at 1.5250 and it could rise to 1.5550. It was at 1.5282/92 against 1.5175/85 at its Asian close on Thursday. 

 The Philippine peso slipped to 30.365/415 to the dollar from its opening 30.30 and Thursday's 30.07 close. 

 Dealers said the central bank offered dollars at the higher level of 30.45 pesos, suggesting tolerance for a weaker peso, but there was no sign of actual intervention. 

 The central bank intervened on Wednesday when the peso fell to a record low of 30.45. It also raised bank liquidity reserves to siphon off funds that could be used for speculation. 

 The South Korean won edged down to 901.90 against Thursday's 901.60 close, but dealers said trade was lacklustre, partly due to fears the central bank would intervene again after doing so repeatedly this week. 

 The normally stolid Hong Kong dollar slipped to a low of 7.7475/85 to the U.S. dollar while overnight interest rates shot up to 10 percent on spillover concerns.

title: Singapore Dlr Up Late Vs U.S. Dlr: Sharp Afternoon Reversal
text:

 Profit-taking in the U.S. currency after at least two or three rounds of suspected central bank intervention, which began in late morning trading, has triggered the Singapore dollar's turnaround, dealers said.

title: S.E. Asian  currencies  show signs of divergence.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 25 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies showed more signs of divergence on Monday as several revived despite the Thai baht being sold down, dealers said. 

 They said the baht eased on mounting perceptions that its international bailout package might not be sufficient and talk of renewed opposition planning for a vote of no-confidence against the government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh. 

 "People are shifting out of Thailand because the country's reserves look bad and its IMF (International Monetary Fund) loan may not be enough to bail it out of its economic troubles," a foreign dealer said. 

 Dollar buying for loan repayments also affected the market and the baht drifted past the key 34 per dollar level to 34.05/15 on the onshore market at 0400 GMT. 

 Offshore, the baht was at 33.550/750 against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the baht would remain under pressure from heavy commercial demand for the U.S. unit to repay foreign loans. 

 Over the past few weeks, weakness in one Southeast Asian currency spilled over into others as the market lumped them together. But that did not happen on Monday. 

 Indonesia's rupiah was seen stable on relatively tight liquidity. Dealers said the market was cautious about selling it as the prospect of tight liquidity loomed with some central bank forward intervention transactions last month maturing soon. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,690/2,700, compared with an opening of 2,685/2,715 on Monday. It touched a high of 2,705 and low of 2,670. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was rangebound with most of the action at midday centred on the ringgit/Sing cross, dealers said. 

 "There's some buying just below the 54 level coming mainly from long-term players," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 The ringgit was at 2.7710/40 to the dollar compared with its close of 2.7640/80 in Kuala Lumpur on Friday. 

 Some dealers said comments over the weekend from U.S. financier George Soros denying involvement in Southeast Asia currency markets, would lend psychological support. 

 Soros also said he believed stability would return soon and that some regional units might be due for a rebound. 

 The Singapore dollar firmed moderately to 1.4968/78, inspired somewhat by its safe haven status in the wake of the baht's slide, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was still vulnerable to selling, but the pace of sales would slacken if markets remained wary of events in Thailand, prompting flight-to-quality buying, they said. 

 In South Korea, the won hit an all-time low despite the central bank's repeated intervention. 

 It broke through 900 to the dollar and then slipped to a new low of 903.80. One Singapore dealer said the central bank was seen intervening around 902. 

 The Philippine peso traded slightly weaker and looked likely to test 30 to the U.S. dollar, but banks were adopting a wait-and-see attitude on regional currency volatility, dealers said. 

 The peso was quoted at 29.880/960 against the dollar. 

 The Taiwan dollar was barely changed with the central bank showing no sign of easing its recent defence. It hovered around T$28.727 to the U.S. dollar, the level at which the central bank has defended it from speculative attack. On Saturday, it closed at T$28.726.

title: Asian regionals stumble as Indonesian rupiah reels.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 19 (Reuter) - Asian regional currencies had another traumatic day on Tuesday with the rupiah under severe pressure, serious enough to prompt a massive rise in interest rates by Bank Indonesia. 

 The rupiah's dive below 3,000 per dollar spurred the central bank into action and dragged other currencies lower. 

 Also under the gun was the Hong Kong dollar where forwards and short-term interest rates shot up amid a mounting belief that a full scale speculative attack on the currency was in the offing. 

 The rupiah's problems began when the authorities last week decided to lift the old intervention bands and allow it to float. With the bands in place onshore companies had felt relatively safe but now they find themselves underhedged. 

 "The locals have come on stream and it's a lot harder to contain locals than it is to contain the offshore players," said Chiang Yao Chye, Head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 "The locals are hedging and in that sense it's real demand and therefore more difficult to deal with, speculators are just in there for a quick buck and they get out." 

 The rupiah regained some lost ground in late business after the rate hikes to 2,890.00 per dollar compared with its day's low of 3,030.00. 

 "So far all we saw were Jakarta names out there," a Singapore dealer said. There was no sign of central bank intervention, he said. 

 It was this kind of seemingly unstoppable pressure which prompted the Indonesian authorities to say enough is enough and rates for central bank certificates (SBIs) were raised sharply. 

 One-week SIBs rose to 20 percent from 10.5, two-week to 22 percent from 11, one-month to 30 from 11.625 and three-months to 28 from 11.5. 

 "If the onshore guys are doing it, it is a cause for concern. You are then going against local demand some of this is obviously commercial in nature," said one analyst, noting that the same thing happened in Thailand when capital controls were first introduced local firms still wanted U.S. dollars so the pressure remained. 

 In Hong Kong, forwards remained firm and short-term rates hit 10 percent plus with the authorities pledging that speculators would be "burned" with high interest rates that would make it too expensive to launch a major attack on the currency. 

 The spot Hong Kong dollar ended firmer at 7.7385 after edging down to 7.7430. Most in the market do not expect a speculative attack to succeed given Hong Kong's access to substantial reserves and the political embarrassment of a devaluation so soon after the handover to China. 

 Also the competitive trade advantage that other Asian countries have got through allowing their currencies to fall does not apply to Hong Kong. 

 It simply does not depend on exports as much as Southeast Asian countries. 

 "Hong Kong is more like a re-import and export hub for China. And most of its competitiveness is in the service industry. The strength of the Hong Kong dollar is not really a dominant factor," said a Singapore based U.S. bank dealer. 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht was still looking weak with the onshore rate down at 32.70 to the dollar compared with Monday's late level of 32.10. 

 The Thai central bank said on Tuesday it would lift the two-tier system "only at an appropriate time and when conditions in the money market are stable." 

 The market still suspects this will be sooner rather than later and has for a long time speculated that when the three month forward contracts put on in mid-May had matured the controls would be lifted.

title: Indonesian rupiah slides, takes others with it.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 19 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies carried on sliding on Tuesday as the Indonesian rupiah dropped through a key level and the hitherto sanguine Hong Kong dollar edged toward the spotlight. 

 The rupiah fell back through the 3,000 to the dollar level on selling by Jakarta players in thin lunch time markets and at 0425 GMT was quoted at 3,010/20 against an opening of 2,960/80. The rupiah briefly touched a low of 3,005 on Monday afternoon. 

 "So far all we saw were Jakarta names out there," a Singapore dealer said. There was no sign of central bank intervention, he said. 

 Dealers said the rupiah had strengthened earlier as U.S. funds booked profits in dollar/rupiah around the 2,990 level and bought the dollar/baht. 

 "The funds believe there are signs Thailand's two-tier market may be lifted and then the onshore market would want to grab dollars from the offshore," said the head of Asian currencies at a European bank in Singapore. 

 He said the cross play in the rupiah/baht had pushed dollar/baht to a high of 32.75 in offshore markets. 

 "The funds probably see more signs of problems in Thailand. The baht behaved quite well after the attack on the rupiah last week, but its current weakness is mainly due to political uncertainty in Thailand," he said. 

 Dealers said the market was nervous about an internal conflict in Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's New Aspiration Party after last week's cabinet reshuffle. 

 The baht was quoted at 32.44/54 to the dollar onshore against 32.05/32.15 late on Monday. It was at 32.65/32.75 offshore against 32.20/32.40. 

 The rupiah fall tipped the Malaysian ringgit over the 2.80 to the dollar level. It was quoted at 2.7970/8020 at 0425 GMT after being sandwiched between dollar bids at 2.79 and offers from Malaysian exporters at 2.80. 

 The Singapore dollar also suffered some spillover weakness from the rupiah, but activity was subdued, dealers said. 

 They said the Hong Kong dollar, Asia's strongest currency peg, was attracting growing attention from speculators. 

 "Once all these regional currencies find a suitable level, the speculators will target the Hong Kong dollar," the European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "Hong Kong's economy is still sound and the stock market is stronger than most in the region. But the market is looking at relative competitiveness and Hong Kong is a big exporter," he said. 

 The continuing weakness of the region's currencies could increase pressure on Hong Kong to abandon its U.S. dollar peg, the dealer added. 

 But Hong Kong was adamant the peg would be protected and speculators who attacked it would be "burned" with high interest rates that would make it too expensive to launch a major operation against the currency. 

 Government chief Tung Chee-hwa said on Monday any speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar was "bound to fail". 

 Hong Kong interbank rates shot up on Monday on fears of a speculative attack. Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) might tighten liquidity to make it expensive for speculators to fund their positions. 

 The Taiwan dollar was weak, but the central bank's continued defence of the T$28.727 level limited its decline. 

 The Taiwan dollar was quoted at T$28.726/727 at 0425 GMT against Saturday's T$28.720 close. A range of T$28.710-727 was expected for the day.

title: Asian  currencies  off lows in London, more pain seen.
text:
LONDON, Aug 15 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies got a brief respite in London trade on Friday after tumbling to new lows in the Far East but foreign exchange dealers predicted more turmoil next week. 

 The renewed slide in Asian units, triggered by Indonesia's decision to move to a managed float system for the rupiah, saw increased trade in the exotic currencies in London after another hectic session in Singapore. 

 The Malaysian ringgit pulled back to 2.7800/7850 against the dollar by 1500 GMT after tumbling on the local market earlier to 2.8210. 

 There was talk of fund profit-taking in the currency, but dealers said they had seen no evidence of rumoured intervention from Bank Negara, the central bank. 

 The Singapore dollar was also off its lows, pulling back to 1.5150/1.5170 after earlier breaching 1.52 while the Indonesian rupiah was sitting under 2,900 after hitting 2,940. 

 But the Hong Kong dollar was fragile, hovering around the key support level of 7.75 to the dollar which dealers said could well fall on Monday, a holiday in Hong Kong. 

 "The market seems to be targeting the Hong Kong dollar as the last peg left in Asia," said one dealer at an Australian bank in London. 

 Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said markets were likely to remain rocky. 

 "We'll probably see more pressure next week. Fundamentals have gone out of the window so it's very difficult to judge at what level the market is going to let these currencies stop," he said. 

 Gregory Cronie, a trader at Indover Bank in Amsterdam, reiterated the view that the economic fundamentals for the rupiah remained strong and did not justify current weakness. 

 But he said there were concerns that Indonesian corporates with foreign loans had been caught short of dollars following this week's currency plunge, adding further uncertainty to the market mix.

title: FOCUS - Ringgit hits weakest level since flotation.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit took a fresh beating on Friday, hitting its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the currency was officially floated in 1973, dealers said. 

 Fresh speculative selling out of Singapore pushed the currency to a record low of 2.8250 to a dollar, dealers said. It had recovered to 2.8000/50 by 0635 GMT. 

 Dealers said the weakness in the Indonesian rupiah has spilled over to the ringgit. 

 The rupiah dropped to a record low of 2,890 to the dollar on Friday after the central Bank of Indonesia allowed it float the day before. 

 Dealers said thin market liquidity had made it easier to push the dollar/ringgit across the key psychological level of 2.8000. 

 "Most of the selling came out of Singapore. Volume is thin which makes it easy to move the market," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 "For now, it is likely that some players who were already long on the dollar may want to take some profits which may see the dollar/ringgit back to 2.8000 over the short term," said another Singapore dealer. 

 Talk of intervention by the central Bank Negara Malaysia at around 2.7910 earlier in the day could not be confirmed. 

 Dealers said the worst may not be over as regional currencies remained under pressure. 

 "So long as the regional crisis is not over, weakness will remain," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. "European players are likely to react when they enter later." 

 The ringgit, like the Thai baht, the Philippine peso and the rupiah, has been hit by speculative attacks over the past month. It has lost nearly 13 percent of its value. 

 Technically, the ringgit is seen heading for 2.8385 with support for the dollar seen at 2.7950, dealers said.

title: S.E. Asia  currencies  hit again after rupiah float.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah dropped to a new low on Friday after its effective float and brought other Southeast Asian currencies down with it. 

 The rupiah quickly lost an early firmness and fell to a record low of 2,890 to the dollar as overnight rates dropped back to 30 percent from an early high of 125 percent. 

 At 0430 GMT, the rupiah was at 2,875/80 at against its opening at 2,770/90. 

 Overnight rates shot up due to the central bank's tight short-term monetary policy and the maturity on Friday of its intervention on Wednesday, when it sold about $500 million to defend the rupiah from a speculative onslaught. 

 "People are just toying around with the rupiah and it's affecting the other currencies as well. We're looking for 3,000 on dollar/rupiah at some point," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 On Thursday, Bank Indonesia gave up its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of an intervention band. 

 Analysts hailed the move as a welcome response to currency and economic turmoil in the region, which has highlighted the need for greater exchange rate flexibility. 

 The International Monetary Fund (IMF) welcomed the float, saying it would allow the Indonesian economy to continue a recent impressive performance. 

 "In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said acting IMF managing director Stanley Fischer. 

 Dealers said the rupiah's decline pushed the Singapore dollar to a 37-month low of 1.5220 to the U.S. dollar. 

 "Nowadays, the regional currencies are traded as a group so if any one of them is being attacked, the rest of them will be pushed down as well," the Singapore dealer said. 

 Speculation of intervention by Singapore monetary authorities helped the Singapore dollar recover from its lows, but dealers said it was still heading for 1.53. 

 The rupiah fall also hit the Malaysian ringgit, which fell 2.7900/30 to the dollar against 2.7650/700 late on Thursday. 

 Dealers said the worst was not over for the ringgit given weak sentiment and the volatility in regional currencies. 

 They said the risk to the 2.80 level and beyond remained intact though the dollar was expected to face strong resistance at 2.7950. 

 The Thai baht eased on continued commercial demand for the dollar, but activity was relatively muted as the market awaited an official announcement of a reported cabinet reshuffle, even though it was expected to have only a limited impact. 

 The baht was at 31.60/31.70 to the dollar in the domestic market against 31.50/31.60 late on Thursday. It was at 31.50/60 in offshore markets. 

 The Philippine peso fell to 29.71/81 to the dollar at 0430 GMT against its previous close at 29.49. 

 Manila traders said the central bank continued to quote offer rates for the dollar at 10 centavos above the best market offer. The peso was expected to test a record low of 30, but dealers said some support was likely at 29.85. 

 The Taiwan dollar's decline was cushioned by central bank sales of the U.S. dollar near T$28.727 in the face of persistent demand from importers. 

 The Taiwan dollar was at T$28.726/727 against Thursday's T$28.725 close.

title: FOCUS - Singapore dollar weakness seen persisting.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 13 (Reuter) - The newly beleaguered Singapore dollar could be in for a spell of sustained weakness if the U.S. dollar stays bullish internationally and turmoil in Asian currency markets persists, economists said on Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to an early low of 1.5175 to the U.S. dollar, levels not seen since July 1994, before talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) near that level prompted a slight recovery. 

 It stood at 1.5140/50 at 0910 GMT, but foreign exchange dealers and analysts said it could slide towards the 1.53, and eventually, 1.55 levels. 

 The latest bout of selling of the usually sturdy Singapore dollar was attributed to an MAS official's comments that the current Singapore dollar level was appropriate to what was happening in the market. 

 The official of the de facto central bank told reporters on Tuesday that the U.S. dollar had been rising in currency markets and the Singapore dollar had depreciated by about five percent against the U.S. unit since the start of 1997. 

 Her comments sparked active sales of the Singapore dollar, pushing it abruptly through the psychological support level of 1.50 against the U.S. dollar. 

 "Obviously, those comments gave the market a green light," said Daniel Lian, head of Asian bond and currency research at NatWest Markets. 

 But he said market players, particularly large hedge funds, had already been gearing up to test the 1.50 level. 

 "What the funds in New York are tracking very closely is our export numbers and whether we can convincingly tell them we're able to engineer a recovery in exports," Lian said. 

 Singapore's non-oil exports, long used to double-digit growth, have been struggling with a downturn in global electronics demand since last year. 

 Non-oil domestic exports expanded by 4.4 percent in the second quarter of 1997 after contracting 4.1 percent in the previous quarter, according to the latest official figures. 

 Electronics account for around 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports. 

 Most economists said the Singapore dollar's weakness could help exports while having only a mild inflationary impact. 

 "Given the benign state of international price trends now, there's further potental for the Singapore dollar to weaken in the medium term without threatening a large rise in price instability," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia. 

 He said Singapore's policy of managing its exchange rate on a trade-weighted basis made a weakening of its currency inevitable in the context of a robust U.S. dollar and declines in neigbouring currencies after the effective devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso last month. 

 "We could quite easily see the weakness extending to the 1.55 levels further down the line. And I wouldn't view that as a sign the MAS was diluting its commitment to keeping inflation low," Supple said. 

 But Jacqueline Ong, economist at independent research house I.D.E.A., said a decline to the 1.55 level would be overdone in view of Singapore's sound fundamentals. 

 "On a trade-weighted basis, levels from 1.48 to 1.51 may be a little bit painful in terms of making imports more expensive," Ong said. 

 "If we're talking about prolonged weakness, I think 1.50 is already the limit," she added.

title: Indonesian rupiah under siege,  central bank  acts.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 13 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah fell prey to the malaise afflicting Southeast Asia's currencies on Wednesday, tumbling to a historic low before the central bank provided some support by raising rates. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 2,665/75 at 0420 GMT after plunging to a low of 2,679 in morning trade against an opening 2,674/76. The rupiah's previous low was 2,665 on July 21. 

 Dealers attributed the slide to lingering spillover weakness from other regional currencies and to a local newspaper report quoting an economist as saying Bank Indonesia should allow the rupiah to find its own level. 

 Sjahrir, an economist and brokerage firm owner, was quoted in the Kompas daily as saying the market would ultimately decide a fair value for the rupiah. 

 "According to me, just let the rupiah fall to 2,700 or 2,800. The central bank does not have to do anything. Once they (speculators) realise the central bank hasn't done anything, the dollar is already overvalued," Sjahrir was quoted as saying. 

 Singapore dealers said there were market rumours Bank Indonesia might widen or remove its intervention band for the rupiah. 

 The rupiah received a brief lift after the central bank raised interest rates for central bank certificates (SBIs) of all maturities by 100 basis points. 

 Analysts said the move, which followed a 50-basis-point cut in SBI rates for paper above one week last Friday, was inevitable in the face of the rupiah's slide and could be a prelude to the removal of the intervention band. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar remained under pressure but recouped some of its losses on talk of possible central bank intervention near its low of 1.5175 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The domestic unit was quoted at 1.5127/37 at 0420 GMT and dealers said the U.S. dollar continued to draw strong bids near the low end of 1.5100. 

 They said local banks were seen selling the U.S. dollar near its highs earlier, often an indication of the central bank's presence, but no confirmation was available. 

 "The market still seems to be quite biddish on the U.S. dollar," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 A European bank dealer said the U.S. dollar would be bought on any dips to 1.5100 or 1.5050 for an eventual move up to 1.53. 

 The Malaysian ringgit moved narrowly but showed persistent signs of weakness and dealers said the market was likely to take a crack at the 2.80 level, a low not seen since the ringgit was officially floated in 1973. 

 "Dollar/ringgit could still reach 2.80 and probably go above that level," said a Malaysian bank dealer. "But I'm expecting some resistance at 2.7850." 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.7720/50 to the dollar at 0420 GMT against 2.7645/75 at the close of Kuala Lumpur trade on Tuesday. It hit a new 42-month low of 2.7930 earlier on Tuesday. The Thai baht opened weaker in domestic markets as players returned from a one-day holiday and bought the dollar on concern about weakness in regional markets. 

 The baht was quoted at 31.59/64 to the dollar in onshore markets and at 31.10/20 in offshore markets. 

 Dealers said there were some sales of dollars offshore ahead of the expected mid-August maturity of short baht positions, established when the Thai currency came under speculative attack three months ago. 

 The Philippine peso remained weak as banks bought up the dollar in volatile regional currency markets. Corporate demand for the dollar also weighed on the peso, which was at 28.925/29.050 against its previous close at 28.66.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - RUPIAH UNDER SIEGE, BI HIKES RATES.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 13 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah fell prey to the malaise afflicting Southeast Asia's currencies on Wednesday, tumbling to a historic low before the central bank provided some support by raising rates. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 2,665/75 at 0420 GMT after plunging to a low of 2,679 in morning trade against an opening 2,674/76. The rupiah's previous low was 2,665 on July 21. 

 Dealers attributed the slide to lingering spillover weakness from other regional currencies and to a local newspaper report quoting an economist as saying Bank Indonesia should allow the rupiah to find its own level. 

 Sjahrir, an economist and brokerage firm owner, was quoted in the Kompas daily as saying the market would ultimately decide a fair value for the rupiah. 

 "According to me, just let the rupiah fall to 2,700 or 2,800. The central bank does not have to do anything. Once they (speculators) realise the central bank hasn't done anything, the dollar is already overvalued," Sjahrir was quoted as saying. 

 Singapore dealers said there were market rumours the Indonesian central bank might widen or remove its intervention band for the rupiah. 

 The rupiah received a brief lift after Bank Indonesia raised interest rates for central bank certificates (SBIs) of all maturities by 100 basis points. 

 Analysts said the move, which followed a 50-basis-point cut in SBI rates for paper above one week last Friday, was inevitable in the face of the rupiah's slide and could be a prelude to the possible removal of the intervention band. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar remained under pressure but recouped some of its losses on talk of possible central bank intervention near its low of 1.5175 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The domestic unit was quoted at 1.5127/37 at 0420 GMT and dealers said the U.S. dollar continued to draw strong bids near the low end of 1.5100. 

 They said local banks were seen selling the U.S. dollar near its highs earlier, often an indication of the central bank's presence, but no confirmation was available. 

 "The market still seems to be quite biddish on the U.S. dollar," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 A European bank dealer said the U.S. dollar would be bought on any dips to 1.5100 or 1.5050 for an eventual move up to 1.53. 

 The Malaysian ringgit moved narrowly but showed persistent signs of weakness and dealers said the market was likely to take a crack at the 2.80 level, a low not seen since the ringgit was officially floated in 1973. 

 "Dollar/ringgit could still reach 2.80 and probably go above that level," said a Malaysian bank dealer. "But I'm expecting some resistance at 2.7850." 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.7720/50 to the dollar at 0420 GMT against 2.7645/75 at the close of Kuala Lumpur trade on Tuesday. It hit a new 42-month low of 2.7930 earlier on Tuesday. The Thai baht opened weaker in domestic markets as players returned from a one-day holiday and bought the dollar on concern about weakness in regional markets. 

 The baht was quoted at 31.59/64 to the dollar in onshore markets and at 31.10/20 in offshore markets. 

 Dealers said there were some sales of dollars offshore ahead of the expected mid-August maturity of short baht positions, established when the Thai currency came under speculative attack three months ago. 

 The Philippine peso remained weak as banks bought up the dollar in volatile regional currency markets. Corporate demand for the dollar also weighed on the peso. 

 The peso was at 28.925/29.050 against its previous close at 28.66. Manila traders said the central bank might have sold dollars at the 28.70/28.78 levels earlier but no confirmation was available from the central bank. 

 The Taiwan dollar was weak but its decline was expected to be slowed by fears of central bank intervention and tight liquidity in domestic money markets. 

 It was at T$28.723/726 against Tuesday's T$28.718 close.

title: FOCUS-Ringgit firms, Malaysia swipes at speculators.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 4 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit rebounded strongly on Monday after the authorities moved to prevent any further speculative pressure on the currency with a mild form of capital controls. 

 The move to limit non-trade swap transactions saw the ringgit rally to 2.5800 per U.S. dollar from Friday's late level of around 2.6350 but later it settled around 2.6030. 

 This together with the news the Thai government talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) were "going well" helped Asian currencies across the board. 

 The long-awaited package from Thailand is expected to get cabinet approval this week and finance minister Thanong Bidaya was upbeat. On emerging from seven days of talks with the IMF one reporter remarked that he looked sad. 

 "You call this face sad? I'm smiling," Thanong told the reporter. "I am confident it's going to be approved by the cabinet and it's going to be good news." 

 Thailand is braced for a fairly painful austerity package and IMF demands might be hard to swallow. 

 "The most painful issue will be related to disclosure," Russell Kopp, head of research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Bangkok, told Reuters Financial Television. 

 "A flexible currency and capital exchange controls, those will have to go, but the real issue at the heart of these problems is political reform and a great part of what the IMF will do here is pry open disclosure." 

 The onshore baht firmed to 31.550 per dollar from Friday's late 31.750 with the offshore rate at 31.550 against 31.85. 

 In Malaysia, Bank Negara, the central bank announced that from Monday local banks have to limit non-trade-related currency swaps with overseas customers to $2.0 million. 

 A swap is an exchange of fixed interest payments in one currency for those in another, in this case the U.S. dollar and the Malaysian ringgit, with a commitment to exchange the principal amount at the end of the swap agreement at a set rate. 

 By imposing a $2.0 million ceiling, overseas players will be limited in the amount of ringgit they can obtain, thereby limiting the scope for speculation. 

 The move helped the ringgit but hit investor confidence on the stock market where prices of blue-chip issues fell sharply. 

 "I don't think the move in itself will have too much impact but what people are worried about is that it could put Malaysia a step back in terms of trying to be a financial centre," said Chaing Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 Also, Malaysia's move may be seen as a little over the top given that since the beginning of July, when pressure really started to mount on Asian currencies, the ringgit's fall has been far from spectacular and certainly not in the Thai baht's league. 

 The ringgit has come down only 3.0 percent on the dollar since July 1 and a lot of that must be due to the fact that the dollar itself has been firm around the world. 

 Since July 1 the yen has fallen over 3.0 percent against the dollar and the deutschemark has dropped 6.0 percent. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was underpinned by tight money market liquidity on Monday but trade was slow, with interest centered on the swap market where players were wary of Indonesia imposing controls similar to those announced by Bank Negara. 

 But traders thought that unlikely at this stage and noted that of all the Asian currencies the rupiah had weathered the recent storm well. 

 "Indonesia has a policy to liberalise exchange controls as much as they can and they have already widened the intervention band," said one trader at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "President Suharto has made it pretty clear that he is happy with the liberal system that's in place for the rupiah." 

 Spot rupiah was a little firmer at 2,595.00 per dollar against Friday's late 2,604.00. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended slightly firmer but was below an earlier high on continued heavy demand for dollars. Taipei dealers said central bank intervention on Saturday signalled that the authorities thought there had perhaps been enough of a correction. 

 It was at T$28.654 after opening at T$28.631 against Saturday's T$28.705 close. The Taiwan dollar tumbled more than four percent last week after the central bank gave up on its long-standing defence of the T$28 level. 

 The Philippine peso was expected to firm as banks needed to sell dollars to improve their liquidity after the central bank ordered a two percentage point increase in liquidity reserves to curb speculation last week. 

 One Manila trader said the central bank had sold $1 million at 29 pesos in Monday's first deal. The peso was at 29.00 per dollar against its previous close of 28.99.

title: Asian  currencies  firm as Malaysia gets tough.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 4 (Reuter) - Asian currencies received a boost on Monday after Malaysia squared up and came out fighting against speculators by limiting non-trade swap transactions. 

 The ringgit rallied to 2.5800 per U.S. dollar from Friday's late level of around 2.6350 and while the scale of the rise was not mirrored elsewhere, Asian currencies were generally firmer. 

 The Malaysian central bank, Bank Negara, announced on Sunday that from Monday, local banks will have to limit non-trade related currency swaps with overseas customers to $2.0 million. 

 A swap is a forward rate agreement to exchange one currency for another. By imposing a $2.0 million ceiling, overseas players will be limited on the amount of ringgit they can get hold of. 

 As they stand, the controls are somewhat mild in nature and after much tough talking from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad against currency speculators they came a little surprise. 

 "I don't think this move in itself have too much impact but what people are worried about is that it could put Malaysia a step back in terms of trying to be a financial centre," said Chaing Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 Analysts doubted much of a squeeze would result from the move as offshore players are not too short of ringgit. 

 They said most had learned from the Thai experience, where shortsellers of baht were left stranded when their supply of the currency was cut off by capital controls imposed by the government. 

 This meant that in the last couple of months, players had actually borrowed in the swap market before they sold the ringgit off, although analysts said there will be upward pressure on offshore forward rates because of the move. 

 "I don't think it's Bank Negara's aim to squeeze the offshore market the way Thailand did. This is more to prevent people getting cheap ringgit offshore to put on new positions," CIBC's Chaing said. 

 The news boosted regional currencies, with the Singapore dollar up at 1.4580 per U.S. dollar from Friday's 1.4750, the Indonesia rupiah up at 2,592.0 from 2.610.0 and the onshore baht up slightly at 31.700 from 31.900. 

 The move by Malaysia is similar to the Singapore system whereby a swap involving a forward sale of U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar to non-residents requires offical approval if the amount exceeds 5.0 million Singapore dollars and the transaction is unrelated to trade. 

 So apart from Singapore and the Philippines, where controls already exist, could this happen anywhere else in Southeast Asia? The answer would seem to be no. 

 There is much speculation that Thailand will in fact lift existing capital controls as part of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) sponsored economic package due this week. 

 In Indonesia, no end is in sight to the liberal exchange rate system. 

 "Indonesia has a policy to liberalise exchange controls as much as they can and they have already widened the intervention band," said one trader at a European bank in Singapore. "President Suharto has made it pretty clear that he is happy with the liberal system that's in place for the rupiah." 

 While Malaysia's move was fairly mild and was good news for the ringgit, it hammered the stock market, with Malaysian blue chip stocks diving 4.5 percent in early trading. 

 "It's not the actual control they have put in place which is worrying investors, it's the fact they have done it at all," said one Singapore based analyst. 

 "If you keep changing the rules you are bound to put people off, you can't do things like this and not expect people to worry that there are toughter measures to come."

title: Profit taking pushes S.E Asian  currencies  higher.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 1 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies, rocked by weeks of turmoil, firmed on Friday morning as players cashed in some of their gains on the dollar ahead of the weekend. 

 Dealers said players were reluctant to establish new positions ahead of the release of Thailand's economic rescue plan, due by August 5, which is expected to include assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 "Everybody wants to see what the IMF will do in Thailand on the fifth because that will indirectly affect all the other regional currencies," a Singapore-based trader said. 

 Vague rumours of an impending military coup in Thailand hit New York markets overnight, causing sales of dollar/baht and a rise in swap premiums. But the rumours had been around for weeks and little credence was attached to them, dealers said. 

 One said there was talk the Bank of Thailand had intervened to sell the dollar around 32.10 baht in Singapore markets on Friday. No confirmation was available. 

 The baht slipped back a notch from morning highs after Standard & Poor's Corp placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch. 

 That was further bad news for the Thai economy, implying greater than expected loan losses in the crisis-torn financial sector. 

 The baht was quoted at 31.85/31.95 to the dollar onshore at 0435 GMT against 31.700/9500 late on Thursday. The offshore rate was at 31.80/32.00. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit showed little immediate reaction to news Bank Negara Malaysia had asked banks to hold their base lending rates steady. 

 Banking sources in Kuala Lumpur said the central bank had asked them to hold their base lending rates at 9.67 percent despite a recent spike up in interbank rates. 

 The ringgit was at 2.6245/95 to the dollar after firming through the 2.63 level earlier on profit-taking in the dollar by funds. 

 Dealers said the dollar looked firm against the ringgit, but talk of large orders to sell the dollar at the 2.6400 level was likely to limit its rise. 

 The market was awaiting Malaysia's trade data for June, expected next week, amid talk of a 1.5 billion ringgit deficit after May's surplus of 157 million ringgit. 

 The Singapore dollar rose through the key 1.47 level to the U.S. dollar but dealers said its rise was likely to be capped around 1.4650. 

 "This is probably just profit-taking. I'm still looking at a higher dollar/Sing," a dealer said, adding that the market continued to expect the Sing to drop to around 1.50. 

 Trade in the Indonesian rupiah was slow, dominated by covering of short dollar positions for the weekend. Spot rupiah was at 2,605/15 against an opening of 2,613/23. 

 The Philippine peso was firmer as banks scrambled to meet a deadline to cut long dollar positions after the central bank slashed the long dollar limit of banks to five percent of capital from 10 percent, or 10 million, whichever is lower. 

 Newspapers quoted central bank governor Gabriel Singson as saying he expected banks to unload $200 million due to the new ruling. The peso was at 28.960/29.060 against its previous close at 29. 

 The Taiwan dollar slipped back from an early high of T$28.590, inspired by the central bank's move to raise two key interest rates after the market's close on Thursday. 

 The central bank raised the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 percent and accomodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375 percent, effective from Friday. 

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said the rate hikes were aimed at maintaining stability in the forex market. 

 The Taiwan dollar was at T$28.653/660 against Thursday's close at T$28.70, its weakest finish since 1988.

title: Asian central banker talks damp  currency  market.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 25 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies were on slightly firmer footing on Friday morning as the market paused from its recent frantic selling just in case an Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai sprang a surprise. 

 The one-day meeting was expected to yield little more than warnings against currency speculation and talk of cooperation, but dealers said the market was taking nothing for granted. 

 "The market is cautious in case anything happens. I would advise customers to trim down their positions or just square up," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said there were still some fears of concerted intervention to counter the recent series of attacks on regional currencies, but most were unconvinced. 

 "In general, it looks like the central banks have decided not to waste foreign exchange reserves intervening against market forces," a senior dealer at another European bank said. 

 The Thai baht remained weak as companies sought the dollar to meet payments and the market worried about the battered financial sector. 

 But dealers said trade was calmer than in recent days and the baht stayed above the low of 32.70 to the dollar it hit on Thursday. 

 Some Bangkok dealers said they saw strong support for the baht around the 32.30 level, but they were not sure whether the central bank had intervened in the market. 

 "The market was quite calm this morning with only small buying. There was light commercial demand and the baht moved in a very tight band," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar bounced back sharply from a morning low of 1.4765 at the open, prompting talk of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). 

 But most dealers attributed the move to nervous profit-taking by a market that had bought up the U.S. dollar aggressively in the last two days. 

 "The MAS wouldn't come in at this level, especially as the Finance Minister has said market forces should determine the exchange rate," said one. 

 Finance Minister Richard Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective. 

 The Singapore dollar was expected to trade a 1.4700-1.4760 range for the day. It was at 1.4729/39 at 0440 GMT. 

 Selling of the Malaysian ringgit subsided but the currency's recovery was blocked around the 2.64 level to the dollar and dealers continued to predict more weakness. 

 "I don't think dollar/ringgit has seen a top yet. It should go to 2.70 eventually and the recent low of 2.6180/2.6200 should hold," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 "The market is very quiet today, kind of in a squarish mode. They are probably waiting to see if any concrete measures emerge from Shanghai," said another Singapore dealer. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained depressed below the 2,600 level to the dollar, but dealers said activity had slowed. 

 "It's still a regional factor. Fund managers who are playing in Jakarta have also exposures in Thailand and the ringgit. Once they move, all those currencies are affected," one said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,610/20 at 0440 GMT compared with an opening of 2,601/09. 

 The Philippine central bank sold dollars in the face of heavy commercial demand, helping stem the peso's fall. 

 The Hong Kong dollar calmed down, but tension lingered after forwards shot up on Thursday, sparking fears of a speculative attack on Asia's most strongly pegged currency. 

 Hong Kong Monetary Authority released figures after the market closed on Thursday, showing it held HK$569 billion at June 30, up 6.4 percent from December 31, 1996. 

 Analysts saw the move as aimed at scaring off speculators.

title: S.E. Asia  currency  war truce for bankers meeting.
text:

 "It's still a regional factor. Fund managers who are playing in Jakarta have also exposures in Thailand and the ringgit. Once they move, all those currencies are affected," one said.

title: Singapore stocks a good buy as economy firms - DBS.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 24 (Reuter) - Singapore equities are on the brink of recovery as the economic outlook improves in the second half of the year and regional currency volatility recedes, DBS Investment Research director Mano Sabnani said on Thursday. 

 The stock market stands to capture more interest as recent sterling performers, such as property investments, stay depressed, he said. 

 "The market could recover about 25 percent for the next six to nine months starting in October," Sabnani told investors over lunch. Many stocks were trading at the lower end of their valuations, Sabani said. 

 He said the Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) would crawl out of its 1,900-2,100 trading band in the fourth quarter and could rise as high as 2,500 points. 

 The STII sank to its lowest level since 1995 in mid-July, dragged down by weak confidence in Asia and the flight of foreign funds on concerns over Thailand's economic woes and regional currencies. 

 But Sabnani said he based his sanguine outlook on the assumption that volatile regional currency markets were in the process of stabilising. 

 He said recent speculative attacks on the Singapore dollar were more a function of the lack of central bank intervention than poor fundamentals. 

 The Singapore dollar's slide to a low of 1.47 against the U.S. dollar could in fact boost market sentiment as a softer currency would help exporters, he said. 

 Singapore's electronics sector, which makes up a hefty 70 percent of exports, should also enjoy better demand as U.S. orders for electronic components picks up and filters through. 

 Sabani said investors were likely to stay sidelined ahead of the corporate reporting season in September but the overall market should benefit from improved liquidity later. 

 The DBS report said some newly-listed stocks held promise, U.S. dollar stocks listed locally could gain from a strong currency, and electronic issues rise on the back of the sector's recovery. 

 And the foreign exchange risk of the Singapore dollar was limited, given a Singapore $115 billion foreign reserve and a current account surplus, Sabani said. 

 "We expect the fall of the Singapore dollar to stabilise around these levels," he said. 

 An economic recovery was also well underway and would gather steam into the second half of the year, he added. 

 A DBS Investment Research forecast gross domestic product (GDP) would steadily rise and see an average of 6.2 percent for 1997. 

 Sabnani said a lack of pressure on interest rates was also favourable to the stock market. 

 "The turnaround has begun. It began on July 17 when the market reached 1,920," he said. Now was the time to pick up good quality stocks which had fallen to attractive levels, he said. 

 DBS recommended buys on issues like automotive parts firm GPE Industries due to its investments in China, printed circuit board maker Gul Technologies because of major expansion plans and Hotel Properties, on its property earnings and foreign hotel prospects.

title: Singapore Dollar Sharply Lower Late Against U.S. Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar was again sharply lower against the U.S. dollar at the close of Asian trading Thursday, as commercial interests, investors and speculative traders all sought to buy the U.S. dollar against the Singapore currency. 

 In afternoon trading the U.S. dollar breached resistance at S$1.4750 to hit S$1.4773 at 1000 GMT (6:00 a.m. EDT), up from S$1.4740 around 0140 GMT (9:40 p.m. EDT), and higher than S$1.4690 in early morning dealings. 

 Few traders were prepared to call a short-term top for the U.S. dollar against the Singapore currency, and most fully expect further falls Friday and in the following week. 

 The latest fall in the Singapore dollar was sparked by comments made by Richard Hu, Singapore's finance minister. Speaking in Singapore's parliament Wednesday afternoon, Hu said the Singapore dollar's exchange rate is determined by market forces, and the recent weakness in the Thai baht and the Philippine peso 'should not pose a significant threat to (Singapore's) competitiveness.' 

 The market interpreted the remarks as an indication that the Singapore government was prepared to allow the Singapore dollar to weaken against the U.S. dollar in line with other regional currencies, and that the Monetary Authority of Singapore would not intervene to prevent depreciation. 

 With the threat of MAS intervention seen lifted from the market, U.S. funds and banks, as well as domestic banks and corporations, were all seen buying the U.S. dollar against Singapore's currency. 

 Meanwhile, the ringgit is at S$0.5580, up from S$0.5566 earlier and S$0.5550 in late trading Wednesday. 

 Local money market rates have not changed since late Wednesday despite the Singapore dollar's weakness against the U.S. dollar. The overnight rate on Singapore dollar deposits is unchanged from late Wednesday at 4%-4.125%. Three-month interbank rates are also steady at 4.125%-4.375%.

title: Shanghai central bankers meet seen as 'G7' of Asia.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuter) - A meeting of Asian central bankers in Shanghai on Friday is being hailed as the region's 'G7'by foreign exchange dealers in the wake of weeks of the recent currency turmoil. 

 In a still jittery market keen to hold U.S. dollars rather than regional currencies, the meeting could be something of a watershed given the possibility of central bank cooperation on foreign exchange intervention. 

 "This meeting will be like the G7 equivalent for this region," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore. 

 "The big issue for the market at the moment is this meeting in Shanghai as there is the possibility of concerted intervention or a statement that they are willing to join hands to support currencies." 

 The meeting is being hosted by the People's Bank of China and the participants are due to arrive in Shanghai on Thursday evening. 

 Those attending include Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, The Philippines, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, China and Indonesia. 

 It is a one-day meeting followed by a sight-seeing trip on Saturday before the bankers leave on Sunday. 

 However, sources in Shanghai say there are no plans to allow media access to the meeting and no briefing or communique is scheduled. 

 Regional central banks have helped each other out in the past. As the Thai crisis intensified in May, the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the market to help shore up the sagging baht. 

 On Tuesday, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Japan would keep in close contact with Asian economies such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand to promote the stability of currency markets in the region. 

 Although Mitsuzuka said "that does not necessarily mean we are in a special cooperative alliance", statements such as this are enough to frighten the market given the huge foreign exchange reserves held by the Bank of Japan. 

 "Although we've seen some big moves lately the actual selling behind them has been light and in some cases extremely light," said one Singapore-based trader. 

 "This meeting is certainly a golden opportunity for some major league jawboning from these guys about intervention and cooperation. In markets this thin it will have an impact." 

 Traders said if there were anything forthcoming from the Friday meeting, it would most likely be after Asian market hours and give the market the whole weekend to digest any news. 

 But region currencies could react to any news during European and U.S. time zones, they said. 

 The need for fresh regional cooperation on currencies was thrown into sharp relief on Tuesday when Malaysia reported an 8.8 billion ringgit, or 12.5 percent, fall in foreign exchange reserves to 61.9 billion in the first two weeks of July. 

 "This was a very nasty figure and just goes to show that in parts of the region there simply isn't the firepower to protect currencies if there is another panic," said one Singapore based trader.
